abstract: This study investigated the prevalence of computer anxiety by area of practice, hours of weekly use, access to equipment,, availability of training for social workers (N = 244) in South Carolina, Georgia,, North Carolina. Measured by the Computer Anxiety Index (CAIN), levels of anxiety were found to be lowest for those who have computers in their work areas, received training,, use computers to accomplish work tasks. Statistically significant positive correlations were found between anxiety levels, high levels of training need as well as the number of hours of weekly use, training received. A significant negative correlation was found between anxiety levels, weekly hours of use.

title: Computer anxiety, its correlates: a meta-analysis
authors: Chua, Siew Lian, Chen, Der-Thanq, Wong, Angela F L
abstract: In this study we report results from a meta-analysis of relationships between computer anxiety, its three correlates—age, gender,, computer experience. Only studies published between 1990, 1996 were included in the analysis. Findings of this meta-analysis are: (1) female university undergraduates are generally more anxious than male undergraduates, but the strength of this relationship is not conclusive; (2) instruments measuring computer anxiety are generally reliable, but not compatible with one another;, (3) computer anxiety is inversely related to computer experience, but the strength of this relationship remains inconclusive. Limitations of the methodology, implications of the findings are discussed. Directions for future studies are suggested.

title: Violence risk factors in stalking, obsessional harassment: A review, preliminary meta-analysis
authors: Rosenfeld, Barry
abstract: The fear of violence is among the most common, debilitating concerns faced by stalking victims. This review summarizes the extant literature on stalking-related violence, highlighting risk factors unique to stalking as well as those common to most offender populations. In total, 13 published studies were found, encompassing 11 unique samples, 1,155 individuals. The overall rate of violence was 38.7\%. Significant correlates of stalking-related violence included the presence of threats, substance abuse,, the absence of a psychotic disorder. Other strong correlates included a prior intimate relationship between victim, offender, a history of violent behavior. Results are discussed with respect to risk assessment strategies, future directions for stalking risk assessment research.

title: Characterizing sexual violence in intimate relationships: An examination of blame attributions, rape acknowledgment
authors: Jaffe, Anna E, Steel, Anne L, DiLillo, David, Messman-Moore, Terri L, Gratz, Kim L
keywords: intimate partner sexual assault; marital rape; sexual coercion; victim-offender relationship; violence;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Rape by an intimate partner frequently involves a precedence of sexual consent between victim, perpetrator, often does not include the use of physical force,, may not fit societal definitions of rape. Given these unique characteristics, women who are assaulted by an intimate partner may be less likely to acknowledge the experience as a rape. In turn, they might make fewer blame attributions toward themselves, their perpetrators than victims of rape by a nonpartner. Consistent with these expectations, results from 208 community women reporting rape in adulthood revealed the presence of indirect effects of perpetrator type (nonpartner vs. intimate partner) on both behavioral self-blame, perpetrator blame through rape acknowledgment, even when controlling for both victim substance use at the time of the assault, coercion severity. Compared with women who experienced a rape by a nonpartner, women who experienced rape in the context of a marital or dating relationship were less likely to blame themselves or the perpetrator for the assault, in part because they were less likely to label their experience as a rape. Overall, these findings highlight the unique nature of intimate partner rape, provide further information about the relatively underresearched area of sexual violence in intimate relationships.

title: Just art for a just city: Public art, social inclusion in urban regeneration
authors: Sharp, Joanne, Pollock, Venda, Paddison, Ronan
abstract: In this article, it is shown how cultural policy,, in particular public art, intersects with the processes of urban restructuring, how it is a contributor, but also antidote, to the conflict that typically surrounds the restructuring of urban space. The particular focus of the paper is on investigating how public art can be inclusionary/exclusionary as part of the wider project of urban regeneration. The first part of the paper examines examples in which public art intervention has attempted to generate inclusion. Subsequently, attention focuses more on examples in which the public art has been perceived as an aspect of cultural domination, has thus provoked resistance. Throughout, it is argued that the processes through which artworks become installed into the urban fabric are critical to the successful development of inclusion.

title: The life, death of five spaces: public art, community regeneration in Glasgow
authors: Sharp, Joanne
abstract: This article discusses the role of public art in the built form of western cities. Increasingly public art is being seen as an unquestionably good thing in urban regeneration discourse, in particular for its ability to (re)create urban communities. In part, this reflects the influence of `new genre public art' approaches which privilege art as process over art as product. However, this reading of new genre public art works can overlook the wider networks through which presence is facilitated, the very materiality of the artistic things produced,, how they are subsequently incorporated into everyday life. These agendas for the critical appreciation of public art will be developed through the example of the Five Spaces public art project in Glasgow, Scotland.

title: Post-apartheid public art in Cape Town: Symbolic reparations, public space
authors: Minty, Zayd
abstract: This essay considers public art practice in post- apartheid Cape Town within the notion of symbolic reparations-a concept deriving out of South Africa's Trust Reconciliation Commission. The paper situates developments in public arts practice in the context of developments in cultural politics in South Africa, globally. More especially, it discusses new genre arts projects, which focus on a range of issues related to identity, space, place. The projects-the District Six Museum, District Six Sculpture Project, PTO, Y30, BLAC, Returning the Gaze,, the In Touch Poetry Bus Tour-focus on issues such as rethinking monuments, the memorialising of 'hidden histories', engagements with racism, the abuse of power,, the reimagining of the city. The paper asks how these contemporary, often ephemeral projects, critically engage with issues of history, geography, memory, transformation and, in so doing, mark the landscape of Cape Town, making spaces for dialogue and/or standing as poetic symbols, challenges to the inequalities of the city.

title: More active living-oriented county, municipal zoning is associated with increased adult leisure time physical activity-United States, 2011
authors: Chriqui, Jamie F, Nicholson, Lisa M, Thrun, Emily, Leider, Julien, Slater, Sandy J
keywords: active living; biking; land use; physical activity; walking; zoning;z\_gakushin2018;Environment, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: Although zoning is recognized for its role in facilitating healthy communities, no study has examined whether active living-oriented zoning codes are associated with adult leisure time physical activity (PA). This study sought to fill this gap, hypothesized that adult leisure time PA would be greater in communities with more progressive zoning code reforms, more active living-oriented zoning. Zoning codes for 1,617 county, municipal jurisdictions located in 30 states (covering ~40\% of the U.S. population) were evaluated for code reform zoning, 11 active living markers. County-aggregated zoning measures were created for linking with five adult PA behaviors obtained from the 2011 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System controlling for individual, county sociodemographics. Zoning elements most associated with adult PA included requirements for mixed use, active, passive recreation, bike parking/street furniture,, bike-pedestrian trails/paths. This study provides new insights as to the role that zoning can play in facilitating adult PA.

title: Geographies of displacement in the creative city: The case of Liberty Village, Toronto
authors: Catungal, John Paul, Leslie, Deborah, Hii, Yvonne
abstract: Creative industries are increasingly associated with employment, tourism, the attraction, retention of talent in economic development discourse. However, there is a need to foreground the interests involved in promoting the creative city, the political implications of such policies. This paper analyses new industry formation in Liberty Village—a cultural industry precinct in inner-city Toronto, Canada. The focus is on the place-making strategies at work in constructing Liberty Village. In particular, the paper explores a series of displacements associated with creative districts, focusing on three scales in particular—the level of the city, the neighbourhood, the precinct itself. An examination of these displacements foregrounds the contested nature of the creative city script.

title: Storying community: Re-imagining regional identities through public cultural activity
authors: Bromley, Roger
abstract: This article is designed to stimulate discussion around a number of related topics. Sceptical that governments, regional or otherwise, are capable of producing regional identities in any other but rhetorical or formulaic terms, it is argued that, in the past decade or so, a number of potentially popular, democratizing tendencies have developed in the wake of new media technologies, but also in different forms of public, community-based cultural activity. Drawing upon models of such activity like the 1993 Chicago Culture in Action project, other examples of a new genre of public art in Manchester, London, together with television-based initiatives, it will be shown how active communities, however tentative, provisional, can be brought into being through interests held in common. On the other hand, new social media are explored for their potential for producing ‘network communities’ in online, offline modes. One prominent, widespread example is digital storytelling, which, at local, regional, national, international levels, has recognized the power of the complex, multiple narratives that shape people’s lives, has harnessed these in ways that bring together narrative, technology, community-building as part of a development strategy, particularly for those alienated or otherwise excluded from access to media. Linked to the focus on digital storytelling will be a brief consideration of citizen media sites, initiatives as a means of possibly helping to open up, legitimate, construct regional identity in a multilayered fashion.

title: Do seats, food vendors,, sculptures improve plaza visitability?
authors: Abdulkarim, Dina, Nasar, Jack L
abstract: Building on Whyte’s work on livable places, the present study developed a four-item scale to assess visitability, used it to test whether three attributes identified by Whyte—seating, food,, triangulation—increase visitability. The study used color slides of three plazas altered for the presence or absence of each attribute. Sixty participants (23 men, 37 women) rated slides of the plazas on each of four items on the Perceived Visitability Scale (PVS). The four items had high interitem reliability,, each item, their composite had high interobserver reliability. The visitability ratings showed that plazas with seats, food, or sculpture had higher scores than plazas without those elements;, the combination of seats, sculpture had higher scores than either element alone. Contradicting Whyte, there was no statistically significant effect of gender. Seats, sculpture,, the perceived compatibility of elements with one another may improve plaza visitability.

title: Crime mapping on-line: Public perception of privacy issues
authors: Kounadi, Ourania, Bowers, Kate, Leitner, Michael
journal: European journal on criminal policy, research
abstract: The Web 2.0 technology introduced dynamic web mapping, which in turn has dramatically changed the distribution, use of geographical information in our society. Some of the many advantages of online mapping include the fast information dissemination to the public, the interactivity between the users, the map interface, as well as the frequent, easy database updates. However, the theme of these maps may entail privacy risks at times. Such examples include the crime mapping initiatives where crime information is considered as private, sensitive. With respect to privacy disclosure risks, this study employs a survey design to investigate the public’s perception of location privacy when information about crimes is being displayed on public maps. Participants from the London Borough of Camden were recruited, their views were analysed by means of a questionnaire accompanied by mapping material ( n = 201). Participants expressed a clear concern when practical implications related to the crime maps were revealed to them. Further, the majority of participants, if given the choice, would opt for a medium-risk protection method in terms of risk of privacy violation. Lastly, in regards to the impact that different visualizations may have on local crime perception the study revealed that the current police.uk cartographic technique creates the perception of more unsafe neighbourhoods than an alternative hot routes density map.

title: Responses to prison for environmental criminals: Impacts of incident, perpetrator,, respondent characteristics
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Mason, Robert J
keywords: environmental criminal; prison; sanctions; polluter; morality; seriousness; college students; criminal history; incident damage; perpetrator \& respondent traits; cooperativeness; structured discretion; Crime; Environment; Environmental Attitudes; Personality Traits; Prisons; Cooperation; Perpetrators; Punishment; Recidivism; Student Attitudes;z\_kakenhi2008
abstract: Qualitative work with water quality inspectors suggests that structured discretion shapes the transition from informal to administrative sanctions, depends both on impressions formed about the morality of the polluter, the seriousness of the incident. Undergraduates ( n = 118) at a diverse, urban university judged vignettes based on an actual prosecution. In a fully between 2 × 2 × 2 randomized design, the authors manipulated incident damage, polluter criminal history,, polluter-regulator relationship. These features influenced respondents’perceptions of offender cooperativeness, event seriousness. Cooperativeness influenced reactions to the appropriateness of prison; event seriousness influenced reactions to the appropriateness of a long prison term. Results suggest the factors influencing reactions to the transition from civil to severe criminal sanctions are somewhat similar to the factors influencing regulators’transitioning from informal to administrative sanctioning; in both sets of processes impressions formed of the incident, the offender mediate the relevant dynamics.

title: Fear of crime, collective action: An analysis of coping strategies
authors: Reid, Lesley Williams, Roberts, J Timmons, Hilliard, Heather Monro
keywords: FEAR of crime; CRIME prevention; GENDER-based analysis; FEAR; BEHAVIOR; RESEARCH;z\_kakenhi2008
abstract: Recent research addressing fear of crime largely concerns the causes of that fear; this article expands our understanding of fear of crime by examining whether people cope with their fear individually or collectively. Our guiding questions were two: Do coping strategies differ by those individual‐level characteristics established in the fear‐of‐crime literature? And do strategies differ based upon conceptually distinct types of fear? This research, based on a 1995 telephone survey of a random sample of New Orleans residents, suggests that the answer to both questions is yes. Commodified, individual‐level precautionary techniques are explained primarily by characteristics that reflect differential abilities to pay for such precautions. Conversely, collective‐level coping strategies are predicted primarily by degree of affective fear based on emotional reactions, regardless of actual levels of victimization.

title: Punitive reactions to completed crimes versus accidentally uncompleted crimes
authors: Oswald, Margit E, Orth, Ulrich, Aeberhard, Marianne, Schneider, Eliane
keywords: CRIME; PUNISHMENT; RAPE; FRAUD; WOMEN -- Crimes against; BLAME; Attribution;z\_kakenhi2008
abstract: Previous studies have shown that the harm caused by crime affects punitive reactions even if differences in the degree of harm are merely accidental. However, it remains unclear whether the effect is direct or whether it is mediated by attributed responsibility or blame. Participants were 303 university students who listened to 4 case vignettes (between-subjects design). Half received information about a completed crime, half about an accidentally uncompleted crime. Crime type was either fraud or rape. The results suggest that individuals consider the actual harm to a significantly greater extent than attribution theory would predict. Moreover, the link between harm, punishment was virtually not mediated by attributed blame, not moderated by individual differences in morality. Future studies should investigate whether the harm-punishment link is a result of an automatic act of retaliation or a desire to compensate for the harm done to the victim (restorative justice).

title: Received, perceived social support in times of stress: A test of the social support deterioration deterrence model
authors: Norris, Fran H, Kaniasty, Krzysztof
keywords: receipt of social support, subsequent perceived social support \& psychological distress, hurricane victims, test of deterioration deterrence model; Models; Psychological Stress; Social Perception; Social Support; Natural Disasters;z\_kakenhi2008
abstract: The authors evaluated the impact of receiving social support on subsequent levels of perceived social support, psychological distress in 2 independent samples of victims of severe natural disasters: Hurricane Hugo ( n = 498), Hurricane Andrew ( n = 404). A social support deterioration deterrence model was proposed that stipulated that postdisaster mobilization of received support counteracts the deterioration in expectations of support often experienced by victims of major life events. LISREL analyses of data collected 12, 24 months after Hugo, 6, 28 months after Andrew provided strong evidence for the hypothesized model: Perceived support mediated the long-term effects on distress of both scope of disaster exposure, postdisaster received support. Theoretical, application issues of social support are discussed.

title: Thinking about the implementation of citizen, community anti-crime measures
authors: Lavrakas, Paul J, Bennett, Susan F
journal: Communities \& Crime Reduction. London: Home Office Research, Planning Unit, Her Majesty’s Stationery Office
keywords: Community crime prevention programs; Program implementation; Services effectiveness;z\_kakenhi2008
abstract: Community crime prevention programs have a logical appeal, but evaluation studies have not found strong evidence that these efforts achieve their intended goals. In fact, some studies suggest that these programs have increased the fear of crime. However, it is not clear whether the lack of success stems from flaws in the underlying theory or from the lack of proper implementation. Program planners must recognize the level of prevention to be achieved: primary, secondary, or tertiary. Efforts to involve citizens in primary prevention should recognize that few citizens are likely to take part. A shared understanding of the underlying causes of crime, a strong leader are both crucial to the success of primary prevention efforts. In contrast, participation in some secondary crime prevention measures also arises from public-minded motives, while other measures are privately motivated. Thus, the need to build a consensus of values is less critical for secondary crime prevention efforts. Furthermore, tertiary crime prevention involves mostly private motives, are reactive in nature. The majority of tertiary prevention efforts seem to offer material incentives. Planners should keep these distinctions in mind as they develop programs. Recommendations for further research, 24 references. title: Reacting to crime, disorder in inner-city neighborhoods: Processes, mechanisms,, the functioning of fear, of other reactions to crime
authors: Carvalho, Irene
keywords: Crime; Disorders; Fear; Life Experiences; Neighborhoods; Urban Environments; crime reaction; disordered neighborhoods; fear reduction; inner city neighborhoods; local experiences; neighborhood conditions;z\_kakenhi2008
abstract: The purpose of this work is to offer a naturalistic approach to fear, other reactions to crime in order to provide an understanding of the mechanisms, processes,, the functioning of these reactions. This study examines the relationship between fear, crime by situating this relationship within the contexts in which it emerges: In the words of those who experience these phenomena, within the broad scope of their everyday lives,, in their areas of residence, inner-city neighborhoods, where crime, related problems are very visible. A group of 69 welfare recipients, randomly selected from a sample of Chicago residents, was interviewed, at two different points in time, regarding experiences of their areas of residence, as well as experiences with,, reactions to, local crime, related problems. The semi-structured interviews were conducted in a conversational style in the neighborhoods of residence of the participants,, interviewers took extensive field notes on these neighborhoods. A grounded theory approach was applied to both interviews, field observations. Results suggest that reactions to crime, disorder depend on distinct types of relationships established with these problems. Fear is not the most prevalent reaction to crime; anger and, most commonly, a sense of safety emerge too, even when crime, related problems exist. Fear appears dissociated from neighborhood conditions, related with sources other than crime or similar problems. Precautionary behaviors are enacted to ensure everyday courses of action, do not seem to ``imprison'' residents in their homes. The processes uncovered in this analysis suggest that crime, related phenomena are not fear-inspiring when they are integrated, understood within a system of life. However, common crimes, disorders appear to justify, legitimize other fears. Based on these conclusions, some reflections on policies are offered, in particular, the seeming advantages of integrating, rather than accentuating, problematizing, crimes, similar phenomena within the scope of everyday life as a way to reduce fear. title: Adolescents' sense of community, feeling of unsafety in the urban environment
authors: Zani, Bruna, Cicognani, Elvira, Albanesi, Cinzia
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: TEENAGERS; URBAN ecology; SOCIAL networks; NEIGHBORHOOD; FEAR; LIFE style; SOCIAL perception; HAZARDS; SEX differences; SAFETY; PEER relations; RISK perception; ITALY; Community attitudes; Community facilities; Dangerousness; Geographical mobility; Parent child communication; Social support networks; Stranger reactions; Vulnerability;z\_mera2010;J Community Appl Soc Psychol
abstract: The purpose of this research was to explore adolescents' feeling of unsafety associated with living in the urban context, their perceptions of the quality of social relations (social support from different persons), sense of community,, the differences according to the size of the city, adolescent gender. A second aim was to analyse the antecedents of feeling of unsafety. In particular, we considered the influence of sense of community, perception of social support, personal involvement in negative experiences in the urban environment. A questionnaire was submitted to 823 adolescents aged 14 to 19 years (43.3\% male, 56.7\% female), living in cities of different sizes in north‐central Italy. Results show the presence of differences in feeling of unsafety, sense of community according to the size of the urban context, adolescent gender. Personal involvement in negative situations is a strong predictor of feeling of unsafety, whereas sense of community plays a limited role in reducing it. The picture concerning the effect of social support is mixed. Copyright © 2001 John Wiley \& Sons, Ltd.

title: Mapping urban revitalization: using GIS spatial analysis to evaluate a new housing policy
authors: Perkins, Douglas D, Larsen, Courtney, Brown, Barbara B
journal: Journal of prevention \& intervention in the community
keywords: Housing; Information Systems; Neighborhoods; Policy Making; Urban Environments; Community Development; Computer Software; Evaluation; Geography; Human; Male; Female; US; mapping urban revitalization; geographic information system; spatial analysis; housing policy; Revised Block Environmental Inventory;z\_mera2010
abstract: This longitudinal, multimethod study uses geographical information system (GIS) software to evaluate the community-wide impact of a neighborhood revitalization project. Unsystematic visual examination, analysis of GIS maps are offered as a complementary tool to quantitative analysis, one that is much more compelling, meaningful,, effective in presentation to community, nonscientific professional audiences. The centerpiece of the intervention was the development of a new, middle-class housing subdivision in an area that was declining physically, economically. This represents three major urban/housing policy directions: (1) the emphasis on home ownership for working-class families, (2) the deconcentration of poverty through development of mixed-income neighborhoods,, (3) the clean up, redevelopment of contaminated, former industrial brownfields. Resident survey responses, objective environmental assessment observations,, building permit data were collected, geocoded at the address level,, aggregated to the block level on 60 street blocks in the older neighborhoods surrounding the new housing in two waves: during site clearing, housing construction (Time 1: 1993-95), three years post-completion (Time 2: 1998-99). Variables mapped include (a) Time 1-2 change in self-reported home repairs, improvements, (b) change in the assessed physical condition of yards, exteriors of 925 individual residential properties, (c) change in residents' home pride,, (d) a city archive of building permits at Time 2. Physical conditions improved overall in the neighborhood, but spatial analysis of the maps suggest that the spillover effects, if any, of the new housing were geographically limited, included unintended negative psychological consequences. Results argue for greater use of GIS, the street block level in community research, of psychological, behavioral variables in planning research, decisions.

title: Residential preferences, life plans
authors: Howell, Frank M
abstract: Discusses a study which examined the relationship of residential preferences to plans for other life cycle behaviors. Review of related literature on social-psychological processes; Methodology; Results of the study.

title: Affect, risk,, decision making
authors: Slovic, Paul, Peters, Ellen, Finucane, Melissa L, Macgregor, Donald G
journal: Health psychology: official journal of the Division of Health Psychology, American Psychological Association
keywords: Emotions; Heuristics; Medical Treatment (General); Neoplasms; Prevention; affect heuristic; cancer prevention; cancer treatment; communication; decision making; evaluation; rationality; risk analysis; risk perception;z\_pmt2009\_dual
abstract: Risk is perceived, acted on in 2 fundamental ways. Risk as feelings refers to individuals' fast, instinctive,, intuitive reactions to danger. Risk as analysis brings logic, reason,, scientific deliberation to bear on risk management. Reliance on risk as feelings is described with ``the affect heuristic.'' The authors trace the development of this heuristic across a variety of research paths. The authors also discuss some of the important practical implications resulting from ways that this heuristic impacts how people perceive, evaluate risk, and, more generally, how it influences all human decision making. Finally, some important implications of the affect heuristic for communication, decision making pertaining to cancer prevention, treatment are briefly discussed.

title: The empirical case for two systems of reasoning
authors: Sloman, Steven A
keywords: distinction between \& properties of associative vs rule based systems of reasoning; Associative Processes; Reasoning;z\_pmt2009\_dual;\_\_work\_pdf登録
abstract: Distinctions have been proposed between systems of reasoning for centuries. This article distills properties shared by many of these distinctions, characterizes the resulting systems in light of recent findings, theoretical developments. One system is associative because its computations reflect similarity structure, relations of temporal contiguity. The other is ule based because it operates on symbolic structures that have logical content, variables, because its computations have the properties that are normally assigned to rules. The systems serve complementary functions, can simultaneously generate different solutions to a reasoning problem. The rule-based system can suppress the associative system but not completely inhibit it. The article reviews evidence in favor of the distinction, its characterization.

title: What does it mean to know a cumulative risk? Adolescents' perceptions of short‐term, long‐term consequences of smoking
authors: Slovic, P
keywords: perceptions of short- \& long-term consequences of smoking, 14-20 yr olds; Adolescent Attitudes; Tobacco Smoking; Risk Assessment;z\_pmt2009\_dual
abstract: A particularly important aspect of risk is its cumulative nature, when exposure to a hazard occurs repeatedly over time. The degree to which people understand cumulative risk has important theoretical, social implications. The latter play a role in disputes about whether those who smoke cigarettes know the risks of that activity. Proponents of the view that cigarette smoking reflects rational choices made by people well informed about the risks assume that knowledge of smoking risks is adequately assessed in terms of perceptions of the long-term risks. However, there is reason to question this assumption. The risks of smoking cumulate, one cigarette at a time. The present study demonstrates that a high percentage of adolescent smokers see no health risk from smoking the next cigarette or even from smoking regularly for the ‘first few years’. This denial of ‘short-term’ risks, coupled with a tendency observed in other studies for young smokers to underestimate the addictive properties of tobacco, indicates that many young people do not really understand the risks from smoking cigarettes. title: The singularity effect of identified victims in separate, joint evaluations
authors: Kogut, Tehila, Ritov, Ilana
keywords: singularity effect; identified victims; preference reversals; emotional responses; judgments; Judgment; Preferences; Victimization;z\_pmt2009\_dual
abstract: People’s greater willingness to help identified victims, relative to non-identified ones, was examined by eliciting real contributions to targets varying in singularity (a single individual vs. a group of several individuals),, the availability of individually identifying information (the main difference being the inclusion of a picture in the “identified” versions). Results of the first, second experiments support the proposal that for identified victims, contributions for a single victim exceed contributions for a group when these are judged separately, but preference reverses when one has to choose between contributing to the single individual, contributing to the group. In a third experiment, ratings of emotional response were elicited in addition to willingness to contribute judgments. Results suggest that the greater contribution to a single victim relative to the group stems from intensified emotions evoked by a single identified victim rather than from emotions evoked by identified victims in general.

title: Exploring the relationship between drug, alcohol treatment facilities, violent, property crime: A socioeconomic contingent relationship
authors: Taniguchi, Travis A, Salvatore, Christopher
abstract: Siting of drug, alcohol treatment facilities is often met with negative reactions because of the assumption that these facilities increase crime by attracting drug users (and possibly dealers) to an area. This assumption, however, rests on weak empirical footings that have not been subjected to strong empirical analyses. Using census block groups from Philadelphia, PA, it was found that the criminogenic impact of treatment facilities in, near a neighborhood on its violent, property crime rates may be contingent on the socioeconomic status (SES) of the neighborhood. Paying attention to both the density, proximity of facilities in, around neighborhoods, results showed that the criminogenic impact of treatment facilities depended largely on neighborhood SES. Under some conditions more treatment facilities nearby was associated with lower crime. Reasons why the presumed criminogenic impact of treatment facilities appears only under some conditions were suggested.

title: Crime, response in rural Japan
authors: Takahashi, Yoshiko
booktitle: The Routledge International Handbook of Rural Criminology
abstract: The community policing system, which has long been a defining feature of Japan's low-crime society, no longer has sufficient staffing, resources in rural areas to maintain its prior levels of efficiency, effectiveness. The population trends have left rural Japan with a number of challenges. Senior citizens in rural Japan are more likely to live alone without ties to family, which makes them more vulnerable to new types of fraud such as Ore ore sagi, aggressive home-visit sales. In response to Ore ore sagi, the police also held workshops involving case studies, advised how to prevent such frauds,, distributed a newsletter to increase citizens' awareness. The aging concentration is closely correlated to rural depopulation, with the areas of highest aging also being the areas of the most significant depopulation. To improve community safety, people expected the police to patrol the community,, provide information about crime prevention, crimes that have taken place.

title: The Routledge international handbook of rural criminology
authors: Donnermeyer, Joseph
abstract: Forty-nine per cent of the world’s population lives in small towns, villages, farms, yet until recent years criminological scholarship has focused almost exclusively on urban crimes. The Routledge International Handbook of Rural Criminology is the first major publication to bring together this growing body of scholarship under a single cover. For many years, rural criminology has remained marginalized, often excluded from the mainstream, with precedence given to urban criminology. This volume intends to address that imbalance.
