title: Willingness to report sexual offenses to the police in Ghana
authors: Boateng, Francis D, Lee, Heeuk D
abstract: This study examined reasons why women in Ghana would report or not report sexual offenses to the police. Using a representative field survey, data were collected during summer of 2011 (N = 431) in the capital, Accra. We found that women would report sexual offenses because they want the offender to be caught, punished,, because crimes should be reported. Reasons for not reporting include when women consider the incident not serious enough, the perpetrator is known,, family will solve it. A multivariate analysis shows that only previous sexual victimization is a significant predictor of sexual offense reporting among women in Ghana.

title: The merging of criminology, geography into a course on spatial crime analysis
authors: Althausen, John D, Mieczkowski, Thomas M
abstract: This article discusses the development, implementation of a course in spatial crime analysis, an interdisciplinary course merging together materials from geographic information systems (GIS), criminology. The article explains the rationale for the course, the topical substance of the lectures,, the nature of the laboratory, computer-based exercises. There is a brief discussion of the pedagogy, the problems encountered in offering the course.

title: Measurement of public opinions on security: the case from Malaysia
authors: Sidek, Noor Zahirah Mohd, Shaharudin, Mohd Rizaimy, Abdullah, Wan Nailah, Hamid, Nur Zainie Abd, Noor, Norazam Mohd, Arsad, Ab Rahaman
abstract: The measurement of security perception is necessary as one of the tools to assess the effectiveness of security policies, enforcement in a country. The aim of the paper is two-fold. Firstly, the study presents an attempt to develop the Security Perception Index (PSI) based on Malaysia’s specific context. Secondly, the study purports to measure the perception of Malaysia’s security for the year 2021 using the developed PSI framework. Six domains were utilised based on the country's national policies on security, public order, such as the National Security Policy (2021–2025), the Security, Public Order Policy (2019). A total of 15,461 samples were collected within the period of three months. The perception index score is 64.67\%, which falls into the ``perceived as safe'' category, implies that the public perceives Malaysia as a safe country to live, work in. The scores are also calculated for each state, the Federal Territories, with Johor obtaining the highest score (72.37\%), Sabah with the lowest score (54.3\%). Implications of the study include prevention, monitoring, law enforcement,, community engagement. Future studies should consider integrating secondary data such as crime, crime scene frequency,, visualisation using geographical information systems (GIS) to provide more integrated, real-time information.

title: Media consumption, fear of crime: Evidence of the need for an intersectional approach
authors: Rosenberger, Jared S, Dierenfeldt, Rick, Ingle, Hannah
abstract: Race/ethnicity, gender,, exposure to various types of media have been identified as important predictors of fear of crime. However, previous research largely fails to take a truly intersectional approach when testing this relationship. Utilizing a unique data source that oversamples for minority respondents, includes measures for social media, Internet,, traditional media consumption the current study attempts to fill this gap. Our research finds evidence that the link between media consumption, fear of crime varies significantly across intersectional subsamples of race/ethnicity, gender. This identifies a need for future intersectional research on fear of crime.

title: Tourists’ safety in the risk society: Explaining perceptions of safety regarding future vacations
authors: Mawby, Rob, Ozascilar, Mine
abstract: While the risk of crime, perceptions of safety have been regularly addressed by criminologists, this has rarely extended to asking how those considering or taking vacations perceive their security. In contrast, tourism researchers regularly focus on perceptions of safety but define this more broadly to include, inter alia, safety from health risks, natural disasters. This paper melds the two disciplines by considering which destinations US residents perceived as unsafe, focusing on risks from crime, political unrest or terrorism,, health concerns. The research used a crowdsourcing platform to collect citizens’ perceptions of safety with regard to crime, terrorism/political disorder,, health problems at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings suggest that health problems were seen as the greatest risk, but not excessively so. Mexico, China were seen as the most risky countries to visit, although US residents also considered the USA a relatively dangerous place to spend a vacation. Variations in perceptions of safety between subgroups of respondents were greatest for health problems, least for crime, suggesting that fear of crime is associated with features of everyday life that are less relevant to tourism destinations. The paper concludes by discussing the relevance of the findings for both the tourism sector, criminology.

title: Understanding the fear of crime, perceived risk across immigrant generations: Does the quality of social ties matter?
authors: Yuan, Yue, McNeeley, Susan, Melde, Chris
abstract: The current study examines the relationships between immigration, social ties,, perceptions of safety. We estimated immigrant generation by race/ethnicity interactions to uncover unique patterns across subpopulations of immigrants while controlling for important neighborhood contextual factors. Immigrant generation was negatively associated with feelings of fear. First-generation Asian immigrants reported the greatest level of fear in the sample. High-quality social ties were negatively associated with fear of crime, while the number of social ties was unrelated to fear. Results suggest first-generation immigrants are in a precarious position in society with respect to feeling safe in their neighborhoods. Local officials should seek ways to provide accurate messaging on the threat of victimization in immigrant communities.

title: Ways of perceiving safety: From interpretative registers to mechanisms of interpretation
authors: Noble, Julien
abstract: In the study of fear of crime, perception of safety with respect to the risk of victimization is often viewed as the mere consequence of the absence of perceived risk. This paper takes the opposite view: that it is a complex phenomenon resting on a plurality of interpretative registers. Analysis of some thirty interviews of students at a French university shows three different ways of perceiving safety (fragility, self-confidence, tranquility), each rests on a specific relationship to oneself, toward supposed aggressors. Having shown this, we then look at how these interpretations emerge, evolve over time. Interpretations are by no means attached to individuals, rather, they fluctuate with the situations encountered, with past experiences, whence the importance of bringing out the two dimensions - synchronic, diachronic - of this phenomenon.

title: The effect of victimization severity on perceived risk of victimization: Analyses using an international sample
authors: Abbott, Jessica, McGrath, Shelly A
abstract: In this article, we explored the effect of prior victimization severity on perceived risk using a cross-national sample. We extracted data for all variables from the International Criminal Victimization Survey (ICVS), the European Survey on Crime Safety (EU ICS). Using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression for both pooled data, individual countries, we found that, in addition to numerous control, prior victimization variables, our key independent variable—perceived severity of victimization—generally influences levels of perceived risk. Discussion of the results, limitations of the study are also included.

title: Effect of public housing redevelopment on reported, perceived crime in a Seattle neighborhood
authors: Albertson, Elaine Michelle, Chen, Roxana, Matheson, Alastair, Ursua, Maria Guillermina, Fliss, Mike Dolan, Farquhar, Stephanie
abstract: Although research indicates that developing new public housing typically does not increase neighborhood crime, little is known about the impact of revitalizing existing public housing properties, also known as redevelopment. This study evaluates the effect of a multi-component physical, social redevelopment project on reports, perceptions of neighborhood crime in Seattle, Washington. We compare administrative police data with findings from a community survey to assess trends during early-to-mid redevelopment. While perceptions of safety improved over the study period, most crime-specific trends were not significantly different at the redevelopment site relative to comparison sites where no redevelopment occurred. Results suggest that this project did not have obvious adverse effects on crime rates. Although this redevelopment may have had a positive effect on perceptions of crime, safety in the short-term, it may take longer to realize beneficial effects on actual experiences or reports of crime.

title: Crime victimization distress, neighbourhood social cohesion, perceived police effectiveness
authors: Avery, Eileen E, Hermsen, Joan M, Towne, Katelynn
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
abstract: Despite important policy implications, there is scant research on the relationship between distress from victimization, perceptions of police effectiveness. This study investigates the relationship between extent of distress due to violent victimization, perceptions of local law enforcement. In addition, we examine the way that perceived neighbourhood social cohesion accounts for the relationship. We use data from a U.S. statewide victimization survey to estimate regression models that compare victims of violent crime with no/mild distress, victims with moderate/severe distress, nonvictims of violent crime on ratings of police effectiveness. Models include controls for local crime, poverty rates, demographic characteristics, property crime victimization, respondents' exposure to negative policing via media, their own contact with law enforcement. Results show that 10\% of respondents are victims of violent crime,, among victims, 40\% report no/mild distress, 60\% report moderate/severe distress. While victims with greater distress rate police lower on the effectiveness scale, these differences can be accounted for by controls for neighbourhood context, especially the level of perceived social cohesion. Results suggest neighbourhood social environments should be incorporated into models of perceptions of police effectiveness, policing more broadly, that increasing social cohesion may improve police‐community dynamics.

title: A predictive model for psychological reactions to crime in Italy: an analysis of fear of crime, concern about crime as a social problem
authors: Amerio, Piero, Roccato, Michele
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: CRIME; PSYCHOLOGY; SOCIAL problems; VICTIMS of crimes; APPLIED sociology; ITALY; Social concerns; Feeling of unsafety; Victimization; Mass media; Fear of crime;301\_ComCrm;J Community Appl Soc Psychol
abstract: AbstractIn this study a model for predicting fear of crime (FC), concern about crime as a social problem (CC) in Italy has been built, using three sets of independent variables concerning: (a) the sociodemographic, criminal victimization domain; (b) the psychosocial domain;, (c) the mass media. A secondary analysis on data gathered by the Observatory of the North‐West (N = 3262, a mail panel that is representative of the Italian population over 18) has been performed. Results showed that FC, CC are related yet distinct constructs: FC is less widespread than CC,, has different predictors. FC predictors are sociodemographic, psychosocial and, above all, victimization variables; whereas mass media, psychosocial variables predict CC. Results were compared with the literature on the topic. Implications, limitations,, future directions are discussed. Copyright © 2004 John Wiley \& Sons, Ltd.

title: Can security beget insecurity? Security, crime prevention awareness, fear of burglary among university students in the East Midlands
authors: Barberet, Rosemary, Fisher, Bonnie S
keywords: university security; crime; crime prevention; awareness; FEAR of crime; university students; victimization; student attitudes; Fear; Safety; College Students; Crime Victims;301\_ComCrm;Security Journal
abstract: Contrary to the heightened awareness surrounding university student safety, security in the United States, it is only recently that attention has been given to these issues in England. In 2002, the Home Office of England, Wales commissioned a study of student victimisation, fear of crime at nine universities in the East Midlands region. Using self-report data from this study, the present study examined the influence of student awareness of institutional security, crime prevention efforts on levels of student fear of burglary in university-owned or -operated accommodation. Awareness of some types of security features, crime prevention efforts was related to students being less fearful, whereas for others, students were more fearful of burglary. Awareness of measures designed to increase the efforts of would-be offenders generated mixed fear results, whereas measures to increase their risks were associated with less fear among those students who were aware of them. The awareness–fear of burglary relationship was particularly pronounced for women students. The implications for university security, crime prevention are discussed.

title: Predicting fear of crime: Results from a community survey of a small city
authors: Bolger, Michelle A, Bolger, P Colin
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: Several studies have examined predictors surrounding fear of crime. Fear of crime has generally been conceptualized as an affective emotional state regarding concern over victimization or as a cognitive state of perceived risk of victimization. While there are many potential predictors of fear of crime, there are two main groups of predictors: individual demographics, neighborhood physical, social disorder. Previous research has predominantly focused on large, urban cities. Less research has been published surrounding smaller cities, towns. As such, the current study involved a mailed household survey of a small city of around 80,000 residents in Pennsylvania. The study examined demographic predictors in line with the vulnerability model, neighborhood contextual predictors of residents’ fear of crime associated with the incivilities model. While the main analyses employed a more affective measure of fear of crime, a supplementary analysis using a measure of perceived neighborhood crime problems was examined as well. Findings revealed that in line with previous research, females, minorities were more likely to be fearful of crime. However, less favorable views of local police, more physical disorder,, more social disorder were also related to greater fear of crime, accounted for a much larger proportion of the variance explaining fear of crime. Supplementary findings strongly supported the importance of neighborhood contextual factors in predicting perceptions of crime problems, including the views of police, physical,, social disorder. However, no demographic factors predicted perceived neighborhood crime problems. Implications, limitations of the study findings are discussed.

title: How do individuals deal with victimization, victimization risk? Longitudinal evidence from Mexico
authors: Braakmann, Nils
keywords: Cost of crime; Victimization; Avoidance behavior; Dwelling protection;301\_ComCrm
abstract: This paper uses variation in victimization probabilities, past victimization between individuals living in the same community to shed new light on the costs of crime. I use panel data from the Mexican Family Life Survey for 2002, 2005, look at the impact of within-community differences in victimization risk on changes in (avoidance) behavior, time-allocation. My results from fixed effects, instrumental variable estimations point towards a number of behavioral changes, including individuals arming themselves, with marked gender differences in the reactions of individuals. Crime victims also suffer from sleep deprivation indicating welfare losses.

title: How collective is collective efficacy? The importance of consensus in judgments about community cohesion, willingness to intervene: How collective is collective efficacy?
authors: Brunton-smith, Ian, Sturgis, Patrick, Leckie, George
keywords: collective efficacy; mixed‐effects; location‐scale model; neighborhood effects; multilevel model; consensus effects;301\_ComCrm;criminology
abstract: AbstractExisting studies have generally measured collective efficacy by combining survey respondents’ ratings of their local area into an overall summary for each neighborhood. Naturally, this approach results in a substantive focus on the variation in average levels of collective efficacy between neighborhoods. In this article, we focus on the variation in consensus of collective efficacy judgments. To account for differential consensus among neighborhoods, we use a mixed‐effects location‐scale model, with variability in the consensus of judgments treated as an additional neighborhood‐level random effect. Our results show that neighborhoods in London differ, not just in their average levels of collective efficacy but also in the extent to which residents agree with one another in their assessments. In accord with findings for U.S. cities, our results show that consensus in collective efficacy assessments is affected by the ethnic composition of neighborhoods. Additionally, we show that heterogeneity in collective efficacy assessments is consequential, with higher levels of criminal victimization, worry about crime,, risk avoidance behavior in areas where collective efficacy consensus is low.

title: Violence, worry, trust in the emergence of weapon-carrying
authors: Brennan, Iain R
abstract: This paper identifies longitudinal predictors of weapon-carrying in a sample of 10–25 year olds in England, Wales. It conceptualises weapon-carrying as anticipation of an adverse event, proposes hypotheses about the origins of weapon-carrying derived from the field of risk analysis. Specifically, it tests if worry about victimisation, experience of violence predict later weapon-carrying, assesses the moderating influence of trust in the police. The results indicate that worry about victimisation does not predict weapon-carrying, but experience of violence does. Distrust of police, peer criminality were also identified as important precursors to weapon-carrying. The study provides further evidence that, at least over longer periods, weapon-carrying is a product of experience of violence, criminogenic factors rather than a response to concern about victimisation.

title: Social disorganization, theories of crime, delinquency: Problems, prospects
authors: Bursik, Jr, Robert J
abstract: After a period of decline in the discipline, the social disorganization model of Shaw, McKay is again beginning to appear in the literature. This paper examines five criticisms of the perspective, discusses recent attempts to address those issues, problems that are still in need of resolution.

title: Examining collective efficacy, perceptions of policing in East Baltimore
authors: Cantora, Andrea, Wasileski, Gabriela, Iyer, Seema, Restivo, Lauren
abstract: This study examines how residents from a high-crime, high-poverty neighborhood in East Baltimore interact with one another, participate in their community,, perceive police. Using community surveys collected from 191 respondents, the study empirically measures collective efficacy, community participation,, police services, encounters. We predict that high levels of collective efficacy lead to more positive perceptions of police, an increased willingness to work with law enforcement. The results indicate that neighborhood trust is an important factor in shaping a community’s overall perception of police. Furthermore, older residents who own their homes are more likely to report a more positive perception of police, specifically police response.

title: Bonding social capital, collective action: Associations with residents' perceptions of their neighbourhoods
authors: Carbone, Jason T
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: bonding social capital; citizen participation; collective action; community development; community/civic engagement; neighbourhood perceptions;301\_ComCrm
abstract: AbstractNeighbourhood perceptions have important implications for individual well‐being, yet there is limited research focused on variables that predict these perceptions. This study proposes that previous engagement in collective action mediates the relationship between neighbourhood bonding social capital, neighbourhood perceptions. Structural equation modelling with a large, nationally representative sample (N = 25,370) is used to test the hypotheses. The findings suggest that bonding social capital has a positive, direct effect on both neighbourhood perceptions, collective action. Collective action has a negative, direct association with neighbourhood perceptions, bonding social capital has a negative, indirect effect on neighbourhood perceptions via collective action. Although the full model explains 28\% of the variance in neighbourhood perceptions, bonding social capital only explains 5\% of the variance in collective action.

title: Factors affecting crime, fear of crime, satisfaction with police: focusing on policing, the neighborhood context
authors: Cho, Joon Tag
abstract: PurposeThe purpose of this study is to explore factors affecting police performance, such as violent crime, fear of crime, satisfaction with police, using objectively measured policing, neighborhood characteristics.Design/methodology/approachThis study combined four data sources, including police statistics, a crime victimization survey, local government statistics, a public service satisfaction survey. Negative binomial regression, ordinary least squares models were estimated using data from 135 city governments.FindingsViolent crime was negatively associated with arrest, while fear of crime was negatively associated with patrol, positively correlated with disorder, public places. In addition, satisfaction with police had a positive association with level of patrolling, disorder policing, whereas residents receiving public assistance, ethnic heterogeneity, entertainment establishments were negatively associated with it.Research limitations/implicationsThis paper identified the different factors that impact each type of police performance, indicating its unique characteristics. Further research should be conducted to analyze data from non-urban areas to improve external validity.Practical implicationsThis study suggests that police managers need to choose the means of policing carefully depending on which performance indicators they are focusing on improving in the region.Originality/valueFew studies to date have examined the correlation between objectively measured policing, neighborhood context factors, police performance at the macro level.

title: Multi-level analysis of disorder policing, fear of crime in South Korea
authors: Cho, Joon Tag, Park, Jisun
abstract: Numerous studies have analyzed the relationship between disorder, fear of crime, but few have focused on the impact of policing against disorder on fear of crime. In order to fill in the gap of research, this study performs a preliminary analysis on the disorder policing, fear of crime in South Korea using a hierarchical linear model. The results showed that disorder policing was negatively associated with fear of crime. In addition, policing against disorder may be effective in reducing fear of crime in young females, who have the greatest fear of crime. Age was found to be inversely associated with fear of crime,, this effect was stronger in regions with more disorder policing. The results indicate a need for increased policing against disorder to reduce fear of crime, complete consideration of a region’s sociodemographic characteristics in the process of disorder policing,, more problem-oriented police activities where social disorder is prevalent.

title: Fear of crime, community concerns: Mediating effect of risk, pragmatic fear
authors: Chadee, Derek, Ali, Stacia, Burke, Ariel, Young, Jason
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: community concerns; pragmatic fear; risk of victimisation; fear of crime; incivilities; infrastructure;301\_ComCrm
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between community concerns (i.e., perceived crime, incivilities,, infrastructure), fear of crime (FOC) while examining the mediating role of risk of victimisation, pragmatic fear. Gender, ethnic differences were also explored. Data were collected using a proportionate multistage random sample of 3,003 participants from a southern Caribbean island in 2015. The following self‐reported measures were used: risk of victimisation, FOC scales, a general (noncrime) fear scale measuring pragmatic fear,, a community concern scale. Data were analysed using path analysis, Sobel tests,, multiple group analysis. Findings revealed that perceived crime, incivilities significantly predicted FOC, whereas infrastructure was insignificant as a direct predictor. Females had higher FOC,, among ethnic groups, Indo‐Trinidadians had the highest FOC than Afro‐Trinidadians, Mixed participants. Risk of victimisation, pragmatic fear had significant mediating effects on community concerns, FOC. Findings are discussed in the context of the social psychology of social disorganisation, previous research.

title: Explaining fear of crime in Queensland
authors: Carcach, Carlos, Frampton, Peta, Thomas, Kaye, Cranich, Mathew
keywords: statistical model of fear of crime, 15 yrs old \& older, Australia; Crime; Fear; Mathematical Modeling
abstract: A model to explain fear of crime in Queensland is developed, fitted to data from the 1991 Queensland Crime Victims Survey. Fear of crime is measured from the answers to the question about respondents' feelings of safety when walking alone in their area after dark. The results suggest that factors such as gender, age, poverty, educational level, labor force status, level of incivility in the area, perceived amount of crime in the area,, neighborhood cohesion all make an impact on fear of crime in a way that is consistent with the theory. The results also show that fear of crimein Queensland is explained by very concrete factors that can be subject to intervention, policy formulation by relevant bodies.

title: Victims' emotional distress, preventive measures usage: Influence of crime severity, risk perception,, fear
authors: Chadee, Derek, Williams, Diana, Bachew, Raecho
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: crime severity; emotional distress; fear of crime; perceived risk of victimization; preventive measures; Trinidad; victimization experience;301\_ComCrm
abstract: AbstractThe central thesis of this study is that crime victims' emotional distress, influenced by the severity of the offence experienced, impacts their propensity to utilize preventive measures via its influence on perceived risk of victimization, fear of crime. Path analysis was conducted to test a model of these relationships, utilizing data from a crime victimization survey conducted on the Caribbean Island, Trinidad, in 2015. Results suggest a direct predictive relationship between crime severity, emotional distress, indirect effects of emotional distress on preventive measures through risk perception, fear of crime. Findings were discussed in the context of prior research, comparability,, variances,, practical implications were noted.

title: Fear of crime in Brisbane city: revisiting the importance of ‘context’ in the development of fear of crime
authors: Chataway, Michael L, Mellberg, Jacques
abstract: Fear of crime can have significant consequences for physical, mental wellbeing. Although our understanding of the causes of fear of crime has improved over the years, there remains a lack of research examining the connections between individual, situational,, social factors that may contribute to concerns about crime within an individual’s immediate environment. The current study examines fear of crime as a context dependent experience, in order to better understand these connections. Data are collected from a sample of N = 180 residents living, working in Brisbane City, Australia. Using Factor Score Path Analysis, we show that signals of crime (i.e., physical, social disorder) in the immediate environment increase the likelihood of worry about crime. Results of this study indicate that in order to reduce concerns about crime researchers should consider dynamic signals of disorder in the immediate environment when designing interventions.

title: Fear of property crime: examining the effects of victimization, vicarious victimization,, perceived risk
authors: Cook, Carrie L, Fox, Kathleen A
keywords: Criminal statistics; Gender differences; Research \& development--R\&D; Social interaction; bicycle theft;301\_ComCrm;Violence Vict
abstract: Fear of crime research has primarily focused on fear of crime in general or on fear of specific types of violent crimes. This study builds from this line of research by focusing exclusively on the night fear of six types of property crimes, including fear of burglary while away from home, vehicle theft, bicycle theft, property theft, vandalism,, vehicle burglary. This study examines the effects of victimization, vicarious victimization,, perceived risk on fear of property crime. Survey data from college students reveal that victimization, vicarious victimization were not significant predictors of fear of property crime, whereas perceived risk was a consistent, significant predictor of fear of all property crimes.

title: Regional, structural,, demographic predictors of violent victimization: A cross-national, multilevel analysis of 112 countries
authors: Corcoran, Katie E, Stark, Rodney
abstract: Routine activities, lifestyles theories emphasize structural, demographic predictors that affect the opportunity to commit crime, the likelihood of being victimized. Past research tends to focus on either the individual- or country-level with few studies incorporating both. Additionally, past research primarily draws on the International Crime Victimization Survey, which results in small country samples that are biased toward developed nations. The current study uses data from a larger, more diverse sample that allow us to test whether findings from prior studies are generalizable. We are also able to theorize, test the effect of region on victimization. We find some differences between our findings, past research; we also identify that region is one of the strongest predictors of violent victimization.

title: Collective efficacy, violent crime in suburban housing estates
authors: Danielsson, Petri
abstract: Collective efficacy theory states that neighbourhood variation in crime can be attributed to social cohesion, informal social control. Despite a substantial body of work, the theory has been subject to little testing in Europe, few studies have compared different outcomes. The current study employed a cluster sampling design to study violent crime in a sample of 70 suburban housing estates built in the 1960s, 1970s throughout Finland. Police-recorded violent crime in public, private space, survey-based measures of neighbourhood violence were studied using register data on neighbourhood characteristics, the residents’ perceptions of social cohesion, perceived capacity for informal control. The results showed that, in a sample of Finnish suburban housing estates, collective efficacy was negatively associated with violence in private space, a survey-based measure of neighbourhood violence, while the association between collective efficacy, violence in public space was not significant. Neighbourhood disadvantage was directly associated with police-recorded violence in private surroundings but not violence in the public sphere.

title: Testing a multilevel opportunity theory of crime (place in neighborhood theory)
authors: Duru, Haci, Kim, Moonsun
abstract: This research aims to empirically test a newly developed “place in neighborhood (PIN)” theory, proposed by Wilcox, Tillyer recently. Using secondary data, the authors generate measures of crime, opportunity factors in street blocks nested in neighborhood clusters in Chicago. Hierarchical non-linear models are used to assess the impact of factors in street block level, neighborhood level,, their cross-level interactions on residential burglary. The results show that all four street block level variables are associated with levels of burglary,, two of three neighborhood level variables (social control, delinquency rate) are significantly associated with lower, higher levels of residential burglary, respectively. Five of the twelve cross-level interaction terms are significantly associated with residential burglary rates. Two of the main effects, one of the cross-level interaction terms show unexpected opposite directions. The findings lend partial support to PIN theory.

title: Environmental design, neighborhood context: A multi-level analysis of crime at apartments in Cincinnati neighborhoods
authors: Deryol, Rustu, Payne, Troy
abstract: The present study examines the role of opportunity on crime counts within the multicontextual opportunity theoretical framework. We used weighted multilevel regression modeling of site observation data from a Cincinnati-based sample of 1003 apartments nested within 228 census block groups. Results indicate that only a couple of environmental design features are associated with crime in the expected direction,, some of these associations are neighborhood-context-dependent. We conclude that the results support the propositions of multicontextual opportunity theory suggesting that neighborhood level factors condition the relationship between micro level opportunity factors, crime. Since there is a scant literature on this topic, more research is needed to see if the findings hold true in other places.

title: Fear of crime in Israel : A multidimensional approach
authors: Fishman, G, Mesch, Gustavo S
