title: Early academic skills, childhood experiences across the urban–rural continuum
authors: Miller, Portia, Votruba-Drzal, Elizabeth
keywords: Urbanicity; Early academic skills; Home environment;306\_Rural
abstract: The urban–rural continuum provides unique contexts for development. Differences in access to resources, childrearing norms, practices in urban, suburban,, rural areas may be linked to disparities in early achievement. Yet, few studies examine associations between urbanicity, children's early academic skills. Using nationally representative data from the Early Childhood Longitudinal Study, Birth Cohort (N ≈ 6050) this study examined differences in academic skills at kindergarten entry across large urban, small urban, suburban, rural areas. Additionally, it considered whether home environments, child care experiences explained disparities in early achievement. Results showed that children in large urban, rural areas entered kindergarten with less advanced academic skills than children in small urban areas, suburbs. Lower achievement for rural children was partly explained by less advantageous home environments, increased use of home-based, rather than center-based, preschool. Parents living in large urban areas had less knowledge of child development, which helped explain their children's lower achievement.

title: A process, outcome evaluation of an Agricultural Crime prevention initiative
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Scott, Michelle L, Bhati, Avinash S
abstract: Agricultural crime victimization—including theft of farm crops, livestock, pesticides,, equipment—and efforts to address it remain largely ignored despite the potential of such crime to adversely affect the lives, businesses of farmers, increase the costs of food to consumers. The Agricultural Crime, Technology, Information,, Operations Network (ACTION) initiative, located in California's central valley, was recently developed to combat such crime. The authors present findings from a process, outcome evaluation of this program. The findings are limited by the design of the study but nonetheless suggest that efforts to increase guardianship measures among farmers (e.g., marking equipment, livestock, using surveillance equipment), to “harden targets” (e.g., locking tractors, storing chemicals in locked storage sheds),, to arrest, prosecute offenders may help reduce agricultural crime victimization.

title: Opportunity theory, agricultural crime victimization
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Scott, Michelle L, Bhati, Avinash S
abstract: Abstract A growing body of research lends support to opportunity theory, its variants, but has yet to focus systematically on a number of specific offenses, contexts. Typically, the more crimes, contexts to which a theory applies, the broader its scope, range, respectively,, thus generalizability. In this paper, we focus on agricultural crime victimization— including theft of farm equipment, crops, livestock,, chemicals—an offense that opportunity theory appears well‐situated to explain. Specifically, we examine whether key dimensions of the theory are empirically associated with the likelihood of victimization, also examine factors associated with farmers' use of guardianship measures. In contrast to much previous research, we combine multiple individual‐level measures of these dimensions. We conclude that the theory partially accounts for variation in agricultural crime victimization, depending on the type of crime,, that greater work is needed investigating how key dimensions of opportunity theory should be conceptualized, operationalized in rural contexts. The study's implications for theory, practice are discussed.

title: Using evidence of empirical research to understand the nature, extent of stock theft: Lessons from Limpopo Province of South Africa
authors: Maluleke, Witness
journal: International Journal of Social Science Research, Review
abstract: Using evidence of empirical research to understand the nature, extent of stock theft in the Limpopo Province of South Africa was the objective of this study. This qualitative study collected data through semi-structured Key Informant Interviews (KIIs), by purposively selecting prominent South African Police Service (SAPS) members, this was aided by the adoption of non-empirical research design: Systematic review, closely looking at recent reputable reports across globe, while using South Africa as a case study, restricted to 2000-2021 [Not in sequence]. The inductive Thematic Content Analysis (TCA) was applied for data analysis.This study established that the current relationship between the local livestock farmers, community members nor relevant stakeholders [Anti-Stock theft structures] is in current disarray state, further positively contributing to the increase of this crime, moreover, adequate deterrent (Combative, Preventative, Investigative) strategies seem to be ineffective. The relevant parties unclearly understand the nature, extent of stock theft in the study locations. It was concluded, recommended that the existing stock theft combating, prevention, investigation strategies be integrated with empirical research studies to enhance current practices. The SAPS Stock Theft Units (STUs) in the Limpopo Province should be strengthened by emphasing closer collaboration, interaction, information exchange amongst these stakeholders, to promote greater awareness, pertaining the nature, extent of this crime across the province, as understanding stock theft phenomenon, prevalence, is critical to its prevention.

title: Protective orders in rural, urban areas: a multiple perspective study: A multiple perspective study
authors: Logan, T K, Shannon, Lisa, Walker, Robert
keywords: Adolescent; Adult; Community Networks/organization \& administration; Female; Focus Groups; Health Services Accessibility/statistics \& numerical data; Health Services Research; Humans; Kentucky/epidemiology; Law Enforcement; Middle Aged; Patient Acceptance of Health Care/statistics \& numerical data; Rural Health Services/statistics \& numerical data; Rural Population/statistics \& numerical data; Spouse Abuse/legislation \& jurisprudence/prevention \& control/statistics \& numerical data; Urban Health Services/statistics \& numerical data; Urban Population/statistics \& numerical data; Women's Health Services/statistics \& numerical data;306\_Rural;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: This study is one of the first to examine the protective order process, barriers,, outcomes by combining qualitative, quantitative research in rural, urban areas. State statutes suggest the protective order process should be fair, consistent,, accessible to all women in the state. However, study results suggest that (a) the process of obtaining protective orders varies depending on community context; (b) although there are barriers to obtaining, enforcing protective orders regardless of geographic region, rural women appear to have more barriers;, (c) differences exist in victimization experiences, protective order stipulations, violations,, perceived effectiveness among rural, urban women.

title: Stock theft: Rural livestock farmers’ entrepreneurial perspectives
authors: Mabunda, Mkateko Vivian, Maluleke, Witness, Barkhuizen, Jaco, Clack, Willie Johannes
abstract: The collation between stock theft, rural livestock farmers’ entrepreneurial perspectives receive limited attention in the field of Criminology, Criminal Justice, as well as ‘Business Administration’ nor entrepreneurial dominance industry. Conventionally, stock theft is nothing new in South Africa, traditional interpretations, recorded cases can be reportedly traced back to 1806. This study reflects the duality of stock theft, offering criminological [Theoretical] explanations, glimpses of attractive business enterprises by adopting the three elements of ‘Timmons Model of Entrepreneurial Process’ through the use of non-empirical research design: Systematic review, while featuring the most affected areas by stock theft in the Eastern Cape (EC), KwaZulu-Natal (KZN), Mpumalanga (MP) Provinces respectively, while focusing on 2014-2020 financial years. This study establishes provides that this crime, instead of making more business avenues for rural livestock farmers, will continue to decrease the number of job opportunities. It is recommended that the South African government (I.e. national, provincial, local levels), agricultural industries,, the local South African Police Service Stock Theft Units (SAPS STUs) as a collective, commodity organisations will have to gravely consider offering adequate services required to bring workable solutions for initiation of entrepreneurial activities in the selected provinces.

title: Civic community, population change,, violent crime in rural communities
authors: Lee, Matthew R, Thomas, Shaun A
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: This analysis investigates the relationships between measures of civic community, population change,, violent crime rates in rural communities. Rural communities that are civically robust are hypothesized to have lower violent crime rates, to experience less change in violent crime over time. Alternatively, sustained population change is hypothesized to elevate violent crime rates, to moderate the protective effect that civic robustness provides against violent crime over time. Results from both lagged panel, cross-sectional negative binomial regression models of county-level data support these expectations. In substantive terms, these findings suggest that civically robust communities are much better positioned to weather population change than civically weak communities, but continuous change over time compromises the protective effect that civic robustness provides against serious crime.

title: Rural policing, youth, overlapping fields of youth justice
authors: Hepburn, Taryn, Spencer, Dale, Ricciardelli, Rosemary
abstract: In the current article, we document the changing roles, responsibilities related to the implementation of the Canadian Youth Criminal Justice Act ( YCJA). Police officers’ experiences, responses to the implementation of the YCJA reveal a disparity between the officers’ idealised role, their actual tasks involving youth. Drawing on Bourdieu’s theory of the habitus, field, we consider the field of youth justice, its effects on rural policing strategies in Canada. We consider the shifting standard for police behaviours from data gathered through interviews, focus groups with police officers. We find standards in the field of policing shift to reflect new realities enacted with the YCJA.

title: Creating demand: influencing information technology diffusion in rural communities
authors: Hollifield, C Ann, Donnermeyer, Joseph F
abstract: In the 21st century, access to information technologies will be necessary for rural communities to attract, retain businesses and, therefore, remain economically viable. However, low population density makes it difficult for rural areas to support expensive technology investments such as are required for broadband. In addition, history shows rural adoption timelines significantly lag those in urban areas, which slows development of the demand economically necessary to support infrastructure construction.This study examined variables that influenced rural residents’ comparatively early adoption of information technologies at a time when the rural-urban digital divide in the use of basic online services was still growing. The study found employment by a company that was using specific information technologies was the strongest predictor of individual adoption. The effect was particularly strong among those with less formal education. The findings suggest rural development specialists should focus on encouraging locally owned rural businesses to adopt information technologies as a means of maximizing local diffusion, increasing demand levels.

title: Using geographic information systems to assess community-level vulnerability to housing insecurity in rural areas
authors: Gleason, Kristen D, Dube, Matthew, Bernier, Elizabeth, Martin, Jennifer
keywords: geographic information systems; homelessness; housing insecurity; prevention; rural community; rural population;306\_Rural
abstract: Research examining homelessness in rural areas has been sparse. The current study aims to expand conceptions of rural homelessness by mapping community-level risk factors related to housing insecurity. Geographic information systems (GIS) techniques were used to map the distribution of select community-level risk indicators in the State of Maine. Three methodological choices related to this process are demonstrated: (1) selection, distribution of housing insecurity risk indicators; (2) use of location quotients;, (3) use of spatial lags. After examining, mapping selected risk factors against the location of homeless service supports, four areas in Maine were identified as communities of concern for housing insecurity. Better understanding the extent, location of areas of high need that are resource poor can help service, funding agencies to plan for the more efficient, effective distribution of homeless prevention, mitigation services. Implications for research in rural areas are discussed.

title: The rural/urban divide: Examining different types of assault through a social disorganization lens
authors: Goodson, Amanda, Bouffard, Leana A
keywords: intimate partner violence; rural/urban divide; social disorganization;306\_Rural;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Most studies of social disorganization theory focus on urban communities. In addition, these studies largely ignore more intimate crimes, such as intimate partner violence. Yet, results from extant studies are often generalized to explain all types of crime in all types of communities, thus potentially ignoring the dynamics surrounding intimate crimes, rurality. The current study expands on previous research in two ways. First, this study examines whether characteristics of social disorganization can predict assault across various victim-offender relationships. Second, this study applies social disorganization predictors to both metropolitan (or urban), nonmetropolitan (or rural) counties. The sample consisted of 690 counties located across 13 different states. Results from the Poisson regression models indicate higher levels of ethnic heterogeneity, concentrated disadvantage were associated with increased rates of assault across various victim-offender relationships. Furthermore, the measures of social disorganization functioned in the expected direction in both metropolitan, nonmetropolitan counties. These results highlight the importance of controlling for community structures when examining rates of violence, including intimate partner violence. Programs, policies designed to reduce intimate partner violence should include neighborhood components as these affect rates of violence within a community.

title: Crime, Alabama farms : victimization, subjective assessment,, protective action
authors: Dunkelberger, John Edward, Clayton, J Mark, Myrick, Rebecca Suzan, Lyles, Gladys

title: Beyond education, employment: Exploring youth experiences of their communities, place attachment, reasons for migration
authors: Eacott, Chelsea, Sonn, Christopher C
abstract: The population in rural areas of Australia has been declining for many decades, it has become common practice to blame this decline on the migration of young people due to structural limitations (e.g. education, employment). This study explores factors associated with migration of youth from rural Victoria looking at their experience of place attachment, community satisfaction, rural culture, migration. Ten participants, four males, six females, were interviewed using a semi-structured guide; they had all relocated from rural Victorian communities to Melbourne. Thematic analyses of data led to the identification of two major thematic categories: migration dynamics, rural culture. Participants confirmed the lack of educational, employment opportunities as the main influences on rural youth migration. Interestingly it was found that all participants felt a sense of community satisfaction, attachment to place but still decided to relocate. Most expressed a desire to return to rural Victoria in the future. The potential of attachment to place, community are discussed as important points for community development initiatives aimed at addressing rural out-migration.

title: Toward a gendered Second Generation CPTED for preventing woman abuse in rural communities
authors: DeKeseredy, Walter S, Donnermeyer, Joseph F, Schwartz, Martin D
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Violence; Women; Social networks; Theory; Sex crimes; Schools; Law enforcement; Evidence; Cultural values; Criminal justice;306\_Rural;Security Journal
abstract: Informed by several studies of woman abuse in rural settings, the main objective of this paper is to discuss how key principles of Second Generation Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) can be applied to help design appropriate community-based prevention strategies for improving the security of women living in rural places from abuse by spouses, partners in both ongoing, terminated relationships. The gender-sensitive version of CPTED recognizes that communities are contested places where differing strands of values, norms, beliefs, tolerance for crime influence the security of rural women. Hence, some forms of social organization or collective efficacy (not social disorganization) may promote, condone rural woman abuse,, other forms serve to prevent, deter it. We propose a Second Generation CPTED framework that considers the utilization of four main strategies, each tailored to directly address feminist concerns, enhance a locality's collective efficacy to increase women's security: community culture; connectivity, pro-feminist masculinity; community threshold, social cohesion.

title: Areal policing, public perceptions in a non‐urban setting: one size fits one
authors: Crank, John P, Giacomazzi, Andrew L
abstract: PurposeA neighborhood‐based notion of the distribution of policing services is a hallmark of community policing philosophy. The purpose of this research is to focus on two policy issues: are there significant differences in important policing issues among the different communities,, what factors within the Sheriff's control might account for these differences?Design/methodology/approachIn 2002, the Ada County Sheriff's Office (ACSO), servicing the area around Boise, Idaho, carried out a survey of citizens stratified across four areas: two contract communities, one non‐contract community,, the unincorporated remainder of the county.FindingsThe survey found significant variation in perceptions of crime, disorder, in perceptions of safety, in social cohesion,, in attitudes toward deputies, to the sheriffs office. Findings suggested the importance of local policy through the tailoring of services to local needs. However, some community factors appeared to provide limits on the extent to which the police could respond to dissatisfaction with their services, regardless of adaptive strategy.Originality/valueOnly limited empirical research has studied neighborhood variation in citizens' perceptions of differences pertinent to policing services,, virtually no such research has been carried out outside urban areas. This research fills this gap.

title: The spatial pattern of suicide in the US in relation to deprivation, fragmentation, rurality
authors: Congdon, Peter
abstract: Analysis of geographical patterns of suicide, psychiatric morbidity has demonstrated the impact of latent ecological variables (such as deprivation, rurality). Such latent variables may be derived by conventional multivariate techniques from sets of observed indices (for example, by principal components), by composite variable methods or by methods which explicitly consider the spatial framework of areas and, in particular, the spatial clustering of latent risks, outcomes. This article considers a latent random variable approach to explaining geographical contrasts in suicide in the US;, it develops a spatial structural equation model incorporating deprivation, social fragmentation, rurality. The approach allows for such latent spatial constructs to be correlated both within, between areas. Potential effects of area ethnic mix are also included. The model is applied to male, female suicide deaths over 2002–06 in 3142 US counties.

title: Violence in the rural global south: Trends, patterns,, tales from the Brazilian countryside
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Ceccato, Heloise
abstract: The aim of this article is to discuss the trends, nature of rural violence in Brazil. Assuming the hypothesis of an increase in violence rates, urban–rural violence rates are compared at three geographical levels: national (Brazil), state (São Paulo),, municipal (Rio Claro). The study combines the analyses of official statistics with newspaper reports, videos,, articles published by the national media. Findings indicate an increase in violence in rural areas in recent decades but such a rise is far from homogenous across the country; it shows links to patterns of population change, economic expansion,, organized crime. Although violence has long being an inherent characteristic of rural Brazil—a place of conflicts, struggles—it is argued here that the more recent rise in violence is distinct from the past, at least in its portrayal by the media. The article finalizes by suggesting a research agenda to improve the understanding of the dynamics of violence in the Brazilian context.

title: Crime prevention in rural Sweden
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Dolmen, Lars
abstract: In this article we report examples of crime prevention (CP) experiences using case studies in rural municipalities in Sweden. Data from three different sources were analysed: semi-structured interviews with representatives of CP groups in eight rural municipalities, responses from an email survey,, a database of CP projects receiving funding from the Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention. Findings show that youth-related problems are the major CP concern, which are translated into projects against violence, alcohol, drug addiction. National CP guidelines overlook the nature of rural crime, its seasonality, what happens outside the urban core. Although CP groups in rural Sweden face a number of challenges, they show indications of being well prepared to address youth-related problems. The article concludes with a summary of results, flags the need to extend the international evidence on crime prevention to include experiences that go beyond large city problems.

title: The role of state programs in NIBRS data quality: A case study of two states
authors: Barnett-Ryan, Cynthia, Swanson, Gregory
abstract: This study explores the question of how the organization of state programs might positively influence the data quality of the state's incident-based reporting data, its National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) data submissions. To investigate this topic, the programs of two states (Tennessee, Vermont) identified as adept at resolving data quality issues are described. These descriptions show that these two state programs have taken measures to implement the quality assurance programs, procedures recommended in The Blueprint for the Future of the Uniform Crime Reporting Program: Final Report of the UCR Study. Given that some states have undertaken very different, very aggressive quality control programs, subsequent research should be done to assess the effects of these programs on the quality of NIBRS submissions.

title: Rural policing: Patterns, problems of “micro” departments
authors: Bass, Jay
abstract: Scholarly interest in policing concentrates on a few giant urban departments; very little is known about small agencies, although they are far more typical. This is an exploratory investigation designed to address that neglected area. The data source was in-depth interviews with law enforcement officials, primarily chiefs of micro departments in rural Oklahoma. The objectives were: to learn about the rural police officer, his job - qualifications, daily tasks, functions; see how small towns are sewed by their police; find out how rural police departments relate to other law enforcement agencies, to city government,, discover why tiny rural communities choose to maintain a police department. Explicit descriptive or explanatory findings were not the main goal; rather, this study explores a relatively unresearched area to obtain insights, information that may be useful in continuing more in-depth study. Among the research topics that might emerge from this inquiry are questions of power relationships between small town elected officials, police department appointees. The literature review introducing this study may also contribute to encouragement of scholarly work in rural policing.

title: Crime, security on agricultural operations
authors: Barclay, Elaine, Donnermeyer, Joseph F
abstract: Agriculture is big business, especially in market-oriented countries like Australia, Great Britain, the United States. Yet, little is known about crime, security issues related to agriculture. This article reviews the literature on agricultural crime, reports on results from a farm victimization, security survey in New South Wales, Australia, using place-based theories to guide the research. Incidents of burglary, the theft of fuel, equipment, machinery were inversely related to the visibility of farm buildings to the farm residence; stock theft was directly related to the distance of a farm to a town, to farms with a hilly terrain; malicious damage, illegal trespassing occurred more often on farms near highways or close to towns;, illegal dumping of trash was inversely associated with unoccupied properties, those closer to town. The implications for security on agricultural operations, for future research on agricultural crime, security are discussed.

title: Determinants of volunteers’ perceptions of crime, disorder: Do perceptions reflect reality?
authors: Wang, Xinting, Lee, Jae-Seung, Zhao, Jihong Solomon
abstract: Perceptions of crime, disorder are conducive to the quality of life in a neighborhood, closely related to social stability, residents’ psychological health. If residents’ perceptions overestimate the reality of neighborhood crime, disorder, it can generate a significant amount of personal fear, stress. To identify factors associated with public perceptions of crime, disorder, the current study investigated a sample of 394 volunteers who participated in a community policing program in Houston, Texas. Results from the structural equation modeling analysis indicated that volunteers’ crime, disorder perceptions were not influenced by the reported crime in their neighborhoods. The findings showed that the significant predictors were associated with collective efficacy in the neighborhood, their attitudes toward the police. Moreover, perceptions of crime had different predictors from perceptions of disorder. Implication for future research was discussed in the end.

title: Neighbourhood policing, community safety: Researching the instabilities of the local governance of crime, disorder, security in contemporary UK
authors: Hughes, Gordon, Rowe, Michael
journal: Criminology \& criminal justice: the international journal of policy, practice
abstract: `Community' continues to be at the heart of political, policy discourses surrounding policing, security, community safety. While recognizing that there are powerful retrogressive, repressive elements to such contemporary debates, it is argued here that this is an unstable, contestable policy terrain, that there are opportunities to develop notions of community that offer more progressive possibilities. This article examines policy developments relating to Neighbourhood Policing, Crime, Disorder Reduction Partnerships in Britain to explore these issues. The latter developments emphasize that community engagement, co-production are centrally important. However, it is clear that there are dangers that already identified tensions will persist. The need to meet performance targets will continue to detract from community-oriented work, unless the two coincide. Additionally cultural, institutional factors are likely to prove inimical to efforts to respond effectively to community needs. None of this ought to be taken as an argument in favour of jettisoning the idea of community, but it does mean that the participation of publics needs to be couched in broad, inclusive, often conflictual terms, understood that such efforts offer only limited guarantees in terms of establishing progressive agendas for community safety, neighbourhood policing.

title: Police in the community: Community involvement in japan in the prevention, solution of crimes
authors: Ames, Walter L

title: Generating, using community intelligence: The case of neighbourhood policing
authors: Bullock, Karen
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper examines the role that community-generated information plays in ‘neighbourhood policing’ — a key component of the UK police reform agenda. The neighbourhood policing agenda is concerned with the delivery of a consistent presence of dedicated neighbourhood teams which should be visible, accessible to the community. However, it also calls for the generation of community intelligence which should be used for local problem-solving, should be incorporated into National Intelligence Model (NIM) tasking. At the time of writing the principle of incorporating information generated from the public into policing intelligence, priority setting thus has strong resonance, at least at the level of rhetoric of policy, practice. It is contended that difficult questions are posed in thinking through what it means to consult with the ‘public’, the nature of community generated information, how it is translated into operational decisions, resource deployment. This paper explores the conceptual foundations of neighbourhood policing — which are found in reassurance policing, problem-oriented policing, the National Intelligence Model. It then examines the current mechanisms for generating community information, prioritising problems,, delivering responses as they are applied in neighbourhood policing. It finishes with a critical discussion of the concept, practice of generating, using community information for setting local policing priorities.

title: Assessing the emotional, behavioral impact of community, extra curricular activities, police contact,, collective efficacy among youth
authors: Gearhart, Michael C, Littman, Danielle Maude
abstract: A broad body of research suggests that interactions with the police can have a negative impact on emotional, behavioral outcomes among youth. Therefore, developing interventions that simultaneously reduce youth involvement in criminalized activities, promote positive outcomes for youth are foundational to creating a just society. The present study examines the emotional, behavioral impact that police contact, community, extracurricular activities,, collective efficacy have on youth. Our findings suggest that participation in community, extracurricular activities is associated with positive youth outcomes. Of the two components of collective efficacy, social cohesion had a strong association with emotional, behavioral outcomes whereas informal social control did not. Our findings emphasize the importance of community engagement, community involvement when developing community-level interventions that simultaneously address participation in criminalized behaviors, promote positive emotional, behavioral outcomes for youth.

title: Crime Prevention through Social Finance, Social Impact Bonds
authors: University of Chieti-Pescara, Galluccio, Caterina
abstract: The rate of adoption of the Social Impact Bonds (SIBs) remains substantially low despite the perceived public attention. Even considering widespread interest in the SIBs model, the low adoption mode suggests that the program is still in its early diffusion phase. In a bid to reduce or control crime rates, the SIBs model represents one of the strategies geared toward social reforms. It was initially piloted in 2010 at Peterborough prison with private financing for crucial social programs. The government could only pay returns to successful programs as an underlying condition. Besides its adoption in the United Kingdom, several states in the United States borrowed similar SIBs programs. This paper examined various aspects of measures of converting cases of recidivism into valuable financial assets, the shortcomings of such programs within the domain of the criminal justice department.

title: Cleaning up the neighborhood: White influx, differential requests for services
authors: Dahir, Nima, Hwang, Jackelyn, Yu, Ang
journal: Socius : sociological research for a dynamic world
abstract: Visible signs of disorder serve as markers of difference across urban space. Sociological theory suggests that variation in collective social control efforts contributes to variation in physical disorder. However, how structural characteristics shape differences in informal social control remains underexplored because of limited data on disorder, social control. Using city service request data, a novel dataset drawing on Google Street View imagery, computer vision methods, the authors examine the neighborhood characteristics associated with propensities to request trash-related services across five large U.S. cities. The authors find that socioeconomically advantaged neighborhoods, those with fewer minority, foreign-born residents have higher propensities. However, an increase in White residents, but not necessarily an increase in high–socioeconomic status residents, is strongly associated with greater propensities. The authors argue that incoming White residents introduce unique dynamics of social control that are not necessarily collective, thereby affecting spatial inequality, power relations within their new neighborhoods.

title: Increasing Community Involvement in Law Enforcement Through Procedural Justice to Improve Ties with The Community
authors: Modise, John Motsamai
abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to review the “state of the art” in research on police legitimacy. The authors consider two bodies of theory, empirical research on police legitimacy: one rooted in social psychology, concerned with individual attitudes,, the other based on organizational institutionalism. The authors contrast the theories, discuss the methods with which propositions have been examined,, take stock of the empirical evidence. The authors then turn to a direct comparison of the theories, their predictions. Design/methodology/approach Critical review, comparison of two bodies of literature. Findings Police legitimacy is a phenomenon that can be properly understood only when it is addressed at both individual, organizational levels. A large body of social psychological research on police legitimacy has been conducted at the individual level, though it has dwelled mainly on attitudes,, the empirical evidence on the relationships of attitudes to behavior is weak. A much smaller body of research on organizational legitimacy in policing has accumulated,, it appears to have promise for advancing our understanding of police legitimacy. Originality/value The understanding of police legitimacy can be deepened by the juxtaposition of these two bodies of theory, research.

title: Community-based crime prevention programs, central American migration: A difference in differences analysis
authors: Iesue, Laura T
abstract: Community-based crime prevention programs are emerging as a crucial alternative for addressing violence in Central America, a significant driver of migration from the region to the United States. Comprehensive analyses of the impact of the adoption of programs on migration intentions, especially among individuals who have been victims of crime, are lacking. Using a distinctive survey dataset derived from randomized-controlled experiments conducted in Guatemala, El Salvador,, Honduras, this study shows that community-based crime prevention programs are associated with an increase in migration intentions in Guatemala but are not linked to migration intentions in El Salvador, Honduras. This finding holds even when considering whether these programs address neighborhood factors, perceived risk of future victimization. Further examination of these programs is warranted.

title: Analysing the levels of fear of crime before, after the implementation of security box: A community policing case study in Chiba prefecture, japan
authors: Suzuki, Ai, Shimada, Takahito, Yamamoto, Isao
keywords: 307\_CP市民参加;業績一覧\_01論文;police visibility;Japan
abstract: Community policing plays an important role in Japanese policing. One prefecture in Japan installed a security box to facilitate community-based crime prevention activities, encouraging interactive partnerships with community neighbours. This study aimed to determine the time-course impact of the implementation of the security box on fear of crime. A questionnaire survey was conducted before, immediately after,, a few years after the implementation of the security box at two different locations. A series of analyses revealed that (1) the number of respondents who knew about the security box, passed by the security box,, saw security advisors staffed at the security box increased from immediately after the introduction to three, a half years after the introduction, (2) levels of fear of crime increased from Wave 1 to Wave 3,, (3) the security box was not associated with levels of fear of crime. Although this study did not provide empirical support for the effects of the security box on lowering fear, many respondents expect its effectiveness in improving neighbourhood safety, community crime prevention; moreover, it is necessary to determine its long-term impact.

title: The role of normative age-graded transitions, human agency in patterns, variations of financial exploitation of older adults
authors: Brancale, Julie, Blomberg, Thomas G
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 307\_CP市民参加;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage;340\_Excelに追加
abstract: Objectives: Drawing from normative age-graded transitions, human agency, this study provides a theoretical, empirical exploration of the patterns, variations of financial exploitation of older adults. Methods: The study employs qualitative methods with data collected from focus groups, interviews with residents of a large retirement community. Results: Normative age-graded transitions—such as retirement, residency relocations, changes in social support networks, medical events, death or incapacitation of a spouse, grief, declines in brain, physical health, cognition—lead to assessments of older adults’ sense of self-efficacy regarding their abilities to deal with everyday tasks, challenges,, decisions. If these assessments result in lowered self-efficacy, that reaches a threshold, cognitive transformations can occur, producing an increased vulnerability for financial exploitation. For those whose assessments of self-efficacy remained stable, financial exploitation was avoided. Conclusions: The role of normative age-graded transitions, general assessments of self-efficacy, thresholds,, cognitive transformations provides a promising theoretical approach for explaining patterns, variations of financial exploitation of older adults. These findings, if confirmed with more representative samples, can help validate the role of normative age-graded transitions, human agency in explaining why some, but not other, older adults fall victim to financial exploitation.

title: Empowerment, collective efficacy: Insights for community-based crime prevention
authors: Gearhart, Michael
journal: Journal of human behavior in the social environment
abstract: ABSTRACTThe current climate surrounding policing in the United States indicates a need to develop more community-based solutions to crime in order to create a more just society. Collective efficacy theory is a widely studied framework that explores how communities mobilize to address crime through informal social control. Though collective efficacy is associated with lower levels of crime, research suggests that developing effective interventions based on the theory is difficult. The present study examines collective efficacy through the lens of empowerment, tests mutual efficacy, self-efficacy as predictors of informal social control among community members,, within respondents? households. Findings from the study increase our understanding of how, why empowered individuals, communities mobilize to prevent crime,, identify practice behaviors that make collective efficacy theory more actionable for social work practice.

title: The effect of community policing on fear, crime reduction, police legitimacy, job satisfaction: an empirical review of the evidence
authors: Crowl, Justin N
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: AbstractSince the 1970s, community policing strategies or the language thereof have been purportedly initiated by a number of police departments nationwide to address notable issues such as crime, neighborhood disorder,, fear of crime. This policing philosophy has received considerable attention, support among scholars, police administrators,, criminal justice practitioners. This article synthesizes the available empirical evidence on the effectiveness of community policing initiatives using a variety of outcome measures. An overview of community policing is first provided with particular attention paid to its essence, objectives. Prior studies that have analyzed community policing effectiveness are then reviewed, assessed in terms of their methodological rigor, scientific merit. A discussion, future research considerations are presented to conclude.

title: Social cohesion, mutual efficacy, informal social control: Collective efficacy, community-based crime prevention
authors: Gearhart, Michael C
journal: International journal of law, crime, justice
keywords: Collective efficacy; Communities; Informal social control; Mutual efficacy; Policing; Social cohesion;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: Collective efficacy, which examines how social cohesion is activated in communities as informal social control, is a commonly used framework for community-based crime prevention. Previous research suggests that mutual efficacy, defined as group members’ perceptions that collective action can be successful, mediates the relationship between social cohesion, informal social control. However, previous research was limited in its measurement of mutual efficacy. The present study examines how mutual efficacy can facilitate participation in community-based crime prevention using a newly developed mutual efficacy scale. Findings suggest that social cohesion, mutual efficacy,, informal social control are distinct, though positively correlated constructs. Mutual efficacy partially mediates the relationship between social cohesion, informal social control. Findings suggest that building social cohesion, raising mutual efficacy are key goals for community-based crime prevention. Thus, practitioners should blend community practice principles with criminal justice goals to increase the effectiveness of interventions.

title: Collective efficacy, the built environment
authors: Lanfear, Charles C
keywords: built environment; collective efficacy; routine activities; situational opportunity;307\_CP市民参加;criminology
abstract: Collective efficacy is a prominent explanation for neighborhood crime concentrations. Just as crime is concentrated in particular neighborhoods, within-neighborhoods crime is concentrated in particular criminogenic locations. Research suggests criminogenic locations are determined by features of the built environment. This study links collective efficacy with situational opportunity to propose that collective efficacy facilitates the removal of criminogenic features of the built environment. I test this by examining associations 1) between past collective efficacy, present criminogenic features of the built environment, as well as 2) between those built environment features, crime, net of present collective efficacy. These are modeled using piecewise structural equations with generalized linear mixed-effect regressions on data from 1,641 blocks in 343 Chicago neighborhoods. Four types of police-reported crime are modeled using eight block-level built environment features in the 2003 Chicago Community Area Health Study (CCAHS; N = 3,074), neighborhood collective efficacy from the CCAHS, the 1995 Project in Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods (PHDCN) Community Survey (N = 7,672). Findings suggest neighborhoods with high collective efficacy maintain low rates of crime in part by limiting criminogenic built environment features, in particular, abandoned buildings. This crime control pathway is important because changes to the built environment are long lasting, reduce the need for future interventions against crime.

title: Community policing does not build citizen trust in police or reduce crime in the Global South
authors: Blair, Graeme, Weinstein, Jeremy M, Christia, Fotini, Arias, Eric, Badran, Emile, Blair, Robert A, Cheema, Ali, Farooqui, Ahsan, Fetzer, Thiemo, Grossman, Guy, Haim, Dotan, Hameed, Zulfiqar, Hanson, Rebecca, Hasanain, Ali, Kronick, Dorothy, Morse, Benjamin S, Muggah, Robert, Nadeem, Fatiq, Tsai, Lily L, Nanes, Matthew, Slough, Tara, Ravanilla, Nico, Shapiro, Jacob N, Silva, Barbara, Souza, Pedro C L, Wilke, Anna M
abstract: Is it possible to reduce crime without exacerbating adversarial relationships between police, citizens? Community policing is a celebrated reform with that aim, which is now adopted on six continents. However, the evidence base is limited, studying reform components in isolation in a limited set of countries,, remaining largely silent on citizen-police trust. We designed six field experiments with Global South police agencies to study locally designed models of community policing using coordinated measures of crime, the attitudes, behaviors of citizens, police. In a preregistered meta-analysis, we found that these interventions led to mixed implementation, largely failed to improve citizen-police relations,, did not reduce crime. Societies may need to implement structural changes first for incremental police reforms such as community policing to succeed.

title: A systematic review, meta-analysis of the relationship between policing, collective efficacy
authors: Yesberg, Julia A, Costi, Francesca, Chan, Angus, Bradford, Ben
abstract: Abstract Objectives To systematically review the evidence of the relationship between policing, collective efficacy. Methods A systematic review, meta-analysis synthesising data from 16 studies (4 experimental/quasi-experimental, 12 observational) assessing the relationship between policing, collective efficacy. Results Overall, police trustworthiness was the only measure of policing that was significantly associated with collective efficacy. People who thought the police were an effective, supportive resource perceived greater collective efficacy in their neighbourhoods. Conclusions The contribution of policing to collective efficacy seems to be about supporting communities by providing a trustworthy presence, which may reassure people that the police will be there if needed.

title: Increasing collective efficacy, social capital at crime hot spots: New crime control tools for police
authors: Weisburd, David, Davis, Michael, Gill, Charlotte
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: There is strong evidence that focussing police resources at 'crime hot spots'—small geographic places at which crime is concentrated—is an effective crime control strategy. Generally, hot spots policing strategies focus on formal social controls such as police crackdowns, often ignore the social context of the places that are targeted. Our article describes an approach that recognizes the importance of police community collaboration to improve public safety, reinforce informal social controls,, the emerging empirical evidence that social disorganization, collective efficacy may influence crime patterns at the micro-geographic level. We argue for the relevance of informal social controls in place-based policing, describe an innovative Smart Policing collaboration between the Brooklyn Park (Minnesota) Police Department, the Center for Evidence-Based Crime Policy at George Mason University that implements a department-wide programme in which police lead interventions to increase collective efficacy in hot spots.

title: Volunteering for community crime prevention: examining guardianship, the Block Parent program of Canada
authors: Varma, Kimberly N
abstract: This article considers the concept of guardianship, examines volunteerism using an example of a Canadian crime prevention program that has been in operation over the past five decades. The Block Parent program of Canada started in 1968, was a large scale, volunteer run, child safety program, which was initiated in response to a tragic child abduction in Ontario, Canada. “Block Parent” volunteers comprised mostly of stay-at-home mothers would place signs in their window to indicate a safe refuge for children. The program became national in 1986 and, at its height, had over 500,000 participating homes in the early 1990s. Just under two decades later that number dropped to 25,000 homes, continues to decline. This study reports the findings of a survey of 1297 Canadians carried out in 2021, which examined volunteerism, civic engagement,, child protection concerns using a Block Parent approach. Findings indicate that while only a small proportion of respondents volunteer in crime prevention programs, these programs appear to provide symbolic, instrumental purposes. Furthermore, findings indicate that volunteerism is linked to community cohesion.

title: Community policing during the pandemic
authors: Smylie, Christina, Duxbury, Linda, Bennell, Craig
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: ABSTRACTCommunity-oriented policing (COP) is a policing philosophy that focuses on the co-production of public safety by police officers, the community members they serve. This paper utilized the extreme context presented by the COVID?19 pandemic to test the theoretical assumptions on which COP is based. The data presented in this paper were collected from 32 community police officers (CPOs) from a Canadian police service who attended six focus group sessions during the fourth wave of the pandemic (July to November 2021). We summarize key findings, insights from these focus groups, provide insights relating to the underlying mechanisms essential to the delivery of effective COP programs. Future studies should continue to examine COP in diverse contexts to understand its benefits, challenges more fully.

title: 環境ボランティア団体における活動継続意図・積極的活動意図の規定因
authors: 安藤, 香織, 広瀬, 幸雄

title: Tailoring model in reforming police organizations towards community policing
authors: Yilmaz, Sefer
abstract: PurposeThis paper aims to suggest that a police organization should prefer change management approaches, methods that would not only lead the organization towards an effective position in preventing crime, fighting terrorism but also enable it to be in harmony with the organizational environment that answers both the expectations of the organization's employees, of the public.Design/methodology/approachThis is a discussion paper.FindingsThe goal will be achieved through developing a new approach, namely the “Tailoring model”, setting out from the similarities between the change manager, a tailor, who designs, prepares a garment taking into consideration both the physical characteristics, personal preferences of the client with the environmental conditions where the suit will be worn.Originality/valueThe paper not only adds significant perspectives for police organization managers in conducting reform initiatives to adapt community policing successfully but also contributes to the literature by developing a model for adapting change management approaches on a specific field of police organizations.

title: Community policing
authors: Williamson, Tom
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology

title: Community policing in comparison
authors: Wisler, Dominique, Onwudiwe, Ihekwoaba D
abstract: If community policing in Western democracies is often a unilateral action of the police promoting community self-rule, in most of the rest of the world, informal policing in communities is ubiquitous, popular,, sometimes excessive. Bracketing the Western ideology of community policing as state-initiated, -controlled (top-down) allows to discover a rich field of informal policing widely practiced by communities in Asia, Latin America, or Africa (bottom-up). Using secondary data as material, the article suggests accounting for these patterns of community policing with a state-centered model. Key variables identified by the authors are the service delivery capacity of the state, the dominant ideology, indirect or dual rule, political alliances as well as the framing of opportunites by civil society enterpreneurs or police managers,, available cultural repertoires of policing.

title: The effect of a community policing management style on officers' attitudes
authors: Wycoff, Mary Ann, Skogan, Wesley G
abstract: Quality management, a form of participatory management modeled on the theories of Edwards Deming, was implemented in the Madison, Wisconsin Police Department as a basis for the implementation of community policing. Personnel surveys conducted in 1987, 1989 found a significant increase over time in the belief that the organization practiced participatory management. The increase in this belief was positively, significantly related to (a) satisfaction with work, the organization, supervision,, job growth potential; (b) perceived significance of work; (c) task identity;, (d) work autonomy. A composite measure of satisfaction was, in turn, significantly related to officers' receptivity to change.

title: Patrol officer responses to citizen feedback: An experimental analysis
authors: Wells, William, Horney, Julie, Maguire, Edward R
abstract: Police organizations that implement community policing often seek new ways to measure officer performance. One important way to measure officer, organizational performance is through surveys of citizens. Although many police departments survey citizens, research has generally overlooked the manner in which this information is used, the effects of citizen feedback. This research describes one program that provides citizen feedback to patrol officers in hopes of increasing the quality of service that they provide. Using a randomized design, the authors test the effects of providing citizen feedback to officers on their job performance, attitudes. Results show that citizen feedback does not alter officers’ performance, attitudes toward the communities they serve,, activities that put them in close contact with those communities. The authors discuss potential explanations for finding no effects of the feedback intervention, pose directions for future research.

title: Volunteer engagement, organizational commitment in nonprofit organizations: What makes volunteers remain within organizations, feel happy?: Volunteer engagement, organizational commitment
authors: Vecina, María L, Chacón, Fernando, Marzana, Daniela, Marta, Elena
abstract: This study was conducted in order to determine whether commitment to organizations, work engagement are distinguishable constructs among volunteers from 18 nonprofit organizations. The strategy used addresses their distinctiveness, demonstrating that they relate differently to outcomes of interest. It is expected that organizational commitment will predict intention to remain, work engagement will predict psychological well-being. Results indicate that the pattern of relationships is clearly different: the relationship between engagement, intention to remain is entirely mediated by commitment,, the relationship between commitment, psychological well-being is fully mediated by engagement. Regression analyses confirm that commitment,, not engagement, predicts intention to remain,, that engagement,, not commitment, predicts psychological well-being in the sample of 232 active volunteers. These results are useful to differentiate between both concepts,, to develop specific nonprofit organization management strategies.

title: Dropout predictors for volunteers in non-profit organizations: A 7-year survival analysis
authors: Vecina, M L, Chacón, Fernando
abstract: This study focused on sustained volunteerism, examined potential dropout predictors because volunteerism is, by definition, a sustained helping behavior, because volunteers' dropout has organizational, social negative repercussions. Thirteen potential predictors from different theories, models were included in a survival analysis, using a sample of 700 volunteers. Results indicated that, controlling for age, sex, the probability of dropping out is lower among volunteers who have developed a strong volunteer identity, have a greater degree of organizational commitment,, do not have satisfied their career motivation. In parallel, they tend to dedicate more hours per week to volunteering yet spend less time commuting to the organization. In light of these results, some management strategies can be drawn. title: Community policing: The middle manager’s perspective
authors: Vito, Gennaro F, Walsh, William F, Kunselman, Julie
abstract: Community policing has evolved as the new organizational orthodoxy of policing. Volumes have been written on the subject by academics, research scholars. However, the voices of those who are charged with the reorganization of their departments, the implementation of community policing have been relatively silent. This article presents data drawn from the content analysis of the written views of community policing held by a select sample of middle managers from across the country. The respondents were attending the administrative officers course at the Southern Police Institute at the University of Louisville. During the course of their studies, they read current anthologies on community policing research. These findings identify, discuss a number of problems that they have encountered in the implementation of community policing. As such, they represent a practitioner’s assessment of community policing.

title: Community Policing
authors: Waddington, P A J
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: This issue of Policing: A Journal of Policy, Practice is devoted to the topic of community policing, its latest incarnation as ‘reassurance policing’. There is no need to apologise for this recycling of the ‘community policy’ approach: no policy falls from the drawing board, onto the production–line without the need for prototypes, modification. In a constantly changing world, it is important that policies are reviewed, adjusted to suit the prevailing conditions. If criticism is called for, it is that policing policy, practice fails to stay the course: a novel or engaging idea is heralded as the panacea for all ills, only to be unceremoniously dumped when it falls short of the unrealistically high aspirations that initially inspired it. The fortunes of community policing have waxed, waned over the past quarter of a century, but has outlasted many of its competitors.

title: Police community support officers in schools: Findings from an evaluation of a pilot training programme for school liaison officers
authors: Trotman, Dave, Thomas, Lorraine
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: This article reports the findings of an evaluation of a pilot training programme for Police Community Support Officers working as School Liaison Officers (SLOs) in secondary schools in two urban authorities in the West Midlands, England. Commissioned by West Midlands Police in response to their concerns about the inadequate preparation of SLOs, a training programme was co-designed by an officer from the Local Policing Unit, the School of Education at Newman University. Using focus group discussions with serving SLOs, individual interviews with key stakeholders, a short questionnaire, the evaluation reveals the complexities of community policing in contemporary urban school contexts, the challenges of professionalising the work of the SLO as a core issue in neighbourhood policing. The possibilities afforded through the Teaching, Learning Academy national professional recognition, the pivotal role of effective school-based mentorship emerge as particularly positive features of the evaluation.

title: Communicating our way to engaged volunteers: A mediated process model of volunteer communication, engagement,, commitment
authors: Trent, Sheridan B, Allen, Joseph A, Prange, Kelly A
abstract: Retaining productive volunteers is an essential issue nonprofit organizations face, as volunteers help extend nonprofits' services to their target populations. The current study examined two facets of communication, perception of voice (i.e., upward communication), satisfaction with communication (i.e., downward communication), as well as training, as important volunteer management practices with respect to facilitating volunteer engagement, commitment using both psychological contract, social exchange theories as the framework. One-hundred, seventy-one volunteers from two nonprofit organizations were surveyed to assess their satisfaction with the communication processes at their respective agencies, as well as their level of engagement, commitment,, perception of the training they received for their volunteer roles. Volunteer perceptions of both upward, downward communication were found to be indirectly related to organizational commitment through engagement. In addition, results indicated that volunteer training practices moderated the effects of upward, downward communication on engagement, commitment. Findings suggested that upward, downward communication are important predictors of volunteer engagement, commitment. Furthermore, providing training may help to strengthen these indirect effects.

title: Community policing 'light': On proximity, distance in the relationship between neighbourhood coordinators, citizens
authors: van Caem, B, van Steden, R, Boutellier, H, van Stokkom, B
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Community policing is currently a leading paradigm in Western police forces, not least in the Netherlands. However, in agreement with a mounting body of empirical research around the globe, our conclusion is that community policing strategies in the Netherlands (more precisely in Amsterdam) do not meet the basic principle of close relationships between citizens, the police. Nevertheless, if we were to lower our expectations to a more realistic level, then a modest (or ‘light’) version of community policing might emerge. This version calls for a small number of active citizens, a visible community police officer,, open communication channels between all stakeholders. We argue that such a view of community policing still offers promise, since proximity between police officers, citizens enhances their mutual understanding, cooperation.

title: The impact of crime on social ties, civic participation: The impact of crime on civic participation
authors: Takagi, Daisuke, Ikeda, Ken'ichi, Kobayashi, Tetsuro, Harihara, Motoko, Kawachi, Ichiro
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: social ties; civic participation; generalized trust; neighbourhood crime; multilevel model;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: AbstractThe present study examined associations of neighbourhood crime with residents' social ties, civic participation using multilevel models. We hypothesized that crime is indirectly associated with residents' low civic participation by negatively relating to their acquaintanceship ties because of fear of neighbours. By contrast, we predicted that crime is indirectly related to frequent civic participation by positively associating with more intimate friendship ties as a response to combat external threats. Additionally, we hypothesized that high crime rates in the neighbourhood increases the importance of generalized trust towards others. Therefore, we examined the interaction effects of neighbourhood crime, trust on social ties, participation. The study is based on a postal questionnaire mailed to residents aged between 20, 69 years, residing in Musashino City, Kiyose City, in Tokyo. Rates of larceny reported by the Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department were used as indices of neighbourhood crime. As hypothesized, our results showed that crime is positively associated with friendship ties, is negatively related to acquaintanceship ties. Through these opposing relationships, crime showed both positive, negative associations with civic participation. Moreover, we found that generalized trust buffered the adverse relationships between crime, broader social ties, participation. Copyright © 2015 John Wiley \& Sons, Ltd.

title: Community policing in practice: Ambitions, realization
authors: Terpstra, J
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: This paper deals with the question of the extent to which the ambitions of community policing are realized in practice. Five elements may be considered as the main ambitions of community policing: proximity, a focus on a wide range of problems in the neighbourhood, prevention, cooperation with other agencies, the promotion of citizen involvement. This observational study of community policing in the Netherlands shows that in practice, these ambitions are only realized to a limited extent. This implementation deficit is a result of several factors: the vague, blurred professional image of community policing (in many cases also for community police officers themselves), its open, indefinite nature, the way this work is often embedded within police organizations, the limited capacities, skills, expertise of community police officers, the increasing managerial emphasis in the Dutch police on so-called core business tasks.

title: Building community: The neighborhood context of social organization
authors: Swaroop, S, Morenoff, J D
journal: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study, interpretation
keywords: NEIGHBORHOOD; SOCIAL groups; SOCIAL structure; CHICAGO (Ill.); ILLINOIS;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: This study explores how neighborhood context influences participation in local social organization through a multilevel-spatial analysis of residents in Chicago neighborhoods. We construct a typology of community participation based on two dimensions: instrumental vs. expressive motivations for participation, formal vs. informal modes of participation. Both instrumental, expressive participation are generally higher in more disadvantaged neighborhoods. However, the association is nonlinear for instrumental organization, such that beyond a certain threshold, additional increases in disadvantage are associated with diminishing rates of participation. Rates of instrumental participation are also higher in neighborhoods where residents perceive more disorder. Rates of expressive participation are higher in more stable neighborhoods. These findings suggest that theories of urban poverty, social need are more applicable to instrumental forms of social organization, whereas the systemic perspective is more applicable to expressive forms. Finally, most forms of participation are related to the characteristics of both the immediate neighborhood, surrounding geographic areas.

title: Community organizations, agencies, group: Significance for children, teens
authors: Speer, Paul W, Perkins, Douglas D

title: Urban, rural attitudes toward participating in an auxiliary policing crime prevention program
authors: Smith, Georgia, Lab, Steven P
keywords: crime prevention efforts;307\_CP市民参加;Criminal Justice, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: Researchers, practitioners have noted the importance of citizen crime prevention, but little attention has been focused on the crime prevention behavior of rural residents. This article compares urban, rural attitudes toward participation in an auxiliary policing program. Using data from the 1982 ABC News Poll of Public Opinion on Crime, a probit regression analysis reveals that the models explaining participation for urban, rural respondents are similar. Differences between the present results, those of past studies suggest that the present results are more reliable than past analyses.

title: Community policing, the work routines of street-level officers
authors: Smith, Brad W, Novak, Kenneth J, Frank, James
keywords: COMMUNITY policing; CRIMINAL justice personnel; LAW enforcement; POLICE; PEACE officers; UNITED States;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: Most of the literature on community policing suggests, either implicitly or explicitly, that the daily activities of community police officers will differ from the activities traditionally engaged in by police officers. The majority of studies examining officer work routines were conducted prior to the rapid proliferation of community policing throughout police departments in the United States. Any attempt to determine the nature, extent of community policing needs to include an examination of the daily activities of line-level personnel charged with its implementation. The current study, using systematic social observation data, provides a description, comparison of the work routines of both community-oriented, traditional police officers in a city implementing community-oriented policing. Many of the findings are similar to those of previous workload studies. However, the findings also indicate that community officers devoted significantly more time to nontraditional policing activities than beat officers. Further, 911 beat officers spent significantly more time engaged in traditional policing activities than community officers.

title: Measuring capacities for community resilience
authors: Sherrieb, Kathleen, Norris, Fran H, Galea, Sandro
keywords: Social Capital; ECONOMIC development; COMMUNITIES; RESILIENCE (Personality trait); DISASTERS; MISSISSIPPI; Community resilience; Resilience; collective efficacy;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: The purpose of this study was to measure the sets of adaptive capacities for Economic Development, Social Capital in the Norris et al. (2008) community resilience model with publicly accessible population indicators. Our approach involved five steps. First, we conducted a literature review on measurements of the capacities. Second, we created an exhaustive “wish list” of relevant measures that operationalized the concepts presented in the literature. Third, we identified data sources, searched for archival, population-level data that matched our indicators. Fourth, we systematically tested correlations of indicators within, across the theoretical elements, used this information to select a parsimonious group of indicators. Fifth, we combined the indicators into composites of Economic Development, Social Capital, an additive index of Community Resilience using Mississippi county data,, validated these against a well-established index of social vulnerability, aggregated survey data on collective efficacy. We found that our measure of community resilience capacities correlated favorably, as expected when validated with the archival, survey data. This study provides the first step in identifying existing capacities that may predict a community's ability to “bounce back” from disasters, thereby reducing post-trauma health, mental health problems.

title: Assessing the relationship between police-community coproduction, neighborhood-level social capital
authors: Scott, Jason D
keywords: Capital Punishment; Neighborhoods; Police Personnel; Human; community policing; neighborhood social captial; police \& communities;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: Some have argued that community policing represents a reform that is capable of increasing neighborhood social capital. Collaborative relationships between police, communities are expected to enhance the capacity of residents to collectively ameliorate neighborhood conditions. This study examines the relationship between police-community coproduction, neighborhood-level social capital using data from a survey of neighborhood leaders. Results provide partial support for the claim that community policing is related to social capital. More specifically, collective social capacity was shown to be higher in neighborhoods where residents perceive the police to be more accessible. Future considerations for the study of community policing, social capital are discussed.

title: Organizational obstacles to participation in community crime prevention programs
authors: Schneider, Stephen
abstract: The term ``organizational obstacles'' refers to impediments to participation in community crime prevention groups, activities that stem from program implementation weaknesses. Given the importance that community-based organizations (CBOs) play in mobilizing neighborhoods, these weaknesses can be fatal to collective crime prevention efforts. Based upon research in a poor, high-crime neighborhood in Vancouver, Canada, this article identifies, examines how CBOs may actually inhibit participation in collective crime prevention groups, activities. Program implementation deficiencies that contributed to low participation rates in this neighborhood include weak, ineffectual community outreach, communication, a lack of strong leadership, inadequate resources, a technical, instrumental approach to crime prevention,, the nurturing of a narrow sociodemographic identity of crime prevention program participants that may be exclusionary. The inadequacies of the dominant crime prevention theories, the failure of applied models in promoting a broad-based mobilization of disadvantaged neighborhoods expose the need to develop, apply alternative theories to these unique environments. These alternative theories must pay greater attention to essential collective action processes underlying community crime prevention, emphasizing emotionally based organizing approaches (such as political advocacy, social development,, community development), which may appeal more to the poor, other marginalized groups.

title: Citizen participation in public administration: investigating open government for social innovation: Citizen participation in public administration
authors: Schmidthuber, Lisa, Piller, Frank, Bogers, Marcel, Hilgers, Dennis
abstract: In recent years, public sector organizations have increasingly focused on citizen contribution by adopting instruments known from open innovation. By collaborating with the periphery, leveraging external knowledge, government institutions initiate social innovation, stimulate a positive change for society. This article examines the involvement of citizens in an ideation platform initiated by a local government, investigates the motivations affecting participation intensity. Drawing on self‐determination theory, we analyze what motivates citizens to participate in an open government platform, how these motivations influence participation quantity. Based on a survey among platform users, the analysis of usage data from the platform operator, we find that motivations of citizen participation in public administration greatly vary across forms of participation. Whereas, intrinsic motivation is positively associated with producing, consuming platform content, external, introjected regulation negatively relate to individuals’ active contribution. At the same time, external regulation is positively associated with evaluation behavior.

title: Crime prevention in a low-crime nation: an enquiry into Japanese bōhan initiatives
authors: Schimkowsky, Christoph
abstract: Despite high public safety levels, crime prevention (bōhan) is a common concern in Japanese society. In the early-2000s, the Japanese government set out to create a crime-resistant society, giving rise to a flurry of crime prevention initiatives involving not only state institutions but also citizen volunteers, private companies. Between 2003, 2008, the number of bōhan volunteers grew by over 1200\% to 2.5 million citizens. In Japanese cities, neighbourhood patrols as well as bōhan posters, signs present frequent reminders of significant societal attention to crime, crime prevention. This paper asks why crime prevention gained so much traction in a relatively safe country. It sets out by identifying the responsibilisation of non-state actors, the incorporation of bōhan measures into the urban environment as core themes of contemporary Japanese crime prevention efforts. Based on an analysis of government, police documents as well as Japanese scholarship, it then discusses two factors that facilitated the spread of crime prevention initiatives in Japan in the mid-2000-2010s: current crime prevention campaigns as a continuation of national currents, governance strategies,, the versatility, adaptability of crime prevention ideas, initiatives. As an in-depth account of bōhan initiatives in contemporary Japan, their roots, this paper provides insights into the governance of deviance, the integration of crime deterrence, surveillance into everyday life in Japanese cities.

title: Building community capacity for violence prevention
authors: Sabol, William J, Coulton, Claudia J, Korbin, Jill E
keywords: collective efficacy;307\_CP市民参加;J Interpers Violence
abstract: The capacity of communities to prevent violence is examined from three perspectives: youth violence, child maltreatment,, intimate partner violence. The analysis suggests that community social control, collective efficacy are significant protective factors for all three types of violence, but these need to be further distinguished for their relationships to private, parochial,, state controls. It is argued that strong interpersonal ties are not the only contributor to collective efficacy, violence prevention. Weak ties, including those outside the community,, organizational ties are also seen as necessary. Violence prevention programs should be structured in ways that contribute to the communities' own capacity to prevent violence.
