abstract: Although not a panacea, community organizations have particular strengths that they bring to crime prevention: generating, sustaining participation, generating a broader understanding of community crime, developing programs that address broader social causes of crime,, forming partnerships for community policing. Questions about the efficacy of community-based crime prevention programs may be due to several limitations of prior evaluations. First they fail to acknowledge the fluid, political planning process of community organizations, which results in changing goals, objectives. Second, the need of community organizations to balance the production of outcomes, the process of developing activists makes it difficult to assess their accomplishments. Third, the emphasis on outcomes forces organizations to shorten the necessary social learning process, undermissing the programs' effectiveness. Finally, the evaluations' conceptual model ignores the political, institutional dimensions of communities, assumes only one means of producing safe communities.

title: Mobile police community office: a vehicle for reducing crime, crime harm, enhancing police legitimacy?
authors: Bennett, Sarah, Newman, Mike, Sydes, Michelle
abstract: Objectives A key objective for police is to develop innovative, adaptive methods to efficiently maintain public safety, foster strong police–community relations. The Queensland Police Service (QPS) designed the Mobile Police Community Office (MPCO), a purpose-built van with many of the same facilities of a police station,, trained MPCO officers to engage with members of the public using principles of procedural justice. This paper reports on whether the MPCO can be a “vehicle” to reduce crime, crime impact, enhance police legitimacy in crime hot spots in Brisbane, Australia. Methods We matched 24 hot spots based on crime, location characteristics. Within pairs, hot spots were randomly assigned to either the existing police response or the existing response plus the MPCO for two days at prevalent crime times/days. A public survey assessing perceptions of police legitimacy was administered during deployment. Our study compared official crime counts for a period of two months pre-/post-deployment date for experimental, control hot spots. We developed a crime impact score using QPS offense level descriptions, corresponding Queensland legislation penalties as an additional efficacy measure. Results We found a modest yet insignificant decrease in crime between the pre-, post-intervention period, no significant difference in crime impact scores. While some argue that hot spot policing can reduce legitimacy, we found no evidence to support this claim. Conclusions The MPCO is well received by the community, further research is needed to better understand its potential deterrent effect on crime.

title: Effect of communication practices on volunteer organization identification, retention
authors: Bauer, Steven, Lim, Dongkuk
keywords: volunteering; organization identification; retention; relationship with supervisor; internal communication; social media; mission statement; leader-member exchange theory; absorption capacity theory;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: Volunteering has taken on growing significance as a benefit to society, in initiatives to promote sustainability; it is therefore important to understand the factors driving its success. One increasingly studied variable with a positive effect on volunteer behavior, retention is organization identification. The antecedents influencing the organization identification variable, however, have not yet been explored in the volunteer literature. We address this gap by implementing a survey among volunteers at the OUR HOUSE Grief Support Center in Los Angeles, analyzing results via simple, multivariate linear regression analyses. Specifically, we investigate whether or not communication factors affect both organization identification, volunteer intention to continue. We find that specific communication factors, including a relationship with one’s supervisor, internal communication,, external social media postings significantly increase the level of organization identification, retention. Our findings are consistent with the theories of leader-member exchange, absorption capacity. Practitioners, nonprofits can improve the organizational environment of volunteers by optimizing these communication practices.

title: Home is where the heart is: The effect of place of residence on place attachment, community participation
authors: Anton, Charis E, Lawrence, Carmen
keywords: Place attachment; Place dependence; Place identity; Rural communities; Urban communities; Western Australian wildfire;307\_CP市民参加;J Environ Psychol
abstract: This study explores the relationships between place of residence, living in a threatened place, the subsets of place attachment: place identity, place dependence. Six hundred participants living in south-west Western Australia in rural, urban areas with varying degrees of bushfire risk responded to surveys asking about their reasons for living in their local area, their place attachment, their socio-demographic details. MANOVAs revealed a significant effect of place of residence on place identity with rural residents reporting higher place identity than urban dwellers. Urban dwellers reported lower place dependence than rural dwellers except when they lived in a fire prone area, in which case their place dependence was on par with that of rural residents. Socio-demographic predictors of both place identity, place dependence to the home, local area were also explored, these included length of residence, education,, owning one's home.

title: Application of geospatial analysis in health research: A systematic review of methodological aspects of studies on violence against children, young people
authors: Shinyemba, Tobias Willem, Shiode, Shino, Devries, Karen
keywords: Child abuse; Children; Geospatial modelling; Physical abuse; Small area estimate; Violence against children;308\_STC
abstract: BACKGROUND: Geographical variation exists in violence experienced by children, young people; however, there is limited research applying geospatial techniques to study this variation,, the methodological quality of this body of work is unclear. OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to review the application of geospatial analysis in research on violence against children (VAC), evaluate how essential methodological aspects are reported. METHODS: Twelve databases were searched for studies on VAC using geospatial techniques. Two independent reviewers screened the papers for eligibility. Findings were narratively synthesised. RESULTS: Sixty studies were included. Six studies estimated the prevalence of VAC, 54 investigated the associations between VAC, covariates. Most studies were conducted in the US (68 \%),, the broad definition of 'child maltreatment' (53 \%) was the most common form of violence explored. Most studies (83 \%) used administrative data, whereas 23 \% used an ecological study design to estimate the associations between risk factors, official reports of VAC. Frequentist modelling approaches were used in 54 \% of the studies,, 47 \% investigated VAC at census tract level. Model fit metrics were reported in 69 \% of studies. CONCLUSIONS: Current knowledge of the geographical distribution of VAC is severely limited because of the reliance on administrative data, which vastly underestimates the prevalence of VAC compared with self-reports, poor reporting of quality characteristics. There is a huge opportunity for applying geospatial methods in VAC research in diverse geographic contexts. Future research must adopt rigorous, standardised approaches to model fitting, validation, make better use of self-reported data.

title: From neighborhood to household: connections between neighborhood vacant, abandoned property, family violence
authors: Fleckman, Julia M, Ford, Julie, Eisenberg, Sophia, Taylor, Catherine A, Kondo, Michelle, Morrison, Christopher N, Branas, Charles C, Drury, Stacy S, Theall, Katherine P
keywords: Family violence; child maltreatment; intimate partner violence; neighbourhood disorder; vacant property;308\_STC
abstract: Rates of family violence, including intimate partner violence (IPV), child maltreatment, remain high in the U.S., contribute to substantial health, economic costs. How neighborhood environment may influence family violence remains poorly understood. We examine the association between neighborhood vacant, abandoned properties, family violence,, the role collective efficacy may play in that relationship. Data were used from a longitudinal cohort of 218 maternal-child dyads in a southern U.S. city known for elevated rates of violence. Women were matched on their propensity score, for living in a neighborhood with elevated vacant, cited properties. Analyses accounting for clustering in neighborhood, matched groups were conducted to examine the association between neighborhood vacant, abandoned property, family violence,, the potential mediating relationship of collective efficacy. The likelihood of experiencing child maltreatment at 12-months of age was more than twice as high for children living in neighborhoods with a high vacant, cited property rates compared to women living in neighborhoods with fewer vacant, cited properties (OR=2.11, 95\% CI=1.03, 4.31). Women living in neighborhoods characterized by high levels of vacant, cited properties were also more than twice as likely to report IPV (OR=2.52, 95\% CI=1.21, 5.25). Associations remained mostly stable after controlling for key covariates. Collective efficacy did not act as a mediator in the relationship between vacant, cited properties, family violence. Reducing neighborhood vacant, cited properties may be an important target for interventions focused on reducing family violence.

title: Investigating the impact of prior criminal justice contact on labor market outcomes during the COVID-19 pandemic: A propensity score analysis
authors: Widdowson, Alex O, Kyser, Anna M
abstract: Using data from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 (NLSY97), a supplemental COVID sample of NLSY97 respondents, we examined the associations between three measures of criminal justice contact, several indicators of labor market participation during the first year of the COVID-19 pandemic. Findings indicated that a history of adult criminal justice contact was associated with higher odds of being out of the labor market during the pandemic. However, among those in the workforce, criminal justice contact was also associated with higher odds of stopping work, working reduced hours, experiencing decreased wages, not working from home,, having close contact with others at work. Additional analyses suggest that deeper levels of contact were sometimes associated with worse outcomes.

title: The spatial dynamics of local violence, 2017–2021: examining the distribution, predictors of changes in street segment violence during the “crime surge”
authors: Drawve, Grant, Harris, Casey T
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Aggravated assault, homicide both increased in 2020, 2021 in the United States, generating considerable public concern. As such, the current study examines whether (1) the increase in violence during the 2020–2021 period uniquely affected some local street segments more so than others when compared to the previous years 2017–2019 and, in turn, (2) whether specific socio-demographic characteristics are associated with different changes in local violence during the 2020–2021 period. The current study focuses on the City of Little Rock, Arkansas, examining violence across streets nested within block groups. Descriptive analyses are followed by mixed-effect models to examine the potential change (increase, decrease) or stability in violence occurrence, including whether a first incident occurred in the years 2020–2021. The central finding was that the violence surge only impacted a small number of street segments – just over 14\% of the total sample in Little Rock –, roughly the same proportion experienced a decrease in violence during this same period of time. The results are further discussed from a crime prevention, policing perspective.

title: Explaining the extraordinary decline in Chicago’s homicide arrest rates, 1965 to 1994, beyond: Trends in case mix versus standards for arrest
authors: Cook, Philip J, Lopez, Javier
abstract: Chicago’s homicide arrest rate dropped from 91\% in 1965 to 57\% in 1994, dropped still lower in recent years. This pattern mirrors the trend in the national homicide clearance rate. A plausible explanation for this great decline is the trend in homicide case mix, which arguably has made it intrinsically more difficult to solve homicide cases. Our analysis describes the change in case mix for the period 1965 to 2020, analyzes the effect on the arrest rate for the first 30 years of this period, all by use of a unique homicide case microdata set. We document the large changes in case mix: for example, the percentage of all homicides in which a male victim was shot outdoors increased from 18\% (1965) to 69\% (2020). But the change in case mix does not account for Chicago’s great decline during the earlier decades, as we demonstrate by use of a novel arrest rate index. In fact, the arrest rates in each of the categories defined by location, sex,, weapon type exhibited similar declines through 1994. (Subsequent years of arrest data are unavailable for now.) Our preferred explanation for the great decline is that the operational standard for making an arrest increased during this period. That interpretation is well supported by evidence explaining the corresponding national trend, though direct evidence is lacking for Chicago. This interpretation challenges the use of the arrest rate as a police performance indicator, offers a positive interpretation of the great decline.

title: Violence, the crime drop
authors: Ganpat, Soenita M, Garius, Laura, Tseloni, Andromachi, Tilley, Nick
abstract: According to the Crime Survey for England, Wales, violence fell dramatically between 1995, 2013/14. To improve understanding of the fall in violent crime, this study examines long-term crime trends in England, Wales over the past two decades, by scrutinizing the trends in (a) stranger, acquaintance violence, (b) severity of violence, (c) age groups,, (d) sexes. It draws on nationally representative, weighted data from the Crime Survey for England, Wales,, examines prevalence, incidence, crime concentration trends. The overall violence fall was driven by a decline in the victimization of young individuals and/or males perpetrated by acquaintances since 1995. Stranger, acquaintance violence followed different trajectories, with the former beginning to drop post 2003/4. Falls in both stranger, acquaintance violence incidence rates were led by a reduction in victims over time. Counting all incidents reported by the same victim (instead of capping at five incidents) significantly affects trends in stranger violence but not in acquaintance violence. In relation to the distributive justice within the crime drop, this study provides unique evidence of equitable falls in acquaintance violence but inequitable falls in stranger violence. These findings highlight the need to examine violence types separately, point to a number of areas for future research.

title: The impact of alcohol consumption on homicide: A time-series analysis of three Nordic countries
authors: Lehti, Martti, Sirén, Reino
abstract: The article explores the statistical association between annual alcohol consumption, homicide mortality in Finland, Sweden, Norway from the early 19th century to 2013. The results show statistically significant impacts on overall, male homicide mortality in Finland, on male homicide mortality in Sweden. In Norway, we found no significant impacts. The results suggest that changes in the level of alcohol consumption have had a stronger impact on homicide rates in Finland, characterized by a heavier drinking culture, than in Norway or Sweden. The strength of the association between alcohol consumption, homicide levels seems also to vary over time, to be conditioned by economic, socio-political factors.

title: Does education affect environmental crime? A dynamic panel data approach at provincial level in Italy
authors: Castaldo, Angelo, Germani, Anna Rita, Pergolizzi, Antonio
abstract: This article investigates the role of education on environmental crime in Italy using a panel of 110 Italian provinces over the period 2010–2015. We employ a system-GMM (Generalized Method of Moments) dynamic panel data approach to tackle the endogeneity that might arise in the estimations from the environmental crime dynamic path, to consider time-invariant effects on provinces. Our empirical results, even after controlling for socioeconomic, judicial efficiency characteristics, support the existence of a U-inverted relationship between education, environmental crime, which depicts an unconventional finding: At the margin, a higher level of education endowment offsets the propensity to commit environmental crimes, which are confirmed to be white-collar type of crimes. The results are robust to model specifications, endogeneity. Furthermore, to check the robustness of nonmonotonicity in the relationship between environmental crime, education, to control for unobserved provincial heterogeneity, we also exploit a semiparametric fixed effects model. There is wide room for efficiency gains that could arise from policy interventions aiming to put environmental crimes into perspective.

title: The systemic model of social disorganization, homicide, suicide trajectories in South Korean community areas: Testing the stream analogy of lethal violence
authors: Cho, Sujung, Harper, Shannon B
abstract: The stream analogy of lethal violence (SALV) argues that homicide, suicide are similarly driven by frustration, aggression. SALV research has examined forces of production (i.e., lethal violence rate [LVR]), forces of direction (i.e., suicide-homicide ratio [SHR]). The current study applies 6 foundational social disorganization theory (i.e., the systemic model) structural predictors, 3 unique social controls to help explain the LVR, SHR. Using data from 229 South Korean community areas, the study tracked lethal violence for 6 years for each area, yielding 1,374 observations for analysis. Findings reveal mixed support for the systemic model. Urban area was negatively associated with the SHR’s initial level, but positively associated with increased SHR rates of change. Variations in the residential instability, divorce rates had positive effects on only the initial LVR level. Children’s nursery facilities fully mediated the link between structural characteristics, increased SHR rates of change.

title: Firearm dealers, local gun violence: A street network analysis of shootings, concentrated disadvantage in Atlanta
authors: Semenza, Daniel C, Griffiths, Elizabeth, Xu, Jie, Stansfield, Richard
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objectives Examine the spatial relationship between firearm dealers, shootings in Atlanta. Methods We combine data from the Atlanta Police Department (APD), the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms,, Explosives (ATF),, the American Community Survey (ACS) to conduct a street network analysis from 2016 through 2018. We employ the Network Cross K Function to assess whether firearm dealers attract shootings in the city. We examine whether this spatial relationship differs by level of concentrated disadvantage in neighborhoods. Results Without consideration of concentrated neighborhood disadvantage, firearm dealers, shootings are spatially unrelated to one another. Tract-level disadvantage influences the relationship between firearm dealers, shootings wherein dealers significantly attract shootings in disadvantaged neighborhoods. Conversely, shootings are located further from gun stores in non-disadvantaged communities. Shootings related to manslaughter, assault, but not robbery, are spatially associated with firearm dealers in disadvantaged neighborhoods. Conclusions Building on prior research regarding firearm dealers, gun violence, we find support for an attraction effect in disadvantaged neighborhoods for certain types of shootings. We contextualize these findings within a broader discussion of how firearm dealers contribute to the complex ecology of local gun violence. This is important in light of federal policies, investments related to the prevention of, response to gun crime.

title: Neighborhood interventions to reduce violence
authors: Kondo, Michelle C, Andreyeva, Elena, South, Eugenia C, MacDonald, John M, Branas, Charles C
keywords: alcohol outlets; built environment; crime; housing; neighborhood environment; neighborhood interventions; schools; urban blight; violence;308\_STC
abstract: Violence is a widespread problem that affects the physical, mental,, social health of individuals, communities. Violence comes with an immense economic cost to its victims, society at large. Although violence interventions have traditionally targeted individuals, changes to the built environment in places where violence occurs show promise as practical, sustainable,, high-impact preventive measures. This review examines studies that use quasi-experimental or experimental designs to compare violence outcomes for treatment, control groups before, after a change is implemented in the built environment. The most consistent evidence exists in the realm of housing, blight remediation of buildings, land. Some evidence suggests that reducing alcohol availability, improving street connectivity,, providing green housing environments can reduce violent crimes. Finally, studies suggest that neither transit changes nor school openings affect community violence.

title: Space-time dynamics of cargo theft: evidence from São Paulo, Brazil
authors: Aransiola, Temidayo James, Justus, Marcelo, Ceccato, Vania
abstract: AbstractThe objective of this study is to contribute to the growing literature on cargo theft by empirically testing four specific hypotheses of its causes – the space-time dynamics hypothesis, the economic attractiveness hypothesis, the social structure hypothesis,, the deterrence hypothesis. This study investigates the case of the economic core of one of the most severe regions regarding cargo theft worldwide – São Paulo state. As novelty in crime studies, we estimate Autorrregressive Distributed Lag models (ARDL). We found that the number of cargo thefts of a geographic area can be predicted by itself, that of neigbouring areas. This is an unprescendeted empirical evidence that cargo theft time series are autoregressive, cointegrated. Regarding economic attractiveness, social structure, the results are inconclusive. However, police activity reduces cargo theft in the large metropolitan area, inland municipalities of São Paulo state.

title: The effect of pretrial detention on labor market outcomes
authors: Grau, Nicolás, Marivil, Gonzalo, Rivera, Jorge
abstract: To study the effect of pretrial detention on post-verdict labor market outcomes.

title: Exploring the neighborhood-level impact of retail marijuana outlets on crime in Washington state
authors: Thacker, John, Martin, Maggie Elliott, Cristy, Yvonne, Rabideau, Deirdre, Shively, Michael, Kling, Ryan
abstract: Since 2012, the production, sale,, use of marijuana, its derivatives for recreational consumption have been legalized in 15 states, Washington, DC, but remain controversial nationwide. Critics argue that marijuana retail outlets attract criminal activity in surrounding areas, promote social disorganization. This paper examines this issue by analyzing secondary data from Washington State, one of the first states to legalize the medical, recreational use of marijuana.

title: Clandestine dumpsites, crime in Mexico city: Revisiting the broken windows theory
authors: Massa, Ricardo, Fondevila, Gustavo, Gutiérrez-Meave, Raúl, Bonilla Alguera, Gerardo
abstract: This paper revisits the broken windows theory with a particular focus on one sign of social disorder: clandestine dumpsites. To explore whether these are predictors of different types of crimes at a neighborhood level, two classification methods were used. Results suggest that clandestine dumpsites have a high predictive capacity for the crimes of dispossession, property damage, house robbery, vehicle theft,, robbery,, have almost none for environmental crimes or robberies of businesses. It is suggested that clandestine dumpsites should be the object of a comprehensive public policy that, in addition to reducing or eliminating the associated health, environmental risks, seeks to reconstitute the social fabric, motivates the long-term recovery of the public space.

title: Policing, labor market,, crime in japan: Evidence from prefectural panel data
authors: Nomura, Tomokazu, Mori, Daisuke, Takeda, Yoshiki
abstract: The study analyzed long-term changes in Japanese crime rates, their relationship with policing, labor market conditions, focusing on the increase in crime rates around 2000. The study used yearly prefectural panel data from 1978 to 2018, estimated econometric models to explore the factors related to the crime rate. Fixed effects models were used to control for unobservable heterogeneity across prefectures. We addressed the endogeneity problem in the number of police officers with the instrumental variable approach, employing the number of traffic fatalities, the number of firefighters as instruments. Instrumental variable estimation revealed that increasing the number of police officers reduced the crime rate. We also confirmed that crime decreased when the labor market was tight, that increasing minimum wages reduced crime. The model窶冱 variables largely explain crime rate declines since 2002 but do not account for increased crime up to 2002. Policing, labor market conditions do matter in crime rates. In Japan, the number of local police officers increased against the explosion of crime around 2000. Such policing significantly reduced crime after 2002. At the same time, increasing job opportunities, income from legal work also contributed to the decline. In contrast, crime expansion until 2002 was not attributed to the model窶冱 variables, so we need further research.

title: Absence of street lighting may prevent vehicle crime, but spatial, temporal displacement remains a concern
authors: Tompson, Lisa, Steinbach, Rebecca, Johnson, Shane D, Teh, Chun Siong, Perkins, Chloe, Edwards, Phil, Armstrong, Benedict
abstract: Abstract Objectives This paper estimates the effect of changes in street lighting at night on levels of crime at street-level. Analyses investigate spatial, temporal displacement of crime into adjacent streets. Methods Offense data (burglaries, robberies, theft of, theft from vehicles,, violent crime) were obtained from Thames Valley Police, UK. Street lighting data (switching lights off at midnight, dimming,, white light) were obtained from local authorities. Monthly counts of crime at street-level were analyzed using a conditional fixed-effects Poisson regression model, adjusting for seasonal, temporal variation. Two sets of models analyzed: (1) changes in night-time crimes adjusting for changes in day-time crimes, (2) changes in crimes at all times of the day. Results Switching lights off at midnight was strongly associated with a reduction in night-time theft from vehicles relative to daytime (rate ratio RR 0.56; 0.41–0.78). Adjusted for changes in daytime, night-time theft from vehicles increased (RR 1.55; 1.14–2.11) in adjacent roads where street lighting remained unchanged. Conclusion Theft from vehicle offenses reduced in streets where street lighting was switched off at midnight but may have been displaced to better-lit adjacent streets. Relative to daytime, night-time theft from vehicle offenses reduced in streets with dimming while theft from vehicles at all times of the day increased, thus suggesting temporal displacement. These findings suggest that the absence of street lighting may prevent theft from vehicles, but there is a danger of offenses being temporally or spatially displaced.

title: Analysis of burglary hot spots, near-repeat victimization in a large Chinese city
authors: Wang, Zengli, Liu, Xuejun
abstract: A hot spot refers to numerous crime incidents clustered in a limited space-time range. The near-repeat phenomenon suggests that every victimization might form a contagion-like pattern nearby in terms of both space, time. In this article, the near-repeat phenomenon is used to analyze the risk levels around hot spots. Utilizing a recent burglary dataset in N (a large city located in southeastern China), we examine the near-repeat phenomenon, the results of which we then use to test the contributions of hot spots. More importantly, we propose a temporal expanded near-repeat matrix to quantify the undulation of risk both before, after hot spots. The experimental results demonstrate that hot spots always form. Space-time areas of high risk are always variable in space, time. Regions in the vicinity of hot spots simultaneously share this higher risk. In general, crime risks around hot spots present as a wave diffusion process. The conclusions herein provide a detailed analysis of criminal patterns, which not only advances previous results but also provides valuable research results for crime prediction, prevention.

title: A quantile panel examination of the moderation effects of guardianship on residential burglary
authors: Vilalta, Carlos, Fondevila, Gustavo, Lopez-Ramirez, Pablo
journal: Journal of housing, the built environment
keywords: Guardianship; Mexico; Quantile panel regression; Residential burglary;308\_STC
abstract: Do informal, formal mechanisms of guardianship work together to reduce residential burglary? In this article we argue that informal guardianship moderates the relationship between formal mechanisms of guardianship, residential burglary. Formal guardianship requires some level of social cohesion, trust to be effective against residential burglary. We test this argument with the use of robust panel quantile methods controlling for time effects, spatial effects,, alternative explanations. Using Mexico City neighborhood crime, census data, we show evidence of a moderating weakening effect of informal guardianship on the previous relationship, particularly in deprived neighborhoods, only in the upper quantiles of the residential burglary distribution. In addition, the moderation effects seem to have weakened over time. In sum, the combination of guardianship mechanisms seems to have been more effective in high burglary risk deprived neighborhoods, although their combination seems to have become less relevant.

title: Time series robustness checks to test the effects of the 1996 Australian firearm law on cause-specific mortality
authors: Ukert, Benjamin, Andreyeva, Elena, Branas, Charles C
abstract: Objectives Many studies utilize time series methods to identify causal effects without accounting for an underlying time trend. We show that accounting for trends changes the conclusions in the study of Chapman et al. (JAMA, 316(3), 291â299, 2016), who evaluated the impact of the Australian firearm law in 1996. We also introduce a new empirical method that tests whether their empirical strategy can actually identify a causal effect that is also useful for panel analyses. Methods We use national data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, assembled in annual counts of: total firearm deaths, firearm suicides,, firearm homicides. These data are used in an independent re-analysis of the impact of the 1996 Australian firearm law that accounts for underlying stochastic trends. We then estimate a series of artificially created interruptions using interrupted times series analysis in a time frame before 1996, to test for changes in the slope of mortality across several years prior to the actual regulatory changes. This tests whether the empirical model produces effects in years other than the year of the intervention, thereby testing if the results can simply be replicated at random using other interruption years. Results Controlling for stochastic trends produces less statistical evidence of the impact of the firearm law on firearm mortality than previously reported by Chapman et al. (JAMA, 316(3), 291â299, 2016). Introducing artificial interruptions in 1990 through 1995 produces statistically significant decreases in all firearm-related mortality measures well above the expected type 1 error. Overall, 19 out of the 36 artificial interruption models we tested were found to be statistically significant, suggesting that the empirical model can be implemented in multiple non-intervention years with results similar to the true 1996 interruption year. Conclusions Current evidence showing decreases in firearm mortality after the 1996 Australian national firearm law relies on an empirical model that may have limited ability to identify the true effects of the law.

title: 戦後日本の犯罪減少の説明における経済的圧迫低減の役割（課題研究「現代日本社会のマクロ変動と犯罪動向」）
authors: ロバーツ, アキ, ラフリー, ゲーリー

title: Deterrence, incapacitation: An interrupted time‐series analysis of California's three‐strikes law$^1$
authors: Ramirez, Juan R, Crano, William D
abstract: Using uniform crime statistics, this research investigates the impact of California's three‐strikes law on instrumental, violent, minor,, drug‐related crimes over the first 5 years of the law's implementation. Autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) models reveal little immediate impact of the law, but significant effects on instrumental crime over time, suggesting an incapacitation effect. After correcting for autocorrelation distortions, less restrictive multiple regression models that test simultaneously for immediate, gradual intervention effects disclose immediate (deterrent) effects on instrumental, minor crimes, arrests,, long‐term (incapacitation) effects on these, violent crimes as well. Drug‐related crimes appear impervious to the three‐strikes law under any analytic model, suggesting the unresponsiveness of such crimes to increasingly severe legal sanctions.

title: The effect of the CARES Act on property crime
authors: Cassino, Peter P
abstract: As a means of reducing the effects of COVID-19, governments implemented mitigation policies, including economic stimulus bills. Nearly all known research in the criminal justice literature examines the impact of local lockdown measures on different forms of crime. Studies have not been conducted on the effect of the CARES Act on crime. The purpose of the present study is to examine the impact of the CARES Act on property crime. The dependent variables were total property, burglary, larceny, theft,, auto theft rates. The control variables were the population structure, southern state, concentrated disadvantage, non-White,, lockdown. The independent variable was the CARES Act. OLS regression analyses were conducted to test for relationships between the CARES Act, property crime. The models indicated significant negative relationships between the CARES Act, the total property crime rate, the burglary rate,, the larceny, theft rate.

title: Space–time clustering of crime events, neighborhood characteristics in Houston
authors: Zhang, Yan, Zhao, Jihong, Ren, Ling, Hoover, Larry
abstract: Spatial–temporal interaction analysis is employed to identify repeat, near-repeat patterns of crime in time, space. Most research to date addresses burglary, shooting incidents. Using the Knox method for space–time interaction, this study analyzes crime data in 12 “super neighborhoods” located in Houston’s crime-heavy southwest quadrant to explore spatial–temporal clustering of three types of crime, namely, residential burglary, street robbery,, aggravated assault. The findings suggest that each type of crime event has a unique clustering signature. Residential burglaries show significant space–time clustering in a relatively longer time range (up to 90 days), distance interval (up to 1.55 miles). In contrast, street robberies present significant clustering only up to 6 days, a quarter of a mile. For aggravated assault, the clusters of pairs occur within the interval of 7 days, within a little more than 1 mile of an initial assault. Examination of the socioeconomic characteristics of the neighborhoods indicates that crime events cluster more often in low income, racially/ethnically diverse neighborhoods. Significant spatial correlations of crime clusters are detected. The findings offer insight into potential suppression of crime events that are time, space correlated.

title: Addressing unobserved heterogeneity in the relationship between crime, consumer confidence
authors: Zhang, Ting
abstract: Objectives This study revisits the relationship between property crime, economic conditions with the latter being represented by a collective economic perception variable in the form of the Index of Consumer Confidence (ICC). The present work takes this application to assess the severity of cross-sectional dependence, nonstationarity, two issues that are deemed pervasive in macro panels but have not been given sufficient consideration in previous research. Methods The dataset comprises information for five Canadian regions over a time period of 24 years from 1982 to 2005. The study compares the parameter estimates, residual properties of the commonly used two-way fixed effects (2FE) model, the augmented mean group (AMG) estimator where the latter can accommodate nonstationarity, cross-sectional dependence that potentially arise from unobserved common factors. Results In contrast to the 2FE approach, when using the AMG estimator one can reject the null hypothesis that the current ICC has no impact on crime. Some of the effects still hold when an alternative economic indicator, the unemployment rate of young males, is added to the model. Diagnostic tests confirm that the commonly used 2FE estimator yields nonstationary, cross-sectional dependent residuals, whereas the heterogeneous parameter model produces more favorable diagnostic results. Conclusions The findings provide evidence supporting the hypothesis that subjective measures of economic conditions are linked to financially-motivated crime rates. Through this application, the study demonstrates the importance of examining underlying data properties, regression residuals in empirical work to ensure the validity of estimates.

title: Analyzing the dynamics of homicide patterns in Chicago: ESDA, spatial panel approaches
authors: Ye, Xinyue, Wu, Ling
keywords: Homicide; Social disorganization theory; ESDA; Hot spot; Spatial panel; Chicago;308\_STC
abstract: This paper studies the relationship between homicide rate, socioeconomic factors at community area level in Chicago from 1960 to 1995. Most of prior studies of social disorganization theory are based on cross-sectional spatial regression or longitudinal studies. This research integrates space, time in testing social disorganization theory. First, exploratory spatial data analysis (ESDA) is used to examine dynamic spatial patterns of these indicators. This investigation justifies the estimation of homicide rates across community areas through panel-data models that extend to include spatial lag, spatial error autocorrelation.

title: Assessing the generalizability of the near repeat phenomenon
authors: Youstin, Tasha J, Nobles, Matt R, Ward, Jeffrey T, Cook, Carrie L
abstract: The “near repeat” phenomenon suggests that when a crime occurs in a given area, the surrounding area may exhibit an increased risk for subsequent crime in the days following the original incident. The present study assesses the extent to which near repeats generalize across three different crimes, including shootings, robbery,, auto theft. A series of near repeat models was estimated to further specify the temporal proximity of near repeats for each crime type under investigation. Results showed that a near repeat pattern exists across crime types; however, each crime type has a unique spatiotemporal pattern. Implications for police strategies, such as geographical profiling, future research connecting near repeat patterns to repeat offenders, are discussed.

title: Spatio-temporal change of crime at provincial scale in China—since the economic reform
authors: Yijing, L I
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Economic reform; Crime; Spatial scale; Temporal scale; Relationship; Province; Social change; Spatial analysis; Criminal statistics; Economic development; China;308\_STC
abstract: China has undergone tremendous social changes during the transition since the Economic Reform,, this paper did a comparative study on crime change patterns among provinces both spatially, temporally. The results indicated that (1) regional differences on crime levels, temporal change trends were largely influenced, or even been shaped, by the outcomes brought by economic reform, such as priority developmental policies, geographical location, transportation facilities, etc. For example, spatially, more developed areas with more governmental policy supports not only saw dramatic development during the economic reform but also showed higher criminal rates, greater criminal rate variation. (2) The relationships between criminal rates, corresponding contextual conditions vary by temporal scales (long-run, short-run), regions, target areas’ features, their different development policy priorities; (3) experiences from Western theories, empirical studies cannot be applied directly into the Chinese society, without taking into consideration of the spatial-temporal scales, target’s specialities; it is also suggestive to local policy-makers, governmental agencies that crime reduction, prevention measures should not be identical to other places, need to be made according to local characteristics.

title: A longitudinal examination of building demolitions on neighbourhood crime rates
authors: Wo, James C, Kim, Young-An
abstract: AbstractCriminological research shows that vacant, dilapidated buildings contribute to higher neighbourhood crime rates. Therefore, the implication is that by physically removing these buildings from a neighbourhood, there will subsequently be a reduction in crime within that neighbourhood. In this study, we focus on the potential crime-reducing benefits of building demolitions—a change in the physical landscape, which may initiate or sustain neighbourhood revitalization. Accordingly, we examine the influence of building demolitions on crime within Philadelphia block groups from 2008 to 2018, controlling for a range of social-ecological factors known to be associated with crime rates. We also differentiate between city, private demolitions to examine the possibility that not all demolitions are created equal in relation to crime.

title: The shape of neighborhoods to come: Examining patterns of gentrification, holistic neighborhood change in Los Angeles County, 1980–2010
authors: Williams, Seth A, Hipp, John R
abstract: The present study examines holistic neighborhood change in Los Angeles County across three decades between 1980, 2010. Using Census tract data, we conduct a latent class analysis to identify classes of neighborhood change for each decade according to housing dynamics, age structure, racial-ethnic composition, churning,, socioeconomic characteristics,, describe latent classes indicative of gentrification. Further, we assess the degree to which tracts experience sustained or repeated gentrification over the 30 year period. In line with more recent conceptualizations of gentrification as a broad urban process, we find that gentrification occurs in a wide range of neighborhoods,, manifests itself differently according to shifts in population characteristics, with many tracts experiencing more than one successive period of gentrification over the 30 year period.

title: Using space–time analysis to evaluate criminal justice programs: An application to stop-question-frisk practices
authors: Wooditch, Alese, Weisburd, David
abstract: Objectives Effects of place-based criminal justice interventions extend across both space, time, yet methodological approaches for evaluating these programs often do not accommodate the spatiotemporal dimension of the data. This paper presents an example of a bivariate spatiotemporal Ripley’s K-function, which is increasingly employed in the field of epidemiology to analyze spatiotemporal event data. Advantages of this technique over the adapted Knox test are discussed. Methods The study relies on x–y coordinates of the exact locations of stop-question-frisk (SQF), crime incident events in New York City to assess the deterrent effect of SQFs on crime across space at a daily level. Results The findings suggest that SQFs produce a modest reduction in crime, which extends over a three-day period. Diffusion of benefits is observed within 300 feet from the location of the SQF, but these effects decay as distance from the SQF increases. Conclusions A bivariate spatiotemporal Ripley’s K-function is a promising approach to evaluating place-based crime prevention interventions,, may serve as a useful tool to guide program development, implementation in criminology.

title: The impact of street lights on spatial-temporal patterns of crime in Detroit, Michigan
authors: Xu, Yanqing, Fu, Cong, Kennedy, Eugene, Jiang, Shanhe, Owusu-Agyemang, Samuel
keywords: Crime analysis; Detroit; Neighborhoods; Spatial-temporal pattern analysis; Street lights;308\_STC
abstract: The importance of understanding crime in the United States assumed enhanced protrusion in the wake of the increased crime rates year by year in certain cities. Neighborhood social demographic variables have been largely used to measure their associations with crime. Other than those social factors, street lighting is a feature of urban, suburban settlement which is widely thought to be a necessary element in preventing crime. Previous research has drawn mixed conclusions about the relationship between street lighting, crime,, the effect of streetlights on neighborhood crime is not entirely definitive. To address this challenge, we examined the spatial associations between street light density, neighborhood social disorganization characteristics, crime (e.g., burglary, vehicle theft, weapons offenses, etc.) in Detroit, Michigan in 2014. Using the street lighting data from the Detroit Public Lighting Authority, crime data from the City of Detroit, supplemented with Census 2010 data, we conducted a Generalized Least Squares model of neighborhood crime in 879 census block groups to test the random effects of the spatial variables, different hours of day on crime. The results show an inverse relationship between street light density, crime rates across census block groups in Detroit, the effects of time period of a day vary according to different types of crime. These findings provided more credible evidence for researchers, policy makers to effectively optimize scarce public safety resources, such as improving street lighting in disadvantaged neighborhoods.

title: Formal, informal deterrents of crime in Japan: Roles of police, social capital revisited
authors: Yamamura, Eiji
keywords: CRIME; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; Social Capital; JAPAN;308\_STC;Japan
abstract: Using Japanese prefecture-level panel data, this paper examines how the crime rate is affected by formal, informal deterrents as reflected by police, social capital, respectively. Both, however, suffer from the endogeneity problem, therefore the estimation results are biased when regression analysis is conducted. Hence, the fixed effects 2SLS method is employed to control for the endogeneity bias as well as for unobservable fixed effects. As well, the relationship between inequality, crime is examined. The main findings are: (1) police, social capital reduce the crime rate, their effects increase when the endogeneity bias is controlled for through fixed effects 2SLS estimation. (2) The effects of social capital, which is smaller than that of police, is however is reinforced by police through the complementary relationship existing between them.

title: Repeat, near-repeat burglaries, offender involvement in a large Chinese city
authors: Wu, Ling, Xu, Xiao, Ye, Xinyue, Zhu, Xinyan
abstract: Repeat, near-repeat phenomena indicate that victimization might form a contagion-like pattern in both near space, near time. The research community has built abundant empirical evidence of repeat, near-repeat patterns over the past 10 years. Along with these pattern analyses, scholars have also proposed theoretical explanation of the mechanisms of near-repeat burglaries. However, the empirical study of mechanisms is very limited, almost absent in China due to the data unavailability. Utilizing a recent burglary dataset in Wuhan (a large Chinese city), the current research examines repeat, near-repeat burglary patterns as well as the underlying theoretical hypotheses. Consistent with prior findings, the current study found significant, meaningful near-repeat patterns of burglary. In addition, the police detection data indicate that pairs of detected burglaries occurring close in space, time are more likely to involve the same offender than distant pairs. Finally, the implications of the findings, limitations are discussed.

title: Exploring the impact of floating population with different household registration on theft
authors: Xu, Chong, Chen, Xi, Chen, Jianguo, Chen, Debao
keywords: household registration; floating population; spatial distribution; crime; negative binomial regression;308\_STC
abstract: The floating population is frequently treated as a homogeneous whole to explore its impact on crime in numerous crime studies in China. However, there are different compositions within the floating population, significant differences in the effects on crime. In this study, the floating population was divided into three types based on household registration (i.e., Hukou): the floating population from other districts in the same city (FPFOD), the floating population from other cities in the same province (FPFOC), the floating population from other provinces (FPFOP). The Moran index was used to analyze their spatial distribution patterns, aggregation, respectively,, several negative binomial regression models were constructed to explore the influence of different types of floating populations on theft. The results show that the three types of floating populations are mainly distributed in different urban areas, implying differences in their impact on theft. Among them, the proportion of the FPFOD shows insignificant negative correlation on theft, while the proportion of the FPFOC, the FPFOP present a significant positive correlation. Meanwhile, the proportion of the FPFOP creates a stronger effect on theft than the proportion of entire floating population. Overall, the model performs best when variables of the proportion of the FPFOC, the FPFOP are included. The research conclusions can provide a meaningful reference for precisely measuring the floating population in crime research.

title: The multilevel effects of changes in disadvantage on changes in crime
authors: Wenger, Marin R
abstract: While social disorganization theory suggests the importance of change, most prior research examining macro-level criminological associations uses cross-sectional data. The current study examines the multilevel relationship between changes in disadvantage, changes in crime over time using four data sources: the National Neighborhood Crime Study, the 2000 U.S. Census, crime-incidents occurring between 2005, 2009,, the 2005–2009 American Community Survey. Analyzing 6,068 census tracts within 53 large U.S. cities using multilevel models with time nested within tracts nested within cities, I parse out the contribution of changes in tract-level disadvantage from city-level disadvantage to changes in robbery, burglary rates. Results indicate the importance of both static, dynamic associations between disadvantage, crime, at both the neighborhood, city level.

title: Replicating group-based trajectory models of crime at micro-places in Albany, NY
authors: Wheeler, Andrew P, Worden, Robert E, McLean, Sarah J
abstract: Objectives Replicate two previous studies of temporal crime trends at the street block level. We replicate the general approach of group-based trajectory modelling of crimes at micro-places originally taken by Weisburd et al. (Criminology 42(2):283–322, 2004 ), replicated by Curman et al. (J Quant Criminol 31(1):127–147, 2014 ). We examine patterns in a city of a different character (Albany, NY) than those previously examined (Seattle, Vancouver), so contribute to the generalizability of previous findings. Methods Crimes between 2000, 2013 were used to identify different trajectory groups at street segments, intersections. Zero-inflated Poisson regression models are used to identify the trajectories. Pin maps, Ripley’s K, neighbor transition matrices are used to show the spatial patterning of the trajectory groups. Results The trajectory solution with eight classes is selected based on several model selection criteria. The trajectory of each those groups follow the overall citywide decline,, are only separated by the mean level of crime. Spatial analysis shows that higher crime trajectory groups are more likely to be nearby one another, potentially suggesting a diffusion process. Conclusions Our work adds additional support to that of others who have found tight coupling of crime at micro-places. We find that the clustering of trajectories identified a set of street units that disproportionately contributed to the total level of crime citywide in Albany, consistent with previous research. However, the temporal trends over time in Albany differed from those exhibited in previous work in Seattle but were consistent with patterns in Vancouver.

title: Federal civil litigation as an instrument of police reform: A natural experiment exploring the effects of the Floyd ruling on stop-and-frisk activities in New York city
authors: White, Michael D, Fradella, Henry F, Morrow, Weston J, Mellom, Doug
abstract: Stop-and-frisk has emerged as a popular crime control tactic in American policing. Though stop-and-frisk has a long, established legal history, the recent experiences in many jurisdictions demonstrate a strong disconnect between principle, practice. Arguably, stop-and-frisk has become the next iteration of a persistent undercurrent in racial injustice in American policing, perhaps best demonstrated by the recent police killings of Eric Garner, Michael Brown,, Freddie Gray — all during stop-and-frisk encounters. Recent events have facilitated a national dialogue on police accountability, police reform,, federal civil litigation has been central to that discussion. Although federal court relief can be pursued through a variety of avenues (most frequently by individuals or class actions under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 or by the U.S. Department of Justice pursuant to 42 U.S.C § 14141), very little research has examined the impact of federal civil litigation on unconstitutional police practices. The current study examines the New York City confluence of racial injustice in policing, misuse of stop-and-frisk by officers,, federal civil litigation designed to precipitate police reform. Authors employ a natural experimental design to conduct a year-to-year comparison of stop-and-frisk activities, outcomes conducted by the NYPD in 2011, during the height of their stop-and-frisk program,, 2014, one year after a federal court deemed the program unconstitutional, ordered reforms. Results show substantial improvement in stop-and-frisk practices following the federal civil litigation, including reduced prevalence, geographic concentration, as well as increased rates of arrest, weapon, contraband seizures. Moreover, crime continued to decline in New York as the NYPD reformed its stop-and-frisk program. Even though racial disparities in those subjected to stops by the NYPD persist, the overall findings show positive progress in New York, highlight the role of federal civil litigation as an instrument of police reform.

title: Patterns of near-repeat gun assaults in Houston
authors: Wells, William, Wu, Ling, Ye, Xinyue
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: The study assesses the extent to which gun assaults are clustered in space, time using crime data from Houston, Texas. The analysis examines patterns of gun assaults at the city-level as well as more localized levels in order to understand the spatial distribution of near-repeats within the city. Consistent with prior research, the city-level analysis shows significant, meaningful near-repeat patterns. The localized analysis indicates that the risk of near-repeats is not evenly distributed across space within the city, but is concentrated among a small portion of incidents, four relatively small spatial clusters. In addition, an examination of crime types, locations,, gang involvement shows slight differences between gun assaults with, without near-repeat follow-up shootings.

title: Does increasing women's education reduce their risk of intimate partner violence? Evidence from an education policy reform: Compulsory schooling, intimate partner violence
authors: Weitzman, Abigail
keywords: intimate partner violence; Latin America; family violence; victimization;308\_STC;20240717\_IVde一次予防;criminology
abstract: Although scholars have employed rigorous causal methods to examine the relationship between education, crime, few studies have taken a causal approach to the study of education, intimate partner violence (IPV) specifically. From a social causation perspective, improving women's education should protect them from violence, yet from a social selection perspective, education could proxy for unobserved factors that explain negative associations between education, IPV. This study adjudicates between the two possibilities using an exogenous source of variation in education-a 1990s compulsory schooling reform in Peru. Specifically, the author conducts an instrumented regression discontinuity that implicitly controls for women's unobserved endowments by comparing women who were aged just above (N=8,195), below (N=6,645) the school-age cutoff at the time of the reform. Consistent with the social causation perspective, increasing women's schooling reduced both their recent, longer-term probabilities of psychological, physical,, sexual IPV,, their recent, longer-term probabilities of experiencing any IPV, poly-victimization. Supplemental mediation analyses provide support for three interrelated causal pathways-improvements in women's personal resources, delayed family formation,, changes in partner selection. These findings confirm the protective effects of women's education, further illuminate mechanistic processes by which this occurs.

title: Proactive policing effects on repeat, near-repeat shootings in Houston
authors: Wells, William, Wu, Ling
abstract: The spatial analysis of crime, community problems can inform police operations by revealing where resources can be most effectively deployed. Advances in understanding the spatial concentrations of crime show that some locations are repeatedly victimized, that some nearby locations are at an elevated risk for a subsequent crime during a relatively short period of time. These are known as repeat, near-repeat phenomena. Police may be able to have a strong preventive impact on crime if these risk patterns can be identified, disrupted. This analysis reports on whether a specialized, proactive patrol unit deployed to high-crime areas was effective in disrupting repeat, near-repeat patterns of shootings. Results suggest the proactive unit did not disrupt concentrations of shootings in a meaningful way. To improve effectiveness, police practitioners, researchers should seek to understand the factors driving these patterns, then design specific interventions to address them.

title: Trajectories of crime at places: A longitudinal study of street segments in the city of Seattle
authors: Weisburd, David, Bushway, Shawn, Lum, Cynthia, Yang, Sue-Ming
keywords: CRIME; CRIME prevention; SEATTLE (Wash.); SOCIAL history; SOCIAL problems; UNITED States; WASHINGTON (State); crime drop; crime places; hot spots; routine activities; spatial analysis; trajectory analysis;308\_STC
abstract: Studies of crime at micro places have generally relied on cross-sectional data, reported the distributions of crime statistics over short periods of time. In this paper we use official crime data to examine the distribution of crime at street segments in Seattle, Washington, over a 14-year period. We go beyond prior research in two ways. First, we view crime trends at places over a much longer period than other studies that have examined micro places. Second, we use 444group-based trajectory analysis to uncover distinctive developmental trends in our data. Our findings support the view that micro places generally have stable concentrations of crime events over time. However, we also find that a relatively small proportion of places belong to groups with steeply rising or declining crime trajectories, that these places are primarily responsible for overall city trends in crime. These findings are particularly important given the more general decline in crime rates observed in Seattle, many other American cities in the 1990s. Our study suggests that the crime drop can be understood not as a general process that occurred across the city landscape but one that was generated in a relatively small group of micro with declining crime trajectories over time. In this chapter, the authors use official crime data to examine the distribution of crime at street segments in Seattle, Washington, over a 14-year period. They examine crime trends at places over a much longer period than other studies that have examined micro places. The authors consider group-based trajectory analysis to uncover distinctive developmental trends in their data. They suggest that the crime drop can be understood not as a general process that occurred across the city landscape but one that was generated in a relatively small group of micro with declining crime trajectories over time. The authors show that a relatively small proportion of the total number of places belong to groups that have steeply rising or declining crime trajectories,, that these places are primarily responsible for overall city trends in crime. The finding of stability of crime at micro places over time is mirrored in early research on the nature of longitudinal patterns of crime within communities.

title: The spatial distribution of random gunfire: A block-level investigation of physical, social structural conditions
authors: Watkins, R Cory, Mazerolle, Lorraine Green, Rogan, Dennis
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Shootings; Social conditions \& trends; Crime;308\_STC
abstract: This paper examines the environmental, social structural correlates associated with random gunfire incidents. The study group consists of 273 face blocks, intersections in a selected portion of Dallas, Texas. The data show some locations routinely generate random gunfire, while others remain gunshot-free. The analysis suggests environmental factors are not sufficient to explain random gunfire. Implications for future inquiries are offered.

title: Coronavirus disease 2019: What could be the effects on Road safety?
authors: Vingilis, Evelyn, Beirness, Doug, Boase, Paul, Byrne, Patrick, Johnson, Jennifer, Jonah, Brian, Mann, Robert E, Rapoport, Mark J, Seeley, Jane, Wickens, Christine M, Wiesenthal, David L
abstract: In March 2020, the World Health Organization declared COVID-19 a world-wide pandemic. Countries introduced public health measures to contain, reduce its spread. These measures included closures of educational institutions, non-essential businesses, events, activities, as well as working from, staying at home requirements. These measures have led to an economic downturn of unprecedented proportions. Generally, as economic activity declines, travel decreases, drivers are exposed to a lower risk of collisions. However, research on previous economic downturns suggests economic downturns differentially affect driver behaviours, situations. COVID-19 pandemic effects on road safety are currently unknown. However, preliminary information on factors such as the increased stress, anxiety brought about by the COVID-19 pandemic, more ``free'' (idle) time, increased consumption of alcohol, drugs,, greater opportunities for speeding, stunt driving, might well have the opposite effect on road safety. Using an interactionist model we identify research questions for researchers to consider on potential person, situation factors associated with COVID-19 that could affect road safety during, after the pandemic. Collaborative efforts by researchers,, public, private sectors will be needed to gather data, develop road safety strategies in relation to the new reality of COVID-19.

title: The (in)stability of residential burglary patterns on street segments: The case of Antwerp, Belgium 2005–2016
authors: Vandeviver, Christophe, Steenbeek, Wouter
abstract: Objectives To examine the spatial concentration, spatial stability of residential burglary at micro places in the context of a substantial city-level burglary drop in Antwerp, Belgium. Methods 51,337 police recorded home burglary incidents for the period 2005–2016 are geo-referenced to 26,875 street segments. Longitudinal trends in spatial concentrations of burglary are considered using descriptive statistics, generalized Gini coefficients,, local Getis–Ord statistics. Andresen’s (Appl Geogr 29(3):333–345, 2009 ) non-parametric spatial point pattern test (SPPT) is used to identify spatial stability in burglary point patterns, evaluate the ubiquity of a city-level burglary drop across street segments. A longitudinal extension of the SPPT is implemented. Results Residential burglary is substantially concentrated in street segments. Burglary point patterns exhibit a moderate to high degree of spatial stability over time. Local analyses show that 91\% of street segments with burglary experienced a net decrease in crime, under 1\% of street segments with burglary experienced a net increase. Absolute spatial stability over time is found for just 1.43\% of street segments with burglary, minor increases are consistently observed for as few as 11 street segments with burglary. Conclusions The citywide home burglary drop manifested itself uniformly across street segments with burglary, the majority of street segments that experienced burglary contributed relatively equally to the crime drop. In other words, we find no strong evidence that the city-level crime drop can be tied to substantial decreases in a few specific places, nor do we find that the reductions in burglary are spatially concentrated.

title: The effectiveness of burglary security devices
authors: Tseloni, Andromachi, Thompson, Rebecca, Grove, Louise, Tilley, Nick, Farrell, Graham
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; burglary; security devices; Crime Survey for England, Wales; security impact assessment tool; security protection factor; burglary rates;308\_STC;Security Journal
abstract: This study measures the effectiveness of anti-burglary security devices, both individually, in combination. Data for 2008–2012 from the Crime Survey of England, Wales are analysed via the Security Impact Assessment Tool to estimate Security Protection Factors (SPFs). SPFs indicate the level of security conferred relative to the absence of security devices. It finds that, for individual devices, external lights, door double locks or deadlocks, are most effective but, counter-intuitively, burglar alarms, dummy alarms confer less protection than no security. Combinations of devices generate positive interaction effects that increase protection more than additively. In particular, combinations with door, window locks plus external lights or security chains confer at least 20 times greater protection against burglary with entry than no security. Although further research is needed, the findings are consistent with improved security playing an important role in long-term declines in burglary rates.

title: Do sports stadiums generate crime on days without matches? A natural experiment on the delayed exploitation of criminal opportunities
authors: Vandeviver, Christophe, Bernasco, Wim, Van Daele, Stijn
abstract: Crime pattern theory claims that busy places generate crime through immediate, delayed exploitation. In delayed exploitation, offenders notice criminal opportunities during opening hours but return to exploit them later. This study investigates delayed exploitation by testing whether soccer stadiums locally increase police-recorded property crime on non-game days. A soccer stadium closure created a natural experiment. We estimate linear regression difference-in-difference models to compare crime rates on non-game days around the stadium, before, after the closure. The closure reduced non-game day property crime beyond the citywide property crime drop. We conclude that criminogenic effects of busy places extend beyond their opening hours, confirming the delayed exploitation mechanism, that crime-prevention strategies should also target these places outside opening hours.

title: A time for a crime: Temporal aspects of repeat offenders’ crime location choices
authors: van Sleeuwen, Sabine E M, Ruiter, Stijn, Menting, Barbara
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objectives: This article examines to what extent repeat offenders’ crime location choices are conditional on the timing of the offenses within the week, within the day. Extending crime pattern theory, we argue that offenders acquire time-specific rather than general knowledge of their environment. We hypothesize that offenders are more likely to offend in previously targeted areas at similar than at different days, times. Methods: Data on 12,639 offenses committed by 3,666 repeat offenders in the Netherlands are analyzed using discrete spatial choice models. Results: Offenders are most likely to offend in areas they already targeted before at similar parts of the week, similar times of the day, especially when the previous offense was committed on exactly the same weekend day or weekday, at the same hour of day. Offenders are less likely to return to previously targeted areas at different times of the week, day,, least likely to offend in areas they never targeted before. The effects were stronger for the same than for different types of crime. Conclusions: Assessing cyclic time patterns in crime location choice not only enhances our understanding of spatial criminal decision-making, but could also improve predictive policing methods.

title: Domestic burglary drop, the security hypothesis
authors: Tseloni, Andromachi, Farrell, Graham, Thompson, Rebecca, Evans, Emily, Tilley, Nick
keywords: Crime Survey for England, Wales; Crime drop; Data signatures; Domestic burglary; Security hypothesis;308\_STC;old;\_\_\_202403\_自動車盗論文
abstract: This study examines the role of household security devices in producing the domestic burglary falls in England, Wales. It extends the study of the security hypothesis as an explanation for the 'crime drop'. Crime Survey for England, Wales data are analysed from 1992 to 2011/12 via a series of data signatures indicating the nature of,, change in, the relationship between security devices, burglary. The causal role of improved security is strongly indicated by a set of interlocking data signatures: rapid increases in the prevalence of security, particularly in the availability of combinations of the most effective devices (door, window locks plus security lighting); a steep decline in the proportion of households without security accompanied by disproportionate rises in their burglary risk;, the decline being solely in forced rather than unforced entries to households. The study concludes that there is strong evidence that security caused the decline in burglary in England, Wales in the 1990s. Testing the security hypothesis across a wider range of crime types, countries, forms of security than examined to date, is required both to understand the crime drop, to derive lessons for future crime prevention practice, policy.

title: Crime, regional economic growth in Mexico: A spatial perspective: Crime, regional economic growth in Mexico
authors: Torres-Preciado, Víctor Hugo, Polanco-Gaytán, Mayrén, Tinoco-Zermeño, Miguel A
journal: Papers in regional science: the journal of the Regional Science Association International
keywords: Crime; regional economic growth; Mexico; spatial panel econometrics;308\_STC
abstract: The aim of this paper is to examine the effects of crime on regional economic growth in Mexico. We estimate a growth model using a spatial panel data model, test for the presence, type of spatial interaction, as proposed by Elhorst. Our results suggest that a two-way spatial Durbin model best fits the data, crime exerts a negative total effect on economic growth across Mexican states, particularly homicides, robbery,, significant spillover effects seem to reinforce the negative impact on regional growth.

title: Linking different types of crime using geographical, temporal proximity
authors: Tonkin, Matthew, Woodhams, Jessica, Bull, Ray, Bond, John W, Palmer, Emma J
abstract: In the absence of forensic evidence (such as DNA or fingerprints), offender behavior can be used to identify crimes that have been committed by the same person (referred to as behavioral case linkage). The current study presents the first empirical test of whether it is possible to link different types of crime using simple aspects of offender behavior. The discrimination accuracy of the kilometer distance between offense locations (the intercrime distance), the number of days between offenses (temporal proximity) was examined across a range of crimes, including violent, sexual,, property-related offenses. Both the intercrime distance, temporal proximity were able to achieve statistically significant levels of discrimination accuracy that were comparable across, within crime types, categories. The theoretical, practical implications of these findings are discussed, recommendations made for future research.

title: Spatial, temporal patterns of violent crime in a Brazilian state capital: A quantitative analysis focusing on micro places, small units of time
authors: Valente, Riccardo
keywords: Violent crime; Florianópolis; Crime concentration; Spatial point pattern test;308\_STC
abstract: The present research analyses a local variation of the problem of violence in Brazil, focuses on Florianópolis, the capital of the state of Santa Catarina, long considered the flagship of security in the country, although currently seeing an increase in violent crimes. A quantitative analysis has been implemented to test whether the law of crime concentration, the assumption of spatial-temporal dissimilarity of crime events were consistent for the specific case under study. The results show that crime concentration in Florianópolis is more accentuated than even previous literature would suggest, that the degree of concentration of street robberies, homicides is temporally stable. However, the specific locations where crime took place change over time depending on temporal dimensions such as the season, day of the week,, the hour of the day. Yet, homicide spatial patterns have shown to be less sensitive to seasonal variations. Although this conclusion challenged the initial expectations derived from previous literature, it provides a meaningful explanation of current trends of violent crime in Florianópolis, which are increasingly linked to organized crime, illegal drug trade. •Crime concentration in Florianópolis is more accentuated than in other contexts.•In discontinuous urban settings, geographic constraints accentuate spatial concentration.•Street robberies' hotspots change across space depending on the time of the day or the year.•Spatial patterns of homicides appeared to be less influenced by seasonal variations.

title: Barriocide: Investigating the temporal, spatial influence of neighborhood structural characteristics on gang, non-gang homicides in East Los Angeles
authors: Valasik, Matthew, Barton, Michael S, Reid, Shannon E, Tita, George E
keywords: 308\_STC;Homicide Studies;社会経済・空間変数と犯罪
abstract: This study explored how changes in neighborhood structural characteristics predicted variation in gang versus non-gang homicides in a policing division of the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD). Longitudinal negative binomial models were examined to test the relationship between-neighborhood structural covariates with gang, non-gang homicides over a 35-year period. This study highlights the potential to estimate temporal effects not captured by cross-sectional analyses alone. The results underscore a unique feature that distinguishes gang homicides from other forms of non-gang violence, its tenacious clustering,, spatial dependence over time.

title: Risky business: Examining the 80-20 rule in relation to a RTM framework
authors: Steinman, Hannah, Drawve, Grant, Datta, Jyotishka, Harris, Casey T, Thomas, Shaun A
abstract: The spatial elements of crime occurrence, the identification of crime generators/attractors have remained a prominent area of research. We focus on the utility of the 80-20 rule, the labeling of risky facilities in crime forecasting models with risk terrain modeling (RTM). We first examine whether the rule holds across types of crime generating places including liquor stores, department stores, hotels/motels, restaurants/bars,, apartment complexes. Next, we use our findings to test whether conducting preliminary analyses to identify risky facilities increases the predictive power of RTM versus using all possible facilities. When restricting the RTM approach to only risky facilities, results were more accurate than a traditional RTM approach. Findings, implications are nested in the utilization of the wider body of environmental criminology research to increase our understanding of where crime is likely to occur.

title: The effect of reduced street lighting on road casualties, crime in England, Wales: controlled interrupted time series analysis
authors: Steinbach, Rebecca, Perkins, Chloe, Tompson, Lisa, Johnson, Shane, Armstrong, Ben, Green, Judith, Grundy, Chris, Wilkinson, Paul, Edwards, Phil
abstract: BACKGROUND: Many local authorities in England, Wales have reduced street lighting at night to save money, reduce carbon emissions. There is no evidence to date on whether these reductions impact on public health. We quantified the effect of 4 street lighting adaptation strategies (switch off, part-night lighting, dimming, white light) on casualties, crime in England, Wales. METHODS: Observational study based on analysis of geographically coded police data on road traffic collisions, crime in 62 local authorities. Conditional Poisson models were used to analyse longitudinal changes in the counts of night-time collisions occurring on affected roads during 2000-2013,, crime within census Middle Super Output Areas during 2010-2013.
