abstract: In this article we test the hypothesis about the impact of oil prices shocks on the unemployment, crime rate on the example of oil-exporting country. According to the hypothesis, there exist a dependence of the labor market on oil revenue. A negative oil price shock should lead to a decrease in the employment rate, which in turn should lead to a rise in illegal forms of behavior. Illegal behavior is measured as an average of registered crimes (bribery, drug dealing). Based on data for 1990-2017 we study a case of Russia, using vector error correction model for detecting short-, long-term effects. Results show that oil prices, unemployment affect crime rate in the long-run in a case of oil-exporting country. Yet, in the short-run both negative oil shocks, a rise in unemployment rate lead to a statistically significant increase in bribery, drug dealing. A 1\% decrease in oil price will lead to a 1,14\% rise in bribery, drug dealing, a 1\% increase in the unemployment rate leads to a 2,72\% increase in drug dealing, bribery.

title: The accuracy of crime statistics: assessing the impact of police data bias on geographic crime analysis
authors: Buil-Gil, David, Moretti, Angelo, Langton, Samuel H
abstract: Abstract Objectives Police-recorded crimes are used by police forces to document community differences in crime, design spatially targeted strategies. Nevertheless, crimes known to police are affected by selection biases driven by underreporting. This paper presents a simulation study to analyze if crime statistics aggregated at small spatial scales are affected by larger bias than maps produced for larger geographies. Methods Based on parameters obtained from the UK Census, we simulate a synthetic population consistent with the characteristics of Manchester. Then, based on parameters derived from the Crime Survey for England, Wales, we simulate crimes suffered by individuals,, their likelihood to be known to police. This allows comparing the difference between all crimes, police-recorded incidents at different scales. Results Measures of dispersion of the relative difference between all crimes, police-recorded crimes are larger when incidents are aggregated to small geographies. The percentage of crimes unknown to police varies widely across small areas, underestimating crime in certain places while overestimating it in others. Conclusions Micro-level crime analysis is affected by a larger risk of bias than crimes aggregated at larger scales. These results raise awareness about an important shortcoming of micro-level mapping,, further efforts are needed to improve crime estimates.

title: The concentration, stability of gun violence at micro places in Boston, 1980–2008
authors: Braga, Anthony A, Papachristos, Andrew V, Hureau, David M
abstract: Boston, like many other major U.S. cities, experienced an epidemic of gun violence during the late 1980s, early 1990s that was followed by a sudden large downturn in gun violence in the mid 1990s. The gun violence drop continued until the early part of the new millennium. Recent advances in criminological research suggest that there is significant clustering of crime in micro places, or hot spots, that generate a disproportionate amount of criminal events in a city. In this paper, we use growth curve regression models to uncover distinctive developmental trends in gun assault incidents at street segments, intersections in Boston over a 29-year period. We find that Boston gun violence is intensely concentrated at a small number of street segments, intersections rather than spread evenly across the urban landscape between 1980, 2008. Gun violence trends at these high-activity micro places follow two general trajectories: stable concentrations of gun assaults incidents over time, volatile concentrations of gun assault incidents over time. Micro places with volatile trajectories represent less than 3\% of street segments, intersections, generate more than half of all gun violence incidents,, seem to be the primary drivers of overall gun violence trends in Boston. Our findings suggest that the urban gun violence epidemic,, sudden downturn in urban gun violence in the late 1990s, may be best understood by examining highly volatile micro-level trends at a relatively small number of places in urban environments.

title: It's F**ing chaos: COVID-19's impact on juvenile delinquency, juvenile justice
authors: Buchanan, Molly, Castro, Erin D, Kushner, Mackenzie, Krohn, Marvin D
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
keywords: COVID-19; Delinquency; Juvenile justice; Juvenile justice reform;308\_STC
abstract: An early examination of the impact of COVID-19 on juvenile delinquency, juvenile justice in America, this review provides initial scholarship to rapidly evolving areas of research. Our appraisals of these topics are made after nearly 2 months of national COVID-19 mitigation measures, like social distancing, limited ``non-essential'' movement outside the home but also as states are gradually lifting stricter directives, reopening economic sectors. We consider the impact of these pandemic-related changes on twenty-first century youths, their behaviors,, their separate justice system. To forecast the immediate future, we draw from decades of research on juvenile delinquency, the justice system, as well as from reported patterns of reactions, responses to an unprecedented, ongoing situation. As post-pandemic studies on juvenile delinquency, juvenile justice proliferate, we urge careful consideration as to how they might influence societal, the system responses to youths' delinquency. Additional practical implications are discussed.

title: Gang-related crime in Los Angeles remained stable following COVID-19 social distancing orders
authors: Jeffrey Brantingham, Paul, Tita, George E, Mohler, George
keywords: coronavirus; gangs; hot spots; street workers; violence prevention; violent crime;308\_STC
abstract: Research Summary: The onset of extreme social distancing measures is expected to have a dramatic impact on crime. Here, we examine the impact of mandated, city-wide social distancing orders aimed at limiting the spread of COVID-19 on gang-related crime in Los Angeles. We hypothesize that the unique subcultural processes surrounding gangs may supersede calls to shelter in place, allow gang-related crime to persist. If the normal guardianship of people, property is also disrupted by social distancing, then we expect gang violence to increase. Using autoregressive time series models, we show that gang-related crime remained stable, crime hot spots largely stationary following the onset of shelter in place. Policy Implications: In responding to disruptions to social, economic life on the scale of the present pandemic, both police, civilian organizations need to anticipate continued demand, all while managing potential reductions to workforce. Police are faced with this challenge across a wide array of crime types. Civilian interventionists tasked with responding to gang-related crime need to be prepared for continued peacekeeping, violence interruption activities, but also an expansion of responsibilities to deal with ``frontline'' or ``street-level'' management of public health needs.

title: The importance of space, time in aggravated assault victimization
authors: Breetzke, Gregory D
keywords: New Zealand; aggravated assault; environmental criminology; place, time; victimization;308\_STC;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Interpersonal crimes such as aggravated assault greatly impacts upon an individuals' sense of personal safety, security as the crime results in a physical injury. Understanding where, when aggravated assaults are most likely to occur is therefore vital to minimize the victimization risk associated with this crime. The main aim of this study is to explore the relative importance of space, time in aggravated assault victimization. This was done using national level aggravated assault data (2008-2010) obtained from New Zealand Police, census data from Statistics New Zealand. Both the spatial, temporal distribution of aggravated assault are outlined to examine their association with aggravated assault victimization. Aggravated assault is found to cluster in space but not in time. The relationships between aggravated assault risk in space, time, a suite of social, economic,, lifestyle variables was then examined. A clear socioeconomic gradient was found between aggravated assault risk by space, all neighborhood characteristics with high-risk neighborhoods having greater residential mobility, ethnic/racial diversity, as well as being more deprived, having higher rates of unemployment,, lower median household incomes. No clear pattern emerged between aggravated assault by time, the selected neighborhood characteristics. The policy implications of these findings in terms of policing, diversity conclude.

title: Coronavirus, quarantine: Catalysts of domestic violence
authors: Bouillon-Minois, Jean-Baptiste, Clinchamps, Maëlys, Dutheil, Frédéric
keywords: COVID-19; SARS-CoV-2; domestic violence; pandemic; quarantine;308\_STC;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: The pandemic of COVID-19 has resulted in quarantines imposed all around the world; these, other restrictions could produce an increase in domestic violence.

title: Measuring the resilience of criminogenic ecosystems to global disruption: A case-study of COVID-19 in China
authors: Borrion, Hervé, Kurland, Justin, Tilley, Nick, Chen, Peng
abstract: This paper uses resilience as a lens through which to analyse disasters, other major threats to patterns of criminal behaviour. A set of indicators, mathematical models are introduced that aim to quantitatively describe changes in crime levels in comparison to what could otherwise be expected,, what might be expected by way of adaptation, subsequent resumption of those patterns. The validity of the proposed resilience assessment tool is demonstrated using commercial theft data from the COVID-19 pandemic period. A 64 per cent reduction in crime was found in the studied city (China) during an 83-day period, before daily crime levels bounced back to higher than expected values. The proposed resilience indicators are recommended as benchmarking instruments for evaluating, comparing the global impact of COVID-19 policies on crime, public safety.

title: Has COVID-19 changed crime? Crime rates in the United States during the pandemic
authors: Boman, 4th, John H, Gallupe, Owen
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
keywords: Coronavirus COVID-19; Crime rates; Group-based offending; Intimate partner violence; Law enforcement; Lockdown orders;308\_STC
abstract: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, state-level governments across the United States issued mandatory stay-at-home orders around the end of March 2020. Though intended to stop the spread of the COVID-19 virus, the lockdowns have had sweeping impacts on life in ways which were not originally planned. This study's purpose is to investigate the extent to which governmental responses to COVID-19 have impacted crime rates in the U.S. Compared to the pre-pandemic year of 2019, crime - as measured by calls for service to law enforcement - has decreased markedly. However, there are multiple indications that the crime drop is being driven by decreases in minor offenses which are typically committed in peer groups. At the same time, serious crimes which are generally not committed with co-offenders (namely homicide, intimate partner violence) have either remained constant or increased. As such, the crime drop appears to be hiding a very disturbing trend where homicides remain unchanged, intimate partner batteries are increasing. Since many offenders would presumably be committing less serious crimes in a non-pandemic world, we raise attention to the possibility that mandatory lockdown orders may have taken minor offenders, placed them into situations where there is rampant opportunity for intimate partner violence, serious batteries,, homicides. While crime in the U.S. appears to be down overall, this good news should not blind us to a troubling co-occurring reality - a reality that paints a dim picture of unintended consequences to public health, criminal justice finances as a result of COVID-19 lockdowns.

title: Take the car keys away: Metropolitan structure, the long road to delinquency
authors: Bichler, Gisela, Orosco, Carlena A, Schwartz, Joseph A
abstract: This research fulfills a void in offender mobility discourse. Metropolitan socioeconomic, spatial structure, defined in crime pattern theory as the urban backcloth, plays a significant role in shaping travel behavior;, yet, current analysis of offender mobility continues to favor individual characteristics to account for travel range.Using a large sample of juveniles, both delinquent, at-risk youth (N = 2,552), this study compared the predictive utility of individual characteristics against indicators of urban backcloth.Delinquent youth were found to be more sensitive to the environmental conditions exerted by community-level socioeconomic characteristics than their at-risk counterparts. However, two factors—intercity hierarchical structure, motor vehicle access—accounted for travel variability among all youth.Offending behavior must be examined within the context of a dynamic environmental context formed by the metropolitan socioeconomic, spatial structure. Delinquents constitute an identifiable subgroup of youth.

title: Greenness, crime in the city: An investigation using remote sensing, spatial panel models
authors: Bhatia, Shaun, Jason, Leonard
abstract: Evidence has suggested that healthy environmental greenness is associated with lower rates of crime. The goal of this study was to explore this phenomenon from a longitudinal perspective while accounting for spatial dependency,, utilizing precision estimation for greenness, refined unit of place. Spatial panel fixed effects estimation was implemented to determine the association between greenness, crime rates in Chicago. Greenness was measured seasonally during the study period (2014–2018) using remote-sensed normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI). Using a spatial error specification with census block group, seasonal effects, higher levels of NDVI were significantly associated with lower overall crime rate (β = -0.24; p < 0.001), non-violent crime rate (β = -0.31; p < 0.001) after adjusting for neighborhood, land-use covariates. Extensions of the current work may focus on more granular units of geography (e.g., city blocks or street segments) using ground-truthing,, cross-validation using alternative measures of greenness.

title: Spatial panel data models using Stata
authors: Belotti, Federico, Hughes, Gordon, Piano Mortari, Andrea
abstract: xsmle is a new command for spatial analysis using Stata. We consider the quasi-maximum likelihood estimation of a wide set of both fixed-, random- effects spatial models for balanced panel data. Of special note is that xsmle allows to handle unbalanced panels thanks to its full compatibility with the mi suite of commands, to use spatial weight matrices in the form of both Stata matrices, spmat objects, to compute direct, indirect, total effects according to the procedure outlined in LeSage, Pace (2009),, to exploit a wide range of postestimation features, extending to the panel data case the predictors proposed by Kelejian, Prucha (2007). This paper describes the command, all its functionalities using both simulated, real data.

title: Close-ups, the scale of ecology: Land uses, the geography of social context, crime: The scale of ecology
authors: Boessen, Adam, Hipp, John R
abstract: Whereas one line of recent neighborhood research has placed an emphasis on zooming into smaller units of analysis such as street blocks, another line of research has suggested that even the meso‐area of neighborhoods is too narrow, that the area surrounding the neighborhood is also important. Thus, there is a need to examine the scale at which the social ecology impacts crime. We use data from seven cities from around the year 2000 to test our research questions using multilevel negative binomial regression models (N = 73,010 blocks, 8,231 block groups). Our results suggest that although many neighborhood factors seem to operate on the microscale of blocks, others seem to have a much broader impact. In addition, we find that racially, ethnically homogenous blocks within heterogeneous block groups have the most crime. Our findings also show the strongest results for a multitude of land‐use measures, that these measures sharpen some of the associations from social characteristics. Thus, we find that accounting for multiple scales simultaneously is important in ecological studies of crime.

title: Them again?: Same-offender involvement in repeat, near repeat burglaries
authors: Bernasco, Wim
abstract: Burglary victimization is associated with a temporary elevated risk of future victimization for the same property, nearby properties. Previous research suggests that often the initial, subsequent burglaries involve the same offenders. This paper tests this assertion, using data on detected residential burglaries during the period 1996—2004 in The Hague, its environs, in the Netherlands. It demonstrates that pairs of detected burglaries occurring in close proximity in space, time are much more likely to involve the same offenders than pairs that are not so related. Topics for future research, implications for the detection of burglaries are addressed.

title: The crime kaleidoscope: A cross-jurisdictional analysis of place features, crime in three urban environments
authors: Barnum, Jeremy D, Caplan, Joel M, Kennedy, Leslie W, Piza, Eric L
keywords: Crime pattern theory; Risk terrain modeling; Spatial influence; Robbery;308\_STC
abstract: Research identifies various place features (e.g., bars, schools, public transportation stops) that generate or attract crime. What is less clear is how the spatial influence of these place features compares across relatively similar environments, even for the same crime. In this study, risk terrain modeling (RTM), a geospatial crime forecasting, diagnostic tool, is utilized to identify place features that increase the risk of robbery, their particular spatial influence in Chicago, Illinois; Newark, New Jersey;, Kansas City, Missouri. The results show that the risk factors for robbery are similar between environments, but not necessarily identical. Further, some factors were riskier for robbery, affected their surrounding landscape in different ways that others. Consistent with crime pattern theory, the results suggest that the broader organization of the environmental backcloth affects how constituent place features relate to, influence crime. Implications are discussed with regard to research, practice.

title: Concentrations of railway metal theft, the locations of scrap-metal dealers
authors: Ashby, Matthew P J, Bowers, Kate J
keywords: Metal theft; Scrap-metal dealers; Market-reduction approach;308\_STC
abstract: Metal theft has become a substantial crime problem in many areas. In response, several countries have introduced legislation to regulate scrap-metal recycling yards. However, at present there is little evidence to support this use of the market reduction approach (MRA) in preventing metal theft. The present study sought to test the underlying assumption of the MRA that the presence of a market for stolen property (in this case provided by scrap yards) drives thefts in a local area. This study tested for a spatial association between the locations of scrap yards, those of metal thefts. The density of industry, local burglary rate, road-accessibility of an area were controlled for. Metal thefts from railway lines in England were shown to be significantly more common in areas with more scrap-metal yards, high road accessibility, high population density. The results support the use of the MRA in relation to metal theft.

title: Changes in police calls for service during the early months of the 2020 Coronavirus pandemic
authors: Ashby, Matthew P J
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Abstract The coronavirus pandemic poses multiple challenges for policing, including the need to continue responding to calls from the public. Several contingency plans warned police to expect a large, potentially overwhelming increase in demand from the public during a pandemic, but (to the author’s knowledge) there is no empirical work on police demand during a major public health emergency. This study used calls-for-service data from 10 large cities in the USA to analyse how calls for service changed during the early months of the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak, compared to forecasts of call volume based on data from previous years. Contrary to previous warnings, overall the number of calls went down during the early weeks of the pandemic. There were substantial reductions in specific call types, such as traffic collisions,, significant increases in others, such as calls to dead bodies. Other types of calls, particularly those relating to crime, order maintenance, continued largely as before. Changes in the frequency of different call types present challenges to law enforcement agencies, particularly since many will themselves be suffering from reduced staffing due to the pandemic. Understanding changes to calls in detail will allow police leaders to put in place evidence-based plans to ensure they can continue to serve the public.

title: Intra-week spatial-temporal patterns of crime
authors: Andresen, Martin A, Malleson, Nick
abstract: Since its original publication, routine activity theory has proven most instructive for understanding temporal patterns in crime. The most prominent of the temporal crime patterns investigated is seasonality: crime (most often assault) increases during the summer months, decreases once routine activities are less often outside. Despite the rather widespread literature on the seasonality of crime, there is very little research investigating temporal patterns of crime at shorter time intervals such as within the week or even within the day. This paper contributes to this literature through a spatial-temporal analysis of crime patterns for different days of the week. It is found that temporal patterns are present for different days of the week (more crime on weekends, as would be expected), there is a spatial component to that temporal change. Specifically, aside from robbery, sexual assault at the micro-spatial unit of analysis (street segments) the spatial patterns of crime changed. With regard to the spatial pattern changes, we found that assaults, theft from vehicle had their spatial patterns change in predictable ways on Saturdays: assaults increased in the bar district, theft from vehicles increased in the downtown, recreational car park areas.

title: Initial evidence on the relationship between the coronavirus pandemic, crime in the United States
authors: Ashby, Matthew P J
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic led to substantial changes in the daily activities of millions of Americans, with many businesses, schools closed, public events cancelled, states introducing stay-at-home orders. This article used police-recorded open crime data to understand how the frequency of common types of crime changed in 16 large cities across the United States in the early months of 2020. Seasonal auto-regressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) models of crime in previous years were used to forecast the expected frequency of crime in 2020 in the absence of the pandemic. The forecasts from these models were then compared to the actual frequency of crime during the early months of the pandemic. There were no significant changes in the frequency of serious assaults in public or (contrary to the concerns of policy makers) any change to the frequency of serious assaults in residences. In some cities, there were reductions in residential burglary but little change in non-residential burglary. Thefts of motor vehicles decreased in some cities while there were diverging patterns of thefts from motor vehicles. These results are used to make suggestions for future research into the relationships between the coronavirus pandemic, different crimes.

title: Druglords don’t stay at home: COVID-19 pandemic, crime patterns in Mexico city
authors: Balmori de la Miyar, Jose Roberto, Hoehn-Velasco, Lauren, Silverio-Murillo, Adan
abstract: Objective: To investigate the effect of the COVID-19 pandemic on conventional crime, organized crime in Mexico City, Mexico.Methods: Mexico City’s Attorney General’s Office reported crime data, covering domestic violence, burglary, robbery, vehicle-theft, assault-battery, homicides, kidnapping,, extortion. We use an event study for the intertemproal variation across the 16 districts (municipalities) in Mexico City for 2019, 2020.Results: We find a sharp decrease on crimes related to domestic violence, burglary,, vehicle theft; a decrease during some weeks on crimes related to assaultbattery, extortion,, no effects on crimes related to robbery, kidnapping,, homicides.Conclusions: While our results show a decline in conventional crime during the COVID-19 pandemic, organized crime remains steady. These findings have policy implications for catastrophic events around the world, as well as possible national security issues in Mexico

title: Fast food restaurants, convenience stores: Using sales volume to explain crime patterns in Seattle
authors: Askey, Amber Perenzin, Taylor, Ralph, Groff, Elizabeth, Fingerhut, Aaron
abstract: This study investigates how convenience stores, fast food restaurants influence crime patterns over time. Using sales volume data from fast food restaurants, convenience stores, we examine streetblock crime levels over a seven year period in Seattle using multilevel models. Results demonstrate that high sales volume links to high crime, even after controlling for local socio-economic status, the effects of retail businesses,, local crime trends. In addition, street segment crime trajectories were spatially clustered in a significant way. The dynamics that explain why specific types of commercial facilities link to street crime need further theoretical clarification. This is the first study demonstrating significant spatio-temporal patterning of streetblock crime trends.

title: The trajectories of crime at places: Understanding the patterns of disaggregated crime types
authors: Andresen, Martin A, Curman, Andrea S, Linning, Shannon J
abstract: Objectives Investigate the spatial concentrations, the stability of trajectories for disaggregated crime types on street segments, intersections in Vancouver, Canada. Methods A longitudinal analysis of 16 years of crime data using street segments, intersections as the units of analysis. We use the k-means non-parametric cluster analysis technique considering eight crime types: assault, burglary, robbery, theft, theft of vehicle, theft from vehicle, other,, total crime. Results The overall results for the individual crime types versus overall crime are similar: crime is highly concentrated regardless of crime type, most street segment, intersection trajectories are stable over time with the others decreasing,, most decreasing trajectories are in the same general areas. However, there are notable differences across crime types that need to be considered when attempting to understand spatial pattern changes, implement crime prevention initiatives. Conclusions The law of crime concentration at places holds in Vancouver, Canada for disaggregated crime types in the context of spatial concentrations, their stability over time. However, notable differences exist across crime types that should be accounted for when developing theory or policy.

title: Exploring the impact of arson-reduction strategies: Panel data evidence from England
authors: Andrews, R
keywords: England; arson; crime prevention; disorder; empirical analysis;308\_STC;自然実験・準実験;British Journal of criminology
abstract: In 2001, the UK government funded the introduction of a series of targeted situational preventive schemes, multi-agency partnerships to reduce deliberate fire-setting in vehicles. This paper explores the impact of these alternative arson-reduction strategies on vehicle arson in the areas served by fire authorities in England utilizing panel data for an eight-year period (1999—2006). The statistical results suggest that both forms of intervention have been successful in reducing vehicle arson,, that higher input intensity is also responsible for better outcomes. Theoretical, practical implications of the findings are discussed.

title: Toward a test of the “Law of Crime Concentration” in Japanese cities: a geographical crime analysis in Tokyo, Osaka
authors: Amemiya, Mamoru, Ohyama, Tomoya
abstract: Abstract This brief report aims to reveal crime concentration at the district level in Tokyo, Osaka, Japan, two cities characterized by low crime rates. Eight types of property crimes that occurred between 2008, 2017 in Tokyo, Osaka, had been aggregated by the census enumeration district were analyzed using the Gini coefficient based on the Poisson-Gamma method. The results indicated three patterns. First, crime concentration was identified. Second, the degree of concentration depended upon crime type. Commercial burglary was the most concentrated crime type,, theft from vehicle, theft from vending machine were the most dispersed. Third, crime concentration patterns either remained stable or became more concentrated over time. Additionally, while theft of bicycle was found to display stable concentration levels over time, the concentration level of purse snatching was fluid. On the basis of the results, this report discusses the possibility of establishing the “Law of Crime Concentration” (LCC) in two Japanese cities.

title: Novel evaluation metrics for sparse spatio-temporal point process hotspot predictions - a crime case study
authors: Adepeju, Monsuru, Rosser, Gabriel, Cheng, Tao
abstract: Many physical, sociological processes are represented as discrete events in time, space. These spatio-temporal point processes are often sparse, meaning that they cannot be aggregated, treated with conventional regression models. Models based on the point process framework may be employed instead for prediction purposes. Evaluating the predictive performance of these models poses a unique challenge, as the same sparseness prevents the use of popular measures such as the root mean squared error. Statistical likelihood is a valid alternative, but this does not measure absolute performance, is therefore difficult for practitioners, researchers to interpret. Motivated by this limitation, we develop a practical toolkit of evaluation metrics for spatio-temporal point process predictions. The metrics are based around the concept of hotspots, which represent areas of high point density. In addition to measuring predictive accuracy, our evaluation toolkit considers broader aspects of predictive performance, including a characterisation of the spatial, temporal distributions of predicted hotspots, a comparison of the complementarity of different prediction methods. We demonstrate the application of our evaluation metrics using a case study of crime prediction, comparing four varied prediction methods using crime data from two different locations, multiple crime types. The results highlight a previously unseen interplay between predictive accuracy, spatio-temporal dispersion of predicted hotspots. The new evaluation framework may be applied to compare multiple prediction methods in a variety of scenarios, yielding valuable new insight into the predictive performance of point process-based prediction.

title: Disorder, decline: The state of research
authors: Skogan, Wesley
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 310\_BW\_総説;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Objectives:A significant, diverse body of research has built up during the 30+ years since the publication of Wilson, Kelling’s seminal “broken windows” article. They affected research, policy,, politics around the world. This article summarizes some of the main strands of research that have since sprung up around these, other claims.Results:This article discusses approaches to conceptualizing, measuring disorder, weighs the strengths, weaknesses of various measurement modalities. It summarizes what this research has revealed about the apparent causes, effects of disorder.Conclusion:Research documents that disorder has broad implications for public health, safety, that it is deeply implicated in the dynamics of neighborhood stability, change. Further, there is evidence that—directly, via its impact on other features of community life—disorder stimulates conventional crime.

title: Negotiated consent or zero tolerance? Responding to graffiti, street art in Melbourne
authors: Young, Alison
abstract: This paper critically considers the recent history of graffiti regulation in one municipality. It draws upon my experience of being appointed to develop a Draft Strategy on Graffiti for the City of Melbourne in 2004. My appointment was based upon the several years I had spent as a criminologist, socio‐legal researcher, engaging with the communities of graffiti writers, street artists in Melbourne, internationally. The aim was to develop a Strategy that would take a more progressive approach to graffiti, street art management,, the proposed policy focused upon notions of ‘negotiated consent’ to the presence of graffiti or street art, ‘zones of tolerance’ with varying degrees of self‐regulation by graffiti writers or external regulation by police, council authorities. Despite widespread support for the Strategy, the Council elected instead to pursue a policy of zero tolerance combined with a discretionary permit system. The paper examines the fate of this particular attempt to think differently about graffiti,, engages critically with the more conventional approaches put in place instead. It considers the policy‐making process in a manner informed both by autobiographical experience, by some recent writings on graffiti, the city, community, communication.

title: Neighborhood physical features, relationships with neighbors: Does positive physical environment increase neighborliness?
authors: Wilkerson, Amy, Carlson, Nichole E, Yen, Irene H, Michael, Yvonne L
abstract: The objective was to investigate associations between features of the physical environment, neighborliness. Measures of the physical environment, including sidewalks, front porches, traffic-calming devices, bars on windows,, the presence of litter or graffiti, were collected using a systematic audit instrument in 10 neighborhoods in Portland, Oregon. Generalized linear regression models were created to model the odds of increasing neighborliness given access to the physical-environment factors of interest. The authors observed a greater probability of higher levels of neighborliness as the total number of positive physical-environment characteristics increased (cumulative odds ratio [95\% confidence interval] = 1.69 [1.16, 2.45]), the results were unchanged after controlling for race, self-reported health, perception of safety, years of neighborhood residence, age of house, market value of house,, proportion of homeowners in neighborhood. Modifiable features of the physical environment may be one mechanism through which people can enhance neighborliness.

title: Reimagining Broken Windows: From Theory to policy
authors: Welsh, Brandon C, Braga, Anthony A, Bruinsma, Gerben J N
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 311\_BW\_社会調査;310\_BW\_総説;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage;pop
abstract: This article serves as a substantive introduction, guiding post for the journal’s special issue on “Reimagining Broken Windows: From Theory to Policy.” It describes the core concepts of the broken windows perspective, examines its theoretical underpinnings,, sets out priorities for future research, policy development. Important advancements have been made in the intellectual development, programmatic application of the broken windows perspective over the last 30 years. Some of these advancements include the measurement of disorder, experimentation of community, problem-solving strategies for policing disorder. There are also many challenges, including the need for a more consistent operationalization of disorder, a better understanding of potential mechanisms,, concerns about policy overreach in the name of broken windows. We predict that the broken windows perspective will be around for many more decades to come—its enduring qualities far exceed a smartly coined phrase.

title: The association between the physical environment of primary schools, active school transport
authors: Van Kann, D H H, Kremers, S P J, Gubbels, J S, Bartelink, N H M, de Vries, S I, de Vries, N K, Jansen, M W J
abstract: This study examined the relationship between the physical environment characteristics of primary schools, active school transport among 3,438 5- to 12-year-old primary school children in the Netherlands. The environmental characteristics were categorized into four theory-based clusters (function, safety, aesthetics,, destination). The correlations between the clusters, active school transport were examined,, multilevel regression analyses were used to examine the association between the clusters, active school transport. No correlations were found between environmental clusters, active school transport for younger children (age 5-9), but for older children (age 9-12), strong positive correlations were found between aesthetics, active transport as were found for safety, active transport. School neighborhood aesthetics were related to active transport for older primary school children. Presence of parks, good maintenance of green spaces,, absence of litter in the school environment contributed most to the positive association between aesthetics, active school transport.

title: The relationship between residential yard management, neighborhood crime: An analysis from Baltimore City, County
authors: Troy, Austin, Nunery, Ashley, Grove, J Morgan
keywords: Crime; Environmental design; Residential landscaping; Yards; Spatial analysis;311\_BW\_社会調査
abstract: We analyzed the relationship between crime, indicators of residential yard management in Baltimore City, County. Data came from a survey we conducted of over one thousand front yards that included more than 40 indicators relating to lawns, trees, shrubs, beds, other features. These indicators were related to point counts of crime at the 150 m scale using a combination of ordinary least squares, spatial error,, Poisson regressions. After controlling for income, population density, block-scale tree canopy,, housing type, we found a consistently significant relationship between crime, a number of indicators of yard management. Yard-level variables that were negatively associated with crime included: the presence of yard trees, garden hoses/sprinklers,, lawns, in addition to the percentage of pervious area in a yard. Those positively associated with crime included presence of litter, desiccation of the lawn, lack of cutting of the lawn,, number of small trees in front of or adjacent to the property. While these results do not establish causality, they add evidence to a growing literature that suggests the possibility of several mechanisms by which environmental design may reduce crime: “cues to care” (the inverse of the “broken window” hypothesis) can lead to reduced crime by signaling to criminals the presence of social capital, the active involvement of neighbors in community spaces;, more appealing landscaping draws more “eyes on the street,” which in turn deters criminals.

title: A twenty-first century graffiti classification system: A typological tool for prioritizing graffiti removal
authors: Taylor, Myra F, Cordin, Robin, Njiru, Joseph
keywords: Telephone hotlines; Graffiti; Hip hop culture; Social research; Criminology; Crime prevention;311\_BW\_社会調査;CPCS2008-2016;Crime Prevention, Community Safety
abstract: Graffiti removal is a prolific, costly problem for Australian municipal authorities. In Western Australia, new incidents of graffiti are reported through the state government's dedicated graffiti hotline. The aim being to have all highly offensive graffiti removed within a 24-hour time frame, all other graffiti within 48 hours. The flaw in the system is that individuals reporting graffiti incidents have diverse understandings as to what forms of graffiti constitute the state government's highly offensive classification. This confusion has led to removal contractors being sent to remove non-highly offensive graffiti ahead of highly offensive graffiti. To address this problem, this article reports on the development, validation of a graffiti classification system. This system provides authorities with a typological tool for prioritizing the removal of graffiti.

title: Paying attention to minor offenses: order maintenance policing in practice
authors: Sousa, William H
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Order maintenance policing is often equated with the term ‘zero tolerance,’ which implies that officers exercise little discretion when enforcing minor offenses. Few researchers, however, have explored the extent to which order maintenance actually limits officer discretion, creates a zero‐tolerance atmosphere. This paper draws on field observations of police officers in NYPD – a department with a reputation for its order maintenance strategy – to explore officer decision making when enforcing minor offenses. Ethnographic data suggest that while officers acknowledge the importance of maintaining order, they possess, utilize a high degree of discretion when managing minor offenses.

title: The transsituational influence of social norms
authors: Reno, Raymond R, Cialdini, Robert B, Kallgren, Carl A
keywords: *Pollution; *Social Approval; *Social Norms; Stimulus Salience;311\_BW\_社会調査
abstract: Three studies examined the behavioral implications of a conceptual distinction between 2 types of social norms: descriptive norms, which specify what is typically done in a given setting,, injunctive norms, which specify what is typically approved in society. Using the social norm against littering, injunctive norm salience procedures were more robust in their behavioral impact across situations than were descriptive norm salience procedures. Focusing Ss on the injunctive norm suppressed littering regardless of whether the environment was clean or littered (Study 1), regardless of whether the environment in which Ss could litter was the same as or different from that in which the norm was evoked (Studies 2, 3). The impact of focusing Ss on the descriptive norm was much less general. Conceptual implications for a focus theory of normative conduct are discussed along with practical implications for increasing socially desirable behavior.

title: Emotional, behavioural responses to everyday incivility: Challenging the fear/avoidance paradigm
authors: Phillips, Tim, Smith, Philip
keywords: EMOTIONS; CRIMINAL law; SOCIOLOGY; CRIMINOLOGY; SOCIAL sciences -- Philosophy; AVERSION; collective efficacy; broken windows; Sage;311\_BW\_社会調査
abstract: Although antisocial behaviour has become an issue of political, policy concern, social science lacks basic information on such events. This article explores one aspect of such everyday incivility - how people react emotionally, behaviourally to the badly behaved stranger. Mainstream criminology, as well as the social theory of Goffman, Bauman, is oriented around a fear/avoidance vision. This dominant paradigm is unnecessarily restrictive on intellectual inquiry. A raft of other options including anger/intervention; disgust/aversion, indifference/do nothing are analytically reconstructed from the classical social theory of Durkheim, Elias, Simmel. These various models are applied to incidents coded from the transcripts of the Melbourne Everyday Incivility Project. The results show that emotions, behaviours tend to pair up as predicted. Fear/avoidance, however, is a relatively uncommon response to incivil encounters. Anger/intervention, indifference/do nothing are more frequent. The former is especially associated with events where the respondent is a ‘victim’,, the latter with those where the respondent is an onlooker. These findings suggest the limitations of current criminological research in areas related to incivility, fear of crime,, have implications for collective efficacy, social capital, broken windows criminology.

title: Ecometrics in the age of big data: Measuring, assessing “broken windows” using large-scale administrative records
authors: O'Brien, Daniel Tumminelli, Sampson, Robert J, Winship, Christopher
abstract: The collection of large-scale administrative records in electronic form by many cities provides a new opportunity for the measurement, longitudinal tracking of neighborhood characteristics, but one that will require novel methodologies that convert such data into research-relevant measures. The authors illustrate these challenges by developing measures of “broken windows” from Boston’s constituent relationship management (CRM) system (aka 311 hotline). A 16-month archive of the CRM database contains more than 300,000 address-based requests for city services, many of which reference physical incivilities (e.g., graffiti removal). The authors carry out three ecometric analyses, each building on the previous one. Analysis 1 examines the content of the measure, identifying 28 items that constitute two independent constructs, private neglect, public denigration. Analysis 2 assesses the validity of the measure by using investigator-initiated neighborhood audits to examine the “civic response rate” across neighborhoods. Indicators of civic response were then extracted from the CRM database so that measurement adjustments could be automated. These adjustments were calibrated against measures of litter from the objective audits. Analysis 3 examines the reliability of the composite measure of physical disorder at different spatiotemporal windows, finding that census tracts can be measured at two-month intervals, census block groups at six-month intervals. The final measures are highly detailed, can be tracked longitudinally,, are virtually costless. This framework thus provides an example of how new forms of large-scale administrative data can yield ecometric measurement for urban science while illustrating the methodological challenges that must be addressed.

title: Custodians, custodianship in urban neighborhoods: A methodology using reports of public issues received by a city’s 311 hotline
authors: O'Brien, Daniel Tumminelli
abstract: The paper introduces a methodology for using a city’s administrative data to study custodianship, or those behaviors aimed at preventing physical disorder in the public space. Custodianship was operationalized through requests for city services regarding public maintenance (e.g., potholes), provided by the database generated by Boston, MA’s hotline for requesting city services (i.e., 311). Users can register with the system, permitting analysis of individual differences in custodianship ( N = 12,361), including frequency of reports, variety of issues reported,, geographical range of reports. Home location (available for N = 7,433) was combined with Census statistics to infer demographic characteristics. Most (76\%) reported one case. There was no evidence that individuals specialize on a single type of issue. Most reported issues over a narrow geographic range (80\% within 2 blocks of home). Homeowners were three times more likely than renters to report public issues. A technique for estimating the home locations of users is also tested.

title: Adverse neighborhood conditions, sanction risk perceptions: Using SEM to examine direct, indirect effects
authors: Kim, Byungbae, Pratt, Travis C, Wallace, Danielle
keywords: Adverse neighborhood conditions; Sanction risk perceptions; Structural equation modeling;311\_BW\_社会調査
abstract: Objectives The present study examines how individuals' sanction risk perceptions are shaped by neighborhood context. Methods Using structural equation modeling on data from waves 6, 7 of the National Youth Survey, we assess the direct, indirect relationships between adverse neighborhood conditions, two dimensions of sanction risk perceptions: the certainty of punishment, perceived shame. In addition, the role of shame as a mediator between neighborhood context, certainty of punishment is also investigated. Results The results indicate that adverse neighborhood conditions indirectly affect both forms of sanction risk perceptions,, additional results show that perceived shame fully mediates the effect of neighborhood conditions on perceptions of the certainty of punishment. Conclusions The perceptual deterrence/rational choice perspective will need to be revised to accommodate more explicitly the role of neighborhood context in shaping sanction risk perceptions.

title: Official graffiti of the everyday
authors: Hermer, Joe, Hunt, Alan
keywords: SIGNS \& symbols; SIGNS \& signboards; GRAFFITI; VISUAL communication; UNITED States -- Social conditions -- 1980-; UNITED States;311\_BW\_社会調査
abstract: This article focuses attention on official graffiti or regulatory signs typified by highway signs, the most invasive, emblematic piece of official graffiti, the prohibition circle with its diagonal red slash used in the iconic representation No Smoking. Establishing the range, pervasiveness of official graffiti in everyday life (as prohibitions, warnings, advisories, instructions, etc.), the authors approach these visual manifestations from the standpoint of the sociology of governance, analyze them as important instances of government at a distance. They explore the varieties, forms of such regulation, trace their expansion from public space to quasi-public space, to the private realm. Locating the texts, icons of official graffiti within implied or express discursive frameworks, the authors point to the construction of objects, subjects of regulation, to regulatory agents as absent experts, address the key role of the construction of danger, the link to insurance principles in a isk society. They also examine resistance through actions of defacement, avoidance that result in the complex order, disorder of surfaces, spaces. Official graffiti manifests a distinctive form of hegemony that is exercised through the small, daily acts of everyday governance.

title: Norms, Neighborhoods: Explaining Variation in Social Control
authors: Horne, Christine, Hoffman, J
booktitle: Experiments in Criminology, Law: A Research Revolution

title: A social norms approach to legitimacy
authors: Horne, Christine
abstract: Rulers seek to develop legitimacy. Legitimacy is a murky concept, however,, just how rulers might attain it is not well understood. This article explores the implications of conceptualizing legitimacy as a social norm that encourages people to support the ruler. This conceptualization points to the importance of social relations as well as characteristics of the ruler, his or her behavior. These factors together are argued to affect the extent to which norms supporting the ruler are enforced and, in turn, the extent to which people obey, respond to calls to action by the ruler. On this view, a ruler seeking legitimacy should consider (a) the messages he or she sends to citizens about himself or herself, (b) the ways in which his or her policies affect ties between citizens.

title: Built environment, violent crime: An environmental audit approach using Google Street View
authors: He, Li, Páez, Antonio, Liu, Desheng
keywords: Built environment; Violent crime; Spatial filtering; Environmental audit; Google Street View;311\_BW\_社会調査;GSV
abstract: Recent studies empirically support the role of the built environment in inducing or hindering violent crime. Particularly, studies of the broken window theory have provided evidence that physical disorder is an environmental correlate of crime. This includes broken windows, vacant/abandoned housings, abandoned cars on street, graffiti,, decayed street lighting, among other things. Current studies are limited by the difficulty involved in collecting fine-scale quantitative environmental data. The conventional environmental audit approach, which aims to assess environmental features, is costly, time-consuming,, burdensome. In this study, we use Google Street View to study the relationship between violent crime, physical features of urban residential environment. More concretely, a Poisson regression model with spatial filtering is used to identify socio-economic correlates of violent crime. Parting from the hypothesis that omission of built environmental factors results in systematic residual pattern, we proceed to analyze the spatial filter to select sites for virtual environmental audits. A series of physical environmental factors are identified using contingency table analysis. The results provide both theoretical, practical implications for several theories of crime, crime prevention efforts.

title: Preventing neighborhood disorder: Comparing alternative models of collective efficacy theory using structural equation modeling
authors: Gearhart, Michael C
keywords: Collective efficacy; Informal social control; Mutual efficacy; Neighborhood disorder; Social cohesion; Theory;311\_BW\_社会調査;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: Collective efficacy is a widely studied theoretical framework. Originally operationalized as the combination of social cohesion, informal social control, collective efficacy theory is a predictor of multiple positive outcomes. Conceptual, empirical critiques of collective efficacy theory suggest that social cohesion, informal social control should be modeled as unique constructs. Further, the current model of collective efficacy theory does not include an explicit measure of efficacy. Mutual efficacy, defined as community members' beliefs that collective action will be successful at attaining group goals, will be developed in this manuscript. The purpose of mutual efficacy was to make efficacy an explicit component within collective efficacy theory. Three models of collective efficacy theory are compared in this study: (a) a one-factor model of collective efficacy that combines social cohesion, informal social control, (b) a two-factor model of collective efficacy that models social cohesion as a predictor of informal social control,, (c) a mutual efficacy model where the relationship between social cohesion, informal social control is mediated by mutual efficacy. Results suggest that the two-factor model, the mutual efficacy model both fit the data better than the current model of collective efficacy.

title: Investigating the spatiotemporal links between disorder, crime,, the fear of crime
authors: Doran, Bruce J, Lees, Brian G
journal: The Professional geographer: the journal of the Association of American Geographers
abstract: Abstract While links between social, physical disorder, crime,, the fear of crime have long been areas of research interest, few studies have looked at these links from a spatiotemporal viewpoint. This is somewhat surprising, as many of the factors associated with disorder, crime,, fear are known to vary over time, space. This paper uses GISystems to investigate potential spatiotemporal links between these areas in Wollongong, New South Wales, with specific focus on links between graffiti, the fear of crime. The results reveal that the distribution of fear of crime varies considerably over time, is often spatially coincident with concentrations of disorder. Graffiti was found to be one of the most prevalent types of physical disorder. The results are discussed in the context of the ?broken windows? thesis, strategic intervention at the community level.; Abstract While links between social, physical disorder, crime,, the fear of crime have long been areas of research interest, few studies have looked at these links from a spatiotemporal viewpoint. This is somewhat surprising, as many of the factors associated with disorder, crime,, fear are known to vary over time, space. This paper uses GISystems to investigate potential spatiotemporal links between these areas in Wollongong, New South Wales, with specific focus on links between graffiti, the fear of crime. The results reveal that the distribution of fear of crime varies considerably over time, is often spatially coincident with concentrations of disorder. Graffiti was found to be one of the most prevalent types of physical disorder. The results are discussed in the context of the ?broken windows? thesis, strategic intervention at the community level.

title: The crucial ‘where’ of graffiti: A geographical analysis of reactions to graffiti in New York
authors: Cresswell, T
abstract: This paper is an examination of the reactions to graffiti in New York during the early 1970s. It is argued that the reactions of the media, government present a discourse of disorder, a discourse in which graffiti is presented as a symptom of disorder, thus a threat to the image of New York City, civilization itself. Simultaneously the art establishment reacts to graffiti by (dis)placing it in Manhattan galleries, describing it as creative, ‘primitive’,, valuable. These discourses play an important role in the formation, maintenance of the meaning of a place. Simultaneously the place—New York, the subway, the gallery—plays a role in affecting the nature of the discourses, judgements of the value of graffiti. This case study is framed in the context of a wider discussion of the relation between place, ideology in which it is suggested that each plays a role in structuring the other.

title: A risk-based model of public perceptions of crime, disorder
authors: Crank, John P, Irlbeck, Dawn M, Giacomazzi, Andrew L
abstract: Incivilities research, related 'broken windows' crime control policies are based on the notion that citizens causally distinguish between crime, disorder. Subjective measures of crime, disorder, however, have (1) failed to supportive evidence of the two as distinctly separate constructs, (2) have shown divergent findings in different research frames. This paper argues that the public does not differentiate among these concepts - or in community conditions associated with criminogenic outcomes - in the same way that researchers have. Instead, the subjective interpretation of specific risks, their concrete circumstances by community members is a pragmatic assessment of associated conditions,, varies according to local community dynamics. However, these concepts share a central organizing principle, logic, that of perceived risk. We first assess the underlying structure of citizens' perceptions of perceived risks, assessing the latent structure of 24 measures of perceived risk. We then assess, using a second-order factor analysis, whether a unifying risk concept ties together the first-order factors in a meaningful way.

title: Littering reduction: A systematic review of research 1995-2015
authors: Almosa, Yara, Parkinson, Joy, Rundle-Thiele, Sharyn
abstract: Littering continues to be a problem worldwide. The purpose of this article is to update earlier systematic reviews on littering, using a scorecard of seven social marketing components, assess the extent of social marketing use in identified littering programs. Following Center for Reviews, Dissemination guidelines, the search included all peer-reviewed studies published between 1995, 2015 in the English language available through 10 databases. A total of 1,220 articles were initially identified, resulted in a final set of 17 that met the study criteria. The analysis revealed key insights including a lack of social marketing use in litter prevention efforts to date providing an opportunity for future research. Limitations of the current study, opportunities for future research are outlined.

title: Investigation of the differences between factors affecting vandalism in urban green areas
authors: Yilmaz, Tahsin, Olgun, Rifat
abstract: This study aimed to identify the factors that have an effect on a variety of vandalism incidents involving urban equipment located in urban green areas in the city of Antalya. For this aim, the urban equipment (benches, lighting fixtures, picnic tables,, waste bins) were observed in situ on a monthly basis for 12 months,, the vandalism incidents were photographed 2028 times, recorded in the information forms. Data obtained through observation, photography were evaluated using nonlinear canonical correlation analysis. The results showed that the variables examined within the content of this study were the factors that influence the occurrence of vandalism incidents. Certain solution suggestions were developed based on the obtained results.

title: The pen or the sword: A situated spatial analysis of graffiti, violent injury in Vancouver, British Columbia
authors: Walker, Blake Byron, Schuurman, Nadine
journal: The Professional geographer: the journal of the Association of American Geographers
abstract: Graffiti is a ubiquitous feature of the urban landscape commonly perceived to be a symptom of disorder, deprivation,, violence. Broken windows theory asserts that it is also a cause. To examine this, we conduct a geographic correlation study of graffiti, violence using geographic information systems. A strong spatial covariation is observed, with spatially dependent residual clusters suggesting that the graffiti–violence relationship is context dependent, varied. Ferrell, Weide's spot theory provides a lens for situating hot spots, facilitating a more nuanced interrogation of graffiti, violence in several Vancouver neighborhoods. We advocate for situated spatial analyses of interpersonal violence to inform public health interventions, advance policymaking beyond the popular aesthetic symbolism of urban space.

title: The differential impact of physical disorder, collective efficacy: a geographically weighted regression on violent crime
authors: E. Stein, Rachel, Conley, Jamison F, Davis, Clinton
abstract: While much of the research on neighborhood crime considers the neighborhood as a whole, this study utilizes spatial analysis techniques to examine how the presence of disorder, collective efficacy create unique pockets of opportunities for criminal behavior within neighborhoods. This spatial perspective reveals how the effect of disorder, efficacy upon crime patterns itself varies across a neighborhood. Physical disorder is measured through systematic social observations, the level of collective efficacy is evaluated through survey responses of neighborhood residents. The indices of disorder, efficacy are compared to crime data from police call logs using geographically weighted regression. Our findings demonstrate a complex spatial relationship between disorder, efficacy. The effects of disorder, efficacy are not consistent across an entire neighborhood, but rather display local variations in small geographical areas within neighborhoods, including some pockets of the neighborhood where the relationships between disorder, efficacy,, crime were contrary to the expected relationships. Based upon these findings, we conclude opportunity is central to understanding crime,, emphasize the role of informal social control in neighborhoods.

title: Where broken windows should be fixed: Toward identification of areas at the tipping point
authors: Steenbeek, Wouter, Kreis, Christian
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 312\_BW\_観察SSO;310\_BW\_総説;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Objectives: Introduce a systematic method to identify areas with similar levels of disorder (from serene, to “tipping,” to crime-ridden) which is crucial for a valid empirical test of Broken Windows Theory (BWT). Methods: Systematic social observation data are used of almost 2,000 locations in the city of Amsterdam, the Netherlands. Spatially constrained hierarchical agglomerative clustering is used to aggregate individual observation locations to form homogeneous areas. Davies–Bouldin index, intraclass correlation coefficient are used to objectively identify the optimum number of clusters. Results: The newly identified areas differ from administrative neighborhoods as well as hot spots of disorder. The regionalization method provides a tentative solution to both the “zonation”, “aggregation” problems of the modifiable areal unit problem liable to affect empirical studies of BWT. Conclusions: Hot spot analysis fails to identify areas with moderate levels of disorder, which impedes testing the basic precept of BWT. Our results may partly explain why the evidence on the effectiveness of order maintenance policing remains inconclusive. We suggest that randomized controlled trials of order maintenance policing should be performed on these new areas rather than in hot spots of disorder.

title: Zero graffiti for a beautiful city: the cultural politics of urban space in San Francisco
authors: Shobe, Hunter, Banis, David
abstract: San Francisco, like many cities in the United States, across the world, has an official zero-tolerance policy on graffiti. In this article, we examine the academic literature concerned with graffiti, then present a case study of zero-tolerance abatement policies in San Francisco. Our analysis yields three main findings. First, zero-tolerance policy stimulates an anti-graffiti industry with vested interest in perpetuating an endless war for control of public space. Second, zero tolerance may generate an unintended result—the proliferation of tags, other forms of graffiti that people tend to dislike the most. Third, we find little evidence that the general public shares the same desire for zero tolerance as the San Francisco Government. Ultimately, we believe that more nuanced readings of graffiti allow greater numbers of people to make sensible, local, place-specific policies regarding graffiti.

title: Assessing physical disorder in urban neighborhoods: Reliability, validity of the parcel maintenance observation tool: Assessing physical disorder in urban neighborhoods
authors: Reischl, Thomas M, Krusky, Allison M, Zimmerman, Marc A, Aiyer, Sophie M, Kruger, Daniel J, Franzen, Susan P, Lipton, Robert
abstract: Research on neighborhood factors that influence health, crime often use neighborhood measures of geographic areas such as census tracts, wards,, postal sectors. These administratively defined areas, however, may mask the heterogeneity of neighborhood influences. In response to calls for more specific measures, we tested the reliability, validity of the Parcel Maintenance Observation Tool (PMOT)–a new measure of physical disorder on property parcels. The results included baseline assessments of 6134 parcels in 2 urban neighborhoods, inter-correlations, inter-rater reliability,, tests of concurrent validity. Most of the measures had high or adequate inter-rater reliability. The PMOT measures differentiated between (a) parcels with occupied, unoccupied buildings, (b) vacant lots included in a property maintenance program, no-program vacant lots. The discussion focuses on potential uses of the PMOT for understanding the effects of neighborhood physical disorder, for evaluating health promotion, crime prevention programs.

title: Systematic social observation of children's neighborhoods using Google Street View: a reliable, cost-effective method: SSO in street view
authors: Odgers, Candice L, Caspi, Avshalom, Bates, Christopher J, Sampson, Robert J, Moffitt, Terrie E
journal: Journal of child psychology, psychiatry,, allied disciplines
abstract: BACKGROUND: Children growing up in poor versus affluent neighborhoods are more likely to spend time in prison, develop health problems, die at an early age. The question of how neighborhood conditions influence our behavior, health has attracted the attention of public health officials, scholars for generations. Online tools are now providing new opportunities to measure neighborhood features, may provide a cost effective way to advance our understanding of neighborhood effects on child health. METHOD: A virtual systematic social observation (SSO) study was conducted to test whether Google Street View could be used to reliably capture the neighborhood conditions of families participating in the Environmental-Risk (E-Risk) Longitudinal Twin Study. Multiple raters coded a subsample of 120 neighborhoods, convergent, discriminant validity was evaluated on the full sample of over 1,000 neighborhoods by linking virtual SSO measures to: (a) consumer based geo-demographic classifications of deprivation, health, (b) local resident surveys of disorder, safety,, (c) parent, teacher assessments of children's antisocial behavior, prosocial behavior,, body mass index. RESULTS: High levels of observed agreement were documented for signs of physical disorder, physical decay, dangerousness, street safety. Inter-rater agreement estimates fell within the moderate to substantial range for all of the scales (ICCs ranged from .48 to .91). Negative neighborhood features, including SSO-rated disorder, decay, dangerousness corresponded with local resident reports, demonstrated a graded relationship with census-defined indices of socioeconomic status,, predicted higher levels of antisocial behavior among local children. In addition, positive neighborhood features, including SSO-rated street safety, the percentage of green space, were associated with higher prosocial behavior, healthy weight status among children. CONCLUSIONS: Our results support the use of Google Street View as a reliable, cost effective tool for measuring both negative, positive features of local neighborhoods.

title: “litterers”: How objects of physical disorder are used to construct subjects of social disorder in a suburb
authors: Murphy, Alexandra K
journal: The annals of the American Academy of Political, Social Science
keywords: 312\_BW\_観察SSO;ANNALS of the American Academy of Political, Social Science
abstract: How do people get constructed as “litterers” through objects of litter on the ground? Middle-, working-class white, black homeowners of the suburb under ethnographic study believe that litter is a significant problem in their community. Despite rarely seeing anyone actually litter, they develop folk theories that blame this problem on black, poor renters moving into the suburb. This article documents the structural features that sustain litter accumulation across different spaces. It then examines how longtime residents interpret these patterns, use their own behavior toward litter (picking it up) to claim a moral status for themselves as community insiders while constructing those they perceive as outsiders as disreputable litterers. The author considers the relationship between physical, social disorder as they construe it, the consequences of this process for theories of ecological contamination, the reinforcement of racial, class distinctions.

title: Social behavior in public space: An analysis of behavioral adaptations to CCTV
authors: Mazerolle, Lorraine, Hurley, David, Chamlin, Mitchell
keywords: CCTV; social behavior; hotspots; deterrence;312\_BW\_観察SSO;Security Journal
abstract: This paper explores how people behave when CCTV cameras operate in public space. We examine how behavioral patterns change over time,, assess the short-term influence of CCTV on behavior in public space. Using videotape footage of four CCTV sites, we document pro-social, anti-social, traffic, guardianship behaviors over a four-month study period. Our study of CCTV in Cincinnati found that surveillance cameras create somewhat of an initial deterrent effect in the month, perhaps two months, following implementation. We conclude that erecting signs to notify people about the cameras could possibly increase the level of deterrence of CCTV. Signs about CCTV cameras in operation would also address some of the fairness issues raised by civil libertarians. We also suggest that shifting CCTV cameras around on a frequent basis could solve two dilemmas: first, it would increase the number of hotspots under surveillance,, hence remove some of the inequities observed in CCTV deployment; second, short, periodic, as opposed to permanent, deployment of CCTV cameras would capitalize upon some of the initial deterrent effects of the cameras that are observed in our data.

title: Disorder in the eye of the beholder: Black, White residents’ perceptions of disorder on high‐crime street segments
authors: Hinkle, Joshua C, White, Clair, Weisburd, David, Kuen, Kiseong
keywords: broken windows; disorder; perceptions; race; street segments;312\_BW\_観察SSO
abstract: AbstractResearch SummaryAlthough broken windows theory has had strong influence on policy, practice in policing, there are still many questions, debates about the nature of disorder itself and, particularly, how people perceive, define it. The current study aims to examine whether Black, White residents living on the same street segments in Baltimore City, Maryland perceive similar levels of social, physical disorder. We find strong, significant differences between Black, White residents after controlling for key sociodemographic variables, street‐level covariates.Policy ImplicationsOur findings suggest that police efforts to reduce disorder are less likely to be noticed by Black residents, that any benefits from targeting disorder may vary across places depending on the racial composition of streets. In this context, police must recognize racial differences in perceptions of disorder when developing disorder policing interventions.

title: Measuring disorder: Observer bias in systematic social observations at streets, neighborhoods
authors: Hoeben, E M, Steenbeek, W, Pauwels, L J R
abstract: Objectives The present study focuses on Systematic Social Observation (SSO) as a method to investigate physical, social disorder at different units of analysis. The study contributes to the aggregation bias debate, to the ‘social science of ecological assessment’ in two ways: first, by presenting a new model that directly controls for observer bias in ecological constructs, second, by attempting to identify systematic sources of bias in SSO that affect the valid, reliable measurement of physical, social disorder at both street segments, neighborhoods. Methods Data on physical disorder (e.g., litter, cigarette butts), social disorder (e.g., loitering adults) from 1422 street segments in 253 different neighborhoods in a conurbation of the greater The Hague area (the Netherlands) are analyzed using cross-classified multilevel models. Results Neighborhood differences in disorder are overestimated when scholars fail to recognize the cross-classified data structure of an SSO study that is due to allocation of street segments to observers, neighborhoods. Not correcting for observer bias, observational conditions underestimates the disorder–crime association at street segment/grid cell level, but overestimates this association at the neighborhood level. Conclusion Findings indicate that SSO can be used for measuring disorder at both street segment level, neighborhood level. Future studies should pay attention to observer bias prior to their data collection by selecting a minimum number of observers, offering extensive training,, collecting information on the urban background of the observers.

title: The social ecology of public space: Active streets, violent crime in urban neighborhoods: The social ecology of public space
authors: Browning, Christopher R, Jackson, Aubrey L
abstract: Drawing on one element of Jacobs' (1961) discussion of the social control benefits of ``eyes on the street,'' this paper explores the link between the prevalence of active streets, violence in urban neighborhoods. Three distinct data sources from the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods are merged to explore the functional form, potential contingency of the active streets-violence relationship: (1) video data capturing the presence of people on neighborhood streets; (2) longitudinal data on adolescents (ages 11 to 16), their self-reports of witnessing severe violence;, (3) community survey data on neighborhood social organizational characteristics. Results from multilevel models indicate that the proportion of neighborhood streets with adults present exhibits a nonlinear association with exposure to severe violence. At low prevalence, the increasing prevalence of active streets is positively associated with violence exposure. Beyond a threshold, however, increases in the prevalence of active streets serves to reduce the likelihood of violence exposure. The analyses offer no evidence that the curvilinear association between active streets, violence varies by levels of collective efficacy,, only limited evidence that it varies by anonymity. Analyses of data on homicide, violent victimization corroborate these findings.

title: Avoidance responses to alternative alcohol warning labels$^1$
authors: MacKinnon, David P, Nemeroff, Carol, Nohre, Liva
abstract: A preference‐based measure of responses to warning labels was used to study alternative alcohol warning labels that differed in: (a) length, (b) presence of qualifier words, (c) alternative content,, (d) specific beverage. The specific risks mentioned were more important than the overall label length, qualifier words reduced avoidance responses, various alternative warnings elicited more avoidance responses than the existing alcohol warning label,, more avoidance responses were made to labels on a whiskey bottle than on a beer bottle. Warnings with the words “poison,”“cancer,” or “health problems” were the most powerful. The results for college students in Study 1 were replicated in a high‐school sample in Study 2.

title: The impact of communications on the self-regulation of health beliefs, decisions,, behavior
authors: Leventhal, H, Safer, M A, Panagis, D M
abstract: The models used in the study of communication, health behavior have changed from those describing how to impose health actions on relatively passive respondents to models describing how respondents regulate their own health practices. We have traced the change from the fear-drive model, which described how fear induced change, to the parallel response model, which described how subjects processed information, generated coping responses to solve the problem posed by both the objective health threat, by their subjective fear. The data supporting this change showed that increasing fear led to more favorable attitudes but that fear alone was insufficient to create action: Specific action instructions had to be added to both high, low fear, both combinations produced the same level of health action. Neither the data nor the parallel model specified what subjects learned about the threat that made exposure to a high or low fear message necessary for behavior change. The parallel response model has been elaborated into a more complete systems model, new studies show how health threats are represented. They have found attributes such as IDENTITY (label, symptoms), CAUSES, TIME LINES or duration,, CONSEQUENCES, that set goals, criteria to generate, evaluate problem solving (coping) behavior.
