keywords: Intimate partner violence; threat assessment; risk tools; test scoring; Risk Factors; Test Scores; Risk Assessment;320\_ST実証研究;Police Practice, Research
abstract: Threat assessment services help police by identifying risk, recommending ways to mitigate risk for cases perceived to have a high potential for intimate partner violence (IPV). However, research has yet to show that cases referred for threat assessment score higher on IPV risk tools than routine policing samples, which would show whether referrals are appropriate. Furthermore, it is unknown whether these tools can be scored reliably from documents gathered by threat assessors without contacting perpetrators or victims. We scored the Spousal Assault Risk Assessment Guide (SARA), its revision (SARA-V3), Brief Spousal Assault Risk Evaluation Form (B-SAFER),, Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment (ODARA) from threat assessment files of 238 men referred for IPV offenses. Cases scored higher than previously reported routine policing samples. Inter-rater reliability coefficients for total scores, most subscales were ≥.70. Findings support appropriateness of referrals, capacity to reliably score IPV risk tools. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)

title: A brief actuarial assessment for the prediction of wife assault recidivism: the Ontario domestic assault risk assessment
authors: Hilton, N Zoe, Harris, Grant T, Rice, Marnie E, Lang, Carol, Cormier, Catherine A, Lines, Kathryn J
keywords: wife assault recidivism; prediction; actuarial assessment; Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment; marital violence; Actuarial Analysis; Adult; Crime; Female; Humans; Logistic Models; Male; Middle Aged; Personality Assessment; Psychometrics; Reproducibility of Results; Risk Assessment; Secondary Prevention; Social Support; Spouse Abuse; Statistics as Topic; Substance-Related Disorders; Violence; Domestic Violence; Intimate Partner Violence; Rating Scales; Recidivism; Wives;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: An actuarial assessment to predict male-to-female marital violence was constructed from a pool of potential predictors in a sample of 589 offenders identified in police records, followed up for an average of almost 5 years. Archival information in several domains (offender characteristics, domestic violence history, nondomestic criminal history, relationship characteristics, victim characteristics, index offense), recidivism were subjected to setwise, stepwise logistic regression. The resulting 13-item scale, the Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment (ODARA), showed a large effect size in predicting new assaults against legal or common-law wives or ex-wives (Cohen's d = 1.1, relative operating characteristic area =.77), was associated with number, severity of new assaults, time until recidivism. Cross-validation, comparisons with other instruments are also reported.

title: An indepth actuarial assessment for wife assault recidivism: the Domestic Violence Risk Appraisal Guide
authors: Hilton, N Zoe, Harris, Grant T, Rice, Marnie E, Houghton, Ruth E, Eke, Angela W
keywords: actuarial assessment; wife assault recidivism; domestic violence risk appraisal guide; Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment; Adult; Female; Health Planning Guidelines; Humans; Male; Risk Assessment; Risk Factors; Spouse Abuse; Surveys, Questionnaires; United States; Correctional Institutions; Domestic Violence; Recidivism;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: An actuarial tool, the Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment (ODARA), predicts recidivism using only variables readily obtained by frontline police officers. Correctional settings permit more comprehensive assessments. In a subset of ODARA construction, cross-validation cases, 303 men with a police record for wife assault, a correctional system file, the VRAG, SARA, Danger Assessment,, DVSI also predicted recidivism, but the Hare Psychopathy Checklist (PCL-R) best improved prediction of recidivism, occurrence, frequency, severity, injury,, charges. In 346 new cases, ODARA, PCL-R independently predicted recidivism. An algorithm was derived for a combined instrument, the Domestic Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (DVRAG),, an experience table is presented (N=649). Results indicated the importance of antisociality in wife assault.

title: The effect of arrest on wife assault recidivism: Controlling for pre-arrest risk
authors: Zoe Hilton, N, Harris, Grant T, Rice, Marnie E
keywords: domestic violence; wife assault; recidivism; arrest; risk assessment; Legal Arrest; Wives; Battered Females;320\_ST実証研究;Criminal Justice, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: Prior research on the effect of arrest on wife assault recidivism had equivocal results, mixed reception. Arrest is not always used in wife assault cases,, several studies suggest that arrest is influenced by incident severity rather than risk of recidivism. The present study examined the effect of arrest controlling for pre-arrest actuarial risk of recidivism, which was measured retrospectively, independently of arrest decision using the Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment. In an archival study of 522 wife assault incidents with police attending, arrest was associated with pre-arrest risk for recidivism, with victim injury, incident severity,, other sample characteristics. In multivariate regression, survival analyses, arrest had no overall effect on recidivism but a small beneficial effect in lower risk cases, mostly in terms of a delayed time until recidivism. Arrest of higher risk cases could be increased by police use of a validated tool for risk assessment.

title: The step-father effect in child abuse: Comparing discriminative parental solicitude, antisociality
authors: Hilton, N Zoe, Harris, Grant T, Rice, Marnie E
keywords: antisociality; step-father; child abuse; domestic violence; intimate partner violence; Fathers; Stepchildren; Stepparents; Antisocial Behavior; Biological Family;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Objective: The greater risk of abusing a step-child than a genetically related child has been attributed to discriminative parental solicitude. We tested whether it is better explained by antisociality, whereby more antisocial fathers are more likely both to have step-children, to be generally more violent. Method: We studied police reports of assaults on children by 387 domestically violent men who had a minor child,, their bivariate association with genetic relatedness, offender antisociality,, opportunity to assault step-children. In the subsample of 118 men with the opportunity to assault both step, genetically related children, we tested whether fathers were more likely to assault step-children, overall, among more antisocial men. Results: Number of step-children was associated with both child abuse, 2 of 3 measures of antisociality. When opportunity was controlled, fathers showed evidence of discriminative parental solicitude, being twice as likely to assault step-children as genetically related children. This step-father effect was observed at all levels of antisociality. Conclusion: Antisociality alone cannot explain the step-father effect. Discriminative parental solicitude remains a viable explanation for the step-father effect observed in this study. Research is needed to explore more proximal causes of the step-father effect. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Non-specialization of criminal careers among intimate partner violence offenders
authors: Hilton, N Zoe, Eke, Angela Wyatt
keywords: intimate partner violence (IPV); domestic violence; criminal careers; specialization; prediction; Intimate Partner Violence; Recidivism; Criminal Offenders;320\_ST実証研究;Criminal Justice, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: Many men arrested for intimate partner violence (IPV) commit other types of criminal offenses as well. We examined 93 IPV offenders’ general offending, tested the ability of criminal career trajectory, an IPV-specific risk assessment (Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment [ODARA]) to predict post-index recidivism 7.5 years later. Most (71\%) had pre-index criminal charges,, most (62\%) had post-index criminal recidivism, although fewer (24\%) committed post-index IPV. Pre-index criminal career (defined as none, non-violent, violent, IPV) did not predict post-index IPV, whereas the ODARA predicted post-index IPV, area under the curve (AUC = .67), as well as other offenses with a moderate or large effect size, including stalking (AUC = .78), sexual assault (AUC = .67),, non-violent offenses (AUC = .74). In line with prior research findings, we conclude that many men arrested for IPV do not specialize in their criminal careers, that risk assessment in these cases could include risk of both IPV, other offenses. Furthermore, the ODARA holds promise for assessing general risk of recidivism among IPV offenders.

title: Prioritizing police investigations of intimate partner violence using actuarial risk assessment
authors: Henning, Kris, Campbell, Christopher M, Stewart, Gregory, Johnson, Jennifer
keywords: Risk assessment; Intimate partner violence; Domestic violence; Policing; Law Enforcement; Police Personnel; Data Collection; Predictive Validity; Recidivism;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) accounts for a large proportion of police calls for service, criminal offenses in most jurisdictions, families often experience significant harm from these incidents. In an effort to rationally allocate investigative resources, police departments are turning to risk assessment scales to identify suspects, victims at greatest risk for further incidents. The existing measures suffer from a number of issues including limited predictive validity, lengthy scoring procedures,, the requirement of supplemental data collection. The current study uses a sample of IPV cases from a large US city to assess whether recidivism can be predicted using factors that are already available in most law enforcement records management systems (RMS). A series of multivariate regression analyses demonstrate that domestic recidivism was predicted (AUC = .72) using a combination of suspect, victim,, index offense characteristics obtained from the local RMS. Additional analyses found that victim-reported risk factors obtained via supplemental interviews did not further benefit predictive validity. The findings suggest that additional data collection for the purpose of IPV risk assessment may be unnecessary for most law enforcement agencies. Moreover, the use of currently available records supports the automation of risk triage tools, which could yield further improvements in predictive accuracy, decision-making efficiency. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Children living with domestic violence: A differential response through multi-agency collaboration
authors: Humphreys, Cathy, Healey, Lucy, Kirkwood, Debbie, Nicholson, Deb
keywords: Child Abuse; Child Protection; Domestic Violence; Practice Research; Risk Assessment; Violence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Developing appropriate pathways to assist children living with domestic, family violence (DFV) is challenging, particularly given the rise in police notifications to Child Protection (CP) relating to exposure to domestic violence. In this article, the argument is put that strong collaboration between organisations can provide a differential response in which only those children requiring an investigation are referred into CP, while all other children, their families are diverted to community-based organisations. This is foundational for the development of a more ethical, supportive response to children, their families living with DFV. The article draws on findings from a case study of the Multi-Agency Triage project in Melbourne, which developed through a collaborative risk assessment process a differential response to manage referrals of children living with DFV. The case study drew from observations of the triage, nine interviews,, analysis of administrative data.IMPLICATIONSStrong collaborations between organisations need to provide the foundation for differentiated referral pathways for children living with DFV based on informed risk assessment.Through multi-agency risk assessment, children, their families who do not meet the threshold for a child protection investigation can be diverted early into a community sector organisation for attention.

title: Responding to domestic violence: A comparison of social workers', police officers' interventions
authors: Home, Alice
keywords: contextual variables; intervention decisions for domestic violence; social workers vs police officers; Canada; Decision Making; Domestic Violence; Police Personnel; Social Workers; Treatment;320\_ST実証研究;99\_文献なし
abstract: Compared intervention decisions of 188 social workers, 235 police officers in response to a domestic violence incident. The differential impact of 8 contextual variables was also studied. Social workers referred women more often than did police to shelters, social services,, legal aid as well as taking more action to ensure their safety. Presence of physical violence, child abuse led to their making more referrals to family counseling as did absence of alcohol. Police took more decisive action when physical violence was part of the scenario than when it was absent. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Comparison of six models for violent romantic relationships in college men, women
authors: Hendy, Helen M, Weiner, Kristen, Bakerofskie, John, Eggen, Doreen, Gustitus, Cheryl, McLeod, Kelli C
abstract: Six types of parent, partner violence were compared as possible models for violence in the romantic relationships of 608 college students (164 men, 444 women). Participants used the Conflict Tactics Scale to report violence to, from the present partner, as well as violence from mother to father, father to mother, mother to participant, father to participant,, past partners to participant. Stepwise multiple regression revealed that violence to the present partner was explained by both partner, parent models of violence for men (R2 = .39), women (R2 = .51), with violence from the present partner found to be the most powerful model. Violence received from the mother was the most powerful parental model for violence in the present romantic relationship, but for women it was associated with receiving violence, whereas for men it was associated with both receiving, inflicting violence.

title: An inside view of police officers’ experience with domestic violence
authors: Horwitz, Susan H, Mitchell, Despina, LaRussa-Trott, Michelle, Santiago, Lizette, Pearson, Joan, Skiff, David M, Cerulli, Catherine
keywords: police officers; domestic violence; health issue; emotional reactions; Emotions; Health Complaints; Police Personnel;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Since the recognition of domestic violence (DV) in the late 1970s, police officers have been frontline providers. Despite their changing role as a result of the criminalization of DV, little is known about their experiences, responses to this public health issue from their unique perspective. Via focus groups, 22 police officers discussed their scope of practice, emotional reactions to DV calls. Participants reported frustration with the recurring nature of DV, with the larger systems’ lack of accountability (e.g., courts, prosecution, community) that follow their initial interventions. Participants discussed the limitations of their role as protectors of public safety, attitudes that evolve over time, their beliefs as to contributing factors that perpetuate DV. Additionally, the officers recommend: more professional training, counseling, incident debriefing for officers including feedback on case disposition, better collaboration across professional groups,, evidence-based prosecution. Harsher penalties were also recommended. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Professional help-seeking for adolescent dating violence in the rural south: The role of social support, informal help-seeking
authors: Hedge, Jasmine M, Sianko, Natallia, McDonell, James R
keywords: adolescent dating violence; help-seeking; mediation; social support; structural equation modeling;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Structural equation modeling with three waves of data was used to assess a mediation model investigating the relationship between perceived social support, informal help-seeking intentions,, professional help-seeking intentions in the context of adolescent dating violence. The sample included 589 adolescents from a rural, southern county who participated in a longitudinal study of teen dating violence victimization, perpetration. Results suggest that informal help-seeking intentions are an important link between perceived social support, professional help-seeking intentions. Findings highlight the importance of informal help-seeking, informal help-giving in fostering professional help-seeking for adolescent victims, perpetrators of dating violence.

title: Experiences with intimate partner violence among Latina women
authors: Hazen, Andrea L, Soriano, Fernando I
abstract: This study examined experiences with intimate partner violence in 292 Latina women classified as U.S. born, immigrant, or migrant-seasonal workers. High lifetime rates of violence were found, with 33.9\% reporting physical violence, 20.9\% reporting sexual coercion,, 82.5\% reporting psychological aggression. Rates of violence in the preceding year were also high, with 18.5\% experiencing physical violence, 14.4\% experiencing sexual coercion,, 72.6\% experiencing psychological aggression. Participants' marital status, partners' substance use were associated with victimization. The present findings suggest the need for screening for intimate partner violence, associated risk factors in settings that serve Latina women.

title: Perceived risk for future intimate partner violence among women in a domestic violence shelter
authors: Harding, Hilary G, Helweg-Larsen, Marie
keywords: Sociology; Women; Perceptions; Risk assessment; Domestic violence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Research investigating women's risk assessments for intimate partner violence (IPV) shows that women can predict future violence with relative accuracy. Limited research has investigated factors that are associated with perceived risk, the potential behavioral consequences of victim risk perception. Results from a survey of women in a domestic violence shelter (N=56) indicated that women perceive lower risk of future violence if the abusive relationship were to end, higher risk of violence if it were to continue. Certain abuse experiences were related to elevated perceptions of personal risk for future violence. Further, perceived personal risk predicted the women's intention to terminate their relationship upon leaving shelter. Results are discussed as they may inform interventions preventing IPV. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: Violent stalkers. Detecting risk factors by the police
authors: Groenen, Anne, Vervaeke, Geert
journal: European journal on criminal policy, research
abstract: In the experience of stalking victims a common element is the fear of physical violence. Until now risk factors that predict physical violence within stalking contexts have been carried out in relatively small, clinical-forensic samples. Consequently, the validity, practical utility of these risk factors in the law enforcement context remains unknown. Furthermore some risk factors have been identified in this research on the basis of information that is not available for or difficult to detect by the police in an early stage of the law enforcement process. The identification of risk factors of physical violence in stalking incidents in an early stage by the police was the subject of the presented study. Risk factors are identified based on literature, content analysis of police records, by testing interaction terms. Therefore 204 judicial files were analyzed, resulting in a five factor model predicting physical violence. Theoretical, practical implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Factors associated with stalking duration among a nationally representative sample: Results from the 2010 National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey
authors: Hayes, Brittany E, Kopp, Phillip M
keywords: National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey; intimate partner violence; stalking duration; stalking victimization;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: The current study examined the duration of stalking episodes among a nationally representative sample. Analyses of the National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey estimated if the victim-perpetrator relationship, other types of victimization experienced were associated with (a) if the stalking episode lasted over a year (N = 1,509), (b) the length of stalking episodes, in days, for episodes <1 year (N = 506). Findings indicate coercive control was associated with higher odds the stalking episode lasted over a year, increased the length of episodes lasting <1 year. The intersection of stalking, coercive control is discussed.

title: Impact of victim, offender,, relationship characteristics on frequency, timing of intimate partner violence using life history calendar data
authors: Hayes, Brittany E
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 320\_ST実証研究;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Objectives:To examine whether victim, offender,, relationship characteristics increase the risk, frequency of intimate partner violence (IPV). The effect of separation length on the risk of IPV is also evaluated.Methods:Using abuse incident data ( N = 4,960) from IPV victims ( n = 497), who accessed a health-care facility over a one-year period, between-individual differences in the frequency, timing of abuse were assessed. Dependence of event times within respondents was accounted for with conditional risk set “gap time” models, which stratified participants across event number, failure order.Results:Employment of both partners, only the victim decreased the risk, frequency. Employment of only the abuser, length of separation decreased frequency but was not significantly associated with timing of abuse. Separated, non-separated respondents were not significantly different in frequency (incident risk ratio = 1.06, p > .05), timing of abuse, (exp ( b) = 0.95, p > .05).Conclusions:By capturing the timing between abuse incidents, insight into the long-term risk of abuse is provided, accounts for selection effects. Findings call for an improvement in measuring relationship status indicators, including relationship length, time since separation. Future research should examine within-individual changes in separation, IPV risk.

title: Relations among intimate partner violence, maternal depressive symptoms,, maternal parenting behaviors
authors: Gustafsson, Hanna C, Cox, Martha J, the Family Life Project Key Investigators
keywords: depression; intimate partner violence; parenting;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: The authors examined the relations among intimate partner violence (IPV), maternal depressive symptoms,, maternal harsh intrusive parenting. Using a cross-lagged, autoregressive path model, they sought to clarify the directionality of the relations among these 3 variables over the first 2 years of the child's life. The results indicated that, in this diverse sample of families living in predominantly low-income rural communities (N = 705), higher levels of early IPV were associated with increases in maternal depressive symptoms, which in turn were associated with increases in maternal harsh intrusive parenting behaviors. These findings suggest that interventions aimed at improving the parenting of women exposed to domestic violence may want to simultaneously target IPV, depressive symptomatology.

title: Men's, women's use of intimate partner violence in clinical samples
authors: Hamberger, L Kevin, Guse, Clare E
keywords: intimate partner violence; relationship violence; court-ordered abuse abatement counseling; gender comparison; shelters; Human Sex Differences; Violence; Adjudication; Counseling;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Experiences, impact of intimate partner violence on men, women court ordered to attend abuse abatement counseling, women in a shelter were examined. Whereas court-ordered men, women appeared similar in expressed violent acts, violence frequency,, injurious outcome, court-ordered women initiated significantly fewer violent episodes than did men, were less likely to start the overall pattern of relationship violence. Court-ordered women were less likely than were shelter women to call police, try to escape, or acquiesce to their partners' violence. The two groups of women reported more fear, anger,, insult, less amusement when their partners were violent than did men. Court-ordered men were significantly more likely than were women to laugh at partner-initiated violence, exhibit dominating, controlling behaviors.

title: Beyond deficits: intimate partner violence, maternal parenting,, child behavior over time
authors: Greeson, Megan R, Kennedy, Angie C, Bybee, Deborah I, Beeble, Marisa, Adams, Adrienne E, Sullivan, Cris
keywords: 320\_ST実証研究;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: Exposure to intimate partner violence (IPV) has negative consequences for children's well-being, behavior. Much of the research on parenting in the context of IPV has focused on whether, how IPV victimization may negatively shape maternal parenting,, how parenting may in turn negatively influence child behavior, resulting in a deficit model of mothering in the context of IPV. However, extant research has yet to untangle the interrelationships among the constructs, test whether the negative effects of IPV on child behavior are indeed attributable to IPV affecting mothers' parenting. The current study employed path analysis to examine the relationships among IPV, mothers' parenting practices,, their children's externalizing behaviors over three waves of data collection among a sample of 160 women with physically abusive partners. Findings indicate that women who reported higher levels of IPV also reported higher levels of behavior problems in their children at the next time point. When parenting practices were examined individually as mediators of the relationship between IPV, child behavior over time, one type of parenting was significant, such that higher IPV led to higher authoritative parenting, lower child behavior problems [corrected]. On the other hand, there was no evidence that higher levels of IPV contributed to more child behavior problems due to maternal parenting. Instead, IPV had a significant cumulative indirect effect on child behavior via the stability of both IPV, behavior over time. Implications for promoting women's, children's well-being in the context of IPV are discussed.

title: Sex disparities in arrest outcomes for domestic violence
authors: Hamilton, Melissa, Worthen, Meredith G F
keywords: sex disparities; arrest outcomes; domestic violence; gender differences; police officers; Alcohol Drinking; Databases, Factual; Female; Humans; Law Enforcement; Logistic Models; Male; Rhode Island; Sex Factors; Street Drugs; Human Sex Differences; Legal Arrest; Police Personnel;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Domestic violence arrests have been historically focused on protecting women, children from abusive men. Arrest patterns continue to reflect this bias with more men arrested for domestic violence compared to women. Such potential gender variations in arrest patterns pave the way to the investigation of disparities by sex of the offender in domestic violence arrests. This study utilizes data from a quantitative dataset that includes responses by police officers who completed a specially mandated checklist after responding to a domestic dispute. The results showed that while females are arrested quite often in domestic disputes, there remains a significant difference in the arrest outcome whereby male suspects were more likely to be arrested than female suspects. Regression models further indicated differences based on sex, certain predictors of arrest, which supported sex-based rationales in arrests for domestic violence.

title: In dubious battle: The politics of mandatory arrest, dominant aggressor laws
authors: Hamel,, John
keywords: domestic violence; criminal justice; primary aggressor laws; dominant aggressor laws; gender bias; intimate partner violence; law enforcement; Laws; Sex Role Attitudes; Perpetrators;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: A major component of in the effort to reduce domestic violence in our communities has been a vigorous criminal justice response, one that holds perpetrators accountable for their actions, helps victims feel safe. In light of research finding higher rates of arrest per calls made to police, a corresponding decline in domestic violence crimes, mandatory arrest, pro-arrest laws were initially welcomed by advocates. When, however, it was apparent that these same laws led to a large number of dual arrests,, a proportionately greater increase in arrests of women compared to men, advocates started calling for primary aggressor or dominant aggressor laws. These laws, adopted in several states, including California, direct police officers to consider context, abuse history so that victims are not wrongfully arrested. A review of the relevant literature is conducted, as well as an examination of two law enforcement training programs, suggesting that primary aggressor, dominant aggressor laws, although written in gender-neutral language, are gender biased (mostly against men), are difficult to properly implement,, may, at times, be counterproductive in reducing domestic violence. Alternatives are then presented for consideration.

title: Predictors of treatment dropout from a spouse abuse abatement program
authors: Hamberger, L K, Lohr, J M, Gottlieb, M
keywords: predictors of dropout from cognitive-behavioral spouse abuse abatement counseling program; male batterers; Adult; Counseling; Follow-Up Studies; Humans; Male; Mental Disorders; Patient Dropouts; Spouse Abuse; Cognitive Therapy; Intimate Partner Violence; Perpetrators; Prediction; Treatment Dropouts; Spouses;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: This study evaluated predictors of dropout among men who began, attended at least 1 session of a cognitive-behavioral, skills training oriented spouse abuse abatement counseling program. Based on prior research, a number of demographic, criminal justice, partner violence pattern,, personality characteristics were studied. Dropout prediction was assessed at 2 phases of program participation, during assessment (early drop), during intervention (late drop). Overall, few of the variables studied predicted dropout. Early dropout was predicted by high rates of police contact for violent crimes, failure to self-report an alcohol problem,, paranoid personality characteristics. Late dropout was predicted by both high, moderate levels of police contact for violent crimes,, borderline personality characteristics. An Age x Violent Crime interaction suggested that young violent offenders are more likely to complete treatment. The overall model accounted for only 7.15\% of the variance. Clinical, research implications are discussed.

title: A large sample empirical typology of male spouse abusers, its relationship to dimensions of abuse
authors: Hamberger, L K, Lohr, J M, Bonge, D, Tolin, D F
keywords: A. Holtzworth-Munroe \& G. L. Stuart model; nonpathological vs antisocial vs passive aggressive-dependent personality subtypes as predictor of violence; adult male batterers; Adult; Antisocial Personality Disorder; Cluster Analysis; Counseling; Humans; Male; Passive-Aggressive Personality Disorder; Personality Disorders; Personality Inventory; Psychometrics; Spouse Abuse; Violence; Intimate Partner Violence; Models; Perpetrators; Psychodiagnostic Typologies; Human Males; Passive Aggressive Personality Disorder; Psychopathology;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: A number of studies have described typologies of domestically violent men. Holtzworth-Munroe, Stuart (1994) recently proposed a theoretical model for predicting violence severity, generality from personality ``type.'' The present study, using data from 833 identified abusive men, tested the model. Personality types were determined from cluster analysis of data from the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory,, resulted in a three-cluster solution consistent with the Holtzworth-Munroe, Stuart model. The three main clusters included nonpathological, antisocial,, passive aggressive-dependent groups. Three other, smaller types were also identified. Multivariate, chi-square analyses comparing the main clusters on other variables generally supported the Holtzworth-Munroe, Stuart model. Nonpathological men had the lowest maximum violence, frequency. They restricted their violence primarily to intimate relationships, had the fewest police contacts. Antisocial, passive aggressive-dependent men did not differ in maximum violence, but antisocial men were the most generally violent, had the most police contacts. Passive aggressive-dependent men had the highest frequency of violence. Clinical, theoretical, methodological implications are discussed.

title: Running the risk: police officer discretion, family violence in New Zealand
authors: Grant, Stephanie, Rowe, Michael
keywords: domestic violence; policy; risk assessment techniques; family violence; violence escalation; police officer attitudes; marginalization of bureaucratic procedures; barriers; Attitudes; Government Policy Making; Law Enforcement; Police Personnel; Risk Assessment;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: As in other jurisdictions, the police in New Zealand have a poor record of responding to domestic violence, a category of crime widely perceived within New Zealand to be a particularly extensive problem relative to other societies. Against that background policy developments have focused on developing risk assessment techniques as a basis for identifying cases of family, domestic violence that are likely to escalate. Using interviews with frontline police officers, this article explores police officers' attitudes towards these investigating methods, their experiences of interviewing victims of family violence in order to gain information about risk. It is argued that while officer attitudes towards risk assessment in general terms might vary, in practice the majority of officers do not complete risk assessment processes in accordance with police policy, even if they support the practice in principle. The reasons for this, it is argued, have more to do with officer negotiation of the demands of routine patrol work, time-management processes that contribute to the marginalisation of bureaucratic procedures. Supervisors, managers compound the perception that these tasks are of second-order importance. In these ways there are cultural, managerial barriers to the more effective policing of family violence; however, the reduction of officer discretion through policy, procedure seems unlikely to provide a viable solution. A professional practice model might be more effective if officers can be trained, educated about the role of risk assessment in this context, the importance of their role as data collectors; although this does not fit easily with traditional concepts of ‘real policework’.

title: Police involvement in cases of intimate partner violence against women: the influence of perceived severity, personal responsibility: The influence of perceived severity, personal responsibility
authors: Gracia, Enrique, García, Fernando, Lila, Marisol
abstract: The influence of perceived severity, sense of personal responsibility of police officers on their level of involvement in cases of intimate partner violence against women is analyzed. Three levels of police involvement are considered: low, medium,, high. The sample consists of 143 Spanish police officers. A 2 x 2 x 3 factorial design is conducted to test hypotheses. Effects of perceived severity, personal responsibility are found only at the highest level of police involvement. For low, medium levels of involvement, no differences in perceived severity, personal responsibility of police officers are found.

title: Women's opinions about domestic violence screening, mandatory reporting
authors: Gielen, A C, O'Campo, P J, Campbell, J C, Schollenberger, J, Woods, A B, Jones, A S, Dienemann, J A, Kub, J, Wynne, E C
keywords: Empirical Approach; Health Care, Public Health;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: BACKGROUND: The purpose of this paper is to describe women's opinions, policy preferences concerning domestic violence screening, mandatory reporting. METHODS: This case-control study included 202 abused women, 240 randomly selected non-abused women recruited from a large metropolitan health maintenance organization who were interviewed by telephone. Of these women, 46.6\% had a college degree, 53.4\% were white,, 60\% had a household income of \$50,000 or more. RESULTS: Forty-eight percent of the sample agreed that health care providers should routinely screen all women, with abused women 1.5 times more likely than non-abused women to support this policy. For mandatory reporting, 48\% preferred that it be the woman's decision to report abuse to the police. Women thought it would be easier for abused women to get help with routine screening (86\%), mandatory reporting (73\%), although concerns were raised about increased risk of abuse with both screening (43\%), reporting (52\%) policies. Two thirds of the sample thought women would be less likely to tell their health care providers about abuse under a mandatory reporting policy. Interventions offered in managed care settings that would be well received, according to the women in this study, include counseling services, shelters,, confidential hotlines. CONCLUSIONS: Women expressed fears, concerns about negative consequences of routine screening and, even more so, for mandatory reporting. Domestic violence policies, protocols need to address the safety, autonomy,, confidentiality issues that concern women.

title: Predictors, outcomes of community agency use in abused mothers
authors: Gilroy, Heidi, Maddoux, John, Symes, Lene, Fredland, Nina, McFarlane, Judith
keywords: intimate partner violence; mental health; vulnerable populations; women's health;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To identify characteristics of abused mothers that predict use, difficulty of use of community agencies for intimate partner violence (IPV), to describe the outcomes of community agency use. DESIGN AND SAMPLE: A prospective study design was used. Three hundred mothers who had experienced physical or sexual IPV, were seeking services for the first time at either a safe shelter for abused women or applying for a protection order. MEASURES: Data were collected, analyzed by the research team. Predictors were tested using binary logistic regression, outcomes were tested using a series of Mann-Whitney U nonparametric test of difference on change scores between baseline, 24-month scores. RESULTS: No individual predictors were statistically significant and/or meaningful for use or difficulty using community agencies. There were significant differences in change scores for severity of violence after women used counseling, the police, or legal services. There were also significant change scores for anxiety after women used legal services, social services. CONCLUSIONS: Abused women need individualized attention to assure that they can access the services they need to recover from IPV. Evidence-based practice is needed for community agencies to treat abused women to facilitate safety, health.

title: Providing support to victims: Police officers’ service referral provision, advocate involvement in domestic violence incidents
authors: Goodson, Amanda, Garza, Alondra D, Franklin, Cortney A
abstract: Limited research has investigated police service provision, advocate involvement in domestic violence (DV) incidents. This study used a stratified random sample of 368 cases from an urban police department to assess police officers’ decisions to provide service provision, to involve an advocate in formally-reported DV incidents. Multivariate binary logistic regression models revealed decreased suspect age, presence of physical abuse significantly increased service referral. Advocate involvement significantly decreased when the victim, suspect were married, when the suspect used alcohol and/or drugs,, when there was physical evidence present in the case. Alternatively, suspect weapon use, victim injury,, service referral by police increased later advocate involvement. Implications, future research directions are discussed.

title: Police responses to intimate partner sexual violence in south Asian communities
authors: Gill, Aisha K, Harrison, Karen
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Recognition of sexual violence as a serious problem has been reflected in the wide range of initiatives that over the past 20 years in the UK have been designed to tackle this problem. Emphasis on prevention, protection,, redress has enabled criminal justice, other responses to become increasingly embedded. Nevertheless, a significant lacuna remains in terms of the contours, context,, consequences of intimate partner sexual violence in South Asian communities. Despite victim-survivors’ offering solid evidence of the prevalence of sexual violence in these communities, this kind of abuse is generally not reported to criminal justice agencies (Gilligan, P., Akhtar, S. (2006). ‘Cultural Barriers to the Disclosure of Child Sexual Abuse in Asian Communities: Listening to What Women Say.’ British Journal of Social Work 36(8): 1361–1377; Hohl, K., Stanko, E. (2015). ‘Complaints of Rape, the Criminal Justice System: Fresh Evidence on the Attrition Problem in England, Wales.’ European Journal of Criminology 12(3): 324–341). Anecdotally, however, this type of violence does appear to have been increasing over time. With that backdrop in mind, this article looks at how four police areas are currently responding to intimate partner sexual violence where the victim-survivor of it is from a South Asian community. In particular, the article evaluates police officers’ levels of understanding with regard to pertinent cultural values and, in turn, assesses the level of training given to help with this awareness,, the appropriateness of front-line police practice. Finally, consideration is also given to what needs to change in order to encourage more victim-survivors from South Asian communities to come forward.

title: Enhancing police responses to domestic violence incidents: Reports from client advocates in new South Wales: Reports from client advocates in new South Wales
authors: Goodman-Delahunty, Jane, Crehan, Anna Corbo
keywords: apprehended violence order; complaints; domestic violence; police practice; procedural justice;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: In an online survey about experiences with the police complaint system, 239 client advocates described a recent incident in which a client with grounds to lodge a complaint declined to do so. Almost one third of those incidents involved domestic violence. Thematic analysis of case descriptions revealed that many police did not take domestic violence reports seriously. A typology of problematic police conduct was developed. Many officers failed to observe current procedures, appeared to lack knowledge of relevant laws. Citizens feared retaliatory victimization by police and/or perceived that complaining was futile. Implications of these findings are reviewed in light of procedural justice theory.

title: The Intimate Partner Violence Strategies Index: Development, application
authors: Goodman, Lisa, Dutton, Mary Ann, Weinfurt, Kevin, Cook, Sarah
abstract: Although research has documented the myriad ways that victims of IPV struggle to keep themselves safe, little research has gone the next step to investigate patterns in women’s use of strategies, the factors that influence choice of strategies, or which strategies are most effective. One obstacle to conducting such research is the absence of an instrument to measure the nature, extent of battered women’s strategic responses to violence across specific domains of strategies. This article describes the development of such an instrument, the Intimate Partner Violence Strategies Index, in the context of a longitudinal study of battered women’s experience over time.

title: Women's resources, use of strategies as risk, protective factors for reabuse over time
authors: Goodman, Lisa, Dutton, Mary Ann, Vankos, Natalie, Weinfurt, Kevin
abstract: Using a longitudinal, ecological approach, we investigated the relationships between women's material, emotional resources, strategies, their ability to stay safe over time in a sample of 406 help-seeking African American women. The multivariate analysis demonstrated that social support served as a protective factor, resistance strategies as risk factors for reabuse during a 1-year period. It also showed an interaction between social support, history of violence such that for participants who had experienced the most severe violence, social support did not serve as a protective factor; however, for the other participants, those with the least amount of social support had a 65\% predicted probability of reabuse during the next year, compared to a 20\% predicted probability for women reporting the highest level of social support. Policy, programmatic implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Screening for risk factors associated with violence in pediatric patients presenting to a psychiatric emergency department
authors: Giggie, Marisa A, Olvera, Rene L, Joshi, Meghna N
keywords: screening; risk factors; violence; pediatric patients; psychiatric emergency department; treatment planning; risk assessments; psychiatry; Adolescent; Child; Documentation; Domestic Violence; Emergency Services, Psychiatric; Female; Firearms; Homicide; Humans; Internship, Residency; Juvenile Delinquency; Male; Mass Screening; Medical History Taking; Medical Records; Peer Group; Recurrence; Retrospective Studies; Suicide; Texas; Pediatrics; Risk Assessment; Emergency Services; History; Psychiatric Training;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This exploratory study was a chart review that examined whether risk factors for violence were adequately reported in 425 pediatric patients assessed by psychiatry residents in a psychiatric emergency room. RESULTS: Overall, psychiatric residents rarely documented asking about important risk factors such as gun access, gang affiliation, history of police contact,, domestic violence; however, high rates of positive endorsement were found when queries concerning risk factors were documented in the chart. Despite being the most common method of homicide/suicide in youth, gun access was assessed by residents in only 3\% of patients. Domestic violence was endorsed as positive 100\% of the time when it was documented. Pediatric patients presenting with violence were more likely to be screened for past violence than those with suicide, other complaints. Males were more likely to have a history of prior violence. CONCLUSIONS: Most psychiatric residents failed to document thorough risk assessments for violence in pediatric patients in an emergency setting. This has important medical-legal, treatment planning implications.

title: Obstacles to victims’ cooperation with the criminal prosecution of their abusers: The role of social support
authors: Goodman, Lisa, Bennett, Lauren, Dutton, Mary A
keywords: Adolescent; Adult; Conflicts; Cooperative Behavior; Criminal Law; District of Columbia; Domestic violence; Families \& family life; Female; Humans; Judges \& magistrates; Middle Aged; Personality Inventory; Police; Prospective Studies; Research \& development--R\&D; Sample size; Self esteem; Social Control, Formal; Social support; Sociology; Spouse Abuse -- legislation \& jurisprudence; Spouse Abuse -- psychology; Wounds \& Injuries -- psychology;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Over the last 20 years, diminishing tolerance for domestic violence has triggered significant criminal justice reforms designed to facilitate the prosecution of abusers. Prosecutors, for example, have adopted policies requiring that cases go forward even if the victim later has second thoughts. Although increasingly common, these “no drop” policies reflect a profound irony about domestic cases that is well known but little understood: the most formidable problem in prosecuting such cases is often the victim’s own unwillingness to bring the abuser to justice. This prospective study explored a range of factors potentially predictive of domestic violence victims’ cooperation with the prosecution of their abusers. Although the study focused on interpersonal, institutional social support, it also investigated the influence of violence severity, victim demographic factors,, victim mental health characteristics, including the presence of depressive symptoms, emotional dependence on the abuser,, substance abuse. Findings showed that tangible support, severity of violence in the relationship,, the presence of children in common with the abuser all significantly predicted victims’ cooperation with the prosecution of their abusers. Substance abuse significantly predicted victims’ noncooperation with prosecution. The research, policy implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Informal social control of intimate partner violence against women: Results from a concept mapping study of urban neighborhoods: Informal social control of intimate partner violence against women
authors: Frye, Victoria, Paul, Margaret M, Todd, Mary-Justine, Lewis, Veronica, Cupid, Jane Coleman, Malik, Salmon, Christina, O'Campo, Patricia
keywords: SOCIAL control; INTIMATE partner violence; WOMEN -- Crimes against; METROPOLITAN areas; PREVENTION; CONCEPT mapping; NEW York (N.Y.); NEW York (State); collective efficacy;320\_ST実証研究;J Community Psychol
abstract: How the neighborhood environment relates to intimate partner violence against women has been studied using theories applied originally to general violence. Extending social disorganization, collective efficacy theories, they apply a traditional measure informal social control that does not reflect behaviors specific to partner violence. We conducted a concept mapping study in two New York City neighborhoods, to understand what behaviors neighborhood residents might enact to prevent partner violence, how feasible, effective residents believed them to be. Results revealed a range of “preventive intervention behaviors.” Cluster analysis revealed that these behaviors grouped into four general areas, corresponding to the victim, perpetrator, community,, formal systems. Preventive intervention behaviors rated by participants as most feasible focused on the victim, whereas those rated most effective involved formal systems. Results have theoretical, practical implications for future research, programs to engage neighbors, neighborhoods in intimate partner violence prevention.

title: The victims of court-ordered batterers: Their victimization, helpseeking,, perceptions
authors: Gondolf, Edward W
keywords: helpseeking behavior; Human; Female; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Thirties (30-39 yrs); Empirical Study; Adult Attitudes; Help Seeking Behavior; Partner Abuse; Crime Victims; Court Referrals; Battered Females; Victimization; Domestic Violence; US; 3236:Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; 4270:Crime Prevention;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: There is relatively little research describing the victims of court-ordered batterers, compared to the extensive descriptions of the batterers themselves. The partners of men ordered to batterer programs in four cities were interviewed about their backgrounds, victimization, helpseeking,, perceptions of the batterers (N = 482). These battered women tend to be from lower economic status, educational levels. A substantial portion have also suffered severe assaults, injury. More than half of these women have previously contacted the criminal justice system in response to abuse, but only about a quarter have received any counseling for domestic violence,, less than 10\% have previously visited a battered women's shelter. The women's perceptions of their batterers are overly optimistic, despite the severe abuse, information from batterer programs. The victims of court-ordered batterers appear to be different at least in terms of their helpseeking than battered women in shelters, may therefore warrant special program, research attention.

title: The nexus between intimate partner violence, stalking: Examining the arrest decision
authors: Garza, Alondra D, Franklin, Cortney A, Goodson, Amanda
abstract: The present study used a stratified random sample of 332 case files from a sizable, urban police department located in one of the five largest, most diverse U.S. cities to examine the effect of previous stalking on arrest decisions among intimate partner violence (IPV) cases. Relevant extralegal, legal case factors were estimated in a multivariate binary logistic regression model to determine correlates of arrest. Findings revealed that previous stalking behavior was not related to arrest. Evidence, physical injury significantly increased the odds of arrest. Presence of witnesses, alcohol involvement,, history of IPV also significantly increased the odds of arrest. Future research, policy implications are discussed.

title: Using the stages of change model to counsel victims of intimate partner violence
authors: Frasier, P Y, Slatt, L, Kowlowitz, V, Glowa, P T
keywords: Abuse; Stages of change; Counseling; Domestic violence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Medical expenses from intimate partner violence (IPV) total between $3, $5 billion annually. Many abuse victims are exposed to serious injuries,, are likely to see their physicians more frequently than other patients. Practitioners must have a reliable, realistic approach to counseling patients who are victims of IPV. This paper presents the stages of change model as a practical guide for counseling victims. Through patients' responses to a series of questions, the practitioner can identify which of five stages of change (precontemplation, preparation, contemplation, action, maintenance) the patient is in. The practitioner can then employ stage-specific strategies for counseling the patient. Using this model shifts the definition of successful outcome from the traditional focus of trying to 'fix the problem' to a patient-centered focus, working with the patient to explore the most effective strategies given his/her stage of change.

title: Predicting case conviction, domestic violence recidivism: measuring the deterrent effects of conviction, protection order violations
authors: Frantzen, Durant, San Miguel, Claudia, Kwak, Dae-Hoon
keywords: Sociology; Domestic violence; Assaults; Sanctions; Violations; Jurisdiction; Arrests; Convictions; Plea bargaining; Domestic Violence -- statistics \& numerical data; Dangerous Behavior; United States; Humans; Risk Factors; Male; Socioeconomic Factors; Recurrence -- prevention \& control; Spouse Abuse -- legislation \& jurisprudence; Female; Law Enforcement; Criminals -- statistics \& numerical data; Interpersonal Relations; Crime Victims -- statistics \& numerical data; Crime Victims -- legislation \& jurisprudence; Criminals -- legislation \& jurisprudence; Domestic Violence -- legislation \& jurisprudence; Women's Health -- legislation \& jurisprudence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Previous research offered little guidance on sentencing outcomes for protection order (PO) violations in cases of domestic assault, whether PO violation charges affected offender recidivism rates. Using data from local court records, this study examined the effect of PO violation charges on the odds of case conviction relative to dismissal,, whether case conviction or a PO violation charge results in lower domestic violence rearrest rates compared to offenders not receiving these sanctions. The models indicate that PO violation charges has no significant effect on the odds of conviction or recidivism rates,, these trends were not significantly different for convicted versus dismissed offenders. Findings are discussed in relation to previous research with recommendations for future areas of study.

title: Symptoms, subjective quality of life in post-traumatic stress disorder: a longitudinal study
authors: Giacco, Domenico, Matanov, Aleksandra, Priebe, Stefan
abstract: BACKGROUND: Evidence suggests that post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is associated with substantially reduced subjective quality of life (SQOL). This study aimed to explore whether, how changes in the levels of PTSD symptom clusters of intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal are associated with changes in SQOL. METHODS: Two samples with PTSD following the war in former Yugoslavia were studied, i.e. a representative sample of 530 people in five Balkan countries, a non-representative sample of 215 refugees in three Western European countries. They were assessed on average eight years after the war, re-interviewed one year later. PTSD symptoms were assessed on the Impact of Event Scale - Revised, SQOL on the Manchester Short Assessment of Quality of Life. Linear regression, a two-wave cross lagged panel analysis were used to explore the association between PTSD symptom clusters, SQOL. RESULTS: The findings in the two samples were consistent. Symptom reduction over time was associated with improved SQOL. In multivariable analyses adjusted for the influence of all three clusters, gender, time since war exposure, only changes in hyperarousal symptoms were significantly associated with changes in SQOL. The two-wave cross-lagged panel analysis suggested that the link between hyperarousal symptoms, SQOL is bidirectional. CONCLUSIONS: Low SQOL of patients with war-related PTSD is particularly associated with hyperarousal symptoms. The findings suggest a bidirectional influence: a reduction in hyperarousal symptoms may result in improved SQOL,, improvements in SQOL may lead to reduced hyperarousal symptoms.

title: Help-seeking experiences of immigrant domestic violence survivors in Australia: A snapshot of Muslim survivors
authors: Ghafournia, Nafiseh, Easteal, Patricia
keywords: Muslim immigrant women; battered women; cultural contexts; disclosure of domestic violence; domestic violence; perceptions of domestic violence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: There has been significant research on women's experiences of domestic violence (DV) as well as on the women's help-seeking behaviors when living with partner abuse. Most of the Australian literature has focused on nonimmigrant women. We know that help seeking can include informal sources such as family, friends, religious leaders,, colleagues or formal assistance from police, doctors, social workers, counselors,, DV agencies. The current study aims to contribute to the literature on help seeking by looking at what has been found concerning immigrant DV survivors, complementing that with interview material from a sample of 14 Muslim immigrant DV survivors in New South Wales. First, we look at barriers that these women may encounter in seeking help, the non-help-seeking strategies they may employ. We then see what may trigger seeking help (including before, after leaving the abusers). Next, we look at how the two types of help seeking are used to better understand the positives, negatives of these pathways. This article ends with some suggestions for developing more appropriate, targeted strategies to assist abused immigrant DV survivors, their children.

title: Assessing the discrimination, calibration of the Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment in Switzerland
authors: Gerth, Juliane, Rossegger, Astrid, Bauch, Elisabeth, Endrass, Jérôme
keywords: intimate partner violence; partner abuse; validity; screening; police; Recidivism; Risk Factors; Test Validity; Risk Assessment;320\_ST実証研究;99\_文献なし
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a major public health issue; worldwide, almost 1 in 3 women is affected. Police involvement in IPV cases has substantially increased because of “proarrest”, “procharging” policies, the enforcement of laws protecting victims of domestic violence. In the course of these changes, several front-line instruments have been developed to structure police risk assessment, decision-making strategies in such cases. One of those is the Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment (ODARA). To investigate its validity in a Swiss police setting, a total cohort of male IPV offenders was retrospectively assessed for a fixed time at risk of 5 years. The recidivism base rate was 32\% when recidivism was defined as subsequent police-registered IPV. Although ODARA scores were significantly correlated with IPV recidivism, they showed poor discrimination, calibration. Despite comparable base rates of recidivism, the Zurich sample scored significantly higher on the ODARA than the development sample. This mismatch of the expected, observed recidivism rates resulted in an overestimating of risk, especially in the two highest risk bins. Several reasons for those deviations, such as level of intervention, victim’s reporting behavior,, the dynamic nature of IPV, are discussed.

title: Das Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment (ODARA) – Validität und autorisierte deutsche Übersetzung eines Screening-Instruments für Risikobeurteilungen bei Intimpartnergewalt
authors: Gerth, J, Rossegger, A, Urbaniok, F, Endrass, J
keywords: ODARA; intimate partner violence; risk of recidivism; validity; German translation; Adult; Domestic Violence; Female; Germany; Humans; Reproducibility of Results; Risk Assessment; Spouse Abuse; Spouses; Foreign Language Translation; Test Validity; Screening;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: On average one third of all women are victimised by intimate partner violence at least once in their life. Many women are affected repeatedly. To efficiently reduce the risk of repeated violence a reliable, valid risk assessment is needed. To date several risk assessment tools have been published in the field of intimate partner violence. There is a strong demand for such tools to be applicable by a wider range of practitioners (e.g., police officers, hospital, victim services' staff) to reliably assess cases of intimate partner violence, recommend further interventions. By developing the Ontario Domestic Assault Risk Assessment (ODARA) it was the authors' aim to provide a brief risk assessment tool which can be scored on the basis of only few, easily collectable information, which efficiently discriminates between low-risk, high-risk offenders of intimate partner violence. Previous replication studies found moderate to good, on average higher power of discrimination of the ODARA compared to other risk assessment tools in the field. However, for the German speaking countries robust findings are still lacking. In the present publication a scientific, authorised translation of the ODARA is provided.

title: After rape: Mexican women’s help-seeking, access to emergency health care in public prosecutor’s offices
authors: Frías, Sonia M, Ríos-Cázares, Alejandra
abstract: Using a mixed-methods design, this study examines the prevalence of women’s rape by someone other than an intimate partner in Mexico, women’s formal help-seeking strategies, their access to emergency healthcare in state attorney agencies. 18 out of every 10,000 Mexican women were raped during 2011. Only 8.37\% of them sought help in law-enforcement agencies, less than 1\% in public health services. Specialized agencies in sexual crimes tend to lack attention protocols (70\%),, medical examiners (26.7\%). Emergency medical care for victims is not guaranteed nor are referrals to public healthcare services for emergency contraception, treatment for STDs, pregnancy interruption.

title: Differential effects of gender on Canadian police officers’ perceptions of stalking
authors: Finnegan, Heather A, Timmons Fritz, Patti A, Horrobin, Barry
abstract: Stalking (also known as ``criminal harassment'' in Canada) is broadly defined as repeated contact with another individual that elicits fear. By manipulating the details of an actual stalking case, the present study examined the role of actor sex (man-woman [M-W], woman-man [W-M]) on perceptions of stalking in a sample of local police officers. Consistent with previous research, officers who read the M-W case anticipated more physical, emotional, psychological,, economic harm, as well as greater likelihood of a prison sentence by judges, than officers who read the W-M case. Actor sex did not influence officers' perceptions of seriousness, likelihood of a jury conviction, or identification of criminal harassment. The findings may be used to develop intervention programs aimed at educating law enforcement, social support workers,, community agencies to ensure appropriate protection, treatment of individuals stalked by former partners.

title: Unprepared for information interactions: abuse survivors, police
authors: Finn, Jeanine, Westbrook, Lynn, Chen, Tiffany, Mensah, Priscilla
journal: The Journal of documentation; devoted to the recording, organization, dissemination of specialized knowledge
abstract: PurposeWorking towards a broader understanding of information provision by agencies responding to crisis situations, the aim of this paper is to examine mandated information provision on the part of law enforcement to survivors of intimate partner violence at the scene of an emergency response.Design/methodology/approachThe authors conducted a detailed content analysis of 1,851 documents supplied by local law enforcement agencies from 755 US cities. A 29‐element coding framework was developed to identify five key content areas of information: the nature of abuse, survivor norms, police information, legal options,, community resources.FindingsThe best represented content areas related to police information, legal options,, community resources. Information on the nature of abuse, survivor hood was dramatically less well represented. Law enforcement understandably privileges that information which involves immediate, concrete action, within which the officer may have a responsibility (for example, to obtain a temporary restraining order). Correlations between city size, the presence of information elements were minimal, while several significant correlations based on region were noted.Originality/valueThis is the first nationwide study of the information that police are required to provide to survivors of intimate partner violence. Understanding the features of this seldom‐discussed yet vital interaction can help IS professionals support practices, protocols of other agencies responding to crisis situations who may be struggling with minimal preparation for information interactions.

title: Family abduction in a national sample of US children
authors: Finkelhor, David, Henly, Megan, Turner, Heather, Hamby, Sherry
keywords: Child abuse; Child maltreatment; Custody disputes; Missing children;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: This study examined the prevalence, characteristics of family abduction episodes occurring in a nationally representative sample of US children ages 0-17. It drew on the experiences of 13,052 children, youth from the aggregation of three cross-sectional waves (2008, 2011,, 2014) of the National Surveys of Children Exposed to Violence. The overall prevalence rate was 4.1\% for a lifetime, 1.2\% for a past year episode. Rates were higher for younger than older children. Parents constituted 90\% of the abductors with females outnumbering males 60\% to 40\%, although men outnumbered women as perpetrators for certain types of abductions. A bit less than half of the episodes (43\%) were reported to police. The experience of a lifetime family abduction had an independent association with traumatic stress symptoms independent of exposure to other kinds of victimization including child maltreatment, witnessing family violence.

title: The process of adapting a universal dating abuse prevention program to adolescents exposed to domestic violence
authors: Foshee, Vangie A, Dixon, Kimberly S, Ennett, Susan T, Moracco, Kathryn E, Bowling, J Michael, Chang, Ling-Yin, Moss, Jennifer L
keywords: dating abuse prevention; exposure to domestic violence; program adaptation;320\_ST実証研究;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Adolescents exposed to domestic violence are at increased risk of dating abuse, yet no evaluated dating abuse prevention programs have been designed specifically for this high-risk population. This article describes the process of adapting Families for Safe Dates (FSD), an evidenced-based universal dating abuse prevention program, to this high-risk population, including conducting 12 focus groups, 107 interviews with the target audience. FSD includes six booklets of dating abuse prevention information,, activities for parents, adolescents to do together at home. We adapted FSD for mothers who were victims of domestic violence, but who no longer lived with the abuser, to do with their adolescents who had been exposed to the violence. Through the adaptation process, we learned that families liked the program structure, valued being offered the program, that some of our initial assumptions about this population were incorrect. We identified practices, beliefs of mother victims, attributes of these adolescents that might increase their risk of dating abuse that we had not previously considered. In addition, we learned that some of the content of the original program generated negative family interactions for some. The findings demonstrate the utility of using a careful process to adapt evidence-based interventions (EBIs) to cultural sub-groups, particularly the importance of obtaining feedback on the program from the target audience. Others can follow this process to adapt EBIs to groups other than the ones for which the original EBI was designed.

title: Longitudinal predictors of serious physical, sexual dating violence victimization during adolescence
authors: Foshee, Vangie Ann, Benefield, Thad Steven, Ennett, Susan T, Bauman, Karl E, Suchindran, Chirayath
keywords: sexual dating violence; risk factors; victimization; adolescence attitudes; Human; Male; Female; Childhood (birth-12 yrs); School Age (6-12 yrs); Adolescence (13-17 yrs); Empirical Study; Followup Study; longitudinal analysis; Quantitative Study; Social Dating; Violence; Adolescent Attitudes; US; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: BACKGROUND: This study identifies potentially modifiable risk factors for the onset of, chronic victimization from serious physical, sexual dating violence. METHODS: One thousand two hundred ninety-one 8th, 9th graders from a county in North Carolina were assessed annually for 5, 4 years, respectively. RESULTS: For males, having been hit by an adult with the intention of harm, having low self-esteem,, having been in a physical fight with a peer predicted onset of serious physical dating violence victimization. Those variables, plus having a friend who has been a victim of dating violence, alcohol use,, being white, predicted chronic victimization for males. For females, onset of serious physical dating violence victimization was predicted by having been hit by an adult; that variable, plus living in a single-parent household, predicted chronic victimization from serious physical violence. Also for females, onset of sexual violence victimization was predicted by having a friend who has been the victim of dating violence, being depressed; those variables, gender stereotyping predicted chronic victimization from sexual dating violence. CONCLUSIONS: The findings identify high-risk groups, risk factors to target for intervention, have implications for approaches to delivering dating violence prevention programs.

title: Contextual factors impacting battered women's intentions to reuse the criminal legal system
authors: Fleury-Steiner, Ruth E, Bybee, Deborah, Sullivan, Cris M, Belknap, Joanne, Melton, Heather C
keywords: situational factors; relational factors; systems-level factors; domestic violence; relationship with perpetrator; community supports; intent to reuse criminal legal system; battered women; Battered Females; Criminal Justice; Intention; Interpersonal Relationships; Adjudication; Criminal Behavior; Intimate Partner Violence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: While a small number of past studies have examined either situational, relational, or systems-level factors that influence battered women's use of either the police, prosecutorial, or court systems, no study to date has examined how these factors each influence women's intentions to reuse these systems. To address this gap, in-person interviews were conducted with 178 women whose assailants had been charged with a domestic violence-related crime against them. Survivors of intimate partner violence were asked about the violence itself, their relationship with the perpetrator (including financial dependence on him), community supports, their expectations,, desires regarding the criminal legal response,, their prior experiences with the police, prosecutors, legal advocates,, the courts. Regression analyses were conducted to examine women's intentions to reuse the criminal legal system in the event of future violence. Consistent with an ecological perspective on behavior (e.g., Bronfenbrenner, 1979), the context of women's lives, the violence they had experienced,, their experiences with the police, the legal system all impacted their intentions. Specifically, women were more likely to want further involvement with these systems if they were employed, felt supported by their communities, had received information about services from the police, had experienced case outcomes consistent with their desires,, had been treated well by the criminal legal system. Women were less inclined to intend to use the system in the future if they were legally or financially tied to their perpetrators, if they had been assaulted again before the court case was closed, if court proceedings had been cancelled at least once,, if they had been pressured rather than supported by the criminal legal system. Implications of the findings are discussed. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2020 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Intimate partner violence, the relation between help-seeking behavior, the severity, frequency of physical violence among women in Turkey
authors: Ergöçmen, Banu Akadli, Yüksel-Kaptanoğlu, İlknur, Jansen, Henrica A F M Henriette
keywords: help-seeking; intimate partner violence; severity, frequency of physical violence;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: This study explores the severity, frequency of physical violence from an intimate partner experienced by 15- to 59-year-old women, their help-seeking behavior by using data from the ``National Research on Domestic Violence Against Women in Turkey.'' Chi-square tests, logistic regression analyses were conducted to compare the relationship between severity, frequency of violence, women's characteristics. Of all ever-partnered women, 36\% have been exposed to partner violence; almost half of these experienced severe types of violence. Women used informal strategies to manage the violence instead of seeking help from formal institutions. Help-seeking behavior increases with increased severity, frequency of violence.

title: Risk factors, correlates of dating violence: the relevance of examining frequency, severity levels in a college sample
authors: Follingstad, D R, Bradley, R G, Laughlin, J E, Burke, L
abstract: To determine whether categorizing levels of violence along dimensions of frequency, severity would result in informative distinctions among individuals using dating violence, reported use of physical violence, along with variables theorized to be related to use of force in intimate relationships, was assessed in a sample of 617 college students (males = 290; females = 327). When participants' scores were analyzed by dichotomizing them along the lines of ever versus never using dating violence, numerous past findings were replicated. However, participants using a higher frequency of force were distinguished by needing to control their partner, by less inhibition in expressing their anger. Higher severity of force by an individual was predicted only by a need to control his/her dating partner. Implications for these findings were discussed.

title: A model for predicting dating violence: anxious attachment, angry temperament,, need for relationship control
authors: Follingstad, Diane R, Bradley, Rebekah G, Helff, Cynthia M, Laughlin, James E
abstract: Structural equation modeling (SEM) was used to test a model incorporating anxious attachment, angry temperament,, attempts to control one's partner as predictors of the severity, frequency of dating violence. To date, these concepts have not been clearly established as having direct or indirect effects on dating violence. It was hypothesized that anxious attachment, angry temperament would influence the need for, attempts to control one's partner which, in turn, would predict a person's actual use of force. College students (213 males; 199 females) completed measures assessing these constructs. Cross-validation was accomplished through using two successive freshmen samples. Statistics indicated the application of the model fit well to both samples. All specified paths were significant except for the direct path from anxious attachment to need for control in the second sample. While exploratory, this model seemed satisfactory for explaining potentially causal relationships of attachment, anger,, attempts to control one's partner leading to dating violence.

title: Weapon use increases the severity of domestic violence but neither weapon use nor firearm access increases the risk or severity of recidivism
authors: Folkes, Stephanie E F, Hilton, N Zoe, Harris, Grant T
keywords: weapon usage; domestic violence severity; recidivism severity; risk factor; firearms usage; lower education; Adult; Confidence Intervals; Crime Victims; Databases, Factual; Domestic Violence; Female; Firearms; Humans; Male; Middle Aged; Odds Ratio; Ontario; Risk Assessment; Recidivism; Risk Factors; Educational Background; Weapons;320\_ST実証研究;repeat\_victim\_intervention
abstract: Use of weapons is a risk factor for domestic violence severity, especially lethality. It is not clear, however, whether access to firearms itself increases assault severity, or whether it is characteristic of a subgroup of offenders who are more likely to commit severe, repeated domestic assault. This reanalysis of 1,421 police reports of domestic violence by men found that 6\% used a weapon during the assault, 8\% had access to firearms. We expected that firearm use would be rare compared to other weapons, that actual weapon use rather than firearm access would increase the severity of domestic assaults. Firearm access was associated with assault severity, but this was mostly attributable to use of nonfirearm weapons. Weapon use was associated with older age, lower education,, relationship history as well as to assault severity. Victims were most concerned about future assaults following threats, actual injuries.
