title: Engaging Bystanders to Prevent Sexual Harassment in Public Transportation: Learnings from an Intervention in Mexico City
authors: Gennari, Floriza Freire
keywords: 0344:Social research; 0453:Womens studies; 0709:Transportation; Bystander intervention; Mexico City Mexico; Psychosocial factors; Public transportation; Sexual Harassment; Social research; Transportation; Victim-blaming; Violence against women; Womens studies;321\_SA実証研究;327;330\_SAEnv
abstract: The sexual harassment (SH) of women in public transportation is a widespread issue, yet research is sparse on how to prevent this type of violence from occurring. In three papers, this dissertation evaluates the impact of the Hazme el Paro! project, a quasi-experimental study that employed a bystander intervention approach to encourage witnesses to intervene in incidents of SH. The study was conducted in Mexico City, Mexico from 2014 to 2016. Papers 1, 2 are exploratory studies of the psychosocial variables associated with perceived risk of SH, bystander willingness to intervene, while Paper 3 examines the effect of the Hazme el Paro! intervention.Paper 1 explored the correlates of SH risk perception,, the extent to which psychosocial variables moderated the relationship between experiencing or witnessing SH, the perceived risk of being sexually harassed. Among women, results suggest a positive association between risk perception, a) acceptance of SH norms as pervasive, b) the belief that most women disapprove of SH (injunctive norms),, c) witnessing or experiencing SH. The results indicate that risk perception is higher for women with a history of SH when victim-blaming beliefs are present. Among men, injunctive norms were negatively associated with risk perception. The findings suggest campaigns seeking to reduce SH in public transport should consider the role of risk perception antecedents in the framing of messages intending to motivate bystanders to action.Paper 2 then seeks to examine the extent to which risk perception, along with other barriers, facilitators, affected willingness to intervene. As hypothesized, scoring high on self-efficacy to intervene attenuated the negative relationship between holding victim-blaming beliefs, the intention to help a victim of SH. Similarly, those with greater outcome expectations scored higher on willingness to intervene, despite their strong victim-blaming beliefs, than those who reported low outcome expectations. The findings suggest that promoting self-efficacy, outcome expectations may be a viable strategy for increasing bystander intention to intervene, specifically among those with stronger victim-blaming beliefs – the group least likely to express a desire to intervene.Paper 3 documents the extent to which the intervention mattered in significantly improving willingness to intervene, actual intervening behaviors. When examining the overall impact of the intervention bus route, controlling for changes in the comparison bus route as per the difference-in-difference method, the analyses showed statistical significance with the intervention being effective in increasing willingness to intervene at end-line. Based on end-line data only, male respondents in the intervention bus route were more likely to report prosocial bystander behaviors. Findings indicate a dose response effect; greater exposure to the intervention was associated with increased willingness to intervene (among men only), bystander behavior. Paper 3 also sought to examine the pathway of influence of the intervention; results suggest outcome expectations, victim-blaming were pathways for both men, women.Overall, the findings from this dissertation suggest that a low-resource bystander intervention initiative in public transportation can indeed influence the intention of bystanders to step in, interrupt an incident of SH.

title: Behavioral economics, empirical public policy: Empirical public policy
authors: Hursh, Steven R, Roma, Peter G
journal: Journal of the experimental analysis of behavior
keywords: behavioral economics, demand curve, exponential model, essential value, reinforcer interactions, choice, public policy;321\_SA実証研究;99\_文献なし
abstract: The application of economics principles to the analysis of behavior has yielded novel insights on value, choice across contexts ranging from laboratory animal research to clinical populations to national trends of global impact. Recent innovations in demand curve methods provide a credible means of quantitatively comparing qualitatively different reinforcers as well as quantifying the choice relations between concurrently available reinforcers. The potential of the behavioral economic approach to inform public policy is illustrated with examples from basic research, pre-clinical behavioral pharmacology,, clinical drug abuse research as well as emerging applications to public transportation, social behavior. Behavioral Economics can serve as a broadly applicable conceptual, methodological,, analytical framework for the development, evaluation of empirical public policy.

title: On the actual risk of bystander intervention: A statistical study based on naturally occurring violent emergencies
authors: Liebst, Lasse Suonperä, Heinskou, Marie Bruvik, Ejbye-Ernst, Peter
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objectives: Bystander studies have rarely considered the victimization risk associated with intervention into violent, dangerous emergencies. To address this gap, we aim to identify factors that influence bystanders’ risk of being physically victimized. Method: We observed bystander behavior from video surveillance footage of naturally occurring violence in nighttime economy settings,, data were analyzed with a logistic regression model. Results: Data show that approximately one of the six interventions results in some type of victimization, typically with a relatively low degree of severity. The bystander’s social group membership, the setting of the emergency,, the bystander’s intervention type are estimated as risk factors for victimization. Conclusions: Previous research suggests that a bystander’s social group membership with victims promotes intervention behavior. Our results expand the role of social group membership as being a factor that also influences whether the intervening bystander is victimized.

title: Naming the unspeakable harm of street harassment: A survey-based examination of disclosure practices
authors: Fileborn, Bianca
keywords: LGBT; disclosure; street harassment;321\_SA実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Street harassment may be considered an ``unspeakable'' harm on account of the routine silencing, trivialization of victims' experiences. Disclosing street harassment is vital in making its harms visible, in working to transform social, cultural attitudes. Despite a recent resurgence of interest in street harassment via online activist groups, there is scant research on disclosure practices. Drawing on findings from an online, mixed-methods survey with 292 participants who have experienced street harassment, I examine disclosure practices using an intersectional lens. I argue that disclosure is an epistemological process, through which a limited, partial understanding of street harassment is produced.

title: Sexual violence against women in India: Daily life, coping strategies of young women in Delhi
authors: Nieder, Christina, Muck, Christoph, Kärtner, Joscha
keywords: India; individual coping strategies; sexual violence; violence against women;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: This study assesses the current situation concerning sexual violence against women in India, women's individual coping strategies. We conducted 15 semistructured interviews with 17- to 22-year-old Indian college students. First, results about the current situation showed threatening circumstances for women, revealed how deeply sexual violence affects women's lives. Second, to cope with sexual violence women mentioned three types of strategies, namely (a) safety, (b) avoidance,, (c) empowerment strategies. In the discussion, we suggest that women's use of safety, avoidance strategies are safety behaviors that play a key role in maintaining women's fear, societal dynamics.

title: Conceptual understandings, prevalence of sexual harassment, street harassment
authors: Fileborn, B
abstract: This resource sheet provides an overview of the existing research on women's experiences of sexual harassment, street harassment. It also considers conceptual models of sexual violence that are inclusive of these experiences.

title: Risk factors for, behavioral consequences of direct versus indirect exposure to violence
authors: Zimmerman, Gregory M, Posick, Chad
abstract: Research suggests that direct exposure (personal victimization), indirect exposure (witnessing or hearing about the victimization of a family member, friend, or neighbor) to violence are correlated. However, questions remain about the co-occurrence of these phenomena within individuals. We used data on 1915 youths (with an average age of 12 years at baseline) from the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods to examine this issue. Results indicated that youths who tended to be personally victimized were also likely to witness violence; conversely, youths who disproportionately witnessed violence were relatively unlikely to experience personal victimization. In addition, direct, indirect exposures to violence were associated with subsequent adverse outcomes in similar ways. The key distinguishing factor was, rather, the cumulative level of violence (both direct, indirect) to which youths were exposed.

title: Teenagers' perceptions of online privacy, coping behaviors: A risk–benefit appraisal approach
authors: Youn, Seounmi
keywords: teenagers perceptions; online privacy; coping behavior; protection motivation theory; risk benefit appraisals; website; Adolescent Attitudes; Internet; Privacy; Websites;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Applying Rogers's (1975, 1983) protection motivation theory to the online privacy context, this study determined that risk, benefit appraisals explain teenagers' willingness to provide information to a Web site, which, in turn, affected their risk-lowering behaviors. Survey data from 326 high school students revealed that a higher level of risk perception of information disclosure led to less willingness to provide information. In contrast, as teenagers perceived more benefits from information disclosure, they were more willing to provide information. Subsequently, as teenagers were less likely to give out their information, they tended to engage in several risk-reducing strategies such as falsifying information, providing incomplete information, or going to alternative Web sites that do not ask for personal information. Implications for public policies, self-regulations to protect teenagers' online privacy were discussed.

title: Unintentional exposure to online sexual content, sexual behavior intentions among college students in China
authors: Zhang, Jingwen, Jemmott, 3rd, John B
keywords: China; college students; internet sexual content; sex education; sexual behavior; survey;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: This study examined the relations of unintentional exposure to Internet sexual content to intentions for sex, condom use, potential mediators of these relations, including attitudes, norms,, self-efficacy, among college students in China. A sample of 524 Chinese college students completed an online questionnaire. Mediation path analyses were conducted to test the theory of planned behavior as a model of the relations between unintentional exposure, intentions to have sex, use condoms. On average, students reported being unintentionally exposed to Internet sexual content about 3 to 4 times during the past month. Unintentional exposure was indirectly associated with intention to have sex, mediated through descriptive, injunctive norms. Descriptive norm was a stronger mediator for females than males. In contrast, unintentional exposure was unrelated to condom-use intention, mediators. The theory of planned behavior provides a model for the development of Internet-based interventions with these students.

title: Addressing fear of crime in public space: gender differences in reaction to safety measures in train transit
authors: Yavuz, Nilay, Welch, Eric W
abstract: Research has identified several factors that affect fear of crime in public space. However, the extent to which gender moderates the effectiveness of fear-reducing measures has received little attention. Using data from the Chicago Transit Authority Customer Satisfaction Survey of 2003, this study aims to understand whether train transit security practices, service attributes affect men, women differently. Findings indicate that, while the presence of video cameras has a lower effect on women's feelings of safety compared with men, frequent, on-time service matters more to male passengers. Additionally, experience with safety-related problems affects women significantly more than men. Conclusions discuss the implications of the study for theory, gender-specific policies to improve perceptions of transit safety.

title: Bystander intervention behavior as function of victimization history, opportunity,, situational context
authors: Woods, William C, Kistler, Tylor A, Stuart, Gregory L, Cornelius, Tara L
keywords: dating violence; domestic violence; intervention; intervention/treatment; sexual assault;321\_SA実証研究;CampusCrime
abstract: Preliminary research has demonstrated the utility of bystander interventions in reducing sexual assault,, initial research has begun extending this type of intervention to intimate partner violence more broadly. However, the extant research is limited by methodological issues that fail to examine opportunity for intervention relative to intervention behaviors as well as a failure to examine intervention rates across differing risk situations. Further, there are many unexplored factors that may impact bystander intervention behavior, notably previous experiences with intimate partner violence, sexual assault. Thus, the current study examined bystander opportunities, intervention across situations of varying risk to the bystander, as well as the relationship of opportunity/intervention relative to victimization history. Given the rates of sexual assault, IPV on college, university campuses, the research examined the number of times college students (N = 393) encountered a range of situations in which bystander intervention may be indicated,, their intervention behavior across varying risk levels to the bystander. Results demonstrated that individuals with a history of psychological victimization were more likely to intervene across all situation types, but sexual, physical victimization provided mixed support for hypotheses. No differences in witnessing or intervening were found as a function of gender. These results replicate previous findings,, further provide evidence for a more nuanced approach to examine bystander behavior intervention. Implications, directions for future research are discussed.

title: A systematic review of experimental studies investigating attitudes towards sexual revictimization: Findings, ecological validity,, scientific rigor
authors: Wager, Nadia M, Goodson, Simon, Parton, Loren E
keywords: Attrition; Sexual revictimization; Attributions; Victim-blame; Believability; Vignettes; Experimental methods; Mock-juror studies;321\_SA実証研究;J Crim Justice
abstract: Background Evidence from attrition studies indicates that complainants who experience sexual assault on more than one occasion, by different perpetrators (i.e. sexual revictimization) are unlikely to have their cases progress through to prosecution. Purpose The aim of this systematic review was to ascertain what can be learned from experimental studies to aid the understanding of this real-world phenomenon. Specifically, to investigate the attributions made to hypothetical cases of sexual revictimization in mock-juror-type, (quasi)experimental studies. Methods This systematic review entailed searching 13 electronic databases. Over 6000 potential sources were generated, of which 24 met the criteria for full-text reading. Application of the inclusion criteria, led to this review being based on 12 articles published between 1976, 2020. These referred to 16 studies involving 4021 participants. Findings The findings, except for one study, revealed consistent evidence of bias towards victims of sexual revictimization, which related to higher levels of disbelief, victim-blame,, other factors. Complainants were blamed most by women when the context was perceived as risky. Conclusions There were several methodological issues with many of the studies which compromised their ecological validity, applicability. Recommendations are made for future research in this area,, police training, practice.

title: Offender–victim relationship, offender motivation in the context of indirect cyber abuse: A mixed-method exploratory analysis
authors: Vakhitova, Zarina, Webster, Julianne, Alston-Knox, Clair, Reynald, Danielle, Townsley, Michael
abstract: Cyber abuse can be executed directly (e.g. by sending derogatory emails or text messages addressed to the victim) or indirectly (e.g. by posting derogatory, private or false information, documents, images or videos about the victim online). This exploratory, mixed-method triangulated study examines cyber abuse crime events with the goal of identifying factors associated with the increased risk of personal victimization from both direct, indirect methods of cyber abuse. First, in-depth qualitative interviews with cyber abuse victims ( n = 12) were conducted. The interviews were analysed using thematic analysis to generate hypotheses. These hypotheses were then tested using content analysis of newspaper reports ( n = 110), victims’ posts on online forums ( n = 91) describing incidents of cyber abuse. Logistic regression using Bayesian Model Averaging analysis revealed that the combination of a prior offender–victim relationship, expressive motivation best predicts the use of indirect methods of cyber abuse, while direct methods of cyber abuse are more likely to occur when the offender does not know the victim, is motivated by instrumental ends. Implications for crime prevention are also discussed.

title: Not all behind closed doors: Examining bystander involvement in intimate partner violence
authors: Taylor, Elizabeth, Banyard, Victoria, Grych, John, Hamby, Sherry
keywords: bystander; bystander behavior; intimate partner violence; rural communities; violence;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: It is often said that intimate partner violence (IPV) happens ``behind closed doors''; however, research on IPV, other crimes suggests that witnesses are sometimes present. This suggests that bystanders may be in a position to help victims or potential victims of violence. Bystander behavior has been studied primarily in school settings,, consequently, little is known about how often it occurs or what its effects may be in the broader community. This study examined IPV incidents in a rural sample to assess the presence, potential impact of bystanders on victim-reported outcomes. One thousand nine hundred seventy-seven adult participants completed a questionnaire that asked about five violent behaviors (my partner threatened to hurt me; pushed, grabbed, or shook me; hit me; beat me up; sexually assaulted me), bystander characteristics,, victim outcomes (fear; injury; disruption of daily routines; mental health). Adult or teen bystanders were present for each IPV approximately one third of the time, except in the case of sexual assault (14.3\%). When a bystander was present, victims reported higher rates of injury, greater disruption in their routines,, poorer mental health. When a bystander's safety was threatened, victims reported more physical injury, more routine disruption. A considerable number of IPV incidents do not happen behind closed doors,, the presence of a bystander was associated with worse outcomes for victims. Prevention efforts for adult IPV may need to take a more cautious or nuanced approach to encouraging bystander action, especially when confronted with more severe incidents. Bystander safety should be a priority for violence prevention.

title: Predictors of female sexual aggression among a U.s. mturk sample: The protective role of sexual assertiveness
authors: Struckman-Johnson, Cindy, Anderson, Peter B, Smeaton, George
abstract: We studied predictors of female sexual aggression (FSA) among a U.S. Mechanical Turk sample (from Amazon’s online crowdsourcing platform) of 634 adult women ( median age = 32). A logistic regression analysis revealed that five measures contributed significantly to a model predicting past use of a tactic of post-refusal sexual persistence (PRSP), accounting for 19\% of variance. Women’s use of a PRSP tactic was associated with lower scores on two sexual assertiveness measures (the ability to refuse sex, the ability to ask questions about a partner’s sexual health history), higher scores on measures of acceptance of heterosexual male rape myths, early courtship rehearsal (number of others called, texted, tweeted, sexted due to attraction before the age of 18),, sexual sensation seeking. Based on our results, we suggest that sexual assertiveness training may be a useful addition to anti-sexual assault programming. For better prediction, potential prevention of FSA, we recommend continued research on the variables in this study, additional factors related to maladaptive personality (e.g., psychopathy, narcissism,, antisocial values), the use of alcohol, drugs.

title: Women's security: Critical perspectives on assessment techniques, preventive responses
authors: Smith, Martha J, Fisher, Bonnie S
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Transgender persons; Security personnel; Risk factors; Homosexuality; Conflicts; Community; Colleges \& universities; Audits;321\_SA実証研究;Security Journal
abstract: The authors demonstrate how the number of assessment tools currently being used to examine women's security can be expanded to deal with new populations (for example, gays, lesbians, transgender individuals) or emerging security problems (for example, domestic violence in rural areas). According to Robinson, Rowlands, these comparisons suggest that risk assessment instruments developed for use with heterosexual partners may not be able to identify risk factors for violence among other types of relationships, such as those involving gay, lesbian, transgender partners.

title: Assessing the Student Right-to-Know, Campus Security Act of 1990: An analysis of the victim reporting practices of college, university students
authors: Sloan, III, John J, Fisher, Bonnie S, Cullen, Francis T
keywords: CRIMINAL statistics; CITIZEN crime reporting; Campus crime; Federal Code; NIJ grant-related documents; Victim-witness legislation;321\_SA実証研究;Crime Delinquency\_●Sage;CampusCrime
abstract: In the late 1980s, celebrated victimizations of college students, grassroots efforts by victims, their families prompted Congress to pass the Student Right-to-Know, Campus Security Act of 1990 that requires postsecondary institutions to disseminate crime statistics for their campuses annually. Using data from a victimization study of more than 3,400 college students, the authors examine whether statistics generated by this policy initiative provide an accurate portrait of on-campus crime. Results of their analyses cast serious doubt on the validity, reliability of the statistics generated by the act.

title: Improving formal support after sexual assault: Recommendations from survivors living in poverty in Canada
authors: Sit, Victoria, Stermac, Lana
keywords: formal support providers; help-seeking; poverty; sexual assault;321\_SA実証研究;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Despite the extensive, often long-lasting sequelae of sexual assault, a significant majority of survivors do not seek assistance from formal support sources, such as police, medical or mental health professionals,, community-based agencies. While growing attention has been directed toward understanding the help-seeking barriers faced by sexual assault survivors, few studies have explored the experiences of survivors living in poverty, how help-seeking can be improved for this marginalized population. The present study sought to understand these issues from perspectives of survivors themselves. Women sexual assault survivors who self-identified as living in poverty (n = 15) were recruited from community-based agencies in the Greater Toronto Area,, participated in semistructured interviews focused on their personal decisions around help-seeking, broader views on access to, quality of formal assistance. Two research questions were of interest. First, what can be done to encourage service use among survivors living in poverty? Second, what is needed to improve the quality of assistance they receive? Thematic analysis revealed three key themes around which participants' recommendations centered: (a) increased accessibility of information, (b) improved training for formal support providers,, (c) greater opportunities for empowerment. Practical implications of these findings improving the service utilization rates, experiences of formal help-seeking among marginalized women survivors of sexual assault are discussed.

title: Campus violence preparedness of US college campuses
authors: Seo, Dong-Chul, Torabi, Mohammad R, Sa, Jaesin, Blair, Earl H
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; College campuses; Emergency preparedness; Firearms; Violence; School violence; College students; United States--US;321\_SA実証研究;Security Journal;CampusCrime
abstract: This study investigates the impact of the 2007 Virginia Tech shootings on college emergency procedures of US college campuses. College administrators, security officers from a cross-sectional representative sample of 161 US colleges participated in an online survey in 2008–2009 academic year. Whereas a majority of college campuses reported having appropriate emergency procedures in place, only 25 per cent (n=40) of the surveyed campuses agreed that students understood the emergency procedures of their campuses. Another 25 per cent (n=41) of the campuses reported that if a dangerous crisis situation occurred, the entirety of students, employees would likely be notified within 5 min. Data indicate that a substantial number of colleges across the nation do not realize the importance of emergency drills, do not engage in campus-wide practice of them on a regular basis.

title: Facilitating Violence: A Comparison of Gang-Motivated, Gang-Affiliated,, Nongang Youth Homicides
authors: Rosenfeld, Richard, Bray, Timothy M, Egley, Arlen
keywords: VIOLENCE; GANGS; CRIMINALS; HOMICIDE; CRIME; GANG members; facilitation; youth homicide;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: It is well established that gangs facilitate violent offending by members,but the mechanisms by which that facilitation occurs remain unclear. Gangsmay promote violence indirectly by facilitating members' access to riskysituations such as drug markets or directly through gang functions such asturf defense. We explore alternative modes of facilitation in a comparisonof gang-affiliated homicides (which involve gang members but do not resultfrom gang activity), gang-motivated homicides (which result from gangactivity),, nongang youth homicides in St. Louis. We find importantdifferences as well as similarities in the time trends, eventcharacteristic of the two types of gang homicide; in key respects thegang-affiliated homicides more closely resemble the nongang events. Thegang-motivated events exhibit a somewhat distinctive spatial patterning,as might be expected from their connection to turf conflicts. However, allthree homicide types are highly concentrated in racially isolated,disadvantaged neighborhoods, which remain the fundamental socialfacilitators of both gang, nongang violence.

title: Do women's coping responses to unwanted pursuit behaviors reduce future victimization? A prospective exploration
authors: Richards, Elizabeth, da Silva, Emily Simões, Dardis, Christina M
keywords: coping responses; intimate partner violence; stalking; unwanted pursuit behaviors; victimization;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: While some studies have assessed perceptions of the effectiveness of coping responses to unwanted pursuit behavior (UPB) victimization, there is limited research assessing the prospective effectiveness of various coping responses in reducing victimization. The current study assessed the effectiveness of a range of coping responses in reducing UPB victimization over an 8-week timeframe. Undergraduate women who had reported experiencing two or more incidents of UPB following the break-up with a man within the past 3 years (N =181) completed measures on coping responses. Whereas Moving Against, Moving Toward responses were bivariately correlated with increases in UPB victimization across the 8-week interim, in a multivariate model, none of the coping responses were associated with Time 2 UPB victimization; rather, higher frequencies of both Time 1 UPB victimization, concurrent Time 2 intimate partner violence predicted Time 2 UPB victimization. More research, replication studies are needed since the results here suggest that current UPB response recommendations (e.g., changing social media accounts, maintaining a log of contact from the perpetrator) do not result in reductions in victimization; further research is needed to identify responses that do result in a reduction of unwanted pursuit.

title: Coping strategies as predictors of distress in survivors of single, multiple sexual victimization, nonvictimized controls
authors: Proulx, Jocelyn, Koverola, Catherine, Fedorowicz, Anne, Kral, Michael
keywords: Canadians; Child Abuse; College Students; Coping Behavior; Effects; Females; Incest; Rape; Revictimization; Survivors; Young Adults; Beck Depression Inventory (Beck et al); History of Unwanted Sexual Contact (Koverola et al); Manifest Anxiety Scale (Taylor); Symptom Checklist 90 Revised (Derogatis et al); Ways of Coping Questionnaire (Folkman, Lazarus); coping with crime; coping;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: This study investigated the relationship between coping strategies, distress symptomatology in survivors of sexual revictimization. Coping strategies were assessed with the revised Ways of Coping Scale (Aldwin \& Revenson, 1987). Distress symptoms included global distress, depression, anxiety,, somatization. Subjects were 44 survivors of sexual victimization in both childhood, adulthood; 54 survivors of a single incident of sexual victimization in childhood;, 256 nonvictimized individuals. All were drawn from a subject pool of female undergraduate students. Multivariate analysis of variance revealed significant differences between groups on reported symptomatology, coping strategies. Victimized groups reported more distress than did the nonvictimized group. The multiple victimization group indicated greater use of coping strategies than did the nonvictimized group,, both victimized groups reported greater use of the escapism strategy than did the nonvictimized group. Multiple backward regression analysis found that coping strategies were predictive of distress symptomatology in all three groups, with escapism as the most potent predictor of distress for each group. Coping strategies were the most powerful predictors of distress in the multiply victimized group. The results of this study provide strong support for the importance of addressing coping strategies in clinical intervention of distress, particularly with survivors of multiple sexual victimization.

title: Evaluating the mentors in Violence Prevention program: A process examination of how implementation can affect gender-based violence outcomes
authors: Pagani, Stefania, Hunter, Simon C, Elliott, Mark A
keywords: Mentors in Violence Prevention; anticipated outcome changes; bystander intervention; gender-based violence; implementation effects; program evaluation;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Gender-based violence is a global public health issue, major human rights concern. It is also a type of violence that is disproportionately experienced by women, girls. This study is the first to examine multiple implementation process (dosage, fidelity,, adaptation) effects on changes in anticipated outcomes of a school-based bystander program targeting gender-based violence, Mentors in Violence Prevention (MVP). Data were collected from two participant groups: mentees (students receiving MVP), mentors (students delivering MVP), across nine participating high schools. The mentee sample comprised 698 students (about 48.9\% males, 49.7\% females), aged 11 to 14 years old (M = 11.86, SD = 0.64). The mentor sample comprised 118 students (17.80\% males, 82.20\% females), aged 15 to 18 years old (M = 16.42, SD = 0.60). Anticipated outcomes were changes in bystanders' attitudes, social influences, control perceptions, intentions, willingness,, intervention behavior, measured using mentees' self-reports at two time points approximately 1 year apart. Implementation processes were measured using mentors' self-reports. Analyses revealed no effects for any of the implementation variables across changes in any of the outcomes measured. These results highlight important implications for the implementation of the MVP program going forward, given its widespread implementation in the United Kingdom. Possible ways that MVP may be enhanced in future are discussed. For example, furthering understanding into how gender-based violence, bystander intervention are addressed, framed during MVP lessons would give more insight into how the current implementation of the program can be improved to maximize its potential benefits.

title: Evaluation of a sexual assault risk reduction, self-defense program: A prospective analysis of a revised protocol
authors: Orchowski, Lindsay M, Gidycz, Christine A, Raffle, Holly
keywords: Rape; Risk Factors; Self Defense; Sexual Abuse; Social Dating; Evaluation; Human; Female; US; sexual assault risk reduction; self-defense program; risky dating; Dating Self-Protection Against Rape Scale; Sexual Communication Survey; Self Efficacy Scale; Rape Attribution Scale; Ohio University Sexual Assault Risk Reduction Program Knowledge Measure; Sexual Experiences Survey;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: The current study extends the development, evaluation of an existing, previously evaluated sexual assault risk reduction program with a self-defense component for college women ( N = 300). The program protocol was revised to address psychological barriers to responding assertively to risky dating situations,, a placebo-control group was utilized rather than a wait-list control group. Relative to the placebo-control group, the program was effective in increasing levels of self-protective behaviors, self-efficacy in resisting against potential attackers,, use of assertive sexual communication over a 4-month interim. Results also suggested reduction of incidence of rape among program participants over the 2-month follow-up. Implications for future development, evaluation of sexual assault risk reduction programming are presented.

title: Community characteristics, child sexual assault: Social disorganization, age
authors: Mustaine, Elizabeth, Tewksbury, R, Huff-Corzine, Lin, Corzine, J, Marshall, Hollianne
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Community; Child abuse \& neglect; Sex offenders; Law enforcement; Children \& youth; Sex crimes; Socioeconomic factors; Orange County Florida; collective efficacy;321\_SA実証研究;J Crim Justice
abstract: This study examines the utility of social disorganization theory as an explanation for community rates of child sexual assault. We explore the sources of preteen (<=12), teen (13-17) sexual assault victimization. Drawing on 1,172 child sexual assault incidents reported to law enforcement agencies in Orange County, Florida in 2004-2006, the present study assesses whether social disorganization theory can explain variation in amounts of preteen, teen sexual assault across census tracts. Social disorganization is assessed using measures of economic disadvantage, collective efficacy,, social cohesion, along with measures of population density, violent crime, presence of sex offenders in the community,, gender-related socioeconomic standing. Economic disadvantage is positively related to the amount of both preteen, teen sexual assault. Surprisingly, immigrant concentration is negatively related to both preteen, teen sexual assault. Housing density is positively related to preteen sexual assault, the presence of registered sex offenders is positively related to teen sexual assault. Social disorganization provides a moderate explanation for community variance in the amount of preteen, teen sexual assault. Also, sources of child sexual assault are different between younger children, older adolescents.

title: The gender safety gap: Examining the impact of victimization history, perceived risk,, personal control
authors: Logan, T K, Walker, Robert
keywords: domestic violence; fear of crime; safety planning; sexual assault; violence exposure;321\_SA実証研究;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Previous research has documented that, in general, women are more concerned about their personal safety, take more safety precautions than men. However, this study looks beyond gender by examining the association of three overall factors including victimization history, perceived risk of future victimization,, personal control with worry about safety, safety responses,, bystander intervention intentions for 270 men, 821 women. There were four main findings from this study including the following: (a) The two most consistently associated factors with worry about safety, safety responses,, bystander intervention intentions were higher perceived risk of violent victimization, safety efficacy; (b) recent victimization, rather than victimization history, played an important role in safety responses particularly for women; (c) different patterns of factors are associated with different safety responses demonstrating the importance of examining a wide variety of safety responses;, (d) the pattern of factors associated with worry about safety, safety responses do differ by gender but also had some important similarities. Implications for future research, prevention as well as safety planning interventions are discussed.

title: The interplay between poly-victimization, sexual assault in late life in the context of life course perspective
authors: Lev, Sagit, Harel, Dovrat, Goldblatt, Hadass, Band-Winterstein, Tova
keywords: life-course perspective; poly-victimization; sexual assault;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: The aim of this article is to explore the interplay between poly-victimization, sexual assault against women in late life (SAWLL) according to the life-course perspective. Two themes emerged from qualitative interviews with 18 experienced welfare, health care professionals who intervened in cases of SAWLL: sexual assault by a spouse co-occurring with other types of abuse within marital relationships,, sexual assault, other types of abuse by two or more perpetrators along the life course. In many cases, SAWLL is an expression of a broader experience of poly-victimization, which relates to vulnerability in old age.

title: SNS online victimization, fear of crime: Including the moderating effects of disorder, collective efficacy,, gender difference
authors: Lee, Seong-Sik, Park, Cheong Sun
abstract: ABSTRACTThis study aims to investigate the relationship between social network site (SNS) online victimization, fear of crime. It is well known that fear of crime is not only affected by the victimization experience in itself but also influenced by the online environment wherein individuals are involved in diverse SNS activities. Thus, the role of victimization on fear of crime is differentiated by the SNS environment, irrespective of whether it is well ordered or not. The research outcome based on the analysis of university students in Seoul, Korea clearly shows that the more they are victimized online, the higher the levels of online disorders, the more they exhibit fear of crime. However, online trust, informal social control, representing online collective efficacy, fail to show any significant effect on fear of crime. Regarding the role of male, female differences in these interaction processes between online victimization with disorder, collective efficacy, respectively, interesting, significant, albeit differentiating, outcomes are found between males, females. The interaction effect between online victimization, environment shows a mingled outcome for male, while it is wholly insignificant for female implying that victimization experience is sufficient to incur fear of crime.

title: Building a model to predict sexual assault victimization frequency among undergraduate women
authors: Kirwan, Mitchell, Lanni, Daniel J, Nagy, Samantha, Pickett, Scott M
keywords: alcohol consumption; impulse control difficulties; sexual assault victimization; sexual refusal assertiveness; sexual risk behaviors;321\_SA実証研究;CampusCrime
abstract: Previous research has identified several factors, including sexual risk behaviors, alcohol consumption, sexual refusal assertiveness, impulse control difficulties, drinking to cope,, sex to cope, as being associated with sexual assault victimization. Data were collected from 465 adult, undergraduate women,, analyzed using structural equation modeling to determine how these variables related to one another. Results showed that together, these factors predicted 17.1\% of the variance in victimization frequency. These findings may help future researchers better understand the etiology of sexual assault victimization on college campuses, prove crucial to the development of future intervention programs which reduce victimization.

title: Predicting the effects of sexual assault research participation: Reactions, perceived insight,, help-seeking
authors: Kirkner, Anne, Relyea, Mark, Ullman, Sarah E
keywords: ethics; help-seeking; research participation; trauma research; victimization;321\_SA実証研究;J Interpers Violence;helping behavior
abstract: This study examined effects of participating in survey research for women sexual assault survivors with other trauma histories to understand the role of study participation on perceived insight, long-term help-seeking behaviors. A diverse sample of 1,863 women from a large Midwestern city participated in a 3-year study on women's experiences with sexual assault. Regression analyses were conducted to (a) examine predictors of immediate positive, negative reactions to survey participation, (b) assess the impact of the survey on perceived insight, women's long-term help-seeking behavior. Overall, most women in the study had a higher positive than negative reaction to the survey (92\%), with a significant proportion indicating they sought additional services as a result of participation (55\%). Women with child sexual abuse (CSA), more emotion dysregulation,, more characterological self-blame had more negative reactions to the survey, whereas those with more education, individual adaptive coping had more positive reactions. Women who said they gained insight from answering survey questions were most likely to seek additional help. This study extends the literature by examining cumulative trauma, postassault symptoms in relation to the effects of survey participation. This is also the first study of women sexual assault survivors to find a relationship between gaining perceived insight from research, subsequent help-seeking. Participating in sexual assault research may help survivors gain greater insight into their recovery, which can lead them to seek out more resources for their ongoing trauma-related problems.

title: Violent victimization, the routine activities/lifestyle of active drug users
authors: Koo, Dixie J, Chitwood, Dale D, Sánchez, Jesús
abstract: The present study examines violent victimization among a sample of active drug users. Two theoretical perspectives are combined to form the underlying conceptual framework of the study: One draws upon routine activities/lifestyle theory, the other incorporates the street addict role theory. While routine activities/lifestyle theory addresses victimization in general, the street addict role theory explains the specific lifestyle characteristics of an active drug abuser which are relevant to the victimization of illicit drug users. We find the prevalence of violent victimization to be high. Approximately 22\% of respondents reported being victimized within a 30 day period. We also find support for combining the two perspectives to help explain violent victimization. Demographic, personal networks, drug use,, street business domain factors are associated with violent victimization for this high risk population. Our study extends the investigation of violent victimization among illicit drug users by identifying characteristics that differentiate drug users who are recent victims of violence from others who have not been similarly victimized.

title: Schools as criminal “hot spots”: Primary, secondary,, beyond
authors: Kautt, Paula M, Roncek, Dennis W
keywords: YOUTH crime; JUVENILE delinquency; JUVENILE delinquents; SCHOOL violence; YOUTH -- Crimes against; SCHOOLS; burglary; hot spots; police strategy; school crime; spatial analysis; Tobit analysis;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Americans are deeply concerned about crime. Increasing crime problems in America's schools, expanding youth involvement in crime are two reasons. These trends should be linked to criminological developments regarding crime incidents, the places where they occur. Routine Activities Theory emphasizes the conditions, locations where crime occurs. Research also indicates crime is concentrated in small areas called “hot spots,” often centered on locations integral to the offender's routine activities. Schools are one focal point for the routine activities of youth. Accordingly, using Tobit analysis of block-level burglary rates, this research examines the importance of different types of schools as focal points of acquisitive crime.

title: The role of neighborhood disadvantage, physical disorder,, collective efficacy in adolescent alcohol use: a multilevel path analysis
authors: Jackson, Nicki, Denny, Simon, Sheridan, Janie, Zhao, Jinfeng, Ameratunga, Shanthi
keywords: Adolescent; Alcohol; Collective efficacy; Neighborhood; Path analysis;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Research into the salient exposures which explain neighborhood variation in adolescent alcohol use remains inconclusive. The Social Disorganization Theory suggests that neighborhood-level disadvantage may reduce collective efficacy to control adolescent risky behavior. Collective perceptions of physical disorder are also implicated in this neighborhood pathway. Drawing on data from a nationally-representative survey of urban high school students in New Zealand, multilevel path analysis was used to estimate the direct, mediating effects of neighborhood disadvantage, physical disorder,, collective efficacy on current drinking, frequency of binge drinking,, typical quantity of alcohol consumed. The findings supported an indirect pathway from disadvantage to binge drinking, high typical quantities in young adolescents (<16 years), mediated by physical disorder, reduced collective efficacy. Collective efficacy was not associated with current drinking in young adolescents. An opposing indirect effect was evident among older adolescents (≥16 years), whereby collective efficacy was positively associated with drinking outcomes. Implications for future research are discussed.

title: Preventing sexual violence through bystander intervention: Attitudes, behaviors, missed opportunities,, barriers to intervention among Australian university students
authors: Kania, Rachel, Cale, Jesse
keywords: barriers; bystander; intervention; missed opportunities; sexual assault; sexual victimization;321\_SA実証研究;J Interpers Violence
abstract: The concept of bystander intervention is gaining popularity in universities as a mechanism to prevent sexual violence. Prior research has focused on correlates of bystanders' intentions to intervene, intervention behaviors in situations where there is a risk of sexual violence. The current study builds on this literature by exploring the nature of missed opportunities, including perceived barriers to intervention. In all, 380 Australian undergraduate university students completed an online survey. Measures included a rape myth acceptance scale, bystander intentions to intervene, actual intervention behaviors, missed opportunities for intervention,, perceived barriers for missed opportunities. Promisingly, students reported high levels of intentions to intervene in situations where there was a risk of sexual violence, reported relatively few missed opportunities to do so when these situations did occur. Intervention behaviors varied by important demographic characteristics such as gender, age, attitudes toward sexual violence,, the nature of the situation. Younger female students, with lower levels of rape myth acceptance, who had previously engaged in bystander intervention behaviors were more likely to report intentions to intervene in future risky situations,, female international students reported fewer missed opportunities for intervention. The most common barrier to intervention for identified missed opportunities was a failure to recognize situations as having a potential risk for sexual violence,, students were most likely to intervene in situations when the opportunity to help a friend in distress arose. This study provides some preliminary empirical evidence about bystander intervention against sexual violence among Australian university students,, identifies unique contexts for intervention, what current barriers to intervention may be.

title: Online dating applications, risk of youth victimization: A lifestyle exposure perspective
authors: Kaakinen, Markus, Koivula, Aki, Savolainen, Iina, Sirola, Anu, Mikkola, Marko, Zych, Izabela, Paek, Hye-Jin, Oksanen, Atte
keywords: adolescents; cybercrime; lifestyle exposure theory; online dating applications; victimization;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Based on lifestyle exposure theory (LET), this study examined online dating application (ODA) use, victimization experiences among adolescents using large cross-national samples of Finnish, American, Spanish,, South Korean young people between ages 15, 18. According to logistic regression analyses in two substudies, ODA use was associated with more likely victimization to online harassment, online sexual harassment,, other cybercrimes, sexual victimization by adults, peers. According to mediation analyses, this relationship was mainly accounted for by the fact that ODA users engage in more risky activities in online communication, information sharing. Attention should be paid to the risks ODAs pose to vulnerable groups, such as young people, with insufficient skills to regulate their social relationships online.

title: Implicit, explicit evaluations of sexual aggression predict subsequent sexually aggressive behavior in a sample of community men
authors: Hermann, Chantal A, Nunes, Kevin L
journal: Sexual abuse: a journal of research, treatment
keywords: evaluations; explicit attitudes; implicit attitudes; rape; sexual aggression against adults;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: The current longitudinal study explored the extent to which implicit, explicit evaluations of sexual aggression predict subsequent sexually aggressive behavior. Participants (248 community men recruited online) completed measures of implicit, explicit evaluations, self-reported sexually aggressive behavior at two time points, approximately 4 months apart. Implicit, explicit evaluations of sexual aggression at Wave 1 had small significant, independent predictive relationships with sexually aggressive behavior at Wave 2, while controlling for sexually aggressive behavior at Wave 1. This is the first study to test whether implicit, explicit evaluations predict subsequent sexually aggressive behavior. Our findings are consistent with the possibility that both implicit, explicit evaluations may be relevant for understanding, preventing subsequent sexually aggressive behavior. If these findings can be replicated, evaluations of sexual aggression should be studied with more rigorous methodology (e.g., experimental design), correctional/forensic populations,, possibly addressed in risk assessment, interventions.

title: Crime victims' experiences of police interviews, their inclination to provide or omit information
authors: Holmberg, Ulf
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This research concerns crime victims' experiences of Swedish police interviews, their inclination to provide or omit information in such interviews. A group of rape or aggravated assault victims, consisting of 178 women, men, answered a questionnaire in this explorative study, which revealed that police officer behaviour in interviews was mainly calm, obliging. Results from factor analyses show that these crime victims perceived police attitudes to be characterised by either dominance or humanity. While being interviewed, crime victims either responded with feelings of anxiety or feelings of being respected, the latter of which encouraged them to be cooperative. Logistic regressions revealed that interviews marked by dominance, responses of anxiety are significantly associated with crime victims who omit information. Interviews marked by humanity, responses of feeling respected,, cooperation are significantly associated with crime victims who provide information.

title: College women's rape awareness, use of commonly advocated risk reduction strategies
authors: Hertzog, Jodie L, Yeilding, R
keywords: Awareness; Colleges; Human Females; Rape; Sexual Abuse; Human; Female; college women; rape awareness; risk reduction strategies; sexual violence; Date, Acquaintance Rape Survey; Risk Behavior Scale; Peer Communication Scale; Sexual Experiences Survey;321\_SA実証研究;CampusCrime
abstract: Despite national efforts to create awareness about acquaintance rape, substance- facilitated sexual assault on college campuses, little empirical research investigates whether college women are incorporating these messages into their social behavior. This exploratory study adds to the existing literature by investigating college women's awareness of rape drugs, incorporation of widely advocated risk reduction strategies, communication with same sex peers about risk, protective factors,, perceptions of vulnerability to sexual violence. One hundred thirty-four women at a metropolitan university in the Midwest completed the web based survey. Findings suggest alcohol use affects the incorporation of risk reduction strategies, while class standing, peer disclosure, sexual assault history, receiving sexual assault education affect perceptions of vulnerability. In addition, perceived vulnerability is positively correlated with same-sex peer communication. Implications for possible prevention initiatives, future research directions are noted. title: University student attitudes to prosocial bystander behaviours
authors: Hennelly, Sarah E, Hussain, Sofia, Hale, Tristan, Cadle, Martha, Brooke, Joanne, Davies, Emma
abstract: Purpose Half of British university students experience assault, harassment behaviours; few report them. Bystander intervention training has been recommended as a means of reducing these behaviours, but there is little evidence about their potential effectiveness in UK contexts. The purpose of this paper is to understand UK students’ attitudes towards reporting, intervening in sexual assault, harassment, hate crimes. Design/methodology/approach A mixed methods cross-sectional survey (n=201; 75.6 per cent women) was conducted in one British university. Open text data were analysed using thematic analysis. Findings Students considered harassment, assault unacceptable,, were confident to intervene in, likely to report incidents. However, fear of backlash was a barrier to intervening, reporting,, they felt that victims should decide whether to report incidents. Students perceived perpetrators as being ignorant about what constitutes consent, harassment, assault. They identified a need for university community education about this, how to report incidents, support peers. Research limitations/implications This cross-sectional survey was conducted at one UK University. The data might not reflect other students’ attitudes,, may be subject to response bias. University community bystander training should be acceptable, report, support systems might be utilised by students. This may have potential to reduce prevalence, increase reporting. Practical implications University community bystander training should be acceptable, report, support systems might be utilised by students. This may have potential to reduce prevalence, increase reporting. Originality/value This is the first study to investigate UK student attitudes to prosocial bystander behaviours.

title: Adding the temporal, spatial aspects of routine activities: A further test of routine activity theory
authors: Groff, Elizabeth R
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Studies; Behavior; Software packages; Simulation; Robbery; Research \& development--R\&D; Law enforcement; Changes;321\_SA実証研究;Security Journal
abstract: Routine activity theory identifies the routine activities of individuals as important to understanding the convergence of elements necessary for a crime to occur. Two recent studies have demonstrated how geographically aware agent-based models can be used to provide a virtual rather than empirical laboratory for testing theory. Those studies trace the development of three versions of a basic street robbery model with different representations of routine activities (random, temporal constraints,, spatio-temporal constraints). This research uses the existing model to test whether the core premise of routine activity theory (i.e., as time away from home increases so will street robbery) holds true under the different versions of activity spaces. The findings indicate that temporal, spatial constraints have separate, unequal influences on the incidence of crime. These results substantiate the key role of spatio-temporal constraints in determining the opportunities for, incidence of street robbery events.

title: Experts’ views on improving the quality of non-stranger rape complainants’ accounts
authors: Gajadhar, Sharita, Bull, Ray
abstract: Recent research consistently indicates that poor justice outcomes for non-stranger rape cases are caused in large part by limitations in the evidential relevance, judicial usefulness of accounts provided by complainants. As direct, other objective corroborating evidence is usually absent, the success of most police investigations, prosecutions of non-stranger rape relies heavily on complainants’ accounts. However, no study to date seems to have directly examined how the evidential relevance, judicial usefulness of such accounts can be improved. The present study explored the views of 16 American, Australian, British experts who work in the fields of sexual violence, investigative interviewing, criminal justice, on (a) information that needs to be elicited by police interviewers in order to obtain an evidentially relevant account from non-stranger rape complainants during their investigative interview; (b) requirements regarding a judicially useful account provided by non-stranger rape complainants, how these can be achieved;, (c) whether the current level of police interviewers’ knowledge of evidentially relevant, judicially useful accounts employed by them during investigative interviews with non-stranger rape complainants can be improved. And if so, how? Thematic analysis revealed three broad areas for improvements: (i) focus police interviewers’ questioning specifically on the legal elements, context of non-stranger rape; (ii) elicit clear, chronological, concise accounts;, (iii) provide evidence-based training, interview guidance. These areas, along with participants’ recommendations, are outlined. The implications of the present study, suggestions for future research are discussed.

title: Reporting Sexual Victimization to the Police, Others: Results From a National-Level Study of College Women
authors: Fisher, Bonnie S, Daigle, Leah E, Cullen, Francis T, Turner, Michael G, Bartol, Curt R, Bartol, Anne M

keywords: reporting sexual victimization; police; third parties; college women; rape; sexual assault; Abuse Reporting; College Students; Human Females; Sex Offenses; Victimization; Police Personnel; Natl crime surveys;321\_SA実証研究;CampusCrime
abstract: Figures have revealed that the majority of female rape, sexual assault victims are between the ages of 16, 24 (Rennison, 1999). It is not surprising, then, that considerable attention has been given to the sexual victimization of college women. Existing research has shown that college women are at an elevated risk for victimization. This study attempted to build on existing information in several ways. First, this study analyzed national-level data with detailed measures to uncover sexual victimization-reporting practices by college women. A second advance this study attempted to make was methodological, by employing a two-stage measurement strategy used by the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS). Third, this study examined the likelihood of reporting across multiple forms of sexual victimization. Fourth, it focused simultaneously on characteristics of offenders, victims,, incidents that influence reporting of sexual victimization, explored the impact of multiple factors within each category. Fifth, this study investigated reporting to police as well as reporting to campus officials, to third parties. Finally, the results of this study have implications for the ongoing debate between feminist, conservative scholars over the extent to which sexual victimization is a problem that warrants intervention. Accordingly, the closing sections of this article discuss the salience of the findings for these competing perspectives.
