keywords: Air Force; intimate partner violence; partner maltreatment; routine activities theory; spouse abuse; Psychology; Empirical Study; Quantitative Study; Human; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Air Force Personnel; Spouses; Daily Activities; US; article; 3800:Military Psychology; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior; Prevalence; Military Personnel; United States; Humans; Periodicity; Male; Time; Holidays; Female; Substance-Related Disorders; Seasons; Alcoholic Intoxication; Databases, Factual;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Routine activities (RA) theory posits that changes in people's typical daily activities covary with increases or decreases in criminal behaviors, including, but not limited to, partner maltreatment. Using a large clinical database, we examined temporal variations among 24,460 incidents of confirmed partner maltreatment across an 11-year period within the U.S. Air Force (USAF). Specifically, we created regression models that predicted the number of partner maltreatment incidents per day. In addition to several control variables, we coded temporal variables for days of the week, month, year,, several significant days (e.g., holidays, Super Bowl Sunday), which allowed us to examine the independent influence of these variables on partner maltreatment prevalence. While accounting for the influence of all other study variables, we observed significant increases in partner maltreatment for weekend days, New Year's Day, Independence Day,, Super Bowl Sunday. Similar results were found for partner maltreatment incidents involving offender alcohol/drug use. Furthermore, the proportion of incidents involving offender alcohol/drug use increased on New Year's Day, Independence Day. Consistent with RA theory, data from civilian samples, the current results indicate that certain days are associated with increased incidents of partner maltreatment within the USAF. These findings should be used to inform future preventive efforts.

title: Changes in economic hardship, intimate partner violence: A family stress framework
authors: Lucero, Jessica L, Lim, Sojung, Santiago, Anna Maria
keywords: Psychology; Intimate partner violence; Economic hardship; Family stress; Fragile families; Child well-being; Studies; Domestic violence; Families \& family life; Stress; Psychological aspects; Social research; Economic conditions; United States--US; 1220:Social trends \& culture; 9190:United States; 9130:Experimental/theoretical; 1110:Economic conditions \& forecasts; 5400:Research \& development;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Issue Title: Special Section: Uneven Recoveries from the Great Recession While recent studies underscore how financial stress, lack of tangible assets significantly increase the odds of intimate partner violence (IPV) among couples, little is known about these effects over time. Theoretically informed by family stress theory, this study examines the influence of changing subjective reports of economic hardship over time on the risk for IPV. Specifically, we test two hypotheses: (1) change in economic hardship significantly predicts IPV; and, specifically, (2) increased economic hardship or unstable economic conditions increases the risk of IPV. Using longitudinal data from the Fragile Families, Child Well-being Study, we assess the incidence of IPV for 941 women in committed relationships. Results from our logistic regression analyses suggest that after controlling for numerous demographic factors, women who never experienced economic hardship had lower odds of experiencing IPV than those who did. Further, women who experienced high levels of economic hardship over time had the highest odds of experiencing IPV. However, the effects of changing economic hardship on IPV were attenuated once maternal depression, parenting stress were controlled. Results are discussed in terms of practice, policy implications.

title: Mediating effects of risk perception on association between social support, coping with COVID-19: An online survey
authors: Li, Dian-Jeng, Ko, Nai-Ying, Chang, Yu-Ping, Yen, Cheng-Fang, Chen, Yi-Lung

abstract: Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is a novel infectious disease which has had a great impact on the public. Further investigations are, therefore, needed to investigate how the public copes with COVID-19. This study aimed to develop a model to estimate the mediating effects of risk perception, confidence on the association between perceived social support, active coping with the COVID-19 pandemic among people in Taiwan. The data of 1970 participants recruited from a Facebook advertisement were analyzed. Structural equation modeling was used to verify the direct, indirect effects between variables. The mediation model demonstrated that lower perceived social support was significantly associated with a higher level of active coping with COVID-19,, this was mediated by a higher level of risk perception. The present study identified the importance of risk perception on the public's coping strategies during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Banking options, neighborhood crime: Does fringe banking increase neighborhood crime?

abstract: In the past few years, scholars interested in neighborhoods, crime have turned their attention to the role of neighborhood organizations. Recently, (Kubrin, Squires, Graves,, Ousey, Criminology \& Public Policy , 10(2), 437–466, 2011 ) examined the impact of payday lenders on neighborhood crime. title: Residential foreclosure rates, calls for service for domestic disputes: An exploratory analysis
authors: Lersch, Kim, Sellers, Christine, Cromwell, Paul

abstract: Over the past 10 years the U.S. has experienced a sharp increase in the number of foreclosures. The problem has been particularly severe in a number of states, including Florida. title: Revisiting the link between economic distress, race,, domestic violence
authors: Leguizamon, J Sebastian, Leguizamon, Susane, Howden, Wesley

abstract: Male unemployment may decrease the incidence of domestic violence, due to loss of economic power in the relationship, or increase the incidence of domestic violence, due to emotional outbursts fueled by increased stress. We hypothesize that Black men may face a greater loss of expected future earnings after an unemployment shock due to a more unfavorable labor market relative to White men. Consequently, we would expect that Black men would, on net, exhibit a greater reduction (or a smaller increase) in incidences of domestic violence following an employment shock. This study uses mass layoff events reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) at the county level (N = 3,377) for the years 2003-2008. Mass layoff events occur when a firm lays off at least 50 workers, are uncorrelated with individual-level characteristics (N = 28,939 events, affecting N = 5,337,481 individuals). Domestic violence data are taken from the National Archive of Criminal Justice, defined as occurring when an accused perpetrator is charged, but not necessarily convicted. We use a multivariate regression model to estimate how differences in the change in reported incidences of domestic violence by race correlate with changes in mass layoffs by race. We control for the poverty rate, real per capita income, percent Black, percent women,, percent of females laid off. The standard errors are clustered at the county level, include county, time dummies to account for regional, time specific trends. We observe that an increase in the number of Blacks subject to a mass layoff event do exert a negative associated influence on domestic violence while layoffs of White men exert a positive influence. Our results shed light on how the influence of economic uncertainty on incidences of domestic violence has been found to be positive in some previous research but negative in other research.

title: Clinically significant fear, anxiety of COVID-19: A psychometric examination of the Coronavirus Anxiety Scale
authors: Lee, Sherman A, Mathis, Amanda A, Jobe, Mary C, Pappalardo, Emily A

abstract: The present study examined the psychometric properties of the Coronavirus Anxiety Scale (CAS) using an online survey of 398 adult Amazon MTurk workers in the U.S. Confirmatory factor analyses demonstrated that the CAS measures a reliable (α = 0.92), unidimensional construct with a structure that was shown to be invariant across gender, race,, age. Construct validity was demonstrated with correlations between CAS scores, demographics, coronavirus diagnosis, history of anxiety, coronavirus fear, functional impairment, alcohol/drug coping, religious coping, hopelessness, suicidal ideation, as well as social attitudes (e.g., satisfaction with President Trump). The CAS also demonstrated solid discrimination ability for functional impairment (AUC =0.88), while the original cut score of ≥9 (76\% sensitivity, 90\% specificity) showed the strongest diagnostic effectiveness among scores. Overall, these findings are largely consistent with the results of the first CAS investigation, support the validity of this mental health screener for COVID-19 related research, practice.

title: Working, but not for a living: a longitudinal study on the psychological consequences of economic vulnerability among German employees
authors: Klug, Katharina, Selenko, Eva, Gerlitz, Jean-Yves
journal: European journal of work, organizational psychology
abstract: ABSTRACTDespite the rise of in-work poverty across Europe, the psychological consequences of individual economic vulnerability are still rather unknown. Drawing on both objective, subjective conceptualizations of economic vulnerability, we investigate the effects of individual low labour income, perceived financial strain on mental well-being. We argue that economic vulnerability restricts workers? agency, propose sense of control as a mediator in the relationship between economic vulnerability, mental well-being ? irrespective of the household?s financial situation. Multilevel analyses across 19 years based on a sample of N = 7,107 employed adults from the German Socio-economic Panel (SOEP) demonstrated that a) persons reporting low income, higher financial strain showed lower health, life satisfaction,, b) intra-individual changes in income, financial strain were associated with corresponding changes in mental health, life satisfaction, respectively. These relationships were mediated by sense of control, both on the between-, the within-person level. The findings emphasize the importance of individual income, financial strain for mental well-being,, underline sense of control as an important psychological mechanism explaining individual consequences of economic vulnerability.

authors: Kelley, Heather H, LeBaron, Ashley B, Hill, E Jeffrey

abstract: This study explores the negative relationship between financial stress, marital quality, examines couple communication as a moderator in this relationship. Using a sample of 373 married U.S. couples from the Flourishing Families Project, an Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) was run to determine the influence of husbands’, wives’ financial stress on both their own, their partner’s reports of marital quality. Results found negative associations between both actor, partner reports of financial stress, marital quality. Couple communication did not moderate the associations between husbands’, wives’ financial stress, wives’ marital quality. However, it did moderate the negative associations between both husbands’, wives’ financial stress, husbands’ marital quality. Specifically, the deleterious relationship of financial stress to marital quality for husbands was significantly less severe when coupled with positive couple communication. title: Changes in intimate partner violence during the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic in the USA
authors: Jetelina, Katelyn K, Knell, Gregory, Molsberry, Rebecca J

abstract: The objective of this study is to describe intimate partner violence (IPV) severity, types of victimization during the early states of the COVID19 pandemic. A survey was distributed through social media, email distribution lists. The survey was open for 14 days in April 2020, 2441 participated. Information on IPV, COVID19-related IPV severity, sociodemographics,, COVID19-related behaviors (eg, job loss) were collected. Regression models were used to evaluate COVID19-related IPV severity across victimization types, sociodemographics. 18\% screened positive for IPV. Among the respondents that screened positive, 54\% stated the victimization remained the same since the COVID19 outbreak, while 17\% stated it worsened, 30\% stated it got better. The odds of worsening victimization during the pandemic was significantly higher among physical, sexual violence. While the majority of IPV participants reported victimization to remain the same, sexual, physical violence was exacerbated during the early stages of the pandemic. Addressing victimization during the pandemic (and beyond) must be multi-sectorial.

title: Impact of the Great Recession on mental health, substance use, violence in families with children: A systematic review of the evidence
authors: Hiilamo, Aapo, Hiilamo, Heikki, Ristikari, Tiina, Virtanen, Petri
keywords: great recession; mental health; substance use; violence; families; children; COVID-19 pandemic; Domestic Violence; Drug Usage; Economy; Family; Pandemics; Parents; COVID-19;322\_経済圧力
abstract: •We summarised the evidence on the Great Recession, mental health, substance use, violence in families with children.•Peer-reviewed articles published in English between January 2010, August 2020 were identified.•High-quality studies provided evidence that the economic recession of 2008 did hurt children’s mental wellbeing.•Evidence on substance use, child maltreatment was more uncertain.•Counter-cyclical investments in social, education, health services targeted also at families with children are crucial in alleviating human suffering in economic recessions. This review summarises the existing evidence on the effects of the Great Recession on mental health, substance use, violence in families with children, discusses the policy, service-system implications of this evidence. Peer-reviewed articles published in English between January 2010, August 2020 were identified through a systematic search of the main scientific databases, citation records,, manual searches of individual journal sites. Studies focusing on children, or their parents, that included an exposure variable measuring the Great Recession, had an outcome related to mental health, substance use or violence were included. A risk of bias assessment, narrative synthesis were provided. In total 40 studies were analysed. Most of the studies were deemed to have a moderate risk of bias (29), nine had a high risk of bias, two had a low risk of bias. High-quality studies provided evidence that the economic recession of 2008 (termed ‘the Great Recession’ in this paper) did hurt children’s mental wellbeing. The evidence regarding substance use in families with children was scarce but there were some indications that the recession increased drug, alcohol use among economically vulnerable subgroups. Studies with individual level data from the US showed that the Great Recession increased the risk of child maltreatment, but little evidence of this was found in several ecological, population level time-trend analyses. Counter-cyclical investments in, further integration of social, education, health services targeted not only at adults but also at families with children are crucial in alleviating human suffering in economic recessions. Subsequent research with the combination of high-quality individual, aggregated level data is warranted to assess the potential effects of recessions on substance use, violence in families with children. During the unprecedented economic changes following the COVID-19 pandemic, it is crucial to monitor timely mental health, substance use, violence in families at risk.

title: Measuring financial strain in the lives of survivors of intimate partner violence
authors: Hetling, Andrea, Stylianou, Amanda Mathisen, Postmus, Judy L

abstract: Agencies serving survivors of intimate partner violence (IPV) often include economic empowerment programs, approaches as a way to assist survivors struggling with avoiding poverty, gaining financial independence. Indeed, survivors' ability to manage their finances, any financial stress or strain should also be assessed to fully understand their needs. The Financial Strain Survey (FSS) provides a useful tool for screening, understanding survivors' complex financial needs. Using data from 457 IPV survivors from seven U.S. states, Puerto Rico, the current study evaluates the factor structure, reliability,, validity of using the FSS with IPV survivors. Findings indicate that the FSS is a reliable instrument for use with IPV survivors. The conclusion discusses the FSS as a practical tool for both practice, research with this population.

title: Do psychiatric patients experience more psychiatric symptoms during COVID-19 pandemic, lockdown? A case-control study with service, research implications for immunopsychiatry
authors: Hao, Fengyi, Tan, Wanqiu, Jiang, Li, Zhang, Ling, Zhao, Xinling, Zou, Yiran, Hu, Yirong, Luo, Xi, Jiang, Xiaojiang, McIntyre, Roger S, Tran, Bach, Sun, Jiaqian, Zhang, Zhisong, Ho, Roger, Ho, Cyrus, Tam, Wilson
keywords: Anxiety; COVID-19; Coronavirus; Depression; Epidemic; Immunopsychiatry; Insomnia; Lockdown; PTSD; Pandemic; Psychiatric illness; Stress; Suicide;322\_経済圧力
abstract: This study aimed to assess, compare the immediate stress, psychological impact experienced by people with, without psychiatric illnesses during the peak of 2019 coronavirus disease (COVID-19) epidemic with strict lockdown measures. Seventy-six psychiatric patients, 109 healthy control subjects were recruited from Chongqing, China, completed a survey on demographic data, physical symptoms during the past 14 days, a range of psychiatric symptoms using the Impact of Event Scale-Revised (IES-R), Depression, Anxiety, Stress Scale (DASS-21), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI). IES-R measures PTSD symptoms in survivorship after an event. DASS-21 is based on tripartite model of psychopathology that comprise a general distress construct with distinct characteristics. The mean IES-R, DASS-21 anxiety, depression, stress subscale, ISI scores were higher in psychiatric patients than healthy controls (p < 0.001). Serious worries about their physical health, anger, impulsivity, intense suicidal ideation were significantly higher in psychiatric patients than healthy controls (p < 0.05). More than one-third of psychiatric patients might fulfil the diagnostic criteria post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). More than one-quarter of psychiatric patients suffered from moderately severe to severe insomnia. Respondents who reported no change, poor or worse physical health status, had a psychiatric illness were significantly more likely to have higher mean IES-R, DASS depression, anxiety, stress subscale scores, ISI scores (p < 0.05). This study confirms the severity of negative psychological impact on psychiatric patients during the COVID-19 epidemic with strict lockdown measures. Understanding the psychological impact on psychiatric patients during the COVID-19 pandemic has the potential to provide insight into how to develop a new immunopsychiatry service. Further research is required to compare pro-inflammatory cytokines between psychiatric patients, healthy controls during the pandemic.

title: Two-way risk communication, public value consensus,, citizens’ policy compliance willingness about COVID-19: Multilevel analysis based on a nudge view
authors: Guan, Bin, Bao, Guoxian, Liu, Qingchuan, Raymond, Raduziner Gary
abstract: COVID-19 has spawned a surge in the number of public epidemic prevention policies. More important than active policy-making is how to increase citizens’ policy compliance willingness. Based on public value theory, nudge theory, this study adopts a multilevel mediation, moderation model to analyze the relationships among the government’s authoritarian control, two-way risk communication, public value consensus, nudge,, citizens’ policy compliance willingness. A sample of 2,616 citizens nested in 86 Chinese cities was collected. The study found that (a) local governments can improve citizens’ policy compliance willingness by adopting both “stick” (authoritarian control), “sermon” (two-way risk communication) policies, whereas two-way risk communication demonstrates a uniquely positive effect on public value consensus;, (b) the effect of two-way risk communication on policy compliance willingness is mediated by public value consensus. By enhancing public value consensus, two-way risk communication helps establish consensus between citizens, the government on “what needs/needs not to be done”, “what should/should not be done” to slow down the pandemic, thus coalescing efforts in a cooperative spirit; (c) nudge intervention positively moderates the effect of two-way risk communication on public value consensus, but has no effect on the authoritarian control–policy compliance willingness relationship. In other words, nudge intervention is a better companion to “sermons,” not “sticks.” Findings of the nuanced relationship manifested the differentiated effect of authoritarian control, two-way risk communication on citizens’ policy compliance willingness during a pandemic. The results provide theoretical implications for scholars to unlock the “black box” of public values, practical implications for strategies from behavioral public administration aspects to curb the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Social suffering, the psychological impact of structural violence, economic oppression in an ongoing conflict setting: The Gaza Strip
authors: Hammad, Jeyda, Tribe, Rachel
keywords: economic oppression; occupied Palestinian territories; political conflict; psychosocial wellbeing; structural violence;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Structural violence, economic oppression (e.g. control over resources, politically engineered poverty, unemployment) are common features of warfare, yet there is a lack of research exploring the impact this has on civilian wellbeing in conflict-affected areas. This study, embedded within a human rights, community liberation psychology framework, aims to address this need by studying young Palestinian university graduates living under military blockade, occupation in the Gaza Strip. Semi-structured interviews were conducted. Thematic analysis indicated that economic, political domains adversely affected multiple aspects of civilian life, wellbeing. The findings revealed the deleterious effects of structural violence, economic oppression which created: human insecurity; poor psychological wellbeing, quality of life; existential, psychological, social suffering; humiliation; injuries to dignity; multiple losses;, led to life being experienced as 'on hold'. Local expressions, idioms to express distress were identified. The findings contributed to unique insights regarding how continual, systemic,, structural oppression can be potentially more psychologically detrimental than specific incidents of conflict, violence. The implications, the relevance of the findings to mental health, disaster relief are considered. Interventions providing human security, economic security should be prioritised.

title: Prospective interactive influence of financial strain, emotional nonacceptance on problematic alcohol use during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Gratz, Kim L, Scamaldo, Kayla M, Vidaña, Ariana G, Richmond, Julia R, Tull, Matthew T
journal: The American journal of drug, alcohol abuse
keywords: COVID-19; alcohol use; economic problems; emotion regulation; financial strain;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Background: Researchers have highlighted the risk for alcohol use problems in the context of COVID-19, although the factors associated with this risk remain unclear.Objectives: This study examined the prospective relation of baseline financial strain (reported at the beginning of the pandemic) to problematic alcohol use one month later, as well as the moderating role of emotional nonacceptance. We hypothesized that financial strain would be more strongly associated with problematic alcohol use one month later among participants with high (vs. mean or low) levels of nonacceptance.Methods: Shortly after COVID-19 was declared a pandemic by the WHO, national emergency by the U.S. President (on March 11, 13, 2020, respectively), a U.S. nationwide community sample completed a prospective online study, including an initial assessment from March 27-April 5, 2020, a one-month follow-up from April 27-May 21. Measures included the Family Economic Strain Scale, Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale,, Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test. Participants included 254 adults reporting some alcohol use (50.4\% women; mean age = 41.8).Results: Baseline financial strain was significantly positively associated with problematic alcohol use one month later only among participants with high (b =.06, SE =.03, p =.037) versus mean (b =.01, SE =.02, p =.677) or low (b = -.04, SE =.02, p =.110) emotional nonacceptance.Conclusion: Individuals experiencing financial strain in the context of COVID-19 may be at risk for problematic alcohol use if they are not accepting of their emotional distress.

title: The relationship between stress, strain, social capital
authors: Gächter, Martin, Savage, Davd A, Torgler, Benno

abstract: PurposeThe purpose of this study is to examine the relationship of social capital with the negative externalities associated with stress, or the psychological, physiological strains experienced by police officers.Design/methodology/approachUsing data collected in 1999 from a survey of Baltimore Police officers designed to examine questions about the relationship between police stress, domestic violence in police families, using multivariate regression analysis, the paper focuses on five different proxies for stress, strain,, two proxies for social capital, conducting several robustness checks.FindingsResults show that an increase in social capital is significantly correlated to a decrease in the level of strain, in the psychological, physical, burnout, health areas.Research limitations/implicationsWhile this study examines the social capital/strain relationship with US officers, more research is needed, as these findings may not extrapolate well into other national settings. Additionally, the data may be dated and, as major changes, events have occurred since the survey, a newer study of officers would be needed to observe whether these changes have had significant impact.Practical implicationsFrom a policy perspective, the findings suggest that stress reduction programs should actively engage employees to build stronger social networks.Originality/valueThis study comprehensively examines the ability of social capital at negating the impacts of strains,, significantly reduces the impact of major trauma events. This paper adds to the literature as there are few multivariate analyses of the social capital/strain relationship.

title: Social capital dimensions are differentially associated with COVID-19 vaccinations, masks,, physical distancing
authors: Ferwana, Ibtihal, Varshney, Lav R
abstract: BACKGROUND: Social capital has been associated with health outcomes in communities, can explain variations in different geographic localities. Social capital has also been associated with behaviors that promote better health, reduce the impacts of diseases. During the COVID-19 pandemic, social distancing, face masking,, vaccination have all been essential in controlling contagion. These behaviors have not been uniformly adopted by communities in the United States. Using different facets of social capital to explain the differences in public behaviors among communities during pandemics is lacking. OBJECTIVE: This study examines the relationship among public health behavior-vaccination, face masking,, physical distancing-during COVID-19 pandemic, social capital indices in counties in the United States. METHODS: We used publicly available vaccination data as of June 2021, face masking data in July 2020,, mobility data from mobile phones movements from the end of March 2020. Then, correlation analysis was conducted with county-level social capital index, its subindices (family unity, community health, institutional health,, collective efficacy) that were obtained from the Social Capital Project by the United States Senate. RESULTS: We found the social capital index, its subindices differentially correlate with different public health behaviors. Vaccination is associated with institutional health: positively with fully vaccinated population, negatively with vaccination hesitancy. Also, wearing masks negatively associates with community health, whereases reduced mobility associates with better community health. Further, residential mobility positively associates with family unity. By comparing correlation coefficients, we find that social capital, its subindices have largest effect sizes on vaccination, residential mobility. CONCLUSION: Our results show that different facets of social capital are significantly associated with adoption of protective behaviors, e.g., social distancing, face masking,, vaccination. As such, our results suggest that differential facets of social capital imply a Swiss cheese model of pandemic control planning where, e.g., institutional health, community health, provide partially overlapping behavioral benefits.

abstract: The present study is a systematic review of empirical literature from the last 35 years on families' responses to economic distress in the context of macroeconomic crises. Thirty-nine studies published between 1983, 2015 in 12 countries were identified, resulting in 3 main findings. First, economic distress was associated with negative changes in family dynamics, specifically couple relationships, parenting. Second, protective factors were found to buffer the adverse effects of economic distress on family, individual outcomes. Third, the results suggest that individual responses to macroeconomic crises may be moderated by sex. Implications for future research encompass using validated assessment instruments, including participants beyond 2-parent families with adolescent children, conducting both longitudinal, qualitative studies that focus on the processes, meanings of adaptation within this risk context. Conclusions highlighted the need to assist families dealing with macroeconomic crises' demands, encouraging the development, validation of macrosystemic intervention programs. authors: Falconier, Mariana K, Jackson, Jeffrey B

abstract: The purpose of this meta-analysis was to quantitatively consolidate the literature on the association between economic strain, couple relationship functioning (negative interactions, positive interactions, satisfaction,, stability) using the family economic stress model (FESM; Conger, Ge, \& Lorenz, 1994) as a theoretical framework, evaluate report, methodological,, sociodemographic factors for moderating effects. Consistent with FESM, results from 29 independent samples with a combined total of 34,007 participants indicated a moderate negative relationship between economic strain, relationship functioning ( r = −.24). Negative interaction was positively associated with economic strain ( r = .25), whereas positive interactions ( r = −.17), satisfaction ( r = −.25),, stability ( r = −.20) were negatively associated with economic strain. Moderator analyses indicated no gender differences but significant effects of some report, sociodemographic factors (e.g., income level, nationality). Clinical, research implications are discussed. title: Crime at home, in the streets: the relationship between family, stranger violence
authors: Fagan, J, Wexler, S
keywords: Sociology; Families \& family life; Behavior; Violent crime; Socialization; Sex roles; Sex crimes; Law enforcement; Criminal justice; Child welfare; Assaults; Humans; Risk Factors; Adult; Child; Interpersonal Relations; Child Abuse -- psychology; Violence; Social Environment; Criminal Psychology; Aggression -- psychology; Spouse Abuse -- psychology;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Research, theory on violent behavior have treated aggression between intimates, aggression between strangers as separate phenomena. Major criminological works on violence, aggression have generally overlooked violence in the home. As a result, independent, distinct bodies of theoretical, practical knowledge exist regarding family violence, aggression toward strangers,, the relationship between family violence, violence directed against strangers is little understood. Estimates of the intersection of these behaviors vary extensively. Severity of domestic violence is associated with violence outside the home. Exposure to violence as a child consistently emerges as a strong explanatory factor for both domestic violence, the behavior of ``generally'' violent men. Behavior patterns appear to shift over time, from domestic violence only to violence toward both strangers, family members. However, an integrated theory of violent behavior by males provides explanations of both stranger, family violence. Early childhood socialization toward violence, modified by social, cultural supports during adolescence, adulthood, suggests a social learning paradigm. Hypotheses are developed that integrate, unify theories of stranger, family violence.

authors: Reeb, Ben T, Conger, Katherine J, Martin, Monica J

abstract: The effects of community characteristics on well-being were examined among 709 African American women. Direct, moderating effects of neighborhood characteristics on distress were tested. Aggregate-level ratings of neighborhood cohesion, disorder were significantly related to distress, although the relation between cohesion, distress became nonsignificant when individual risk factors were statistically controlled. Magnusson \& N. S. Endler, 1977 ). Community cohesion intensified the benefits of a positive life outlook. authors: Chesterman, A, de Battista, M, Causse, E

abstract: In France, the COVID-19 pandemic, ensuing lockdown measures have created unprecedented circumstances that increase stress, anxiety, thus leading individuals experiencing home confinement to adopt various coping strategies that contribute to building resilience. Given the novelty, recency of the COVID-19 lockdown, factors of coping, resilience in this specific context of home confinement remain undefined. Based on some recent observations, we conducted a study on a convenience sample in France (N = 809) in order to investigate two potential factors of lockdown resilience, coping: social position, household affordances, while also exploring some complementary hypotheses based on the literature. Social position, household affordances were identified as significant predictors of lockdown coping, resilience,, low social position was found to coincide with less social support coping strategies. Results are discussed in relation to the theory, the limits identified in this study. Recommendations are made for potential second waves of COVID-19 spread or similar pandemics in the future.

authors: Buttell, Frederick, Cannon, Clare E B, Rose, Katherine, Ferreira, Regardt J

abstract: COVID-19 is a pandemic event not seen in a century. This research aims to identify the group differences regarding resilience, perceived stress for those who identified as single, in a relationship not experiencing intimate partner violence (IPV),, those in a relationship experiencing IPV during the COVID-19 pandemic. This study uses a cross-sectional design, with purposive snowball sampling, for primary survey data collected over 10 weeks starting the first week in April 2020 ( n = 374). Participants completed a self-administered questionnaire on demographics, behavioral factors. Resilience was assessed using the 10-item Connor Davidson Resilience Scale,, perceived stress was assessed using the 10-item Perceived Stress Scale. Two one-way analysis of variance procedures were performed to identify statistically significant differences across 3 groups, those not in a relationship, those in a relationship not experiencing IPV,, those in a relationship, experiencing IPV. Analyses indicate that those experiencing IPV reported lower resilience, greater perceived stress. Analyses also show those in the experiencing IPV group were statistically significantly different from those in a relationship without IPV, those in the single group with respect to resilience. Those in the IPV experiences group were also statistically significantly different from the group of participants in relationships without reported IPV experiences with respect to perceived stress. These findings provide empirical support for the contention that public health measures put in place to combat the spread of COVID-19 might have negative, unintentional consequences for people experiencing IPV, mental health issues. title: The bright, dark sides of social media usage during the COVID-19 pandemic: Survey evidence from Japan
authors: Cato, Susumu, Iida, Takashi, Ishida, Kenji, Ito, Asei, Katsumata, Hiroto, McElwain, Kenneth Mori, Shoji, Masahiro

abstract: The spread of misinformation on the internet regarding the COVID-19 pandemic, such as unproven or fake cures, has been a serious concern. However, the extent to which social media usage affects individuals' health behavior, particularly when reliable information is scarce, is not well understood. This study evaluates the impact of social media usage on individuals' responses to the COVID-19 pandemic, such as demand for necessities, social distancing. We conduct an original online survey of 1804 Japanese respondents in March 2020. Japan is suitable because it confirmed COVID-19 cases earlier than most other countries. Scientific evidence about the coronavirus, protective measures was scarce in the initial pandemic phase, despite the spread of unconfirmed rumors. Our analysis focuses on the usage of Twitter, Facebook,, Instagram. We use the entropy balancing method to control for heterogeneity in observed characteristics between social media users, non-users. The results show that while users are more likely to maintain social distancing practices, they are also more likely to take measures whose reliability is not scientifically confirmed, such as eating fermented soybeans. Although previous studies emphasize the negative effects of social media, our results suggest that it has both bright, dark sides.

abstract: BACKGROUND: Mental health problems are increasingly recognized as a significant, concerning secondary effect of the COVID-19 pandemic. Research on previous epidemics/pandemics suggest that families, particularly mothers, may be at increased risk, but this population has yet to be examined. The current study (1) described prevalence rates of maternal depressive, anxiety symptoms from an online convenience sample during the COVID-19 pandemic, (2) identified risk, protective factors for elevated symptoms,, (3) described current mental health service use, barriers. METHODS: Participants (N = 641) were mothers of children age 0-8 years, including expectant mothers. Mothers completed an online survey assessing mental health, sociodemographic information,, COVID-19-related variables. RESULTS: Clinically-relevant depression was indicated in 33.16\%, 42.55\%,, 43.37\% of mothers of children age 0-18 months, 18 months to 4 years,, 5 to 8 years, respectively. Prevalence of anxiety was 36.27\%, 32.62\%,, 29.59\% for mothers across age groups, respectively. Binary logistic regressions indicated significant associations between risk factors, depression/anxiety across child age groups. LIMITATIONS: Cross-sectional data was used to describe maternal mental health problems during COVID-19 limiting the ability to make inferences about the long-term impact of maternal depression, anxiety on family well-being. CONCLUSIONS: Maternal depression, anxiety appear to be elevated in the context of COVID-19 compared to previously reported population norms. Identified risk factors for depression, anxiety across different child age ranges can inform targeted early intervention strategies to prevent long-term impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on family well-being, child development.

title: Safely examining complex dynamics of intimate partner violence
authors: Burge, Sandra K, Becho, Johanna, Ferrer, Robert L, Wood, Robert C, Talamantes, Melissa, Katerndahl, David A
journal: Families, systems \& health: the journal of collaborative family healthcare
keywords: spouse abuse; battered women; domestic violence; nonlinear dynamics; longitudinal studies; research methods; participant safety; recruitment; retention; Medical Sciences; Empirical Study; Longitudinal Study; Quantitative Study; Human; Female; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Young Adulthood (18-29 yrs); Thirties (30-39 yrs); Middle Age (40-64 yrs); Battered Females; Experimental Subjects; Methodology; Intimate Partner Violence; Experimentation; Data Collection; Safety; article; US; 2260:Research Methods \& Experimental Design; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior; Humans; Middle Aged; Adult; Male; Spouses; Interpersonal Relations;322\_経済圧力
abstract: The overall goal of this study is to use complexity science to gain a deeper understanding of the nonlinear day-to-day dynamics of intimate partner violence, with implications for clinical interventions. This report describes research methods for gathering information about partner violence in real time, assesses recruitment, retention, adherence to study protocol, data validity,, participant safety. Research assistants enrolled 200 women in moderately violent intimate relationships, asked them to report about their relationships every day for 12 weeks. Daily, participants telephoned an Interactive Voice Response (IVR) system, responded to 34 survey questions. They also completed baseline, end-of-study surveys, maintained telephone contact with the study team weekly. Forty-two participants completed qualitative end-of-study interviews to describe their relationships, the impact of the study on their lives. Of 200 enrollees, 145 women provided enough data for nonlinear analyses, averaging 63.5 daily reports of 84 possible. Participants submitted 9,201 daily reports, documenting partner's verbal or physical aggression on 39.4\% of days,, their own aggression on 23.1\%. Two women were withdrawn from the study for safety reasons; the remainder reported that study participation posed no additional threat. Eighty women sought assistance from community resources. Violence severity did not appear to change over the 12 weeks. The research team successfully, safely recruited, retained 145 women who provided valuable data for a study of complex dynamics of intimate partner violence.

title: Associations among state-level physical distancing measures, suicidal thoughts, behaviors among U.S. adults during the early COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Bryan, Craig J, Bryan, Annabelle O, Baker, Justin C
keywords: COVID-19; coronavirus; stress; suicide;322\_経済圧力
abstract: PURPOSE: The purpose of this study was to identify leading sources of stress, describe rates of mental health outcomes,, examine their associations among U.S. adults during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic. METHOD: In a cross-sectional, general population survey conducted from March 18 to April 4, 2020, U.S. adults (n = 10,625) were recruited through Qualtrics Panels using quota sampling methods. RESULTS: Life stressors, probable depression, past-month suicide ideation,, past-month suicide attempts were not elevated among participants subject to state-level stay-at-home orders and/or large gathering bans. Multiple life stressors were associated with increased rates of probable depression. Past-month suicide ideation was significantly higher among participants reporting ongoing arguments with a partner, serious legal problems. Past-month suicide attempt was significantly higher among participants reporting concerns about a life-threatening illness or injury, but was significantly lower among participants reporting an unexpected bill or expense. CONCLUSIONS: Results failed to support the conclusion that physical distancing measures are correlated with worse mental health outcomes. Concerns about life-threatening illness or injury were uniquely associated with increased risk of suicide attempt.

title: Strain, coping,, socioeconomic status: Coping histories, present choices
authors: Botchkovar, Ekaterina V, Tittle, Charles R, Antonaccio, Olena
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Socioeconomic factors; Criminology; Households;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Objectives Using household survey data from three major cities in foreign countries, we add to research concerning General Strain Theory (GST) by focusing on aspects that have been ignored or under-researched. First, we address questions concerning SES variations in the operation of the processes of GST, with particular focus on whether various relationships specified by the theory are more likely in the lower SES group. Second, we explore the extent to which prior coping strategies influence subsequent coping choices. Finally, we seek to determine the links between SES, coping histories,, subsequent coping choices. Methods The study analyzes the effects of past, contemporaneous strain/negative emotions, prior coping efforts on various coping strategies across three SES groupings using negative binomial, ordered logit,, OLS regression. Results We find that, with some variations, the basic processes of GST are operative across all SES categories. However, whereas strain appears to have a moderate association with alcohol-related, criminal coping strategies, avoidant coping appears to be largely irrelevant for anybody who faces strain. Our data also demonstrate that specific forms of prior coping partially influence the types of coping employed later. But, with few exceptions, these effects are not more pronounced among those of lower SES. Conclusion In sum, our findings suggest that individuals in various SES groupings may prefer certain types of coping, whereas different types of attempted coping may predispose individuals to specific forms of subsequent adaptation.

title: Using couple data to determine domestic violence rates: an attempt to replicate previous work

abstract: Research methodology using only one spouse to report for the couple has been questioned. Szinovacz (1983) reported higher rates of violence when both spouses responded to six items on Straus's Conflict Tactics Scale (CTS). The purpose of this study was to replicate her methodology by using all items measuring severe violence in the latest CTS scale with 94 military couples, to see if couple reports of violence indicated higher rates of violence compared to individual spouses' reports. Results were similar to Szinovacz's findings,, support the advisability of using both spouses to report violence in marriages.

title: Suffering in silence: How COVID-19 school closures inhibit the reporting of child maltreatment
authors: Baron, E Jason, Goldstein, Ezra G, Wallace, Cullen T
keywords: COVID-19; Child maltreatment; School closures;322\_経済圧力
abstract: To combat the spread of COVID-19, many primary, secondary schools in the United States canceled classes, moved instruction online. This study examines an unexplored consequence of COVID-19 school closures: the broken link between child maltreatment victims, the number one source of reported maltreatment allegations-school personnel. Using current, county-level data from Florida, we estimate a counterfactual distribution of child maltreatment allegations for March, April 2020, the first two months in which Florida schools closed. While one would expect the financial, mental,, physical stress due to COVID-19 to result in additional child maltreatment cases, we find that the actual number of reported allegations was approximately 15,000 lower (27\%) than expected for these two months. We leverage a detailed dataset of school district staffing, spending to show that the observed decline in allegations was largely driven by school closures. Finally, we discuss policy implications of our findings for the debate surrounding school reopenings, suggest a number of responses that may mitigate this hidden cost of school closures.

title: ‘It feels like money’s just flying out the window’: financial security, stress, health in gentrifying neighborhoods
authors: Binet, Andrew, Zayas del Rio, Gabriela, Arcaya, Mariana, Roderigues, Gail, Gavin, Vedette
abstract: ABSTRACTThe health consequences of gentrification are little-understood,, researchers have called for qualitative studies to uncover potential causal pathways between gentrification, health. Resident Researchers in a Participatory Action Research study of community health in nine gentrifying neighborhoods across the Boston area hypothesized that financial insecurity is one pathway through which gentrification might harm health. We analyze qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with 40 financially vulnerable respondents to understand how the experience of living in a gentrifying neighborhood produces feelings of financial insecurity,, how such feelings may be harmful to health. Results indicate that experiencing gentrification exacerbates respondents? sense of exposure to financial risk, while simultaneously reducing the perceived efficacy of available buffers against financial risks. The threats to an individual?s financial security introduced by gentrification-related changes in the neighborhood environment are stressful because they are appraised as taxing, exceeding the coping resources available to individuals. This gentrification-related financial insecurity is a meso-level phenomenon, produced by interactions between respondents, the contexts in which they live, with uncertain, uneven outcomes. Based on our findings, we argue that feelings of financial insecurity are one pathway through which the experience of living in a gentrifying neighborhood shapes health.

title: Bad news, bad times,, violence: The link between economic distress, aggression
authors: Barlett, Christopher P, Anderson, Craig A
keywords: aggression; economic strain; frustration; hostility; stress; distress; violence; Psychology; Empirical Study; Quantitative Study; Human; Male; Female; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Economics; Aggressive Behavior; Financial Strain; article; US; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Objective: The current research applied the general aggression model (GAM) to explain the relation between negative societal changes (e.g., indicators of a poor economy) on aggression-related outcomes. One correlational, one experimental study tested the relationships between these variables as well as possible mediating mechanisms. Method: In Study 1 (N 193), participants completed several measures to assess aggression, stress from current economic crises,, trait hostility. In Study 2( N 101), participants were randomly assigned to view stressful news videos (clips suggesting the economy is poor) or neutral news videos prior to completing state measures of stress, hostility. Results: Study 1 found significant positive relations between stress from negative societal changes, aggression, mediated by hostility. Study 2 showed that viewing stressful news videos increased state hostility, which was mediated by state levels of stress. Conclusions: Overall, results suggest that indicators of poor economic times are related to aggression, hostility. These findings offer theoretical implications for the utility of the GAM in explaining how societal-level shifts in economy-related variables can influence aggression levels at the individual level.

title: Depressed, anxious,, stressed: What have healthcare workers on the frontlines in Egypt, Saudi Arabia experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic?
authors: Arafa, Ahmed, Mohammed, Zeinab, Mahmoud, Omaima, Elshazley, Momen, Ewis, Ashraf
keywords: Anxiety; COVID-19; Depression; Healthcare workers; Sleeping hours; Stress;322\_経済圧力
abstract: INTRODUCTION: As the Novel Corona Virus Disease (COVID-19) was declared by the world health organization a pandemic in March 2020, thousands of healthcare workers (HCWs) worldwide were on the frontlines fighting against the pandemic. Herein, we selected two Middle East countries; Egypt, Saudi Arabia to investigate the psychological impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on their HCWs. METHODS: In this cross-sectional study, a Google survey was used to access HCWs in many hospitals in Egypt, Saudi Arabia between the 14th, 24th of April 2020. The survey assessed HCWs regarding their sociodemographic, occupational features, sleeping hours,, psychological impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic using the Depression Anxiety Stress Scale-21 (DASS-21). RESULTS: This study included 426 HCWs (48.4\% physicians, 24.2\% nurses,, 27.4\% other HCWs). Of them, 69\% had depression, 58.9\% had anxiety, 55.9\% had stress,, 37.3\% had inadequate sleeping (<6 h/day). Female sex, age ≤30 years, working in Egypt, attending emergency, night shifts, watching/reading COVID-19 news ≥2 h/day,, not getting emotional support from family, society,, hospital were associated with a high likelihood of depression, anxiety, stress,, inadequate sleeping. LIMITATIONS: the cross-sectional design restricted our ability to distinguish between preexisting, emerging psychological symptoms. CONCLUSION: HCWs on the frontlines in Egypt, Saudi Arabia experienced depression, anxiety, stress,, inadequate sleeping during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Comparing decision making between cancer patients, the general population: thoughts, emotions, or social influence?
authors: Yang, Z Janet, McComas, Katherine A, Gay, Geri K, Leonard, John P, Dannenberg, Andrew J, Dillon, Hildy
abstract: This study extends a risk information seeking, processing model to explore the relative effect of cognitive processing strategies, positive, negative emotions,, normative beliefs on individuals' decision making about potential health risks. Most previous research based on this theoretical framework has examined environmental risks. Applying this risk communication model to study health decision making presents an opportunity to explore theoretical boundaries of the model, while also bringing this research to bear on a pressing medical issue: low enrollment in clinical trials. Comparative analysis of data gathered from 2 telephone surveys of a representative national sample (n = 500), a random sample of cancer patients (n = 411) indicated that emotions played a more substantive role in cancer patients' decisions to enroll in a potential trial, whereas cognitive processing strategies, normative beliefs had greater influences on the decisions of respondents from the national sample.

title: Information seeking, information sharing related to Hurricane Harvey
authors: Yang, Janet Z, Zhuang, Jun
abstract: This study is focused on social cognitive variables that motivate information seeking, information sharing related to Hurricane Harvey. Survey results from a nationally representative sample, a quota sample of Houston residents indicate that climate change beliefs, issue salience are consistent predictors of risk perception, which increases individuals’ negative emotions, information insufficiency. This need for information subsequently motivates information seeking, information sharing. Informational subjective norms are significantly related to seeking, sharing in the Houston sample, whereas perceived information gathering capacity, trust in media are significant predictors in the national sample.

title: Risk aversion in information seeking
authors: Wakebe, Toshihiro, Sato, Tomomi, Watamura, Eiichiro, Takano, Yohtaro
abstract: The information gain model argues that participants select alternatives with a larger expected value of information gain. The present study investigated risk aversion in information seeking to examine whether the expected value always determines information-seeking behaviour. For this investigation, we used a scale method selection task in which participants were required to select one of two scales for weighing coins in order to find an underweight coin. Two experiments showed that participants more frequently selected the alternative that provided information gain without risk, although its expected information gain was smaller. This finding indicates the presence of risk aversion in information seeking, suggesting that information-seeking behaviour is affected by risk associated with obtaining information gain.

title: Ritualisation of Crisis Communication: Crowd-enabled responses to the Stockholm terror attack on Twitter: Crowd-enabled responses to the Stockholm terror attack on Twitter
authors: Tikka, Minttu
journal: The NORDICOM review of Nordic research on media \& communication
abstract: Abstract Digital connectivity enables ordinary people to participate in the social construction of crises. This article explores the crisis responses of common people through the prism of ritual communication in the case of the 2017 Stockholm terror attack. The ritual approach has helped to produce a nuanced understanding of the social functions of patterned, performative communication in crises, conflicts. However, the crisis communication of ordinary people has remained understudied from the viewpoint of ritualisation. Drawing from digital media ethnography, content analysis of a Twitter feed created around the hashtag \#openstockholm, it is claimed that the ritualisation of crisis responses illustrates the active agency of ordinary people, contributes to ephemeral social cohesion.

title: Proxemic effects on information seeking after the September 11 attacks
authors: Spence, Patric R, Westerman, David, Skalski, Paul D, Seeger, Matthew, Ulmer, Robert R, Venette, Steve, Sellnow, Timothy L
abstract: This research investigated the relationship between proximity to a crisis event, the desire for information to reduce uncertainty. The dataset was collected between two, five days after the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001. It included 1329 responses from three different cities in the USA. Results indicate that as proximity to a crisis event increases, individuals report significantly higher levels of emotional response. Differences were also found among geographic region as to types of information desired.

title: Information-seeking in the wake of tragedy: An examination of public response to mass shootings using Google Search data
authors: Semenza, Daniel Charles, Bernau, John A
journal: Sociological perspectives: SP: official publication of the Pacific Sociological Association
abstract: Mass shootings are a highly visible form of violence in the United States, although public response to these events varies considerably. Drawing on social problems, collective threat perception literature, we use search data for all Google-using Americans following mass shootings since 2004 to examine how event attributes such as the number of victims, venue,, type of weapon(s) predict public information-seeking related to gun control, gun rights. The results demonstrate that the number of victims, news coverage, school venue,, the use of certain weapons all significantly increase public interest in gun control, gun rights. These key predictors interact with one another to further influence information-seeking behaviors related to both gun control, gun rights. We conclude with a discussion of our findings, the potential for Google Search data in social science research.

title: The action suited to the word? Use of the framework of risk information seeking to understand risk-related behaviors
authors: Kievik, Milou, ter Huurne, Ellen F J, Gutteling, Jan M
abstract: Although a growing body of risk communication research focuses on how people process risk information, one question that is overlooked is how the seeking of information contributes to behavioral adaptation toward the risk issue. How are people’s behavioral responses to risks affected by the search for risk information? Building on the Framework of Risk Information Seeking (FRIS), this paper reports on two studies that focus on the experimental testing of several of the basic FRIS assumptions. In study 1, a 2 (involvement: high vs. low) × 2 (risk perception: high vs. low) between-subjects experiment was conducted to test the assumption that higher levels of involvement, risk perception stimulate the intention to seek additional risk information as well as the actual risk information. Study 2 is a partial replication of study 1. In study 2, a 2 (involvement: high vs. low) × 2 (fear appeal: present vs. absent) × 2 (response efficacy: high vs. low) between-subjects experiment was conducted to test how varying the levels of involvement, risk perception,, response efficacy influence actual, intended information seeking, as well as the intention to adopt risk-mitigating actions. The results showed that the high-involvement, high-risk perception, high-response efficacy group was most likely to actually seek information, make behavioral changes. The results are in accordance with basic FRIS assumptions. Implications for risk communication are discussed.

title: Risk here vs. Risk there: Intention to seek information about gulf coastal erosion
authors: Huang, Jialing, Ells, Kevin
abstract: ABSTRACTThe Gulf coast is losing land to erosion at a rapid rate. Applying the planned risk information seeking model (PRISM; Kahlor, L. (2010). PRISM: A planned risk information seeking model. Health Communication, 25(4), 345?356), this survey research examines the cognitive, affective determinants of individuals? intention to seek information about Gulf coastal erosion,, the moderation effect of geographic distance on the proposed relationships through multigroup Structural Equation Modeling. Results showed that PRISM performs well in this novel context, confirming its robustness. Further, the relationship between knowledge insufficiency, information seeking intent was stronger for Gulf residents than residents of other states. The results suggested that PRISM can increase its explanatory power by including a psychological distance factor. Also, communication about Gulf coastal erosion to local residents should focus on their lack of knowledge of this risk.

title: Information needs, risk perception as predictors of risk information seeking
authors: Huurne, Ellen Ter, Gutteling, Jan
abstract: This paper introduces a theoretical framework that describes the importance of public's information sufficiency, risk perception,, self‐efficacy as predictors of intended risk information seeking behaviour. Based on theoretical assumptions, measurement instruments for relevant concepts were developed, validated using data from a mail questionnaire. Relationships among selected determinants of risk information seeking behaviour were analysed. Results indicate that information needs, risk perception,, current knowledge are direct predictors of intentions to seek information. Trust, engagement, social influence,, self‐efficacy affect risk perception, the need for information is influenced by engagement, social influence.

title: Procedures, collaborative information seeking: A study of emergency departments
authors: Hertzum, Morten, Reddy, Madhu
abstract: Information seeking is a central, inherently collaborative activity in the emergency department (ED), which is the common entry point to hospitals for nearly all acute patients. In this paper, we investigate how ED clinicians’ collaborative information seeking (CIS) is shaped by the procedures that they follow in the ED. Based on observations in two Danish EDs, we identify four procedures prominent to how CIS is accomplished: the triage procedure, the timeouts, the coordinating nurse,, the recurrent opportunities for information seeking at the whiteboard. We then discuss how CIS activities are impacted by these procedures, the challenges to effective CIS in these settings. We conclude with some thoughts about future studies of CIS in healthcare settings.

title: Personal cancer knowledge, information seeking through PRISM: the planned risk information seeking model
authors: Hovick, Shelly R, Kahlor, Leeann, Liang, Ming-Ching
abstract: This study retested PRISM, a model of risk information seeking,, found that it is applicable to the context of cancer risk communication. The study, which used an online sample of 928 U.S. adults, also tested the effect of additional variables on that model, found that the original model better fit the data. Among the strongest predictors of cancer information seeking were seeking-related subjective norms, attitude toward seeking, perceived knowledge insufficiency,, affective risk response. Furthermore, risk perception was a strong predictor of an affective risk response. The authors suggest that, given the robustness across studies, the path between seeking-related subjective norms, seeking intention is ready to be implemented in communication practice.

title: Impact of information seeking, disaster preparedness, typhoon emergency response on perceived community resilience in Hong Kong
authors: Guo, Chunlan, Sim, Timothy, Ho, Hung Chak
journal: International journal of disaster risk reduction: IJDRR
abstract: Gentrification, urban development in coastal megacities have increased community resilience due to better physical, socioeconomic conditions to cope with natural hazards. However, perceived community resilience, namely public belief regarding the ability of society to recover, is under-researched. In particular, specific pathways between information seeking, perceived community resilience during extreme storm events are rarely discussed. Therefore, this study applied structural equation modelling to examine the associations between the use of traditional, new information channels in typhoon-related information seeking, individual perceived community resilience, with disaster preparedness, typhoon emergency response as mediators. This analysis was based on a population-based cohort (n = 1015), the Cantonese version of the Conjoint Community Resiliency Assessment Measure (CCRAM-10). Generally, CCRAM-10, four of the five sub-dimensions were rated lower than average, although 89.8\% of the respondents used at least two channels to acquire typhoon-related information. Direct associations were found between the use of traditional information channels (e.g., television), greater perceived community resilience (β = 0.096; SE = 0.035),, two indirect associations were found via individual disaster preparedness behaviours, typhoon emergency response behaviours. However, we found only indirect associations between the use of new information channels (e.g., social media), greater perceived community resilience via individual, household disaster preparedness behaviours. These associations suggest that community-based programmes should consider improving perceived community resilience by making more information-seeking channels available for residents. To increase urban resilience in coastal areas, new information channels should also be synergised with both top-down, bottom-up typhoon-related information as well as physical, socioeconomic conditions of the urban environment for urban governance, community-based disaster management.

title: Policing Katrina: Managing law enforcement in New Orleans
authors: Deflem, M, Sutphin, S
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Hurricane Katrina impacted the Gulf Coast of the USA on a scale, intensity that was unprecedented for the region. Special problems of policing were posed before, during,, after the hurricane. Focusing on the law enforcement dimensions of the effects of Hurricane Katrina in the city of New Orleans, this paper reviews the organizational, functional adaptations of the New Orleans Police Department in view of the storm. Revealing the social implications of natural disasters, Hurricane Katrina presented a variety of police concerns, ranging from shifting duties involving crime control, emergency relief to the destruction of essential elements of the police infrastructure, the breakdown of police communication, transportation systems,, the need for coordination between police, other first responders. The police experiences of Katrina in New Orleans can serve as a guide for the management of law enforcement organizations to be prepared for similar disasters.

title: Employee variables influencing ‘Run Hide Fight’ policy knowledge retention, perceptions of preparedness in the hospital setting
authors: Darais, Mallory, Wood, Mckenzie
abstract: Nationally, there has been a large increase in the number of active shooter events within healthcare facilities such as hospitals. Due to this upturn, government organizations have recently released documents to guide healthcare facilities on implementing active shooter policies, updating emergency operation plans. Currently, recommendations from government entities, such as the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security, suggest the ‘Run, Hide, Fight’ approach during an active shooter incident. The current study uses data collected from hospital employees via a survey to determine, assesses variables that influence whether hospital employees retain knowledge related to the ‘Run Hide Fight’ policy, as well as employee perception of whether the training was adequate. Results reveal that level of education, clinical versus non-clinical work role,, work schedule are significant variables in determining successful program implementation.

title: Trust, affect: how do they impact risk information seeking in a health context?
authors: Allen Catellier, Jennifer R, Yang, Z Janet
abstract: This study examines college students’ intention to seek information about the H1N1 flu vaccine. We specifically focused on the relationship between trust, affect, whether they work together to influence risk information seeking. Results indicated that positive affect moderated the relationship between trust, information seeking, but negative affect did not. While both positive affect, negative affect influenced risk information seeking, when combined with trust, only positive affect remained as a significant predictor. These results suggest that by understanding the role that trust, affect play, medical professionals, disease control agencies can tailor their communication efforts to increase an individual’s intention to seek information about preventive measures. Specifically, maintaining the public’s trust, positive feelings toward these entities is key to successful communication about prevention measures such as vaccination.

title: Juvenile willingness to report: correlates, implications for procedural justice
authors: Hurst, Y Gail, Ilchi, Omeed S, Frank, James, Dai, Mengyan
abstract: Taylor \& Francis Online Top Full Article Figures \& data References Citations Metrics Reprints \& Permissions Read this article XFacebookLinkedInEmail共有 ABSTRACT One of the positive consequences of procedurally just behavior by the police during interactions with citizens is alleged to be citizen willingness to cooperate with the police. While there have been numerous studies that have examined this issue, many have involved samples of adults, assessed citizen willingness to engage in certain behaviors in the future. Using data collected from a sample of high school aged youth, the present study explores the extent to which they report engaging in behaviors supportive of the police when given the opportunity,, the factors associated with reporting suspicious and/or criminal behaviors to the police. Implications for law enforcement policy, for understanding citizen engagement in the coproduction of police outputs are discussed.

title: Crime reporting in Chicago: A comparison of police, victim survey data, 1999–2018
authors: Rezey, Maribeth L, Lauritsen, Janet L
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency

abstract: Objectives A critical unknown in any jurisdiction is the scope of crime that is not brought to the attention of police. This study provides a unique comparison of Chicago crime rates using both police, victimization survey data. Levels of crime reporting, the reasons victims provide for or against reporting crime to the police are examined. Patterns are compared to those found for other large U.S. cities. Methods Data for Chicago residents from the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) are used to estimate serious violence, burglary rates, levels of reporting to the police,, residents’ justifications for reporting or not reporting. Levels, trends in NCVS, Chicago Police Department rates of serious violence, burglary are compared. Results The NCVS data show that while Chicago residents typically experience higher rates of these crimes than residents of other large cities, they report these crimes to the police at mostly similar rates. Reasons for, against reporting these crimes to the police are generally similar to victims elsewhere. Conclusions Despite a documented history of distrust in the police, Chicago residents do not appear to have notably lower rates of reporting serious violence or burglary to the police than residents of other large cities.

title: Coping with victimization: The effects of police intervention on victims' psychological readjustment
authors: Rosenbaum, Dennis P
abstract: Beginning with the premise that police-victim interactions shortly after victimization mediate the psychological impact of criminal victimization, the Detroit Victims Experiment was designed to test the notions that (a) new police officers could be sensitized to the psychological needs of victims,, (b) this sensitivity would ameliorate the severity of the victims' stress reactions, facilitate readjustment,, improve the prospects of cooperation with the criminal justice system. In a randomized experimental design, police recruits who received the victim-focused training reported significantly more favorable attitudes, perceptions,, behavioral intentions vis-à-vis victims than did the control group. However, victims were largely unaffected by this police intervention across a wide range of outcome measures. Implications for crisis theory, policy are discussed.

title: The effects of interior design on communication, impressions of a counselor in a counseling room
authors: Miwa, Yoshiko, Hanyu, Kazunori
abstract: This study aimed to investigate effects of the interior design of a counseling room on participants' self-disclosure, impressions of a counselor. The authors examined the effects of lighting, decorations. It tested four conditions crossing decorations (with or without home-like decorations), type of lighting (bright or dim). Eighty undergraduate students (clients) were randomly assigned to one of the conditions, individually underwent a structured interview with an interviewer (a counselor), then completed a questionnaire. The results showed that dim lighting yielded more pleasant, relaxed feelings, more favorable impressions of the interviewer,, more self-disclosure than did the bright lighting. However, the authors found no predominant pattern of the decorations. Thus, the pleasant, relaxed feelings related to dim lighting may well enhance the perceived attractiveness of a counselor, self-disclosure from clients. The results imply that interior design could influence communication, other relationships in counseling rooms.

title: A coping theory framework toward preventing sexual revictimization
authors: Macy, Rebecca J
keywords: Coping Behavior; Human; Prevention; Sexual Abuse; Victimization; coping; coping theory; interventions; sexual revictimization; sexual violence;325\_Vic介入;repeat\_victim\_intervention
abstract: A substantial body of research demonstrates the problem of repeated sexual victimization. However, what is less clear is what can be done to prevent revictimization. The most pressing needs in the development of revictimization knowledge are for prevention theories, interventions to address this problem. Building on theoretical, empirical research, this paper helps to address this critical knowledge gap by presenting a coping theoretical framework toward revictimization prevention. This framework, which is composed of three related coping theories, adaptive, proactive,, resistive-defensive, can be used to form the basis of interventions to prevent revictimization. In combination, the three coping theories provide a framework to organize, sequence women's coping efforts in the aftermath of sexual victimization in order to mitigate the negative aspects of the assault, reduce the likelihood of revictimization. The framework described here provides an organizing heuristic that will help guide coping-based revictimization prevention efforts.

title: Police \& Civilian Help for Crime Victims: Can It Make a Difference? Executive Summary
authors: Lurigio, Arthur J, Rosenbaum, Dennis P, Northwestern University
keywords: MICHIGAN; Services effectiveness; Victim attitudes; Victim reactions to CJS; Victim services;325\_Vic介入
abstract: The project also examined the adverse emotional consequences of victimization on the so-called 'forgotten victims' of residential burglary, personal robbery,, assault. The research used two experimental designs. In the first, police recruits were assigned randomly to a special victim sensitivity training program. In the second, victims were assigned randomly to receive a home visit from trained civilian volunteers who were prepared to offer counseling, support,, referrals for social services. Finally, samples of victims, non-victims were compared on a variety of outcome variables. Results showed that the police training was very successful in changing officers beliefs, intentions, although some effects declined over time, the training had few measurable effects on victim attitudes. In addition, the civilian intervention had several positive effects on victims. Both the police training, the civilian intervention had more favorable effects on older victims. Finally, crime victims reported more negative psychological impacts than did non-victims.
