title: Counseling interactions as a function of spatial-environmental conditions
authors: Lecomte, Conrad, Bernstein, Bianca L, Dumont, Florent
keywords: *Counselor Trainees; *Environmental Effects; *Personal Space; *Psychotherapeutic Processes; *Self-Disclosure; Counselor Characteristics;325\_Vic介入
abstract: Investigated the effects of interpersonal distance, intensity of lighting,, time on counselor communication of affective, cognitive self-disclosure. Excerpts from initial sessions conducted by 18 counselors-in-training with 54 clients were randomly selected, rated. Results indicate significant effects of Distance on counselor concreteness, of Lighting on counselor communication of cognitive sets in the last third of the interviews. Additionally, Distance had a significant effect on counselee affective self-disclosure in the 2nd third of the interviews. (12 ref)

title: Effects of contrasting degrees of privacy on client self-disclosure in a counseling setting
authors: Holahan, Charles J, Slaikeu, Karl A
abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of reduced privacy in a counseling setting on client self-disclosure. The study involved a laboratory analogue simulating an invasion of privacy by a third party in a counseling setting. The experimental design included 74 subjects randomly assigned to three experimental conditions: private-an interviewer, subject were alone in an interview setting; invasion-a third party (an experimental confederate) invaded the privacy of the interview; spatial divider-a third party again invaded the interview, but spatial dividers were introduced to enhance privacy. The results strongly demonstrated that reduced privacy decreases client self-disclosure. Spatial dividers influenced the client's perception of privacy but failed to increase self-disclosure.

title: Coordinated community efforts to respond to sexual assault: A national study of sexual assault response team implementation: A national study of sexual assault response team implementation
authors: Greeson, Megan R, Campbell, Rebecca
keywords: coordinated community response; coordinating council; rape; sexual assault response team;325\_Vic介入;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Sexual Assault Response Teams (SARTs) bring together sexual assault responders (e.g., police, prosecutors, medical/forensic examiners, rape victim advocates) to coordinate, improve the response to sexual assault. Ultimately, SARTs seek to improve sexual assault victims' experiences of seeking help, sexual assault case outcomes in the criminal justice system. To date, there are hundreds of SARTs across the United States, yet, there has been no nationally representative study of how SARTs are implemented. Therefore, the current study used a multistep process to create the first sampling frame of SARTs, then studied how SARTs are structured, function within a random sample of SARTs. Findings reveal commonalities as well as variation across SARTs. Most SARTs rated improving legal outcomes, improving victims' help-seeking experiences,, prevention/education as important goals, yet most prioritized their time, energy toward victims' experiences. SARTs' membership varied, with an average of 12 organizations involved in the SART,, 75\% of SARTs having active membership from police, prosecutors, rape victim advocates,, medical/forensic examiners. SARTs were moderately formalized, most SARTs engaged in most collaborative processes (e.g., multidisciplinary cross-training, case review, policy/protocol development,, review) on an as needed basis. Finally, results revealed that some types of cross-system coordination in responding to victims/cases were quite frequent, whereas other types of coordination were quite infrequent. Implications for future research, supporting the development, sustainability of SARTs are discussed.

title: The impact of environmental design on teamwork, communication in healthcare facilities: A systematic literature review
authors: Gharaveis, Arsalan, Hamilton, D Kirk, Pati, Debajyoti
keywords: communication; healthcare design; healthcare facility; teamwork;325\_Vic介入
abstract: The purpose of this systematic review is to investigate the current knowledge about the impact of healthcare facility design on teamwork, communication by exploring the relevant literature. Teamwork, communication are behavioral factors that are impacted by physical design. However, the effects of environmental factors on teamwork, communication have not been investigated extensively in healthcare design literature. There are no published systematic reviews on the current topic. Searches were conducted in PubMed, Google Scholar databases in addition to targeted design journals including Health Environmental Research \& Design, Environment, Behavior, Environmental Psychology,, Applied Ergonomics. Inclusion criteria were (a) full-text English language articles related to teamwork, communication, (b) involving any healthcare built environment, space design published in peer-reviewed journals between 1984, 2017. Studies were extracted using defined inclusion, exclusion criteria. In the first phase, 26 of the 195 articles most relevant to teamwork, 19 studies of the 147 were identified, reviewed to understand the impact of communication in healthcare facilities. The literature regarding the impact of built environment on teamwork, communication were reviewed, explored in detail. Eighteen studies were selected, succinctly summarized as the final product of this review. Environmental design, which involves nurses, support staff,, physicians, is one of the critical factors that promotes the efficiency of teamwork, collaborative communication. Layout design, visibility,, accessibility levels are the most cited aspects of design which can affect the level of communication, teamwork in healthcare facilities.

title: The effects of lighting, interpersonal distance on counseling interactions
authors: Dumont, Florent, Lecomte, Conrad
abstract: This study investigated the effect of intensity of lighting andinterpersonal distance in an analog counseling situation on an array ofcounseling variables: e.g., communication of empathy, duration of silence,duration of speech, number of interactions. Excerpts from initial sessionswere randomly selected, rated,, analyzed. Results showed a significantinteractive effect of lighting, distance on the communication of empathy.Both significant, non-significant results were discussed.

title: Environmental factors, clients' self-disclosure in counseling
authors: Cohen, B N, Schwartz, R C
abstract: Self-disclosure by clients is regarded as a fundamental component of counseling, with increased self-disclosure being related to positive outcome of treatment; however, scant attention has focused on environmental characteristics that may facilitate self-disclosure among clients. An evaluation of prior research in this area leads to suggestions for studies on environmental factors, self-disclosure.

title: The problem behavior model: the development of a stalkers clinic, a threateners clinic
authors: Warren, Lisa J, MacKenzie, Rachel, Mullen, Paul E, Ogloff, James R P
abstract: Traditionally, forensic mental health services have focused on the assessment, treatment of offenders with serious mental disorders. In recent years, there has been growing recognition that forensic clinicians have an important role to play for those offenders who engage in criminal acts driven by psychological or/and social problems, which may, or may not, occur in conjunction with a major mental disorder. This is especially true for specific offenses such as stalking, threatening. This article describes the innovation of the problem behavior model. This model uses a reductionist approach, the nexus between psychiatry, psychology to address the complex phenomena associated with specific problem behaviors that often culminate in offenses. The model is illustrated by describing the development of specialist clinics for the problem behaviors of stalking, threatening.

title: Dialectical behavior therapy for the treatment of stalking offenders
authors: Rosenfeld, Barry, Galietta, Michele, Ivanoff, André, Garcia-Mansilla, Alexandra, Martinez, Ricardo, Fava, Joanna, Fineran, Virginia, Green, Debbie
journal: International journal of forensic mental health
abstract: The need for effective mental health interventions for specific offender populations has become clear in recent decades. In particular, individuals who engage in stalking, harassment have increasingly attracted the attention of the public, mental health, criminal justice professionals, however no evidence-based treatment currently exists for this population. We adapted Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) for the treatment of this offender group, in part because of the high prevalence of personality disorders. This study describes the application of a 6-month treatment program to a sample of 29 individuals, 14 of whom completed treatment. Treated offenders were significantly less likely to re-offend with another stalking offense (0 of 14) compared to treatment drop-outs (26.7\%) or to published recidivism data (47\%). Measures intended to help determine the nature of changes revealed increased thought suppression, but are qualified by the high degree of defensive responding. These preliminary data suggest that DBT holds promise for reducing stalking behaviors, warrants further study.

title: Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) for the treatment of stalking offenders: A randomized controlled study
authors: Rosenfeld, Barry, Galietta, Michele, Foellmi, Melodie, Coupland, Sarah, Turner, Zoe, Stern, Stephanie, Wijetunga, Charity, Gerbrandij, Jacomina, Ivanoff, Andre
keywords: *Anger Control; *Recidivism; *Stalking; *Dialectical Behavior Therapy; *Criminal Offenders; Behavior; Intervention; Treatment Effectiveness Evaluation;326\_ST介入
abstract: The objective was to evaluate the relative efficacy of dialectical behavior therapy modified for stalking offenders (DBT-S) versus a cognitive-behavioral anger management intervention for the treatment of stalking offenders. We expected DBT to result in significantly lower rates of renewed stalking behavior, significantly greater improvements in impulsivity, aggression, anger,, empathy. We randomly assigned individuals charged with stalking-related offences (N = 109) to one of two study interventions: DBT-S, anger management. Recidivism (renewed stalking, violence,, other offences) was monitored for 1 year following the baseline assessment,, participants completed a battery of self-report questionnaires before, after treatment, at a 1-year follow-up assessment. We found relatively low rates of reoffence when compared to past studies of untreated stalking offenders in the U.S., but type of treatment had no impact on the likelihood of reoffence, nor did completion of the treatment program. Likewise, there was no between-groups difference in rates of treatment completion, or on changes in self-report measures. Intensive treatment focused on reducing problematic behaviors in stalking offenders may be effective regardless of treatment modality, but the mechanism by which treatment impacts criminal behavior is not yet clear. title: The emergence, persistence of stalking during hospitalization: Application of the Offense Paralleling Behaviour framework
authors: Daffern, Michael
journal: The journal of behavior analysis of offender, victim treatment, prevention
keywords: *Mental Disorders; *Psychiatric Hospitalization; *Psychiatric Patients; *Stalking; Risk Assessment;326\_ST介入
abstract: Mental disorder is common amongst those who engage in stalking. When mentally disordered patients with a history of stalking are admitted to hospital for psychiatric treatment their stalking behavior may persist. Stalking behavior might also have its onset during hospitalization, continue following discharge. Stalking may emerge following dissatisfaction with treatment providers or because patients misinterpret treatment as affection. In both situations mental health staff may be victimized. This paper considers the application of the Offense Paralleling Behavior (OPB) framework to stalking behavior in hospitalised mentally disordered patients. Application of this framework may result in increase awareness of the relevance of behavior occurring within hospital to pre-admission, post-discharge criminal behavior. It is recommended that individuals with a known history of stalking, those patients with personal characteristics associated with stalking be assessed on admission, monitored during their hospital stay for stalking related OPB. Monitoring, analysis of contingencies associated with OPB may help identify the determinants of persistent, emergent stalking so that treatment, risk management interventions can be developed. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Using remote sensing data in urban crime analysis: A systematic review of English-language literature from 2003 to 2023
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Ioannidis, Ioannis
abstract: Drawing from environmental criminology principles, this article explores the existing literature to assess the utility of remote sensing data in detecting, analysing features in the urban environment that are associated with crime occurrence. A systematic review of the literature in the English language from 2003 until the first half of 2023 from two major databases, Scopus, Science Direct, is carried out. As many as 910 publications were selected, from which 36 publications satisfied the selection criteria. Findings show that neighborhood's design has a quantifiable imprint that is possible to be observed with very high spatial-resolution imagery. Given its high spatial, temporal resolution, remote sensing data can to different degrees support the identification of criminogenic features in urban environments (streets, roads, property boundaries, housing density, characteristics, density of vegetation as well as luminosity levels), but when it is used for the detection of potentially illegal activities, infringement of people's privacy, methods lacking validation still present serious concerns. The article concludes with a discussion of the opportunities, challenges of using remote sensing data in crime analysis.

title: Pornography use, sexual scripts among men who have committed sexual offenses
authors: Osuna, Amanda Isabel, Holt, Karen
abstract: Drawing from sexual scripting theory, the present study employed semi-structured interviews with 101 individuals incarcerated for sexual offenses in a Midwestern minimum-security prison to explore: (1) Do individuals who have committed sexual offenses report that porn scripts influenced or informed their sexual behavior?, (2) How do participants understand the norms, values inherent in porn? Through a qualitative analysis, several themes were identified which included living the porn, transforming sex, porn as grooming, offending,, porn as risk. For some individuals, porn serves as a salient factor in how they navigate their sexual behaviors, relationships, however, most did not report relying on these scripts in their offenses. We discuss treatment, supervision implications related to pornography use.

title: The journey to crime, victimization
authors: Luo, Fei, Zhang, Yan, Hoover, Larry T
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The offender’s journey to crime has attracted much attention in mobility triangle research, whereas the journey to victimization, the spatial distance between the offender’s, the victim’s residences have been relatively less examined. This research fills this gap in the literature by examining spatial comparisons of variations in journey to crime, journey to victimization,, the distance between victim’s, suspect’s residences for five types of offenses. Crime data from the Houston Police Department from 2010 to 2013 were used to analyze the mobility triangle in five types of crime. The results show that the dynamics of travel pattern vary by demographic characteristics of the suspects, victims. It is also contingent on the types of crime. The proximity of offender’s, victim’s residences is closely related to the chance of crimes. The findings provide important implications for theory, policy, policing practice.

title: ``You're just constantly on alert'': Women, Gender-Diverse People's Experiences of Sexual Violence on Public Transport
authors: Ison, Jessica, Forsdike, Kirsty, Henry, Nicola, Hooker, Leesa, Taft, Angela
keywords: GLBT; sexual assault; sexual assault < GLBT; sexual harassment; stalking;330\_SAEnv;public\_transportation\_334
abstract: Sexual violence is a public health issue that can be experienced across the life course. Public transport is a key site of sexual violence, harassment experienced by women, gender-diverse people in Australia, although victim-survivor voices have rarely been sought in addressing this issue. Through in-depth qualitative interviews with 41 diverse female, gender-diverse victim-survivors who were staff or students at two Australian universities, we sought to understand their experiences of sexual violence, harassment on public transport. We found that women, gender-diverse people, while often reporting on a significant experience of sexual violence or harassment on public transport, also had other, ``everyday'' experiences across their life course that impacted how they traveled, their confidence in the world. Overall, we argue that the significant impact of sexual violence, harassment on public transport should be addressed through targeting public transport as a key site for primary prevention of sexual violence, harassment.

title: Evacuation behavior in a subway train emergency: A video-based analysis
authors: Philpot, Richard, Levine, Mark
abstract: How do people behave in the seconds after they become aware they have been caught up in a real-life transport emergency? This paper presents the first micro-behavioral, video-based analysis of the behavior of passengers during a small explosion, subsequent fire on a subway train. We analyzed the behavior of 40 passengers present in the same carriage as the explosion. We documented the first action of the passengers following the onset of the emergency, described evidence of pro-, anti-social behavior. Passengers’ first actions varied widely. Moreover, anti-social behavior was rare, displays of pro-sociality were more common. In a quantitative analysis, we examined spatial clustering of running behavior, patterns in passenger exit choices. We found both homogeneity, heterogeneity in the running behavior, exiting choices of passengers. We discuss the implications of these findings for the mass emergency literature, for evacuation modeling.

title: Formation of fear, adaptive behavior in young ethnic minority women riding public transport
authors: Chowdhury, Subeh, Patel, Priya, Giridharan, Varun, Ceccato, Vania
abstract: Young ethnic minority women face unique challenges when riding public transport. The present study contributes by providing a narrative-based examination of young ethnic minority women’s formation of fear, adaptive behavior when using public transport. Twenty-nine ethnic minority women, under the age of 30, participated in a semi-structured interview in Auckland, New Zealand. Findings show that adaptive behavior commonly includes pre-planning nighttime trips, relying on their phones to act confident, engage in communication with family en-route,, appearing disinterested to reduce unwanted attention. These measures are expressions of women’s agency, their capacity to prevent victimization, manage fear, particularly in places where they feel unsafe, such as empty stations, dark or enclosed environments. Their lived experiences highlight the level of anxiety they experience on a regular basis. Participants discussed how they are acutely aware of their ethnicity (and appearance) when using public transport at all times of the day. They remain near exits, are constantly on high alert. They also discussed how, from an early age, women are educated in a culture of “stranger-danger” which in the long term erodes their confidence to travel independently, safely. These findings show that the current design of public transport systems does not adequately meet the travel needs of certain groups of women. Public transport authorities are encouraged to gain deeper insights into these issues, develop design strategies which promote inclusiveness.

title: Women-only transportation: How “pink” public transportation changes public perception of women’s mobility
authors: Dunckel-Graglia, Amy
abstract: It is well documented that women often face sexual harassment, violence during their daily commutes, particularly in countries with extreme levels of gender inequality. A popular reaction to this problem is to issue women-only transit services. Despite this growing trend, we know very little about it. Looking at the case of Mexico City, this study examines, analyzes,, evaluates women-only transportation, focusing on the roles of culture, public opinion. Drawing from both qualitative, quantitative data, it finds that the violence women face in public transit leads them to always opt for women-only services, encouraging local policy makers to increase their numbers. Local feminist groups have advanced this system by arguing that violence in regular public transit is gender discrimination. Consequently, they have positioned themselves as administrators of women-only transportation, using it as a campaign to defend womenâs equal right to urban mobility.

title: Harassment of low-income women on transit: A photovoice project in Oregon, Utah
authors: García, Ivis, Albelson, Miriam, Puczkowskyj, Nicholas, Maheruma Khan, Sadika, Fagundo-Ojeda, Kevin
journal: Transportation research. Part D, Transport, environment
keywords: Ethnicity; Gender; Harassment; Photovoice; Race; Transportation;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Scholarship on gendered mobilities has shown that women experience transit differently than men do, particularly regarding personal safety. Not enough studies have considered the everyday interaction of women of color with transit systems. This research employs a photovoice methodology which includes in-depth interviews, phone texting with 22 low-income women of color who ride transit at least a few times a month in Oregon, Utah.Like other gender mobility research, participants discussed sexual harassment on buses, streetcar,, light rail while walking or waiting for public transportation in either crowded areas downtown or desolated spaces outside of it. At the same time, this article makes a unique contribution to this body of literature because it shows that women feel targeted also based on their racial or ethnic identity, not only their gender. The article discusses womenâs actions every day to increase their sense of safety.

title: Transportation professionals' visions of transit sexual assault: The problem of deproblematizing beliefs
authors: Kash, Gwen
journal: Transportation research. Part A, Policy, practice
abstract: This study examines plannersâ views of transit sexual assault in two transit systems where sexual assault is widespread, but little action has been taken: TransMilenio Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) system in BogotÃ¡, Soacha, Colombia, informal transit in El Alto, Bolivia. In both cases, many planners lack information about transit sexual assault in their city,, the agencies do not systematically measure its frequency. Additionally, plannersâ views of transit sexual assault are shaped by five widespread deproblematizing beliefs: (1) victims of sexual assault on transit are often mistaken or lying; (2) groping, sexual rubbing do not seriously harm victims; (3) victims brought the attack on themselves; (4) assault is natural, unchangeable;, (5) planners should not be responsible for addressing sexual assault because they did not create the problem. These beliefs, which were more common among male planners, pose a significant barrier to action because they support an attitude that sexual assault on transit is not a problem to which planners should devote resources; either there is no problem to solve or attempting to solve it is so difficult as to be futile. Additionally, deproblematizing beliefs reduce openness to new data about transit sexual assault. The belief that women are likely to mistake innocent actions for sexual assault renders some planners dismissive of survey data based on the self reports of (ostensibly) unreliable narrators. The results indicate that in the long term, a gender mainstreaming approach that includes training for planners is needed. In the short term, one critical task is to convince reluctant reformers that transit sexual assault is a problem on which planners can, should take action.

title: Social context, personal norms, the use of public transportation: Two field studies
authors: Bamberg, Sebastian, Hunecke, Marcel, Blöbaum, Anke
keywords: Norm-activation model; Personal norm; Social norm; Theory of planned behavior; Travel mode choice;330\_SAEnv;J Environ Psychol
abstract: The paper concentrates on the role personal norms play in the decision to use public transportation means instead of the car. An integrative theoretical framework is presented from which hypotheses concerning the social, psychological processes activating personal norms, mediating their impact on behavior are derived. These hypotheses are tested, cross-validated with two independent data sets collected in two German urban agglomerations with different economic, social–cultural backgrounds. In both samples, personal norm is a significant predictor of PT-use intention even after checking for the impact of attitude, perceived behavioral control. Furthermore, there is evidence that the reported personal norms are based on two related but distinct processes: anticipated feelings of guilt, perceived social norms. These two processes provide an explanation how different social contexts may influence people's judgment of PT as well as their actual PT-use.

title: Framing safety of women in public transport: A media discourse analysis of sexual harassment cases in Bangladesh
authors: Mowri, Seama, Bailey, Ajay
abstract: This paper analyzes the role of print media in framing incidences of sexual harassment in public transport; particularly in the context of Bangladesh, where gender-based violence is highly prevalent in the public sphere. This article uses Douglas’ cultural theory to reflect on media practices, its institutional power to reframe the social problem through risk, blame attribution. We conducted a discourse analysis of 71 news articles extracted from four of the widely circulated, influential newspapers of Bangladesh. Our findings reveal that the hegemonic discourse of gender-based violence in public transport is systemic and/or primarily reliant on legal recourse. By contrast, discourses presenting sexual harassment as symptomatic of broader gender inequality is less frequent. Moreover, these media platforms belong to an assemblage of patriarchal social-power holders that collaborate with established law, order to facilitate a blame game, thereby relieving the same stakeholders of ownership, accountability. Given the power of news media in constructing meta-narratives of safety (and nudging policymakers), journalists must tread responsibly on issues of blame, women’s safety,, their rights to the city.

title: Sexual harassment in public spaces: Examining gender differences in perceived seriousness, victimization
authors: Madan, Manish, Nalla, Mahesh K
abstract: In this article, we examine the situational conditions of female sexual victimization in public spaces. Using survey questionnaire methodology, we explore gender differences in perceptions of the occurrence, location of sexual harassment in public spaces as well as the extent to which such behaviors are considered serious. The study’s methodology relies on using multistage cluster, quota sampling technique, where we interviewed nearly 1,387 respondents (both men, women) from the capital city of India, New Delhi. This study finds an overall congruence between perceived likelihood of female sexual harassment victimization, actual self-reported victimization in most public transportation modes, but there is a significant gap between these two indicators for occurrences that take place in certain transportation modes, such as taxis, auto-rickshaws. There are statistically significant gender differences in the seriousness ratings of various behaviors that constitute sexual harassment to women. Policy implications include adoption of a zero-tolerance policy toward any form of sexual harassment in public spaces.

title: Reducing gender-based violence in public transportation: Strategy design for Mexico City, Mexico
authors: Rivadeneyra, Aldo Tudela, Dodero, Abel Lopez, Mehndiratta, Shomik Raj, Alves, Bianca Bianchi, Deakin, Elizabeth
abstract: Gender-based violence on public transportation in Mexico City, Mexico, is a growing concern. Current efforts to counteract the violence have focused on transit vehicles for exclusive use by women, children, campaigns to promote the report of offenses. To characterize the problem, this study conducted a transit user survey, workshops with transit users, interviews with operators,, interviews with experts in the field. The study found that, even though transit users believed that the gender-exclusive transport service reduced problematic encounters, they did not view the service as a solution to the problem of gender-based violence. Transit users would prefer to see the problem addressed through a combination of interventions including social marketing, mobile phone reporting systems,, transit service upgrades. Government agencies acknowledged that gender segregation, current reporting systems were only partially successful,, nongovernmental organizations, private operators agreed. Those agencies added that they were ready to contribute to the effort to find solutions to the problem. Study recommendations included (a) a communication campaign to foster better social behavior by passengers; (b) the use of technology, such as cell phone applications, to enable users to report offenses;, (c) the further investigation of the potential for new technology-based niche transportation services to address particular markets that were unsafe.

title: From harassment to disappearance: Young women's feelings of insecurity in public spaces
authors: Almanza Avendaño, Ariagor Manuel, Romero-Mendoza, Martha, Gómez San Luis, Anel Hortensia
abstract: BACKGROUND: There are processes of gender socialization that increase the vulnerability of young women against a continuum of threats in the public space. This study explored the feeling of insecurity in public spaces among young women in a city located near the northern border of Mexico. METHODS AND FINDINGS: This study was based on the tradition of grounded theory. Purposive sampling was used,, 24 group interviews were conducted with junior high school, high school, university students to understand the conditions that favour the emergence of the feeling of insecurity, its psychosocial consequences, management strategies. A computer-assisted qualitative analysis was performed using MAXQDA 18 software. The study showed that street harassment was manifested mainly as sexual harassment but generated a continuous threat of feminicide, disappearance. Young women experienced discomfort, restrictions on mobility,, they had to assume individual responsibility for their safety in the absence of support from the state. CONCLUSIONS: The interaction between gender, age determines the vulnerability to crime in urban spaces. Future studies could analyse the chronic impact of this continuum of threats, develop psychosocial interventions that promote the empowerment of young women.

title: A spatio-temporal analysis of crime at Washington, DC metro rail: Stations’ crime-generating, crime-attracting characteristics as transportation nodes, places
authors: Irvin-Erickson, Yasemin, La Vigne, Nancy
abstract: Transit stations are acknowledged as particularly criminogenic settings. Transit stations may serve as crime “generators,” breeding crime because they bring together large volumes of people at particular geographies, times. They may also serve as crime “attractors,” providing well-known opportunities for crimes. This paper explores the node, place characteristics that can transform Washington DC, Metro stations to generators, attractors of different crimes at different times of the day. The crime-generating, crime-attracting characteristics of stations are modeled with Negative Binomial Regression analysis. To reflect the temporal trends in crime, crime counts are stratified into three temporal groups: peak hours, off-peak day hours,, off-peak night hours. The findings from this study not only suggest that stations assume different nodal, place-based crime-generating, crime-attracting characteristics, but also these roles vary for different crimes, different times. The level of activity, accessibility of a station, the level of crime at a station,, the connectedness of a station to other stations are consistent indicators of high crime rate ratios. Different characteristics of a station—such as being a remote station or belonging to a high or low socioeconomic status block group—are significant correlates for particular crime outcomes such as disorderly conduct, robbery,, larceny.

title: Fear, safety in transit environments from the women’s perspective
authors: Loukaitou-Sideris, Anastasia
abstract: While the relationship between women’s fear of crime, public space has been the focus of considerable research, transit environments have received less attention. This study examines women’s safety in transit environments through a comprehensive review of the literature, in-depth interviews with representatives of 16 national women’s interest groups in the United States. It finds that women have distinct safety/security needs, are often fearful of certain transit environments, frequently adjust their behaviour, travel patterns to avoid them. This is particularly true for certain groups of women who feel more vulnerable to victimization, harassment than others. The women interviewed outlined design, policing, security technology, education/outreach strategies that would make women riders feel safer in transit settings.

title: Crime, safety in transit environments: a systematic review of the English, the French literature, 1970–2020
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Gaudelet, Nathan, Graf, Gabin
abstract: AbstractThis article reviews five decades of English, French literature on transit safety in several major databases, with the focus on Scopus, ScienceDirect. The review explores the nature, frequency of transit crime, passengers’ safety perceptions in transport nodes, along the trip using bibliometric analysis, a systematic review of the literature. The number of retrieved documents was 3137,, 245 were selected for in-depth analysis. Transit safety as a research area took off after the mid-1990s, peaked after the 2010s. The body of research is dominated by the English-language literature (mostly large cities), with a focus on the safety of rail-bound environments, examples of interventions to improve actual, perceived safety for public transportation (PT) users. Highlighting the importance of transit environments along the whole trip, the article also helps advocate for more inclusion of passengers’ safety needs, the involvement of multiple stakeholders in implementing PT policies.

title: Crime, bus stops: An examination using transit smart card, crime data
authors: Zahnow, Renee, Corcoran, Jonathan
journal: Environment, planning. B, urban analytics, city science
abstract: Bus stops are considered “risky places” given their propensity to generate opportunities for crime, attract would-be offenders. In this study we examine crime across a large network of bus stops (n = 7170) in Brisbane, Australia. We use smart card, land use data to measure the influence of passenger presence, features of the immediate bus stop environs on theft, property damage at bus stops during peak, off-peak travel periods. We find that when more passengers are present at stops, there is greater risk of theft but there is no effect of passenger presence on property damage. We conclude that factors associated with crime at bus stops vary based on time of day.

title: Commuters using public transit in New York City: Using area-level data to identify neighbourhoods with vulnerable riders
authors: Yu, Sung-Suk Violet, Smith, Martha J
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Theory; Government agencies; Robbery; Women; Victims of crime; Pragmatism;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal
abstract: This study uses routine activity theory, research on victimization, fear of crime to contextualize the importance of examining characteristics related to crime-target vulnerability among public transit commuters. A principal component analysis was conducted using 5-year data from the American Community Survey 2010. New York City (NYC) Police Department Compstat data for 2010 were used to provide a backcloth for understanding the types of crime problems vulnerable transit commuters may confront in their local areas. Findings show that a majority (55.3 per cent ) of the NYC commuters used public transit to travel to work, with more females, youths, ethnic minorities, non-naturalized immigrants commuting by public transit. Two distinct types of transit commuters were found to cluster in different parts of NYC, where the types of local-area crime problems also differed. These findings can help transit operators, policymakers build guardianship, assist place management in areas where potentially vulnerable commuters live.

title: Journey-to-crime distances of residential burglars in China disentangled: Origin, destination effects
authors: Xiao, Luzi, Liu, Lin, Song, Guangwen, Ruiter, Stijn, Zhou, Suhong
keywords: journey to crime; residential burglary; origin, destination effects; cross-classified multilevel model;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Research on journey-to-crime distance has revealed the importance of both the characteristics of the offender as well as those of target communities. However, the effect of the home community has so far been ignored. Besides, almost all journey-to-crime studies were done in Western societies,, little is known about how the distinct features of communities in major Chinese cities shape residential burglars’ travel patterns. To fill this gap, we apply a cross-classified multilevel regression model on data of 3763 burglary trips in ZG City, one of the bustling metropolises in China. This allows us to gain insight into how residential burglars’ journey-to-crime distances are shaped by their individual-level characteristics as well as those of their home, target communities. Results show that the characteristics of the home community have larger effects than those of target communities, while individual-level features are most influential. Older burglars travel over longer distances to commit their burglaries than the younger ones. Offenders who commit their burglaries in groups tend to travel further than solo offenders. Burglars who live in communities with a higher average rent, a denser road network, a higher percentage of local residents commit their burglaries at shorter distances. Communities with a denser road network attract burglars from a longer distance, whereas those with a higher percentage of local residents attract them from shorter by.

title: Adolescents’ fears of violence in transit environments during daily activities
authors: Wiebe, Douglas J, Richmond, Therese S, Poster, Jed, Guo, Wensheng, Allison, Paul D, Branas, Charles C
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Studies; Teenagers; Students; Behavior; Violence; Perceptions; Walking;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal
abstract: We investigated children’s perceived safety from assault risk while in different transportation modes. Children 10–18 years old were interviewed in Philadelphia, PA, USA, using a Geographic Information System (GIS) interface, reporting how safe they felt using a 10-point item (1=very unsafe, 10=very safe) during recent daily activities. Results show that among 153 subjects, 75.8 per cent felt less than very safe (that is, 8, for example, was 0.84 while in a car, 0.84 on a bus, but 0.66 on foot, 0.40 on a subway (P<0.05). Targeting transportation environment-related factors is warranted to help children feel safe during daily activities.

title: Shooting on the Street: Measuring the spatial influence of physical features on gun violence in a bounded street network
authors: Xu, Jie, Griffiths, Elizabeth
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Spatial influence; Physical features of place; Street network; Network Cross K Function; Gun violence; Alcoholic beverages; Measurement; Grocery stores; Violence; Pedestrians; Roads \& highways; Firearms; Bias; Crime; Walkways; Shooting; Density; Attraction;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Objectives Accurately estimate the strength, extent (distance) of the spatial influence of physical features on gun violence using a street network measurement strategy. Methods Treating disaggregated point locations as the unit-of-analysis, the spatial influence of various physical features of place on all 2012 incidents of gun violence in Newark, NJ is estimated along a street network plane rather than a planar plane,, using a continuous operationalization of street network distances as opposed to Euclidean or Grid distances. Network-based computation methods clarify the path distances over which physical features of place, or shooting attractors, exert a significant spatial influence on gun violence. Segmented regression models estimate feature-specific distance decay patterns by demarcating the exact network distances at which the strength of attraction weakens or dissipates entirely. Results Findings show that liquor stores, grocery stores, bus stops,, residential foreclosures are shooting attractors in Newark, NJ. The magnitude of spatial influence is strongest in the immediate vicinity of each physical feature,, declines precipitously thereafter; yet the nature, strength of the decay varies by feature. A comparison of results analyzed on a street network plane to those based on an unbounded plane illustrates the potential biases in traditional approaches. Conclusions Determining whether, how strongly physical features operate as crime attractors requires constraining the analyses to the street network plane, accurately measuring continuous distances along the street network. The methodology articulated in this study can be used to more precisely estimate the spatial influence, distance decay of various physical features of place on crime density.

title: Burglars blocked by barriers? The impact of physical, social barriers on residential burglars' target location choices in China
authors: Xiao, Luzi, Ruiter, Stijn, Liu, Lin, Song, Guangwen, Zhou, Suhong
keywords: China; Discrete choice; Physical, social barriers; Residential burglary;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Based on an offender spatial decision-making perspective, this burglary target location choice study aims to understand how physical, social barriers affect why residential burglars commit their crimes at particular locations in a major Chinese city. Using data on 3860 residential burglaries committed by 3772 burglars between January 2012, June 2016 in ZG city, China, conditional logit (discrete choice) models were estimated to assess residential burglars' target location choice preferences. Three types of physical barriers were distinguished: major roads with access control, major roads without access control,, major rivers. Social barriers were constructed based on the Hukou system to reflect how local, nonlocal residents live segregated lives. Results show that residential burglars are less likely to target areas for which they have to cross a physical barrier, even less likely to do so if they have to cross multiple rivers. Local burglars are more likely to target communities with a majority of local residents than communities with a majority nonlocal population or a mixed community. Such a social barrier was less pronounced for nonlocal burglars. These findings add new insight that physical, social barriers affect, to various degrees, where residential burglars in China commit their crimes. •This study aims to understand how barriers affect why residential burglars commit their crimes at particular locations in a major Chinese city.•All burglars are less likely to target areas separated by rivers, major roads.•Local burglars are more likely to target communities with a majority of local residents than the other ones.•Such social barrier effect is less pronounced for nonlocal burglars.

title: Decision to commit crime: rational or nonrational
authors: Walters, Glenn D, Kutztown University, USA
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Rationality; Emotions; Criminology; Decision making; England;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Objective to prove the necessity to take into account the influence of emotions on decision making to describe a combined model of the decision making process which unites rational, irrational components of choice in crime commitment. Methods dialectic systemic historicallegal formaljuridical methods summarization. Results the paper gives a complex analysis of the criminal decisionmaking process, reveals the factors increasing the probability of antisocial actions. The value of the combined cognitiveemotive model is that emotions can give more significant information to the decisionmaker than reasoning. Scientific novelty the author proposes a theory of decision making which says that a person chooses to act or not to act under hedonistic or moral emotions while the irrelevant emotions are increased, the relevant ones are suppressed by cognitive, situational factors serving as a basis for criminal decision making. Practical significance studying the role of emotions in the criminal, noncriminal decision making will significantly contribute to the development of criminology. The research results will be useful for researchers, lawenforcement bodies as well as for all those who are interested in the issues of crime control, prevention.

title: Rational misbehavior? Evaluating an integrated dual-process model of criminal decision making
authors: van Gelder, Jean-Louis, de Vries, Reinout E
abstract: Objectives Test the hypothesis that dispositional self-control, morality relate to criminal decision making via different mental processing modes, a 'hot' affective mode, a 'cool' cognitive one. Methods Structural equation modeling in two studies under separate samples of undergraduate students using scenarios describing two different types of crime, illegal downloading, insurance fraud. Both self-control, morality are operationalized through the HEXACO model of personality (Lee, Ashton in Multivariate Behav Res 39(2): 329-358, 2004). Results In Study 1, negative state affect, i.e., feelings of fear, worry evoked by a criminal prospect,, perceived risk of sanction were found to mediate the relations between both dispositions, criminal choice. In Study 2, processing mode was manipulated by having participants rely on either their thinking or on their feelings prior to deciding on whether or not to make a criminal choice. Activating a cognitive mode strengthened the relation between perceived risk, criminal choice, whereas activating an affective mode strengthened the relation between negative affect, criminal choice. Conclusion In conjunction, these results extend research that links stable individual dispositions to proximal states that operate in the moment of decision making. The results also add to dispositional perspectives of crime by using a structure of personality that incorporates both self-control, morality. Contributions to the proximal, state, perspectives reside in the use of a new hot/cool perspective of criminal decision making that extends rational choice frameworks.

title: Geographic mobility, criminal behavior
authors: Tittle, Charles R, Paternoster, Raymond
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: CRIMINAL behavior; CRIMINAL psychology; CRIMINALS; MIGRATION, Internal; GEOGRAPHIC mobility;330\_SAEnv;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: A structural model portraying the processes through which geographic mobility presumably affects individual criminal behavior is derived by amalgamating twelve theoretical statements from the literature. The model is then estimated using self-report data from a three-state survey, focusing on four self-projected offenses, change in residence over a ten-year period. The results show no direct influences of mobility but they do indicate the presence of a fairly general indirect effect through the intervening linkage of moral commitment to conventional norms. Thus, in general, mobility appears to reduce moral commitments that, in turn, increase the chances of offense. Yet the discovery of an inverse effect of mobility on the offense of marijuana smoking suggests that the effects of mobility may vary somewhat by type of offense under consideration. We conclude that the mobility/crime linkage merits further attention, especially in an effort to build more specific, conditional theory.

title: All offenders are equal, but some are more equal than others: Variation in journeys to crime between offenders
authors: Townsley, Michael, Sidebottom, Aiden
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; CRIMINAL careers; CRIMINAL behavior, Prediction of; CRIME forecasting; CRIMINAL behavior; DEVIANT behavior; CRIMINOLOGICAL theory; GEOGRAPHICAL offender profiling; aggregation fallacy; journey to crime; Multilevel analysis; nested data; repeated measures;330\_SAEnv;criminology;20250703\_Aiden
abstract: The results of this study reveal a major methodological problem with an established body of criminological literature-the journey to crime. The dominant finding of such research is that most crimes occur close to an offender's home. Consequently, journeys to crime typically display a distance-decay function that is assumed to exist between, within offenders. However, most journey-to-crime studies use nested data-individual offenders contributing multiple crime trips-yet employ analytic methods that fail to account for this property, leading to inference, aggregation concerns. In the study outlined in this article , we demonstrated the implications of using nested data for analyzing the journey to crime. We showed that once controlling for nesting, only a few (prolific) offenders display a distance decay pattern. Implications of the findings for theory, future research are discussed.

title: Traveling to violence: The case for a mobility-based spatial typology of homicide
authors: Tita, George, Griffiths, Elizabeth
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: VIOLENCE; HOMICIDE; INTERPERSONAL relations; VICTIMS of crimes; CRIME; CRIMINALS; NEIGHBORHOODS; PITTSBURGH (Pa.); PENNSYLVANIA; Crime, Criminal Justice,, Law Enforcement; mobility triangles; victim/offender mobility;330\_SAEnv;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: According to routine activities theory, crime is the result of an intersection between victims, offenders in both time, space. We introduce a spatial typology that identifies five combinations of victim, offender mobility to homicide incident locations: internal, predatory, intrusion, offense mobility,, total mobility types. The authors’ argue that the joint mobility pattern of the victim, offender is the mechanism underlying routine activities theory,, made explicit by the spatial typology. Using information on the 420 homicides in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, between 1987, 1995, we demonstrate that the majority of homicides involve at least some mobility on the part of victims and/or offenders. Our results also indicate that mobility to homicide incident locations is most associated with event characteristics such as motive, rather than with characteristics of the participants. With most offenders committing the homicide outside of their own neighborhood, levels of lethal violence in a community are influenced more by the interaction among nonlocal participants than by the violent actions of local residents.

title: The consequences of queueing: Crowding, situational features, aggression in entertainment precincts
authors: Townsley, Michael, Grimshaw, Robert
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Studies; Emotional abuse; Theory; Licenses; Cultural change; Risk assessment; Behavior; Crime; Liquor industry; Wage \& price controls; Violence; Computer simulation; Councils; Criminal statistics; Australia;330\_SAEnv;CPCS2008-2016;Crime Prevention, Community Safety
abstract: Alcohol-related violence has long been regarded a serious social problem in Australia. Extensive research has been conducted analysing the relationship between alcohol, crowding, aggression inside licensed premises, consistently finding that situational, social factors play significant roles. However, there has been a dearth of empirical research into these relationships in the public space outside licensed premises, around transport nodes. This study provides such an analysis. A systematic observational measurement was employed on six street segments in the Valley Entertainment Precinct, Brisbane, Queensland that recorded aspects of the physical, social environment, levels of intoxication, street population, queueing practices, crowding, aggression. Over 96 hours of observation, 42 acts of high-level, 94 acts of low-level aggression were witnessed, a far higher rate than previous studies. The relationships between levels of crowding, aggression were observed, even after controlling for major correlates. The results of the study strengthen arguments about the need to consider crowding, queue management issues as well as the design of public spaces in entertainment precincts to reduce aggression.

title: Target selection models with preference variation between offenders
authors: Townsley, Michael, Birks, Daniel, Ruiter, Stijn, Bernasco, Wim, White, Gentry
abstract: Objectives: This study explores preference variation in location choice strategies of residential burglars. Applying a model of offender target selection that is grounded in assertions of the routine activity approach, rational choice perspective, crime pattern, social disorganization theories, it seeks to address the as yet untested assumption that crime location choice preferences are the same for all offenders. Methods: Analyzing detected residential burglaries from Brisbane, Australia, we apply a random effects variant of the discrete spatial choice model to estimate preference variation between offenders across six location choice characteristics. Furthermore, in attempting to understand the causes of this variation we estimate how offenders’ spatial target preferences might be affected by where they live, by their age. Results: Findings of this analysis demonstrate that while in the aggregate the characteristics of location choice are consistent with the findings from previous studies, considerable preference variation is found between offenders. Conclusions: This research highlights that current understanding of choice outcomes is relatively poor, that existing applications of the discrete spatial choice approach may underestimate preference variation between offenders.

title: Examining the disorder–crime connection in Philadelphia parks
authors: Tower, Sondra M, Groff, Elizabeth
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Crime; Studies; Dissertations \& theses; Research; Law enforcement; Parks \& recreation areas; Playgrounds; Outdoor activities;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal
abstract: Recent research on urban parks, crime in Philadelphia has shown that some parks have higher crime densities than other places within the city. Why that relationship exists is an open question. Here, field survey data collected through primary observation, along with official Philadelphia crime data from 2008 to 2009, is used to evaluate one possible explanation: the relationship between assessed physical disorder, crime. Regression models are used to examine both the influence of crime on incivilities, the inverse relationship, over an approximate 1-year time period. Findings show that contrary to what theories of incivilities would suggest, assessed physical disorder in parks in 1 year has no significant connection to crime in the next. However, both disorder, violent crime counts are significantly related to subsequent levels of observed incivilities. Results suggest that increasing the police presence in urban parks may serve to reduce both future criminal activity, physical disorder. The findings have implications for residents, park managers, police.

title: Crime generators in context: Examining ‘place in neighborhood’ propositions
authors: Tillyer, Marie Skubak, Wilcox, Pamela, Walter, Rebecca J
abstract: Objectives The present study tests hypotheses regarding the moderating influence of neighborhood-level criminal opportunity on the relationship between crime generators, block-level crime. Methods We first estimated multilevel negative binomial regression models for violent, property,, drug crimes to identify crime-type specific crime generators on each block. We then estimated a series of crime-type specific models to examine whether the effects of violent, property,, drug crime generators are moderated by three census block group-level indicators of neighborhood criminal opportunity—concentrated disadvantage, vehicular traffic activity,, civic engagement. Results The positive relationship between crime generators, crime on blocks was exacerbated in census block groups with high levels of concentrated disadvantage, high levels of traffic activity for all three crime types. The effects of crime generators on block-level crime were significantly tempered in census block groups with high levels of civic engagement. Conclusions Particular place types do not generate crime similarly across varying neighborhood contexts. Rather, the criminogenic effects of micro-places appear to be exacerbated in neighborhoods with extensive criminal opportunity, tempered in neighborhoods with less criminal opportunity.

title: Busy businesses, busy contexts: The distribution, sources of crime at commercial properties
authors: Tillyer, Marie Skubak, Walter, Rebecca J
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objective: Examine the distribution, sources of crime across freestanding businesses in San Antonio. We test hypotheses about the main, interactive effects of neighborhood, business characteristics on crime at the business, with a focus on busy contexts, busy businesses. Method: Police crime incident data are spatially joined to study area business parcels. Additional data sources include Infogroup USA Business Data, the American Community Survey,, an Environmental Protection Agency traffic activity indicator. Multilevel negative binomial regression models are estimated to observe the main, interactive effects of census block group, business variables on crime at the parcel. Results: Businesses located in block groups with more commercial property, high levels of vehicular traffic experience more crime. In addition, crime is higher at “busy” businesses, as indicated by employee size, sales volume,, square footage. Busy contexts, busy businesses do not appear to interact to increase crime at the parcel beyond their main effects. Conclusions: Crime is clustered at relatively few businesses,, this variation cannot be explained by business type alone. Both neighborhood, business characteristics are associated with crime at freestanding businesses, with busy businesses, those within busier block groups experiencing more crime.

title: Urban park crime: Neighborhood context, park features
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Haberman, Cory P, Groff, Elizabeth R
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Social cohesion; Socioeconomic status; Structural models; Social disorganization; Urban areas; Motivation; Violent crime; Urban crime; Structural equation models; Criminology; Communities; Neighborhoods;330\_SAEnv;J Crim Justice
abstract: This work examined the determinants of park crime, drawing together into one conceptual frame three threads from community criminology - community demographic structural crime determinants; community cultural crime determinants, focusing specifically on social cohesion;, park features that are potentially crime and/or disorder relevant. Generalized structural equation models using data for 249 urban parks, their surrounds show: in the preferred model of disorder crime two aspects of nearby crime,, community social cohesion, both drive park crime; in the preferred model of violent crime, one aspect of nearby crime, community socioeconomic status,, one park feature, security fencing, all shape park crime. Implications for several domains within community criminology merit mention. •Find crime levels in small urban parks affected by neighborhood, park features,, nearby crime.•Links depend on type of crime, violent crime or disorder.•Neighborhood structural, cultural features can both prove relevant.•Work contributes to ongoing discussions about healthy living, risky facilities,, community criminology.

title: Does the configuration of the Street network influence where outdoor serious violence takes place? Using space syntax to test crime pattern theory
authors: Summers, Lucia, Johnson, Shane D
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Street networks; Crime pattern theory; Offender awareness spaces; Violence; Space syntax; Crime; Violent crime; Layout; Spatial distribution; Syntax; Murders \& murder attempts;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Objectives To examine the effect of the physical layout of the street network on the spatial distribution of outdoor serious violence. Crime pattern theory predicts crime would be more prevalent on more connected, accessible or traveled street segments, as these will be more likely to fall within an offender’s awareness space. Methods The distribution of incidents of outdoor murder, attempted murder, other near-lethal violent crimes that occurred in one London (UK) borough (N = 447 offenses) was analyzed. The space syntax methodology was used to estimate the to-, through-movement potential of individual street segments. Results Regression analyses showed higher levels of integration (a measure of to-movement potential), choice (through-movement potential) were associated with greater odds of a street segment containing at least one crime. Risk was also higher for segments located near to segments with the highest global choice values. In contrast, connectivity (the number of other segments a street segment is adjacent to) was negatively associated with crime occurrence. Conclusions As predicted, the configuration of the street network was associated with the spatial distribution of outdoor serious violence. Crime reduction measures should be targeted at high-choice street segments (typically main arteries), segments nearby.

title: Crime feeds on legal activities: Daily mobility flows help to explain thieves’ target location choices
authors: Song, Guangwen, Bernasco, Wim, Liu, Lin, Xiao, Luzi, Zhou, Suhong, Liao, Weiwei
abstract: Objective: According to routine activity theory, crime pattern theory, crime feeds on the legal routine activities of offenders, unguarded victims. Based on this assumption, the present study investigates whether daily mobility flows of the urban population help predict where individual thieves commit crimes. Methods: Geocoded tracks of mobile phones are used to estimate the intensity of population mobility between pairs of 1616 communities in a large city in China. Using data on 3436 police-recorded thefts from the person, we apply discrete choice models to assess whether mobility flows help explain where offenders go to perpetrate crime. Results: Accounting for the presence of crime generators, distance to the offender’s home location, we find that the stronger a community is connected by population flows to where the offender lives, the larger its probability of being targeted. Conclusions: The mobility flow measure is a useful addition to the estimated effects of distance, crime generators. It predicts the locations of thefts much better than the presence of crime generators does. However, it does not replace the role of distance, suggesting that offenders are more spatially restricted than others, or that even within their activity spaces they prefer to offend near their homes.

title: Offender-target redistribution on a new public transport system
authors: Sedelmaier, Christopher M
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Low income groups; Robbery; Hypotheses; Neighborhoods; Light rail transportation; New Jersey;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal
abstract: This study seeks evidence that a newly introduced light rail system has altered the crime opportunity structure in a north-eastern United States city. New public transport systems may affect crime opportunities in their constituent neighborhoods, either by introducing non-local offenders to previously unexplored ‘hunting grounds’, or by delivering new opportunities to local offenders already active in station neighborhoods. Chi-square analyses of arrest data connected to offenses committed in station areas before, after service introduction found little evidence that the new system had either introduced non-local offenders to its constituent neighborhoods or contributed with new targets to local offenders. These findings are important to transport planners, crime scientists alike, as this evidence may help to both reframe public discourse about potential transport system effects on local crime, aid law enforcement in crafting crime prevention strategies.

title: Super controllers, crime prevention: A routine activity explanation of crime prevention success, failure
authors: Sampson, Rana, Eck, John E, Dunham, Jessica
abstract: Why does crime prevention fail? And under what conditions does it succeed? Routine Activity Theory provides the foundation for understanding crime, its patterns by focusing on variations in the convergence of offenders, targets, controllers in space, time. But Routine Activity Theory does not provide a full understanding of why the controllers may be absent or ineffective. This article expands Routine Activity Theory to explain controllers. It claims that the behaviors of controllers can be understood in the context of their relationship with super controllers – those who regulate controllers’ incentives to prevent crime. The article lists, describes types of super controllers. Drawing on a rational choice perspective, Situational Crime Prevention, the article examines the methods super controllers use to regulate the conduct of controllers. Examples are used throughout to illustrate specific points, to show the diversity of super controlling. This article concludes with a discussion of the implication of super controllers for the practice of crime prevention, research into crime reduction methods.

title: Is travel actually risky? A study of situational causes of victimization
authors: Ruiter, Stijn, Bernasco, Wim
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Victimization risk; Time use; Travel mode; Smartphone; Fixed effects; Victimization; Travel; Public transportation; Smartphones; Risk assessment; Tourism;330\_SAEnv;Journey to crime/victimization
abstract: ObjectiveWe present a first test using a smartphone time use survey app for whether the risk of criminal victimization is higher while traveling than during other activities,, assess risk heterogeneity between public transport, private transport by car,, private open-air transport.MethodsA sample of 1334 young adults completed a time-use survey on their smartphones with additional items on criminal victimization. Participants reported their time use, victimization experiences (vandalism, theft, threat, or assault) per 10-min timeslot for 4 days. To prevent potential confounders from affecting the results, we analyzed the data with a fixed effects logit model that exclusively relies on within-person variation between timeslots.FindingsA total of 78 victimization situations were reported by 45 participants. Although these numbers are too low to draw definitive conclusions, with respect to the four types of victimization measured, sleeping appeared to be the safest activity. The risk of victimization was considerably larger during travel, but also during many other activities. We found shopping to be the activity with the highest risk of victimization. No victimization was observed during private transport by car, but the risk of victimization was significantly higher in private open-air, public transport than during sleep.ConclusionUsing a state-of-the-art instrument, a rigorous statistical design, we tentatively conclude that the risk of criminal victimization is not higher during travel than during most other activities, only sleeping is safer. Larger samples are needed to assess the robustness of our findings. We discuss practical implications, strengths, weaknesses of the study,, new research challenges.

title: Global warming, U.s. crime rates: An application of routine activity theory
authors: Rotton, James, Cohn, Ellen G
abstract: Two archival analyses were performed to examine the association between annual temperatures, U.S. crime rates. The first was based on area-averaged temperatures in the United States as a whole for the years 1950 through 1999. Box-Jenkins time-series analyses indicated that annual temperatures were associated with assault but not murder rates in analyses that controlled for yearly population, ethnicity,, three economic variables. The second analysis was based on state-centered crime rates from 1960 through 1998, included the same controls. Contrary to the general aggression model, cross-sectional time-series analyses indicated that annual temperatures were associated with rates for assault, rape, robbery, burglary,, larceny, but not murder or motor vehicle theft. The results are consistent with a routine activity theory interpretation of everyday, criminal behavior.

title: Outdoor temperature, climate control,, criminal assault: The spatial, temporal ecology of violence
authors: Rotton, James, Cohn, Ellen G
abstract: Based on the negative affect escape (NAE) model of heat, aggression, it was hypothesized that relationships between temperature, aggravated assaultswould be moderated by access to air conditioning. This hypothesis was tested by subjecting calls for service received by police in Dallas, Texas, to multivariate analyses of covariance that employed weather variables as predictors, controlled for the temporal variables of holidays, time of day, day of the week,, season of the year. As the NAE model predicts, assaults in probably climate-controlled settings were a linear function of temperature, whereas assaults in settings that probably lacked climate control declined after peaking at moderately high temperatures. The results are consistent with recent attempts to use the concept of social avoidance to integrate routine activity theory, psychological theories of aggression.

title: Bars, blocks,, crimes revisited: Linking the theory of routine activities to the empiricism of “hot spots”
authors: Roncek, Dennis W, Maier, Pamela A
keywords: CRIME; BARS (Drinking establishments); CRIME scenes; CRIMINOLOGY; BLOCKS (City planning); TAVERNS (Inns);330\_SAEnv;criminology
abstract: Anticipating recent developments in routine activities theory, Roncek, Bell (1981) found that bars, taverns had detrimental effects on crime on residential city blocks in Cleveland for 1970. We replicate, extend their work by examining the effects of recreational liquor establishments (i.e., taverns, cocktail lounges) on crime from 1979 to 1981 on Cleveland's residential city blocks. The number of such businesses on residential city blocks has positive, statistically significant effects on the amount of crime. The effects on crime are compounded when the businesses are located in areas with physical characteristics that are associated with more anonymity, lower guardianship. Our results reaffirm the value of new developments in routine activities theory that now stress the importance of facilities. They also extend recent work attempting to identify, analyze “hot spots” of crime.

title: Factors associated with the guardianship of places: Assessing the relative importance of the spatio-physical, sociodemographic contexts in generating opportunities for capable guardianship
authors: Reynald, Danielle M
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Routine activity theory can be applied to places in which a motivated offender encounters a suitable target that is not effectively guarded. The focus of this article was on the third aspect of this theory as the explanatory power of guardianship was examined, compared to other related contextual factors in explaining criminal victimization at micro-places. This empirical study used an observational measure of guardianship in action in residential places by observing household occupancy, monitoring by residents,, direct intervention during the daytime, nighttime. The results demonstrated the significant role of active guardianship compared to other spatio-physical, sociodemographic factors in explaining the amount of property crime recorded at the street segment level. This article is concluded by highlighting the ways in which these contextual factors help generate opportunities for capable guardianship, while simultaneously blocking opportunities for property crime.

title: Street crime strategies: The changing schemata of streetwalkers
authors: Riccio, R
abstract: Streetwalkers have unique transactions with the urban environment. They must be aware of the shifting environmental stimuli, react accordingly in order to remain in business, avoid arrests. The transactions, schemata of streetwalkers are explored in light of various sociocultural factors by use of police arrest records, field observations, survey results from arrested prostitutes, a multiple regression,, a multidimensional scaling technique. Women of different races are found to be using similar street crime strategies, however their schemata differ. Black, White street-walkers appear to work at different times,, sometimes places, during the day. The interrelationships between behavior, space,, time are apparent, reveal the dynamic, multifaceted nature of criminal transactions.

title: Analyzing victimization determinants for the city of Barcelona: The role of public infrastructures
authors: Planells-Struse, S
journal: Contemporary readings in law, social justice
keywords: Law; Sports facilities; Robbery; Health facilities; Cities; Spain;330\_SAEnv
abstract: In recent decades the increase in the number of crime victimization surveys conducted across countries has allowed researchers to examine the determinants of crime victimization by applying both the routine activity/opportunity theory, social disorganization theory. In this paper we apply a multilevel model to test both theories for the first time in Barcelona, a city that has undergone a massive socio-economic change over the last decade. We also introduce the effect of the public infrastructure built by the public sector in this period to determine its impact on the probability of victimization. The results show that both theories partially explain victimization probabilities for the case of Barcelona, that, depending on the type of public infrastructure, proximity to the facility may either increase or decrease a citizen's probability of victimization.

title: Assessing macro-level predictors, theories of crime: A meta-analysis
authors: Pratt, Travis C, Cullen, Francis T
abstract: The macro-level approach reemerged as a salient criminological paradigm in the late 1970s, early 1980s. Prompted by new theories, reformulations of existing ones, over 200 empirical studies explored ecological correlates of crime. Few efforts have been made, however, to make sense of this literature. A meta-analysis was undertaken to determine the relative effects of macro-level predictors of crime. Indicators of concentrated disadvantage (e.g., racial heterogeneity, poverty,, family disruption) are among the strongest, most stable predictors. Except for incarceration, variables indicating increased use of the criminal justice system (e.g., policing, get-tough policy effects) are among the weakest. Across all studies, social disorganization, resource/economic deprivation theories receive strong empirical support; anomie/strain, social support/social altruism,, routine activity theories receive moderate support;, deterrence/rational choice, subcultural theories receive weak support.

title: Crime script analysis for adult image-based sexual abuse: a study of crime intervention points for retribution-style offenders
authors: O'Hara, Abigail C, Ko, Ryan K L, Mazerolle, Lorraine, Rimer, Jonah R
abstract: AbstractObjectiveThis research uses crime scripts to understand adult retribution-style image-based sexual abuse (RS-IBSA) offender decision-making, offending in offline, online environments. We explain the crime-commission process of adult RS-IBSA, identify crime intervention points at eight crime script stages.MethodsPublicly released court transcripts of adult RS-IBSA prosecution cases (n = 18) in New Zealand from 2015 to 2018 were utilised to examine the crime-commission process of adult RS-IBSA. We analysed the court transcripts thematically at offence-level prior to constructing the crime scripts.FindingsThe study identified four types of adult RS-IBSA acts including the non-consensual dissemination of a victim’s intimate images, violent cyber sextortion, covert intimate photography,, unauthorised access of a victim’s phone/media. From our analysis, we identified three script tracks, constructed three distinct crime scripts: (1) threats, sextortion, dissemination; (2) unauthorised access of a victim’s mobile device, dissemination;, (3) covert intimate filming. We highlight areas for potential intervention for law enforcement agencies, policy makers to increase deterrence, personal security in online, offline spaces.ConclusionAdult RS-IBSA occurs in a range of dating, domestic contexts. This study develops crime scripts for adult RS-IBSA, advances our understanding of how the Internet/smartphones/digital media translates into virtual crime scenes with opportunities for maximum harm infliction. We offer several policy implications including revising current RS-IBSA legislation, supporting law enforcement agencies with policing online, offline intimate relationship spaces through situational prevention.

title: Expert decision making in burglars
authors: Nee, Claire, Meenaghan, Amy
keywords: THIEVES; CRIME prevention; CRIMINOLOGY; COGNITIVE development; BURGLARS; GREAT Britain;330\_SAEnv;British Journal of criminology
abstract: This paper begins by reviewing research on the cognitive processing used by residential burglars when choosing targets.
