It is imperative that aging services, allied professionals who work with older persons lacking financial capacity learn how to prevent, detect,, remedy exploitation,, to collaborate with each other to achieve those goals.``,

title: Credulity rather than general trust may increase vulnerability to fraud in older adults: a moderated mediation model
authors: Shao, Jingjin, Du, Weiping, Lin, Tian, Li, Xiying, Li, Jiamei, Lei, Huijie
keywords: Credulity; general trust; greed; persuasion; vulnerability to fraud;340\_Frauds
abstract: The present study aimed to clarify whether it is credulity or general trust that specifically affects vulnerability to fraud, as well as investigating the mediating role of susceptibility to persuasion, the moderating role of greed in this relationship. 254 Chinese older adults completed measures of credulity, general trust, susceptibility to persuasion, greed,, vulnerability to fraud. The results showed that credulity, but not general trust, was positively correlated with vulnerability to fraud, after controlling for demographic covariates. Susceptibility to persuasion partially mediated the effect of credulity on vulnerability to fraud. In addition, this mediating effect of susceptibility to persuasion was only significant in older adults with higher levels of greed. Our findings suggest that credulity, rather than general trust, is a risk factor in vulnerability to fraud among older adults,, may inform the development of supportive interventions to reduce this population's risk of falling victim to fraud.

title: The psychology of the internet fraud victimization of older adults: A systematic review
authors: Shang, Yuxi, Wu, Zhongxian, Du, Xiaoyu, Jiang, Yanbin, Ma, Beibei, Chi, Meihong
keywords: cognitive function; internet fraud victims; older adults; personality traits; technology, experience;340\_Frauds
abstract: Criminals targeting, exploiting older adults in online environments are of great concern. This study systematically retrieved, analyzed articles on the psychological characteristics of older adult victims of online fraud. First, we found that there was no evidence that older adults were more prevalent than other individuals of other ages among online fraud victims,, current researchers have focused more on why older adults are easy targets for fraud (susceptibility to being cheated). Second, research on psychological factors of older adults' susceptibility to online fraud has mainly focused on cognitive function, trust traits,, other personality traits, such as social loneliness, the Big Five personality traits,, self-control. Among them, most researchers claim that the cyber-cheating of older adults may be due to a decline in their cognitive function. However, there has not been a consensus on how cognitive function, physical, mental conditions affect older people who are cheated. Third, techniques (i.e., methods, techniques used by fraudsters), experience (i.e., familiarity with internet technology or fraud) may be related to the susceptibility of older adults to fraud,, these studies have also not yet generated a consensus supported by reliable data. Based on the above research uncertainties, we propose that fraud prevention, control strategies for older adults should be applied with caution.

title: Forewarning reduces fraud susceptibility in vulnerable consumers
authors: Scheibe, Susanne, Notthoff, Nanna, Menkin, Josephine, Ross, Lee, Shadel, Doug, Deevy, Martha, Carstensen, Laura L
keywords: Telemarketing fraud; aging; decision making; forewarning; prevention;340\_Frauds;02\_高齢者詐欺被害についての教育プログラム;Basic Appl Soc Psych;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: Telemarketing fraud is pervasive, older consumers are disproportionally targeted. Given laboratory research showing that forewarning can effectively counter influence appeals, we conducted a field experiment to test whether forewarning could protect people who had been victimized in the past. A research assistant with prior experience as a telemarketer pitched a mock scam two or four weeks after participants were warned about the same scam or an entirely different scam. Both warnings reduced unequivocal acceptance of the mock scam although outright refusals (as opposed to expressions of skepticism) were more frequent with the same scam warning than the different scam warning. The same scam warning, but not the different scam warning, lost effectiveness over time. Findings demonstrate that social psychological research can inform effective protection strategies against telemarketing fraud.

title: Information network model query processing
authors: Song, Xiaopu
abstract: The accidents of Fukushima nuclear power stations produce too much of information about risk from nuclear power accidents. It generally assumed that after the people try to interpret the information by utilizing the specific mode of information process, they judge the risk. Our study will test the heuristic-systematic information-processing model (HSM) suggested by Shelly Chaiken. HSM suggested two information process modes in heuristic or systematic ways; the heuristic mode used the least amount of cognitive processing governed by availability, accessibility,, applicability whereas the system mode did the effortful processing, depending on comprehension, analysis, reliability of information. To test the workings of those two modes in judging the risk information related with Fukushima nuclear power accident, we will collect the data with survey method. The main topics in analysis will include as follow; first, examine the tendency of using two modes, relationships between those two modes; Second, analyze the impact of determinants of two modes on information processing, such as ability for judgment, motivation to make judgment,, information relevance; Third, investigate the contextual variables, e.g., information attributes or source credibility, to moderate the relationships between the determinant, two modes of information processing. Question \& Propose 1) Question A lot of previous studies in the information processing have focused on not only role of recipient's characteristics but also attributes of information, source's characteristics. However, there are few studies to integrate the recipient, information, source. Thus we elaborate this information processing model both by building the more comprehensive theoretical model, by testing it through empirical analyze of the survey data related with Fukushima nuclear power accidents. Especially, we investigate how the attributes of information, source's characteristics to moderate the relationships between the determinant, two modes of information processing. 2) Propose ① We examine the tendency of using two modes (heuristic-systematic information-processing), relationships between those two modes in judging nuclear power accidents in Fukushima, Japan. ② We analyze the impact of recipient's characteristics, e.g., receipt's ability for judgment, motivation to make judgment,, information relevance, on using two mode information processing, ③ We investigate how the contextual variables , e.g., information attributes or source credibility, to moderate the relationships between the determinant, two modes of information processing. Theoretical Background Heuristic-Systematic Information Processing Model (HSM) assumes that heuristic, systematic information processing can occur simultaneously. Heuristic information processing depends on the availability, accessibility, reliability of judgmental heuristics. But systematic information processing is more effortful, capacity limited than heuristic processing. Heuristic information processing can proceed in either a more or less self-conscious manner. The principles of least effort, sufficiency are crucial motivational determinants of information processing mode (Eagly \& Chaiken, 1993, p. 341). Heuristic-systematic model Developed to apply to ``validity seeking'' persuasion settings in which people's primary motivational concern is to attain accurate attitudes that square with relevant facts In these settings, the primary processing goal of accuracy-motivated recipients is to assess to validity of persuasive messages,, that both heuristic, systematic processing can serve this objective (Chaiken, 1980, 1987) Research Model \& Data 1) Model We set the demographic variables, attributes of information, recipient's characteristics, source's characteristics as independent variables in explaining Dual Information Processing (Heuristic-systematic information processing) about nuclear power. As we state above, important determinants for Dual Information Processing (HSM) consisted of not only recipient's characteristic Variables but also attribute of information, source's characteristics. In this view point, it is important that we inspect for relationships between recipient's characteristics, attributes of information,, source's characteristics. Research Model of Dual Information Processing 2) Data We will use the survey data which are collected in 2012 with samples of 564. The following is a regression analysis on determinant of choice of systematic processing model against heuristic processing model, related with processing the information about nuclear power accident, Fukushima. As you can see from below Model 1, 2, 3, demographical factor (gender, age), recipient factor (ability, motivation), source factor (credibility), information factor (ambiguity, usefulness, attraction) were showed the significant influences. Also in model 4, several interaction terms showed significant impact on HSM Findings 1 Below Table 1 clearly shows that each independent variables have a different impact on systemic information processing. Also it means that Dual Information Processing has different determinants. → Demographic : The male, the older show more systematic information processing than the female, the younger. → Recipient : The higher recipient's ability, motivation appear, the more systemic information processing occurs. → Source : More credible sources about information is, the more people process information systematically. → Information : More useful or interested information is, the more people process information systematically whereas more ambiguous information is, the more people process information heuristically. Hierarchical Regression Analysis In table 2, we analyze the correlation between HSM, systemic information processing, contrasted with heuristic one,, independent variables. The table show all of correlation coefficients significant. The relationship between HSM, Determinant variables Note: *. Correlation is significant at the 0.1 level (2-tailed) ;**. Correlation is significant at the 0.05 level (2-tailed) ; Correlation is significant at the 0.01 level (2-tailed) Findings 2 The ability, relevance, motivation, credibility, accuracy, usefulness, attraction has positive relation with systemic information processing. The ambiguity, however, represented opposite impaction (non-significant). It assumed that the attribute of information, source credibility intervene between receipts' motivation, choice of information processing model. So we will analyze the moderating effect. In Table1, Model 4 showed that that there are significant interactions between attributes of information, i.e, accuracy, usability, attractiveness of information, sources credibility, receipt's motivation. Moderating effects were presented in below Figures. Findings 3 Moderating effect exists between motivation, information usefulness. In other words, the information usefulness plays to suppress the effect of recipient's motivation on the systemic information processing. Summery Demographical factor (gender (-), age (+)), recipient factor (ability (+), motivation (+)), source factor (credibility (+)), information factor (ambiguity (-), usefulness (+), attraction (+)) significantly influence the systemic information processing. Moderating effect by information usefulness exists, which attenuate the motivation's impact on the systemic information processing .

title: Contrary to psychological, popular opinion, there is no compelling evidence that older adults are disproportionately victimized by consumer fraud
authors: Ross, Michael, Grossmann, Igor, Schryer, Emily
journal: Perspectives on psychological science: a journal of the Association for Psychological Science
keywords: aging, decision making; cognitive aging; consumer fraud; emotional regulation, aging; successful aging;340\_Frauds
abstract: According to psychological, popular opinion, older persons are especially susceptible to consumer fraud. Research on cognitive, affective aging reveals age-related changes that could increase the vulnerability of older persons to consumer fraud. However, this research does not show that consumer fraud actually is more prevalent among older persons. In generalizing from laboratory findings of cognitive decline to age differences in the prevalence of consumer fraud, psychologists may underestimate the influence in everyday life of possible protective factors associated with old age, including increased experience, changes in goals, lifestyle, income, as well as purchasing, risk behaviors. We review evidence on the prevalence of consumer fraud, conclude that there is no clear indication that it is more prevalent among older persons. Aggregating across all consumer frauds, there is evidence that consumer fraud is less common among older persons than adults of other ages. This evidence is potentially flawed, however, because of failings inherent in the methodologies. In the absence of irrefutable data, it is premature to conclude that consumer fraud is less prevalent among older adults, but it is also premature to conclude that consumer fraud is more prevalent among older persons, as is assumed in conventional, psychological wisdom.

title: Online routines, identity theft victimization: Further expanding routine activity theory beyond direct-contact offenses
authors: Reyns, Bradford W
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objectives: The purpose of the current study was to extend recent work aimed at applying routine activity theory to crimes in which the victim, offender never come into physical proximity. To that end, relationships between individuals' online routines, identity theft victimization were examined. Method: Data from a subsample of 5,985 respondents from the 2008 to 2009 British Crime Survey were analyzed. Utilizing binary logistic regression, the relationships between individuals' online routine activities (e.g., banking, shopping, downloading), individual characteristics (e.g., gender, age, employment),, perceived risk of victimization on identity theft victimization were assessed. Results: The results suggest that individuals who use the Internet for banking and/or e-mailing/instant messaging are about 50 percent more likely to be victims of identity theft than others. Similarly, online shopping, downloading behaviors increased victimization risk by about 30 percent. Males, older persons,, those with higher incomes were also more likely to experience victimization, as were those who perceived themselves to be at greater risk of victimization. Conclusions: Although the routine activity approach was originally written to account for direct-contact offenses, it appears that the perspective also has utility in explaining crimes at a distance. Further research should continue to explore the online, offline routines that increase individuals' risks of identity theft victimization.

title: A routine activity perspective on online victimisation
authors: Reyns, Bradford W
keywords: Business And Economics--Banking And Finance; Hacking; Victimization; Phishing; Malware; Routine activities; Computer viruses; Studies; Criminology; Canada; United States--US;340\_Frauds
abstract: Purpose – The purpose of this study is to test a comprehensive routine activity framework on three types of online victimization. Prior research has utilized routine activity theory to explain varied online forms of victimization, but most have focused on its person-based forms. The present study, therefore, expands upon this research to examine the effects of online exposure, online target suitability, online guardianship upon phishing, hacking, malware infection victimization. Design/methodology/approach – Secondary data from the 23rd Cycle of the Canadian GSS were used to address the study’s research questions using binary logistic regression analyses. Findings – Particular online behaviors were consistently, positively related to all three types of online victimization, including booking/making reservations, social networking, having one’s information posted online. Other online routines exhibited unique effects on online victimization risk. Originality/value – In support of the theory, the results suggest that online exposure, target suitability increase risks for phishing, hacking, malware victimization. Online guardianship was also positively related to victimization, a finding that runs counter to theoretical expectations.

title: Preventing crime online: Identifying determinants of online preventive behaviors using structural equation modeling, canonical correlation analysis
authors: Reyns, Bradford W, Randa, Ryan, Henson, Billy
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Studies; Internet crime; Economic models; Theory; Social research; Behavior; Social networks; Computer viruses; Victimization;340\_Frauds;CPCS2008-2016;Crime Prevention, Community Safety
abstract: The purpose of the present research was to identify determinants of online crime prevention behaviors by examining the relationships between online victimization, online exposure, online communication behaviors, online prevention within an opportunity framework. Utilizing a large national sample of residents of Canada from the General Social Survey, structural equation modeling, canonical correlation analysis were used to assess the effects of opportunity-based routines upon preventive behaviors as well as the effects of individual elements of each construct on the relationship between the constructs. Results from the structural equation models indicate that there is a positive, significant relationship between online victimization, the adoption of online preventative routines, while the canonical correlation analyses suggest that these relationships are complex, that specific types of victimization are related to particular prevention efforts. The present research provides early evidence that online lifestyles influence the theorized cycle of online victimization, preventative efforts. We find that indicators of online exposure, communications routines were positive predictors of online victimization,, that online victimization is positively associated with taking precautionary measures.

title: Can you hear me now? Telemarketing fraud victimization, lifestyles
authors: Policastro, Christina, Payne, Brian K
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: Researchers have used lifestyle theory to delineate patterns surrounding various forms of victimization. Much of this research focuses on conventional crimes, demonstrates a seemingly consistent pattern in terms of victim age: older victim’s lifestyles reduce their risk for conventional victimization, but may increase their risk for other forms of victimization. Using lifestyle/routine activity theory as a guide, this study explores whether the lifestyles, activities of older persons are tied to their risk of being targeted for telemarketing fraud. Our findings suggest that victimization risk for telemarketing fraud does not vary across the life-course,, that lifestyles of older persons are not tied to telemarketing fraud victimization. Factors tied to victimization include neighborhood disorder, being employed part-time. Implications are provided.

title: Shopping fraud victimization among the elderly
authors: Reisig, Michael D, Holtfreter, Kristy
keywords: 340\_Frauds;20240717\_IVde一次予防;条件該当性が特に高い論文
abstract: PurposeThis study aims to investigate whether low self‐control, routine activity theories explain fraud outcomes among the elderly. Specifically, the effects of low self‐control, remote purchasing behaviors on shopping fraud targeting, victimization are empirically assessed.Design/methodology/approachCross‐sectional survey data from telephone interviews conducted in Arizona, Florida are used. A total of 2,000 adults aged 60, over were surveyed. Because selection bias was observed, a two‐stage probit regression model was estimated to assess theoretical hypotheses in a multivariate context.FindingsThe results demonstrate that two forms of remote purchasing – telemarketing purchase, mail‐order purchase – increase the probability of shopping fraud targeting. Infomercial purchase, mail‐order purchase are significant correlates of shopping fraud victimization. The probability of becoming a target, victim is affected positively by reduced levels of self‐control. The effects of demographic characteristics on fraud outcomes are null.Research limitations/implicationsThis research lends support to the argument that low self‐control, routine activity theories shed light on fraud victimization among elderly consumers. Future research should examine the influence of low self‐control, individual routines, lifestyles on other forms of victimization that the elderly experience.Practical implicationsThe findings underscore the need for fraud prevention, increasing public awareness among elderly consumers.Originality/valueThis is the first study to examine shopping fraud targeting, victimization of the elderly in a broad theoretical context.

title: Fraud victimization, confidence in Florida's legal authorities
authors: Reisig, Michael D, Holtfreter, Kristy
abstract: Purpose – This study seeks to identify personal characteristics that help to explain variation in consumer confidence in legal authorities' ability to effectively deal with fraud victimization in the State of Florida. Design/methodology/approach – The study uses cross‐sectional survey data from 918 adults who participated in a telephone interview in 2004, 2005. Univariate statistics are used to describe the distribution of the dependent variable (i.e. consumer confidence in legal authorities). Hypotheses are tested using bivariate, multivariate statistical techniques. Findings – Results show that less than one‐half of respondents (48.2 percent) report that they have either “a great deal” or “quite a bit” of confidence in the ability of legal authorities to respond to consumer fraud victimization. Bivariate correlations show that younger respondents, those with more formal education, recent fraud victims,, individuals inclined to take risks with their financial assets report lower levels of confidence. These findings persist in a multivariate context. Research limitations/implications – Because these data were collected from survey respondents living in a single state, one should exercise caution when generalizing these findings to other settings. Practical implications – The findings can be used to target public awareness efforts, educational campaigns to consumer groups with low levels of confidence in legal authorities. Doing so may not only help bolster confidence, but also potentially increase rates of fraud victimization reporting. Originality/value – This study extends the literature on confidence in legal authorities to the previously unexplored crime‐related context of consumer fraud victimization.

title: The distillation of national crime data into A plan for elderly fraud prevention: A quantitative, qualitative analysis of U.s. postal inspection service cases of fraud against the elderly
authors: Rebovich, Donald, Corbo, Leslie
abstract: ABSTRACTThe following article represents the product of a research study funded by the United States Postal Inspection Service (USPIS), conducted by researchers from the Identity Management, Information Protection Center (CIMIP) of Utica College. The study focuses on frauds committed against victims aged 55 years, older. The primary objective was to uncover as much key empirical information on characteristics of victims of elderly fraud, those who commit these crimes,, the methods they employ to commit these fraudulent acts. For this study, researchers were afforded the opportunity to examine criminal case investigation data from the USPIS national criminal case database on elderly frauds. The data that supplies the foundation for this study relies on information from criminal case investigators transposed to a national database reflecting critical characteristics of cases of fraud against the elderly. Recommendations are offered as to how the analysis of this information can be beneficial in the development of effective public awareness campaigns for helping to prevent elderly fraud victimization.

title: The effect of message credibility, need for cognitive closure,, information sufficiency on thought-induced attitude change
authors: Pfeiffer, Bruce E, Deval, Hélène, Silvera, David H, Cronley, Maria L, Kardes, Frank R
abstract: Self-generated thought has been shown to have a significant impact on attitude change. Merely thinking about an attitude can result in more extreme attitudes. Although research in this area has investigated several moderating factors, most of the research looks at constraints that attenuate but do not reverse the effect (depolarization). The current research investigates source effects as a depolarizing variable while testing two additional moderating variables. The results provide important new insights into self-generated persuasion. Source effects can result in polarizing effects if the source is credible but depolarizing effects if the source is less credible (experiment 1). Further, thought-induced attitude change depends on varying levels of need for cognitive closure (experiment 2, experiment 3), information sufficiency (experiment 3).

title: Routine online activity, Internet fraud targeting: Extending the generality of routine activity theory
authors: Pratt, Travis C, Holtfreter, Kristy, Reisig, Michael D
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Routine activity theory predicts that changes in legitimate opportunity structures (e.g., technology) can increase the convergence of motivated offenders, suitable targets in the absence of capable guardianship. The Internet has fundamentally changed consumer practices, has simultaneously expanded opportunities for cyber-fraudsters to target online consumers. The authors draw on routine activity theory, consumer behavior research to understand how personal characteristics, online routines increase people’s exposure to motivated offenders. Using a representative sample of 922 adults from a statewide survey in Florida, the results of the regression models are consistent with prior research in that sociodemographic characteristics shape routine online activity (e.g., spending time online, making online purchases). Furthermore, indicators of routine online activity fully mediate the effect of sociodemographic characteristics on the likelihood of being targeted for fraud online. These findings support the routine activity perspective, provide a theoretically informed direction for situational crime prevention in a largely unexplored consumer context.

title: Age differences in dual information-processing modes: Implications for cancer decision making
authors: Peters, Ellen, Diefenbach, Michael A, Hess, Thomas M, Västfjäll, Daniel
keywords: Age Factors; Aging/psychology; Decision Making; Humans; Neoplasms/psychology/therapy;340\_Frauds
abstract: Age differences in affective/experiential, deliberative processes have important theoretical implications for cancer decision making, as cancer is often a disease of older adulthood. The authors examined evidence for adult age differences in affective, deliberative information processes, reviewed the sparse evidence about age differences in decision making,, introduced how dual process theories, their findings might be applied to cancer decision making. Age‐related declines in the efficiency of deliberative processes predict poorer‐quality decisions as we age, particularly when decisions are unfamiliar, the information is numeric. However, age‐related adaptive processes, including an increased focus on emotional goals, greater experience, can influence decision making, potentially offset age‐related declines. A better understanding of the mechanisms that underlie cancer decision processes in our aging population should ultimately allow us to help older adults to better help themselves. Cancer 2008;113(12 suppl):3556–67. © 2008 American Cancer Society.

title: Can adults discriminate between fraudulent, legitimate e-mails? Examining the role of age, prior fraud experience
authors: O'Connor, Alison M, Judges, Rebecca A, Lee, Kang, Evans, Angela D
abstract: The present study assessed how accurate adults are at detecting fraudulent e-mail activity. A total of 100 younger (18-26 years), 96 older adults (60-90 years) categorized a series of e-mails as legitimate or fraudulent phishing schemes, self-reported their fraud experiences. Younger, older adults did not differ in accuracy rates when categorizing the e-mails (72\%), but older adults used a ``high-suspicion'' strategy where they were more likely to mislabel a legitimate e-mail as fraudulent compared to younger adults. Younger adults were less likely to be targeted by fraud than older adults, but the groups were victimized at similar rates. Being a prior fraud victim negatively related to e-mail detection performance, but this differed across age groups, the extent of fraud experience. Together, these results provide insight into the relation between fraud experience, the ability to detect e-mail scams, can inform fraud prevention, education initiatives.

title: Efforts to reduce consumer fraud victimization among the elderly: The effect of information access on program awareness, contact
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Reisig, Michael D, Scaggs, Samuel, Holtfreter, Kristy
abstract: Concern about the risk of consumer fraud victimization among the elderly has led to programs that disseminate fraud prevention information, provide services. However, little is known about how seniors access such information or learn about or contact these programs. Drawing on scholarship on fraud, media consumption,, the fear of crime, this study contributes to efforts to understand, reduce consumer fraud victimization. Analyses of data from adults age 60, above demonstrate that certain segments of the elderly population access a greater variety of information sources to learn about fraud prevention. In turn, such access is associated with greater fraud prevention program awareness, contact.

title: Elderly victimization: An examination beyond the FBI's index crimes
authors: Mccabe, Kimberly A, Gregory, Sharon S
abstract: Most of the research on elderly victimization has focused primarily on the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI)'s major index crimes of murder, rape,, robbery; however, this restricted approach to the study of crime only depicts a portion of the actual crime against the elderly. This research was conducted to capture a more encompassing view of elderly victimization. The data were obtained from the FBI's National Incident Based Reporting System (NIBRS) in the state of South Carolina. Results of the study suggest that the elderly (age 65, older) are more at risk than are younger segments of the population for crimes of robbery, intimidation, vandal-ism,, forgery/fraud, with the sex, race of the elderly victim also associated with specific types of criminal victimization.

title: Relationship between socioeconomic conditions, financial fraud victimization among older adults in China: Do financial literacy, financial attitudes matter?
authors: Mao, Xupeng, Liu, Yuerong
keywords: China; financial attitudes; financial fraud victimization; financial literacy; socioeconomic conditions;340\_Frauds;20240717\_IVde一次予防
abstract: Using data from the 2015 wave of the China Household Finance Survey (N ≈ 12,100), this study used structural equation modeling to examine the relationship between socioeconomic conditions (i.e., educational attainments, hukou status,, household financial assets per capita), financial fraud victimization among Chinese older adults, the mediating roles of financial literacy, financial attitudes (i.e., interest in financial matters, risk tolerance). We found that although neither educational attainment nor hukou status was directly related to financial fraud victimization, household financial assets per capita was postively associated with the risk of financial fraud victimization. In addition, higher educational attainment, urban hukou,, more financial assets per capita were associated with more risk of financial fraud victimization through higher levels of financial literacy, higher interest in financial matters. Implications for preventing, protecting Chinese older adults from financial fraud victimization are discussed.

title: Organized fraud, organizing frauds: Unpacking research on networks, organization
authors: Levi, Michael
journal: Criminology \& criminal justice: the international journal of policy, practice
abstract: This article examines the settings for frauds in the context of crime networks, fraud opportunities, of a victim-centric typology of fraud. It demonstrates the variety of actors, settings, the variable need for knowing collaboration between co-offenders in frauds of different types. It explores what is known about those involved in the organization of some forms of frauds; how they find both co-offenders, victims in face-to-face, remote settings;, the barriers to growth of the `fraud business'. It concludes that the globalization of crime is part of contingent relationships between settings, with their rich, varied opportunities (reflecting patterns of business, consumer, investment activities), the variable abilities of would-be perpetrators to recognize, act on those opportunities (the `crime scripts' perspective),, their interactions with controls (including, but not restricted to, law enforcement). Constructs of `organized crime' are becoming less obsessed with the structure of groups than with what people need from the largely illicit, largely licit worlds before they commit fraud. Although some frauds are committed by generic transnational `organized crime' networks, others are merely mobile small groups or individuals who can transplant techniques wherever they go;, others still commit very large one-off frauds without a need for long-term or any involvement in `organized crime'.

title: Psychological, functional vulnerability predicts fraud cases in older adults: Results of a longitudinal study
authors: Lichtenberg, Peter Alexander, Sugarman, Michael A, Paulson, Daniel, Ficker, Lisa J, Rahman-Filipiak, Annalise
abstract: Using cross sectional data Psychological vulnerability was identified as a correlate of older adult's being defrauded. We extend that research by examining fraud prevalence using longitudinal data from the Health, Retirement Study,, to identify the best predictors of fraud longitudinally across a 4-year time frame. Whereas reported fraud prevalence was 5.0\% in a 5-year look-back period in 2008, it increased to 6.1\% in 2012. The rate of new-incident fraud across only a 4-year look-back was 4.3\%. Being younger-old, having a higher level of education,, having more depression significantly predicted the new cases of fraud reported in 2012. Psychological vulnerability was a potent longitudinal predictor of fraud, with the most vulnerable individuals being more than twice as likely to be defrauded. Results indicate that fraud victimization among older adults is rising,, that vulnerability variables, along with some demographic variables, predict new cases of fraud.

title: Consumer vulnerability to fraud: Influencing factors
authors: Lee, Jinkook, Soberon-ferrer, Horacio
abstract: Using the 1993 Survey of Older Consumer Behavior commissioned by the American Association of Retired Persons, consumer vulnerability to market fraud was investigated. Consumer vulnerability was determined based on consumers' market knowledge, awareness of unfair business practices. Using an ordered logit analysis, it was found that consumers were more susceptible to fraud if they were older, poor, less educated, and/or living without spouse. Neither gender nor race was found to be a significant predictor of consumer vulnerability. Implications for consumer educators, policy makers were drawn.

title: Elderly consumers' receptiveness to telemarketing fraud: JPP\&M
authors: Lee, Jinkook, Geistfeld, Loren V
keywords: 1200:Social policy; 4300:Law; 45439:Other Direct Selling Establishments; 54186:Direct Mail Advertising; 62412:Services for the Elderly, Persons with Disabilities; 7000:Marketing; 9130:Experimental/theoretical; 9190:United States; Age; Business And Economics--Marketing And Purchasing; Cognitive ability; Consumer fraud; Consumers; Direct marketing; Fraud; Investigations; Memory; Older people; Public policy; Regression analysis; Social exchange theory; Social integration; Social interaction; Social isolation; Studies; Telemarketing; United States--US;340\_Frauds
abstract: Data from the 1996, 1997 EXCEL Omnibus Survey commissioned by the American Association of Retired Persons is used to investigate the receptiveness of consumers 50 years of age or older to telemarketing fraud. Elderly consumers' receptiveness to telemarketing fraud, as reflected by a consumers' psychological orientation (willingness to listen to sales pitch, attitude toward callers), actual engagement in risky behavior (responding to unknown callers) is investigated using setwise regression. Policy implications are provided.

title: Consumer vulnerability to scams, swindles,, fraud: A new theory of visceral influences on persuasion
authors: Langenderfer, Jeff, Shimp, Terence A
abstract: Scams exact a huge toll on consumers, society at large, with annual costs in the United States alone exceeding \$100 billion. The global proliferation of the Internet has enabled con artists to export their craft to a rapidly expanding market, reach previously untapped consumers. In spite of the prevalence of scams around the world, there has been virtually no academic attention devoted to understanding the factors that might account for why individuals differ in their scamming vulnerability. Building on the background of elder consumer disadvantage, informed by the authors' own survey of expert opinion, this article presents a tentative theory of scamming vulnerability. The proposed theory incorporates the effects of visceral influences on consumer response to scam offers, hypothesizes a role for various moderating factors such as self-control, gullibility, susceptibility to interpersonal influence,, scam knowledge. Theoretical propositions are provided for future empirical investigation. © 2001 John Wiley \& Sons, Inc.

title: Seeking, processing information about impersonal risk
authors: Kahlor, Leeann, Dunwoody, Sharon, Griffin, Robert J, Neuwirth, Kurt
abstract: Attempts to model risk response tend to focus on risks that pose a direct personal threat. This study examined the applicability of one risk response model to impersonal risks—risks that threaten something other than the self, in this case, the environment. This study utilized a section of the Griffin et al. risk-information seeking, processing model, which depicts relationships between informational subjective norms, information seeking, processing as being mediated by perceptions of information insufficiency. The results indicate that while those relationships do hold for impersonal risk, informational subjective norms (perceived social pressure to be informed) may play an even more complex role than initially anticipated. These norms may be a powerful predictor of seeking, processing when individuals face impersonal risks.

title: Fraud against businesses both online, offline: crime scripts, business characteristics, efforts,, benefits
authors: Junger, Marianne, Wang, Victoria, Schlömer, Marleen
keywords: 340\_Frauds;20240717\_IVde一次予防;条件該当性が特に高い論文
abstract: AbstractThis study analyses 300 cases of fraudulent activities against Dutch businesses, 100 from each of the following three categories: CEO-fraud, fraudulent contract,, ghost invoice. We examine crime scripts, key characteristics of targeted businesses,, the relationship between input criminal effort, output financial benefit. Results indicate that whilst all CEO-frauds are conducted online, most of the fraudulent contracts, ghost invoices are undertaken via offline means. Both Routine Activity Theory, Rational Choice Model are evidenced-fraudsters clearly take the business size, seasonality into account,, the input criminal effort, output criminal benefit are positively correlated. Having vigilant employees is evidenced as the most effective way of fraud prevention, both online, offline.

title: Sociolegal change in consumer fraud: From victim-offender interactions to global networks
authors: Holtfreter, Kristy, Van Slyke, Shanna, Blomberg, Thomas G
abstract: Advances in technology have transformed fraud against consumers from face-to-face, victim-offender interactions to a crime that now transcends international boundaries. Although consumer protection issues have been of interest to investigative journalists, literary scholars for centuries, the topic has only recently been subject to serious criminological inquiry. Employing the American consumer protection movement as an historical framework, we examine the evolution of consumer fraud. Our review documents that progressive social, legal changes in consumer protection, corporate regulation, as well as developments in criminological research, correspond to prominent literary exposes of the time. In today's technological age, such a reactive response to consumer fraud is neither efficient nor effective. Contemporary criminologists need to simultaneously address the questions of 'how' fraud is perpetrated, 'why' it occurs. Toward this end, we identify methodological strategies, data sources to promote empirical, theoretical understanding of consumer fraud,, to ultimately contribute to multi-national crime control policy.

title: Low self‐control, routine activities,, fraud victimization
authors: Holtfreter, Kristy, Reisig, Michael D, Pratt, Travis C
keywords: Crime; Criminal Behavior; Female; Fraud; Human; Lifestyle; Male; Self Control; US; Victimization; fraud victimization; low self-control; routine activities;340\_Frauds;20240717\_IVde一次予防;criminology;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: Recent research has used both routine activity/lifestyle frameworks, self‐control theory to explain victimization. Thus far, combined tests of these theories have focused on offending populations, street crime victimization. Whether these frameworks also explain exposure to, likelihood of nonviolent victimization (e.g., fraud) in general‐population samples remains an open empirical question. Building on prior work, we assess the independent effects of routine consumer activities (i.e., remote purchasing), low self‐control on the likelihood of fraud targeting, victimization. Using a representative sample of 922 adults from a statewide survey in Florida, the results confirm our expectation that remote‐purchasing activities increase consumers' risk of being targeted for fraud. Low self‐control has no effect on whether consumers are targeted, but it does significantly increase the likelihood of fraud victimization.

title: Testing the robustness of a risk information processing model
authors: Griffin, Robert J, Powell, Maria, Dunwoody, Sharon, Neuwirth, Kurt, Clark, David, Novotny, Vladimir

title: Information Sufficiency, Risk Communication
authors: Griffin, Robert J, Neuwirth, Kurt, Dunwoody, Sharon, Giese, James
abstract: In an effort to better understand individuals' use of information in risky situations, in this article we propose a new variable, information sufficiency, as an important component of people's information-seeking behaviors. We surveyed residents of 2 Great Lakes cities to test the ability of a group of factors often employed in risk communication studies to predict information sufficiency, defined as a person's sense of how much information he or she needs to cope with a risk. We found that 2 predictors of this perceived gap in information were an individual's worry about the risk, the perception that others would expect one to keep abreast of information about the risk.

title: Fundraising, the elderly: A content analysis
authors: Gregory, Lynn Dee
abstract: Direct marketing, as an avenue for fundraising, provides nonprofit organizations with the ability to fulfill their missions, donors the opportunity to support a worthy cause. There are concerns, however, when sophisticated marketing practices target potentially at-risk consumers. Demographic studies clearly show that the percentage of elderly Americans, aged 65, over, is rising with a corollary increase in the incidence of Alzheimer’s disease, dementia. These facts suggest this may be a group whose defining characteristics make them especially vulnerable. This exploratory study identifies, qualifies persuasive tactics used by several linked nonprofit organizations targeting one elderly Alzheimer’s victim over a 14-month period. The carefully designed direct mail solicitations utilize appeals that engender low elaboration likelihood, peripheral route processing. In addition, there is some evidence that even those appeals that might encourage high elaboration likelihood become heuristic cues for individuals with cognitive decrease. Taken together, the incorporation of multiple tactics within each solicitation, an approach referred to here as shotgunning, may have significant implications for future research, practice in communication, ethics,, public policy.

title: Online consumer fraud victimization, reporting: A quantitative study of the predictors, motives
authors: Fonseca, Catarina, Moreira, Samuel, Guedes, Inês
abstract: ABSTRACTOnline consumer fraud is one of the most fast-growing crimes. It corresponds to situations where, for instance, the products that are bought, but are not delivered. The present study (N = 1710) aimed at exploring, on the one hand, the predictors of online fraud victimization and, on the other hand, to examine the reporting to the police. Even though 223 were victims of online consumer fraud, only 20 reported to the police. Moreover, while individual variables were not predictors of victimization, online routines were relevant to its explanation. Finally, monetary loss was the most important predictor of reporting to the police.

title: Understanding aging, consumer fraud victimization in the Chinese context: A two-stage conceptual approach
authors: Fan, Jessie X, Yu, Zhou
keywords: China; Consumer financial fraud; fraud exposure; fraud victimization; methods of contact;340\_Frauds;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: The relationship between aging, consumer fraud victimization is mixed in the literature. Most studies based on survey data have found older consumers less likely to be fraud victims, while a few studies have found older consumers more likely to be victimized, especially with certain fraud types. We developed a two-stage conceptual framework to differentiate fraud exposure from fraud victimization once exposed. Using nationally representative Chinese data, controlling for confounders, we found that consumers between 65, 74 face similar risks of being targeted by perpetrators compared to younger groups, while consumers 75+, older are less likely to be exposed to fraud. However, once exposed, both groups of older consumers are significantly more likely to become fraud victims. In the Chinese context, these two opposing effects led to an overall higher risk of consumer financial fraud victimization by older consumers.

title: Decision strategies, susceptibility to phishing
authors: Downs, Julie S, Holbrook, Mandy B, Cranor, Lorrie Faith
booktitle: Proceedings of the second symposium on Usable privacy, security - SOUPS '06
abstract: Phishing emails are semantic attacks that con people into divulging sensitive information using techniques to make the user believe that information is being requested by a legitimate source. In order to develop tools that will be effective in combating these schemes, we first must know how, why people fall for them. This study reports preliminary analysis of interviews with 20 non-expert computer users to reveal their strategies, understand their decisions when encountering possibly suspicious emails. One of the reasons that people may be vulnerable to phishing schemes is that awareness of the risks is not linked to perceived vulnerability or to useful strategies in identifying phishing emails. Rather, our data suggest that people can manage the risks that they are most familiar with, but don't appear to extrapolate to be wary of unfamiliar risks. We explore several strategies that people use, with varying degrees of success, in evaluating emails, in making sense of warnings offered by browsers attempting to help users navigate the web.

title: Cyber-victimization preventive behavior: A health belief model approach
authors: Dodel, Matias, Mesch, Gustavo
keywords: Victimization; Safety; Preventive behavior; Health belief model; Security; Cybercrime;340\_Frauds
abstract: Cyber-victimization has extensive economic, personal consequences for Internet users as well as negative consequences for economies, the cyber infrastructure. This paper investigates the determinants of cyber-safety behaviors, particularly the factors associated with using anti-virus software in the general Internet user population, through a conceptual model about the determinants of non-digital preventive actions. We tested the Health Behavior Model, which considers perceptions about threats, expectations about behavior as the main determinants of health-related preventive behaviors, using a survey of Israeli Internet users 18 years old, older (N = 1850). Findings show that gender, age, education, seniority online, frequency of Internet use are basic determinants of anti-virus preventive behaviors. Nevertheless, similar to preventive health behaviors, beliefs about digital threats, actions to thwart them appear to account for more variance in anti-virus preventive behaviors than socio-demographic characteristics, Internet use. Our findings provide an innovative conceptual model, imply that the fight against cybercrime can take cues from health behavior studies demonstrating the role of perceptions, beliefs in reducing online threats. Furthermore, health behavior models are useful frameworks to conceptualize behavioral reactions to threats, to study cyber-safety.

title: Elder fraud, financial exploitation: Application of routine activity theory
authors: DeLiema, Marguerite
keywords: Adult protective services; Elder abuse forensic center; Forensic neuropsychologist; Retrospective review; Victimization;340\_Frauds;01\_高齢者の詐欺被害の現状;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験;\_\_\_202501\_fraud
abstract: Background, Objectives: Elder financial exploitation, committed by individuals in positions of trust,, elder fraud, committed by predatory strangers, are two forms of financial victimization that target vulnerable older adults. This study analyzes differences between fraud, financial exploitation victims, tests routine activity theory as a contextual model for victimization. Routine activity theory predicts that criminal opportunities arise when a motivated offender, suitable target meet in the absence of capable guardians. Research Design, Methods: Fifty-three financial exploitation, fraud cases were sampled from an elder abuse forensic center. Data include law enforcement, caseworker investigation reports, victim medical records, perpetrator demographic information,, forensic assessments of victim health, cognitive functioning. Results: Fraud, financial exploitation victims performed poorly on tests of cognitive functioning, financial decision making administered by a forensic neuropsychologist following the allegations. Based on retrospective record review, there were few significant differences in physical health, cognitive functioning at the time victims' assets were taken, although their social contexts were different. Significantly more fraud victims were childless compared with financial exploitation victims. Fraud perpetrators took advantage of elders when they had no trustworthy friends or relatives to safeguard their assets. Discussion, Implications: Findings support an adapted routine activity theory as a contextual model for financial victimization. Fraud most often occurred when a vulnerable elder was solicited by a financial predator in the absence of capable guardians. Prevention efforts should focus on reducing social isolation to enhance protection.

authors: Cross, Cassandra
keywords: Social Services And Welfare; Vulnerability; Fraud; Cybercrime; Victimisation; COVID-19; Older persons; Social isolation; Offenders; Victimization; Loneliness; Internet crime; Older people; Well being; Research fraud; Singapore; United Kingdom--UK; Hong Kong; United States--US;340\_Frauds
abstract: PurposeThe purpose of this paper is to understand how COVID-19 may alter the vulnerability levels of older persons,, how this may change their potential for fraud victimisation. This is particularly focused on the government’s use of isolation, restrictions on activity, physical distancing to combat the virus.Design/methodology/approachIn the absence of statistics, this paper examines what is currently known about older persons, fraud, as well as the recent knowledge of COVID-19-related fraud. On this basis, the paper hypothesises the conceivable changes to vulnerability that potentially expose older persons to fraud.FindingsThis paper argues that COVID-19 has not seen “new” fraudulent approaches, rather offenders have used COVID-19 as a context to their existing schemes. Further, the current response to COVID-19 can substantially increase the number of older persons experiencing levels of vulnerability,, therefore increase their fraud risk.Research limitations/implicationsThe current paper applies existing knowledge into the current circumstances of COVID-19, lays the foundations for empirical work to be conducted in this area.Practical implicationsThis paper provides an impetus to target the well-being, connectivity of older persons, (regardless of the COVID-19 context), to reduce their vulnerability to fraud victimisation.Social implicationsThis paper highlights the importance of connectivity for older persons,, the need to focus on overcoming social isolation, loneliness.Originality/valueThis paper is the first to hypothesise the effects of COVID-19, its associated government responses to the overall vulnerability of older persons, with a focus on the potential for fraud victimisation.

title: Using artificial intelligence (AI), deepfakes to deceive victims: the need to rethink current romance fraud prevention messaging
authors: Cross, Cassandra
abstract: Romance fraud uses the guise of a genuine relationship to deceive a victim for a financial gain. Each year, millions of individuals globally lose money to these approaches. Current prevention messaging focuses heavily on promoting the use of internet searches (specifically reverse image searches) to verify or refute the identity/scenario that one is being presented with. For those who choose to do this, it can be successful, avoid initial financial losses or reduce the overall amount of money lost to an offender. However, as technology evolves, it is likely offenders will alter their methods to deceive victims. This is already evident through the rapid progression, improvements of artificial intelligence, deepfakes to create unique images. This article argues that the adoption of these new techniques requires a need to rethink current prevention messaging, as the utility of conducting reverse image searches may become somewhat redundant into the future.

title: Effective forewarning requires central route processing: Theoretical improvements on the counterargumentation hypothesis, practical implications for scam prevention
authors: Daiku, Yasuhiro, Kugihara, Naoki, Teraguchi, Tsukasa, Watamura, Eiichiro
keywords: Sciences: Comprehensive Works; Psychometrics; Pilot studies; Cognition; Emotions; Finance; Memory recall; Questionnaires; Police; Damage prevention; Memory; Research methodology; Theory; Hypotheses; Experiments; Studies; Prevention; Researchers; Peripheral processing; Victimization; Consent; Fraud; Japan;340\_Frauds
abstract: Financial scams have caused tremendous financial damage globally. In Japan, the police forewarn people by equipping them with scam-prevention techniques or providing awareness regarding examples of previous scams; however, this does not appear to effectively prevent the damage, as many scam victims do not remember these warnings when faced with actual scam encounters. Considering that scammers often use appeal to emotion techniques, peripheral processing during scam attempts might disturb people's abilities to recall the warnings on scammers' modus operandi, thus leading to failed counter-arguing efforts. We verified this hypothesis in an experimental setting by asking 162 participants to remember given forewarnings, resist deceptive advertisements. The results showed that participants gave the advertisers' manipulative intent a higher rating only when they processed the advertisement through a central route, in addition to being forewarned. This means that forewarning had no effect when participants processed the advertisement through a peripheral route. Moreover, forewarning recollection levels mediated the effect of processing route on this rating, which suggests that remembering forewarnings is necessary to generate counterarguments. This result expands the theory on forewarning effects, explains why people are susceptible to scam victimization. Furthermore, it provides implications for scam prevention.

title: Confronting online extremism: The effect of self-help, collective efficacy,, guardianship on being a target for hate speech
authors: Costello, Matthew, Hawdon, James, Ratliff, Thomas N
abstract: Who is likely to be a target of online hate, extremism? To answer this question, we use an online survey ( N = 963) of youth, young adults recruited from a demographically balanced sample of Americans. Adapting routine activity theory, we distinguish between actor-initiated social control (i.e., self-help), other-initiated social control (i.e., collective efficacy),, guardianship, show how self-help is positively related to the likelihood of being targeted by hate. Our findings highlight how online exposure to hate materials, target suitability,, enacting social control online all influence being the target of hate. Using social networking sites, encountering hate material online have a particularly strong relationship with being targeted with victim suitability (e.g., discussing private matters online, participating in hate online), confronting hate also influencing the likelihood of being the target of hate speech.

title: Automated teller machine fraud in south-west Nigeria: Victim typologies, victimisation strategies, fraud prevention
authors: Tade, Oludayo, Adeniyi, Oluwatosin
abstract: Extant studies have not examined the unintended consequences of automated teller machine (ATM) subscription, particularly factors making individuals susceptible to fraud. To address this gap in the literature, this study investigated ATM fraud victims in south-west Nigeria. Using the in-depth interview method, data were collected from 20 victims of ATM fraud in the states of Lagos, Oyo. The results showed that victims were young, elderly, included both males, females. Fraudsters were typically lovers, friends, relatives, sometimes the children of the victims. Card cloning, card swapping, physical attacks at ATMs were reported tactics for defrauding. Vulnerability factors included illiteracy, ill health, routine activity, time of withdrawal. As means of mitigating fraud, it was found that banks employed an assortment of strategies including, but not limited to, improvements in staff welfare, stringent penalties for culpable staff, enhanced fraud awareness through customer alerts. The paper reveals the limits of trust in cashless policy. It raises salient policy issues concerning the need for the governance of trust to engender adoption, ensure victim compensation.

title: The fraud review, the policing of fraud: Laying the foundations for a centralized fraud police or counter fraud executive?
authors: Button, M, Johnston, L, Frimpong, K
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: The recent United Kingdom (UK) Fraud Review Final Report made 62 recommendations on a wide range of issues across the breadth of the criminal justice system, all of which were accepted by the government. This paper aims to generate further debate on the recommendations vis-a-vis the future of fraud investigation. The paper begins by examining some of the main recommendations of the UK Fraud Review before exploring the growing pressures on fraud investigation in the UK. The paper argues that the Fraud Review, combined with these growing pressures, is laying the foundations for the further centralization of fraud investigation. The authors argue that there are two potential models for the centralization of the policing of fraud: a National Fraud Police or National Counter Fraud Executive,, the authors also argue that the latter offers the best model for the longer term, for effectively tackling fraud in the UK.

title: Taking time seriously: A theory of socioemotional selectivity
authors: Carstensen, Laura L, Isaacowitz, Derek M, Charles, Susan T
keywords: *Emotions; *Goal Setting; *Learning; *Motivation; *Time Perception; Age Differences; Theories;340\_Frauds;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Socioemotional selectivity theory claims that the perception of time plays a fundamental role in the selection, pursuit of social goals. According to the theory, social motives fall into 1 of 2 general categories-those related to the acquisition of knowledge, those related to the regulation of emotion. When time is perceived as open-ended, knowledge-related goals are prioritized. In contrast, when time is perceived as limited, emotional goals assume primacy. The inextricable association between time left in life, chronological age ensures age-related differences in social goals. Nonetheless, the authors show that the perception of time is malleable,, social goals change in both younger, older people when time constraints are imposed. The authors argue that time perception is integral to human motivation, suggest potential implications for multiple subdisciplines, research interests in social, developmental, cultural, cognitive,, clinical psychology.

title: Applying the Theory of Planned Behaviour to predicting online safety behaviour
authors: Burns, Sarah, Roberts, Lynne
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Internet; Privacy; Internet crime; Identity theft; Electronic commerce;340\_Frauds;CPCS2008-2016;Crime Prevention, Community Safety
abstract: A widely promoted preventative measure against becoming a victim of cybercrime is the control of personal information online; however, little is known about what predicts the use of this type of protective safety behaviour. This study examines the utility of the Theory of Planned Behaviour in predicting online protective behaviours. Participants (N=150) completed measures of online privacy attitudes, normative influence, perceived behavioural control (PBC), intention to use, actual use of online protective behaviours. Path analysis indicated the effects of online privacy attitudes, normative beliefs on online protective safety behaviours were mediated through intention, while PBC had a significant direct effect on online protective safety behaviours. The model explained 81 per cent of the variance in protective online safety behaviours. The results of this study facilitate understanding of the psychological processes underlying the use of online protective behaviours,, can be used in the development of educational materials, cyber-identity theft prevention strategies.

title: Aging, the neuroeconomics of decision making: A review
authors: Brown, Stephen B R E, Ridderinkhof, K R
abstract: Neuroeconomics refers to a combination of paradigms derived from neuroscience, psychology,, economics for the study of decision making, is an area that has received considerable scientific attention in the recent literature. Using realistic laboratory tasks, researchers seek to study the neurocognitive processes underlying economic decision making, outcome-based decision learning, as well as individual differences in these processes, the social, affective factors that modulate them. To this point, one question has remained largely unanswered: What happens to decision-making processes, their neural substrates during aging? After all, aging is associated with neurocognitive change, which may affect outcome-based decision making. In our study, we use the subjective expected utility model—a well-established decision-making model in economics—as a descriptive framework. After a short survey of the brain areas, neurotransmitter systems associated with outcome-based decision making—and of the effects of aging thereon—we review a number of decision-making studies. Their general data pattern indicates that the decision-making process is changed by age: The elderly perform less efficiently than younger participants, as demonstrated, for instance, by the smaller total rewards that the elderly acquire in lab tasks. These findings are accounted for in terms of age-related deficiencies in the probability, value parameters of the subjective expected utility model. Finally, we discuss some implications, suggestions for future research.

title: Policing fraud in England, Wales: examining constables’, sergeants’ online fraud preparedness
authors: Bossler, Adam M, Holt, Thomas J, Cross, Cassandra, Burruss, George W
abstract: The significant economic, emotional consequences of online fraud have not been equally matched by the policing response to these offenses. This paper examines constables’, sergeants’ perceived preparation to respond to online fraud through a quantitative analyses of survey data collected from over 1300 officers from 35 local police agencies across England, Wales. The findings demonstrated that constables, sergeants being prepared to respond to online fraud was related to agencies having clear policies, procedures, constables having computer skills, online incident experiences,, being able to relate to fraud victims. The implications of this study for first responder training, resource development to respond to cybercrimes are considered.

title: The interplay of heuristic, systematic processing of social information
authors: Bohner, Gerd, Moskowitz, Gordon B, Chaiken, Shelly
abstract: The heuristic-systematic model (HSM) provides a general theory of social information processing. It features two modes of social information processing, a relatively effortless, top-down heuristic mode, a more effortful, bottom-up systematic mode. The model assumes that social perceivers strike a balance between effort minimization, achieving confidence in their social judgments. The HSM emphasizes three broad motivational forces: accuracy, defence,, impression motivation. Both heuristic, systematic processing can serve either of the three motives, are capable of co-occurring in an additive or interactive fashion under specified conditions. In this chapter, we describe the HSM, present illustrative research based on the model in the areas of mood, persuasion as well as minority influence.

title: Safeguarding consumers against identity-related fraud: examining data breach notification legislation through the lens of routine activities theory
authors: Anandarajan, M, D'Ovidio, R, Jenkins, A
abstract: With the proliferation of network technologies, data breaches of consumer personal information continue to become an ever-increasing part of the information age in which we live.In the USA 46 states have responded by enacting data breach notification statutes designed to help consumers protect their information by providing organizations with guidelines to follow in reporting data breaches.In this paper Cohen, Felson's routine activity theory is used to explain why it is that these breaches or personal information occur.Next, data breach security notification statutes are broken into five dimensions—data, personal information, notification content, notification method,, penalty—and operationalized into a data breach notification statute index (DBNSI) designed to indicate which of the enacted state data breach statutes may be most effective, which may be least effective.Finally, the DBNSI is applied in a regression model to test to what extent the constructs can explain variance in three dependent variables.

title: Searching for the unexpected - understanding information-seeking behaviours of people new to prison visits
authors: Ryan, Nicole R, Ryan, Nathan C
journal: Psychiatry, psychology,, law: an interdisciplinary journal of the Australian, New Zealand Association of Psychiatry, Psychology, Law
keywords: flexible pattern matching analysis; information seeking; prison visitation; prison visitors; uncertainty management theory;351\_選択行動
abstract: Often, when an offender is sentenced their family, friends find themselves in a state of uncertainty. At this point, family, friends of prisoners need support, often find themselves alone to navigate, learn the correctional system to gain visitation approval. It is unknown how people new to visitation learns the rules, processes of prison visits to gain visitation access. This study explores 21 prison visitors' information-seeking behaviour to understanding how people new to prison visitation learns to navigate the system to obtain visitation approval, identify any factors that might imped their ability to information-seek, thus delaying or preventing visitation. Using Flexible Pattern Matching Analysis we identified five factors that can occur prior to individual's need to information-seek,, one key factor that was common during the visit experience that can impact peoples 'ability to information seek'. Implications for prison visitation policy, practice are discussed.

title: Fear of crime, the willingness to report crime to police: A case study of model policing in Meta-Mercado, Coatepeque, Guatemala
authors: Iesue, Laura, Pitts, Wayne, Inkpen, Chris
journal: International journal of comparative, applied criminal justice
abstract: ABSTRACTCommunity-oriented policing has been a mainstay of policing over the past quarter century. In March 2019, the municipality of Coatepeque in Guatemala, with the assistance of Research Triangle Institute (RTI) International, implemented a new community policing plan called Vivir y Prosperar in the Meta Mercado. Vivir y Prosperar was designed to improve security, reduce crime,, promote economic prosperity. This study utilises the pre-test, baseline, 6-months post-test, endline survey data of market vendors in the Meta Mercado to assess whether Vivir y Prosperar reduced fear of crime, increased someone?s willingness to report crime to police as tenets of community policing would anticipate. Results show that Vivir, Prosperar did not directly contribute to a decrease in fear of crime or improve one?s willingness to report crimes to the police. However, improving personal victimisation experiences, bribery payments,, other factors may indirectly promote a reduction in fear of crime, increase the willingness to report a crime among market vendors.
