title: Viewing things differently: The dimensions of public perceptions of police legitimacy: Public perceptions of police legitimacy
authors: Tankebe, Justice
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Criminology; Cooperation; Citizens; Obligations; Police; London England;360\_Trust;criminology
abstract: Legitimacy (or “the right to exercise power”) is now an established concept in criminological analysis, especially in relation to policing. Substantial empirical evidence shows the importance of legitimacy in securing law‐abiding behavior, cooperation from citizens. Yet adequate theorization has lagged behind empirical evidence,, there has been a conflation of legitimacy with the cognate concepts of “trust”, of “obligation to obey the law.” By drawing on the work of Beetham (1991), others (e.g., Bottoms, Tankebe,), this study tests the hypothesis that the contents of the multiple dimensions of police legitimacy comprise procedural fairness, distributive fairness, lawfulness,, effectiveness. The study also investigates the relative influence of legitimacy, feelings of obligation on citizens’ willingness to cooperate with the police. Using data from London, the results substantiate the hypothesized dimensions of police legitimacy. In addition, legitimacy was found to exhibit both a direct influence on cooperation that is independent of obligation, an indirect influence that flows through people's felt obligations to obey the police. Implications for future research are discussed.

title: An integrated contextual model of confidence in local police
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Lawton, Brian A
abstract: Current work tests an integrated contextual model of confidence in local police. The model addresses four questions. (a) Do incivilities, procedural justice,, local social climate each affect confidence? (b) Do incivilities more powerfully corrode confidence at some points along the urban versus rural continuum? (c) Where on the continuum is confidence weakest? (d) Does confidence in local police bolster confidence in the broader justice system? Surveys from households across the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania were supplemented with municipality-level census, reported crime data,, county-level urban versus rural continuum codes. Findings showed significant net effects of both procedural justice, incivilities on the outcome; strongest corrosive impacts of incivilities in rural counties; lowest confidence in rural counties;, connections between confidence in local police, confidence in the broader criminal justice system. Results underscore the broad importance of police simultaneously maintaining order, treating citizens fairly.

title: Internal procedural justice, moral alignment,, external procedural justice in democratic policing
authors: Sun, Ivan Y, Wu, Yuning, Van Craen, Maarten, Hsu, Kevin Kuen-Lung
abstract: Notwithstanding the popularity of the process-based model of policing among social scientists, research on factors that encourage police officers to engage in procedurally fair behavior is relatively scarce. Based on the fair policing from the inside out framework, survey data collected from Taiwan police officers, this study explored the connection between internal procedural justice, external procedural justice through the mechanisms of moral alignment with both supervisors, citizens, perceived citizen trustworthiness. Fair supervision was found to build up moral alignment between officers, supervisors, between officers, citizens, which in turn led to stronger commitment to responsiveness, fair treatment of the public. Internal procedural justice, moral alignment also cultivated officers’ perceptions of public trustworthiness, which similarly strengthened officers’ response, fair treatment toward the public.

title: Procedural justice, legitimacy,, public cooperation with police: Does western wisdom hold in China?
authors: Sun, Ivan Y, Wu, Yuning, Hu, Rong, Farmer, Ashley K
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objectives: The principal objective of the current study is to test the applicability of Tom Tyler’s process-based model of policing in China. A secondary objective of this research is to examine the internal consistency, discriminant validity of key composite constructs in Tyler’s model. Methods: Using survey data collected from approximately 1,000 residents in a Chinese city, ordinary least squares regression was employed to assess the direct, indirect (through legitimacy) effects of procedural justice, specific distributive justice,, police effectiveness on willingness to cooperate with the police. Results: The internal consistency, discriminant validity of key composites in Tyler’s original model appear questionable with the Chinese data. Procedural justice, just like in the West, plays a significant role in predicting Chinese views on police legitimacy, willingness to cooperate with the police. Meanwhile, the strongest predictor of Chinese perceptions of police legitimacy is police effectiveness. The impact of both distributive justice, effectiveness on Chinese willingness to cooperate is mainly indirect through police legitimacy. Conclusions: Key arguments of Tyler’s model are largely supported by the Chinese data. Future research needs to develop culture-specific measures to further elaborate Tyler’s process-based model of policing.

title: Public attitudes toward auxiliary police in China: A preliminary investigation
authors: Sun, Ivan Y, Wu, Yuning, Hu, Rong
abstract: Despite their colossal size, importance in policing, China’s auxiliary police forces have garnered very little research attention. This study attempts to fill our knowledge gap by first describing key features that distinguish the auxiliary police from the regular police in China, their counterparts in Western societies, followed by an empirical investigation of public attitudes toward the auxiliary police in China. Based on survey data collected from a coastal city in China, we reported the general patterns of people’s evaluations of auxiliary officers, assessed whether variables representing institutional trust, media exposure,, neighborhood context are predictive of Chinese attitudes toward the auxiliary police. We found that Chinese citizens rated their local auxiliary officers very positively. Trust in the government, police, known negative reports about the auxiliary police are linked to Chinese’ global satisfaction with the auxiliary police. Trust in the police, exposure to, belief in negative media reports about the auxiliary police,, perception of neighborhood collective efficacy are associated with people’s specific attitudes toward auxiliary officers. Implications for future research, policy are discussed.

title: Social disorganization, legitimacy of local institutions, neighborhood crime: An exploratory study of perceptions of the police, local government
authors: Sun, Ivan Y, Triplett, Ruth A, Gainey, Randy R
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite a tendency in the past to emphasize the role of social networks in understanding neighborhood rates of social control, crime, recent work in social disorganization has begun to theorize about the role of institutions. In particular, in his 2002 presidential address Sampson (2002) argued that perceptions of institutions as legitimate are particularly important in shaping neighborhood levels of collective efficacy. In addition, Triplett, Gainey, Sun (2003) have argued that institutional strength is an important predictor of neighborhood crime rates. Within this framework, they predict that institutional strength is predictive of perceptions of public institutions as legitimate which in turn are predicted to affect neighborhood rates of crime. The purpose of this study is to provide an initial empirical assessment of the role of perceptions of two institutions - the police, local government - as legitimate on neighborhood rates of crime. Findings support the prediction that these perceptions are important, suggest the need for further research.

title: Beyond measuring 'how good a job' police are doing: The MPS model of confidence in policing
authors: Stanko, E A, Bradford, B
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: In England, Wales, the 'public confidence agenda' has enjoined the police service together with their key local partner, local authorities (Home Office, 2008). Yet before the police can consider this partnership to reduce crime, local disorder, they must know what people think about policing itself. This paper presents a model built around the question 'do police do a good job in your local area?', which serves as the foundation of the Metropolitan Police Service's (MPS) strategic direction for achieving local confidence. This model is derived from a multi-layered analysis of the MPS's local survey, the Public Attitude Survey. Four key elements-perceptions of police effectiveness, fairness of personal treatment, the level of police engagement with the community,, local people's concerns about local disorder-have strongly significant effects on 'overall' confidence. Taken together these four elements indicate that public confidence can be influenced by 'what police do'. We conclude with a discussion of the implications of the model, how it can be used as a strategic guide for improvement.

title: Assessing police stops of pedestrians: Toward a new generation of benchmarks
authors: Smith, Michael R, Tillyer, Rob, Smith, Mitchell, Lloyd, Caleb D
abstract: This paper extends the stop, frisk literature from New York City by examining pedestrian stops made by San Jose, California, police officers from January 2013 through March 2016 with a particular focus on benchmarking. Using violent crime suspects, nuisance-related calls for service (CFS) as comparators, we consider whether San Jose Police Department (SJPD) officers disproportionately stopped individuals from the city’s dominant racial, ethnic groups citywide, in certain police beats with high levels of nuisance calls. Using violent crime suspects citywide as a benchmark, Whites were significantly overrepresented among those stopped by the police while Hispanics, Asians,, Blacks were underrepresented. The CFS findings at the beat level were consistent with the citywide findings for Blacks but reversed direction for Hispanics, varied for Asians depending upon beat, call type. We discuss possible reasons for this divergence across benchmarks, racial/ethnic groups, consider the implications for future research.

title: Television dramas, support for controversial public policies: Effects, mechanisms
authors: Slater, Michael D, Rouner, Donna, Long, Marilee
abstract: In this experiment, we examine effects of television dramas on support for controversial public policies (gay marriage, the death penalty), explore mechanisms that may explain such effects. The dramas influenced support for death penalty but not gay marriage. As predicted, exposure to the relevant drama eliminated the relationship between prior ideology (conceptualized as a continuous variable), death penalty support. Moreover, the valence of the relationship between prior (increasingly liberal) ideology, salience of a relevant value (perceived importance of a safe, crime-free society) went from negative in the comparison condition to positive after exposure to the relevant drama. These, other results suggest that a television narrative can influence policy support by reframing the dramatic situation to reduce the effect of prior ideology, values, by minimizing processing of the story as intentionally persuasive discourse.

title: Victimization, fear of crime,, trust in criminal justice institutions: A cross-national analysis
authors: Singer, Alexa J, Chouhy, Cecilia, Lehmann, Peter S, Walzak, Jessica N, Gertz, Marc, Biglin, Sophia
abstract: Prior studies demonstrate that victimization, fear of crime independently affect criminal justice attitudes, but few have examined trust in criminal justice institutions. In addition, research has been primarily confined to the United States. Using data from the AmericasBarometer survey collected in the United States, Mexico, Argentina,, Brazil, the current study investigates the direct, indirect effects of criminal victimization, fear of crime on (a) perceived fairness of the courts, (b) trust in the police,, (c) overall trust in the criminal justice system. Results show that while the direct effects of victimization are mixed across countries, outcomes, fear of crime consistently mediates the effects of victimization on trust in criminal justice institutions.

title: Public confidence in the police: A time-series analysis
authors: Sindall, K, Sturgis, P, Jennings, W
keywords: PUBLIC support; POLICE; EMPIRICAL research; CROSS-sectional method; SOCIAL cohesion; CRIMINAL statistics; TIME series analysis; British Crime Survey; confidence in policing; time-series regression analysis;360\_Trust;British Journal of criminology;police visibility
abstract: Empirical analyses of the causes of public confidence in policing have been based almost entirely on cross-sectional survey data, with a consequent focus on between-group differences in levels of confidence at a single point in time. Our aim here is to introduce a time dimension to this area of investigation. Employing repeated cross-sectional survey data from the British Crime Survey, we apply time-series regression methods to show how confidence in policing changes over time for the aggregate population. Counter to cross-sectional findings, time-series analyses reveal that confidence in the police is not related to aggregate worry about crime, perceptions of social cohesion, nor informal social control, but only to perceptions of crime, the property crime rate.

title: A casual model explaining the perception, acceptance of gene technology
authors: Siegrist, Michael
abstract: This study examined factors affecting perceived risks, acceptance of gene technology. Based on the reviewed literature, a causal model was proposed. The plausibility of the postulated model was tested using structural equation modeling procedures. Participants were randomly selected students from a Swiss university (N = 837). Results indicated that trust in companies, scientists performing gene manipulations have a strong effect on the benefits, risks perceived. When trust was controlled for the inverse relationship between perceived risk, perceived benefit vanished. Furthermore, world views, perceived benefit,, perceived risk each are found to contribute independently to the prediction of acceptance of gene technology. World views, trust appear to play an important role in perceptions of gene technology. この研究は遺伝子技術の perceived risks と受容に影響を与えて因子を調べた。 再検討された文献に基づいて、原因となるモデルが提案された。 仮定されたモデルのもっともらしさは構造的な方程式モデリング手続きを使ってテストされた。 参加者はスイスの大学（ｎ ＝ ８３７）からのランダムに選ばれた学生たちであった。 結果が会社でその信頼を示した、そして遺伝子扱いを行なっている科学者が利益と認知されるリスクに強い影響を与える。 信頼がそうであったときコントロールされて、リスク認知と認知される利益の間の逆の関係は消失した。 さらに、世界観、認知される利益とリスク認知はそれぞれ独立して遺伝子技術の受容の予測に寄与することが判明する。 世界観と信頼は遺伝子技術の知覚における重要な役割を果たすように思われる。

title: Police trust-building strategies. A socio-institutional, comparative approach
authors: Schaap, Dorian
abstract: Police require public trust to do their work well. Recognising this, police organisations across Europe implement various methods to gain trust: trust-building strategies. Surprisingly, the field of trust in the police, police legitimacy has paid scant attention to what the police actually do to improve trust. The present contribution outlines an approach to understanding police trust-building strategies in their social, institutional context applying a comparative, dynamic perspective. Departing from the assumption that trust, legitimacy exist in a dialogue between the public, the police, the author argues that trust-building strategies develop in an unpredictable, dynamic complex of interrelated social, institutional factors. What is seen as a suitable trust-building strategy is determined by dominant 'rationalised myths', ways of thinking about what good police work should look like. These are shaped by a diverse range of different actors, factors. This complex affects each phase in the development of police trust-building strategies: problem recognition, generation of strategies,, adoption of strategies. Illustrating the value of the socio-institutional approach towards trust-building strategies, each of these phases is discussed in the context of a comparative, dynamic study of police trust-building strategies in England, Wales, Denmark,, the Netherlands. It is argued that this more sophisticated understanding of trust-building in its social, institutional context does not just tell us something about the police, but also helps us understand how state institutions shape, maintain their position in the complex environments of our changing societies.

title: Seeking 'civilianness': Police complaints, the civilian control model of oversight
authors: Savage, S P
abstract: The 'civilian control' model of police complaints systems is premised on a clear separation between 'civilian-led', 'police-led' investigative processes. This paper examines the nature of 'civilianness' in civilian control-based oversight agencies by examining the cultural profiles, internal dynamics of three police oversight bodies within the British, Irish islands. Based on over 100 interviews, it presents findings relating to the motivations behind oversight work, the dynamics associated with the joint workings of investigators with both non-police, police backgrounds. It concludes that civilian control may be seen as a differentiated space with varying degrees of civilianness, including remnants from, continuities with police culture.

title: The influence of race/ethnicity, social class,, neighborhood context on residents' attitudes toward the police
authors: Schuck, Amie M, Rosenbaum, Dennis P, Hawkins, Darnell F
abstract: The purpose of this study is to extend our understanding of attitudes toward the police by examining how race/ethnicity, social class,, neighborhood context interact to influence four different dimensions of attitudes: neighborhood, global, police services,, fear of the police. The results showed significant racial/ethnic variation in perceptions of the police, with African-Americans reporting the most negative attitudes. The magnitude of the racial/ethnic gap, however, varied across the different attitude dimensions with the largest difference between African-Americans, Whites in terms of fear of the police. The findings also suggested that African-Americans', Hispanics' perceptions of the police are moderated by the interaction of social class, neighborhood socioeconomic composition. Middle-class African-Americans, Hispanics who resided in disadvantaged neighborhoods reported more negative attitudes toward the police than those who resided in more advantaged areas. Overall the study findings highlight the complex interplay between experiences, community context, social class,, type of attitudinal assessment in understanding within, across racial, ethnic variation in residents' perceptions of the police.

title: Global, neighborhood attitudes toward the police: Differentiation by race, ethnicity, type of contact
authors: Schuck, Amie M, Rosenbaum, Dennis P
keywords: POLICE; RACE; ETHNICITY; SOCIAL groups; MENTAL representation; PEACE officers; citizens attitudes; community policing; demeanor; racial differences;360\_Trust
abstract: This study focused on a series of hypotheses regarding residents' attitudes toward the police: (1) residents' attitudes toward the police are better represented by a two-dimensional model that differentiates global perceptions of the police from assessments of the police in the respondents' neighborhood; (2) the structure of residents' attitudes toward the police is different for Whites, African Americans,, Latinos; (3) direct experiences with the police in the respondents' neighborhood will be more strongly associated with the respondents' assessment of police in their neighborhood than global perceptions of the police;, (4) the influence of direct experiences with the police will be stronger for African Americans, Latinos than for Whites. Results based on structural equation modeling offer strong support for the need to differentiate between global, neighborhood perceptions of the police. The underlining measurement structure of attitudes toward the police was similar for Whites, African Americans,, Latinos. However, the relationship between global, neighborhood attitudes was stronger for African Americans, Latinos. Negative contact with the police was associated with both negative global, neighborhood assessments of the police. Non-negative contact was associated with positive neighborhood perceptions of the police; however, only when it occurred within the neighborhood. The influence of direct experiences with the police (both inside, outside the neighborhood) was similar for Whites, African Americans,, Latinos.

title: The impact of procedurally-just policing on citizen perceptions of police during traffic stops: The Adana randomized controlled trial
authors: Sahin, Nusret, Braga, Anthony A, Apel, Robert, Brunson, Rod K
abstract: Objectives The process-based model of police legitimacy suggests, when police are perceived to make fair decisions, treat people with respect, they will be viewed as legitimate authorities. A randomized controlled trial was used to test the impact of a procedural justice policing intervention, relative to routine police behavior, during traffic stops for excessive speeding in Adana, Turkey. Methods Drivers stopped by traffic officers for speeding violations were randomly assigned to treatment, control groups. Subjects in the treatment group received the procedural justice policing intervention during traffic stops, while subjects in the control group experienced business-as-usual traffic stops. Treatment officer behavior was guided by a script that helped to ensure that key components of a procedurally-just encounter were delivered. After completion of the traffic stop, drivers were interviewed on the encounter, general perceptions of traffic police. Results The experimental analyses show that the infusion of procedural justice principles into police traffic stops does improve citizens’ perceptions of the specific encounter relative to routine police traffic stops. However, the procedural justice treatment did not generate a robust improvement in citizens’ general perceptions of traffic officers. Conclusion These results indicate it might be overly optimistic to suggest a single positive encounter can exert a strong influence on durable citizen perceptions of confidence, trust in the police. In addition to ensuring procedurally-just encounters, police executives, police makers should also pay attention to other relevant performance dimensions such as crime control effectiveness, distributive fairness,, lawfulness to change global perceptions of the police.

title: Media, confidence in the police: Differences across race/ethnicity
authors: Rosenberger, Jared S, Dierenfeldt, Rick
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: A substantial body of literature connects direct experience with crime, the criminal justice system to public confidence in the police (Bradford Policing, Society, 24(1): 22-43, 2014; Gibson et al. American Journal of Political Science 47: 354-367, 2003, Political Research Quarterly, 58: 187-201, 2005; Sargeant Policing, Society 27: 927-940, 2017). However, most citizens have limited direct interaction with the police (Roberts \& Doob Law, Human Behavior 14: 451-468 , 1990; Surette, 2007), justifying research exploring the impact of media consumption on attitudes toward the police. This study examines the impact of news consumption through television, the internet,, social media on confidence in the police across race/ethnicity. The study utilizes a national non-full probability sample of 500 White, Black,, Hispanic/Latinx respondents. Findings suggest that race/ethnicity mediates the relationship between news source, attitudes toward the police. Implications are discussed.

title: Attitudes toward the police: The effects of direct, vicarious experience
authors: Rosenbaum, Dennis P, Schuck, Amie M, Costello, Sandra K, Hawkins, Darnell F, Ring, Marianne K
abstract: Researchers have emphasized the importance of direct encounters with the police as a determinant of attitudes toward the police, yet cross-sectional studies allow for limited causal inference. This study includes the measurement of attitudes before, after encounters with the police among African American, Hispanic,, White residents of Chicago. Contrary to previous research, direct contact with the police during the past year is not enough to change attitudes, but vicarious experience (i.e., learning that someone else has had a good or bad encounter with the police) does influence attitudes in a predictable manner. Also, residents’ initial attitudes about the police play a critical role in shaping their judgments of subsequent direct, indirect experiences as well as their future attitudes. The findings are discussed in terms of stereotypes about the police that are resistant to change.

title: Public confidence in criminal justice in Canada: A comparative, contextual analysis
authors: Roberts, Julian V
journal: Canadian journal of criminology, criminal justice
keywords: CONVICTION rates; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; CRIMINAL law; ECONOMIC trends; OPPOSITION (Political science); POLITICAL attitudes; PUBLIC opinion; PUBLIC support; SITUATION ethics; confiance du grand public; opinion du grand public; public confidence;360\_Trust
abstract: Public confidence in criminal justice has emerged as an important issue in most western nations. Several jurisdictions have made promoting public confidence a policy priority,, governments in many countries have recently conducted public opinion surveys to gauge levels of confidence in criminal justice. However, little is known about levels of public confidence in criminal justice in Canada. This article reviews the empirical research on this issue, attempts to explain current trends. Although a significant plurality of the public expresses little confidence in the justice system, more people are positive than are negative. In comparison to other countries, confidence levels in criminal justice are generally higher in Canada. This said, the public has less confidence in the justice system than in other public institutions such as the health care system. Consistent with findings elsewhere, the police attract most,, the prison system the least amount of public confidence. The article places these findings in context,, discusses their implications for research, policy.

title: Compliance with the law in Slovenia: The role of procedural justice, police legitimacy
authors: Reisig, Michael D, Tankebe, Justice, Mesko, Gorazd
journal: European journal on criminal policy, research
keywords: LEGITIMACY of governments; OPERATIONAL definitions; PROCEDURAL justice; ENDOGENEITY (Econometrics); SURVEYS; SLOVENIA; Compliance; Endogeneity; Legitimacy; Self-control; TYLER, Tom;360\_Trust
abstract: The empirical status of Tom Tyler’s ( 1990 ) process-based model of regulation is frustrated by the fact that most studies are conducted in the US, leaving open the question of whether similar effects can be observed in countries with different historical, political contexts. The current study tests two process-based model hypotheses using cross-sectional survey data from 683 young adults in Slovenia. The results reveal: (1) procedural justice judgments significantly shape individual perceptions of police legitimacy,, (2) perceived police legitimacy explains self-reported compliance with the law. Though slightly diminished in magnitude, the legitimacy effect persists when using an instrumental variable to address possible endogeneity bias, after statistically controlling for known correlates of law violating behavior (i.e., personal morality, low self-control). The findings also show that the legitimacy effect on compliance with different laws (e.g., littering, buying stolen property) varies depending on the operationalization of legitimacy (i.e., additive scale versus instrumental variable). While the findings indicate that the process-based model of regulation is germane to post-socialist countries such as Slovenia, more research focusing on the explanatory breadth of the model is necessary.

title: Geographies of trust
authors: Rahn, Wendy M, Yoon, Kwang Suk, Garet, Michael, Lipson, Steven, Loflin, Katherine
abstract: Generalized social trust is an important component of social capital, has been linked to a variety of individual-, community-level outcomes, including low crime rates, effective government,, healthy, happy citizens. Drawing on a multicommunity survey conducted in several American towns, cities in 2002, the authors examine the individual, contextual origins of general social trust using the techniques of Hierarchical Linear Modeling. Based on prevailing theoretical understandings of social trust, the authors posit a comprehensive model to account for the contextual variation that remains after controlling for individual-level variables. Two community-level variables, voter turnout, commute times, emerge as important contextual predictors of social trust. The authors explore community attachment as a potential mediator of these effects, finding that it partially mediates the impact of commuting but not voter turnout, results consistent with their distinction between “experiential”, “cultural” theories of social trust formation.

title: The effects of justice judgments on police legitimacy across urban neighborhoods: A test of the invariance thesis
authors: Reisig, Michael D, Flippin, Michaela, Meško, Gorazd, Trinkner, Rick
abstract: The invariance thesis posits that the effects of procedural justice judgments on police legitimacy beliefs are consistent across a variety of contexts, including urban neighborhoods. An alternative argument, one steeped in the relational model of authority, holds that procedural justice effects are weaker in high-crime communities where residents do not identify with the police, where they place more weight on instrumental concerns. This study used survey data from 1,000 adults in Ljubljana, Slovenia. The regression models showed that the association between procedural justice, police legitimacy was stronger in low-risk neighborhoods. In high-risk areas, distributive justice was a stronger correlate of legitimacy. Overall, the findings highlight how neighborhood context can moderate the influence of fairness judgments on supportive beliefs.

title: The effects of police performance on agency trustworthiness, citizen participation
authors: Porumbescu, Gregory A, Neshkova, Milena I, Huntoon, Meghan
abstract: We examine the effect of performance information on citizens’ willingness to engage with government. We hypothesize that when performance information is positive, citizens perceive government as trustworthy, which increases proclivity for participation. To validate this framework, we conduct an experiment that tests the effect of police performance on citizens’ perceptions of police trustworthiness, intentions to participate in a neighbourhood watch programme. We find that information about police performance strongly affects perceptions of police trustworthiness. Yet, citizen decisions to participate in the community watch programme are more complex, can be triggered by either positive or negative police performance.

title: When is policing fair? Groups, identity, judgements of the procedural justice of coercive crowd policing
authors: Radburn, Matthew, Stott, Clifford, Bradford, Ben, Robinson, Mark
abstract: Procedural justice theory (PJT) is now a widely utilised theoretical perspective in policing research that acknowledges the centrality of police ‘fairness’. Despite its widespread acceptance this paper asserts that there are conceptual limitations that emerge when applying the theory to the policing of crowd events. This paper contends that this problem with PJT is a result of specific assumptions that are highlighted by two studies using a novel experimental approach. Study 1 systematically manipulated the social categories used to describe crowd participants subjected to police coercion. The experiment demonstrates how these social categories dramatically affected participants’ perceptions of the same police action, that it was participants’ relational identification with the police, rather than a superordinate category, that mediated the association between judgements of procedural fairness, intentions to cooperate. In Study 2, using a quasi-experimental design, we then replicated, extended these findings by demonstrating how perceptions of procedural fairness are also influenced by levels of in-group identification. The paper concludes by exploring the implications of the data for reconceptualising the social psychological processes mediating these judgements, impacts of police legitimacy.

title: Expectations, effectiveness, trust,, cooperation: Public attitudes towards the Israel police during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Perry, Gali, Jonathan-Zamir, Tal
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: AbstractThe COVID-19 pandemic significantly affected the work of police agencies worldwide. Within a short period of time, the police were assigned new responsibilities, were required to change their priorities, focus on enforcing unusual emergency orders. These new tasks, as well as the emergency atmosphere, its socio-psychological implications, raise a series of questions about public expectations from, trust in the police during the pandemic period. In this article, we report the views of majority communities in Israel (non-Orthodox Jews), as expressed in a survey carried out in the midst of the pandemic. We find that this population supports police enforcement of the new orders, trusts them to do so with integrity, believes the police have been successful in this arena,, is willing to report violations of emergency regulations. Overall, responses indicate more favourable attitudes towards the police, echoing previous findings on policing emergencies.

title: Fear of retaliation, citizen willingness to cooperate with police
authors: Papp, Jordan, Smith, Brad, Wareham, Jennifer, Wu, Yuning
abstract: Qualitative research has shown that fear of retaliation influences an individual’s willingness to cooperate with the police. This research has shown that those who are fearful of being retaliated against are less likely to cooperate with the police (Clayman, C., Skinns, L., 2012. To snitch or not to snitch? An exploratory study of the factors influencing whether young people actively cooperate with the police. Policing, society: an international journal of research, policy, 22 (4), 460–480; Rosenfeld, R., Jacobs, B.,, Wright R., 2003. Snitching, the code of the street. British journal of criminology, 43, 291–309; Whitman, J., Davis, R., 2007. Snitches get snitches: youth, gangs,, witness intimidation in Massachusetts. Washington, DC: National Center for Victims of Crime). This study examined this topic quantitatively so as to gain an understanding of the influence of fear of retaliation relative to other known correlates of cooperation with the police. Data for this study were collected from 408 Detroit households from 3 different neighbourhood clusters. Results indicated that fear of retaliation reduces an individual’s willingness to cooperate with the police. However, even more salient was trust in the police, which showed that citizens who are more trustful of the police report greater willingness to cooperate with them.

title: Citizen attitudes toward the police in Canada
authors: O'Connor, Christopher D
abstract: PurposeCitizens' opinions of the police are important indicators of how well the police are performing their duties, can help to shape police practice as well as public policy. However, little research exists in Canada on people's opinions of the police. This paper aims to provide a more robust understanding of citizen attitudes toward the police in Canada by examining a variety of factors that have been deemed important in shaping people's attitudes in other countries (predominantly from research conducted in the USA).Design/methodology/approachThe paper utilizes path analysis to decompose, better understand the relationships between sociodemographic/non‐sociodemographic variables, attitudes toward the police. Data were drawn from the 1999 General Social Survey conducted by Statistics Canada. A random sample of Canadians was surveyed regarding victimization, personal safety, attitudes toward the criminal justice system.FindingsSeveral distinct groups of people (i.e. young people, visible minorities, males, those who have experienced criminal victimization, those dissatisfied with their safety, those who perceive their neighborhoods as being high in crime) emerged as having negative views toward the police, which is consistent with much of the research conducted in the USA.Originality/valuePolice practice should more closely resemble the principles inherent in community policing if certain groups' negative views of the police are to be improved. This can be partly accomplished by the police being more inclusive of diverse opinions in the community, actively seeking out this opinion in order to better inform policing practices, strategies.

title: Do fair procedures matter? The effect of procedural justice on spouse assault
authors: Paternoster, Raymond, Brame, Robert, Bachman, Ronet, Sherman, Lawrence W
keywords: ASSAULT \& battery; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; LAW enforcement; MARITAL violence; POLICE -- United States; UNITED States;360\_Trust
abstract: In a reanalysis of the Milwaukee Domestic Violence Experiment, the authors examine whether the use of fair procedures on the part of police officers called to the scene of a domestic assault inhibits subsequent assault. Consistent with expectations, they found that procedural justice did suppress subsequent violence, even in the face of adverse outcomes. When police acted in a procedurally fair manner when arresting assault suspects, the rate of subsequent domestic violence was significantly lower than when they did not. Moreover, suspects who were arrested, perceived that they were treated in a procedurally fair manner had subsequent assault rates that were as low as those suspects given a more favorable outcome (warned, then released without arrest). The suppression effect of procedural justice did not depend on the personal characteristics of suspects

title: Are trustworthiness, legitimacy ‘hard to win, easy to lose’? A longitudinal test of the asymmetry thesis of police-citizen contact
authors: Oliveira, Thiago R, Jackson, Jonathan, Murphy, Kristina, Bradford, Ben
abstract: Abstract Objectives Test the asymmetry thesis of police-citizen contact that police trustworthiness, legitimacy are affected more by negative than by positive experiences of interactions with legal agents by analyzing changes in attitudes towards the police after an encounter with the police. Test whether prior attitudes moderate the impact of contact on changes in attitudes towards the police. Methods A two-wave panel survey of a nationally representative sample of Australian adults measured people’s beliefs about police trustworthiness (procedural fairness, effectiveness), their duty to obey the police, their contact with the police between the two waves,, their evaluation of those encounters in terms of process, outcome. Analysis is carried out using autoregressive structural equation modeling, latent moderated structural models. Results The association between both process, outcome evaluation of police-citizen encounters, changes in attitudes towards the police is asymmetrical for trust in police effectiveness, symmetrical for trust in procedural fairness,, asymmetrical (in the opposite direction expected) for duty to obey the police. Little evidence of heterogeneity in the association between encounters, trust in procedural fairness, duty to obey, but prior levels of perceived effectiveness moderate the association between outcome evaluation, changes in trust in police effectiveness. Conclusions The association between police-citizen encounters, attitudes towards the police may not be as asymmetrical as previously thought, particularly for changes in trust in procedural fairness, legitimacy. Policy implications include considering public-police interactions as ‘teachable moments’, potential sources for enhancing police trustworthiness, legitimacy.

title: Trust in the police: The influence of procedural justice, perceived collective efficacy
authors: Nix, Justin, Wolfe, Scott E, Rojek, Jeff, Kaminski, Robert J
abstract: Tyler’s process-based model of policing suggests that the police can enhance their perceived legitimacy, trustworthiness in the eyes of the public when they exercise their authority in a procedurally fair manner. To date, most process-based research has focused on the sources of legitimacy while largely overlooking trust in the police. The present study extends this line of literature by examining the sources of trust in the police. In particular, emerging research has revealed that neighborhood context influences attitudes toward the police but much less attention has been given to exploring the role individuals’ perceptions of their neighborhood play in shaping such evaluations. Therefore, the present study considers whether individuals’ perceptions of collective efficacy serve as a social-psychological cognitive orientation that influences levels of trust in the police. Using data from a recently conducted mail survey of a random sample of 1,681 residents from a metropolitan city, we find that procedural justice evaluations are a primary source of trust in the police. At the same time, however, level of perceived collective efficacy is positively associated with trust even after accounting for procedural justice. The findings suggest that police procedural fairness is vitally important to establishing trust from the public but peoples’ cognitive orientation toward their neighborhood context partially shapes the level of trustworthiness they afford to the police.

title: Nurturing regulatory compliance: Is procedural justice effective when people question the legitimacy of the law?
authors: Murphy, Kristina, Tyler, Tom R, Curtis, Amy
keywords: compliance; legitimacy; motivational postures; procedural justice; regulation;360\_Trust
abstract: AbstractProcedural justice generally enhances an authority's legitimacy, encourages people to comply with an authority's decisions, rules. We argue, however, that previous research on procedural justice, legitimacy has examined legitimacy in a limited way by focusing solely on the perceived legitimacy of authorities, ignoring how people may perceive the legitimacy of the laws, rules they enforce. In addition, no research to date has examined how such perceptions of legitimacy may moderate the effect of procedural justice on compliance behavior. Using survey data collected across three different regulatory contexts – taxation (Study 1), social security (Study 2),, law enforcement (Study 3) – the findings suggest that one's perceptions of the legitimacy of the law moderates the effect of procedural justice on compliance behaviors; procedural justice is more important for shaping compliance behaviors when people question the legitimacy of the laws than when they accept them as legitimate. An explanation of these findings using a social distancing framework is offered, along with a discussion of the implications the findings have on enforcement.

title: Procedural justice, compliance behaviour: the mediating role of emotions
authors: Murphy, Kristina, Tyler, Tom
abstract: AbstractProcedural justice researchers have consistently found that if authorities treat people with trust, fairness, respect, neutrality, people will not only be more willing to cooperate with authorities, but they will also be more likely to comply with authority decisions, rules. New research in this area has gone on to explore the role that emotions play in response to procedural justice, injustice. What this new research has neglected to do, however, is examine whether emotions mediate the effect of procedural justice on subsequent compliance behaviour in real life settings. Using longitudinal survey data collected in two real‐life contexts (Study 1: a taxation dispute (N = 652),, Study 2: workplaces (N = 2366)), the present study will show that perceptions of procedural justice influence the emotions experienced by people, but more importantly these emotional reactions (i.e. anger, happiness) mediate the effect of justice on subsequent compliance behaviour. In other words, it is these positive, negative emotional reactions to perceived justice or injustice that go on to predict who will, will not comply with authority decisions, rules.
