This paper furthers our understanding of information sharing by city police departments as well as public redistribution of this information through the use of social media tools.

title: Law enforcement agency adoption, use of Twitter as a crisis communication tool
authors: Heverin, Thomas, Zach, Lisl
keywords: crisis informatics; crisis communications; technology adoption;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: Abstract: This chapter describes the results of a research study investigating the adoption, use of Twitter as a crisis communication tool by law enforcement agencies from large US cities (cities with populations greater than 300,000). The study consisted of two parts – an analysis of Twitter use based on publicly available posts authored by 30 law enforcement agencies that have active Twitter accounts, an analysis of data collected through 17 semi-structured interviews with law enforcement public information officers, public media specialists.

title: Twitter adoption, use in mass convergence, emergency events
authors: Hughes, Amanda Lee, Palen, Leysia
abstract: This paper offers a descriptive account of Twitter (a microblogging service) across four high-profile, mass convergence events - two emergency, two national security. We statistically examine how Twitter is being used surrounding these events,, compare, contrast how that behaviour is different from more general Twitter use. Our findings suggest that Twitter messages sent during these types of events contain more displays of information broadcasting, brokerage,, we observe that general Twitter use seems to have evolved over time to offer more of an information-sharing purpose. We also provide preliminary evidence that Twitter users who join during, in apparent relation to a mass convergence or emergency event are more likely to become long-term adopters of the technology.

title: The evolving role of the public information officer: An examination of social media in emergency management
authors: Hughes, Amanda L, Palen, Leysia
journal: Journal of homeland security, emergency management
abstract: This work examines how the introduction of social media has affected the role of the Public Information Officer (PIO)—the public relations component of the National Incident Management System (NIMS). Through analysis of 25 PIO interviews, we examine the work practice of PIOs, find that social media expand not only the scope, type of PIO work activity, but also the “information pathways” that exist between PIOs, the media,, members of the public. We model these changes, examine how the presence of social media challenges previous conceptualizations of PIO work. Lastly, we present a view of how PIO work could be better imagined for the future of emergency management organizations.

title: CDC's use of social media, humor in a risk campaign—“preparedness 101: Zombie apocalypse”
authors: Fraustino, Julia Daisy, Ma, Liang
journal: Journal of applied communication research: JACR
abstract: This is a multiple methods study that highlights the tension between awareness-, behavioral-based campaign successes, particularly when communicating using social media, pop-culture-referencing humor. To illustrate, it examines the Centers for Disease Control, Prevention's (CDC) “zombie apocalypse” all-disaster-preparedness campaign. An interview with a CDC campaign manager, campaign document analysis,, a 2 (information form: social vs. traditional media) × 2 (message strategy: humorous vs. non-humorous) experiment uncovers benefits, pitfalls of using social media, humorous messaging for risk communication. Findings show social media can quickly spread information to new publics for minimal costs; however, experiment participants who received the humorous (i.e., zombie) risk message reported significantly weaker intentions to take protective actions in comparison to those who received the traditional, non-humorous risk message.

title: Facebook, twitter in crisis communication: A comparative study of crisis communication professionals, citizens
authors: Eriksson, Mats, Olsson, Eva-Karin
abstract: This mixed-methods study presents a comparative analysis of the use, perceived usefulness of Facebook, Twitter, among Swedish citizens, crisis communication professionals, as crisis communication tools, information sources. The use, perceived usefulness of Facebook, Twitter are not congruent, consistent between the two different groups, according to the overall study. Communication professionals, for example, report higher levels of perceived usefulness regarding Facebook's potential as a crisis communication tool than do the citizens. Taken together, the results show that researchers (within social media, crisis communication), crisis managers both need to deal with the fact that social media is not a homogenous phenomenon with a single coherent role in crisis management, communication research, practice.

title: What are the police doing on Twitter? Social media, the police, the public
authors: Crump, Jeremy
abstract: AbstractThis article examines the growing interest since 2008 of UK police forces in the use of social media as a basis for engagement with the public. This interest is set in the context of a political agenda for increasing public trust, confidence in the police, enlistment of the public as jointly responsible for crime reduction. An ambitious national police agenda led by the Association of Chief Police Officers has promoted the use of social media to engage groups previously uninvolved in discussion of local policing,, has envisaged its use as a basis for deliberation about priorities. This article investigates how successful this endeavour has been,, how far a hierarchical organisation ‐ the police service ‐ has been able to exploit the networked characteristics of social media, the potential of user created content. The paper analyses the police use of one particular platform, Twitter, including the structure of networks, the content of the messages. The article concludes that the constraints of police culture have meant that Twitter has been used cautiously, as a reinforcement for existing means of communication. It puts forward key issues which need to be addressed if the more ambitious aims for social media are to be achieved.

title: Potential of social media as a tool to combat foodborne illness
authors: Chapman, Benjamin, Raymond, Benjamin, Powell, Douglas
abstract: The use of social media platforms, such as Facebook, Twitter, has been increasing substantially in recent years, has affected the way that people access information online. Social media rely on high levels of interaction, user-generated context shared through established, evolving social networks. Health information providers must know how to successfully participate through social media in order to meet the needs of these online audiences. This article reviews the current research on the use of social media for public health communication, suggests potential frameworks for developing social media strategies. The extension to food safety risk communication is explored, considering the potential of social media as a tool to combat foodborne illness.

title: Pandemics in the age of Twitter: content analysis of Tweets during the 2009 H1N1 outbreak
authors: Chew, Cynthia, Eysenbach, Gunther
abstract: BACKGROUND: Surveys are popular methods to measure public perceptions in emergencies but can be costly, time consuming. We suggest, evaluate a complementary ``infoveillance'' approach using Twitter during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. Our study aimed to: 1) monitor the use of the terms ``H1N1'' versus ``swine flu'' over time; 2) conduct a content analysis of ``tweets'';, 3) validate Twitter as a real-time content, sentiment,, public attention trend-tracking tool. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: Between May 1, December 31, 2009, we archived over 2 million Twitter posts containing keywords ``swine flu,'' ``swineflu,'' and/or ``H1N1.'' using Infovigil, an infoveillance system. Tweets using ``H1N1'' increased from 8.8\% to 40.5\% (R(2) = .788; p<.001), indicating a gradual adoption of World Health Organization-recommended terminology. 5,395 tweets were randomly selected from 9 days, 4 weeks apart, coded using a tri-axial coding scheme. To track tweet content, to test the feasibility of automated coding, we created database queries for keywords, correlated these results with manual coding. Content analysis indicated resource-related posts were most commonly shared (52.6\%). 4.5\% of cases were identified as misinformation. News websites were the most popular sources (23.2\%), while government, health agencies were linked only 1.5\% of the time. 7/10 automated queries correlated with manual coding. Several Twitter activity peaks coincided with major news stories. Our results correlated well with H1N1 incidence data. CONCLUSIONS: This study illustrates the potential of using social media to conduct ``infodemiology'' studies for public health. 2009 H1N1-related tweets were primarily used to disseminate information from credible sources, but were also a source of opinions, experiences. Tweets can be used for real-time content analysis, knowledge translation research, allowing health authorities to respond to public concerns.

title: Temporal analysis of social media response to live events: The Milano fashion week
authors: Brambilla, Marco, Ceri, Stefano, Daniel, Florian, Donetti, Gianmarco
abstract: Social media response to catastrophic events, such as natural disasters or terrorist attacks, has received a lot of attention. However, social media are also extremely important in the context of planned events, such as fairs, exhibits, festivals, as they play an essential role in communicating them to fans, interest groups,, the general population. These kinds of events are geo-localized within a city or territory, are scheduled within a public calendar. We consider a specific scenario, the Milano Fashion Week (MFW), which is an important event in our city.

title: Neighborhood disadvantage, residents' distress,, online social communication: Harnessing Twitter data to examine neighborhood effects
authors: Booth, Jaime M, Lin, Yu-Ru, Wei, Kai
abstract: This study aims to examine the role of place-based online social communications in buffering the relationship between neighborhood disadvantage, psychological distress using geo-located Twitter feeds. We collected 1,981,802 geo-tagged tweets posted within the physical boundaries of 78 neighborhoods located in Pittsburgh for 16 consecutive months, beginning July 15, 2013. Psychological distress was measured using sentiments expressed in tweets,, within-, between-neighborhood online social communications were assessed using users' Twitter activity. This study reveals differential effects of within-, between-neighborhood online social communications. More online social communications within a neighborhood were associated with increased psychological sadness, anxiety,, distress in high-poverty neighborhoods; a relationship that was not found in low-poverty neighborhoods. This study suggests the buffering effects of online social communications may follow the same patterns as off-line social support in disadvantaged neighborhoods. Considering the interactions between online spaces, neighborhoods may be important for planning, implementing neighborhood-level interventions.

title: Quantitative approaches to comparing communication patterns on twitter
authors: Bruns, Axel, Stieglitz, Stefan
journal: Journal of technology in human services
abstract: To date, available literature mainly discusses Twitter activity patterns in the context of individual case studies, while comparative research on a large number of communicative events, their dynamics, patterns is missing. By conducting a comparative study of more than forty different cases (covering topics such as elections, natural disasters, corporate crises,, televised events) we identify a number of distinct types of discussion which can be observed on Twitter. Drawing on a range of communicative metrics, we show that thematic, contextual factors influence the usage of different communicative tools available to Twitter users, such as original tweets, @replies, retweets,, URLs. Based on this first analysis of the overall metrics of Twitter discussions, we also demonstrate stable patterns in the use of Twitter in the context of major topics, events.

title: Policing, social media: A mixed-method investigation of social media use by a small-town police department
authors: Boateng, Francis D, Chenane, Joselyne
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: In recent times, police departments across all social contexts have undergone tremendous changes,, a major catalyst of these changes has been the emergence of social media. This technological innovation has provided departments with a platform to communicate effectively, share information with the public. Social media have impacted policing, transformed the way the police do their job. The current analysis focused on understanding social media usage by small college-town police departments. Twitter, interview data were collected from the Oxford Police Department, were analyzed qualitatively, quantitatively to achieve the study’s objective. Results of these analyses revealed six main types of information that the department shared with the public on Twitter. Recommendations for improving the police’s use of social media are offered.

title: Effectiveness of police social media use
authors: Beshears, Michael L
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: Specifically, this study was an examination of the role of social media for, by Arkansas sheriff offices with respect to community relations efforts, the solving of crimes. A review of the literature led to an examination of the relationship between predictor variables frequency, quality of social media communication, while using county population density, county social economic status (SES) as control variables. A hierarchical multiple linear regression model was used to evaluate the data that had been collected via a phone, online survey. All statistical requirements to use this regression model were met. Careful adherence to ethical standards was practiced. The relatively small sample resulting from the small population was cited as a concern. However, responses from 52 of the 75 Arkansas county sheriff offices provided sufficient data for the study. The predictor variable, frequency, accounted for a significant degree of variation in both dependent variables. The predictor variable, quality or variety of social media sources, was not significant, so the null hypothesis was not rejected. However, more social media sources increase the significance of the frequency. Overall, Arkansas sheriff offices surveyed supported the use of social media for both community relations, crime solving. The social media platforms identified as being used by one or more sheriff office or individual sheriff to connect with residents in their community included, a Basic Website, Electronic Newsletters, FaceBook, Twitter, Instagram,, YouTube.

title: Twitter for crisis communication: lessons learned from Japan's tsunami disaster
authors: Acar, Adam, Muraki, Yuya
journal: International Journal of Web Based Communities
abstract: Two weeks after the Great Tohoku earthquake followed by the devastating tsunami, we have sent open-ended questionnaires to a randomly selected sample of Twitter users, also analysed the tweets sent from the disaster-hit areas. We found that people in directly affected areas tend to tweet about their unsafe, uncertain situation while people in remote areas post messages to let their followers know that they are safe. Our analysis of the open-ended answers has revealed that unreliable retweets (RTs) on Twitter was the biggest problem the users have faced during the disaster. Some of the solutions offered by the respondents included introducing official hash tags, limiting the number of RTs for each hash tag, adding features that allow users to trace information by maintaining anonymity.

title: ‘No one wants to end up on YouTube’: sousveillance, ‘cop-baiting’ in Canadian policing
authors: Huey, Laura, Ferguson, Lorna

title: Engaging Citizens via Twitter: A Comparative Analysis of Social Media Strategies in Community Policing by Greater
authors: Ali, Muhammad, Zia, Mehwish
abstract: The widespread acceptance of social media platforms has compelled police departments worldwide to utilize Twitter for community policing. Proponents of this new policing model argue that fostering partnerships between community members, police can strengthen bond between citizens, law enforcement. Community policing necessitates of cers to establish direct, close links with public, a task facilitated by Twitter's network-building, one-on-one interaction capabilities. Furthermore, Twitter empowers citizens to voice their opinions on matters of public importance, thereby exercising their democratic rights. Direct communication via Twitter also enables police to consider Citizens feedback when reviewingpolicies,ultimately enhancing their effectiveness.However,the challenge of low online citizen engagement remains. Effective collaboration between citizens, police requires law enforcement agencies to create an environment that encourages increased citizen engagement. This research evaluates the citizen engagement strategies employed by Islamabad Capital Territory Police, the Greater Manchester Police on Twitter. Through a comparative analysis, this study identi es the most commonly used media, content types by both police forces, measures the citizen engagement generated by each. The ndings reveal that despite having a larger number of followers, tweets, the citizen engagement generated by GMP on Twitter is relatively low

title: Policing social media: Are procedural justice principles guiding Canadian police interactions online?
authors: Zaidi, Huda, O'Connor, Christopher D
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Police presence on social media has become increasingly common in recent years, has arguably altered policing in many ways. Although research in this area is increasing, the growing presence of police on a range of social media platforms requires further examination of the various nuances that continue to emerge regarding this symbiosis. To that end, only a small number of studies have examined this topic from the perspective of police personnel in the Canadian context. Accordingly, drawing on in-depth interviews with police personnel overseeing police social media sites, this article examines how Canadian police services manage negativity, conflict online. The findings suggest that police services address negativity, conflict on their social media sites by drawing on the principles of procedural justice to guide their interactions. We discuss the implications of these findings, how police–public social media interactions might be improved.

title: Understanding the risk of Sexual Reoffending in adult men: A network-Based Model
authors: van den Berg, Jan Willem, van Beek, Daan J, Bouman, Yvonne H A, Janssen, Erick, Smid, Wineke J, Gijs, Luk
journal: Sexual abuse: a journal of research, treatment
keywords: causal network; dynamic risk factors; network approach; risk of sexual reoffending; sexual recidivism;362\_SNA
abstract: The predominant approach to understand dynamic risk factors of sexual reoffending has been referred to as the Propensities Model (Thornton, 2016). According to this model, dynamic risk factors can be conceptualized as latent constructs whose change alters the risk of sexual reoffending. Despite its strengths, contributions to research, this model does not offer answers to the question of how dynamic risk factors contribute to the risk of sexual reoffending, or of how sustained change in risk might take place. In this paper we introduce the Network-Based Model of Risk of Sexual Reoffending (NBM-RSR), which addresses several limitations, constraints of the Propensities Model, offers empirically testable propositions regarding the nature, development of the risk of sexual reoffending. The NBM-RSR considers risk of sexual reoffending to involve a self-sustaining network of causally connected dynamic risk factors. Consistent with this, an increased risk of sexual reoffending is characterized through a network that contains more, stronger interconnected dynamic risk factors with a higher strength. Sustained change in risk of sexual reoffending occurs when activity in the network exceeds a critical point resulting in a new self-sustaining network. Propositions based on the NBM-RSR are introduced, translated into testable hypotheses. These propositions revolve around (a) risk of sexual reoffending resulting from the construction of a network of causally connected dynamic risk factors, (b) network stability, sudden changes,, critical transitions,, (c) dynamic risk factors' relative influence on risk of sexual reoffending.

title: Online neighborhood networks: The relationship between online communication practices, neighborhood dynamics
authors: Robaeyst, Ben, Baccarne, Bastiaan, Meulenaere, Jonas De, Mechant, Peter
abstract: This article builds upon communication infrastructure theory, investigates how communication practices on online neighborhood networks (ONNs) relate to the social cohesion of neighborhood communities. Specifically, we study the hyperlocal social media platform Hoplr, which provides ad-free ONNs in which neighbors can communicate with one another. Local governments can subscribe to Hoplr to communicate with their residents, engage them for community, public participation purposes. This study is based on an online survey of Hoplr members (N = 3,055) from 150 randomly selected ONNs. Social cohesion is disentangled as a combination of social support, a sense of community, reciprocal exchange,, social trust. We investigated social cohesion differences at the neighborhood level in relation to self-reported types of ONN communication practices (shared interest, supportive communication,, both tangible, informational support mobilization). The results reveal the limited value of quantified behavioral data to explain differences in neighborhood social cohesion. However, interesting patterns are revealed between different communication practices, neighborhood social cohesion, such as the importance of trivial storytelling, information exchange practices for enhancing trust, reciprocal support,, a sense of community. At the same time, a reversed relation appears when ONNs are considered explicit information exchange platforms. With these insights, we enhance the theoretical understanding of ONNs in relation to neighborhood social cohesion, within a broader repertoire of neighborhood communication infrastructures.

title: Dynamic individual risk networks: Personalized network modelling based on experience sampling data
authors: Smid, Wineke J, Wever, Edwin C, Van den Heuvel, Nathalie
journal: Sexual abuse: a journal of research, treatment
keywords: experience sampling; network analysis; personalized network modeling; risk assessment;362\_SNA;\_\_work\_pdf登録
abstract: Following a network perspective, risk of sexual reoffending can be understood as a construct that emerges from the interactions between risk factors. If these interrelationships are validly mapped out, this leads to an increased understanding of the risk, thus may contribute to more effective and/or more efficient interventions. This paper reports on personalized network modeling mapping the interrelationships of dynamic risk factors for an individual convicted of sexual offenses, using experience sampling (ESM) based on Stable-2007 items. The longitudinal character of ESM enables both the assessment of interrelations between risk factors within a timeframe, the relationships between risk factors over time. Networks are calculated, compared to the clinical assessment of interrelationships between the risk factors.

title: Officer networks, firearm behaviors: Assessing the social transmission of weapon-use
authors: Ouellet, Marie, Hashimi, Sadaf, Vega Yon, George G
abstract: We reconstruct the networks of officers co-involved in force incidents to test whether interactions with weapon-prone peers impact firearm use.

title: Investigating the role of neighborhood youth organizations in preventing adolescent violent offending: Evidence from Chicago
authors: Zimmerman, Gregory M, Welsh, Brandon C, Posick, Chad
keywords: Neighborhood; Self-control; Violence prevention; Youth organizations; Youth violence;362\_SNA
abstract: Objectives: Neighborhood youth organizations are a salient community-level resource in the lives of children, adolescents, but empirical research on the aggregate-level relationship between neighborhood crime rates, neighborhood organizations is mixed. This study attempts to clarify, extend prior research by examining (1) whether there is a contextual effect of neighborhood youth organizations on individual violent offending,, (2) whether neighborhood youth organizations have conditioning, beneficial effects that extend beyond the youths who participate in these organizations. Methods: Data from two components of the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods were utilized in this study: the Community Survey, the Longitudinal Cohort Study. A three-level logistic item response model nested 15,242 violent crime item responses within 1,912 subjects from cohorts aged 9, 12,, 15 years; subjects were nested within 79 neighborhoods across the city of Chicago. Results: Neighborhood youth organizations did not have a direct, contextual effect on adolescent violent offending. But, the effects of neighborhood youth organizations were heterogeneous in that they reduced the effects of low self-control on violent crime. Moreover, the conditioning role of neighborhood youth organizations operated partly through child-centered informal social control.Conclusions Neighborhood organizations matter in the etiology of youthful offending, but the ways in which these organizations are relevant are nuanced. Research must continue to grapple with the various mechanisms through which neighborhood organizations operate. Illuminating these processes may hold key insights for designing, implementing neighborhood organizations to prevent adolescent violent offending.

title: Social networks in ‘neighbourhood Tokyo’
authors: Wissink, Bart, Hazelzet, Arjan
abstract: The loss of community worries academics, politicians the world over,, Japan is no exception. Over recent decades, in response to an outcry over diminishing social cohesion, Japan has seen a wave of neighbourhood projects, aiming to restore local social networks. At the same time, some argue that here urban neighbourhoods still function as organisers of social life. These contrasting views make Japanese cities interesting case studies. Unfortunately, despite a host of studies on aspects of neighbourhood involvement, there is limited general research into local social networks as a neighbourhood effect. The authors aim to fill this gap with evidence from a household survey in Tokyo. They conclude that neighbourhoods in Tokyo are relatively mixed, that, for some groups, the neighbourhood is an important source for social relations. However, the study does not show that this supports cross-group relations.

title: Alcohol's role in social reactions to sexual assault disclosures: A qualitative study of informal support dyads
authors: Ullman, Sarah E, Lorenz, Katherine, Kirkner, Anne
keywords: alcohol; dyad; qualitative; sexual assault; social reactions;362\_SNA;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Studies of informal support dyads are lacking to understand the disclosure of sexual assaults, social reactions informal supporters make to survivors. This study of 19 informal support dyads using interview data examined how three relationship types-significant others (i.e., romantic partners), family,, friends-differ in social reactions to sexual assaults in the context of drinking or alcohol problems. It was expected that alcohol's role in responses to such disclosures would differ depending on relationship type as well as role alcohol played in the assault and/or in the survivor's life or those in her social network, including the perpetrator. Results show that alcohol has mixed effects, that alcohol-related assaults as well as contexts where survivors, perpetrators, and/or their support networks have alcohol problems need further study to understand how such disclosures, social reactions occur, the impact they have on survivors, their relationships,, recovery.

title: Spatializing the social networks of gangs to explore patterns of violence
authors: Tita, George E, Radil, Steven M
keywords: AUTOCORRELATION (Statistics); CALIFORNIA; GANGS; Gang violence; LOS Angeles (Calif.); Neighborhood effects; SOCIAL influence; SOCIAL networks; SPATIAL analysis (Statistics); Spatial analysis; VIOLENCE;362\_SNA
abstract: The majority of spatial studies of crime employ an inductive approach in both the modeling, interpretation of the mechanisms of influence thought to be responsible for the patterning of crime in space, time. In such studies, the spatial weights matrix is specified without regard to the theorized mechanisms of influence between the units of analysis. Recently, a more deductive approach has begun to gain traction in which the theory of influence is used to model influence in geographic space. Using data from Los Angeles, we model the spatial distribution of gang violence by considering both the relative location of the gangs in space while simultaneously capturing their position within an enmity network of gang rivalries. We find that the spatial distribution of gang violence is more strongly associated with the socio-spatial dimensions of gang rivalries than it is with adjacency-based measures of spatial autocorrelation.

title: Incarceration, personal networks: Unpacking measures, meanings of tie strength
authors: Rengifo, Andres F, DeWitt, Samuel E
abstract: Objectives The advent of mass incarceration has reinvigorated calls for a deeper understanding of how the “quality of relationships” is shaped by imprisonment (Travis J, Western B, Redburn S (eds), The growth of incarceration in the United States: exploring causes, consequences, National Academies Press, Washington DC, 2014 ). We address this issue by describing how imprisonment relates to four dimensions of tie strength in a sample of South Bronx residents. Methods We draw on a series of survey-based multilevel models to examine how tie strength relates to characteristics of respondents, their self-reported contacts (N 1 = 585 ties, N 2 = 97 egos) regarding (a) frequency, (b) duration, (c) multiplexity,, (d) reciprocity. Results Ties of formerly-incarcerated persons are of shorter duration, exhibit less overlap relative to other respondents. However, markers of general association across the sample to currently/formerly incarcerated persons correlate with alter-ego ties that are more frequent, long-lasting,, multi-dimensional. Conclusions There is some support for the notion that direct exposure to incarceration is linked to a weakening of ties akin to a “knifing-off” process (Maruna, Roy, J Contemp Crim Justice 23(1):104–124, 2007 ). Indirect exposure to incarceration may follow an inverse pattern, strengthening the ties among those “left behind”.

title: Spatializing social networks: Using social network analysis to investigate geographies of gang rivalry, territoriality,, violence in Los Angeles
authors: Radil, Steven M, Flint, Colin, Tita, George E
journal: Annals of the Association of American Geographers. Association of American Geographers
abstract: Social network analysis is an increasingly prominent set of techniques used in a number of social sciences, but the use of the techniques of social network analysis in geography has been challenged because of a perceived lack of geographic nuance or consideration of spatialities of context in social networks. The concept of social position, the associated technique of structural equivalence in social network analysis are explored as a means to integrate two different kinds of embeddedness: relative location in geographic space, structural position in network space. Using spatialized network data, this article compares the geography of rivalry relations that connect territorially based criminal street gangs in a section of Los Angeles with a geography of the location of gang-related violence. The technique of structural equivalence uses the two different spatialities of embeddedness to identify gangs that are similarly embedded in the territorial geography, positioned in the rivalry network, which aids in understanding the overall context of gang violence. The technique demonstrated here has promise beyond this one study of gang crime as it operationalizes spatialities of embeddedness in a way that allows simultaneous systematic evaluation of the way in which social actors' positions in network relationships, spatial settings provide constraints on, possibilities for their behavior.

title: The company you keep? The spillover effects of gang membership on individual gunshot victimization in a co‐offending network: Gang membership, networks, \& victimization
authors: Papachristos, Andrew V, Braga, Anthony A, Piza, Eric, Grossman, Leigh S
keywords: street gangs; social networks; gun violence;362\_SNA;criminology
abstract: The effects of gang membership on individual social, behavior, cognitive,, health outcomes are well documented. Yet, research consistently has shown that gang membership, the boundaries of gangs are often fluid, amorphous. The current study examines how social proximity to a gang member in one's co‐offending network influences the probability of being a gunshot victim. We re‐create, analyze the social network of all individuals who were arrested, summonsed for a quality‐of‐life violation,, subjected to noncustodial police contacts in Newark, New Jersey, during a 1‐year time period (N = 10,531). A descriptive network analysis finds an extreme concentration of fatal, nonfatal gunshot injuries within a small social network: Nearly one third of all shootings in Newark occur in a network that contains less than 4 percent of the city's total population. Furthermore, a series of logistic regression models finds that being directly or indirectly linked to a gang member in one's co‐offending network has a significant effect on one's probability of being a gunshot victim. Implications of these findings for the study of gangs, gun violence,, a public health approach to violence are discussed.

title: Understanding the structure of a large heroin distribution network: A quantitative analysis of qualitative data
authors: Natarajan, Mangai
keywords: Drug trafficking; Electronic eavesdropping; Heroin; Social sciences; Entrepreneurs; New York City New York;362\_SNA
abstract: An analysis is reported of 2,408 wiretap conversations gathered in the course of prosecuting a heroin dealing organization in New York City in the 1990s. The five-step analysis, which included a social network analysis of phone contacts, revealed a large, loosely structured group of 294 individuals, most of whom had very limited contacts with others in the group. The group's active core comprised 38 individuals with extended contacts, little status differentiation, some task specialization. A smaller more tightly connected group of 22 individuals was somewhat independent of the remainder of the core, appeared to constitute a communal business. The existence was not confirmed of the large criminal conspiracy described by the prosecution that operated at all levels of trafficking, dealing, from wholesale distribution to street sales. Rather, it appeared that the 294 individuals comprised one segment of the heroin market in the city. However, the discrepancy could be due to the fact that the prosecution drew upon a wider set of information about the individuals concerned than provided by the wiretap data. The study supports recent analyses that see organized crimes, such as drug trafficking, as mostly the work of small groups of loosely linked entrepreneurs rather than large, highly structured criminal syndicates.

title: Social Network Analysis: A case study of the Islamist terrorist network
authors: Medina, Richard M
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Leadership; Terrorism; Research; Social networks; Recruitment; Afghanistan; Iraq; Bin Laden, Osama;362\_SNA;Security Journal
abstract: Social Network Analysis is a compilation of methods used to identify, analyze patterns in social network systems. This article serves as a primer on foundational social network concepts, analyses, builds a case study on the global Islamist terrorist network to illustrate the use, usefulness of these methods. The Islamist terrorist network is a system composed of multiple terrorist organizations that are socially connected, work toward the same goals. This research utilizes traditional social network, as well as small-world,, scale-free analyses to characterize this system on individual, network, systemic levels. Leaders in the network are identified based on their positions in the social network, the network structure is categorized. Finally, two vital nodes in the network are removed, this version of the network is compared with the previous version to make implications of strengths, weaknesses, vulnerabilities. The Islamist terrorist network structure is found to be a resilient, efficient structure, even with important social nodes removed. Implications for counterterrorism are given from the results of each analysis.

title: More than just friends: Online social networks, offending
authors: McCuddy, Timothy, Vogel, Matt
abstract: The study of peer-group processes has a rich history in criminology. The dramatic growth in online social network websites has fundamentally changed peer-group interaction; however, relatively little research has considered how socialization processes observed in traditional interaction translate to online interaction. Using a sample of 583 undergraduate students from a mid-southern university, this study explores the concurrency between self-reported offending, exposure to criminal behavior in social network websites. Results demonstrate a strong, positive association between individual behavior, exposure to criminal behavior in online networks, suggesting that the processes underlying traditional social interaction also characterize online interaction. These results underscore the importance of online networks for understanding the etiology of criminal behavior.

title: Social network, distance correlates of criminal associates involved in illicit drug production
authors: Malm, Aili E, Kinney, J Bryan, Pollard, Nahanni R
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Social networks; Surveillance; Hazardous substances; Data bases; Criminal investigations; Crime prevention;362\_SNA;Security Journal
abstract: This research examines the relationship between demographic, social network,, criminal history variables,, the distance between the home, locations of individuals (associates) involved in an illicit drug production network. The authors integrate principals from environmental criminology, routine activities theories, journey to crime research,, social network analysis in order to explore the geographic, social space of criminal associates. The results show that the distance between individuals in the drug production criminal network, their associates vary systematically with network characteristics (centrality measures) but not with demographics or criminal history variables.

title: Does the spatial distribution of social ties impact neighborhood, city attachment? Differentials among urban/rural contexts
authors: Luo, Xiaoshuang Iris, Hipp, John R, Butts, Carter T
keywords: Attachment; Neighborhoods; Social ties; Spatial; Urban/Rural;362\_SNA
abstract: Using social network data from the American Social Fabric Project (ASFP), this study examines how the distance to social alters may lead to different perceptions of neighborhood, city attachment among urban versus rural residents,, considers which types of relations play influential roles in shaping attachment. Overall, a key finding is that having more local neighborhood ties is positively associated with attachment at both the neighborhood level, city level, holding for any social relationship in our sample, for urban, rural environments. Notably, long distance ties are not irrelevant for attachment; rather, we see that long distance ties are associated with greater neighborhood, city attachment. Among different social relations measured, neighborhood safety ties consistently show the strongest positive relationship with neighborhood, city attachment. Surprisingly, we find that the spatial distribution of social ties appears more consequential for attachment in the rural sample than it does in the urban sample. Further, geographically dispersed ties also matter for urban versus rural settings: physically close, midrange core discussion ties are associated with weaker attachment for urban residents, whereas they do not affect rural residents’ perceptions of attachment.

title: Social network connections, increased preparation intentions for a disaster
authors: Losee, Joy E, Webster, Gregory D, McCarty, Christopher
keywords: Disaster preparedness; Social Norms; Social network analysis; Threat perception;362\_SNA;J Environ Psychol
abstract: The present research examined the role of social context—social network structure, composition—in people's intentions to prepare for a hurricane. We examined whether social network structure, composition would relate to hurricane threat responses. We randomly assigned 300 Florida resident homeowners to either a hypothetical Category 1 or 3 hurricane condition. Participants also provided information about 30 alters (other people) from their real-life social networks via an online interview, which yielded information on 130,500 total dyads (435 dyads per participant). People with more dense social networks, more emotionally close network compositions were more likely to prepare for a hurricane regardless of its severity. People with dense networks, people who perceived an evacuation norm in their network also reported being more likely to evacuate regardless of the severity. These results suggest that interventions that strengthen human connections may effectively increase people's preparedness.

title: Beyond social capital: Triad organized crime in Hong Kong, China
authors: Lo, T W
keywords: ORGANIZED crime; COMMERCIAL crimes; Social Capital; HISTORY; TRIADS (Gangs); TIANANMEN Square Incident, 1989; HONG Kong (China); CHINA; financial crime; triad society;362\_SNA;British Journal of criminology
abstract: In view of the smuggling out of democratic leaders after the Tiananmen crackdown in 1989, China's resumption of sovereignty of Hong Kong in 1997, China applied a ‘united front’ tactic to recruit Hong Kong triad societies to the Communist camp. Consequently, triad leaders were able to set foot in China, bridge up with officials, state enterprises. Against this backdrop, this paper argues that when political dynamics is involved, both the traditional structural, social network approaches are insufficient to explain triad-organized crime. Therefore, social capital perspective is proposed. Using two case studies, it was discovered that the triad leaders converted the social capital they developed in mainland China into economic capital through illegitimate means in the stock market. The paper concludes by highlighting the similarities, differences between this triad-organized crime, other forms of Chinese organized crime.

title: Agents shaping networks shaping agents: Integrating social network analysis, agent-based modeling in computational crime research
authors: Lettieri, Nicola, Altamura, Antonio, Malandrino, Delfina, Punzo, Valentina
abstract: The paper presents a recent development of an interdisciplinary research exploring innovative computational approaches to the scientific study of criminal behavior. The attention is focused on an attempt to combine social network analysis, agent-based modelling into CrimeMiner, an experimental framework that seamlessly integrates document-enhancement, visualization, network analysis techniques to support the study of criminal organizations. Our goal is both methodological, scientific. We are exploring how the synergy between ABM, SNA can support a deeper, more empirically grounded understanding of the complex dynamics taking place within criminal organizations between the individual/behavioral, social/structural level.

title: Measurement of repeat effects in Chicago’s criminal social network
authors: Kump, Paul, Alonso, David Haro, Yang, Yongyi, Candella, Joseph, Lewin, Jonathan, Wernick, Miles N
keywords: Crime analysis; Social network analysis; Violent crime; Predictive policing;362\_SNA
abstract: The “near-repeat” effect is a well-known criminological phenomenon in which the occurrence of a crime incident gives rise to a temporary elevation of crime risk within close physical proximity to an initial incident. Adopting a social network perspective, we instead define a near repeat in terms of geodesic distance within a criminal social network, rather than spatial distance. Specifically, we report a statistical analysis of repeat effects in arrest data for Chicago during the years 2003–2012. We divide the arrest data into two sets (violent crimes, other crimes) and, for each set, we compare the distributions of time intervals between repeat incidents to theoretical distributions in which repeat incidents occur only by chance. We first consider the case of the same arrestee participating in repeat incidents (“exact repeats”), then extend the analysis to evaluate repeat risks of those arrestees near one another in the social network. We observe repeat effects that diminish as a function of geodesic distance, time interval,, we estimate typical time scales for repeat crimes in Chicago.

title: Network structure, influence, selection,, adolescent delinquent behavior: Unpacking a dynamic process
authors: Jose, Rupa, Hipp, John R, Butts, Carter T, Wang, Cheng, Lakon, Cynthia M
abstract: This study uses National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health (Add Health) data to explore the co-evolution of friendship networks, delinquent behaviors. Using a stochastic actor–based (SAB) model, we simultaneously estimate the network structure, influence process,, selection process on adolescents in 12 small schools ( N = 1,284), 1 large school ( N = 976) over three time periods. Our results indicate the presence of both selection, influence processes. Moderating effects were tested for density, centrality,, popularity, with only a weak interaction effect for density, influence in the small schools ( p

title: Nested loyalties: Local networks' effects on neighbourhood, community cohesion
authors: Hipp, John R, Perrin, Andrew
abstract: Recent scholarship has suggested that cohesion at the neighbourhood level may not translate into greater cohesion for the broader community, may even have detrimental effects. Employing a sample from a recently developed 'new urbanist' community within a southern US city, the paper simultaneously explores the determinants of perceived cohesion with the local neighbourhood, with the broader community. It is found that there is indeed a positive relationship between the two in this sample. However, the determinants of the two differ: while both strong, weak informal ties in the neighbourhood increase perceived neighbourhood cohesion, only weak ties foster perceived cohesion with the broader community. No effect is found of residents' structural positions within local networks on perceived cohesion beyond the effect of strong, weak ties. The paper ends with a discussion of the implications of the findings for the broader literature viewing the effects of bridging, bonding social capital.

title: Social network characteristics, alcohol use by ethnic origin: An ego-based network study on peer similarity, social relationships,, co-existing drinking habits among young Swedes
authors: Gustafsson, Nina-Katri, Rydgren, Jens, Rostila, Mikael, Miething, Alexander
abstract: The study explores how social network determinants relate to the prevalence, frequency of alcohol use among peer dyads. It is studied how similar alcohol habits co-exist among persons (egos), their peers (alters) when socio-demographic similarity (e.g., in ethnic origin), network composition, other socio-cultural aspects were considered. Data was ego-based responses derived from a Swedish national survey with a cohort of 23-year olds. The analytical sample included 7987 ego-alter pairs, which corresponds to 2071 individuals (egos). A so-called dyadic design was applied i.e., all components of the analysis refer to ego-alter pairs (dyads). Multilevel multinomial-models were used to analyse similarity in alcohol habits in relation to ego-alter similarity in ethnic background, religious beliefs, age, sex, risk-taking, educational level, closure in network, duration,, type of relationship, as well as interactions between ethnicity, central network characteristics. Ego-alter similarity in terms of ethnic origin, age, sex was associated with ego-alter similarity in alcohol use. That both ego, alters were non-religious, were members of closed networks also had an impact on similarity in alcohol habits. It was concluded that network similarity might be an explanation for the co-existence of alcohol use among members of peer networks.

title: Targeting the most harmful co-offenders in Denmark: A social network analysis approach
authors: Frydensberg, Christian, Ariel, Barak, Bland, Matthew
abstract: Is there a ‘power few’ individuals in Denmark who, through consistent co-offending, produce the highest frequency of crimes, the most harm to society amongst all co-offenders?

title: Social network position of gang members in schools: Implications for recruitment, gang prevention
authors: Gallupe, Owen, Gravel, Jason
abstract: Schools are venues in which gang, non-gang involved youth converge. It is therefore a likely venue for gang recruitment. The extent to which this occurs depends upon the ability of gang members to connect with non-gang members. In this study, we compare the social network positions of high social status gang members who are well integrated into school networks with low status members who are not. Using network data from the Add Health study (n = 1,822), we find that not only are high status gang members strongly embedded within school networks, but that this status is driven by their ability to connect with non-gang members rather than other gang members (indicated by the high number of friendship nominations they receive from non-gang members). These gang members are potentially in optimal positions to influence others to join gangs. The implications of these results for school-based gang prevention programs are discussed.

title: Beyond police boundaries: network analysis of multi-jurisdictional crime
authors: Fox, Andrew M, Washington State Department of Children, Youth,, Families, Ogaki, Mutsumi, Pickering, Jordan C, University of California, Irvine, California State University, Fresno
abstract: In spite of the long - standing belief that crime is not restricted by arbitrary city or law enforcement jurisdictional boundaries, with a few exceptions, previous network studies relying on law enforcement data have been limited to criminal networks in one jurisdiction (Marshall et al., 2004). Using incident, arrest data from seven law enforcement agencies in King County, Washington, the current study constructed crime specific multi - jurisdictional co - offending networks for four categories of crime: 1) vi olent, 2) property, 3) sex,, 4) domestic violence. Results indicate the existence of highly socially connected criminal networks in the county, with a higher percentage of offenders committing violent, property crime in two or more jurisdictions (16. 8, 29\% respectively). Moreover, logistic regression models indicate that network position of an individual is a significant predictor of engaging in multi - jurisdictional offending. For violent crime, offenders with high betweenness centrality are likely to operate multi - jurisdictionally. These findings support the existence of a sizeable portion of offenders that cross jurisdictional boundaries to commit crime, implying the importance of sharing data among law enforcement jurisdictions.

title: Use of social network analysis to identify popular opinion leaders for a youth-led sexual violence prevention initiative
authors: Edwards, Katie M, Banyard, Victoria L, Waterman, Emily A, Hopfauf, Skyler L, Shin, Hee-Sung, Simon, Briana, Valente, Thomas W
keywords: prevention; sexual assault; social network analysis; youth;362\_SNA
abstract: In the current article, we describe an innovative sexual violence (SV) prevention initiative that used social network analysis to identify youth, adult popular opinion leaders who were subsequently trained in best practices in SV prevention (e.g., bystander intervention) at a kickoff event (i.e., camp) of the initiative. We provide information on recruitment strategies, participation rates, how those rates varied by some demographic factors, reasons for nonattendance, the initial impact of the camp,, lessons learned. Despite challenges with youth, adult engagement, this innovative approach has the potential to transform the way we approach SV prevention among youth.

title: Exploring the user base of online neighborhood networks: Determinants of online neighborhood network membership, uses
authors: De Meulenaere, Jonas, Courtois, Cédric, Walrave, Michel, Pauwels, Lieven J R, Hardyns, Wim, Ponnet, Koen
abstract: ABSTRACTThis paper aims to determine the prevalence of the use of online neighborhood networks (ONNs), explores which socio-demographic, socioeconomic status (SES), social integration,, media use determinants predict ONN membership, uses. Drawing on a stratified random sample (Ghent, Belgium), we found that over a third of the population are ONN members, that membership was mainly predicted by socio-demographic characteristics. Also, in contrast to prior research, our results show that ONNs are the local online territory of residents of lower SES, to whom these ONNs are a means of connecting with, capitalizing on neighborhood connections.

title: A social network approach to understanding community partnerships in a nontraditional destination for Latinos: Social network approach to understanding community partnerships
authors: Eiler, Brian A, Bologna, Daniele A, Vaughn, Lisa M, Jacquez, Farrah
abstract: Cincinnati, like other new migration areas, has recently experienced tremendous growth in the Latino immigrant population. Because greater health disparities exist for Latinos compared to both majority, other minority groups, it is essential to understand how migratory patterns, healthcare infrastructure are related. In this study, social network analysis (SNA), which quantitatively assesses, evaluates network formation, network relationships, was used to investigate the structure of the Greater Cincinnati Latino health network. Referral, collaboration networks were assessed for 29 individuals serving the Latino community. Results indicated the desired collaboration network was nearly twice as dense as either the physical or the mental health referral networks. The physical network was also denser than the mental health network. Similar results were found when analyzing network centralization. Taken together,

title: Responses to mass shooting events: The interplay between the media, the public
authors: Croitoru, Arie, Kien, Sara, Mahabir, Ron, Radzikowski, Jacek, Crooks, Andrew, Schuchard, Ross, Begay, Tatyanna, Lee, Ashley, Bettios, Alex, Stefanidis, Anthony
abstract: Research SummaryPublic mass shootings tend to capture the public's attention, receive substantial coverage in both traditional media, online social networks (OSNs), have become a salient topic in them. Motivated by this, the overarching objective of this paper is to advance our understanding of how the public responds to mass shooting events in such media outlets. Specifically, it aims to examine whether distinct information seeking patterns emerge over time, space,, whether associations between public mass shooting events emerge in online activities, discourse. Towards this objective, we study a sequence of five public mass shooting events that have occurred in the United States between October 2017, May 2018 across three major dimensions: the public's online information seeking activities, the media coverage,, the discourse that emerges in a prominent OSN. To capture these dimensions, respectively, data was collected, analyzed from Google Trends, LexisNexis, Wikipedia Page views,, Twitter. The results of our analysis suggest that distinct temporal patterns emerge in the public's information seeking activities across different platforms,, that associations between an event, its preceding events emerge both in the media coverage, in OSNs.Policy ImplicationStudying the evolution of discourse in OSNs provides a valuable lens to observe how society's views on public mass shooting events are formed, evolved over time, space. The ability to analyze such data allows tapping into the dynamics of reshaping, reframing public mass shooting events in the public sphere, enable it to be closely studied, modeled. A deeper understanding of this process, along with the emerging associations drawn between such events, can then provide policy, decision‐makers with opportunities to better design policies, communicate the significance of their goals, objectives to the public.

title: Exploring internal child sex trafficking networks using social network analysis
authors: Cockbain, E, Brayley, H, Laycock, G
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: This article explores the potential of social network analysis as a tool in supporting the investigation of internal child sex trafficking in the UK. In doing so, it uses only data, software,, training already available to UK police. Data from two major operations are analysed using in-built centrality metrics, designed to measure a network’s overarching structural properties, identify particularly powerful individuals. This work addresses victim networks alongside offender networks. The insights generated by SNA inform ideas for targeted interventions based on the principles of Situational Crime Prevention. These harm-reduction initiatives go beyond traditional enforcement to cover prevention, disruption, prosecution, etc. This article ends by discussing how SNA can be applied, further developed by frontline policing, strategic policing, prosecution,, policy, research.

title: Social network analysis as a tool for criminal intelligence: understanding its potential from the perspectives of intelligence analysts
authors: Burcher, Morgan, Whelan, Chad
abstract: Over the past two decades an increasing number of researchers have applied social network analysis (SNA) to various ‘dark’ networks. This research suggests that SNA is capable of revealing significant insights into the dynamics of dark networks, particularly the identification of critical nodes, which can then be targeted by law enforcement, security agencies for disruption. However, there has so far been very little research into whether, how law enforcement agencies can actually leverage SNA in an operational environment, in particular the challenges agencies face when attempting to apply various network analysis techniques to criminal networks. This paper goes some way towards addressing these issues by drawing on qualitative interviews with criminal intelligence analysts from two Australian state law enforcement agencies. The primary contribution of this paper is to call attention to the organisational characteristics of law enforcement agencies which, we argue, can influence the capacity of criminal intelligence analysts to successfully apply SNA as much as the often citied ‘characteristics of criminal networks’.

title: Social network analysis, the characteristics of criminal networks
authors: Burcher, Morgan
abstract: This chapter examines what Sparrow (1991, Soc. Networks 13(3), 251–274) describes as the ‘characteristics of criminal networks’. In his push for social network analysis (SNA) to be applied to criminal networks, Sparrow (1991, Soc. Networks 13(3), 251–274) also identified four key challenges: size, incompleteness, fuzzy boundaries, the dynamic nature of social networks. This chapter examines each of these challenges in detail as well as several other data challenges, incorrectness, inconsistencies, data transformation, from the perspective of intelligence analysts. This chapter is focused on how these challenges impact on the ability of intelligence analysts to apply SNA in operational environments.

title: Introduction: Intelligence-led policing, crime intelligence, social network analysis
authors: Burcher, Morgan
abstract: This chapter introduces the book, outlines its intention to examine both the capabilities, challenges of applying social network analysis in operational law enforcement environments. The chapter introduces different conceptual frameworks of law enforcement, examines in detail the latest iteration, intelligence-led policing, in order to understand the context in which intelligence analysts operate. Network analysis concepts are introduced, the analytical approach of social network analysis is outlined. The chapter explains the research design utilised in this study, semi-structured interviews with intelligence analysts from two Australian state law enforcement agencies,, concludes with an outline of the books structure.

title: Social network analysis, crime prevention
authors: Berlusconi, Giulia
abstract: Social network analysis (SNA) has proven its value in refining criminological concepts, theories to aid the understanding of social processes behind crime problems, to assist law enforcement agencies in enforcing crime. Social network methods, techniques have a great value for crime prevention as well. SNA can be adopted to study crime epidemics, gang-related violence to identify proper violence reduction strategies. Furthermore, the adoption of a network approach can help understand the etiology, dynamics of criminal groups, assess the implications of different disruption strategies, thus limiting network reorganization. This chapter discusses the network approach in criminology, its value for crime prevention.

title: Tactical social network analysis: Using affiliation networks to aid serial homicide investigation
authors: Bichler, Gisela, Lim, Steven, Larin, Edgar
abstract: Integrating crime pattern theory with tenets of social network theory, we argue that linking people who frequent the same places reveals intersecting behavioral patterns illustrative of case connectivity. Using the Green River serial murder investigation as a case study, we demonstrate that structural statistics may be useful in focusing investigative efforts. Significant shifts in the centrality of suspects emerge when we track the evolution of this case at 6-month increments, suggesting that the initial working case hypothesis misled investigators. Continued exploration into the utility of social network analysis (SNA) for tactical purposes will help advance applied criminology.

title: Integrating social network data into GISystems
authors: Andris, Clio
abstract: Our goal is to facilitate a guide for analyzing SNs as derived from online social media, telecommunications, surveys, etc. within geographic space by combining the mature fields of social network analysis SNA, GISystems. First, we describe why modeling socialization in geographic space is essential for understanding human behavior. We then outline best practices, techniques for embedding SN nodes, edges in GISystems by introducing terms like ‘social flow’, ‘anthrospace’,, categorizations for data, spatial aggregation types. Finally, we explore case study vignettes of SNA within GISystems from diverse regions located in Bolivia, China, Cote d’Ivoire, Singapore, the United Kingdom,, the United States, using concepts such as geolocated dyads, ego–alter relationships, node feature roles, modularity,, network transitivity.

title: Victims, offenders, victim-offender overlaps of knife crime: A social network analysis approach using police records
authors: Bailey, Laura, Harinam, Vincent, Ariel, Barak
abstract: Knife crime is a source of concern for the police in England, Wales, however little published research exists on this crime type. Who are the offenders who use knives to commit crime, when, why? Who are their victims,, is there a victim-offender overlap? What is the social network formation for people who are exposed to knife crime? Using a multidimensional approach, our aim is to answer these questions about one of England, Wales' largest jurisdictions: Thames Valley. We first provide a state-of-the-art narrative review of the knife crime literature, followed by an analysis of population-level data on central tendency, dispersion of knife crimes reported to the police (2015-2019), on offences, offenders, victims, victim-offender overlaps, gang-related assaults. Social network analysis was used to explore the formations of offender-victim networks. Our findings show that knife crime represents a small proportion of crime (1.86\%), is associated largely with violence offenses. 16-34 year-old white males are at greatest risk of being the victims, offenders or victim-offenders of knife crime, with similar relative risks between these three categories. Both knife offenders, victims are likely to have a criminal record. Knife crimes are usually not gang-related (less than 20\%),, experienced mostly between strangers, with the altercation often a non-retaliatory 'one-off event'. Even gang-related knife crimes do not follow 'tit-for-tat' relationships-except when the individuals involved have extensive offending histories, then are likely to retaliate instantaneously. We conclude that while rare, an incident of knife crime remains predicable, as a substantial ratio of offenders, victims of future knife crime can be found in police records. Prevention strategies should not be focused on gang-related criminals, but on either prolific violent offenders or repeat victims who are known to the police-and therefore more susceptible to knife crime exposure.

title: Understanding, preventing the advertisement, sale of illicit drugs to young people through social media: A multidisciplinary scoping review
authors: Fuller, Ashly, Vasek, Marie, Mariconti, Enrico, Johnson, Shane D
keywords: adolescent; harm reduction; illicit drugs; scoping review; social media;363\_publicity
abstract: ISSUES: The sale of illicit drugs online has expanded to mainstream social media apps. These platforms provide access to a wide audience, especially children, adolescents. Research is in its infancy, scattered due to the multidisciplinary aspects of the phenomena. APPROACH: We present a multidisciplinary systematic scoping review on the advertisement, sale of illicit drugs to young people. Peer-reviewed studies written in English, Spanish, French were searched for the period 2015 to 2022. We extracted data on users, drugs studied, rate of posts, terminology used, study methodology. KEY FINDINGS: A total of 56 peer-reviewed papers were included. The analysis of these highlights the variety of drugs advertised, platforms used to do so. Various methodological designs were considered. Approaches to detecting illicit content were the focus of many studies as algorithms move from detecting drug-related keywords to drug selling behaviour. We found that on average, for the studies reviewed, 13 in 100 social media posts advertise illicit drugs. However, popular platforms used by adolescents are rarely studied. IMPLICATIONS: Promotional content is increasing in sophistication to appeal to young people, shifting towards healthy, glamourous, seemingly legal depictions of drugs. Greater inter-disciplinary collaboration between computational, qualitative approaches are needed to comprehensively study the sale, advertisement of illegal drugs on social media across different platforms. This requires coordinated action from researchers, policy makers, service providers.

title: A 10-year retrospective of research in health mass media campaigns: where do we go from here?
authors: Noar, Seth M
abstract: Mass media campaigns have long been a tool for promoting public health. How effective are such campaigns in changing health-related attitudes, behaviors, however,, how has the literature in this area progressed over the past decade? The purpose of the current article is threefold. First, I discuss the importance of health mass media campaigns, raise the question of whether they are capable of effectively impacting public health. Second, I review the literature, discuss what we have learned about the effectiveness of campaigns over the past 10 years. Finally, I conclude with a discussion of possible avenues for the health campaign literature over the next 10 years. The overriding conclusion is the following: The literature is beginning to amass evidence that targeted, well-executed health mass media campaigns can have small-to-moderate effects not only on health knowledge, beliefs,, attitudes, but on behaviors as well, which can translate into major public health impact given the wide reach of mass media. Such impact can only be achieved, however, if principles of effective campaign design are carefully followed.

title: Framing fear: An analysis of the fear-based framing styles of serial homicide news articles
authors: Marceaux, Hope, Jeanis, Michelle N, Stearns, Ami E
abstract: The portrayal of offenders, crime is often viewed through the framing of news stories in traditional media. This shaping of crime to fit preconstructed perspectives can result in the spread of fear-based ideals. This study assesses use of fear-based media framing in serial homicide news articles. Taking a mixed methods approach, results suggest prolific use of fear-based framing methods, with six dominant fear-based themes identified. Fear-based frames of provoking, dehumanizing, magnifying, validating,, sensationalizing fear were found, a new frame, sanctifying fear, was identified. Variability among use of frames by offender characteristics were also assessed.

title: Nudging, manipulation
authors: Wilkinson, T M
keywords: nudge; manipulation; autonomy; social psychology; behavioural economics;363\_publicity
abstract: Behavioural economics, social psychology have shown that humans have all sorts of psychological quirks. Policy makers have become enthusiastic about taking advantage of these quirks through what Thaler, Sunstein call ‘nudges’. This article asks: when would nudging be manipulative? The article has six parts: (1) publicity, transparency, which claims that Thaler, Sunstein's own attempt to deal with evil nudges is inadequate; (2) manipulation, autonomy, where the nature, wrongness of manipulation is connected to a conception of autonomy; (3) the perversion of the decision-making process – a piecemeal approach, which sorts nudges into easy, hard cases, assesses attempts to pick out certain methods, such as temptation, as manipulative; (4) the perversion of the decision-making process – general accounts, which shows why we do not have a clear, complete, correct account of what such perversion is; (5) intentions, nudging's escape clause, where it is shown that governments that nudge as Thaler, Sunstein would wish do not manipulate because they do not have the intention to manipulate;, (6) consensual manipulation, where it is claimed that manipulation can, with the right consent, be consistent with autonomy.

title: University policies, programs for crime prevention, awareness: An examination of online reports, resources
authors: Woodward, Vanessa H, Pelletier, Dylan, Griffin, III, O Hayden, Harrington, John R
abstract: Crime on college campuses has increasingly become an area of public concern. While the Clery Act requires universities to disclose crime statistics, provide some methods of prevention, crimes on university campuses still appear to be a common problem. The purpose of this study was to examine how institutions were using the Internet to provide students with resources to promote crime prevention, awareness. Specifically, we assessed what online resources, programs institutions provided to students, then evaluated whether these resources met the general requirements of Clery. The accessibility of resources was also examined as well as how both accessibility, compliance with Clery varied across regions, student populations. The findings indicate that while most universities, colleges provide some methods of prevention or disclosure, few universities, colleges go beyond mere compliance by proactively attempting to prevent crime and/or educate their students about crime.

title: Kids, crime,, local television news
authors: Yanich, Danilo
abstract: The vast majority of crime reporting occurs on local television news, in newspapers. Although crimes are extraordinary events, they assume an ordinariness that only daily reporting can give them. The obvious question is what does the news tell us about crime. This article compares the coverage of adult crime, the coverage of what the author has termed “KidsCrime,” defined as a story in which a juvenile was either the suspect or the victim (or both). What is the nature of that coverage? How consistent is it with official statistics? Are there differences between adult crime, KidsCrime coverage regarding offenses, victimization, production techniques,, other attributes? This examination of the crime coverage revealed (a) significant differences between KidsCrime, adult crime coverage, (b) a portrait of crime that was consistent, inconsistent with official statistics,, (c) a presentation approach that discouraged critical viewing.

title: Fear of crime, mass media crime reports testing similarity hypotheses
authors: Willem Winkel, Frans
abstract: One function of the mass media is to provide the public with news on the discovery, tracking, prosecution of criminal offenses. In this paper, we discuss the effects such reporting may have on their audiences’ fear of crime. We begin with a brief survey of theories dealing with the relation between (ear, crime reports. It is of interest to observe that in the literature one finds references to a positive relationship (increase of fear), to a negative relationship (reduction of fear), to claims that no relationship exists at all (zero effects). Our theoretical survey leads us to formulate five hypotheses, each of which will be tested experimentally. In closing we offer a summary of the more important test results, of the conclusions derived from them.

title: Community newspaper use promotes social cohesion
authors: Yamamoto, Masahiro
abstract: The analysis of survey data from the northwestern United States shows that newspaper reading correlates with respondents' sense of social cohesion, indicating that community newspapers are important to community engagement.

title: Primary definitions of crime, moral panic: A content analysis of experts' quotes in feature newspaper articles on crime
authors: Welch, Michael, Fenwick, Melissa, Roberts, Meredith
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: CRIME; NEWSPAPERS; IDEOLOGY; LAW enforcement; POLICE; POLITICIANS; INTELLECTUALS; CRIME, CRIMINAL JUSTICE, AND LAW ENFORCEMENT;363\_publicity;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Research on crime news continues to generate scholarly interest, particularly in the realm of social constructionism. From this perspective, researchers have documented the process by which crime is shaped into news—especially the pivotal role played by law enforcement officials. In this study, the authors contribute to this area of inquiry by administering a content analysis of 105 feature articles on crime published in four national newspapers between 1992, 1995. In addition to exploring the topics of crime, they systematically examined the nature of quotes offered by two groups of experts, namely, state managers (e.g., police, politicians), intellectuals (e.g., professors). Their findings support previous research demonstrating the media's heavy reliance on law enforcement officials in formulating primary definitions of crime. The significance of primary definitions of crime within the context of the dominant ideology, moral panic is discussed at length.

title: Things like that don't happen here: Crime, place, real estate in the news
authors: Wallace, Aurora
abstract: This article investigates the construction of place in crime reporting through bystander quotes in recent crime stories in newspapers from the north-eastern US. These quotes are part of a larger pattern of reporting that highlights environmental features of serenity, peacefulness as antidotes to crime. Against claims that crime in the media is always exaggerated, this research demonstrates how the impact of crime is moderated by declaring it unlikely, by discursively shifting it to other geographic locations. It is argued that crime reporting shares a structural similarity with fictional representations of place found in film,, that this pattern of crime reporting helps to reinforce a suburban consumption ethos.

title: Attitudes to domestic violence: School students’ responses to a television drama
authors: Tulloch, M, Tulloch, J
keywords: comprehension of \& attitudes toward TV portrayal of domestic violence, 4th \& 7th \& 10th graders, Australia, implications for educational programs; Comprehension; Domestic Violence; Student Attitudes; Television Viewing; Educational Programs; Elementary School Students; High School Students; Junior High School Students;363\_publicity;PDFなし
abstract: SynopsisThis study sought to examine the responses of 216 primary, high school students to a television narrative excerpt portraying domestic violence. Comprehension was tested by unprompted summaries, structured questions. Semantic differentials assessed students’ evaluation of the program, the main protagonists. Students were also asked to choose between alternative behaviours open to aggressor, victim, third party in the violence scenario. The program was generally well understood, especially by high school students. A strong rejection of domestic violence in all age, gender, social class groupings was revealed in response to behavioural alternatives, character evaluations. While involvement with the program was greater for girls, working class students, the generally positive, serious responses indicated the Value of television in exploring attitudes, its potential in education programs aimed at increasing awareness of domestic Violence.

title: Assessing the risk of crime victimization: The integration of personal victimization experience, socially transmitted information
authors: Tyler, Tom R
keywords: VICTIMS of crimes; CRIME; CRIMINOLOGY; FEAR of crime; VICTIMS; SOCIOLOGY; CRIME, CRIMINAL JUSTICE, AND LAW ENFORCEMENT;363\_publicity
