abstract: To adapt effectively to environmental hazards such as the risk of crime victimization, individuals should not rely solely upon their direct personal experience. Instead, they should use information about the environment gained from others' experiences in estimating risks, in determining the appropriate type, number of behaviors to undertake in order to avoid victimization. Such information can come either through social networks (i.e., through talking to friends, family, or neighbors) or via the mass media (newspapers, television, radio, magazines,, pamphlets). Although experiences conveyed by family, friends,, neighbors have been found to influence risk estimates, prevention behaviors, mass media experiences have not been found to influence such judgments or behaviors. This lack of mass media influence has been found both in studies of naturally occurring crime‐risk judgments, in evaluations of media campaigns, such as the recent national campaign urging citizens to “take a bite out of crime.” This paper reviews the literature concerning the influence of indirect experiences upon fear of crime, with a focus on trying to understand why citizens fail to use the mass media as a source of information about personal crime risk.

title: The mass media, judgments of risk: Distinguishing impact on personal, societal level judgments
authors: Tyler, Tom R, Cook, Fay L
keywords: Mass Media; Probability Judgment; Public Opinion; Threat;363\_publicity
abstract: Recent research findings about whether mass media reports influence risk-related judgments have not been consistent. One reconciliation of the differing findings is the impersonal impact hypothesis, which suggests that media impact occurs with societal level judgments about general problem importance or frequency but not with judgments about personal risks. Three studies, with 465 undergraduates were conducted to test this hypothesis. Results support the impersonal impact hypothesis by suggesting that personal, societal level judgments are distinct, that media reports exert their primary influence on societal rather than personal judgments. Although media reports influenced judgments about societal risks but not about risks to one's self under the conditions examined in the present research, personal judgments may be affected under other conditions. Conditions under which media reports may have differential or similar effects on personal, societal-level judgments are considered in relation to the base rates of an event occurring, the strength of the media case that a problem exists,, the individual's identification with the problem. (55 ref)

title: Impacts from repeated mass media campaigns to promote sun protection in Australia
authors: Smith, Ben J, Ferguson, Claire, McKenzie, Jeanie, Bauman, Adrian, Vita, Philip
abstract: Campaigns using television, radio, print media were conducted over three summers in New South Wales, Australia, aiming to increase the use of sun protection measures among children under 12 years. The evaluation entailed cross-sectional telephone surveys before, after each of the first two campaigns, following the third campaign. The study group were parents of children under 12 years. Random digit dialling yielded samples of approximately 800 for each survey. Measures addressed campaign recall, sun protection knowledge, attitudes, behaviours. The surveys revealed significant levels of campaign recall. Knowledge about the protective benefits of sunscreens, hats, protective clothing was high at baseline, showed little improvement over the campaigns. Knowledge levels about the benefits of shade cover, of the relative risks of skin cancer from childhood sun exposure were lower,, also did not show improvement. Just one of the four attitude factors showed significant improvement,, this concerned the importance that parents placed on the issue of child sun protection. After the final campaign there were increases compared with baseline in childrens' use of sunscreen, protective clothing, shade, but it was notable that between campaigns levels of these behaviours were similar to or below those at baseline. There was no evidence of a campaign-related increase in hat wearing by children. All sun protection measures were used less often by adults than children, but these showed similar trends. Mass media campaigns may contribute to short-term increases in some sun protection behaviours; however, as their impact is not sustained they should be repeated, supplemented by educational, policy, environmental strategies.

title: Crime victimization, exposure to crime news, social trust among adolescents
authors: Salmi, Venla, Smolej, Mirka, Kivivuori, Janne
keywords: CRIME; VICTIMS of crimes; CULTIVATION theory (Communication); TEENAGERS; SOCIAL sciences; Social Capital; CRIMINOLOGISTS; SOCIAL interaction; SOCIAL support; FINLAND; adolescence; crime news; cultivation theory; trust; victimization;363\_publicity
abstract: Interpersonal trust has recently emerged at the centre of research in social science as an important component of social capital. Earlier, it has been theorized that exposure to media cultivates a suspicious, distrusting ‘mean–world’ outlook on life (cultivation theory). In this article, we aim to bind these separate but obviously interconnected theoretical discussions in a combined empirical analysis, by exploring several potential correlates of social trust. As criminologists, our main interest lies in the possible association between victimization, fear of crime, use of crime news media, trust. We categorize victimization experiences as either persistent or occasional ones. In addition, we add a set of social, structural factors to our analysis. Our cross–sectional survey data consists of a nationally representative sample of 15–16 year–old Finnish adolescents (N = 5142). The results of the multivariate analyses indicate that both victimization, fear of crime are related to lower levels of interpersonal trust. As expected, there is a more robust association between persistent victimization, the level of trust than is the case with occasional victimization. Viewing regularly television crime reality programmes is also robustly related to lower levels of trust, a finding that supports the cultivation theory. Of social interaction variables, social support, supervision by parents, teachers are positively related to trust. Contrary to this, participation in civic life (such as religious, various secular associations) is not related to social trust among Finnish adolescents. This, other results are here discussed applying social capital theory, cultivation theory of media effects.

abstract: It is argued that the efficacy of such programs is dependent upon the successful application of several empirically based communication principles. In addition, the attempt is made to analyze several general problems concerning the meaning, measurement of program success. Issues relating to both the operation, the evaluation of crime prevention through mass media programs are discussed in terms of their practical implications for public policy. (Author abstract)

title: Media constructions of crime
authors: Sacco, Vincent F
journal: The annals of the American Academy of Political, Social Science
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; VICTIMS; CRIME \& the press; CRIME in mass media; UNITED States; Media coverage; Public attitudes toward crime;363\_publicity;ANNALS of the American Academy of Political, Social Science
abstract: The news media are a vital part of the process by which individuals' private troubles with crime—as victims or offenders—are transformed into public issues. The social construction of crime problems may be understood as reflecting the types of relationships that link news agencies to their sources,, the organizational constraints that structure the news-gathering process. The ways in which the news media collect, sort,, contextualize crime reports help to shape public consciousness regarding which conditions need to be seen as urgent problems, what kinds of problems they represent, and, by implication, how they should be resolved. While much attention has been focused on the ways in which media attention to crime influences the fear of crime, it is likely that the most significant effects of media reporting are broadly ideological rather than narrowly attitudinal. By restricting the terms of discussion, the news media facilitate the marginalization of competing views regarding crime, its solution.

title: THE EFFECTS OF MASS MEDIA ON PERCEPTIONS OF CRIME: A reanalysis of the sues
authors: Sacco, Vincent F
keywords: MASS media \& crime; PERCEPTION; TELEVISION; NEWSPAPERS; MASS markets;363\_publicity;PDFなし;99\_文献なし
abstract: The argument that mass media exert a direct causal influence upon perceptions of crime is critically examined. Employing data collected in the province of Alberta in 1979, an attempt is made to detect relationships involving respondents' patterns of newspaper, television consumption, their views on crime. Consistent with earlier research findings, the analysis of the Alberta data reveals no evidence of a significant media effect. Some of the issues that must be considered if such findings are lobe reconciled with the commonsense expectation of a direct effect of media consumption upon perceptions of crime are discussed. title: Crime prevention, public opinion
authors: Roberts, Julian V, Grossman, Michelle G
journal: Canadian journal of criminology. Revue canadienne de criminologie
keywords: CRIME prevention -- Citizen participation; NEIGHBORHOOD watch programs; MASS media; VIOLENT crimes; SOCIAL groups; CRIMINOLOGY; RESEARCH; UNITED States; CANADA; CRIME, CRIMINAL JUSTICE, AND LAW ENFORCEMENT;363\_publicity
abstract: Public views of crime prevention are explored through a review of recent survey research in Canada, the United States, elsewhere. First, however the role of the media is reviewed. Content analyses of the news media indicate that crime prevention stories are rare, relative to stories describing individual crimes (particularly crimes of violence). Notwithstanding this indifference on the part of the news media, the most recent surveys reveal widespread public awareness of the major crime prevention programs in Canada (such as Neighbourhood Watch). As well, attitudes towards crime prevention initiatives appear to be positive. A second paradox also emerges: research shows that this favourable reaction on the part of the public is not always matched by active participation in crime prevention programs. The article concludes by advocating further research into the reasons for low active participation rates,, through this the ways in which participation can be increased. title: News media influences on public views of sentencing
authors: Roberts, Julian V, Doob, Anthony N
abstract: Opinion polls in Canada, the United States, Great Britain, Australia,, elsewhere suggest that most members of the public would like their criminal courts to be harsher. Does media coverage of criminal sentencing contribute to a preference for harsher sentencing? Most people derive their information about sentencing from the news media,, content analyses of news stories in Canada, the United States demonstrate that crimes of violence, sentences of imprisonment are overrepresented. Moreover, the news media provide little systematic information about the sentencing process or its underlying principles. This article reports the results of three studies examining the effects of media coverage on public opinion about sentencing. Subjects who read actual newspaper stories about sentencing that appeared in Canadian newspapers rated most reported sentences as too lenient. However, the specific account they read influenced their leniency judgments. Furthermore, in one experiment, participants assigned to read a newspaper account of a sentencing decision supported harsher sentences than participants who read a summary of actual court documents from the sentencing hearing.

title: Prevention of child sexual abuse: evaluation of a community media campaign
authors: Rheingold, Alyssa A, Campbell, Carole, Self-Brown, Shannon, de Arellano, Michael, Resnick, Heidi, Kilpatrick, Dean
abstract: Given that mass media techniques have been an effective tool within the public health field for affecting behavioral change, these strategies may prove successful for the primary prevention of child sexual abuse (CSA). This study was an independent evaluation of a CSA media campaign. Two hundred parents were recruited from eight sites across the United States. Results indicated that the combined mass media campaign affected knowledge about CSA at the time of intervention compared to no intervention. No significant differences were found in regards to CSA attitudes. A significant positive impact on primary prevention response behaviors assessed using hypothetical vignettes was found; however, no significant findings were noted for several other behavioral responses. Knowledge, behavioral gains were not maintained at the one-month follow-up. Small sample size at follow-up may have affected findings. Results of this study imply that media campaigns alone may not significantly affect primary prevention of CSA.

title: Designing, implementing,, evaluating a media campaign illustrating the bystander role
authors: Potter, Sharyn J, Stapleton, Jane G, Moynihan, Mary M
journal: Journal of prevention \& intervention in the community
abstract: Recent research found that training men, women to understand the role of bystanders in situations where violence against women (VAW) is occurring may reduce the incidence of VAW (Moynihan \& Banyard, 2004). Therefore a public awareness campaign to increase understanding of the prosocial role of bystanders in reducing VAW was developed, implemented. The current article discusses the role of media campaigns in addressing public health issues, describes the initial development, implementation,, evaluation of a media campaign focused on the bystander role in reducing the incidence of VAW. Conclusions, future directions of this exploratory project are discussed.

title: Using a multimedia social marketing campaign to increase active bystanders on the college campus
authors: Potter, Sharyn J
journal: Journal of American college health: J of ACH
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the campus-wide administration of the Know Your Power bystander-oriented social marketing campaign. PARTICIPANTS: Undergraduate students at a public college were invited to participate in a public awareness survey before, after the 6-week campaign administration in February, March 2009. METHODS: Pretest, posttests were administered (N = 353) to examine if exposure to the campaign changed students' stage of scale scores. RESULTS: Exposure to the social marketing campaign increased participants' awareness of their role in reducing sexual, relationship violence, stalking, increased their expressed willingness to get involved in reducing the incidence these types of violence,, resulted in participants being more likely to report having taken action to reduce these types of violence. CONCLUSIONS: As college students explore their role as community members, it is an opportunity for college educators to design, administer prevention messages highlighting behavioral norms to be explored, adopted.

title: The public perception of crime prevalence, newspaper readership, ‘mean world’ attitudes
authors: O'Connell, Michael, Whelan, Anthony
keywords: Crime; News Media; Risk Perception; Social Perception; Victimization; Age Differences; Demographic Characteristics; Human Sex Differences;363\_publicity
abstract: Surveying an Irish sample, the authors asked respondents (N=623) to give their views on the seriousness of, appropriate penalties for 10 offence scenarios. They also assessed the respondents' risk perception of crime by asking for estimates of the prevalence of the same 10 offence scenarios compared to five years previously. Experience of crime victimization, socio‐demographic data were also gathered. Beliefs about crime prevalence were found to be independent of official crime rates, personal experience of victimization, some socio‐demographic categories. Sex, age, newspaper readership were found to be the strongest predictors of crime prevalence estimates. Additional support for the role of the media was suggested by the clustering of a number of ‘mean world’ attitudes towards crime.

title: Communication, health beliefs: Mass, interpersonal influences on perceptions of risk to self, others
authors: Morton, Thomas A, Duck, Julie M
keywords: Health Attitudes; Interpersonal Communication; Mass Media; Risk Perception; Social Influences; Health Promotion; Interpersonal Influences; Judgment; Human; Male; Female; Australia; mass media coverage; health beliefs; judgements; social influence; Australian college students;363\_publicity
abstract: This study investigated the impact of media coverage of a health issue (skin cancer) on judgements of risk to self, others, the role of related communication processes. Consistent with predictions derived from the impersonal impact hypothesis, the effects of mass communication were more evident in perceptions of risk to others rather than in perceptions of personal risk. Perceptions of personal risk were more strongly correlated with interpersonal communication. However, as suggested by media system dependency theory, the relationship between mass communication, beliefs was complex. The impact of mass communication on both personal, impersonal perceptions was found to be moderated by self-reported dependence on mass mediated information. The effect of this two-way interaction on perceptions of personal risk was partially mediated through interpersonal communication. Results point to the interdependence of mass, interpersonal communication as sources of social influence, the role of media dependency in shaping media impact.

title: What works in public awareness campaigns? A scoping review
authors: McGuire, James, Evans, Emily, Kane, Eddie
abstract: How effective are public awareness campaigns focused on criminal justice? The objective of the review was to locate, briefly summarize the range of empirical studies relevant to this question but not to extract detailed information, identify effective methods, but simply to outline the range of work in the field. Seven electronic databases were searched, the contents tables of four journals inspected, identifying a set of 551 potentially relevant records. After screening, 52 items were retained for fuller analysis. The retained studies, reports were divided into three categories: (1) general crime prevention materials, research studies, (2) a smaller group of reports describing responses to specific crime prevention initiatives or exercises, (3) research reports focused on prevention of specific types of offences. There is evidence that public awareness campaigns work better when they are aligned with changes in the law, accompanied by effective enforcement. Campaigns are more likely to be effective when a range of methods is used to ensure publicity. The relationship between policing, criminal justice awareness campaigns has been compared with analogous work in the field of public health,, the relation between the two is briefly discussed.

title: News about murder in an African American newspaper: Effects of relative frequency, race, gender typifications
authors: Lundman, Richard J, Douglass, Olivia M, Hanson, Jason M
keywords: AFRICAN Americans; HOMICIDE; MURDER; RACE relations; GENDER stereotypes; AFRICAN American newspapers;363\_publicity
abstract: Previous scholarly research on selection bias in news about murder indicates that race, gender stereotypes and, to a much lesser extent, the relative frequency of particular murders explain why some homicides are made into news, others are not. However, previous research has directed nearly exclusive attention to white newspapers. The present research remedies this omission by directing attention to the factors that shape selection bias in news about murder in a big-city African American newspaper. The results indicate that the relative frequency dimension of newsworthiness is a weak, inconsistent explanation of selection bias in news about murder in the black newspaper examined. Race, however, has profoundly different effects in white, African American newspapers. Whereas white newspapers use long-standing race stereotypes to filter news about murder, the data from the African American newspaper signal a firm rejection of the black image in the white mind (Ent- man, Rojecki 2000). Newspaper images of women, men are another matter. In both black, white newspapers, gender stereotypes uniformly filter news about murder, fundamentally distort gender effects. The implications of these findings are discussed including the clear need, ample scholarly room for replicative analyses of news about murder in other African American newspapers, with a keen eye on both ``raced ways of seeing'' (Hunt 1999, pp. 181-215), gendered ways of seeing. title: Media Cooperation With Police: The Case of Crime Stoppers
authors: Lavrakas, Paul J, Rosenbaum, Dennis P, Lurigio, Arthur J
keywords: Media support; Private sector-government cooperatn;363\_publicity;PDFなし
abstract: Crime Stoppers offers monetary incentives (typically ranging from $100 to $1,000), the protection of anonymity to persons who provide information that leads to the arrest, indictment, or conviction of suspected offenders. Since its beginning in Albuquerque, N.M., in 1976, Crime Stoppers has spread across the United States with more than 70 programs operational in 1988. The study reported in this chapter used two mail surveys to determine the extent of media cooperation with the police in the Crime Stoppers program. The first survey, conducted in 1984, yielded 203 questionnaires completed by the police coordinators of local Crime Stoppers programs. The second survey produced 237 questionnaires completed by media executives. The police coordinators rated radio stations, weekly newspapers,, cable companies as more cooperative than UHF, VHF television stations, daily newspapers; however, all types of media were rated as 'cooperative.' title: CRIME COMMUNICATION AT INFORMATION MEETINGS

abstract: The present study examined whether media coverage was likely to have an effect on burglars' emotional, cognitive,, behavioral responses to the offense. Implications for police use of the media as well as limitations of the study are discussed.

title: Finding one’s way on the roads to social change: The metamodel of the impact of FOPH communication campaigns
authors: Kammer, Adrian, Niessen, Sebastian, Schmid, Lukas, Schwendener, Norina
abstract: Many theories, models attempt to explain the mechanisms underlying human behavior. In order to maintain an overview of the many aspects involved in communication campaigns, social marketing,, behavior change, the Swiss Federal Office for Public Health has created a metamodel of the impact of its campaigns. This metamodel does not claim to contribute any new findings to behavioral research. Its purpose is primarily to summarize the current state of research in the field in a comprehensive, comprehensible way, with reference to a range of relevant communications, social marketing,, behavior change theories. Dimensions addressed include strategy, processes,, impact, with the final dimension demonstrating the possible ranges of impact from individual to societal, from information to behavior. Social marketers, campaign planners may find this model useful as a planning, evaluation tool for campaigns, programs, or interventions that seek to increase awareness or change behavior. Its focus lies on communication campaigns, while also indicating the limits of campaign efficacy. It makes it clear that campaigns are most effective at the early stages of the behavioral change process, such as capturing attention, while other interventions are more effective at later stages.

title: Mass media, fear of crime
authors: Heath, Linda, Gilbert, Kevin
abstract: Charges that the mass media create unwarranted levels of fear of crime are almost as old as the media themselves. Researchers entered the fray in large numbers in the 1960s, documenting the effects of television, newspapers,, movies on perceptions of crime, fear of criminal victimization. Recent developments in mass media, such as the rise in popularity of crime reenactment television programs, the access to more violence via cable, VCR,, satellite dish,, the interactive nature of electronic games, raise even greater concern about the fear-generating potential of these media. In addition, the real-world increase in the occurrence of stranger crimes, mass attacks could make the media image even more potent, because of the prevalence of random or random-appearing crimes reported by the media. This article provides an overview of the research on the mass media, its effects on perceptions of crime danger, personal fear of crime,, reactions to crime risk. In addition, we examine the modifiers of the relationships between media, fear.

title: Preventing Alcohol-Related Problems in the US Through Policy: Media Campaigns, Regulatory Approaches, Environmental Interventions

title: Security at the 2012 London Olympics: Spectators’ perceptions of London as a safe city

abstract: The build-up to the 2012 Olympics was fraught with problems, attracted considerable negative publicity in both the British, international press. One key component of this involved security at the Games, with the inability of G4S, the private security firm awarded the contract for Games security, to fulfil its obligations, resulting in a major shift in security provision in the weeks leading up to the Games. Our research on spectators’ perceptions of safety, security in London during the Games attains particular significance in this context. However, while previous studies have suggested a heightened crime, disorder problem associated with tourism, at mass public events, the findings here demonstrate that visitors to the Olympics saw London,, the Olympic venues, as safe, in terms of both crime, terrorism, with positive consequences for their future plans to revisit London. title: Canadian news coverage of intimate partner homicide: Analyzing changes over time
authors: Fairbairn, Jordan, Dawson, Myrna
abstract: News coverage of intimate partner homicide can reveal, reproduce societal assumptions, beliefs that may influence social, political responses to violence against women. This study analyzes all male-perpetrated intimate partner homicides reported in three daily newspapers in Toronto, Canada within two separate time periods (1975-1979, 1998-2002) to explore if, how this coverage has changed over time. Results suggest that, in more recent years, news coverage is more likely to report a previous history of intimate partner violence, less likely to employ news that excuses or justifies the perpetrator’s actions. However, coverage continues to employ victim-blaming news frames, to portray intimate partner homicide as an individual event, in part, through the absence of the voices of violence against women organizations, researchers,, service providers as legitimate authorities in both time periods. Thus, news coverage fails to encourage social, political responses to violence against women in intimate relationships that emphasize the need for social structural changes focusing on gender equality.

abstract: The experience of transportation—being absorbed in a narrative—and its relationship to persuasion were considered in two studies exploring responses to health-promoting mass media messages. title: Comparing American, Canadian local television crime stories: A content analysis

abstract: Crime is a staple of local television newscasts. However, there is debate regarding the differences between Canadian, U.S. crime coverage on local television broadcasts. abstract: Two experiments examined the extent to which U.S. viewers’ perceptions that Blacks face structural limitations to success, support for the death penalty,, culpability judgments could be influenced by exposure to racialized crime news. title: Television viewing, fear of victimization: Is the relationship causal?
authors: Doob, Anthony N, Macdonald, Glenn E

abstract: Previous findings have suggested that people who watch a lot of television are more likely to fear their environment than are those who report being less frequent viewers of television. From this simple correlation, previous authors have suggested that television causes people to overestimate the amount of danger that exists in their own neighborhoods. The present study attempted to replicate this finding, to determine if the apparent effect was due to a previously uncontrolled factor: the actual incidence of crime in the neighborhood. Respondents to a door-to-door survey indicated their media usage, estimated the likelihood of their being a victim of violence. Neighborhoods were chosen so as to include a high-, a low-crime area in downtown Toronto, a high-, a low-crime area in Toronto’s suburbs. However, the average within-area correlation was insignificant, suggesting that when acicual incidence of crime is controlled for, there is no overall relationship between television viewing, fear of being a victim of crime. A multiple regression analysis, a canonical correlation analysis confirmed these findings. This chapter focuses on the relationship between television viewing, fear of criminal victimization. It attempts to replicate the finding, to determine if the apparent effect was due to a previously uncontrolled factor: the actual incidence of crime in the neighborhood. A variety of social problems have been attributed to television viewing. One can assume that there exists in these cities some variability in the dangerousness of different neighborhoods. title: Bias in the newspaper reporting of grime news

abstract: Members of the general public pay for crime in two different ways. As victims they suffer the direct consequences,, as tax-payers, rate payers they finance the police, courts, prisons to control it. For both these reasons it seems that the general public has a right to know on what,, how successfully, their money is spent. However, the responsibility for informing them rests almost exclusively with a competitive, commercial press. Indeed, it has been noted by Hauge (1965) that `` the near monopoly of the daily press as a source of crime news therefore presumably makes it an important influence on public opinion on the subject of crime '' (p. 148). Accordingly, it is important to monitor regularly the newspaper coverage of crime to assess whether or not the overall picture of crime which news papers collectively produce is informative, balanced. Previous research in this field has frequently discovered that the news paper coverage of crime news is, in some way, biased. Hauge (1965), Roshier (1973), Croll (1974), Beardsworth (1975) have discovered an over-emphasis on crimes of violence,, Sherizen (1978) discovered an additional over-emphasis on crimes involving indecency. Yet whilst there has been an upsurge in analytic interest in the media in the last decade (Glasgow University Media Group, 1976, 1980; Murphy, 1976; Chibnall, 1977; Brunsdon, Morely, 1978; Hall et al., 1978; Hurd, 1979; Jones, 1980), systematic analysis of the newspaper coverage of crime has been relatively neglected. title: The cultivation of fear of sexual violence in women: Processes, moderators of the relationship between television, fear

abstract: AbstractThrough this study, we shed new light on a key line of inquiry for criminologists: the way the media influence the public's understanding of crime, justice. abstract: Elder abuse, including emotional, physical, sexual, financial,, neglectful mistreatment is widespread in the United States, with as much as 11\% of community-residing older adults experiencing some form of abuse in the past year. title: Why less is more: exploring affect‐based value neglect
authors: Wilson, R S, Arvai, J L
abstract: Previous research indicates that the affective nature of the problem context can override gains in the evaluability of risk attributes brought on by side‐by‐side comparisons of two problems. Specifically, in a joint evaluation, an affect‐rich problem will be given greater management preference than an affect‐neutral problem even when the risk is significantly greater for the neutral problem. A series of new experiments were conducted to explore the relevance of this concept (i.e., affect‐based value neglect) for the evaluation of two affect‐rich problems. Consistent with previous research, the results indicated no preference for either problem evaluated in isolation, given that both the affective impression, the level of risk were hard to evaluate. Again, consistent with previous research, there was no preference for either problem in a joint evaluation when the difference in risk between the two problems was small (one problem posing 1.5‐times greater risk than the other). However, when the risk difference was large – 3‐times greater – preference was given to managing the higher‐risk problem. Additional evidence indicates that joint evaluations may increase the significance of probabilities as a form of risk communication,, that increased availability of one problem may dominate both initial affective impressions, the presentation of risk attributes.

title: ‘Nobody is sure of tomorrow’: using the Health Belief Model to explain safety behaviours among Boko Haram victims in Kano, Nigeria

abstract: The further advancement of privacy models depends upon clarifying two issues: the relationship between privacy, territoriality, the degree to which different types of privacy have distinct behavioral, cognitive correlates. keywords: COVID-19; anxiety; coping strategies; coronavirus pandemic; depression; perceived support;370\_Isolation
abstract: The coronavirus pandemic represents a severe global crisis, affecting physical,, psychological health. Lockdown rules imposed to counteract the rapid growth of COVID-19, mainly social restrictions, have represented a risk factor for developing depressive, anxious symptoms. The research aims are to explore the effect of coping strategies, perceived social support on depressive, anxious symptomatology during the COVID-19 pandemic. Ninety-six healthy people (46 males, mean age = 39.3; SD = 16.6) completed through on-line platform: Socio-demographic questionnaire, Coping Inventory for Stressful Situations (CISS), Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support (MSPSS), Symptom Checklist-90-Revised (SCL-90-R), 3 weeks after the imposition of lockdown restrictions. SCL-90-R Depression scores showed significant positive correlation with CISS Emotion (r = 0.85; p = 0.001), Avoidant (r = 0.34; p = 0.018), a significant negative correlation with MSPSS Family support (r = -0.43; p = 0.003). SCL-90-R Anxiety scores showed a significant positive correlation with CISS Emotion (r = 0.72; p = 0.001), Avoidant (r = 0.35; p = 0.016). No significant correlations between both CISS Emotion, Avoidant scales with social support emerged. Two Multiple Linear Regression analysis were performed using, respectively, SCL-90-R Depression, Anxiety scores as dependent variables,, the CISS, MSPSS scales, age,, gender as predictors. The first regression model (R 2 = 0.78; adjusted R 2 = 0.75) revealed CISS Emotion (β = 0.83; p = 0.001), MSPSS Family support (β = -0.24; p = 0.004) had a predictive effect on SCL-90-R Depression scores. The second regression model (R 2 = 0.52; adjusted R 2 = 0.472) revealed that only CISS Emotion (β = 0.71; p = 0.001) predicted the SCL-90-R Anxiety scores. In conclusion, during the COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns, coping focus on emotions seemed to increase anxious, depressive symptoms, probably due to the uncontrollable nature of the stressful event, the high emotional response. Family support which reduces the sense of loneliness had an exclusive role in mitigating depressive symptoms. These results highlight the importance of promoting psychological strategies to improve emotional regulation skills, reducing isolation from family, to prevent mood symptomatology in healthy citizens during large-scale health crises.

title: Social disorganization, drug market activity,, neighborhood violent crime
authors: Martínez, Ramiro, Rosenfeld, Richard, Mares, Dennis
abstract: Although illicit drug activity occurs within local communities, past quantitative research on drug markets, violent crime in the United States has been conducted mainly at the city level. The authors use neighborhood-level data from the city of Miami to test hypotheses regarding the effect of drug activity, traditional indicators of social disorganization on rates of aggravated assault, robbery. The results show that drug activity has robust effects on violent crime that are independent of other disorganization indicators. The authors also find that drug activity is concentrated in neighborhoods with low rates of immigration, less linguistic isolation, ethnic heterogeneity,, where nondrug accidental deaths are prevalent. The authors find no independent effect of neighborhood racial composition on drug activity or violent crime. The results suggest that future neighborhood-level research on social disorganization, violent crime should devote explicit attention to the disorganizing, violence-producing effects of illicit drug activity.

title: The need for comprehensive crime prevention planning: The case of motor vehicle theft
authors: Linden, Rick, Chaturvedi, Renuka
journal: Canadian journal of criminology, criminal justice
abstract: Most crime prevention programs are poorly planned, implemented,, therefore do little or nothing to prevent crime. Programs are typically fragmented, with little communication among the groups who share a common interest in reducing crime. Most programs operate in isolation rather than being linked to a broader community-wide prevention strategy. Communities that have been able to make meaningful reductions in crime rates have done so by taking a comprehensive approach to crime prevention in which they implement an integrated series of programs that coordinate the efforts of a broad range of partners, participants. To be comprehensive, effective, crime prevention programs must analyse the crime problems in their community context, involve a broad group of people, organizations, consider a diverse range of prevention strategies, carefully implement the programs most suited to a particular community,, assess the results. This article illustrates how this process can be applied to the prevention of motor vehicle theft.

title: Contextualizing community crime control: Race, geography,, configurations of control in four communities: Contextualizing community crime control
authors: Leverentz, Andrea, Williams, Monica
keywords: community; informal social control; new parochialism; systemic theories;370\_Isolation;criminology
abstract: Criminology, urban sociology have long‐standing interests in how neighborhoods, communities respond to, control crime. We build on the literature on social disorganization, collective efficacy,, new parochialism to develop a framework that explains how, why communities respond differently to crime. We draw on more than 2 years of comparative ethnographic data, 56 resident, stakeholder interviews on responses to crime in four communities in two states. We find that the intersections of racial composition, geography,, crime narratives in each place contributed to distinct community responses to crime. By analyzing these dynamics across the four sites, we propose three types of public–parochial partnerships that communities use to respond to crime: public alliances that rely primarily on public forms of control, tentative public–parochial partnerships that rely on tenuous connections with public institutions,, grassroots engagement with public institutions. We explain the emergence of these three approaches as patterned responses rooted in characteristics of local contexts, including racial composition, geographic isolation.

title: Violence against women in Papua New Guinea
authors: Lewis, Ione, Maruia, Bessie, Walker, Sharon
keywords: women; Papua New Guinea; domestic violence; HIV status; HIV; Human Females;370\_Isolation
abstract: The spread of HIV in Papua New Guinea is influenced by the social, cultural context. This study has aimed to develop knowledge about the different forms of domestic violence experienced by PNG women, their HIV status,, to give women a voice by asking them about their experiences of violence, their recommendations for services, community responses for women experiencing violence. The study has used a mixed method approach to collect quantitative, qualitative data through structured interviews with a sample of 415 women who accessed antenatal, Voluntary Counselling, Testing services across four provinces of Papua New Guinea. Participants were asked about violence they had experienced in their relationships,, the impact of the violence on their lives. The quantitative data were analysed using SPSS,, the qualitative data were coded, themes identified using a grounded theory approach. Physical, emotional abuse in relationships were reported by 58\% of women, financial abuse was reported by 47\%, sexual abuse was reported by 44\%,, social isolation by 38\%. Women who reported violence in their relationships were, on average, 2 years older than women who said they had not been abused, were more likely to be HIV positive. Sexual abuse in relationships was strongly associated with HIV positive status. Level of school education, post-school education, paid employment were not found to influence the rates at which women reported domestic violence. Women spoke about the negative impact of violence on their lives. Women's attitudes towards the violence included acceptance because of financial dependence on husbands, partners, cultural customs, such as payment of bride price, polygamy. Seventy-five percent of the sample had never accessed support services. Participants in the study called for changes to legislation to protect women's rights, more informed responses to violence against women by police, strengthening of court responses to offenders, empowerment of women, employment opportunities to reduce financial dependence on men,, education of men in the need to care for women. There was also a strong recommendation for making community, counselling services available, accessible for women who are victims of violence. The study concludes that programs which are concerned with the prevention of HIV in PNG must include interventions to counter domestic violence, increasing the social status of women through greater access to education, employment.
