The case is argued that if geography teaching starts from children’s own geographies, then geography teaching is important in the enhancement of personal well-being.

title: The consequences of race for police officers' responses to criminal suspects
authors: Plant, E Ashby, Peruche, B Michelle
abstract: The current work examined police officers' decisions to shoot Black, White criminal suspects in a computer simulation. Responses to the simulation revealed that upon initial exposure to the program, the officers were more likely to mistakenly shoot unarmed Black compared with unarmed White suspects. However, after extensive training with the program, in which the race of the suspect was unrelated to the presence of a weapon, the officers were able to eliminate this bias. These findings are discussed in terms of their implications for the elimination of racial biases, the training of police officers.

title: The bounty of buffers: Spatial measurement of displacement, diffusion of benefits of alarms on burglary
authors: Lee, Seungmug (zech), McCrie, Robert D
abstract: This study analyzes the extent to which alarm systems impact geographical displacement and/or diffusion of benefits on burglary, which regards as a substitute for the absence of capable guardians. A quasi-experimental design with three nested concentric zones—target, buffer,, control—are utilized by incorporating the WDQ conceptual approach with GIS, a parcel map. The datasets include burglary incidents, alarm permit records. Alarms produce a sizeable impact on burglary reduction. No indication of spatial displacement is observed from protected houses to nearby houses. Alarms create a short geographic ambit, a wider spatial range of diffusion of benefits. A burglar alarm can protect the house without displacing burglary to nearby houses, provides neighboring houses with protection as well.

title: The effects of community-infused problem-oriented policing in crime hot spots based on police data: a randomized controlled trial
authors: Taylor, Bruce G, Liu, Weiwei, Maitra, Poulami, Koper, Christopher S, Sheridan, Jackie, Johnson, William
keywords: Community policing; crime hot spots; Policing experiment; Problem-oriented policing; Randomized controlled trial;357\_POP\_training;357-04\_POP;357-99\_未分類;J Exp Criminol;pop
abstract: Objectives: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) assessed the effectiveness of a community-infused problem-oriented policing (CPOP) intervention on reducing property/violent crime. Methods: In two mid-Atlantic cities, a total of 102 crime hot spots were randomly assigned to receive CPOP or standard patrol. Analyses examine changes in crime the year before, during,, one year after the intervention. We used hierarchical Poisson regression models. Results: We found no main effects for the CPOP intervention on property, violent crimes in either site. In site B, the violent crime count in low treatment hot spots was 200\% higher than controls post-intervention but this likely reflected officers paying less attention to treatment locations with lower levels of crime. Conclusions: Our results suggest that CPOP was not effective in the unusual context of the COVID-19 pandemic, post-George Floyd killing. Given the challenges of implementing CPOP during this unique time, caution is needed in interpreting these findings.

title: Changing environments to promote safety in libraries
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Ariel, Barak, Ercin, Emrah, Sampaio, Adriana, Hazanov, Julia, Elfström, Sara
abstract: The purpose of this article is to investigate how changes in the environment of a library affect the safety conditions of both visitors, staff. Using principles of Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design, crime, incidents of public disturbance from 2017 to 2020 from libraries in Stockholm, Sweden, are analyzed, later mapped using 3D models in CAD. These findings are inspected via fieldwork visits, then compared with answers from a safety survey with library visitors ( N = 112), interviews with library personnel ( N = 6). Analysis of variance shows that crime, incidents of public disturbance decrease after these interventions, with clear impacts on their geography. A third of visitors indicate that there have been fewer problems after changes in the library are introduced while staff suggests that training prepares them to manage conflict situations more efficiently. The study concludes with a critical assessment of the methodology, makes suggestions to improve safety conditions in libraries.

title: Revisiting the tautology problem in rational choice theory: What it is, how to move forward theoretically, empirically
authors: Steinmetz, Kevin F, Pratt, Travis C
abstract: Criminological rational choice theory is blighted by tautology—that if a crime occurs, then by definition the benefits must exceed the costs. The current analysis details the nature of this tautology as well as its theoretical, philosophical implications concerning the circumstances under which offenders make rational (thoughtful, reflective) or irrational (habitual, intuitive, or instinctual) choices. In short, rational choice theorists appear to side-step the problems presented by this tautology by attempting to coerce observations, theorizing to conform with assumptions about cost–benefit rationality. This essay concludes by setting forth an agenda for the continued empirical investigation of the rational choice perspective—one where the perceived cost/benefit analysis itself for criminal behavior is treated as the outcome of interest.

title: Neighborhood disadvantage, social groups,, adolescent violence: Assessing mechanisms in structural-cultural theories
authors: Thomas, Kyle J, O'Neill, Jennifer, Vogel, Matt
abstract: Structural-cultural perspectives link contextual characteristics to interactions with associates who transmit definitions favorable to crime, thus influencing behavior. Drawing on this, we predict that: (1) adolescents in disadvantaged neighborhoods will be more likely to have parents, friends,, schoolmates who hold violent rationalizations, (2) exposure to associates who hold violent rationalizations will increase an adolescent?s own violent rationalizations,, (3) one?s willingness to rationalize violence will be associated with self-reported violent conduct. Using panel data from the University of Missouri ? St. Louis Comprehensive School Safety Initiative, structural equation models, our findings indicate that respondents residing in disadvantaged neighborhoods are more likely to be exposed to associates who report a greater willingness to rationalize violence, which in turn predicts an adolescent?s own rationalizations. Further, one?s willingness to rationalize violence is predictive of violent conduct, mediates the effects of associates? attitudes on self-reported violence.

title: Predictors of vulnerability, aggression in severe intimate partner violence
authors: Aguilar Ruiz, Raúl, Calderón, María José González
keywords: No terms assigned; Vulnerability; battered women; male batterers; risk factors;370\_Isolation;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Understanding the characteristics of victim vulnerability as well as the violence perpetrated by abusers against women in relationships is essential for professionals in the field who are adopting intervention measures. The current study aimed to examine the differences between severe (n = 805), less severe (n = 805) intimate partner violence (IPV) as well as to identify the variables that predict severe IPV. Chi-square test, logistic regression analysis were used to examine the information from police reports on IPV in Catalonia (Spain) between 2016, 2017, obtained through the Police Risk Assessment Questionnaire (PRAQ). In relation to the victims, isolation, minimization of abuse, fear of being seriously assaulted, substance abuse, pregnancy increased the risk of suffering severe IPV, while being in a new relationship, the existence of prior police reports diminished it. As for the aggressor, previous sexual aggression, abuse, degrading treatment, threats, harassment, control,, jealousy increased the probability of committing severe IPV. Some implications for intervening between aggressors, victims of IPV are discussed.

title: Domestic violence amid COVID-19 pandemic: Pakistan's perspective
authors: Baig, Mirza Altamish Muhammad, Ali, Sajjad, Tunio, Numra Altaf

abstract: While the coronavirus pandemic has spread around the world like wildfire since almost 7 months of its emergence, domestic violence has been breeding endlessly like a ``silent pandemic'', is similarly globally persevered. Violence against women exacerbates during such emergencies on account of heightened tension, close living conditions due to lockdowns regulated by state orders. In Pakistan, where domestic violence is a ``taboo'' object of discussion, help is not provided from neighboring citizens, or even by law enforcers, leaving victims to endure in solitude acts of verbal, physical, psychological,, sexual abuse in the name of alleged supremacy of the assailant.

title: Social norms, rank-based nudging: Changing willingness to pay for healthy food
authors: Aldrovandi, Silvio, Brown, Gordon D A, Wood, Alex M
keywords: *Attitudes; *Choice Behavior; *Food Preferences; *Health Behavior; *Social Norms; Consumer Behavior; Food; Intervention;370\_Isolation;351\_選択行動
abstract: People's evaluations in the domain of healthy eating are at least partly determined by the choice context. We systematically test reference level, rank-based models of relative comparisons against each other, explore their application to social norms nudging, an intervention that aims at influencing consumers' behavior by addressing their inaccurate beliefs about their consumption relative to the consumption of others. Study 1 finds that the rank of a product or behavior among others in the immediate comparison context, rather than its objective attributes, influences its evaluation. Study 2 finds that when a comparator is presented in isolation the same rank-based process occurs based on information retrieved from memory. Study 3 finds that telling people how their consumption ranks within a normative comparison sample increases willingness to pay for a healthy food by over 30\% relative to the normal social norms intervention that tells them how they compare to the average. We conclude that social norms interventions should present rank information (e.g., ``you are in the most unhealthy 10\% of eaters'') rather than information relative to the average (e.g., ``you consume 500 calories more than the average person'').

title: When will adolescents tell someone about dating violence victimization?
authors: Black, Beverly M, Tolman, Richard M, Callahan, Michelle, Saunders, Daniel G, Weisz, Arlene N
abstract: This study examined factors that influence help-seeking among a diverse sample of adolescents who experienced dating violence. A sample of 57 high school students in an urban community reported on the prevalence, characteristics of dating violence in their relationships. Someone observing a dating violence incident, a survivor's attaching an emotional meaning to the event significantly influenced adolescents to talk to someone. When dating violence occurred in isolation, survivors were more likely to receive no support from others in the aftermath of the incident. Differences between boys', girls' help-seeking, implications for dating violence intervention, prevention programming are discussed.

title: The ecology of privacy, mood in a shared living group
authors: Brown, B
keywords: Emotional States; Home Environment; Interpersonal Interaction; Living Arrangements; Privacy;370\_Isolation;jep\_org;J Environ Psychol
abstract: Demonstrated that social, physical,, behavioral aspects of context contributed to the experience of privacy regulation, mood in a shared living group. The study tracked social contacts, physical settings, activities, privacy regulation,, mood at random times over 1 wk for 20 women (aged 20-22 yrs) who resided in a 10-student shared living facility during the fall or winter. Solitude was a frequent experience even when Ss were in the shared facility. The most aversively experienced solitude occurred when Ss desired to be alone. Thus, aversive experiences when alone did not signal times of desired but unattained contact. Ss were not socially overloaded: they were frequently alone, often desired greater intimacy. Yet they also reported positive experiences of place attachment in both the family home, the private apartments, but not in the shared living spaces outside the apartments. title: Perceived social isolation, cognition
authors: Cacioppo, John T, Hawkley, Louise C
abstract: Social species, from Drosophila melanogaster to Homo sapiens, fare poorly when isolated. Homo sapiens, an irrepressibly meaning-making species, are, in normal circumstances, dramatically affected by perceived social isolation. Research indicates that perceived social isolation (i.e. loneliness) is a risk factor for,, may contribute to, poorer overall cognitive performance, faster cognitive decline, poorer executive functioning, increased negativity, depressive cognition, heightened sensitivity to social threats, a confirmatory bias in social cognition that is self-protective, paradoxically self-defeating, heightened anthropomorphism, contagion that threatens social cohesion. These differences in attention, cognition impact on emotions, decisions, behaviors, interpersonal interactions that can contribute to the association between loneliness, cognitive decline, between loneliness, morbidity more generally.

title: Trust in emergency management authorities, individual emergency preparedness for tornadoes
authors: Choi, Junghwa, Wehde, Wesley
journal: Risk Hazards \& Crisis in Public Policy
keywords: FEMA; confianza en el gobierno; emergency management; gobierno local; local government; manejo de emergencias; preparación para tornados; tornado preparedness; trust in government; 地方政府; 对政府的信任; 应急管理; 联邦紧急事务管理局(FEMA); 龙卷风预备;370\_Isolation;360\_Trust
abstract: The risks associated with disasters can be significantly reduced if individuals are well prepared according to the orders, recommendations of emergency management authorities such as the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), local government. Despite this fact, there is evidence that individuals are not cooperative with these authorities, are therefore underprepared for an emergency. This article argues that individual trust in emergency management authorities may affect their cooperation with emergency preparedness recommendations. Using unique survey data, this study finds a nuanced relationship between individual emergency preparedness for tornadoes, trust in emergency management authorities. Although trust in FEMA in isolation does not explain variations in individual preparedness for tornadoes, increased preparation for a tornado is explained by trust in local government contingent upon a low baseline level of trust in FEMA. This article concludes with some practical, theoretical implications for emergency management authorities, scholars.

title: Students under lockdown: Comparisons of students' social networks, mental health before, during the COVID-19 crisis in Switzerland
authors: Elmer, Timon, Mepham, Kieran, Stadtfeld, Christoph
abstract: This study investigates students' social networks, mental health before, at the time of the COVID-19 pandemic in April 2020, using longitudinal data collected since 2018. We analyze change on multiple dimensions of social networks (interaction, friendship, social support, co-studying), mental health indicators (depression, anxiety, stress, loneliness) within two cohorts of Swiss undergraduate students experiencing the crisis (N = 212),, make additional comparisons to an earlier cohort which did not experience the crisis (N = 54). In within-person comparisons we find that interaction, co-studying networks had become sparser,, more students were studying alone. Furthermore, students' levels of stress, anxiety, loneliness,, depressive symptoms got worse, compared to measures before the crisis. Stressors shifted from fears of missing out on social life to worries about health, family, friends,, their future. Exploratory analyses suggest that COVID-19 specific worries, isolation in social networks, lack of interaction, emotional support,, physical isolation were associated with negative mental health trajectories. Female students appeared to have worse mental health trajectories when controlling for different levels of social integration, COVID-19 related stressors. As universities, researchers discuss future strategies on how to combine on-site teaching with online courses, our results indicate the importance of considering social contacts in students' mental health, offer starting points to identify, support students at higher risk of social isolation, negative psychological effects during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Rural isolation, small towns,, the risk of intimate partner violence
authors: DuBois, Kathryn O
keywords: NCVS; intimate partner violence; prevalence; settlement type;370\_Isolation;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Ethnographic research from the United States on gender-based violence showing that rural isolation exacerbates intimate partner violence (IPV) is at odds with estimates from nationally representative victimization surveys which indicate that the incidence of IPV in settlements conventionally characterized as rural is similar to or less than the incidence for urban settlements. One possible reason for this discrepancy-that the conventional metropolitan statistical area-based measure of settlement type fails to distinguish isolated rural areas from other nonmetropolitan places-is put to test in this study. Pooled data from 578,471 women interviewed a total of 1,672,999 times in the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) between 1994, 2015 were used in this study to consider the risk of IPV across a measure of settlement type that differentiates nonmetropolitan settlements into dispersed rural areas or residentially concentrated small towns. Logistic regression estimates of semiannual IPV prevalence were modeled using generalized estimating equations, robust standard errors to compensate for repeated measures, for the complex sample design of the NCVS. After adjusting for age, race/ethnicity, year,, time in sample, these analyses indicated that women from dispersed rural settlements had a lower semiannual risk of IPV (2.31 per 1,000 [95\% confidence interval [CI] = [2.02, 2.64]]) than women from small towns (3.30 per 1,000 women [95\% CI = [2.82, 3.87]]) or women from the urban core (2.60 per 1,000 [95\% CI = [2.44, 2.77]]). title: Intimate partner violence in small towns, dispersed rural areas,, other locations: Estimates using a reconception of settlement type: Estimates using a reconception of settlement type
authors: DuBois, Kathryn O, Rennison, Callie Marie, DeKeseredy, Walter S
abstract: Current understanding of victimization of those in rural settlements compared to other types of settlements is limited by inadequate classifications of settlement types. To investigate this, we detail problems with following the typical approach,, then describe an alternative measure of settlement type. We next use this alternative settlement type measure to estimate the incidence of intimate partner violence (IPV) against women from 1992–2015 National Crime Victimization Survey data. Over the period examined, the incidence of IPV was highest for women living in small towns (11.4 per 1,000). In contrast, women living in dispersed rural settlements (7.9 per 1,000) shared rates with those in suburbs (7.9 per 1,000), exurbs (7.1 per 1,000) while reporting rates lower than those of women residing in the urban core (9.7 per 1,000). These results provide clarity to earlier research on the incidence of IPV across settlement types, they call into question the salience of geographic isolation as a determinant of IPV in nonmetropolitan locales.

title: Changes in self-reported health, alcohol consumption,, sleep quality during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States
authors: French, Michael T, Mortensen, Karoline, Timming, Andrew R
abstract: ABSTRACTWhen the novel coronavirus entered the US in early 2020, the initial response to protect the health-care system capacity, slow transmission,, associated morbidity, mortality has been stay-at-home orders, social distancing,, proper hygiene. However, extended social isolation can result in unintended consequences. To examine possible unintended consequences, we fielded a longitudinal survey with the same sample of respondents ? the first at the end of March 2020, the second one month later at the end of April 2020. We calculated changes over time in physical health status, mental health status, alcohol consumption,, sleep quality. Random-effects logit models were estimated to identify statistically significant predictors for each outcome. Results show that individuals reported significantly worse outcomes in all four areas as the pandemic progressed, especially for alcohol consumption, sleep quality. In general, age, non-White race, religiosity,, resiliency are protective factors while being female, having greater fear of the coronavirus are risk factors. If these trends continue as we enter future stages of the pandemic, then the full societal costs could become extreme.

abstract: Why is neighborhood racial composition linked so strongly to police-reported crime? Common explanations include over-policing, negative interactions with police, but police reports of crime are heavily dependent on resident 911 calls. Using Sampson's concept of legal cynicism, Vaisey's dual-process theory, we theorize that racial concentration, isolation consciously, nonconsciously influence neighborhood variation in 911 calls for protection, prevention. The data we analyze are consistent with this thesis. Independent of police reports of crime, we find that neighborhood racial segregation in 1990, the legal cynicism about crime prevention, protection it engenders have lasting effects on 911 calls more than a decade later, in 2006-2008. Our theory explains this persistent predictive influence through continuity, change in intervening factors. A source of cumulative continuity, the intensification of neighborhood racial concentration, isolation between 1990, 2000, predicts 911 calls. Likewise, sources of change-heightened neighborhood incarceration, home foreclosures during the financial crisis in 2006-2008-also predict these calls. Our findings are consistent with legal cynicism theory's focus on neighborhood disadvantage, racial isolation,, concerns about police protection, crime prevention; they correspond less with the emphasis of procedural justice theory on police legitimacy.

title: Policing, community safety in northern Canadian communities: challenges, opportunities for crime prevention
authors: Griffiths, Curt Taylor
abstract: Although there is an emerging body of research literature on rural policing, less is known about policing in small communities in Canada’s territories populated largely by Indigenous peoples. These communities are often situated in geographically isolated areas, are subjected to harsh weather conditions,, may experience high rates of crime, disorder. Drawing on interviews conducted with RCMP officers in the two Canadian territories of Yukon, Nunavut, this paper examines the dynamics of policing in northern communities, how these might affect efforts to create sustainable, effective crime prevention initiatives. The findings reveal that geographic isolation, social problems,, history of distrust of the police, combined with the structure through which police services are delivered, present significant challenges to the development, sustainability of crime prevention initiatives. The unique environments of northern communities, however, also provide opportunities for the creation of police–community partnerships built on mutual trust that can provide the basis for effective crime prevention programs.

title: Sheltering in place, domestic violence: Evidence from calls for service during COVID-19
authors: Leslie, Emily, Wilson, Riley

abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic has led to an economic slowdown as more people practice social distancing, shelter at home. The increase in family isolation, unemployment,, economic stress has the potential to increase domestic violence. We document the pandemic's impact on police calls for service for domestic violence. The pandemic increased domestic violence calls by 7.5\% during March through May of 2020, with effects concentrated during the first five weeks after social distancing began. The increase in reported domestic violence incidents began before official stay-at-home orders were mandated. title: Resistance among domestic violence offenders: measurement development, initial validation: Measurement development, initial validation
authors: Levesque, Deborah A, Velicer, Wayne F, Castle, Patricia H, Greene, R Neil
abstract: Batterers' resistance to traditional intervention programs has been well documented. Within a Transtheoretical Model of Change (stage of change) framework, a measure of processes of resistance was developed, administered to 346 adult male domestic violence offenders in treatment. The study yielded a 38-item measure that assesses eight dimensions of resistance: (a) System Blaming, (b) Problems with Partner, (c) Problems with Alliance, (d) Social Justification, (e) Hopelessness, (f) Isolation, (g) Psychological Reactance,, (h) Passive Reactance. title: Hearing impairment, loneliness, social isolation,, cognitive function: Longitudinal analysis using English Longitudinal Study on Ageing

abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study examines the relationships between hearing impairment, cognitive function among older adults,, whether that association is mediated by loneliness, social isolation. METHODS: Data were drawn from English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) wave two (2004/2005) until wave seven (2014/2015). The study sample consisted of 8,199 individuals aged 50 years or older. Cognitive function was measured using episodic memory. We performed analysis using a generalized structural equation modeling (GSEM) technique. RESULTS: GSEM analysis shows that the direct effect of hearing impairment on episodic memory was negative, significant (β = -0.29, p <0.001). Loneliness, social isolation mediated that effect. Hearing impairment was positively associated with loneliness (β = 0.10, p <0.001), social isolation (β = 0.04, p <0.001). CONCLUSION: The link between hearing impairment, episodic memory was partly mediated by loneliness, social isolation. Interventions to improve the social networks of older adults with hearing impairment are likely to be beneficial in preventing cognitive decline. Thus, the importance of maintaining social relationships among older adults, especially those with hearing impairment is highlighted.

title: The ``golden thread'': Coercive control, risk assessment for domestic violence
authors: Myhill, Andy, Hohl, Katrin

abstract: Research on risk assessment for domestic violence has to date focused primarily on the predictive power of individual risk factors, the statistical validity of risk assessment tools in predicting future physical assault in sub-sets of cases dealt with by the police. This study uses data from risk assessment forms from a random sample of cases of domestic violence reported to the police. An innovative latent trait model is used to test whether a cluster of risk factors associated with coercive control is most representative of the type of abuse that comes to the attention of the police. Sub-lethal physical violence-choking, use of weapons-was also consistent with a course of controlling conduct. Whether a physical injury was sustained during the current incident, however, was not associated consistently either with the typical pattern of abuse or with other context-specific risk factors such as separation from the perpetrator. title: Barriers to the implementation of the ward-based outreach team program in Mpumalanga Province: Results from process evaluation

abstract: BACKGROUND: South Africa adopted the ward-based outreach team (WBOT) program as one aspect of the three-stream approach to primary health care (PHC) re-engineering. title: Personality characteristics of victims of intimate partner violence: A systematic review

abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is global public health issue, refers to the violence committed by a partner in the context of an intimate relationship, regardless of whether or not it is legally recognized. title: Social guardianship, social isolation: An application, extension of lifestyle/routine activities theory to rural adolescents

title: Using dynamic contextual factors to better understand the etiology, escalation of stalking violence

abstract: Stalking is dynamic, influenced by targets’ reactions, stalkers’ circumstances. Consequently, the risk of violence in stalking cases is likely dynamic. title: Unintended consequences of neighbourhood restructuring: Uncertainty, disrupted social networks, increased fear of violent victimization among young adults

abstract: The unprecedented outbreak, continuous spread of the COVID-19 virus starting in December 2019 resulted in a strict lockdown, nationwide long-term home isolation, which has possibly led to increased levels of family violence in China. This commentary aims to explore two issues related to the impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic on family violence in China, with intimate partner violence as its most common form. abstract: Reports on road rage/aggressive driving imply that most everyone who drives could be involved, affected by such emotions. abstract: Communication studies increasingly recognize the audience's critical role in receiving, interpreting media messages. Research into audience attributes that distinguish media effects, on the fear of crime (FEAR) has been limited-particularly as it relates to the reception of news. This study is based on a survey of 2,092 adults in Tallahassee, Florida at the height of a media driven panic about violent crime. Controlling for age, gender, race, victim experience, other perceptions of crime, the frequency of watching television news, listening to news on the radio is significantly related to FEAR. Reading newspapers, newsmagazines, recall of detail concerning specific highly publicized violent crimes are unrelated to FEAR. When audiences are disaggregated by gender, race,, a series of third attributes, television news consumption is significantly related to FEAR only for white females between the ages of thirty, fifty-four. This finding holds regardless of victim experience, income or perceived safety. Several explanations derived from previous research are applied to this finding. Both esonance, substitution have possible explanatory relevance, but the affinity of audience members with victims most often seen on television news may best account for the concentration of media effects among white women.

title: Exploring anti‐gang advertisements: Focus group discussions with gang members, at‐risk youth
authors: Chapel, Gage, Peterson, Kristin M, Joseph, Roy
journal: Journal of applied communication research: JACR
abstract: Abstract In the highly debated issue concerning the use of advertising to discourage gang membership, the responses of the gang members, at‐risk youth for whom the ads are intended have been overlooked. This study explores the usefulness of anti‐gang advertising by seeking the opinion of young people living in a gang environment. Participants verbally responded to seven anti‐gang ads created, broadcast by a Fox television network affiliate. Based on participant responses, seven generic advertising strategies were suggested that hold the possibility of creating more effective anti‐gang ads.

title: NCCD research review : Crime, the mass media: A selective review of research
authors: Garofalo, James
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: MASS media \& crime; JUSTICE; VIOLENT crimes; DEVIANT behavior; CRIMINAL law; UNITED States;363\_publicity;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;121\_Lane2014;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: The mass media are pervasive in the United States,, accusations about the media's role in eliciting deviant behaviors are common. Yet criminologists have paid scant attention to the media in their theories, research. There is, however, a body of research conducted by psychologists, political scientists,, sociologists that bears, directly or indirectly, on the issues of crime, justice. This article draws on that research in reviewing the major findings on a selected set of topics. In general, the available research shows that crime is a relatively staple topic in the media's news, entertainment presentations. The amount of crime depicted has little relationship to the amount of crime occurring,, violent crimes are high ly overrepresented by the media. The effects of these distorted portrayals on public attitudes, beliefs are unclear because conflicting research results have emerged. On the other hand, the research strongly supports the notion that the viewing of violence increases the probability of behaving aggressively. The review concludes with several broad suggestions for media-related research that would be relevant to issues in criminology, crimincel justice.

title: Television news magazine crime stories: A functionalist perspective
authors: Grabe, Maria Elizabeth
journal: Critical studies in mass communication: CSMC: a publication of the Speech Communication Association
abstract: More than a century ago, Emile Durkheim argued that the rituals of processing, punishing crime are functional in constructing a society's morality, teaching its members to abide by certain rules,, promoting cohesion among members by making it public when individuals have violated shared moral values. This content analysis investigates network, syndicated news magazine crime stories for their potential to promote these three social Junctions. Programs were exhaustively sampled over a six month period (October 1, 1994 to March 31, 1995). Three coders content analyzed 272 hours of television programs. Results indicate patterns in the data set to support the Durkheimian notion that social systems ritualize crime events with functional implications for the maintenance of social order.

title: Fear of crime: A review of the literature
authors: Hale, C
keywords: CRIME; SOCIAL problems; SOCIAL groups; ECONOMICS; SOCIAL sciences; MEDIA buying services;363\_publicity;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;121\_Lane2014;international Review of Victimology;police visibility
abstract: The literature on fear of crime has grown rapidly in the last three decades. This paper examines the reasons for this growth, attempts to put some structure on the work to date. The inadequacies of measures of fear of crime are discussed, alternative approaches suggested. Alternative explanatory theories are compared, strategies for reducing fear reviewed.

title: Impact of newspaper crime reports on fear of crime: Multimethodological investigation
authors: Heath, Linda
keywords: Attribution; COLLEGE students; CRIME \& the press; FEAR of crime; INTERPERSONAL relations; SOCIAL groups; SOCIAL participation;363\_publicity;315\_介入実験\_情報提示
abstract: Investigated the impact of components of newspaper crime reports on fear of crime in an examination in which key newspaper components were based on theorizing in the areas of downward comparison, attribution,, normative behavior. In Study 1, 36 newspapers were classified according to the proportion of crime reports that involved local crimes, sensational crimes,, random crimes; the levels of fear of crime among 335 readers of these newspapers were assessed through telephone interviews. Results indicate that Ss who read newspapers that printed a high proportion of local crime news reported higher levels of fear if the crimes were predominantly sensational or appeared to be random, whereas Ss whose newspapers printed a low proportion of local crime news reported lower levels of fear if the crimes were predominantly sensational or random. These findings were replicated in Study 2: college students ( N = 80) who read reports of local crimes expressed higher levels of fear if the crimes were random rather than precipitated, whereas the opposite pattern emerged in regard to nonlocal crimes. Implications for psychologists, journalists are discussed. (35 ref)

title: On interpretative risk perception research: Some reflections on its origins; its nature;, its possible applications in risk communication practice
authors: Horlick-Jones, Tom, Prades, Ana
keywords: EMERGENCY management; RISK perception; RISK communication; COMMUNICATION in medicine; PRACTICAL reason; GREAT Britain; interpretative risk perception research; risk; risk, practical reasoning; thick description;363\_publicity;J\_TF1505
abstract: The use of risk communication as a policy tool has become increasingly important in areas as diverse as emergency planning, health communication,, including aspects of many of the leading issues of the day. Its use, as a part of institutional attempts to inform, influence lay behaviour, is predicated upon a variety of models of how people make sense of risk-related issues. Many such models are based upon a cognitive information-processing metaphor,, have an underlying instrumental nature that assumes recipients 'would behave responsibly if only they knew the facts'. In this paper, we discuss some alternative, sociological, approaches to risk perception that have developed over the last decade, in which resulting lay behaviours are recognised as being embedded within a matrix of everyday associations, preferred ways of life, trust relations, economic constraints, emotional commitments. In particular, we will be concerned with the emergence of so-called 'interpretative' risk perception research. In so doing, we draw particular attention to the relevance of Ryle's notion of 'thick description' in seeking to investigate the nature of practical reasoning about risk issues. We illustrate some of these themes by revisiting,, re-analysing, a particularly rich 10-year-old corpus of largely unpublished comparative UK, Spanish data, generated by citizens living in communities geographically close to potentially hazardous industrial facilities.

title: An evaluation of the short‐term impact of a media‐based substance abuse prevention programme
authors: Jason, Leonard A, Pokorny, Steven B, Kohner, Katherine, Bennetto, Loisa
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: Media; prevention; substance abuse;363\_publicity;317\_介入実験\_集団地域
abstract: AbstractA state‐wide substance abuse prevention programme, entitled KidsInTouch, incorporated a multifaceted approach involving: (a) media‐based interventions;, (b) parent training workshops. KidsInTouch was targeted at parents, their children, ages five to 12 years. The media‐based interventions attempted to increase children's, parents' awareness, knowledge about substance abuse, prevention. In addition, the intervention advertised, solicited audience participation in parent training workshops. Parents participating in the parent training workshops, in comparison to the control parents, evidenced significant improvement in both alcohol, other drug knowledge, parenting skills. The implications of using the media, involving children, their parents in substance abuse prevention programmes are discussed.

title: Crime prevention, the attitude toward the criminal justice system
authors: Kuttschreuter, Margôt, Wiegman, Oene
keywords: criminal justice system; crime prevention; multimedia campaign; residential burglary; violence; Criminal Behavior; Criminal Justice; Mass Media;363\_publicity;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;J Crim Justice
abstract: This study concerns the effects of a multimedia campaign regarding residential burglary, violence on the streets in The Netherlands that can be characterised as a tell-the-truth campaign. The mass media component of the campaign consists of editorials in the regional dailies, local weeklies,, items on the regional radio station. The audience was given the opportunity to personally contact an information officer (via information meetings, “Crime Prevention Van,” or stands). The campaign led to a more positive attitude towards the criminal justice system among the general public. There was no effect on knowledge of burglary, violence, the image of local crime, risk assessment, fear of crime, outcome expectation, self-efficacy expectation, preventive behaviour,, the attitude towards crime reporting.

title: Ethnicity, information sources,, fear of crime
authors: Lane, Jodi, Meeker, James W
keywords: ETHNICITY; INFORMATION resources; CRIME; MASS media; ORANGE County (Calif.); CALIFORNIA; UNITED States; Ethnic, Cross-Cultural Relations;363\_publicity;J\_TF1505;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root
abstract: Using data from a 1997 random digit dial survey of Orange County, California residents, this article examines the ``indirect victimization'' thesis regarding the effects of mass media on perceived risk, fear of crime among whites, Latinos. Using structural equation models, we analyze the differential effects of television, newspapers when used as the primary source of information about crime. For whites, relying on the newspaper has a negative indirect impact on fear through perceived risk, but television has no effects. For Latinos, newspaper has no effects on fear, but televisionhas both a positive direct effect, indirect effect on fear through perceived risk.

title: Routine activities, television viewing: An exploration of the influences of fear of crime in Lisbon, Portugal
authors: Lobo Antunes, Maria Joao
journal: International journal of comparative, applied criminal justice
abstract: In 1999, the Centre of Public Opinion Surveys (CESOP) of the Portuguese Catholic University, in collaboration with the Mayor of Lisbon's Security Department, formed the Lisbon Safety Observatory (LSO). The Centre was to conduct a series of annual surveys aimed at assessing victimization, safety issues in the city of Lisbon. The analyses revealed surprising information regarding fear of crime, victimization. Victimization was found to be extremely low; only 7 in every 100 persons surveyed had been the victim of a personal crime, yet over 60\% expressed concern for their safety. Viewed in the light of recent developments in routine activities (Wilcox, et al., 2003), the effect these have on fear of crime, this paper proposes an explanatory model of fear using elements from this theory, incorporating other potential explanations including media exposure (Chiricos, et al., 2001), prior victimization. The results are analyzed using OLS regression. Contrary to popular expectation, victimization has little influence on fear of crime; rather, it is primarily mediated by routine activities, variables of guardianship, exposure to motivated offenders, target attractiveness,, to a lesser extent exposure to media, specifically television.

title: Visibility, transparency, police‐media relations
authors: Mawby, Rob C
abstract: The relationship between the British police service, the media has a chequered history, is one of complexity. Whilst the media has been a main contributor to promoting favourable images of policing, mystifying police work, conflict is endemic to the relationship, the level of trust between the parties is constantly in the balance. Commentators have suggested that the police are the dominant party in the relationship, managing the media to their own advantage, not in the interests of democratic policing. This paper examines the police‐media relationship in the context of the media advances in the 1990s. Drawing on research carried out across the police service in England, Wales, it concludes that although the police service has become more professional in the way it handles media relations, the complexity of the media world coupled with police organisational characteristics prevent police domination of the media to the extent feared.

title: Taking a bite out of crime: The impact of the national citizens' crime prevention media campaign
authors: O'Keefe, Garrett J, Rosenbaum, Dennis P, Lavrakas, Paul J, Reid, Kathaleen, Botta, Renee A
keywords: CRIME; CRIME prevention; LAW enforcement; MASS media; PREVENTION; SOCIAL problems; Advertising; Public Opinion; Marketing \& Advertising; Human; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); development \& content \& public impact of National Crime Prevention media campaign, citizens \& law enforcement officers \& media gatekeepers;363\_publicity;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;301\_5;PDFなし
abstract: This book examines how well a national public information program worked at getting citizens more involved in protecting themselves from crime. We examine the development, content, and, in particular, the public impact of the National Crime Prevention media campaign--better known as the McGruff or Take a Bite Out of Crime campaign. We present findings from national survey studies of reactions to the campaign by citizens, law enforcement officers,, media gatekeepers. /// We attempt to portray the campaign in the context of critical crime prevention, law enforcement issues of the 1990s. Our contention is that public information programs are--and need to be--deeply embedded in the issues, culture of the societal problems they address. title: Keeping an eye on the neighbours: Police, citizens,, communication within mobile neighbourhood crime prevention groups
authors: Pridmore, Jason, Mols, Anouk, Wang, Yijing, Holleman, Frank
abstract: Mobile neighbourhood crime prevention has become increasingly popular in the Netherlands. Since 2015, 7,250 WhatsApp neighbourhood crime prevention (WNCP) groups have been registered online, most of which are initiated, moderated by citizens. This entails a form of participatory policing aimed at neighbourhood crime prevention, which may provoke increased feelings of anxiety, interpersonal surveillance. Community police officers, citizens need to adapt to changed interactions, trust relations in the neighbourhood. This mixed-methods research examines both the mediation of messaging applications, its implementation by both citizens, police, indicating the tensions, negotiations around formal, informal ‘policing’.

title: Shoplifting prevention: The role of communication-based intervention strategies
authors: Sacco, Vincent F
journal: Canadian journal of criminology. Revue canadienne de criminologie
keywords: shoplifting; Crime Prevention; Literature Review; Mass Media;363\_publicity;332\_Retail
abstract: Reviews the research concerning the feasibility of anti-shoplifting information programming, focusing on prevention through the mass media. It is argued that programs directly oriented toward juvenile shoplifters are likely to suffer problems in design, implementation; results of these programs are uncertain because of the complex psychological, social patterns characteristic of juvenile retail theft. Indirect deterrence programs aimed at the general public must overcome widespread apathy, ambivalence regarding appropriate behavioral, attitudinal responses before they can be effective. Evidence suggests that anti-shoplifting campaigns are more likely to modify attitudes than to affect behavior, that the organizational victims of shoplifting elicit a relatively low degree of public concern. It is concluded that crime prevention through mass media is a costly, difficult social undertaking that has limited applicability, only a moderate capacity for problem amelioration. title: The relation between crime news, fear of violence
authors: Smolej, Mirka, Kivivuori, Janne
journal: Journal of Scandinavian studies in criminology, crime prevention
keywords: CRIME; Crime news; FEAR of crime; FINLAND; MASS media \& crime; Media exposure; VICTIMS of crimes; VIOLENCE; Victimization;363\_publicity;J\_TF1505
abstract: In this article, we explore the relationship between the use of crime news, fear of violence through multivariate analyses. Our main objective is to examine whether exposure to crime news is related to avoidance behaviour, fear of crime when personal, vicarious victimization experiences, as well as a number of other relevant factors, are held constant. Using the 2003 sweep of the Finnish National Victimization Surveys, we focus on two types of crime news exposure: exposure to crime‐related tabloid headlines,, the scope of exposure to different sources of crime news. Our main finding is that reading tabloid front pages is associated with both avoidance behaviour, with higher levels of worry about becoming a victim of violence. We also found that people who expose themselves to many sources of crime news are more likely to fear violence. As an interesting by‐product of our analyses, we observed that being unemployed was quite strongly associated with fear of violence.

title: Zero tolerance, the media,, a local community
authors: Törrönen, Jukka
journal: Journal of Scandinavian studies in criminology, crime prevention
abstract: The article examines a one?year zero tolerance project launched by the City of Tampere in southern Finland in August 1999 with a view to discouraging drunken, disorderly behaviour in public places. The analysis is anchored to the context of publicity produced by the local daily Aamulehti. The project is approached from a constructionist vantage point by asking what kinds of techniques, programmes of responsibilization, punishment were articulated for the programme in Aamulehti, which of them gained a dominant position in the local publicity, how the different ?versions' of the programmes, techniques were articulated as part of the local actors' self?understanding. The tools of analysis are mainly borrowed from positioning theory. The articles appearing in Aamulehti on zero tolerance are analysed in terms of a struggle over meaning in which the community position of zero tolerance, the social identities of the actors involved are shaped by deconstructing, reconstructing categories, by redirecting the objectives of the campaign, by manipulating identification mechanisms. title: Breaking news: How local TV news, real-world conditions affect fear of crime
authors: Weitzer, Ronald, Kubrin, Charis E
abstract: Many Americans report that they are fearful of crime. One frequently cited source of this fear is the mass media. The media,, local television news in particular, often report on incidents of crime,, do so in a selective, sometimes sensational manner. This paper examines the role of the media in shaping crime fears, in conjunction with both demographic factors, local crime conditions. Unlike most previous research in this area, which typically focuses on only one medium, the present study examines the effects of several—local, national television, radio, newspapers,, the Internet. The findings address four theoretical perspectives on the relationship among the media, real-world conditions,, fear of crime.

title: Mass media as a macrolevel source of social control: A new direction in the community structure model
authors: Yamamoto, Masahiro
abstract: A community structure model is grounded in the structural model of mass media originally formulated by the Minnesota team of Tichenor, Donohue,, Olien. Although recent theoretical, empirical work has led to major refinements of the community structure research, there remain substantive, promising issues that deserve to be examined by mass communication scholars. This article recasts the original structural model by integrating a community-oriented approach to social control, formulates a set of hypotheses with regard to the role of local mass media in community social control.

title: Policing cyber-neighbourhoods: tension monitoring, social media networks
authors: Williams, Matthew L, Edwards, Adam, Housley, William, Burnap, Peter, Rana, Omer, Avis, Nick, Morgan, Jeffrey, Sloan, Luke
abstract: We propose that late modern policing practices, that rely on neighbourhood intelligence, the monitoring of tensions, surveillance, policing by accommodation, need to be augmented in light of emerging ‘cyber-neighbourhoods’, namely social media networks. The 2011 riots in England were the first to evidence the widespread use of social media platforms to organise, respond to disorder. The police were ill-equipped to make use of the intelligence emerging from these non-terrestrial networks, were found to be at a disadvantage to the more tech-savvy rioters, the general public. In this paper, we outline the development of the ‘tension engine’ component of the Cardiff Online Social Media ObServatroy (COSMOS). This engine affords users with the ability to monitor social media data streams for signs of high tension which can be analysed in order to identify deviations from the ‘norm’ (levels of cohesion/low tension). This analysis can be overlaid onto a palimpsest of curated data, such as official statistics about neighbourhood crime, deprivation, demography, to provide a multidimensional picture of the ‘terrestrial’, ‘cyber’ streets. As a consequence, this ‘neighbourhood informatics’ enables a means of questioning official constructions of civil unrest through reference to the user-generated accounts of social media, their relationship to other, curated, social, economic data.

title: Fear of crime: Read all about it?
authors: Williams, Paul, Dickinson, Julie
keywords: prominence \& space \& qualitative aspects of newspaper crime reporting, fear of crime, adults, Great Britain; Crime; Fear; Newspapers;363\_publicity;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;121\_Lane2014;British Journal of criminology
abstract: This article reports a three-stage study of the relationship between newspaper reporting of crime, fear of crime. The first stage measured the amount of space, prominence given to crime, particularly violent crime, in ten British daily newspapers. The second stage of the study was a questionnaire survey of the relationship between newspaper reporting of crime, fear of crime. A significant positive correlation was found which appeared to be independent of demographic factors associated with readership. The third stage examined qualitative aspects of reporting styles in these newspapers. Consistent differences were found between newspapers. Those newspapers classified as 'broadsheets' carried proportionally fewer crime reports, reported crimes in a less sensational fashion than the 'tabloids', particularly low-market ones.

title: Disentangling social support mobilization via online neighborhood networks
authors: De Meulenaere, Jonas, Baccarne, Bastiaan, Courtois, Cédric, Ponnet, Koen
keywords: community involvement; community networks; community participation; cooperative behavior; help-seeking behavior; social behavior; social support;362\_SNA;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: This paper proposes, tests a theoretical model to investigate the mechanism underpinning local social support exchange via online neighborhood networks (ONNs). We drew on community psychology, social support,, social media literature, used a survey conducted in the Dutch-speaking part of Belgium among 561 ONN users (nfemales = 409; 72.9\%) between 18, 82 years old (Mage = 43.73; SDage = 15.37). We found that engaging in online neighboring behaviors was associated to both online, offline neighborhood sense of community. Subsequently, these provide access to perceived local social support, the intention to mobilize local social support online. The latter was predominantly explained via the path along online sense of community. ONNs facilitate local bridging behavior, connecting otherwise distinct local networks, ties. At the same time, online neighboring behaviors provide the normative context that supports the exchange process.

title: People, places,, adolescent substance use: Integrating activity space, social network data for analyzing health behavior
authors: Mennis, Jeremy, Mason, Michael J
journal: Annals of the Association of American Geographers. Association of American Geographers
abstract: This research investigates the influence of place, social network characteristics on substance use among a sample of 215 urban, primarily African American, adolescents in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. We utilize survey data that capture the places that adolescents perceive to be risky, safe, as well as their home location. The survey also captures the egocentric social network characteristics that are associated with each type of place for each adolescent. Place-characterization data included indicators of a variety of physical features we theorize might enhance or mitigate the likelihood of substance use, such as the locations of alcohol outlets, recreation centers,, violent crime. We employ multivariate Tobit regression to investigate the relationships of place, social characteristics with substance use behavior. Substance use was greater for males, older adolescents but was associated with few physical features of adolescents’ homes or perceived safe places. Substance use was enhanced by several characteristics of adolescents’ perceived risky places, such as commercial activity in distressed neighborhoods. In addition, the presence of substance users at an adolescent's perceived risky place was associated with an increase in substance use. Substantial differences concerning gender, age were also observed. Girls, older adolescents tend to be more sensitive to social, place characteristics as compared to boys. This study highlights the importance of capturing activity space characteristics, perceptions of places,, social network data for investigating substance use, as well as for studies of other health, crime behaviors.

title: The social network of victims of domestic violence: A network-based intervention model to improve relational autonomy
authors: Nolet, Anne-Marie, Morselli, Carlo, Cousineau, Marie-Marthe
keywords: domestic violence; intervention; relational autonomy; social networks;362\_SNA;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: This study aims to understand when, how domestic violence victims' relational autonomy changes, to propose an intervention model stemming from the findings. Using qualitative, social network analysis, we study the actions of network members, as well as changing features of victims' networks. Results show that victims base their decisions on their expectations toward others,, on a desire to preserve their autonomy. Their relational autonomy tends to increase when they leave abusive partners, stay in shelters, but maintaining relational diversity proves challenging once they exit shelters. A network-based model of intervention that aims to improve the victims' relational autonomy is proposed.

title: Explaining gang homicides in Newark, New Jersey: Collective behavior or social disorganization?
authors: Pizarro, Jesenia M, McGloin, Jean Marie
abstract: Although numerous studies examined the distinction between gang, non-gang homicides, there is nonetheless a continued need for research in this domain. Specifically, few studies investigated the etiological differences between these homicides at the multivariate level or attempted to examine the relative robustness of the primary explanations of gang homicides—social disorganization, Decker's (1996) collective behavior hypothesis of gang violence. This article therefore addresses this void by focusing on gang-related homicides in Newark, New Jersey over a sixty-six month period. The findings of this study suggested that there were significant differences between gang, non-gang homicides at the incident level. At the multivariate level, the authors found that homicides precipitated by the operationalization of Decker's (1996) escalation hypothesis were more likely to be gang-related. Conversely, the social disorganization measure did not predict gang homicide, while poverty was a significant predictor. When measures of both potential explanations were entered into the same model only the micro-level escalation hypothesis retained its significance.

title: Does police use of Twitter align with, enhance community policing objectives? An analysis of the New York City Police Department’s Twitter activity
authors: Thomas, Amanda L, Hatten, David N, Connealy, Nathan T
abstract: Prior research has examined how social media has been integrated into law enforcement operations; however, this research has not fully explored the potential for this technology to function as an effective community policing strategy. Through the creation of a uniquely large dataset constructed with individual “tweets,” the current study analyzed Twitter use by the New York City Police Department (NYPD) in 2016. Using a mixed-methods approach, this research identified linkages between social media, community policing, the level of adherence to community policing objectives, the potential for heterogeneity in usage across different NYPD patrol boroughs,, the degree of public engagement. Our findings suggest Twitter is inimitably positioned to contribute to each aspect of community policing, although its effectiveness varied across dimension typology. Second, heterogeneity was also observed across patrol boroughs, indicating both the objectives, application of social media varies within the agency. Lastly, engagement metrics reveal a few notable trends concerning police-community relations.

title: The use of Twitter by police officers in urban, rural contexts in Sweden
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Solymosi, Reka, Müller, Oskar
abstract: The aim of this article is to investigate the nature of information sharing via Twitter by police officers. We examine the content of Tweets in urban, rural contexts using a sample of 20 police-related Twitter accounts, comparing official, personal accounts active in Southern Sweden. Exploratory data analysis, in-depth content analysis of a sample of Tweets compose the underlying methodology. We find a distinct pattern of consistency in the content of the information shared via the official police accounts compared to the personal accounts, regardless of if they are from urban or rural areas. However, some urban–rural differences were observed between official, personal accounts regarding public engagement, operationalized as likes, Retweets. The study calls for a discussion of new models of police engagement using social media by a society that is increasingly shaped by the internet.

title: Social media engagement tactics in U.S. community policing: Potential privacy, security concerns
authors: Carter, Alexander E, Hoy, Mariea, DeSimone, Betsy Byrne
abstract: Despite law enforcement’s best efforts to use social media as a means of community policing, some engagement tactics may lead citizens to disclose personally identifiable information (PII). We coded 200 tweets with the popular \#9PMRoutine that tagged @PascoSheriff (Florida) for participant PII. We found numerous postings of adults’, children’s PII that are problematic including pictures, health information, security-related comments about their routines or vacations. Implications for law enforcement to protect their communities are discussed as well as opportunities to continue to cultivate their online relationships in a more secure forum. We also provide future research directions.

title: Potential, challenges for social media in the neighborhood context
authors: Johnson, Bonnie J, Halegoua, Germaine R
abstract: Many studies have focused on new media's role in connecting interest-based communities across vast geographic distances; fewer studies have examined how viable social media is as a communication tool within the neighborhood context. This study investigates the ways in which established modes of place-based neighborhood association, connection,, communication coincide or conflict with the perceived affordances of connection, association available in social networking sites. As a case study, we identified a neighborhood association that had seen its participation rates dwindle. The association's steering committee decided to turn to popular social media platforms (Facebook, Twitter) to revitalize. After the initial launch, they garnered only five “likes,” three Twitter followers,, two members for the e-mail listserv out of a possible 550 households. A survey of neighborhood residents showed some potential for social media use but also significant mismatches between the perceived affordances of social media, residents’ understanding of the place-based context, condition of the neighborhood. We found three main categories where perceptions, expectations of neighborhood communication did not mesh with social media affordances: perceived intimacy within the neighborhood; desired attributes of neighborhood communication;, expectations of digital, physical space, place.

title: Reading the riots: whatwerethe police doing on Twitter?
authors: Procter, Rob, Crump, Jeremy, Karstedt, Susanne, Voss, Alex, Cantijoch, Marta
abstract: The widespread adoption of new forms of digital communication platforms such as micro-blogging sites presents both an opportunity, a challenge for researchers interested in understanding people's attitudes, behaviours, especially in the context of unfolding crises, the need for government agencies such as the police to inform the public, act swiftly to ensure public order, safety. In this paper, we use a study of a recent public order crisis in England to explore how the police, other organisations, individuals used Twitter as they responded to this event.

title: Police presentational strategies on Twitter in Canada
authors: Schneider, Christopher J
abstract: This empirically driven paper explores police presentational strategies on popular micro-blogging social media site Twitter. A total of 105,801 tweets from Canadian Toronto Police Service Twitter accounts were examined using qualitative document analysis. Thematic issues associated with police professionalism, community policing are identified. A finding that runs throughout each thematic includes official police officer use of Twitter while off duty. A basic argument advanced herein is that official off duty use of Twitter delineates the individual officer from the policing institution but does so in an official capacity, a presentational strategy that diminishes the appearance of authoritarian relations traditionally associated with police. Suggestions for future research are noted.

title: Tweeting the spill: Online informal communications, social networks,, conversational microstructures during the Deepwater Horizon oilspill
authors: Sutton, Jeannette, Spiro, Emma, Butts, Carter, Fitzhugh, Sean, Johnson, Britta, Greczek, Matt
journal: International journal of information systems for crisis response, management
abstract: Informal online communication channels are being utilized for official communications in disaster contexts. Channels such as networked microblogging enable public officials to broadcast messages as well as engage in direct communication exchange with individuals. Here the authors investigate online information exchange behaviors of a set of state, federal organizations during the Deepwater Horizon 2010 oil spill disaster. Using data from the popular microblogging service, Twitter, they analyze the roles individual organizations play in the dissemination of information to the general public online,, the conversational aspects of official posts. The authors discuss characteristics, features of the following networks including actor centrality, differential mixing, as well as how structural features may affect information exchange in disasters. This research provides insight into the use of networked communications during an event of heightened public concern, describes implications of conversational features,, suggests directions for future research.

title: Warning tweets: serial transmission of messages during the warning phase of a disaster event
authors: Sutton, Jeannette, Spiro, Emma S, Johnson, Britta, Fitzhugh, Sean, Gibson, Ben, Butts, Carter T
abstract: Serial transmission-the passing on of information from one source to another-is a phenomenon of central interest in the study of informal communication in emergency settings. Microblogging services such as Twitter make it possible to study serial transmission on a large scale, to examine the factors that make retransmission of messages more or less likely. Here, we consider factors predicting serial transmission at the interface of formal, informal communication during disaster; specifically, we examine the retransmission by individuals of messages (tweets) issued by formal organizations on Twitter. Our central question is the following: How do message content, message style,, public attention to tweets relate to the behavioral activity of retransmitting (i.e. retweeting) a message in disaster? To answer this question, we collect all public tweets sent by a set of official government accounts during a 48-hour period of the Waldo Canyon wildfire. We manually code tweets for their thematic content, elements of message style. We then create predictive models to show how thematic content, message style,, changes in number of Followers affect retweeting behavior. From these predictive models, we identify the key elements that affect public retransmission of messages during the emergency phase of an unfolding disaster. Our findings suggest strategies for designing, disseminating messages through networked social media under periods of imminent threat.

title: A preliminary investigation of risks for adverse outcomes of relationship seeking on social network sites (SNS): a descriptive study of women over 50 seeking relationships on MySpace in Hillsborough County, Florida
authors: Vandeweerd, Carla, Corvin, Jaime, Coulter, Martha, Perkins, Elizabeth, Telford, Robin, Yalcin, Ali, Myers, Jaime, Yegidis, Bonnie
abstract: In contrast to younger populations, little attention has been paid to the increase in seniors using Internet-based venues to find relationships, the potential risk for adverse outcomes this poses. This study examined data collected via an online survey from 45 ethnically diverse women aged 50+ ``seeking relationships'' on MySpace. The majority of women reported a relationship with someone they met online (85\%). They also reported experiencing adverse events including financial exploitation (40\%), threats (55\%),, physical harm (38\%) by someone they met online at levels greater than traditional relationship seeking in the general population. Directions for future research are explored.

title: Police message diffusion on Twitter: analysing the reach of social media communications
authors: van de Velde, Bob, Meijer, Albert, Homburg, Vincent
abstract: Social media are becoming increasingly important for communication between government organisations, citizens. Although research on this issue is expanding, the structure of these new communication patterns is still poorly understood. This study contributes to our understanding of these new communication patterns by developing an explanatory model of message diffusion on social media. Messages from 964 Dutch police force Twitter accounts are analysed using trace data drawn from the Twitter™ API to explain why certain police tweets are forwarded, others are not. Based on an iterative human calibration procedure, message topics were automatically coded based on customised lexicons. A principal component analysis of message characteristics generated four distinct patterns of use in (in)personal communication, new/versus reproduced content. Message characteristics were combined with user characteristics in a multilevel logistic general linear model. Our main results show that URLs or use of informal communication increases chances of message forwarding. In addition, contextual factors such as user characteristics impact diffusion probability. Recommendations are discussed for further research into authorship styles, their implications for social media message diffusion. For the police, other government practitioners, a list of recommendation about how to reach a larger number of citizens through social media communications is presented.

title: Information sharing in community policing in Europe: Building public confidence
authors: Aston, Elizabeth V, O'Neill, Megan, Hail, Yvonne, Wooff, Andrew
abstract: The literature on the importance of procedural justice in policing is extensive. Using the context of information sharing in community policing, this paper argues that interactional, procedural, distributive justice are salient in interactions between the police, the public, both online, face-to-face. Structured interviews ( n = 161) were conducted with members of young minority groups, intermediaries (who work with minorities, police agencies) across nine countries in Europe. Our analysis of barriers, facilitators to sharing information with the police highlights processes of interactional, procedural, distributive justice in building public confidence. We highlight theoretical, practical implications of relevance to policing internationally. Our findings show that demonstrating aspects of interactional justice (attitude, behaviour, accessibility, communication, personal contact, relationships); procedural justice (responsiveness, efficiency, data protection, security);, distributive justice (outcomes, effectiveness, equity in distribution of policing services) have a role in building public confidence, facilitating information sharing with police online, face-to-face. We conclude that in addition to micro-level interactions, meso-level social processes (e.g. community policing models, data protection, security procedures) can be useful in enhancing public confidence.

title: Exploring the sanction–crime relationship through a lens of procedural justice
authors: Augustyn, Megan Bears, Ward, Jeffrey T
keywords: Defiance; Deterrence; Labeling; Procedural justice; Recidivism;360\_Trust;J Crim Justice
abstract: Research overwhelmingly explores “kinds of people” as moderators of the sanction–crime relationship (Piquero et al., 2011). This work, on the other hand, focuses on the sanction experience, draws upon the procedural justice doctrine, key ideas in Sherman's (1993, 2014) defiance theory to test whether individual evaluations of procedural justice condition the effect of legal sanctions on subsequent criminal behavior.Using a sample of serious adolescent offenders, generalized linear regression models with interaction terms are employed to test whether the effect of legal sanctions on involvement, variety,, frequency of offending is conditioned by procedural justice. Significant interaction effects of legal sanction, procedural justice are illustrated with graphical methods.Results suggest that evaluations of procedural justice condition the sanction–crime relationship. Sanctions lead to a higher likelihood of offending among individuals with low evaluations of procedural justice. However, among those with higher evaluations of procedural justice, there is no significant relationship between sanctions, subsequent offending.Increasing perceptions of procedural justice reduces unintended consequences of sanctioning experiences. In an era of heightened focus on interactions between citizens, criminal justice professionals, enhancing procedural justice is not only ethical but also protects against deviance amplification processes.

title: Procedural justice policing, citizen compliance behaviour: the importance of emotion
authors: Barkworth, Julie M, Murphy, Kristina
abstract: Research consistently finds that if authorities use procedural justice in encounters with the public then this will promote citizen cooperation, compliance with the law. Recently, the importance of people's emotional reactions in response to procedural justice, injustice,, the subsequent effect this has on behaviour have been examined. This paper utilises a multi-method approach to examine the mediating role that negative affect plays in the effect of procedural justice policing on citizen compliance behaviour. Study 1 utilises both cross-sectional, longitudinal field survey data collected from Australian citizens who have had a recent contact with a police officer. Study 2 utilises an experimental vignette study designed to assess the causal mechanisms involved in the procedural justice–emotion–compliance relationship. Both studies find that procedural justice is linked to people's self-reported propensity to comply with police. Study 1, 2 also find that negative affect mediates this relationship. These findings have important implications for training police to interact with the public in a manner that reduces negative emotions, ensures the highest level of compliance from the public.

title: Cynical streets: Neighborhood social processes, perceptions of criminalinjustice: Neighborhood cynicism, perceived injustice
authors: Berg, Mark T, Stewart, Eric A, Intravia, Jonathan, Warren, Patricia Y, Simons, Ronald L
keywords: violence against women; trends; status of women; gender inequality; victim—offender relationship;360\_Trust;15\_天津;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;z\_2018\_mera;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;301\_ComCrm;301\_3;308\_STC;318\_介入実験\_Policing;320\_ST実証研究;criminology
abstract: KEYWORDS: neighborhood organization, social control, perceptions of crime, disorder , urban China By drawing on the two streams of Western literature on ``neighborhood effects'', perceptions of neighborhood disorder adapted to the distinctive organizational infrastructure of neighborhoods in contemporary urban China, we examine the con-textual effects of different forms of neighborhood social control (i.e., collective efficacy, semipublic control, public control,, market-based control) on different types of perceived disorder (i.e., criminal activity, social disorder, physical disorder,, total disorder) across neighborhoods. The analyses are based on data collected in the year 2013 from a survey of approximately 2,500 households in 50 neighborhoods across the city of Tianjin. Collective efficacy as a form of informal control has a significant effect only for perceived social disorder. Public control as measured by the activities of neighborhood police stations has a significant contextual effect on all forms of perceived disorder, whereas the role of market-based control as represented by contracted community services is limited to perceived physical disorder. Finally, semipublic control as measured by the activities of neighborhood committees significantly affects all forms of perceived disorder, but the direction of the effect is positive. We interpret this positive effect with reference to the complex processes surrounding the ``translation'' of neighborhood disorderly conditions into perceptions of disorder. A key development in criminology over the course of the past few decades has been the resurgence of interest in ``neighborhood effects'' to understand disorderly conditions , including criminal activity (Sampson, Morenoff,, Gannon-Rowley, 2002). As Skogan (2012: 174; 2015) has observed, the accumulated evidence is difficult to summarize succinctly because the concept of disorder encompasses a wide range of concrete

title: Contact, confidence: revisiting the impact of public encounters with the police
authors: Bradford, Ben, Jackson, Jonathan, Stanko, Elizabeth A
