title: Linking burglary, target hardening at the property level: New insights into victimization, burglary protection
authors: Hirschfield, Alex, Newton, Andrew, Rogerson, Michelle
keywords: 331\_Burglary;z\_2015MERA;9\_310\_外出時無施錠\_2016\_MERA(6章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;Crim Justice Policy Rev\_●Sage
abstract: This article draws on a recent study that examined the impact of target hardening on domestic burglary in the City of Liverpool, England, between July 2005, December 2007. Individual property-level data, from a range of sources, were collated for each residential property in the City enabling details about burglaries (timing, location, modus operandi) to be linked to data on the nature, timing,, location of target-hardening activity. Properties were grouped according to the presence or absence of burglary and/or target hardening at each address, the sequence of events. Groups included properties burgled, target hardened,, not subsequently burgled; no prior burglary, target hardened, subsequent burglary; burgled, never target hardened,, other combinations.The results suggest that property-level data give a richer picture of the relationship between burglary, target hardening than is possible using aggregate data at an area level.

title: Territorial cues, defensible space theory: The burglar's point of view
authors: MacDonald, Julia E, Gifford, Robert
keywords: Crime Prevention; Criminals; Home Environment; Theft; Territoriality;331\_Burglary;jep\_org;J Environ Psychol
abstract: This study tests the defensible space hypotheses that surveillability, evidence of territorial concern will deter burglars. Fifty photographs of single-family dwellings were assessed for many individual cues, five cue categories,, for economic value. Forty-three male subjects (20 youths, 23 adults), who had been convicted of residential breaking, entering, sorted the photographs along a 7-point scale of Vulnerability (likelihood of being a burglary target). As the theory predicts, easily surveillable houses were rated as the least vulnerable targets. Contrary to the theory, evidence of territorial concern had no effect (traces of occupany, actual barriers) or actually increased vulnerability (symbolic barriers). Burglars apparently assume that occupants who care for the exterior of their house possess goods that make the house a profitable target. Concept-based cue categories were more useful in predicting Vulnerability than were individual cues or cue category scores based on simple summations of individual cues. Over half of the variance in Vulnerability could be accounted for by a revised model of defensible space for burglary in single-family dwellings.

title: New patterns in residential burglary: The method of deadbolt lock picking
authors: Mercan, Boran Ali
abstract: This article examines the adaptability of burglars, tactical displacement in Ankara, the capital of Turkey, as part of an ‘arms race’ escalating in response to the sophistication of offensive, preventive measures. It describes the current method of picking deadbolt locks on steel doors inside apartment buildings, a procedure requiring a more complicated, collaborative effort. Following a Bourdieusian criminological reading determining the script, resources of a group of active offenders that function as criminal capital, this article reveals that recently, residential burglary has been displaced from the ‘outside’ to the ‘inside’ of multi-storey apartment buildings due to the proliferation of CCTV, alarm systems, spotlights. Ethnographic findings suggest that a decade ago burgling a residence was far easier for most offenders than it would be today, with numerous similarities in the script of offenders in the non-Western, Western contexts.

title: Vulnerability, risk: some lessons from the UK Reducing Burglary Initiative
authors: Millie, Andrew
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Various police, partnership schemes claim to address vulnerability, either as an end in itself, or as a means of crime reduction. However, project staff do not articulate always what is meant by ‘vulnerability,’ or relate it necessarily to victimization risk. This paper considers what the notions of ‘vulnerability’, ‘risk’ mean,, how they are tackled, prioritized. Some lessons are provided from the UK Reducing Burglary Initiative. The paper argues that un‐evidenced assumptions of vulnerability, risk need to be avoided. Additionally, a decision to focus on vulnerability is, mostly, one to reduce disadvantage rather than crime.

title: The relation between residential property, its surroundings, day-, night-time residential burglary
authors: Montoya, Lorena, Junger, Marianne, Ongena, Yfke
keywords: 331\_Burglary;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;Stability;Environment, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: This article examines how residential property, its surroundings influence day-, night-time residential burglary. Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) principles of territoriality, surveillance, access control, target hardening, image maintenance,, activity support underpin the study. Data were collected by observing 851 houses in the city of Enschede, half of which were burgled, half representing a random selection of houses not burgled. Multilevel multinomial regression models were estimated for predicting day-, night-time burglaries. The findings show that territoriality, access control predict daytime burglary while access control, target hardening predict night-time burglary. The analysis controls for offender availability, target attractiveness,, residential stability. The conclusion is that two separate burglary prevention frameworks are needed: one for day-and another one for night-time burglary.

title: New methods for examining expertise in burglars in natural, simulated environments: preliminary findings
authors: Nee, Claire, White, Martin, Woolford, Kirk, Pascu, Tudor, Barker, Leon, Wainwright, Lucy
abstract: Expertise literature in mainstream cognitive psychology is rarely applied to criminal behaviour. Yet, if closely scrutinised, examples of the characteristics of expertise can be identified in many studies examining the cognitive processes of offenders, especially regarding residential burglary. We evaluated two new methodologies that might improve our understanding of cognitive processing in offenders through empirically observing offending behaviour, decision-making in a free-responding environment. We tested hypotheses regarding expertise in burglars in a small, exploratory study observing the behaviour of experienced offenders (ex-burglars), novices (students) in a real, in a simulated environment. Both samples undertook a mock burglary in a real house, in a simulated house on a computer. Both environments elicited notably different behaviours between the experts, the novices with experts demonstrating superior skill. This was seen in: more time spent in high value areas; fewer, more valuable items stolen;, more systematic routes taken around the environments. The findings are encouraging, provide support for the development of these observational methods to examine offender cognitive processing, behaviour.

title: The efficacy of home security measures
authors: O'shea, Timothy C
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
keywords: 331\_Burglary;z\_2015MERA;9\_310\_外出時無施錠\_2016\_MERA(6章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root
abstract: Crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) assumes criminal acts are influenced by their inherent costs, benefits. Policy implications drawn from CPTED suggest home security measures increase these costs, reduce the likelihood of burglary.This paper tests the efficacy of home securitv measures. A telephone survey of 566 residents in Mobile Countv, Alabama. inquired abow security measures burglary victims, nonvictims employed. A logistic regression solution found some, but not all, of these security measures to be quite effeclive.

title: LIFESTYLES, ROUTINE ACTIVITIES, AND RESIDENTIAL BURGLARY VICTIMIZATION
authors: Robinson, Matthew B
abstract: This paper reports findings from an exploratory, place specific study of the relationship between victims’ lifestyles, routine activities,, residential burglary victimization. A telephone survey differentiated people with various lifestyles in terms of daily obligatory, discretionary activities. These differential lifestyles were related to variations in routine activities (i.e., pedestrian, automotive traffic) on street segments around residential areas. In a pooled cross-sectional design, street segments with higher volumes of routine activities between 1992-1996 had significantly lower burglary rates over this time period, as did street blocks with irregular periods of routine activities in 1997. Implications are discussed for the lifestyle / exposure, routine activity theories, for the movement in criminology away from explaining why individual offenders commit crimes, toward explaining why crimes happen at particular places at particular times, not others.

title: Scandinavian prospects for a place‐based randomized experiment on burglary reduction
authors: Sorensen, David W M
journal: Journal of Scandinavian studies in criminology, crime prevention
abstract: Despite their widespread implementation, there is a surprising absence of clear‐cut, unambiguous evidence concerning the effectiveness of situational crime prevention approaches (e.g. alarms, neighborhood watch, property‐marking) on residential burglary. This absence of evidence—which should not be confused with a presence of contradictory evidence—stems most notably from the fact that very few of the programs enacted to date have been evaluated under controlled, experimental conditions. The current article describes problems with previous evaluations, advocates the use of a place‐based, randomized experimental design—which this author argues should be easier to implement in Scandinavia than elsewhere.

title: Where, when? Examining spatiotemporal aspects of sexual assault events
authors: Balemba, Samantha, Beauregard, Eric
abstract: Abstract This research investigates the where, when of sexual assaults to determine what types of sexual crimes are committed at different time, place classifications. Exhaustive CHAID (chi-squared automatic interaction detection) analyses are conducted, examining factors associated with crimes that were committed indoors or outdoors, in private or public places, during the day or at night,, during the week or on the weekend. These methods are applied to a sample of 361 sexual crime events committed by 72 serial sex offenders. The results are strikingly different dependent on which spatial or temporal aspect of the crime is examined, which implies the complexity of sexual crime events, their situational components. This research brings to light possible policy implications with respect to situational crime prevention.

title: Emergent regularities of interpersonal victimization: An agent-based investigation
authors: Birks, Daniel, Townsley, Michael, Stewart, Anna
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: Repeat Victimization;330\_SAEnv;304\_RepeatVic;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage;Journey to crime/victimization
abstract: Objectives: Apply computational agent-based modeling to explore the generative sufficiency of several mechanisms derived from the field of environmental criminology in explaining commonly observed patterns of interpersonal victimization. Method: Controlled simulation experiments compared patterns of simulated interpersonal victimization to three empirically derived regularities of crime using established statistical techniques: (1) spatial clustering (nearest neighbor index), (2) repeat victimization (Gini coefficient),, (3) journeys to crime (Pearson’s coefficient of skewness). Results: Large, statistically significant increases in spatial clustering, repeat victimization,, journey to crime skewness are observed when virtual offenders operate according to mechanisms proposed by the routine activity approach, rational choice perspective,, geometry/pattern theories of crime. Conclusion: This research provides support for several propositions of environmental criminology in explaining why interpersonal victimization tends to be spatially concentrated, experienced by a small number of repeat victims,, why aggregate journey to crime curves tend to follow a distance decay relationship. By extending previous work in agent-based modeling of property victimization, it also demonstrates that the same core mechanisms are sufficient to generate plausible patterns of crime when examining fundamentally different types of offending.

title: Do street robbery location choices vary over time of day or day of week? A test in Chicago
authors: Bernasco, Wim, Ruiter, Stijn, Block, Richard
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: Chicago; day of week; location choice; street robbery; time of day;330\_SAEnv;308\_STC;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This article examines the hypothesis that in street robbery location choices, the importance of location attributes is conditional on the time of day, on the day of the week. METHOD: The hypothesis is assessed by estimating, comparing separate discrete location choice models for each two-hour time block of the day, for each day of the week. The spatial units of analysis are census blocks. Their relevant attributes include presence of various legal, illegal cash economies, presence of high schools, measures of accessibility,, distance from the offender's home. RESULTS: The hypothesis is strongly rejected because for almost all census block attributes, their importance hardly depends on time of day or day of week. Only the effect of high schools in census blocks follows expectations, as its effect is only demonstrated at the times, on the days that schools are open. CONCLUSIONS: The results suggest that street robbers' location choices are not as strongly driven by spatial variations in immediate opportunities as has been suggested in previous studies. Rather, street robbers seem to perpetrate in the environs of cash economies, transit hubs most of the time irrespective of how many potential victims are around.

title: An application of the rational choice approach to the offending process of sex offenders: A closer look at the decision-making
authors: Beauregard, Eric, Leclerc, Benoît
journal: Sexual abuse: a journal of research, treatment
abstract: Although the study of both offense processes, implicit theories provides in-depth knowledge about the decision-making of sex offenders, these studies focus solely on the internal psychological processes of the offender leading to the commission of a sexual assault. These studies neglect to look specifically at the offender's decision-making during the offense in interaction with the immediate situations encountered at the offense scene, such as the choices of behavior while interacting with the victim in a specific context. Based on a rational choice approach, this study investigates the decision-making involved in the offending process of 69 serial sexual offenders who have committed their crimes against stranger victims. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with offenders in order to identify the rationale behind their actions during the pre-crime phase (premeditation of the crime, estimation of risk of apprehension by the offender,, forensic awareness of the offender), crime phase (use of a weapon, use of restraints, use of a vehicle,, level of force used),, the post-crime phase (event leading to the end of crime, victim release site location choice). Results show that sex offenders, even if traditionally described as irrational, impulsive individuals, are capable, up to a certain point, of an analysis of the costs/benefits related to their actions. Moreover, results emphasize the important role of situational factors, such as victim resistance, on the decision-making process of sex offenders. Implications of the results are briefly discussed in regard of clinical practice, crime prevention.

title: Spatial patterns of sex offenders: Theoretical, empirical,, practical issues
authors: Beauregard, Eric, Proulx, Jean, Rossmo, D Kim
keywords: Geographic profiling; Hunting patterns; Routine activities; Sex offenders; Spatial analysis; Typologies;330\_SAEnv
abstract: The aim of the current article is to review the theoretical, empirical,, practical issues related to the spatial behavior of sex offenders. After describing three theoretical models related to geographic profiling, empirical studies are presented that investigate the links between offender characteristics, modus operandi variables,, the distances traveled by sex offenders. Different spatial typologies of sex offenders, investigative strategies that take into account the spatial component of criminal behavior are discussed.

title: Nodes, paths, edges: Considerations on the complexity of crime, the physical environment
authors: Brantingham, Patricia L, Brantingham, Paul J
keywords: Crime; Environment; Criminals; Decision Making; Environmental Effects; Human; physical environment, criminal decision making \& crime location \& pattern, criminals;330\_SAEnv;jep\_org;jep;327;J Environ Psychol
abstract: Crime has long been thought to be intimately associated with the physical environment in which it occurs. Theoretical, empirical developments over the past 20 years demonstrate that this relationship is complex, varies substantially at different levels of spatial, temporal resolution. Research on the distribution of property crimes in time, space resonates with research on the target selection processes of offenders to suggest that crime is strongly related to aggregate elements of the perceived physical environment: nodes, paths, edges, an environmental backcloth. The relationship between crime, the physical environment is mediated through individual awareness, action spaces. This implies a series of research issues, crime control policies for future exploration.

title: Longitudinal change in women's sexual victimization experiences as a function of alcohol consumption, sexual victimization history: A latent transition analysis
authors: Bryan, Amanda E B, Norris, Jeanette, Abdallah, Devon Alisa, Stappenbeck, Cynthia A, Morrison, Diane M, Davis, Kelly C, George, William H, Danube, Cinnamon L, Zawacki, Tina
keywords: alcohol consumption; latent class analysis; latent transition analysis; sexual victimization;330\_SAEnv;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Women's alcohol consumption, vulnerability to sexual victimization (SV) are linked, but findings regarding the nature, direction of the association are mixed. Some studies have found support for the self-medication hypothesis (i.e., victimized women drink more to alleviate SV-related distress); others have supported routine activity theory (i.e., drinking increases SV vulnerability). In this study, we aimed to clarify the interplay between women's prior SV, typical drinking,, SV experiences prospectively over one year. METHOD: Participants (N = 530) completed a baseline survey, weekly follow-up surveys across Months 3, 6, 9,, 12. RESULTS: Latent class analysis (LCA) suggested that women could be classified as victimized or non-victimized at each assessment month; 28\% of participants were classified as victimized at one or more assessment months. Latent transition analysis (LTA) revealed that childhood sexual abuse, adult SV history each predicted greater likelihood of being victimized during the year. Typical drinking during a given assessment month was associated with (1) greater likelihood of victimized status at that assessment month, (2) greater likelihood of having transitioned into (or remained in) the victimized status since the previous assessment month. Furthermore, victimized status at a given assessment month predicted a higher quantity of subsequent drinking. CONCLUSION: These findings indicate a reciprocal relationship between typical drinking, SV, supporting both the self-medication hypothesis, routine activity theory,, suggesting that hazardous drinking levels may be one important target for both SV vulnerability reduction, interventions for women who have been sexually victimized.

title: Fear of sexual harassment, its impact on safety perceptions in transit environments: A global perspective
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Loukaitou-Sideris, Anastasia
keywords: \#MeToo! movement; fear of crime; gender; public transportation; sexual crime; university students;330\_SAEnv;321\_SA実証研究;public\_transportation\_334
abstract: This study reports variation in safety perceptions in transit environments, based on samples of university students in 18 cities on six continents who responded to an identical 45-question survey (N= 13,323 university students). We explore potential links between students' fears, sexual victimization, conclude that sexual harassment affects their behavior, mobility. Student mobility was affected by avoidance strategies prompting some transit riders to travel at particular times, on travel routes, settings that are deemed especially risky, or even avoiding using transit completely. Findings highlight the importance of city-country contexts for transit safety.

title: Routine activities, sexual assault: an analysis of individual-, school-level factors
authors: Cass, Amy I
keywords: RAPE; COLLEGE students -- Sexual behavior; DATING violence; DATE rape victims; VICTIMS of crimes; VIOLENCE -- Forecasting; UNIVERSITIES \& colleges; MARITAL status; DATE rape; campus crime; routine activities; sexual assault; victimization;330\_SAEnv;z\_2012\_jacp;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;321\_SA実証研究;327;Violence Vict;CampusCrime;250109\_multilevel
abstract: The efficacy of routine activities theory is examined to explain sexual assault on the college campus. Although many research studies have utilized routine activities theory to predict sexual assault using individual-level factors, little is known about the effect of school-level factors on a student's risk of sexual assault. Based on interviews from 3,036 randomly selected students, surveys from 11 randomly selected colleges in the United States, a hierarchical linear model was created to predict student victimizations by school characteristics. For the individual, results reveal that being female, drug use,, marital status are statistically significant for predicting the probability of a sexual assault. At the institutional level, however, none of the variables are significant in predicting sexual assault among college coeds. Policy implications for prevention measures on college campuses are discussed.

title: Homicide in São Paulo, Brazil: Assessing spatial-temporal, weather variations
authors: Ceccato, Vânia
keywords: HOMICIDE; VIOLENT deaths; CRIME; BRAZIL;330\_SAEnv;jep\_org;jep;J Environ Psychol
abstract: Although São Paulo is one of the most dangerous cities in the world, very little is known about the variations of levels of crime in this Brazilian city over time. This article begins by investigating whether or not homicides are seasonal in São Paulo. Then, hypotheses based on the principles of routine activities theory are tested to evaluate the influence of weather, temporal variations on violent behaviour expressed as cases of homicides. Finally, the geography of space–time clusters of high homicide areas are assessed using Geographical Information System (GIS), Kulldorff's scan test. The findings suggest that central, peripheral deprived areas show the highest number of killings over the year. Moreover, homicides take place when most people have time off: particularly during vacations (hot months of the year), evenings, weekends. Overall, the results show that temporal variables are far more powerful for explaining levels of homicide than weather covariates for the Brazilian case—a finding that lends weight to the suggested hypotheses derived from routine activity theory.

title: A typology of multiple-perpetrator rape
authors: Chambers, Jemma C, Horvath, Miranda A H, Kelly, Liz
abstract: Some consistency in existing typologies of rape has been found, which have extended from lone to multiple perpetrator offenses. The current study sought to explore the facets of multiple-perpetrator rape (MPR) in a sample representative of one geographical area. Seventy-five victim statements of MPR reported to an urban police force in the United Kingdom were classified into a qualitative model denoting offender actions in MPR. Four types from pathways through the model were produced: violence, criminality, intimacy,, sexuality. Analysis of the crime scene variables provided additional evidence of the four types. Finally, the associations between the four types, offense characteristics, such as victim, perpetrator age, were explored. Implications of these findings for the prevention, investigation of MPR are discussed along with suggestions for future research directions.

title: The role of land use, walkability in predicting crime patterns: A spatiotemporal analysis of Miami-Dade County neighborhoods, 2007–2015
authors: Cowen, Christopher, Louderback, Eric R, Roy, Shouraseni Sen
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Metropolitan areas; Regression analysis; Urban planning; Crime; Land use; Walking; Statistical analysis; Regression models; Harmonic analysis; Fourier analysis; Miami-Dade County Florida;330\_SAEnv;308\_STC;Security Journal
abstract: This study investigates the relationship between land use, walkability,, the outcomes of neighborhood crime rates of larceny, aggravated assault. We use a combination of OLS regression models, harmonic analysis of diurnal patterns,, geospatial statistical techniques to examine the spatial patterning of larceny, aggravated assault in 782 Census blocks in Miami-Dade County, Florida with long-term data from 2007 to 2015. The results show that neighborhoods (i.e., Census block clusters) with higher levels of walkability have greater levels of aggravated assault. We also find that the increasing land-use diversity increases both aggravated assault, larceny. Finally, aggravated assault peaks during late night hours, while larceny peaks during daytime hours. Based on the results of our study using conventional, geospatial analyses, routine activity, social disorganization theories of neighborhood crime are partially supported, in that more motivated offenders, potential targets increase crime rates, while increased guardianship, informal social control reduce crime rates. The results of this study have important implications for security experts, law-enforcement agencies,, urban planning policy specialists focused on reducing crime in metropolitan areas. It is also relevant for theoretical frameworks designed to explain, predict temporal, spatial crime patterning.

title: A CCTV-based analysis of target selection by guardians intervening in interpersonal conflicts
authors: Ejbye-Ernst, Peter, Lindegaard, Marie Rosenkrantz, Bernasco, Wim
abstract: Guardians are a potential resource of conflict de-escalation but we still know little about their actual behaviour. In this article we investigate whom among the antagonists a guardian selects as a target when they intervene in an interpersonal conflict. We investigate this using CCTV footage from Amsterdam (the Netherlands) of 46 interpersonal conflicts in public spaces involving 641 interventions by 176 individuals. We find that guardians are more likely to target antagonists: (1) who have performed the most aggressive behaviours, (2) who are not simultaneously targeted by other guardians, (3) who are from their own social group, (4) who are men. The analysis shows that the behaviour of intervening guardians is shaped by multiple aspects of the complex, often ambiguous conflict situations.

title: What distinguishes single from recurrent sexual victims? The role of lifestyle‐routine activities, first‐incident characteristics
authors: Fisher, Bonnie S, Daigle, Leah E, Cullen, Francis T
keywords: SEXUAL abuse victims; RAPE victims; VICTIMS of crimes; COLLEGE students; CAMPUS violence; ACTIVITIES of daily living; campus crime; lifestyle; recurrent victims; self-protective behaviors; sexual victimization; state dependence;330\_SAEnv;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303;Justice Q
abstract: An unsettling reality is that a substantial proportion of women who have been sexually victimized are recurrent victims who experience more than one sexual victimization while young adults. What is not well understood is why some women experience a single sexual victimization whereas others experience recurrent sexual victimizations. Using a sample of 4,399 college women from the National College Women Sexual Victimization study, we examine lifestyle‐routine activities, first‐incident characteristics that could place women at risk of being recurrent sexual victims during an academic year. Our results show that none of the lifestyle‐routine activities variables differentiated single, recurrent victims; the factors that predicted being a single victim are similarly predictive of being a recurrent victim. However, women who used self‐protective action during the first incident reduced their likelihood of being a recurrent victim. Implications for the development of sexual victimization risk‐reduction, prevention programs are also discussed.

title: Does spending time in public settings contribute to the adolescent risk of violent victimization?
authors: Felson, Richard B, Savolainen, Jukka, Berg, Mark T, Ellonen, Noora
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Teenagers; Violence; Victims of crime; Criminology;330\_SAEnv;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Objectives Using data from a nationally representative survey of adolescents in Finland this research examined the influence of spending time in public settings on the risk of physical assault, robbery victimization. Methods Binary, multinomial regression models were estimated to disaggregate associations between hours spent in public settings, characteristics of the victimization incident. The amount of causality/spuriousness in the association was examined using a method of situational decomposition. Results Our findings indicate that: (1) an active night life (any time after 6 pm) has a strong effect on victimization for boys, whereas much of the association between night life, victimization is spurious for girls; (2) after-school activity is not a risk factor; (3) adolescents who frequent public places at night increase their risk of victimization by people they know as well as strangers;, (4) much of the risk of night time activity in public settings is alcohol-related. Conclusions Our research suggests that a good deal of the risk associated with spending time in public settings is a function of the victim's own risky behavior rather than inadvertent physical contact with motivated offenders in the absence of capable guardians. In addition, this lifestyle is significantly more victimogenic for males.

title: Risky lifestyles, routine activities,, the General Theory of Crime
authors: Forde, David R, Kennedy, Leslie W
abstract: Gottfredson, Hirschi's A General Theory of Crime proposes that low self-control is a cause of criminal behavior. Several recent studies, showing mixed support, test this theory for understanding crime, imprudent behavior. In this paper we reassess the general theory of crime, highlight the importance of proximate causes, including routine conflict, in explaining the propensity toward violence. Drawing from the insights provided by routine activities theory, we operationalize risky behavior. We analyze data collected in 1994 in a survey of respondents from two Canadian provinces. Our results show that elements of low self-control do not directly affect crime, although measures of self-control have strong effects on imprudent behavior which relate, in turn, to offending. Adding measures of proximate causes, we are better able to understand criminal offending, victimization by respecifying the general theory of crime.

title: Offender searches, crime events
authors: Gialopsos, Brooke Miller, Carter, II, J W
abstract: This article explores how several prominent theories explain how, where crime events occur. In particular, rational choice, lifestyle-routine activities, crime pattern,, multilevel opportunity theories are applied to offender searches for targets. Examples from qualitative, quantitative works are used to illustrate these theoretical concepts as applied to offenders’ target selection, journey to crime. While both of these types of studies help to shed light on these topics, the ethnographic works have been particularly instrumental in understanding offenders’ searches for targets. Finally, new directions or suggestions for future research are discussed, mainly the application to school shootings (or other mass murders), online crimes.

title: Criminal directionality, the structure of urban form
authors: Frank, Richard, Andresen, Martin A, Brantingham, Patricia L
keywords: 3236:Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; criminal directionality; Human; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Criminology; Urban Environments; Quantitative Study; decision making; Spatial Perception; spatial criminology; Empirical Study; Criminal Behavior; Canada; urban form;330\_SAEnv;jep\_org;jep;J Environ Psychol
abstract: Spatial criminology has three interrelated elements: place, distance,, direction. Though directionality has had theoretical support for many years, very few empirical verifications of this component of crime have emerged. In this article, we investigate the strength of directionality by comparing a simulated randomized dataset, a large incident-based dataset of repeat offenders. We find strong evidence for a strong presence of directionality in criminal spatial decision-making. This aspect of the spatiality of crime must be considered in any attempts to understand the aetiology of crime.

title: Assessing the effect of routine activity theory, self-control on property, personal,, sexual assault victimization
authors: Franklin, Cortney A, Franklin, Travis W, Nobles, Matt R, Kercher, Glen A
abstract: This study used a sample of 2,230 female university students to assess the applicability of routine activity theory, self-control on property, personal,, sexual assault victimization. Results indicate that (a) both self-control deficits, participation in drug sale behavior were significantly correlated with increased property, personal,, sexual assault victimization; (b) increased partying, shopping frequency, off-campus housing significantly, substantively correlated with increased property victimization; (c) off-campus housing was correlated with increased personal victimization;, (d) increased number of days spent on campus, increased frequency of partying significantly increased sexual assault victimization, net of controls. Future directions for the integration of feminist theory, strategies for crime prevention are discussed.

title: Assessing the risk of nonsexual, sexual victimization using incident-based police reports
authors: Gilliard-Matthews, Stacia, Nolan, III, James J, Haas, Stephen M
keywords: nonsexual victimization; sexual victimization; risk assessment; black women; intimate partner violence; Human Females; Physical Abuse; Sexual Abuse; Victimization; Blacks;330\_SAEnv;J\_TF1505;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;320\_ST実証研究;Victims \& Offenders
abstract: Current research has affirmed that black women are most at risk for rape, assault,, intimate partner violence in the United States. These findings are often based on statistics from surveys like the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS). The NCVS collects data from a stratified sample of households in the United States from which one can establish victimization risk, rates at the national level. We know very little about a person’s risk of violent crime victimization from police records at the local, state level because until recently the data were not available. This study, therefore, adds to current victimization research by utilizing state-level police data to examine violent crime victimization patterns. Specifically, using data from the U.S. Census Bureau, West Virginia Incident-Based Reporting System (WVIBRS), we construct a model to examine the risk of nonsexual, sexual victimization over a lifetime by sex, race. Our findings indicate that black females in West Virginia have the highest probability of experiencing a nonsexual, sexual victimization over their lifetime. They also have the highest risk of multiple victimizations for these crimes. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2016 APA, all rights reserved)

title: Sexual crime, place: The impact of the environmental context on sexual assault outcomes
authors: Hewitt, Ashley, Beauregard, Eric
abstract: Using the rational choice perspective, the current study investigates the impact that the environment, offending behavior have on serial sexual crime event outcomes.The effects of time, place factors, as well as offender modus operandi strategies, on sexual crime event outcomes are tested using Generalized Estimating Equations on a sample of 361 crime events committed by 72 serial sex offenders.Time, place do impact serial stranger sexual offenders’ modus operandi strategies, but the place characteristics of the crime have more of an effect on the offender’s behavior than do the temporal conditions during which the event occurs. Subsequent analyses indicate that temporal, place factors, as well as offender modus operandi strategies, predict whether the offender completes the rape, his reaction to victim resistance,, the level of physical force that he inflicts on the victim, but not whether the victim is forced to commit sexual acts on the offender.Serial stranger sexual offenders are effective decision-makers who adapt their strategies to the physical environment in which they commit their crimes, but their degree of rationality can vary as some outcomes are more dependent on the context than the offender, his actions.

title: General theory of spatial crime patterns: General theory of spatial crime patterns
authors: Hipp, John R
abstract: I propose a general theory for examining the spatial distribution of crime by specifically addressing, estimating the spatial distribution of the residences of offenders , targets, guardians,, their respective expected movement patterns across space, time. The model combines information on the locations of persons, typical spatial movement patterns,, situational characteristics of locations to create estimates of crime potential at various locations at various points in time, makes four key contributions. First, the equations make the ideas involved in the theory explicit,, they highlight points at which our current state of empirical evidence is lacking. Second, by creating measures of spatial ``potentials'' of offenders, targets,, guardians, this theory provides a precise grounding for operationalizing spatial effects in studies of place, crime. Third, the equations provide an explicit consideration of offenders, where they might travel and, therefore, incorporates offenders into crime-and-place research. Fourth, these equations suggest ways that researchers could use simulations to predict stable patterns, as well as changes, in the levels of crime at both micro, macro scales. Finally, I provide an empirical demonstration of the added explanatory power provided by the theory to a study of place, crime. A burgeoning field of research has been focusing on the spatial distribution of crime. One large research area has emanated from the Chicago School, has focused on the ecological distribution of crime in meso units such as neighborhoods (Browning et al.

title: The social ecology of violence against women
authors: Lauritsen, Janet L, Schaum, Robin J
abstract: Despite more than three decades of research on the topic of violence against women, the relative contribution of individual, family, community factors to victimization risk remains unknown. We use self‐report data from the Area‐Identified National Crime Victimization Survey to study the correlates of stranger, nonstranger, intimate‘partner violence against women. Regardless of victim‐offender relationship, we find that the risk for victimization is highest among young, single women with children, particularly those who have lived in the current home for relatively shorter periods. Area family, age composition appear to have stronger direct relationships with women's violence than poverty or racial composition measures. We also find there to be more similarities than differences in the individual, family,, community correlates of stranger, nonstranger, intimate partner violence. We discuss these findings as part of the growing body of multilevel literature on violence, on violence against women.

title: Getting away with the stolen vehicle: An investigation of journey-after-crime
authors: Lu, Yongmei
journal: The Professional geographer: the journal of the Association of American Geographers
abstract: Analyses of criminals' travel patterns can provide significant suggestions to improve crime management. This study extends the investigation of criminals' travel behavior from journey-to-crime to journey-after-crime. Moreover, new methods are developed to examine the spatial patterns of location pairs when restricted by the underlying geographical process. The methods are employed to investigate criminals' journey-after-auto-theft in the city of Buffalo, New York. The analyses reveal that auto thieves' trips from vehicle-theft locations to the corresponding vehicle-recovery locations are local in nature. The travel distances are significantly shorter than the randomly simulated trips; the travel directions are biased from the random directions as well.

title: The geography of transit crime: Documentation, evaluation of crime incidence on, around the Green line stations in Los Angeles
authors: Loukaitou-Sideris, Anastasia, Liggett, Robin, Iseki, Hiroyuki
abstract: The link between the social, physical environment, transit crime is an important one, but it is not well understood or explored. This study explores the environmenttransit crime connection by examining in depth the relation between crime incidence at the stations along a light-rail line in Los Angeles, the social, physical characteristics of the stations, their neighborhoods. The study employs a mix of qualitative, quantitative methods to analyze crime statistics, census, ridership data,, built environment data. It documents, evaluates the geography of crime along this light-rail line as well as the impact of sociodemographic, environmental attributes on crime incidence at the station.

title: Journey to murder: examining the correlates of criminal mobility in sexual homicide
authors: Martineau, Melissa, Beauregard, Eric
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Although the empirical research on the journey to crime seems to indicate that most crimes are committed close to home, only a few studies have specifically examined the journey to crime in cases of sexual homicide. Using a sample of 214 sexual homicide cases, the current study investigates, using logistic regression, offenders who travel during the crime to those offenders who commit their crime, all at the same location. Current findings suggest that sexual murderers who engage in intra-crime travel tend to use a vehicle in the commission of their offence, target adult victims who are involved in the sex trade, move the body post murder.

title: The demographic, spatial patterns of recorded rape in a large UK metropolitan area
authors: Muir, Grant, Macleod, Malcolm D
abstract: The present study details a social contextual analysis of 172 rapes, attempted rapes that occurred in a large metropolitan area in the UK. The main focus of the present study concerns the demographic characteristics of rape victims, offenders, including their age, ethnicity, vis-à-vis their relationship. The study also considers the geographic distribution of offences, their relationship to ethnicity, socio-economic status. Our data clearly indicate that the age of offenders is significantly associated with the nature of the victim–offender relationship,, that rape tends to be intra-racial. The data also provide unique comparisons to be made with contextual data on rapes in rural settings. The implications of these findings for the prevention, deterrence of rape, the recording of rape by the police,, the impact of such findings on public education are considered.

title: Victimization risks at leisure: a gender-specific analysis
authors: Mustaine, E E, Tewksbury, R
keywords: Sociology; Research methodology; Research \& development--R\&D; Behavior; Alcohol use; Models, Theoretical; Humans; Risk Factors; Questionnaires; Sex Factors; Adult; Female; Logistic Models; Male; Substance-Related Disorders; Alcohol Drinking; Leisure Activities; Crime Victims;330\_SAEnv;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Based on two central propositions-(1) that routine daily activities create criminal opportunity structures by increasing the frequency, intensity of contacts between motivated offenders, suitable victimization targets,, (2) that the subjective value of a target, together with its level of guardianship, determines victim selection-this theoretical perspective incorporates both structural aspects of environments, contexts, free will in explaining criminal victimization (Miethe \& Meier, 1990). The British Crime Survey, which is recognized as perhaps the most thorough, large-scale study to examine leisure domain victimization (Lasley, 1989; Maxfield, 1987) includes only a handful of questions about drinking behaviors, amount of alcohol consumed, identification of principal leisure activity; there are no other measures of leisure activities.\n Given recent literature that applies a feminist critique to routine activity theory, we should not be surprised about this.

title: Journey to crime, victimization: An application of routine activities theory, environmental criminology to homicide
authors: Pizarro, Jesenia M, Corsaro, Nicholas, Yu, Sung-Suk Violet
keywords: Crime; Criminology; Environment; Homicide; Victimization; Demographic Characteristics; Lifestyle; Human; Male; Female; US; Routine activity theory; environmental criminology; suspect characteristics; Deviant Lifestyle Scale;330\_SAEnv;J\_TF1505;2012\_jsep\_review\_root;z\_kyoto2015;Victims \& Offenders;Journey to crime/victimization
abstract: Despite the attention the crime of homicide has received by the academic community there are still gaps in the literature. One of these gaps pertains to the examination of the mobility patterns of homicide victims, offenders. This study addresses this gap by focusing on three research questions-(1) Does the distance traveled by homicide suspects, victims from their residence to the incident location vary by homicide motive type? (2) Does the reason why homicide victims, suspects travel to the incident location vary by homicide motive type? (3) What victim, suspect characteristics significantly predict the distance traveled from the residence to the incident location? The analyses show that there are statistically significant differences among the homicide types in terms of the length of the journey of victims, suspects to the incident location. In addition, there is variation by motive in terms of why the victims, suspects traveled to the incident location. Finally, the findings suggest that the demographic, lifestyle characteristics of victims, suspects have an impact on their journey to crime, victimization.

abstract: Examines the applicability of the `routine activities' theory to women's risk of non-spousal multiple victimization. Using data collected through Statistics Canada's national Violence Against Women Survey, both bivariate, multivariate analyses are used to examine the impact of lifestyle, proximity, exposure to crime,, physical, social guardianship on women's multiple non-spousal victimization. Also compares stranger multiple victimization, multiple victimization by known men in order to delineate differences in the applicability of routine activities theory. (Original abstract-amended)

title: Contextualizing the sexual assault event: Images from police files
authors: Sherley, Alison J
keywords: RAPE; CRIME; SOCIAL problems; OFFENSES against the person; CRIMINOLOGY; ALCOHOL;330\_SAEnv;J\_TF1505;z\_kyoto2015
abstract: This study focuses on sexual assault from a criminal event perspective, using case files to examine why elements of a crime emerge. Beyond how elements of a crime converge, as proposed by routine activities theory, statements extracted from police files shed light on the precursors to the criminal transaction, contextual elements, allowing insight into questions such as: Why are the offenders motivated? Why are the victims vulnerable? And, why are guardians absent? Results show that actors bring with them unique sets of circumstances that influence the progression of the sexual assault event. Alcohol and/or drugs, broken relationships,, anger were common factors.

title: Individual, structural opportunities: A cross-national assessment of females’ physical, sexual assault victimization
authors: Stein, Rachel E
abstract: Opportunity theories are suited to cross-national research on victimization that incorporates a multilevel approach. Comparative research on non-lethal victimization often combines several types of violence into a single category of expressive crime. While expressive crimes do indeed share some characteristics, opportunities leading to specific types of victimization may vary. The current research uses the International Crime Victimization Survey (ICVS) to examine two types of expressive victimization: sexual, physical assault. These data are limited to female victims, as sexual assault in the ICVS is assessed only for females. These data provide a rich source of comparative information on opportunities leading to victimization. Opportunities have been traditionally examined at the individual level through routine activities, lifestyles theories. Opportunity at the structural level of analysis is less commonly employed; however, routine activities theory offers a framework for measuring structural opportunity. The results indicate a multilevel approach of opportunities on victimization is appropriate. Differences in opportunity leading to sexual, physical assault are most evident in the opportunities provided by the development level of the country. The impact of country development on physical assault victimization is moderated by the involvement in leisure activities outside of the home.

title: Violent victimization, hooking up among strangers, acquaintances on an urban campus: an exploratory study
authors: Tomsich, Elizabeth A, Schaible, Lonnie M, Marie Rennison, Callie, Gover, Angela R
abstract: College students anticipating a competitive labor market, arrested economic independence increasingly elect to delay romantic commitment, reproduction. Casual sexual relationships provide an alternative to the commitment required in traditional romantic relationships. Although committed, casual sexual relationships each have their benefits, both likewise have respective risks. The present exploratory study adds to the growing literature on 'hookups' among strangers, acquaintances by examining experiences with (a) hookups, (b) sexual violence,, (c) relationship violence in a nontraditional urban university sample. Findings from logit regression models indicate that gender, race, ethnicity, employment, relationship status, housing, class standing, psychological relationship abuse,, sexual assault by force significantly vary between students who report hooking up with strangers, acquaintances, those who do not. Gender-specific logit models find unique patterns of variables associated with hooking up. Findings are discussed with consideration of policy implications, the direction of future research.

title: Examining the relationship between sexual offenders, their victims: Interpersonal differences between stranger, non-stranger sexual offences
authors: Woods, Laura, Porter, Louise
abstract: Abstract The present study examined the behavioural differences in sexual assault offences in relation to the offender–victim relationship (stranger versus non-stranger). These differences were examined specifically in the context of four interpersonal themes of interaction: dominance, submission, hostility, cooperation. The details of 100 sexual offence cases (50 stranger, 50 non-stranger) were content-analysed, generating 58 dichotomous variables, covering offender, victim behaviour during the offence. χ2 tests comparing the two samples found that offenders who were strangers to their victims were more likely than non-stranger offenders to display behaviours that indicate a hostile, violent offence style. In contrast, those offenders who knew their victims were more likely than strangers to display a less violent, more personal, compliance-gaining offence style. These findings are discussed in terms of their implications for offender rehabilitation, victim support.

title: Transforming mobility justice: Gendered harassment, violence on transit
authors: Lubitow, Amy, Abelson, Miriam J, Carpenter, Erika
keywords: Mobilities; Mobility justice; Transgender; Public transit; Violence;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Mobility justice scholarship has shown that socially disadvantaged people experience uneven access to movement through various spaces, even 'immobility' based on their differential hold on resources, power. Scholarship on gendered mobilities demonstrates that public spaces, such as public transit, are structured in ways that serve to reproduce gender hierarchies. While much important work on gendered mobilities has focused on the unique limitations to mobility women experience in spaces such as public transport, there is little work that considers how other gender minorities experience mobility in these spaces. Drawing from 25 qualitative interviews with transgender, gender nonconforming public transit users in Portland, Oregon, this paper demonstrates that gender minorities experience significant challenges to their routine mobility on public transit. The consistency with which participants in this study experienced harassment, discrimination,, violence while attempting to use public transit suggests that scholarship on gendered mobilities must begin to theorize from a more expansive understanding of gender. Transport justice studies broadly,, the scholarship on gendered mobilities specifically, must move toward a more comprehensive understanding of the spectrum of gendered experiences that impact mobility, accessibility. The paper concludes with specific policy recommendations that could make direct impacts on the safety, comfort of transgender riders. While larger cultural, societal change is necessary to fully address these inequities, these smaller efforts would likely increase transgender people's use of public transportation.

abstract: This study identifies the first crime script for unsolved stranger sexual offenses against women. The purpose is to better understand the crime-commission process of solved, unsolved stranger sexual offenses, identify potential points of intervention for prevention purposes. Crime script analysis was performed on 542 solved (n = 265), unsolved (n = 277) cases based on police data in Queensland, Australia, followed by a comparison between solved, unsolved crime scripts. Results showed that unsolved offenses tended to be associated with the following factors: the offender fleeing/desisting, using minimal force, less intrusive sexual outcomes,, less verbal engagement with the victim. In these cases, there was a lack of information regarding forensic evidence, behavioral clues,, eyewitness leads. This highlights the relevance of focusing on situational crime prevention, policing strategies that may deter stranger sexual crimes at the earliest stages of the script.

abstract: Background: Karachi, London as megacities face huge challenges of providing safe environment for women in public spaces. Fear of sexual harassment on buses may cause domestic, transit captivity in women as public space is regarded as male domain. Purpose: The purpose of this study is to expose the perils of public sexual harassment; women encounter on public transport in the megacities-Karachi \& London. Findings: Comparative review evinced the gravity of sexual harassment in the megacities-Karachi, London, formulated baseline evidences for the law enforcement agencies to take strict action against the perpetrators to attenuate the jeopardy of sexual harassment on public transport. Literature on sociological studies, psychiatric assessments reveals that the crime leaves the victims in havoc of psychological, physical, emotional distresses which in turn damages their mental, social, personal wellbeing. title: Sexual harassment, assault in transit environments: A review of the English-language literature
authors: Ding, Hao, Loukaitou-Sideris, Anastasia, Agrawal, Asha Weinstein
abstract: The \#MeToo movement has brought much attention to crimes of sexual harassment in the workplace, but less attention has been given to such crimes taking place in transit environments. Reviewing international literature on sexual harassment, assault,, rape in transit environments, this article explores questions that relate to the nature, frequency,, impact of these crimes,, the strategies, interventions adopted by, recommended to public agencies to improve actual, perceived safety for riders. Highlighting an issue that primarily affects women, the article helps advocate for a better inclusion of women’s needs in planning for safety, mobility.

title: Routinising police-security collaborations: A prospective, mixed-methods experiment in British train stations
authors: Ariel, Barak, Gregory, Allan, Cronin, Luke, Ebbs, Benjamin, Wiffin, Melanie, Michel, Nicholas
abstract: Interagency cooperation may increase efficiency, cost-effectiveness in an era of resource austerity, increased workload for both the police, their partners. Yet the effect of a strategic police-security collaboration on routine operations across multiple sites is unknown. In a controlled experiment, we introduced an interagency collaboration between state, non-state guardianships to train stations across England. A mixed-methods approach, with multiple crime indicators, a survey administered with police officers, security partners, was applied through a series of before-and-after comparisons with staggered start dates to control for confounding variables. Crime recording, police proactivity, crisis intervention increased compared to controls. Security staff, officers valued collaboration, saw it as beneficial, efficient. The findings support police-private-security collaboration on crime, disorder, but more research with larger, more diverse samples, stricter control over rival explanations is needed.

title: Management, treatment of stalkers: problems, options,, solutions
authors: MacKenzie, Rachel D, James, David V
abstract: Legal sanctions alone are often ineffective in preventing stalking because, in the absence of treatment, the fundamental problems driving the stalker remain unresolved. Criminal justice interventions can be problematic because of difficulties in framing anti-stalking legislation, inconsistencies in their application. Civil remedies in the form of restraining orders may be ineffective or counterproductive. Treatment of stalkers involves pharmacotherapy when mental illness is present, but the mainstays of treatment for non-psychotic stalkers are programmes of psychological intervention. These depend on accurate assessment of the risks inherent in stalking, on the identification of psychological deficits, needs,, responsivity factors specific to the individual. Treatment can then be tailored to suit the stalker, thereby enhancing therapeutic efficacy. Developing a framework for identifying the risk factors, shaping the delivery of treatment is crucial. Two service innovations developed specifically to work with stalkers are presented as options to overcome current management deficiencies.

title: Understanding victim support as crime prevention work: The construction of young victims, villains in the dominant crime victim discourse in Sweden
authors: Hansen Löfstrand, Cecilia
journal: Journal of Scandinavian studies in criminology, crime prevention
abstract: Starting from the observation that a new victim category has emerged in the form of the ?young crime victim?, this article explores the notion of support to young crime victims as crime prevention work, considering it as an important constituent of the dominant crime victim discourse among support professionals. In the context of the support work, the (young) ?victim?, the (young) ?villain? provide mutually necessary counterparts constructed in relation to each other. Corresponding to this division, two approaches in criminal, crime prevention policy, practice are then analysed using Garland's notions of ?the criminology of the self?, ?the criminology of the other?. The first of these strategies is generally associated with rehabilitative measures (with the resulting normalization of the crime, its victims,, villains), while in the second punitive measures remain the norm (with the crime, its victims,, villains becoming ?Otherized?). Yet, as shown within the context of rehabilitation organized as support to young crime victims, both of these (at first glance mutually contradictory) discourses are drawn upon, operationalized by the professional support staff constructing images of young victims, villains in their daily work. Help-seeking youths resistant to identifying as victims remain represented as (possible future) villains.

title: Facilitating problem-, emotion-focused coping in victims of burglary: Evaluating a police crisis intervention program
authors: Winkel, F, Vrij, A
keywords: ADJUSTMENT (Psychology); BURGLARY; CRIME prevention; CRIMINAL investigation; EMOTIONS (Psychology); POLICE; coping; coping with crime;325\_Vic介入;318\_介入実験\_Policing;J Community Psychol
abstract: The impact of a police crisis intervention program on problem-, emotion- focused coping with burglary victims was assessed. Major program components included: conducting a criminal investigation in the victim's home, providing oral, written crime prevention information,, performing a security check. All participating police officers were trained in utilizing interview techniques facilitating emotion-, problem-focused coping with the event. Results suggested that the program actually facilitated coping with the event: Victims' perceived police protection against crime was enhanced; concern about crime was reduced; while preventive cognitions, prevention awareness, responsibility,, preventive intentions were strengthened, more extreme preventive options were generally rejected. Criminal investigations per se, however, may backfire, hamper coping processes. Several implications for future studies on victim intervention programs are discussed.

abstract: Intimate partner violence is one health-related outcome that has received growing attention from those interested in the role of neighborhood context. A limitation of existing contextual health research is its' failure to look beyond urban settings. Because suburban, rural areas have received so little attention, it is not clear whether data generated from urban samples can be generalized to non-urban geographic settings. We began to explore this issue using concept mapping, a participatory, mixed method approach. Data from 37 urban, 24 suburban women are used to explore, compare perceptions of neighborhood characteristics related to intimate partner violence. While several similarities exist between the perceptions of participants residing in urban, suburban areas, some differences were uncovered. These results provide valuable information regarding the perceived relationship between neighborhood context, intimate partner violence, suggest future avenues for research interested in examining the role of geographic setting.

title: An increasing risk of family violence during the Covid-19 pandemic: Strengthening community collaborations to save lives
authors: Campbell, Andrew M
keywords: Animal control; Child abuse; Coronavirus; Covid-19; Domestic violence; Multi-Disciplinary; Pet abuse; Prevention;322\_経済圧力;308\_STC
abstract: Though necessary to slow the spread of the novel Coronavirus (Covid-19), actions such as social-distancing, sheltering in-place, restricted travel,, closures of key community foundations are likely to dramatically increase the risk for family violence around the globe. In fact many countries are already indicating a dramatic increase in reported cases of domestic violence. While no clear precedent for the current crisis exists in academic literature, exploring the impact of natural disasters on family violence reports may provide important insight for family violence victim-serving professionals. Improving collaborations between human welfare, animal welfare agencies, expanding community partnerships,, informing the public of the great importance of reporting any concerns of abuse are all critical at this time.

title: Psychological distress, anxiety, family violence, suicidality,, wellbeing in New Zealand during the COVID-19 lockdown: A cross-sectional study
authors: Every-Palmer, Susanna, Jenkins, Matthew, Gendall, Philip, Hoek, Janet, Beaglehole, Ben, Bell, Caroline, Williman, Jonathan, Rapsey, Charlene, Stanley, James
keywords: Sciences: Comprehensive Works; COVID 19; Suicide; Pandemics; Anxiety; Mental health, psychiatry; Surveys; Ethnicities; Clinical psychology; Population; Mental health; Domestic violence; Essential workers; Psychological factors; Young adults; Violence; Anxieties; COVID-19; Viral diseases; Ethnicity; Economic impact; Mental disorders; Aggression; Coronaviruses; Medicine; Minority \& ethnic groups; Public health; Data collection; Mental depression; Alcohol; Reporting; Glutamate decarboxylase; Suicides \& suicide attempts; New Zealand;322\_経済圧力;308\_STC
abstract: New Zealand's early response to the novel coronavirus pandemic included a strict lockdown which eliminated community transmission of COVID-19. However, this success was not without cost, both economic, social. In our study, we examined the psychological wellbeing of New Zealanders during the COVID-19 lockdown when restrictions reduced social contact, limited recreation opportunities,, resulted in job losses, financial insecurity. We conducted an online panel survey of a demographically representative sample of 2010 adult New Zealanders in April 2020. The survey contained three standardised measures-the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), the GAD-7,, the Well-Being Index (WHO-5)-as well as questions designed specifically to measure family violence, suicidal ideation,, alcohol consumption. It also included items assessing positive aspects of the lockdown. Thirty percent of respondents reported moderate to severe psychological distress (K10), 16\% moderate to high levels of anxiety,, 39\% low wellbeing; well above baseline measures. Poorer outcomes were seen among young people, those who had lost jobs or had less work, those with poor health status,, who had past diagnoses of mental illness. Suicidal ideation was reported by 6\%, with 2\% reporting making plans for suicide, 2\% reporting suicide attempts. Suicidality was highest in those aged 18-34. Just under 10\% of participants had directly experienced some form of family harm over the lockdown period. However, not all consequences of the lockdown were negative, with 62\% reporting 'silver linings', which included enjoying working from home, spending more time with family,, a quieter, less polluted environment. New Zealand's lockdown successfully eliminated COVID-19 from the community, but our results show this achievement brought a significant psychological toll. Although much of the debate about lockdown measures has focused on their economic effects, our findings emphasise the need to pay equal attention to their effects on psychological wellbeing.

title: Abuse, self-harm, suicidal ideation in the UK during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Iob, Eleonora, Steptoe, Andrew, Fancourt, Daisy

The reported frequency of abuse, self-harm, thoughts of suicide/self-harm was higher among women, Black, Asian, minority ethnic (BAME) groups, people experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage, unemployment, disability, chronic physical illnesses, mental disorders, COVID-19 diagnosis. Psychiatric medications were the most common type of support being used, but fewer than half of those affected were accessing formal or informal support.

title: Strengthening community-level understanding of, responses to intimate partner violence using geographic information systems (GIS)

abstract: Purpose – Recently, there has been increased attention to community-, neighborhood-level influences on rates, experiences of intimate partner violence (IPV). The purpose of this paper is to describe the use of geographic information systems (GIS) to geographically analyze these influences in order to enhance community-level understanding of, responses to IPV. Design/methodology/approach – The authors review existing literature supporting the needs for this level of analysis,, then they present eight steps for researchers, practitioners to use when applying GIS to analyze IPV. Findings – This is a conceptual paper. Research limitations/implications – This paper offers researchers, practitioners suggested strategies for using GIS analyses to examine community-level influences on IPV in future research. Practical implications – The practical implications of using GIS analyses are discussed, including ways that the findings of these analyses can be used to enhance community-level resources to prevent, respond to IPV. Social implications – This innovative, interdisciplinary approach offers new insights into understanding, addressing IPV at a community level. Originality/value – To date, there has been minimal research used to apply GIS analyses to the problem of IPV in communities. This paper presents a framework for future researchers, practitioners to apply this methodology to expand on community-level understanding of IPV.

title: Employment, crime: A longitudinal follow-up of organized crime offenders
authors: van Koppen, Vere, van der Geest, Victor, Kleemans, Edward, Kruisbergen, Edwin
abstract: Employment is considered to help offenders desist from crime. Studies focusing on organized crime offenders, however, have suggested that employment may promote rather than inhibit crime for these offenders, but lacked quantitative individual-level data to confirm this finding. Using a large sample of organized crime offenders ( N = 1921), longitudinal individual data on offending, employment, income, financial support, the current study aims to clarify the role of employment in the offending careers of these offenders. Fixed effects models show the effects of employment, self-employment, employment on the payroll. For organized crime offenders, being employed is associated with a 10 percent increase in offending, having their own business is associated with a 23 percent increase in offending. For organized crime offenders in leadership positions, employment is associated with a 47 percent increase in offending, owning a business is associated with a 68 percent increase in offending.

abstract: Purpose The purpose of this paper is to reflect upon the challenges posed for the ongoing implementation of multi-agency risk assessment conferences (MARACs) for police forces in England, Wales during the 2020 pandemic. Design/methodology/approach This is rapid response research involving qualitative methods primarily online semi-structured interviewing with a sample of police domestic abuse leads in England, Wales. Findings The findings point to increased use of virtual platforms particularly for MARACs, that this has beneficial consequences both for the police, in their view also for victim-survivors. Research limitations/implications The findings reported here are from policing domestic abuse leads. More work needs to be done to explore the value of engaging in virtual MARACs for all the agencies concerned but also whether MARACs continue to be the best way to ensure the victim-survivor is kept in view. Practical implications The use of virtual platforms carries a range of practice implications for the future of MARACs for the foreseeable future. These range from ensuring attendance of the appropriate agencies to the range, frequency of meetings, to infrastructural support for all agencies to engage. Originality/value This is an original study funded by the Economic, Social Research Council examining police, court responses to domestic abuse during the covid-19 pandemic.

title: Strain, violence: Testing a general strain theory model of community violence
authors: Warner, Barbara D, Fowler, Shannon K
abstract: Agnew's General Strain Theory (GST) has come to be recognized as an increasingly important explanation for violence at the individual level. Drawing on this individual level theory, Agnew [Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency 36 (1999) 123] recently suggested that GST might also be applicable to explaining variations in community crime rates. This macro level General Strain Theory (MST) has, however, rarely been empirically examined. This article provides an examination of some of the central ideas in Agnew's MST using data from sixty-six neighborhoods in a southern state. The findings presented here suggest that neighborhood disadvantage, stability significantly affect neighborhood levels of strain. In turn, strain significantly affects levels of violence. The extent to which the effects of strain on violence are conditioned by levels of informal social control, social support/capital are also examined in this article. The results are partially supportive of MST.

title: Sexual assault victimization, fear of sexual assault,, self-protective behaviors: A test of general strain theory
authors: Archer, Robert Joseph Lee
abstract: ABSTRACTAccording to Agnew?s General Strain Theory, many individuals who experience strain are more likely to engage in crime or become delinquent. To date, past research has examined the relationship between victimization, fear of crime, as well as the corresponding relationship between fear of crime, self-protective behaviors. Yet, the mediating role fear of sexual assault may have in accounting for the association between prior sexual assault victimization, self-protective behaviors has not been evaluated. The current study addresses this gap in the literature using data collected from a random sample of college students from 12 universities in the United States. The results indicated that the relationship between prior sexual assault victimization, self-protective behavior is partially mediated by fear of sexual assault. The study concludes with a discussion of implications, limitations, as well as directions for future research.

title: Crime dynamics under COVID-19 emergency measures in Nigeria: An exploration of residents’ perception
authors: Badiora, Adewumi I, Dada, Olanrewaju T, Odufuwa, Bashir O, Adeniyi, Adeyemi S, Omoniyi, Sunday S

abstract: This study examines how the COVID-19 emergency has impacted crime across different locations in Nigeria. Data were collected from a sample of residents from across Nigeria, analysed using mean ratings, percentages, chi-square. Based on the residents' perceptions, certain crime types have decreased (e.g. home break-ins, assaults), some remain unchanged (e.g. stealing, pilfering), others have increased (e.g. cybercrime, domestic violence). The findings show concentrations of crime in urban centres, states on total lockdown, geographical areas with poor economic indicators. The times that most crimes are perpetrated remain unchanged, except for the night time, where there has been a significant increase. Generally, individual responses to crime remain unchanged, although the use of security guards, special security door locks has changed significantly. Conversely, neighbourhood-level responses have changed significantly, particularly with the use of vigilante groups, police, military patrols as well as restrictions of human, vehicular movement. Although some of the causes of this crime change existed before COVID-19, new crime opportunities are also acknowledged. The findings suggest that Nigerian cities may face a severe battle to recover from crime even after the COVID-19 emergency has passed. Policy, further research implications are discussed.

title: Routine activity theory, the risk of rape: Analyzing ten years of national crime survey data
authors: Belknap, Joanne

abstract: This analysis applies routine activity theory to the risk of rape, using 10 years (1973-82) of NCS data. In addition to univariate analysis describing characteristics of the victimization itself, bivariate, multivariate (discriminant) analyses are employed to assess the risk of rape, comparing 762 rape, attempted rape victims with 2,523 randomly selected non-rape victims. Most characteristics concerning the rape incident itself (e.g., time of day, season) were consistent with routine activity theory. However, the place of occurrence was not. Additionally, discriminant analysis showed that marital status, age, family income,, the number of living units per structure appear to be the strongest predictors of the risk of rape. Unlike most prior research, race was not a factor in the risk of rape, although race was correlated with those factors influencing the risk of rape. Given the fundamental level of these predictor variables, the likelihood of affecting the level of rape through policy appears limited.

title: Youth exposure to community violence: Association with aggression, victimization,, risk behaviors

abstract: ABSTRACT The purpose of this study was to examine the association between exposure to community violence, aggression, victimization,, risk-taking behaviors among young adolescents. Secondary analysis was conducted on data from a cross-sectional survey of 8,259 sixth, seventh,, eighth grade students from eight urban schools in Texas. Results indicated that students exposed to a high level of community violence were 7.7 times more likely to carry a handgun, 5.2 times more likely to be involved in a gang were 6.4 times more likely to use marijuana, 5.3 times more likely to binge drink,, 2.8 times more likely to be injured as a result of fighting. This suggests the need for an interdisciplinary approach to violence prevention that targets all the environments of youth, including schools, homes, neighborhoods,, other community units.

title: Youth behavior, school structure,, student risk of victimization
authors: Burrow, John D, Apel, Robert
