abstract: Although a growing body of research on student safety focuses on school disorder, school climate,, the intersection of community/situational factors, comparatively less research has focused specifically on the individual‐, school‐level factors that put students at risk of victimization in the immediate school environ. The present study is an attempt to broaden our understanding of the contribution of schools, school behavior to the victimization experiences of students. We compare traditional routine activity constructs to understand whether, how they differentially influence the risk of community, school victimization. Additionally, we investigate what school‐related variables (behavioral, structural) explain variation in young people’s risk for school victimization.

title: Who are the mavens of bystander intervention? Implications for the social diffusion of intervention norms

abstract: A recent randomized controlled trial reported that Green Dot (GD)-a bystander intervention training program that targets popular opinion leaders for intensive training-reduced school-level interpersonal violence perpetration, victimization. Expanding GD's targeted group members to include ``mavens'' of bystander intervention-those who spread bystander intervention norms to others by communicating with peers-may increase the effectiveness of such training. Self-report data collected from students at the 13 intervention high schools in Kentucky are analyzed to identify characteristics of those who engage in discussions with peers about preventing interpersonal violence. Findings show that students who engage in more frequent bystander behaviors are more likely to have such conversations with peers, but GD participants were no more likely than nonparticipants to discuss preventing interpersonal violence with peers.

title: Does change in binge drinking reduce risk of repeat sexual assault victimization? Evidence from three cohorts of freshman undergraduate women
authors: Butler, Leah C, Fisher, Bonnie S, Reyns, Bradford W
abstract: Many college students who experience sexual assault experience subsequent (i.e., repeat) sexual assault incidents. There is also an established relationship between sexual assault, binge drinking. The “once bitten, twice shy” (OBTS) hypothesis suggests that those who experience alcohol- or drug-related (AOD) sexual assault would reduce how frequently they binge drink in an effort to avoid repeat victimization. We test this hypothesis by analyzing two years of survey data collected from a panel of three cohorts of freshmen women. Supportive of OBTS, our analyses reveal that students who experienced an AOD-related sexual assault at time 1 only reduced the number of days they binge drank from time 1 to time 2, that this change significantly differed from repeat victims. Implications for efforts to reduce sexual victimization against college women are discussed.

title: Change matters: Binge drinking, drugging victimization over time in three college freshman cohorts
authors: Butler, Leah C, Fisher, Bonnie S, Schilling, Rachael, Lasky, Nicole V, Swan, Suzanne C
abstract: The once bitten, twice shy (OBTS) hypothesis argues that crime victims who change their involvement in risky lifestyle behaviors reduce their likelihood of experiencing repeat victimization. Tests of this hypothesis have yielded weak to mixed results, which may be due to methodological issues. We address these methodological issues by testing the OBTS hypothesis for repeat drugging victimization with survey data from a panel of three freshman cohorts at three large, public universities. Supportive of the OBTS hypothesis, the multivariate results show that, on average, those not drugged at Time 1 or Time 2, those drugged at Time 1, Time 2 increased the number of days they binge drank in the past month significantly more than those who were drugged at Time 1 only. Our findings have implications for both victimology theory, drugging prevention programming.

title: Reconstructing, sequencing behaviours in multiple perpetrator rape
authors: Chambers, Jemma C, Horvath, Miranda A H, Kelly, Liz
abstract: Abstract Much of the existing knowledge base of multiple perpetrator rape (MPR) comes from studies undertaken more than 20 years ago,, thus fails to integrate contemporary perspectives on sexual violence. The current study used Grounded Theory methodology to construct a holistic model of MPR from 15 victim accounts. The model of multiple perpetrator rape (MMPR) included both the actions of the perpetrators, the reactions of the victim in a temporal sequence of 13 categories, 9 of which had sub-categories that allowed for individual differences. Broad themes of MPR were then explored using a total of 101 cases. Each case was coded in the 9 sub-categories where individual differences were allowed from the model. An associative analysis of these sub-categories was then performed using Smallest Space Analysis. Two dominant themes were displayed. The Manipulate theme included two perpetrators who offended sequentially, socialised with the victim. The Force theme did not involve any social interaction, as the force, teamwork of the group enabled the victim to be physically overpowered.

title: Sorority affiliation, sexual assault victimization: Assessing vulnerability using path analysis: Assessing vulnerability using path analysis
authors: Franklin, Cortney A
keywords: peer support; routine activity theory; self-control; sexual assault; social learning theory; sorority affiliation; victimization;321\_SA実証研究;z\_2012\_jacp;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: The current research used survey data from 282 college women to investigate the relationship between female Greek membership, sexual assault victimization. Drawing from routine activity theory, low self-control,, social learning theory, this study tested a theoretical model that identified pertinent factors present among sorority environments to determine the relationships between Greek affiliation, sexual assault. Path analyses revealed that sorority women reported consuming more alcohol, with greater frequency, increased risk-taking behavior, delayed assessments of threat, responses to risk,, increased contact with fraternity men-all of which significantly predicted sexual assault. Future theory, research,, policy directions are proposed.

title: Feminist self-defense, resistance training for college students: a critical review, recommendations for the future: A critical review, recommendations for the future
authors: Gidycz, Christine A, Dardis, Christina M
abstract: There remains resistance to feminist self-defense, resistance training programming for women, despite (a) documented effectiveness of rape resistance strategies in avoiding rape, (b) consistently high rates of sexual victimization on college campuses,, (c) limited evidence of lasting change in sexual assault perpetration reduction within existing men's prevention programs. The current article seeks to discuss (1) the rationale for feminist self-defense, resistance training for women, (2) key components of feminist self-defense, resistance training, (3) barriers to its implementation, (4) outcomes of self-defense, resistance training programming,, (5) recommendations for future work. Such suggestions include increasing funding for large-scale self-defense, rape resistance outcome research to examine program effectiveness. Specifically, outcome research that examines the role of contextual factors (e.g., alcohol use), women's victimization histories is needed. Finally, self-defense training, resistance training should be combined with bystander intervention, men's programs with the goal of providing synergistic effects on rape reduction.

title: Is the use of protective behavioral strategies associated with college sexual assault victimization? A prospective examination
authors: Gilmore, Amanda K, Maples-Keller, Jessica L, Pinsky, Hanna T, Shepard, Molly E, Lewis, Melissa A, George, William H
keywords: college women; protective behavioral strategies; sexual assault;321\_SA実証研究;z\_2012\_jacp;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Sexual assault protective behavioral strategies (PBS) may be negatively associated with sexual assault victimization. However, no studies to date have prospectively examined whether the use of sexual assault PBS is negatively associated with subsequent sexual assault experiences. The current study examined the association between the use of sexual assault PBS, subsequent sexual assault victimization severity. College women who reported engaging in heavy episodic drinking ( n = 77) were assessed online for their use of sexual assault PBS, history of sexual assault victimization. In addition, a 3-month follow-up survey was given assessing sexual assault victimization severity in the past 3 months. The use of sexual assault PBS was negatively associated with sexual assault severity in the 3-month follow-up period. Future research should further examine these PBS to create more college-specific PBS, to determine whether they are useful as risk-reduction strategies.

title: Prediction of women's utilization of resistance strategies in a sexual assault situation: a prospective study: A prospective study
authors: Gidycz, Christine A, Van Wynsberghe, Amy, Edwards, Katie M
keywords: College Students; Females; Rape; Survivors; Americans; Drug Abuse; Inappropriate Sexual Behavior; Suicidality; Eating Disorders; Young Adults; Sexual Experiences Survey (Koss, Oros); National College Health Risk Behavior Survey;321\_SA実証研究;z\_2012\_jacp;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;J Interpers Violence
abstract: The present study prospectively explored the predictors of resistance strategies to a sexual assault situation. Participants were assessed at the beginning of an academic quarter on a number of variables, including past history of sexual victimization, perceived risk of sexual victimization,, intentions to use specific types of resistance strategies. Only women who reported being victimized over the interim (N=68) were included in the analyses, which suggested that women's Time 1 intentions to utilize assertive resistance strategies (e.g., physically fight, run away), offender aggression predicted women's use of assertive resistance strategies in response to the assault that occurred over the follow-up. Women's utilization of nonforceful verbal resistance (e.g., reason, plead, quarrel) was predicted by perpetrator aggression, previous sexual victimization. Women's immobility (e.g., turn cold, freeze) during the assault that took place over the interim was predicted by experiences of childhood sexual victimization, previous sexual victimization.

title: Commitment, crime,, the responsive bystander: effect of the commitment form, conformism
authors: Guéguen, Nicolas, Dupré, Mickaël, Georget, Patrice, Sénémeaud, Cécile
abstract: Research has shown that eliciting commitment is a valuable way of inciting people to act, even in emergencies, dangerous situations. The purpose of the two studies presented here was to explore the relation between the form of commitment used to prevent a crime, the moderating effect exerted by the number of passive observers of this crime. At a bus stop, a first confederate put a bag down on the ground upon arriving, immediately left to withdraw money from an automated teller machine near the bus stop. Two male participants were present at the bus stop. In Study 1, the confederate said nothing (control), directly asked one participant to watch his bag (direct commitment), or asked all present to watch his bag (indirect commitment). About 30 seconds later, a male confederate walked up to the victim's bag, picked it up,, quickly walked away in the opposite direction of the victim. A total of 150 participants (50 per condition) were observed. It was found that 34\% intervened in the control condition, 88\% in the direct commitment condition,, 56\% in the indirect commitment condition. In Study 2, 150 participants (50 per condition) were observed while two male confederates were present at the bus stop with the instruction not to react to the theft. It was found that more intervention was found in the direct commitment condition (88\%) than in the control condition (18\%). However, the indirect commitment condition did not elicit higher intervention (22\%). Variation in the level of personal responsibility to help the victim is used to explain these differences.

title: Exploring bystander presence, intervention in nonfatal violent victimization: when does helping really help?
authors: Hart, Timothy C, Miethe, Terance D
keywords: BYSTANDER effect; HELPING behavior; ASSISTANCE in emergencies; VIOLENCE; VICTIMS; HUMAN behavior; bystander intervention; conjunctive analysis; quantitative comparative analysis; situational context; third-party involvement; Natl crime surveys;321\_SA実証研究;301\_ComCrm;Violence Vict
abstract: The current research explores two important issues related to the study of bystander intervention during nonfatal violent victimization. First, using data from the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS), conjunctive analysis of case configurations is conducted to identify the most dominant situational contexts in which a bystander is present during violent crime. Second, the prevalence of responses in which a bystander helps or hurts during these events is determined. Results, the analytical approach used in this investigation are discussed in terms of their implications for future research on the normative, deviant reactions to crime by third parties, its victims.

title: Perceived risks, crime prevention strategies of Japanese high school, university students
authors: Honda, Akio, Yamanoha, Tsuyoshi
keywords: 321\_SA実証研究;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;9\_001\_intro;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Crime Prevention, Community Safety;CPCS2008-2016;Japan
abstract: This study was undertaken to investigate Japanese high school, university students’ perceived risks, their crime prevention strategies. Gender differences, the effects of their type of residence were also examined. Six types of crime prevention strategy were identified: vigilance, avoiding dangerous areas, risk management, avoiding dangerous routes, self-monitoring, avoiding going out at night. The results of our study indicate that women have greater perceived risks, more awareness of avoidance-related strategies than men. University students reported greater perceived risks than did high school students but were aware of fewer crime prevention strategies. Data on university students showed similar effects of type of residence: residents of single-family dwellings reported greater perceived risks than did those of multiple-family dwellings, although the former type of residence exerts negative impacts on their awareness of precautionary behaviors. These findings suggest that adolescents’ housing choices might increase perceived risks, but decrease or restrict their awareness of crime prevention strategies.

title: College women's fears, precautionary behaviors relating to acquaintance rape, stranger rape
authors: Hickman, Susan E, Muehlenhard, Charlene L
keywords: fear of crime; precautionary behaviors; acquaintance rape; stranger rape, female college students; Attitudes; Behavior; Fear; Rape; Female Attitudes; Human Females;321\_SA実証研究;z\_pmt2009\_crime;9\_2012\_心研(10章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2012心研;99\_文献なし
abstract: Past research on women's fear of rape has focused on women's fears relating to stranger rape, even though most rapes are acquaintance rapes. In this study, 139 undergraduate women completed a questionnaire concerning their fears, precautionary behaviors,, beliefs relating to acquaintance, stranger rape. Women reported being more fearful of rape by strangers than by acquaintances,, they reported engaging in more precautionary behaviors because of fear of stranger rape than of acquaintance rape. When asked to self-generate situations in which they feared rape, they generated more situations in which they feared stranger rape than acquaintance rape. Paradoxically, they estimated that acquaintance rape was more common. Precautionary behaviors were best predicted by level of fear. A history of acquaintance rape had no effect on women's responses. Theoretical, educational implications are discussed.

title: Criminology, criminal justice, law \& society avoidance behaviors in a campus residential environment
authors: Hibdon, Julie, Hibdon, Julie, Schafer, Joseph, Lee, Charern, Summers, Monica
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Research; Behavior; Theory; School safety; Perceptions; Studies; College campuses; Gender; College students; Victimization; Self help; Crime prevention; Criminology; Learning;321\_SA実証研究;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;301\_5;CampusCrime
abstract: Over the last several decades, campus crime, victimization,, incidents of violence have been a focal concern for campus administrators, have generated interest in the research community. Studies have provided insight into the nature of campus crime, victimization, as well as whether these concerns relate with fear of crime, perceptions of risk. Less consideration has been given to the relationship between these variables, the use of protective action among college students, especially those residing in student housing environments. This study uses survey data from students residing in campus housing at a Midwestern university to examine how fear of crime, perceived risk of victimization,, other relevant concepts predict student protective action and, more specifically, the use of avoidance behaviors. The findings suggest that White, female residents, as well as those who were more fearful of crime, had prior victimization experiences, were more likely to engage in avoidance behaviors.

title: Health, sexual outcomes of women who have experienced forced or coercive sex
authors: Jozkowski, Kristen N, Sanders, Stephanie A
abstract: Previous research has linked women's history of experiencing sexual assault with negative health outcomes; however, much of this research is over a decade old. Furthermore, little research has examined the relationship between sexual assault, women's sexuality. In the current study the authors aimed to assess the relation of experiencing sexual assault to women's health, sexuality, the relation of repeat victimization by multiple different perpetrators to such outcomes. Data were collected from a convenience sample of 2,915 women using an online questionnaire. Nearly half (n = 1,394, 47.8\%) indicated having experienced forced or coercive sex. Women who had experienced forced or coercive sex were more likely to report negative health outcomes (Adj. OR = 1.56; 95\% CI: 1.35-1.82, p < .001), some negative sexual outcomes compared to women without a history of forced or coercive sex. Similarly, women who experienced repeat victimizations by multiple different perpetrators were even more likely to report negative health outcomes (Adj. OR = 1.43; 95\% CI: 1.28-1.59, p < .001) as well as some negative sexual outcomes. Healthcare providers should be aware of the relation of sexual assault to health, sexuality, continue to address health, sexuality issues associated with sexual assault for their patients.

title: A multi-level approach to investigating neighborhood effects on physical aggression among urban Chicago youth
authors: Jennings, Wesley G, Maldonado-Molina, Mildred M, Reingle, Jennifer M, Komro, Kelli A
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
keywords: Adolescence; Aggression; Multilevel; Neighborhood; Urban;321\_SA実証研究;z\_urban\_socio\_root;10\_英語の研究;12\_Chicago;301\_ComCrm
abstract: The current study evaluates neighborhood effects, individual-level effects,, demographic characteristics that influence physically aggressive behavior among urban youth. Using data derived from 5,812 adolescents from Project Northland Chicago (PNC), Heirarchical Linear Modeling (HLM) techniques, the results suggested that neighborhood problems significantly predicted physical aggression, before, after adjustment for individual-level risk factors (alcohol use, peer alcohol use, lack of adult supervision,, depression), demographics. After accounting for baseline physical aggression, however, neighborhood problems were no longer a significant predictor of physical aggression. Implications for intervention at both the neighborhood, individual-level, study limitations are also discussed.

title: Violence against women: Conditions, consequences,, coping
authors: Löbmann, Rebecca, Greve, Werner, Wetzels, Peter, Bosold, Christiane
abstract: This article gives a structured summary of current research on violence against women from a European perspective. First, some thought is given to the correct definition of violence against women. Then, different manifestations of violence are presented along with prevalence data. Next, the paper discusses risk markers for victimization, goes on to describe the consequences for the victims. Particular emphasis is placed on coping processes, their relevance for research in this field. Finally, conclusions are drawn from a prevention, intervention perspective.

title: Intimidation, street gangs: Understanding the response of victims, bystanders to perceived gang violence
authors: Melde, Chris, Rennison, Callie Marie
abstract: While research routinely examines the influence of gang membership on the quantity of violent crime involvement, less is known about the influence of gang violence on the situational characteristics of violent victimization. Felson’s discussion of street gangs highlights the possible functional role gang membership plays in the commission of violent crime; what he terms “the street gang strategy.” This study examines the functionality of gang membership during violent crimes by investigating the influence of perceived gang membership on the likelihood of victim resistance, bystander intervention,, police reporting using data from the National Crime Victimization Survey. Findings offer little support for the idea that gang members intimidate victims, bystanders to the extent that their behavior during, after violence differs systematically from responses resulting from non‐gang violence. Results are discussed in terms of their policy relevance, implications for future research.

title: The use of drinking, sexual assault protective behavioral strategies: Associations with sexual victimization, revictimization among college women
authors: Neilson, Elizabeth C, Gilmore, Amanda K, Pinsky, Hanna T, Shepard, Molly E, Lewis, Melissa A, George, William H
keywords: alcohol use; college women; protective behavioral strategies; sexual assault;321\_SA実証研究;z\_2012\_jacp;J Interpers Violence;CampusCrime
abstract: Despite consistent high rates of campus sexual assault, little research has examined effective strategies to decrease sexual assault victimization. Sexual assault, drinking protective behavioral strategies (PBS) may be important means of reducing sexual assault victimization risk on college campuses but need further examination. The current study examined the relationship among sexual assault in childhood, before college,, since college to evaluate the mitigating roles of both sexual assault PBS, drinking PBS on sexual assault victimization. Participants (n = 620) were undergraduate women, 18 to 20 years old. The current study was a cross-sectional online survey assessing participants' sexual assault PBS, sexual assault history. Sexual assault history was positively associated with future sexual assault experiences. Pre-college sexual assault was associated with increased since-college sexual assault, increased drinks per week. Since-college adolescent/adult sexual assault was associated with less use of sexual assault PBS. These findings suggest that PBS may have an important role in sexual assault victimization, future research should examine their usefulness in risk reduction programs for college women.

title: College women's perceived risk to experience sexual victimization: a prospective analysis
authors: Orchowski, Lindsay M, Creech, Suzannah K, Reddy, Madhavi K, Capezza, Nicole M, Ratcliff, Tanya
keywords: Sociology; Women; Sex crimes; Rape; College students; Teenagers; United States; Young Adult; Questionnaires; Students -- statistics \& numerical data; Humans; Health Status; Peer Group; Spouse Abuse -- statistics \& numerical data; Life Style; Prospective Studies; Risk Factors; Adult; Social Support; Female; Substance-Related Disorders -- epidemiology; Sexual Behavior -- statistics \& numerical data; Students -- psychology; Aggression -- psychology; Crime Victims -- psychology; Interpersonal Relations; Spouse Abuse -- psychology;321\_SA実証研究;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303
abstract: This study implemented a prospective design to explore college women's perceived risk to experience sexual victimization over a 2-month interim (N = 143). Compared to women without such histories, women with a history of unwanted sexual contact via arguments/ pressure, or a history of unwanted sexual intercourse via administration of alcohol/drugs reported higher perceived risk to subsequently experience these forms of victimization. Compared to women who were not victimized, women who subsequently experienced unwanted sexual intercourse via administration of alcohol/drugs or arguments/pressure reported higher levels of risk to experience these forms of victimization. Controlling for victimization history, higher levels of risk to experience sexual intercourse over the interim via arguments predicted this form of victimization over the follow-up. Implications are discussed.

title: College women's likelihood to report unwanted sexual experiences to campus agencies: Trends, correlates
authors: Orchowski, Lindsay M, Meyer, Douglas H, Gidycz, Christine A
abstract: The present study examined college women's likelihood to report sexual victimization to the police, a friend, the counseling center, their resident advisor, or on a survey (N = 300). In comparison to other forms of reporting, women perceived themselves to be most likely to report victimization on a survey. Women also indicated a higher likelihood to report to friends rather than to other agencies. Likelihood to report on a survey did not vary as a function of history of sexual victimization; however, women with a victimization history indicated a lower likelihood to report to all agencies compared to women without a victimization history. Correlates of women's likelihood to report were also documented.

title: Whither women's fear? Perceptions of sexual violence in public, private space
authors: Pain, R
abstract: This paper assesses explanations for women's fear of sexual violence. Many existing analyses share a common theoretical basis, but certain conflicts arise in the empirical evidence. These concern a number of paradoxes between fear, violence, in terms of their extent, their nature, in particular their spatial situation. A research project on women's fear of crime in Edinburgh aimed to improve understanding of these. Evidence from the questionnaire survey showed a further mismatch between women's common sense knowledge about general risks, their perceptions of personal risk. Many women know that the usual location of violence is private space, yet only fear attack in public places. Data from qualitative interviews suggest that this contradiction is preserved by the tendency to distance violence from the self, a process which is central to the management of danger, consequent lifestyle adaptation.

title: Safety concerns, fear, precautionary behavior among college women: An exploratory examination of two measures of residency
authors: Pritchard, Adam J, Jordan, Carol E, Wilcox, Pamela
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Women; Studies; Sex crimes; College students; College campuses; Crime; United States--US;321\_SA実証研究;301\_ComCrm;Security Journal;CampusCrime
abstract: This study examines the impact of two distinct measures of residency on college women's perceptions of safety, fear of crime, precautionary behaviors within both on-campus, off-campus areas. A student's current residency either on- or off-campus, a student's prior residency in a metropolitan, micropolitan or rural county prior to college are compared across these three aspects of campus safety. Current residency is found to be significantly related to a student's perceptions of safety in off-campus areas around campus, as well as the likelihood of engaging in precautionary behaviors such as avoiding specific locations on campus or carrying or keeping something (for example, weapons) for protection. Prior residency, on the other hand, was not found to impact perceptions of safety, fear of crime or precautionary behaviors.

title: Cyberbullying victimization, adaptive avoidance behaviors at school
authors: Randa, Ryan, Reyns, Bradford W
abstract: Using data from the 2009 National Crime Victimization Survey, School Crime Supplement (NCVS-SCS) the current study explores the relationships between traditional bullying victimization, cyberbullying victimization,, victim adaptive avoidance behaviors. Like traditional forms of bullying, the cyberbullying literature base is developing, growing into a targeted area of emphasis in 21st century victimology. We explore the effects of these online victimization experiences, net of the impacts of traditional bullying, fear of victimization at school. Based on logistic regression analysis the results indicate that cyberbullying victimization experiences are significantly related to avoidance behaviors at school.

title: Routine activities, criminal victimization: The significance of gendered spaces
authors: Savard, Dennis M, Kelley, Thomas M, Merolla, David M
keywords: criminal victimization; gender; gendered spaces; routine activity theory;321\_SA実証研究;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Gender is arguably the most prominent correlate of criminal victimization. Few studies, however, examine gender-specific dynamics that might help advance criminology's understanding of the persistent gender gap in criminal victimization. We attempt to help fill this research void by examining data from the 2012 National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) through the lens of routine activity theory to investigate the relationship between ``gendered spaces'', criminal victimization. We propose that gendered spaces constructed by people's routine activities may increase their exposure to motivated offenders, which in turn may increase their risk of victimization. Our findings appear to support our proposition, to shed new light on the nature of the victimization gender gap. The results showed that females were significantly more likely than males to be victimized at each of the three ``feminine gendered spaces'' (i.e., bank, shopping center,, grocery store). However, the relationship between gendered space, criminal victimization varied by crime type. Females were significantly more likely than males to be robbed at each of the three feminine gendered spaces. For sexual assault, aggravated assault, females were significantly more likely than males to be victimized at a ``masculine gendered space'' (i.e., bar/nightclub). For simple assault, females were significantly less likely than males to be victimized at two of the three feminine gendered spaces (i.e., bank, shopping center). Our findings appear to highlight the importance of gendered spaces in helping explain the gender gap in criminal victimization, suggest that future researchers should investigate how other gendered spaces formed by people's routine activities affect their risk of victimization.

title: College students' lifestyles, self-protective behaviors: Further considerations of the guardianship concept in routine activity theory
authors: Tewksbury, Richard, Mustaine, Elizabeth Ehrhardt
keywords: college students; lifestyle; self-protective behaviors; self-protective devices; routine activity theory; Victimization risk; targets for crime; criminal events; Crime Prevention; Self Defense; Victimization; Activity Theory; Crime; Crime Victims; Daily Activities; Risk Factors;321\_SA実証研究;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303;Criminal Justice, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: Routine activity theory has traditionally emphasized identifying victimization risks, suitable targets for crime. Assessments of the role of guardianship in criminal events are less emphasized. Explorations of who uses guardianship to attempt to reduce their chances for victimization have been developed only minimally, typically relying on demographics. This research goes further in assessing who uses self-protective strategies, considering lifestyles related to proximity to motivated offenders, the suitability of individuals as targets,, how these characteristics influence the use of self-protective devices. Results show the most influential lifestyle characteristics, behaviors on use of self-protective measures are exposure to potential offenders, neighborhood characteristics. Fear of crime, substance use,, individual demographics show only small relationships to guardianship.

title: Examining the role of gender in the prevalence of campus victimization, perceptions of fear, risk of crime,, the use of constrained behaviors among college students attending a large urban university
authors: Tomsich, Elizabeth A, Gover, Angela R, Jennings, Wesley G
keywords: 321\_SA実証研究;J\_TF1505;301\_ComCrm;J Criminal Justice Education;J Crim Justice Educ;CampusCrime
abstract: The incidence, the impact of crime on college campuses are important issues for students, administrators alike. This study examines experiences with victimization, perceptions of crime on campus with a convenience sample of 997 students attending an urban university in Colorado. Approximately 8\% of the student respondents indicated they had been victimized by at least one type of crime since first enrolling at the university. Respondents indicated low‐to‐moderate levels of fear, perceived risk of victimization on campus, viewed the campus as being moderately safe. Male, female respondents did not significantly differ in victimization rates, although gender differences were found in levels of fear, perceived risk of victimization, constrained behavior,, perceptions of overall safety on campus. The results from this study are compared to findings from the work of Jennings, Gover,, Pudrzynska in 2007, which examined campus crime among students at a traditional university, published in the Journal of Criminal Justice Education.

title: A 10-year update of “review, critique of empirical studies of rape avoidance”
authors: Ullman, Sarah E
keywords: Prevention; Rape; Self Defense; Sexual Abuse; Training; Human; rape avoidance; sexual assaults; interventions; self defense training;321\_SA実証研究;z\_2012\_jacp
abstract: Ullman’s review of empirical studies of rape avoidance is updated to illuminate what has been learned in the past 10 years, what is needed to continue to promote this important form of secondary prevention. Following a brief historical review, empirical studies of resistance strategies to sexual assaults since 1997 are reviewed. Studies of the effects of situational factors, rapist types,, victim-offender relationships on women’s resistance are included. Selected literature on self-defense training, rape prevention related specifically to women’s resistance also are reviewed, as these related areas of research have grown substantially in the past decade, can inform intervention, prevention efforts with women. Recommendations for future research, practice are offered.

title: Individual, behavioral,, situational correlates of the drugging victimization experiences of college women
authors: Warner, Tara D, Allen, Christopher T, Fisher, Bonnie S, Krebs, Christopher P, Martin, Sandra, Lindquist, Christine H
abstract: Interest in “drugging” has increased, with much focus on drugging victimization within the context of sexual assault, particularly among college students. This study uses data from the Campus Sexual Assault (CSA) Study, the Historically Black College, University Campus Sexual Assault (HBCU-CSA) Study to explore college women’s drugging victimization experiences beyond those limited to drug-facilitated sexual assault. We draw on a lifestyle-exposure/routine activity theory approach to personal victimization integrated with scholarship on gendered opportunities, the campus party culture to examine the individual, behavioral,, situational characteristics embedded in the campus environment that place college women at increased risks of being drugged. We pay particular attention to cultural, institutional differences shaping experiences, risks at predominantly White institutions (PWIs), Historically Black Colleges, Universities (HBCUs). Findings show that 5\%, 4\% of women at PWIs, HBCUs, respectively, report drugging victimization, that exposure to risky situations (e.g., fraternity party attendance) is a risk factor primarily for women at PWIs.

title: Fear of crime on campus: Gender differences in use of self-protective behaviours at an urban university
authors: Woolnough, April D
keywords: 321\_SA実証研究;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Security Journal;CampusCrime
abstract: Research establishes that female college students are more fearful of crime on campus, are more likely to believe they will be victimized than male students. However, little is known about how students’ fear of crime, their perceptions of risk influence their use of self-protective behaviours. Undergraduates at an urban university were surveyed about fear, perceived likelihood of being the victim of various crimes, their use of self-protective behaviours. This study examines students’ use of self-protective behaviours, compares sex differences in fear, perceived likelihood of different types of crime, score on a self-protective behaviours index. Results suggest that women engage in self-protective behaviours more than men,, do so based upon their fear of crime, perceived likelihood of victimization; in addition, women are more likely to engage in self-protective behaviours than men even after fear, perceived risk are held constant.

title: Experiences of sexual assault, financial stability: Sense of control as a potential mechanism
authors: Furlong, Courtney, Hinnant, Ben
keywords: financial stability; perceived constraints; sense of control; sexual assault; trauma; trauma theory;321\_SA実証研究;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: This investigation utilized the Midlife in the United States Survey (N = 3,258) to assess the relationships between sexual assault, sense of control,, financial stability. Age of first sexual assault, sexual assault revictimization were also considered in analyses of sexual assault survivors' data. Results revealed consistent associations between experiences of sexual assault, revictimization with lower financial stability, suggest that sense of control may be an indirect mechanism linking these variables. Findings have policy relevance, practical implications for practitioners. Restoring sexual assault victims' internal loci of control may promote more positive financial outcomes.

title: Crime control or just theater? An experimental test of the effects of a mobile safety app on crime prevention intentions, behaviors
authors: Kettrey, Heather Hensman, Tidwell, Michael L, Burke, Savannah R, Duncan, Sarah, Nwajei, Monika, Reynolds, Noah Samuel, Waddell, Claire, Scott, Sam, Imbody, Cadi, Jerge, Mary, Young, Joffrey, Nishan, Noor, Rathi, Akanksha, Jackson, Jauhar
abstract: Objectives We examined whether mobile safety apps constitute a form of crime control theater that thwarts actions that have the potential to prevent crime. Methods Using an experimental research design with a sample of college students (N = 210), we measured the effects of a safety app (i.e., Rave Guardian) on trust in mobile technology, fear of crime victimization, self-protective behavior,, bystander intentions to help someone at risk of victimization. Results Findings indicate that safety app access is associated with increased selfprotective behavior, bystander intentions. However, participants who actually used the app exhibited increased trust in mobile technology that slightly inhibited bystander intentions. We found no effect of app access or usage on fear of victimization. Conclusions Safety app usage, but not access, may function as a form of crime control theater. Until future research further explores differences between app access, usage, widespread uptake seems premature. Keywords Bystander • Crime control theater • Fear • Mobile safety app • Prevention • Trust • Campus victimization Young Americans place a great deal of trust in mobile devices,, they tend to believe that these devices can keep them safe from crime (Cumiskey, Brewster

title: The importance of proximity, target congruence,, guardianship of Korean youth victims: Applying latent class analysis to identify subtypes of poly-victimization
authors: Cho, Sujung, Lee, Claire Seungeun
abstract: Poly-victimization, or exposure to multiple types of victimization, is particularly common among children, adolescents. This study uses Lifestyle-Routine Activity Theory, Target Congruence Theory to examine distinct subgroups of Korean youth who have experienced poly-victimization through the estimation of a latent class analysis. This study uses a nationally representative sample—the 2018 National Survey on the Rights of Children, Youth ( N = 9,060, Grades 4–12). Results found four distinct subgroups of Korean youth who have experienced violent victimization: low risk/non-victims (54.1\%), poly-victims (4.1\%), verbal bullying victims (10.5\%),, victims of parental abuse (31.3\%). Distal outcomes such as suicidality, dropout were also examined regarding victimization experiences. Policy implications such as detecting victimization, early intervention/prevention programs are also discussed.

title: Domestic violence, housing problems: A contextual analysis of women's help-seeking, received informal support,, formal system response
authors: Baker, Charlene K, Cook, Sarah L, Norris, Fran H
abstract: This study examined housing problems, homelessness after separation in a sample of 110 women who had experienced domestic violence. Of the sample, 38\% reported homelessness. Similar percentages reported housing problems (e.g., late paying rent, skipping meals, threatened with eviction). Predictors of more housing problems included experiencing a greater severity of violence, contacting fewer formal systems, having less informational support,, receiving a negative response from welfare. Women's odds of reporting homelessness were reduced by 30\% if police officers responded positively. These findings highlight the importance of changing system responses in an effort to reduce women's housing problems, risks for homelessness after separation.

title: Factors predicting dating violence perpetration among male, female college students
authors: Baker, Colleen R, Stith, Sandra M
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examined the importance of witnessing parental violence, experiencing childhood violence, problems with alcohol, length of relationship, relationship satisfaction, anger management skills,, partner's use of physical, psychological aggression for male, female perpetrators of dating violence in college. For males, partner's use of physical aggression, low anger management skills,, high relationship satisfaction were the strongest predictors of physical aggression. For females, partner's uses of physical, psychological aggression were the most important predictors of their use of physical aggression. The model in this study was a good predictor of male violence, accounting for 81\% of the variance; however, it only accounted for 51\% of the variance in female violence.

title: Putative secrets, conflict in romantic relationships over time
authors: Aldeis, Desiree, Afifi, Tamara D
abstract: When people discover their romantic partner is keeping a secret from them but allow their partner to believe the secret is still unknown (creating what Caughlin, Scott, Miller,, Hefner referred to as a putative secret), this can have negative implications for their relationship. This study examined how putative secrets influence conflict in romantic relationships over time, whether certain factors (including perceived reasons for the secrecy, use of deception,, relationship satisfaction) moderate this association. The sample consisted of 305 dating individuals. Participants reported on a current putative secret, a putative secret kept in the past, or no secret,, then completed 3-week online diary entries tracking their conflict. The results revealed that individuals who were currently managing a putative secret had higher levels of conflict, more changes in conflict in their relationship over time than individuals who experienced a putative secret in the past or no putative secrets at all. Although individuals' attributions for their partner's secret keeping were important, they often depended on relationship satisfaction, currency of the putative secret. Relationship satisfaction significantly moderated the association between putative secrets, conflict, such that individuals who reported current putative secrets, were more dissatisfied reported the most intense conflict, the greatest changes in conflict over time.

title: The decision to leave the abusive partner by women survivors of intimate partner violence, risk of further revictimization: The role of gratitude, risk perception
authors: Costanza Baldry, Anna, Cinquegrana, Vincenza
keywords: IPV revictimization; gratitude; risk perception;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Being able to perceive the risk of further violence can be an essential step toward seeking help, leaving the abuser,, eventually reducing the risk of revictimization. The current study looks at the individual, contextual risk factors related to perception of risk and, subsequently, their influence on the decision of 83 battered women to leave the abusive partner after 1 year as well as on revictimization. Results indicated that perceiving more risk is a predictive factor in the decision to leave the partner. A dangerous side of gratitude emerged about future revictimization. Results are discussed for clinical implications.

title: Adopting a Stages of Change Approach for Individuals Who Are Violent with Their Intimate Partners
authors: Begun, Audrey L, Shelley, Gene, Strodthoff, Terri, Short, Lynn
abstract: The Stages of Change principles related to individuals' attempts to change problem behaviors provides a useful framework for illuminating the processes by which individuals may be able to successfully eliminate violence directed toward intimate partners. In this article, the five stages, relapse phenomenon are discussed, along with implications for developing standards for violence prevention interventions, the potential of stage-matched interventions,, the importance of addressing the ongoing risk of violence.

title: Validation of the Stalking Assessment, Management checklist (SAM) in law enforcement: A prospective study of 153 cases of stalking in two Swedish police counties
authors: Belfrage, Henrik, Strand, Susanne
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The overall aim of this study was to test the validity, the practical usefulness of the Stalking Assessment, Management checklist (SAM) within the police. Police officers in two police counties in Sweden were trained in using the Stalking Assessment, Management checklist (Kropp, Hart, \& Lyon, 2007) in real-life cases of reported stalking during the period May 2005 to December 2006 (N = 230). Results showed that the SAM was easy to code for the police, since there were very few cases of missing information coded by the police. Most importantly, the validity of the SAM was found to be very strong in terms of a strong correlation between factors included in the SAM, the degree of risk assessed by the police officers. The more SAM risk factors coded by the police officers concerning the alleged perpetrators, the higher the risk assessed for repeated stalking, violence. The same results were found concerning victim vulnerability factors. Those victims that were assessed to be at higher risk than others generally had more of the SAM victim vulnerability factors. We conclude that the SAM seems to be a valid, useful tool for use by law enforcement professionals in cases of alleged stalking.

title: Assessment, management of risk for intimate partner violence by police officers using the Spousal Assault Risk Assessment Guide
authors: Belfrage, Henrik, Strand, Susanne, Storey, Jennifer E, Gibas, Andrea L, Kropp, P Randall, Hart, Stephen D
keywords: 3236:Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; 4200:Forensic Psychology \& Legal Issues; Adolescence (13-17 yrs); Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Aged (65 yrs \& older); Crime; Empirical Study; Female; Human; Law; Male; Middle Age (40-64 yrs); Police Personnel; Prospective Study; Quantitative Study; Recidivism; Risk Assessment; Risk Management; SARA; Spousal Assault Risk Assessment Guide; Sweden; Thirties (30-39 yrs); Very Old (85 yrs \& older); Young Adulthood (18-29 yrs); crimes; intimate partner violence; longitudinal analysis; police;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a crime that is present in all countries, seriously impacts victims,, demands a great deal of time, resources from the criminal justice system. The current study examined the use of the Spousal Assault Risk Assessment Guide, 2nd ed. (SARA; Kropp, Hart, Webster, \& Eaves, 1995), a structured professional judgment risk assessment, management tool for IPV, by police officers in Sweden over a follow-up of 18 months. SARA risk assessments had significant predictive validity with respect to risk management recommendations made by police, as well as with recidivism as indexed by subsequent contacts with police. Risk management mediated the association between risk assessment, recidivism: High levels of intervention were associated with decreased recidivism in high risk cases, but with increased recidivism in low risk cases. The findings support the potential utility of police-based risk assessment, management of IPV,, in particular the belief that appropriately structured risk assessment, management decisions can prevent violence.

title: The prevalence of stalking among Finnish university students
authors: Björklund, Katja, Häkkänen-Nyholm, Helinä, Sheridan, Lorraine, Roberts, Karl
keywords: stalking;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;1\_複数尺度と因子分析;2\_親密非親密の比較;J Interpers Violence
abstract: The present study examined the prevalence, nature of stalking among university students in Finland. The prevalence of stalking was analyzed in relation to stalking episodes, violent stalking victimization, the stalker-victim relationship,, stalking duration. A group of Finnish university students were contacted by e-mail, asked to participate in a stalking survey. In total, 615 students participated. Almost one fourth of the respondents (22.3\%) had experienced one episode (i.e., period of time) of stalking,, more than one fourth (26.2\%) reported being stalked two or more episodes (i.e., periods of time) in their lifetime. More than half (55\%) of the stalkers were acquaintances, 25\% were ex-partners,, 19\% were strangers. The mean duration of stalking was 10 months. Stalking duration was significantly associated with stalker gender, prior victim-stalker relationship. Almost half of those being stalked (46\%) had been exposed to violent or threatening behavior. Ex-partner stalkers were most likely to use violence as well as a wide range of violent stalking methods. Logistic regression analysis revealed significant independent associations between stalking violence, stalking behaviors. Stalking is highly prevalent among Finnish university students; it is maintained, on average, for a relatively long period;, it often includes some form of violence and/or threats. The results suggest that health care professionals require screening methods, schooling concerning stalking.

title: Coping with stalking among university students
authors: Björklund, Katja, Häkkänen-Nyholm, Helinä, Sheridan, Lorraine, Roberts, Karl
keywords: ADJUSTMENT (Psychology); SOCIAL adjustment; VICTIMS of crimes; STALKING; OFFENSES against the person; HARASSMENT; LAW enforcement; stalker violence; victim-stalker relationship; coping with crime; coping;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;2\_親密非親密の比較
abstract: The present study examined behavioral coping actions, coping strategies in relation to specific contextual factors (e.g., victim-stalker relationship, stalking violence, duration of stalking,, prior victimization) among Finnish university students. Participants completed a stalking survey, also including items concerning coping. Victims of violent stalking threatened the stalker with the use of certain legal actions significantly more compared with victims of nonviolent stalking, but no difference in the actual use of formal help was found. Instead victims of stalking tried to avoid the stalker or turned to friends, family for help. Victim-stalker relationship, stalker violence,, number of stalking episodes had a significant main effect on certain coping strategies (e.g., positive reappraisal, escape-avoidance,, problem-solving), while no interaction effect was found. The findings suggest that knowledge of victim-coping behavior, strategies is crucial for health care, law enforcement professionals when devising appropriate support for victims, developing multidisciplinary approaches.

title: Latent profile approach to duration of stalking: Stalking duration
authors: Björklund, Katja, Häkkänen-Nyholm, Helinä, Sheridan, Lorraine, Roberts, Karl, Tolvanen, Asko
keywords: forensic science; forensic psychology; stalking; duration of stalking; latent profile analysis; university students;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;1\_複数尺度と因子分析;2\_親密非親密の比較;Violence Vict
abstract: Stalking behavior, victim-stalker relationship are often the principal known factors in a stalking case. Thus, they are of great importance when trying to identify factors contributing to stalking duration. The present study aims to identify distinct subgroups of stalking victims based on measures of behavioral stalking dimensions. These victim subgroups, stalking dimensions,, victim-stalker relationship are examined in relation to stalking duration. Using a sample of 137 university students, latent profile analysis (LPA) revealed five distinct victim subgroups based on stalker behavior dimensions: surveillance, low-profile, social lurker, wide scope,, baseline stalkers. The subgroups were significantly related to stalking duration, explained a considerable amount of the variance along with the stalking dimensions, victim-stalker relationship. Connections to stalking literature, utility of person-orientated methods in stalking research are discussed.

title: Changes in police notification for rape, 1973–2000
authors: Baumer, Eric P, Felson, Richard B, Messner, Steven F
keywords: CRIME; Natl crime surveys; POLICE; RAPE; VICTIMS of crimes; VICTIMS of crimes surveys; WOMEN -- Crimes against; police notification; victim-offender relationship.; victimization;320\_ST実証研究;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）;criminology
abstract: We use data from the National Crime Survey (NCS), the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) to explore changes in the likelihood of police notification in rape incidents. The findings indicate that during the 1970s, 1980s there was a significant increase in police notification by third parties, by victims raped by non‐strangers. During the 1990s the increase in rates of police notification in rape incidents accelerated, broadened in scope. In addition, differences in police notification between stranger, non‐stranger incidents diminished during the 1970s, 1980s and, by the early 1990s there was no significant difference.

title: Legal help—seeking experiences of former intimate—stalking victims
authors: Brewster, Mary P
abstract: Few researchers have explored the experiences of stalking victims in the legal system. Data for this study were gathered through extensive interviews with 187 women who were stalked by former intimate partners. Content analyses of interview transcripts revealed that most victims initially attempted to handle the situation themselves, but the majority ultimately sought assistance from the legal system. Logistic regression analyses examined predictors of legal help seeking. Predictors of seeking any type of legal help, filing for a protection from abuse order or temporary restraining order, and/or seeking police assistance included age (i.e., older women were more likely to seek help), race (i.e., White women were most likely to seek assistance), the presence of threats of violence, violent acts by the stalker,, length of stalking. Likert-type scale ratings by victims of the police, prosecutors',, judges' handling of their cases revealed greatest satisfaction with judges, followed by prosecutors. Suggestions for ways in which the system can better respond to the needs of stalking victims are made. Policy recommendations include greater criminal justice responsiveness to victims of stalking, more coordinated efforts between the police, courts.

title: Stalker typologies: A law enforcement perspective
authors: Boon, Julian C W, Sheridan, Lorraine
abstract: In the last ten years diverse attempts have been made to produce classificatory systems of stalkers, each with a different objective. The classificatory system advanced in this study was developed to serve the needs of law enforcement professionals. Based on a large number of documented, real-life cases (n = 124), the system was designed to identify, partition offenders according to motivational orientation. Specifically, four principal classifications were identified: (1) ex-partner harassment/stalking; (2) infatuation harassment; (3) delusional fixation stalking;, (4) sadistic stalking. The implications for assessing threat, preliminary recommendations for case management were advanced for each type. Inter-rater reliability among forensic, non-forensic psychologists in the application of the system was high (pairwise minimum > 92\%), supporting the view that this system could be readily assimilated, consistently applied by professionals working in the field.

title: The span of collective efficacy: Extending social disorganization theory to partner violence
authors: Browning, Christopher R
keywords: collective efficacy; conflict disclosure; neighborhood effects; partner violence;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: This research applies the social disorganization perspective on the neighborhood‐level determinants of crime to partner violence. The analysis brings data from the 1990 Decennial Census together with data from the 1994–1995 Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods Community Survey, the 1994–1995 Chicago homicide data,, data from the 1995–1997 Chicago Health, Social Life Survey. The findings of this study indicate that collective efficacy—neighborhood cohesion, informal social control capacity—is negatively associated with both intimate homicide rates, nonlethal partner violence. Collective efficacy exerts a more powerful regulatory effect on nonlethal violence in neighborhoods where tolerance of intimate violence is low. Collective efficacy also increases the likelihood that women will disclose conflict in their relationships to various potential sources of support.

title: The social ecology of red-light districts: A comparison of Antwerp, Brussels
authors: Weitzer, Ronald
abstract: Research on modern red-light districts (RLDs) is deficient in some key respects. Centered largely on street prostitution zones, nations where prostitution is illegal, this literature gives insufficient attention to settings where RLDs consist of a cluster of indoor venues that are legal, regulated by the authorities. Using classic Chicago School research on vice districts as a point of departure, this article examines the physical structure, social organization of red-light zones in two Belgian cities: Antwerp, Brussels. The comparative analysis identifies major differences in the social ecology of the two settings. Differences are explained by the distinctive ways in which each municipal government manages its respective RLD, which are related to the contrasting social backgrounds, political capital of the population residing in the vicinity of each district. Policy implications are briefly discussed.

title: Night moves: A qualitative investigation of street-level sex work
authors: Dalla, Rochelle L
abstract: The subculture of street-level sex work including the social environment, drug use, abuse,, violence was examined. Personal interviews were conducted with 43 women involved in streetwalking prostitution. Data were analyzed using Phenomenological Descriptive Analysis (Colaizzi, 1978). Several participants reported developing emotional relationships, having children with clients, former clients, or pimps; some participants were married to men who pimped them. Supportive relationships with other streetwalkers were largely nonexistent; streetwalking constitutes a solitary business for most. The majority reported drug addiction, although less than half entered prostitution to support an already established drug habit. Financial need propelled many into the streets. Victimization, subjection to multiple forms of abuse were commonly reported but did not constitute justification for leaving the streets. Implications of this investigation are discussed.

title: Examining the association between massage parlors, neighborhood crime
authors: Huff, Jessica, Wallace, Danielle, Riggs, Courtney, Katz, Charles M, Choate, David
abstract: Although massage parlors have been associated with illicit activities including prostitution, less is known about their association with neighborhood crime. Employing the Computer Automated Dispatch/Record Management System (CAD/RMS), online user review, licensing, Census,, zoning data, we examine the impact of massage parlors on crime in their surrounding neighborhoods. Using spatial autoregressive models, our results indicate the total number of massage parlors was associated with increased social disorder. The presence of illicit massage parlors in adjacent neighborhoods was associated with crime, physical disorder in the focal neighborhoods. This study has consequences for how police address crime associated with massage parlors. Specifically, the use of online user review forums could be an effective way to identify illicit massage parlors. Recommendations for policing, code enforcement are discussed.

title: Controlling the ‘anti sexual’ city: Sexual citizenship, the disciplining of female street sex workers
authors: Sanders, Teela
journal: Criminology \& criminal justice: the international journal of policy, practice
abstract: This article makes connections between the politics, policies relating to prostitution, anti social behaviour, with the construction of sexual citizenship. Through an analysis of what I have termed policing the ‘anti sexual’ city, I argue that new social technologies of control applied by a range of policing agencies include a gendered, sexual dimension to enforce ‘appropriate’ conduct among those considered to be sexually ‘disordered’, ‘uncivil’. I apply the concept of public patriarchy to the case of the management of female street prostitution, through New Labour’s insistence on an eradication, ‘exiting’ agenda. I argue that ‘forced welfarism’, through anti social behaviour mechanisms, are used to enforce ‘correct’ sexual citizenship through the tools of public patriarchy. Mechanisms of coercion, rehabilitation,, responsibilization are applied to sex workers through the contradictory narratives of ‘victim’, ‘offender’ that are played out in policy, practice. In summary, I argue that anti social behaviour policies that implement contractual governance have become a vehicle for ensuring that the benchmarks of sexual citizenship are maintained through the politics of inclusion, exclusion.

title: Neighborhood assessment of prostitution as a pressing social problem, appropriate responses: Results from a community survey
authors: Shdaimah, Corey S, Kaufman, Benjamin R, Bright, Charlotte Lyn, Flower, Shawn M
abstract: Concerns arising from three Baltimore, Maryland community groups advocating for more effective responses to prostitution led to the creation of the Specialized Prostitution Diversion program (SPD), a therapeutic model within the traditional criminal justice system. This mixed methods study used survey, interview,, field observations to ascertain neighborhood concerns about prostitution. Findings show that one neighborhood is notably different from the others in that respondents consider prostitution less of a problem, are less likely to believe police should respond to prostitution,, are less likely to indicate that prostitution causes a nuisance or could lead to additional criminal behavior. Neighborhood residents’ assessment of appropriate responses to prostitution, however, was not significantly different. Most believe that jail and/or treatment are appropriate for individuals engaging in prostitution, suggesting community support for hybrid responses combining punitive, rehabilitative components such as the SPD, regardless of the types or level of concern about prostitution

title: A predictive theory of intentions to exit street-level prostitution
authors: Cimino, Andrea N
abstract: Street-level prostitution is notoriously difficult to escape, rarely do women exit prostitution on their first attempt or without experiencing serious negative consequences to their physical or mental health. Unfortunately, few theories exist that explain the exiting process, those that do exist are difficult to test quantitatively. This article applies the integrative model of behavioral prediction to examine intentions to exit prostitution through attitudes, norms,, self-efficacy beliefs that underlie a woman's intention to exit prostitution. Constructs unique prostitution--agency, societal context--enhance the model. This theory may explain, predict an exit from street-level prostitution.

title: Weighing the consequences of a deviant career: Factors leading to an exit from prostitution
authors: Oselin, Sharon S
journal: Sociological perspectives: SP: official publication of the Pacific Sociological Association
abstract: Research on how individuals leave sex work examines this transition by focusing on either structural/economic conditions that keep them in the trade or internal changes that prompt exiting. Leaving certain roles, such as those deemed criminal, deviant, may be more challenging due to labeling, stigma,, a lack of resources. In this study, the author analyzes the particular factors that lead women to exit street prostitution via enrollment in “helping” organizations. The author finds extant theories do not fully capture how multiple factors combine to pull women off the streets. Rather, the author contends it is both internal, external factors that lead women to initially exit prostitution. This study draws on interviews with thirty-six street prostitutes from four different U.S. cities to address these concerns.

title: Gentrification, the flexibilisation of spatial control: Policing sex work in Germany
authors: Künkel, Jenny
abstract: Gentrification has often been linked to the spatial displacement of the marginalised, including prostitutes. However, in Germany, the legal spaces of prostitution are to a certain extent defensible,, gentrification processes often cover larger parts of inner cities, leaving little room for displacement. Using the example of prostitution in Frankfurt, this paper analyses how police make sense of, shape the shifting geographies of gentrification. It shows how spatial displacement is partially subsumed by two additional police strategies: intensifying attempts to discursively appease protesting citizens,, flexibilising the containment of prostitution in the inner city (e.g. by keeping street scenes on the move, lobbying for temporary brothel licenses).

title: Difficulties in revitalizing public space by CCTV: Street prostitution surveillance in the Swiss city of Olten
authors: Klauser, Francisco R
abstract: This article critically assesses the adequacy of CCTV as an instrument to revitalize urban areas suffering from concentrated social disadvantage. Empirically, it focuses on the video-surveillance of street prostitution in the Swiss city of Olten. This CCTV system was installed at the beginning of 2001, focuses on an urban `hot spot' used by different types of marginalized social groups. In the Olten case-study, video-surveillance is examined as it is understood, perceived both by the population at large, by daily users of the monitored area. In investigating whether surveillance cameras render monitored areas accessible to people erstwhile excluded from that space because of their negative subjective perception of risks, this article puts particular emphasis on the phenomenon of `distanciation' caused by CCTV. By showing that CCTV is forgotten very quickly, felt to be somehow unreal against the background of everyday social activities in monitored areas, this approach also stresses that CCTV is very limited as an instrument to revitalize public places of fear.

title: Intimate partner violence victims’ accuracy in assessing their risk of re-abuse
authors: Cattaneo, Lauren Bennett, Bell, Margret E, Goodman, Lisa A, Dutton, Mary Ann
keywords: PARTNER violence; VICTIMS of family violence; MARITAL violence; FAMILY violence; HELP-seeking behavior; INTERPERSONAL relations; RISK assessment; MULTIVARIATE analysis; Danger assessment; Intimate partner violence; Optimistic bias; Re-abuse; Risk perception; Victim accuracy; stalking;320\_ST実証研究;301\_ComCrm;302\_CogBias
abstract: Using four categories of accuracy (true positive, false positive, true negative, false negative), this study explored (1) how accurately intimate partner violence (IPV) victims are able to assess their risk of re-abuse;, (2) potential predictors of accuracy. Women seeking help for IPV (N=246) rated the likelihood that they would experience physical re-abuse in the coming year, then reported 18 months later whether those risks had been realized. Victim assessments were more likely to be right than wrong,, were subject to neither a pessimistic nor optimistic bias. In the multivariate analysis, significant/marginally significant predictors of the accuracy categories were the history of violence from this, former partners, level of substance use, PTSD symptoms,, the recency of the violence. Among the more robust findings were the connection between level of stalking, true positives,, between substance use, false negatives. This study suggests that victim assessments have significant potential to inform practice,, deserve further exploration. Adapted from the source document.

title: Women's reporting of sexual, physical assaults to police in the National Violence Against Women Survey
authors: Chen, Yingyu, Ullman, Sarah E
keywords: 320\_ST実証研究;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Previous research has assumed that rape reporting is unique, but no study has systematically tested this assumption. The present study used a probability sample of female victims from the National Violence Against Women Survey to compare factors affecting rape, physical assault reporting using multinomial logit regression. Overall, results suggested that there was similarity in reporting decisions between rapes, physical assaults in terms of main effects. However, interactions suggested that age, marital status,, physical force each influenced reporting differently by assault type. Implications of these results are discussed, directions for future research are offered.

title: Self-perceptions of stalking victimization, impacts on victim reporting
authors: Campbell, Julie, Moore, Robert
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Stalking as a behavior is not new; however, less than two decades have passed since the behavior was criminalized. First recognized in the USA in 1990 as a criminal behavior, the study of stalking, its impact on victims is also relatively new. The current study examined the various stalking-related behaviors, whether exposure to these behaviors was related to respondents' self-perception of being a stalking victim. This is important as stalking continues to be a crime in which victims are less likely to report their victimization. The results of the current study revealed that being followed, spied upon, having property vandalized,, receiving unwanted emails were significant predictors of a respondent self-identifying themselves as a stalking victim. However, only a small percentage of respondents in the current study actually reported their victimization (10\%), with feeling threatened, purchasing personal protection devices being the only significant predictors of whether a victim would report their victimization to law enforcement.

title: Optimistic bias about dating/relationship violence among teens
authors: Chapin, John R, Coleman, Grace
abstract: A survey of American adolescents documented optimistic bias regarding intimate partner violence (IPV). Teenagers believe they are less likely than peers to become victims of violence by a boyfriend or girlfriend, despite reporting some first-hand experience with violence. Optimistic bias was predicted by prior knowledge of dating, relationship violence, perceptions about media influence. The findings indicate that optimistic bias is more than an esteem-preserving mechanism, point to new directions in research by exploring linkages to cultivation effects. The study also extends the optimistic bias literature by utilizing an adolescent sample, exploring IPV as a context.

title: The victim‐offender relationship, calling the police in assaults
authors: Felson, Richard B, Messner, Steven F, Hoskin, Anthony
keywords: CRIME; CRIMINALS; POLICE; VICTIMS of crimes; VICTIMS of crimes surveys; Natl crime surveys;320\_ST実証研究;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）;criminology
abstract: The revised National Crime Victimization Survey is used to examine the effects of the victim's relationship to the offender on whether assaults are reported to the police by either the victim or by third parties. The results indicate that the offender‐victim relationship affects third‐party but not victim reporting. The former effect occurs in part because third parties are unlikely to witness assaults involving people in ongoing relationships, particularly couples,, in part because third parties are reluctant to report minor assaults (i.e., those assaults that involve a threat but no actual attack, no weapon). We discuss possible explanations for why no effect of relationship on victim reporting was found.

title: The reporting of domestic violence, sexual assault by nonstrangers to the police: (535952006-001)
authors: Felson, Richard, Pare, Paul-Philippe
keywords: assault; crime reporting; domestic violence; gender; police; sexual assault;320\_ST実証研究;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）
abstract: We examine the effects of the gender of the victim, offender, their relationship to each other on whether sexual, physical assaults are reported to the police. We also examine the reasons victims give for not reporting assaults, whether reporting patterns have changed over time. The analyses are based on a sample of 6,291 physical assaults, 1,787 sexual assaults from the National Violence Against Women Survey. The results suggest that victims are just as likely to report domestic assaults as they are to report assaults by other people they know. Male victims are particularly reluctant to report assaults by their intimate partners, whereas third parties are particularly unlikely to report assaults by partners of either gender. Sexual assaults, particularly those that involve acquaintances, are less likely to be reported. These patterns have not changed since the 1960s.

title: Household, neighborhood contexts of intimate partner violence
authors: Fox, Greer Litton, Benson, Michael L
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Two sources of contextual risk on the prevalence, severity of intimate partner violence (IPV) are investigated: household economic condition, neighborhood disadvantage. There is debate about whether each context is an independent source of IPV risk, whether risks cumulate over contexts. METHODS: Data from the second wave of the National Survey of Families, Households are combined with tract level data from the 1990 U.S. Census. A sub-sample of co-resident couples with a child aged 5-17 in the household was selected for analysis (n=2,273). IPV is measured in three ways: as any physical violence reported by either partner in the year prior to the survey, as gendered violence in which both partners are identified as aggressors,, as severe violence in terms of injury, frequency. RESULTS: Regardless of how IPV is assessed, couples with IPV are more likely to present a vulnerable economic risk profile, to live in neighborhoods of high disadvantage. When economically vulnerable couples living in advantaged versus disadvantaged neighborhoods are compared, there are no significant differences in rates of IPV, regardless of the measure of IPV that is used. Neighborhood context matters, however, in comparisons among economically advantaged couples: rates of IPV are significantly higher among those in disadvantaged neighborhoods. CONCLUSIONS: The consistency of effect for economic vulnerability, its invariance across neighborhood settings suggests that reducing economic vulnerability is likely to have beneficial effects in both disadvantaged, non-disadvantaged neighborhoods.

title: Experiences of stalking victims, requests for help in three European countries. A survey
authors: Galeazzi, Gian M, Bučar-Ručman, Aleš, DeFazio, Laura, Groenen, Anne
journal: European journal on criminal policy, research
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Stalking; Government agencies; Community support; Support groups; Law; Western Europe; Eastern Europe; 9175:Western Europe; 1200:Social policy; 4300:Law; 9176:Eastern Europe;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jssp2018
abstract: Issue Title: Stalking in Europe / Guest Editor: Laura De Fazio Previous research by the Modena Group on Stalking (MGS) regarding awareness, recognition of stalking by police officers, general practitioners using case scenarios showed significant differences across three countries. It was also hypothesized that victims used different pathways when seeking help. To explore the experience of requesting help by victims of stalking in different European countries a detailed survey was completed by 391 victims of stalking in Belgium (n=145), Italy (n=126), Slovenia (n=120). The research confirmed the significant intensity, duration of stalking, psychological distress for victims. Victims used several pathways to survive stalking. Some victims reported that informal interventions they or family/friends implemented were effective, but the majority had to have recourse to helping agencies. Significant differences in help seeking behaviour were found between the three countries. In Belgium victims contacted the police, as well as other helping agencies, more often, more precociously than in Italy, Slovenia.
