title: Dyadic correlates of the perpetration of psychological aggression among intimate partners
authors: Johnson, Wendi L, Taylor, Bruce G, Mumford, Elizabeth A, Liu, Weiwei
keywords: aggression; gender; dyadic data analysis; Psychology; Empirical Study; Quantitative Study; Human; Male; Female; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Young Adulthood (18-29 yrs); Thirties (30-39 yrs); Drug Usage; Aggressive Behavior; Risk Factors; Dyads; Human Sex Differences; Perpetrators; Partners; Test Construction; Psychodynamics; Intimacy; Alcohol Abuse; Statistical Analysis; article; US; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior;320\_ST実証研究
abstract: Objectives: Using couple-level data, a multilevel actor-partner interdependence model, this study examined correlates of psychological aggression including problem drinking, illicit drug use, anxiety, depression, recent life stressors, love, caring, adverse childhood experiences (ACE) of emotional, physical abuse, with particular emphasis on the adoption of a street code perspective/attitude, low self-control. Method: Using a diverse sample derived from a national sample, self-reports of psychological aggression, its correlates were analyzed across 800 individuals (400 dyads) who were in a current heterosexual intimate partnership. Results: In multilevel analyses, psychological aggression was correlated with the individual's risk factors, that of their partner for all variables except for problem drinking, illicit drug use. Although associations for both actor, partner were generally similar, partners' reports of love, caring were more protective against respondents' perpetration of psychological aggression. Furthermore, associations between psychological aggression, its covariates did not vary by gender. With the exception of self-control, actor effects did not interact with partner effects to buffer or amplify associations with psychological aggression. Conclusion: Our findings suggested that risk factors associated with the individual, those associated with the partner both contributed to each individual's psychological aggression independent of the other. Future intimate partner violence studies should continue to explore dual interactive risk factors for both members of the intimate relationship in predicting aggression.

title: Partner covictimization, post-breakup stalking, pursuit,, violence: A retrospective study of college women
authors: Katz, Jennifer, Rich, Hillary
abstract: Covictimization involves experiencing both physical, sexual forms of intimate partner violence (IPV). It was hypothesized that covictimization during a dating relationship would predict stalking, ongoing pursuit,, continued partner violence after the relationship ended. Undergraduate women ( N = 99) provided self-report data regarding experiences of IPV both during, after their most recent breakup, ongoing pursuit after the breakup. As expected, covictimized women reported elevated rates of post-breakup IPV, both physical, sexual. In addition, covictimized women reported elevated rates of ongoing pursuit involving intimidation/threats, but not involving approach/contact or surveillance. Ongoing intimidation/threat pursuit was also associated with post-breakup IPV, even after controlling for pre-breakup IPV. Covictimized women are at risk for continued intimidation, violence from ex-partners.

title: Serious assault victim, incident characteristics associated with police notification, treatment in emergency rooms in rural, suburban,, urban areas
authors: Kaylen, Maria, Pridemore, William Alex
abstract: Two common sources of violence rates are police data, hospital data on injuries. It is unclear, however, if violence rates calculated using these sources have the same meaning across location types like rural, suburban,, urban areas. We know that characteristics of assault victims, incidents are associated with whether or not the victim reports the incident to the police. If community type moderates this help-seeking behavior—for example, if the impact of sex, age, race, victim–offender relationship, or injury severity on reporting to the police or being treated in an emergency room (ER) is different in rural relative to urban areas—then this selection bias is problematic for comparisons across location type, for including different location types in the same sample. The goal of this study was to determine which victim, incident characteristics are associated with police notification, ER treatment, to see if these characteristics are the same across rural, suburban,, urban areas. We used National Crime Victimization Survey data on reporting serious assaults to the police, being treated in an ER as a result of a serious assault. Results revealed that (1) police notification is much more likely to occur than ER treatment, (2) a majority of victim, incident characteristics are significantly associated with police notification, (3) few victim, incident characteristics are significantly associated with ER treatment,, (4) there is only chance moderation by location type. Findings suggest that both police, hospital data on serious assaults can be used to make comparisons across rural, suburban,, urban communities without being limited by disproportionate inclusion or exclusion of incidents associated with victim, incident characteristics. However, comparisons between the two data sources should be made with caution due to the different victim, incident characteristics associated with police notification, ER treatment.

title: The help-seeking strategies of female violent-crime victims: the direct, conditional effects of race, the victim-offender relationship: The direct, conditional effects of race, the victim-offender relationship
authors: Kaukinen, Catherine
keywords: 320\_ST実証研究;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）;J Interpers Violence
abstract: The author used national data to examine the help-seeking strategies of female crime victims. The research has two objectives. First, to determine whether help seeking exists as isolated choices or whether there is a discernable set of help-seeking strategies used by victims. Second, the author examined the effects of race, the victim-offender relationship on these help-seeking decisions. Findings identify three help-seeking strategies: (a) minimal or no help seeking, (b) family, friend help seeking,, (c) substantial help seeking (includes help from family, friends, psychiatrists, social service providers,, police). The author found that White women, victims of intimate partner violence are more likely to engage in increasing levels of help seeking. She also found that White women victimized by an intimate partner or other known offender are more likely (as compared to other victims) to seek increasing levels of help, social support.

title: The help-seeking decisions of violent crime victims: An examination of the direct, conditional effects of gender, the victim-offender relationship
authors: Kaukinen, Catherine
keywords: 320\_ST実証研究;z\_2018\_jav（被害者学会）;z\_jssp2018;J Interpers Violence
abstract: National data are used to examine the help-seeking strategies of male, female crime victims. Victims who seek help from family, friends, the users of mental health, social services,, self-help groups tend to be female. In contrast, most male victims do not seek help. When men do seek help, they are more likely to call the police than to call on family, friends. This study also finds that attacks by known offenders lead to help-seeking strategies that rely primarily on family, friends. Finally, the author finds that the victim-offender relationship conditions the effect of gender on help-seeking decisions. Help-seeking strategies are unique to particular gender/victim-offender relationship categories. Women victimized by known offenders rely on family, friends. In contrast, men victimized by strangers most often do nothing, but some men who have been victimized by a stranger will report the victimization to the police

title: Sexual assault, current mental health: the role of help-seeking, police response
authors: Kaukinen, Catherine, Demaris, Alfred
abstract: We examine the extent to which seeking help from social service agencies, family, friends, reporting to the police, or responses by the police might buffer or exacerbate the impact of sexual assault on mental health outcomes among sexual assault victims.The trend in many cases was for help-seeking, police response to exacerbate the impact of sexual assault victimization. With respect to depression, we found that the association of rape penetration was greater among those seeking help from social services, those reporting their victimization to the police. Although arresting the offender appears to be associated with higher levels of depression, it actually results in a lower probability of heavy episodic drinking.

title: Domestic violence: Predictors of victim support for official action
authors: Kingsnorth, Rodney F, Macintosh, Randall C
abstract: In this paper, using a sample of 5,272 domestic violence cases processed through the Sacramento County District Attorney's Office between July 1, 1999, December 31, 2000, we analyze the predictors of victim support for official action. We test the impact of victim, offender characteristics, situational variables,, official behavior on whether it was the victim or some third party who called for assistance, whether the victim desired the arrest,, whether the victim was willing to prosecute. The multiple significant effects found include race/ethnicity, gender, cohabitation, co-parenthood, attack severity, victim injury, prior incidents, reporting of prior incidents, presence of a protective order, provision of victim services, victim substance use,, suspect injury. Especially important from a policy perspective is that prosecutor charging practice (i.e., filing as a felony rather than a misdemeanor or violation of probation) was negatively associated with levels of victim support for prosecution.

title: Mediating influence of crime type on victim satisfaction with police services: A comparative analysis across victims of property crimes, violent crimes in India
authors: Kumar, T K Vinod
abstract: Different crimes have their own unique characteristics. Victim needs, experiences vary across crime types. However, there has been a tendency for the criminal justice system to treat victims as a homogeneous entity, respond to victims of different types of crimes in a routine manner. This is especially true in a developing country like India. This study, using victim survey data from India, examines whether the crime type (property crime or violent crime) has a mediating influence on the relation between the quality of procedure, outcome of police response on the one hand,, victim satisfaction on the other. The study concludes that the type of crime has a mediating effect on the relation between interpersonal justice, information justice, outcome,, the satisfaction of victims with services provided by the police.

title: Impact of demographic characteristics of crime victim on interaction with police in India—gender, caste, class, police response
authors: Vinod Kumar, T K
abstract: Demographic characteristics of crime victims have an impact on their interaction with the police. The initial mindset of the victim before contact with the police, post interaction assessment of satisfaction with police services are important indicators of the social dynamics, functioning of the criminal justice system. The first indicating individual perception of social location, accessibility to police,, the latter the levels of professionalism in police response to victims of crime. This study examines the influence of demographic characteristics on the state of mind of victims when they approach police in India, further on their assessment of police after the interaction,, on the basis of the findings comments on the state of police services in India.

title: The development, validation of the guidelines for stalking assessment, management
authors: Kropp, P Randall, Hart, Stephen D, Lyon, David R, Storey, Jennifer E
abstract: International research has established that stalking is a prevalent problem with serious, often life-threatening consequences for victims. Stalking is also a unique form of violence due to its nature, diversity, making it difficult for criminal justice, health professionals to establish which perpetrators, victims have the greatest need for services, protection. Risk assessment is one way to address these problems but few tools exist. This article describes the development of the Guidelines for Stalking Assessment, Management (SAM), the first risk assessment instrument designed specifically for the stalking situation. Preliminary data are presented, indicating that the SAM has promise for use by professionals working with stalkers, their victims. Results indicated that interrater reliabilities for the SAM risk factors, total scores range from fair to good,, the structural reliability of the SAM is sound. Moreover, the SAM showed good concurrent validity when compared with two other measures of violence propensity: the Psychopathy Checklist Screening Version (PCL:SV), the Violence Risk Appraisal Guide (VRAG). Limitations of the study are discussed, especially those related to the difficulties inherent in file-based research,, suggestions for future research are offered.

title: Women's decisions to not seek formal help for partner violence: A comparison of intimate terrorism, situational couple violence: A comparison of intimate terrorism, situational couple violence
authors: Leone, Janel M, Lape, Megan E, Xu, Yili
keywords: coercive control; criminal justice system; formal help-seeking decisions; male partner violence; minority women;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jssp2018
abstract: This study examined the help-seeking decisions of low-income women (n = 389) in two types of physically violent heterosexual relationships-intimate terrorism (i.e., physical violence used within a general pattern of coercive control), situationally violent (i.e., physical violence that is not part of a general pattern of coercive control). Intimate terrorism victims were significantly more likely than situational couple violence victims to cite fear as a reason for not seeking help from the police, medical centers,, counselors/agencies. In contrast, situational couple violence victims more often said that they did not need help. Regression analyses also indicate that additional violence-related factors predict women's help-seeking. Findings emphasize the importance of distinguishing between types of male partner violence, recognizing women's exertions of personal choice, perceptions of dangerousness when examining their decisions about seeking help from service providers.

title: Stalking victimization in the context of intimate partner violence
authors: Logan, T K, Shannon, Lisa, Cole, Jennifer
abstract: This article is one of the first to extensively compare characteristics of women who do, do not report stalking by a violent partner or ex-partner using a large sample of women with civil protective orders. Specifically, the purpose of this study was to examine similarities, differences in relationship, victimization history characteristics, mental health symptoms, help-seeking,, protective order violations for women who report being stalked in the past year (n = 345) by the partner they received a protective order against compared to women who received a protective order against a violent partner but who report no stalking by that partner ever in the relationship (n = 412). Results indicate that women who report partner stalking have more severe partner violence victimization, histories, increased distress, greater fear,, more protective order violations, suggesting that partner stalking victimization warrants more research, practice attention.

title: Toward a deeper understanding of the harms caused by partner stalking
authors: Logan, T K, Walker, Robert
abstract: This study examined stalking prevalence, patterns,, harm among 210 women with civil protective orders (PO) against violent male partners or ex-partners. Results suggest that stalking is associated with PO violations, almost every other type of partner violence. Also, women who have been stalked by violent partners report significantly more distress, harm than even women who experience PO violations but not stalking. Results of key informant perceptions suggest many victim service (n=116), criminal justice professionals (n=72) do not seem to understand the extent or gravity of the harms caused by partner stalking especially when contrasted with victim reports of harm. Furthermore, key informant reports of their advice to women being stalked by an ex-partner were not consistent with recommendations for stalking victims in general.

title: The process of leaving an abusive relationship: the role of risk assessments, decision certainty
authors: Martin, Andrea J, Berenson, Kathy R, Griffing, Sascha, Sage, Robert E, Madry, Lorraine, Bingham, Lewis E, Primm, Beny J
keywords: WIFE abuse; FAMILY violence; RISK assessment; abusive relationships; battered women; Risk assessments;320\_ST実証研究;302\_CogBias
abstract: Seventy female residents of an urban domestic violence shelter were interviewed to examine a series of hypotheses concerning two factors relevant to the process of leaving an abusive relationship: risk assessments, decision-certainty. Participants' subjective estimates of their own risk of returning to the batterer were examined relative to their perceptions of the likelihood that most battered women will return to the batterer, their certainty regarding the decision to leave the batterer,, their status on known risk factors for returning to an abusive relationship. As hypothesized, battered women's perceptions of personal risk for returning to the batterer were biased by unrealistic optimism; specifically, personal risk was estimated as significantly lower than the risk of most battered women, was not correlated with actual risk factors. Further, the magnitude of the optimistic bias was significantly greater among women expressing high certainty about their decision to leave than among women who expressed less certainty. The clinical implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Stalking victimization, labeling,, reporting: Findings from the NCVS Stalking Victimization Supplement: Findings from the NCVS Stalking Victimization Supplement
authors: Ménard, Kim S, Cox, Amanda K
keywords: labeling; reporting to police; stalking;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;z\_jssp2018;0\_代表性被害調査;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Using the National Crime Victimization Survey 2006 Stalking Victimization Supplement (NCVS-SVS), guided by Greenberg, Ruback's social influence model, this study examines the effects of individual (e.g., severity, sex, victim-offender relationship), contextual (e.g., location) factors on stalking victimization risk, victim labeling, help seeking,, victim, third-party police contacts. Logistic regression results suggest individual, contextual characteristics matter. Consistent with prior research, the theoretical model, the positive effects of severity, sex (female) were significant across all dependent variables, whereas the interaction effect of victim-offender relationship, location held only for third-party police contacts.

title: The Relationship Between Threats, Violence in Juvenile Stalking
authors: Mccann, Joseph T
abstract: The relationship between threatening behavior, victim-directed violence was examined in a convenience sample of 26 stalking cases involving a child or adolescent perpetrator. Overall, the base rate for violence in the sample was 38\%, the base rate of threatening behavior was 65\%. When threatening behavior directed toward the victim was used as a predictor of subsequent violence, the sensitivity was 0.80, specificity was 0.44, positive predictive power was 0.47,, negative predictive power was 0.78. The overall classification rate of violence was only 58\% when threats were used as a predictor. There was a non-significant, negative relationship between threats, violence. Results are compared with findings that have emerged in stalking research on adult populations, various suggestions are offered for further study of the potential for violence in cases involving children, adolescents.

title: The prevalence of stalking among college students: the disparity between researcher-, self-identified victimization
authors: McNamara, Corinne L, Marsil, Dorothy F
journal: Journal of American college health: J of ACH
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Researchers examined the prevalence of self-identified, researcher-identified stalking victimization among college students. PARTICIPANTS AND METHODS: A representative sample of 1,573 (70.1\% female; 29.9\% male) student respondents completed an online stalking questionnaire. RESULTS: Overall, 12\% self-identified as having been stalked. Additionally, 42.5\% (45.4\% female; 35.7\% male) of students reported experiencing at least 1 behavioral indicator of stalking victimization; however, only 24.7\% of those self-identified as being stalked (25.6\% female; 22.0\% male). CONCLUSIONS: Stalking is a serious problem in the college community. A concern that needs to be addressed is the disparity between the number of those who met the behavioral criteria for stalking victimization, but who did not self-identify as a victim. The consequences of stalking victimization are highlighted. Recommendations for addressing this issue on campus are detailed in a plan that may help improve the retention, progression,, graduation rates for stalking victims.

title: The time course of repeat intimate partner violence
authors: Mele, Marie
keywords: repeat intimate partner violence; repeat victimization; victim offender contact; Human; Male; Female; Adolescence (13-17 yrs); Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Young Adulthood (18-29 yrs); Thirties (30-39 yrs); Middle Age (40-64 yrs); Aged (65 yrs \& older); Empirical Study; Quantitative Study; Partner Abuse; Intimate Partner Violence; Recidivism; Victimization; Criminals; US; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior;320\_ST実証研究;304\_RepeatVic
abstract: This study examines the time course of repeat victimization by assessing whether the opportunity for victim/offender contact influences the time lapse between successive incidents of intimate partner violence. Several measures of opportunity for victim/offender contact are used, including cohabitation, co-parenting, restraining order status,, victim unemployment. The study finds that some victims (i.e., those who live with the offender) are at risk of repeat victimization in a shorter period of time than other victims. However, the study yields conflicting findings about the relationship between other opportunity variables (i.e., co-parenting, victim unemployment), the time lapse between successive incidents of intimate partner violence. Policy implications are discussed, suggestions are offered for future research on repeat intimate partner violence. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2012 APA, all rights reserved)(journal abstract)

title: Parent blaming, parent power,, the start of real research
authors: Waltz, Mitzi
abstract: As the 1970s moved forward, many adults like Jimmy Jones remained on locked wards, but far fewer children were being shunted into long-stay institutions. In any case, there had always been some families who resisted the advice to institutionalise. For example, the Edge family, from a small coastal village in England, struggled to keep their son Michael in the family during the 1960s. It was help from friends, relatives,, eventually support services started by the National Autistic Society (NAS), that made this possible (Stevens, 2011).

title: The tactical face of stalking
authors: Nicastro, Alana M, Cousins, Amber V, Spitzberg, Brian H
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; MENTALLY ill offenders; CRIMINAL methods; STALKERS; STALKING; VICTIMS of crimes; CALIFORNIA; Crime specific countermeasures; Harassing telephone calls; Offender attitudes; Offender profiles; Personal security; Psychological victimization effects; Victim attitudes; Victim-offender relationships; coping with crime; coping;320\_ST実証研究;J Crim Justice
abstract: The empirical literature on stalking was reviewed,, found wanting for greater descriptive detail of the process of stalking. For this study, fifty-five stalking case files from the city attorney's Domestic Violence Unit in a major western metropolitan area were coded for over one hundred variables each. Multiple victimization factors were examined to ascertain the characteristics of stalking victims, to analyze the relationship between victimization, symptomology,, coping strategies. Results indicate that the most common coping strategy was “hung up when they called,”, that victims reported feeling “threatened” more than any other symptom. In addition, as the number and/or breadth of perpetrator tactics increased, the victims experienced more symptoms. A history of violence was reported in the majority of the case files,, the presence of restraining orders had a strong correlation with victimization. Implications for refining current theory, research on stalking, strategies for successful intervention were examined.

title: Police response to domestic violence: A case study of TecSOS mobile phone use in the London metropolitan police service
authors: Natarajan, Mangai
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Police forces are constantly seeking to improve their service to victims of domestic abuse, to facilitate reporting of these offenses. Using a variety of police data, this case study describes the London Metropolitan Police Service's use of TecSOS mobile phone technology in responding to domestic abuse. The case study indicates that the rapid response made possible by TecSOS activations reduces the risk of repeat victimization. It also results in victim protection, empowerment, it increases the risk of apprehension for the offender, it strengthens evidence for prosecution by apprehending perpetrators in action, whether or not in the victim's home. The case study also suggests that TecSOS has potential for wider cost-saving public benefits. Most importantly, it was found that only a small minority of victims ever activated their phones suggesting that these serve as a powerful deterrent to would-be perpetrators.

title: Stalking, gender,, coping strategies: A partial test of broidy, Agnew's gender/general strain theory hypotheses
authors: Ngo, Fawn T, Paternoster, Raymond
abstract: Using data from the Supplemental Victimization Survey (SVS) of the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS), relying on theoretical direction provided by Broidy, Agnew's gendered strain theory, we examine gender differences in the emotional reactions, behavioral outcomes to one type of serious strain: stalking. We found females experienced significantly higher levels of stalking strain than males for only one type of stalking strain, the experience of stalking appeared to elevate anger among male victims, reduce anger among female victims,, female victims were more likely to express a variety of nonangry emotions in response to stalking stress as well as adopt a variety of legitimate coping mechanisms in order to deal with their victimization. We also uncovered that one emotional reaction to strain, fear, was more prominent for females than males. The implications of our findings are also discussed.

title: Career dimensions of stalking victimization, perpetration
authors: Nobles, Matt R, Fox, Kathleen A, Piquero, Nicole, Piquero, Alex R
abstract: Prior literature concerning stalking, particularly in the field of criminology, finds wide variation in fundamental trends regarding stalking victimization, perpetration. There seems to be little consensus regarding when, how stalking is manifested. Furthermore, prior research to date has not addressed the etiology of stalking‐related behaviors by applying principles from criminal career research, including participation, frequency, onset,, duration. The present study builds upon prior research by addressing trends in age of onset for stalking victimization, perpetration, the duration of stalking‐related behaviors,, the relationship between those behaviors, other types of crime over the life course using primary data from a sample of young adults. Findings indicate that stalking victimization, perpetration share important career attribute similarities,, that self‐reported history of intimate partner violence, sexual assault are strongly associated with stalking outcomes.

title: The role of perceptions, attributions in battered women's intentions to permanently end their violent relationships
authors: Pape, Karen T, Arias, Ileana
abstract: The purpose of the current investigation was to examine the mediational role of attributions, emotional reactions to partner violence in the relationship between violence severity, frequency,, women's intentions to leave abusive relationships permanently. The results of separate regression analyses indicated that perceived increases in the frequency, severity of violence over time, but not absolute levels of violence, were significantly related to women's attributions for the violence, the severity of nervousness reported subsequent to a violent episode,, the intention to leave the abusive partner permanently. Attributions of partner causality, responsibility for violence were significantly related to nervous reactions, the intention to leave the abusive partner permanently. As predicted by the attributional model tested, the relationship between perceived increases in violence over time, the intention to leave the abusive partner permanently was completely mediated by the extent to which women explained or attributed the causes of the violence to the partner that were stable, global,, attributed blameworthiness, malicious intent,, selfish motivations to the partner for his use of violence.

title: What makes police officers act? Police response to instances of intimate partner violence
authors: Peirone, Amy, Barrett, Betty Jo, Cheung, Chi Ho, Habibov, Nazim
keywords: intimate partner violence; law enforcement; police contact; police response; spousal violence;320\_ST実証研究;300;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Using data from the 2009 General Social Survey (GSS Cycle 23: Victimization main file), this study assessed the relationship between individual, neighborhood-level factors, police response to spousal violence in Canada. A total of 890 participants in the GSS reported experiences of spousal violence within the previous 5 years, with approximately 22\% of these victims reporting direct contact with the police because of the violence. Among this subsample of victims who had police contact, we evaluated the extent to which individual-level factors (sociodemographic, violence characteristics), neighborhood-level factors (perceptions of social disorder, the presence of police facilities in one's community) were related to distinct types of police response to reported spousal violence. Regression analyses suggest variations in police response based on sociodemographic, violence,, neighborhood characteristics; however, overall satisfaction with police actions taken were not found to be significantly different among victims based on these characteristics. Implications are relevant for policing practice as results suggest that different victims may have different safety needs, abilities to communicate these needs to the police.

title: Intimate partner violence, women’s help-seeking behaviour: Evidence from India
authors: Paul, Sohini
abstract: This study examines the role of socio-economic characteristics that influence a battered woman in India to either remain silent or approach someone for help in response to domestic violence. We investigate the influence of socio-economic factors on choosing between formal, informal sources of seeking help. The dataset used for the analysis is a nationally representative, community-based survey database—the National Family Health Survey-3 (NFHS-3). A logistic regression framework was used to analyze the data. The results suggest that education, economic empowerment play a crucial role in deciding whether to seek help to stop domestic violence. Women exposed to violence attempts utilize both formal, informal sources of help; however, informal sources of help are more popular compared with formal sources in India. JEL: J12

title: Police response to domestic violence: making decisions about risk, risk management: Making decisions about risk, risk management
authors: Perez Trujillo, Monica, Ross, Stuart
keywords: Police Personnel; decision making; domestic violence; judgment; police officers; risk assessment;320\_ST実証研究;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Assessing, responding to risk are key elements in how police respond to domestic violence. However, relatively little is known about the way police make judgments about the risks associated with domestic violence, how these judgments influence their actions. This study examines police decisions about risk in domestic violence incidents when using a risk assessment instrument. Based on a sample of 501 risk assessments completed by police in Australia, this study shows that a limited number of items on the risk assessment instrument are important in police officers' decisions about risk. Statistical analyses show that the victim's level of fear contributes to police officers' judgment on the level of risk, their decisions on which risk management strategy should be used. These findings suggest that research on police responses to domestic violence needs to pay greater attention to situational dynamics, the task requirements of risk-based decision making.

title: The Intimate Partner Violence Stigmatization Model, barriers to help-seeking
authors: Overstreet, Nicole M, Quinn, Diane M
keywords: Anticipated Stigma; Barriers; Cultural Stigma; Disclosure; Help-Seeking; Intimate Partner Violence; Stigma; Stigma Internalization;320\_ST実証研究;J\_TF1505;Basic Appl Soc Psych
abstract: The Intimate Partner Violence (IPV) Stigmatization Model identifies how three stigma components hinder IPV help-seeking behaviors: cultural stigma, stigma internalization,, anticipated stigma. Cultural stigma highlights societal beliefs that de-legitimize people experiencing abuse. Stigma internalization involves the extent to which people come to believe that the negative stereotypes about those who experience IPV may be true of themselves. Anticipated stigma emphasizes concern about what will happen once others know about the partner abuse (e.g., rejection). We provide an integrative literature review that supports the IPV stigmatization model, its role in reducing help-seeking behaviors.

title: Why definitions matter: Stalking victimization in the United States: Stalking victimization in the United States
authors: Owens, Jennifer Gatewood
keywords: NCVS; methods; national victimization estimates; stalking; victimization;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Although there is a growing understanding of stalking victimization, it remains difficult to define,, characterizations of the phenomenon vary within the literature. As such, research is needed to understand how variations in the definition of stalking may change who is defined as a victim, thereby limit the generalizability of findings across previous studies. The focus of this study is the inclusion or exclusion of subjective, reasonable measures of fear for 1,430 victims identified by the 2006 Supplemental Victimization Survey. Results suggest that the definition of stalking is important,, prior research has potentially excluded stalking victims due to restrictive operationalizations. Victims who report different types of fear appear to be similar to each other in some respects but differ in others, particularly with regard for gender representation, suggesting some definitions of stalking may be gendered, under-represent male stalking victims. Finally, using complex stratified survey weights, the impact of these varying operationalizations is examined. Using the same data but different definitions resulted in estimates of just over 1 to 5.3 million persons who are stalked in the United States each year.

title: Rural Australian women's legal help seeking for intimate partner violence: women intimate partner violence victim survivors' perceptions of criminal justice support services: Women intimate partner violence victim survivors’ perceptions of criminal justice support services
authors: Ragusa, Angela T
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a widespread, ongoing,, complex global social problem, whose victims continue to be largely women. Women often prefer to rely on friends, family for IPV help, yet when informal support is unavailable they remain hesitant to contact formal services, particularly legal support for many reasons. This study applies a sociological lens by framing the IPV, legal help-seeking experiences of rural Australian women gained from 36 in-depth face-to-face interviews as socially contextualized interactions. Findings reveal police, court responses reflect broader social inequalities, rurality exacerbates concerns such as anonymity, lack of service. Cultural differences, power imbalances between survivors, formal support providers are manifested to inform future research seeking to improve survivors' willingness to engage, satisfaction with formal services. Finally, the important role police, the criminal justice system play in de-stigmatizing IPV, legitimating its unacceptability is argued a crucial, yet unrecognized, key to social change.

title: The prevalence, nature of stalking in the Australian community
authors: Purcell, Rosemary, Pathé, Michele, Mullen, Paul E
journal: The Australian, New Zealand journal of psychiatry
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study examines the extent, nature of stalking victimisation in a random community sample. METHOD: A postal survey was distributed to 3700 adult men, women selected from the electoral roll in the State of Victoria. Outcome measures included the lifetime, annual cumulative incidence of stalking, the duration, methods of harassment, rates of associated violence, responses to victimisation. RESULTS: Almost one in four respondents (23.4\%;432) had been stalked, the unwanted behaviour they were subjected to being both repeated, fear-provoking. One in 10 (197) had experienced a protracted course of stalking involving multiple intrusions spanning a period of at least one month. Women were twice as likely as men to report having been stalked at some time in their lives, though the rates of victimisation in the 12 months prior to the study did not differ significantly according to gender. Younger people were significantly more likely than older respondents to report having been stalked. Victims were pursued by strangers in 42\% of cases. The most common methods of harassment involved unwanted telephone calls, intrusive approaches, following. Associated threats (29\%), physical assaults (18\%) frequently arose out of the stalking. Significant social, economic disruption was created by the stalking for 63\% of victims. Most sought assistance to manage their predicament (69\%). CONCLUSIONS: The experience of being stalked is common, appears to be increasing. Ten percent of people have been subjected at some time to an episode of protracted harassment. Assaults by stalkers are disturbingly frequent. Most victims report significant disruption to their daily functioning irrespective of exposure to associated violence.

title: The overlap between teen dating violent offending, violent victimization
authors: Pusch, Natasha, Reisig, Michael D
abstract: Teen dating violence (TDV) affects both males, females,, the negative consequences associated with such violence last into adulthood. This study had three objectives: (a) determine the extent of overlap in TDV offending, TDV victimization, (b) test whether social ties explain the TDV overlap,, (c) assess whether the effects of social ties on teen dating violence are invariant between sexes. This study used data from the 2018 Arizona Youth Study ( N = 5,189). The findings confirmed that TDV overlap exists. In addition, social ties appeared to partially explain this overlap. Finally, some social ties appeared more general, predicting TDV for both sexes, whereas others were not. For instance, Paternal Attachment was found to reduce the probability of dating violence among female participants only. The findings lend support to prevention programs that aim to strengthen ties between parents, teens.

title: A gendered lifestyle-routine activity approach to explaining stalking victimization in Canada
authors: Reyns, Bradford W, Henson, Billy, Fisher, Bonnie S, Fox, Kathleen A, Nobles, Matt R
keywords: Canada; criminal harassment; routine activity theory; stalking; victimization;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;0\_代表性被害調査;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Research into stalking victimization has proliferated over the last two decades, but several research questions related to victimization risk remain unanswered. Accordingly, the present study utilized a lifestyle-routine activity theoretical perspective to identify risk factors for victimization. Gender-based theoretical models also were estimated to assess the possible moderating effects of gender on the relationship between lifestyle-routine activity concepts, victimization risk. Based on an analysis of a representative sample of more than 15,000 residents of Canada from the Canadian General Social Survey (GSS), results suggested conditional support for lifestyle-routine activity theory, for the hypothesis that predictors of stalking victimization may be gender based.

title: Stalking, Related Harassment of Secondary School Counselors
authors: Romans, John S C, Hays, Joni R, Pearson, Christy, Duroy, L Chris, Carlozzi, Barbara
abstract: In a study of stalking in secondary schools, 140 respondents reported they had been stalked, with perpetrators being evenly distributed between students, non-students. The largest non-student group of perpetrators was parents of students. Harassing phone calls, threatening correspondence constituted most of the stalking behaviors, but respondents also reported being followed, being watched, encountring a student with a weapon,, being victims of assault, property crimes. Although a number of negative consequences were reported to have resulted from the stalking incidents, most surprising considering the amount of violence, threatening experiences reported was that the majority of victims (57.9\%) reported no concern for their safety. Prevention strategies for individuals, schools are suggested.

title: Changing stalking patterns, prosecutorial decisions: Bridging the present to the future
authors: Roberts, Albert R, Dziegielewski, Sophia F
abstract: This article reviews sixty cases from prosecutor's files in two New Jersey counties. These cases are used to examine, help better define the phenomena of stalking. Selected sample case examples are presented, described in regard to the typology of stalking behavior originally proposed by Dziegielewski, Roberts (1995). Based on these cases, application, modification, refinement of the typology criteria are suggested. The critical need for crisis intervention protocols, specialized anti-stalking units, training are emphasized. It is hoped that this information will help the criminal justice, forensic professional to better understand, assess the dangerousness of,, intervene rapidly, effectively in the phenomena of stalking,, to provide technology to protect victims.

title: Informal, formal help-seeking decisions of stalking victims in the United States
authors: Reyns, Bradford W, Englebrecht, Christine M
abstract: A large body of criminal justice research has investigated the decisions made by system actors, especially police, judges,, prosecutors. A growing area of research interest has focused on the decisions made by crime victims in response to criminal victimization. Many times, victims decide to seek help from informal sources such as friends or family in overcoming their criminal victimization, a decision that may influence the likelihood of reporting to more formal outlets, including the police. These decisions, the factors that influence a victim’s decision to seek help are not well understood, particularly for victims of stalking. The present study examines the situational, victim characteristics that affect informal help-seeking decisions among stalking victims while also exploring the impact of informal help-seeking on the decision to report the crime to law enforcement (formal help-seeking). Results suggest that dimensions of offense seriousness, fear of victimization,, victimization acknowledgment are among the factors affecting decision-making,, that these informal, formal victim decisions are unrelated despite having similar predictors.

title: Experiences of intimate partner violence victims with police, the justice system in Canada
authors: Saxton, Michael D, Olszowy, Laura, MacGregor, Jennifer C D, MacQuarrie, Barbara J, Wathen, C Nadine
keywords: domestic violence; justice system response; police response; survey design;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jssp2018
abstract: Legal responses to intimate partner violence (IPV) can determine whether, how those exposed to IPV seek help. Understanding the victim's perspective is essential to developing policy, practice standards, as well as informing professionals working in policing, the justice system. In this survey study, we utilized a subset of 2,831 people who reported experiencing IPV to examine (a) rates of reporting to the police; (b) experiences with,, perceived helpfulness of, police; (c) rates of involvement with the criminal, family law systems, including protection orders;, (d) experiences with,, perceived helpfulness of, the justice system. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics for closed-ended survey questions, content analysis of text responses. More than 35\% of victims reported a violent incident to the police,, perceptions of helpfulness were mixed. Fewer victims were involved with the criminal, family law systems,, their satisfaction also varied. Text responses provided insight into possible reasons for the variability found in experiences, for example, the proposed role of victim, system expectations,, respondents' perception that getting help depends on ``being lucky'' with the officials encountered.

title: ‘Reasonable’ perceptions of stalking: the influence of conduct severity, the perpetrator–target relationship
authors: Scott, Adrian J, Sheridan, Lorraine
abstract: Abstract Ex-partner stalkers are more persistent, dangerous than stranger stalkers, but are less likely to be convicted of an offence. This research considers whether the just world hypothesis (JWH) can account for this apparent contradiction. An experimental 3×3 independent factorial design was used to investigate the influence of conduct severity, the perpetrator–target relationship on perceptions of stalking. Three hundred, thirty-four students were presented with one of nine vignettes, asked to complete five scale items relating to the situation described. Conduct severity, the perpetrator–target relationship produced significant main effects for the combined scale items. The perpetrator's behaviour was perceived to constitute stalking, necessitate police intervention and/or criminal charges,, cause the target alarm or personal distress to a greater extent when the perpetrator, target were depicted as strangers rather than ex-partners. Conversely, the target was perceived to be less responsible for encouraging the perpetrator's behaviour in the stranger condition compared to the ex-partner condition. The JWH provides a possible explanation for the influence of the perpetrator–target relationship on perceptions of stalking. Future research could utilize more realistic vignettes to increase the impact of the perpetrator's behaviour.

title: Perceptions, prevalence of stalking in a male sample
authors: Sheridan, Lorraine, Gillett, Raphael, Davies, Graham
keywords: stalking;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;1\_複数尺度と因子分析
abstract: Abstract Most research into stalking has focused on males as perpetrators, females as victims. The present study investigated firstly how males perceive the crime of stalking, secondly the prevalence of stalking, other intrusive activities in a male population. A sample of 210 British men was asked to indicate which of a continuum of 42 behaviours they believed to represent stalking. Clear subtypes of perceived stalking were identified,, these did not significantly differ from those produced by a female sample in earlier work (Sheridan, Davies, Boon, 2001). Thus, male, females hold similar views on which activities do, do not constitute ‘stalking’, Respondents were then asked to indicate whether they had personal experience of the same 42 behaviours, if they had, to provide free narrative on their ‘worst experience’. As expected, males reported substantially less experience of intrusive behaviour than females,, just 5.2\% were judged to have suffered ‘stalking’. Whilst this figure is significantly below estimates made for females, it still indicates a notable risk for males, suggests that complaints of stalking made by males should be taken as seriously as those made by females.

title: Initial courtship behavior, stalking: how should we draw the line?
authors: Sinclair, H C, Frieze, I H
keywords: Adolescent; Adult; Adults; Attitude; Behavior; Courtship; Diagnosis, Differential; Fear; Female; Humans; Male; Obsessive Behavior -- diagnosis; Obsessive Behavior -- psychology; Older people; Rejection (Psychology); Sociology; Surveillance; Violence; Violence -- psychology;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;1\_複数尺度と因子分析
abstract: As noted by Schaum, Parrish (1995), stalking blurs the boundaries between normal courtship, obsessive behavior. Consequently, stalking proves an elusive phenomenon to define, to study. Where does courtship end, stalking begin? To address this question, 197 women, 44 men from the University of Pittsburgh who had loved someone who did not love them in return were surveyed about their feelings, actions in response to this rejection. Factor analyses revealed six groupings of behaviors in response to unrequited courtship: approach, surveillance, intimidation, harming oneself, verbal abuse/mild physical harm,, extreme physical harm. Approach behavior was reported to be used more often by men, but there were no significant differences between men, women in the self-reported prevalence of other types of courtship behaviors. Correlations reveal that feelings of anger, depression were the most common predictors of violent behavior for both men, women. Pursuer-perceptions of what behaviors connoted ``going too far'' in pursuit of a relationship proved unreliable. However, when pursuers were asked whether their love interest was afraid of them, fear was a reaction perceived in response to intimidation. Although it is likely that pursuer perceptions of where to draw the line would differ from the view of the love object, these results suggest that engaging in intimidation would be an appropriate place to draw the line between courtship, stalking.

title: Obsessive relational intrusion, coping,, sexual coercion victimization
authors: Spitzberg, Brian H, Marshall, Linda, Cupach, William R
abstract: Both obsessive relational intrusion (ORI), sexual coercion can be viewed as unwanted forms of excessive relational intrusion. ORI is a pattern of persistent invasion of another's sense of privacy for the purpose of advancing a relationship that the target of pursuit does not desire. This study examined first if ORI, sexual coercion victimization tend to correspond,, second, if coping responses tended to correspond with both forms of victimization. Both expectations were strongly supported. Implications for formulating better models of victimization are discussed.

title: Exploring the interactional phenomenon of stalking, obsessive relational intrusion
authors: Spitzberg, Brian H, Nicastro, Alana M, Cousins, Amber V
keywords: 320\_ST実証研究;J\_TF1505;1\_複数尺度と因子分析;z\_jasc2017\_root
abstract: Obsessive relational intrusion (ORI),, its more extreme relative, stalking, are significant social problems. However, to date, most research is relatively crude, anecdotal in nature. Further, most of the stalking literature has focused on aspects of the perpetrators rather than characteristics of the victims. This study sought to examine the nature, extent of victimization, employing new measures of ORI, stalking developed by Spitzberg, Cupach (1997). Multiple victimization factors were examined to ascertain the characteristics of obsessive intrusion victims, to analyze the relationship between victimization, symptomology,, coping strategies. The ORI‐VSF (victim short form) was administered to 69 male, 93 female college students. Exploratory factor analysis indicated two factors, suggestive of general pursuit, aggression. Analyses indicate that males, females were not differentially victimized. Further, coping responses were more predictive of symptomology than amount of victimization. Discussion explores issues about the nature of presumed sex differences in victimization, the role of coping responses in mediating the effects of stalking, obsessive relational intrusion.

title: Obsessive relational intrusion, sexual coercion victimization
authors: Spitzberg, Brian H, Rhea, Jill
abstract: A study was conducted to identify the extent to which people self-identified as victimized by obsessive relational intrusion are also victimized by sexual coercion by a given relational partner. Respondents were asked to rate the extent to which they had experienced any 1 of 23 clusters of obsessive relationally intrusive activities, to focus on the worst relationship in which such behaviors were experienced,, indicate the extent to which that same person had engaged in any of 36 sexually coercive activities. Results indicate that obsessive relational intrusion, sexual coercion tend to co-occur in relationships,, that both are unique, relatively equivalent predictors of psychological symptoms, accounting for extensive variance in general distress, sense of loss,, resilience symptoms. Implications are discussed for developing more predictive models of the factors sustaining intrusive relationships.

title: Victim experiences, perspectives on police responses to verbal violence in domestic settings
authors: Stewart, Catherine Carolyn, Langan, Debra, Hannem, Stacey
abstract: This interdisciplinary, qualitative study explores why individuals called the police in noncriminal, verbally aggressive situations, how they perceived police responses. In-depth interviews were conducted with 30 individuals, mostly women. While some reported positive perceptions of the police response, the participants’ accounts underscored the seriousness of verbal violence, revealed that when women seek help from police they often perceive the resulting response as inadequate and/or unfair. This study highlights the importance of recognizing that verbal violence is often part of a “fabric of abuse” that may include criminal behavior, considers implications for police practice.

title: Providing victims of crime with information on police response activity: The challenges faced by the police non-emergency call-handler
authors: Stafford, Andrew B
abstract: Police policy in England, Wales is to always explain to a member of the public who contacts the police what will happen as a result of them doing so. During initial contact between a victim of crime, the police, this task often falls to police call-handlers. This article examines information on police response activity provided to victims by police non-emergency call-handlers during such instances of contact. Empirical analysis highlights the importance that call-handlers place on providing accurate information on response activity to those who call the police,, the various challenges that they can encounter when attempting this.

title: Assessment, management of risk for intimate partner violence by police officers using the Brief Spousal Assault Form for the Evaluation of risk
authors: Storey, Jennifer E, Kropp, P Randall, Hart, Stephen D, Belfrage, Henrik, Strand, Susanne
keywords: intimate partner violence; Brief Spousal Assault Form for the Evaluation of Risk; B-SAFER measure; risk assessment; police officers; risk management; test validity; psychometrics; test reliability; risk evaluation; Domestic Violence; Evaluation; Police Personnel; Threat;320\_ST実証研究;Criminal Justice, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: The management of intimate partner violence (IPV) typically falls to police. For assistance, officers are increasingly using violence risk assessment tools like the Brief Spousal Assault Form for the Evaluation of Risk (B-SAFER). This study replicates the methodology of Belfrage et al. but examines the B-SAFER as used by Swedish police officers when assessing, managing IPV. Results revealed a positive relationship between risk, management. Total scores, overall risk ratings predicted recidivism (AUC [Area under the curve] = .70, .69, respectively). Finally, a pattern where management recommendations were associated with decreased recidivism in high risk perpetrators but increased recidivism in low risk perpetrators was found. Results validate the use of the B-SAFER by police, reveal mostly comparable findings between the B-SAFER, the Spousal Assault Risk Assessment Guide, as examined by Belfrage et al., but suggest that the B-SAFER may be better suited for police.

title: Defining relational stalking in research: Understanding sample composition in relation to repetition, duration of harassment
authors: Thompson, Carleen M, Dennison, Susan M
journal: Psychiatry, psychology,, law: an interdisciplinary journal of the Australian, New Zealand Association of Psychiatry, Psychology, Law
abstract: Due to ambiguities in stalking laws, the concept of stalking more generally, it is difficult for researchers to operationalize stalking for the purpose of selecting samples of perpetrators or victims. In an attempt to develop an empirical basis for operationalizing relational stalking, this study examined unwanted intrusions in a community, student sample. Participants (N = 1738) completed a questionnaire assessing the repetition, duration of their unwanted intrusive behaviour following the termination of a relationship or pursuit of a romantic relationship. The consequences of applying different cut-offs of repetition, duration of harassment were examined in relation to the proportion of participants who self-reported intent to frighten, intimidate or harm the target, perceived target fear or harm, the use of violence and/or threats. Engaging in some form of unwanted pursuit was almost normative (75\% of the sample). When higher levels of repetition were used to define stalking, the sample comprised participants who reported engaging in more serious forms of intrusive behaviour. Applying different cut-offs of duration appeared to have less of an effect on sample composition than did repetition. Criteria that may help to capture more serious forms of stalking behaviour, as opposed to normative behaviour, are discussed.

title: The nonlinear effect of informal social control on repeat intimate partner violence victimization
authors: Valentine, Colby L, Stults, Brian J, Hasbrouck, Matthew
keywords: informal social control; intimate partner violence; neighborhood context; nonlinear;320\_ST実証研究;304\_RepeatVic
abstract: Prior research has examined the effects of neighborhood context on intimate partner violence (IPV) with mixed results. While most studies find that neighborhood disadvantage is positively associated with risk of IPV, the effects are less consistent for characteristics such as social ties, informal social control. One possible explanation for these mixed findings draws from theoretical, empirical literature arguing that a high level of collective efficacy can aid in the control of criminal behavior, but it can also deter residents from acting against crime committed by neighbors. This suggests the possibility of a nonlinear effect of collective efficacy where the risk of IPV may be high in areas with very low levels of collective efficacy because of the inability of neighborhoods to collectively control residents, but it may also be high in areas with very high levels of collective efficacy where residents are less willing to report on the criminal behavior of fellow residents. We test this possibility using survey data for female victims of IPV in Chicago merged with neighborhood characteristics. Findings suggest that the risk of repeat victimization is highest in areas with either very high or very low levels of informal social control.

title: The prevalence of stalking in The Netherlands
authors: Van Der Aa, Suzan, Kunst, Maarten
keywords: stalking;320\_ST実証研究;z\_jasc2017\_root;0\_代表性被害調査;international Review of Victimology
abstract: Over eight years after the enactment of the Dutch anti-stalking provisions there are still no figures detailing the prevalence of stalking in The Netherlands. This article aims to estimate the lifetime, annual prevalence of this form of victimisation within the Dutch population. Questionnaires were distributed in July 2007 to visitors to the annual Tilburg fun fair. Of the 1,027 respondents 16.5 percent reported a lifetime rate of stalking victimisation, 3.9 percent had experienced stalking within the past twelve months. With more than one in five women (20.7\%), almost one in seven men (13.4\%), women were significantly more likely to report having been subjected to stalking at some time during their lives. This would concern approximately 1.4 million women, 0.9 million men nationally. In line with previous research, age was significantly related to life-time stalking, with younger people having greater odds of reporting victimisation.

title: Intimate partner violence in u.S. Metropolitan areas: The contextual influences of police, social services: Intimate partner violence in the u.S
authors: Xie, Min, Lauritsen, Janet L, Heimer, Karen
keywords: National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS); intimate partner violence; mandatory arrest laws; police; social services;320\_ST実証研究;z\_urban\_socio\_root;criminology
abstract: Although community responses to the problem of intimate partner violence typically focus on increasing, improving policing, social services, few studies have examined the relationship among police force size, social service providers,, women's safety at home. To address this issue, we use data from the National Crime Victimization Survey to examine patterns of intimate partner violence for 40 metropolitan statistical areas (MSAs) over a 16‐year period (1989–2004). We analyze the data using three‐level multilevel models, with individual respondents (N = 487,166) nested within years, nested within MSAs. Net of other important individual, contextual factors, the results show that women's likelihood of victimization is significantly lower in MSAs that employ more sworn officers per capita, whereas the states’ mandatory arrest laws are not found to have significant independent effects. Above, beyond the effects of police force size, we also find a significant negative relationship between the size of the social service workforce, intimate partner violence. Future research should develop collaborative data collection efforts to examine the specific activities of police, social service workers in dealing with intimate partner violence so that the mechanisms underlying these significant relationships can be understood more clearly.

title: The relationship between social support, intimate partner violence in neighborhood context
authors: Wright, Emily M
abstract: Social support has been recognized as a protective factor associated with reduced intimate partner violence (IPV). A question that few studies have examined, however, is whether the effectiveness of social support on IPV is conditioned by the neighborhood in which it occurs. This study investigated whether the separate effects of support from friends, family members on partner violence were conditioned by neighborhood disadvantage. Results indicated that social support from family significantly reduced the prevalence, frequency of IPV, whereas support from friends was associated with higher frequencies of partner violence. Importantly, the effects of social support were contextualized by neighborhood disadvantage, with the impact of both forms of social support on IPV being diminished in neighborhoods characterized by higher levels of disadvantage.

title: Relational aggression, intimate partner violence,, gender: An exploratory analysis
authors: Wright, Emily M, Benson, Michael L
abstract: This study explores the effects of romantic relational aggression on intimate partner violence. The concept of relational aggression denotes a type of nonphysical aggression that is specific to relationships, that has only recently been recognized in the psychological literature. Using responses to the Conflict Tactics Scale from adults participating in the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods, romantic relational aggression is examined with regard to male, female intimate partner violence perpetration, victimization. Results indicate that romantic relational aggression is a predictor of partner violence perpetration, victimization among both males, females.

title: The cycle of violence in context: Exploring the moderating roles of neighborhood disadvantage, cultural norms: Cycle of violence in context
authors: Wright, Emily M, Fagan, Abigail A
keywords: child abuse; culture; disadvantage; family violence; neighborhoods;320\_ST実証研究;z\_urban\_socio\_root;criminology
abstract: Although the cycle of violence theory has received empirical support (Widom, 1989a, 1989b), in reality, not all victims of child physical abuse become involved in violence. Therefore, little is known regarding factors that may moderate the relationship between abuse, subsequent violence, particularly contextual circumstances. The current investigation used longitudinal data from 1,372 youth living in 79 neighborhoods who participated in the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods (PHDCN),, it employed a multivariate, multilevel Rasch model to explore the degree to which neighborhood disadvantage, cultural norms attenuate or strengthen the abuse-violence relationship. The results indicate that the effect of child physical abuse on violence was weaker in more disadvantaged communities. Neighborhood cultural norms regarding tolerance for youth delinquency, fighting among family, friends did not moderate the child abuse-violence relationship, but each had a direct effect on violence, such that residence in neighborhoods more tolerant of delinquency, fighting increased the propensity for violence. These results suggest that the cycle of violence may be contextualized by neighborhood structural, cultural conditions.

title: Nonfatal strangulation during domestic violence events in new South Wales: Prevalence, characteristics using text mining study of police narratives
authors: Wilson, Mandy, Spike, Erin, Karystianis, George, Butler, Tony
keywords: domestic violence; intimate partner violence; nonfatal strangulation; police; text mining;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Nonfatal strangulation (NFS) is a common form of domestic violence (DV) that frequently leaves no visible signs of injury, can be a portent for future fatality. A validated text mining approach was used to analyze a police dataset of 182,949 DV events for the presence of NFS. Results confirmed NFS within intimate partner relationships is a gendered form of violence. The presence of injury and/or other (non-NFS) forms of physical abuse, emotional/verbal/social abuse,, the perpetrator threatening to kill the victim, were associated with significantly higher odds of NFS perpetration. Police data contain rich information that can be accessed using automated methodologies such as text mining to add to our understanding of this pressing public health issue.

title: The life History Calendar method, multilevel modeling: Application to research on intimate partner violence
authors: Yoshihama, Mieko, Bybee, Deborah
keywords: Asian women; domestic violence; intimate partner violence; life history calendar; multilevel modeling; self-report;320\_ST実証研究;Violence Against Women\_Sage
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is prevalent, often recurrent in women's lives. To better understand the changing risk of IPV over the life course, which could guide more effective policies, program responses, methodological innovations are needed. Life History Calendar methods enhance respondents' recall of the timing of specific types of IPV experienced over the life course. Multilevel modeling provides a way to analyze individual, collective trajectories, examine covariates of IPV risk. We apply these complementary methods to examine IPV trajectories for a sample of women of Filipina descent living in the United States, examining life course timing, cohort effects.

title: The importance of social learning, critical incident stressors on police officers’ perpetration of intimate partner violence
authors: Zavala, Egbert, Melander, Lisa A, Kurtz, Don L
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) perpetrated by police officers has been largely attributed to the unique critical incident stressors encountered in the field. While a large body of studies has documented a link between critical incident stressors, IPV among law enforcement, these studies have not examined whether experiencing child maltreatment, witnessing interparental violence also contribute to IPV perpetration. The current study uses data from the study Police Stress, Domestic Violence in Police Families in Baltimore, Maryland: 1997-1999 to examine the effects child maltreatment, interparental violence,, critical incident stressors have on IPV perpetration within a social learning, general strain framework. Results indicate that personally experiencing child maltreatment was associated with police officers perpetrating IPV later in life. In addition, women were more likely to report perpetrating IPV when compared to men. Studies that have not controlled for child maltreatment may not have provided a comprehensive test of the correlates of IPV in police families.
