title: Helping citizens help themselves: Neighborhood improvement programs, the impact of social networks, trust,, norms on neighborhood-oriented forms of participation
authors: Lelieveldt, Herman
abstract: This article analyzes the relationship between social capital, neighborhood-oriented forms of participation within the context of an innovative Dutch neighborhood improvement program. On the basis of a survey among 307 residents, the author studies the link between three dimensions of social capital (neighborliness, trust in neighbors,, sense of duty), three neighborhood oriented forms of participation: informal governance, the conversion of specific neighborhood problems into action,, participation in the program. Neighborliness, a sense of duty are positively related to the various forms of participation, whereas the impact of trust is somewhat more ambiguous. A subsequent analysis of the residents’ proposals shows that although some of them explicitly refer to the importance of social capital, the bulk of their plans simply demand resources (money, personnel, or policies) to address concrete issues. The author concludes that social capital is an important facilitator of people’s capacity to prevent, solve such problems themselves but that at the same time a whole range of problems still needs to be addressed through direct governmental action.

title: The impact of crime rate, experience of crime,, fear of crime on residents’ participation in association: studying 25 districts in the City of Seoul, South Korea
authors: Lee, Juheon, Cho, Sarah
keywords: 307\_CP市民参加;16\_ソウル;10\_英語の研究;301\_ComCrm;Crime Prevention, Community Safety
abstract: While the majority of studies on community crime have focused on socio-economic characteristics that lead to high or low rates of crime, the impact of crime on community residents’ social ties has received less attention. This study examines the impact of district-level crime rate, experience of crime,, fear of crime on individual community residents’ participation in association—which has been widely seen as an indicator of social capital—in the city of Seoul, South Korea. Moreover, as recent social capital studies look deeper into the different types of neighborhood crime connected to different types of associations, this study separately examines the impact of total crime, violent crime,, property crime on the respondents’ social, civic engagement, reward-based,, online associations. We find that district-level crime rates negatively correlated with all types of associations, but the difference between violent crime, property crime was minimal. Additionally, individual-level experience of crime significantly decreased residents’ participation in social, online associations. However, fear of crime did not show a significant effect on any type of association.

title: Citizen participation in neighborhood crime prevention
authors: Lavrakas, Paul J, Herz, Elicia J
keywords: CITIZENSHIP; COMMUNITIES; CRIME prevention; CRIMINOLOGY; METROPOLITAN areas; TELEPHONE surveys;307\_CP市民参加;z\_kakenhi2008;20240717\_IVde一次予防;criminology
abstract: ABSTRACTThe importance of citizen involvement in crime prevention was stressed throughut the 1970s and, with looming service cutbacks, grows in potential importance for the coming decades. While many programs have been developed to encourage the public to get involved, especially in community‐based crime prevention efforts, not much was known about the underlying motivational dynamics. On the basis of a random‐digit‐dial telephone survey of 1803 residents in an entire metropolitan area, we conclude that most citizens become involved in neighborhood anticrime activities not because of fear of crime, but rather as an extension of their general tendency for community‐based voluntary action.

title: Can we speak in confidence? Community intelligence, neighbourhood policing v2.0
authors: Lowe, Trudy, Innes, Martin
abstract: Informed by empirical data collected in the London Borough of Sutton (LBS) in four sweeps between 2007, 2010, this article examines the impact of a community engagement methodology encouraging citizens to articulate their local security needs to Neighbourhood Policing teams (NPTs). By acting on this community intelligence police are able to ‘tune’ their interventions towards those problems generating most social harm. In so doing, the data suggest police are able to improve public confidence, increase overall community well-being. This case study of Sutton is used to illuminate some broader patterns, trends in how policing in England, Wales is being reconfigured in response to a set of economic, ideological pressures. It is suggested that the combination of forces are liable to induce a revised version of the principles, practices associated with the initial model of Neighbourhood Policing (NP).

title: Violence, hyperviolence: The rhetoric, practice of community policing
authors: Manning, P K, Singh, Mahendra P
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: The postmodernism perspective, used here to illuminate the rhetoric, practice of community policing, draws attention to the role of violence in sustaining social order, the increasing role of symbolic or representational violence in shaping interpersonal relations. When societies valorize violence in some public contexts, it can be suppressed or effaced in others. The media‐driven spectacle of violence uses representations of violence as a means to increase ratings, sell goods, services,, maintain its salience by diminishing it to cartoon‐parody status. Focus on symbolic violence distracts public attention from the grinding everyday violence, the infrequent excesses of governmental social control. The rhetoric of community policing is “postmodern”, displays “hyperviolence” (rhetoric that denies the role of violence, yet indicates its presence in practice) in that it suppresses the centrality of violence to the police mandate, displaces attention to a notional “community.” A case study of community policing in one western city, based on interviews, observations,, focus groups, reveals that although community policing rhetoric is used as public discourse, the practice of patrol officers is little changed,, the absence of a crime control emphasis creates ambiguity in the police role, raises morale questions,, alters public expectations. A quite different future is imagined, depending on the scenario one adopts: the spread of community policing, increasing punitive crime control, a rising prison population, multiple modes of “soft control” partially obscuring the dramatic rise in the incarcerated population,, the use of the death penalty or some dialectic between representational, hyperviolence, rising violence on the part of the excluded lower classes.

title: Situational policing: neighbourhood development, crime control
authors: Nolan, III, James J, Conti, Norman, Mcdevitt, Jack
keywords: Communities; Crime Prevention; Law Enforcement; Psychosocial Development; Human; situational policing; neighbourhood development; crime control; SOCIAL disorganization; collective efficacy; broken windows;307\_CP市民参加;J\_TF1505
abstract: Over the past two decades, the Broken Windows version of social disorganization theory has had a significant impact on law enforcement practices in the United States. Contemporary sociologists, however, have demonstrated that neighbourhood‐level collective efficacy (or a lack thereof) is a more significant predictor of violent crime than are physical, social disorder (i.e., broken windows). Collective efficacy is viewed as an evolving neighbourhood‐level property. We posit that neighbourhoods pass through, regress to, or get stuck in identifiable stages of development as they move toward (or away from) higher levels of collective efficacy. Giving consideration to both stage of neighbourhood development, level of neighbourhood crime, disorder, we construct four neighbourhood types: Strong, Vulnerable, Anomic, Responsive. The concept of “situational policing”, then, is introduced as a way to address effectively both the development of collective efficacy,, the occurrence of crime, disorder in each neighbourhood type.

title: How officers spend their time with the community
authors: Parks, Roger B, Mastrofski, Stephen D, DeJong, Christina, Gray, M Kevin
abstract: Using data from field observation of police patrol officers at work in two American cities, we explore similarities, differences between the tasks undertaken by generalist patrol officers, community policing specialists. As expected, community policing specialists are much more able to choose the work they do, the people they encounter. Specialists use their discretion to spend less “face time” with the public, more time “behind the scenes” than do patrol generalists,, to engage a higher-status, less problem-ridden clientele. Implications for adoption of community policing are discussed.

title: Police culture, individualism,, community policing: Evidence from two police departments
authors: Paoline, III, Eugene A, Myers, Stephanie M, Worden, Robert E
abstract: According to the conventional wisdom, the police culture consists of a set of values, attitudes,, norms that are widely shared among officers, who find in the culture a way to cope with the strains of their working environment. Some research implies that the conventional wisdom is overdrawn,, recent research has begun to question it more directly. Changes in the composition (i.e., the race, sex,, education) of police personnel, as well as philosophical, organizational changes associated with community policing, could be expected to further fragment police culture, to shift the distribution of police attitudes. Here we examine variation in outlooks that, according to conventional wisdom, are part of the police culture, using survey data collected in two police departments. We also examine the relationships between these outlooks, characteristics of officers—sex, race, education, length of service, community-policing training,, community-policing specialist assignment—that are associated with the changes in policing. We find that officers' outlooks do not conform to the pattern that we would expect on the basis of conventional wisdom. We also find that the variation in officers' occupational attitudes is not patterned to a great extent by their characteristics. We conclude with directions for future research on police attitudes.

title: Community policing, social service partnerships: lessons from New England
authors: Peaslee, Liliokanaio
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Partnerships between police, social service agencies are an important but understudied component of community policing. This paper looks at why – despite the adoption of community, problem‐solving policing nationwide – police–social service partnerships are not routine. I draw from case studies of youth‐focused partnerships in four US cities to examine how police can better collaborate with municipal, community‐based agencies,, to address the organizational, leadership challenges confronting reformers. The findings of this paper illustrate that while police are valuable partners for social service agencies, one should use caution in conceptualizing too large a role for police in juvenile prevention, intervention initiatives.

title: An examination of citizen involvement in crime prevention in high-risk versus low- to moderate-risk neighborhoods
authors: Pattavina, April, Byrne, James M, Garcia, Luis
keywords: citizen involvement; citizen participation; crime prevention; high risk neighborhoods; BOSTON (Mass.); At Risk Populations; Community Involvement; Crime; Neighborhoods;307\_CP市民参加;z\_2009jasc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;Crime Delinquency\_●Sage
abstract: In the following study, the authors examine factors that explain citizen participation in crime prevention activities in Boston. Using survey data from a random sample, census data,, official crime, arrest data, the authors identified a wide range of individual-, community-based indicators that could potentially explain citizen involvement in crime prevention. Findings revealed that citizen involvement in collective crime prevention does indeed vary by the risk level of a particular neighborhood, with high-risk neighborhoods demonstrating higher rates of involvement than low- to moderate-risk neighborhoods. The authors also found that the factors that explained citizen participation varied by the risk level of the neighborhood. Overall, this research demonstrated that in high-risk neighborhoods, citizen involvement in crime prevention activities is affected by the unique blend of personal, parochial,, public social control mechanisms operating in these areas.

title: Style of policing adopted by rural police, deputies: An analysis of job satisfaction, community policing
authors: Pelfrey, Jr, William V
abstract: Purpose– The purpose of this paper is to show that policing research frequently commits two errors: focusing on urban police units, failing to incorporate theory. The current research considers the policing style adopted by officers in a rural setting, tests the utility of Work Redesign, a theory that explains the importance, role of satisfaction with work.Design/methodology/approach– Rural police officers in community policing, traditional motorized patrol assignments were surveyed regarding policing style, the perceived importance of various tasks,, time allocation.Findings– Findings suggest that community policing has a role in rural areas; however, officers generally endorse the practices of traditional motorized patrol uniformly while only community policing officers endorse COP practices.Research limitations/implications– Although generalizing findings derived from several police agencies to other agencies should be done with caution, the findings are potentially important to agency decision makers regarding assignment, implementation of community policing programs.Originality/value– This paper is of interest to those investigating: the impacts of assignment at the officer level, community policing, the influence of job satisfaction on work,, rural law enforcement.

title: The relationship between citizen participation, organizational processes, outcomes, the benefits of citizen participation in neighborhood organizations
authors: Ohmer, Mary L
abstract: ABSTRACT A major resource of neighborhood organizations is the voluntary participation of residents who give their time, energy to improve their communities. In recent years, there has been a revitalization of strategies to engage residents to volunteer for neighborhood-based organizations. Guided by organizational empowerment theory, the ecological perspective, the current study examined the relationship between citizen participation, organizational characteristics, effectiveness, the benefits received by residents participating in neighborhood organizations in poor communities. The data were gathered through a survey of resident volunteers in four neighborhood organizations in Pennsylvania, were analyzed using hierarchical multiple regression analyses. The results showed that volunteers' level of involvement in their neighborhood organization influenced their self-efficacy. However, volunteers' perceptions of their neighborhood organizations' characteristics, effectiveness were the most strongly related to the benefits of citizen participation, contributing to residents' self efficacy, collective efficacy,, sense of community. Implications for social work research, practice are discussed.

title: Citizen participation in neighborhood organizations, its relationship to volunteers' self-, collective efficacy, sense of community
authors: Ohmer, M L
abstract: Citizen participation is the active involvement of individuals in changing problematic conditions in communities, influencing policies, programs that affect the quality of their lives. Neighborhood organizations in poor communities often rely on volunteers to accomplish their goals. Therefore, social workers must understand how engaging residents in volunteer activities in their neighborhood benefits them individually, collectively. This study examined the relationship between resident involvement in neighborhood organizations, volunteers' self-efficacy, collective efficacy,, sense of community by surveying members, participants of four neighborhood organizations in poor communities in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Results demonstrated that volunteers involved in the organization's everyday activities, in decision making received the most benefits, including increased self-efficacy (leadership, policy control, neighborhood policy control,, knowledge, skills), organizational collective efficacy,, sense of community. Involvement in the everyday activities alone increased volunteers' self-efficacy, organizational collective efficacy. Implications for social work practice, strategies for developing the volunteer capacity of community-based organizations are discussed.

title: Settlement typology, community participation in participatory landscape ecology of residents
authors: Peng, Li-Pei, Hsieh, Yeu-Sheng
abstract: Numerous scholars have emphasised the importance of providing participatory landscape ecology (PLE) that local residents deem acceptable. However, the complexity of PLE may require promoting the understanding of settlement types, community participation in PLE of residents. Our empirical study contributes to the critical PLE by adopting physical, social environments to determine the community participation of residents. The physical environments are classified into four settlement types: high-rise/urban, low-rise/urban, high-rise/rural, low-rise/rural. Survey data collected from 495 residents in the Taipei metropolitan area revealed the typology of physical environments, which can be used to substantially explain community participation. Perceived residential satisfaction (PRS), neighbouring behaviour (NB), derived from the social environment, were tested for describing community participation. We observed an indirect relationship between settlement typology, community participation through the two intervening roles of PRS, NB. This affirms the importance of social environment to the relationship between settlement types, community participation.

title: Perceptions of police, participatory behavior for crime prevention: a multilevel analysis of formal, informal behaviors
authors: Pyo, Jimin
abstract: This study examines relationships between attitudes toward police, informal as well as formal participatory behaviors for neighborhood crime prevention, while considering neighborhood influences on individuals’ behaviors. Utilizing data from Ross Matsueda’s Seattle Neighborhoods, Crime Survey of 2220 households, this study examined relationships between perceptions of police—satisfaction, cynicism about police activities in dealing with residents’ concerns—and participatory behaviors. Consistent with the legitimacy argument, results demonstrated that individuals with more positive perceptions of police service participate more in neighborhood crime prevention in both formal, informal ways. One notable neighborhood factor was community social ties which potentially moderates associations between perceptions of police, participatory behaviors. Implications for crime prevention policy are discussed.

title: Broken windows theory, citizen engagement in crime prevention
authors: Ren, Ling, Zhao, Jihong “solomon”, He, Ni “phil”
abstract: According to broken windows theory, heightened perceptions of disorder, increased fear of crime, diminished community social control are significant inhibitors of public participation in crime prevention arising directly from concerns for personal safety, sense of futility associated with the effort required. The purpose of this study is to partially test these hypothesized links between conditions, perceptions, behaviors. The data were derived from a telephone survey of approximately 1,100 residents in Houston, Texas. In addition to the traditional survey data, social nuisance crime/disorder incidents recorded by the police in the immediate neighborhood of each respondent’s residence were documented by using a GIS spatial analysis tool. The use of structural equation modeling enables us to examine the related effects of key elements of broken windows theory on citizen engagement in public safety promotion. Study results indicate that disorder incidents had a significant impact on perceptions of disorder, while perceptions of disorder tend to increase fear for personal safety, which in turn reduces sense of collective efficacy. Finally, citizen engagement in crime prevention was significantly related to collective efficacy. These findings hold true across various neighborhood contexts classified by an index of concentrated disadvantage. The findings reported here lend support to propositions derived from broken windows theory to a major extent. Study limitations, relevant implications are discussed in some detail.

title: Volunteer street patrols: responsibilised, motivated volunteering in community safety
authors: Westall, Adam
abstract: Purpose This paper aims to contribute towards our knowledge, understanding of volunteer street patrols working within community safety, pluralised policing. Through the increased responsibilisation of communities, individuals, volunteers are taking to the streets to help others in need, support the community safety infrastructure. The example of volunteer street patrols is used to explore the motivations of individuals participating in the local delivery of community safety, policing. Design/methodology/approach This research is drawn from ethnographic research consisting of 170 hours of participant observation on the streets of a northern UK city, Manchester, supported by 24 semi-structured interviews with volunteers, stakeholders who participate in a street patrol, those working alongside them. Findings Using a three-paradigm perspective for volunteer motivations, the themes altruism, civil connection, volunteering for leisure are applied to explore volunteer motivations. Through their actions, volunteers in the street patrol are motivated volunteers who can offer an additional, important resource within the local community safety, pluralised policing infrastructure. Originality/value This paper highlights volunteer street patrols offer a caring, supportive function to people in need on the street, one in support of the police, other agencies. It contributes to the growing understanding of those who volunteer in policing, community safety landscapes. As responsibilised citizens, they have an increased awareness of social problems. They are motivated individuals who wish to create, maintain safety, play an important role in policing the night-time economy.

title: The theory, research behind Neighborhood Watch: Is it a sound fear, crime reduction strategy?
authors: Rosenbaum, Dennis P
keywords: Block watch; COMMUNITY Involvement; CRIME prevention -- Citizen participation; Community crime prevention programs; FAMILY; FEAR of crime; Families with special problems -- families with criminal offenders; NEIGHBORHOOD watch programs; Organizations, services to families -- community groups; Psychology, sociology, anthropology -- psychology; Theory, research methodology -- family theory;307\_CP市民参加;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;301\_5;Crime Delinquency\_●Sage
abstract: This article takes a critical look at the theory, research behind the highly touted community crime prevention strategy known as Neighborhood Watch. While correlational studies of neighborhoods, citizen participation are numerous, there is a paucity of rigorous experimental evaluations that test the proposed “Implant Hypothesis,” that is, that collective citizen participation (and the social processes it allegedly activates) can be implanted in neighborhoods where it does not currently exist. However, there are both theoretical, empirical reasons to challenge some of the basic assumptions underlying the Neighborhood Watch approach to reducing crime, reducing fear of crime,, restoring a sense of community. The hypothesis that Watch programs increase fear of crime, may have other effects is examined. The implications of this assessment for theory development, public policy are explored.

title: Crime, social capital,, community participation
authors: Saegert, Susan, Winke, Gary
keywords: Social Capital; SOCIAL networks; NEIGHBORS; SOCIAL control; SOCIOLOGY; SOCIAL groups; community organization: tenant organizing; crime; Multilevel analysis; urban; collective efficacy;307\_CP市民参加;z\_2013\_コミュニティの社会心理学;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: Social disorganization at the neighborhood, community levels has been consistently linked to various forms of criminal activity. However,a very much smaller body of literature addresses the effects of crime on community organizations. In some studies, crime appears to energize communities while in others, crime leads to withdrawal from community life. Using department of health crime victimization data, interviews with 2,985 low-income inner city residents living in 487 multi-family dwellings, a multi-level model examined the relationships among crime victimization, social organization,, participation in neighborhood organizations. Social organization at the individual, building levels was measured using recent formulations of social capital theory. Findings regarding crime suggested more signs of a chilling effect on participation than of an energizing effect, especially at the building level. Social capital at the building level was more strongly, consistently related to participation in community organizations than was crime.

title: Citizen perceptions of police services: Race, neighborhood context,, community policing
authors: Schafer, Joseph A, Huebner, Beth M, Bynum, Timothy S
abstract: Studies considering perceptions of the police have traditionally focused on very broad outcome measures (e.g., global views of the police). In an era of community policing, it is imperative to consider how the public perceives the police, police services using measures reflecting this alternative paradigm of policing. In addition, recent research suggests that perceptions of the police are formed within the context of respondents’neighborhood cultures, contexts. This research examines factors predicting citizen perceptions of police services in a Midwestern community, incorporating variables reflecting respondents’ demographic traits, experiences,, neighborhood contexts. The analysis tests the predictive power of these factors using both traditional outcome measures, perceptions of police services based on community-policing criteria. The findings demonstrate the need for multidimensional constructs of citizen perceptions of police services, highlight important dimensions of public perceptions of community policing.

title: Civilian policing, legitimacy, vigilantism: findings from three case studies in England, Wales
authors: Sharp, Douglas, Atherton, Susie, Williams, Kate
abstract: The growth of civilian policing is indicative of public concerns regarding crime, community safety, the performance of the police, along with the recognition of the need for communities to engage in reducing crime, disorder. This paper examines three examples of ‘civilian policing’, including two ‘Street Watch’ schemes, a private security firm. It explores the legitimisation of civilian policing schemes by the police, along with the extent of public support, the impact upon crime reduction. Two of the case studies demonstrate the difficulties for the police in legitimising schemes that engage in the use of or threat of violence, what could be termed ‘vigilantism’. Such activities can clearly undermine the legitimacy of the police,, more specifically the ideals of community policing.

title: Contacts between police, public: Findings from the 1992 British crime survey: Home office research study 134: (450532008-001)
authors: Skogan, Wesley G
abstract: It is widely believed that voluntary action by neighborhood residents can play an important role in maintaining order. However, the ability of individuals to act in defense of their community is constrained by the opportunities for action that are available to them. Participation in collective efforts against crime is confined to places where the existence of local organizations makes that possible. The distribution of group activity across the metropolitan landscape thus defines the “opportunity structure” for local collective action. This article examines the impact of serious crime, the economic, social resources residents have to draw upon to deal with neighborhood problems,, their characteristic relationships with the police, upon those opportunities to participate in organized efforts to combat crime.

title: Volunteer retention: The importance of organisational support, psychological contract breach: Volunteer psychological contracts
authors: Walker, Arlene, Accadia, Rebecca, Costa, Beth M
abstract: Volunteer organizations face issues related to the retention of volunteers, not unlike those found in the paid workforce; however, management, authority structures, practices are different. In previous research, support factors, psychological contracts have been found to contribute to retention of employees. Few studies of volunteers have investigated the appropriateness of these variables. Survey data from 721 Australian volunteers from diverse organizations were analyzed to learn to what degree perceived organizational support, coworker support,, psychological contract breach explained volunteer intention to remain, having controlled for age, tenure. Psychological contract breach explained much more of the variance in volunteer intention to remain than tenure, coworker support, or perceived organizational support. The relationship between psychological contract breach, volunteer intention to remain is similar to that found in the paid workforce, despite the differences in management in the 2 sectors.

title: Linking informal social control, restorative justice: moving social disorganization theory beyond community policing
authors: Warner, Barbara D, Beck, Elizabeth, Ohmer, Mary L
abstract: Much of what is at the heart of social disorganization theory’s approach to neighborhood crime prevention has been ignored in favor of policies that are more closely associated with deterrence, rational choice theories. Specifically, ideas of informal social control, collective efficacy have often been translated into policies of community surveillance, the reporting of suspicious behaviors to the police. While these policies may make neighborhoods less attractive to offenders because they create higher certainty levels of recognition,, subsequently arrest, social disorganization theory, at its heart, suggests crime prevention policies of a very different nature: policies that are more closely associated with restorative justice, re‐integrative shaming, peacemaking criminology. These associations are highlighted, provide a conceptual model for a community crime prevention program that is more consistent with the underlying nature of social disorganization theory.

title: Generating action, responding to local issues: Collective efficacy in context
authors: Wickes, Rebecca L
journal: The Australian \& New Zealand journal of criminology
abstract: Recent research suggests that communities can be collectively efficacious without dense networks, kith, kinship relations. Yet few studies examine how collective efficacy is generated, sustained in the absence of close social ties. Using in-depth interviews with local residents, key stakeholders in two collectively efficacious suburbs in Brisbane, Australia, this study explores the role of social ties, networks in shaping residents' sense of active engagement, perceptions of community capacity. Results suggest that strong social bonds among residents are not necessary for the development of social cohesion, informal social control. Instead, collective representations or symbols of ‘community’ provide residents with a sense of social cohesion, trust, a perceived willingness of others to respond to problems of crime, disorder. Yet there is limited evidence that these collectively efficacious communities comprise actively engaged residents. In both communities, participants report a strong reliance on key institutions, organisations to manage, respond to a variety of problems, from neighbourhood nuisances to crime, disorder. These findings suggest a more a nuanced understanding of collective efficacy theory is needed.

title: Voluntary organizations, neighborhood crime: A dynamic perspective: Voluntary organizations, neighborhood crime
authors: Wo, James C, Hipp, John R, Boessen, Adam
keywords: neighborhood crime; voluntary organizations; organizational life course; social services; social capital;307\_CP市民参加;301\_ComCrm;301\_1;criminology
abstract: Although numerous theories suggest that voluntary organizations contribute to lower crime rates in neighborhoods, the evidence for this proposition is weak. Consequently, we propose a dynamic perspective for understanding the relationship between voluntary organizations, neighborhood crime that involves longitudinal analyses, the measurement of the age of organizations. By using longitudinal data on a sample of census blocks (N = 87,641) located across 10 cities, we test the relationship between age‐graded measures of different types of voluntary organizations, neighborhood crime rates. We use fixed‐effects negative binomial regression models that focus on change within neighborhoods of the relationship between voluntary organizations, neighborhood crime. Our results show that although each type of voluntary organization is found to exhibit crime‐reducing behavior in neighborhoods, we find that many of them are consistent with what we refer to as the “delayed impact scenario”—there is a pronounced delay between the placement of a voluntary organization, a neighborhood subsequently experiencing a reduction in crime. With protective effects of organizations typically not demonstrated until several years after being in the neighborhood, these patterns suggest a need for long‐term investment strategies when examining organizations.

title: Citizen patrol projects, national evaluation program, phase I summary report
authors: Yin, R K, Vogel, M E, Chaiken, J M, Both, D R
journal: Washington, DC: National Institute of Law Enforcement, Criminal Justice
keywords: SURVEYS; EVALUATION; APARTMENT houses; SECURITY measures; Citizen patrols; Community crime prevention programs; Crime seriousness measures; National Evaluation Program; Summaries; Vertical patrol;307\_CP市民参加;z\_2009jasc;z\_岩波エビデンス;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root

title: Reactions to crime: a multilevel analysis of fear of crime, defensive, participatory behavior
authors: Yuan, Yue, McNeeley, Susan
keywords: 307\_CP市民参加;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;9\_001\_intro;301\_ComCrm;301\_3
abstract: This study examines the associations between fear of crime, individual constrained behavior. Specifically, to address the inconsistent findings of previous research, we investigate how emotional fear of crime, perceived risk of victimization are associated with the use of defensive behaviors. We also extend previous research by examining the relationships between fear of crime, perceived risk, participatory behavior. The results of multilevel models based on survey data from Seattle show that fear of crime was positively associated with three individual defensive behaviors,, perceived risk was negatively associated with two participatory behaviors. The results suggest that emotional fear increases individualistic target-hardening behaviors, while perceptions of risk reduce participation in community-wide crime-prevention activities.

title: Participation in community crime prevention: Are volunteers more or less fearful of crime than other citizens?
authors: Zhao, Gibson, Lovrich, Gaffney
keywords: 307\_CP市民参加;J\_TF1505;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);301\_ComCrm;202408\_IndependentMobility
abstract: Fear of crime is one of many quality of life issues that community crime prevention strategies have attempted to identify, address. Little is known, however, about the perceptions of fear of criminal victimization among citizens who volunteer in community crime prevention programs. This study assesses fear of violent crime, property crime victimization among 192 police volunteers, 421 general citizens, controlling for known correlates of fear of crime in the comparison. Multivariate regression analyses show that police volunteers fear violent crime victimization substantially more than general citizens. Likewise, police volunteers fear property victimization more than general citizens, however, the effect on fear of violent crime was markedly more robust than for property crime. The findings drawn from this study lend support to Pepinski's (1989) cautions concerning community crime prevention programs. Directions for future research are discussed.

title: The effect of police presence on public fear reduction, satisfaction: A review of the literature
authors: Zhao, Jihong “soloman”, Schneider, Matthew, Thurman, Quint
keywords: FEAR of crime; POLICE; SOCIAL integration;307\_CP市民参加;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2009jasc;301\_ComCrm;318\_介入実験\_Policing;police visibility
abstract: This paper attempts to answer two questions. First, we are interested in the extent to which the presence of the police reduces public fear of crime. Second, we examine the link between police presence, public satisfaction with the police. We explore both of these topics from the existing research literature where studies were conducted using a quasi-experimental design to measure police presence. More specifically, we include research where police presence is depicted according to either targeted patrol practices, proactive/aggressive arrest projects,, /or comprehensive, integrating police strategies (i.e., community policing ). Our examination of the research literature leads us to conclude that police presence does have a strong impact on public fear reduction. In addition, proactive or/and community policing strategies appear to us to demonstrate the strongest impact on fear reduction among residents. Simultaneously, we found that public satisfaction is strongly associated with the success of a fear reduction program. In other words, a successful fear reduction program can increase public satisfaction with police services.

title: Community policing in China: old wine in new bottles
authors: Zhong, Lena Y
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: Policing in China is by nature in the community, for the community,, by the community, as manifested in the ?mass line?. With crime soaring, fear of crime growing in the reform era, policing in China encountered numerous challenges,, community policing was imported from the West. This paper first delineated the history of policing in China since 1949, then used an example to illustrate what community policing is, how it could be implemented in China. It argued that community policing per se in China since 2002 is no more than ?old wine in new bottles.?; Policing in China is by nature in the community, for the community,, by the community, as manifested in the ?mass line?. With crime soaring, fear of crime growing in the reform era, policing in China encountered numerous challenges,, community policing was imported from the West.
