title: The relationship between citizen perceptions of collective efficacy, neighborhood violent crime
authors: Armstrong, Todd A, Katz, Charles M, Schnebly, Stephen M
keywords: collective efficacy;307\_CP市民参加;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_3;Crime Delinquency\_●Sage
abstract: The current work assesses the relationship between respondent perceptions of collective efficacy, neighborhood violence. Data used in the analysis combined a community survey from Mesa, Arizona, with census data. Factor analysis provided mixed evidence regarding the factor structure of collective efficacy; therefore, separate regression models were used to test the influence of collective efficacy, social cohesion,, willingness to intervene on levels of neighborhood violence. Analyses found that community structural characteristics including concentrated disadvantage, residential instability significantly predicted perceptions of collective efficacy, social cohesion,, willingness to intervene. In turn each of these variables was related to violent crime after controlling for levels of concentrated disadvantage, residential instability,, individual demographic characteristics. When social cohesion, willingness to intervene were included in a single regression model, only social cohesion was predictive of neighborhood violence. Social cohesion, violent crime had reciprocal effects that were both negative, statistically significant.

title: The effects of community policing on fear of crime, perceived safety: findings from a pilot project in Trinidad, Tobago
authors: Maguire, Edward R, Johnson, Devon, Kuhns, Joseph B, Apostolos, Robert
abstract: Using findings from a quasi-experiment, this study examines whether the implementation of community policing in Gonzales, a distressed Caribbean community, reduced fear of crime, increased perceptions of safety. We use a pre-post, comparison group design with two groups. Data are based on three waves of citizen surveys carried out in both groups. Our findings reveal that from wave 1 to wave 2, the treatment area experienced an increase in fear relative to the comparison area; the effect size was small, positive, but was not statistically significant. The change in perceived safety from wave 1 to 2 in the treatment area was trivial, non-significant. From wave 2 to 3, the treatment area experienced a significant positive increase in perceptions of safety relative to the comparison area. The treatment area also experienced a small reduction in fear relative to the comparison area, but the effect was not statistically significant. Overall, we conclude that the early stages of implementing community policing in Gonzales may have increased fear but had no effect on perceived safety. Later, more robust implementation was associated with a significant increase in perceived safety, possibly a small reduction in fear.

title: Crime in rural Sweden
authors: Ceccato, Vânia, Dolmen, Lars
keywords: Violence; Thefts; Countryside; Regional patterns of crime; GIS; Modelling;306\_Rural;z\_rural2020;301\_ComCrm
abstract: The objective of this article is to assess the levels, spatial patterns of crime in rural Sweden. This involves a summary of the changing levels, composition of a selected group of offences from 1996 to 2007 in two groups of rural areas (remote, accessible) in relation to urban areas. Crime rates are modelled cross-sectionally as a function of the municipalities’ structural indicators. Geographical information systems (GIS), spatial statistics techniques are used to assess shifting patterns of concentration of thefts, violence as well as for modelling crime rates. Findings show that rural areas have become more criminogenic than they were a decade ago. Changes in the rates, geography were found using cluster techniques for both violence, theft. Although models of rural crime do not show any special ‘rural dimension’, the predicting variables in models containing both urban, rural areas are not exactly the same as in models with rural areas only. Crime is often linked to the presence of alcohol-selling premises, characteristics of family structure, proportion of young male population.

title: The impact of rural policing on the private lives of New Zealand police officers
authors: Buttle, John, Fowler, Corrine, Williams, Mei Wah
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article is concerned with perceived differences between rural, urban policing in New Zealand. More specifically with how officers view the effect that rural, urban policing has on their private lives, those of their family members. Using grounded theory as a research method because of its reflexivity in regard to generating questions from emergent data, 16 participants were interviewed. Seven of these participants were stationed in an urban location while nine were recruited from rural stations. The results suggest that rural policing has a greater, often more stressful impact on the private lives of police officers, their families. This suggests a need for the New Zealand Police as an organisation to engage in policy-making that gives greater recognition to the rural aspects of policing, with a particular focus being the provision of support for the families of rural officers.

title: The psychological determinants of attitudes toward relocation in the elderly: A survey study in urban, rural environments
authors: Cerina, Veronica, Fornara, Ferdinando
abstract: The aim of the study is to analyze, compare different individual, psycho-social,, psycho-environmental responses of elderly living in different environments. The conceptual frame of reference is the Complementary-Congruence Model of person-environment fit (Carp \& Carp, 1984), which focuses on relevant changes in person-environment relationship during the lifespan , with particular attention to the processes of ageing. Participants (N = 201 aged over-65 recruited in urban, rural places) filled in a questionnaire including an array of measures. Significant differences emerged between urban, rural elderly residents in psychological well-being, social network, collective identity,, attitudes to relocate. Psycho-social, psycho-environmental dimensions were more influent than individual, intra-personal dimensions on attitudes toward short-and long-term relocation. In particular, a higher environmental competence, a lower home attachment, perceived social network are associated with attitudes toward both short-term, long-term relocation. Finally, environmental competence resulted also as the strongest antecedent of psychological well-being. Los determinantes psicológicos de las actitudes hacia el traslado en las personas mayores: una encuesta en entornos urbanos y rurales Resumen El propósito de este estudio es analizar y comparar las distintas respuestas individuales, psicosociales y psico-ambientales de personas mayores que residen en diferentes entornos. El marco conceptual de referencia es el Mode-lo de Complementariedad-Congruencia entre la persona y su entorno (Carp y Carp, 1984), que examina los cambios importantes en la relación entre una persona y su entorno a lo largo de su vida, prestando especial aten-ción a los procesos de envejecimiento. Los participantes (N = 201 de más de 65 años, procedentes de entornos urbanos y rurales) rellenaron un cuestionario que evaluaba una serie de medidas. Se encontraron diferencias significativas entre las personas mayores de procedencia rural y las de procedencia urbana en bienestar psicológi-co, entorno social, identidad colectiva, y actitudes hacia el traslado. La dimensión psicosocial y la psicoambien-tal ejercen mayor influencia que la dimensión individual y la intrapersonal sobre las actitudes hacia los tras-lados por períodos cortos y largos. En concreto, una mayor competencia ambiental, un menor apego al lugar y un entorno social más pobre se asocian con actitudes hacia el traslado, tanto por períodos largos como por períodos cortos. Por último, la competencia ambiental resultó ser el antecedente más importante del bienestar psicológico. Palabras clave: Bienestar de las personas mayores, traslado de domicilio por períodos cortos y lar-gos, estrategias de afrontamiento proactivas, competencia ambiental, apego al hogar.

title: Rural to urban population density scaling of crime, property transactions in English, welsh Parliamentary Constituencies
authors: Hanley, Quentin S, Lewis, Dan, Ribeiro, Haroldo V
abstract: Urban population scaling of resource use, creativity metrics,, human behaviors has been widely studied. These studies have not looked in detail at the full range of human environments which represent a continuum from the most rural to heavily urban. We examined monthly police crime reports, property transaction values across all 573 Parliamentary Constituencies in England, Wales, finding that scaling models based on population density provided a far superior framework to traditional population scaling. We found four types of scaling: i) non-urban scaling in which a single power law explained the relationship between the metrics, population density from the most rural to heavily urban environments, ii) accelerated scaling in which high population density was associated with an increase in the power-law exponent, iii) inhibited scaling where the urban environment resulted in a reduction in the power-law exponent but remained positive,, iv) collapsed scaling where transition to the high density environment resulted in a negative scaling exponent. Urban scaling transitions, when observed, took place universally between 10, 70 people per hectare. This study significantly refines our understanding of urban scaling, making clear that some of what has been previously ascribed to urban environments may simply be the high density portion of non-urban scaling. It also makes clear that some metrics undergo specific transitions in urban environments, these transitions can include negative scaling exponents indicative of collapse. This study gives promise of far more sophisticated scale adjusted metrics, indicates that studies of urban scaling represent a high density subsection of overall scaling relationships which continue into rural environments.

title: HUMAN ecology, rural policing: A grounded theoretical analysis of how personal constraints, community characteristics influence strategies of law enforcement in rural New South Wales, Australia
authors: Jobes, Patrick
journal: Police practice \& research: an international journal
abstract: This research employs a grounded theoretical perspective to describe factors that affect police officers, techniques of policing in rural Australia. A random sample of rural officers in New South Wales (NSW) described local problems, the characteristics of people most likely to cause those problems. Two themes emerged. First, officers incorporated a human ecological perspective. Second, effective officers used traditional community policing. Most officers identified persistent tensions between formal expectations imposed by the police service, government agencies,, effective procedures for policing small towns. Effective policing occurred only after officers became integrated into informal community structures, exercised discretion regarding community standards.

title: A comparison of aggravated assault rate trends in rural, suburban,, urban areas using the UCR, NCS/NCVS, 1988–2005
authors: Kaylen, Maria, Pridemore, William Alex, Roche, Sean Patrick
abstract: Between the 1980s, 2000s, the USA experienced wide swings in violence rates. These swings were not experienced equally across urban, suburban,, rural areas. We employed UCR, NCS/NCVS data to compare aggravated assaults rates in rural, suburban,, urban areas between 1988, 2005. As expected, urban aggravated assault rates tended to remain the highest. However, the crime decline was much greater for urban relative to suburban, rural areas. Further, NCS/NCVS rates were not always higher than UCR rates for a given time, location. In the latter years, UCR–NCVS rate ratios were close to one for suburban, rural areas but remained about 1.5–2.0 in urban areas. This urban–nonurban difference has implications for testing criminological theories in non-urban areas.

title: Assessing community capacity, social capital in rural America: lessons from two rural observatories
authors: Marré, Alexander W, Weber, Bruce A
abstract: This paper reviews the work of two rural observatories: the New Rural Economy project in Canada, the Ventures program in the state of Oregon. These observatories collect data to better understand the assets, liabilities of a selection of rural communities. Both observatories attempt to measure the social capital or capacity of each observed community.After a brief review of the theoretical literature on social capital, community capacity,, development, we draw on publications, reports,, personal communication with the principals of these observatories to review their efforts in measuring social capital, community capacity. Our aim is to look for lessons that can inform the design of a rural observatory to assess community capacity, social capital in rural communities in the United States.

title: Myth, reality in rural policing: Perceptions of the police in a rural county of England
authors: Mawby, R I
abstract: In England, Wales, concern over policing often reflects a perception of a halcyon period, epitomised by community policing, when the police operated on a local level, were well known to the communities they policed. To some extent, images of rural policing are a modern‐day representation of this idyll,, studies certainly show that those living in rural areas hold more favourable views of the police than do their metropolitan counterparts. This paper, however, based on a postal survey in Cornwall, a rural county in England, demonstrates that rural dwellers are also critical of certain aspects of policing, particularly the inaccessibility of the police. It then considers differences between different subsections of the Cornish people. Taken together, the findings indicate that rural residents' concerns over public safety are accentuated by their concerns that the police in Cornwall are less accessible than those in urban areas, are less able to respond in an emergency. This has implications for policy.

title: Explaining patterns of victimization within A rural county of England
authors: Mawby, Rob I, Jones, Carol
abstract: This article reports on victim surveys carried out in a rural county of England, using a postal questionnaire. Surveys in rural areas are uncommon, but many patterns of risk that were identified here were found to be similar to those identified in national, urban surveys. This suggests both that postal surveys provide a valid measure of variations in risk, that similar explanations for variations in risk apply. Routine activity theory is used to explain the patterns identified. Although the impact of residential location was seen to be less important in the rural context than studies in urban areas have indicated, the question of where people spent their time, including the town or city that they frequented, was significant in predicting victimization. The relationship between location, risk thus appears to be stronger in terms of where people spend their time outside the home than in terms of where they live.

title: Emotional, behavior problems in urban, rural adjudicated males: Differences in risk, protective factors
authors: Nelson, D Margo, Coleman, Daniel, Corcoran, Kevin
abstract: Emotional, behavior problems in rural adjudicated youth have received scant research attention. The association of risk, protective factors with emotional, behavioral problems were examined in samples of urban, rural adjudicated youth. Urban youth had higher levels of personal, peer risk. For both samples, family, community risk were strong risk factors. The effects of family, school variables on emotional, behavioral problems were stronger for rural youth. The closer social ties of rural communities provide protective effects. Programs that facilitate more supportive family, community networks are consistent with the results of this study.

title: Community policing in small town rural America: A comparison of police officer attitudes in Chicago, Baldwin county, Alabama
authors: O'Shea, Timothy C
abstract: Much has been written about policing in America. We know a good deal about its structure, function, operations, culture, etc. Based on this wealth of knowledge, we have drawn conclusions about the causes of observed dysfunctions in the institutional arrangements of policing. This has led, from time to time, to a variety of police reform efforts, the most recent of which is the furor over community policing. Some have argued that police policy has been driven by research conducted for, in urban American police departments, that the portability of those policies to rural American police departments may be inappropriate. This paper seeks to explore the urban/rural divide by comparing the attitudes of police officers from a large urban American police department with those of police officers from five small town rural American police departments. Significant differences in the attitudes between the urban, rural American police officers are found, the implications, pursuant to the limited generalizability of these findings, are examined.

title: Situational contexts of rural violence: A comparison of male, female perpetration
authors: Rennison, Callie Marie, DeKeseredy, Walter S
abstract: The amount of social scientific knowledge about rural violence pales in comparison with that of urban violence,, even less is known about the situational contexts of rural violence. Using National Crime Victimization Survey data, we explore situational contexts of rural violence in general, as well as compare male-, female-perpetrated violence contexts. Results indicate that the contexts of violence committed by females are characterized by main effects (i.e., no weapons, no injuries across a variety of contexts), while male-perpetrated violence is highly contextual. An important finding emerged from studying contexts associated with male offenders, female victims—in every dominant context with one exception, male perpetrators were engaged in woman abuse. These findings highlight the need for greater attention to rural violence, variation in how this violence is perpetrated.

title: Intimate relationship status variations in violence against women: urban, suburban,, rural differences: Urban, suburban,, rural differences
authors: Rennison, Callie Marie, DeKeseredy, Walter S, Dragiewicz, Molly
keywords: National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS); nonfatal intimate violence; relationship status; rural;306\_Rural;z\_rural2020
abstract: Woman abuse varies across intimate relationship categories (e.g., marriage, divorce, separation). However, it is unclear whether relationship status variations in violence against women differ across urban, suburban,, rural areas. We test the hypothesis that rural females, regardless of their intimate partner relationship status, are at higher risk of intimate violence than their urban, suburban counterparts. Results indicate that marital status is an important aspect of the relationship between intimate victimization, geographic area, that rural divorced, separated females are victimized at rates exceeding their urban counterparts.

title: A contextual model of adolescent alcohol use across the rural-urban continuum
authors: Rountree, P W, Clayton, R R
keywords: Alcohol Abuse; Alcohol Drinking Patterns; Individual Differences; Models; Rural Environments; School Environment; Social Control; Urban Environments;306\_Rural;J\_TF1505;z\_rural2020
abstract: In the research presented here, we develop, test with respondents from a broad range of contexts a multilevel social control model of adolescent substance use, integrating macro-, microsociological, criminological perspectives. Specifically, this research examines the individual-level social control processes or mechanisms thought to lead to alcohol use embedded in school contexts in different community settings along the rural-urban continuum. In this way we determine 1) the main effects of individual-, contextual school-level variables, 2) the conditioning or moderating influences of school climate on individual alcohol use, on individual-level processes leading to alcohol use. Furthermore, given that our sample contains students from a broad range of settings along the rural-urban continuum, our findings address the appropriateness of conceptualizing rural, urban drug use, their respective etiologies as dichotomous. In this respect our findings suggest that heterogeneity in drug use exists within rural school settings as well as within urban school settings,, that examining rural drug use as separate from urban drug use is not justified.

title: Rurality-urbanism, protective order service: A research note
authors: Wilcox, Pamela, Jordan, Carol E, Pritchard, Adam J, Randa, Ryan
abstract: ABSTRACT Examination of contextual effects on legal case processing has a long tradition. However, that tradition largely emphasizes jurisdiction-level variation in outcomes at the point of arrest, prosecution, or adjudication within the criminal justice system. In the area of domestic violence specifically, however, additional stages of “justice” come into play, including those surrounding the processing of civil protective orders. There has been a recent call for attention to jurisdiction-level variation in the issuing, serving of such protective orders, with particular emphasis placed on understanding more fully apparent contextual differences that correspond with rural-urban court location. This paper responds to that call with a county-level analysis of non-service of issued protective orders using data from every county in one state. Findings suggest that rurality is positively associated with rates of non-service. The effect of rurality, however, appears substantially mediated by an SES index presumed to tap resource deprivation. Measures of population heterogeneity/instability play less of a mediating role but have significant associations with non-service nonetheless.

title: Crime concern, policing in the countryside: Evidence from Parish councillors in West Mercia Constabulary, England
authors: Yarwood, Richard
keywords: RURAL crimes; CRIME; SOCIOLOGY, Rural; POLICE; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; ENGLAND; Crime concern; Parish councils; Partnerships; Policing; Rural; United Kingdom;306\_Rural;J\_TF1505
abstract: It has been recognized that the fear of crime is problematic for people living in the countryside, but less is known about society, policing in rural areas. This article focuses on parish councillors in West Mercia Constabulary, England,, examines their attitudes towards fear of crime, policing. The article reveals that crime concern is lower than recent media reports have implied,, that satisfaction with policing is relatively high. It notes that many concerns about crime reflect broader perceptions of rural change rather than criminal threat. Consideration is given to how these discourses may affect, reflect the development of multi-agency policing in rural areas of the United Kingdom.

title: Criminal victimization during one's life course: The effects of previous victimization, patterns of routine activities
authors: Wittebrood, Karin, Nieuwbeerta, Paul
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: VICTIMS of crimes; VICTIMS of crimes surveys; AUTOMOBILE theft; SEX crimes; REGRESSION analysis; NETHERLANDS; bicycle theft;304\_RepeatVic;301\_ComCrm;301\_2;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: This study focuses on the effects of previous victimization, patterns of routine activities on the risk of falling victim to seven types of crime: sexual offense, assault, threat, burglary, personal larceny, car theft, bicycle theft. To examine these effects' individual life-course data on marital, fertility, residential, educational, employment, criminal histories were related to histories of criminal victimization. These data derived from a nationally representative survey administered in the Netherlands in 1996 to 1,939 individuals age 15 years or older. Logistic multilevel models were used in the analysis of the data. The results of the analyses suggest that individuals who have once been victims suffer a substantial higher risk of subsequent victimization. This effect of previous victimization can partly be explained by a real effect of previous victimization (state dependence), but more largely by the effects of patterns of routine activities (heterogeneity in the population).

title: Repeat criminal victimization, vulnerability for coping failure: A prospective examination of a potential risk factor
authors: Winkel, Frans Willem, Blaauw, Eric, Sheridan, Lorraine, Baldry, Anna Constanza
keywords: VICTIMS of crimes surveys; DISTRESS (Psychology); Repeat Victimization; coping with crime; coping;304\_RepeatVic;J\_TF1505;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh
abstract: The psychological impact of repeat victimization is commonly assessed via victimization surveys that are retrospective in nature. Associations between repeat victimization, coping failure may then easily be inflated due to memory biases, such as mood-congruence effects. This study examined the status of repeat victimization as a resilience or vulnerability factor for psychological distress on the basis of a prospective design, which included measures administered prior to the first victimization,, follow up measures of repeat victimization. Analyses revealed a series of significant differences in both the personal (e.g. in perceptions of pre-victimization comparative vulnerability,, prior life stress), social risk (e.g. insufficient social support) profiles of repeat versus singular victims. Analyses suggested that re-exposure within a short time interval negatively influenced post-victimization functioning: this impact was only partly mediated by other risk factors. The validity of police decisions to refer victims to victim support can be enhanced through incorporating repeat victimization as an additional referral criterion.

title: Multilevel modelling of the number of property crimes: household, area effects
authors: Tseloni, Andromachi
journal: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society. Series A
keywords: Multilevel analysis; Negative binomial; Property crimes; Random effects; British Crime Survey;304\_RepeatVic;301\_ComCrm
abstract: This study examines household, area effects on the incidence of total property crimes, burglaries, thefts. It uses data from the 2000 British Crime Survey, the 1991 UK census small area statistics. Results are obtained from estimated random-effects multilevel models, with an assumed negative binomial distribution of the dependent variable. Both household, area characteristics, as well as selected interactions, explain a significant portion of the variation in property crimes. There are also a large number of significant between-area random variances, covariances of household characteristics. The estimated fixed, random effects may assist in advancing victimization theory. The methods have potential for developing a better understanding of factors that give rise to crime, so assist in framing crime prevention policy. Copyright 2005 Royal Statistical Society.

title: Joining up research, policy, practice about crime
authors: Tilley, Nick, Laycock, Gloria
abstract: Evidence-based policy in relation to crime, as in other policy areas, is all the rage. It looks like plain common sense. Yet getting good evidence to policy, policy to good evidence faces an uphill struggle. Ideology is important in any consideration of crime, crime policy, limiting the potential of hard evidence. Common sense ideas about crime are also powerful influences on policy,, they are not easily overturned by research evidence, which may contradict them. Even where there is space for research to impact on policy, practice, it can easily mislead, if treated uncritically, unreflectively. Much research is technically weak. Single studies that appear to be methodologically sound can generate findings that subsequent investigations contradict. Programmes shown by evaluation studies to work in one context may not work in another. It is often not clear what it is about a programme which has worked, hence what needs to be replicated to produce the same effects. Yet, there are examples of studies,, series of studies, yielding valid, useable policy-relevant findings. Examples relating to property marking, to repeat victimization, its prevention are given. Ways in which members of the policy-making, research communities can facilitate the appropriate production, use of evidence in policy-development, practice are suggested. More generally, evidence-based policy calls for a more policy-literate research community,, a more research-literate policy community. Policy-making, however, can, should be informed by more than research evidence alone.

title: Area, individual differences in personal crime victimization incidence: The role of individual, lifestyle/routine activities, contextual predictors
authors: Tseloni, Andromachi, Pease, Ken
abstract: This article examines how personal crime differences between areas, between individuals are predicted by area, population heterogeneity, their synergies. It draws on lifestyle/routine activities, social disorganization theories to model the number of personal victimization incidents over individuals including routine activities, area characteristics, respectively, as well as their (cross-cluster) interactions. The methodology employs multilevel or hierarchical negative binomial regression with extra binomial variation using data from the British Crime Survey, the UK Census. Personal crime rates differ substantially across areas, reflecting to a large degree the clustering of individuals with measured vulnerability factors in the same areas. Most factors suggested by theory, previous research are conducive to frequent personal victimization except the following new results. Pensioners living alone in densely populated areas face disproportionally high numbers of personal crimes. Frequent club, pub visits are associated with more personal crimes only for males, adults living with young children, respectively. Ethnic minority individuals experience fewer personal crimes than whites. The findings suggest integrating social disorganization, lifestyle theories, prioritizing resources to the most vulnerable, rather than all, residents of poor, densely populated areas to prevent personal crimes.

title: “can’t stop, won’t stop”: Self-control, risky lifestyles,, repeat victimization
authors: Turanovic, Jillian J, Pratt, Travis C
abstract: Objectives Drawing from lifestyle-routine activity, self-control perspectives, the causal mechanisms responsible for repeat victimization are explored. Specifically, the present study investigates: (1) the extent to which self-control influences the changes victims make to their risky lifestyles following victimization,, (2) whether the failure to make such changes predicts repeat victimization. Methods Two waves of panel data from the Gang Resistance Education, Training program are used (N = 1,370), direct measures of change to various risky lifestyles are included. Two-stage maximum likelihood models are estimated to explore the effects of self-control, changes in risky lifestyles on repeat victimization for a subsample of victims (n = 521). Results Self-control significantly influences whether victims make changes to their risky lifestyles post-victimization,, these changes in risky lifestyles determine whether victims are repeatedly victimized. These changes in risky lifestyles are also found to fully mediate the effects of self-control on repeat victimization. Conclusions Findings suggest that future research should continue to measure directly the intervening mechanisms between self-control, negative life outcomes,, to conceptualize lifestyles-routine activities as dynamic processes.

title: Repeat burglary victimization in Malawi, the influence of housing type, area-level affluence
authors: Sidebottom, Aiden
keywords: burglary victimization; housing type; developing countries; Human; Empirical Study; Quantitative Study; Housing; Victimization; Malawi; 3230:Behavior Disorders \& Antisocial Behavior; Repeat Victimization;304\_RepeatVic;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303;Security Journal;20250703\_Aiden
abstract: There is little research on repeat victimization in developing countries. This article reports the first study of repeat domestic burglary victimization in Malawi. Secondary analysis of data from a large multipurpose survey finds burglary to be highly concentrated. The influence of housing type – measured here as the building materials used –, area-level affluence is explored. Homes constructed of permanent materials, indicative of greater wealth, experienced higher rates of repeat victimization than those made of mud, thatch. This pattern is most pronounced in less affluent areas, although the variation in risk is less than that reported in comparable studies. Implications for preventing repeat burglaries in resource-limited settings are discussed.

title: The blameworthy victim: Domestic violence myths, the criminalization of victimhood
authors: Policastro, Christina, Payne, Brian K
keywords: Psychology; College students; Perceptions; Domestic violence; Criminal justice; Repeat Victimization;304\_RepeatVic;J\_TF1505
abstract: Prior research shows that individual perceptions of victims play an integral role in the societal response to domestic violence, as well as victims' responses to their own victimization. However, little research has specifically examined individual perceptions of domestic violence victims who remain in abusive relationships. This study begins to fill the void in the literature by examining college students' attitudes toward battered women. Specifically, the study considers whether students adhere to common myths associated with battering, if myths lead college students to view domestic violence victims as “blameworthy.” The study relies on a sample of 370 university students attending a large Southern metropolitan university. Findings indicate that students moderately support domestic violence myths, that myth promotion is associated with support for increased criminal justice penalties such as prosecution of mothers, approval of delayed police response in cases of repeat victimization. Implications for policy, theory,, practice are provided.

title: Repeat, multiple victimizations: the role of individual, contextual factors
authors: Outlaw, Maureen, Ruback, Barry, Britt, Chester
keywords: Crime; Models; Role Perception; Victimization; Human; Male; Female; hierarchical modeling; role of individual; repeat violence; SOCIAL disorganization; Repeat Victimization;304\_RepeatVic;13\_Seattle;330\_マルチレベル被害\_2018\_JPA(8章)\_root;9\_320\_構造的選択モデル\_2019\_犯社研(7章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;301\_ComCrm;301\_2;Violence Vict
abstract: The present research uses hierarchical modeling to examine the relative contributions of factors about the person, factors about the context, and, most important the interaction of factors about the person, factors about the context in models of both repeat victimization (more than one of the same type of crime), multiple victimization (two or more different types of crime). Using telephone survey data from a multistage sample of Seattle residents, we estimate separate hierarchical models for repeat property, repeat violent, multiple victimization. Results indicate that repeat victimization of both types varies substantially by neighborhood, whereas multiple victimization seems more determined by individual-level factors. Implications for social disorganization theory, routine activity/lifestyle exposure theory,, future work on repeat victimization are discussed.

title: Understanding the random effect on victimization distributions: A statistical analysis of random repeat victimizations
authors: Park, Seong Min, Eck, John E
abstract: The notion of repeat victimization has been a growing interest of crime prevention policies, portrayed as a practical solution to prevent crimes. One stochastic characteristic of repeat victimization, however, has not been fully considered in understanding the distribution of victimizations: random repeat victimization, which indicates a concentration of victimizations solely by chance. This lack of consideration has resulted in misleading interpretations of victimization data, erroneous arguments. Through simulating the 2008–2009 British Crime Survey, employing mathematical demonstrations, this study investigates the statistical characteristics of random repeat victimization, reviews the arguments of previous studies on repeat victimization.

title: The “normality” of repeat victimization from adolescence through early adulthood
authors: Menard, Scott
abstract: The research presented here is essentially descriptive, but includes new empirical findings on repeat victimization. Based on data from nine waves of the National Youth Survey (NYS), encompassing the years 1976–1992, respondents' ages ranging from 11 to 33, the present study examines the seriousness of victimization incidents reported in the NYS; the distribution of annual, cumulative,, repeat victimization by age, gender,, ethnicity; the extent to which victimization tends to be concentrated, with a relatively small proportion of victims accounting for a relatively large proportion of the victimization incidents; the extent to which victimization tends to be repeat victimization as opposed to isolated incidents;, the extent to which repeat victimization tends to be continuous rather than intermittent. Differences between patterns for violent victimization, property victimization are highlighted.

title: Repeat victimization in the ICVS, the NCVS
authors: Farrell, Graham, Tseloni, Andromachi, Pease, Ken
keywords: SURVEYS; CRIME; RESEARCH; VICTIMS; VICTIMS of crimes; Repeat Victimization; International Crime Victims Survey; Natl crime surveys;304\_RepeatVic;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;Crime Prevention, Community Safety
abstract: Overall, 40 per cent of crimes reported to the International Crime Victims Survey (ICVS) in 2000 were repeats against the same target within a year, with variation by crime type, country. However, policy makers have yet to realise the potential of victim-oriented crime reduction strategies. A preliminary comparison of repeat victimization uncovered by the ICVS, the US National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) finds ICVS rates are double those of the NCVS. The NCVS may be seriously flawed in the manner in which it measures repeat victimization,, hence crime overall. Further study is needed, but since the NCVS is an influential survey, the possibility that it is misleading may have widespread implications for crime-related research, theory, policy, practice in the United States, elsewhere.

title: A victim is a victim is a victim?
authors: Ellingworth, Dan, Farrell, Graham, Pease, Ken
keywords: Multiple victimization; Crime; Crime Victims; Victimization; Statistical Data; Surveys; Theft; Repeat Victimization; British Crime Survey;304\_RepeatVic;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303;British Journal of criminology
abstract: This paper builds on previous work which identified the importance of multiple victimization in determining crime rates. Using the first four sweeps of the British Crime Survey, patterns of property, personal crime victimization are investigated,, the interdependence of incidents is established: the probability of a further victimization increases with each subsequent victimization. A comparison is made between the observed distribution,, a hypothetical distribution which assumes that crime incidents are randomly distributed throughout the population. Given the extent of concentration of incidents amongst a small number of chronic victims, recommendations are made for the way official crime statistics are recorded.

title: The violent, sexual victimization of college women: is repeat victimization a problem?: Is repeat victimization a problem?
authors: Daigle, Leah E, Fisher, Bonnie S, Cullen, Francis T
keywords: Sociology; Sexual Assault; College Students; Females; Victimization; Repeat Victimization;304\_RepeatVic;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;303
abstract: Little attention has been given to repeat violent, sexual victimization among college women. Using two national-level data sets, the authors find that a small proportion of college women experience a large proportion of violent, sexual victimizations. Women are more likely to experience repeat sexual victimization than repeat violence incidents. Repeat victimization tends to happen in the same month of the initial victimization,, the most likely next type of victimization is by far the same type of victimization. Comparing incident-level characteristics of repeat incidents to single incidents, there are few differences, with the exception that, in a larger proportion of single incidents, women took self-protective action. Implications for prevention, educational programs are discussed.

title: Citizen recourse to self protection: Structural, attitudinal, experiential factors
authors: Ziegenhagen, Eduard A
keywords: FEAR of crime; SELF-DEFENSE; Personal security;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Crim Justice Policy Rev\_●Sage
abstract: At least one fourth of the New York City subway riders surveyed in a 1986 study carry some form of self protection ranging from guns, knives to mace. The tendency of citizens to carry self protective devices is a source of concern to law enforcement officials who denounce such behavior as needless, potentially harmful. Criminal justice practitioners assert that the likelihood of becoming a victim of violent crime is small, that victims, prospective victims are incompetent in their efforts to protect themselves,, that protection against crime is primarily an area reserved to the state regardless of whether it is effective or not. How is one to explain the practice of carrying devices dedicated to self protection when it persists contrary to the advice, disapproval of criminal justice practitioners?

title: Crime victims' attributional activities, differential psychological responding to victimisations: the influence of behaviour, character, external explanations
authors: Winkel, F, Vrij, A
keywords: Coping Behavior; Empirical Study; Attribution; 3236:Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; Crime Victims; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Human; attributional style \& problem vs emotion focused coping behavior, burglary victims, Netherlands; coping with crime; coping;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);301\_ComCrm;301\_4;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh
abstract: Examined, in 165 victims of burglary, the precise relation between indicators of emotion-focused coping (external, behavioral,, character attributions; aspects of fear responses; intentions to choose extreme preventive options to avoid future victimization), indicators of problem-focused coping (cognitive, attitudinal,, connative aspects of taking precautionary measures). Janoff-Bulman, 1979) suggesting that internal attributions,, behavior attributions in particular, are associated with more successful coping. Behavior attributors reported the lowest levels of fear, fear-related cognitions, exhibited the weakest intentions to engage in fight or flight responses. title: Crime victims, their social network: A field study on the cognitive effects of victimisation, attributional responses, the victim-blaming model
authors: Winkel, Frans Willem, Denkers, Adriaan
keywords: 3236:Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; Attribution; 680; 7419; 5760; Cognitions; 1494; Crime Victims; 1887; Internal External Locus of Control; 4040; 5829; 5817; Social Support; 7439; 615; 4068; 7406; 7375; 825; cognitive effects; locus of control; social network responses; validity of victim blaming model; Netherlands; Human; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Empirical Study;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: A field study is reported focusing on the cognitive effects of criminal victimisation, on the types of responses victims encounter in their social network,, on the validity of the ‘victim blaming model’. Data reveal that victimisations have a negative impact on the perceived benevolence of the world. Perceptions of self control, control over outcomes are reduced,, victims consider themselves less as persons having luck in life. These cognitive effects appear to stretch out beyond those directly involved. Results generally do not support the theoretically dominant position in the victimological literature on ‘blaming the victim’. Empathical responses, external attributions from the social network are much more common than internal responses to victimisation. Moreover, internal attributions from the social network appear to work more positively on the wellbeing of victims than external attributions. These outcomes - which are in line with the Janoff-Bulman model - are clearly in contrast to the ‘victim blaming model’. Some implications for future studies are discussed.

title: Comparing psychological images of the social perceiver: Role of perceived informativeness, memorability,, affect in mediating the impact of crime victimization
authors: Tyler, Tom R, Rasinski, Kenneth
keywords: SOCIAL perception; CRIME prevention; VICTIMS of crimes; MEMORY; BEHAVIOR; FEAR of crime; crime prevention efforts;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: Recent research in social cognition has been concerned with the inferences people draw from their experiences. The research reported here is concerned with one inference--the judged risk of crime victimization--and with heightened levels of crime prevention behavior that result from such an inference. Two surveys of 315 Ss who had at least 1 experience with crime, an experiment with 360 undergraduates were conducted to test the role of 3 psychological characteristics of victimization in mediating the impact of being a victim of crime. In the experiment, Ss read a pamphlet describing a person's experience with crime; Ss' perceived informativeness, availability in memory of the information, affect, fear of crime,, crime prevention behavior were later assessed. Results suggest that the perceived informativeness, availability in memory,, affect aroused by a crime victimization were distinct aspects of the event. Though distinct, however, perceived informativeness, affect were not statistically independent. Those events judged to be more informative were also more upsetting. Availability in memory, on the other hand, was independent of both perceived informativeness, affect. When the mediation of impact was considered, the results suggest independent influences of both perceived informativeness, affect on both fear of crime, crime prevention behavior. Availability apparently does not have an important role in mediating impact on either inferences or behaviors. (130 ref)

title: Impact of directly, indirectly experienced events: The origin of crime-related judgments, behaviors
authors: Tyler, Tom R
keywords: CRIMINAL behavior; CRIMINAL psychology; CRIMINOLOGY; JUDGMENTS; SOCIAL surveys; VICTIMS of crimes;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: Used data collected from 1,862 adults in 2 surveys of crime victimization to examine the integration of 1st-hand, indirect experiences with crime into crime-related judgments, behaviors. Analysis revealed 2 independent levels of judgment: general judgments of the base rate of crime, individual judgments of personal vulnerability to crime. Examination of the effect of 1st-hand, indirect experiences on these judgments counters the conventional wisdom that 1st-hand experiences have greater influence than indirect experiences, suggests that the relative influence of different modalities of experience depends on the level of the judgment being considered. The role of the perceived informativeness, memorability,, affectivity of a crime victimization experience in mediating its impact was also explored. Results suggest that informativeness was generally the most important mediator of impact. Results also suggest that different characteristics mediated the impact of experiences on judgments, on behaviors. (46 ref)

title: Perceived control, behavioral reactions to crime
authors: Tyler, Tom R
keywords: perceptions of controllability of crime vs own probability of victimization, crime prevention behavior, Los Angeles; Crime; Prevention; Social Perception; Victimization;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: In a recent survey of New Yorkers, Miransky, Langer (1978) found that residents who believed that crime could be controlled made only minimal efforts to utilize door locks. Miransky, Langer argue that this failure to exert potential control represents a relinquishment of responsibility for crime prevention motivated by a fear of the psychological consequences of accepting responsibility for a potentially uncontrollable event. This article suggests the alternative interpretation that Miransky, Langer have confused perceptions of the controllability of crime, perceptions of the controllability of one's own probability of victimization. Results of this study suggest that perceptions of the controllability of one's own probability of victimization are strongly related to crime-prevention behavior. These results do not support the motivational theory of Miransky, Langer.

title: An assessment of change in risk perception, optimistic bias for hurricanes among Gulf Coast residents: Change in risk perception, optimistic bias
authors: Trumbo, Craig, Meyer, Michelle A, Marlatt, Holly, Peek, Lori, Morrissey, Bridget
journal: Risk analysis: an official publication of the Society for Risk Analysis
keywords: Demographics; Gulf Coast; hurricanes; optimistic bias; risk perception;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;302\_CogBias;RiskAnalysis
abstract: This study focuses on levels of concern for hurricanes among individuals living along the Gulf Coast during the quiescent two-year period following the exceptionally destructive 2005 hurricane season. A small study of risk perception, optimistic bias was conducted immediately following Hurricanes Katrina, Rita. Two years later, a follow-up was done in which respondents were recontacted. This provided an opportunity to examine changes,, potential causal ordering, in risk perception, optimistic bias. The analysis uses 201 panel respondents who were matched across the two mail surveys. Measures included hurricane risk perception, optimistic bias for hurricane evacuation, past hurricane experience,, a small set of demographic variables (age, sex, income,, education). Paired t-tests were used to compare scores across time. Hurricane risk perception declined, optimistic bias increased. Cross-lagged correlations were used to test the potential causal ordering between risk perception, optimistic bias, with a weak effect suggesting the former affects the latter. Additional cross-lagged analysis using structural equation modeling was used to look more closely at the components of optimistic bias (risk to self vs. risk to others). A significant, stronger potentially causal effect from risk perception to optimistic bias was found. Analysis of the experience, demographic variables' effects on risk perception, optimistic bias,, their change, provided mixed results. The lessening of risk perception, increase in optimistic bias over the period of quiescence suggest that risk communicators, emergency managers should direct attention toward reversing these trends to increase disaster preparedness.

title: The impact of victimization on fear
authors: Skogan, Wesley G
keywords: FEAR of crime; VICTIMS of crimes; Families with special problems -- families with criminal offenders; Psychological victimization effects; Psychology, sociology, anthropology -- psychology; Victim reactions to crime;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_210\_大田調査\_2004\_犯社研(3章);301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Crime Delinquency\_●Sage
abstract: This report examines the relationship between criminal victimization, fear of crime. Past research has been surprisingly inconclusive about this issue,, some people's fears have been branded “irrational” because the two did not appear to be tightly linked. However, the data analyzed here indicate that victimization affects both fear-related attitudes, behavior in a clear, consistent manner. This report also suggests that the impact of victimization is relatively uniform. Some research has indicated that certain groups are especially affected by crime, a claim that might be used to justify special treatment for selected victims, has been used to support demands for special “treatment” of selected offenders. However, the strong effects of victimization registered in these data were not differentially distributed across subgroups. In sum, most people do learn from their experiences, although other kinds of learning are rational as well.

title: What do we know about the effects of crime on victims?
authors: Shapland, Joanna, Hall, Matthew
abstract: In order to create an economic measure of the direct, indirect effects of crime, it is necessary to consider the effects of crime on victims. The article reviews the state of research into the effects of crime on individuals, in respect of personal, household victimisation,, the effects of crime on businesses. General population surveys have concentrated upon the common property offences, minor violence, have tended to ignore the dimension of the course of victimisation over time. Longitudinal studies are rare, have concentrated upon serious violent crime. Because of the element of clinical judgment, much work on PTSD is unsuitable for creating an economic measure of effects over all types of crime. There needs to be a marriage of survey methodology with time measures, possibly using a panel design.

title: Self-protective behaviours against crime in urban settings: An empirical approach to vulnerability, victimization models
authors: San-Juan, César, Vozmediano, Laura, Vergara, Anabel
abstract: Previous research on the relationships between age, sex, ethnic group or previous victimization experience, fear of crime is controversial, as inconsistent results have been obtained, many of them attributable to a lack of methodological, conceptual consensus. We propose the study of self-protective behaviours motivated by fear of crime as a useful alternative that pays attention to the consequences of fear for urban quality of life. A survey with a representative sample of residents in a major city in Spain provides evidence about sex, age differences in self-protective behaviours against crime. Results from the ‘classical’ vulnerability, victimization models are discussed, the suitability of the evolutionary, the routine activities perspectives is also considered.

title: Correlates of earthquake cognitions, preparedness behavior in a victimized population
authors: Rüstemli, Ahmet, Karanci, A Nuray
keywords: NATURAL disasters; COGNITION; ENVIRONMENTAL policy; RESEARCH; EARTHQUAKES; EARTH movements; CRISIS management; INCONSISTENCY (Logic);303;J\_TF1505;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;The J Soc Psychol
abstract: Abstract A survey of earthquake victims in Erzincan (a town in Eastern Anatolia, Turkey) was conducted 16 months after a major earthquake to explore the relations of earthquake-related cognitions, preparedness behavior to a set of personal, residential, experiential,, affect variables. Data from a sample of 461 adults representing different households indicated that earthquake expectations, preparedness could be predicted by fear, perceived control,, educational background. Results also indicated that damage anticipation was related to height, perceived strength of residence as well as to perceived control, trust in officials. Severity of past experience did not appear to have the predicted effect on quake cognitions, preparedness.

abstract: We interviewed residents of 4 southeastern cities that differed in the nature of their exposure to Hurricane Hugo 2 years following the hurricane about their current precautionary behaviors, attitudes in the domains of hazard preparedness, crime prevention, vehicular safety,, health maintenance. Earlier interviews provided data on individual differences in severity of exposure. Both individual-, community-level measures of exposure predicted hazard preparedness. The effects of exposure on behavior were largely mediated by exposure's effects on the perceived usefulness of those behaviors. Although smaller in magnitude, effects of exposure generalized to self-protective acts other than hazard preparedness. The findings contradict earlier conclusions in the literature that the effects of personal experience on self-protective behavior are modest, transient,, specific.

title: Psychological distress following criminal victimization in the general population: Cross-sectional, longitudinal,, prospective analyses
authors: Norris, Fran H, Kaniasty, Krysztof
abstract: Samples of 105 violent crime victims, 227 property crime victims,, 190 nonvictims provided normative data regarding levels of psychological distress following criminal victimization. At points approximately 3 months, 9 months,, 15 months postcrime, symptoms of depression, somatization, hostility, anxiety, phobic anxiety, fear of crime,, avoidance were assessed. Although crime victims showed substantial improvement between 3, 9 months, thereafter they did not. Over the course of the study, violent crime victims remained more distressed than did property crime victims who, in turn, remained more distressed than nonvictims. Regression analyses revealed that the effects of crime could not be accounted for by precrime differences between victims, nonvictims in either social status or psychological functioning. However, lasting effects were often contingent on the occurrence of subsequent crimes.

title: THE EFFECTS OF “SELF-HELP” PRECAUTIONARY MEASURES ON CRIMINAL VICTIMIZATION AND FEAR: Lmplications for crime-prevention policy
authors: Norris, Fran H, Johnson, Knowlton W
keywords: 303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;301\_ComCrm;301\_2;301\_4
abstract: “Self-help” precautionary measures taken at the individual or household level are widely used by citizens to confront the problems of crime, fear. In this article, we assess the effectiveness of precautionary behavior as it varies naturally within a general population sample. Using data from a two-wave panel study of victims, nonvictims in Kentucky,, controlling for the effects of nine other “vulnerability factors” in hierarchical regression analyses, the findings were as follows: Precaution in the first year did not prevent victimization in the second year. Compared to nonvictims, victims were More likely to be victimized in the second year, were also more fearful Compared to other victims, victims who practiced high precaution after the first incident were no less likely to be revictimized, were no less fearful. From these findings, the policy of promoting precaution independently of other crime-prevention tactics would appear to be an insufficient strategy for both general, victim populations. Implications of findings for urban policies on crime prevention are discussed Co-production policies through which governments share responsibility for crime prevention with citizens (e.g., block watches) are distinguished from policies that transfer the responsibility to individual citizens (e.g., “target hardening”).

title: British Television Animation 1997-2010: Drawing Comic Tradition
authors: Norris, Van
keywords: frequency \& structure of precautionary behavior \& preparedness for hazards or accidents or illness or crime, 18-60+ yr olds; Accident Prevention; Crime Prevention; Hazards; Health Promotion; Safety;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;9\_001\_intro;z\_jpa2014;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: British Television Animation 1997-2010 charts a moment in TV history where UK comic animation graduated from the margins as part of a post-Simpsons broadcast landscape. Shows like Monkey Dust, Modern Toss, Stressed Eric not only reflected the times but they ushered in an era of ambition, belief in British adult animation.

title: Adjustment to Rape: (332232004-001)
authors: Meyer, C B, Taylor, S E
keywords: Coping Behavior; Rape; Empirical Study; Attribution; Crime Victims; Psychology; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Human; Adjustment; causal attributions; psychological adjustment; rape victims; causal attribution; coping with crime; coping;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: This questionnaire stud) of rape victims' reactions, causal attributions for the rape, coping behaviors after the rape,, psychological adjustment to the rape were examined. As in previous research, high levels of behavioral, characterological self-blame for rape were found. Contrary to prior hypotheses, behavioral self-blame was not associated with good adjustment. Rather, both behavioral, char-acterological self-blame were associated with poor adjustment. Societal blame was the only causal attribution for rape that was unassociated with adjustment. Remaining at home, withdrawing from others were both associated with poor adjustment,, the use of stress reduction techniques was associated with good adjustment. The implications of the results for theories of victimization, for clinical interventions with rape victims are discussed.

title: Fear of crime, individual crime protective actions in Israel
authors: Mesch, Gustavo S, Fishman, Gideon
keywords: FEAR of crime; SOCIAL problems; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; VICTIMS of crimes; SOCIAL security; SAFETY;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;international Review of Victimology
abstract: The inability of the police, the criminal justice system to contain crime at low levels has led people to use personal protective measures to reduce victimization risks. Recent studies on fear of crime indicate that fear for others' safety is more prevalent than fear for oneself. Using a representative sample drawn from the third largest city in Israel, this study investigates the hypothesis that fear for others more than fear for one's own safety may elicit the use of precautionary measures. The findings support the hypothesis only for personal protective behaviour. The implications of the findings are discussed.

title: A gendered assessment of the ‘‘threat of victimization’’: Examining gender differences in fear of crime, perceived risk, avoidance,, defensive behaviors
authors: May, David C, Rader, Nicole E, Goodrum, Sarah
abstract: Rader has called for a change in how researchers study fear of crime, suggesting that fear of crime, perceptions of risk,, experiences with victimization are interrelated dimensions of the larger ‘‘threat of victimization’’ concept. In this study, the authors examine how each independent dimension affects additional theoretical dimensions of the ‘‘threat of victimization’’, how these relationships vary by gender. Using data from residents of Kentucky, the authors estimate a series of multivariate linear, logistic regression models. The findings presented here suggest that gender differences do exist in the components of the threat of victimization, that many of the relationships in the Rader model are multifaceted, including the relationship between perceived risk, fear of crime,, avoidance, defensive behaviors. Implications of these findings for future research regarding predictors of the threat of victimization are discussed.

title: Social disorganization perceptions, fear of gang crime,, behavioral precautions among Whites, Latinos,, Vietnamese
authors: Lane, Jodi, Meeker, James W
keywords: GANGS; COMMUNITY; PERCEPTION; SOCIAL disorganization;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_3;301\_4;J Crim Justice
abstract: Gangs were an important media, policy topic during the 1990s, but few studies focused on fear of gangs specifically. Even fewer studies examined ethnic differences in perceptions of community problems, fear,, behavioral precautions due to gangs. Using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) techniques, this article examines differences among Whites, Latinos,, Vietnamese in perceptions of community disorder, diversity, perceived risk, fear of gang crime,, resulting behavioral precautions. Results indicated that Vietnamese were most concerned about community problems, felt most at risk, afraid of gang crimes. Latinos also felt more concerned, more at risk, afraid than Whites did. Most people in all three groups practiced avoidance behaviors to avoid gang crime, but few turned to weapons for protection. Results confirmed that minorities were more afraid, point to the importance of focusing limited policy resources on populations most affected by gangs.

title: Perceptions of neighborhood problems, fear of crime,, resulting behavioral precautions: Comparing institutionalized girls, boys in Florida
authors: Lane, Jodi
keywords: neighborhood disorder perceptions; crime fear; behavioral precautions; institutionalized girls; institutionalized boys; Florida; streets; Behavior; Crime; Disorders; Fear; Neighborhoods; Human Females; Human Males;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: Researchers rarely study perceptions of disorder, fear of crime,, behavioral precautions among youths, especially juvenile offenders. This study examines perceptions of neighborhood disorder, fear of general, gang crimes,, resulting precautionary behaviors while on the street among a sample of 149 incarcerated youths in Florida. The results show that neither girls nor boys perceived neighborhood disorder. Most are also not afraid. There are few significant differences between girls, boys on disorder, precautionary behaviors, but no significant differences on fear. These unexpected results may be due to sample characteristics, pointing to the need for more research.

title: Esteem, control bases of blame: ``Adaptive'' strategies for victims versus observers
authors: Janoff-Bulman, Ronnie
keywords: PERSONAL criticism; VICTIMS; RESPECT; SELF-esteem; BEHAVIOR; BLAME; OBSERVABILITY (Control theory); CONTROL theory (Mathematics); METHODOLOGY;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: An experiment was conducted to determine the esteem, control correlates of behavioral, characterological blame for victims, observers. On the basis of a proposed motivation to minimize perceptions of vulnerability, it was predicted that behavioral self‐blame would be “adaptive” for victims, whereas both behavioral, characterological blame of the victim would be “adaptive” for observers. As hypothesized, behavioral self‐blame by victims was associated with high self‐esteem, perceptions of future avoid ability of the victimization, whereas both behavioral, characterological blame by observers were associated with high self‐esteem. Behavioral blame was more likely to be engaged in by victims than by observers,, characterological blame was more likely to be engaged in by low esteem victims, high esteem observers. The study employed a role‐playing/observer methodology. The adequacy of this methodology, the generalizability of results to actual victim/observer populations are discussed.

title: Once a victim, always A victim? A study of how victimisation patterns may change over time
authors: Hopkins, Matt, Tilley, Nick
abstract: The evaluation of the Small Business, Crime Initiative in Leicester involved before, after victimisation surveys of all businesses in the two target areas. The second was conducted exactly two years after the first. Each sweep achieved a response rate of 65\%. A panel sample of 483 businesses took part in both surveys. The results afford an opportunity to track crime experience over time. This paper reports findings about the patterns of continuity, change in victimisation amongst members of the panel sample. Four groups are distinguished: those with low crime levels in both sweeps, those with high crime levels in both sweeps, those going from relatively high to relatively low levels,, those going from relatively low to relatively high levels. Identifying triggers leading from low to high rates of victimisation, from high to low ones clearly has implications for prevention. There may be scope usefully also to track victimisation careers of non-business victims of crime.

title: (the lack of) optimistic biases in response to the 1994 Northridge earthquake: The role of personal experience
authors: Helweg-Larsen, Marie
keywords: OPTIMISM; EXPERIENCE; PSYCHOLOGY, Applied; SOCIAL psychology; PREJUDICES; COLLEGE students; NORTHRIDGE Earthquake, Calif., 1994; RESEARCH; EARTHQUAKES -- California; RISK assessment; DISASTER victims;303;J\_TF1505;520\_研究成果の応用に向けて(13章)\_root;510\_実証研究のまとめと意義(12章)\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;302\_CogBias;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;Basic Appl Soc Psych
abstract: The tendency to believe that one's risk is less than that of one's peers is a well-documented, pervasive tendency. This optimistic bias is reduced in certain circumstances, such as when people have personal experience with an event, although it may reappear with time. University students who experienced the 1994 Northridge, CA earthquake were asked 1 week after the quake about their optimistic biases concerning earthquakes, a variety of other events. Students were followed every 2 weeks over the next 5 months. In addition, two new groups of students were surveyed at 2, 4 months after the earthquake. As expected, no optimistic bias for earthquakes was present immediately after the earthquake (but other events did show the bias). Contrary to previous research, no bias for earthquakes was present even 5 months after the earthquake. Those who had personal experience with injury or monetary loss as a result of the earthquake showed less optimism about injury in future earthquakes than those with no personal experience of injury or loss. Results are discussed in terms of the moderators of the optimistic bias.

title: Emotions about crime, attitudes to punishment
authors: Hartnagel, Timothy F, Templeton, Laura J
abstract: Various polls, surveys seem to indicate that a substantial proportion of the Canadian public desires harsher penalties for crime. While various explanations have been offered for this punitiveness, emotional reactions to crime have been under-researched. The present research draws on a Canadian data set to test the hypothesis that the emotions of fear, particularly anger about crime are significant predictors of punitive attitudes once crime victimization, economic insecurity, internal attributions of crime causation, other variables are controlled for. This research also examines the possible indirect effects of economic insecurity, victimization, internal attributions of crime causation on punitiveness through their impact on fear, anger. The multiple regression results support the role of emotions, particularly anger, in explaining punitive attitudes. While indirect effects of victimization, economic insecurity were insignificant, 14 per cent of the effect of internal attributions was through anger.

title: Explaining victim self-protective behavior effects on crime incident outcomes: A test of opportunity theory
authors: Guerette, Rob T, Santana, Shannon A
abstract: Prior research on victim self-protective behavior (VSPB) has largely been void of a theoretical basis. Accordingly, it remains unclear why it would be expected that victim actions might mitigate crime incident outcomes or under which circumstances such actions might be most successful. Using data from the National Crime Victimization Survey for periods 1992 to 2004, this study uses a nested logistic regression analysis to test the predictive utility of opportunity theory in explaining outcomes of VSPB during incidents of robbery, rape. The results suggest that opportunity theory provides a useful framework for understanding the effect of victim resistance on crime outcomes. Greater levels of victim resistance increase the effort needed by offenders, resulting in some cases in a 93\%, 92\% decrease in the odds of a robbery, rape being completed, respectively, compared to when no resistance is used. Implications for crime prevention practice are discussed.

title: Examining personal security, avoidance measures in a 12-city sample
authors: Giblin, Matthew J

keywords: 303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage;police visibility
abstract: Existing research has recognized the multidimensional nature of self-protective behaviors. Using secondary data collected by the Bureau of Justice Statistics, this study examined the predictive ability of measures related to policing, lifestyles, victimization, neighborhood conditions,, demographic characteristics in explaining six types of protective behavior. Results suggest that factors such as awareness of community policing, satisfaction with police, perceptions of disorder,, sex are consistently related to protective measures, whereas the influence of other factors (e.g., personal victimization, race) varies according to the behavior analyzed.

title: The behavioural, emotional, psychological effects of street robbery on victims
authors: Gale, Julie-Anne, Coupe, Timothy
abstract: This paper is concerned with the emotional, psychological impact of street robbery on its victims. Findings are presented from two sets of interviews with robbery victims sampled from police incident records,, conducted within three weeks, again nine months after victimisation. A majority of victims found street robbery to be a very frightening experience, and, as a result, fear of crime increased, many victims suffered serious psychological distress. While the effects had moderated 9 months after the crime, the robberies were still having a serious, enduring effect on victims' fear, social behaviour, psychological health, particularly for women, those who possessed a less hardy personality.

title: Victim attributions, post-rape trauma
authors: Frazier, Patricia A
keywords: POST-traumatic stress disorder; WOMEN -- Crimes against; INDIVIDUAL differences; MENTAL depression; SEX crimes; RAPE trauma syndrome; SEXUAL ATTITUDES, BEHAVIOR, AND PROBLEMS; Attribution;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: This study assessed (a) the kinds of attributions victims make, (b) whether behavioral, characterological self-blame are associated with other variables as hypothesized (e.g., perception of future avoidability of being raped),, (c) whether behavioral self-blame is associated with better post-rape adjustment ( Janoff-Bulman, 1979 ). Attributions, adjustment were assessed in a sample of adult female rape victims seen at a hospital-based rape crisis program. Many victims blamed themselves but tended to place more blame on external factors. The pattern of relations between behavioral, characterological self-blame, other attributional measures did not support the hypothesized distinctions between them. Both kinds of self-blame were significantly associated with increased post-rape depression (all p s < .05). Attributions strongly predicted adjustment, accounting for up to 67\% of the variance in 3-day post-rape depression. The theoretical, clinical implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Crime victims' well-being, fear in a prospective, longitudinal study
authors: Denkers, Adriaan J M, Winkel, Frans Willem
keywords: FEAR of crime; VICTIMS of crimes; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; MENTAL health; SOCIAL psychology; longitudinal analysis;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;international Review of Victimology
abstract: A study is presented on the influence of criminal victimization on well-being, fear within a nationwide sample of the Dutch population. The study focused on differences between victims, non-victims,, on the causality between crime, psychological upheaval. The design of the study was prospective, it included victims of several crime-types,, a matched sample of non-victims. The reactions of victims were measured before,, within two weeks, one month, two months after the crime. Results indicated that victims of crime systematically report lower levels of well-being, and, to some extent, higher levels of fear. Next, some indications were found supporting the notion that victims of violent crimes suffer more psychological distress than victims of property crimes. And finally, the data imply that, after the incident victims were ‘unhappier’ than non-victims, but, at least partly, already were so before the crime took place.

title: The aftermath of criminal victimization: Race, self-esteem,, self-efficacy
authors: DeLisi, Matt, Jones-Johnson, Gloria, Johnson, W Roy, Hochstetler, Andy
abstract: Criminal victimization is associated with a cascade of negative effects on social development, but research has primarily focused on children, adolescents. Less is known about the effects of criminal victimization on psychosocial functioning of Americans age 50, older. Relying on individual-level data from Waves 1, 2 of a longitudinal panel study of older adults—the Americans’ Changing Lives study—the current study explored the effects of criminal victimization on self-esteem, self-efficacy separately for Whites, African Americans. Net of the effects of employment, income, depression, age, sex, self-esteem,, self-efficacy, criminal victimization reduced self-esteem, self-efficacy among African Americans but not Whites. However, Whites who had greater difficulty dealing with their victimization evinced lower subsequent self-esteem. Greater difficulty with their victimization was also modestly associated with subsequent self-efficacy for Whites, African Americans. Implications, directions for future research are provided.
