title: The influence of perceptions of social disorder, victimization on business owners' decisions to use guardianship strategies
authors: Casten, John A, Payne, Brian K
keywords: Crime Prevention; Decision Making; Guardianship; Ownership; Victimization; Business; Crime; Criminals; Human; Male; Female; US; perceptions; social disorders; business owners; guardianship strategies; crime prevention strategies; broken windows;303;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;J Crim Justice
abstract: Using social disorganization, broken windows,, routine activities theories as guides, this study considered how perceptions of crime in the neighborhood influenced business owners' decisions on the use of various crime prevention (guardianship) strategies. The analysis revealed that perceptions of a crime problem were influenced by the presence of disorder. Drug offenses, vandalism were particularly tied to disorder with drug offenses more often related to guardianship strategies than other offenses. In addition, several strategies were used as prevention measures counter-intuitively for crimes not affected by these strategies, suggesting the need for increased awareness, training for business owners on effective guardianship strategies.

title: Use of protection motivation theory to assess fear of crime in rural areas
authors: Cates, James A, Dian, Donald A, Schnepf, Greg W
keywords: FEAR of crime; MOTIVATION (Psychology);303;J\_TF1505;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;315\_介入実験\_情報提示
abstract: Fear of crime has long been the purview of sociology, with attitudes more extensively researched in higher risk urban populations. A sample of 184 rural participants from 36 states in the USA responded to a questionnaire on experiences of crime victimization,, attitudes toward crime, using the multidimensional Protection Motivation Theory (PMT) model. For the entire sample, perceived noxiousness of crime, personal risk corresponded to a recent history of victimization. Yet, victimization did not appear to alter perceptions of efficacy of proposed response or self efficacy in response to crime. When sorted by gender, women did express differences in perceptions of efficacy based on experience. The findings argue for fear of crime as a multidimensional construct, with implications for both research, applied programs.

title: The impact of anonymity on responses to sensitive questions1
authors: Ong, Anthony D, Weiss, David J
keywords: BOMBINGS; VICTIMS of violent crimes; VICTIMS of crimes; VIOLENT crimes; ADJUSTMENT (Psychology); MENTAL depression; coping;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: To estimate frequencies of behaviors not carried out in public view, researchers generally must rely on self‐report data. We explored 2 factors expected to influence the decision to reveal: (a) privacy (anonymity vs. confidentiality), (b) normalization (providing information so that a behavior is reputedly commonplace or rare). We administered a questionnaire to I55 undergraduates. For 79 respondents, we had corroborative information regarding a negative behavior: cheating. The privacy variable had an enormous impact; of those who had cheated, 25\% acknowledged having done so under confidentiality, but 74\% admitted the behavior under anonymity. Normalization had no effect. There were also dramatic differences between anonymity, confidentiality on some of our other questions, for which we did not have validation.

title: Reciprocal effects of victimization, routine activities
authors: Averdijk, Margit
keywords: VICTIMS of crimes; CRIMINOLOGY; RESEARCH; SURVEYS; longitudinal analysis; DATABASES -- Research; DATA analysis; Victimization; Victims of crime; Natl crime surveys;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);301\_ComCrm;301\_4;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;international Review of Victimology;londitudunal\_vic\_survey
abstract: Although there is much research on the relationship between routine activities, victimization, we have little knowledge about the reciprocal effects of victimization, routine activities. The current paper is framed within the Once Bitten Twice Shy perspective proposed by Hindelang et al. (Victims of personal crime: an empirical foundation for a theory of personal victimization. Ballinger, Cambridge, 1978) which argues that victimization decreases risky routine activities, that this in turn decreases the risk of victimization. The current paper tests these propositions by using longitudinal data from the National Crime Victimization Survey, which allows us to tease out victimization, routine activities over time. Both violent, household victimization are examined. Variables pertaining to how often respondents go out for shopping, how often they go away at night, whether they have household devices are used as indicators for routine activities. Results indicate that the reciprocal effects of victimization, routine activities are limited. Consequences for routine activities theory are discussed.

title: Unrealistic optimism about future life events
authors: Weinstein, Neil D
keywords: LIFE change events; OPTIMISM; COLLEGE students; PERSONALITY; MOTIVATION (Psychology); SOCIAL desirability;302\_CogBias;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: Two studies investigated the tendency of people to be unrealistically optimistic about future life events. In Study 1, 258 college students estimated how much their own chances of experiencing 42 events differed from the chances of their classmates. Overall, they rated their own chances to be above average for positive events, below average for negative events, ps<.001. Cognitive, motivational considerations led to predictions that degree of desirability, perceived probability, personal experience, perceived controllability,, stereotype salience would influence the amount of optimistic bias evoked by different events. All predictions were supported, although the pattern of effects differed for positive, negative events. Study 2 tested the idea that people are unrealistically optimistic because they focus on factors that improve their own chances of achieving desirable outcomes, fail to realize that others may have just as many factors in their favor. Students listed the factors that they thought influenced their own chances of experiencing eight future events. When such lists were read by a second group of students, the amount of unrealistic optimism shown by this second group for the same eight events decreased significantly, although it was not eliminated.

title: Preface
authors: Gilovich, Thomas, Griffin, Dale, Kahneman, Daniel
keywords: risk perception; risk factors; risk judgments; optimistic bias; college students; health hazards; health problems; Cognitive Processes; Health; Judgment; Optimism; Prejudice;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Study 1 tested whether alerting participants to relevant risk factors would reduce optimistic biases with 222 subjects (Ss). Study 2 tried to reduce optimistic biases by presenting risk factors in such a way that the 164 Ss would see their own attributes as less than ideal. In Study 3, 190 college students formed a mental image of someone at high or low risk for having a weight problem. Study 4 attempted to alter risk judgments by having 374 college students generate their own list of factors that might lead themselves to develop (or that would keep them from developing) a weight or drinking problem. These 4 studies, testing a variety of approaches, using a variety of health hazards, were unsuccessful in reducing optimistic biases about familiar health hazards. The findings strongly suggest that, at least for familiar health problems, reminding people of risk factors or encouraging people to compare themselves with a low-risk target has little impact on personal risk perceptions, does not reduce people's tendency to claim that they are less at risk than their peers. title: College students' perceived risk of sexual victimization, the role of optimistic bias
authors: Saling Untied, Amy, Dulaney, Cynthia L
keywords: optimistic bias; perceived similarity; sexual assault;302\_CogBias;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Many college women believe that their chances of experiencing a sexual assault are less than their peers. This phenomenon, called optimistic bias, has been hypothesized to be one important element to address in sexual assault risk reduction, awareness programs aimed at reducing women's chances of experiencing a sexual assault. The present study examined the role that participants' (N = 89) perceived similarity to a narrator (portraying a sexual assault survivor) describing an assault plays in reducing this bias. The age of the narrator was manipulated (similar or dissimilar to age of participants) with the aim of assessing whether the program could produce reductions in optimistic bias for those participants who watched a video of someone similar to them in age. A significant interaction between pre-, post-program, age similarity indicated a significant decrease in optimistic bias from pre- to posttest for the similar group. Furthermore, an exploratory analysis indicated optimistic bias for White participants decreased from pre- to posttest, whereas optimistic bias for the Black participants increased. These results suggest that some factors such as age similarity may reduce optimistic bias in sexual assault risk reduction, awareness programs. However, a race dissimilarity may increase optimistic bias. Thus, more research is needed to understand the factors that affect optimistic bias with regard to sexual assault awareness.

title: The role of perceived control in alcohol prevention campaigns
authors: Krieger, Janice L, Parrott, Roxanne L, Afifi, Walid A
abstract: Optimistic bias provides a framework in this study to consider college students' knowledge about, perceptions of control over the effect of alcohol consumption on genes, health. Participants were 339 college students who completed a survey on genetics in the spring of 2001. This study confirmed that there is a significant relationship between knowledge, perceived control. In addition, the prediction that there are no differences between heavy, light drinkers with respect to their perceived knowledge, perceived control was supported. These results suggest the need to reconsider how prevention programs promote control over alcohol's use, effects because of the perceptions of invulnerability that may accompany feelings of control.

title: Event frequency, comparative optimism: Another look at the indirect elicitation method of self-others risks
authors: Klar, Yechiel, Ayal, Shahar
keywords: perceived event frequency; optimistic bias; two-process model; peer \& personal risk judgments; Risk Taking; life events; Life Experiences; Models; Optimism; Risk Perception; Peers; Social Perception;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Price, Pentecost,, Voth (2002) argue that common rather than rare negative future life events elicit greater indirect self-others comparative optimism. We argue that this finding may reflect a measurement effect: Rare events generate small differences (but large ratios), whereas common events produce larger differences (but smaller ratios). In Study 1, we show that the greater is event's perceived frequency, the greater is the numerical value assigned to express a given degree of risk discrepancy. In Study 2, we found weak negative rather than positive relations between perceived event frequency, the sense of risk discrepancy. Thus, it is crucial to understand how participants relate the two risk probabilities to each other to estimate their indirect comparative optimism.

title: Perceived breast cancer risk: heuristic reasoning, search for a dominance structure
authors: Katapodi, Maria C, Facione, Noreen C, Humphreys, Janice C, Dodd, Marylin J
keywords: CANCER; HEALTH risk assessment; BREAST; RISK assessment; RISK factors; RESEARCH; Breast cancer; Dominance structure; Heuristic reasoning analysis; Optimistic bias; Perceived risk; USA;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Studies suggest that people construct their risk perceptions by using inferential rules called heuristics. The purpose of this study was to identify heuristics that influence perceived breast cancer risk. We examined 11 interviews from women of diverse ethnic/cultural backgrounds who were recruited from community settings. Narratives in which women elaborated about their own breast cancer risk were analyzed with Argument, Heuristic Reasoning Analysis methodology, which is based on applied logic. The availability, simulation, representativeness, affect,, perceived control heuristics,, search for a dominance structure were commonly used for making risk assessments. Risk assessments were based on experiences with an abnormal breast symptom, experiences with affected family members, friends, beliefs about living a healthy lifestyle,, trust in health providers. Assessment of the potential threat of a breast symptom was facilitated by the search for a dominance structure. Experiences with family members, friends were incorporated into risk assessments through the availability, simulation, representativeness,, affect heuristics. Mistrust in health providers led to an inappropriate dependence on the perceived control heuristic. Identified heuristics appear to create predictable biases, suggest that perceived breast cancer risk is based on common cognitive patterns.

title: Do Moderators of the Optimistic Bias Affect Personal or Target Risk Estimates? A Review of the Literature
authors: Helweg-Larsen, Marie, Shepperd, James A
journal: Personality, social psychology review: an official journal of the Society for Personality, Social Psychology, Inc
keywords: 302\_CogBias;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;520\_研究成果の応用に向けて(13章)\_root;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: The optimistic bias is defined as judging one's own risk as less than the risk of others. Researchers have identified numerous personal, situational factors that moderate the extent to which people display the bias. It is unclear, however, whether these moderators affect the bias by influencing people's personal risk estimates or their risk estimates for a target. A review of moderators of the optimistic bias reveals evidence for both influences. Moderators associated with negative affect (negative mood, dysphoria, trait, state anxiety, event severity,, proximity of feedback), control related moderators (perceived control, prior experience) appear primarily to affect personal risk estimates. Positive mood affects target risk estimates. Finally, moderators that surround the comparison process appear to have different effects. Specifically, the type of comparison target appears to affect target risk estimates, whereas attention to personal risk-related behaviors affects personal risk estimates.

title: Self-affirmation, the biased processing of threatening health-risk information
authors: Harris, Peter R, Napper, Lucy
keywords: ALCOHOL; BREAST -- Cancer; DISEASES -- Risk factors; DRINKING of alcoholic beverages; HEALTH; IMAGINATION; Perceived risk; Optimistic bias; Persuasion; Self-affirmation defensive processing;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Self-affirming before reading about the link between alcohol, breast cancer promoted increased message acceptance among young women at higher risk. Differences were maintained on variables measured up to 1 month later. Relative to their nonaffirmed counterparts, higher risk, self-affirmed participants had higher ratings of risk, imagination, intention to reduce alcohol consumption,, negative affect, such as fear, while reading the leaflet. In contrast, there were no differences between the groups on measures of broader message acceptance (belief in the link, evidence strength). Thus, self-affirmation promoted acceptance of the personal relevance of the message, a critical step in the precaution adoption process. Overall, the findings support the view that self-affirmation in an unrelated domain can offset defensive processing of a threatening health message, promoting central route persuasion, producing consequential, durable increases in message acceptance.

title: Optimistic bias, sexual assault,, fear
authors: Chapin, John R, Pierce, Mari
keywords: optimistic bias; risk perception; sexual abuse;302\_CogBias;J\_TF1505;301\_ComCrm
abstract: A survey of 431 adults documents optimistic bias regarding people's perceived risk of sexual victimization. The findings extend optimistic bias to crime victimization, contribute to the literature by considering a motivational factor, fear, as a predictor of optimistic bias. The study also yielded significant relationships between optimistic bias, demographic variables, including age, gender,, family structure.

title: Knowledge is power: A theory-based approach to reducing school violence
authors: Chapin, John, Coleman, Grace
keywords: theory based approach; school violence reduction; middle high school students; optimistic bias; High School Students; Middle School Students; Prevention; School Based Intervention; School Violence; Student Attitudes;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: The study assesses the impact of a theory-based school violence program though a survey of 1,500 middle, high school students. It is the first to apply the concept of optimistic bias within the school violence context. Despite high profile school shootings, the students maintained the belief that violence was less likely to happen to them (personally) or in their schools than elsewhere in the country. Findings indicate that optimistic bias can be reduced through educational campaigns,, suggest a means of reducing violence by first reducing optimistic bias. [PUBLICATION ABSTRACT]

title: It won't happen to me: An investigation of optimism bias in occupational health, safety
authors: Caponecchia, Carlo
keywords: Human; Male; Female; occupational health; optimistic bias; occupational safety; safety hazards;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Optimism bias is the tendency to think that negative events are less likely to happen to oneself than to one's peers. Optimism bias concerning occupational health, safety (OHS) hazards was assessed in 105 postgraduate students, university employees. Significant levels of optimism bias were found for several events (e.g., suffering/causing injury). Though optimism bias was not related to perceived controllability, administration of OHS by management may explain why this observation differs from findings in other domains. While further study is required, the present study demonstrates that people tend to think hazardous events at work are less likely to happen to themselves compared to others doing the same job, which has important implications for management of safety at work.

title: Personality, emotionality,, risk prediction
authors: Borkenau, Peter, Mauer, Nadine
keywords: optimistic bias; negative emotionality; positive emotionality; risk estimates; prediction bias; individual differences; Cognitive Bias; Estimation; Prediction; Risk Perception; Emotionality (Personality); Optimism;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: We suggest a new approach for measuring individual differences in optimistic bias that adjusts risk estimates for oneself for: (1) risk estimates for other persons to control for response tendencies,, (2) risk estimates by knowledgeable informants to control for differences in actual risk. In two studies, we measured Positive, Negative Emotionality by self-reports, reports by knowledgeable informants. Moreover, likelihood estimates that pleasant, unpleasant events will occur to oneself, to an average other person were collected,, the knowledgeable informants provided risk estimates for the research participants. Risk estimates by knowledgeable informants were even more optimistic than self-estimates,, optimistic bias was related directly to Positive Emotionality, inversely to Negative Emotionality. These effects of personality on optimistic bias were not mediated by current mood.

title: Accuracy, error,, bias in predictions for real versus hypothetical events
authors: Armor, David A, Sackett, Aaron M
keywords: optimism; optimistic bias; prediction; accuracy; construal level theory; uncertainty; Performance; Prediction Errors; Reality;302\_CogBias;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Participants made predictions about performance on tasks that they did or did not expect to complete. In three experiments, participants in task-unexpected conditions were unrealistically optimistic: They overestimated how well they would perform, often by a large margin,, their predictions were not correlated with their performance. By contrast, participants assigned to task-expected conditions made predictions that were not only less optimistic but strikingly accurate. Consistent with predictions from construal level theory, data from a fourth experiment suggest that it is the uncertainty associated with hypothetical tasks,, not a lack of cognitive processing, that frees people to make optimistic prediction errors. Unrealistic optimism, when it occurs, may be truly unrealistic; however, it may be less ubiquitous than has been previously suggested.

title: Resident, police perceptions of the neighborhood: Implications for community policing
authors: Stein, Rachel E, Griffith, Candace
keywords: 301\_5;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;301\_ComCrm;Crim Justice Policy Rev\_●Sage
abstract: The successful implementation of community policing programs is dependent on police, residents understanding the needs of their communities. Differences between resident, police perceptions can affect the success of crime prevention strategies. Much neighborhood research highlights residents’ perceptions of their neighborhoods; the perceptions of police officers are often not taken into account. The current research examines police, resident perceptions of three high crime neighborhoods in a Midwestern city in the United States. Results indicate residents, police have different interpretations of the neighborhoods. Resident perceptions of neighborhood measures are relatively consistent across the three neighborhoods. Police perceptions of their relationship with residents, the close-knit structure of the community, however, are more positive in the primarily White neighborhood that has an active crime prevention program. The findings suggest that what the officers see in the neighborhood is driving perceptions, while actual problems might play a secondary role.

title: The impact of citizen perceptions of community policing on fear of crime: Findings from twelve cities
authors: Scheider, Matthew C, Rowell, Tawandra, Bezdikian, Veh
keywords: SURVEYS; COMMUNITY policing; CRIME prevention; CRIMINAL justice, Administration of; CRIMINOLOGY; crime prevention efforts; Natl crime surveys;301\_5;z\_2018jssc;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_3;Police Quarterly
abstract: Under the community policing philosophy, reducing citizen fear of crime has become a legitimate objective for police. Using the Twelve Cities Survey, a 1998 supplement to the National Crime Victimization Survey, this study examines the relationship between citizen perceptions of community policing, fear of crime, including other factors such as satisfaction with police, crime prevention behaviors by citizens. It is found that perceptions of community policing have strong positive effects on satisfaction with police, crime prevention behaviors. However, citizen perceptions of community policing do not directly affect levels of fear. In half of the cities examined, crime prevention behaviors had a positive (not negative) relationship with fear of crime. Implications for community policing efforts are discussed.

title: Perceptions of police work by the police, by the public
authors: Munn, James R, Renner, K Edward
keywords: a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;Criminal Justice, Behavior\_●Sage;360\_Trust
abstract: Three distinctions are proposed to determine what types of efforts are necessary to improve the quality of the relationship between the police, the public: first, whether there are different groups within the public which have contrary expectations that are impossible for the police to satisfy simultaneously or whether the disagreements are between the police, the nonpolice in general; second, whether the content, psychological significance of the disagreements can be specified;, third, whether negative evaluations of the police represent conflicting beliefs about what are proper police functions, services or emotional reactions arising from contact with regulatory power of the police.

title: The conceptualization, measurement of citizens' crime prevention behaviors
authors: Lavrakas, Paul J, Lewis, Dan A
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: CRIMINAL statistics; NEWSLETTERS; FEAR of crime; ILLINOIS; Community crime prevention programs; Program evaluation; Public information;301\_5;z\_kakenhi2008;9\_001\_intro;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: During the last decade scholars have begun to investigate crime prevention behav iors among citizens. Various classification schemes have been proposed in implicit, explicit attempts to conceptualize ``what people do to reduce the likelihood and/or impact of criminal victimization.''A review of four such classification sys tems—avoidance/mobilization activities; access control/surveillance/territori ality; individual/collective behaviors;, public-minded/private-minded activities—finds that in no case was the validity of the distinctions sup ported by empirical evidence. The present paper offers the results of secon dary analyses of data from four surveys—a 1972 Kansas City survey, a 1974 Portland survey, a 1975 Hartford survey,, a 1977 Philadelphia-Chicago-San Francisco survey—each of which included items that measured various crime pre vention behaviors by citizens. A factor analysis, internal consistency check were performed on the relevant set of items from each survey. Results provide pre liminary evidence of what a reliable conceptualization of citizens' crime prevention behaviors may include,, how the dimensions can be measured. It is suggested that future policy making, program planning, research,, evaluation in crime prevention by citizens should consider more fully the uncertain validity of past conceptualizations.

title: The effectiveness of a police-initiated fear-reducing strategy
authors: Bennett, Trevor
keywords: program of continuous police presence \& resident contacts, fear of crime \& quality of life, community residents, England, 1 yr followup; Community Attitudes; Crime; Fear; Law Enforcement; Quality of Life; Followup Studies; Police Personnel;301\_5;z\_2009jasc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);z\_jssp2009;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;z\_岩波エビデンス;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;British Journal of criminology
abstract: The paper presents the results of a quasi-experimental evaluation of the impact of a policing initiative which aimed to reduce fear of crime, to improve the quality of life of residents in two chosen areas. The results show that the programme was fully implemented during the experimental period. There was no evidence that the programme achieved its major outcome goal of directly reducing the fear of crime. There was evidence, however, that the programme achieved its secondary goals, improving some aspects of the quality of life in the programme areas. The results showed significant improvements, in both programme areas, in respondents' involvement with neighbours in home protection, in satisfaction with the police,, in contact with the police. The results also showed significant improvements in at least one of the programme area* in satisfaction with the area, sense of community,, informal control of crime.

title: A multilevel analysis of the risk of household burglary in the city of Tianjin, China
authors: Zhang, L, Messner, S F, Liu, J
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; BURGLARY; CRIMINAL law; PRESSURE groups; SOCIAL conflict; SOCIAL control; SOCIAL groups; TIANJIN (China); CHINA; collective efficacy;301\_4;z\_2015MERA;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;123\_1\_社会関係（集合的効力感）;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;z\_jssp2009;z\_bsj2011;z\_bsj2010\_past;9\_310\_外出時無施錠\_2016\_MERA(6章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;15\_天津;z\_urban\_socio\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_2;British Journal of criminology;police visibility
abstract: This study applies the integrated, multilevel framework developed in the West to explain variation in the risk of household burglary within the city of Tianjin, China. The analytic framework consists of three sets of determinants: household variables, neighbourhood structural factors,, neighbourhood social control processes. The selection of variables is guided by routine activities/lifestyle theories, the social disorganization perspective, adapted to reflect features of urban China. The results of multilevel regression modeling reveal that indicators of target attractiveness (household income), guardianship (length of residence, somebody home ) exhibit the predicted effects on the risk of household burglary. Similarly, the effects of two of the neighbourhood process variables-collective efficacy, public control-conform to theoretical expectations, findings in Western research. The results for the neighbourhood structural factors are inconsistent with those widely reported in the West. These analyses demonstrate the applicability of elements of Western criminological theory to contemporary urban China but also reveal important differences in the ecological dynamics of crime across contexts.

title: Weapons at school: Are the predictors generalizable across context?
authors: Rountree, Pamela Wilcox
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
keywords: STUDENTS; CONDUCT of life; CRIMINAL behavior; CULTURE; WEAPONS;301\_4;J\_TF1505;301\_ComCrm;Sociological Spectrum
abstract: This study addresses the reasons for school-based weapon carrying across three diverse county-level contexts. Weapon carrying among students at school has been, until very recently, neglected in research. Further, much of the information that is available is non-comparative. Hence, whether the etiology of in-school weapon carrying is generalizable across diverse settings remains largely an unanswered question. The present study moves toward a test of generalizability by comparing student weapon possession, its antecedents in three geographically, economically,, culturally distinct communities in Kentucky. Findings suggest that few differences exist across context regarding the etiology of school-based weapon carrying. Regardless of community context, peer weapon carrying as well as criminal lifestyle are important predictors of adolescents carrying weapons to school.

title: Criminal victimization in cross-national perspective: An analysis of rates of theft, violence, vandalism across 27 countries
authors: van Wilsem, Johan
abstract: This research examines the effect of resource deprivation, criminal opportunities, social disorganization on national rates of homicide, non-lethal violence, theft, car vandalism. Previous cross-national research has concentrated on homicide variation, owing to the comparative problems associated with rates for other crimes. In the present article, International Crime Victims Survey (ICVS) data on various contact crimes, as well as homicide figures from the World Health Organization (WHO), are analysed across 27 East European, Western countries. First, a comparison of homicide levels with victimization rates for theft, non-lethal violence indicates considerable overlap, which suggests that countries with high levels of homicide tend to have high levels of other violence, theft too. Second, results from multivariate analyses indicate that income inequality is the most consistent structural correlate of victimization rates for homicide, theft, non-lethal violence, car damage across this selection of countries. Also, homicide, theft show negative relations with GDP per capita. This may indicate that societal development goes together with lower levels of exposure to likely homicide offenders (family, friends). However, the results provide no support for the crime-inducing impact of high target attractiveness, thereby challenging predictions derived from routine activity theory on theft.

title: Burglary victimization in England, wales, the United States, the Netherlands: A cross-national comparative test of routine activities, lifestyle theories
authors: Tseloni, A
keywords: Crime; Theft; Victimization; Human; Male; Female; Netherlands, England, US, Wales; burglary victimization; burglary incidence; British Crime Survey;301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;9\_001\_intro;301\_ComCrm;British Journal of criminology
abstract: This study examines factors relating to burglary incidence in England, Wales, the United States,, the Netherlands. Negative binomial regression models are developed based on routine activities theory. Data are drawn from national victimization surveys of about the same time: the 1994 British Crime Survey, the 1994 National Crime Victimisation Survey,, the 1993 Police Monitor, respectively. Relative to the two European countries, US households have more idiosyncratic patterns of burglary victimization. Despite differences across the three data sets, several similar effects emerge of variables tapping lifestyle characteristics on burglary victimization. Four variables had significant effects in the same direction in two or more countries where the third country showed a non-significant effect in the same direction. These were age, lone parent household status, urbanization,, the presence of security measures in the home. Some variables had significant effects in opposite directions according to country: rented accommodation was associated with higher burglary rates in the UK but lower rates in the Netherlands; household affluence was linked with higher rates of burglary in the UK, lower rates in the United States.

title: Examining rates of sexual offenses from a routine activities perspective
authors: Tewksbury, Richard, Mustaine, Elizabeth Ehrhardt, Stengel, Kenneth M
keywords: SEX offenders; COMMUNITY psychology; VICTIMS of crimes; GUARDIAN \& ward; SEX crimes; CRIMINALS; Routine activity theory; sex offenses;301\_4;J\_TF1505;z\_kyoto2015;301\_ComCrm;Victims \& Offenders
abstract: Recent policies enacted regarding sex offenders include the formation of a publicly accessible sex offender registry, community notification,, residential restrictions. Often the motivation behind these policies is to get information out about sex offenders to community members so that these communities can effectively guard against any revictimization by the sex offenders among them. Theoretically, the premise for this type of legislation corresponds to relationships specified by routine activities theory. The theory states that if guardians can interrupt potential offenders as they are preying on suitable targets, these crimes-in-the-making will not occur. The present study assesses routine activities theory via a study of the presence of potential offenders (as measured by the number of registered sex offenders in the area), as well as community, resident characteristics that measure the presence, types of suitable targets, the existence of guardians, guardianship structures. We find that only the presence of certain types of suitable targets has an influence on the variation in the rate of sex offenses across these communities. Policy implications are discussed.

title: Routine Activities And Vandalism: A Theoretical And Empirical Study
authors: Tewksbury, Richard, Mustaine, Elizabeth Ehrhardt
abstract: Using routine activity theory this paper examines vandalism victimization rates among a sample of 1,513 American college students at nine institutions. Relying on a sophisticated set of measures of community structures, conditions, victims’ alcohol, drug, other illegal activities, lifestyle activities,, security precautions, there is strong support found for the theory. Significant predictors of vandalism victimization risks include measures of target suitability, exposure to potential offenders, victim's offending behaviors,, measures of community structure, organization, cohesion.

title: The utility of country structure: A cross-national multilevel analysis of property, violent victimization
authors: Stein, Rachel E
abstract: Routine activities, lifestyle theories focus on the opportunities that lead to victimization experience. Routine activities theory considers a micro-, macro-level approach to understanding victimization, which suggests the utility of this theory in cross-national research. However, few cross-national studies applying a routine activities framework address both the individual, structural levels of analysis. Additionally, much research adhering to this theoretical perspective does not distinguish between instrumental, expressive crimes. Because of these limitations, the full explanatory value of the theory has not been adequately explored. In this study, the author focuses on a cross-national multilevel analysis of violent, property victimization across 47 developed, developing nations. The author uses the International Crime Victimization Survey (ICVS), the European Survey on Crime, Safety (EU ICS) for individual-level measures, incorporates information on country structure from sources including the United Nations, World Bank,, the International Labor Organization. The results indicate individual-level measures of routines, lifestyles are differentially related to expressive, instrumental victimization,, these relationships maintain significance when structural opportunity measures are considered. Moreover, the measures of structural opportunity as captured by the level of development, sex ratio,, female employment are differentially associated with violent, property victimization.

title: Residential burglary victimization: Household-, country-level mixed modeling
authors: Soo Chon, Don
keywords: 301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;330\_マルチレベル被害\_2018\_JPA(8章)\_root;301\_ComCrm;international Review of Victimology
abstract: The current study employed the International Crime Victimization Survey for 142,665 subjects in 35 countries to compare residential burglary patterns across countries by their developmental levels. The mixed-level modeling shows that households in less developed countries were more likely to experience residential burglary than those in highly developed countries. In addition, married status, low income levels were positively, while living in a detached house was negatively, related to burglary victimization. These findings are consistent with routine activity theory.

title: Sources of informal social control in Chicago Neighborhoods
authors: Silver, Eric, Miller, Lisa L
keywords: communities, crime; informal social control; social disorganization; social ecology; urban sociology;301\_4;12\_Chicago;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;301\_ComCrm;301\_3;criminology
abstract: Why do youth in structurally disadvantaged neighborhoods experience lower levels of informal social control? To answer this question, we examined multilevel data from the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods. Using hierarchical regression, we found that (1) neighborhood attachment, satisfaction with police contributed significantly to neighborhood levels of informal social control;, (2) neighborhood attachment, satisfaction with police mediated a substantial portion of the association between informal social control, neighborhood levels of concentrated disadvantage, immigrant concentration.

title: Coping with urban crime: women's use of precautionary behaviors
authors: Riger, S, Gordon, M T, LeBailly, R K
keywords: neighborhood conditions \& psychological factors \& life circumstances, crime precautionary behaviors, surveyed female urban residents; Avoidance; Crime; Fear; Human Females; Urban Environments; Coping Behavior; Demographic Characteristics; Personality Correlates; coping with crime; coping;301\_4;z\_kakenhi2008;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;z\_2013\_コミュニティの社会心理学;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: This investigation examines the impact of three sets of variables, neighborhood conditions, psychological factors,, life circumstances, on women's use of behaviors designed to protect themselves from criminal victimization. Participants in the study were 299 women living in Philadelphia, Chicago,, San Francisco. Two types of precautionary behaviors were identified: avoiding dangerous situations (e.g., by not going out alone at night), managing risks in the face of possible danger (e.g., by asking repairmen for identification). The three sets of variables were better able to predict avoidance than risk-management behavior. Commonality analyses revealed that psychological factors uniquely accounted for the largest proportion of the variance in the use of both types of precautions. In multiple regression analyses, fear, perceived physical competence, race,, education were significant predictors of avoidance, while fear, perceptions of local social disorder had significant regression effects on risk-management. Implications of the results for research, social policies regarding the impact of crime on communities are discussed,, this area is suggested as a rich context for the exploration of styles of coping with environmental stressors.

title: Routine activities, fear of crime: Specifying individual-level mechanisms
authors: Rengifo, Andres F, Bolton, Amanda
keywords: FEAR of crime; CRIMINAL behavior; CRIMINOLOGICAL research; Routine activity theory; DAS-Naglieri Cognitive Assessment System; INDIVIDUAL measures (Psychology); MATHEMATICAL models; DATA analysis; risk interpretation model; routine activities; British Crime Survey;301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Studies have examined individual-level associations between fear of crime, various environmental, cognitive assessments but have largely dismissed the relationship between various dimensions of fear, broad behavioural adaptations. Drawing on the risk interpretation model, we specify path models to assess the nature of relationships between perceptions of risk of crime, disorder, the patterning of voluntary, compulsory routine activities. We also explore whether these activities influence the relationship between disorder, risk, fear. Using data from the 2007–8 British Crime Survey, we find support for the proposed distinction between types of routine activities. Although we also find that the various manifestations of fear exhibit different associations with these activities, our models offer marginal support for the proposed mediating role of behavioural policies.

title: Risky neighbourhood or individuals at risk? The significance of neighbourhood conditions for violent victimization in residential areas
authors: Nilsson, Anders, Estrada, Felipe
journal: Journal of Scandinavian studies in criminology, crime prevention
keywords: At Risk Populations; Psychosocial Factors; Risk Factors; Victimization; Violence; Human; Male; Female; Sweden; social determinants; violent victimization; risky neighborhoods;301\_4;J\_TF1505;z\_bsj2010\_past;301\_ComCrm;301\_2
abstract: The objective of this study is to examine the social determinants of violent victimization, with the principal focus being directed at the significance of neighbourhood conditions. By combining data from victim surveys with information on the neighbourhoods in which the survey respondents live, we have been able to study both the individual, household characteristics,, also the factors specific to different neighbourhoods that are associated with violent victimization. What we are able to show is that the violence that occurs in the residential neighbourhood constitutes only a small fraction of the violent incidents to which people are exposed. Further, the violence that occurs within the neighbourhood takes place to a large extent within the victim's home. This suggests that exposure to violence is associated with neighbourhood conditions only to a limited extent. More detailed analyses of the violence that does occur within the neighbourhood show no effects of neighbourhood conditions when controls are included for individual, household characteristics. The conclusion, therefore, is that we are unable to find any clear neighbourhood effects in relation to violent victimization. The differences that we initially note between different types of neighbourhood in the proportions reporting exposure to violence are too a large degree the result of selection processes. These do not, however, in themselves increase the risk for violent victimization. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2009 APA, all rights reserved) (journal abstract)

title: Routine leisure activities, rates of crime: A macro-level analysis
authors: Messner, S F, Blau, J R
journal: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study, interpretation
keywords: CRIME; HOUSEHOLDS; LEISURE; HYPOTHESIS; REGRESSION analysis; UNITED States;301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;9\_001\_intro;301\_ComCrm
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to apply a “routine activities” approach to explain the relations between macro-level indicators of leisure activities, rates of serious crime. We hypothesize that indicators of the volume of leisure activities that typically take place within households will exhibit negative relations with rates of crime, whereas indicators of the volume of leisure activities that are usually conducted away from households will yield positive associations with rates of crime. Regression analyses for a sample of the largest Standard Metropolitan Statistical Areas (SMSAs) in the United States provide strong support for these hypotheses. A “household activities” index, a “nonhousehold activities” index exhibit negative, positive associations, respectively, with SMSA crime rates. We suggest that while these results are fully consistent with the routine activities approach, they are not readily interpretable with reference to other general perspectives on the relations between leisure, crime.

title: Lifestyle, rational choice,, adolescent fear: A test of a risk‐assessment framework
authors: Melde, Chris
keywords: CRIME; CRIMINOLOGY; FEAR of crime; HUMAN behavior; lifestyle; JUVENILE delinquency; CRIMINAL behavior, Prediction of; VICTIMS of crimes; RESEARCH; fear; opportunity; perceived risk; routine activities; victimization;301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;121\_Lane2014;301\_ComCrm;criminology
abstract: Criminological research on fear of crime primarily has been based on,, supportive of, an opportunity framework. The current research tests an expanded risk‐assessment model of fear, which is rooted in an opportunity framework, by incorporating a measure of delinquent lifestyle, which is a known risk factor for victimization, using a sample of youth aged 10–16 years. The findings from longitudinal structural equation models do not support the applicability of a risk‐assessment model of fear in adolescence. Namely, although increased involvement in a delinquent lifestyle is associated strongly with an increase in victimization over time, no such association exists with the perceived risk of victimization. Most importantly, as adolescents become more involved in a delinquent lifestyle, are victimized at a higher rate than nondelinquent youth, their fear of victimization actually decreases at a significantly higher rate than more prosocial youth.

title: Perceptions of risk, lifestyle activities,, fear of crime
authors: Mesch, Gustavo S
keywords: PERCEPTION; ACTIVITIES of daily living; FEAR of crime; GENDER; AGE; RISK; NIGHT;301\_4;J\_TF1505;122\_3\_リスク解釈モデル;121\_Lane2014;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm
abstract: This study explored the relationship between perceptions of risk, routine night time activities,, fear of crime. The hypothesis that the effect of gender, age on fear of crime is mediated by individuals' perception of risk, the extent that they engage in night time routine activities was tested. Data from a survey of a representative sample of the population in Israel were used,, LISREL models were estimated. Individuals with previous experience of victimization, women reported higher levels of perceived risk. The higher the perceived risk, the less likely was the person to engage in routine night time activities, the more likely to fear crime. A salient finding was that gender had a direct effect on fear, indirect effects through perceived risk, routine activities. The implications of the findings are discussed.

title: Property crime, the routine activities of individuals
authors: Massey, James L, Krohn, Marvin D, Bonati, Lisa M
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;330\_マルチレベル被害\_2018\_JPA(8章)\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_2;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: The risk of property crime victimization is examined from a routine activities approach using data from six neighborhoods in Atlanta, Georgia. Indicators of the concepts of motivated offenders, suitable targets,, capable guardians are identified,, their individual, combined explanatory power are examined. The findings reveal that measures of neighborhood crime, housing type are the only variables that consistently relate to victimization in the hypothesized direction; employment status is the only guardianship measure that has the predicted effect on victimization. The analyses provide limited support for the routine activities approach, but are also consistent with hypotheses derived from other theoretical perspectives on criminal victimizations.

title: Exploring the overlap between individualistic, collective crime prevention
authors: Madero-Hernandez, Arelys, Fisher, Bonnie S, Wilcox, Pamela
abstract: Crime prevention behaviors range from private-minded or individualistic actions citizens take to protect themselves from crime, to public-minded or collective behaviors aimed at protecting entire neighborhoods. Although these behaviors may be overlapping, few studies have examined the extent to which citizens engage in individualistic, collective crime prevention simultaneously. This study examines the co-occurrence, predictors of crime prevention behaviors with data from Canada’s General Social Survey. Results indicate that citizens who engage in individualistic crime prevention behaviors are somewhat likely to engage in collective ones. But when looking at the etiology of these behaviors, individualistic behaviors are largely influenced by concerns about victimization, while collective behaviors are driven more by concerns with neighborhood conditions.

title: Risky behaviors, personal victimization in Taiwan
authors: Kuo, Shih-Ya, Cuvelier, Steven J, Sheu, Chuen-Jim
journal: International journal of comparative, applied criminal justice
abstract: Western studies have consistently shown that risky behaviors are associated with personal victimization. In Taiwan, little is known about such behaviors in relation to personal victimization. This study utilized data from the 2000 Taiwan Areas Criminal Victimization Survey to examine whether the relationship between risk-taking behaviors, personal victimization that have been established in the Western literature also applied to Taiwan. This study generally found that the aspects of risky activities have great applicability for modeling criminal victimization risks. The findings from gender, marital status to victimization, however, do not meet the expectations derived from Western research. Based upon the inconsistent results, we agree with the conclusion of Messner, colleagues that it is necessary to apply the Western model flexibly in order to reflect the broader social–cultural context that shapes people's routine daily life, their differential risks of victimization in non-Western societies.

title: Evaluating the influence of fear of crime as an environmental mobility restrictor on women's routine activities
authors: Keane, Carl
keywords: 301\_4;eb;121\_Lane2014;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;301\_ComCrm;330\_SAEnv;Environment, Behavior\_●Sage
abstract: Although fear of crime is a topic that has received considerable research interest, less attention has been paid to the behavioral consequences of fear. Conducting secondary data analysis on a national survey of Canadian women, this article examines whether women would frequent certain environments more often, that they currently perceive as unsafe, if they felt safer. The article concludes that fear may be limiting women's movement around their environment,, by reducing fear, lifestyle options should increase.

title: Modeling Fear of Crime, Perceived Victimization Risk: The (In)Significance of Neighborhood Integration
authors: Kanan, James W, Pruitt, Matthew V
keywords: FEAR of crime; VICTIMS of crimes; NEIGHBORHOOD; CRIME; SAFETY;301\_4;z\_2009jasc;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;122\_3\_リスク解釈モデル;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm
abstract: The bulk of fear–of–crime research has been limited to one questionnaire item that asks respondents to assess their personal safety by answering “how safe they feel alone in their neighborhoods at night.” More recently, however, studies have pointed to the multidimensional nature of fear of crime, perceived risk of victimization. Following this line of inquiry, we investigate the potential impact of several variable sets on three measures of fear of crime or risk perception—the traditional risk assessment of being alone at night, a measure of worry about crime,, a more general assessment of neighborhood safety. Of particular interest are the relative effects of neighborhood integration variables on the measures of fear/risk. A comparison of the effects of neighborhood integration variables with a set of perceived neighborhood disorder, routine activities, socio–demographic characteristics,, victimization experience variables reveals that the neighborhood disorder (incivilities), income,, crime prevention measures produce the most consistently significant effects on fear of crime, perceived risk. Contrary to our expectations, neighborhood integration variables appear to be relatively unimportant.

title: Sexual revictimization: A routine activity theory explanation
authors: Culatta, Elizabeth, Clay-Warner, Jody, Boyle, Kaitlin M, Oshri, Assaf
keywords: depression; revictimization; routine activity theory; sexual victimization; substance use;301\_4;301\_ComCrm;J Interpers Violence
abstract: Research has shown that victims of sexual assault are at a significant risk of revictimization. We use routine activity theory to predict how sexual victimization in adolescence relates to depression, substance use,, ultimately revictimization as a young adult. We frame our research within routine activity theory, predict that sexual victimization increases substance use, depressive symptoms, both of which increase the likelihood of revictimization. We test the hypotheses with three waves of data from the Longitudinal Study of Violence Against Women. Using structural equation modeling, we examine the direct, indirect effects of previous sexual victimization, depressive symptoms,, substance use on the odds of victimization during the sophomore year of college. Results suggest that sexual victimization during the sophomore year of college is predicted directly by previous sexual victimization, also indirectly through depressive symptomology, though not substance use. Although understudied in the literature, depression is shown to mediate the relationship between victimization, revictimization,, this finding is consistent with routine activity theory, as well as the state dependence perspective on revictimization. Our findings suggest that depressive symptoms, a long acknowledged consequence of sexual victimization, should also be understood as a source of revictimization risk, indicating the importance of depression screening, intervention for decreasing sexual victimization.

title: Auto+burglaries+in+an+entertainment+district\%3A+patron+perceptions+of+risks+and+precautionary+behaviors
authors: Cochran, John K;, Bromley, Max L
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Cities; Burglary; Automobile theft; Risk assessment;301\_4;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Cochran, Bromley examine the perceptions of risks, precautionary behaviors of patrons concerning auto burglaries in an entertainment district, evaluate the applicability of SARA, a crime problem-solving model. In the entertainment district known as Ybor City, located in Tampa FL, auto burglaries are considered to be an important problem by the police, security officials,, local merchants. While not as serious as crimes of violence, auto burglaries in Ybor City were occurring on a consistently frequent basis, coupled with the small size of the city area, this geographic entity is considered a hot spot.

title: Differences between men’s, women’s monetary valuation of crime avoidance behavior
authors: Bitton, Yifat, Shavit, Tal
abstract: In this article, we focus on the monetary value of the “female fear,” namely, women’s precautionary, avoidance behaviors, which they use to protect themselves against crimes, compare it with the monetary value of similar behaviors taken by men. Using scenario questionnaires that allude to the risks of being alone in dark surroundings, we tested the willingness of men, women to pay for what is perceived as a means for reducing the potential of being the victim of a crime in these risky situations. The results reveal that females are willing to pay higher amounts of money for actions they perceive as having a positive effect on lowering the danger of victimization. This finding shows that the monetary cost of female fear is yet another harm inflicted upon women within the social framework of gendered power relationships. More to the point, the gender-based comparison this article undertakes re-conceptualizes female fear not only as women-focused but also as a cost being unevenly borne by women. Relevant policy implications are discussed. This is the first study to put a price tag on female fear, illuminating its financial implications, yet to be explored, next to its acknowledged behavioral implications.

title: Assessing Risk of Victimization through Epidemiological Concepts: An Alternative Analytic Strategy Applied to Routine Activities Theory
authors: Arnold, Robert, Keane, Carl, Baron, Stephen
journal: The Canadian review of sociology, anthropology. La Revue canadienne de sociologie et d'anthropologie
keywords: VICTIMS of crimes; EPIDEMIOLOGY; PUBLIC health; MEDICAL model; CRIME; HEALTH \& welfare funds;301\_4;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;9\_001\_intro;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Cet article fait appel aux concepts et aux techniques de l'epidemiologie pour examiner la capacite de la theorie des activites routinieres a expliquer le risque de victimisation criminelle. En allant au-dela de l'identification des facteurs de risque de victimisation, les auteurs se demandent comment les changements des facteurs de causalite pourraient influer sur ce risque dans la population generale. lis trouvent que les predicteurs etablis avec des methodes plus traditionnelles expliquent la plus grande partie du risque, mais que certains sont moins importants pour la comprehension du risque de la population dans l'ensemble en raison du petit nombre de personnes qui leur est associe, tandis que d'autres sont plus utiles parce qu'ils s'appliquent a un plus grand nombre de personnes. This paper draws upon concepts, techniques from epidemiology to examine the ability of routine activities theory to account for the risk of criminal victimization. Moving beyond the identification of risk factors for victimization, we ask how changes to causal factors might affect the risk of victimization in the general population. We find that predictors identified with more traditional methods account for the bulk of the risk, but that some are less important for understanding overall population risk because of the small numbers of people associated with them, while others are more helpful because they apply to larger numbers.

title: Coping with crime: Individual female responses
authors: Ade, Catherine M
journal: International journal of comparative, applied criminal justice
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; APARTMENT houses; SECURITY measures; RISK management; Behavior patterns; Citizen crime precautions; Female victims; Personal security; Reactions to crime; Victimization risk;301\_4;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Freedom from personal attack, security of one's personal possessions are goals to which almost everyone subscribes ¾ from the derelicts clutching their bottles of cheap wine to millionaires worried about intrusions into their mansions. Reducing the risk of crime against our homes, our property, ourselves is a goal about which much consensus exists (Levine, et al., 1980: 22). Since formal means of crime control through the Criminal Justice Agencies only have been found to be ineffective, women must turn to community‐oriented policing as a welcome alternative for self‐protection. This article discusses the strategies women employ to cope with the rising incidence of crime.

title: Social ties, collective efficacy,, crime-specific fear in Seattle neighborhoods
authors: Yuan, Yue, McNeeley, Susan
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; fear of crime/perceived risk; theories; social disorganization; social capital; victimization; Social integration; Crime; Violence; Perceptions; Neighborhoods;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);301\_ComCrm;Victims \& Offenders
abstract: While research suggests that individuals' interactions with their communities-such as their social integration into the community, perceptions of collective efficacy-impact their perceived risk of victimization, only a handful of studies have examined the influence of these characteristics on crime-specific, emotional fear. Using the Seattle Neighborhoods, Crime Survey, we conduct multilevel models to examine whether social ties, collective efficacy are associated with perceived risk, emotional fear of violence, burglary. The results show that individuals' social ties to the community are negatively associated with perceived risk, but not emotional fear of violence or burglary, while perceived collective efficacy is negatively related to both cognitive, emotional fear. Moreover, the results suggest that individuals' social integration into the community functions through perceptions of collective efficacy to predict perceived risk; however, this process does not extend to emotional fear of either violence or burglary.

title: Multilevel impacts of perceived incivilities, perceptions of crime risk on fear of crime: Isolating endogenous impacts
authors: Wyant, Brian R
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 301\_3;z\_2018jssc;122\_3\_リスク解釈モデル;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;9\_001\_intro;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_urban\_socio\_root;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);301\_ComCrm;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Past work has linked incivilities to fear of crime but has left open two questions: Do multilevel impacts of incivilities persist after simultaneously controlling for sociodemographics, perceptions of crime risk, neighborhood fabric,, violent crime? Is neighborhood fear spatially lagged,, if so, does controlling for nearby fear alter endogenous impacts on fear? Survey data from 45 Philadelphia neighborhoods showed that those perceiving more incivilities, more crime risk than their neighbors were more fearful. Furthermore, neighborhoods where residents on average saw more crime risk were on average more fearful, even after controlling for significantly auto-correlated nearby neighborhood fear. The results suggest that impacts of incivilities on fear at the individual level are not completely mediated by perceived risk, that average fear levels in nearby neighborhoods correlate significantly, suggesting that some localized processes are operating above the neighborhood level. What these are,, how they link to neighborhood-, individual-level dynamics, remains to be investigated.

title: The built environment, community crime risk interpretation
authors: Wilcox, Pamela, Quisenberry, Neil, Jones, Shayne
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 301\_3;13\_Seattle;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;author\_Wilcox;10\_英語の研究;301\_ComCrm;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: In this article, the authors examine whether subjective perceptions of community safety are informed by the built environment. They posit that the built environment serves as a heuristic device, providing cues about likely levels of neighborhood crime, independent of the effects of neighborhood crime itself. Using data on 4,456individuals nested within 100 census tracts, the authors estimate hierarchical logistic models of perceived community crime risk. They focus on the role of the neighborhood built environment in the form of aggregated perceptions of nonresidential land use, while controlling for individual-level criminal opportunity, community-level social structural antecedents,, community-level objective crime. The findings indicate that the neighborhood-level presence of businesses, parks, playgrounds increases individual perceptions of community danger, but these effects disappear once neighborhood crime rates are controlled. The presence of schools has no effect on subjective interpretations of community crime, regardless of whether actual area crime is considered.

title: Discovering the impact of community policing: The broken windows thesis, collective efficacy,, citizens’ judgment
authors: Xu, Yili, Fiedler, Mora L, Flaming, Karl H
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: community policing; collective efficacy; citizens judgment; fear; perceived disorder; crime; quality of life; Collective Behavior; Communities; Police Personnel; Judgment;301\_3;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2018\_mera;332\_collectiveefficacy;301\_ComCrm;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage;307\_CP市民参加
abstract: The main purpose of the present study is to demonstrate the structure, mechanisms,, efficacy of community policing, its impact on perceived disorder, crime, quality of life in the community, citizens’ fear,, satisfaction with the police. It compares traditional, community policing paradigms on three dimensions: goal, measurement of outcome,, approach to crime. It concludes that community policing has a comprehensive, community-oriented goal, targets both disorder, crime,, emphasizes both organizational, community measures in police evaluation. It also addresses the criticisms of community policing, tests the heatedly debated relationships concerning community policing, disorder, crime, citizen’s fear,, collective efficacy. The major findings of the study include (1) Harcourt’s falsification of Skogan’s findings is invalid because of the methodological flaws,, therefore does not negate the disorder-crime nexus; (2) Sampson, Raudenbush unintentionally demonstrate, through their reciprocal feedback models, that crime, disorder are indirectly related; (3) disorder has strong direct, indirect,, total effects on crime even with collective efficacy being controlled for; (4) contrary to intuition, disorder elicits more fear than crime; (5) community policing reduces crime indirectly; (6) collective efficacy plays a far less significant role in controlling disorder, crime,, fear than community policing;, (7) citizens’ fear, perceived life quality are significant predictors of citizen satisfaction with the police.

title: Neighborhood residents' production of order: The effects of collective efficacy on responses to neighborhood problems
authors: Wells, William, Schafer, Joseph A, Varano, Sean P, Bynum, Timothy S
keywords: neighborhood residents; neighborhood problems; communities; citizen response; collective efficacy; crime; policing; Community Involvement; Crime Prevention; Neighborhoods; Police Personnel; Responses;301\_3;z\_2013\_コミュニティの社会心理学;301\_ComCrm;Crime Delinquency\_●Sage
abstract: Community policing agencies seek to engage communities to build working partnerships, solicit the input of neighborhood residents,, stimulate informal control of crime. A common barrier to these efforts is a lack of citizen participation. The purpose of this article is to assess the relationship between neighborhood-level variables, citizen response to neighborhood problems. The authors'predictions are guided by recent research on collective efficacy, the relationship between neighborhood conditions, citizen actions. Accordingly, the authors expect neighborhood variables will affect residents'responses to perceived problems. Results show that residential-unit variables do not have significant effects on the likelihood that residents respond to neighborhood problems they identified. Methodological limitations must be overcome before it can be concluded that collective efficacy is not predictive of citizen responses to neighborhood problems, but research must consider this important outcome variable.

title: Social cohesion, criminal victimization, perceived risk of crime in Brazilian neighborhoods
authors: Villarreal, A, Silva, B F A
journal: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study, interpretation
keywords: Sociology; Neighborhoods; Crime; Urban areas; Community organizations; Poverty; Brazil;301\_3;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Ecological theories linking community characteristics to the level of crime have rarely been tested outside the context of the United States, Western Europe. In this study we examine the effects of social cohesion, neighborhood disorder on crime using data from a survey of neighborhoods in Brazil. We find that lower-income neighborhoods, including irregular settlements known as favelas, have higher levels of social cohesion. Contrary to the results of research in U.S. urban areas, we find that greater cohesion among neighborhood residents is not significantly associated with lower levels of crime,, is in fact associated with a higher perceived risk of victimization. By contrast, neighborhood social, physical disorder increases violent victimization, but does not affect residents' perceived risk of being victimized. We argue that the effect of social cohesion on risk perception is explained by the greater spread of information regarding crimes occurring in more cohesive neighborhoods where residents interact more frequently with each other.

title: A test of the routine activities, neighborhood attachment explanations for bias in disorder perceptions
authors: Wallace, Danielle
abstract: “Neighborhood disorder” refers to how people perceive neighborhoods as unsafe, disorganized. However, certain disorder cues may indicate disorder to some residents but not to others. There are many explanations for disorder perception bias, though few have been tested. This article uses data on 4,721 residents in 100 neighborhoods in Seattle to assess two explanations for biases: neighborhood attachment, routine activities. Using fixed-effect models, this article shows that neighborhood attachment, routine activities provide additional insight into disorder perceptions. Hanging out with teens, engaging in protective neighborhood activities, like watching neighbors’ property, have a strong positive influence on disorder perceptions. This study concludes by discussing alternative explanations for disorder perception bias, their impact on disorder theory as a whole.

title: Racially homophilous social ties, informal social control: Racially homophilous social ties
authors: Warner, Barbara D, Swartz, Kristin, Hawk, Shila René
keywords: communities, crime; informal social control; social disorganization theory; interracial friendships; racial homophily;301\_3;301\_ComCrm;criminology
abstract: Social disorganization theory argues that racial/ethnic heterogeneity is a key neighborhood characteristic leading to social disorganization and, consequently, higher levels of crime. Heterogeneity's effect is argued to be a result of its fragmentation of social ties along racial/ethnic lines, which creates racially homophilous social networks with few ties bridging racial/ethnic groups. Most studies of social ties in social disorganization models, however, have examined their quantity, left unaddressed the extent to which ties are within or across different racial groups. This study goes beyond previous studies by examining the effects of both racially homophilous, interracial friendship networks on informal social control. Using multilevel models, data from 66 neighborhoods with approximately 2,300 respondents, we found that heterogeneity actually increased the average percentage of residents with interracial friendship networks, but the percentage of residents with interracial networks decreased the likelihood of informal social control. In contrast, the percentage of residents with White racially homophilous networks increased the likelihood of informal social control. Examining the microcontext of individuals’ networks, however, we found residents with interracial ties reported higher likelihoods of informal social control, that this effect was enhanced in neighborhoods with higher percentages of non‐White racially homophilous networks.

title: Neighborhood factors related to the likelihood of successful informal social control efforts
authors: Warner, Barbara D
keywords: Informal social control; Collective efficacy theory; Responses to social control; Crime prevention;301\_3;301\_ComCrm;J Crim Justice
abstract: To expand conceptualizations of informal social control in social disorganization, collective efficacy theories to include responses to informal social control,, to examine neighborhood level predictors of responses to informal social control.The study uses surveys of approximately 2300 residents across 66 neighborhoods, supplemented with census data at the block group level.Neighborhood mobility decreased the odds of positive responses to informal social control, measured as both “giving in”, “talking it out” when you have a disagreement with your neighbor. Disadvantage was found to decrease only the odds of “giving in.” Neighborhood level measures of social cohesion, faith in the police were also found to increase the odds of responding positively to informal social control efforts. In contrast, social ties were not found to significantly affect the likelihood of positive responses to informal social control.The findings from this study broaden support of collective efficacy theory, concepts related to efficacious neighborhoods. While previous studies have raised questions about the measurement of informal social control, the findings in this paper offer support to earlier studies by providing a different approach to the conceptualization, measurement of informal social control.

title: Testing alternative models of fear of crime
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Hale, Margaret
journal: The journal of criminal law \& criminology
keywords: FEAR of crime; CRIME; FEAR; VICTIMS of crimes; SOCIAL problems;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;9\_001\_intro;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;author\_Taylor;10\_英語の研究;z\_urban\_socio\_root;z\_2009jasc;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Studied the explanatory power of 3 models of fear of crime (FOC) via interviews with 523 Atlanta residents, in crime rate, land use data. The indirect victimization model (IVM) views vulnerable groups that are more likely to be victimized, have more local social ties as related to FOC. The perceived disorder model (PDM) posits that lower socioeconomic status (SES), a higher incidence of physical, social incivilities heighten perceptions of local problems, elevate FOC. The community concern model (CCM) posits that community conditions lead to perceived problems that lead to community concern, which elevates FOC. Path analyses show that all of the models explain about 10\% of worry. Key social, psychological variables in the IVM, PDM were major predictors of worry. Community concern made no independent contribution to predicting worry. The models varied in predicting FOC, with the CCM predicting best, PDM slightly less well,, IVM least well.

title: Local businesses as attractors or preventers of neighborhood disorder
authors: Steenbeek, Wouter, Völker, Beate, Flap, Henk, van Oort, Frank
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: While businesses may attract potential offenders, thus be conducive to disorder, the number of employees could offset this by exercising social control on offenders. This study uses data from different sources to test this expectation across 278 Dutch neighborhoods in the four largest cities of the Netherlands, using multivariate multilevel analysis to disentangle individual perception differences of disorder, neighborhood effects. Attention is paid to traditional explanations of disorder (i.e., poverty, residential mobility,, ethnic heterogeneity). Results show a positive relationship between business presence, neighborhood disorder. We do not find consistent results of the number of employees (i.e., bigger businesses are not always better or worse). Our research demonstrates that the presence of neighborhood businesses could rival the effects of social disorganization theory.

title: A longitudinal test of social disorganization theory: Feedback effects among cohesion, social control,, disorder: Cohesion, social control,, disorder
authors: Steenbeek, Wouter, Hipp, John R
keywords: SOCIAL disorganization; FEEDBACK (Psychology); SOCIAL control; SOCIAL cohesion; NEIGHBORHOODS; SOCIAL status; HOMOGENEITY; RESPONSIBILITY; CROSS-sectional method; longitudinal analysis; UTRECHT (Netherlands); NETHERLANDS;301\_3;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;Stability;z\_2013\_コミュニティの社会心理学;301\_ComCrm;criminology
abstract: Social disorganization theory holds that neighborhoods with greater residential stability, higher socioeconomic status,, more ethnic homogeneity experience less disorder because these neighborhoods have higher social cohesion, exercise more social control. Recent extensions of the theory argue that disorder in turn affects these structural characteristics, mechanisms. Using a data set on 74 neighborhoods in the city of Utrecht in the Netherlands spanning 10 years, we tested the extended theory, which to date only a few studies have been able to do because of the unavailability of neighborhood‐level longitudinal data. We also improve on previous studies by distinguishing between the potential for social control (feelings of responsibility), the actual social control behavior. Cross‐sectional analyses replicate earlier findings, but the results of longitudinal cross‐lagged models suggest that disorder has large consequences for subsequent levels of social control, residential instability, thus leading to more disorder. This is in contrast to most previous studies, which assume disorder to be more a consequence than a cause.
