This study underlines the importance of longitudinal data, allowing for simultaneously testing the causes, consequences of disorder, as well as the importance of breaking down social control into the two dimensions of the potential for social control, the actual social control behavior.

title: Block crime, fear: Defensible space, local social ties,, territorial functioning
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Gottfredson, Stephen D, Brower, Sidney
keywords: CRIME; NEIGHBORHOOD; FEAR of crime; SOCIAL problems; CITY dwellers; BLOCKS (City planning); CRIME, CRIMINAL JUSTICE, AND LAW ENFORCEMENT;301\_3;z\_urban\_socio\_root;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;2012\_jsep\_review\_root;author\_Taylor;10\_英語の研究;11\_Baltimore;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Why do some blocks have more crime, or their residents have higher fear levels, than other blocks? In an effort to answer this question we proposed a model that incorporated physical defensible space features, local social ties,, territorial functioning. The model was tested using data from a multistage, stratified sample of687 Baltimore households on 63 blocks. At each household, surveys were completed, on-site physical features were photographed, subsequently rated. Records of police activity on each block were also obtained. Our model explained significant portions of crimes of violence to persons (18\%)and block fear (37\%). It was also able to predict a significant amount (13\%) of the variation in individual-level fear. At the block level: defemible space features dampened crime, fear but not as strongly as expected;, local social ties dampened crime, fear directly,, indirectly via an enhancement of territorial functioning. A model predicting individual fear levels, controllingfor block context, was abo supported. Our successful modeling of block dynamics suggests that these entities may profitably be treated as small-scale social units or groups. The pattern of findings has also confirmed suggestions made by others that physicalfactors alone cannot be relied on to preserve local order, feelings ofsecurity. Finally, the block-level linkages between local social ties, territorial attitudes clarify how territorial attitudes reflect,, may contribute to, the development of group-based norms regarding appropriate behaviors in on-block settings. As crime in the urban residential environment has mounted in the last twenty years or so, so has concern about crime control. The latter area of inquiry spans a sizable literature in the areas of criminology, economics, geography, planning, psychology,, sociology. Defensible space features, which in the residential environment would include real barriers, symbolic barriers,, surveillance opportunities, may have some types of causal impacts. Crime is a powerful, omnipresent stressor,, thusly, of considerable practical interest. Each survey included sections on household composition, residence history, demographics, local social ties, perception of local crime, problems, fear, neighborhood identification,, territorial attitudes. Social climate, strength of territorial functioning on the block are both conditioned by the larger sociocultural context—racial composition, neighborhood stability,, so on. As social bonds—perhaps even of a superficial nature such as acquaintanceship—evolve, residents' interest, involvement in the public spaces of the block is increased.

title: Attachment to place: Discriminant validity,, impacts of disorder, diversity
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Gottfredson, Stephen D, Brower, Sidney
keywords: local disorders levels; Contextual Associations; Diversity; Neighborhoods; Territoriality;301\_3;11\_Baltimore;author\_Taylor;10\_英語の研究;301\_ComCrm;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: We sought to establish the discriminant validity of related concepts: territoriality, attachment to place. Further, we investigated the contextual determinants of attachment. We hypothesized that persons living in more heterogeneous neighborhoods would be less attached. We also hypothesized that levels of perceived or objective disorder would be negatively associated with attachment levels. The hypotheses were tested using data from a survey of 687 heads of household in Baltimore, Maryland. Data on police activity, neighborhood characteristics were also gathered. A clear territorial dimension, two attachment dimensions (Rooted, Involved; Acquaintanceship) were identified. Regressions of each dimension supported the distinctness of territoriality, attachment, as well as the hypothesized impacts of diversity, disorder on attachment. Not only are some people more attached to place than others but there are also some places to which people can become attached more easily. This study is the first to establish the direct impacts of diversity on attachment to place.

title: Community structural change, fear of crime
authors: Taylor, Ralph B, Covington, Jeanette
keywords: COMMUNITIES; NEIGHBORHOOD; CORPORATE culture; SOCIAL groups; ECOLOGY; CORRECTIONS;301\_3;301\_ComCrm;11\_Baltimore;author\_Taylor;10\_英語の研究
abstract: This paper examines how unexpected neighborhood changes influence fear of crime. It focuses on the roles of population composition, signs of incivility,, unsupervised peer teen groups. Survey, physical assessment,, census data for 1,622 residents in 66 Baltimore city neighborhoods form the basis of contextual models of daytime, nighttime fear levels. Fear was high in neighborhoods experiencing unexpected increases in minority, youth populations. Unexpected ecological change does not by itself set in motion a broad array of consequences undermining neighborhood viability. Rather, ecological change influences racial composition; other structural dynamics, independent of these ecological changes, subsequently determine the specific consequences of neighborhood racial composition.

title: Fear of crime, criminal victimization: Gender-based contrasts
authors: Schafer, Joseph A, Huebner, Beth M, Bynum, Timothy S
keywords: VICTIMS of crimes; FEAR of crime; SEX differences; OFFENSES against the person;301\_3;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;301\_ComCrm;J Crim Justice
abstract: Extant research on the fear of crime, criminal victimization had generally found that women express greater levels of fear than men. Using survey data, this study contrasted perceptions of safety, the fear of personal, property victimization among male, female respondents. Specifically considered was the relationship between demographic characteristics, fear facilitators, fear inhibitors, neighborhood context,, crime-related fear. Results indicated some gender differences in the influence explanatory variables had on fear, although not all achieved statistical significance. For both gender groups, respondents' perceptions of their neighborhood as orderly, satisfactory had the largest effect on perceptions. Gender-based differences in the outcome of the analyses further supported that males, females experienced fear based upon different factors.

title: Different actions for different crimes: Explaining individual action in local crime problems
authors: Schaefer, Lacey, Mazerolle, Lorraine, Kapnoulla, Marianne
abstract: The crime prevention literature finds extensive support for crime-specific approaches to organized interventions in crime problems. Yet within the communities, crime literature, little is known about the crime-specific (or generalized) way that individuals respond to different types of crime problems in their neighborhood. Using data from the Australian Community Capacity Study, this paper examines how individual characteristics, perceptions of agents of formal social control,, perceptions of informal community processes influence the decision a person makes to do something about different types of local crime problems. Results indicate that individual characteristics (prior police contact, previous victimization), positive perceptions of informal community processes (frequency of neighboring) are positively associated with action; yet when people perceive agents of formal social control as effective, they are less likely to take informal crime control action. We conclude that the mechanisms that prompt community action are best understood from a crime-specific approach.

title: Predicting perceptions of crime: Community residents’ recognition, classification of local crime problems
authors: Schaefer, Lacey, Mazerolle, Lorraine
journal: The Australian \& New Zealand journal of criminology
keywords: 301\_3;14\_Brinbane;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;301\_ComCrm
abstract: In the scholarship of crime prevention, little is understood regarding the prompts for individual observation, classification of local crime problems. Moreover, studies that evaluate individuals’ perceptions of crime tend to emphasise the risk of victimisation rather than the probability of crime controller behaviour. In order to predict whether, how a community resident combats neighbourhood crime, disorder, we first require a greater understanding of how individuals recognise, categorise those same neighbourhood phenomena. To explore these processes, the current project uses large-scale multilevel survey data from the Australian Community Capacity Study to test the predictive influence of individual characteristics, local social processes,, suburb features on a resident’s identification, categorisation of minor, moderate,, major neighbourhood crime problems. Results indicate that lived experiences with prior victimisation, interactions with the police, greater frequencies of neighbouring behaviours but lower levels of collective efficacy, socioeconomic disadvantage,, ethnic homogeneity are all associated with a greater likelihood of reporting serious local crime problems.

title: Beyond social capital: Spatial dynamics of collective efficacy for children
authors: Sampson, Robert J, Morenoff, Jeffrey D, Earls, Felton
keywords: CHILDREN; INFRASTRUCTURE (Economics); SOCIAL conflict; SOCIAL control; SOCIOLOGY; collective efficacy;301\_3;301\_ComCrm
abstract: We propose a theoretical framework on the structural sources, spatially embedded nature of three mechanisms that produce collective efficacy for children. Using survey data collected in 1995 from 8,782 Chicago residents, we examine variations in intergenerational closure, reciprocal local exchange,, shared expectations for informal social control across 342 neighborhoods. Adjusting for respondents' attributes, we assess the effects of neighborhood characteristics measured in the 1990 census, the role of spatial interdependence. The results show that residential stability, concentrated affluence, more so than poverty, racial/ethnic composition, predict intergenerational closure, reciprocal exchange. Concentrated disadvantage, by contrast, is associated with sharply lower expectations for shared child control. The importance of spatial dynamics in generating collective efficacy for children is highlighted-proximity to areas high in closure, exchange,, control bestows an advantage above, beyond the structural characteristics of a given neighborhood. Moreover, spatial advantages are much more likely to accrue to white neighborhoods than to black neighborhoods.

title: Social safety, self-rated general health, physical activity: changes in area crime, area safety feelings, the role of social cohesion
authors: Ruijsbroek, Annemarie, Droomers, Mariël, Groenewegen, Peter P, Hardyns, Wim, Stronks, Karien
keywords: General health; Neighbourhood crime; Physical activity; Social cohesion; Social safety;301\_3;301\_ComCrm
abstract: The aim of this study was to examine whether changes over time in reported area crime, perceived area safety were related to self-rated general health, physical activity (PA), in order to provide support for a causal relationship between social safety, health. Additionally, we investigated whether social cohesion protects the residents against the negative impact of unsafe areas on health, PA. Multilevel logistic regression analyses were performed on Dutch survey data, including 47,926 respondents living in 2974 areas. An increase in area level unsafety feelings between 2009, 2011 was associated with more people reporting poor general health in 2012 in that area, but was not related to PA. Changes in reported area crime were not related to either poor general health or PA. The social cohesion in the area did not modify the effect of changes in social safety on health, PA. The results suggest that tackling feelings of unsafety in an area might contribute to the better general health of the residents. Because changes in area social safety were not associated with PA, we found no leads that such health benefits were achieved through an increase in physical activity.

title: Perceived risk versus fear of crime: Empirical evidence of conceptually distinct reactions in survey data
authors: Rountree, P W, Land, K C
journal: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study, interpretation
keywords: CRIME; FEAR of crime; SOCIAL surveys; VIOLENCE; COGNITION; PSYCHOLOGY;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;121\_Lane2014;9\_001\_intro;110\_序論(1章)\_root;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_2016\_事典\_08犯罪不安;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;author\_Wilcox;10\_英語の研究;13\_Seattle;z\_urban\_socio\_root;z\_2009jasc;301\_ComCrm
abstract: The conceptualization, measurement of fear of crime have received considerable attention in the research literature. Nevertheless, most sample surveys use indicators that only tap a general, cognitive assessment of safety - assumed to represent fear of violence. This article examines whether there are conceptually, empirically distinct dimensions offear of crime by comparing the micro-, macrolevel antecedents of such a general, cognitive ``fear'' - which we call ``perceived risk'' - with thosefor a more emotionally based, burglary-specific fear. Hierarchical logistic regression models for both types offear are presented. Some similarities were found between fear, risk in terms of various predictors, but results generally provide further empirical evidence that the two constructs are quite distinct. At the individual-level, the effect of gender is different across models,, routine-activities variables are somewhat better predictors of burglary-specific fear in comparison to risk perception. At the contextual level, neighborhood integration serves to diminish respondents' perceptions of neighborhood danger, yet this variable is positively related to burglary-specific fear.

title: Neighborhood disorder, fear,, mistrust: the buffering role of social ties with neighbors
authors: Ross, C E, Jang, S J
keywords: perceived disorder in neighborhood \& alliances \& connections with neighbors; fear of victimization \& mistrust of others; 18–92 yr olds; Crime; Fear; Neighborhoods; Social Support; Victimization; Drug Abuse; Trust (Social Behavior); Vandalism;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;9\_001\_intro;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_2018\_mera;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: This paper proposes that individuals who report that they live in neighborhoods characterized by disorder--by crime, vandalism, graffiti, danger, noise, dirt,, drugs--have high levels of fear, mistrust. It further proposes that an individual's alliances, connections with neighbors can buffer the negative effects of living in a neighborhood characterized by disorder on fear, mistrust. Results from a representative sample of 2482 Illinois residents collected by telephone in 1995 support the propositions. Living in a neighborhood with a lot of perceived disorder significantly affects mistrust, the fear of victimization, adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. Perceived neighborhood disorder, social ties significantly interact: informal social ties with neighbors reduce the fear-, mistrust-producing effects of disorder. However, formal participation in neighborhood organizations shows little buffering effect.

title: Effects of community policing upon fear of crime: Understanding the causal linkage
authors: Roh, Sunghoon, Oliver, Willard M
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Community policing; Crime; Fear \& phobias; Behavior; Perceptions; Police; Effects; Citizens; Causality;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;9\_001\_intro;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_2018\_mera;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm
abstract: PurposeTo identify intervening factors between perceptions of community policing, reduction of crime fear among citizen, which can provide a better understanding of the causal linkage between these two variables.Design/methodology/approachThe present study employs the research data from the 1998 study “Criminal Victimization, Perception of Community Safety in 12 United States Cities,” which was conducted as a supplement to the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS). This study used only the personal data, which included information on respondents' demographic characteristics, personal crime, victimization experiences, perceptions of neighborhood crime,, experience, satisfaction with local police.FindingsThe finding reveals that while vulnerability variables (indirect victimization model) do not affect the relationship between community policing, fear of crime, the perception of incivilities (perceived disorder model), the dissatisfaction with life‐quality (community concern model) in the neighborhood intervene between community policing, fear of crime.Originality/valueDespite the abundant research in the area of community policing, less attention has been paid to the causal process between community policing activities, its presumed effect, reduction of crime fear in communities. This study helps us to understand how fear of crime is reduced by the implementation of community policing.

title: Community policing, fear of crime in Seoul: a test of competing models
authors: Roh, Sunghoon, Kwak, Dae-Hoon, Kim, Eunyoung
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Community policing; Crime prevention; Social research; Society; Civil rights; Community; Citizens; Criminal investigations; Quality of life; Kim Dae Jung;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;16\_ソウル;301\_ComCrm
abstract: PurposeThe purpose of this paper is to examine the complex constellation of underlying factors between community policing, fear of crime by embracing various exogenous variables identified through accumulated empirical research. Another important purpose of the current study is to examine the association between community policing, fear of crime in the Korean context.Design/methodology/approachThe data originated from a survey administrated by the Korean Institution of Criminology in the area of Seoul, South Korea, in an attempt to examine citizens’ fear of crime, perceptions of public safety, environment. Using a stratified sampling method, a total of 654 respondents were selected. Structural equation modeling was used to examine direct, indirect relationships among exogenous, endogenous variables, to test the authors’ hypothesized structural model of the citizen's fear of crime.FindingsThe current study found that the four proposed models between community policing, fear of crime were not supported in the Korean context. Neither direct nor indirect relationships between community policing, fear of crime were statistically significant. On the other hand, community policing was found to be significantly, indirectly associated with perceived risk of crime; those who more perceived community policing activities felt a greater risk of crime. A logical explanation for these findings requires understanding of the characteristics of community policing practice, the unique crime environment in South Korea.Originality/valueThis study shows unique characteristics in the community policing‐fear of crime nexus in Korean society in relation to the implementation of community policing, the level of fear of crime, perception of community‐based crime control.

title: A reexamination of the crime-fear linkage
authors: Rountree, Pamela Wilcox
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: FEAR of crime; CRIME; FEAR; VICTIMS of crimes; RISK perception;301\_3;z\_urban\_socio\_root;z\_bsj2010\_past;author\_Wilcox;10\_英語の研究;13\_Seattle;301\_ComCrm;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Various recent developments in the fear-of-crime literature have led scholars to the general conclusion that fear is a multidimensional concept. For instance, methodological work in the fear-of-crime tradition has recognized various dimensions of the concept of “fear,” suggesting that there are cognitive (e.g., risk perception), emotional (e.g., being afraid) components that need to be theoretically, empirically distinguished from one another. Related to this, the fear literature has also established the value in examining crime-specific fears, recognizing that the proximate causes of fear can vary depending on the crime fear in question. This article extends the notion of “the multidimensional nature of fear of crime” by comparing multilevel models of fear of violence versus fear of burglary with a specific focus on the crime-fear relationship for each type of fear. Using data from 4,638 individuals living in 100 Seattle neighbor-hoods, hierarchical logistic models of fear of violent victimization, fear of property victimization are estimated. Findings suggest that individual-, neighborhood-level crime experiences have differential effects on fear of violence in comparison to fear of burglary, thus providing further evidence of the multidimensional nature of fear of crime.

title: Predicting perceived risk of crime: a multilevel study
authors: Russo, Silvia, Roccato, Michele, Vieno, Alessio
keywords: CRIME; VICTIMS of crimes; SOCIAL problems; CRIMINAL liability; RISK perception; Disorder; Multilevel analysis; Perceived risk of crime; Psychological reactions to crime; Social peripherality; Victimization;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;9\_001\_intro;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;American Journal of Community Psychology
abstract: With a sample of Italians selected from 71 Italian counties (N = 1,868), we performed two multilevel analyses aimed at predicting the perceived risk of crime at local (i.e., in the participants' county of residence), at societal (i.e., in the context of Italian society) levels. A significant proportion of the variation in local risk perception was at the county level. The following individual variables predicted higher levels of this variable: indirect victimization, the perception of social, physical disorder, being a woman, being poorly educated,, being an older person. Among the ecological predictors, the crime rate, unemployment rate predicted higher levels of local crime risk perception, while the immigrant rate did not. Perceived risk of crime at the societal level did not show significant variation at the county level. Education, being a man, trusting people,, adhesion to post-materialistic values predicted lower levels of societal crime risk perception, while number of sons/daughters, exposure to television news increased it. The limitations, possible development of this study are discussed.

title: Criminal victimization, crime risk perception: A multilevel longitudinal study
authors: Russo, Silvia, Roccato, Michele, Vieno, Alessio
keywords: 301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm
abstract: In a national sample of the Italian population, surveyed four times between October 2002, January 2007 (N = 2,008), we performed a multilevel longitudinal study aimed at predicting the increase in crime risk perception as a function of three families of independent variables, respectively lying at the within individual level (direct victimization, indirect victimization), at the between-individuals level (being a woman, being an older person, being a poorly educated person, size of area of residence), at the ecological level (county's crime rate, unemployment rate, immigration rate). Direct, indirect victimization, being a woman, being an older person, living in a large town, in a context characterized by high crime, unemployment rates positively influenced the change in crime risk perception, while the other individual, ecological predictors we used in our predictive model did not. Strengths, limitations, implications, future developments of this research are discussed.

title: How long does victimization foster fear of crime? A longitudinal study
authors: Russo, Silvia, Roccato, Michele
keywords: 301\_3;z\_2018jssc;9\_001\_intro;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_2013\_コミュニティの社会心理学;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;J Community Psychol
abstract: AbstractWe studied the relationship between victimization, fear of crime longitudinally, analyzing data from the Observatory of the North‐West (Italian national sample, N=1,701, two waves: January 2006, January 2007). We modeled fear of crime at T2 using as independent variables: (a) the main sociodemographic variables, fear of crime, as assessed at T1; (b) direct victimization;, (c) indirect victimization. Recent direct victimization was the most effective victimization predictor of both concrete, abstract fears, followed by multiple or repeat direct victimization. On the other hand, direct victimization occurring in the 12 months before the first wave did not influence fear. Recent indirect victimization and, above all, multiple or repeat indirect victimization influenced concrete, but not abstract, fear of crime, while direct victimization occurring in the 12 months before the first wave did not foster fear. We discuss the limits of this work, possible further directions. © 2010 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.

title: Multilevel Longitudinal Impacts of Incivilities: Fear of Crime, Expected Safety,, Block Satisfaction
authors: Robinson, Jennifer B, Lawton, Brian A, Taylor, Ralph B, Perkins, Douglas D
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; FEAR of crime; CRIMINAL behavior; SELF; SATISFACTION; CRIMINAL psychology; broken windows theory; incivilities; Multilevel analysis;301\_3;z\_社会と調査;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_bsj2010;z\_bsj2010\_past;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;author\_Taylor;10\_英語の研究;11\_Baltimore;z\_urban\_socio\_root;z\_2018jssc;z\_kakenhi2008;z\_mera2010;301\_ComCrm;londitudunal\_vic\_survey
abstract: Several aspects of the incivilities thesis, or the role of social, physical disorder in encouraging crime, fear, deserve further testing. These include examining individual-, streetblock-level impacts on reactions to crime, local commitment over time,, testing for lagged, co-occurring impacts at each level. We model these four types of impacts on three reactions to crime, community satisfaction using a panel study of residents (n = 305) on fifty streetblocks, interviewed two times a year apart. At the individual level, incivilities showed unambiguous, lagged impacts on satisfaction, fear,, worry; furthermore, changes in perceived incivilities accompanied changes in resident satisfaction, fear. At the streetblock level: incivilities failed to demonstrate expected lagged impacts on either of the two outcomes where data structures permitted such impacts; changing incivilities, however, were accomp-anied by changing community satisfaction, changing perceptions of relative risk. Before we conclude that lagged ecological impacts of incivilities are weaker than previous theorizing suggests, we must resolve some outstanding theoretical, methodological issues.

title: Social disorganization, neighborhood fear: Examining the intersection of individual, community,, county characteristics
authors: Porter, Jeremy R, Rader, Nicole E, Cossman, Jeralynn S
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Criminal justice; Fear \& phobias; Crime; Neighborhoods;301\_3;301\_ComCrm
abstract: Fear has long been studied as a consequence of crime given the consistent, ubiquitous nature of fear as a reaction, the systematic variations in its consequences. Past research has shown significant variations in fear of crime at both the individual, ecological level. Here we implement a multi-level approach to understanding potential interactions between perceived safety in one’s neighborhood in relation to social disorganization indicators at the neighborhood level, crime rates at the county level. The nationally representative sample data ( n = 2,610) used in this analysis combines individual level data collected in 2006 from the Panel Study of Religion, Ethnicity (PS-ARE) with ecological level data at the tract, county level from the 2000 US Census. The findings suggest a three level interaction negating the well known protection hypothesis of marriage, crime; this essentially means that as being married or cohabitating decreases the negative effects of being in a community with a high level of familial disruption (percent of divorced) increases, but that effect is substantively negatively tempered as the violent crime rate of the county rises.

title: Making neighborhoods safer: Examining predictors of residents’ concerns about neighborhood safety
authors: Pitner, Ronald O, Yu, Mansoo, Brown, Edna
keywords: US; Crime; Human; Adulthood (18 yrs \& older); Safety; Neighborhoods; Interview; Quantitative Study; crime areas; Middle Age (40-64 yrs); Empirical Study; Aged (65 yrs \& older); Young Adulthood (18-29 yrs); 4270:Crime Prevention; Vigilance; Male; Female; Thirties (30-39 yrs); collective efficacy;301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;jep;jep\_org;301\_ComCrm;J Environ Psychol
abstract: This study examined what factors best predict residents’ concerns about neighborhood safety. One-hundred, twenty-two participants were selected from a large, Midwestern metropolitan area. All participants lived in high crime areas. Participants completed a 22-item questionnaire that assessed their perceptions of neighborhood safety, vigilance. These items were clustered as: 1) Community care, vigilance, 2) neighborhood safety concerns, 3) physical incivilities,, 4) social incivilities. Police crime data were also used in the analyses. Our findings suggest that aspects of the broken window theory, collective efficacy,, place attachments/territoriality play a role in affecting residents’ concerns about neighborhood safety.

title: Incivilities in nonmetropolitan communities: The effects of structural constraints, social conditions,, crime
authors: Reisig, Michael D, Cancino, Jeffrey Michael
keywords: Antisocial Behavior; Communities; Crime; Demographic Characteristics; Sociocultural Factors; Urban Environments; Human; Male; Female; incivilities; nonmetropolitan communities; structural constraints; social conditions; sociodemographic characteristics; collective efficacy;301\_3;301\_ComCrm;J Crim Justice
abstract: Guided by social disorganization theory, the emerging concept of collective efficacy, this study used three sources of data, including community surveys administered to 1,125 citizens nested in thirty-one residential units,, hierarchical modeling techniques to examine the effects of structural features, collective social processes, net of property crime (i.e., burglary), citizen-level sociodemographic characteristics, on perceived incivilities (i.e., signs of physical decay, social disorder) in nonmetropolitan communities. The results showed that respondents living in economically disadvantaged geographic areas were significantly more likely to perceive their immediate surroundings in more negative terms (i.e., higher levels of incivilities). Respondents living in residential units characterized by higher levels of collective efficacy (i.e., a composite measure consisting of both cohesion, control), however, reported significantly fewer incivility problems. When assessed separately, social cohesion partially mediated the effects of economic disadvantage. The findings indicated that social disorganization theory generalizes to less densely populated, nonmetropolitan communities.

title: The Cohort-Size Sample-Size Conundrum: An Empirical Analysis, Assessment Using Homicide Arrest Data from 1960 to 1999
authors: O'Brien, Robert M, Stockard, Jean
keywords: Communities; Crime; Job Performance; Police Personnel; Work Load; Poverty; Size; Human; Canada; community size; crime type; crime clearance; workload; police officers; police performance;301\_3;z\_bsj2010\_past;301\_ComCrm
abstract: A number of studies use the Age-Period-Cohort Characteristic (APCC) model to address the impact of cohort related factors on the age distribution of homicide offending. Several of these studies treat birth cohorts as spanning several years, an operationalization that most closely matches tenets of cohort theory, yet sharply reduces the number of observations available for analysis. Other studies define birth cohorts as those born within a single year, an operationalization that is theoretically problematic, but provides many more observations for analysis. We address the sample size problem by applying a time-series-cross-section model (panel model) with age-period-specific homicide arrest data from the United States for each year from 1960 to 1999, while operationalizing cohorts as five-year birth cohorts. Our panel model produces results that are very similar to those obtained from traditional multiyear APCC models. Substantively, the results provide a replication of work showing the importance of relative cohort size, cohort variations in family structure for explaining variations in age-period-specific homicide rates. The additional observations provided by our approach allow us to examine these relationships over time,, we find substantively important changes. The year-by-year estimates of the age distribution of homicide offending help us to examine the model during the epidemic of youth homicide.

title: Aging, neighborhood attachment,, fear of crime: testing reciprocal effects
authors: Oh, Joong-Hwan, Kim, Sangmoon
keywords: 301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;10\_英語の研究;12\_Chicago;z\_2009jasc;301\_ComCrm;J Community Psychol
abstract: AbstractThis study attempts to examine the reciprocal effects between fear of crime, neighborhood attachment because aging is a critical factor in both discussions of fear of crime, neighborhood attachment (friendship, neighboring, social cohesion, trust, informal social control,, participation in neighborhood watch program). Using data from the Project on Human Development across 343 Chicago neighborhoods, this study tests the impact of aging combined with five measures of neighborhood attachment on fear of crime. Our analyses confirm that all five interaction variables are insignificant in explaining fear of crime. In contrast, this study tests another argument that aging coupled with fear of crime (urban elderly's fear of crime) affects neighborhood attachment. The findings show that rising fear of crime among urban elderly residents helps increase their interactions with neighbors (neighboring), their perceived level of social cohesion to, trust of neighbors. In short, this study supports a model where an interaction predictor of aging, fear of crime increases neighborhood attachment. © 2008 Wiley Periodicals, Inc.

title: Neighbourhood disorder, worry about criminal victimization in the neighbourhood
authors: Mellgren, Caroline, Pauwels, Lieven, Levander, Marie Torstensson
keywords: 301\_3;z\_2018jssc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_2018\_mera;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;international Review of Victimology
abstract: This study tested a cross-level integrated model of neighbourhood level disorder, individual level vulnerability, in relation to explaining individual differences in worry about criminal victimization1. The aim of the present study is (1) to establish if there is unique neighbourhood level variation in worry about criminal victimization, independent of neighbourhood composition, and(2) to establish the extent to which two proposed mechanisms at the individual level, prior local victimization, perceived disorder, act as mediators of a hypothesised effect of neighbourhood level disorder. Given the hierarchical structure of the research question a series of multilevel analyses based on data from a survey of more than 4,000 residents of a Swedish urban are a was performed. Findings by, large indicate that there are significant neighbourhood level differences in worry about criminal victimization, that these differences are not completely due to compositional effects. Neighbourhood disorder has effects on worry about criminal victimization, independent of the composition of neighbourhoods. The present study suggests that neighbourhood disorder has consequences for worry about criminal victimization, that prior victimization, perceived disorder are key mediators of the contextual effect of neighbourhood disorder. The implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Victimization, risk perception,, the desire to move
authors: McNeeley, Susan, Stutzenberger, Amy
keywords: 301\_3;J\_TF1505;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;Victims \& Offenders
abstract: A small body of research indicates that victims of personal, property crimes are more likely to change residence. Scholars assume that this decision to move after suffering victimization is driven by the increase in perceptions of risk of subsequent victimization. The current study examines the effect of victimization, perception of safety on the desire to move. Using Matsueda's Seattle Neighborhoods, Crime Survey, we test the hypothesis that risk perception increases the desire to change residence, that this effect explains the relationship between victimization, the desire to move. As expected, property victimization affected the extent to which individuals considered moving from their current home; this relationship was indirect through an increase in risk perception. However, violent victimization was not related to the desire to move.

title: A multilevel examination of the code of the Street’s relationship with fear of crime
authors: McNeeley, Susan, Yuan, Yue
abstract: Research suggests that youths adopt the code of the street to reduce potential victimization, but it may increase actual risk of victimization. Because of this contradiction, the relationship between the code of the street, fear of crime may be an important component; however, fear of crime is an understudied component in the code of the street literature. This study conducts multilevel models to examine whether the code of the street is associated with perceived risk of victimization, emotional fear of crime. Individual belief in the code of the street was positively related to emotional fear of violent crime. At the neighborhood level, the code of the street was associated with higher perceived risk.
