abstract: It is argued that most travel mode choices are repetitive, made in a stable context. As an example, the everyday use of public transport is analyzed based on a panel survey with a random sample of about 1300 Danish residents interviewed up to three times in the period 1998–2000. The use of public transport is traced back to attitudes towards doing so, beliefs about whether or not public transportation can cover one’s transport needs,, car ownership. The influence of these variables is greatly attenuated when past behavior is accounted for, however. For subjects without a car, behavior changes are in the direction of greater consistency with current attitudes, perceptions. For car owners, current attitudes are inconsequential. The temporal stability of transport behavior is also higher for car-owners than for non-owners.

title: Are repeatedly victimized households different?
authors: Osborn, Denise R, Ellingworth, Dan, Hope, Tim, Trickett, Alan
abstract: Much recent victimization research has concentrated on predicting who will be victimized, with relatively little concern for the number of events suffered. This study turns to the latter issue by focusing attention on the prediction of repeat victimization. A statistical methodology is employed which allows for the explicit recognition that an initial victimization must occur prior to any repeat event. When applied to property crime information from the 1984 British Crime Survey, we find little evidence that repeat victims have distinctive characteristics compared with single victims. Nevertheless, households with characteristics which protect from victimization, in the sense of giving rise to a low initial risk, have this protection reduced for a subsequent event. Moreover, comparing two households with different risk characteristics, their repeat victimization probabilities are more similar than were those for the initial occurrence.

title: Personal fraud: The victims, the scams
authors: Titus, Richard M, Gover, Angela R
abstract: The evidence from fraud victimization surveys is unanimous that repeat victimization is common. Greater education is not a protective factor against victimization; the evidence points to the reverse. Much evidence also suggests that older people are not at greater risk of fraud victimization. It may be that younger, better-educated people have wider interests, engage in a broader range of activities,, have more consumer participation in the marketplace than other demographic groups, thereby increasing their exposure to fraudulent solicitations, transactions. Risk heterogeneity, state dependence both appear to contribute to repeat victimization. The present study finds that fraud attempts are less likely to succeed if:(1) the offender is a stranger;(2) the initial contact is by telephone or mail;(3) the potential victim has heard of this type of fraud before; or (4) the potential victim tries to investigate the person or proposition before responding. Targeted campaigns aimed at fraud victims should be mounted. Enhanced, routine data collection on a national level is necessary, together with anticipation of new methods of fraudsters.

title: Problem-oriented policing, drug market locations: Three case studies
authors: Hope, Timothy
abstract: The problem-oriented approach to policing, the sltuattonal approach to crime prevention have much in common, both arising from the search for more effective means of crime control. They share a common perspective in being targeted at specific crime problems, locations. This paper describes three case studies of problem-oriented policing carried out by officers of the St Louis (MO) Metropolitan Police Department, each concerned with reducing crime, disorder at locations where drugs were being sold. In each case, the individual officers played a pivotal role as catalysts in stimulating actions by the community, city agencies,, in achieving reductions in crime, disorder at the problem locations. The cases suggest that at the localized level at which it operates, problem-oriented policing can achieve the kind of coordinated action which may not be so easy at a broader level of community, organizational aggregation.

title: School-based prevention of teen-age pregnancy, school dropout: process evaluation of the national replication of the Teen Outreach Program
authors: Allen, J P, Philliber, S, Hoggson, N
abstract: Examined a program designed to prevent adolescent pregnancy, school failure,, dropout using a process model of evaluation to assess with which groups of participants, under what conditions the program was most effective. Students in the Teen Outreach Program of the Association of Junior Leagues, matched comparison students in 35 schools nationwide participated. Sites that highly utilized a volunteer service component,, sites that primarily served older students reported lower levels of student problem behaviors at program exit, after controlling for problem behaviors at entry. These findings occurred only for program youths, not for comparison youths. The connection of volunteer service to reductions in adolescent problem behaviors is interpreted in terms of helper-therapy, empowerment theories. Limitations of the analytic strategy used in this study, as well as techniques for addressing the limitations, are also discussed.

title: The relationship of information sufficiency to seeking, processing risk information
authors: Griffin, Robert, Dunwoody, Sharon, Neuwirth, Kurt, Giese, James
abstract: Based in part on Eagly, Chaiken’s (1993) Heuristic-Systematic model of information processing, we develop, test part of a model that focuses on characteristics of individuals that might predispose them to seek, process information about health, environmental risks in different ways. Specifically, the part of the model being tested proposes that three main predictors —(1) the need for sufficient information to allow one to deal with the risk, (2) one’s perceived personal capacity to acquire needed information,, (3) beliefs about the usefulness of information in various channels — will influence the extent to which a person will seek out this risk information in both routine, non-routine channels, the extent to which he or she will spend time, effort analyzing the risk information critically. Results indicate that information (in)sufficiency, as hypothesized, is associated positively with non-routine seeking of information, systematic processing of it,, negatively with heuristic processing of information, avoidance of it. Individuals were less likely to avoid risk information,, instead were likely to process it heuristically and, especially, systematically if they believe that the channels contain essential processing cues. Capacity, however, did not relate to information seeking, processing in the manner expected. Results indicate the model is useful for examining audience members’ communication responses to risks.

title: Panic on the streets of London: Police, crime,, the July 2005 terror attacks
authors: Draca, Mirko, Machin, Stephen, Witt, Robert
abstract: In this paper we study the causal impact of police on crime, looking at what happened to crime, police before, after the terror attacks that hit central London in July 2005. The attacks resulted in a large redeployment of police officers to central London as compared to outer London. During this time, crime fell significantly in central relative to outer London. The instrumental variable approach we use uncovers an elasticity of crime with respect to police of approximately -0.3 to -0.4, so that a 10 percent increase in police activity reduces crime by around 3 to 4 percent. title: Social capital, collective efficacy: Resource, operating tools of community social control
authors: Ansari, S
journal: Journal of Theoretical, Philosophical Criminology Social Capital \& Collective Efficacy
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Social capital; Social networks; interventions; Public good; collective efficacy;301\_ComCrm
abstract: ABSTRACTCurrent popularity of social capital, collective efficacy theories in community research has presented some challenges related to definition, measurement,, ontological issues that need to be addressed to facilitate future research. Although scholars have made efforts to clarify the differences between social capital, collective efficacy, the two concepts have been either used interchangeably or presented as competing ideas. The paper, through the review of relevant literatures, addresses some of these issues, argues that social capital, collective efficacy are partly overlapping, complementary to one another with regards to establishing, sustaining community social control. When social capital is activated in the specific direction to develop social control, collective efficacy plays an important role by providing a connection, activating the resource of social capital for the specific goal of safety. Social capital alone cannot guarantee safety, but collective efficacy cannot exist in absence of social capital.Key Words: Social Capital, Collective Efficacy, Crime, Disorder, Social Control, NeighborhoodSocial Capital, Collective Efficacy: Resource, Operating Tools of Community Social ControlINTRODUCTIONThe concepts of social capital, collective efficacy have recently gained popularity in community research in criminology. Both are in the process of getting shaped, re-shaped. Several problems are being encountered in defining, measuring these concepts. First, there are no accepted working definitions as different scholars define these concepts differently. The issue of definition is more challenging in case of social capital because the concept is interdisciplinary, multidimensional. Second, the relationship between social capital, collective efficacy is somewhat confusing. Scholars have attempted to clarify the similarities, differences between them. Some have conceptualized them as competing, conflicting concepts, while others have used them interchangeably. Third, measurements of these concepts remain issues mainly because of lack of consensus on working definitions. Finally, the relationship between social capital, collective efficacy,, informal social control also needs some clarifications. The purpose of the paper is to address these issues by reviewing relevant literatures.Social capital may be defined as a community stock of social trust, norms of reciprocity embedded in social networks that facilitates collective actions. This definition integrates the elements of several definitions of social capital provided by scholars. Collective efficacy is defined as a form of social organization that combines social cohesion, shared expectations for social control (Sampson, Raudenbush, \& Earl, 1997; Sampson, 2006). Currently, the theories of social capital, collective efficacy are used in criminology in community research (Kubrin \& Weitzer, 2003; Morenoff, Sampson, \& Raudenbush, 2001; Putnam, 2001, 2002; Rose \& Clear, 1998; Rosenfeld, Messner, \& Baumer, 2001; Sampson et al., 1997; Sampson \& Raudenbush, 1999). Several studies have reported that either social capital is positively related with crime, disorder or it is insufficient to activate social control at neighborhood level (Sampson, 2006; Cancino, 2005; Pattillo, 1998). This is probably due to the narrow conceptualization of the definition of social capital in social disorganization literature where social capital is equated with social networks, early works in social disorganization assumed that networks alone directly affect the community social control (Bursik, 1988; Kubrin \& Weitzer 2003). The recent research in collective efficacy, while accepting the necessity of some networking for activation of neighborhood collective efficacy, reports potential negative externalities of dense ties, argues for dispensability, undesirability of dense ties (Pattillo, 1998; Sampson, 2006). …

title: An analysis of the mediating effects of social relations, controls on neighborhood crime victimization
authors: Rhineberger-Dunn, Gayle, Carlson, S
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Social control; Criminology; Theory; Neighborhoods; Crime prevention; Violent crime;301\_2;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;301\_ComCrm;police visibility
abstract: Abstract: Recent tests of systemic social disorganization theory focus on specifying types of informal, formal controls, their ability to mediate the impact of negative structural conditions on neighborhood crime rates. However, a majority of these studies use measures that confound the quality of the relationships needed to develop both informal, formal control with the willingness to exercise these controls. We contribute to this body of literature by making a distinction between the quality of relationships that facilitate the ability to use controls (e.g., social cohesion, police-citizen relations), the willingness to exercise informal, formal control. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that social cohesion, informal control, police-citizen relations,, formal control differentially mediate the impact that neighborhood structural characteristics have on interpersonal violence, specific types of property crime victimization. Further, we argue that the effects of informal control will be stronger than the effects of formal control,, that the impact of social cohesion, police-citizen relations will be partially mediated by their influence on the exercise of these controls. The results of our hierarchical generalized linear models show that social cohesion, informal control, police-citizen relations,, formal control differentially mediate the impact of neighborhood structural conditions on violent crime, property crime victimization. Our results suggest that strategies needed to prevent violent crime are different than those needed to prevent property crime. Keywords: social disorganization, collective efficacy, informal control, formal control, crime, victimization (ProQuest: ... denotes formulae omitted.) INTRODUCTION Since the early 1980s, social disorganization theory has experienced a revitalization in the academic literature. Much of the recent research focuses on extending systemic social disorganization theory by attempting to specify the factors that mediate the impact negative social structural characteristics (e.g., poverty, racial/ethnic heterogeneity, residential mobility) have on neighborhood crime. Most of these studies test the mediating effects of social cohesion, relational ties, attachments, or networks (e.g., Bellair 1997; Lowenkamp, Cullen,, Pratt 2003; Markowitz et al. 2001; Sampson, Groves 1989; Warner, Rountree 1997). More recent research has turned to specifying the sources of informal and/or formal controls (Renauer 2007; Silver, Miller 2004; Triplett, Gainey,, Sun 2003; Wells et al. 2006), assessing the impact that informal, formal controls have on mediating structural conditions on neighborhood crime rates (Clear et al. 2003; Goudriaan, Wittebrood,, Nieuwbeerta 2006; Sampson, Raudenbush,, Earls 1997; Triplett, Sun,, Gainey 2005; Velez 2001). Although a growing body of literature has focused on specifying types of informal, formal control, their ability to mediate the impact of negative structural conditions, many of these studies have created measures that focus on either the ability or the willingness of residents to enact control (Triplett et al. 2005). Furthermore, it has been argued that some studies use measures that confound the quality of the relationships that foster the ability to use social controls with the willingness to exercise them (Kubrin, Weitzer 2003; Lowenkamp et al. 2003; Rhineberger-Dunn, Carlson 2009; Triplett et al. 2005). Similarly, a variety of policing-related variables have been used to measure formal control, albeit most confound the issue of relationships between police, neighborhood residents with the exercise of formal control itself (Rhineberger-Dunn, Carlson 2009). The basic tenets of systemic social disorganization theory suggest that relational variables, control variables should differentially mediate the effects of structural conditions on neighborhood crime rates (Bursik, Grasmick 1993). …

abstract: Incidence of harassment on, around public transit is widely reported in grey literature, particularly for women, members of marginalised groups. Given the international evidence that harassment, subsequent fear of crime may increase car use over public transport use, fear of crime may be compromising efforts to increase the share of public transport in Australian cities. This paper reviews international literature on harassment, transit behaviour, focusing on its prevalence, transport-behavioural impacts within a fear of crime framework. Potential solutions that are relevant to planning are reviewed. The applicability of international examples to the Australian context highlights potential research opportunities for understanding the public impacts, potential solutions for transit-related harassment in Australia.

title: \textitThe presentation of police in everyday life: Police–press relations, impression management, the Leveson Inquiry
authors: Mawby, Rob C
abstract: In 2012 the Leveson Inquiry investigated relations between the police, the press, examining the routine systems, processes of police–press relations in the UK and, more specifically, the conduct of senior Metropolitan Police Service officers during an investigation into phone-hacking (Operation Caryatid). The Inquiry is notable in that it shone a light on a normally hidden policing function; it brought the backstage processes of police–media relations, part of police ‘image work’, to the frontstage area. This article considers the Leveson Inquiry, the data it collected as a case study of police impression management; it examines how the police sought to manage impressions about how they manage impressions. It takes a dramaturgical approach drawing on the work of Erving Goffman, Peter K Manning, combined with impression management concepts drawn from management, organisational studies. The article concludes that the identified impression management tactics used by different police ‘teams’ combined to protect the collective police image, to reinforce, for the present, the dominant position of the police in their relationship with the press.

abstract: Objectives. To examine the degree of association between newspaper readership, perception of crime, whether a causal relationship favouring a top‐down model (i.e. media shapes public opinion) of media‐audience interaction found support rather than a bottom‐up model (i.e. media responds to public opinion).Methods. The study involved the triangulation of three methods. Study 1 was a quantitative analysis of 2000 newspaper articles involving crime. Study 2 was a number of semi‐structured interviews with newspaper crime correspondents. Study 3 was a two‐part experimental investigation of the causal model.Results. Study 1 demonstrated a correspondence between misperception of crime, key quantitative measures of crime presentation in four newspapers. Study 2 found a correspondence between the newspaper values of crime journalists, the views of their readers. The experimental work in Study 3 did not demonstrate one‐off presentation effects as predicted by a simple top‐down model.Conclusions. There appeared to be evidence confirming an association between readers' views, the presentation of crime in their newspapers. However, the results of the experimental study do not permit an exclusive top‐down interpretation of this association.

title: Creating, validating GIS measures of urban design for health research
authors: Purciel, Marnie, Neckerman, Kathryn M, Lovasi, Gina S, Quinn, James W, Weiss, Christopher, Bader, Michael D M, Ewing, Reid, Rundle, Andrew
abstract: Studies relating urban design to health have been impeded by the unfeasibility of conducting field observations across large areas, the lack of validated objective measures of urban design. This study describes measures for five dimensions of urban design - imageability, enclosure, human scale, transparency,, complexity - created using public geographic information systems (GIS) data from the US Census, city, state government. GIS measures were validated for a sample of 588 New York City block faces using a well-documented field observation protocol. Correlations between GIS, observed measures ranged from 0.28 to 0.89. Results show valid urban design measures can be constructed from digital sources.

title: Use of mass media campaigns to change health behaviour
authors: Wakefield, Melanie A, Loken, Barbara, Hornik, Robert C
abstract: Mass media campaigns are widely used to expose high proportions of large populations to messages through routine uses of existing media, such as television, radio,, newspapers. Exposure to such messages is, therefore, generally passive. Such campaigns are frequently competing with factors, such as pervasive product marketing, powerful social norms,, behaviours driven by addiction or habit. In this Review we discuss the outcomes of mass media campaigns in the context of various health-risk behaviours (eg, use of tobacco, alcohol,, other drugs, heart disease risk factors, sex-related behaviours, road safety, cancer screening, prevention, child survival,, organ or blood donation). We conclude that mass media campaigns can produce positive changes or prevent negative changes in health-related behaviours across large populations. We assess what contributes to these outcomes, such as concurrent availability of required services, products, availability of community-based programmes,, policies that support behaviour change. Finally, we propose areas for improvement, such as investment in longer better-funded campaigns to achieve adequate population exposure to media messages.

title: Unintended effects of a domestic violence campaign
authors: Keller, Sarah N, Wilkinson, Timothy, Otjen, A J
abstract: This paper reports findings from a media intervention designed to raise awareness about domestic violence, to prevent abuse. The campaign included four television advertisements, one billboard, a poster,, newspaper ads. A quasi-experimental, in-field approach was used to assess campaign effects. The study analyzes the effects of campaign exposure on awareness, perceived threat,, efficacy. Results obtained using analysis of covariance indicate that male, female attitudes were significantly different following campaign exposure. Women (but not men) increased their perceived severity of domestic violence, awareness of services from pretest to posttest. The campaign appeared to have effectively reached women. By contrast, male attitudes moved in the opposite direction from pre- to posttest, or did not change. A comparison of means confirmed these findings, also showed that women increased their belief in the effectiveness of services. The authors draw comparisons between male, female reactions, offer some suggestions for new strategies to address audience beliefs about domestic violence.

abstract: Research Summary:Data concerning burglary rates and, among other things, the timing, intensity of publicity campaigns were acquired for 21 burglary reduction schemes. Statistical analyses showed clear effects of publicity as follows: (1) schemes that employed stand‐alone publicity campaigns were the most effective in reducing burglary; (2) time‐series analyses demonstrated that burglary reduction was coincident with intense periods of publicity;, (3) across the 21 schemes, there was evidence of a drop in the burglary rates prior to the implementation of the schemes, a so‐called anticipatory benefit.Policy Implications:The results suggest that the effectiveness of crime reduction schemes may be significantly enhanced by publicity. Promoting schemes prior to their implementation may also produce an anticipatory benefit, as was observed here. This suggests that carefully planned publicity campaigns may represent a powerful yet cost‐effective tool in crime prevention.

abstract: Despite a recent surge in research on procedural justice in organizational contexts, little work has systematically investigated how employees define procedural justice. This lack of attention to construct definition is problematic, since it prevents an understanding of what underlies employees' fairness evaluations, leaves several issues regarding the definition, conceptualization of procedural justice unresolved. To address these issues, this article describes the four-component model of procedural justice [Blader, S. L., \& Tyler, T. R. (in press). A four component model of procedural justice: Defining the meaning of a “fair” process. Personality, Social Psychology Bulletin; Tyler, T. R., \& Blader, S. L. (2000). Cooperation in groups: procedural justice, social identity, behavioral engagement. Philadelphia, PA: Psychology Press.], which posits four components that are believed to underlie overall procedural justice evaluations. The model differentiates between both justice type (decision making, quality of treatment), justice source (formal, informal) in developing these components. Research supporting the four-component conceptualization is discussed, the utility of this approach for procedural justice research is reviewed.

title: A four-component model of procedural justice: Defining the meaning of a “fair” process

title: Obeying the rules of the road: Procedural justice, social identity,, normative compliance
authors: Bradford, Ben, Hohl, Katrin, Jackson, Jonathan, MacQueen, Sarah
abstract: Why do people comply with traffic laws, regulations? Road traffic policing tends to be premised on the idea that people comply when they are presented with a credible risk of sanction in the event of non-compliance. Such an instrumental model of compliance contrasts with the normative account offered by procedural justice theory, in which compliance is encouraged by legitimate legal authorities. Comparing these two accounts, we find evidence that both instrumental, normative factors explain variance in motorists’ self-reported propensity to offend. Extending the standard procedural justice account, we also find that it is social identity—not legitimacy—that forms the “bridge” linking procedural fairness, compliance, at least according to a definition of legitimacy that combines felt obligation, moral endorsement. Fair treatment at the hands of police officers seems to enhance identification with the social group the police represent,, in turn, identification seems to motivate adherence to rules (laws) governing social behavior. These findings have implications not only for understandings of legal compliance but also for our understanding of why procedural justice motivates compliance, the role of procedural justice in promoting social cohesion.

title: Effectiveness of citizen police academies in changing the attitudes, beliefs,, behavior of citizen participants
authors: Brewster, Joanne, Stoloff, Michael, Sanders, Nicole
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: The purpose of this study was to determine whether the citzen police academies (CPA) in two cities were effective in changing participants’ attitudes, beliefs,, behavior toward police. Pre-and post-test questionnaires were used to obtain participants’ ratings of their attitudes, beliefs concerning police officers, their willingness to cooperate with police. Participants were also asked to indicate what cooperative behaviors they had actually engaged in before and/or during the CPA. At the end of the CPA, participants in both cities rated themselves as having more positive attitudes toward police,, more willingness to engage in behaviors that would help police. There was also an increase in actual performance of some cooperative behaviors during the CPA. These changes did not seem to be overly dependent on the jurisdiction (large versus small city), the demographics of the CPA participants, or the specific characteristics of the CPA curriculum.

title: On the importance of a procedurally fair organizational climate for openness to change in law enforcement
authors: Brimbal, Laure, Bradford, Ben, Jackson, Jonathan, Hartwig, Maria, Joseph, Emily
keywords: *Law Enforcement; *Openness to Experience; *Organizational Change; *Organizational Climate; *Procedural Justice; Compliance; Interrogation; Interviewing; Police Personnel;360\_Trust;30\_英米での普及・トレーニング
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Drawing on recent work in policing, organizational psychology, we examined factors related to openness to organizational change, to adopting evidence-based interview techniques among law enforcement investigators. HYPOTHESES: We hypothesized that a procedurally fair organizational climate would predict outcomes tied to organizational change, mediated by organizational identification, perceived legitimacy. We also predicted that procedural justice factors would be stronger predictors than outcome-oriented factors (i.e., rewards, sanctions). METHOD: Study 1 surveyed law enforcement investigators (N = 711) about their attitudes toward, behaviors within their organization (i.e., perceived procedural fairness of one's organization, identification, legitimacy, compliance, empowerment,, extra-role behavior). Study 2 conceptually extended this survey to interviewers (N = 71) trained in a new, evidence-based interviewing approach adding likelihood of future use of the novel interviewing approach as an outcome. RESULTS: In Study 1, the more investigators thought their organization had a procedurally fair climate, the more they identified with the organization, perceived it as legitimate. Framing compliance, empowerment, extra-role behavior as associated with openness to change, we found that legitimacy predicted compliance, tendency toward extra-role behavior (i.e., going ``above, beyond''), while level of identification predicted feelings of empowerment, extra-role behavior. Study 2 partially replicated findings from Study 1, found that motivation to attend the training also predicted likelihood of future use. CONCLUSIONS: These studies highlight the value of a procedurally just organizational climate framework in understanding law enforcement interrogators' propensity toward implementing new evidence-based interrogation techniques. title: Differences in citizen perceptions of interactions with police officers
authors: Clark, Nick, Werling, Robert, Chintakrindi, Sriram, Randol, Blake
abstract: The topic of this study is how different demographics, crime rates in police beats differ in their perceptions of interactions with police officers. The research questions for this study are: ‘Do citizens of a mid-sized city in California differ in their perceptions of interactions with police based on demographic?’, ‘Do differences in neighbourhood crime rates affect different perceptions of the police?’ The participants in this study were 307 residents from households of an anonymous city in California, chosen through stratified random sampling. Mailed surveys were sent out to 1,500 households, with canvassing done several months later to increase response rate. The results of the study were determined using frequency distributions to determine the descriptive statistics of the study, Kruskal–Wallis H tests, Mann–Whitney U tests for determining differences in predictor variable groups,, crosstabs, Spearman’s Rho to determine any correlations between the predictor, outcome variables. The results show that, outside two weak correlations, demographics, crime rates do not cause differences in people’s perceptions of interactions with the police.

title: EXPLORING THE BASIS OF CITIZENS'ATTITUDES TOWARD THE POLICE
authors: Frank, James

title: Trust in government regarding COVID-19, its associations with preventive health behaviour, prosocial behaviour during the pandemic: a cross-sectional, longitudinal study
authors: Han, Qing, Zheng, Bang, Cristea, Mioara, Agostini, Maximilian, Bélanger, Jocelyn J, Gützkow, Ben, Kreienkamp, Jannis, PsyCorona Collaboration, Leander, N Pontus
abstract: BACKGROUND: The effective implementation of government policies, measures for controlling the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic requires compliance from the public. This study aimed to examine cross-sectional, longitudinal associations of trust in government regarding COVID-19 control with the adoption of recommended health behaviours, prosocial behaviours,, potential determinants of trust in government during the pandemic. METHODS: This study analysed data from the PsyCorona Survey, an international project on COVID-19 that included 23 733 participants from 23 countries (representative in age, gender distributions by country) at baseline survey, 7785 participants who also completed follow-up surveys. Specification curve analysis was used to examine concurrent associations between trust in government, self-reported behaviours. We further used structural equation model to explore potential determinants of trust in government. Multilevel linear regressions were used to examine associations between baseline trust, longitudinal behavioural changes. RESULTS: Higher trust in government regarding COVID-19 control was significantly associated with higher adoption of health behaviours (handwashing, avoiding crowded space, self-quarantine), prosocial behaviours in specification curve analyses (median standardised β = 0.173, 0.229, p < 0.001). Government perceived as well organised, disseminating clear messages, knowledge on COVID-19,, perceived fairness were positively associated with trust in government (standardised β = 0.358, 0.230, 0.056,, 0.249, p < 0.01). Higher trust at baseline survey was significantly associated with lower rate of decline in health behaviours over time (p for interaction = 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: These results highlighted the importance of trust in government in the control of COVID-19.

title: Public attitudes toward the police: Findings from a dual-frame telephone survey
authors: He, Ni Phil, Ren, Ling, Zhao, Jihong Solomon, Bills, Matthew A
journal: International journal of offender therapy, comparative criminology
keywords: cell-phone-only sample; dual-frame survey; landline-phone sample; public attitudes toward the police;360\_Trust;police visibility
abstract: Using telephone survey data collected in Houston, Texas, this study explores the feasibility of a dual-frame (landline, cell-phone-only household samples) design survey in police studies, compares the corresponding characteristics of survey respondents, multiple measures of citizens' attitudes toward the police. It was found that a cell-phone interview with the same scope, length of a landline interview is indeed operationally feasible, albeit at higher cost, lower response rate. Compared with their landline counterparts, respondents in our cell-phone-only sample are younger, males, members of ethnic minority, renters, mobile,, less educated. No appreciable attitudinal differences among the respondents are observed between the two samples. In addition, substantive outcomes from multivariate regression models do not seem to be impacted by the types of phones used. Implications for future studies are included.

title: Centering race in procedural justice theory: Structural racism, the under-, over-policing of Black communities
authors: Jackson, Jonathan, McKay, Tasseli, Cheliotis, Leonidas, Bradford, Ben, Fine, Adam, Trinkner, Rick
abstract: Objective: To centre race in procedural justice theory by incorporating perceptions of the under-, over-policing of Black communities into the framework. Hypotheses: Perceptions of the under-, over-policing of Black communities predict legitimacy, adjusting for perceptions of procedural justice, distributive justice, bounded authority. Identification with the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement moderates the partial associations between legitimacy, perceptions of the under-, over-policing of Black communities. Findings pertain to both Black, White research participants alike.Method: A cross-sectional quota sample survey of 1,500 US residents was conducted just after the police killing of George Floyd in 2020. In addition to fielding relatively standard measures of legitimacy, procedural justice, distributive justice, bounded authority, we used new measures of under-, over-policing of Black communities, identification with the BLM cause. Data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM), latent moderated SEM.Results: Perceptions of under-, over-policing of Black communities predicted legitimacy, alongside procedural justice, distributive justice, bounded authority. When people identified with BLM, the relationships between legitimacy, perceptions of the under-, over-policing of Black communities were stronger compared to when people did not identify with BLM. All these results held among Black, White study participants.Conclusions: Incorporating perceptions of the under-, over-policing of Black communities into procedural justice theory is one way to include racialised policing into the framework. The under-, over-policing of Black communities may carry racially-directed messages of diminishment, domination, neglect as well as general messages of unfairness, exclusion that delegitimize the police themselves, the state they represent.

title: “when they come for you”: Legal mobilization in new authoritarian Russia: “when they come for you”
authors: van der Vet, Freek

title: Public attitudes toward the police
authors: Jesilow, Paul, Meyer, J'ona, Namazzi, Nazi
abstract: Surveys attitudes to police (ATP) in Santa Ana, California by asking respondents what they most like or dislike about police. Finds inter alia that the primary indicator of ATP is how people feel about their location. Contrasts sharply with previous research in finding that ethnicity is not a very good predictor of ATP. Points out that unrealistic expectations for law enforcement may be ameliorated by community policing, which involves citizens in decision making, neighborhood improvement.

title: Accountability, transparency as levers to promote public trust, police legitimacy: findings from a natural experiment
authors: Kochel, Tammy Rinehart, Skogan, Wesley G
abstract: PurposeThis paper examines the President's Task Force on 21st Century Policing's recommendation that police promote trust, legitimacy by creating a culture of transparency, accountability.Design/methodology/approachThe study is based on a panel survey of 841 Chicago residents that was interrupted between the waves by a momentous local policing event that proved to be known to virtually every participant. The reinterview period encompassed this event, its political repercussions, subsequent efforts to hold Chicago Police accountable, increase transparency. The authors examine whether these events, reform efforts improved African Americans' assessments of police legitimacy, trust relative to other respondents.FindingsTrust in Chicago Police improved by 21\%,, trust in neighborhood police increased 30\% among Black residents. In contrast, views of Whites became more negative, declining by 62\% in their assessments about Chicago Police, by 39\% regarding neighborhood police.Originality/valueEvents occurring between the waves of a panel survey created an opportunity to examine the impact of events on residents of a large, diverse city. The authors discuss why reforms promoting transparency, police accountability can alter levels of trust in the police but in different, politically consequential ways.

title: Race, attitudes toward police: the mediating effect of social distance
authors: Lee, Joongyeup, Gibbs, Jennifer C
abstract: Purpose – Given the consistent finding in the literature that members of minority groups hold less favorable views of the police than white citizens, social distance may be an important, yet untested, mediator. The purpose of this paper is to examine the mediating effect of social distance net of other established correlates. Design/methodology/approach – A sample of students attending a university in the northeastern USA completed an online survey in 2013. The survey was about their contact with the police, attitudes toward the police,, lifestyles, among others. Findings – Race, along with other predictors, significantly influenced confidence in police. However, race is the only factor that turns nonsignificant when social distance is included in the model. Mediation tests confirmed that social distance mediates the relationship between race, confidence in the police. Research limitations/implications – To maximize confidence in the police, administrators should focus on closing the social distance between the public, the police through initiatives like community policing. Originality/value – While there is extensive research on public attitudes toward the police, social distance has been neglected as a determinant, despite movements like community policing that promote citizens’ relational closeness to the police – that is, to decrease the social distance between police, the public. The current study would be an exploratory study, reference for future studies.

title: Social modeling effects on perception of the police: Focus on indirect police contact experience among college students
authors: Lim, Hyeyoung
abstract: Purpose– The purpose of this paper is to investigate whether indirect police contacts through observational learning models impact students’ trust in the police, their perceptions of police bias.Design/methodology/approach– The study is based on a survey at two public universities in the mid-western, southern regions of the USA (921 out of 1,089 responses were retained for this study). The empirical analysis relied on a principle component factor analysis, a multivariate regression analysis.Findings– Results show that three observational learning models (live, verbal,, symbolic) significantly influence perceptions of the police. In particular, the symbolic model is significant regardless of students’ direct, indirect contact experiences with the police.Originality/value– This study is the first to examine the modeling effects on attitudes toward the police applying the classic social learning theory developed by Albert Bandura. The results highlight the importance of indirect police contact experiences in shaping young citizens’ perceptions of the police.

title: The anatomy of police legitimacy: Dialogue, power, procedural justice
authors: Martin, Richard, Bradford, Ben
abstract: In a series of recent influential papers, Anthony Bottoms, Justice Tankebe make the case for a ‘dialogic model’ of police legitimacy, wherein legitimacy is envisaged as emergent in a process through which the police, as power-holders, make claims to authority which are, in turn, responded to by audiences. Our aim in this article is to analyse this model. We argue that while it has the potential to direct legitimacy research along paths hitherto poorly explored, there is a need for conceptual refinement, development in three key respects. First, through recognition of micro-, meso-levels of legitimation. Second, acknowledgement that police claims-making is contingent on the authorization, endorsement of other actors. Third, a fuller consideration of the qualified role of dialogue—i.e. communication between police, policed—in public audiences’ legitimacy assessments. In the spirit of critical engagement, conceptual exploration, this article develops these three insights to propose a modified version of the dialogic model.

title: The police service quality in rural Taiwan: A comparative analysis of perceptions, satisfaction between police staff, citizens
authors: Min Chen, Chien, Tau Lee, Hong, Hua Chen, Sheu, Hsien Tsai, Tsung
abstract: Purpose– The purpose of this paper is to investigate the perceptions, satisfaction between police officers, citizens on Kinmen Island (of Taiwan), using an analytical framework that combines five primary dimensions, 25 corresponding determinants.Design/methodology/approach– It considers recent developments in the application of performance measures, management to public and, particularly, police services. It goes on to assess comparative rural police performance which suggests that the application of targets could ultimately serve to provide the overall satisfaction with police services.Findings– The findings of the study suggest that perceptions, satisfaction of both citizens, police staff may result in the success of the policing management,, that police managers have to satisfy their citizens with a high level of service quality based on different localities.Practical implications– From managerial perspectives, police managers should consider both the service quality, customer satisfaction constructs as determinants of behavioural intentions, based on the fact that satisfaction can be a strategic key to maintain long term relationship with citizens as it is found of significant impact on the intentional behaviour.Originality/value– This research adds empirical support to this vein of literature, has identified the five main dimensions, the 25 sub-dimensions as important constructs for police service quality.

title: Does procedural justice reduce the harmful effects of perceived ineffectiveness on police legitimacy?
authors: Nam, Yongjae, Wolfe, Scott E, Nix, Justin
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: Objectives: Judgments about police procedural fairness consistently have a stronger influence on how the public ascribes legitimacy to the police than evaluations of police effectiveness. What remains largely underexplored, however, is the potential moderating effect of procedural justice on the relationship between effectiveness, legitimacy, whether this moderation varies by citizen race. Method: We administered two separate surveys to determine whether procedural justice's moderating effect on the relationship between police ineffectiveness, legitimacy varies by citizen race. The first was a mail survey of a random sample of citizens in a southern US city (N = 1,681) conducted in 2013; the second, a national survey of adults (N = 972) administered via Qualtrics in 2022. Results: We found that procedural justice could help protect against the harmful influence of perceived ineffectiveness on police legitimacy in Study 2. However, contrary to expectations, this moderation effect held only for White Americans. Conclusions: The effect of perceived ineffectiveness on legitimacy evaluations does not vary depending on citizens’ perceptions of procedural justice. Yet, police still do have control over how they treat people with whom they interact, which is one mechanism that can improve citizens’ views on police legitimacy.

title: Relation between police image, police visibility
authors: Salmi, Satu, Voeten, M, Keskinen, E
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
keywords: model for the public image \& visibility of the police, 19+ vs 14-19-yr-olds from 2 Finnish cities; Community Attitudes; Police Personnel; Public Opinion; Age Differences; Models;360\_Trust;z\_2009jasc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);z\_岩波エビデンス;510\_13\_近隣防犯対策;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;J Community Appl Soc Psychol;police visibility
abstract: The purpose of this study was to build a model for the public image, visibility of the police. These variables were seen as central to successful community policing. Explanatory variables included were contacts with the police, victimisation, background characteristics of the respondents. Questionnaire data were obtained from a sample of 3271 adults (mean age 42), 986 youngsters (mean age 15.5) in two Finnish cities. Using multi-sample structural equation modelling, a four-factor model with two image factors (Friendliness, Closeness), two visibility factors (Patrol-Car-Related, Police-on-Foot Activities) was confirmed by the data. As hypothesised, for both adults, youngsters, seeing police-on-foot activities was positively correlated with both image factors, while seeing Patrol-Car-Related Activities was negatively correlated with police image. Relationships of explanatory variables with image factors were to a large extent but not completely mediated by the visibility factors. Some differences were found between adults, youngsters in factor means, in regression relationships. Quality of police visibility proved to be an important factor from the point of view of community policing, in which one of the main purposes is to improve the relationship between the police, the public. title: Assessment of public attitudes towards sex offenders in an Australian population
authors: Shackley, Michaela, Weiner, Carlye, Day, Andrew, Willis, Gwenda M
abstract: Public attitudes towards sex offenders are believed to play a key role in the development of legislation, public policy designed to manage the risks posed by known sex offenders who live in the community. There have, however, been few previous attempts to validate methods by which public attitudes can be measured. The current study aims to address this issue by establishing the factor structure of the Community Attitudes Towards Sex Offenders (CATSO) scale with an Australian community sample, examine the extent to which demographic variables, support for sex offender management policies influence these attitudes. A sample of 552 participants recruited through online social media sites completed the CATSO as well as a number of items developed by the researchers designed to assess individuals' support for specific sex offender policies. Results of an exploratory factor analysis suggested the presence of four distinct factors which were labelled ‘social tendencies’, ‘treatment, punishment’, ‘crime characteristics’, ‘sexual behaviour’. Individuals with higher levels of educational attainment rated sex offenders less negatively than those with lower educational attainment, while those who reported being supportive of community notification reported more negative attitudes towards sex offenders.

title: Moral motives, police legitimacy, acceptance of force
authors: Silver, Jasmine R
abstract: PurposeThis study extends legitimacy theory by examining individualizing, binding moral motives, perceptions of police.Design/methodology/approachData are drawn from an online survey of the public (N = 961). OLS regression is used to predict global perceptions of legitimacy, as well as department legitimacy, acceptance of force in an experimental vignette that manipulates procedural justice.FindingsThe binding moral motive is associated with greater global, department legitimacy, acceptance of force. The individualizing moral motive is associated with reduced global legitimacy, acceptance of force,, with department legitimacy when procedural justice is low. Perceptions of legitimacy mediate the effects of the binding moral motive on acceptance of force, of the individualizing moral motive when procedural justice is low.Research limitations/implicationsThis study identifies novel antecedents of police legitimacy, acceptance of force (i.e. binding, individualizing moral motives).Social implicationsThis study provides insight into public attitudes regarding use of force.Originality/valueThis study is the first to propose, test a link between binding, individualizing moral motives, perceptions of police.

title: Understanding knife crime, trust in police with young people in east London
authors: Skarlatidou, Artemis, Ludwig, Lina, Solymosi, Reka, Bradford, Ben
abstract: We explore young people’s experiences, perceptions of knife crime,, we compare these to the understanding of police experts, to explore the perceptions shaping trust in the police, policing. We carry out an experience sampling survey deployed using a mobile application reflecting on safety, knife crime, to understand young people’s daily lived experiences. We then use the mental models approach to interview young people, police experts, construct a shared mental model which identifies mismatches between the two groups, key areas of discord related to breakdown of trust, communication. We identify gaps, misconceptions, expectations for re-establishing trust, propose strategies to tackle knife crime, improve trust between young people, the police.

title: Does trust in citizens mediate the relationship between internal, external procedural justice: A comparison between China, Taiwan police
authors: Sun, Ivan Y, Liu, Jianhong, Wu, Yuning, Van Craen, Maarten
journal: International journal of offender therapy, comparative criminology
keywords: Chinese police; Taiwanese police; compliance with agency policies; external procedural justice; internal procedural justice; trust in citizens;360\_Trust
abstract: This study investigates the roles of trust in citizens, compliance with agency policies in mediating the direct, indirect relationships between internal procedural justice, external procedural justice among Chinese, Taiwanese police officers. Based on survey data collected from 1,253 police officers, this study comparatively analyzes whether supervisory treatment of officers is predictive of trust in citizens, willingness to follow agency policies, which in turn is linked to their willingness to act fairly, justly toward citizens on the street. The results indicate that officer trust in citizens mediates the relationship between internal, external procedural justice in both China, Taiwan, but compliance with agency policies does not. Internal procedural justice directly predicts external procedural justice among Taiwanese officers, but such a connection is not found among Chinese officers. Implications for future research, policy are discussed.

title: Distributional, procedural aspects of satisfaction with citizen-police encounters
authors: Tyler, Tom R, Folger, Robert
keywords: COMMUNITY policing; CRIMINAL justice personnel; CRIMINAL procedure; EQUALITY; JUSTICE; LAW enforcement; POLICE; PROCEDURE (Law); SOCIAL psychology; PEOPLE;360\_Trust;Basic Appl Soc Psych
abstract: Using data from a survey of a sample of the residents of Evanston, Illinois, the hypothesis of Thibaut, Walker—that the procedures utilized to resolve a dispute have an impact upon satisfaction that is independent of outcomes received—is tested in the context of police-citizen encounters, It is found that when citizens call the police for assistance or are stopped by the police, their perception of the fairness of their treatment by the police has an impact upon their satisfaction with the police that is independent of whether the police: (1) solve the problem about which the citizen calls; or (2) cite the citizen they have stopped for a violation of the law. These findings suggest that issues of procedural justice have a much broader range of applicability than to the courtroom settings within which they have previously been studied.

title: What is procedural justice?: Criteria used by citizens to assess the fairness of legal procedures
authors: Tyler, Tom R
keywords: COURTS; JUDGMENTS; JUSTICE; PROCEDURE (Law); LEGAL authorities; LEGAL research;360\_Trust
abstract: This paper examines procedural justice in the context of citizen experiences with the police, courts. It is based on interviews of 652 citizens with recent personal experiences involving those authorities. I will consider two issues: first, whether the justice of the procedures involved influences citizen satisfaction with outcomes, evaluations of legal authorities;, second, how citizens define “fair process” in such settings. The results replicate those of past studies, which found that procedural justice has a major influence on both satisfaction, evaluation. They further suggest that such procedural justice judgments are complex, multifaceted. Seven issues make independent contributions to citizen judgments about whether the legal authorities acted fairly: (1) the degree to which those authorities were motivated to be fair; (2) judgments of their honesty; (3) the degree to which the authorities followed ethical principles of conduct; (4) the extent to which opportunities for representation were provided; (5) the quality of the decisions made; (6) the opportunities for error correction;, (7) whether the authorities behaved in a biased fashion. I found that the meaning of procedural justice varied according to the nature of the situation, not the characteristics of the people involved.

title: The role of perceived injustice in defendants' evaluations of their courtroom experience
authors: Tyler, Tom R
keywords: CONDUCT of court proceedings; FAIRNESS; JUDGES; JUSTICE; JUSTICE, Administration of; LAW;360\_Trust
abstract: The purpose of this study is to explore the role of perceived injustice in generating dissatisfaction with legal authorities. Using data collected in interviews with a sample of defendants in traffic, misdemeanor court, I compare the influence of case outcomes upon attitudes toward judges, courts to that of distributive, procedural justice. The results suggest that among the defendants studied the major determinant of satisfaction with legal authorities is perceived fairness. Once the influence of perceived fairness is considered, case outcomes explain no additional variation in attitudes toward courts, judges. In the conclusion, possible implications of this finding are discussed.

title: The political economy of crime: Did Universal Credit increase crime rates?
authors: Tiratelli, Matteo, Bradford, Ben, Yesberg, Julia
abstract: Abstract Interest in the political economy of crime goes back to sociology’s founding fathers, but the nature of the relationship between restrictive social security systems, crime remains contested. This paper exploits exogenous variation in the introduction of Universal Credit (UC) to local areas across England, Wales to address this question. We first use fixed effects models, with a range of controls, to show that as UC enrolments increase in a given area, so does the crime rate. We then use interrupted time series analysis to show that, despite UC being rolled out at different times in different places, its introduction in each local area coincides with a positive shift in the trend in crime. These findings hold for total crime, property crime, violent crime. Borrowing from Strain Theory, Routine Activities Theory, we suggest that changes to the pool of motivated offenders may help to explain these correlations.

title: Opening a window into police internal affairs: Impact of procedural justice reform on third-party attitudes
authors: Kerstetter, Wayne A, Rasinski, Kenneth A
abstract: The study explores the impact of a procedural innovation on justice judgments made by third party observers. The innovation involved the establishment of a review panel with civilian participants to monitor a police department's investigation of allegations of misconduct against its officers. The study distinguishes the impact on racial minority observers from that on racial majority observers. Data suggest that the innovation had a positive, though differing, impact on the justice judgments of both minority, majority observers.

title: Putting the fear back into fear appeals: The extended parallel process model
authors: Witte, Kim
abstract: The fear appeal literature is diverse, inconsistent. Existing fear appeal theories explain the positive linear results occurring in many studies, but are unable to explain the boomerang or curvilinear results occurring in other studies. The present work advances a theory integrating previous theoretical perspectives (i.e., Janis, 1967; Leventhal, 1970; Rogers, 1975, 1983) that is based on Leventhal's (1970) danger control/fear control framework. The proposed fear appeal theory, called the Extended Parallel Process Model (EPPM), expands on previous approaches in three ways: (a) by explaining why fear appeals fail; (b) by re‐incorporating fear as a central variable;, (c) by specifying the relationship between threat, efficacy in propositional forms. Specific propositions are given to guide future research.

title: Preoccupation, affect as predictors of protective action following natural disaster
authors: Weinstein, Neil D, Lyon, Judith E, Rothman, Alexander J, Cuite, Cara L
keywords: Natural Disasters; Responses; Risk Management; Risk Perception; Rumination (Cognitive Process); Emotional Responses; Experiences (Events);\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;303;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);301\_ComCrm;301\_4
abstract: The actions taken by individuals after natural disasters to prepare for future disasters were studied to see whether theories of self‐protective action are missing important variables. Residents of three communities struck by severe tornadoes who did not experience damage or injury (N = 715) were interviewed shortly after the tornadoes, again 14 months later. Initial responses to the tornadoes, details of the tornado experience were used to predict precautions reported at the initial, follow‐up interviews. Preoccupation with tornadoes strongly predicted action independent of affect, perceived risk,, perceived control. Recollections of fear felt during the tornado, negative affect when thinking about tornadoes were also related to action: both negative affect, high fear (if combined with preoccupation) were associated with less action in the initial period following the tornadoes. Our findings suggest that the conceptualization of action as reflecting a decision about the expected costs, benefits of action is inadequate, that theories of self‐protective behaviour need to include measures of preoccupation, affect as well.

title: Self-protection in rural America: A risk interpretation model of household protective measures
authors: Giblin, Matthew J, Burruss, George W, Corsaro, Nicholas, Schafer, Joseph A
keywords: collective efficacy;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh;303;z\_rural2020;121\_Lane2014;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;301\_ComCrm;301\_4;Crim Justice Policy Rev\_●Sage
abstract: Scholarly interest in self-protective behaviors is demonstrated in studies examining victimization; these behaviors are presumed to reduce the likelihood of experiencing crime. Protective behaviors are not taken by all citizens equally, however, so it is critical to explain these behaviors within the population. The current study extends existing works, most of which were based on urban samples, by examining the determinants of protective behaviors in a sample of rural residents in the United States. Predictors are derived from a modified risk interpretation model (Ferraro, 1995), include risk, fear, victimization experiences,, perceived collective efficacy. Results show that household protective behaviors are influenced by perceptions of risk and, indirectly through risk, by perceived collective efficacy, victimization experiences.

authors: Lambert, William W, Lazarus, Richard S

title: The role of the affect, availability heuristics in risk communication
authors: Keller, Carmen, Siegrist, Michael, Gutscher, Heinz
