abstract: This article explores two problems analysts face in determining how to estimate values for children's health, safety risk reductions. The first addresses the question: Do willingness-to-pay estimates for health risk changes differ across children, adults and, if so, how? To answer this question, the article first examines the potential effects of age, risk preferences on willingness to pay. A summary of the literature reporting empirical evidence of differences between willingness to pay for adult health, safety risk reductions, willingness to pay for health, safety risk reductions in children is also provided. The second dimension of the problem is a more fundamental issue: Whose perspective is relevant when valuing children's health effects-society's, children's, adults-as-children, or parents'? Each perspective is considered, followed ultimately by the conclusion that adopting a parental perspective through an intrahousehold allocation model seems closest to meeting the needs of the estimation problem at hand. A policy example in which the choice of perspective affects the outcome of a regulatory benefit-cost analysis rounds out the article, emphasizes the importance of perspective.

title: Testing, expanding a model of cognitive processing of risk information
authors: Johnson, Branden B
journal: Risk analysis: an official publication of the Society for Risk Analysis
abstract: Scholars have begun to explore the role of modes of information processing, related audience characteristics in reactions to risky situations, risk information.((11, 12, 14, 17, 18, 20))``Information processing'' concerns how people attend to, consider available information: systematic processors analyze messages, situations carefully, while heuristic processors skim, use cues (e.g., opinions of trusted reference groups) for quick judgments. This article uses scenarios about a semi-hypothetical industrial facility, in particular risk comparisons being considered by its manager for inclusion in a talk to the community, to explore the impact of information processing. Information insufficiency, self-assessed capacity to understand information,, information-seeking propensities are tested for potential effects on information processing about industrial risks by people living near industry. As well as testing established models, this article explores the additional explanatory value of involvement, relevance,, ability (Earle et al., 1990), objective knowledge. Both existing model variables, new ones have significant effects on information seeking, information processing in this case,, partly confirm earlier results. Trumbo((17,18)) found that heuristic processors saw lower risk, systematic processors higher risk from suspected cancer clusters. In this study, reporting knowledge about local industrial risks as insufficient for one's purposes, self-reported avoidance of such information both raised ratings of the facility's risk, lowered ratings of its acceptability. Neither type of information processing significantly affected risk or acceptability judgments, but both increased risk ratings, heuristic processing had more effect than systematic processing. Positive ratings of risk comparisons' clarity, meaningfulness decreased risk, increased acceptability ratings, dominated other information variables in predictive power,, exceeded risk, benefit,, trust in contribution to acceptability judgments. Despite differences across studies in designs, variables,, the embryonic development of appropriate (self-reported) measures for use in field surveys, these results confirm the potential value of further research in how information seeking, processing affect risk beliefs, reactions to risk communications.

title: Intimate partner violence in Colombia: Who is at risk?
authors: Friedemann-Sanchez, G, Lovaton, R
journal: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study, interpretation
abstract: The role that domestic violence plays in perpetuating poverty is often overlooked as a development issue. Using data from the 2005 Demographic Health Survey, this paper examines the prevalence of intimate partner violence in Colombia. Employing an intrahousehold bargaining framework, a bivariate probit model, it assesses the prevalence of, risk factors for physical, emotional intimate partner violence, including such variables as income, education, gender-based intrahousehold decision making, employment, migration related to armed conflict, child maltreatment. The findings of the study particularly underscore the effects of early childhood maltreatment on domestic violence, the need for policy measures that span the life cycle, include families. Its recommendations for policy makers, researchers take into consideration practical, theoretical, methodological issues.

title: How norms can generate conflict: An experiment on the failure of cooperative micro-motives on the macro-level
authors: Winter, F, Rauhut, H, Helbing, D
journal: Social forces; a scientific medium of social study, interpretation
abstract: Why does the adherence to norms not prevent conflict? While the current literature focuses on the emergence, maintenance, impact of norms with regard to cooperation, the issue of norm-related conflict deserves more attention. We develop a general game theoretical model of ``normative conflict'', explain how transaction failures on the macrolevel can result from cooperative motives on the microlevel. We differentiate between two kinds of conflict. The first results from distinct expectations regarding the way in which general normative obligations should be fulfilled, the second from distinct expectations as to how the norm should restrain actions based on self-interest. We demonstrate the empirical relevance of normative conflict in a version of the ultimatum game. Our data reveal widespread normative conflict among different types of actors - egoistic, equity, equality, cherry picker. Our findings demonstrate how cooperative intentions about how to divide a collectively produced good may fail to produce cooperative outcomes.

title: African-American communities, violent crime: The construction of race differences
authors: Covington, Jeanette
abstract: Abstract Urban poor African-American communities typically have violent crime rates much higher than those of white communities. In explaining this race difference in crime, criminologists have gravitated toward representing high-crime African-American neighborhoods in ways that suggest their residents are different-in-kind from those living in low-crime white neighborhoods. Accounting for crime in terms of a “race difference” has become increasingly problematic because, much like gender, the meaning of the concept of race has come in for increased scrutiny. Indeed some theorists of race are skeptical that “race” can be considered a category capable of differentiating social groups based on their tendency to engage in distinct behaviors. Yet, despite their controversial status in other subareas of sociology, the twin concepts of race, race difference remain important in the study of crime, urban communities. One criminological theory which still treats these concepts uncritically is racial inequality theory. Racial inequality theorists suggest that shared perceptions of racial deprivation have been instrumental in creating a distinct community-based collective black psychological reaction. It is this black-specific psychological reaction which, in theory, has made blacks more aggressive, thus more inclined to engage in violent behavior than whites. In this paper, I will examine how racial inequality theorists go about constructing a race difference based on a collective black psychological reaction to racial deprivation. Problems with the way race differences are constructed in racial inequality theories will also be addressed.

title: Using knowledge of social networks to prevent human immunodeficiency virus infections: The Colorado Springs study
authors: Darrow, William W, Potterat, John J, Rothenberg, Richard B, Woodhouse, Donald E, Muth, Stephen Q, Klovdahl, Alden S
abstract: Abstract The development of an applied social science research project with implications for the management of infectious diseases is described. The project evolved out of a multidisciplinary effort to understand how sexually transmissible agents enter into social systems, are transmitted, can be identified, prevented, controlled. Collaborators began their investigations in the 1970s by looking at the social, behavioral patterns of individuals infected with gonorrhea, then applied similar methods in the late 1980s, early 1990s to examine the ways human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), the pathogen that causes AIDS, might spread among heterosexuals in a mid-sized American community. Concepts of personal, social networks of individuals linked by social, sexual, drug-sharing exposures guided the systematic collection of information from 595 participants in a large, prospective study. Results suggest that HIV did not spread among heterosexuals who engaged in risky sexual, needle-sharing behaviors in Colorado Springs because those infected with HIV (and capable of infecting others) were located in small, relatively isolated network components or in peripheral network regions.

title: A symbolic interaction approach to cigarette smoking: Smoking frequency, the desire to quit smoking
authors: Reitzes, Donald C, Depadilla, Lara, Sterk, Claire E, Elifson, Kirk W
abstract: This study applies a symbolic interaction perspective to the investigation of smoking frequency, a person's desire to quit smoking cigarettes. Data derived from 485 Atlanta area adult smokers provide a diverse, community-based sample of married, single men, women, aged 18 to 70 years old with a range of income, education,, occupational experiences. Multiple regression was used to analyze the data in order to explore the influence of social demographic characteristics, social interaction, subjective assessments of health, self conceptions,, smoker identity on smoking frequency, quitting smoking. Findings include: (1) the relationship with a non-smoker, hiding smoking negatively impacted smoking frequency, while perceiving positive consequences from smoking has a positive effect on smoking frequency;, (2) perceiving positive consequences of smoking was negatively related to the desire to quit smoking, while a negative smoker identity has a positive influence on the desire to quit. Taken as a whole, the symbolic interaction-inspired variables exerted strong, independent effects on both smoking frequency, quitting smoking. Future smoking interventions should focus on meanings, perceived consequences of smoking in general,, on the smoker identity in the development of campaigns to encourage quitting cigarette smoking.

title: Use of time, satisfaction with the psychotherapeutic relationship
authors: Bland, Connie E, Ferraro, Kenneth F, Miller, Jr, Robert K
abstract: Abstract The purpose of this inquiry is to determine how social position affects the quantity, quality of psychotherapeutic care received in outpatient mental health centers. It is posited that use of time in the therapeutic dyad is, in part, a manifestation of the therapist's desire to work with the patient, also a cause of the degree of satisfaction expressed by the patient with the psychotherapeutic relationship. Using data from a random sample of adult community mental health care recipients (N = 179), use of time is assessed by the client's report of waiting time, session length. The results indicate the importance of temporal factors for predicting satisfaction in the psychotherapeutic relationship. Although the sex, race of the respondent did not affect use of time or satisfaction with the psychotherapeutic relationship, socioeconomic status, age effects were observed. The broader implications of this study are that lower class clients express more positive attitudes toward medicine, psychiatric care providers, while the more affluent are more consumer-oriented, skeptical toward medical or psychiatric care.

title: Social capital theory as an integrating theoretical framework in technological disaster research
authors: Ritchie, Liesel Ashley, Gill, Duane A
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: Conceptual, empirical research on technological disasters has produced a number of seminal contributions including concepts of recreancy, collective trauma, lifestyle, lifescape change, corrosive community, secondary trauma,, the ecological-symbolic perspective. This article presents social capital theory as a comprehensive framework that incorporates, integrates these key conceptual elements, theories. After presenting fundamental elements of social capital theory, we demonstrate how key concepts in technological disaster research relate to social capital. We conclude that while social capital theory has merit, potential for improving our understanding of all disaster events, it is particularly useful in comprehending the multifarious impacts of technological disasters.

title: The femA trailer parks: Negative perceptions, the social structure of avoidance
authors: Lee, Matthew R, Weil, Frederick D, Shihadeh, Edward S
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: In recent years, negative media attention has fostered the impression that Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) parks are social wastelands filled with criminal elements, other undesirables. FEMA parks have subsequently come to be viewed by some as a major threat to the safety, quality of life of the local communities in which they are situated. This analysis addresses attitudes toward FEMA trailer parks in Baton Rouge after Hurricane Katrina among Baton Rouge residents. Drawing on the Locally Undesirable Land Use/Not in My Backyard (LULU/NIMBY) literature, the contact hypothesis,, a broad paradigm of social status, social control, we hypothesize that spatial proximity, contact,, social status will influence negative perceptions of the parks, while these same factors along with the negative perceptions will influence avoidance behaviors. The results indicate that living near a FEMA park is associated with less negative perceptions, while actually seeing trailer park residents is associated with more negative perceptions, a greater odds of avoidance, particularly changing driving routes. Whites are particularly concerned about crime associated with the parks, but interracial trust reduces negative perceptions of the parks, the likelihood of avoidance. Those who are likely to end up in a FEMA park if they were in the same situation are more friendly toward the parks, less likely to use avoidance techniques,, negative perceptions themselves are strong predictors of avoidance behaviors. We conclude with a discussion of directions for future research.

title: People, places: Welfare reform, the separate effect of caseload characteristics, local conditions
authors: Zimmerman, Julie N, Goetz, Stephan J, Debertin, David L
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: The shift from hardship alleviation policies to behavior-focused policies in cash assistance highlight competing theoretical approaches to poverty: those focused on individuals' characteristics, those focused on structural factors lying beyond the control of the individual. This research bridges these approaches by examining the question, do local conditions have a separate, independent effect from cash assistance caseload characteristics on affecting caseload declines? The results indicate a separate, independent effect of both local conditions, caseload characteristics in explaining caseload declines suggesting that caseload reductions, the economic sustainability of recipients are affected by individual characteristics, but also by where recipients live.

title: The gender gap in fear: Assessing the interactive effects of gender, perceived risk on fear of crime
authors: Reid, Lesley Williams, Konrad, Miriam
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: In this research we explore the interaction between gender, perceived risk of victimization on levels of fear of crime. Much of the previous research on the effects of gender on fear of crime assumes that crimes are not gendered, that the effects of gender would operate the same regardless of type of crime. Challenging this assumption, we examine crimes that disproportionately victimize women or men. We find that there is greater nuance in both fear of crime, perception of risk when explored in this way. In fact, men's fear of crime actually surpasses women's fear at high levels of perceived risk for those crimes in which men are more likely to be victimized. We offer explanations for this finding, concluding that gendered perceptions of crime, victimization may drive these differences. In sum, our study indicates that future research on fear of crime must be even further attuned to the gender gap in fear.

title: Fear of crime, personal vulnerability: Examining self-reported health
authors: Cossman, Jeralynn S, Rader, Nicole E
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: This research considers the relationship between self-reported health, fear of crime. Fear of crime literature suggests women, the elderly, or the impoverished may experience heightened fear of crime. It is hypothesized that it is a sense of vulnerability that leads individuals to believe they would be unable to protect themselves should an attack occur, increasing their personal fear of crime. We argue in this article that poor self-reported health may also lead to a sense of vulnerability, elevate fear of crime. We test this hypothesis using data from the General Social Survey (GSS). Using a variety of health measures, our results indicate that some indicators of health are related to a heightened fear of crime, that this relationship varies by gender. Women are at a double disadvantage, in that they feel more vulnerable to crime than men,, women also have more negative perceptions of health.

title: The impact of information, risk perception on the hurricane evacuation decision-making of greater New Orleans residents
authors: Burnside, Randolph, Miller, Demond Shondell, Rivera, Jason D
journal: Sociological spectrum: the official journal of the Mid-South Sociological Association
abstract: This article contributes to the current discussion on how residents living in vulnerable areas make the decision to evacuate when they are in harms way. Key in this discussion is the question, what role does information, risk play in shaping evacuation behavior? This study used a sample of respondents from the greater New Orleans region (Orleans, Jefferson,, St. Bernard Parishes) of the Twelve Parish Survey (N = 1,207) conducted prior to Hurricane Katrina. The findings indicate that information sources are vitally important in the evacuation process. By examining the role of information from authorities, family,, friends; visual imagery;, the media we found that individuals use a variety of sources when they decide to evacuate. Further, the importance of visual imagery in the evacuation process is discussed. The article concludes with a discussion of the implications of information dissemination, its importance to members of the media, public policy makers.

title: Black-white differences in perceptions of fear of crime
authors: Parker, Keith D
abstract: Abstract The combined effects of race, social factors on fear of crime were investigated. The sample consisted of 1,835 black, white residents of Mississippi, 15 years old or older. The results indicated that (a) for the pooled sample, race, age,, marital status had significant effects on fear of crime,, (b) with the exception of age, the variables had significantly different effects on fear of crime among black, white respondents.

title: The effect of victim information on causality judgments in a rape trial scenario
authors: Rempala, Daniel M, Geers, Andrew L
abstract: D. M. Rempala, F. B. Bernieri (2005) showed that in a date-rape trial scenario, increasing the amount of neutral, nondiagnostic information (i.e., information unrelated to the case) about the rape victim decreases the percentage of guilt verdicts. The authors attempted to determine the causal mechanism for this phenomenon. Participants read 1 of 4 rape trial scenarios (which differed only in the amount of non diagnostic information about the defendant, victim), then provided a verdict, rated the targets on several dimensions. The authors replicated pattern of guilt verdicts in the Rempala, Bernieri study (p < .05),, a path analysis indicated that increased victim information altered causality judgments, which then affected guilt verdicts.

title: Differences between Japanese, American college students in giving advice about help seeking to rape victims
authors: Yamawaki, Niwako
abstract: In this study, the author investigated differences in Japanese, American college students' tendencies to advise a hypothetical rape victim (their sister) to seek help from police, family members, or mental health professionals. Japanese students tended to encourage the victim to seek help from her family members, whereas American students tended to encourage her to seek help from police, mental health counselors. Cross-cultural discrepancies were marked by the following factors: (a) feelings of shame moderated advice to seek help from police; (b) minimization of rape mediated the likelihood to advise the involvement of police, mental health counselors; (c) attitudes toward mental health counselors mediated advice to seek help from them;, (d) the type of rape (stranger vs. date rape) moderated advice to report the crime to police.

title: Predicting Facebook users' online privacy protection: risk, trust, norm focus theory,, the theory of planned behavior
authors: Saeri, Alexander K, Ogilvie, Claudette, La Macchia, Stephen T, Smith, Joanne R, Louis, Winnifred R
abstract: The present research adopts an extended theory of the planned behavior model that included descriptive norms, risk,, trust to investigate online privacy protection in Facebook users. Facebook users (N = 119) completed a questionnaire assessing their attitude, subjective injunctive norm, subjective descriptive norm, perceived behavioral control, implicit perceived risk, trust of other Facebook users,, intentions toward protecting their privacy online. Behavior was measured indirectly 2 weeks after the study. The data show partial support for the theory of planned behavior, strong support for the independence of subjective injunctive, descriptive norms. Risk also uniquely predicted intentions over, above the theory of planned behavior, but there were no unique effects of trust on intentions, nor of risk or trust on behavior. Implications are discussed.

title: Effects of perpetrator gender, victim sexuality on blame toward male victims of sexual assault
authors: Davies, Michelle, Pollard, Paul, Archer, John
abstract: Most researchers who have investigated attributions of blame toward victims in sexual-assault depictions have considered only female victims of male perpetrators. Few researchers have investigated the effects of perpetrator gender or victim sexual orientation on blame attributions toward male victims. The present authors investigated those two variables. Participants were 161 undergraduates at a British university in social science courses, each of whom read one scenario of a set in which perpetrator gender, victim sexual orientation were varied between subjects,, who completed a questionnaire measuring their blame toward the victim, the perpetrator. The present results showed that male participants blamed the victim more if a person of the gender that he was normally attracted to assaulted him. Male participants also regarded the female perpetrator in more favorable terms than they did the male perpetrator regardless of the victim's sexual orientation. The authors discussed the present results in relation to gender role stereotypes.

title: Fight-seeking motivation in dating partners with an aggressive relationship
authors: Marcus, Robert F
abstract: The author studied aggression among dating couples to determine if partners' fight-seeking motivation could explain the phenomenon. Intact dating couples were classified as aggressive if either partner reported having perpetrated 2 or more acts of assaultive violence in the past year. The author asked participants to rate the extent to which they, their partners intentionally physically or verbally fought with one another, felt calmer after physical or verbal conflict with their partners,, sought to increase sensory stimulation by taking part in high-risk activities. Together, these ratings constituted a measure of fight-seeking motivation. Results of a logistic regression analysis showed that couples classified as aggressive (48\%) had relationships longer in duration than did nonaggressive couples. In addition, both men, women in aggressive relationships had greater fight-seeking motivation than did individuals in nonaggressive relationships.

title: How voluntariness of apologies affects actual, hypothetical victims' perceptions of the offender
authors: Jehle, Alayna, Miller, Monica K, Kemmelmeier, Markus, Maskaly, Jonathan
abstract: Apologies are important in social interactions. Study 1 investigated participants' reactions after being insulted by a confederate, receiving no apology, a voluntary apology, a coerced apology with consequences (i.e., explicitly coerced apology), or a coerced apology without consequences (i.e., implicitly coerced apology). Receiving any apology produced more positive perceptions of the offender, less serious recommended punishments than no apology. Study 2 replicated Study 1, except participants read about the insult, imagined being a victim (instead of being an actual victim as in Study 1). Actual victims distinguished between types of apologies while hypothetical victims did not. Results have implications for court-ordered apologies.

title: Effects of defendant age on severity of punishment for different crimes
authors: Bergeron, Christine E, McKelvie, Stuart J
abstract: After reading a murder or theft vignette in which the perpetrator was a 20-, 40-, or 60-year-old man, 95 undergraduates gave sentence, parole recommendations. Punishment was harsher for the murder than for the theft. For murder, participants treated the 20-, 60-year-old men less harshly than the 40-year-old man, which confirms previous archival findings. However, this inverted U-shaped function occurred for murder only. The authors discussed the results in the context of the just-desert, utilitarian rationales that guide sentencing, gave suggestions for future research.

title: Belief in a just world, social perception: evidence for automatic activation
authors: Murray, John D, Spadafore, Jo Ann, McIntosh, William D
abstract: The authors tested the hypothesis that beliefs in a just world are automatically activated, used in social perception. Under the guise of a perceptual vigilance task, the authors exposed 34 undergraduate women preconsciously to words that were either rape-related or neutral. Immediately after the exposure, participants read a date scenario that was ambiguous with respect to the man's aggressiveness, the extent to which the woman was responsible for the man's behavior. Afterwards, all participants evaluated the target man, woman on an impression task. The primary finding was that participants holding stronger beliefs in a just world perceived the target woman more negatively after experiencing the rape-related prime words than after experiencing the neutral words. This pattern is consistent with a research literature that shows that believers in a just world will often ``blame the victim'' in cases of rape. The present findings are important because they provide evidence that general, orienting beliefs are automatically activated in a manner similar to that shown by stereotype beliefs. The authors discussed implications for social perception.

title: Sexual preference, gender,, blame attributions in adolescent sexual assault
authors: Davies, Michelle, Austen, Kerry, Rogers, Paul
abstract: The study investigated the impact of victim sexual orientation, perpetrator gender,, participant gender on judgements toward a 15-year-old male victim of a depicted sexual assault. One hundred, eight-eight participants (97 male, 91 female) read a hypothetical scenario depicting the sexual assault of a 15-year-old male victim where the victim's sexual orientation, the perpetrator's gender were varied between subjects. Participants then completed a questionnaire assessing their attributions toward both the victim, the perpetrator. Results revealed that male participants blamed the victim more than female participants when the victim was both gay, attacked by a male perpetrator. All participants, regardless of gender, made more positive judgements toward the female as opposed to male perpetrator. Results are discussed in relation to gender role stereotypes, homophobia.

title: Ego depletion increases risk-taking
authors: Fischer, Peter, Kastenmüller, Andreas, Asal, Kathrin
abstract: We investigated how the availability of self-control resources affects risk-taking inclinations, behaviors. We proposed that risk-taking often occurs from suboptimal decision processes, heuristic information processing (e.g., when a smoker suppresses or neglects information about the health risks of smoking). Research revealed that depleted self-regulation resources are associated with reduced intellectual performance, reduced abilities to regulate spontaneous, automatic responses (e.g., control aggressive responses in the face of frustration). The present studies transferred these ideas to the area of risk-taking. We propose that risk-taking is increased when individuals find themselves in a state of reduced cognitive self-control resources (ego-depletion). Four studies supported these ideas. In Study 1, ego-depleted participants reported higher levels of sensation seeking than non-depleted participants. In Study 2, ego-depleted participants showed higher levels of risk-tolerance in critical road traffic situations than non-depleted participants. In Study 3, we ruled out two alternative explanations for these results: neither cognitive load nor feelings of anger mediated the effect of ego-depletion on risk-taking. Finally, Study 4 clarified the underlying psychological process: ego-depleted participants feel more cognitively exhausted than non-depleted participants, thus are more willing to take risks. Discussion focuses on the theoretical, practical implications of these findings.

title: General versus specific victim blaming
authors: Johnson, Lee M, Mullick, Rehan, Mulford, Charles L
keywords: DISCRIMINATION; SOCIAL distance; VICTIMS; SOCIAL psychology; BLAME; general blaming; social responsibility; society blaming; specific blaming; victim blaming; Attribution;The J Soc Psychol;J\_TF1505
abstract: The authors investigated (a) whether victim blaming is a general variable in a person's make-up or (b) whether the extent of blaming depends on the kind of victim considered. The authors evaluated scales for blaming (a) victims in general, (b) society in general, (c) a specific kind of victim (i.e., AIDS),, (d) the society in which AIDS victims live. The general, specific scales had favorable psychometric properties, including reliability. General, specific victim blaming were significantly, positively correlated, whereas victim blaming, society blaming were not significantly correlated. Multiple regression analyses provided evidence of construct validity for the scales. All blaming variables were significantly related in the hypothesized directions to social distance, social responsibility,, discrimination (regarding persons with AIDS). The general, specific scales made significant, unique contributions. Implications for attribution theory, research are specified.

title: Relation of affect control theory to the sentencing of criminals
authors: Tsoudis, O
abstract: Past researchers (A. Blumstein, J. Cohen, S. E. Martin, \& M. H. Tonry, 1983; A. Von Hirsch \& H. Gross, 1981) have explored legal variables, demonstrated the significance of various criteria (e.g., criminal's prior record, seriousness of offense, influence of victim) on the sentencing of criminals. Affect control theory (D. R. Heise, 1979) focuses on inferences about the identity of the criminal. In the present study, the author examined the influence of the foregoing legal variables, affect control theory in sentencing decisions by using U.S. undergraduates' reactions to statements of criminals, of victims. Results of a 2 (criminal's emotion: sad vs. unconcerned) x 2 (victim's emotion: sad vs. unconcerned) x 2 (prior record: none vs. auto theft) factorial design supported affect control theory, demonstrated the significance of the victim's perceived identity in sentencing decisions, even when information about the prior record was provided.

title: Intrapersonal variation in consumer susceptibility to normative influence: toward a better understanding of brand choice decisions
authors: Orth, Ulrich R, Kahle, Lynn R
keywords: COLLEGE students; PSYCHOLOGY; AIDS (Disease); PATIENTS; GENDER; RELIGION; GREEK letter societies; BLAME; UNITED States;The J Soc Psychol;J\_TF1505
abstract: The authors examined intrapersonal variation in consumer susceptibility to normative influence as a key mediator of wine brand choice. On the basis of a consumer sample, the authors found that individual values, social identity complexity affect consumer susceptibility to normative influence with downstream effects on (a) which brand benefits consumers desire in wine, (b) choice. Individuals higher on internal values, with more complex social identities were less susceptible to normative influence, placed less emphasis on social brand benefits. Separate examinations of consumption scenarios with, without salient reference groups showed that reference group salience interacts with personal values, social identity complexity in affecting consumer susceptibility to normative influence, which in turn affects which brand benefits consumers desire, consequently choice.

title: Risk, benefit perceptions, acceptability judgments,, self-reported actions toward nuclear power
authors: Gardner, Gerald T, Tiemann, Adrian R, Gould, Leroy C, Deluca, Donald R, Doob, Leonard W, Stolwijk, Jan A J
abstract: Summary Three-hundred, sixty-seven respondents selected from five widely differing groups in two U.S. communities were administered a questionnaire tapping personal action for or against nuclear power, as well as a variety of attitudinal, cognitive,, sociodemographic variables. Respondents included members of environmental groups, college students, blue-collar workers, business people,, nuclear engineers, other technologists. The results indicated that degree of self-reported action was systematically correlated with the rated “acceptability,” risks, benefits,, qualitative characteristics of nuclear power. The results also pointed to other major correlates of personal action, including confidence in various risk-management institutions, organizations. Emphasis is placed upon general methodological issues involved in the study of risk perceptions, acceptability judgments,, actions.

title: The effects of using identity deception, suggesting secrecy on the outcomes of adult-adult, adult-child or -adolescent online sexual interactions
authors: Bergen, Emilia, Davidson, Julia, Schulz, Anja, Schuhmann, Petya, Johansson, Ada, Santtila, Pekka, Jern, Patrick
abstract: There is a lack of knowledge about effects of behaviors during online sexual solicitations. Our aims were to explore the prevalence of identity deception, wanting to keep the interaction a secret,, how these behaviors relate to the outcome of sexual interactions online. The participants were adults who self-reported online sexual interactions with a stranger during the last year. We separated them into groups based on the age of their contact: (1) those that interacted sexually with adults (n = 640), (2) those that interacted sexually with a child or adolescent (n = 136). Neither the prevalence of identity deception, suggesting secrecy, nor the outcomes of the interactions differed between the two groups. Suggesting secrecy increased the likelihood of receiving a sexual picture with an adult contact, whereas using any identity deception increased the likelihood with a child or adolescent. Several deceptions as well as suggesting secrecy increased the likelihood of cybersex within both groups, while using identity deceptions mostly decreased the likelihood of meeting the contact offline in both groups. Suggesting online, offline secrecy increased the likelihood of sexual contact offline with the child or adolescent but not with adult contacts.

title: Preventing repeat domestic burglary: A meta-evaluation of studies from Australia, the UK,, the United States
authors: Grove, Louise
abstract: Domestic burglary repeat victimization prevention programs are examined across three countries: the UK, Australia,, the United States. The success of these programs is reviewed using a combination of systematic review, scientific realism techniques. Repeat burglary prevention programs in the UK had demonstrable success, while those in Australia, the United States did not. Programs need to be tailored to the specific context of the crime problem, designed to avoid common implementation problems.

title: Blame attribution in court: Conceptualization, measurement of perpetrator blame
authors: Cramer, Robert J, Gorter, Erin L, Cornish Rodriguez, Monique D, Clark, John W, Rice, Amanda K, Nobles, Matt R
abstract: Drawing on legal, psychological theory of blame, the present study evaluates psychometric properties of the Perceptions of Blame Scale (PBS; Rayburn, Mendoza, \& Davison, 2003) across crimes of varying severity (i.e., misdemeanor assault, felony assault,, murder), motivation (gay hate crime victim versus heterosexual victim perceived as gay). Results revealed support for a single-factor model of perceptions of perpetrator blame in a panel of jury-eligible community members. Perceptions of blame in this study moderated the impact of crime motivation on the sentencing decision. Results are discussed with regard to legal, psychological perspectives of blame in a jury research paradigm.

title: DESIGNREVIEWANDPUBLICPREFERENCES:EFFECTSOF GEOGRAPHICALLOCATION, PUBLICCONSENSUS, SENSATIONSEEKING, ANDARCHITECTURALSTYLES
authors: Nasar, Arthure Stampsiiiandjackl

title: Taking woman abuse seriously: A critical response to the Solicitor General of Canada's crime prevention advice
authors: Dekeseredy, Walter S, Burshtyn, Hyman, Gordon, Charles
abstract: While women experience male violence, intimidation in both public, private settings, the most serious, common threats to their physical, psychological well-being are abusive acts committed by known men. However, the Solicitor General of Canada's recent crime advice to women does not address this problem. The principal objective of this paper is to show how this discourse obscures the reality of woman abuse in Canada.

title: A neighborhood business area is hurting: Crime, fear of crime,, disorders take their toll
authors: Fisher, Bonnie
abstract: Neighborhood businesses are essential to the social, economic viability of a community. Research on the effects of crime, fear of crime,, physical, social disorders has focused primarily on the residential area, has ignored the neighborhood business area. This note presents an argument for further research to redress this imbalance, offers survey results from one neighborhood business area that suggest that crime, fear,, disorders are perceived by small business proprietors, landowners to be serious problems. Results indicate that victimization is frequent, has negative financial, operational effects on business.

title: General multilevel opportunity, crime events
authors: Tillyer, Marie Skubak
abstract: General multilevel opportunity theory draws from a range of existing opportunity theories that collectively account for variation in criminal opportunity across various levels of analysis. The theory, which is inclusive in its conceptualization of criminal opportunity, specifies macro-, micro-influences, their interactive effects. There is a growing body of multilevel victimization research that supports the propositions of the theory. To date, however, general multilevel opportunity theory has been underutilized as a theory of crime events, situational prevention. This article describes general multilevel opportunity theory, reviews its empirical status,, offers new extensions, applications of the theory for crime-event research, situational prevention.

title: The Kansas City preventive patrol experiment: A continuing debate
authors: Risman, Barbara J
abstract: This research briefis a methodological critique of Richard Larson's criticism of the Kansas City Preventative Patrol Experiment. The measurement issues, which are the focus of his critique, are reassessed in this brief,, the argument is presented that the experimental conditions were different enough to expect significant results if variability in police presence did indeed affect the dependent measures.

title: Elderly consumers’ receptiveness to telemarketing fraud
authors: Lee, Jinkook, Geistfeld, Loren V
abstract: The authors use data from the 1996, 1997 EXCEL Omnibus Survey commissioned by the American Association of Retired Persons to investigate the receptiveness of consumers 50 years of age or older to telemarketing fraud. The authors investigate elderly consumers’ receptiveness to telemarketing fraud, as reflected by a consumer's psychological orientation (willingness to listen to sales pitch, attitude toward callers), actual engagement in risky behavior (responding to unknown callers) using setwise regression. They conclude with policy implications.

title: Exploring teenage shoplifting behavior: A choice, constraint approach
authors: Lo, Lucia
abstract: This article examines the geography of teenage shoplifting within a choice, constraint framework. Potential offenders indicated spatial, temporal preferences in committing this crime. They tended to shoplift for small amounts from large stores in the neither too busy nor too quiet hours of the day. Although the tendency to shoplift was not found to be related to socioeconomic or moral values, socialization emphasizing the enjoyment, pursuit of fun, thrill likely affected one's tendency to shoplift. Like shopping preferences, the key in shoplifting behavior was accessibility to opportunity.

title: Direct victimization experiences, fear of crime: A gender perspective
authors: Sironi, Emiliano, Bonazzi, Leda Maria
journal: Peace Economics Peace Science, Public Policy
abstract: AbstractUsing data from the sixth round of the European Social Survey, we implement propensity score matching methods in order to test whether the presence of past experiences of direct victimization decreases citizens’ safety perception. Results confirm the hypothesis that victimization strongly increases the fear of crime; furthermore the effect is also gender specific: victimized women show higher decrease in safety perception than men.

title: Victimization, the fear of crime
authors: Garofalo, James
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: FEAR of crime; VICTIMS of crimes; CRIME; CRIMINOLOGY; UNITED States;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章;122\_0\_犯罪不安研究の起こり;9\_001\_intro;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: The determinants of the fear of crime are examined with special attention to how the risk, experience of criminal victimization affect that fear. Us ing data from victimization, attitude surveys in eight American cities, a model of the determinants of the fear of crime is developed, evaluated in a preliminary fashion. The major conclusion is that the fear of crime is not simply a function of the risk of, actual experiences with victimization.

title: Crime, vandalism in university residence halls: A confirmation of defensible space theory
authors: Sommer, Robert
keywords: Crime; 3236:Criminal Behavior \& Juvenile Delinquency; Spatial Organization; Vandalism; Environmental Planning; Human; Dormitories;jep\_org;jep;J Environ Psychol
abstract: University residence halls with good defensible space were found to have substantially lower crime, vandalism than residence halls with poor defensible space characteristics.

title: The dark side of community: Moralistic homicide, strong social ties
authors: Cooney, Mark
abstract: Abstract Contrary to common belief, strong communities do not necessarily enjoy low rates of violence. Applying Baumgartner's (1988) thesis that confrontational forms of conflict management tend to be found where social interaction is intense, this paper argues that conflict-related or “moralistic” homicide is associated with several of the defining characteristics of community. Thus, a considerable amount of evidence, modern, pre-modern, suggests that moralistic homicide flourishes under conditions of proximity, sociability, immobility, publicity, loyalty.

title: Editorial: Asking questions about risk, worry: dilemmas of the pollsters
authors: Sjöberg, Lennart
abstract: The perceived risk of terrorism has been found to have properties similar to those of other risk perceptions. Risk perception research is therefore relevant to a discussion of methods used by polling firms to gauge public opinion with regard to terrorism. Questions used by one firm for this purpose are analyzed in relation to research findings. It is concluded that alternative formulations may be preferable, that more methodological research on risk perception, related attitudes should be conducted. Polling firms working on worry, concerns of the public would profit from taking risk perception research into account.

title: Mobility, perceptions of a hazardous environment
authors: Kiecolt, K Jill, Nigg, Joanne M
abstract: This article focuses on the first stage of the mobility decision-making process-the consideration of moving. A social-ecological model has been developed to analyze the relationship between a stated decision to move, the objective hazardousness of one's present location due to the threat of a damaging earthquake. A unique feature of this model is the inclusion of subjective earthquake-related factors in order to determine the extent to which these mediating variables improve the explanation of mobility plans.

title: Subcultural diversity, the fear of crime, gangs
authors: Lane, Jodi, Meeker, James W
abstract: Fear, gangs were two of the most important factors driving crime policy in the 1990s. Policy makers, the media blamed gangs for much of the violence occurring across the nation, for public fear. This article examines fear of crime, gangs in Orange County, California, as measured by a randomized survey of 1,223 respondents conducted in 1995 by The Orange County Register newspaper. The authors find that the factors predicting fear of crime, fear of gangs are different. In addition, they find that concern about subcultural diversity is a strong predictor of both types of fear.

title: Risk analysis in loss prevention research
authors: Johns, Tracy L
abstract: Conventional risk management models identify risks, assess the probability of their occurrence, potential impact,, then implement steps to reduce the risk or the impact of the risk. Although almost all retailers implement measures to try to eliminate or reduce theft (the end step of risk management), we know little about how many undertake systematic risk assessments of loss to guide solutions, the methods that they may use to do so. This study presents the results of a survey of 22 diverse retail companies about their LP/AP risk management process, including the types of risk data collected, types of risk assessment, analyses conducted,, how these data are used in management decisions.

title: Are all victims alike? The adverse, generalized,, differential impact of crime
authors: Lurigio, Arthur J
abstract: Samples of crime victims (burglary, robbery, felonious assault), nonvictims were compared to examine the short-term differential, generalized effects of crime on psychological, behavioral,, attitudinal measures. Victims were more likely to report experiencing higher levels of vulnerability, fear,, symptomology,, lower levels of self-efficacy. Also, victims were more likely to engage in protective behaviors. There were fewer differences, however, among the three groups of crime victims. Burglary victims were more likely to report feeling vulnerable, fearful, while assault victims were more likely to express more negative views of the police.

title: Clods online : fraud, the global financial crisis – how brain information processes undermine our ability to yield sound decisions
authors: Pniewki, Krystyne
journal: International journal of business, social science
abstract: This is an investigation into the putative link between the processes involved in making judgments, the resultant decisions which prove detrimental. This will be achieved through an examination of two well-known, very troublesome outcomes of these processes. The first is the ease with which people become victims of fraud, the second is the Global Financial Crisis. A possible or partial explanation for errant or unethical decisions lies in the fact that heuristics, which spill over into overconfidence are more likely to be utilized. However, 'reflective introspection', sometimes called 'reflective engagement' or 'reflective problem solving' which is underutilized, is far more conducive to individuals, organisations, institutions in making sound decisions.

title: How helpful is bystander intervention? Perspectives of dating, sexual violence survivors
authors: McMahon, Sarah
keywords: Bystander intervention; college campuses; dating, sexual violence;330\_SAEnv;Violence Against Women\_Sage;CampusCrime
abstract: While bystander intervention education has demonstrated promise as a strategy to reduce dating, sexual violence (DSV) on campus, little is known about whether survivors on whose behalf the interventions take place find these helpful. This paper uses qualitative, in-depth interviews with 33 DSV survivors to explore their perspectives on bystander intervention. Results indicate that while some interventions were identified as helpful, especially those that provided support to the survivor, many were not helpful enough or even harmful. Further work is needed to understand the consequences of bystander action.

title: Violent crime, incentives in the long-run: evidence from England, Wales
authors: Saridakis, George
abstract: This study uses recent advances in time-series econometrics to investigate the non-stationarity, co-integration properties of violent crime series in England, Wales. In particular, we estimate the long-run impact of economic conditions, beer consumption, various deterrents on different categories of recorded violent crime. The results suggest that a long-run causal model exists for only minor crimes of violence, with beer consumption being a predominant factor.

title: Domestic violence: The beginning, continuation, or final act in a criminal career?
authors: Buzawa, Eve S, Hirschel, David
abstract: This paper uses a life-course perspective to examine the extent to which domestic violence is part of a criminal career. Offenders who commit domestic violence as their first criminal act are compared to offenders for whom domestic violence is merely a continuation of a criminal career, for whom the domestic violence relationship provides an opportunity for the commission of still another type of offense. In addition, there is an examination of patterns in offending, reoffending for males, females.

title: Stuck in the past with push-pins on paper maps: Challenges of transition from manual to computerized crime mapping, analysis in Kenya
authors: Baraka, Gachie Eliud, Murimi, Shadrack Kiana
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Although crimes, the modus operandi of perpetrators across the world change constantly, some policing tools, especially in developing countries, remain the same. This study sought to assess Kenyan police officers’ satisfaction with the use of paper maps, push-pins (manual tools) in crime analysis,, identify challenges to the adoption of computerized tools such as geographical information systems (GIS) at a time when most operations are driven by technology. A descriptive survey targeting 120 Kenyan police officers was carried out at the National Police Service (NPS) headquarters in Nairobi, but only 94 (78.3\%) officers responded. The study reveals that 42.3\% of respondents found manual tools to be useful in crime mapping, spatial analysis, whereas 67.8\% felt that they were easy to use. The study indicates that 55.0\% of respondents were satisfied with manual crime mapping, spatial analysis, mainly because it was easy to use. The study also identifies several challenges to the adoption of GIS in crime analysis. The study concludes that majority of respondents found manual crime-mapping tools to be easy to use, but less useful although still usable in the absence of alternatives. The NPS should consider implementing pilot projects of computerized crime mapping, spatial analysis to allow stakeholders to assess police operations against multiple platforms.

title: Identifying, disseminating ‘good’ community safety practice: a problem solving approach
authors: Erol, Rosie, Millie, Andrew
abstract: This paper describes how a problem solving approach was used to identify good practice lessons from four community safety projects implemented in Birmingham,, how these lessons were disseminated to meet the different needs of practitioners, managers, a wider community safety audience.

title: The influence of spatial design characteristics on low-rise residential neighbourhoods in Basra city: Enhancing residents’ social interaction
authors: Alahmed, Hani, Alaghbari, Wa'el, Ibrahim, Rahinah, Salim, Azizah
journal: International Journal of Housing Markets, Analysis
abstract: Purpose - – This paper aims to investigate the ways that could enhance residents’ social interaction in low-rise residential building neighbourhoods of Basra city in Iraq. The lack of social interaction among residents of Basra city prompted the authors to frame a strategy for this case study. Design/methodology/approach - – The spatial design characteristics of low-rise residential building neighbourhoods implicated to support the residents in terms of social interactions in comparison to those exhibited by a single home, traditional neighbourhoods. The statistical data demonstrated that by using this strategy, several unique features of secured, collective, responsive, supportive spaces could enhance the residents’ social interaction. Findings - – This study found that all collective space factors have a significant influence on social interaction. “Fostering proper proximity, accessibility” factor was ranked first, the most significant factor with an influence on social interaction. Secured spaces (hierarchical spatial structure, physical security supports, construct) have a significant influence on social interaction. The most interesting finding in this study is that all factors of the supportive spaces construct have a significant influence on social interaction. Finally, this study showed that two factors of the responsive spaces construct, increasing variety, increasing legibility, have an insignificant influence on social interaction. Originality/value - – The design of low-rise residential building neighbourhoods in Basra city may be used to develop social interaction as the contributing factor for maintaining values of traditional neighbourhood communities. This study highlights certain recommendations for architects, especially urban designers, to reinforce residents’ social interaction in low-rise residential building neighbourhoods in Basra city.

title: An ecological perspective on adolescent sexual offending
authors: Bischof, G H, Rosen, K H
abstract: This paper proposes an ecological perspective for understanding the complex phenomenon of adolescent sexual offending. Pertinent research findings are incorporated within the individual, microsystem, mesosystem, exosystem,, macrosystemic levels as suggested by this model. This perspective is capable of integrating research, treatment approaches from divergent disciplines, varying theoretical perspectives. An ecological perspective suggests consideration of variables, interactions not previously examined that may play a role in the etiology of sexual offenses by adolescents. Implications of this ecological perspective for prevention, treatment, further research are offered.

title: Variations in the recidivism of treated, nontreated sexual offenders in New Jersey: An examination of three time frames
authors: Zgoba, Kristen M, Levenson, Jill
abstract: This study examines the recidivism of sexual offenders in New Jersey at three different time intervals: three years, five years,, ten years after release from prison. The sample is comprised of sexual offenders released from the general prison population (untreated sample, n = 150), the Adult Diagnostic, Treatment Center (ADTC) (treated sample, n = 150), a sex offender specific facility. The goals of this study were twofold: (1) to identify the recidivism rates of sexual offenders, to determine whether sexual offenders who receive treatment demonstrate lower levels of recidivism, (2) to examine whether differences in recidivism exist among the varying time frames, offender subtypes. The results indicate that treated sex offenders maintained decreased nonsexual recidivism rates. Additionally, offenders who committed acts of rape, offenders followed up after six years had increased rates of recidivism.

title: A longitudinal examination of secondary traumatic stress among law enforcement
authors: Craun, Sarah W, Bourke, Michael L, Bierie, David M, Williams, Katria S
abstract: Current research on secondary traumatic stress (STS) has been drawn from cross-sectional data. To determine how STS manifests over time, we conducted a three-year, longitudinal panel survey of investigators at a federal law enforcement agency. We measured STS scores, coping styles, perceptions of the work environment,, subject demographics. We found that STS scores are fairly stable over time. A variety of both positive, negative coping mechanisms, as well as characteristics about the work environment, were found to impact STS. In particular, coping with denial more often in the previous year was related to higher STS scores a year later, while higher scores indicating supervisory support were related to lower STS one year later. Deputy demographic variables were unrelated to STS.
