The findings indicate that the most common barriers to creating change in rural communities include patriarchal mindsets that foster a culture of silence around women's rights, lack of education, digital illiteracy,, lack of access to digital tools, services. Notwithstanding these obstacles, rural Indian women, girls participated in an intervention to create a new narrative informed by technological solutions that addressed gender violence in their communities.

abstract: Following disturbances during the EU summit in Gothenburg in 2001, the Swedish police adopted a new concept, called special police tactics, for the policing of public order. In 2006, the Swedish National Police Board decided to start a 3-year project to develop a long term strategy for knowledge development with regard to these tactics, integrating research, training,, practice. This article reports on the set up, results of this reform project. Changes in the planning, carrying out, evaluation of police operations at major events were observed. The project provided a theoretical foundation for the special police tactics, a practical evaluation method for continuous knowledge development. The project methodology contributed to a developmental climate in the special police tactics organization. The project work also reinforced the basis for public order policing of crowds, to contribute to uphold- ing consitutional rights of assembly, freedom of speech.

abstract: Drawing on data collected from a survey of 334 randomly selected residents in Ile-Ife, Nigeria, this paper explores the perception, factors that contributed to residents’ opinion of the police. The overall result revealed that residents had low satisfaction with the police. It was deducible that satisfaction with the police increases with an increase in residents’ level of education, income status, age. Furthermore, maximum satisfaction was held about the police by residents who felt very much safe in the study area. It was further revealed that satisfaction with the police increases as place of residence changes from a high- to a low-density neighbourhood. The result of multiple ordinary least-squares regression analysis further revealed gender, experience of crime, contact with the police as significant factors in residents’ perception of the police. The study therefore concluded that perception of the police varies between socioeconomic groups, is also influenced by many other contextual factors.

title: Explaining fear of crime
authors: Box, Steven, Hale, Chris, Andrews, Glen
keywords: model of factors for explanation of fear of crime, 16 yr olds \& older, England \& Wales; Crime; Fear; Models; Demographic Characteristics; Psychosocial Factors;360\_Trust;British Journal of criminology;police visibility
abstract: The authors construct a model for explaining ``fear'' of crime by using the relevant literature to identify possible factors, making out a prima facie case for each by examining data from the second British Crime Survey. Using logit analysis this model is tested on data derived from the same survey. The authors show that such factors as gender, age, race, neighbourhood cohesion, confidence in the police, levels of local incivility, experience of victimisation, perception of risk, assessment of offence seriousness all combine toform a theoretical account of ``fear'' which has strong empirical support. On the basis of these findings, they conclude by making some suggestions for policies to reduce this ``fear''.

title: Levels of guardianship in protecting youth against exposure to violence in the community
authors: Ahlin, Eileen M, Lobo Antunes, Maria João
abstract: Using hierarchical generalized linear modeling, the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods data, the authors examine whether different types of guardianship protect youth against exposure to violence in the neighborhood while controlling for situations where exposure is most likely to occur. Protective family management practices, internal locus of control significantly reduce exposure to community violence. Contrary to expectations, however, neighborhood collective efficacy exerted no effect. The findings emphasize the importance of considering family management practices, individual characteristics as protective factors against harmful environments. Further, guardianship is not restricted to external informal agents of control.

title: Fear of crime, victimization among the elderly in different types of communities
authors: Akers, Ronald L, La GRECA, Anthony J, Sellers, Christine, Cochran, John
abstract: The central issue examined here is the effect that community setting, relative to other factors, has on victimization, fear of crime among the elderly. Findings are from 1,410 in‐home interviews in two retirement communities (age homogeneous), two age‐heterogeneous communities. Victimization of elderly is low in all communities,, although nearly half of the respondents have some fear of crime, the percentage reporting great fear of crime is low. Victimization, fear of crime are only weakly related to one another,, the regression model for each does not account for much variance. But both are significantly related to the type of community,, fear of crime is also related to other variables. The greater the age density of the community (greater concentration of elderly), the less crime, less fear of crime. Living arrangements, sociodemographic variables,, health status of the elderly as indicators of personal vulnerability to crime are not related to victimization, but are related to fear of crime,, effects of community setting on fear of crime are reduced when these other variables are taken into account. Suggestions for other, unmeasured, sources of variations, implications for future research are presented.

title: Sense of community, civic engagement, social well‐being in Italian adolescents
authors: Albanesi, Cinzia, Cicognani, Elvira, Zani, Bruna
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
abstract: AbstractThis study investigates the relationship between sense of community, civic engagement, social well‐being in a sample of Italian adolescents. Participants were 14–19 year‐old high school students (N = 566) from two demographically distinct cities. Participants completed a questionnaire assessing sense of community, social well‐being (Keyes, 1998), involvement in structured group activities (group membership), civic engagement. Results showed that involvement in formal groups is associated with increased civic involvement, increased sense of community. Sense of community predicts social well‐being, explains some of the association between civic engagement, social well‐being. Findings suggest that, to increase social well‐being, it is important to provide adolescents with more opportunities to experience a sense of belonging to the peers' group, promote prosocial behaviours in the community context. title: Culpable control, counterfactual reasoning in the psychology of blame
authors: Alicke, Mark D, Buckingham, Justin, Zell, Ethan, Davis, Teresa
abstract: Many counterfactual reasoning studies assess how people ascribe blame for harmful actions. By itself, the knowledge that a harmful outcome could easily have been avoided does not predict blame. In three studies, the authors showed that an outcome's mutability influences blame, related judgments when it is coupled with a basis for negative evaluations. Study 1 showed that mutability influenced blame, compensation judgments when a physician was negligent but not when the physician took reasonable precautions to prevent harm. Study 2 showed that this finding was attenuated when the victim contributed to his own demise. In Study 3, whether an actor just missed arriving on time to see his dying mother or had no chance to see her influenced his blameworthiness when his reason for being late provided a basis for negative evaluations but made no difference when there was a positive reason for the delay. These findings clarify the conditions under which an outcome's mutability is likely to influence blame, related attributions.

title: The spatial distribution of crime, population density in Saudi Arabia
authors: Algahtany, Mofza, Kumar, Lalit, Barclay, Elaine, Khormi, Hassan M
abstract: This study examined the relationship between crime, place across the 13 provinces of Saudi Arabia using geographic information systems techniques based on population density, identifying, visualising the spatial distributions of national, regional crime rates for drug crimes, theft, murder, assault, alcohol, ‘outrageous crimes’ (offences against Islam) over a 10-year period from 2003 to 2012. Social disorganisation theory was employed to guide the study, explain the diversity in patterns in crime across the country. The highest rates of overall crimes were identified in the Northern Border, Jizan areas, located in the north, south of the country, respectively, while the East Area has the lowest crime rate. Most drug offences occurred in Northern Borders, Jizan, high rates of theft were recorded in Northern Borders, Jouf, Makkah, while the highest rates of homicide occurred in Asir.

title: “There goes the fear”: feelings of safety at home, in the neighborhood: The role of personal, social,, service factors: Feeling Safe at Home, in the Neighbourhood
authors: Allik, Mirjam, Kearns, Ade
abstract: Safety has been shown to be an important contributor to mental wellbeing, is often identified as a key element of sustainable communities. Drawing on the fear of crime literature this paper investigates the determinants of feelings of indoor, outdoor safety for people living in deprived areas, using both cross-sectional, longitudinal samples from household surveys in 15 communities in Glasgow. Across the different models social cohesion, satisfaction with services, perceived empowerment emerge as the most robust predictors of feeling very safe indoors, outside. Our findings suggest useful extensions to several theoretical models of the fear of crime: the vulnerability hypothesis should include social vulnerability more generally; environmental models should focus on local amenities, services as well as on disorder;, social-psychological models should consider not only informal social control but resident empowerment in relation to housing, neighbourhood issues.

title: Assessing the impediments to organizational change
authors: Allen, Rhonda Y W
abstract: This article identifies, assesses the impediments to implementing one aspect of community-oriented policing (COP): designated patrol assignments. The research was based on 126 interviews with three different levels of police practitioners (top, middle,, street-level) in three different southwest police departments. While this exploratory study examined several factors that could potentially impede or facilitate change, it was found that individual attitudes towards COP, pressure had the most significant effect on the process of change.

title: Near-repeat victimization of sex crimes, threat incidents against women, girls in Tokyo, Japan
authors: Amemiya, Mamoru, Nakaya, Tomoki, Shimada, Takahito
keywords: 304\_RepeatVic;40\_日本のオープンデータ;業績一覧\_01論文;sexvic\_jp;Japan
abstract: AbstractNear-repeat victimization (NRV) is a phenomenon in which there is a greater likelihood for a subsequent crime to occur within close spatiotemporal proximity of the last occurrence of a similar crime. This study investigated the NRV of sex crimes, threat incidents against women, girls in Tokyo. An analysis using the Knox ratio showed significant near-repeat patterns of sex crimes, two types of threat incidents, with the exception of threat incidents with physical contact against girls. Additionally, the tendency of NRV was revealed as being stronger when the victims were girls.

title: How the COVID-19 pandemic has changed our lives: A study of psychological correlates across 59 countries
authors: Alzueta, Elisabet, Perrin, Paul, Baker, Fiona C, Caffarra, Sendy, Ramos-Usuga, Daniela, Yuksel, Dilara, Arango-Lasprilla, Juan Carlos
keywords: COVID-19; anxiety; depression; mental health; pandemic;322\_経済圧力
abstract: OBJECTIVE: This study examined the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, subsequent social restrictions or quarantines on the mental health of the global adult population. METHOD: A sample of 6,882 individuals (Mage = 42.30; 78.8\% female) from 59 countries completed an online survey asking about several pandemic-related changes in life, psychological status. RESULTS: Of these participants, 25.4\%, 19.5\% reported moderate-to-severe depression (DASS-21), anxiety symptoms (GAD-7), respectively. Demographic characteristics (e.g. higher-income country), COVID-19 exposure (e.g., having had unconfirmed COVID-19 symptoms), government-imposed quarantine level,, COVID-19-based life changes (e.g., having a hard time transitioning to working from home; increase in verbal arguments or conflict with other adult in home) explained 17.9\% of the variance in depression, 21.5\% in anxiety symptoms. CONCLUSIONS: In addition to posing a high risk to physical health, the COVID-19 pandemic has robustly affected global mental health, so it is essential to ensure that mental health services reach individuals showing pandemic-related depression, anxiety symptoms.

title: Assessing the impact of public policy on homicide rates in Brazil: The case of PRONASCI program
authors: de Castro, Talita Egevardt, Justus, Marcelo, Kassouf, Ana Lúcia
abstract: The current study evaluates the impact of the National Public Security with Citizenship Program (PRONASCI) on the homicide rate in Brazilian municipalities. PRONASCI program was implemented in Brazilian metropolitan regions, urban territories with high violent crime rates in 2007. In this study, we have applied a spatial difference-in-differences model with matching approaches. Municipalities that did not receive funds from the program made up the control group. We found that the program was inefficient to reduce the homicide rate in all of the municipalities that had received funds from it, compared to those that had not, even considering their potential spatial spillover effects. This result was expected due to the program complexity, in particular due to its ineffective management, the resistance from municipalities to change with the program.

title: Police foot patrol, crime displacement: A local analysis
authors: Andresen, Martin A, Malleson, Nicolas
abstract: Police patrol, motorized, foot, has a long history of being used as a crime prevention method. Scientific evaluations of this crime prevention technique have been undertaken for at least 40 years, with mixed results. One of the important questions to be answered regarding the implementation of a police patrol is the presence of crime displacement: criminal activity simply moving around the corner, away from the primary patrol area. Previous investigations of this phenomenon have found that, most often, crime displacement is nonexistent or less than crime reductions in the primary area of interest. In this article, we investigate local crime displacement. We use a spatial point pattern test that can identify changes in the spatial patterns/distribution of crime even if crime in all areas has decreased. We find moderate evidence for the presence of this spatial shift, discuss the implications.

abstract: Abstract This paper presents a personal view on some emerging research directions at the interface of social science, spatial analysis. Particular emphasis is placed on methodological challenges presented by developments in social science theory, demands for data manipulation,, the need for education, dissemination.

title: \textitGeoDa: An introduction to spatial data analysis
authors: Anselin, Luc, Syabri, Ibnu, Kho, Youngihn
abstract: This article presents an overview of GeoDa™, a free software program intended to serve as a user‐friendly, graphical introduction to spatial analysis for non‐geographic information systems (GIS) specialists. It includes functionality ranging from simple mapping to exploratory data analysis, the visualization of global, local spatial autocorrelation,, spatial regression. A key feature of GeoDa is an interactive environment that combines maps with statistical graphics, using the technology of dynamically linked windows. A brief review of the software design is given, as well as some illustrative examples that highlight distinctive features of the program in applications dealing with public health, economic development, real estate analysis,, criminology.

title: Effects of eye images on everyday cooperative behavior: a field experiment
authors: Ernest-Jones, Max, Nettle, Daniel, Bateson, Melissa
journal: Evolution, human behavior: official journal of the Human Behavior, Evolution Society
keywords: Eyes; Cooperation; Prosocial behaviour; Field experiment;316\_介入実験\_環境手がかり
abstract: Laboratory studies have shown that images of eyes can cause people to behave more cooperatively in some economic games,, in a previous experiment, we found that eye images increased the level of contributions to an honesty box. However, the generality, robustness of the eyes effect is not known. Here, we extended our research on the effects of eye images on cooperative behavior to a novel context—littering behavior in a university cafeteria—and attempted to elucidate the mechanism by which they work, by displaying them both in conjunction with,, not associated with, verbal messages to clear one's litter. We found a halving of the odds of littering in the presence of posters featuring eyes, as compared to posters featuring flowers. This effect was independent of whether the poster exhorted litter clearing or contained an unrelated message, suggesting that the effect of eye images cannot be explained by their drawing attention to verbal instructions. There was some support for the hypothesis that eye images had a larger effect when there were few people in the café than when the café was busy. Our results confirm that the effects of subtle cues of observation on cooperative behavior can be large in certain real-world contexts.

title: Can evolutionary principles explain patterns of family violence?
authors: Archer, John
abstract: The article's aim is to evaluate the application of the evolutionary principles of kin selection, reproductive value,, resource holding power to the understanding of family violence. The principles are described in relation to specific predictions, the mechanisms underlying these. Predictions are evaluated for physical violence perpetrated by (a) parents to unrelated children, (b) parents to genetic offspring,, (c) offspring to parents, between (d) siblings, (e) sexual partners. Precise figures for risks have been calculated where possible. The major conclusions are that most of the evidence is consistent with evolutionary predictions derived from kin selection, reproductive value: There were (a) higher rates of violence to stepchildren, (b) a decline in violence with the age of offspring,, (c) an increase in violence with parental age, while (d) violence between siblings was generally at a low level, concerned resource disputes. The issue of distinguishing evolutionary from alternative explanations is addressed throughout, is problematic for predictions derived from reproductive value. The main evolutionary explanation for male partner violence, mate guarding as a result of paternity uncertainty, cannot explain Western studies where sex differences in control, violence between partners were absent, although other aspects of male partner violence are consistent with it,, it may explain sex differences in traditional cultures. Recurrent problems in evaluating the evidence were to control for possible confounds, thus to distinguish evolutionary from alternative explanations. Suggestions are outlined to address this, other issues arising from the review.

title: The end of risk communication as we know it
authors: Árvai, Joseph
abstract: According to the US National Research Council, risk communication ought to be viewed as a dialogue among people conducted to help facilitate a more accurate understanding of risks and, related, the decisions they may make to manage them. But, in spite of this widely accepted perspective on risk communication, there is often a disconnect between how it is defined, how it is practiced. Rather than focusing on a true dialogue aimed at improving risk assessments, risk management decisions, risk communication is often viewed as means of simply educating people about existing risk assessments so that, on their own, they might make (or contribute to) better risk management decisions. More worrisome, risk communication is still often seen as a means of ‘correcting’ misconceptions about, or perceptions of, risk; in other words, risk communication is used as a vehicle for attempting to align lay perceptions with their expertly assessed severity. In this paper, I argue that risk communication must become more decision-focused if it is to meet the objectives set forth – in 1989 – by the US National Research Council.

title: The impact of leader personality on new product development teamwork, performance: The moderating role of uncertainty
authors: Aronson, Zvi H, Reilly, Richard R, Lynn, Gary S
abstract: We examined the affect of leader personality on new product development (NPD) project performance under differing conditions of uncertainty. Our model posits teamwork as a mediating variable between leader personality, NPD performance. We hypothesized that the personality variable of openness would have a stronger influence on teamwork, NPD performance when uncertainty was high,, that the personality variables of extraversion, conscientiousness, stability would have a stronger indirect influence on NPD performance through teamwork when uncertainty was low. We used structural equation modeling to test two models of the influence of personality. In our study of 143 development projects, we support the importance of teamwork as a process variable linking leader personality to NPD performance, confirm that the effects of leader personality on these criteria depend on the level of uncertainty operating in NPD projects, thus substantiating all our hypotheses. Recommendations to re-consider hiring criteria, training for NPD project leaders are provided.

title: Self-guardianship at automated teller machines
authors: Ashby, Matthew P J, Thorpe, Adam
abstract: Automated teller machines (ATMs) are central to the functioning of developed economies, but by their very nature operate without human supervision, making them vulnerable to criminal abuse. This study sought to understand how customers protect themselves from theft while using ATMs. Observations of, surveys with ATM customers were used to identify how individuals protect themselves from theft of cash, card or personal details while using an ATM. The most common self-guardianship measure was to use only ATMs believed to be safe. The majority of customers did not cover the ATM keypad while entering their personal identification number, despite long-running publicity campaigns encouraging this behaviour. This suggests that self-guardianship is important at ATMs, but many customers fail to take even basic measures to protect themselves, their money, their bank details from theft. Banks, crime-prevention practitioners should do more to facilitate, encourage self-guardianship at ATMs.

title: Policing Neighbourhoods: Exploring the Geographies of Crime, Policing, Performance Assessment This research was funded under ESRC CASE award PTA-033-2002-00026
authors: Ashby, David I
abstract: Recent developments under the Public Service Reform agenda in the United Kingdom have increasingly focused upon public accountability, the needs of local communities. Similarly, crime, fear of crime, the efficacy of public service delivery have become central to the domestic political debate in recent years, with all three main political parties campaigning on local policing issues in the run up to the 2005 General Election. This article explores the drive for robust performance assessment frameworks across different policing geographies, highlights some of the inconsistencies between the new localism agenda, current data infrastructures, analytical techniques. The significance of neighbourhood composition is expressed,, the potential of local analytical techniques for both performance assessment, resource determination is highlighted. Specifically, the value of geodemographic neighbourhood typologies, spatial analysis, geographical expertise in the evaluation of policing performance, the refinement of local service delivery is discussed.

title: Comparing methods for measuring crime harm/severity
authors: Ashby, Matthew P J
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Ensuring police resources are focused where they are most needed requires understanding of the consequences of crime in relation to offenders, victims, places. Most crime analysis is based on counts of crimes, but not all crimes are equivalent to one another. Researchers have recently developed two methods - the Crime Harm Index, the Crime Severity Score - for weighting crime counts according to the severity of different crime types. This article compares these two methods by applying them to two common crime analysis scenarios: focusing resources on the most important types of crime, in the areas most affected by crime. The two measures are found to produce substantially different results when other factors are held constant. The results of severity-weighted crime analysis (and the decision made based on them) could therefore be greatly influenced by the method chosen. The implications of this are discussed, future research avenues outlined.

title: A virtue ethical account of making decisions about risk
authors: Athanassoulis, Nafsika, Ross, Allison
abstract: Most discussions of risk are developed in broadly consequentialist terms, focusing on the outcomes of risks as such. This paper will provide an alternative account of risk from a virtue ethical perspective, shifting the focus on the decision to take the risk. Making ethical decisions about risk is, we will argue, not fundamentally about the actual chain of events that the decision sets in process, but about the reasonableness of the decision to take the risk in the first place. A virtue ethical account of risk is needed because the notion of the ‘reasonableness’ of the decision to take the risk is affected by the complexity of the moral status of particular instances of risk‐taking, the risk‐taker's responsiveness to these contextual features. The very idea of ‘reasonable risk’ welcomes judgements about the nature of the risk itself, raises questions about complicity, culpability, responsibility, while at its heart, involves a judgement about the justification of risk which unavoidably focuses our attention on the character of the individuals involved in risk‐making decisions.

title: Studying crime, place with the Crime Open Database: Social, behavioural scienes
authors: Ashby, M P J
journal: Research data journal for the humanities, social sciences
abstract: The study of spatial, temporal crime patterns is important for both academic understanding of crime-generating processes, for policies aimed at reducing crime. However, studying crime, place is often made more difficult by restrictions on access to appropriate crime data. This means understanding of many spatio-temporal crime patterns are limited to data from a single geographic setting,, there are few attempts at replication. This article introduces the Crime Open Database (code), a database of 16 million offenses from 10 of the largest United States cities over 11 years, more than 60 offense types. Open crime data were obtained from each city, having been published in multiple incompatible formats. The data were processed to harmonize geographic co-ordinates, dates, times, offense categories, location types, as well as adding census, other geographic identifiers. The resulting database allows the wider study of spatio-temporal patterns of crime across multiple US cities, allowing greater understanding of variations in the relationships between crime, place across different settings, as well as facilitating replication of research.

title: Dynamic systems simulation analysis: A planning tool for the new century
authors: Auerhahn, Kathleen
abstract: Dynamic systems simulation analysis is an analytical technique that allows for the modeling of complex, nonlinear systems. While this technique is currently not widely used in the social sciences or in criminal justice planning, the author argues that more attention should be given to these models in criminal justice. These models can be used in a variety of ways—to gain greater insight into processes of system change, to track the development of specific system populations (e.g., drug offenders, elderly offenders),, to estimate projected system growth, change over a variety of legislative, policy scenarios—making them useful tools for theoretical development, policy evaluation, as well as more pragmatic considerations such as program, facilities,, overall system planning. An overview of the methodology, some examples of analyses are presented.

title: Updating perceptions of (in)justice
authors: Augustyn, Megan Bears
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: Objectives:This study evaluates the malleability of judgments of procedural justice. Drawing upon various literatures, five factors are hypothesized to be related to changes in procedural justice: (1) prior judgments of procedural justice, (2) direct experiences of arrest, (3) vicarious experiences of arrest, (4) individual arrest history,, (5) age.Methods:Using 11 waves of data from the Pathways to Desistance Study ( N = 1,354), multilevel models relate within-person covariates including individual, family,, peer arrests,, age to changes in procedural justice, controlling for stable, individual characteristics.Results:Judgments of procedural justice are anchored in prior perceptions. They are also a function of direct, vicarious experiences of arrests with the effect of individual arrests varying across individual arrest history. Evidence also suggests a developmental component. Age has a direct effect on judgments of procedural justice, conditions the effect of individual arrests on changes in procedural justice.Conclusions:Judgments of procedural justice are not static. Given these results, future research should continue to investigate the varying effects of other interactions with legal authorities on changes in judgments of procedural justice in order to form stronger policies aimed at increasing citizen cooperation.

title: Anxiety, depression,, resilience of healthcare workers in Japan during the Coronavirus disease 2019 outbreak
authors: Awano, Nobuyasu, Oyama, Nene, Akiyama, Keiko, Inomata, Minoru, Kuse, Naoyuki, Tone, Mari, Takada, Kohei, Muto, Yutaka, Fujimoto, Kazushi, Akagi, Yu, Mawatari, Momoko, Ueda, Akihiro, Kawakami, Junko, Komatsu, Junko, Izumo, Takehiro
keywords: anxiety; coronavirus disease 2019; depression; healthcare worker; resilience;322\_経済圧力;Japan
abstract: Objective Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is spreading around the world. The aim of this study was to assess the degree of anxiety, depression, resilience,, other psychiatric symptoms among healthcare workers in Japan during the COVID-19 pandemic. Methods This survey involved medical healthcare workers at the Japanese Red Cross Medical Center (Tokyo, Japan) between April 22, May 15, 2020. The degree of symptoms of anxiety, depression,, resilience was assessed using the Japanese versions of the 7-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder Scale (GAD-7), Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D),, 10-item Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale. Furthermore, we added original questionnaires comprising three factors: (i) anxiety, fear of infection, death; (ii) isolation, unreasonable treatment;, (iii) motivation, escape behavior at work. Results In total, 848 healthcare workers participated in this survey: 104 doctors, 461 nurses, 184 other co-medical staff,, 99 office workers. Among all participants, 85 (10.0\%) developed moderate-to-severe anxiety disorder,, 237 (27.9\%) developed depression. Problems with anxiety, fear of infection, death, isolation, unreasonable treatment,, motivation, escape from work were higher in the depression group than in the non-depression group (total CES-D score ≥ 16 points). Being a nurse, high total GAD-7 scores were risk factors of depression. Older workers, those with higher resilience were less likely to develop depression than others. Conclusion During the COVID-19 epidemic, many healthcare workers suffered from psychiatric symptoms. Psychological support, interventions for protecting the mental health of them are needed.

title: Transformational leadership, organizational commitment in Korean police station: Test of second-order MLQ-6 S, OCQ
authors: Baek, Hyunin, Byers, Edward H, Vito, Gennaro F
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: In comparison with research on the private sector, organizational commitment within the police has been rarely examined. Moreover, the leadership styles of police officials are not equal in all police studies across the world. Using data collected in 2009 from 236 Korean police officers, the purpose of this study is twofold: (a) to determine if the scale (multifactor leadership questionnaire, form 6-S [MLQ-6 S]) is applicable to police agencies internationally;, (b) to examine if leadership influences organizational commitment in law enforcement agencies. Results indicate that transformational leadership is positively linked to organizational commitment in Korean police agencies. However, the applicability of MLQ-6 S is controversial. Future research is required to examine comprehensively whether MLQ-6 S is a valid instrument for various types of organizations across the world.

title: Perceived appropriateness of training, organizational commitment among Korean police
authors: Baek, Hyunin
abstract: Although organizational commitment (OC) generates several beneficial outcomes to law enforcement agencies, the policing literature has underexamined OC. Using data gathered from 11,709 Korean police in 2012, this study conducted analyses of structural equation modeling (SEM) in order to examine the relationship between OC, perceived organizational support. In addition, SEM was conducted to determine whether Allen, Meyer’s three components of OC is appropriate. The results indicated that two predictors of perceived appropriateness of training (i.e., perceived support of training, training needs) strongly accounted for OC. However, unlike previous studies, this study found that hypotheses in the model with the subcomponents of OC (affective, continuous,, normative commitments) could not be verified. In sum, for sturdier examinations, future studies should apply the Allen, Meyer model to diverse agencies.

title: From evaluation to interpretation: Assessing theoretical elements in residential programmes
authors: Baerveldt, Chris, Horjus, Bob, De Winter, Micha
abstract: Impact studies of prevention programmes, in particular meta-analyses, usually interpret outcome, impact statistics as tests of an underlying theory of prevention. However, these programmes usually combine various interventions linked to different theoretical perspectives. Consequently, the effects of the programme can easily be misinterpreted.This article introduces an interpretation method that acknowledges the eclecticism of prevention practice, is also a feasible instrument to enhance the quality of meta-studies. First, the interventions of the programme are identified, analysed separately. Second, an assessment is made of the arguments that link interventions, the espoused theories.Third, each intervention is represented by a set of scores indicating the types of links, core theoretical assumptions.These scores are aggregated to programme scores, included as independent variables in meta-analyses.The method is illustrated by an evaluation of practices in two Dutch crime prevention institutions. The evaluation demonstrated the theoretical value of (eclectic) practices, even when they differ substantially from the official programme theories.The approach also highlighted an `interpretation error' in assessing the impact of one of the programmes, suggests a correction.

title: Intimate partner sexual violence: A review of terms, definitions,, prevalence: A review of terms, definitions,, prevalence
authors: Bagwell-Gray, Meredith E, Messing, Jill Theresa, Baldwin-White, Adrienne
keywords: definitions; domestic violence; intimate partner sexual violence; intimate partner violence; prevalence; rape; sexual assault
abstract: Intimate partner sexual violence (IPSV) is a significant aspect of intimate partner violence (IPV). While intimate partners commit one third of sexual assaults, IPSV is often overlooked in studies about IPV, in research on sexual violence. There are difficulties identifying, defining,, measuring IPSV,, research lacks consistency in terminology, measurement. The purpose of this article is to review the terms, definitions,, measurements associated with IPSV. Academic journals, nonscholarly documents from the United States were searched for articles, reports associated with the study of sexual violence, IPV. Forty-nine documents met the criteria for inclusion. A four-part taxonomy defining IPSV was developed, which included IPSV, intimate partner sexual coercion, intimate partner sexual abuse,, intimate partner forced sexual activity. The average weighted prevalence rates of these various forms of IPSV were calculated across included research studies. However, the measurements generally used to assess IPV do not adequately measure IPSV. Future research should consist terms to ensure consistent conceptualization, measurement of IPSV, to inform practice with survivors.

title: Do (un)certainty appraisal tendencies reverse the influence of emotions on risk taking in sequential tasks?
authors: Bagneux, Virginie, Bollon, Thierry, Dantzer, Cécile
abstract: According to the Appraisal-Tendency Framework (Han, Lerner, \& Keltner, 2007), certainty-associated emotions increase risk taking compared with uncertainty-associated emotions. To date, this general effect has only been shown in static judgement, decision-making paradigms; therefore, the present study tested the effect of certainty on risk taking in a sequential decision-making task. We hypothesised that the effect would be reversed due to the kind of processing involved, as certainty is considered to encourage heuristic processing that takes into account the emotional cues arising from previous decisions, whereas uncertainty leads to more systematic processing. One hundred, one female participants were induced to feel one of three emotions (film clips) before performing a decision-making task involving risk (Game of Dice Task; Brand et al., 2005). As expected, the angry, happy participants (certainty-associated emotions) were more likely than the fearful participants (uncertainty-associated emotion) to make safe decisions (vs. risky decisions).

title: Safety, services for survivors of intimate partner violence: A researcher-practitioner dialogue on the impact of COVID-19
authors: Bagwell-Gray, Meredith E, Bartholmey, Erin
journal: Psychological trauma: theory, research, practice, policy
abstract: This commentary offers a dialogue between a researcher, practitioner on the potential benefits of collaborative research to benefit survivors of intimate partner violence (IPV), a population exposed to high levels of violence, trauma. The dialogue occurred in a written, back-and-forth exchange, with the researcher, practitioner taking turns asking, responding to questions. The questions posed, answered in this commentary include: How are clients at an emergency domestic violence shelter experiencing the pandemic? How do you think a researcher or community member can help during a time like this? What should a researcher consider when engaging in collaborative research partnerships with service providers during this time? The answers offer insights into the importance of developing strong researcher-practitioner partnerships to improve services for trauma survivors during a global crisis.
