title: Sense of community: Advances in measurement, application
authors: Chavis, D, Pretty, G
abstract: This article summarizes theoretical, methodological advances in the study, application of a SOC,, serves as the introduction to a special issue devoted to this subject. Four themes emerged from the review. The first was that there continues to be a search for additional measures, despite the popularity of the SOC Index (SCI). Current investigations have begun to look at individual, group level effects of a SOC. Research continues to find an important, complicated relationship between the neighborhood (as a residential community), a SOC, contrary to the proliferation of communities that are not based on place. Research was also discovered investigating the relationship between a SOC, history, attachment,, identity. A SOC was found to be used as a catalyst for community justice, change in several national, local initiatives. © 1999 John Wiley \& Sons, Inc.

title: Privatisation, security, community: How master planned estates are changing suburban Australia
authors: Cheshire, Lynda, Walters, Peter, Wickes, Rebecca

title: Unpacking spatio-temporal differences of risk for crime: An analysis in Little Rock, AR
authors: Chillar, Vijay F, Drawve, Grant
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Introduction Risk terrain modeling (RTM) is spatial analysis that constructs an assessment of how the built environment influences events, such as crime,, is designed to provide actionable results that move the focus off of people, turn the attention to risky places. Excluded from previous studies utilizing RTM is the inclusion of a temporal element, which should be considered when developing tailored policing strategies. The goal of the current study is to account for police shifts, the modal violent crime within each police division in Little Rock, Arkansas. Using RTM to build division, shift specific models allows results to be translated into actionable intel by Little Rock Police Department (LRPD) to develop crime, risk reduction strategies tailored to their respective divisions, shifts.

title: An assessment of the relationship between private security companies, the police in crime prevention in Lagos Metropolis, Nigeria
authors: Chinwokwu, Eke Chijioke
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This study examined the relationship between private security companies (PSCs), the police during crime prevention in Lagos Metropolis, Nigeria. The study elicited data from 1500 randomly selected respondents to a self-administered survey. Data were further collected through purposive in-depth interviews. Descriptive statistics was used for data analysis. The results showed that operational collaboration, networking between PSCs, the police during crime-prevention strategies in Lagos Metropolis were imperative for achieving a crime-free society. The study shows that PSCs, the police are in a collaborative relationship that has had a positive impact on the reduction in crime; however, synergy between PSCs, the police is weak. The study further found that areas in which PSCs, the police collaborate include: escort duties, static guards, investigation, crowd control, patrol duties. The study also showed that most of the respondents identified areas of future collaboration, improvement between PSCs, the police, including: training, intelligence sharing, investigation, prosecution. The study findings show that both PSCs, the police see their relationship as cordial, complementary, although sometimes unequal, competitive. The study highlights a need to improve interagency collaboration, networking; strengthen collaboration between PSCs, the police;, pool technical resources to fight crime in Lagos Metropolis in particular,, Nigeria in general.

title: Racial typification of crime, support for punitive measures
authors: Chiricos, Ted, Welch, Kelly, Gertz, Marc
abstract: This paper assesses whether support for harsh punitive policies toward crime is related to the racial typification of crime for a national random sample of households (N=885), surveyed in 2002. Results from OLS regression show that the racial typification of crime is a significant predictor of punitiveness, independent of the influence of racial prejudice, conservatism, crime salience, southern residence, other factors. This relationship is shown to be concentrated among whites who are either less prejudiced, not southern, conservative, for whom crime salience is low. The results broaden our understanding of the links between racial threat, social control, beyond those typically associated with racial composition of place. They also resonate important themes in what some have termed modern racism, what others have described as the politics of exclusion.

title: The Health Action Process Approach as a motivational model for physical activity self-management for people with multiple sclerosis: a path analysis
authors: Chiu, Chung-Yi, Lynch, Ruth T, Chan, Fong, Berven, Norman L
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the Health Action Process Approach (HAPA) as a motivational model for physical activity self-management for people with multiple sclerosis (MS). DESIGN: Quantitative descriptive research design using path analysis. PARTICIPANTS: One hundred ninety-five individuals with MS were recruited from the National Multiple Sclerosis Society, a neurology clinic at a university teaching hospital in the Midwest. OUTCOME MEASURES: Outcome was measured by the Physical Activity Stages of Change Instrument, along with measures for nine predictors (severity, action self-efficacy, outcome expectancy, risk perception, perceived barriers, intention, maintenance self-efficacy, action, coping planning,, recovery self-efficacy). RESULTS: The respecified HAPA physical activity model fit the data relatively well (goodness-of-fit index = .92, normed fit index = .91,, comparative fit index = .93) explaining 38\% of the variance in physical activity. Recovery self-efficacy, action, coping planning,, perceived barriers directly contributed to the prediction of physical activity. Outcome expectancy significantly influenced intention, the relationship between intention, physical activity is mediated by action, coping planning. Action self-efficacy, maintenance self-efficacy,, recovery self-efficacy directly or indirectly affected physical activity. Severity of MS, action self-efficacy had an inverse relationship with perceived barriers, perceived barriers influenced physical activity. CONCLUSIONS: Empirical support was found for the proposed HAPA model of physical activity for people with MS. The HAPA model appears to provide useful information for clinical rehabilitation, health promotion interventions.

title: A latent class analysis of family characteristics linked to youth offending outcomes
authors: Chng, Grace S, Chu, Chi Meng, Zeng, Gerald, Li, Dongdong, Ting, Ming Hwa
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: family factors; latent class analysis; youth offending;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage
abstract: OBJECTIVES: There were two aims to this study: firstly, to identify family subtypes of Singaporean youth offenders based on eight family variables. Secondly, the associations of these family subtypes with youth offending outcomes were tested. METHODS: With a sample of 3,744 youth, a latent class analysis was first conducted based on eight family variables. Multivariate analyses, a Cox regression were subsequently performed to analyze the associations of the family classes with age at first arrest, age at first charge,, recidivism. RESULTS: A three-class solution was found to have the best fit to the data: (1) intact functioning families had little family risk; (2) families with criminality had higher probabilities of family criminality, of drug/alcohol abuse,, of being nonintact;, (3) poorly managed families received the poorest parenting, were more likely to be nonintact. Youth offenders from the latter two classes were arrested, charged at younger ages. Additionally, they reoffended at a quicker rate. CONCLUSIONS: Family backgrounds matter for youth offending outcomes. Interventions have to be multifaceted, targeted at the family in order to mitigate the risk of young offenders from developing into pathological adult criminals.

title: Sleepy punishers are harsh punishers: Daylight saving time, legal sentences
authors: Cho, Kyoungmin, Barnes, Christopher M, Guanara, Cristiano L
keywords: daylight saving time; legal sentencing; moral judgment; sleep; third-party punishment
abstract: The degree of punishment assigned to criminals is of pivotal importance for the maintenance of social order, cooperation. Nonetheless, the amount of punishment assigned to transgressors can be affected by factors other than the content of the transgressions. We propose that sleep deprivation in judges increases the severity of their sentences. We took advantage of the natural quasi-manipulation of sleep deprivation during the shift to daylight saving time in the spring, analyzed archival data from judicial punishment handed out in the U.S. federal courts. The results supported our hypothesis: Judges doled out longer sentences when they were sleep deprived.

title: Depression, anxiety in Hong Kong during COVID-19
authors: Choi, Edmond Pui Hang, Hui, Bryant Pui Hung, Wan, Eric Yuk Fai
journal: International journal of environmental research, public health
keywords: COVID-19; Hong Kong; anxiety; depression; mental health;322\_経済圧力
abstract: It has been three months since the first confirmed case of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) in Hong Kong,, people now have a more complete picture of the extent of the pandemic. Therefore, it is time to evaluate the impacts of COVID-19 on mental health. The current population-based study aimed to evaluate the depression, anxiety of people in Hong Kong during the COVID-19 pandemic. Respondents were randomly recruited, asked to complete a structured questionnaire, including the patient health questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9), the generalized anxiety disorder-7 (GAD-7), the global rating of change scale, items related to COVID-19. Of the 500 respondents included in the study, 19\% had depression (PHQ-9 score ≥ 10), 14\% had anxiety (GAD score ≥ 10). In addition, 25.4\% reported that their mental health had deteriorated since the pandemic. Multiple logistic regression analysis found that not experiencing the SARS outbreak in 2003, being worried about being infected by COVID-19, being bothered by having not enough surgical masks, being bothered by not being able to work from home were associated with a poorer mental health status. Psychological support, such as brief, home-based psychological interventions, should be provided to citizens during the pandemic.

title: The mobility crime triangle for sexual offenders, the role of individual, environmental factors
authors: Chopin, Julien, Caneppele, Stefano
journal: Sexual abuse: a journal of research, treatment
keywords: rape; schema; sexual abuse; sexual offender; typology; victim;330\_SAEnv
abstract: This study-based on a national data set (N = 1,447)-focuses on extrafamilial sexual assaults, their mobility. Spatial information about the offender's house, the victim's house,, the crime scene was combined in mobility crime triangles. The findings reveal that most of the assaults fall in the categories of total mobility (42.78\%), offender mobility (33.10\%). Our results also show the validity of the distance decay function with over 50\% of aggressions occurring within 3 km of the offender's house. The analysis did not reveal the existence of buffer zones, probably due to the acquaintance between some of the offenders, their victims. The evidence suggests that environmental risk factors are more significant than individual ones when it comes to explaining the variation among mobility patterns in sexual assaults. Offenders appear to adapt their mobility patterns, modus operandi according to the environmental constraints. Often, offenders choose their own or their victim's house as a safe environment for performed sexual assault.

title: Public versus expert knowledge, perception of climate change-induced heat wave risk: a modified mental model approach
authors: Chowdhury, Parnali Dhar, Haque, C Emdad, Driedger, S Michelle
abstract: Effects of climate change, its induced extreme environmental events have been the object of intense public debate in recent years. Extreme environmental events, such as heat waves,, their impact upon the elderly, the poor are of special concern to policy-, decision-makers. However, how the public views these issues is critical for dealing with the associated risks. Recognizing the importance of risk assessments, implementation of mitigation measures, we adopted a comparative approach to assess, extend a generic methodology to examine diverse sets of beliefs about climate change-induced heat wave hazards. Using a modified mental model approach, this study mapped existing knowledge structures about the risk associated with climate change-induced heat waves in an urban setting of Canada (Winnipeg, Manitoba). ‘Public models’ were developed from open-ended interviews with diverse community groups; ‘influence diagrams’ were formulated based on open-ended discussions with experts in the pertinent fields. An assessment of the juxtaposition of the public, experts’ knowledge, perception of heat wave risk has revealed significant gaps in the perception of: (a) the effects of climate change-induced heat wave, (b) of responsible authority for policy intervention to affect the cause or impacts. It further identifies misconceptions in public perception regarding: (a) thinning of ozone layer to cause a rise in earth’s temperature;, (b) whether precautionary measures can be taken to reduce heat wave mortality; (c) of future heat wave ‘risk estimation’ in the city of Winnipeg. Based on our results, we argue that by developing interactive risk communication tools, practicing public engagement in knowledge enhancement, heat wave risk assessment, mitigation capacity of both public, experts can be improved.

title: Rapists' behaviors to avoid police detection
authors: Chopin, Julien, Beauregard, Eric, Bitzer, Sonja, Reale, Kylie

title: Geocoding child sexual abuse: An explorative analysis on journey to crime, to victimization from French police data
authors: Chopin, Julien, Caneppele, Stefano
keywords: Crime patterns; Journey to crime; Modus operandi; Rational choice; Sexual crime; Spatial behavior;330\_SAEnv;Journey to crime/victimization
abstract: BACKGROUND: For several years, the link between mobility, human behavior, crime have highlighted by criminologists. Nevertheless, due to the difficulty of compiling sensitive geographical data, the spatial behavior of extrafamilial child abusers has received little empirical attention. OBJECTIVE: The purpose of this study is to explore the spatial mobility of victims, offenders of extrafamilial child abuse under the lens of the crime mobility triangle methodology. The main objective is to analyze the distribution of the spatial mobility patterns, determine which factors are associated with these patterns. PARTICIPANTS: This study analyses the characteristics of 612 cases of extrafamilial child abuses recorded by the French police between 1979, 2013. METHODS: By using police data, this research analyses firstly the journey to crime, the victims of child abuse with descriptive analyses. Secondly, geographical data are merged to compute, classify the cases in the geometric, geographic mobility typologies. Thirdly, multivariate analyses are used to identify which factors are associated with each specific mobility pattern. RESULTS: Results suggest that the journeys to crime, victimization are shorter compared to cases of adult sexual abuse. Over 50\% of aggression occurred within 2.5 km of offenders' houses, 0.5 km of victims' residences. Acquaintanceship is more important when the victims are younger while the expansion of routine activities associated with secondary socialization increases the risk of aggression in public spaces. CONCLUSIONS: Journeys to crime are affected by children routine activities, modus operandi parameters, whereas offenders' characteristics were found to have no impact on the spatial behavior.

title: The labeling of convicted felons, its consequences for recidivism
authors: Chiricos, Ted, Barrick, Kelle, Bales, William, Bontrager, Stephanie
abstract: Florida law allows judges to withhold adjudication of guilt for individuals who have been found guilty of a felony, are being sentenced to probation. Such individuals lose no civil rights, may lawfully assert they had not been convicted of a felony. Labeling theory would predict that the receipt of a felony label could increase the likelihood of recidivism. Reconviction data for 95,919 men, women who were either adjudicated or had adjudication withheld show that those formally labeled are significantly more likely to recidivate in 2 years than those who are not. Labeling effects are stronger for women, whites,, those who reach the age of 30 years without a prior conviction. Second‐level indicators of county characteristics (e.g., crime rates or concentrated disadvantage) have no significant effect on the adjudication/recidivism relationship.

title: The impact of residential context on adolescents' Subjective Well being
authors: Cicognani, Elvira, Albanesi, Cinzia, Zani, Bruna
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
abstract: AbstractThe study investigates the impact of residential context on stressful events, Subjective Well being (Emotional, Psychological) in young people living in a deprived geographical area,, the mediating role of personal (Self‐Efficacy), social (Social Support, Sense of Community) variables. A questionnaire was submitted to 297 subjects (48.5\% males): 203 adolescents (14–19 years old), 94 young adults (20–27 years old), from different socio‐economic (SES) levels. Results confirm the significant impact of the residential context on youngsters' perceived residential quality, Stress, Subjective Well being outcomes; such effect partly differs according to participants' gender, age. Adolescents are less satisfied of their living context, enjoy lower well being than young adults. Social resources (Friend, Family Support) significantly buffer the effect of a deprived residential context of youngsters' Well being, whereas personal resources (Self‐Efficacy) directly increase Well being levels. Copyright © 2008 John Wiley \& Sons, Ltd.

title: The role of task demands, processing resources in the use of base-rate, individuating information
authors: Chun, Woo Young, Kruglanski, Arie W
abstract: This article addresses the process that governs the use of base-rate, individuating information. Five experiments demonstrated that, for both, informational length, order of presentation (determining processing difficulty) interact with the recipients' processing resources to determine use. In cases in which the base-rate or the individuating information is brief and/or is presented early, the tendency to use it is greater under limited cognitive resources (cognitive load) than under ample cognitive resources. In contrast, in cases in which the base-rate or the individuating information is lengthy and/or is presented late in the informational sequence, the tendency to use it is greater under ample versus limited resources. These results suggest the appropriateness of conceptually decoupling informational contents (having to do with base rates or individuating descriptions) from the task demands (processing ease or difficulty) that a given judgmental problem presents, that may require different amounts of processing resources.

title: A review of crime prevention activities in an Australian local government area since the late 1980s
authors: Clancey, Garner, Metcalfe, Laura
abstract: To date, there has been limited analysis of local crime prevention approaches adopted in one council or local government area over time. This article seeks to partially address this gap. By reviewing crime prevention initiatives adopted by a single council in New South Wales (Australia) over time, it was possible to identify some continuities, discontinuities, to reflect on the impact of crime trends, changing demography on local approaches to crime prevention. Through a desktop analysis of the demographic profile of the area, crime trends across time,, crime prevention plans drafted by the council from the late 1980s, it became apparent that the council has adopted a myriad of crime prevention measures, many of which have continued over numerous years, complicating evaluation efforts of whole crime prevention plans, individual crime prevention measures; the cultural, linguistic diversity of the area has greatly affected how crime prevention is conceptualised, delivered, that crime trends have impacted crime prevention planning, but perhaps not in as clear a manner as might be expected. This case study highlights the challenges facing local governments with diverse populations, covering large geographic areas, with limited funding to support crime prevention activities,, raises questions about the roles of higher tiers in government in preventing crime.

title: Crime, crime prevention in an Australian growth centre
authors: Clancey, Garner, Kent, Jennifer, Lyons, Adam, Westcott, Harriet
abstract: Drawing on a case study of a growth centre on the fringe of Australia’s most populous city, Sydney, this article considers some of the potential crime generating consequences of urban sprawl, the associated challenges of planning for crime prevention. Significant population growth residing in predominantly detached houses on the urban fringe will potentially increase opportunities for crime. Empty completed dwellings prior to occupation; lengthy commuting to employment for new residents; financial pressures associated with ‘mortgage stress’;, growing numbers of young people are some of the potential crime generators in the area. Through this case study, we illustrate some of the complexities of large-scale, peri-urban, residential development, the challenges of embedding crime prevention during this period of rapid, sustained population growth.

title: Fear in fear-of-crime
authors: Clark, Julie
journal: Psychiatry, psychology,, law: an interdisciplinary journal of the Australian, New Zealand Association of Psychiatry, Psychology, Law
abstract: In this article, fear-of-crime research is integrated with multidisciplinary knowledge on fear, phobias. At present, many of the practical applications stemming from criminological research have treated fear-of-crime as a crime phobia, have attempted to reduce or even eliminate it from the community. Using Rachman's three components of fear to discuss reported experiences of this phenomenon, it is shown that little is known about the fear in fear-of-crime. The difference between a normal fear, a phobia rests on a continuum of emotional intensity. The placement of the fear within fear-of-crime on that continuum cannot be established from current research. It is recommended that further work be done to determine how people respond emotionally to crime, why such a response is elicited. It is also suggested that the assumption that fear-of-crime be treated as a crime phobia, eliminated from the community be tested through greater knowledge of the fear in fear-of-crime.

title: Examination of systematic variations in burglars' domain-specific perceptual, procedural skills
authors: Clare, Joseph
abstract: Abstract This research examines systematic variations in residential burglars' domain-specific perceptual, procedural skills. Utilising a formula incorporating frequency of offending, generation of offending-related income, burglary charges,, estimated duration of burglary career, 53 experts, 53 novices were objectively identified from a sample of 209 interviews conducted with incarcerated burglars. The perceptual, procedural burglary skills of these two groups were compared, the results demonstrated important differences indicative of superior domain-specific performance for objectively classified experts. The theoretical implications of these findings are discussed, along with suggestions for application of this knowledge to crime prevention initiatives.

title: Patterns of police, fire,, ambulance calls-for-service: Scanning the spatio-temporal intersection of emergency service problems
authors: Clare, Joseph, Townsley, Michael, Birks, Daniel J, Garis, Len
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Abstract Independent analysis of police, fire,, ambulance calls for service demonstrates common patterns in emergency service activity. Targeted, place-focused interventions have been demonstrated to prevent future problems for emergency services. This research builds on these findings to examine the spatial, temporal intersection of police, fire,, ambulance incidents to explore the potential utility of enhanced collaboration between emergency-first responders. Using police, fire data from Surrey, BC, Canada, from 2011 to 2013, spatial, temporal patterns of police-, fire-,, ambulance-related incidents were examined. Initial analyses demonstrate that 36\% of the City’s area experienced 72\% of incidents responded to over this 3-year study period. Focusing on this high-volume area, the spatial, temporal intersection of these incident types was explored. Spatially, lattices of varying cell sizes (250 m, 500 m,, 1,000 m) were placed over the study area. Temporally, incident volume was examined across the entire 3-year study period,, at yearly, monthly intervals. Incidents were placed within these spatial, temporal frameworks, visual inspection was utilized to assess the convergence of service demand. Regardless of the cell grid size, police, fire,, ambulance incidents were spatially, temporally concentrated, with the top 10\% of cells accounting for approximately 50\% of all incidents across all services. Furthermore, there was considerable spatio-temporal convergence in cells which account for the top decile of call volume for all incident types. A 2 × 2 typology is proposed to classify locations (in this case grid cells) based on (1) the frequency at which they generate high demand for services (sporadic versus persistent),, (2) the combination of agencies required to respond to high demand problems (single versus convergent). The spatial, temporal convergence of emergency service problems observed in this study suggests that an interagency approach to problem identification will enhance problem analysis processes. Working in conjunction with established problem-focused intervention strategies (such as problem-oriented policing), the volume-service typology provides a framework that can contribute to the development of appropriate problem-responses. This, we hope, will support emerging efforts to increase the extent to which emergency-first responder agencies collaborate to maximize efficiency, effectiveness,, reduce harm.

title: What predicts where sex offenders live? An examination of census tract data in Minnesota
authors: Clark, Valerie A, Duwe, Grant
abstract: Communities across the United States have become increasingly concerned over the presence of sex offenders in their neighborhoods. The purpose of this research is to examine the factors that are associated with the concentration of sex offenders in a large geographic area with few residency restrictions. This research also examines multiple categories of sex offenders subject to varying levels of community notification, allowing for an assessment of what, if any, effect community notification has on the residential patterns of sex offenders. Concentrated disadvantage, concentrated affluence,, housing affordability are all significant factors in explaining the concentration of multiple categories of sex offenders. Concentrated affluence relative to poverty is the most consistent predictor of sex offender concentration, revealing that more affluent communities ward off sex offender residents, regardless of community notification requirements.

title: The impact of child maltreatment, intimate partner violence surveillance initiatives
authors: Clinton-Sherrod, A Monique, Gibbs, Deborah A, Crosby, Alexander, Melanson, Cindi, Loomis, Kellie M, Farris, Tonya, Leeb, Rebecca T
journal: International journal of injury control, safety promotion
abstract: Child maltreatment (CM), intimate partner violence (IPV) take a tremendous toll on communities around the world. Despite the impact of CM, IPV, data on their incidence are drawn from disparate sources of varying quality. To improve data resources in these areas, the Centers for Disease Control, Prevention's (CDC) Division of Violence Prevention funded state-based IPV, CM surveillance activities in nine states between 1994, 2005. This article describes reported outcomes of these surveillance programmes; assesses factors affecting their sustainability;, provides recommendations for similar programmes through document review, interviews with state representatives. Findings indicate that states achieved outcomes with these surveillance initiatives; however, states noted concerns with sustaining systems because of a lack of resources, ineffective collaborations. Highlighted in this article are several lessons that other countries can learn from the experiences of these states in testing CM, IPV surveillance systems.

title: Counteracting the deviance of depression: Peer support groups for victims
authors: Coates, Dan, Winston, Tina
abstract: Early laboratory research has shown that when people are faced with a stressfull situation they prefer the company of those facing the same unpleasant event. In this paper we extend this work by examining the impact that peer support group membership has on the mental health of participants, individuals who have sought the help of similarly afflicted others. We present a theoretical argument which proposes that needs for evaluating the appropriateness of one's emotional reactions to victimization are not likely to be met through normal social interactions, leading to feelings of perceived self deviance which could contribute to depression. We suggest that needs for validation, however, could be fulfilled when a victim is able to share emotional reactions with those having similar experiences in peer support groups. Indirect evidence from other research, relevant data from our pilot study on peer support for rape victims indicates that feelings of deviance do tend to decline after group participation. The findings on the reduction of negative affect of group members are rather limited, but positive outcomes generally have been obtained in groups facilitated by professionals. We conclude by suggesting some of the functions that peer support groups may serve for participants in the hopes of increasing their general effectiveness as vehicles for depression reduction.

title: The legal control of drunken driving: A comment on methodological concerns in assessing deterrent effectiveness
authors: Cohen, Jacqueline
abstract: Appearing in this volume are papers by Votey, Phillips, Ray,, Votey that raise basic questions about the effectiveness of efforts to reduce drunken driving through legal controls implemented in the criminal justice system. The primary issues of extent, source,, duration of any effect are raised by those authors. This paper discusses the concern for deterrence expressed by Phillips, et al.,, particularly focuses on some methodological problems in demonstrating the deterrent effectiveness of criminal sanctions on drunken driving.

title: Multilevel analyses for predicting sequence effects of financial, employment problems on the probability of arrest
authors: Cohen, Patricia, Chen, Henian, Hamigami, Fumiaki, Gordon, Kathy, McArdle, John J

title: The effects of news stories that put crime, violence into context: testing the public health model of reporting
authors: Coleman, Renita, Thorson, Esther
abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine whether changing the way newspaper stories report crime, violence can induce shifts in readers' perceptions of the problem. Using an experiment that manipulates the framing, graphic presentation of newspaper stories on crime, violence, we seek to discover whether the public health model that calls for news stories to incorporate information on context, risk factors,, prevention strategies will help readers learn more about the context in which crime, violence occurs, endorse prevention strategies in addition to punishment,, become more attuned to societal risk factors, causes of crime, violence.

title: Information quantity, communication effectiveness: Low‐impact messages on wilderness trailside bulletin boards
authors: Cole, David N, Hammond, Timothy P, McCool, Stephen F
abstract: This study assessed the attention wilderness visitors gave to environmental messages encouraging low‐impact practices posted on trailside bulletin boards at a national wilderness area, the ability of visitors to retain message content,, their ability to correctly identify agency‐recommended practices. The number of posted messages was varied from two to eight, as well as whether there was a map posted beside the messages, to assess the effect of information quantity, a message attractant. Hikers experienced a significant increase in knowledge levels following exposure to messages, but there was evidence of information overload when numerous messages were posted. As the number of messages increased, total message attention increased, but the attention devoted to each message, the ability to retain message content declined. This finding helps explain why hikers exposed to all eight messages could not identify any more of the agency‐recommended low‐impact practices than those exposed to only two messages. Posting a map had no effect on message attention or message content retention.

title: Assault as a function of time, temperature: A moderator-variable time-series analysis
authors: Cohn, Ellen G, Rotton, James
abstract: The authors hypothesized that relations between temperature, assaults are stronger during evening hours than during other hours of the day, tested this hypothesis by obtaining 3-hr measures of assaults, temperature,, other weather variables for a 2-year interval. The hypothesis was confirmed by autoregressio n analyses that controlled for secular trends, seasonal differences, other weather variables, holidays,, other calendar events. In addition, as predicted by the negative affect escape model, assaults declined after reaching a peak at moderately high temperatures. The inverted Ushaped relation survived tests that controlled for secular trends, seasonality, autocorrelation, outliers,, heteroscedasticity. In addition, consistent with routine activity theory, moderator-variable regression analyses indicated that relations were strongest during evening hours, on weekends.

title: Testing the effect of framing, sourcing in health news stories
authors: Coleman, Renita, Thorson, Esther, Wilkins, Lee
abstract: This study examines whether changing the way news stories report on health can induce shifts in readers' perceptions of problems of obesity, diabetes, immigrant health,, smoking. The authors manipulated two variables in a controlled experiment: the quality of sourcing-the number of sources, their expertise-and the framing-changing from an episodic, traditional frame to a thematic frame that incorporated information on context, risk factors, prevention strategies,, social attributions of responsibility. The authors found that a thematic frame made readers more supportive of public policy changes, encouraged them to improve their own health behaviors. However, it did not alter their attributions of responsibility for health problems from one of blaming individuals to seeing the larger social factors. Adding richer sourcing to the thematic frame did not increase these effects, nor did readers find the thematic stories to be more interesting, relevant, believable, important,, informative. In addition, there were differential results because of story topics that represent uncontrolled effects. The implications for improving health reporting to encourage positive change in society are discussed.

title: Alley-gates, domestic burglary: Findings from a longitudinal study in urban South Wales
authors: Rogers, Colin
abstract: The introduction of Crime Prevention Through Environmental design (CPTED) initiatives such as alley-gating is now widespread across the United Kingdom (UK),, has become part of the urban landscape. For practitioners, policy makers alike, erecting steel gates at entrances to alleys is seen as a major initiative for reducing domestic burglary. In particular, in the current climate of economic austerity, such apparently cost-effective measures may seem more attractive to policy makers, planners alike as they struggle to maintain public confidence in the criminal justice system, reduce levels of criminality. This paper examines one such alley-gate initiative at Cadoc, Barry, South Wales, based on 10 years of data collection,, considers the long-term impact upon recorded domestic burglary. It also probes local community perceptions of the gates in tackling the problem of crime.

title: The relationship between police procedural justice, police legitimacy,, people's willingness to cooperate with law enforcement: A meta-analysis
authors: Colin Bolger, P, Walters, Glenn D

title: Stranger child abduction, guardianship: Accompaniment, surveillance in attempted, completed cases
authors: Collie, Craig J R, Shalev Greene, Karen
abstract: The Routine Activity Theory construct of capable guardianship is used to examine the features of 78 cases of stranger child abduction, using an outcome-based approach to establishing the effectiveness of various potential sources of guardianship in preventing abduction attempts from becoming completed,, to test widely held, taught beliefs on this subject. Results show only direct oversight provided by an adult who sees themselves as personally responsible for a child to be a very effective means of abduction prevention, both dissuading, disrupting offences. Guardianship provided by other actors, such as peers, third-party passers-by, were not effective. Accompaniment by other children could dissuade offending, but failed to disrupt offences in progress. Sources of natural surveillance were ineffective. The finding regarding the ineffectiveness of peers was particularly surprising. The theoretical, practical implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Sense of community, participation in urban contexts
authors: Colombo, Monica, Mosso, Cristina, De Piccoli, Norma
journal: Journal of community \& applied social psychology
abstract: This paper questions the conceptions found in the principal theoretical approaches developed within psychological, social sciences to the problem of community, psychological sense of community. Some core assumptions that are recurrent in the various definitions of the concept of community are discussed. From these assumptions stem the idea of community as a sort of ideal‐type of the forms that social relationships may take, as a type of social collectivity characterized by a high degree of homogeneity, similarity. With reference to urban contexts, a more encompassing definition of community is needed so that the city may be regarded both as a local community, a local society. Copyright © 2001 John Wiley \& Sons, Ltd.

title: Validation of the technology acceptance model for police
authors: Colvin, Caran A, Goh, Angeline
abstract: The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) developed by Davis (1989) was used to develop a basic theoretical model that would explain why patrol officers embraced or rejected new computer technology. Davis identified two factors of technology acceptance: ease of use, usefulness. Items representing each factor were generated in focus groups with patrol officers,, subject matter experts (SMEs) provided evidence of content validity. Exploratory (EFA), confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) were conducted to assess the construct factorial validity of the factor structure. The two-factor model hypothesized by Davis (1989) was not supported. The EFA, however, identified a four-factor model that indicated a good fit to the data. The four factors were labeled as ease of use, usefulness, information quality,, timeliness. The findings suggested that the new factors of information quality, timeliness were the most important components of technology acceptance by patrol officers. Policy implications, future research directions are discussed.

title: Addressing the inconsistencies in fear of crime research: A meta-analytic review
authors: Collins, Rachael E
abstract: A great deal of research has been conducted on the fear of crime (FOC) to date. Despite this attention, there are a wide range of equivocal results in determining the segment of the population most likely to be afraid.A meta-analysis was conducted using 114 studies in order to gauge a quantitative relationship between FOC, several demographic variables at both the individual (e.g., race, gender), neighbourhood (i.e., the presence of incivilities, collective efficacy) level. The current analysis resulted in 572 effect sizes.The results show that 8 of the 12 selected demographic characteristics significantly predicted FOC.While data identifying the most fearful segments of the population are generally robust, a moderator variable analysis revealed several elements in the design of individual studies significantly impact the trends they observe, particularly the way FOC is measured, the phrasing of FOC questionnaires.

title: A spatial analysis of the neighborhood scale of residential perceptions of physical disorder
authors: Conley, Jamison, Stein, Rachel E, Davis, Clinton

title: Policing the platonic cave: Ethics, efficacy in police training
authors: Conti, Norman, Nolan, III, James J
abstract: This article seeks to understand the form, content, broader implications of police academy ethics training. We begin by detailing the mechanisms borrowed from (near) total/greedy institutions that are key elements in the academy training structure. These are noted in an ethnographic account that points out the importance of obedience to authority,, the resultant shame, honour, which function as the core of police socialization. We conclude by explicating the theoretical foundation of the police function, then move on to question how ethics training supports, or resists, this structure. Findings suggest that, even at its best, ethics training is likely to serve in restraining the professional vision of incoming police officers. Despite what can only be assumed to be the best of intentions, a traditional model of police as law enforcers is (re)generated within a recruit cohort while more progressive notions of the police role (i.e., working toward neighbourhood efficacy) are ignored. With this, truly ethical behaviour is structurally inhibited by theatrical efforts at maintaining the collective fiction of the police mandate.

title: Motivational aspects of community support for school‐based comprehensive sexuality education
authors: Constantine, Norman A, Slater, Jana Kay, Carroll, Julie

title: Police, media relations in an era of freedom of information
authors: Cooke, Louise, Sturges, Paul
abstract: Changes to how police forces in England, Wales are working to manage their public image in an environment of heightened accountability, transparency are explored. The locus of control of information shaping the portrayal of the police in the news media is discussed, as is the impact of the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) 2000. The findings from case studies of two police forces in the East Midlands are reported. The case studies indicate that, whilst police, media cooperation is not a new phenomenon, UK police forces are becoming increasingly proactive, strategic, professionalised in their use of the news media. For their part, the media are dependent on the news ‘fed’ to them on a regular basis by police press relations units. Nevertheless, thanks in particular to their use of the FOIA 2000, the media continue to play a role as independent watchdog, reporter of police activity.

title: The micro-situational context of sexual offences against adult women: Unpacking the role of guardianship intensity in disruption
authors: Cook, Alana, Leclerc, Benoit, Reynald, Danielle M, Wortley, Richard
abstract: The current study explores the way guardianship is perceived by offenders, the extent to which it affects the likelihood of disruption in sexual offences against adult females. Specifically, we compare the micro-situational contexts in which sexual offences against adult females are disrupted to those in which these offences are completed. Data on sexual crime events was collected from 138 adult males who were incarcerated for committing a sexual offence against a woman using a self-report questionnaire incorporating a crime-script framework. We found that the presence or availability of a guardian does not guarantee offence disruption. Rather, action taken by the guardian is the critical factor which determines a sexual offender’s decision to cease the offence.

title: The place of public fear in sentencing, correctional policy
authors: Cook, Carrie L, Lane, Jodi
abstract: Public opinion about sentencing, correctional issues has emerged in recent decades as a salient topic in criminology. Empirical studies have suggested that the public has dynamic perceptions about these criminal justice issues. Sentencing, correctional policy have become key issues confronting legislators, policymakers, as correctional budgets, public interest in these areas have increased. Despite the focus on public opinion about sentencing, corrections, previous research has largely ignored how the public feels about the role of policymakers regarding these issues,, what influences opinions about whether public fear should be an important consideration in policy decisions. The current study partly replicated the work of Cullen, colleagues by examining perceptions of crime salience, crime causation, goals of the criminal justice system,, attitudes towards imprisonment, rehabilitation. It uniquely examined perceptions about the importance of legislator consideration of a specific determinant, namely, public fear, in decision making about sentencing, correctional policy.

title: Thoughts on Victimization: If it Happened to Him or Her, Couldn't it Happen to You?
authors: Cooper, H H A, Freiner, Sarn
abstract: This article deals with problems of personal safety, security in current times. It addresses a variety of dangerous situations, their prudent avoidance. Training, education for classes at risk are suggested, along with the kinds of professional help that may be sought, utilized.

title: Crime prevention, young people: Models, future direction for youth night patrols
authors: Cooper, Trudi, Scott, John, Barclay, Elaine, Sims, Margaret, Love, Terence
abstract: This article presents a typology of different approaches to social crime prevention adopted by Australian Indigenous youth night patrols. Research that informed this typology occurred in a specific context, but generic observations about youth crime prevention policy are transferable to community youth crime prevention in other settings. The typology identifies several key points of difference between various service delivery models, in particular, different perceptions of relationships between crime prevention; community safety; community development; community self-determination; child protection;, youth development, welfare. Discussion teases out how political discourse frames concepts such as community governance, self-determination, paternalism,, funding accountability. The discussion illustrates how politicised decision-making has meant that policy makers responded selectively to programme evaluations, in ways that did not always maximise benefit. The typology is intended to be useful to youth crime prevention practitioners, evaluators,, policy makers.

title: Worrying about the future, fear of crime among young adults: a social psychological approach
authors: Cops, Diederik, Pleysier, Stefaan, Put, Johan
abstract: This article builds on recent insights in the fear of crime research tradition which tackle the poor theoretical substructure of most studies on this topic. Recent advances have acknowledged that both a social psychological approach, the interpretation of fear of crime as a ‘sponge’, absorbing more abstract, fundamental concerns about one's place in society, are essential elements to improve the understanding of this complex, multifaceted phenomenon. In this contribution, these suggestions, expressed in the relationship between more general worries about the personal future, fear of crime, are implemented, tested in a sample of Flemish young adults (N=1121) aged 19 to 24 years. The results demonstrate the potential of combining both perspectives in the study of the determinants of fear of crime in the often neglected social category of young people.

title: Effects of validity screening items on adolescent survey data
authors: Cornell, Dewey, Klein, Jennifer, Konold, Tim, Huang, Francis
abstract: In 2 studies, we examined the use of validity screening items in adolescent survey data. In each study, adolescent respondents were asked whether they were telling the truth, paying attention in answering survey questions. In Study 1 (N = 7,801), the prevalence rates of student risk behaviors were significantly lower after inappropriate (invalid) responders were screened out of the sample. In addition, confirmatory, multigroup factor analyses demonstrated significant differences between the factor structures of school climate scales with valid versus invalid responders. In Study 2, student perceptions of school climate were correlated with teacher perceptions in 291 schools. A bootstrap resampling procedure compared the correlations obtained with valid versus invalid responding students in each school, found that valid responders had more positive views of school conditions, produced higher correlations with teacher perceptions. These findings support the value of validity screening items in improving the quality of adolescent survey data.

title: Perceptions of police practice, cynicism of police performance,, persistent neighborhood violence: An intersecting relationship
authors: Corsaro, Nicholas, Frank, James, Ozer, Murat
abstract: A growing literature indicates that legal cynicism at the neighborhood level corresponds with retaliatory homicides, persistent homicide rates, net of controls. However, no study to date has examined: a) how cynicism of police performance might be influenced by specific experiences with, perceptions of the police,, b) whether neighborhood cynicism of police performance is associated with violent crime beyond homicides.This study analyzed citizen, neighborhood data from Cincinnati, Ohio in the late 1990s - a social setting that had antagonistic police-community relationships.The results revealed that perceived unjust policing was the strongest individual level correlate of cynicism of police services,, that aggregate levels of cynicism predicted both homicides, overall violence above, beyond social disorganization as well as previous levels of violence.We speak to the importance of these findings in terms of identifying which police-community factors seemingly have the greatest likelihood to facilitate the association between cynicism, persistent neighborhood violence.

title: Effect of fear of victimization on hazardous alcohol drinking, tobacco,, marijuana use among university students: A tale of two sexes
authors: Couture, Marie-Claude, Garcia, Dellanira, Whaley, Reid, Grinshteyn, Erin
keywords: Fear of victimization; Hazardous alcohol drinking; Marijuana use; Tobacco use; University students
abstract: BACKGROUND: Fear of victimization has been associated with poorer physical, mental health, yet is understudied in public health. Few studies have examined sex differences in the effects of fear of victimization on substance use. We examined associations between fear of victimization, hazardous alcohol drinking, tobacco,, marijuana use among female, male university students. METHODS: A cross-sectional study was conducted among university students in an urban location (n = 1415). Socio-demographics, substance use,, fear related to various crimes were measured using online surveys. All fear types were summed into a total fear score, categorized into quartiles: no/little fear, moderate fear, high fear,, very high fear. Chi-square tests, multiple logistic regression models were used to examine associations between fear of victimization, hazardous alcohol drinking, tobacco, marijuana use, by sex. RESULTS: Females were more likely to report high, very high fear of victimization (26.6\%, 33.1\%) than male students (19.8\%, 16.3\%; p < 0.001). In multiple logistic regression models, associations differed by sex: moderate, high,, very high fear were all independently associated with hazardous drinking among females but not males. Female students with very high fear of victimization were more likely to report tobacco use. High, very high fear was also independently associated with marijuana use among female only. CONCLUSIONS: Higher fear of victimization was associated with substance use among females but not male students. Public health, health care professionals should acknowledge fear of victimization as a potential risk factor for substance use, particularly among women.

title: Environmental criminology, the potential for reducing opportunities for bushfire arson
authors: Cozens, P, Christensen, W
abstract: Since the 1980s, the incidence of wildfires (forest fires), across the World has significantly increased (Jensen), climate change has been implicated in this trend (UNEP). In recent years, major wild fires have occurred in the United States, Canada, Australia, Indonesia, Latin America, Spain, Portugal, Greece, Iran, Russia, most recently, in Israel. In Australia, wildfires or forest fires are known as bushfires,, approximately 60 000 occur each year. Only 6 per cent are ‘natural fires’, while 90 per cent are the result of people's actions. Significantly, deliberate ignitions; incendiary (maliciously lit fires), suspicious fires account for 50 per cent of known fire causes (Bryant). Internationally, research in the field of bushfire arson prevention is currently dominated by offender-based approaches, which largely rely on incomplete, limited insights from a minority (less than 1 per cent) of arsonists who have been apprehended (Ogloff Tomison, Jones). This article explores how theories from environmental criminology can be used to understand, analyse place-based factors associated with deliberately lit bushfires. It also presents findings from a recent workshop conducted at the Australian Symposium on Bushfire Arson Prevention in order to further contextualise the relevance of environmental criminology to the analysis, reduction of bushfire arson.

title: Design strategies for mitigating the impact of anti-social behavior upon suburban rail timetables
authors: Coxon, Selby, Napper, Robbie, De Bono, Arthur
abstract: Train schedules are particularly important during service peak periods, short headways. Miscreant passenger behavior such as the inappropriate or malevolent use of the emergency communication alarm, or the deliberate holding open of doors, has a detrimental effect upon maintaining the service timetable. There is a general absence of literature in the transportation field examining this problem or offering potential solutions. Manipulating the design of the environment to provoke desired behaviors in people is a technique widely used in various disciplines from large architectural projects to more subtle uses of applied psychology. This article discusses a collaborative research project carried out between Monash University’s Department of Design, the French National Railway (SNCF). Two research projects are discussed as they relate particularly to SNCF’s network in the Ile-de-France. However, the design solutions may have pertinence for other networks similarly afflicted around the world.

title: A review, current status of Crime Prevention through Environmental Design (CPTED)
authors: Cozens, Paul, Love, Terence
abstract: This article reviews the current status of the concept of Crime Prevention through Environmental Design (CPTED). It provides an overview of its history, origins, defines how it is commonly understood, conceptualized. Globally, CPTED is an increasingly popular crime prevention strategy supported by governments all over Europe, North America, Australia,, New Zealand, as well as in Asia, South Africa. This review inspects some of the evidence associated with CPTED, provides a detailed overview of the main criticisms facing this field.

title: Modelling high-intensity crime areas: Comparing police perceptions with offence/offender data in Sheffield
authors: Craglia, Massimo, Haining, Robert, Signoretta, Paola
abstract: High-intensity crime areas are areas where high levels of violent crime coexist with large numbers of offenders, thereby creating an area that may present significant policing problems. In an earlier paper, the authors analysed police perceptions of high-intensity crime areas,, now extend that earlier work by comparing the police's perception of where such areas are located with offence/offender data. They also report on the construction of predictive models that identify the area-specific attributes that explain the distribution of such areas. By focusing on the city of Sheffield, the authors draw on a wider range of local area data than was possible in the original paper,, also question how widespread such areas may be in Sheffield.

title: Additional security patrols in residential areas: Notes from the marketplace
authors: Crawford, Adam, Lister, Stuart
abstract: This article presents an overview of an emerging market in residential security patrols in England, Wales. Drawing on recent empirical research, it outlines the fragmented, uneven nature of current developments, highlights coordination deficits, the absence of regulatory oversight. The research illustrates how the growth in competitive relations between different providers of patrol can stymie the development of effective networked security alliances. It demonstrates the capacity of additional policing schemes to fuel unrealistic expectations among local publics, raise security thresholds. Furthermore, it highlights how policing as commodity through residential patrols can foster exclusionary tendencies by serving parochial rather than public interests. This raises important challenges that demand robust forms of governance, accountability to guarantee an equitable, fair distribution of policing, security.

title: Counting woman abuse: a cautionary tale of two surveys
authors: Crocker, Diane
journal: International journal of social research methodology
abstract: This paper describes how the findings of two nationally representative Canadian surveys on woman abuse were taken up by both academics, the media. It puts the surveys in the context of debates about feminist epistemology, measurement. This context does now, however, fully account for the ways in which the findings were mobilized for apparently different purposes. Using a governmentality perspective, the paper illustrates the parallels between the way in which anti‐violence policies, the surveys have constituted the problem of woman abuse in ways that facilitate a particular form of governing gender. The paper argues that the wider shift to neo‐liberal forms of governance must be considered by feminists who count woman abuse in order to avoid contributing to this shift. The paper concludes with ways to undertake survey research on woman abuse.

title: Streets of San Francisco: Brunswik's lens model applied to urban inference, assessment
authors: Craik, Kenneth H, Appleyard, Donald
abstract: Brunswik's probabilistic functionalism, the lens model offers a conceptual framework for linking environmental assessment with environmental perception, cognition in the study of such urban problems as inference, action regarding crime opportunity, crime vulnerability. An adaptation of Brunswik's lens model is applied to analysis of inferences about urban conditions. The ecological validity of cues generated by technical, observational assessments of residential streets in San Francisco is gauged for three conditions: traffic volume, average family income, residents' concern about crime. The functional validity of estimates of these conditions by expert judges is also appraised,, policy capturing is illustrated.

title: Uncovering organized shoplifting, theft networks
authors: Crocker, Ruth, Skidmore, Michael, Webb, Sarah, Garner, Sarah, Gill, Martin, Graham, John
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Abstract This article explores the role of organized crime groups in persistent theft, shop theft. It is based on an analysis of police data using exploratory analytical techniques assessing the extent of connectivity between acquisitive offenders. The research also draws on qualitative data collected from interviews. The findings suggest that shop theft was predominantly committed by UK nationals; although foreign nationals were proportionately more likely to be involved in organized crime, there is some evidence that they may themselves be being exploited. The findings are discussed, suggestions for further research are made.

title: Spatial dynamics of white flight: The effects of local, extralocal racial conditions on neighborhood out-migration
authors: Crowder, Kyle, South, Scott J
abstract: We use longitudinal data from the Panel Study of Income Dynamics, data from three U.S. censuses,, techniques of spatial data analysis to examine how the composition of extralocal areas - those areas surrounding a householder's neighborhood of residence - affect the likelihood that whites will move out of their neighborhood. Net of the influence of local neighborhood conditions, other predictors of residential mobility, high concentrations of minorities in surrounding neighborhoods reduce the likelihood that white householders will move, presumably by reducing the attractiveness of the most likely residential alternatives. This effect suppresses the influence of the racial composition of the immediate neighborhood so that controlling for extralocal conditions provides substantially greater support for the white flight thesis than has previously been observed. We also find that recent growth in the size of the extralocal minority population increases the likelihood of white out-migration, accounts for much of the influence previously attributed to racial change in the local neighborhood. Finally, high levels of minority concentration in surrounding neighborhoods exacerbate the positive effect of local minority concentration on white out-migration. These results highlight the importance of looking beyond reactions to local racial conditions to understand mobility decisions, resulting patterns of segregation.

title: Fear of crime, the police: Exploring lifestyle, individual determinants among university students
authors: Crowl, Justin N, Battin, Joshua R
abstract: Using lifestyle exposure theory as a guide, this study examines the complex relationship between fear of crime, select lifestyle, individual-level constructs. Participants included undergraduate students at two state-funded universities located in Pennsylvania. Student fear of crime at both universities was examined to ascertain what factors influence this emotion-laden phenomenon. Results revealed support for several key fear of crime correlates. Notably, a significant relationship emerged between police visibility, fear of crime in the estimated partial, full models. Results also indicated that student lifestyle choices can impact fear of crime; this relationship can vary across samples, as evidenced in this study. It was also found that multiple individual characteristics, namely gender, race, living arrangement, were positively related to student fear of crime. A discussion, implications are offered to conclude.

title: Alcohol‐related problems, drug use,, male intimate partner violence severity among US couples
authors: Cunradi, Carol B, Caetano, Raul, Schafer, John
abstract: Background: Particularly for women, level of intimate partner violence (IPV) severity is associated with risk of injury. Previous research suggests that male drinking problems, drug use are key risk factors. Few studies, however, have examined the associations between male, female alcohol problems, drug use, risk of moderate, severe male IPV in general household population samples.Methods: A multiethnic sample of 1615 married, cohabiting couples was obtained from the 1995 National Study of Couples, a cross‐sectional study on alcohol, IPV. We assessed the contribution of past year male, female alcohol‐related problems (i.e., drinking consequences, alcohol‐dependence symptoms), illicit drug use to the risk of moderate, severe male IPV. A series of generalized multinomial logit models, with adjustment for sociodemographic, psychosocial covariates, was constructed to assess these associations.Results: Female, male alcohol‐related problems, female drug use, were associated with increased risk of moderate, severe male IPV. Contrary to our expectation, male drug use was not associated with elevated risk for either type of male IPV. Compared with couples residing in low‐unemployment neighborhoods, couples residing in high‐unemployment neighborhoods were at greater risk for severe, but not moderate, male IPV.Conclusions: Alcohol‐related problems among men, women, drug use among women, appear to be important correlates of male IPV severity among couples in the general population. These findings can aid in IPV screening efforts, the formulation of prevention strategies,, help inform batterer, victim treatment programs.

title: Alcohol outlets, neighborhood characteristics,, intimate partner violence: ecological analysis of a California city
authors: Cunradi, Carol B, Mair, Christina, Ponicki, William, Remer, Lillian
journal: Journal of urban health: bulletin of the New York Academy of Medicine
abstract: Neighborhood indicators of social disadvantage, such as poverty, unemployment, are associated with intimate partner violence (IPV). Despite the well-established link between heavy drinking, IPV, few studies have analyzed the contribution of alcohol outlet density to the occurrence of IPV. Greater numbers of alcohol outlets in a community may be a sign of loosened normative constraints against violence, promote problem drinking among at-risk couples,, provide environments where groups of persons at risk for IPV may form, mutually reinforce IPV-related attitudes, norms,, problem behaviors. This study used ecological data to determine if alcohol outlet density (number of bars, restaurants serving alcohol,, off-premise outlets per unit area) is related to rates of IPV-related police calls, IPV-related crime reports in Sacramento, California. Separate analyses for IPV calls, crime reports were conducted using Bayesian space-time models adjusted for area characteristics (poverty rate, unemployment rate, racial/ethnic composition). The results showed that each additional off-premise alcohol outlet is associated with an approximate 4\% increase in IPV-related police calls, an approximate 3\% increase in IPV-related crime reports. Bars, restaurants were not associated with either outcome. The findings suggest that alcohol outlet density, especially off-premise outlets, appear to be related to IPV events. Further research is needed to understand the mechanisms by which neighborhood factors, such as alcohol outlet density, affect IPV behaviors. Understanding these mechanisms is of public health importance for developing environmental IPV prevention strategies, such as changes in zoning, community action, education,, enforcement activities.

title: Mapping crime harm, priority locations in New Zealand: A comparison of spatial analysis methods
authors: Curtis-Ham, Sophie, Walton, Darren
abstract: Despite progress being advanced with spatial approaches to crime, crime control, the geography of crime harm has to date received little attention. The recent development of “Crime Harm Indices”, which weight crimes by an estimate of the relative harm they cause, offers an opportunity to improve on volume based spatial analysis approaches to identify where crime harm concentrates.This study aims to address this issue via the use of a Crime Harm Index (CHI) developed for New Zealand. By contrast to localized ‘harm-spotting’ analysis, we apply a census unit based approach to identify, at a macro level, the neighborhoods, wider communities suffering the highest crime harm in New Zealand. This approach enables harm to be viewed not only as a total Index but as a rate controlled for population, allows for the identification of census based sociodemographic factors which predict harm. Specifically, this paper compares the CHI with the New Zealand Priority Locations Index (PLI), an existing census unit based crime analysis tool which combines crime, demographic variables to identify communities vulnerable to crime, disorder issues.In this study CHI, PLI scores were calculated for Census Area Units (normally containing 3000–5000 population) across New Zealand. Bivariate correlations, a general linear model were used to determine the relationships between the CHI, PLI, additional population related variables. The CHI, PLI were weakly correlated, with population size, urban/rural categorization also accounting for CHI variance. Mapping techniques are used to illustrate outlier locations where the CHI, PLI differ widely, to identify location features which may assist in explaining CHI/PLI differences.This work exemplifies a novel geographic approach to the problem of crime harm with implications for resource allocation at national through to local levels. Wider implications for the theory, practice of crime, crime harm control are discussed, along with limitations of the study, areas for further research.

title: Women’s avoidance behaviours in public transport in the Ile-de-France region
authors: d'Arbois de Jubainville, Hugo, Vanier, Camille
abstract: Adaptive behaviours are an important aspect of personal safety. When feeling unsafe in public transport, women are likely to take avoidance measures. Drawing from a sample of 3188 women who participated in the victimisation survey “Cadre de vie et sécurité” (Living Environment, Security) between 2010, 2013, this study examines whether, how female passengers in the Ile-de-France region change their routines when feeling unsafe in the transit environment. Logistic regressions were conducted to assess the relationship between avoidance behaviours, individual characteristics, transport habits,, personal safety. Results suggest that education, previous victimisation,, declared perceived safety are consistently associated with time-based, space-based avoidance. However, avoidance appears to be constrained by transport habits, such as frequency of use, riding to work.

title: Crime, arrests,, pretrial jail incarceration: An examination of the deterrence thesis
authors: D'alessio, Stewart J, Stolzenberg, Lisa
abstract: Using longitudinal data calibrated in daily intervals, a vector ARMA (VARMA) study design, we investigate the causal relations among the number of crimes reported to the police, the frequency of arrest,, the number of defendants held in pretrial jail confinement. Results show a lagged negative effect of frequency of arrest on reported crime. As the number of wrests made by police increases, the number of index crimes reported to authorities decreases substantially the following day. Additionally the analysis reveals a significant positive contemporaneous relationship between criminal activity, arrest levels. No feedback effects among the three variables are noted. In sum, our findings add empirical support to the thesis that the instantaneous, lagged relationship between crime, clearances are of opposite sign. That is, criminal activity increases arrest levels instantaneously, or at least relatively so, while the negative effect of arrest levels on crime levels transpires more gradually.
