title: A longitudinal perspective on patterns of crime
authors: McCORD, Joan
abstract: AbstractThis article addresses the possibility of prospectively identfying chronic criminal offenders using identifiers available to the criminal justice system. Data were collected as part of a longitudinal study of the lives of men who were in a delinquency prevention program in the early 1940s. For the half who were randomly assigned to the treatment group, a discriminant function correctly identified 67\% of the men as recidivists or nonrecidivists. When tested on the control group, it correctly sorted 76\% of the men. The author argues that although prospective identification of recidivists may be possible, legal action based on predictions would be wrong.

title: Family relationships, juvenile delinquency,, adult criminality
authors: McCORD, Joan
abstract: Home observations during childhood, criminal records 30 years later are used to address questions of relative impact among features of child rearing influencing male criminal outcomes. The results suggest two mechanisms: Maternal behavior appears to influence juvenile delinquency and, through those effects, adult criminality. Paternal interaction with the family, however, appears to have a more direct influence on the probability of adult criminal behavior.

title: Sex-related offenses, fear of crime on campus
authors: McCreedy, Kenneth R, Dennis, Brent G
abstract: This paper is part of a larger study of reported, unreported crime on the campus of East Carolina University. The survey was conducted during the Spring of 1994,, involved a total sample of 760 respondents. Those questions dealing with rape, other sexual offenses, stalking,, lewd phone calls were used to determine the level of both reported, unreported incidents,, the relationship of such experiences to the students' overall fear of crime,, avoidance of night classes. Overall, students exhibited an extremely high concern about crime. Students who reported having received lewd and/or threatening phone calls were the most concerned, reluctant to take night classes.

title: Cops, computers, the curriculum
authors: McCoy, Mark R
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Computers have become an integral tool for use by police officers in performing their daily duties. However, little has been done to incorporate training on the use of these important tools in basic police academies, in-service training. This article details the need for integration of computer training in curricula of police academies to improve computer literacy among police officers. Models for successful curriculum integration are discussed, recommendations are provided for reducing the barriers to computer related training.

title: Energizing, de-motivating effects of norm-conflict
authors: McDonald, Rachel I, Fielding, Kelly S, Louis, Winnifred R
abstract: Norms have a pervasive influence on behavior, yet previous research has not addressed that people often face conflicting norms from multiple ingroups. The current research addresses this gap in the context of proenvironmental behavior, demonstrates two effects predicted by the novel theoretical position we offer: People can be de-motivated by norm-conflict, or conversely, norm-conflict can encourage people to take action. Studies 1, 2 demonstrated that norm-conflict is associated with increased perceived effectiveness for those with positive attitudes to the issue, reduced perceived effectiveness for those with moderate attitudes,, effectiveness perceptions mediated an indirect effect on behavioral intentions. Study 3 found that perceived effectiveness also moderates the effects of norm-conflict such that norm-conflict only influences intentions when perceived effectiveness is high. Norm-conflict is both positively, negatively related to behavioral decision making, suggesting additional considerations in the design of social norms-based interventions.

title: The varieties of religious development in adulthood: a longitudinal investigation of religion, rational choice
authors: McCullough, Michael E, Enders, Craig K, Brion, Sharon L, Jain, Andrea R
abstract: The authors used growth mixture models to study religious development during adulthood (ages 27-80) in a sample of individuals who were identified during childhood as intellectually gifted. The authors identified 3 discrete trajectories of religious development: (a) 40\% of participants belonged to a trajectory class characterized by increases in religiousness until midlife, declines in later adulthood; (b) 41\% of participants belonged to a trajectory class characterized by very low religiousness in early adulthood, age-related decline;, (c) 19\% of participants belonged to a trajectory class characterized by high religiousness in early adulthood, age-related increases. Gender, strength of religious upbringing, number of children, marrying,, agreeableness predicted membership in the trajectory classes. Results were largely consistent with the rational choice theory of religious involvement.

title: Conflicting norms highlight the need for action
authors: McDonald, Rachel I, Fielding, Kelly S, Louis, Winnifred R
abstract: Previous research has not addressed the possibility that people may face conflicting norms of pro-environmental behavior from their multiple in-groups. Across two studies, the authors test competing hypotheses: People may be demotivated by norm conflict, or conversely, norm conflict may motivate people to action. The results of both studies suggest a clearly motivating effect of conflict. Norm conflict was associated with decreased water usage (i.e., increased water conservation) in Study 1,, increased pro-environmental behavior intentions in Study 2. The effects of conflict were partially mediated by perceived effectiveness in Study 2. Although these initial findings indicate that conflict motivates rather than hinders behavioral engagement, future research should investigate whether the nature of the influence of norm conflict depends on factors such as issue importance.

title: The present, possible future of quantitative criminology
authors: McDowall, David

title: Project safe neighborhoods, violent crime trends in US cities: Assessing violent crime impact
authors: McGarrell, Edmund F, Corsaro, Nicholas, Hipple, Natalie Kroovand, Bynum, Timothy S

title: Risk taking from the participant's perspective: the case of driving, accident risk
authors: McKenna, Frank P, Horswill, Mark S
journal: Health psychology: official journal of the Division of Health Psychology, American Psychological Association
abstract: Although perceived health risk plays a prominent role in theories of health behavior, its empirical role in risk taking is less clear. In Study 1 (N = 129), 2 measures of drivers' risk-taking behavior were found to be unrelated to self-estimates of accident concern but to be related to self-ratings of driving skill, the perceived thrill of driving. In Study 2 (N = 405), out of a wide range of potential influences, accident concern had the weakest relationship with risk taking. The authors concluded that although health risk is a key feature in many theories of health behavior, a central focus for researchers, policy makers, it may not be such a prominent factor for those actually taking the risk.

title: Intelligence-led policing as a framework for responding to terrorism
authors: McGarrell, Edmund F, Freilich, Joshua D, Chermak, Steven
abstract: Leading police associations in the United States, the United Kingdom have advocated that law enforcement adopt an intelligence-led policing model (ILP). Much like the situation with community policing, there does not appear to be a commonly accepted definition of ILP nor of the practical implications for police agencies' mission, structure,, processes. This article presents a model of ILP that builds on community policing, problem solving,, continuous improvement business models that have been adopted by police departments. Examples of these practices are reviewed as a method of illustrating the promise of an ILP approach. A broad conceptualization of ILP is presented under the belief that ILP will be most likely integrated into law enforcement, will have the greatest impact if it is adopted from an “all crimes” perspective. The article concludes with illustrations of the utility of ILP for addressing threats of domestic, international terrorism.

title: Attachment, personality, female perpetrators of intimate partner violence
authors: McKeown, Annette
journal: The journal of forensic psychiatry \& psychology

title: “it's not really stalking if you know the person”: Measuring community attitudes that normalize, justify, minimise stalking
authors: McKeon, Bronwyn, McEwan, Troy E, Luebbers, Stefan
journal: Psychiatry, psychology,, law: an interdisciplinary journal of the Australian, New Zealand Association of Psychiatry, Psychology, Law
abstract: It has been hypothesised that attitudes minimising, justifying, normalising stalking exist in the community, influencing whether or not stalking is recognised,, potentially affecting the responses of police, others to whom victims turn for support. This study investigates the nature of these attitudes as measured using the Stalking Related Attitudes Questionnaire (SRAQ). Two hundred, forty-four community members, 280 police officers in Victoria, Australia (total sample 61\% male, mean age=43.3, SD = 13.3) completed the SRAQ. Full information factor analysis identified three underlying stalking-related attitudes: “stalking isn't serious”, “stalking is romantic”, “victims are to blame”. Males endorsed all to a greater extent than females, whereas police, community only differed in that police believed stalking to be more serious. Stronger stereotype endorsement was related to judgements of not guilty in a fictional stalking case. These results indicate that attitudes, beliefs that downplay, excuse, normalise stalking behaviour can be measured,, have some influence on recognition of stalking behaviour.

title: Peer influence on IPV by young adult males: Investigating the case for a social norms approach
authors: McKool, Marissa, Stephenson, Rob, Winskell, Kate, Teten Tharp, Andra, Parrott, Dominic
keywords: intimate partner violence; peer influence; social learning theory; social norms theory
abstract: Nearly 32\% of women report experiencing physical violence from an intimate partner, more than 8\% report being raped by a significant other in their lifetime. Young people's perceptions that their peers perpetrate relationship violence have been shown to increase the odds of self-reported perpetration. Yet, limited research has been conducted on this relationship as individuals begin to age out of adolescence. The present study sought to examine the link between the perception of peer perpetration of intimate partner violence (IPV), self-reported IPV perpetration among a sample of predominately young adult (21-35 years) males. This study also explored the discordance between the perception of peer IPV behavior, self-reported perpetration. Data from 101 male peer dyads (n = 202) were taken from a study on the effects of alcohol, bystander intervention in Atlanta, Georgia. Thirty-six percent (n = 73) of men reported perpetrating physical IPV, 67\% (n = 135) reported perpetrating sexual IPV in the past 12 months. Nearly 35\% (n = 55) of the sample reported that none of their peers had perpetrated physical IPV, which contradicted their friend's self-report of physical IPV perpetration. Similarly, 68\% (n = 115) of the men perceived none of their peers to have perpetrated sexual IPV, which contradicted their friend's self-report of sexual IPV perpetration. Discordance variables were significantly associated with self-reported perpetration for both physical (χ2 = 152.7, p < .01), sexual (χ2 = 164.4, p < .01) IPV. These results point to an underestimation of peer IPV perpetration among young adult males. Findings suggest a traditional social norms approach to IPV prevention, which seeks to persuade individuals that negative behaviors are less common than perceived, may not be the best approach given a significant number of men believed their friends were nonviolent when they had perpetrated violence.

title: Sexual violence on the college campus: a template for compliance with federal policy
authors: McMahon, Patricia Pasky
journal: Journal of American college health: J of ACH
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The author introduces a template, the Model Policy for the Prevention, Response to Sexual Assault, to assist institutions of higher education to benchmark campus policy compliance with federal laws directed at sexual assault. The author presents a detailed review of policy criteria recommended by the National Institute of Justice. The author proposes 2 unique criteria not found in the National Institute of Justice report for consideration for a comprehensive campus sexual assault policy. CONCLUSION: The template provides an inclusive system to benchmark campus sexual assault policies. Conforming to the template provides compliance with federal laws, demonstrates that the campus fosters a climate that does not tolerate sexual violence.

title: Sense of community, pathway to, or bridge from alienation?
authors: McMillan, David W, Lorion, Raymond P
keywords: learning, progressive perspectives; sense of community
abstract: Psychological Sense of Community (PSOC) represents a formative conceptual offering of Community Psychology to the social sciences. Nearly five decades ago, PSOC offered a window into the influence of ecological factors to understanding the emotional, behavioral well-being of members of disenfranchised, underserved segments of the population, especially members of minority, low-income subgroups. Our discipline's founders viewed PSOC as one promising vehicle for pursuing the desired paradigmatic shift from individual to systemically focused interventions to achieve intended outcomes of the emerging community mental health movement. This Commentary reflects the authors' shared thoughts to the adoption of PSOC by conservative spokespersons to explain the resistance of some to the diversification of the population, growing voice of progressive advocates.

title: Risk perceptions, worry about cancer: does gender make a difference?
authors: McQueen, Amy, Vernon, Sally W, Meissner, Helen I, Rakowski, William
abstract: Risk perceptions, worry are important constructs in many theoretical frameworks used to develop cancer screening interventions. Because most cancers for which we have early detection or prevention strategies are gender specific, few investigations have examined gender differences. We examined gender differences in the magnitude of,, associations with, perceived risk, worry by cancer type. Our sample included 939 men, 1,580 women >or= 50 years old with no history of relevant cancers from the 2003 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS). Dependent variables included absolute, comparative perceived risk, worry for gender-specific (breast/prostate), colon cancers. We examined demographics, health status, health behaviors, cancer beliefs,, cancer communication variables as correlates. Linear regression analyses, pairwise contrasts were conducted with SUDAAN. Men reported greater comparative perceived risk for developing cancers, whereas women reported more frequent cancer worry. For both genders, perceived risk, worry were lowest for colon cancer. Correlates of perceived risk, worry varied,, several associations were moderated by gender. Different risk messages, intervention strategies may be needed to influence males', females' perceived cancer risk, worry. All effect sizes were small,, future prospective research is needed to confirm our findings.

title: Predictors of perceived susceptibility of breast cancer, changes over time: a mixed modeling approach
authors: McQueen, Amy, Swank, Paul R, Bastian, Lori A, Vernon, Sally W
journal: Health psychology: official journal of the Division of Health Psychology, American Psychological Association
abstract: OBJECTIVE: To examine predictors of perceived susceptibility to breast cancer, assess differences across three dependent measures. DESIGN: Annual surveys were completed by US women veterans (N = 3,758) participating in a repeat mammography intervention trial. Multivariable non-linear mixed model analyses examined individual-, group-level changes in perceived susceptibility to breast cancer. DEPENDENT MEASURES: Three single-item measures of perceived susceptibility to breast cancer (percent risk, ordinal risk,, comparative risk likelihood). Predictors included demographic, health status, health behavior, affect, knowledge,, subjective norm variables. RESULTS: Breast symptoms, greater cancer worry increased perceived susceptibility for all three measures. Other predictors varied by dependent measure. Random change, indicating individual variability, was observed for percent risk only. CONCLUSION: Despite small model effect sizes, breast symptoms, cancer worry were consistent predictors, may be good targets for messages designed to influence women's perceived susceptibility to breast cancer. Researchers may benefit from using measures of perceived susceptibility with larger response scales, but additional measurement research is needed. Combining indicators of perceived susceptibility may be undesirable when different predictors are associated with different measures.

title: Thinking fast, not slow: How cognitive biases may contribute to racial disparities in the use of force in police-citizen encounters
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Craig, Miltonette O, Stewart, Eric A, Warren, Patricia Y
abstract: To illuminate how racial disparities in police use of force may arise, to guide research aimed at explaining such disparities.We draw on research on policing, racial disparities in criminal justice,, cognitive bias, decision making to argue that police-citizen encounters require rapid assessments that demand reliance on cognitive “shortcuts,” or heuristics, that may influence the use of force.When cognitive shortcuts rely on biases about the dangerousness of racial minorities, they can contribute to disparities in the use of force. These biases may interact with those that citizens hold, which creates a greater potential for disparities. In addition, biases of officers, citizens may be influenced by such factors as officer training, social context,, reaction time.Research is needed that identifies cognitive shortcuts used during police-citizen encounters, conditions under which they are activated,, strategies for minimizing their role in contributing to racial disparities in the use of force.

title: The code of The Street, inmate violence: Investigating the salience of imported belief systems: The code of The Street, inmate violence
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Stewart, Eric A, Siennick, Sonja E, Simons, Ronald L
keywords: importation; incarceration; order violence; street code;criminology
abstract: Scholars have long argued that inmate behaviors stem in part from cultural belief systems that they ``import'' with them into incarcerative settings. Even so, few empirical assessments have tested this argument directly. Drawing on theoretical accounts of one such set of beliefs-the code of the street-and on importation theory, we hypothesize that individuals who adhere more strongly to the street code will be more likely, once incarcerated, to engage in violent behavior, that this effect will be amplified by such incarceration experiences as disciplinary sanctions, gang involvement, as well as the lack of educational programming, religious programming,, family support. We test these hypotheses using unique data that include measures of the street code belief system, incarceration experiences. The results support the argument that the code of the street belief system affects inmate violence, that the effect is more pronounced among inmates who lack family support, experience disciplinary sanctions,, are gang involved. Implications of these findings are discussed.

title: Social ecology, recidivism: Implications for prisoner reentry
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Wang, Xia, Hay, Carter, Bales, William D
abstract: Despite the marked increase in incarceration over the past 30 years, the fact that roughly two thirds of released offenders are rearrested within 3 years of release, we know little about how the social ecology of the areas to which offenders return may influence their recidivism or whether it disproportionately affects some groups more than others. Drawing on recent scholarship on prisoner reentry, macrolevel predictors of crime, this study examines a large sample of prisoners released to Florida communities to investigate how two dimensions of social ecology—resource deprivation, racial segregation—may independently,, in interaction with specific populations, influence recidivism. The findings suggest that ecology indeed is consequential for recidivism,, it differentially influences some groups more than others. We discuss these findings, their implications for theory, research,, policy.

title: Illegal drug cultivation in Mexico: an examination of the environmental, human factors
authors: Medel, Monica, Lu, Yongmei

title: Crime as hazard: Perceptions of risk, seriousness
authors: Meier, Robert F, Short, Jr, James F
abstract: The study of crime suffers from an inattention to the social consequences of criminal acts. Conceiving crimes within the larger context of “hazard,” data are reported on the relative seriousness of conventional, white‐collar crimes, as well as other hazards, using a sample of Washington state respondents. The results indicate that there is an inverse relationship between the perceived likelihood of a hazard, its seriousness. Generally, the more immediate the threat of a hazard, such as white‐collar crimes, the more serious it is perceived to be. There are also implications from these consequences for perceptions of institutional effectiveness, interpersonal relationships. This suggests that future studies of the consequences of criminality, especially white‐collar, corporate violations, might be directed toward the notions of risk and, eventually, social trust.

title: Usefulness of the protection motivation theory in explaining hearing protection device use among male industrial workers
authors: Melamed, S, Rabinowitz, S, Feiner, M, Weisberg, E, Ribak, J
journal: Health psychology: official journal of the Division of Health Psychology, American Psychological Association
abstract: The present study examined the usefulness of personal variables: noise annoyance,, components of the protection motivation theory (R. W. Rogers, 1983) along with social-organizational factors in explaining hearing protection device (HPD) use among Israeli manufacturing workers. Participants were 281 men exposed to harmful noise levels for which routine HPD use is required by regulation. In practice, 3 HPD user groups were identified: nonusers (n = 38), occasional users (n = 125),, regular users (n = 118). HPD use was objectively verified. HPD use was primarily related to the personal variables but not to management pressure, coworker pressure, or family support. The most powerful predictors of HPD use were perceived self-efficacy (for long-term HPD use), perceived susceptibility (to hearing loss),, noise annoyance, together explaining 48\% of the outcome variance. These findings have implications for interventions aimed at motivating workers to use HPDs regularly.

title: Qualitative GIS, the visualization of narrative activity space data
authors: Mennis, Jeremy, Mason, Michael J, Cao, Yinghui
keywords: Activity space; contextual effects; geographic visualization; narrative; qualitative GIS
abstract: Qualitative activity space data, i.e. qualitative data associated with the routine locations, activities of individuals, are recognized as increasingly useful by researchers in the social, health sciences for investigating the influence of environment on human behavior. However, there has been little research on techniques for exploring qualitative activity space data. This research illustrates the theoretical principles of combining qualitative, quantitative data, methodologies within the context of GIS, using visualization as the means of inquiry. Through the use of a prototype implementation of a visualization system for qualitative activity space data,, its application in a case study of urban youth, we show how these theoretical methodological principles are realized in applied research. The visualization system uses a variety of visual variables to simultaneously depict multiple qualitative, quantitative attributes of individuals' activity spaces. The visualization is applied to explore the activity spaces of a sample of urban youth participating in a study on the geographic, social contexts of adolescent substance use. Examples demonstrate how the visualization may be used to explore individual activity spaces to generate hypotheses, investigate statistical outliers,, explore activity space patterns among subject subgroups.

title: An experimental investigation of the influence of deviant peers on own deviancy: A replication study
authors: Mercer, N, Crocetti, E, Meeus, W, Branje, S
keywords: Causality; Delinquency; Deviancy; Experiment; Peer delinquency;J Exp Criminol
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study is a replication of a study examining the causal impact of a brief exposure to deviant peers on own deviant behavior, i.e., Paternoster et al. (Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency, 50:476-503, 2013). This study retested this design using different monetary incentives, a female deviant peer. METHODS: A total of 69 university students (61\% female) from the Netherlands participated in this laboratory-based study (Mage = 20.64; SD = 2.00) under the façade of a study on individual differences predicting memory recall. Participants could earn up to 10 euros. All participants had the opportunity to cheat to illegitimately earn more money (deviancy). Participants in the experimental condition were exposed to a deviant peer who verbalized her intention to cheat, justified this behavior,, then visibly cheated on the memory recall task. RESULTS: Although participants in both conditions engaged in some deviancy, the brief exposure to a deviant peer significantly increased the amount of deviancy compared to participants who were not exposed to a deviant peer. These results were consistent after controlling for different demographic, theoretical control variables that predict deviancy. CONCLUSIONS: Although not identical in magnitude, our results echo those found by Paternoster et al. (2013): Even a brief exposure to a previously unknown deviant peer increases the amount of deviant behavior in young adults. Future research should examine factors predicting the susceptibility to (different types, thresholds of) deviant peer influence.

title: Police, Vietnamese-Australian communities in multi-ethnic Melbourne
authors: Meredyth, D, McKernan, H, Evans, R
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: This paper explores practical solutions to sensitive community policing issues, drawing on an Australian case study of relations between police, Australian-Vietnamese communities. The paper summarizes initial research on the attitudes of Australian-Vietnamese community members, police to one another, to security, crime. Despite three decades of community policing, there is only limited communication flow between Vietnamese-Australian citizens including offenders, victims, police. The question is whether partnership policing can fill the gap. For police, this involves understanding not only ethnic distinctiveness but also intergenerational issues, tensions within cultural groups,, changing complex forms of membership, affiliation.

title: A composite indicator model to assess natural disaster risks in industry on a spatial level
authors: Merz, Mirjam, Hiete, Michael, Comes, Tina, Schultmann, Frank
abstract: In the event of natural disasters, industrial production sites can be affected by both direct physical damage, indirect damage. The indirect damage, which often exceeds the direct ones in value, mainly arises from business interruptions resulting from the impairment of information, material flows as well as from domino effects in interlaced supply chains. The importance of industry for society, the domino effects often result in severe economic, social,, environmental consequences of industrial disasters making industrial risk management an important task for risk managers at the administrative level (e.g. civil protection authorities). Since the possible industrial disaster damage depends not only on hazard, exposure but also on the vulnerability of a system, an effective, efficient industrial risk management requires information about the system’s regionalized vulnerability. This paper presents a new methodology for structural industrial vulnerability assessment based on production factors that enables to assess the regional industrial disaster vulnerability. In order to capture industry-specific vulnerability factors, to account for the processes underlying regional industrial vulnerability, a two-stage approach is developed. This approach combines a composite indicator model to assess sector-specific vulnerability indices (Vs) with a new regionalization method. The composite indicator model is based on methodologies from the field of multicriteria decision analysis (MultiAttribute Value Theory), the Decision-Making Trial, Evaluation Laboratory Method is applied to correct the (Vs) for interdependencies among the indicators. Finally, the developed approach is applied to an exemplar case study, the industrial vulnerability of 44 administrative districts in the German federal state of Baden-Wuerttemberg is assessed.

title: Internet connectivity, community participation,, place attachment: A longitudinal study
authors: Mesch, Gustavo S, Talmud, Ilan
abstract: The effect of Internet connectivity on social involvement, civic participation,, community sentiments has recently received research attention. Mostly, previous studies have been limited in that they did not account for the mechanism that might link Internet connectivity, community participation.This study uses a longitudinal design to examine the effects of Internet connectivity, participation in a local electronic bulletin board on local community involvement, participation. It is hypothesized that Internet connectivity affects community involvement, positive sentiments attached to the locale. Data from a longitudinal survey of two suburban communities in Israel are used to test the hypothesis. The results show that Internet connectivity, attitudes toward technology provide more channels for local civic participation. But, it is the active participation in locally based electronic forums over, above other forms of social capital (such as face-to-face neighborhood meetings, talking with friends,, membership in local organizations) that is associated with multiple measures of community participation. The formation, active participation in local community electronic networks not only adds but also amplifies civic participation, elevated sense of community attachment.

title: Poverty, inequality,, the urban homicide rate: Some unexpected findings
authors: Messner, Steven F
abstract: ABSTRACTThe purpose of this article is to report findings concerning the relationship between poverty, inequality,, the homicide rate for a sample of 204 SMSAs. A measure of family income inequality exhibits a moderate zero order correlation with the homicide rate, but the effect becomes insignificant in the regression analysis. A second economic measure, that of the size of the poverty population, also exhibits a moderate zero order correlation with the homicide rate, but the partial effect is significant, the sign is quite unexpectedly negative. Additional unexpected results include strong partial effects for measures of Southern regional, racial composition. These findings suggest the need for reconsideration of the role of economic, perhaps subcultural factors in the explanation of urban homicide.

title: Regional differences in the economic correlates of the urban homicide rate: Some evidence on the importance of cultural context
authors: Messner, Steven F
abstract: AbstractThis article examines regional differences in the economic correlates of the urban homicide rate. On the basis of cultural variations between the South, other parts of the country, the proportion of the population below the poverty line, the level of income inequality are hypothesized to have stronger positive effects on the homicide rate in nonsouthern than in southern cities. Regression results for a sample of 256 nonsouthern cities, a sample of 91 southern cities do not support the hypothesis for the measure of income inequality, however. The Gini coefficient of family income concentration has no significant effect in either region. In contrast, the results for the poverty measure are consistent with expectations. The proportion below the poverty line has a significant, positive effect on the homicide rate only in the nonsouthern sample. These findings suggest that the impact of economic deprivation on rates of violent crime is likely to vary appreciably depending on the general cultural context.

title: The “dark figure”, composite indexes of crime: Some empirical explorations of alternative data sources
authors: Messner, Steven F
abstract: This paper compares composite crime indexes across two alternative data sources—the Uniform Crime Reports (UCR), the National Crime Survey (NCS). A variety of indexes are constructed based on weights derived from Sellin, Wolfgang's “seriousness” scale. The results reveal that indexes weighted by offense seriousness are not very highly correlated across data sources for a sample of twenty-six American cities. The substantive importance of the discrepancies between UCR, NCS estimates is illustrated by examining the ecological correlates of weighted crime rates for the twenty-six city sample, by assessing changes in weighted crime rates at the national level for the 1973-81 period. The results also reveal that if estimates of homecide are included in the composite indexes by supplementing the NCS data with data from the Center for Health Statistics, then under certain weighting conditions the correlations across data sources are nearly perfect. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of this latter finding for the measurement of overall levels of criminal activity, for the scaling of the relative gravity of different offenses.

title: The social ecology of urban homicide: An application of the “routine activities” approach
authors: Messner, Steven F, Tardiff, Kenneth
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to use the recently developed “routine activities” approach to help interpret patterns of homicide in a major metropolitan area—Manhattan, New York We argue that the routine activities perspective suggests several distinctive hypotheses about the relationships among sociodemographic characteristics of victims, temporal features of the situation,, the probability of being involved in different kinds of homicide. More specifically, we hypothesize that the sociodemographic characteristics of age, sex, race, marital status,, employment status, along with temporal factors such as time of day, day of week, time of year, will be related systematically to the location of homicide (that is, The geographical proximity to the victim's household), to the victim‐perpetrator relationship (that is, the social proximity of participants: family members, friends, strangers). Detailed data on all recorded homicides occurring in Manhattan during 1981 are examined to evaluate the hypotheses. The results are generally consistent with expectations, indicating that the routine activities approach does indeed provide a useful framework for interpreting the social ecology of urban homicide.

title: Economic inequality, levels of homicide: An analysis of urban neighborhoods
authors: Messner, Steven F, Tardiff, Kenneth
abstract: This paper presents an analysis of the relationship between levels of economic inequality, homicide rates for a sample of 26 neighborhoods in Manhattan, New York. It argues that neighborhoods are more appropriate units of analysis for studying inequality, homicide than are larger political, statistical units because neighborhoods are more likely to constitute meaningful frames of reference for social comparisons. The principle hypothesis is that a high degree of economic inequality in a neighborhood will give rise to high levels of relative deprivation, high rates of homicide. The results of a series of multiple regression analyses fail to support this hypothesis. The measure of economic inequality is weakly associated with the observed homicide rates. Similarly, the racial composition of Manhattan neighborhoods exhibits no significant association with levels of homicide, given statistical controls for other sociodemographic variables. Two neighborhood characteristics do emerge as significant predictors of homicide rates: the relative size of the poverty population, the percent divorced or separated. Homicide rates tend to be highest in those neighborhoods characterized by extreme poverty, pervasive marital dissolution.

title: Distinctive characteristics of assaults motivated by bias
authors: Messner, Steven F, Mchugh, Suzanne, Felson, Richard B
abstract: This research examines the ways in which assaults motivated by bias are similar to, different from other types of assault. Analyses are based on data from the National Incident Based Reporting System (NIBRS), pooled across eleven states. We find evidence suggesting that offenders motivated by racial, ethnic bias are more likely to be versatile offenders than specialists: they are more (not less) likely to be using drugs, alcohol during the crime than conventional offenders. Bias offenders are also more likely to seriously injure the victim. Finally, we find that the risks of bias crime victimization (relative to the risk of assault victimization generally) are similar for blacks, other racial minorities.

title: Public consensus on crime seriousness normative structure or methodological artifact?
authors: Miethe, Terance D
abstract: ABSTRACTSResearch on public perceptions of crime seriousness is reviewed. Two explanations for subgroup consensus are advanced as alternatives to the dominant view that ratings of crime seriousness reflect an underlying normative structure. It is argued that a normative explanation is plausible only after dismissing these alternative explanations. Research, data analytic strategies are proposed to evaluate the plausibility of these alternative explanations, suggestions are offered for future research in crim seriousness, the measurement of normative phenomena.

title: Using diaries to understand women’s responses to crime, violence
authors: Meth, Paula
abstract: This paper describes the use of solicited diaries in research on crime, violence in a South African community, drawing on material collected from 15 diary writers. The paper explains the broader aims of the research, describes the circumstances of the diary writers,, relates some of the stories told by these women in their diaries. The importance of triangulation is discussed and, in this particular case, illustrated through a combination of diaries, focus group interviews. The paper concludes by discussing the benefits, drawbacks associated with the use of solicited diaries.

title: Socioeconomic disparities under determinate sentencing systems: A comparison of preguideline, postguideline practices in Minnesota
authors: Miethe, Terance D, Moore, Charles A
abstract: After a brief review of determinate sentencing systems, this study examines the impact of Minnesota's determinate sentencing law on various presentence, sentencing outcomes. Using comparable pre‐, postguideline measures, the results of this study suggest that Minnesota's reform effort was largely successful in reducing disparity within the scope of the new guidelines. However, although the direct impact of socioeconomic attributes of the offender diminished, these characteristics continued to influence sentencing decisions indirectly through various presentence decisions, case attributes not governed by the guidelines Different models of charge bargaining, sentence negotiations are also observed when pre‐, postguideline models are compared. Yet, the determinants of these time‐specific models are not consistent with the assumptions of a circumvention argument. The paper concludes with suggestions for further research evaluating the impact of determinate sentencing systems on achieving social neutrality in the application of criminal sanctions.

title: Exploring the social context of instrumental, expressive homicides: An application of qualitative comparative analysis

title: Prevalence, risk factors of intimate partner violence among women in four districts of the central region of Ghana: Baseline findings from a cluster randomised controlled trial
authors: Ogum Alangea, Deda, Addo-Lartey, Adolphina Addoley, Sikweyiya, Yandisa, Chirwa, Esnat Dorothy, Coker-Appiah, Dorcas, Jewkes, Rachel, Adanu, Richard Mawuena Kofi
abstract: Intimate partner violence (IPV) is a significant global public health problem. Understanding risk factors is crucial for developing prevention programmes. Yet, little evidence exists on population-based prevalence, risk factors for IPV in West Africa. Our objective was to measure both lifetime, past year prevalence of IPV, to determine factors associated with past year physical or sexual IPV experience. This population-based survey involved 2000 randomly selected women aged 18 to 49 years living in 40 localities within four districts of the Central Region of Ghana. Questionnaires were interviewer-administered from February to May 2016. Respondents were currently or ever-partnered,, resident in study area ≥12months preceding the survey. Data collected included: socio-demographics; sexual behavior; mental health, substance use; employment status; 12-month, lifetime experience of violence; household food insecurity; gender norms/attitudes; partner characteristics, childhood trauma. Logistic regression modelling was used to determine factors associated with sexual or physical IPV, adjusting for age, survey design. About 34\% of respondents had experienced IPV in the past year, with 21.4\% reporting sexual, or physical forms. Past year experience of emotional, economic IPV were 24.6\%, 7.4\% respectively. Senior high school education or higher was protective of IPV (AOR = 0.51[0.30-0.86]). Depression (AOR = 1.06[1.04-1.08], disability (AOR = 2.30[1.57-3.35]), witnessing abuse of mother (AOR = 2.1.98[1.44-2.72]), experience of childhood sexual abuse (AOR = 1.46[1.07-1.99]), having had multiple sexual partners in past year (AOR = 2.60[1.49-4.53]), control by male partner (AOR = 1.03[1.00-1.06]), male partner alcohol use in past year (AOR = 2.65[2.12-3.31]), male partner infidelity (AOR = 2.31[1.72-3.09]) were significantly associated with increased odds of past year physical or sexual IPV experience. Male perpetrated IPV remains a significant public health issue in Ghana. Evidence-based interventions targeting women's mental health, disabilities, exposure to violence in childhood, risky sexual behavior, unequal power in relationships will be critical in reducing IPV in this setting.

title: A multilevel analysis of neighbourhood contextual effects on serious juvenile offending: The role of subcultural values, social disorganization
authors: Oberwittler, Dietrich
abstract: The extent, nature of contextual effects on juvenile offending are frequent subjects of current research, mainly in the USA. After a short literature review, this paper presents empirical results of a new study which hints at the existence of neighbourhood contextual effects on serious offending by adolescents. The study is based on three types of cross-sectional data on 61 neighbourhoods in two German cities, a rural area: a self-report survey of students aged about 13 to 16, a separate survey of residents in the survey neighbourhoods,, census, administrative data on the same neighbourhoods. Multilevel analysis is applied to identify, explain the neighbourhood-level variance of selfreported serious juvenile offending. Hypotheses from both main traditions of theoretical reasoning about contextual effects on juvenile delinquency - subcultural, disorganization theories - are supported by the empirical findings. The spatial concentration of adolescents with attitudes typical of delinquent subcultures increases the likelihood of serious offending net of relevant individual predictors, whereas the social capital of neighbourhoods (as measured by the independent survey of residents) reduces it. Methodological problems of applying multilevel analysis to delinquency research are discussed.

title: Public (mis)understanding of crime policy: The effects of criminal justice experience, media reliance
authors: Pickett, Justin T, Mancini, Christina, Mears, Daniel P, Gertz, Marc
abstract: Scholars attribute the public’s low level of knowledge about sentencing, corrections to its lack of extensive criminal justice experience, consequent reliance on the media for justice-related information. However, scant research exists that evaluates how criminal justice experience affects media consumption, or how such consumption may influence knowledge about sentencing laws or the extent of imprisonment. To extend this literature, we develop, test three hypotheses about the relationships between prior criminal justice experience, reliance on the mass media for information about crime, justice,, knowledge about criminal punishment. Analysis of data from a random telephone survey of 1,308 adult Floridians reveals that individuals with prior criminal justice experience are less likely to rely on the media for crime-related information. The evidence also shows that media reliance is associated with lower levels of knowledge about criminal punishment,, that this effect is particularly strong for female respondents.

title: Public perceptions of dangerous places: sources of variability in evaluating criminogenic environments
authors: Miethe, Terance D, Venger, Olesya

title: Police use of force, its video coverage: An experimental study of the impact of media source, content on public perceptions
authors: Miethe, Terance D, Venger, Olesya, Lieberman, Joel D

title: Social conditions, cross-national imprisonment rates: Using set-theoretic methods for theory testing, identifying deviant cases
authors: Miethe, Terance D, Troshynski, Emily I, Hart, Timothy C
abstract: Macro-level theories of punishment suggest that particular social conditions explain national imprisonment rates over place, time. Important causal factors underlying these theories include a country’s level of development, criminality, socioeconomic inequality,, political volatility. Based on a sample of 166 nations, set-theoretical methods, the present study uses the formal logic standards of necessity, sufficiency to evaluate the empirical merits of these widely assumed causal relations. After summarizing the confirmatory evidence, patterns of exceptional cases, results are discussed in terms of their implications for refining current macro-level theories of punishment, future testing of them through the conjunctive analysis of set-theoretic relations.

title: Police authorities, accountability,, citizenship
authors: Millen, F, Stephens, M
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: Policing has recently attracted a great deal of controversy set against the recent wave of student disturbances, the use of paramilitary tactics to disperse, contain,, kettle protestors. Moreover, the controversial application of stop, search powers under the Terrorism Act 2000 has raised further questions about the accountability of the police. The responsibility of holding the police to account currently falls to the 43 police authorities operating across England, Wales. This article draws on ground-breaking research on police authorities using questionnaire, in-depth interview data to outline just how it is that police authority members approach their duties, responsibilities. It outlines the role, potential of police authorities to influence police policy, operations, discusses how the work of police authorities has impacted on participation by local citizens. Our starting position is that citizen participation is a prerequisite for the effective delivery of accountable policing. This has serious consequences for the proposed Police, Crime Commissioners, which are intended to replace police authorities in November 2012.

title: Self-blame in victims of violence

title: Police stations, architecture, public reassurance
authors: Millie, A
abstract: Architecture has for many years been of interest to criminology in terms of its role in social control, crime prevention. This article focuses on architecture as reassurance, the specific example of the police station what is an under-researched topic. Supporting evidence is presented from a study of police stations in three English police forces. The study’s aims were modest, exploratory, to draw on theoretical, empirical evidence to consider whether police stations are a worthwhile area of criminological/architectural study,, to investigate the possibility that police stations could contribute to public reassurance. Using the language of semiotics, the article argues that meanings attached to police stations can contribute to reassurance by affecting people’s emotive ‘readings’ of security, safety; yet, to do this, there has to be a rethink for many existing stations in terms of what these buildings communicate. The article adopts an interpretivist view of meaning acknowledging that buildings can mean different things to different people. It is suggested that numerous police stations can be read as intimidating fortresses; many others are secret places; while others are potentially public buildings where the public are welcomed. Implications for a policy of reassurance are discussed in light of the current cuts to police budgets. An agenda for further systematic research is suggested.

title: Bridging the gap: Understanding reassurance policing
authors: Millie, Andrew, Herrington, Victoria
journal: The Howard journal of criminal justice
abstract: Abstract: While crime rates in England, Wales have been falling, the perception has remained, for many, that crime is rising. It has also been assumed that fear of crime is high, although measures of fear have been declining since the mid‐1990s. Of greater concern is a concurrent decline in confidence in the police. This ‘gap’ underpins the need for reassurance as a means of gaining legitimacy for policing decisions. We consider the background to reassurance policing, examine interpretation at ground level through interviews with officers involved in a strategy trial based upon a ‘signal crimes’ perspective.

title: Argumentativeness, hurtful message type: Their relationship with confrontation, pressure to end conflicts
authors: Miller, Courtney Waite, Roloff, Michael E
abstract: Romantic partners sometimes say hurtful things to each other. After being hurt, individuals vary with regard to whether they confront their partners. This study investigated how argumentativeness, hurtful message type interact to influence whether a confrontation would take place. This study hypothesized that argumentativeness would be positively related to confronting the hurtful message, negatively related to pressure to end the confrontation,, this relationship would be stronger after an insult than a tease. Undergraduate daters were randomly assigned to indicate how they would respond to being teased or insulted by their partners. Argumentativeness was positively related to willingness to confront the partner, but no evidence was found that this relationship was moderated by hurtful message type. However, it was confirmed that the hypothesized interaction was related to pressure to end the conflict. This article discusses the implications of these findings for understanding, investigating hurtful messages, argumentativeness,, confrontations.

title: The relationship between perceived organizational support, perceived coworker support, debriefing, professional quality of life in Florida law enforcement officers
authors: Miller, Anastasia, Unruh, Lynn, Wharton, Tracy, Liu, Xinliang “albert”, Zhang, Ning “jackie”
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The purpose of this study was to examine the relationships between perceived organizational support, perceived coworker support,, debriefing on the one hand,, compassion satisfaction, burnout,, secondary traumatic stress on the other hand in Florida law enforcement officers. To explore the relationships between these constructs, the research examined the relationships of the work environment of Florida law enforcement personnel by administering surveys gaging perceived organizational support, perceived coworker support, psychological resilience,, debriefing activities that the personnel participate in. The Professional Quality of Life: Compassion Satisfaction, Compassion Fatigue Version 5 was also sent out to establish the self-reported levels of compassion satisfaction, burnout,, secondary traumatic stress. A total of 826 surveys were completed by law enforcement personnel across the state of Florida. The study found that there were relationships between perceived organizational support, perceived coworker support,, debriefing activities, the levels of compassion satisfaction, burnout,, secondary traumatic stress in Florida law enforcement personnel.

title: Fear of crime among Korean Americans in Chicago communities
authors: Lee, Min Sik, Ulmer, Jeffery T
abstract: This study examines Korean Americans' perceived incivilities, perceived crime risk,, fear of crime using an explanatory model combining group threat theory of racial hostility, risk interpretation theory of fear of crime. In particular, our hierarchical linear models show strong effects on fear of crime for English proficiency, length of U.S. residence, preference for ethnic Korean media, perceived risk of future black rioting,, anti‐black prejudice. We discuss the importance of cultural factors, the dynamics of race, ethnic conflicts in explaining fear of crime,, suggest directions for future research on race relations, perceived victimization risks,, fear of crime.

title: Gender-based violence during COVID-19 pandemic: A mini-review
authors: Mittal, Shalini, Singh, Tushar
keywords: COVID 19; domestic violence; gender-based violence; pandemic; quarantine
abstract: Purpose: Quarantine is necessary to reduce the community spread of the Coronavirus disease, but it also has serious psychological, socially disruptive consequences. This is known as the quarantine paradox that also includes a surge in the cases of gender-based violence. However, there exists a clear gap of rigorous literature exploring the issue. Hence, the current paper attempts to understand gender-based violence as an aspect of the COVID-19 lockdown. It reviews the pattern of rise in gender violence cases, the resultant psychological, social issues, attempts to create awareness by initiating a discourse urging for change in the response towards the victims of gender-based violence. The paper further attempts to suggest measures to mitigate the issues arising out of gender violence during quarantine. Method: The current paper reviews the literature on the rise of gender-based violence in the times of current, past pandemics. The paper also reviews the published reports in scientific as well as mass media literatures focusing on the rise of gender-based violence during the imposed lockdown, its consequences,, the measures taken by the governments to tackle the issue. Results: The present review reveals that similar to the previous pandemics, epidemics, there has been an alarming rise in the incidents of gender-based violence during the COVID-19 pandemic. The present review further reveals various other risk factors that have been found attributive to the surge of gender-based violence such as economic insecurity, alcohol consumption. The results of the review indicate that despite its global prevalence, gender-based violence has been one of the most neglected outcomes of pandemics. Moreover, the legislatures, services available for such victims are often inadequate and, thus, worsening their situation. Conclusion: Pandemic situations have been found to be associated with advancements in the medical field. However, a part, parcel of this situation is the age-old practice of quarantine that has several negative outcomes. This also includes a surge in gender-based violence that raises serious concerns about the safety of women. As the legislatures provided, measures taken by the governments are falling short in dealing with the issue, a number of non-government organizations are stepping up to provide necessary services to these victims.

title: “Truly free consent”? Clarifying the nature of police legitimacy using causal mediation analysis
authors: Pósch, Krisztián, Jackson, Jonathan, Bradford, Ben, Macqueen, Sarah
abstract: Abstract Objectives To test whether normative, non-normative forms of obligation to obey the police are empirically distinct, to assess whether they exhibit different dynamics in terms of the downstream effects of police-citizen contact. Methods Analysing data from the Scottish Community Engagement Trial of procedurally just policing, we use natural effect modelling for causally ordered mediators to assess causal pathways that include—but also extend beyond—the experimental treatment to procedural justice. Results Normative, non-normative forms of obligation are empirically distinct. Normative obligation to obey the police is sensitive to procedurally just or unjust police behaviour,, influences cooperation with the police, traffic law compliance in a way that is consistent with procedural justice theory. Non-normative obligation to obey the police is ‘sticky’, unresponsive. Conclusions Legitimacy can resonably be defined partly as normative obligation with its expected beneficial downstream effects, so long as it is measured properly.

title: Tonic immobility during sexual assault - a common reaction predicting post-traumatic stress disorder, severe depression
authors: Möller, Anna, Söndergaard, Hans Peter, Helström, Lotti
keywords: Depression; Tonic Immobility Scale; peritraumatic reactions; post-traumatic stress disorder; rape; sexual assault
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Active resistance is considered to be the 'normal' reaction during rape. However, studies have indicated that similar to animals, humans exposed to extreme threat may react with a state of involuntary, temporary motor inhibition known as tonic immobility. The aim of the present study was to assess the occurrence of tonic immobility during rape, subsequent post-traumatic stress disorder, severe depression. MATERIAL AND METHODS: Tonic immobility at the time of the assault was assessed using the Tonic Immobility Scale in 298 women who had visited the Emergency clinic for raped women within 1 month of a sexual assault. Information about the assault, the victim characteristics were taken from the structured clinical data files. After 6 months, 189 women were assessed regarding the development of post-traumatic stress disorder, depression. RESULTS: Of the 298 women, 70\% reported significant tonic immobility, 48\% reported extreme tonic immobility during the assault. Tonic immobility was associated with the development of post-traumatic stress disorder (OR 2.75; 95\% CI 1.50-5.03, p = 0.001), severe depression (OR 3.42; 95\% CI 1.51-7.72, p = 0.003) at 6 months. Further, previous trauma history (OR 2.36; 95\% CI 1.48-3.77, p < 0.001), psychiatric treatment history (OR 2.00; 95\% CI 1.26-3.19, p = 0.003) were associated with the tonic immobility response. CONCLUSIONS: Tonic immobility during rape is a common reaction associated with subsequent post-traumatic stress disorder, severe depression. Knowledge of this reaction in sexual assault victims is important in legal matters, for healthcare follow up.

title: A multilevel study of neighborhoods, parent-to-child physical aggression: results from the project on human development in Chicago neighborhoods
authors: Molnar, Beth E, Buka, Stephen L, Brennan, Robert T, Holton, John K, Earls, Felton
abstract: The majority of children in the United States experience parent-to-child physical aggression (PCPA), a disciplinary strategy out of favor with many experts. Several decades of research have documented a link between community characteristics, severe child maltreatment. None have taken a multilevel approach to study whether neighborhoods affect the amount of corporal punishment and/or physical abuse used by individual families. Data for this article come from the Project on Human Development in Chicago Neighborhoods, were analyzed using hierarchical linear modeling. An interval scale of PCPA was developed. Values obtained show that several neighborhood characteristics were associated with PCPA. Immigrant concentration remained significant after controlling for family composition. A cross-level interaction was found between neighborhood social networks, Hispanic race/ethnicity. The article's conclusion is that neighborhood characteristics may influence the amount of PCPA used by families. Neighborhood intervention strategies hold promise.

title: When police patrols matter. The effect of police proximity on citizens’ crime risk perception
authors: Montolio, Daniel, Planells-Struse, Simón
abstract: Crime risk perception is known to be an important determinant of individual well-being. It is therefore crucial that we understand the factors affecting this perception so that governments can identify the (public) policies that might reduce it. Among such policies, public resources devoted to policing emerge as a key instrument not only for tackling criminal activity but also for impacting on citizens’ crime risk perception. In this framework, the aim of this study is to analyze both the individual, neighbourhood determinants of citizens’ crime risk perception in the City of Barcelona (Spain) focusing on the effect of police proximity, taking into account the spatial aspects of neighbourhood characteristics. After controlling for the possible problems of the endogeneity of police forces, crime risk perception, the potential sorting of individuals across neighbourhoods, the results indicate that crime risk perception is reduced when non-victims exogenously interact with police forces. Moreover, neighbourhood variables, such as proxies of social capital, the level of incivilities, together with individual characteristics have an impact on citizens’ crime risk perception.

title: Disentangling the root causes of COVID-19 related increases in alcohol consumption
authors: Molsberry, Rebecca, Maskaly, Jon, Reingle Gonzalez, Jennifer M
journal: The American journal of drug, alcohol abuse
keywords: Alcohol use; COVID-19; binge drinking; mental health;370\_Isolation;322\_経済圧力
abstract: Recent studies suggest that the COVID-19 pandemic has increased alcohol sales, alcohol related problems. This may be due to the synergistic effects of unemployment, stress from childcare or additional caregiving responsibilities, reduced social interactions, negative coping strategies. Weerakoon, colleagues set out to identify the most robust risk factors for alcohol consumption, binge drinking,, changes in drinking patterns due to the COVID-19 pandemic. One-third of the sample reported consuming more alcohol after COVID-19 compared to pre-COVID-19. In addition, each additional week spent at home under stay-at-home orders was increased the odds of binge drinking by 19\%. Individuals who have been diagnosed with depression, were currently experiencing depressive symptoms were more than three times more likely (OR = 3.37) to have increased their alcohol consumption during COVID-19 compared to those with no history or symptoms of depression. Parents of children was associated with decreased COVID-19 related binge drinking (OR = .74). As many daily life factors have been altered due to the pandemic, a more holistic lifestyle disruption construct may help further investigate the long term effects of social isolation on alcohol use as the pandemic continues. Furthermore, the role of social support in mitigating COVID-19-related stress has yet to be examined, may be a protective factor against alcohol related problems. As stress continues, researchers should continue assessing the longitudinal effects of COVID-19 lockdowns with the goal of early identification for those at the highest risk of problematic alcohol use.

title: Communicating violence risk: Frequency formats, vivid outcomes,, forensic settings
authors: Monahan, John, Heilbrun, Kirk, Silver, Eric, Nabors, Erik, Bone, Jonathan, Slovic, Paul
journal: International journal of forensic mental health
