Colquhoun (2004) is concerned with housing, neighbourhood design, local facilities, using case studies from Britain, overseas. Town et al (2003) also concentrates on residential design, but the Office of the Deputy Prime Minister (2004) gives wide coverage of town centres, commercial, health buildings, schools, parks, car parks, transport.This paper draws out the key findings, recommendations of these three publications, which should be taken seriously, used constructively. What is clear from all three is the need, especially in urban, housing regeneration, for a joined-up approach to planning, design which links physical with cultural, social, economic development. Resident participation is essential, including the involvement of young people, who have such an impact on public safety, its perception. In this way it is possible to create safe, sustainable communities.

title: Design out crime? Using practice-based models of the design process
authors: Gamman, Lorraine, Pascoe, Tim
abstract: This paper compares, contrasts design models associated with ‘design against crime’, ‘crime prevention through environmental design’, so that professionals can better understand, as well as use, each other's methodologies, practices. It teases out the differences between the models of design linked to crime prevention for consumer markets, on the one hand,, on the other for social housing, public space, where building regulations, other public-sector drivers have some sway. The paper is divided into two sections, both of which question what is meant when the word ‘design’ is used in practice by these different methodologies.

title: Seeing is believing: Notes towards a visual methodology, manifesto for crime prevention through environmental design
authors: Gamman, Lorraine, Pascoe, Tim
abstract: Seeing is a great deal more than believing these days. You can buy an image of your house taken from an orbiting satellite or have your internal organs magnetically imaged. If that special moment didn't come out quite right in your photography, you can digitally manipulate it on your computer. At New York's Empire State Building, the queues are longer for the virtual reality New York Ride than for the lifts to the observation platforms. Alternatively, you could save yourself the trouble by catching the entire New York skyline, rendered in attractive pastel colours, at the ‘New York, New York’ resort in Las Vegas. This virtual city will shortly be joined by Paris Las Vegas, imitating the already carefully manipulated image of the city of light. (Mirzoeff, 1998:3).

title: ‘troublemaker’, ‘nothing to lose’ employee offenders identified from a corporate crime data sample
authors: Dodd, Nick J
abstract: Actual employee offender data has rarely been utilised in previous analyses of employees offending against their employer. In this paper such a data source is used,, demonstrates that it has an important role to play in organisations to prevent, investigate employee crime. However, this is only achievable if the organisation in question knows how to harness the potential of the data, use it accordingly. The analysis of the data in this chapter provides support for previous research findings that employee offenders are virtually indistinguishable from their non-deviant colleagues. However, it does establish that there are different types of employee offender within this case study who adopt very different approaches to their deviance in the organisational setting. This has not been demonstrated before,, has implications for future research, for the development of preventative, investigative strategies within organisations.

title: Making links: The auditing of alcohol-related crime, disorder
authors: Tierney, John
abstract: All Crime, Disorder Reduction Partnerships are obliged to conduct three-yearly local audits of crime, disorder. It is clear that particular types of information tend to be lacking in these audits. One such example is data pertaining to alcohol-related crime, disorder. This article examines the conceptual problems associated with the notion of specifically alcohol-related crime, disorder,, assesses the strengths, weaknesses of available data. A distinction is drawn between a ‘direct’, an ‘indirect’ approach,, the key issues, implications of each are analysed. It is argued that an indirect approach is potentially the most productive.

title: Crime-mapping in crime prevention partnerships: Drivers, inhibitors
authors: Organ, Joe
abstract: ‘Crime-mapping’ through GIS has become a major focus for Crime, Disorder Reduction Partnerships in England, Wales. At first glance, accessible technology, data, supporting legislation,, an alignment with the wider ‘e-government’ reform agenda would indicate that crime-mapping has become an easy option in the pursuit of improved crime prevention. Through research into the history of partnerships in crime prevention, criminal justice IT, patterns of government GIS use, this paper argues that the road to successful crime-mapping has been a difficult one. Several factors hindered progress considerably; some of these barriers are still apparent. The paper concludes by questioning central involvement in crime-mapping,, asks whether there can or should be attempts to create a national system,, if so what format such a system should adopt.

title: Understanding the older person's awareness, experience of doorstep crime: Results of a national survey
authors: Thornton, Amanda, Hatton, Chris, Ralph, Lysa, Owen, Tom
abstract: Police records suggest that on average almost 19,000 distraction burglaries are committed across England, Wales per year, although this is likely to under-report actual levels of distraction burglary targeting, victimisation. To investigate in more detail the extent of distraction burglary targeting, victimisation amongst older people, a national telephone survey of 3403 adults aged 60, over across England, Wales, Scotland was conducted. Across the whole sample, 3.3 per cent of respondents reported themselves to have been a target of a potential distraction burglary in the previous year, with 1.1 per cent reporting the theft of property as a result. Older age groups reported themselves as more likely to be both targets, victims. There were also age, gender, socioeconomic differences in awareness of distraction burglary campaigns, home security, concern about answering the door. Scaling-up the responses to this survey would suggest approximately 400,000 distraction burglary attempts, 130,000 successful distraction burglaries in England, Scotland, Wales per year. A number of suggestions are made concerning the discrepancy between these figures, police records, including police recording, under-reporting, methodological issues within the survey. The considerable policy, practice implications of these figures are also discussed.

title: Evaluating the implementation of Indiana area ‘communities that care’
authors: Myers, David L, Arter, Michael
abstract: ‘Communities That Care’ (CTC) is a research-based operating system designed to help communities identify, reduce risk factors, enhance protective factors,, prevent a number of adolescent problem behaviors, including delinquency, violence, substance abuse, school drop-out,, teen pregnancy. Indiana, PA, is one of approximately 125 communities throughout Pennsylvania that have chosen to use the CTC approach to promote the positive development of children, youth in the local area. This paper presents an initial review of Indiana Area CTC, in terms of the planning, implementation efforts that have taken place during the past five years.

title: A letter from Australia: Doing crime prevention research: A personal reflection
authors: Cherney, Adrian
abstract: It is important for the criminologist to be conscious of the challenges policy makers, practitioners face in translating official policy statements, theories of crime prevention into working practices,, to empathise with the crisis they face. Doing so does not diminish one's objectivity, but can actually enhance comprehension of the contingent nuances of crime prevention policy, practice. The work of C. Wright Mills provides a framework for attaining such insights. In a similar vein the ‘what works’ paradigm needs to pay far greater attention to the inherently contingent nature of crime prevention, with the delivery of programmes, strategies being far harder than assumed. The weakness of the position is that it ignores the ‘enabling conditions’ which need to exist to ensure ‘best practice’ is followed in practice. The examination of these issues is grounded in the author's own experience, observations of conducting research on crime prevention in the Australian state of Victoria from the late 1990s to early 2000.

title: Surfing the crime net: Issues, challenges in police-community relations
authors: Garland, Jon

title: What works? A critical note on the evaluation of crime reduction initiatives
authors: Marchant, Paul
abstract: This article discusses the important differences between evaluating area-based crime reduction interventions through comparison of areas,, evaluating treatment effectiveness by a classic randomised controlled trial (RCT). The differences must be respected in the analysis of data. Wrong results will be given for a comparative area- based crime reduction trial if it is thought of as an RCT. The problem with evaluations which compare areas, one with an intervention, one without, is that such studies are neither randomised nor controlled,, the crime events being counted are correlated rather than statistically independent. Wrongly using those methods which are appropriate for an RCT will give misleading results. Statistical uncertainties will tend to be large, poorly determined,, statistical biases problematic because of the lack of equivalence between areas at the outset. Crime studies need to be appropriately designed to avoid such problems if costly mistakes are to be avoided.

title: A little yellow box: The targeting of automatic teller machines as a strategy in reducing street robbery
authors: Holt, Tony, Spencer, Jon
abstract: This article is based on part of a wider research study concerning street robbery. It is concerned with the application of the concept of ‘personal defensible space’ at automatic teller machines (ATMs) in a high-robbery area. The application of personal defensible space in the pilot study area had a significant effect on the number of robberies committed at or in close proximity to identified ATMs. The article also considers how the proximity of drug, stolen goods markets has an effect on the number of robberies committed. Finally, the article suggests that the identification of vulnerable ATMs, the creation of a personal defensible space zone may lead to greater safety, thus prevent crime.

title: Burglary reduction in action: The hartlepool experience
authors: Adamson, Sue
abstract: This paper draws on research for the evaluation of the Home Office Reducing Burglary Initiative to examine one project, assess its success in reducing burglary. Hartlepool chose a variety of interventions which were well targeted with respect to the problems of the area, to the resources available. Implementation was assisted by strong management, close cooperation with the community. Analysis of burglary data showed that Hartlepool met its own target of reducing burglary by 25 per cent in the first two years,, achieved a net reduction of 55 burglaries after trends in the surrounding area had been removed. Further work has shown that this reduction has continued over a further two years, resulting in a total saving of 138 burglaries. As a whole the project was cost-beneficial, with net benefits after two years of £64,000. Effects of individual interventions have not always been clear, but some have had beneficial impacts.

title: Surfing the crime net: A guide to the ‘rest’ of the British isles
authors: Mawby, R I

title: Hotel crime: Who cares?
authors: Jones, C, Mawby, R I
abstract: This paper emanates from an evaluation of a burglary reduction initiative targeting hotels in a tourist area of southern England. In carrying out the evaluation a second, control area was included,, the paper focuses on hotel crime as a problem in these two areas. Police statistics are described to illustrate the extent of the problem. Victim survey data are then used to supplement this picture, to assess the differential risk suffered by different types of hotels. However, despite the extent of crime against hotels, data from structured, semi-structured interviews demonstrate that hoteliers do not perceive crime as a particular problem. The paper thus concludes by discussing the implications of this for crime reduction, community safety initiatives.

title: The impact of a summer camp program as a secondary prevention measure for at-risk youth
authors: Hanes, Carolyn, Rife, Elaine Moyer, Laguna, Louis B
abstract: Based on a developmental model of risk factors unique to children, adolescents, a summer camp program was evaluated with regard to its potential positive impact on at-risk participants who successfully completed the program, compared to at-risk participants who were nominated but did not participate in it. Basic features of the camp included mentoring, problem-solving activities,, the development of pro- social skills. Participants who attended the summer camp obtained significantly higher grades, in the year following camp, than did a non-camp comparison group. Additionally, the camp group had fewer absences, days tardy, number of detentions than the non-camp group. Methodological limitations, recommendations for future research are discussed.

title: Eliminating the visible: Exploring the community response to anti-social behaviour
authors: Moore, Stephen, Scourfield, Peter
abstract: New Labour has identified combating anti-social behaviour as one of its key policies since 1997, has introduced a range of disciplinary measures to tackle it. Included in these measures are policies which set out to involve local communities in decision- making regarding how the policing of anti-social behaviour is to be carried out.This case study focuses on the way in which one community, or at least a vocal minority of that community, has influenced the way in which anti-social behaviour policies have been implemented.Those representing the community had only one interest, which was to ensure that the people with a street lifestyle disappeared from the streets. What happened to them afterwards was of little interest. This contrasted with the police, local council who were interested in a longer-term, reasoned solution to the problem.In this particular study, the more considered approach of the police, local authority was overwhelmed by the demands by the community for the people with a street lifestyle to be expelled from the area. This duly happened through the imposition of a range of disciplinary measures.We suggest however that this exclusionary approach to deviant groups has a long tradition. Using Rutherford's concepts of visibility, elimination, we explore the history of community responses to deviant groups, locate the specific case study within a long tradition of communities' desires to expel deviants. We suggest finally that the more New Labour involves local communities in combating anti-social behaviour, the more prominent these themes are likely to become.

title: Crime prevention strategies in neighborhoods dominated by rental property
authors: Munson, Paul J
abstract: A concern in many older communities is decay in neighborhoods dominated by rental properties. Multiple strategies are being adopted throughout the country to assist police departments, other policy makers to solve the crime problems of these areas. These strategies include the Crime Free Multi-Family Housing Program, zoning regulations, smart growth policies, landlord education programs, neighborhood organizations, drug, gang activity eviction legislation, administrative searches, inspections,, partnering between law enforcement, the rental industry. Legal, social issues need to be addressed, including recent court decisions on administrative regulations, concerns about affordable housing,, housing availability for persons with criminal convictions.

title: Models of local security networks: On the diversity of local security networks in the Netherlands
authors: Terpstra, Jan
abstract: Local security networks are highly diverse in their goals, structure, participants, size, methods of intervention. This diversity is analysed by looking at the underlying network models. Four of these models are distinguished: participatory networks; mixed enforcement networks; preventive institutional networks;, re-active institutional networks. These models differ not only in their main orientation (preventive or reactive), participants (only institutional or also citizens), but also in their style of co-operation, structure, technology. The problems local security networks are confronted with depend to a large degree on the underlying network models. Each model has its specific problems. Moreover, some problems of local security networks result from the tensions between the logic or demands of one or more underlying models.

title: The effectiveness of redeployable CCTV
authors: Waples, Sam, Gill, Martin
keywords: CPCS1999-2009;CPCS815;Crime Prevention, Community Safety;318\_介入実験\_Policing
abstract: Although there is some published research on CCTV almost all of it is on static CCTV. Yet there is emerging a popular different type, one that can be moved around to deal with crime hotspots as they arise. The flexibility, the fact that it is perceived as more cost effective add to its appeal. However, until now redeployable CCTV has attracted very little comment. The paper discusses an empirical research study assessing its effectiveness, then attempts to highlight some of the policy implications. What is clear is that if the potential of this technology is ever to be realized, it will need to be managed very differently.

title: R–E–S–P–E–C–T, Find out What it Means to me: The Connection Between Respect, Youth Crime
authors: McCarthy, Peter, Walker, Janet
abstract: There is a long tradition of linking antisocial behaviour on the part of young people with a breakdown in respect,, the present government's pronouncements about the causes of youth crime, antisocial behaviour are continuing this tradition. This paper, however, argues that respect is a complex commodity, which is not easy to generate. Young people tend to accept that some of their number are disrespectful of their elders, but argue that they are more likely to show respect if they are accorded it themselves. Self-respect is also crucial. Government strategies are premised on a limited definition of respect, an inadequate understanding of how it is generated. They confuse respect with obedience towards authority, propose to generate respect by asserting control, but there is no evidence that this will lead to those being controlled respecting either the controllers or themselves.

title: The nature of British media reporting of hedonistic tourism
authors: Brunt, Paul, Davis, Claire
abstract: This study examines the nature, extent of British media reporting of hedonistic tourism via a study of the resort of Faliraki, Rhodes. The nature of the tourism industry is discussed as well as image formation, its importance to a tourism destination. The role of the media in forming an image is considered, a content analysis of news articles from five British media sources is undertaken, which identified several reporting themes. The occurrence of keywords in the articles was also analysed. Results show how reports are amplified through the use of particular words, but show little difference between the reporting styles of the newspapers sampled. The importance of media in amplifying bad publicity resulting in subsequent reductions in tourism demand is disscussed.

title: How important is “regression to the mean” in area-based crime prevention research?
authors: Farrington, David P, Welsh, Brandon C
abstract: If an area with a relatively high crime rate is chosen to receive a crime prevention programme, its crime rate is likely to decrease after the programme because of fluctuations in crimes over time caused by fluctuations in influencing factors. This is called “regression to the mean”. If this high-crime experimental area is compared with a control area with a lower crime rate, crimes are likely to decrease more in the experimental area than in the control area because of these fluctuations, possibly creating the illusion that the programme had an effect when in fact it did not. This article estimates the importance of “regression to the mean” using recorded crime rates in police Basic Command Units (BCUs) in England, Wales in 2002–03, 2003–04. It is concluded that, in reasonable comparisons between areas with high, moderately high crime rates, this effect may cause a 4\% decrease in crimes. Hence, it could not account for much of the 19\% decrease in crimes following improved street lighting.

title: A question of (dis)engagement? Historical lessons in promoting an effective public interface to address current crime concerns
authors: Rowbotham, Judith, Stevenson, Kim
abstract: What is lacking in the current crime control strategies is any genuine, effective debate between government, the legal world, the wider public about crime related issues. Historically, the Victorian media provided the conduit for an effective interface to address both public, official concern, but today this is absent from the media discourse. This article utilizes two case studies, focusing on the crimes of rape, burglary to demonstrate the problems that this present level of disengagement between the public, the criminal justice system can generate. It suggests ways in which the historical experience can facilitate, promote a more constructive, successful interface between the official, the popular communities. The argument is made that a more effective, influential public forum is a prerequisite to engender public confidence in the criminal justice system's ability to ensure community safety,, that a responsible media is best placed to facilitate this.

title: Social deprivation, rural youth crime: Young men in prison, their experiences of the “rural idyll”
authors: Meek, Rosie
abstract: Within rural communities, young people are highly visible, therefore more readily stigmatized, marginalized. At the same time they tend to be, paradoxically, invisible in terms of research, service delivery, policy. This article explores the experiences of young men in prison who come from rural parts of the south west of England. The results indicate that rural policy, practice have failed to meet the needs of young people, particularly those caught up in the Criminal Justice System. Findings suggest that key issues within rural communities include a lack of services, isolation, inter-generational tensions. It is suggested that these concerns exacerbate the risks of re-offending as young people return to their communities after release from prison. The need for community-wide initiatives, recommendations for policy, practice in the prison, probation services are discussed.

title: Community Policing in Context: Has it Come of Age?
authors: Brookes, Stephen
abstract: This paper identifies some of the critical conditions that help or hinder the development of community policing. The findings are timely given the current political emphasis on neighbourhood policing. The research on which it is based took place in three police forces of varying sizes, was based on a systems approach. Following an extensive literature review that concluded there is “no one best way” of achieving community policing it also established that it may be possible to identify the conditions in which critical success factors can come together to develop what is described as a coactive (community-based) policing style within a process of change. The research sought to test this proposition, asks whether in this sense community policing has really come of age. It concludes that while the conditions are right for community policing, significant barriers still remain before it can be conceived of as the normal way of conducting policing business. Attention to the management of change is required, in particular, the cultural conditions.

title: Target hardening the college campus through stakeholder input: Merging community, the security survey
authors: Hummer, Don, Preston, Pamela
abstract: Physical security surveys have for many years been an integral component of an overall crime prevention plan for post-secondary institutions. As assessment tools, they highlight vulnerable features of design, environment that could potentially put persons or property at risk. Noticeably absent from a majority of these surveys is input from the constituents (community) that regularly use these complexes as students, employees, residents, or visitors. The perceptions of these users give a differing perspective on how those who may perhaps be most familiar with the institution under scrutiny view potential risks. By merging a physical survey of facilities with stakeholder input, a more comprehensive crime control strategy can be developed, implemented that addresses the needs of both users, administrators. The present research illustrates how such a dual method was undertaken at an urban university, discusses the benefits that emerge when two perspectives are taken into account in developing an institutional security plan.

title: A “criminal personas” approach to countering criminal creativity
authors: Hilton, Kev, Irons, Alastair
abstract: This paper describes a pilot study of a “criminal personas” approach to countering criminal creativity. The value of the personas approach has been assessed by comparing the identification of criminal opportunity, through “traditional” brainstorming, then through “criminal personas” brainstorming. The method involved brainstorm sessions with Computer Forensics Practitioners, with Product Designers, where they were required to generate criminal scenarios, select the most serious criminal opportunities,, propose means of countering them. The findings indicated that there was merit in further research in the development, application of the “criminal personas” approach. The generation of criminal opportunity ideas, proposal of counter criminal solutions were both greater when the brainstorm approach involved the group responding through their given criminal personas.

title: Partnership problems: Analysis, re-design
authors: Ellis, Elaine, Fortune, Joyce, Peters, Geoff
abstract: Multi-agency partnership working is becoming increasingly prevalent, particularly within, between the public, voluntary sectors. However, it is widely accepted that while this method of working brings the prospect of benefits, it also has the potential to be problematic. This paper looks at the difficulties experienced by one particular partnership, describes how the partnership used insight into the effectiveness of its structures, processes, to make changes to its design. The approach used to provide this insight was an application of the Systems Failures Method. This method is explained briefly in the paper, a summary of its application in this context is also given. Links are drawn with research work on partnerships in other contexts,, proposals are made about how the Systems Failures Method could be used at different stages of a partnership's life in order to evaluate its design, monitor, improve its methods of working, its effectiveness.

title: Police-Led Proactive Prevention of Youth Crime: A case for the Innovative use of Support Workers?
authors: Barton, Adrian, Teagle, Richard
abstract: The Every Child Matters, Youth Matters legislation have continued the trend of mandating joint working, identifying agencies' responsibilities in dealing with social problems. For many agencies, this is relatively unproblematic, simply means a continuation of current working practices. However, for some it has meant forays into unfamiliar or previously difficult territory. This paper, which is based on some empirical findings, concentrates on how the Devon, Cornwall police have become involved in proactive interventions aimed at preventing youth crime while avoiding charges of net widening, mesh thinning.

title: Public disorder, business victimization: Findings from a survey of female entrepreneurs
authors: Savolainen, Jukka
abstract: Despite a recent surge in research on crimes against the business sector, this literature has generally failed to contribute to the theoretical core of criminology. Drawing on a survey of female entrepreneurs in Finland, our study attends to public incivilities as an environmental source of business victimization. According to an influential article by Sampson, Raudenbush , the link between disorder, crime is mostly spurious, caused by intense levels of poverty, residential segregation. Finland is an example of a society with comparatively low rates of structural disadvantage. As such, it represents an informative national context to examine the empirical merits of the incivilities thesis. Findings from our research support the assumption that public disorder is an important environmental antecedent of business victimization.

title: Professionalizing counter fraud specialists in the UK: Assessing progress, recommendations for reform
authors: Button, Mark, Frimpong, Kwabena, Smith, Geoffrey, Johnston, Les
abstract: This article examines an initiative in the United Kingdom to professionalize counter fraud staff through the creation of the Counter Fraud Specialist (CFS). It describes how common training packages have been created using “Professional Accreditation Boards” which are also accredited by Universities, who embed those awards in specially tailored University programmes. The paper evaluates the success of the initiative so far outlining areas where it could be further enhanced.

title: Fraud, peace: Investigative interviewing, fraud investigation
authors: Shawyer, Andie, Walsh, Dave
abstract: The adaptation, application of the “PEACE” framework for investigative interviewing in public sector counter-fraud was intended to create a more professional body of trained counter-fraud interviewers, a more standardized interview model. This paper discusses the importance of interviewing in the investigation process, with specific reference to fraud. Specifically, it will examine the Department for Work, Pensions public sector agency. It examines how successfully the PEACE model can fit into fraud investigative interviewing,, investigates the attitudes, perceptions of fraud investigators to the PEACE framework as applied to the fraud interview. The paper refers to research indicating that PEACE is not being consistently applied in all interviews,, that some elements of the model might work better than others in relation to fraud interviews. Further, the paper highlights the mixed reaction of investigators to using the model,, leads to the proposition that perhaps the model needs to be adapted to “fit” fraud interviews.

title: Public Sector Corruption: Lessons to be learned from the Ukrainian Experience
authors: Markovska, Anna, Isaeva, Anna
abstract: This paper introduces certain problems of the Ukrainian health-care system,, provides an overview of the local health-care system, pharmaceutical market,, identifies regulatory, legal issues. The authors present the preliminary results of an interview programme with medical practitioners in Ukraine that address the issues of development of relationships between Western pharmaceutical companies, medical practitioners in Ukraine. It also identifies some unique features of these relationships,, discusses the implications for the culture of bribery in this important developing market.

title: “safer homes”: An evaluation of a reorganization to deal with domestic burglary within a UK police force
authors: Warren, Jeremy, Hogard, Elaine, Ellis, Roger
abstract: This paper describes an evaluation of an initiative to improve performance regarding domestic burglary in a police force in the North of England. The force was not performing well in respect of domestic burglary detections, was required to make considerable changes in order to improve levels of performance. The force undertook substantial organizational restructuring to implement the scheme. The evaluation focussed on the process, outcomes, stakeholder views of the initiative. The changes had a significant effect on burglary detection rates, a moderate effect on numbers of incidents, partnership working at practitioner level, but little effect on relationships with partner agencies at a strategic level.

title: Anatomy of riots: A situational crime prevention approach
authors: Verma, Arvind
abstract: The basis of Situational Crime Prevention, Routine Activity Approach, Environmental Criminology, Opportunity Theory, related perspectives is the notion of rational choice. The preventive techniques are based on the assumption that a rational offender is unlikely to act if the efforts of committing a crime are greater than the expected rewards. This paper seeks to extend the notion of rational choice from the individual to the group, suggests the application of situational prevention to a new dimension – that of large-scale disorder problems such as riots, anti-government demonstrations, confrontational religious celebrations. These disorder problems pose serious challenges since these involve vicious mobs violating prohibitory orders, attacking police personnel, indulging in wanton destruction of property, violence. We argue that even though a mob behaves irrationally, indulges in senseless acts of violence, destruction, the individuals comprising the mob are rational, guided by self-interest in their behavior. Therefore, even in riotous situations, rational choice perspective can be profitably exploited to prevent mayhem. We present several cases of handling major riots, group confrontation from different parts of India. We describe the applicability of several situational techniques to controlling disorder, preventing further escalation of violence. The generalization of Situational Crime Prevention techniques to large-scale order maintenance problems is suggested.

title: No escape from the iron cage? Governmental discourse in new labour's community safety policy
authors: Gilling, Daniel, Schuller, Nina
abstract: This article seeks to provide an explanation for why it is that local crime, disorder reduction partnerships (CDRPs), established by the 1998 Crime, Disorder Act, have thus far failed to display the kind of self-governing networked governance that is generally expected of partnership approaches. Rather than searching for explanations that focus upon the “competence” of the CDRPs, the politically inspired “control freakery” of the centre, or the structural influences on late-modern crime control, the concept of grid-group theory is employed to show how CDRPs exist as structures that are vulnerable to the influence of a range of conflicting, competing, contradictory modes of social organization that pull in very different directions. This meso-level focus affords a better understanding of the difficulties faced by CDRPs,, of how they might be overcome in the pursuit of networked governance.

title: “dead in the water”: Is rural violent crime prevention floating face-down because criminology can't handle context?
authors: Bell, Erica, Hall, Rob
abstract: The paper explores the challenges of capturing context in criminology with reference to one kind of small-N situation – violent crime in rural communities. An illustrative analysis of the violent crime prevention research, select adjunct debates about method, including case-based approaches, was undertaken. First, the paper explores the need for methods offering diversity-oriented ways of understanding country, community,, the individual in situ in the community. Second, it examines how the challenges of “context” are being described in wider debates: about the technical limitations of “big Q” methods for criminology; about the relevance of research evidence; about case-based analyses. Third, it sketches the value of Charles Ragin's diversity-oriented, small-N method for enriching understandings of context. The paper concludes that Ragin's method can add value to local rural crime prevention practice, related micro-social policy development by illuminating the “black box” of individual cases.

title: Applying the problem-solving model to a developing world context: The case of murder in Trinidad, Tobago
authors: Miller, Joel, Hendricks, Nicole J
abstract: This article reflects upon the applicability of the problem-solving model of crime prevention, developed within Britain, the US, to murder in Trinidad, Tobago. Murder, along with other serious violence, has experienced a significant upswing in recent years, apparently related to the increasing integration of Trinidad, Tobago into the global drug economy. The article shows that, while the conventional problem-solving approach provides logical strategies for prevention, it would likely face significant challenges because of problems of corruption, capacity within state institutions. Solving these institutional problems would require, among other things, a stronger role for civil society in crime prevention.

title: Dealing with terrorist threats through A crime prevention, community safety approach
authors: Shaftoe, Henry, Turksen, Umut, Lever, John, Williams, Sara-Jayne
abstract: This paper is based on discussion from the first of a series of five seminars organized by the European Forum for Urban Security. The seminar took place in Bristol on 28, 29 September 2006. Over the 2 days, it was attended by 30 people, including police, municipal emergency planning officers, security specialists, academics. The seminar focused on what could be done to prevent terrorism, with some attention given to minimizing the harms, disruption caused by terrorist incidents. There was a critique of a purely “warfare” or deterrence approach, as well as attempts by governments to feed off citizen's fears, legislate their way out of the problem. It was recognized that the media can be counter-productive in their coverage of terrorist attacks, threats by fuelling fear, giving terrorists the publicity they desire. The theme that came out strongly from this seminar is that prevention through both situational, social interventions is the key to a sustainable reduction in terrorism. Another theme was the importance of communication, negotiation, conflict resolution as means to defusing existing terrorist threats. It was understood that there is a need to recognize “difference”, respect, within limits, that people should be allowed to hold different political views, cultural aspirations, as it is prejudice, intolerance that often fuels extremism. As the paper suggests, the skills, knowledge for both prevention, mediation already exist within local authorities, voluntary organizations, they are regularly used for effective crime prevention. However, many local authorities, government departments are hiving off terrorism as a separate topic to be addressed by others (notably the security services, police, emergency planning departments), rather than as dealing with it as a part of what they do already to prevent crime, minimize harms. This paper examines the possibility of an alternative approach based on crime prevention, community safety.

title: Cross-cultural analysis of perceptions of environmental characteristics in the target selection process for residential burglary
authors: Lee, Kyung-Hoon, Lee, Joong-Yeon
abstract: What are the environmental characteristics that constitute the burglars' template used in their target selection? Are there any similarities or differences in a burglar's template for burglary across cultures? This study attempts to answer these research questions by carrying out experiments, developing a simulated model of burglars' target selection processes, in Korea, the United States. In developing the simulation model, 12 imaginary blocks, 109 dwelling units were constructed to test the hypothesis in relation to a burglar's block, dwelling unit selection. The results of the experiments showed that both culture groups had similar patterns in perceiving environmental characteristics suitable for residential burglary, except for a few differences. Both groups showed a similar pattern of balancing risk, ease factors in their target selection. Overall, both groups considered risk factors as relatively more important than ease factors in decision making. However, the Korean group showed a relatively balanced consideration of risk, ease factors in dwelling unit selection than the US group.

title: Understanding, tackling gang violence
authors: Bullock, Karen, Tilley, Nick
abstract: Gang-involved shootings comprise a serious problem. A Manchester-based project addressing the issue was tracked, its development is discussed. The initiative moved from a planned focus on the situational determinants of shootings, drawing on the successful Boston Gun Project, to one that focused instead on the social determinants of gang membership. The term “gang” itself is highly ambiguous. Equally there are difficulties in defining, operationalizing the concept of “gang membership” for preventative, enforcement purposes. Practical uncertainties followed for the identification of individuals who belong to gangs or are at risk of becoming members,, hence warrant special project attention. This intrinsic uncertainty paved the way for disagreements between the practitioners in their estimates of the risks of gang involvement faced by individuals, in the selection of young people to focus on within the project,, in levels of concern about the consequences that might follow from negatively stereotyping young people as gang members. It is concluded that it may be more effective, efficient to target specific patterns of violent behaviour rather than gang membership for preventative, enforcement attention.

title: The use of exile: The revaluation of power between the ancients, modernity
authors: Noah Walsh, Sean
abstract: In the midst of the Peloponnesian War the city of Athens held its last ostrakaphoria, the ritualized ostracism that served to thwart the ambitions of potential tyrants. Now, in the arena of contemporary politics, a new form of exile has emerged, the so-called residency ban enacted against individuals categorized as sex offenders that effectively prohibits them from maintaining domicile within participating municipalities. It is at the site of exile, perhaps more than at the site of even death itself, that the state reveals its failure. The exile is the actor beyond compliance, insufficiently disciplined, improperly socialized. In this paper, I examine the revaluation of power as represented in the comparison of ancient, modern exile. I argue that the futile effort to control sexual predation through the use of exile succeeds in inadvertently creating a new kind of political resistance. Through the lens of exile a notion of modern power emerges that is inverted from its ancient antecedent.

title: Editors' introduction special edition of cpcs
authors: Townsley, Michael, Tompson, Lisa, Sidebottom, Aiden
abstract: This special edition of Crime Prevention, Community Safety: An International Journal comprises selected papers presented at the 15th Environmental Criminology, Crime Analysis (ECCA) seminar held at University College London, UK in July 2007. ECCA appears to be entering a new phase of growth, in terms of both participating members, research agenda. The 2007 seminar served as an international forum to discuss, exchange, reflect on the developments, research direction, advancements in environmental criminology, related areas such as situational crime prevention, offender profiling.

title: Current policy on domestic violence: A move in the right direction or a step too far?
authors: Welsh, Kirsty
abstract: This paper reflects on doctoral research conducted in Northern England to explore understandings about, approaches to domestic violence. Specifically, it considers the problem's increasing popularization as an “…horrific crime…”, wonders whether, how its increasing celebration as a “collective cause” could marginalize the feminist analyses, action that has, for over 30 years, been so central to endeavours to challenge male violence in the home. Focusing on two issues, gender, crime prevention, the paper examines local, national policy, practice on domestic violence in order to explore whether current policy is a move in the right direction or whether it has taken a step too far.

title: An empowered approach to developing a youth violence prevention plan: A case study in a small but growing rural community
authors: Payne, Brian K, Gainey, Randy R, Button, Deeanna M
abstract: This article describes a recent project in which the authors worked with policy makers, practitioners,, citizens to develop a youth violence prevention plan in a small but significantly growing rural city. The authors participated in an “empowered approach” to research youth violence in the city, made recommendations about strategies to prevent future youth violence. Characteristics of the approach are discussed along with the individual, community-level,, empirical themes that arose during the research, planning process. The strengths of using an empowered approach to study crime, develop response mechanisms are considered. The article concludes with recommendations for ways that other criminologists can use a similar approach in other jurisdictions.

title: Mobile phone reprogramming: Its extent, prevention
authors: Kaplankiran, Tulay, Mailley, Jen, Whitehead, Shaun, Farrell, Graham
abstract: Reprogramming involves hacking the software of a mobile phone to change its identity. A handset's international mobile equipment identity number (equivalent to a car's vehicle identification number) is altered to enable illegal re-sale, thus facilitating theft, robbery of mobiles. The extent of the problem has not been adequately measured, so this study presents two approaches. The first was an on-street survey of owners that examined their mobile phones. The second was an examination of mobile phones in lost property offices. A conservative estimate is that 5\% of the sample of mobiles were stolen or reprogrammed. Studies with larger representative samples are needed but, if representative, this suggests that millions of stolen/reprogrammed mobiles are in circulation in the UK. Possibilities for policing, prevention are discussed.

title: Do relaxed trading hours for bars, clubs mean more relaxed drinking? A review of international research on the impacts of changes to permitted hours of drinking
authors: Stockwell, Tim, Chikritzhs, Tanya
abstract: Trading hours of licensed premises have been progressively relaxed since World War II across much of the English-speaking world as part of a global trend towards liquor deregulation. This review was informed by a systematic search of studies published in the English language since 1965 which sought to evaluate the public health, safety impacts of changes to liquor trading hours for on premise consumption – namely ‘pubs’, clubs in the United Kingdom, ‘hotels’, ‘taverns’ in Australia, New Zealand, ‘bars’ in North America. The systematic search was supplemented by materials identified from the ‘grey literature’, mostly government reports. A total of 49 unique studies met the inclusion criteria of which only 14 included baseline, control measures, were peer-reviewed. Among these, 11 reported at least one significant outcome indicating adverse effects of increased hours or benefits from reduced hours. Controlled studies with fewer methodological problems were also most likely to report such effects. It is suggested that differences between findings from Australia, the United Kingdom following the Licensing Act 2003 are most likely due to differences in methodological approach. It is concluded that the balance of reliable evidence from the available international literature suggests that extended late-night trading hours lead to increased consumption, related harms. Further well-controlled studies are required to confirm this conclusion.

title: Tackling violence in the night-time economy on the ground: Putting policy into practice in England, Wales
authors: Burrell, Amy, Erol, Rosie
abstract: Violence in the night-time economy is a key priority for the police, crime, disorder reduction partnerships (CDRPs), local authorities (LAs) across England, Wales,, there have been a plethora of new policies, strategies introduced to help tackle the problem in recent years. This paper discusses the effects of key policy changes, including the introduction of the Licensing Act 2003, the publication of the National Alcohol Strategy, on the day-to-day delivery of frontline services. This paper highlights how national crime reduction initiatives, strategies, such as the tackling violent crime programme (TVCP), alcohol misuse enforcement campaigns (AMECs) were implemented at a local level. Other interventions, such as the use of head-mounted cameras for evidence gathering, the introduction of the Best Bar None scheme are also discussed in relation to reducing night-time economy violence.

title: A review of the impact of the Licensing Act 2003 on levels of violence in England, Wales: A public health perspective
authors: Morleo, Michela, Lightowlers, Carly, Anderson, Zara, Cook, Penny A, Harkins, Corinne, Bellis, Mark A
abstract: Alcohol has long been associated with violence in nightlife environments across England, Wales. In November 2005, the Licensing Act 2003 provided local authorities with increased controls, flexibility to manage licensed venues. This article explores, from a public health perspective, the relationships between such changes, nightlife violence. Combined, the evaluations reviewed point to a number of potential consequences such as shifts towards consumption of alcohol, violence later at night. However, the impacts vary between local areas. The article concludes that more work is needed to provide robust, national data sets that collate intelligence from a range of information sources. These resources, along with a better understanding of how legislation is being implemented, are necessary to examine, interpret how legislative changes affect levels of night-time violence. Such a public health approach would provide a valuable insight into how successful initiatives can be developed to reduce nightlife violence.

title: Shaping the night: How licensing, social divisions, informal social controls mould the form, content of nightlife
authors: Hadfield, Phil, Measham, Fiona
abstract: This paper considers licensing as a governmental tool for controlling crime, disorder in the night-time economy while simultaneously shaping that economy's social mores. Using recent contrasting examples from the English, Welsh experience – the regulation of live music events, lap dancing – the paper shows how licensing frameworks endorse particular social, cultural, economic forms while criminalizing, delegitimizing, suppressing others. Regulation of alcohol sales, entertainment (through licensing) sits in uneasy relationship with contemporary youth/young adult cultures, local leisure scenes. Young people's identities are constructed, in part, by, through their experiences as ‘consumers’ of nightlife. Within this context, heavy sessional alcohol consumption remains an important motif for young people; a culture of intoxication, combined with wider sources of social tension, fragmentation, governs the ‘life of night’ informally, in more subtle, pervasive, effective ways than formal dicta could hope to achieve.

title: The epidemic of petit corruption in contemporary Cambodia: Causes, consequences, solutions
authors: Feinberg, Gary
abstract: This study explores the nature, magnitude, seriousness of ‘unofficial fees’, other forms of corruption in Cambodia, a nation still reeling from the devastating effects of Pol Pot's genocidal regime (1975–1979), one that annihilated its intellectual resources, destroyed its economy, eviscerated its social identity. It continues by profiling unofficial fees, corruption in education, health care, other public agencies, ‘job renting,’ as well as a mammoth tax-evasion problem. In addition, perceived causes of corruption, its manifold, pernicious consequences are addressed. It concludes with a critical analysis of proffered methods for reducing corruption, such as implementing an independent judiciary, improving public officials’ salaries, applying transparent accounting procedures, other collaborative solutions.

title: Household guardians: A multilevel analysis of household-level guardianship, individual-level victimization risks
authors: Shim, Hyunjung, Hayes, Brittany E
abstract: Guardianship is a multidimensional concept that influences the risk of victimization. However, the influence of the household—central to people’s routines—has been overlooked. Using data from the NCVS (2017–2022), this study employs a multilevel analysis of household guardianship to investigate residents’ risk of violent victimization, domestic violence, controlling for individual-level factors. Living in single-unit households, marriage,, owning a home reduce the risk of violent victimization. Conversely, owning a business, residing in urban areas increase this risk. For domestic violence, living in single-unit households increases the risk, whereas gated communities lower the risk. Implications for crime prevention, future directions on guardianship are discussed.

title: Explaining, sustaining the crime drop: Clarifying the role of opportunity-related theories
authors: Farrell, Graham, Tilley, Nick, Tseloni, Andromachi, Mailley, Jen
abstract: Western industrialised countries experienced major reductions in crime for a decade from the early to mid-1990s. The absence of adequate explanation identifies a failing of criminological theory, empirical study. More importantly, it means that none of the forces that reduced crime can confidently be harnessed for policy purposes. Existing hypotheses relating to the crime drops are reviewed, found generally wanting. Many do not stand up to empirical testing. Others do not seem able to explain crime increases (such as phone theft, robbery, internet-related crimes) that occurred alongside the crime drops. It is suggested that the set of opportunity-related theories, or the criminologies of everyday life, present a more promising line of research. The ‘security hypothesis’ is discussed wherein changes in the level, quality of security may have been a key driving force behind the crime drop,, an agenda of crime-specific research is proposed.

title: Towards degarrisonisation in Jamaica: A place for civil society
authors: Johnson, Hume Nicola
abstract: For nearly 50 years, powerful politically connected criminal actors called ‘dons’ (or area leaders) have occupied – Mafia style – some of Jamaica's deprived urban communities,, enacted new, outlaw forms of community leadership. In these communities, notoriously labelled ‘garrisons’, dons have ‘manufactured consent’ for their illicit rule, using coercive tactics, by positioning themselves as legitimate civic leaders. In the process, these rogue actors have not only gained acceptance among significant numbers of the subaltern class but also (tacit) political recognition in the wider society. Genuine civil society has been eclipsed in Jamaica's urban garrisons due to the persistence of this rogue leadership. Still, a more hopeful outlook for Jamaica may be possible. Drawing upon previous research outlining the widespread struggle against the Mafia led by members of Italian civil society,, the ensuing decline in its omnipotence in that country, the paper considers the implications of the positive developments in Italy for the noticeable movement towards degarrisonisation in Jamaica,, contemplates what role a resurrected Jamaican civil society might play in this process.

title: Community responses to tourism, crime
authors: Brunt, Paul, Hooton, Natalie
abstract: Tourism is known to bring about positive, negative changes in destinations. This paper explores how tourism business owners' lives, residents within the tourism area of an English seaside resort respond in their behaviour as a consequence of tourism-related crime, their fear of such crimes. Through a mixture of primary, secondary data analysis it is clear that crime in the case study area increases during the tourism season. The results suggested that these are changes in behaviour made by parking in different locations; socializing differently; bypassing specific streets at night;, carrying out additional security checks in the home. Perceptions of the destination, of criminal activity were found to vary in relation to occupation, involvement with the tourism industry,, there were associations with socio-demographic variables, the level of attachment to the town.

title: A situational crime prevention approach to cyberstalking victimization: Preventive tactics for Internet users, online place managers
authors: Reyns, Bradford W
abstract: Cyberstalking is a specialized form of stalking, which takes place in cyberspace using Internet capable tools. The stalking behavior is carried out using a variety of electronic communication methods across different online domains. These include emails, instant messenger (IM) messages, blog posts, text messages, any other form of electronic communication which is persistent, annoying, alarming or threatening to the victim. Although the more traditional offline forms of stalking have begun to receive some attention by researchers over the last decade, cyberstalking is still little known, largely because the Internet has only made such activities possible in recent years. Limiting its occurrence may be accomplished by limiting opportunities for potential stalkers to gain access to their victims. The techniques of situational crime prevention are ideal for this task,, have proven successful in limiting opportunities for different kinds of crime across a wide range of situations. Tactics for Internet users, place managers are discussed.

title: Direct elections, the local governance of crime in the United Kingdom: A view from the ground
authors: Button, Mark, Loveday, Barry
abstract: In the latter half of 2008, proposals emerged from the Home Office for the creation of a completely new elected office in England, Wales, the Crime, Policing Representative. These were to be directly elected, would chair Crime, Disorder Reduction Partnerships (CDRPs) in England, Community Safety Partnerships (CSPs) in Wales, as well as automatically become members of the police authority. However, before the proposals were even debated in parliament they were dropped because of concerns extremist parties may win them. This article presents findings from interviews with a range of councillors, police officers, other officials working with or for CDRPs/CSPs in a representative mix of authorities. It shows that although extremist parties winning were a concern there were many more compelling reasons to reject this policy. The article ends with a brief discussion of alternative proposals that could be considered.

title: Licence recalls, returns to custody in England, Wales
authors: Bowers, Kate, Pease, Ken
abstract: The Ministry of Justice issued statistics of recalls to custody in July 2009, after media outrage about murders committed by an offender remaining free some 33 days after his recall. A contrast is drawn between the Ministry of Justice recall figures with in many ways analogous cancer survival rates, which provide helpful estimates of probability of succumbing to the disease. The Ministry of Justice figures do not address the key question of the number, proportion of those recalled who remain at liberty 1, 2, 3, so on months after release. Re-analysis of the figures tentatively concludes that a minimum of 330 of those recalled remain at liberty 6 months after their recall, a minimum of 200 12 months after recall. Analyses subsequently released by the Ministry of Justice are liable to the same criticisms as those analysed here.

title: The use of off-trade glass as a weapon in violent assaults by Young Offenders
authors: Forsyth, Alasdair J M, Khan, Furzana, McKinlay, William
abstract: This article aims to highlight the neglected issue of ‘glassing’ injury risk from off-trade alcohol bottles. The study participants included a survey of male Young Offenders (n=172) recruited during their induction into Scotland's only Young Offenders Institution in 2007, an interview sample (n=30) recruited in the same way during 2008. A self-complete questionnaire enquired about respondent's drinking, offending. Face-to-face interviews were conducted to qualitatively investigate issues raised by the 2007 survey. The survey comprised more than a quarter of Scotland's male Young Offenders. Over 80 per cent had been drinking before their current offence. Approximately two-thirds reported using a weapon (80 per cent while under the influence of alcohol). After knives, bottles were their most often ‘used’ weapon. Unlike knives, bottles were seldom reported as being ‘carried’. Interviewees more often gave accounts of using bottles than any other potential weapon, suggesting that bottles may not be considered as a weapon (in the same way as knives), but simply happen to be omnipresent when alcohol-related violence occurs. On-trade glass was never mentioned during this research. There is a clear need to highlight the risks posed by off-trade alcohol glassware,, for this to be replaced with plastic containers where possible.

title: Responding to anti-social behaviour: Analysis, interventions, the transfer of knowledge
authors: Bullock, Karen
abstract: This article examines contemporary responses to anti-social behaviour (ASB) in England, Wales. Drawing on empirical evidence, it examines how ASB problems are understood, prioritised by practitioners; the nature of the interventions developed, implemented to address problems;, the ways in which outcomes are evaluated. The article points to how systematic analysis of ASB problems is unusual, responses are usually reactive; there has been a focus on enforcement interventions rather than on the development of broader solutions to problems;, evaluation of outcomes is weak. These findings are discussed in relation to the development of the ASB agenda in England, Wales. Implications for solving problems are discussed.

title: A university sexual misconduct policy: Prioritizing student victims’ voices
authors: Tamborra, Tracy L, Narchet, Fadia M
abstract: This article discusses the creation of a college campus sexual misconduct policy. Major emphasis is placed on the involvement, input of students at all levels of policy creation. In order to elicit student feedback, a survey was administered to 119 students. Survey results revealed that exposure to sexually aggressive experiences were related to the location of the incident, the perpetrator's group affiliation (for example, athletes). Findings also revealed a relationship between the use of intoxicants, experience with sexual aggression. In addition, findings revealed that respondents who had sexually aggressive experiences did not report their experience to on-campus resources. These findings resulted in specific policy changes, recommendations.

title: Post-emotional man, a community safety with feeling
authors: Davies, Pamela
abstract: This article focuses on the affective dimensions of crime, victimisation. Presupposing that human emotion is important generally in understanding social relations, it operates at two levels. At one level it explores potentially complementary approaches to the study of human emotion in criminological, victimological, community safety research, theory. Flowing from these ideas, I suggest that the subjective, embodied, experiential aspects of doing crime, surviving victimisation are crucial in the search for secure, compassionate communities. Examples of emotions that have the potential to stimulate both negative, positive motivations, actions are considered. At this level the article considers human emotion, feeling as a prominent policy concern. While acknowledging the difficulties in the struggle to establish compassionate communities, the importance of cultivating emotions that are likely to enhance safety, promote security, emotions based on empathy, compassion for others are explored. Arguing that gender-sensitive emotions particularly matter to crime prevention, community safety endeavours, this article contributes to a more developed criminological sociology of emotions.

title: Criminalizing communities of poor, dark women in the Caribbean: The fight against crime through Puerto Rico's public housing
authors: Dinzey-Flores, Zaire Zenit
abstract: In the year 1993, Mano Dura Contra el Crimen [Hard Hand against Crime] was implemented in Puerto Rico with the purposes of fighting crime in the island. Exclusively targeting public housing projects, this policy included a range of environmental interventions. This article questions the policy's targeting mechanism by analyzing whether public housing communities in Puerto Rico were indeed presenting higher criminal activity than other sectors of the island. This article then examines the race, class, gender profile of the public housing communities, examines how the Mano Dura policies served to solidify a profile of public housing communities that was not consistent with the real demographic profile of these communities. This article argues that the policies led to the increased stigmatization, isolation of public housing communities.

title: International travel for purposes of child sexual exploitation: Policies, responses
authors: Thomas, Terry
abstract: The ability of all people to move more easily across international borders has brought with it the spectre of the mobile offender, including the person who might commit sexual offences. This article explores why the sex offender, in particular, might want to travel to commit further offences,, what devices can be employed to minimise the possibilities of such movement, prevent further offending. Taking the United Kingdom as a case study, the article looks at ways of identifying the incoming sex offender, ensuring that the outgoing offender only leaves after notifying the police of his intentions. The ways of preventing a sex offender from travelling from the United Kingdom are also considered.

title: A letter from Cyprus: Migration, policy transference, the piloting of neighbourhood watch
authors: Mawby, R I
abstract: This brief article discusses bottom-up policy transference, using the recent example of a neighbourhood watch pilot project in the Republic of Cyprus. Here, it is argued, British ‘ex-pats’ have been instrumental in persuading the police to cooperate in the formation of an initiative previously unknown to the island.

title: Schooled in democracy? Promoting democratic values as a whole-school approach to violence prevention
authors: Holt, Amanda, Martin, Denise, Hayden, Carol, Nee, Claire
abstract: This article discusses a Europe-wide project that aimed to promote Safer Schools through utilising a Charter of ‘democratic principles’. This included the non-violent resolution of conflicts, the right to equal treatment, respect. The first part of this article discusses the empirical findings from original research conducted with five London schools (and their local partners) who participated in this project. It was found that most participants were positive about the project's potential, with many ‘democratic initiatives’ cited as examples of how the promotion of a principled Charter could produce good practice in combating violence in schools. The second part of this article raises more fundamental questions about the role of democracy in violence prevention programmes. In particular, it questions the assumption of a direct relationship between (non)violence, democratic values,, asks whether it is possible to promote democratic principles within inherently undemocratic institutions such as schools.

title: A letter from Australia: Addressing deficits in venue security officer training in Cairns
authors: Hayes-Jonkers, Charmaine S, Pointing, Shane, Clough, Alan R
abstract: As with other front-line agencies, the role of licensed venue security officers is risky, as they put their bodies on the line at work. As ‘the watchers’ of public behaviour, disorder, security officers are rarely asked about their needs or how to improve their industry, their role within it. A study of alcohol-related assault in, around licensed premises in inner city of Cairns (far North Queensland, Australia) identified the need for basic training in human behaviour, as it is essential to staff safety, protection. As part of the Cairns study researchers provided this training in response to senior management's request. This article describes the training provided, security officers’ responses to it. The industry may be failing licensed venue security officers if rudimentary skills-based learning, workplace health, safety training, support are not addressed.

title: Community safety politics, policy in Europe
authors: Moore, Stephen, Millie, Andrew
abstract: This special issue brings together contributions from across Europe on policy, political rhetoric on community safety. This issue differs from the usual structure for the journal by including a combination of four articles, three shorter commentaries.

title: Crime prevention, community safety policies from a dynamic, comparative perspective: The cases of Rome, London
authors: Lucianetti, Livia
abstract: In the past 30 years, the issue of urban community safety has gained increased social, political relevance, being decisive in the results of national, local elections in Europe, elsewhere. Western countries have responded to increasing levels of fear, insecurity through the diffusion of ‘new prevention’ approaches, giving place to what has been called the ‘preventive turn’. The spread of these new approaches generated a debate around the convergence of policy ideas, solutions. These convergence processes have been widely interpreted as the result of macro-factors such as the deep socio-economic, cultural processes of change impacting post-modern societies, determining a phase of state restructuring rooted on neo-liberal principles. Despite the fact that convergence processes are taking place, significant elements of divergence are still present across Europe. These are attributed to the complexity, heterogeneity of what Hughes defines as ‘geo-histories’ (namely, a place's own geographic, historical context of reference), to a country's institutional infrastructure. The objective of this work is to offer a contribution to the debate around convergence, policy change processes of crime prevention, community safety in Europe through a comparative analysis of community safety policies in Rome, London. The article concludes that different factors may impact upon policy divergence or convergence at different times. In the period of left-wing dominance up to 2008, local discourses, practices were strongly influenced by the different national, local politics on crime prevention, security, as well as by the different normative framework, governance patterns. However, since 2008, the shift to right-wing local governments that assumed power, there has been a convergence based on discourses operating more at a symbolic, emotive level. Furthermore, there may be greater continuity in policy between politically different administrations than is immediately apparent.

title: Commentary on community safety in Germany
authors: Matt, Eduard
abstract: This article summarizes some of the new developments in crime prevention/community safety that have taken place in Germany in the last few decades. It highlights the steps towards cross-governmental cooperation in this area, the increasing attempts to incorporate the broader population in crime prevention activities. Alongside these developments has been the growth in the voluntary sector's involvement.

title: Sustaining evidence-based policing in an era of cuts: Estimating fear of crime at small area level in England
authors: Whitworth, Adam
abstract: Fear of crime has become a major focus of attention both for policy makers, within the academic literature, although geography is considered relevant to fear of crime little is known about how it varies spatially. The present article applies multilevel modelling to a newly available geocoded version of the British Crime Survey to explore the feasibility of estimating fear of crime down to small area level across England. Five of the six models are considered sufficiently powerful in explaining the between-area variance to produce estimates. Estimates of fear of crime for these five crime types are produced (with 95 per cent credible intervals to indicate their likely precision) for small areas, local authorities in England, are placed in the public domain. The models also highlight, however, that most of the variance in individual's fear of crime is within rather than between small areas, questioning the logic of area-based policies to tackle fear of crime. In an era of public sector resource tightening, targeting, it is hoped that these findings will enable practitioners, policy makers, academics to continue to understand, monitor geographical variations in fear of crime.

title: Crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED), the New South Wales crime risk assessment guidelines: A critical review
authors: Clancey, Garner, Lee, Murray, Fisher, Daren
abstract: Crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) guidelines have been adopted in Australia, internationally. In 2001 CPTED guidelines were introduced in New South Wales (NSW). Since their introduction there has been little discussion or scholarly analysis of these guidelines. This article seeks to address this gap through a critical analysis of the NSW guidelines, related crime risk assessment reports. On the basis of this analysis, we argue that the guidelines provide limited direction for the compilation of crime risk assessment reports, little guidance to local authorities (that is councils) assessing development applications. The existing guidelines are based on four CPTED concepts, which limits assessment of crime risks, the lack of diagrams, photos or illustrations reduces their overall utility. While the introduction of the guidelines triggered an increased focus on ways to design out crime, our research suggests the guidelines require revision. Guidelines from other Australian jurisdictions (such as Victoria) provide a potential model for how the NSW guidelines could be improved.

title: When intervention is a load of rubbish: Evaluating the impact of ‘clean-up’ operations
authors: Brown, Rick, Evans, Emily
abstract: This article examines the impact of 10 clean-up operations designed to improve the environment. The findings of environmental visual audits undertaken before, after the operations show that the level of refuse declines in only half the cases, with an increase in the other half of cases. This may be explained by the poor engagement with the community that can accompany such operations. These findings show that even the simplest, most ‘common-sense’ interventions can bring about unintended consequences without careful thought to the way in which the intervention is expected to work.

title: The Cairns Model: Evaluating the context of an open-space, closed circuit television system in an urban centre in tropical Australia
authors: Pointing, E Shane, Hayes-Jonkers, Charmaine S, Clough, Alan R
abstract: Australian, United Kingdom evaluations of open-space, closed circuit television (CCTV) systems in urban areas were reviewed in an attempt to identify elements of good practice, assess the Cairns Regional Council's (CRC) CCTV system against them. Recommended management, operational practices were extracted from peer reviewed public health, criminological literature, government reports. These were grouped by key topics, tabulated. CRC's CCTV manuals were examined. Observational sessions, open-ended discussions, focus groups with operators, stakeholders were used to identify operational, management practices. These were then compared with those found in the literature, the results fed back to Council. We found the Cairns CCTV model generally met recommended guidelines but improvements are possible. This article also situates this study within debate surrounding the adequacy of CCTV evaluation. Our evaluation used a public health ‘continuous quality improvement’ approach incorporating elements of a criminological ‘realist evaluation’ methodology. This identified 10 contexts within which to postulate, test, with further research, the mechanisms through which the Cairns CCTV system operates. Implications for improving our understanding of the effectiveness of CCTV are discussed.

title: Dispatches from the field: Developing community safety in Northern Ireland
authors: Brunger, Mark
abstract: This article critically examines the ongoing development of community safety in Northern Ireland. By drawing upon in-depth interviews with key practitioners, the article assesses the current architecture that is in place to support community safety-based activity, as well as considering the future prospects for community safety in Northern Ireland since the devolution of criminal justice to the Department of Justice in 2010. The article maintains that against the background of transition, where Northern Ireland is moving from a society in conflict to one of peace, the progression towards a holistic, ‘bottom-up’ community safety-based framework to tackle crime, its often damaging social effects continues to be obfuscated by a number of issues. These include: an overarching ‘top-down’ managerialist framework embodied in an array of centrally directed performance targets that, while seemingly providing a de-politicised, neutral discourse, applies a methodology that often denigrates the importance of acute local problems. In addition, the legacy of political violence,, its continuance in some areas, is contributing to inertia in many State agencies to go beyond the symbolism of partnership working, fully engage with the community, which would involve radically changing the nature of their work. The article concludes that community safety, in its more ‘bottom-up’ sense, has simply failed to materialise.

title: Secondary school children, the experience of robbery: A survey in three south London schools
authors: Hayden, Carol, Dlugosz, Gabriela
abstract: This article presents selected results from a victimisation survey of secondary school pupils in three very different schools in south London (n=1590). The focus is on the experience of robbery in school, on the journey to, from school; ‘experience’ includes those who were personally ‘robbed’ when they were alone, as well as those who were with others when they were ‘robbed’. The associations between this experience, perceptions of safety, safe behaviours are explored.
