abstract: Wife assault has proven elusive to attempts to measure its actual incidence. Reliance on police statistics, official records, clinical data appears to present only part of the picture. Societal taboos serve to deter people from calling attention to this behavior,, therefore formal methods of compiling data are somewhat flawed. Surveys appear to provide a more complete portrayal of the incidence of wife assault, in part due to their anonymity, direct nature. Three different types of surveys are critically examined, efforts made to glean rates of severe, recurrent wife assault from each. While surveys may provide more information on this behavior, various factors inherent to the design of the surveys contribute to their own inaccuracies.

title: The impact of crime on international tourist numbers to cape town
authors: George, Richard
abstract: Cape Town, a major tourism destination, is under the spotlight due to its susceptibility to crime committed against tourists. The ‘Mother City’ of South Africa, along with Durban, Johannesburg, is increasingly perceived to be an unsafe place to visit. Street crime, car hijacking, petty crime, muggings, acts of serious violence have continued to increase. Furthermore, there has been a spate of bombings—21 to be exact—in, around Cape Town during the last two years. Between 1998, 2000 these attacks have left three people dead, 105 injured,, have threatened the region's economic development, in particular its tourism industry. The most devastating of these incidences was a pipe bomb at the Planet Hollywood restaurant at the V \& A Waterfront—Cape Town's major tourist venue—which killed two people, seriously injured many, including tourists. This paper examines the effects of this incident, along with the escalation of violent crime in the Cape Town region, on its hospitality sector,, discusses recent crime prevention measures.

title: Workplace violence: ‘the family connection’
authors: Collins, Pam, Scarborough, Kay, Southerland, Mittie
abstract: In the following paper, the authors examine a rare type of lethal workplace violence. Most lethal workplace violence occurs at a single site, time. Yet there are cases which involve multiple sites of violent acts by an offender over a short time-frame. This paper defines the characteristics that distinguish between a multi-site, single-site incident,, also addresses the connections between incident, offender,, victim variables. It meticulously describes these incidents, including offenders, victims of lethal workplace violence, that differ when the incident occurs at multiple sites rather than at a single site.

title: Resolving conflict in the community: A case for mediation?
authors: Simmonds, Lesley
abstract: Neighbour disputes have become increasingly recognised as a problem in that if unresolved they may lead to (serious) crime. This is especially pertinent against the current backdrop of ‘community safety’. However, in England, Wales the Crime, Disorder Act 1998, although concerned with ‘anti-social behaviour’, does not immediately embrace such disputes. Community mediation may, nevertheless, represent a more accessible and, perhaps, more appropriate remedy for this type of conflict, while at the same mirroring the ‘restorative’ shift occurring within criminal justice. In considering the value of mediation this paper uses measures of satisfaction that relate to both outcomes, process. Overall it presents a positive view of the service, but attention is also paid to the potential misuse of community mediation.

title: Crime prevention, planning: Searching for common sense in disorder legislation
authors: Moss, Kate, Seddon, Martin
abstract: It has recently been suggested that Section 17 of the Crime, Disorder Act 1998 did not create an additional material consideration, nor would it affect Home Office Circular 5/94: Planning Out Crime. Reference to published research suggests that Section 17 considerations are already material, according to decided case law,, that Circular 5/94 has already been affected by these, other changes in environmental planning, since DETR has already tendered for its review, update. It is suggested that the appeal decisions cited in support of this claim are not representative of the general trend in planning,, that in support of the government's initiative towards partnerships in crime prevention, joined-up thinking in environmental planning, crime reduction, planners, crime reduction specialists both within, outside the police are currently working together more fully to incorporate crime, design issues into the planning process at an early stage to produce the best possible results.

title: Surfing the crime net: Policing, crime prevention, community safety in Australia
authors: Palmer, Darren
abstract: There can be no doubt that the Internet offers the possibility of increasing access to a range of sources of available information in a timely manner. This is particularly so as we increasingly seek to engage with information from outside our jurisdictional boundaries. While this hints at the effects of globalisation, it is also meant to be suggestive of the practical realities involved in researching (or simply following) developments occurring within emergent federal structures (for instance the European Union) or longer-standing federations such as the United States, Australia. Of course, a department or agency having a homepage, various links is only the start of the process of making information accessible. As will be indicated below, there remain significant limitations in the electronic material available from many agencies. Fortunately, there are also a number of organisations that enable the researcher to access original data, research publications.

title: Crime on campus: A survey of space users
authors: Robinson, Matthew B, Mullen, Kenneth L
abstract: This paper reports findings from a study of perceptions, realities of crime at a regional, comprehensive university campus in North Carolina, USA. Specifically, the study explored perceptions of the primary place users of the campus (ie students, faculty, staff,, university police officers) on matters related to criminal victimization, fear of crime,, perception of crime risk. It also assessed environmental conditions on campus. We sought to identify how students, faculty, staff,, police view crime on campus,, to what degree each group feared crime, how they perceived risks to their personal safety. We also aimed to identify environmental conditions unique to particular areas on campus which may be related to fear of crime, perceptions of crime risk. Finally, we compared perceptions of crime on campus with its reality, as measured by self-reported victimizations of students, faculty,, staff, as well as official police reports. Since crime prevention policy on campus is logically best informed by the primary users of campus space, this study sets forth a model for future research in preventing campus crime.

title: Letter from America: The reality approach to deterring drinking, drug use among juveniles
authors: Witte, Christine, Dundes, Lauren
abstract: Reality, an innovative prevention program that goes beyond teaching facts, makes first-time juvenile drug, alcohol offenders contemplate possible negative outcomes of their behaviour which have repercussions for their entire social circle. The program combats juveniles' rationalizations for adverse consequences resulting from drug, alcohol abuse, addresses their tendency towards short-term personal gratification. Data from 229 participants in Reality reveal that these offenders have few explicit long-term plans that might otherwise help them to focus on their future,, to deter behaviors that could jeopardize their aspirations. Although it is difficult to determine the effectiveness of such programs as Reality, its unique approach, supported by its theoretical foundation (techniques of neutralization, self-control theory) make the curriculum worthy of consideration for youthful drug, alcohol first-time offenders.

title: Policing alcohol-related crime in the UK: Would a public health approach in alcohol-related crime reduction strategies help maximise success?
authors: Deehan, Ann
abstract: The role of alcohol in crime has been long debated. Does alcohol cause crime or is it merely one of a multitude of factors that are associated with crime? In the midst of this debate there is one fact: the police regularly come into contact with individuals as a result of the latter's alcohol consumption—and such contact may offer a window of opportunity for public health interventions. While strategies to combat drug-related crime routinely include a public health approach targeting the individual's drug use, alcohol-related crime reduction strategies rarely target the individual's alcohol consumption. This paper explores the potential benefits of applying alcohol-related public health interventions to police arrestees. It begins by examining the reasons why alcohol public health policy has not filtered into the criminal justice system in the UK. In addition what role, if any, the police could legitimately have is explored. Finally, it argues that an alcohol public health element in a crime reduction strategy should focus on the problematic alcohol users rather than dependent alcohol users alone.

title: The audit culture, crime, disorder reduction partnerships: Exorcising the wicked issue of community safety?
authors: Hughes, Gordon
abstract: There are few areas in criminal justice that have seen such a growth industry as that which has occurred of late in the UK around community safety, local crime, disorder reduction partnerships. In the wake of the 1998 Crime, Disorder Act, we have seen a massive proliferation in posts, teams in local authorities dedicated to the pursuit of the by no means easily reconcilable goals of community safety, of crime, disorder reduction. This overview of recent developments in the audit, strategy process of crime, disorder reduction partnerships (CDRPs) offers a critique of the closely intertwined dominant ‘audit culture’, the ‘what works’ paradigm of policy, practice, whose influence is especially marked in the policy field of ‘crime reduction’. Despite the manifest persistence of punitive populism, the logic of mass-deterrent incarceration in the politics of law, order, the adaptive strategies associated with auditable, managerialised reductive measures, realised through the multi-agency partnerships, are increasingly in the ascendancy in the contemporary UK crime control complex. In the first section of the paper the lessons of the post- Morgan agenda of the 1990s are outlined. In the next section the key findings of current academic research into the immediate post-1998 (‘phase one’) CDRP audits, strategies are summarised. In the final section the likely consequences of the post-2002 ‘phase two’ processes of audit, strategy are outlined, in terms of a series of questions rather than of definite answers. Throughout this paper a central argument is that this new ‘community’-based, multi-agency partnership approach to the governance of crime control is indissolubly linked to political, moral contestations about the nature of the relationship of the state, public authorities, the citizenry, communities in conditions of late modernity,, is accordingly not reducible to either good managerial practice or technical efficiency, however important these may be.

title: The crime, disorder audit process: A post-mortem on the first round
authors: Bowers, Kate, Jennings, Jennifer, Hirschfield, Alex
abstract: This paper reviews crime, disorder audits published following the 1998 Crime, Disorder Act. It specifically examines the audits produced in the North-west, North-east of England, by means of a survey of the partnerships as well as an analysis of the content, design of the audit documents themselves. The primary aim of this exercise was to establish what was best practice, what elements were involved in obtaining this. In general, it has been found that last time round the whole process was an important learning experience, which is likely to require a number of changes not only in organisational matters but also in relation to data issues.

title: Alcohol-related crime, disorder: The first audit, strategy documents from crime, disorder partnerships
authors: Deehan, Ann, Saville, Esther
abstract: The links between alcohol, crime have been extensively explored. While the research evidence points to a link between alcohol, various types of crime, there are no official statistics collected systematically, making it impossible to gain a true picture of the role of alcohol in crime at a national level. However, further evidence is emerging of the presence of alcohol in offending, although this does not prove that alcohol is causal in crime being committed. Local crime audit data collected as a result of the 1998 Crime, Disorder Act, therefore, could be a potentially rich source of information. This paper describes the extent to which alcohol-related crime was raised as an issue in local crime audit documents, how it is dealt with in resulting crime, disorder strategies,, gives some practical recommendations for future work.

title: The land that crime forgot? Auditing the isles of scilly
authors: Mawby, R I
abstract: This paper summarises the main findings from the 2001/2002 Crime Audit for the Isles of Scilly. The islands form the smallest Crime, Disorder Reduction Partnership (CDRP) in England, Wales,, despite their dependence on tourism crime is a rarity. The paper cites police data, other agencies' records,, the results of postal surveys conducted with local residents, the business community. These surveys also demonstrate that fear of crime does not appear a major concern on the islands. Further analysis suggests that crime rates have risen in recent years, that crime, disorder issues are associated with tourism, but that the Isles of Scilly remain ‘the land that crime forgot’. Nevertheless, local residents, the business community demonstrated a willingness to consider a wide range of crime reduction measures, particularly emphasising social crime prevention.

title: Beyond technicism: Broadening the ‘what works’ paradigm in crime prevention
authors: Cherney, Adrian
abstract: Since the 1990s there has been an upsurge in policy-related research that aims to identify ‘what works’ in crime prevention. The principal aim has been to institute an evaluated body of knowledge that delineates ‘best practice’, providing a basis for the design, implementation of evidence-based crime prevention policy. The overall result has been efforts to specify general ‘what works’ principles that have a broad application across, within various jurisdictions, contexts. The main aim of this article is not to stipulate emerging ‘what works’ principles in crime prevention, but rather to provide a critical appraisal of this trend. The article is divided into three interrelated sections. Section one attempts to situate ‘what works’ research in crime prevention, explaining why it has gained prominence, currency. The second section provides a critical appraisal of the trend to specify ‘what works’ in the context of crime prevention's wider political, symbolic significance. The third section canvasses the issue of replication. It is concluded that any ‘what works’ program should be far broader than the current ‘technicist’ agenda being adopted.

title: The victimisation of petrol service stations: Crime patterns, implications
authors: Chakraborti, Neil, Gill, Martin, Willis, Andrew, Hart, Jerry, Smith, Polly
abstract: Whilst the recent growth of research on retail crime has to some degree raised awareness of the considerable impacts of such crime, there remain a number of areas that have yet to be explored. One prime example is the victimisation of petrol service stations. By investigating the nature, extent of crime committed against petrol retail outlets in the UK, the present study was designed to encourage greater understanding of the problem, to assist in the development of preventive measures.The paper focuses on the key crime patterns identified in this research, which highlight the wide range, number of offences committed, their serious financial consequences for petrol retailers. In addition, the research has shown that service stations are vulnerable targets for criminal activity in both urban, rural parts of the country,, at all times of the day, week, year. These findings have serious implications for petrol retailers,, suggest that both improved security measures, increased police intervention are needed to reduce crime, increase safety in service stations across the country.

title: Crime in Russia: Exploring the link between victimisation, concern about crime
authors: Beck, Adrian, Robertson, Annette
abstract: During the past ten to 15 years, political, economic, social transformation has led to unprecedented increases in crime across countries in Eastern, Central Europe, including Russia,, this has resulted in widespread public concern. This article uses survey data to explore the relationship between victimisation, concern about crime among the Russian population. Both the extent, patterns of victimisation are investigated, as are people's concerns about crime in general, about specific types of offences. Having established which groups are more likely to be victimised in Russia, which are more likely to express concern about crime, the article discusses the extent to which victimisation influences people's concerns. It concludes by briefly considering how Russia could begin to tackle these two interrelated problems.

title: Tourists' fear of crime while on holiday in cape town
authors: George, Richard
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to evaluate whether tourists who visited Cape Town in August, September 2001 felt safe while staying in, touring round the ‘Mother City’,, how they perceived safety, security in Cape Town. The findings, which were taken from a survey of 438 visitors to Cape Town, reveal that respondents had reasonably positive perceptions of safety, security, although they felt unsafe going out after dark, using the city's public transport. A number of personal factors, such as nationality, previous experience of crime, were also found to affect respondents' perceptions of crime. These findings are compared with several studies, which include empirical research conducted at other international tourist destinations, the Institute for Security Studies Cape Town Victim Survey,, the South African Tourism data on foreign visitors' perceptions of tourism facilities in the country. In the light of the findings, it is recommended that the tourism industry, law enforcement agencies coordinate efforts to improve crime prevention measures in Cape Town.

title: If you don't call us, we'll call you: The experiences of business crime direct
authors: Douglass, John P, Bowers, Kate J, Young, Chris, Clare, Louise
abstract: Business Crime Direct is an initiative funded by the Home Office's Targeted Policing Programme which aims to reduce crime against small businesses throughout Merseyside. It was envisaged that this initiative would build on the experience of previous research, which had found that it was crucial to access those harder-to reach businesses that saw crime as an inevitable part of everyday life; these were often the most victimised businesses. It was also seen as important to provide a continued support service to those at the greatest risk, to maintain, extend the longevity of the effect of any assistance that was given, to increase the momentum of crime prevention efforts. BCD was therefore set up using a call centre to manage potential recipients of security improvements, to grant assistance. It would so this by receiving inward enquiries, making outward contact with businesses,, referring those of the latter most at risk to Security Advice Officers, who then made site visits. This dual approach to managing the contact between businesses, crime prevention experts, along with accurate recording of the history of this contact, should assist in providing such long-term support to hard-to-reach higher-risk businesses. The extent to which the service achieved these aims,, the problems experienced in implementing such an innovative scheme, are discussed in this paper.

title: DNA, the active criminal population
authors: Leary, Dick, Pease, Ken
abstract: Analysis of rates of submission of crime scene samples from one police force area, of matches with offender DNA samples already on the national database demonstrates, first, an increasing rate of submission, second, a steady state of matching in the West Midlands force during the period studied, at 58 per cent,, third, a reasonable linear fit between number of samples, number of matches, suggesting no diminution in return as the number of submitted samples increased. The results are discussed in terms of the distribution of lengths of criminal career; implications for practice are also discussed, especially the importance of taking criminal justice samples at the first presenting opportunity.

title: The extent of the impact of terrorism on international travel, tourism at specific tourist destinations
authors: Brunt, Paul, Cousins, Karen
abstract: This study reviews the relationships between tourism, terrorism,, in particular their impacts on tourism demand. Following a review of the literature, the effects of specific terrorist incidents involving tourists which occurred in different countries during 1997 are considered. These incidents included: a bomb attack at a shopping mall in Jerusalem, Israel, in September; a truck bomb explosion in the Sri Lankan capital of Colombo in October;, the killing of 58 tourists near Luxor in Egypt in November. To explore the impacts of these incidents on tourism demand, statistical data concerning tourist arrivals in each of the countries concerned were analysed. Whilst, due to the nature of the research, its methodological limitations, the findings were not intended to be applicable to a wider population, the results do indicate that terrorism involving tourists was particularly influential in shaping tourism flows, though in some cases the impact on tourism demand is delayed.

title: The impact of September 11th on the UK business community
authors: George, Bruce, Button, Mark, Whatford, Natalie
abstract: This paper discusses the impact of the events of September 11th on the UK's business community,, the threat from what has been termed the ‘new terrorism’. It summarises, analyses the effect on different sectors of the community, ranging from the public utilities to the financial, insurance sectors,, examines how security has been affected by the impact of September 11th. It also makes reference to the British government's response to the threat of the new terrorism,, to the House of Commons Defence Select Committee's reports The Threat from Terrorism, Defence, Security in the UK. Finally, the paper seeks to outline a number of considerations on how the UK could be better prepared for terrorist attacks.

title: Countryside alliance? An assessment of multi-agency responses to racism in rural Suffolk
authors: Garland, Jon, Chakraborti, Neil
abstract: Recent debates surrounding racialised disorder, integration, multiculturalism have resulted in increased scrutiny of the extent to which anti-racism is incorporated into statutory, voluntary agencies' working practice. However, the examination of agency responses to racism in a rural, as opposed to urban, context is often overlooked, as issues of rural racism tend mistakenly to be dismissed as relatively insignificant problems, due to the comparatively small populations of minority ethnic groups residing in rural parts of Britain.This paper uses the findings of a recent investigation into the nature, extent, impact of racist victimisation in a rural English county to highlight the pressing need for effective intra-, inter-agency working to counter the phenomenon of rural racism. It is argued that agency responses to racist incidents in a rural setting can often be constrained by a tendency to prioritise other problems that appear more visibly in official figures, as well as by other factors that detract from the effectiveness of co-ordinated multi-agency strategies. Unless, until combating racism is seen as a central component of rural community safety work, the process of victimisation suffered by minority ethnic groups in rural areas will continue to be compounded.

title: Can information technology help in the search for money laundering? The views of financial companies
authors: Gill, Martin, Taylor, Geoff
abstract: The fight against money laundering has taken a variety of forms. One crucial element is the production by finance companies of ‘Suspicious Transaction Reports’, which provide information for investigation agencies. Clearly, the greater the grounds of suspicion—or more specifically, the more evidence there is to support a belief that a transaction is illegal—the better the base for enforcement action. Yet very little is known about how finance companies generate intelligence about suspicion from the billions of transactions that pass through accounts each day. This paper considers this issue, reports on finance companies' experiences, views,, specifically assesses the role of IT in this process. The findings suggest that in tackling money laundering IT does not yet play a major role,, many, including users of dedicated systems, are sceptical about its value. The paper concludes that this may reflect more a lack of understanding about ‘suspicion’ than a weakness of IT systems per se.

title: A letter from India: Gender violence in west Bengal
authors: Maiti, Prasenjit
abstract: Gender violence is a significant problem in West Bengal. This paper seeks to establish causal linkages between crimes against women (especially since the 1990s), the changes that Bengali bhadralokian society has undergone during this decade, impacted by globalization, liberalization in terms of culture root paradigms, world views, the philosophy of everyday life. It is argued that the construct of the feminine self as iconized within the perspectives of the dominant male discourse has more often than not been subverted by the compulsions, tensions of transition, which have transcended socio-economic cultural identities in order to establish a different regime, of gender negotiation underscored by violence. Law-and-order maintenance agencies of the state have also contributed to the problematic so far as authorized repression is concerned.

title: Sex offender community notification, its impact on neighborhood life
authors: Zevitz, Richard G
abstract: This paper is based on research that both quantitatively, qualitatively examines the effects of sex offender community notification on neighborhood life—specifically on fear of crime, community morale,, the ability of residents, business owners to preserve, restore their neighborhood. The literature hypothesizes that neighborhoods are stable social entities that react to destabilizing events by finding ways to resist unwanted change, bounce back to a semblance of their former selves. This resiliency factor may be problematic in those neighborhoods beset by a variety of social problems. Data for this paper were derived from an in-person interview survey with households, businesses located within an area officially notified about a convicted sex offender living there. The findings suggest that the state practice of targeting an already fragile neighborhood for sex offender placement, while a blow to the neighborhood, may not be of such magnitude as to weaken its ability to recover.

title: Fear of violence among Australian women
authors: Carcach, C, Mukherjee, S K
abstract: Fear of crime has emerged as one of the most important issues in many communities. Indeed, it appears as serious a problem as crime itself,, many believe the fear is exaggerated. Heightened fear of crime has important implications for the quality of life. It increases psychological distress, restricts outdoor activity. Crime surveys show that women admit to more fear than other population groups. Based on the analysis of an Australian survey, our findings give strong support to social, economic vulnerability, concern for the safety of other family members,, women's experiences of physical violence as being among the main sources of fear of crime among Australian women.

title: Improving multi-agency coordination: Overcoming the barriers to communication – A case study
authors: Finney, Andrea
abstract: This paper explores the relevance, roles of communication processes in the failure of a multi-agency Drug Action Team (DAT) to function effectively, to coordinate the activities of the four participating agencies. In-depth interviews with seven purposely selected public agency staff were analysed according to the principles of grounded theory, of the constant comparative method. Four themes emerged to explain the difficulties experienced by the DAT representatives. These are: the nature of the task for which the representatives meet; the implications of mandated (‘forced’) coordination; the features of modern bureaucratic organisations;, the characteristics of multi-agency relations. The effects of deeply hidden cultural meanings in communication within, between the agencies are hypothesised, explored. The characteristics of occupational cultures proved particularly illuminating. Means for overcoming the DAT's difficulties are suggested and, finally, lessons for best practice in multi-agency bodies are highlighted.

title: The prevention of alcohol-related crime: Operationalising situational, environmental strategies
authors: Deehan, Ann
abstract: Alcohol-related crime, disorder in, around the licensed drinking environment has become an issue of increasing concern. Although there is a strong tradition of research focusing on licensed premises, few efforts have been directed at the practical application of findings. That body of research work, however, has provided the crime prevention field with a range of tools that can predict, manage, contain alcohol-related offences in the licensed environment. This paper reviews this research literature, presents a summary of situational, social, environmental factors that can be influenced to help prevent, reduce alcohol-related crime,, of the available mechanisms to operationalise these tools. What is clear from the literature is that rarely will one single measure be effective in tackling alcohol-related crime. There are, however, a range of tools, strategies that can be successfully employed at the local level to address the issue of alcohol-related violence associated with licensed premises. Partnerships involving law enforcement, licensees, other stakeholders (such as local government, health authorities) have been in operation for some time in Australia,, have the potential to act as a mechanism for operationalising projects aimed at the reduction of alcohol-related crime. The lack of a legal requirement to participate in such groups may have limited their potential. Do the crime, disorder partnerships in the UK have a better chance of tackling this issue?

title: All that glitters isn't gold: Environmental crimes, the production of local criminological knowledge
authors: Whyte, Dave
abstract: The emergence of the discourse of ‘community safety’, regarded by many as a definitive shift in crime control strategy, has in theory renewed prospects for the flourishing of criminological knowledge as to the incidence of ‘crimes of the powerful’ (that is, crimes committed by corporate, state actors). The paper examines this prospect in the light of the current boom in local criminological knowledge production. In particular it discusses the degree to which community safety agendas have taken account of more general crime/safety threats to local populations posed by powerful corporate, state actors. This investigation is based on an analysis of data generated by crime, disorder partnerships in the North West of England, with a particular focus on the visibility of environmental crimes in these data. It concludes with a discussion of the prospects for the inclusion of crimes of the powerful in future crime reduction agendas.

title: Critically reviewing the theory, practice of secured-by-design for residential new-build housing in Britain
authors: Cozens, P M, Pascoe, T, Hillier, D
abstract: The UK government has projected a need for some 4.1 million homes by 2021 (Department of the Environment, Transport, the Regions, 1999a), a stated policy objective of achieving 60 per cent of new-build housing on ‘brownfield’ sites (Department of the Environment, Transport, the Regions, 1999b). The government is clearly committed to ‘designing out crime’ (Department of the Environment, 1994; Crime, Disorder Act 1998),, this paper explores the secured-by-design schemes (SBD), one of the most important community safety initiatives available to planners to assist in achieving these complex aims. The rise in premises liability cases (Hanson, 1998), the Human Rights Act 1998 illustrate the increasing importance of tackling such issues. A critical review of both the theory, practice of SBD is presented as it applies to the new-build residential environment in the British city. The implications of reviewing SBD's theoretical basis, its application are discussed.

title: Petrol service stations as victims of crime: Their risks, vulnerabilities
authors: Taylor, Natalie
abstract: While research into crimes against specific business sectors has begun to grow in recent years, differences in the experience of crime between individual types of business within a sector may remain obscured. This is problematic because it can result in an averaging effect, may mask real differences in levels of crime. This paper builds on recent findings concerning the nature, extent of crimes committed against petrol retail outlets, to provide a more complete picture of their risks of robbery compared with other types of retail business, the psychological consequences of crime, levels of repeat victimisation. Drawing on nationally recorded data plus survey data, it is shown that petrol service stations in Australia have been facing an increased risk of robbery in recent years,, that the financial, psychological costs of crime at petrol station outlets are substantial. It is argued that identifying risk factors which differentiate victims from non-victims is essential if crime prevention strategies are to be appropriately targeted.

title: Surfing the crime net: Victim support, victim assistance programmes
authors: Mawby, R I
abstract: Harm reduction is the bedfellow of crime prevention. Providing services for victims at the time an offence is reported to the police may help alleviate the pain of victimisation, enable crime victims to cope. At the same time, they may be offered advice on crime prevention, access to crime reduction programmes,, help in filling up claim forms, in liaising with the police, other agencies. The availability of services abroad is currently of particular relevance, with both the EU, the US emphasising reciprocity, some degree of uniformity in the way citizens who experience crime or terrorist attacks while abroad are treated. It is also relevant to practitioners, policy makers interested in examples of successful programmes,, academics seeking to understand the emergence of the victims' movement in its various manifestations.

title: A letter from New Zealand: Home detention—emerging issues after the first three years
authors: Gibbs, Anita
abstract: Home detention in New Zealand began on 1st October 1999, having developed from a political climate of punitiveness towards offenders, a desire to introduce tougher parole or post-imprisonment supervision regimes (Gibbs, King, 2002). Home detention had been unsuccessfully piloted in New Zealand in the mid-1990s (Church, Dunstan, 1997), but this made little difference to the National government of the day as it introduced a full-blown scheme through an amendment to the Criminal Justice Act 1985. The current scheme is promoted as a means of reintegration into the community for people who have been in prison, or as a diversion from imprisonment for people given prison sentences of up to two years. This piece will explore the operation, impact of home detention in its first three years (1999 to 2002),, consider some of its successes, limitations, in the light of its aims to reintegrate, divert.

title: Design against crime in Vienna: A feminist approach
authors: Stummvoll, Günter P
abstract: The example of Vienna shows an institutionally fragmented approach to crime prevention, which nevertheless includes a large number of activities in a variety of disciplines: police, social services, medical services, welfare services, urban planning. This paper looks at the field of urban design in Vienna,, presents a feminist approach in the discussion about design-led crime prevention techniques. Some general remarks on crime prevention policy in Vienna are necessary in order to understand the administrative practice of ‘Design Against Crime’ in Vienna. The main section of the paper focuses on a description of the Vienna City Council's work, its distinctively feminist approach towards public safety. The overall philosophy, activities of the council's department for gender-sensitive planning, building, the ‘Leitstelle für Alltags- und Frauengerechtes Planen und Bauen’, are explained, some of their projects described.

title: Flotilla or armada? Interpreting the practices, politics of three Community Safety Partnerships
authors: Skinns, Layla
abstract: This paper is concerned with the practices, politics of three community safety1 partnerships. Community safety has been developing in England, Wales since the late 1980s, but was recently formalized by the Crime, Disorder Act 1998, the Police Reform Act 2002. The paper is based on observation of meetings, interviews undertaken in three partnerships between April 2002, February 2004. I assess the utility of the typologies employed by Liddle, Bottoms,, Belbin,, argue that they cannot take account of changes in the socio-political context of the CSPs. Instead, the paper develops a nine-pronged typology, based on a nautical analogy, which takes account of the likely impact of changes in governance, managerialism, funding, performance monitoring arrangements. The nautical analogy implies that roles, responsibilities within the CSPs are in need of reform, that there are continuities, changes within the CSPs, which are illustrative of the shift towards late modernity. In addition, the analogy suggests that CSPs are more of a collection of loosely affiliated agencies, that is, a flotilla rather than an armada.

title: Predicting, preventing: Developing A risk assessment mechanism for residential housing
authors: Armitage, Rachel
abstract: The introduction of legislative requirements placed upon key agencies to consider the crime, disorder implications of every decision that they make has been a progressive step in crime reduction. Yet this requirement will not achieve its potential unless these partner agencies can agree upon which factors are indeed criminogenic, therefore what impact their decisions will have upon crime. Recognizing the need for clarification within the field of designing out crime within the built environment, this paper presents a comprehensive, yet straightforward, usable crime risk assessment mechanism which Architectural Liaison Officers, Crime Prevention Design Advisors can use to predict the vulnerability of residential housing to future crime, disorder problems.

title: Learning from the 2004 crime audit. An evaluation of the national community safety plan 2006–2008, current impediments to the effective delivery of community safety strategy by local crime reduction partnerships
authors: Loveday, Barry
abstract: This article assesses the current status, efficacy of Crime, Disorder reduction Partnerships (CORPs) based upon the results of crime audits conducted on behalf of three local CDRPs. These results are matched up against the government's National Community Safety Plan, the priorities identified within the Plan particularly those for local authorities the police, CDRPs. The article considers the impact of the failure to establish coterminous boundaries between police force areas, local authorities, the challenge this generates for local partnerships. The article also considers the problematic nature surrounding the delivery of crime reduction strategies within non-metropolitan counties. It argues that the two-tier local authority structure guarantees the likely failure of CDRP partnerships, that a review of local government structure is now needed. The article goes on to evaluate the impact of centrally set performance regimes on CDRP work, the lack of engagement among local authority management with CDRPs, the very low public profile that characterizes local partnerships. It argues for core funding for community safety; for coterminous boundaries for police, CDRPs, for public, effective accountability mechanisms to encourage much greater public awareness of,, participation, in the work of local partnerships.

title: Community social organization as a predictor of mortality: Analyzing Chicago neighborhoods
authors: Feinberg, Seth L
abstract: This research explores the relationship between community social organization, neighborhood rates of mortality. Community social organization is a latent term that captures a variety of social interactions between residents that bring individuals together, providing an opportunity for a collective response to perceived neighborhood problems. Drawing from social disorganization theory, I suggest that more efficacious communities should have lower rates of mortality, particularly for youth. Using survey, secondary data for Chicago neighborhoods, I find that social organization (measured as collective efficacy) has a strong protective effect in terms of reducing youth death rates. The impact of collective efficacy holds for both preventable, health-related youth mortality. Results suggest that neighbors may contribute to protecting the lives of youth by helping mobilize residents to engage in community social organization.

title: A letter from: Healthcare fraud, corruption from A European perspective
authors: Koken-Vossestein, M R
abstract: The feature outlines recent developments in the way several countries in Europe have cooperated to counter fraud, corruption against their healthcare systems. Although the delivery of healthcare differs across Europe, nonetheless the frauds, acts of corruption committed against them are similar, the issues surrounding countering fraud, corruption are familiar ones. As a result, cooperation, sharing best practice can only benefit participants.

title: Feelings of safety: Ironic consequences of police patrolling: Feelings of safety
authors: van de Veer, Evelien, de Lange, Martijn A, van der Haar, Eline, Karremans, Johan C
abstract: Increasing police patrolling is often assumed to be an effective means of enhancing general feelings of safety. This relationship between perceiving police, feelings of safety was tested by having police officers patrol during a field experiment (Study 1), by manipulating the police presence in pictures of neighborhoods in a laboratory experiment (Study 2). Both studies show that in environments that are generally considered to be safe, feelings of safety are not increased by police presence. Moreover, men feel less safe when police are present compared with when police are absent. The results are discussed in terms of possible underlying mechanisms, implications for police patrolling.

title: Police, citizen value systems: Some cross‐sectional comparisons
authors: Griffeth, Rodger W, Cafferty, Thomas P
abstract: Rokeach, Miller,, Snyder (1971) have reported evidence for a “value gap” between samples of police, citizens in the midwest. The objectives of the present study were: (1) to examine the generality of this finding for another section of the country, the southeast; (2) to extend the analysis from the comparisons of individual values to the comparison of configurations of values between police, citizens;, (3) to compare the police sample from the Rokeach et al. study with the police sample from this study. The Rokeach Value Survey was administered to 104 South Carolina police officers, to 316 citizens sampled in a variety of South Carolina community settings. Group comparisons were made on the rank ordered individual values using the median test. In addition, group median rank orders were compared using the Spearman correlation. The results for the individual values generally supported the findings of Rokeach et al. (1971). For the value configurations, the police‐community correlations were uniformly high, indicating general agreement on the relative order of most values. Results of the cross‐sectional comparison of police samples revealed a very high degree of correspondance for both individual values, configurations.

title: Attributions as a function of expertise: The case of the police decision to arrest1
authors: Wortley, Richard
abstract: Using a longitudinal design, this study tested Carroll, Payne's (1977) attributional model on a cohort of 387 police recruits at recruitment\% at the completion of academy training., after I year of police experience. Contrary to expectations, the relationship between causal attributions, other judgments about offenders predicted by the model did not weaken with increasing police experience. However, there was an increase in the extent to which causal attributions also affected judgments about offenders which were not predicted by the model,, this was interpreted as indicating an increase in halo error. It was argued that halo error is indicative of rudimentary schemata which may precede the development of more complex offender typologies.

title: Fearfulness in the community: Empirical assessments of influential factors
authors: Boateng, Francis D
keywords: Ghana; attitudes; fear of crime; police visibility; social disorder;305\_FoC
abstract: Fear of crime has been well studied; however, there has yet not been widespread consideration of the potential impact of both individual-, neighborhood-level factors on residents' level of fear of crime. From a logistic-regression analytical standpoint, the present study empirically explores the contribution of several factors in explaining residents' propensity for being fearful of crime. Precisely, the study tests the applicability, generalizability of three theoretical perspectives of fear of crime in the Ghanaian context, examines the effects of residents' attitudes toward the police on their levels of fear of crime. Using large-scale cross-sectional data collected on more than 1,000 residents from 25 neighborhoods in Ghana, the results demonstrate significant predictive effects of both individual-, neighborhood-level factors on citizens' rate of fearfulness. Findings from this study have both theoretical, practical implications,, provide important insights for the police to reduce levels of fear of crime in the community.

title: Improving police services: Evidence from the French Quarter Task Force
authors: Cheng, Cheng, Long, Wei
abstract: This study sheds light on the improvement of police services by examining the French Quarter Task Force (FQTF) – an anti-crime program in New Orleans' French Quarter. First, we provide new evidence that increasing police presence is effective in crime prevention. Our difference-in-differences estimates suggest that the FQTF, which increased police visibility in the French Quarter, reduced robberies, aggravated assaults,, thefts by 37.4\%, 16.9\%,, 13\%, respectively. Second, our findings imply that the proper use of monitoring, incentive strategies has the potential to further improve police services. Exploiting the program's change in management, we find that providing officers with more monitoring, performance incentives led the FQTF to reduce robberies by 22.12, aggravated assaults by 5.56 each quarter.

title: Canadian Aboriginal peoples victimization, offending, its prevention: Gathering the evidence
authors: Monchalin, Lisa
abstract: It is well documented that Aboriginal peoples have had to endure disproportionately high rates of both victimization, offending for decades. This is largely owing to multiple risk factors that are a product of experiences in residential school systems, the colonization of traditional values, culture,, institutional racism. These issues have been,, continue to be, dealt with primarily through the standard colonial criminal justice system: the police, corrections, the courts. It is evident that this approach has been largely unsuccessful, considering the current high rates of Aboriginal overrepresentation in the system. Efforts to reduce this discrepancy have been minimal, fragmented at best. However, there is a growing body of knowledge that demonstrates that if risk factors are tackled in a culturally appropriate manner, they can be reduced. Given this evidence, it is recommended that Aboriginal organizations, communities, individuals who implement programmes that address the risk factors in a culturally appropriate manner receive adequate support.

title: Partnerships, NSW local government Community Safety Officers
authors: Shepherdson, Patrick, Clancey, Garner, Lee, Murray, Crofts, Thomas
abstract: Local government Community Safety Officers (CSOs) are now common in many jurisdictions. While their roles are diverse, most CSOs are actively engaged in various partnership approaches. This article discusses the nature, scope of inter-agency partnerships CSOs participate in or coordinate in the Australian jurisdiction of New South Wales (NSW). Through a focus group discussion with 13 CSOs (predominantly from councils in the Sydney Metropolitan Area), it was found that each CSO participates in a variety of inter-agency partnership groups, including those that focus on alcohol, licensing issues, drugs, domestic violence, homelessness, general community safety, crime prevention. Respondents suggested that only some of these committees are effective, raising questions about the ongoing need for, utility of the plethora of inter-agency crime prevention, community safety inter-agency structures operating in NSW.

title: Surviving in the shadows of war: Polyvictimised children in post-conflict Angola
authors: Cole, Bankole, Maxwell, Maureen, Chipaca, Adelino
abstract: This article reports on findings from a preliminary study that aims to ascertain the extent to which a group of 30 15–17-year-old Angolan juvenile suspects are polyvictims, as defined by Finkelhor, colleagues,, the degree to which their victimisation might be attributed to the aftermath of the country’s civil war. Analysis of their victimisation identified the majority as being polyvictims. Research into the context of victimisation revealed their neighbourhoods as being of primary importance. Findings confirm a direct link between these children’s victimisation, Angola’s war history. The article concludes that Angolan authorities need to adopt a psychosocial approach to dealing with the traumatic experiences of these children, their social development.

title: Designing in crime prevention, designing out ambiguity: Practice issues with the CPTED knowledge framework available to professionals in the field, its potentially ambiguous nature
authors: Johnson, Derek, Gibson, Victoria, McCabe, Megan
abstract: Crime prevention in the design of an urban setting displays unambiguous links with behavioural geography, the urban setting, development of sustainable communities, being a strategy that has been extant for over 40 years. This article examines how such strategies have been able to develop (or not) within the design of our environments, undertakes ground breaking analysis of academic input jointly with the response of professional practice. Systematic literature analysis, questionnaire responses from professionals in the field extracted a sizeable, diverse number of conflicting terms used to label Crime Prevention through Environmental Design (CPTED) concepts in both academia, professional practice policies. Realising damaging transferability issues, extreme diversity in the understanding, use of CPTED frameworks between research, practice, this research exposes the risk to the sustainability, integrity of the crime prevention response by design to the human use of space. Frameworks from academic literature, professional policies were analysed evidencing the lack of a universally accepted framework, terminology set throughout.

title: A case study of a law enforcement council: Economy of scale, scope or too costly for agencies?
authors: Schnobrich-Davis, Julie
abstract: This research fills some gaps in the literature regarding the viability, sustainability of law enforcement councils for policing in the twenty-first century. The Metropolitan Law Enforcement Council (Metro-LEC) is a non-profit organization comprising 43 law enforcement agencies in the Commonwealth of Massachusetts that have pooled resources, regionalized selected police services. The amalgamation provides services to small-, medium-sized police agencies to address incidents that go beyond their capability in scale/duration, in scope/skills. Results are presented from multi-wave surveys of frontline officers as well as surveys administered to the chief executive officers in member police agencies regarding their perceptions of the organization. In addition, a cost analysis presents a comparison between the costs of operating regionalized police units to the costs of operating those units in-house. The overall findings conclude that a law enforcement council approach provides needed services to area police agencies that are valued, utilized, cost effective, sustainable over time.

title: Crime in neighborhoods: Evidence from Santiago, Chile
authors: Olavarría-Gambi, Mauricio, Allende-González, Claudio
abstract: On the basis of an ecological approach, this article analyzes the crime determinants in neighborhoods of Santiago, Chile. It concludes that the concentration of social disadvantages, disorder, physical deterioration, together with the presence of an oppositional subculture, is associated with a greater occurrence of crimes,, that the development of trust among the neighbors operates as a mechanism for the prevention of criminal activities. The article also identifies the implications that the relationship between crime, the characteristics of the neighborhood would have for the design of public policies aimed at preventing, controlling crime at that level. A representative survey was carried out that collected data from 5861 households belonging to neighborhoods of Greater Santiago. Data have also been collected through direct observation of the characteristics of these neighborhoods. The analyses were carried out at the micro-neighborhood (a small territorial space), neighborhood unit (intermediate territory between the micro-neighborhood, the commune) level,, econometric estimations of count data type were applied.

title: Who are the guardians in product counterfeiting? A theoretical application of routine activities theory
authors: Hollis, Meghan E, Wilson, Jeremy
abstract: Product counterfeiting, as an emerging problem, has seen limited scholarly attention. Although there has been an increase in the scholarly work in this area, much more remains to be done. This article is an attempt to address one considerable gap in the product counterfeiting literature – the application of criminological theory. At this time, no research on product counterfeiting has attempted to apply a theoretical perspective to understand the product counterfeiting phenomenon. This article involves a systematic attempt to view product counterfeiting through a routine activities theory lens. More specifically, this is an exercise in applying the theoretical construct of ‘guardianship’ to the study of product counterfeiting. Implications for prevention, policy are discussed.

title: What works, what does not work in reducing juvenile graffiti offending? A comparison of changes that occurred in the frequency of persistent graffitists’ patterns of offending following the announcement of two successive initiatives aimed at reducing graffiti proliferation
authors: Taylor, Myra F, Khan, Umneea
abstract: Although the reality is that most young people are law-abiding when some juveniles are found to be engaged in acts of antisociality or criminality, a moral panic is often generated. Governments are then faced with the difficult task of implementing crime prevention policy initiatives that not only deter juvenile offending but also do not heighten the general public’s fear of crime. The Western Australian Government’s approach (like many other Western governments) to this dilemma is largely a penal one. As graffiti is a common entry crime, this study examined Western Australia Police records of the offending histories of 629 juvenile graffiti offenders over a 6-year offending time period (2004–2009). In this regard, the time interval (in terms of number of days) was calculated to determine whether Age, Gender offending differences existed. In the final stage of the analysis, a subset of 1056 successively recorded graffiti offences was examined in relation to the announcement of two different graffiti-reduction initiatives, namely, the 2004 increased financial, incarceration penalties for recidivist graffiti offenders, the 2007 graffiti hotline for reporting graffiti, its linked (Crime Stoppers WA) mechanism for reporting a graffiti offender (that is, ‘Bag-a-Tagger’). The study’s results show that no significant decrease occurred in the interval gap (that is, number of days) between the recorded graffiti offences in the two years following the announcement of the 2004 increased penalties initiative, but a significant change did occur in the interval gap between the recorded graffiti offences in the 2 years following the announcement of the 2007 report initiative. The implications of this finding are discussed.

title: Evaluating a fire safety programme
authors: Kennedy, Patrick John, Mason, Claire Louise
abstract: Objective: This study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of a programme in enhancing the knowledge, awareness of fire safety in children in mainstream schools. Method: 226 pupils completed an evaluation questionnaire on three occasions, in order to ascertain whether the programme had enhanced their knowledge of fire safety, whether any enhancement had been retained over a 3-month period. Results: There was a significant increase in knowledge of fire safety between the pre-, post-programme evaluations,, this increase was maintained at the three-month follow-up evaluation. Conclusion: The fire safety programme was successful in its objective to enhance knowledge, awareness of fire safety as evidenced in the post-programme evaluation. It was also successful in that this knowledge was retained over a three-month period, which has implications for the delivery of fire education programmes in schools, the potential effect on deliberate, accidental fire-setting behaviour.

title: ‘See, blind, hear, deaf’: Informerphobia in Jamaican garrisons
authors: Johnson, Hume N, Soeters, Joseph L
abstract: This article aims to describe, analyse the notion of informerphobia in the context of Jamaican society. Informerphobia refers to the fear people have about reporting information on (threatening) violence, crime, terror to the state agencies/agents formally tasked to respond to these threats. The article draws on interviews with garrison residents, law enforcement officials, other citizens, as well as secondary research data. On the basis of this case study, the wider implications of this phenomenon are discussed. The article points to the importance of having properly functioning state agencies, systems that are effective, not part of the problem,, flexible enough to deploy in a decentralized manner, hence generating trust within local populations. In addition, a civic culture of ordinary citizens providing counter-pressure is indispensable for state agencies to be more effectual. The concept of informerphobia is new, as is its conceptual elaboration, application to Jamaica.

title: Some findings from an Australian local crime prevention case study
authors: Clancey, Garner
abstract: Fieldwork in a postcode area of inner-Sydney (New South Wales, Australia) over an 18-month period (mid-2012–December 2013) revealed a number of key findings relevant to crime prevention policies, practices. First, a welter of crime prevention programmes, security-related technologies were observed. Many of these diverse programmes are delivered by various organisations, reflect different methods of prevention,, combine to form a preventative ‘quilt’, which has built up over time. Second, few of these specific initiatives have been thoroughly evaluated, raising questions about the efficacy of the existing evidence-base. Third, despite the seemingly disparate nature of some of these initiatives, there is considerable potential for collective impact from these diverse forms of security, crime prevention. Measuring the potential additive benefits of these programmes, technologies, interventions in combination requires more than just evaluating individual programmes. Together, these findings have implications for approaches to evaluation, for efforts to build an evidence-base, for the development of crime prevention policy.

title: ‘It’s like working away for two weeks’: The harms associated with young drug dealers commuting from a saturated London drug market
authors: Windle, James, Briggs, Daniel
abstract: This article discusses some new developments in British illicit drug markets: the commuting of London-based gang members to sell drugs in other British towns, or in gang member’s parlance: ‘working the country lines’. This is concerning for several reasons, not least because children, young people may be running away from home, putting themselves at significant risk by dealing drugs, including involvement in the distribution of drugs from ‘crack houses’. This article hypothesises that the increased saturation of London drug markets is increasing the chances of drug dealers commuting from their homes, which in turn raises particular harms, including conflict with established dealers in other cities as well as child welfare issues. The article concludes with some policy, research recommendations.

title: Examining perceptions of crime, quality of life by residents living in a drug market intervention neighborhood
authors: Stallings, Robert P, Hawkins, Paul M, Ward, Kyle C
abstract: Evaluations have shown that the Drug Market Intervention (DMI), when implemented correctly, can effectively reduce open-air drug markets (Kennedy, Wong; Rivers et al). Lacking from the research is a quantitative measurement of the impact of DMIs on residents’ perceptions of crime, safety. The Roanoke, VA, Police Department (RPD) surveyed residents living in a target area before, after the implementation of a DMI to gauge potential fluctuations in feelings of safety, concern for crime, the physical environment, sanitation. The current study conducted secondary data analyses of RPD survey results to further explore these relationships. The authors found statistically significant improvements in residents’ concern for crime, sanitation, the physical environment pre to post DMI. Future research, policy implications are discussed with inclusion of the importance of assessing levels of community informal social control before, after implementing DMI in order to strengthen evaluations of the program.

title: Civil committees during the January Revolution in Egypt: Youth safeguarding their neighbourhood
authors: Hussein, Nashaat
abstract: Children, adolescents have long been treated as the products of the socialization process they experience through their families, surrounding communities. They are rarely perceived as ‘social actors’ who can affect their surroundings or the way the society operates. This ethnographic research aims to investigate the role played by a group of children, adolescents who voluntarily formed a civil committee (a term propagated during the January Revolution in Egypt) to defend their neighbourhood against thugs’ attacks. In the absence of law enforcement, they volunteered to defend their homes, families, personal belongings. The research argues that through their interaction together, the development of their peer culture, children were able to develop skills, defence mechanisms to protect their neighbourhood. It concludes that children’s peer culture, in addition to creating social cohesion among the group, helped them to develop their abilities, skills to overcome threats.

title: Crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED), built-environmental manifestations in Accra, Kumasi, Ghana
authors: Owusu, George, Wrigley-Asante, Charlotte, Oteng-Ababio, Martin, Yaa Owusu, Adobea
abstract: Households in Ghanaian cities have responded to crime by fortifying their houses, a practice referred to as crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED). Though little researched in Ghana, Africa in general, this article, based on in-depth interviews with police officers, city planners, community members as well as a household survey, reveal that CPTED through target hardening is a widespread practice across different socio-economic residential neighborhoods of Accra, Kumasi. It was found that rising crime rates, the fear of crime have led to adoption of target hardening measures such as high walls, metal burglar-proofed windows, doors, security doors/special door locks, so on, which tend to create ‘security islands’ with limited impact on community crime incidence. While CPTED has been widely applied in Western cities to restructure the physical layout of communities to reduce crime through community efforts, there are marked differences in the Ghanaian context. In particular, households’ responses to crime through target hardening have the tendency in the long-term to weaken social cohesions, with limited impact on community crime levels. Interestingly, the household survey results show relatively low level of community solidarity in middle, upper-class neighborhoods as measures for fighting crime.

title: Urban, rural residence, its significance on services for victims of domestic violence in Cyprus
authors: Zalaf, Alexia, Kyriakidou, Marilena, Sotos, Maria
abstract: Data from a domestic violence non-governmental organization (NGO) in Cyprus was used to determine whether differences between urban, rural dwellers are present. Previous literature has indicated inconsistency in the actions of service providers in rural, urban settings, as well as a wide range of factors (for example, shame, religion) that may be able to justify any possible differences between rural, urban dwellers in their use of services for domestic violence. On the basis of the existing literature, we expected fewer calls from rural dwellers, no differences between the two samples on the services they would request, receive from the NGO,, finally, rural dwellers would have less access to services than urban dwellers. Data was obtained from SPAVO, the only NGO dealing with domestic violence in Cyprus. This data covered a 2-year period (2011–2012), is gathered by SPAVO’s call centre from people calling the request information or report an incident of abuse. Results indicated no differences in the services the victims from both areas received before contacting the NGO, requested from the NGO, were subsequently recommended. One significant finding was that both rural, urban dwellers reported low levels of requesting services related to domestic violence before contacting the NGO. The discussion centres on possible reasons for this finding, implications for future research.

title: A review of the impact of crime risk assessment reports in New South Wales, Australia
authors: Clancey, Garner, Fisher, Daren, Lyons, Adam, Lee, Murray
abstract: Crime risks assessment reports are prepared for some specific new proposed developments in New South Wales (NSW), Australia. These assessments aim to identify crime risks, should include reference to how the design of the proposed development minimises or mitigates crime risks. In 2010, Clancey et al (2011, 2012) reviewed the content of 33 crime risk assessment reports prepared in NSW. In order to investigate the impact of these crime risk assessments on the subsequent development process, site visits were conducted in February 2015 to 23 locations for which original crime risk assessment reports had been prepared. These site visits sought to determine if developments had been completed,, if so, whether potential crime risks were evident (or not) from a review of the key physical features of the site. It was found that 10 out of these 23 sites (43.5 per cent) had not been developed or construction was still being undertaken, demonstrating the lengthy development process. Of those developments that had been built, they represented a variety of functions which raises questions about the utility of generic crime risk assessment guidelines. For example, the crime, security issues of a major hospital are vastly different to a small suburban residential development. While access control measures were ubiquitous across the diverse sites, greater attention might have been given to natural ladders, the function, maintenance of communal areas. The findings from this research have implications for ongoing policy development in this area.

title: Recognizing the continuum of opportunities for third parties to prevent, respond to sexual assault, dating violence on a college campus
authors: Palmer, Jane E
abstract: A framework proposed by McMahon, Banyard outlines the opportunities college students have to engage in prosocial helping behaviors before, during or after an incident of sexual assault or dating abuse. To build on this framework, this study (i) used confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling to test the proposed framework, (ii) examined the correlates associated with student behaviors along a continuum of opportunities to prevent or respond to these types of crimes in a college setting. The structural equation model results demonstrated that there are different factors associated with whether students engaged in behaviors to prevent sexual assault or dating abuse, whether they engaged in prosocial behaviors after an incident of violence or whether they intervened in risky situations involving alcohol. Observing others engage in similar prosocial behaviors was the most consistent predictor. Past victimization, respondent sex were also associated with different types of interventions. Practical implications of these findings are addressed.

title: Social demographics of crime in a military community in the United States
authors: Hollis, Meghan E
abstract: Prior research has focused on relationships between the socio-demographics of a neighborhood, neighborhood crime levels. The current study contributes to the growing body of neighborhoods, crime research by examining socio-demographics of neighborhoods in a new context – a military community. Military communities provide an interesting context in which to study the connection between socio-demographic features, crime as they tend to be tightly knit, with strong informal, formal ties. This research adds to the neighborhoods, crime research by exploring the influence of the larger context in which neighborhoods are imbedded. The results demonstrate that certain socio-demographic indicators correlate with crime in a manner that is consistent with that found in past research, but that relationship is amplified when models include measurement of the percentage of residents who are military service members. Implications for research, theory are discussed.

title: Welfare fraud prevention in Australia: A follow-up study
authors: Prenzler, Tim
abstract: This article provides an additional 2 years of data to the study by Prenzler (2014b) on reductions in welfare fraud in Australia. The original study covered 14 years, with the number of cases falling by approximately 75 per cent in the final 3 years. Data for 2013–2014 to 2014–2015 show that these large reductions were sustained with a continuing slight downward trend overall. The article also analyses possible explanations, focusing on the maintenance of an ‘early contact’ system assisting customer compliance,, maintenance of an investigative focus on larger suspected frauds. At the same time, the article draws attention to some problematic aspects of the programme, including ambiguities about the influences on the reduction in cases, ongoing opportunities for fraud, major disparities in sentencing, the prosecution of large numbers of women.

title: Reflections on Norway’s juvenile justice model: A comparative context
authors: Winterdyk, John, Antonopoulos, Georgios A, Corrado, Ray
abstract: Juvenile delinquency, its relationship to the complex contemporary challenges that confront (certain) young people remain an enigma for many national juvenile justice systems (JJS). One exception to this global trend is Norway, which has experienced low levels of youth crime even though it processes youth within the adult criminal justice system at age 15. With few such exceptions, most industrialised liberal democratic countries have utilised a variety of distinctive JJS separate from their adult criminal justice systems. In this article, the ‘Norwegian model’ is examined to assess whether it is theoretically unique to Norway and, if so, why. The broader political, social, economic contexts appear essential in explaining the success of a JJS embedded in the adult criminal justice system. The article concludes with several policy observations.

title: Fear of crime on the rail networks: Perceptions of the UK public, British Transport Police
authors: Power, Nicola, McManus, Michelle A, Lynch, Rosa, Bonworth, James
abstract: Counter-terrorism on the rail network is vital to the security of the United Kingdom. The British Transport Police (BTP) employ covert, overt security measures to prevent crime, which includes: closed circuit television, armed police, unarmed polisce, police community support officers, police dogs, stops, searches, awareness campaigns. All security measures aim to deter crime while importantly reassuring the public. We surveyed both members of the public, BTP officers about the perceived effectiveness of current security measures, specifically with regards to fear of terrorism. Feelings of reassurance, the perceived effectiveness of security measures were positively related. The most effective, reassuring security measure was the use of armed police; whereas the least effective, reassuring was the use of awareness campaigns. However, interestingly, qualitative analyses suggested that an increase in armed police without informed awareness campaigns would have a negative impact on public reassurance by increasing fear.

title: ‘I’m anonymous, I’m a voice at the end of the phone’: A Canadian case study into the benefits of providing telephone support to fraud victims
authors: Cross, Cassandra
keywords: CPCS2008-2016;\_\_work\_PDF登録\_CPCS;02\_高齢者詐欺被害についての教育プログラム;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験;Crime Prevention, Community Safety;340\_Frauds
abstract: Globally there are limited support services that specifically target fraud victims. Despite the devastating effects of fraud on an individual, dedicated support programmes are rare. This article examines the ‘Senior Support Unit’ (SSU), a Canadian-based telephone support service for older victims of fraud. The SSU is a unique example of a service that seeks to address some of the specific needs of fraud victims. Using data obtained from interviews with 21 SSU volunteers, this article presents the three main roles of the volunteer: providing advice, warnings; providing a listening ear;, providing reassurance. It argues how these particular roles respond to identified needs of fraud victims,, analyses the perceived effectiveness of this support model, from the perspective of the volunteers, incorporating both harm reduction, crime prevention elements. Overall, this article uses the evidence presented on the SSU as a foundation to advocate increased recognition of the needs of fraud victims, an expansion of support programmes dedicated to addressing these issues.

title: Crime, land use in Pittsburgh: A micro-size grid-cell analysis of the influence of land-uses on area crime
authors: O, Soohyun, Lee, Yongjei
abstract: Though substantial amount of research of routine activities/opportunity theory investigated the relationship between land use, crime, very few studies considered various types of land uses at the micro-scale of area. Using 2013 crime data geocoded on the 500-ft2 grid cells overlaid on Pittsburgh, results from multivariate regression models show that certain types of facility such as retail shops, schools, bus stops increase the number of crimes at grid cells. Further results show that, net of the socioeconomic factors, the number of crimes in a grid cell varies both by facility, crime type. However, potential guardianship, target suitability of the facility are not found to have significant influence on the number of crimes in grid cells. Attention to various types of land uses across the city is required to help effective allocation of social control resources against crime.

title: The ‘art, science’ of preparing crime risk assessment reports
authors: Clancey, Garner, Fisher, Daren, Lee, Murray
abstract: Much has been made of the impact of neo-liberalism on crime control, prevention in recent decades. The privatisation of corrections, security, other criminal justice functions has been the focus of considerable commentary. One feature of this debate that has received little attention has been the work of private consultants. Interviews with a small number of private consultants engaged (among other things) in the preparation of crime risk assessment reports in New South Wales (Australia) shed some light on this dimension of crime prevention through environmental design practice in NSW. In particular, analysis of interview transcripts revealed the striking similarity of approaches to compiling a crime risk assessment, the challenges of maintaining independence, quantifying crime risks, the lack of consistency of councils (local government) to review crime risks of proposed developments, the need for research, professional development.

title: Inspecting the European crime prevention strategy towards incivilities
authors: Di Ronco, Anna
abstract: In recent years the crime prevention (CP) policies of many EU countries have been expanded up to including the regulation of uncivil, disorderly behaviour,, have been implemented at the local level through measures that have often excessively constrained individuals’ rights, freedoms. By drawing on the analysis of EU policy documents retrieved in the database EUR-lex, this article investigates whether the European CP strategy has also focused on the regulation of incivilities.
