In contrast to other studies of focused deterrence programs, chronic offenders who do not specialize in any type of crime, participate in both violent, nonviolent offending behavior were selected to participate in this program based on their social harm index score. The paper details the features on the program. We then examined the social harm committed by the offenders as well as individual level time to arraignment as outcome measures. The results show that the focused deterrence program did not significantly reduce the social harm index nor the time to arraignment for these offenders. The use of focused deterrence for gangs, groups as opposed to chronic offender is discussed.

title: Is there a relationship between fear of crime, attitudes toward gun control?
authors: Verrecchia, P J, Bush, Michael D, Hendrix, Nicole
abstract: Much of the research on fear of crime uses fear as a dependent variable (what causes someone to be afraid of crime). This study uses fear of crime as an independent variable to examine its relationship with attitudes regarding gun control policy. Using a national sampling frame of over 3000 responses (n = 3265), this study explored whether fear of being a victim of crime has a relationship with one’s attitude toward gun control. Fear of crime correlated with attitude toward gun control, but when fear of crime, six other variables were examined together, the relationship between fear of crime, attitude toward gun control disappeared. Several variables such as age, sex, owning a firearm,, political ideology did have an effect on attitude toward gun control.

title: Extending the net: from securitisation to civicisation of migration control
authors: Klaus, Witold, Szulecka, Monika
abstract: The article aims to contribute to the very actual theoretical debate concerning intersection of migration control, crime prevention. Its objective is to review, critically discuss the process of extending control over immigrants. It is based on the analysis of control practices revealed in the countries of the Global North, which are the most common destinations for immigrants, be they forced or voluntary. We apply the three-stage notion of the development of migration control, of which two, i.e. securitisation, privatisation, have been quite extensively commented on in the literature so far. The third level, though, based on civic involvement in migration control practices, named here civicisation of migration control, deserves special attention as possibly prospective tool applied by the states in migration governance. We claim that increasing the net of social agents encouraged or obliged to control, report to authorities “suspicious” migrants or their “suspicious” behaviours raises doubts whether the involvement of citizens of certain kinds of public, private bodies can be assessed positively. To support this argument, we indicate the consequences of unreflexive associations of migration-related phenomena with threats to security, crimes.

title: (Re)Conceptualizing the role of guardianship in preventing child sexual abuse in the home
authors: McKillop, Nadine, Reynald, Danielle M, Rayment-McHugh, Susan
abstract: In criminology, the role of guardianship in preventing crime has received significant international attention because of its focus on the function, importance of regular, informal citizens in controlling, preventing crime across contexts. Initially applied to property crimes, interest in its utility for understanding, preventing crime of an interpersonal nature (including child sexual abuse [CSA]) has increased in recent years. However, the personal nature of CSA highlights layers of complexity that require a more elaborate analysis of the mechanisms that underpin guardianship, especially in the home environment where most CSA occurs. The purpose of this discussion paper is to advance current understanding by applying Felson (1995), Reynald’s (2010) conceptualizations of guardianship to the prevention of CSA in the home. Drawing on current literature, we apply a critical lens to examine factors that serve to promote or impede informal guardianship,, likelihood to intervene, within the home. From this analysis, we: (1) conclude that some (re)conceptualization of the dimensions of guardianship is required for understanding, preventing CSA in the home; (2) recommend proactive (parent, bystander education programs; place-based), reactive (psychoeducation for parents whose children have been abused) prevention strategies;, (3) advocate for further theoretical, empirical investigation on this important issue.

title: Police-led, school-based driver education: a pre-, post-comparison of young driver self-reported behaviour, intentions including gender differences
authors: Anderson, Levi, Bates, Lyndel, Madon, Natasha S
abstract: This study examined the effects of a police-led, school-based young driver education program on the future driving intentions of young, novice drivers. The participants were 294 final-year high school students from the Sunshine Coast region of Queensland (Australia). The study employed a pre-, post-survey design that measured self-reported driving behaviour, sensation seeking,, self-reported future driving intentions of young drivers. T-tests between pre-, post-responses identified statistically significant positive changes in young driver intentions after the program when compared to their previously self-reported behaviours. Further analysis of the changes between the pre-, post-surveys demonstrate that the LAW program has a greater effect on female participants, those with higher levels of sensation seeking. The findings of this study indicate that police-led, school-based driver education programs may be an effective way of altering the driving intentions of young novice drivers, in turn promoting greater road safety.

title: Everyday moral judgements of anti-social behaviour
authors: Adams, Jan, Millie, Andrew
abstract: Over recent decades, there has been a lot of academic, political focus on anti-social behaviour, but less attention on the everyday moral judgements that can inform what we perceive to be anti-social. This is despite politicians’ claims that anti-social behaviour reflects a moral decline. This article draws on a focus group study from the North West of England, on ideas from criminology, philosophy. People’s assessments of anti-social behaviour are found to be informed by judgements of morality, most often in terms of ‘doing what’s right’, having respect,, abiding by the Golden Rule, to ‘do to others what you would have them do to you’. Understandings of anti-social behaviour are stretched so far by the public that they can range from littering through to tax avoidance, but what these behaviours have in common is their perceived breaching of our day-to-day moral standards. Implications are discussed.

title: How prepared are we for the serious violence duty?
authors: Hopkins, Matt, Floyd, Keith
abstract: This paper analyses the delivery of violence reduction, preparations for the Serious Violence Duty in one region in the United Kingdom. Using Bath \& O’ Moore’s 5c’s approach as an analytical framework, we explore the response to the Government Serious Violence Strategy (Home Office, Serious Violence Strategy April 2018.), Public Health approaches to violence reduction, how prepared the region appears to be for the implementation of the Serious Violence Duty. The evidence suggests the development of Violence Reduction Units has led to a two tiered approach to violence reduction, resourcing is a major concern, partnership arrangements will need to evolve in order to deliver the Serious Violence Duty. However, it is also evident that the duty represents an opportunity for the development of new knowledge around the implementation of partnership, public health approaches to violence reduction, ‘what works’ in this space.

title: Attitudes regarding becoming an engaged bystander for targeted violence prevention
authors: Gleicher, Lily, Alderden, Megan, Weine, Stevan M
abstract: The recent increase in mass attacks in the USA has enhanced concerns about how persons in communities might be able to contribute to the prevention of such incidents, other forms of targeted violence. The purpose of this study was to learn about what persons are willing to do regarding individuals exhibiting or vocalizing concerning behaviors,, what factors would impact their actions. This was accomplished through 9 focus groups of 72 persons total, in which participants were asked to provide their perceptions regarding six different behavior-based scenarios involving acquaintances, close friends or family members. The study found that participants were willing to engage someone in a conversation, take some type of action with friends, family, contact law enforcement if there is imminent danger,, use a third-party resource when the behavior viewed was particularly concerning. Implications of these findings for targeted violence prevention efforts are discussed.

title: Local government public space CCTV systems in Australia
authors: Metcalfe, Laura, Morgan, Anthony, Clancey, Garner
abstract: The rapid, sustained growth in use of public space closed-circuit television (CCTV) is well-documented. However, there are mixed findings as to the efficacy of CCTV in public places as a crime prevention or crime control measure. Analysis, exploration of findings from a national online survey of local councils across Australia conducted (by the Australian Institute of Criminology) in mid-2014 was conducted, is reported here. This paper seeks to provide a comprehensive snapshot of the determinative factors in local councils’ decisions to install, maintain CCTV, the corresponding mechanisms of the network,, the prevalence of evaluations of public space CCTV systems across Australia. The findings illustrate a need for greater consideration of the objectives of CCTV which align with the purpose, perceived benefits of the systems, as well as the coverage, operational framework available to support ongoing implementation. Moreover, robust evaluations which assess the benefits of CCTV for deterrence, reduction or investigation of crime in demographically, geographically diverse areas is needed.

title: Peeling back the layers of organised crime in local communities: integrating data, analyses to strengthen the narrative
authors: Skidmore, Michael, Crocker, Ruth, Webb, Sarah, Gill, Martin, Garner, Sarah, Graham, John
abstract: At a national level, the scale, diversity of the threats from organised crime are starting to be understood. Locally, however, police forces remain uncertain how to robustly assess organised crime within their own borders. To address this, contribute to the development of a local ‘narrative’ of organised crime we studied two UK neighbourhoods where organised crime was known to be impacting. Our study brings together data from multiple sources that each offer a distinct perspective: the measurable impact of organised crime as represented in recorded crime, the groups, offenders, activities recorded by the police for the purposes of developing intelligence on organised crime,, finally the qualitative impact on communities as described by local practitioners, community representatives. The implications for developing the perspective of practitioners, their approach to tackling organised crime are discussed. In summary, organised crime groups are responsible for a much wider range of harms than that expressed by the national police intelligence mechanism, much of this harm is local,, this needs to be factored in when considering priority, intervention from police, partners.

title: How Eritreans plan, fund, manage irregular migration,, the extent of involvement of ‘organised crime’
authors: Whittle, Joseph, Antonopoulos, Georgios A
abstract: The increased government, media, public focus on migration from Africa to the EU in the past few years has led to an explosion in reporting from governments, NGOs, academics, quasi-academia. Within this context, there are a number of basic assumptions, discourses in relation to these migratory processes from Africa. The first assumption, often put forward by the media, is that migrants from Africa intend to cross the Mediterranean Sea in an effort to reach Western European countries. The second assumption is that in their effort to cross the Mediterranean, African migrants are facilitated by ‘criminal networks’. The third (and extremely popular in the last few years) assumption is that information, communication technologies have been instrumental in the planning of irregular migration, identifying smugglers to facilitate migration. The final assumption, which has also garnered increasing attention in recent years, is that understanding human smuggling finances can inform policies specifically targeting migrant smuggling. This article, which is based on in-depth interviews with Eritreans, who have migrated illegally in Egypt, aims to add to the understanding about how Eritrean people plan, fund, manage irregular migration journeys. In the process, it will attempt to debunk some of the common assumptions around irregular migration.

title: Place managers for crime prevention: the theoretical, empirical status of a neglected situational crime prevention technique
authors: Douglas, Stephen, Welsh, Brandon C
abstract: Place managers are individuals who are physically, legally able to prevent crime in proprietary places, in addition to their designated functions within these places. They can be apartment complex owners, store managers, bar owners, parking lot attendants, or other individuals who have ownership claims to a place or are employed by that place. Largely informed by the criminal opportunity perspective, recognized as a situational crime prevention technique, place managers benefit from a rich theoretical development, but only limited evaluation research. In examining the theoretical, empirical status of place managers, we were motivated to develop a greater understanding of the potential for place manager interventions to be implemented, evaluated, as well as to explore a promising mechanism—in the form of regulatory frameworks—to help place managers in performing roles related to the prevention of crime.

title: Novice drivers, parents: exploring the feasibility of third-party policing in reducing young driver offending
authors: Belsham, David, Bates, Lyndel, Somoray, Klaire, Lennon, Alexia
abstract: Third-party policing involves police partnering with other individuals or organisations in order to prevent or control crime, disorder. Given the high level of young driver crash rates, offences, an intervention based on third-party policing may reduce both. This study explored the feasibility of using this approach with parents, who would be the third party,, young drivers in the Australian Capital Territory. Semistructured interviews with 16 parents, 11 of their children were conducted. The results suggest that given parents are supportive of the formal policing of young drivers, their willingness to impose additional restrictions on their children, that the introduction of an intervention based on a third-party policing framework is feasible. However, the lack of knowledge of GDL restrictions that apply to their child may make it difficult for parents to act as an enforcement authority in partnership with police. There is also the need to introduce a legal lever to support parents in their interactions with children, enable police to coerce parents into taking action.

title: Exploring the removal of online child sexual abuse material in the UK: Processes, practice
authors: Martellozzo, Elena, DeMarco, Jeffrey
abstract: This paper explores the processes involved in the removal of online child sexual abuse material. It specifically focuses on the work of the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF) in the UK who are partially responsible for the removal of this content. The empirical work was carried out between May 2017, September 2017, explored whether the IWFs processes at removing online child sexual abuse material were both useful, effective to the police, the wider community. The research applied a mixed methods approach: Semi-structured interviews with employees (N = 10), key stakeholders (N = 9), seeking to explore the strengths, challenges of both the task, the IWFs remit. Both employees, stakeholders saw the value in the original, innovative ‘space’, ‘approach’ the IWF took in removing child sexual abuse material. This included the evolving nature of their tools, from the original URL list filter, to the more adaptable image hashing process. However, challenges around transparency, visibility, partnership were also raised. With online child sexual abuse ever evolving, it is important to consider novel ways in which intervention, prevention of victimization, offending can take place. Where a multi-disciplinary approach is needed in supporting victims, this research provides an insight into how one such organisation uses tools, techniques, different to traditional statutory services or law enforcement responses.

title: How vulnerable are people to victimisation of County Lines drug dealing?
authors: Fawell, Lilly, Davies, Joseph L, Stubbings, Daniel, Payne, Libby
abstract: AbstractThe current study examined how willing a non-probability sample of adults were to engage in hypothetical activities typical of County Lines,, whether involvement could be predicted by perceived risk factors. Of the 101 participants; 48\% were willing to engage in activities that could lead to cuckooing, 63\% to a coffee meet up, 50\% to transferring money, 32\% would accept free drugs, 56\% would pay off a friend’s debt, whereas only 1\% were willing to engage in the control scenario (a phone scam). Actual occurrences of these scenarios were also documented, occurred in approximately 1\% of the sample. Males, people with greater drug use scores were more likely to endorse engagement in a County Lines scenario involving drugs, whilst greater drug use scores were only associated with a lower risk of a County Lines scenario involving lending money to a friend. Our findings suggest that drug use may predict endorsement to engage in some County Lines scenarios. However, given a small non-probability sample was used in the current study, further development of methodologies to capture the likelihood to engage in County Lines activities are needed.

title: Alcohol-, drug-impaired e-scooter riding: exploring countermeasures from Australia, Belgium, New Zealand,, Norway
authors: Alexander, Marina, Bates, Lyndel
abstract: AbstractThis article explores the emerging problem of drug-, alcohol-impaired e-scooter riding. Fifteen government, e-scooter hire firm professionals from four jurisdictions (Australia, Belgium, New Zealand, Norway) described, assessed countermeasures designed to deter drug-, alcohol-impaired riding. Government professionals were from local/municipal councils, state, national departments of transport,, policing organisations. We used Braun, Clarke’s (Qual Res Psychol 18(3):328–352, 2020.https://doi.org/10.1080/14780887.2020.1769238) six-step method of thematic analysis, the NVivo qualitative analysis software system to analyse the interviews. All participants said traditional police enforcement is ineffective because laws, regulations are underdeveloped,, police have limited resources for patrols. Thematic analysis grouped countermeasures into four themes: enforcement, education, encouragement,, the road environment. Third-party policing initiatives show promise. For example, local/municipal councils required e-scooter hire firms to ban e-scooters from areas that sell alcohol through GPS-based geofencing. However, geofencing, other regulatory controls do not extend to privately owned e-scooters, a growing sector in the market. Other countermeasures used a combination of education, behavioural change techniques (BCTs) to encourage compliance. For example, innovative nudge methods (a type of BCT) have potential to change dangerous riding behaviours by targeting riding norms. However, participants said some people will continue to ride under the influence of alcohol or drugs either because they are addicted to substances or exhibit high-risk behaviours. Government should therefore adopt laws, regulations that build a more forgiving road environment, based on the safe system approach, to limit injuries when crashes occur.

title: Framing retail crime through an environmental criminological lens: insights from Australia, New Zealand
authors: Townsley, Michael, Hutchins, Benjamin
abstract: AbstractThis article aims to provide insights regarding crime problems affecting the Australian, New Zealand (ANZ) retail sector, focusing primarily on the size, range of criminal behaviours. The research incorporated an online survey of retailers, police statistics. The study finds that the cost of retail crime increased by 28\% over the last 4 years, against 25\% growth in revenue. It also reveals that shoplifting remains the most significant, costly economic problem facing retailers, followed by employee theft. Additionally, fraud, notably in online channels, will remain a concern for the foreseeable future. We examine potential explanations, interpretations for retail crime through an environmental criminological lens. Increased research, involvement of researchers hold tremendous potential for reducing retail crime, preventing its growth in the future.

title: A review of the impacts of Business Improvement Districts on crime, disorder
authors: Moir, Emily, Cairns, Natalee, Prenzler, Tim, Rayment-McHugh, Susan
abstract: AbstractBusiness Improvement Districts (BIDs) are an initiative adopted by some local governments, businesses,, residents to address concerns around crime, disorder in commercial areas, especially open street town centres. BIDs have become popular in the USA since the 1970s; however, no comprehensive review of evaluations has occurred to date. This paper systematically reviewed the academic literature to find 13 BID evaluations. These studies were examined in terms of their impacts on crime, disorder, displacement,, cost-effectiveness. Of the nine studies that quantitatively examined BID impacts on crime rates, eight (88\%) found a reduction in one or more crime types. Six studies explored BID impacts on property crime, with all finding BIDs had a significant negative association with at least one type of property crime, with BIDs particularly effective at targeting vehicle-related offences. BIDs were also found to have a positive impact on reducing disorder, public nuisance type offences, however, had mixed evidence on violent crime, with three out of seven studies on violent crime finding BIDs can help to prevent robbery. Displacement of crime to surrounding areas was found to be rare,, the three studies that examined costs of operating BIDs all concluded they are cost-effective. The challenges of implementing BIDs are discussed, along with the implications for ongoing policy, practice development in the reduction of crime, disorder in commercial areas.

title: Size matters: measuring the private security industry in the United Kingdom
authors: Pazzona, Matteo, White, Adam
abstract: AbstractThe private security industry has become a central feature of the plural policing landscape in the United Kingdom. As such, it has received considerable attention in both academic, policy circles. Yet, perhaps surprisingly, there remain notable question marks over its precise size, shape. With this in mind, the article draws upon data from the Security Industry Authority, the Office of National Statistics Business Register, Employment Survey to measure the sector along three key dimensions: the number of private security officers, the number of companies, turnover. This novel methodological approach reveals a complex, contested picture of what the sector looks like at a fundamental level and, at the same time, allows for a reassessment of commonly deployed indicators such as growth rates, the ratio of private security officers to police officers during key time periods such as the Covid-19 pandemic.

title: ‘It’s a group-on-one’: social disconnection as a tool of, defence against child criminal exploitation in the Republic of Ireland
authors: Sheehan, Katie, Walsh, Colm, Cusack, Alan
abstract: AbstractDespite increasing evidence on the exploitation of young people into criminal activity, their perspectives on, experiences of exploitative processes are not well understood. Despite progress in Great Britain with regard to ‘County Lines’ exploitation,, in the Republic of Ireland regarding youth criminality, grooming, the subjective accounts of how young people understand the phenomenon of child criminal exploitation (CCE) remain under-evaluated. This exploratory study captures the perspectives of Irish youth on CCE, draws on the theory of social capital to explore the social structures that enable CCE, the (limited) choices available to the young people.

title: “Seeing all these shootings at school, this makes me feel unsafe”: a mixed-methods study to explore the impact of social disadvantages on adolescents' unsafe neighborhood perceptions
authors: Yang, Yingwei, Liller, Karen, Salinas-Miranda, Abraham, Chen, Henian, Martinez Tyson, Dinorah, Coulter, Martha
abstract: Community safety is critical for adolescent health, development. This study was to (1) explore social factors contributing to adolescents' unsafe feelings, (2) measure the combined effects of multiple social disadvantages by mixed methods approach. The quantitative analysis using structural equation modeling (N = 24,356) showed that adolescents exposed to high levels of social disadvantages (e.g., gun violence, drug selling, gang activity,, poverty) had up to 19 times greater odds of perceiving their community as unsafe,, concentrated social disadvantages strongly, cumulatively impacted adolescents' unsafe perceptions. The qualitative study applied photovoice to collect photographs, viewpoints from six adolescents. The findings added new insights (e.g., living close to sexual offenders, child abduction) on social disadvantages, confirmed the quantitative results (e.g., mass shooting, tobacco selling). This mixed method study indicates safety promotion programs are highly needed for children, adolescents exposed to gun violence, concentrated social disadvantages.

title: Exactly how dangerous is drink driving? An examination of vehicle crash data to identify the comparative risks of alcohol-related crashes
authors: Love, Steven, Rowland, Bevan, Davey, Jeremy
abstract: AbstractThis study aimed to explore how specific situational variables (remoteness, speed zones, days of the week, hours of the day), risk factors (risky behaviours, road-related conditions) might influence the comparative likelihood, severity of alcohol-related crashes (ARCs). Vehicle crash data (N = 63,226) were analysed, included the details of crashes between 2015, 2019. In comparison to non-ARCs, ARCs were up to two times more likely to occur in rural areas, on weekdays,, two to four times more likely in the late evening, early morning (6 p.m. to 6 a.m.). In addition, risky road conditions, driving behaviours were found to significantly increase both ARC likelihood, severity, with some factors (e.g., speeding) increasing fatality risk by up to nine times. Overall, this study highlights the specific risks associated with drink driving, highlights situational factors that may increase crash risk.

title: Risky business: voluntary sex workers as suitable victims of work-related crimes in a legalised prostitution environment
authors: Molnar, Lorena, Aebi, Marcelo F
abstract: AbstractMany studies have analysed the violence to which sex workers (SWs) are exposed in countries where prostitution is criminalised, but violence in sex work when it is a legal, freelance activity has seldom been studied. This study is based on non-systematic participant observation, 14 interviews conducted with cisgender, transgender freelance SWs exercising their profession in Switzerland. Findings show that all the participants had been victims of work-related offences, that their victimisation can be interpreted through the updated version of Routine Activities Theory. Few reported the victimisation to the police although in general, they said that they appreciated the Swiss police. Most common perpetrators were customers, passers-by,, colleagues. The places where offences occurred can be defined as risky settings. The police, the SWs themselves, other actors such as social workers are identified as controllers, while the legal framework, NGOs themselves can be labelled as super-controllers. Our study suggests that public policies should not be limited simply to regulating prostitution, but also continuing to ensure SW’s safety by developing evidence-based prevention strategies.

title: Child sexual exploitation, the adoption of public health approaches to prevention: critical reflections on evolving processes, practices
authors: Weston, Samantha, Mythen, Gabe
abstract: AbstractIn recent years, the use of public health approaches to address complex social problems has gained popularity. In England, Wales, the rise in low-volume, high-harm crime has accelerated this shift, with calls for public health interventions to tackle knife-crime, extremism, sexual violence made by politicians, policy-makers, welfare workers, the police service. Notwithstanding such appeals, how public health approaches are both operationalised, impact remain largely unknown. Drawing on findings from a qualitative study focused on the implementation of a specific initiative in the UK designed to reduce the risk of Child Sexual Exploitation (CSE) amongst young people, this article attempts to address tangible gaps in these two key areas of knowledge. Although generally supportive of a public health approach to CSE, an analysis of in-depth interviews with members of a multi-agency team reveals a number of quandaries, thorny issues when implemented within a specific policing, criminal justice context.

title: The dangers, distractions of in-vehicle safety, infotainment enhancements: stakeholders’ views on the role of third parties in ways forward
authors: Van Felius, Margo, Bates, Lyndel, Seccombe, John
abstract: AbstractDistracted driving is a leading contributor to road crashes. Distractions can be caused by devices integrated within the vehicle itself or mobile phones. There is limited regulation of most distractions, except mobile phones, therefore providing an opportunity for third parties to take an active role in minimising distractions caused by in-vehicle technology, mobile phones. To date, the role of third parties has received limited attention in the road safety literature. This study uses 14 interviews, written responses from road safety experts, enforcement agencies, regulators in Australia, the United Kingdom to discuss the potential role of third parties in reducing distracted driving. The results indicate car manufacturers, car retailers, employers with commercial fleets, sole operators can play a significant role in reducing distracted driving by more clearly regulating in-vehicle technologies, educating consumers, mobile phone use during worktime.

title: Engaging parents to reduce youth violence: evidence from a youth justice board pathfinder programme
authors: Caulfield, Laura, Brooks-Wilson, Sarah, Booth, Jane, Monaghan, Mark
abstract: AbstractThe Youth Justice Board’s 2019–2022 strategic plan set youth violence as a priority. As part of this, a ‘pathfinder’ approach was launched to assist local authorities, their partners to devise, develop,, disseminate whole systems approaches to serious youth violence (Youth Justice Board in Pathfinder—YJB, https://yjresourcehub.uk/working-with-partners/item/651-pathfinder-yjb.html Youth Justice Board Annual Report, Accounts 2020/21, 2020). In partnership with a regional Violence Reduction Unit, seven local Youth Offending Teams worked together with a programme that facilitated peer support networks for parents of children known to the youth justice system. The programme presented a challenge to a view in statutory youth justice of parents as part of the problem (Burney, Gelsthorpe in Howard J Crimin Justice 47(5):470–485, 2008). The aim of the programme was to engage parents of young people involved in the youth justice system, facilitating peer to peer support through a blend of online, face-to-face meetings. Taking a mixed-method approach, the research sought to investigate the impact of the programme on participants’ well-being, perceived competence with parenting. A secondary aim was to explore experiences of the self-care, peer support activities offered by the programme. The quantitative findings showed statistically significant increases in parents’ self-reported well-being, perceived competence with parenting during engagement with the programme. Effect sizes reached the minimum important difference for all of the quantitative measures, with a large effect for well-being. The qualitative findings highlighted that the self-care focus was important in engaging parents, helps distinguish the programme from statutory services. The findings are combined in the paper to produce a potential model of peer support for parents of children known to the youth justice system. Future research should investigate the impact on the children of parents who took part in this programme with a specific focus on youth violence.

title: An explorative qualitative study of cyberbullying, cyberstalking in a higher education community
authors: Bussu, Anna, Ashton, Sally-Ann, Pulina, Manuela, Mangiarulo, Marta
abstract: AbstractThe literature suggests an increased risk of cybervictimisation during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper explores student, staff experiences in a higher education community as victims of cyberbullying, cyberstalking during the COVID-19 lockdowns. An online semi-structured questionnaire was administered to self-identified students, staff victims within a higher education context. By analysing victim responses, within a qualitative framework, this research identifies perceptions, impacts, support mechanisms. The findings offer insights for the development of effective practices, policies to mitigate risk factors, foster resilience. This research addresses the need for comprehensive understanding in the face of emerging digital challenges, future traumatic events.

title: “Neighborhood fear of crime, disadvantaged areas: a comparative longitudinal study”
authors: Di Rocco, Jennie, Vasiljevic, Zoran, Ivert, Anna-Karin
abstract: AbstractThe current study explores how neighborhood fear of crime (“worry about specific crimes”) changes over time in neighborhoods with different levels of disadvantage. With a comparative design, 81, 123- neighborhoods in two cities in Sweden are followed over a six-year period. Fear of crime trajectories are assessed through growth curve modeling. We consider how differences in neighborhood processes, such as social, physical disorder, might influence fear of crime levels. The results show that fear of crime increased over time in both cities, the increase was related to higher levels of physical disorder in several areas. Furthermore, the change differed depending on the neighborhood type – in highly disadvantaged neighborhoods, the fear was stable at a high level. In contrast, the largest increases in fear could be seen in the areas with the lowest disadvantage in both cities. Theoretical, practical implications are discussed.

title: Is partnership working? Complexities, barriers in the development of community safety practice in Wales
authors: Rabaiotti, Ella, Harrison, Michael
abstract: AbstractCommunity safety in England, Wales underwent significant change a quarter of a century ago when community safety partnerships (CSPs) were introduced as part of the Crime, Disorder Act 1998. Measures to reduce or prevent anti-social behaviour, crime became the responsibility of not just the police but multiple public, third-sector organisations working in partnership. In Wales, additional complexity exists due to most CSP partners operating, working under both the UK,, Welsh Government remit. Findings from mixed-methods research into the training needs of community safety professionals in Wales revealed that support was needed in several areas of practice, including the practicing of meaningful ‘partnership’ working, problem solving. However, given the complex partnership landscape in Wales, lack of clarity around partnership governance, coupled with a seeming overreliance on the police, local government within community safety, the success of collaborative learning, development plans is limited.

title: How do representatives from sporting organisations understand primary prevention of violence against women?
authors: Liston, Ruth, Hamilton, Gemma, McCook, Sarah
abstract: AbstractSports settings have been identified as important locations for the prevention of violence against women, with numerous prevention initiatives currently running in many sports internationally. However, little is known about how those involved in sporting organisations, who are often tasked with delivering such initiatives, conceptualise the prevention of violence against women. This research draws on a survey of people who were invited to participate if they had professional experience in the development or delivery of violence prevention programs in their sporting organisation. We found that a cohort of participants had a limited understanding of primary prevention, how it applies to the prevention of violence against women through sport. Broadly, they were not aware of the difference between primary, secondary, tertiary prevention techniques. These findings suggest that there is a need for better education of those working in sporting organisations about the nature of primary prevention of violence against women as well as deeper consideration of the complex nature of doing violence prevention work through sport.

title: Global crime science: what should we do, with whom should we do it?
authors: Ignatans, Dainis, Aleksejeva, Ludmila, Pease, Ken
abstract: AbstractFollowing on from a previous paper advocating changes in the editorial processes of peer-reviewed journals, the present paper espouses the conduct of multiple local victimisation surveys as an affordable route to a pan-European crime science. Local surveys have a local impact which national surveys lack,, meta-analysis of survey results enable more general conclusions. The Latvian local survey reported in the chapter revealed wide inequality of victimisation at the individual level, an association between high rating of the seriousness of offences suffered, multiple victimisation at the individual level,, alienation from the police of some ethnic groups.

title: Can education influence the public’s vulnerability to county lines?
authors: Hayman, Chloe-Marie, Stubbings, Daniel Robert, Davies, Joseph Lloyd, Payne, Libby
abstract: AbstractThis paper explored the novel use of an educational tool to assess its influence on County Lines victimisation. Participants (n = 122) were randomly assigned to receive either County Lines education or no County Lines education, then, rate their likelihood to engage in five hypothetical scenarios typical of County Lines victimisation verses a text scam. County Lines education did not significantly reduce participant willingness to engage in the scenarios, whilst most participants were not susceptible to a text scam. Demographic data, drug use, social isolation, poor mental health,, financial instability were weak predictors of engagement. Findings suggest that the public may be vulnerable to victimisation, that future research should continue to explore the role that education can have in reducing the likelihood of engaging in County Lines activity.

title: Introduction to the special issue: Implementing environmental criminology for crime prevention
authors: Ceccato, Vania
abstract: AbstractThis introduction aims to showcase the articles of the special issue, highlights the expansive field of environmental criminology, underscoring its role in understanding, preventing crime through situational, environmental strategies. This collection of articles covers a wide array of research from the USA, Sweden, Australia, New Zealand,, Uruguay, demonstrating the global application of environmental criminology principles. Contributions from various disciplines illustrate the field’s multidisciplinary approach to tackling crime, particularly in the face of challenges posed by climate change, the need for social, economic sustainability.

title: One crime wave, three hypotheses: using interrupted time series to examine the unintended consequences of criminal justice reform, computer tablet recording of crime, a long-term hot spots policing programme
authors: Chainey, Spencer P, Estévez-Soto, Patricio R
abstract: AbstractAfter sustained reductions in robberies, thefts in 2016, the city of Montevideo, Uruguay, experienced a sudden increase in these crimes in late 2017. Using interrupted time series regressions,, controlling for seasonality using ARIMA models, we investigated three potential explanations for this increase: (1) the failure of a hot spots policing program to maintain crime decreases; (2) improved crime recording by police patrols using tablet computers;, (3) the change from an inquisitorial to an adversarial criminal justice procedure. We found that the hot spots policing program that began in April 2016 continued to be associated with crime reductions during 2017, that the increases observed after November 2017 were strongly associated with the new criminal justice procedure,, that tablets had a positive, albeit negligible, effect. The findings illustrate that criminal justice reforms, desirable as such reforms may be, can have unintended consequences on crime levels.

title: Comparing responses from a paper-based survey with a web-based survey in environmental criminology
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Gliori, Gabriel, Näsman, Per, Sundling, Catherine
abstract: AbstractThis article aims to compare the pattern of responses obtained by a web-based, a paper-based survey used to investigate the transit safety of travellers in railway stations in Sweden. This aim is achieved by evaluating whether the response, the completion rates change as the surveys progress, assessing the effect of the survey mode on respondents’ answers (after controlling for the surveys’ internal consistency, differences in the samples),, the potential impact of the order of alternatives in multiple-choice questions on the responses. To carry out the study, a sample of 500 responses was taken from each population, later compared using a series of statistical tests. Findings indicate that despite the surveys’ high internal consistency, the prevalence of victimisation, fear of crime,, precautions detected in the web survey was higher than those found in the paper survey. The web survey shows a major drop just after the initial questions, while the paper survey shows a more stable pattern of responses, but was also affected by a single compulsory question that pushed the completion rate down. Finally, the order of alternatives in multiple-choice questions (fixed or random) did not affect the answers given by the respondents, providing a solid base for safety interventions in transit environments, regardless of survey mode. The article concludes by making suggestions for both research, practice.

title: Finding synergies in the built environment between climate change adaptation, crime prevention
authors: Chamard, Sharon
abstract: This article identifies potential synergies between the domains of crime prevention, climate change adaptation within the built environment. It delves into three specific risks associated with climate change—heat, wildfires,, flooding, tidal surges—and investigates how adapting the built environment to these challenges may inadvertently affect crime vulnerability or prevention. It examines how human-controlled nature-based solutions, such as trees, community gardens, can reduce both heat-related problems, crime risks. The article discusses passive cooling through architectural design in hot climates, explores strategies for reducing wildfire risks through landscaping, building design. Additionally, it considers the implications of sea walls, floating structures for crime prevention in the face of tidal surges, flooding. The article concludes by underscoring the need for further research in this intersection of climate change adaptation, crime prevention, the role of crime scientists in shaping safer urban environments amid the challenges of climate change.

title: Uncovering spatial patterns of crime: a case study of Kolkata
authors: Mukherjee, Kasturi, Saha, Sumana, Karmakar, Supratim, Dash, Pratik
abstract: Crime, criminality are global concerns that pose significant risks to societal well-being, quality of life. The urbanization process, the land use of cities profoundly influence the occurrence, types,, intensity of crimes. The design, management of cities play a pivotal role in ensuring overall safety, security. Although Kolkata is considered a safe city, recent reports from the National Crime Records Bureau highlight an increase in crimes against women, placing Kolkata as the second-highest in West Bengal. The crime rate in the city has witnessed a substantial 63.46\% increase over the past three years, categorized as “high” on the rating scale. Little is known about the spatial, temporal patterns of crimes in Kolkata. This study aims to analyze the spatiotemporal patterns of murder, theft, snatching, drugging, pickpocketing,, crimes against women, using regression models. Using geoinformatics, geostatistics, the research also seeks to identify the spatial clustering, significant crime hotspots,, their shifting between 2015, 2020, also attempts to analyze the impact of urban land use on crime rates. The study reveals a significant temporal change in crime patterns over 30 years, with bare land consistently impacting crime across all categories. While thefts, snatching, pickpocketing, drugging,, crimes against women exhibit relatively stable hotspots, murder hotspots have increased, become more dispersed. The unique land use patterns of port areas influence murder, drugging,, crimes against women, while dense built-up spaces contribute to higher rates of pickpocketing.

title: Physical space characteristics, official statistics of crime in the historic centre of Porto, Portugal: the crucial role played by crime prevention through environmental design
authors: Paulo, Daniela, Nunes, Laura M, Dinis, Maria Alzira Pimenta, Sani, Ana Isabel
abstract: Understanding the relationship between physical spaces, crime in the Historic Centre of Porto (HCP), Portugal, is crucial, considering the relevance of this area to the city. This study analyses HCP’s physical space characteristics, its official statistics of crime, identifying the physical space facilitating crime. A mixed methodology comprising exploratory, descriptive design was used. The sample consisted of 410 observation records (2019–2020),, 15,853 official records of criminal occurrences reported to the Public Security Police (PSP) (2015–2019) in charge of safety in this area. Findings suggest that physical space facilitating crime include reduced visibility, night lighting, narrow streets, tunnels, dead end streets, abandoned places, houses allowing hiding,, areas without formal/informal surveillance. The PSP records show that property crime was the most prevalent in all the six HCP parishes. It is absolutely urgent to reform the spaces in the HCP, to prevent crime. Local entities can implement Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design (CPTED) strategies to make the HCP safer for all.

title: Examining cybercrime victimisation among Turkish women using routine activity theory
authors: Özaşçılar, Mine, Çalıcı, Can, Vakhitova, Zarina
abstract: Over the last few decades, the rise in internet usage has led to a transition from traditional crimes to cybercrimes. Using data from a sample of 749 Turkish women, the current study applies the routine activity theory (RAT) framework, focusing on target suitability conceptualised as VIVA (value, inertia, visibility,, accessibility), to cybercrime victimisation, including cyberstalking, computer hacking,, credit card identity theft. This study is the first to adopt this framework to understand the patterns of victimisation of Turkish women—university students. The findings indicate that RAT may be useful regardless of the geographic location of the victim; routine activities that are risky for one type of cybercrime may be harmless in relation to another; RAT could be helpful when examining cybercrime victimisation with a gendered lens.

title: Exploring, developing crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) audits: an iterative process
authors: Cozens, Paul, Babb, Courtney, Stefani, Danielle
abstract: This paper utilizes an ecological perspective to explore the development of a crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) audit tool through an ongoing iterative process. We draw upon existing examples from criminology, research into auditing the built environment for physical activity, active travel. The purpose of the paper is to present a revised CPTED audit tool, process to assist those managing crime, anti-social behaviour in their streets, neighbourhoods, communities. It may also assist those seeking to use audits as part of the CPTED process set out in the recent International Standards on CPTED: ISO22341 (British Standards 2021). Following Ceccato (Crim Justice Stud 32:165–188, 2019), we briefly reflect on the validity, reliability, generalizability of the CPTED audit tool, consider further possible refinements for future iterations.

title: From contextual to criminal harms: young people’s understanding, experiences of the violence of criminal exploitation
authors: Walsh, Colm
abstract: The criminal exploitation of children represents a significant threat to their individual wellbeing as well as to wider community safety. Despite the legacy of conflict, enduring paramilitarism, widespread violent victimisation, there is a paucity of research regarding the criminal exploitation of children (CCE) in the context of Northern Ireland (NI). In this novel exploratory study, forty-four young people engaged in in-depth focus group interviews. The data converged as well as diverged with research on CCE elsewhere suggesting that some distinct features of the mechanisms of CCE exist in the NI context. The study also found that those who experience the greatest contextual harms are at elevated risk to also experience criminal harms. CCE is experienced in a range of ways, from agile to more sustained exploitation. Leveraging mistrust of others; engaging in the mass deception of communities; minimising of the harm caused to victims;, the use of violence as capital all appear to contribute to the phenomenon of CCE in NI. This study suggests that multi-tiered responses could help to prevent CCE, protect victims of CCE; that young people require safer spaces to reflect on their experiences of contextual as well as criminal harm;, that joined up safeguarding across systems is required.

title: Crime prevention research: How can it be shared across language barriers?
authors: Ignatans, Dainis, Aleksejeva, Ludmila, Pease, Ken
abstract: This is the first of two papers addressing language barriers in criminological discourse. The present paper rehearses arguments for comparative criminological research, identifies the administrative processes of journals leading to acceptance or rejection role of language as a contributory factor acting against the interests of those lacking fluency in a journal’s specified language of submission. Revisions of the common editorial practices of peer-reviewed journals are suggested. The potential contribution of machine translation is discussed.

title: Community policing, recovery: a case study following a mass shooting in the UK
authors: Gilling, Dan, Watson, Caroline, McBride, Katie, James, Zoe
abstract: This article draws upon research conducted as part of an officially sponsored evaluation into one part of a recovery programme, put in place following a mass shooting event in the Plymouth city district of Keyham, in the UK, in the summer of 2021. It discusses the contribution made by a dedicated community policing team, focusing on its reception by the local community, aspects of its constitution, operational practices that may be regarded as critical success factors. More critically, the article questions whether this part of the recovery programme was as much about the recovery of the reputation, standing of the local police as it was about the recovery of a putative vulnerable community.

title: CCTV operators’ perspectives on protecting soft target terrorist locations in England
authors: Palace, Marek, Frankel, Rachel, Shortland, Neil, Jinag, Wenping, May, Brandon, Jones, Anthony, Starkey, Jennie
abstract: Despite the significant importance of surveillance in counterterrorism, the CCTV operators’ perspectives appear to be under-researched. To explore such perspectives, we conducted a number of semi-structured interviews with British security professionals tasked with CCTV monitoring of public spaces,, subjected their responses to the thematic analysis. Four themes emerged: challenges to the use of CCTV systems, criticism of operator roles in counterterrorism, need for improvements,, the value of CCTV in counterterrorism. While offering a critical view of current CCTV use in soft target (i.e., vulnerable) locations, these findings also highlight the value of CCTV in terms of deterrence,, support the Actor Actor-Network Theory [Terzi, Tesam Akad Derg 6(1):213–247]. As national security is increasingly looking to even more advanced technology for solutions (e.g., artificial intelligence), this exploratory research highlights the need for closer integration of human, technological actors, operator empowerment, continuous training that must be informed by actual CCTV operators who present themselves as marginalised.

title: Lithuania’s “Bloody Sunday”: a criminological, legal approach
authors: Zaksaitė, Salomėja
abstract: Lithuania’s liberation from the Soviet Union did require certain sacrifices,, one of the biggest of them occurred on the so-called Bloody Sunday—January 13, 1991. Historically, January events in Lithuania might be paralleled to earlier massacres intended to stymie Soviet-era liberation movements: Black Saturday in Baku (1990), The April 9 tragedy in Tbilisi (1989). This topic covers a wide range of legal, criminological themes, including selective justice; the issue of the liability of the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces (i.e., Mikhail Gorbachev);, limitations of criminal law while incriminating the acts falling under Arendt’s term known as the “banality of evil.” Naturally, similar events have a Rashomon-like character, with both facts, interpretations varying wildly depending on the source. In light of this, the article discusses several dichotomous (i.e., opposingly perceived) concepts: the relationship between spontaneous, planned, liberation, status frustration,, crowd, mobs. The aim of the article is to analyze the criminal case, the events of January 13, 1991, to apply criminological theories to this specific case,, last but not the least, to determine whether this legal case can be described as a quest for justice or a quest for criminals.

title: Radioactive isotopes theft in Mexico during 2011–2023: a green criminological approach
authors: Carpio-Domínguez, José Luis, Lampkin, Jack, Castro-Salazar, Jesús Ignacio
abstract: In the last decade, cases of radioactive isotope theft have been observed more frequently in Mexico, endangering human health, biodiversity,, the environment due to the risks of mishandling radioactive isotopes. The aim of this study was to analyze the theft of radioactive isotopes in Mexico in the period 2011–2023 from the perspective of green criminology through official data, radiological emergency bulletins. The results show that the most frequently stolen isotopes were 192Ir, 137Cs,, 131I in this study period,, it was also identified that the isotopes are stolen unintentionally, since it is the vehicles that transport them that are stolen, most of the time without knowing what they contain. It is concluded that the theft of radioactive isotopes in Mexico is a crime linked to vehicle theft, which in turn stems from the conditions of public insecurity but puts the health, safety, well-being of people, biodiversity,, the country's ecosystems at risk, so that institutional actions must be oriented considering the conditions of public insecurity to improve nuclear safety in the country.

title: The impact of parenting style on perceptions of police, offending intentions of young drivers: evidence from Australia
authors: Bates, Lyndel, Seccombe, John, Alexander, Marina, McLean, Rebecca
abstract: Parents are central to many learn to drive programmes internationally. This study surveys young drivers from Victoria, Queensland in Australia to examine if parental style impacts (a) intentions to offend on the road, (b) perceptions of police. Maccoby, Martin’s four parenting styles: (1) Authoritative, (2) Authoritarian, (3) Permissive,, (4) Neglectful inform the survey design. Results suggest that fixed offences like wearing a seatbelt or DUI are not impacted by different parental styles, while transient offences like speeding or dangerous driving are impacted. Specifically, young drivers with Authoritative or Authoritarian parents, who have higher levels of control, were less likely to speed or drive dangerously. Perceptions of police were also affected by parental style. Young drivers with Authoritative or Authoritarian parents had more positive perceptions of police than Neglectful or Permissive parents. The results suggest that parental support, education programmes could be developed to encourage parents to monitor their young person’s early driving career more closely.

title: Catalytic converter theft: An examination of the elasticity of crime
authors: Stickle, Ben, Rennhoff, Adam, Morris, Charles A, Fritts, Samuel
abstract: Catalytic converters are part of a vehicle’s exhaust system, contain valuable metals (i.e., platinum, palladium,, rhodium). The value of these metals has risen dramatically,, so they have the incidents of theft. This study contributes in two important ways: First, it provides insight into an emerging crime trend of catalsytic converter theft,, second, it advances knowledge of the elasticity of crime, specifically how the value of metal impacts thefts. Data on catalytic converter thefts were collected from official police reports, social media complaints in eight California cities for 42 months. We use regression analysis to study the weekly estimated value of catalytic converters, theft. Our regression approach, which we estimate using feasible generalized least squares, accounts for the non-stationarity in weekly metal thefts, allows for autocorrelation in a panel setting. Findings reveal an average price elasticity of 1.98, meaning that a 10\% increase in metal prices results in approximately a 20\% increase in catalytic converter thefts. The results illustrate how the value of metals impacts thefts.

title: Introducing the journal
authors: Fisher, Bonnie, Eck, John, Gill, Martin, Beck, Adrian
abstract: Welcome to the new Security Journal,, it is very much a new journal. Indeed, this publication has merged with, absorbed the International Journal of Risk, Security, Crime Prevention,, this has enabled us to build on the best parts of both journals. The journal has a new publisher: Perpetuity Press are specialists in the area of security publications. We have appointed a new international Advisory Board who are committed to a new Vision for the journal. And we represent a new editorial team with responsibilities for different locations (Bonnie, John for the Americas, Martin, Adrian for the rest of the world). Moreover, responsibility for Reviews (not just books but videos, other outputs), which we hope will become an important part of the journal, has been divided between James Calder (the Americas), Claire Lawrence (rest of the world). And with the help of Sandy Davidson, Michael Stack, others there is a new agreement with the American Society of Industrial Security to promote the journal, help facilitate its new Vision.

title: Relations between police officers, security professionals: A study of perceptions
authors: Nalla, Mahesh K, Hummer, Don
abstract: This paper presents the results of a recent survey of 127 police officers, 109 security professionals in a Midwestern state in the USA, which revealed interesting findings on the working relationship between public law enforcement, private security agencies. Overall, security professionals' perceptions of their relationship with police departments were positive. However, most intriguingly, security professionals felt that police officers do not view working with private security positively, even though police officers indicate the contrary. Written comments from both sides provide insights on the issues that hamper an effective working relationship between them. Also, the findings reveal that both police officers, security professionals believe that they could probably do more to encourage a positive working relationship, thus leading us to conclude that mistaken perceptions, a lack of communication are hindrances as well.

title: Cues, needs, decisions: A ‘lens’ model of security operations
authors: Baron, Viktor, van Zwanenberg, Nigel
abstract: Following from an empirical study, a ‘double lens’ model of security operations, the influences shaping them is proposed. Factors related to the ‘objective’ need for security are depicted in the left-hand lens. These are viewed as ‘cues’ which indicate the potential for criminal or other undesired events to potential perpetrators. The right-hand lens is concerned with cues that influence ‘subjective’ need, as perceived by managers, other stakeholders in the organisation. The effectiveness of a security operation then depends upon the extent to which its members are aware of those cues to which criminals, on the one hand,, stakeholders, on the other, are sensitive. These two sets of cues effectively act as the lenses through which the overall need for security is perceived. It is proposed that the need for security be understood by identifying, quantifying the influence of these cues. The model circumvents the problems involved in dealing with the absence of outcome data where security or deterrence has been successful by concentrating on the potential for events as indicated by the presence of various cues. Ways of seeking, incorporating empirical data are suggested. The potential impact on, benefits to the management of security operations are discussed.

title: Using repeat victimisation to counter commercial burglary: The Leicester experience
authors: Taylor, Geoff
abstract: Much of the discussion about repeat victimisation centres around the opportunity it presents to prevent or reduce crime by offering a prediction of its re-occurrence. In a unique crime prevention project in Leicester the practical implementation of a strategy to reduce commercial burglary by taking positive action with recent victims has shown remarkable results in the space of a few months. The strategy was designed to increase risks for offenders through enhancing detection levels. As an arrest-achieving model the outcome has been inconsequential but as a crime reduction project the results have been encouraging, at remarkably small cost in terms of both personnel, material.

title: Managing, understanding activist demonstration
authors: Coram, Gregory J
abstract: An activist demonstration on company property can be extremely disruptive to normal business operations, cause a negative public relations situation. The role of the security/police department is critical in the control of this situation. The dilemma exists in the need to balance the right of free speech, assembly with the right of a company to conduct business. In order to manage a demonstration effectively, it is essential to have psychological knowledge of the purpose, stages of this action. Understanding the dynamics, functions of an activist group provides a security/law enforcement agency with an opportunity to prepare, manage the demonstration. This psychological knowledge will enhance security preparation, will increase the probability of a successful outcome.

title: Motor vehicle theft at the shopping centre: An application of the routine activities approach
authors: Hollinger, Richard C, Dabney, Dean A
abstract: Using a national survey of self-reported shopping centre crime, this study examines how one of the most commonly reported shopping centre offences, namely, motor vehicle theft, is associated with the three critical elements of the ‘routine activities’ approach to crime distribution. As expected, the presence of motivated offenders, the absence of capable guardians both have a significant effect on the rates of auto theft occurring at 265 major US shopping centres, malls. However, contrary to the model, the availability of suitable targets does not predict auto theft in the regression equation. Theoretical discussion considers several possible explanations for this partial support for the routine activities model.

title: Tackling business crime within companies
authors: Punch, Maurice
abstract: Crime within business is highly damaging, but poorly understood, too often viewed as low-level, individual deviance. Research reveals that crime within companies is often located high in the hierarchy, is fostered by managerial weaknesses or tacit collusion. The author argues that the best guarantee of compliance is not powerful control agencies, hefty sanctions but a business strategy based on self-interest in partnership with stakeholders. Business has the resources to implement effective control, prevention through private ‘justice’ allied to external supervision. This, of course, places considerable demands on the quality of top management, on its ability to shape an ethical climate with positive social control within a learning environment. Failure to follow this path makes companies highly vulnerable to internal business crime.

title: A survey of security legislation, regulatory strategies in Australia
authors: Prenzler, Tim, Sarre, Rick
abstract: This paper reports on the first national survey of legislation regulating the security industry in Australia. In addition to estimating the size of the industry, an assessment was made of legislative statutes, enforcement strategies. The survey found that the industry was up to three times the numerical strength of the police. There was a trend towards comprehensive licensing of security occupations, primarily through controls on entry by criminal record checks, minimum training requirements. However, there was significant inconsistency between the eight jurisdictions. Strategies for monitoring the conduct of licensed personnel were relatively passive, relying largely on complaints. The authors argue that the industry, consumers could greatly benefit from a unified national system, with the implementation of more proactive forms of compliance monitoring, professional development.

title: The levels of orientation security officers have towards a public policing function
authors: Michael, Deborah
abstract: The development of the manned guarding sector of the private security industry has led to speculations surrounding the privatisation of policing or the likelihood of the emergence of a multi-tiered policing service in Britain in the future. Despite a recent growth of interest, research on the private security industry in the UK, there has been little research studying the extent to which security officers are personally motivated towards their work. Drawing on some initial impressions from qualitative research currently being undertaken, this article aims to provide information about the perceptions, motivations of security officers. It is suggested here that the guards were not strongly attracted towards a public policing function, nor were they trained to be so.

title: Research of security, safety culture within an organization. The case study within the Slovak Republic
authors: Veľas, Andrej, Halaj, Martin, Hofreiter, Ladislav, Kampová, Katarína, Zvaková, Zuzana, Jankura, Richard
abstract: AbstractSecurity, safety culture is an increasingly important term in assessing the security, safety of organizations. It is an internal security, safety factor of an organization that can directly influence its overall security, safety. In many cases, however, organizations do not know, nor do they have a way of assessing the level of their security, safety culture. It is therefore necessary to know the content, elements,, sectors in which it can be identified in order to gain a deeper knowledge of security, safety culture in more detail, be able to examine it. Firstly, we focused on creating a model for evaluating the safety, safety culture, its application in selected organizations. Secondly, we devoted to the description, design of an organization’s security, safety culture assessment model. The proposed model is based on the identification of subsectors, indicators of security, safety culture that will gain their value by using information obtained from combining the four proposed methods. Accordingly, six security, safety culture sectors were defined for the purposes of security, safety culture assessment in selected organizations. These were compared to each other to determine their mutual weight. Finally, using these research methods, security, safety culture indicators were also identified, included in the defined security, safety culture sectors. The research needed to design a security, safety culture assessment model was realized in six selected organizations, which wanted to participate in the research. These were divided according to the size of the organization into two small, two medium,, two large organizations. Crucial element in our research was data collection conducted by means of controlled interviews, questionnaire surveys in these organizations. Based on this survey, indicators of security, safety culture could be identified. As a result of this, security, safety culture values are determined for all analyzed organizations. The conclusions will point up the possible way of evaluating security, safety culture in organizations, it also contains a specific example of their usage in the practice. Thus, by using the resulting values, it is possible to decide the further direction for the organizations, focusing on the sectors of the security, safety culture, which yielded unsatisfactory results.

title: Police recruits’ wants, needs in police training in Germany
authors: Staller, Mario S, Koerner, Swen, Heil, Valentina, Abraham, Andrew, Poolton, Jamie
abstract: AbstractPolice recruits undertake mandatory training programmes to prepare for conflict situations. To motivate recruits to engage in what is called “police training” (“Polizeitraining” or “Einsatztraining”) in Germany, police trainers should design activities that align with what the recruitswantfrom training. As such, the current study investigated the wants, subjective training needs of police recruits by asking twenty-seven recruits of a German police force to identify positive, negative aspects of police training, as well as the characteristics of a competent police trainer. The qualitative data was analysed using content analysis. Higher order themes consisted of (a) the relevance of police training; (b) motivating aspects of police training; (c) negative aspects of police training;, (d) characteristics of a competent police trainer. Recruits expressed that police training is an important part of their education, which they perceived as relevant in preparing them for their duty, for upcoming performance tests. Prominent motivating aspects included the perception of competence, being challenged holistically. De-contextualized practice, static repetitions were demotivating factors. The police trainer is perceived to play a prominent role in learning, recruits want police trainers to (a) have sound knowledge of the taught content; (b) effectively deliver the training content;, (c) be mindful of individual differences. By offering insight into the wants, needs of recruits undertaking police training, the current study informs the practice of police trainers, trainer developers.

title: Business e-mail compromise scam, cyber victimization,, economic sustainability of corporate organizations in Nigeria
authors: Okpa, John Thompson, Ajah, Benjamin Okorie, Nzeakor, Ogochukwu Favour, Eshiotse, Emmanuel, Abang, Thelma Aya
abstract: Although numerous studies on cybercrime have been undertaken, very little is known about the BEC scam, its effects on economic sustainability in Nigeria. Using data collected via various methods, this study examines the implications of the BEC scam as cyber victimization on the economic infrastructure of corporate organizations in Cross River State, Nigeria. A specifically structured questionnaire, an in-depth interview with staff (nâ=â1087) was conducted, the data received were analyzed using descriptive statistics, logistic regression,, content analysis. Findings revealed that BEC victimization is increasing,, has adversely affected such corporate organizations as banks, telecommunications firms,, manufacturing companies. The organization one works for is an important factor in determining oneâs vulnerability to BEC scamming. Therefore, a multilateral cybersecurity, cyber-intelligence relationship between the various corporations, government departments is necessary for adequate protection of critical infrastructures. This multi-sectoral approach to cyber-law enforcement requires the installation of uncompromised internal physical, digital access control in order to strengthen targets. This demands robust organizational cyberspace surveillance to complement the existing government counter-cybercrime implementations.

title: Examining the crime prevention claims of crime prevention through environmental design on system-trespassing behaviors: a randomized experiment
authors: Fisher, Daren, Maimon, David, Berenblum, Tamar
keywords: 2022\_2023;316\_介入実験\_環境手がかり;Security Journal
abstract: Crime prevention through environmental design (CPTED) is a non-punitive method for reducing crime through the design of the built environment. The relevance of CPTED strategies, however, is less clear in the context of computing environments. Building upon prior research indicating that computing environments may change computer users’ behaviors, this study tests the effectiveness of CPTED-based approaches in mitigating system-trespassing events. Findings from this randomized controlled field trial demonstrate that specific CPTED strategies can mitigate hacking events by reducing the number of concurrent activities on the target computer, attenuating the number of commands typed in the attacked computer,, decreasing the likelihood of hackers returning to a previously hacked environment. Our findings suggest some novel, readily implemented strategies for reducing cybercrime.

title: A model of citizens’ trust in intelligence services
authors: Hribar, Gašper, Podbregar, Iztok, Rosi, Bojan
abstract: This article addresses a topic that has rarely been addressed in the available scientific literature, according to our knowledge. It comprehensively defines citizens’ trust in the services, identifies the factors influencing this type of trust,, proposes a model for establishing, maintaining holistic trust. The research described in the article is based on the analysed publicly available literature in the field of trust (in general, specific types of trust), intelligence services, while offering its definition of trust (in general), holistic trust.

title: International cooperation in police training: evaluation of a European Union programme for African gendarmes
authors: de Castro, Andrés, Gaona Prieto, Rodrigo, Antón, José-Ignacio
abstract: This research evaluates an onsite training programme for the security forces in Burkina Faso. This scheme is part of the Rapid Action Groups for Surveillance, Intervention in the Sahel Project; an EU initiative for improving the effectiveness of national security forces in counterterrorism actions, policing the territory, its borders. Considering the short, intensive, residential nature of the programme, we use a before-after study design to determine the scheme’s causal effects on participants’ marksmanship skills, physical fitness. Our findings suggest that this scheme has a highly positive impact on these dimensions, even though the benefits differ across participants.

title: ‘We shall triumph like the Jews’: unveiling the implicit side of IPOB’s armed separatism in Southeast Nigeria
authors: Agbo, Paulinus Okechukwu
abstract: This study investigated the impetus for the armed separatism of the Indigenous Peoples Of Biafra (IPOB). Drawing from a mixed method design utilizing a cross-sectional survey, qualitative study, seventy five (75) agitators were purposively sampled to assess the trajectory of revivified armed struggle for the independence of Biafra in Southeast Nigeria. Informed conversations on neo-Biafra movements are mainly constructed around state repression, socio-political exclusion, terrorism. This study focused on how ancient Israel’s providential war victories are renegotiated in IPOB’s armed struggle against the Nigerian state. The article specifically assessed how the influences from Jewish triumphant war narratives, self-rule are re-enacted in the IPOB’s armed struggle towards achieving Biafra’s independence in Southeast Nigeria. The findings indicated that the more religiously motivated participants are, the more their zest, proclivity to armed struggle for an independent state of Biafra (β = 0.25; t = 2.12; P < 0.05). Hence, the renewed armed struggle for an independent state of Biafra was largely traced to religious motivation, proclivity to violence F (2, 74) = 2.26, P < 0.05. In line with the findings, conclusions were drawn, implications were examined. The study uncovers the motivation behind the reinvigoration of the IPOB movement, their perception of Elohim’s (God) backing to have been drawn from the Jews’ past armed insurrection, war successes, eventual political freedom. This account maps into the discourse on how religious beliefs frame the struggle for political independence in postcolonial settings.

title: Introduction to the special issue “environmental criminology in crime prevention: theories for practice”
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Ioannidis, Ioannis
abstract: AbstractIn this special issue, five articles demonstrate the impact of contemporary Environmental Criminology theory on the understanding of crime, the development of crime prevention practices in both urban, rural contexts.
