The study found that “knowledge about laws related to industrial espionage,” “case types, modus operandi,”, “knowledge related to digital forensics, utilization of useful tools” are necessary competencies for the police investigating industrial espionage cases. Several non-essential but beneficial competencies were also found, such as “understanding of the latest technology trends,” “knowledge of internal computer systems, relevant organizations,”, “ability to use programs to design drawings or program source codes.”

title: Perspectives on privacy
authors: Newell, Patricia Brierley
abstract: The nature of privacy is an interesting, complex question which has been addressed in several disciplines. Perspectives on privacy are thus varied, occasionally conflicting,, generally difficult to evaluate in a coherent fashion. There is not, in fact, agreement on what privacy actually is. In this article, studies of privacy from anthropology, ethology, political science, psychology, sociology,, other disciplines, are classified into person-centred, place-centred, interactional perspectives, in all disciplines, rather than examining each discipline independently. The review provides a framework which may be used to facilitate comparison of privacy issues across disciplines, perspectives. A broader concept of privacy results from viewing the very different perspectives under a wider umbrella than that of the more individual viewpoints. At the same time, niceties of interpretation surface, which contribute to the depth, clarity of the concept.

title: Urbanicity, psychotic experiences: Social adversities, isolation, exposure to natural environments predict psychosis
authors: Beyer, Moana, Brick, Timothy R, Kühn, Simone
keywords: Psychotic experiences; Urbanicity; Environment; Predictive modelling; Boruta; Elastic net regression;J Environ Psychol
abstract: Background Research has shown that incidence rates of psychotic experiences are higher in urban areas, defined by their population density,, that an increasing number of people move to cities. Thus, it is critical to understand which characteristics of cities drive this association. To date, efforts to explore urban risk have predominantly focused on a few or single preselected candidate factors, clinical populations. Methods We aimed to identify the best predictors of psychotic experiences (PE) in a subclinical population, considering 26 factors describing the physical, social environment. Two feature selection models were employed, i.e., a Boruta algorithm, a random forests approach,, an elastic net penalised logistic regression model. Results Individual-specific social environment features emerged as the most robust predictors of PE, including childhood adversity, stressful life events, social isolation, low household income. Exposure to natural environments was found to be negatively associated with PE. Conclusions Spending more time in residential natural environments could be an actionable target for preventing, treating psychosis.

title: Assault prevention as social control: Women, sexual assault prevention on urban college campuses
authors: Day, Kristen
abstract: Sexual assault on U.S.A. college campuses is increasingly recognized as an urgent, pervasive national problem. To prevent assault, school administrators, individual women promote, adopt safety strategies that often compromise women's free, independent use of the campus environment. Such strategies may fail to correspond to the actual nature of sexual assault on campus. Based on open-ended interviews with college personnel, women students, this study examines sexual assault, personal crime prevention strategies at two midwestern, urban universities. School, individual strategies are characterized according to type, goals,, orientation. Findings explore the relationship of strategies to sexual assault on campus,, implications of strategies for women's use of public space. Conclusions suggest means to increase real safety while enhancing women's freedom, mobility on, near campus.

title: Homes, homeless women
authors: Bunston, Terry, Breton, Margot
abstract: This paper is based on a study of the problems homeless women face, their attempts at solving these problems. The investigation applied a quality of life framework which enabled the authors to identify the strengths, problems evident in seven life domains relevant to homeless women. The present paper examines the findings in light of several properties of home selected from the literature, asking of the data what it can tell us about the ‘homefulness’ of the respondents former, current housing arrangements.

title: Where do young children in middle-class high-rise housing estates play?A critical analysis of spatial planning, design parameters across seven heterogeneous housing estates in Pune, India
authors: Atmakur-Javdekar, Sruthi
keywords: Children's play; Housing estates; High-rise housing; Architecture; Design, planning;J Environ Psychol
abstract: Play is fundamental to children's physical growth, social development,, mental, emotional well-being;, how we plan,, design high-rise housing estates impacts children's ability to access, use spaces for play, thus impacting their overall growth, development. By using Lefebvre's Spatial Triad (1974/1991) as an analytical framework, this paper investigates (1) ‘Conceptualized Space’ or ‘play areas, materiality of the play areas as conceptualized by design professionals’; (2) ‘Actual Space’ or ‘spaces where children actually play’;, (3) ‘Experienced Space’ or ‘caregivers’ assessment of play spaces, their preferences of play materials, elements, surfaces for young children in high-rise housing estates. Comparative case-study research of seven housing estates from a baseline study of 63 high-rise housing estates was adopted to realize contrasts, patterns, or similarities across the cases. Methods included (1) semi-structured open-ended interviews with design professionals including developers (n = 4), architects (n = 4), landscape architects (n = 2), play equipment manufacturer (n = 1); (2) In-depth field studies;, (3) semi-structured open-ended interviews with parents (n = 27), grandparents (n = 5), nannies (n = 4) of young children. This study generates new knowledge about design, planning considerations for designated play spaces, caregivers', designers ideas around nature based play, caregivers' preferences of play elements, materials, surfaces,, details spatial factors influencing young children's play areas in housing estates. As a way forward, the paper offers 11 guidelines to influence the design, planning of play spaces, open areas in future housing estates to fulfil young children's play needs.

title: The prediction of police calls for service: The influence of weather, temporal variables on rape, domestic violence
authors: Cohn, Ellen G
abstract: Rape, domestic violence are two of the most controversial types of criminal behavior. Both are violent crimes, both are usually directed towards women. This research examines the short-term effect of weather, temporal variations (time of day, day of week, holidays, etc.) on calls for police service in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The influence of these variables on domestic violence, rape is compared, it is found that the two types of crimes are affected in very different ways by the independent variables used. The results suggest that the occurrence of domestic violence is much more highly influenced by immediate temporal, weather variables such as time of day, day of week, ambient temperature. However, rape appears not to be as greatly affected by immediate situational conditions, contexts. Possible explanations for the findings, implications of the research are discussed.

title: Place meanings surrounding an urban natural area: A qualitative inquiry
authors: Spartz, James T, Shaw, Bret R
keywords: Natural resources management; Advocacy groups; Sense of place; Place meaning; Urban natural area;J Environ Psychol
abstract: This article describes a qualitative analysis of place-based meanings held by members of a conservation advocacy, or ``Friends of…,'' group living within watershed boundaries surrounding a public, urban arboretum in South Central Wisconsin. Responses to semi-structured interview questions were analyzed using an iterative analytic method. Indicators of place-based meanings associated with this urban natural area were assessed from interview transcripts. An integrative model of Arboretum Meanings emerged from the analysis highlighting place meanings associated with various attributes of the area. Use of this urban natural area was often associated with a deep appreciation of its biodiversity, as a location for sanctuary or escape, a place for recreation, exercise,, as a meeting place for friends, family. Results are discussed in terms of how place-based meanings can inform land managers, conservation advocacy group leaders to better understand their stakeholders, maintain the most desirable elements of urban natural areas,, reduce potential conflict resulting from divergent place meanings among user groups.

title: Environmental view, color for a simulated telemarketing task
authors: Stone, Nancy J
abstract: In two experiments, task type or a break, environmental color,, environmental view were manipulated to determine their effects on mood, satisfaction, motivation,, performance. Mood, specifically negative mood,, performance satisfaction tended to be affected by what one did, not by the environmental design. Individuals working a high demand task reported more negative mood, less performance satisfaction than individuals working a low demand task. As expected, motivation was not affected by any manipulations. Performance appears to be affected by environmental color or view. When performing a low demand task, performance appears to worsen over time in the blue rather than the red environment. When working a high demand task in a red environment, performance was worse unless either a break or a scenic picture were present. These data suggest that blue is a calming color, red is a stimulating color, which may interact with other environmental factors. The impact of a scenic picture may serve a comparative process.

title: The impact of transit growth on the perception of crime
authors: Spicer, Valerie, Song, Justin
keywords: Perception of crime; Public disorder; Transit; Growth;J Environ Psychol;305\_FoC
abstract: Fear is a pervasive urban problem affecting the quality of life in urban communities. In the urban environment, fear, the perception of crime happen at the nexus that connects people to places. Research linking fear of crime to public transit reveals public disorder as a major contributing factor. This relationship is particularly relevant to transit systems that are forecasting significant growth. This study demonstrates how perception of crime changes over ten years of growth at a large transit hub in western Canada. The results show that perception of crime increases, becomes more concentrated. Cognitive maps (1997: n = 430; 2007: n = 458) from a community survey compare the perception of crime overtime, between males, females,, victims of crime. The micro morphology of the area surrounding the transit hub is discussed, the location of this station on the system is analyzed. Future research directions are presented.
