Results Scripts consist of dominant officer, subject action configurations associated with an increased risk of escalation from soft empty-hand control to more severe types of force, as well as configurations of environmental, demographic characteristics. Conclusions Based on identified scripts, if study results are replicated using a larger sample size, results support the efficacy of persistent calm commands for reducing risk of escalation. Crisis intervention, procedural justice training is recommended for officers. To create a heightened awareness of the presence of a recording device, wearers of BWCs may consider narrating interactions as they unfold. Finally, pending replication, we advocate for immediate physical separation of victim, suspect when in a private space.

title: The code of the street, cooperation with the police: Do codes of violence, procedural injustice,, police ineffectiveness discourage reporting violent victimization to the police?
authors: Kwak, Hyounggon, Dierenfeldt, Rick, McNeeley, Susan
keywords: Code of the street; Crime reporting; Police effectiveness; Procedural justice;J Crim Justice
abstract: Purpose Few quantitative studies have tested Anderson's (1999) suggestion that reliance on codes of violence, mistrust in the police reduce the likelihood of cooperating with the police after being victimized. We examine whether perceived codes of violence, perceived police effectiveness,, perceived procedural injustice influence the decision to report crime to the police. We also examine whether these relationships interact with individual or situational characteristics. Methods This study applies binary logistic regression to a sample of 687 victims of violence from the Seattle Neighborhoods, Crime Survey. Results The results indicated that procedural injustice had significant effects on crime reporting, though this relationship was conditioned by victim injury. Codes of violence, police effectiveness were related to crime reporting, but only among Black crime victims. Conclusions Taken together, the results underscore the importance of police-community relations, as poor perceptions of the police, reliance on oneself for protection, justice reduce cooperation with the police, especially among minorities.

title: The extent, correlates of public support for deterrence reforms, hot spots policing: Deterrence reforms, hot spots policing
authors: Metcalfe, Christi, Pickett, Justin T
abstract: As one approach to prison downsizing, criminal justice reform, scholars recommend altering the nature of policing by reallocating resources toward policing, increasing sentinel patrols, hot spots interventions. Public attitudes toward these reforms are unknown. In the current police crisis, shifting policies in ways disfavored by the public can impact police-community relations, especially among those disproportionately affected. The current study uses survey data from a nationally representative sample of Americans to evaluate whether the public is receptive to the suggested reforms. Our results indicate that the majority of the general public believes policing is more cost-effective than incarceration, supports a focus on sentinel patrols, crime hot spots, although there is less support for hot spots policing among blacks, Hispanics,, lower income individuals. The hot spots policing strategy most preferred is situational prevention,, the least supported is aggressive order-maintenance policing.

title: Gunshot detection technology time savings, spatial precision: An exploratory analysis in Kansas City
authors: Piza, Eric L, Hatten, David N, Carter, Jeremy G, Baughman, Jonas H, Mohler, George O
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: AbstractGunshot detection technology (GDT) is expected to impact gun violence by accelerating the discovery, response to gunfire. GDT should further collect more accurate spatial data, as gunfire is assigned to coordinates measured by acoustic sensors rather than addresses reported via 9-1-1 calls for service (CFS). The current study explores the level to which GDT achieves these benefits over its first 5 years of operation in Kansas City, Missouri. Data systems are triangulated to determine the time, location gunfire was reported by GDT, CFS. The temporal, spatial distances between GDT, CFS are then calculated. Findings indicate GDT generates time savings, increases spatial precision as compared to CFS. This may facilitate police responses to gunfire events, provide more spatially accurate data to inform policing strategies. Results of generalized linear, multinomial logistic regression models indicate that GDT benefits are influenced by a number of situational factors.

title: How, why is crime more concentrated in some neighborhoods than others?: A new dimension to community crime
authors: O'Brien, Daniel T, Ciomek, Alexandra, Tucker, Riley
abstract: Objectives Much recent work has focused on how crime concentrates on particular streets within communities. This is the first study to examine how such concentrations vary across the neighborhoods of a city. The analysis evaluates the extent to which neighborhoods have characteristic levels of crime concentration, then tests two hypotheses for explaining these variations: the compositional hypothesis, which posits that neighborhoods whose streets vary in land usage or demographics have corresponding disparities in levels of crime;, the social control hypothesis, which posits that neighborhoods with higher levels of collective efficacy limit crime to fewer streets. Methods We used 911 dispatches from Boston, MA, to map violent crimes across the streets of the city. For each census tract we calculated the concentration of crime across the streets therein using the generalized Gini coefficient, cross-time stability in the locations of hotspots. Results Neighborhoods did have characteristic levels of concentration that were best explained by the compositional hypothesis in the form of demographic, land use diversity. In addition, ethnic heterogeneity predicted higher concentrations of crime over, above what would be expected given the characteristics of the individual streets, suggesting it exacerbated disparities in crime. Conclusions The extent to which crime concentrates represents an underexamined aspect of how crime manifests in each community. It is driven in part by the diversity of places in the neighborhood, but also can be influenced by neighborhood-level processes. Future work should continue to probe the sources, consequences of these variations.

title: Understanding high-risk behavior among non-dominant minorities: a social resistance framework
authors: Factor, Roni, Kawachi, Ichiro, Williams, David R
abstract: Across different societies, non-dominant minority groups, compared to the dominant group, often exhibit higher rates of involvement in high-risk behaviors, such as smoking, drug, alcohol use, sexual risk behaviors, overeating,, unsafe driving habits. In turn, these behaviors have a well-documented impact on chronic disease, morbidity,, mortality. Previous studies have emphasized macro-structural or micro-agentic explanations for this phenomenon. Such explanations suffer from mirror-image shortcomings, such as, by emphasizing structural barriers, macro-level explanations leave out individual agency (``the over-socialized conception of the individual''), while micro-level theories give short shrift to structural constraints that prevent individuals from engaging in health-promoting behaviors (``the under-socialized conception of the individual''). Moreover, most current theories regard individuals as passive players who are influenced by the social environment or by psychological problems, or who make ``bad'' choices. The current paper develops an integrated theoretical framework that incorporates structural inequalities while leaving intact the role of individual agency. According to the social resistance framework, power relations in society encourage members of non-dominant minority groups to actively engage in everyday resistance practices that include various unhealthy behaviors. The paper develops propositions from which testable hypotheses can be generated,, discusses the implications, contributions of the social resistance framework.

title: Evaluation of the UNREST questionnaire for testing the social resistance framework
authors: Factor, Roni, Kawachi, Ichiro, Williams, David R
abstract: BACKGROUND: The recently developed social resistance framework addresses a widespread pattern whereby non-dominant minority groups, such as ethnic/racial minorities, people of low socioeconomic status, often engage in unhealthy, risky behaviours at higher rates compared with society at large. The framework suggests that power relations within society may encourage members of non-dominant minority groups to actively engage in acts of everyday resistance, which may include risky, unhealthy behaviours. METHODS: The current paper develops, psychometrically evaluates a research tool to test this innovative framework. The UNREST questionnaire measures the key concepts of the framework, along with four high-risk, unhealthy behaviours, as well as demographic, socioeconomic characteristics. A pilot survey was conducted among representative subsamples of a non-dominant group (African-Americans), a dominant group (Caucasians). RESULTS: Consistent with the general premises of the framework, the evaluation of the questionnaire produced six valid, reliable scales, which were significantly correlated with some criterion-related items as well as unhealthy, risky behaviours. CONCLUSIONS: The preliminary results of our pilot study suggest that the new tool may be useful for testing the framework. The results also provide support for the framework in general.

title: “gentefication” in the barrio: Examining the relationship between gentrification, homicide in East Los Angeles
authors: Barton, Michael S, Valasik, Matthew A, Brault, Elizabeth, Tita, George
abstract: Research has increasingly moved toward a consensus that violent crime declines as neighborhoods gentrify, yet some studies find the direction of this relationship varies by type of violent crime. This finding becomes even more important when connected with recent research that finds the structural influences of gang, non-gang homicide are disparate. The current study engages with research in each of these areas by examining the relationship of gentrification with levels of total, gang,, non-gang homicide in Los Angeles Police Department’s (LAPD) Hollenbeck Community Policing Area. We find gentrification was not associated with variation in total or gang homicide, but was positively associated with non-gang homicide.

title: An ecological study of the location of gang “set space”
authors: Tita, George E, Cohen, Jacqueline, Engberg, John
abstract: Previous gang research has focused primarily on the attributes of individuals who join gangs. This ecological study of violent urban youth gangs examines the social, economic,, physical organization of places where gangs locate. Our goal is to understand those features of communities that either facilitate the formation of gangs or insulate an area from gang formation. By interviewing gang members, having them map places where they came together as a sociological group to “hang out,” we study what we label as the “set space” of gangs. Our study is analogous to criminological studies of where criminal acts occur rather than of the factors that lead an individual to commit criminal acts. This study indicates that gang set space is usually a very small geographic area, much smaller than neighborhoods or even census tracts. A probability (logit) model estimates the influence of various local area attributes on the presence of violent youth gangs in census block groups. Diminished social control—in the absence of capable guardians, physical abandonment of place—and underclass features increase the likelihood of observing violent youth gangs hanging out in a particular area.

title: Burglar target selection: A cross-national comparison: A cross-national comparison
authors: Townsley, Michael, Birks, Daniel, Bernasco, Wim, Ruiter, Stijn, Johnson, Shane D, White, Gentry, Baum, Scott
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: discrete spatial choice; offender mobility; replication; residential burglary;331\_Burglary
abstract: OBJECTIVES: This study builds on research undertaken by Bernasco, Nieuwbeerta, explores the generalizability of a theoretically derived offender target selection model in three cross-national study regions. METHODS: Taking a discrete spatial choice approach, we estimate the impact of both environment-, offender-level factors on residential burglary placement in the Netherlands, the United Kingdom,, Australia. Combining cleared burglary data from all study regions in a single statistical model, we make statistical comparisons between environments. RESULTS: In all three study regions, the likelihood an offender selects an area for burglary is positively influenced by proximity to their home, the proportion of easily accessible targets,, the total number of targets available. Furthermore, in two of the three study regions, juvenile offenders under the legal driving age are significantly more influenced by target proximity than adult offenders. Post hoc tests indicate the magnitudes of these impacts vary significantly between study regions. CONCLUSIONS: While burglary target selection strategies are consistent with opportunity-based explanations of offending, the impact of environmental context is significant. As such, the approach undertaken in combining observations from multiple study regions may aid criminology scholars in assessing the generalizability of observed findings across multiple environments.

title: Crime, safety-related concerns in a small community
authors: Austin, D Mark, Woolever, Cynthia, Baba, Yoko
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: This research utilizes social context, personal characteristics as determinants of both perceptions, satisfaction with safety in the local neighborhood. Using survey data obtained from residents of a small town, this analysis examines the impact of satisfaction with the environment, victimization,, social integration on attitudes concerning safety. Consistent with past research, results indicate that victimization, satisfaction with the local area are both significant predictors of perceptions of safety. They also share a significant relationship with satisfaction with safety. Two indicators of social integration yielded differing results. Participation in local organizations, associations played a more significant role in attitudes concerning safety than did the number of friends a respondent has in the neighborhood. When controlling for personal characteristics, participation in organizations was a more significant predictor of perceptions of safety than of satisfaction with safety.

title: A multilevel analysis of collective efficacy, neighborhood disorder,, individual social capital on avoidance behavior
authors: Hardyns, Wim, Snaphaan, Thom, Pauwels, Lieven J R, Vyncke, Veerle, Willems, Sara
abstract: The principal aim of this multilevel study was to assess the impact of collective efficacy, disorder, as neighborhood characteristics,, individual social capital on an individual’s avoidance behavior, independent of the neighborhood composition. The theoretical backdrop to the present study integrates insights from social capital theory, collective efficacy theory,, broken windows theory. The multilevel model is based on an individual-level questionnaire of inhabitants ( N = 2,730), a neighborhood-level questionnaire of key informants in neighborhoods in Ghent, Belgium ( N = 142). The results suggest small but significant neighborhood effects on an individual’s avoidance behavior. Individuals with lower levels of individual social capital, who live in neighborhoods with higher levels of disorder report more avoidance behavior.

title: Are the police primarily responsible for influencing place-level perceptions of procedural justice, effectiveness? A longitudinal study of street segments
authors: Weisburd, David, Jonathan-Zamir, Tal, White, Clair, Wilson, David B, Kuen, Kiseong
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
abstract: While there has been significant study of the relationship between police legitimacy, its key antecedents - procedural justice (PJ), police effectiveness (PE) at the individual level, little attention has been paid to what impacts general evaluations of PJ, PE. Our paper focuses on these perceptions at places. Our analyzes utilize survey data collected on 447 street segments in Baltimore City, MD, in two waves. We first used EFA to determine the latent structure of PJ, PE measures. We then used mixed effects OLS regression modeling techniques to examine the antecedents of a “scorecard” of perceptions of the police. The results of the EFA show a single latent structure that we term the scorecard for PJ, PE. While we find that experiences with the police, street conditions that the police are presumed to impact influence the scorecard, street conditions that are less likely to be influenced by police (collective efficacy, concentrated disadvantage) also have strong influence. Both the research, policy-oriented literature often view the police as primarily responsible for their public image. Our data suggest that at the place level, such perceptions are also strongly impacted by factors primarily outside police influence.

title: Can homicide detectives improve homicide clearance rates?
authors: Braga, Anthony A, Dusseault, Desiree
abstract: The available scientific evidence on the value of detectives in clearing crimes generally suggests that most crimes are solved through the random circumstances of crime scenes rather than special follow-up investigation. Other research, however, suggests that the work of criminal investigators can increase the likelihood that crimes might be cleared through arrest. After years of homicide clearance rates that were lower than the national average, the Boston Police Department engaged a problem-oriented policing approach to improve their post-homicide criminal investigation processes, practices. Our quasi-experimental statistical analyses suggest that the intervention significantly increased key investigative activities, improved Boston homicide clearance rates relative to existing homicide clearance trends in other Massachusetts, U.S. jurisdictions.

title: Deterrence, macro-level perceptions of punishment risks: Is there a “collective wisdom”?
authors: Kleck, Gary, Barnes, J C
abstract: Prior research indicates that individual perceptions of the risk of punishment for criminal behavior are unrelated to actual risks of punishment in the areas in which individuals reside. It could be argued, however, that the relevant policy question is whether variation in actual punishment levels affects average perceptions of risk among aggregates. Scholars have argued that there is “collective wisdom” in the perceptions of collectivities of humans, even if the views of individuals are inaccurate. This thesis is tested using survey data on individual perceptions of the risks of legal punishment for crimes, aggregated up to the level of county populations. The authors find that the aggregate perceptions of county populations are generally not related to actual county levels of the certainty, severity,, swiftness of punishment. Thus, neither the perceptions of individuals nor the average perceptions of populations have any significant association with actual risks of punishment.

title: Do more police lead to more crime deterrence?
authors: Kleck, Gary, Barnes, J C
abstract: Does increasing police strength deter more crime? Some studies have found apparent negative effects of police manpower levels on crime rates,, the most common explanation of such findings is that greater police strength increases perceptions of arrest risk, thus reducing crime via general deterrence mechanisms. The authors directly tested this hypothesis by estimating the association between survey respondents’ perceptions of arrest risk, the level of police strength prevailing in the counties where they live. No relationship between the number of police officers per capita, perceptions of the risk of arrest was found, suggesting that increases in police manpower will not increase general deterrent effects, decreases will not reduce these effects. The authors also considered the possibility that police manpower levels influence the number of criminals incarcerated,, thus affect crime rates via the incapacitative effects of incarceration, but concluded that such an effect is unlikely. These findings point to a need to reconsider previous interpretations of findings as supportive of a deterrent effect of increased police manpower on crime rates.

title: Offender decision-making in criminology: Contributions from behavioral economics
authors: Pogarsky, Greg, Roche, Sean Patrick, Pickett, Justin T
abstract: If there is agency, some decision-making process entailed in criminal behavior, then what are the incentives for crime, for conformity,, what is their role in offending decisions? Incentives have long been the province of economics, which has wide influence in criminology (e.g., Becker 1968 ). However, economics has evolved considerably since Becker's influential model. An important development has been the advent of behavioral economics, which some consider a branch of economics on par with macroeconomics or econometrics ( Dhami 2016 ). Behavioral economics integrates empirical departures from traditional microeconomic theories into a rigorous, more descriptively accurate economic model of choice. This review explains how behavioral economic applications on offender decision-making can help refine criminological theories of choice, identify innovative possibilities for improving crime-control policies.

title: The deterrence effect of criminal sanctions against environmental crime in Finland: an application of the rational choice model of crime
authors: Lindqvist, Riku, Lombardini, Chiara, Suvantola, Leila, Ollikainen, Markku
abstract: AbstractApplying the rational choice model of crime, this study estimates the optimality of sanctions for environmental crimes, the social cost of these crimes, the expected gain to the offender with Finnish court data from 327 criminal cases in the period 2013–2018. Sensitivity analyses are conducted for the optimal fine, the expected gain from the crime, its social cost. The time-lag, uncertainties related to the restoration of the environmental harm are explicitly included in the model, the empirical analysis. The average fine was much lower than the optimal fine even when taking into account the constraint posed by the offenders’ wealth, disregarding the time-lag, uncertainties related to the restoration of the environmental harm. The use of prison sentences was also suboptimal. Even when the illegal gain was fully forfeited, the expected gain from the crime to the offender remained positive. Our results suggest a need to increase the cost of punishment by higher fines, reliable forfeiture of the illegal economic gain. They also point to the importance of systematically estimating both the environmental damage, the illegal gain from the crime as these were available respectively for only 24\% (N = 79), 3\% (N = 11) of all cases.

title: Punishment menus, their deterrent effects: an exploratory analysis
authors: Grolleau, Gilles, Mungan, Murat C, Mzoughi, Naoufel
abstract: Conventional wisdom suggests that allowing offenders to choose alternative punishments to a previously existing punishment cannot enhance deterrence, because offenders can simply select the least costly option available. After reviewing the deterrence research literature, we argue that punishment menus may encourage individuals to focus more on how they construe the wrongdoing, view the ethical gravity of their actions. We experimentally test whether people may perceive punishment menus as more deterrent than stand-alone sanctions available within the same menu. Our results suggest that this is possible,, that changes in people’s perceptions are often mediated by the mindset (e.g., calculative, ethical) they adopt to evaluate punishment schemes as well as their impressions of the seriousness of the illegal act.

title: Cognitive map of perceptions of social networks as a means of justice in sexual offenses
authors: Nadav-Carmel, Hila, Lev-On, Azi
abstract: The decision to share deeply personal experiences of sexual violence publicly is complex, multifaceted. This study provides valuable insights into this phenomenon. Interviews conducted with fifteen victims of sexual assault in Israel provide insights into the decision-making pathways of victims. The existing literature on sexual victims of sexual assault in Israel offers insights into their decision-making pathways but often lacks integration between theoretical concepts, practical outcomes. This article contributes to this field by proposing a detailed cognitive map that illuminates the specific decisions made by victims in choosing where to disclose their assault. The cognitive map presented in this study provides a comprehensive view of victims’ decision-making pathways. This study is part of a larger research project that involves interviewing communication consultants, analyzing posts from the social network platform Instagram to better understand the perceptions, behaviors of sexual assault victims. The interviews brought up four main themes: the existence of communicative justice, its importance as an arena for achieving justice; social media is critical for achieving justice, sometimes even more than the institutional arena; procedural justice is more important than outcome justice; voice is a leading principle in procedural justice principles.

title: Systematic review of empirical studies on cyberbullying in adults: What we know, what we should investigate
authors: Jenaro, Cristina, Flores, Noelia, Frías, Cinthia Patricia
abstract: Cyberbullying is a worldwide phenomenon, most of our knowledge comes from studies with adolescent, younger populations. Adult populations have received scarce attention. The present study is a systematic review of empirical academic papers on cyberbullying in the adult population. An online databases search (CINHAL, PsycInfo, ERIC, Medline, Pubmed,, Web of Science) identified 3986 references that, in successive steps, were reduced to 90 studies published between 2004, 2016 that met the inclusion criteria. Each study was analyzed regarding topic, methods, ages,, other general characteristics. In addition, the measures used to assess cyberbullying, the impact of cyberbullying,, the different roles of those involved in the studies with adult population were explored. Results showed that there is a need for studies conducted in locations other than university settings, that the variety of measures, as well as the different criteria utilized to identify the cyberbullied, cyberbullies,, bystanders makes it difficult to compare findings. There is a need for longitudinal studies, for evidence-based practices to deal with these violent, aggressive behaviors.

title: Attitudes toward police response to domestic violence: a comparison of Chinese, American college students: A comparison of Chinese, American college students
authors: Sun, Ivan Y, Su, Mingyue, Wu, Yuning
abstract: Domestic violence has emerged as a worldwide concern since the 1970s. Although a substantial amount of efforts have been devoted to assessing various aspects of domestic violence, a relatively small number of studies have empirically examined factors that shape public attitudes toward police response to such incidents. Even rarer is investigating the topic from an international, comparative perspective. Based on survey data gathered from approximately 550 college students in China, the United States, this study analyzes the effects of background characteristics, personal, vicarious experiences of crime,, perceptions of gender roles, violence on attitudes toward proactive, traditional police response to domestic violence. Compared to their American counterparts, Chinese students were less likely to favor proactive response, more likely to support traditional response. Chinese, American students' attitudes toward police response to domestic violence were shaped by some different, common factors. Implications for policy, future research are discussed.

title: Self-protection in the social context: A daily-level examination of young adult women's perceived need for, engagement in sexual assault protective behavioral strategies
authors: Zaso, Michelle J, Livingston, Jennifer A, Shaw, Rachael J, Colder, Craig R, Read, Jennifer P
keywords: Routine Activity Theory; alcohol use; protective behavioral strategies; sexual assault
abstract: Objective: Young adult women naturalistically engage in sexual assault protective behavioral strategies (SA-PBS) in an effort to reduce their risk of sexual assault. Despite well-documented sociocontextual risks for sexual assault, it remains largely unknown whether, how social contexts influence SA-PBS use. The present study characterized relations of women's alcohol use, interpersonal contexts with SA-PBS engagement across social events, framed according to Routine Activity Theory. Method: Young adult women from a community sample (N = 174) reported their drinking, social events across 27 daily assessments spanning one year. Multilevel latent class analyses examined variability in SA-PBS,, multinomial regression tested associations of contextual risks with SA-PBS engagement. Results: Results supported three distinct classes of social events characterized by SA-PBS engagement: (1) No or Minimal Use of SA-PBS (``No Use,'' 26\%), (2) No Perceived Reason or Opportunity to Use SA-PBS (``No Reason or Opportunity,'' 44\%),, (3) Any Use of SA-PBS (``Any Use,'' 30\%). Presence of likely offenders (odds ratio [OR] = 4.77, p = .004), absence of capable guardianship (OR = 5.91, p < .001),, greater other's substance intoxication (OR = 1.46, p = .01), as theorized by Routine Activity Theory, increased odds of membership in the ``Any Use'' relative to ``No Use'' class. Women's alcohol consumption was not associated with class membership. Conclusions: Women's perceptions of risk in the social environment relate to their likelihood of engaging in SA-PBS. Findings represent an important step toward understanding the social context's role in sexual assault risk, protection.

title: Intimate partner violence, health conditions among U.s. adults-National Intimate Partner violence survey, 2010-2012
authors: Gilbert, Leah K, Zhang, Xinjian, Basile, Kathleen C, Breiding, Matthew, Kresnow, Marcie-Jo
keywords: domestic violence; intimate partner violence; polyvictimization; sexual violence; stalking
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Few studies of intimate partner violence, health outcomes include multiple forms of intimate partner victimization, so this paper sought to examine health associations with intimate partner violence (IPV), including sexual, physical, stalking,, psychological forms, as well as polyvictimization. METHODS: Data are from the 2010-2012 National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey, an on-going national random-digit-dial telephone survey of U.S. adults. There were 41,174 respondents. Logistic regression was used to compute prevalence ratios for any IPV, adjusted for demographics, non-IPV victimization. For individual forms of IPV, prevalence ratios were further adjusted for other forms of IPV. Tests for linear trend in poly-victimization were performed. RESULTS: Any IPV was associated with all health conditions for both sexes with a few exceptions for males. Female penetrative sexual victimization, male stalking victimization were associated with the most health conditions. For each health condition, a significant linear trend indicated that as the number of forms of IPV experienced increased, prevalence of each health condition increased, with a few exceptions for males. CONCLUSIONS: It is important for service providers to screen for multiple forms of IPV, including psychological aggression, because individual forms or polyvictimization may have unique, cumulative health effects.

title: Sexual violence victimization of U.s. males: Negative health conditions associated with rape, being made to penetrate
authors: Smith, Sharon G, Chen, Jieru, Lowe, Ashley N, Basile, Kathleen C
keywords: PTSD; anything related to sexual assault < sexual assault; male victims < sexual assault; mental health, violence; violence exposure
abstract: Sexual violence is a significant public health problem with long-term health implications. Previous investigations of male victimization have often relied on nongeneralizable samples to examine the health consequences of rape. Furthermore, made to penetrate (MTP) victimization has received very little attention as a specific form of sexual violence. Using data from the 2010 to 2012 National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey, we examined negative impacts (e.g., injury), health conditions associated with experiences of rape, MTP among male victims in the United States. Results indicate that approximately 1 in 4 victims of rape-only, 1 in 12 victims of MTP-only reported physical injuries. An estimated 62.7\% of rape-only victims, 59.8\% of MTP-only victims reported at least one impact due to the perpetrator's violence. Rape victims were significantly more likely than non-rape victims to report 2 of 11 health conditions measured, while MTP victims had greater odds of reporting 6 of 11 health conditions measured compared to non-MTP victims. This article fills gaps in understanding the impacts of rape, MTP on male victims,, it is the only study to do so using a large, nationally representative sample. Sexual violence is linked to serious health effects but is also preventable. Screening for violence victimization, preventing male sexual violence before it happens are both important to reduce the risk for immediate, chronic health impacts.

title: Characteristics, impacts of sexual violence, stalking victimization by the same perpetrator using a nationally representative sample
authors: Basile, Kathleen C, Smith, Sharon G, Wang, Jing, Friar, Norah
keywords: Intimate partner violence; United States; health impacts; polyvictimization; prevalence
abstract: Authors examine prevalence of sexual violence, stalking victimization by the same perpetrator, reporting perpetrator types, intimate partner context, impacts for this combination of victimization. Data are from the 2010-2012 National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey, a nationally representative adult telephone survey. Analyses examined the characteristics of the victimization, presence of other intimate partner violence by the same perpetrator,, victim impacts (e.g., injury). An estimated 8.1\% (9.8 million) of women, 1.6\% (1.9 million) of men in the United States were stalked, sexually victimized by the same perpetrator, most often an intimate partner. Over 90\% of female, male victims experienced sexual violence, stalking, psychological aggression,, physical violence by the same intimate partner perpetrator. Impacts of both intimate partner, non-intimate partner perpetrated victimization were most commonly fearfulness, concern for safety,, posttraumatic stress disorder symptoms. Sexual violence combined with stalking is common in the context of intimate partner violence. Early prevention efforts (i.e., in youth) addressing the context of intimate partner violence may be helpful in reducing these forms of violence, their impacts.

title: Chronic diseases, health conditions,, other impacts associated with rape victimization of U.s. women
authors: Basile, Kathleen C, Smith, Sharon G, Chen, Jieru, Zwald, Marissa
keywords: PTSD; anything related to sexual assault; mental health, violence; violence exposure
abstract: Sexual violence (SV) is an urgent public health issue that is common, has lifelong effects on health. Previous scholarship has documented the association of SV victimization with numerous health conditions, impacts, but much of this past work has focused on negative health outcomes associated with child sexual abuse using non-nationally representative samples. This article used a nationally representative female sample to examine health conditions associated with any lifetime experience of rape. We also examined injury, health outcomes (e.g., fear, injury) resulting from any violence by a perpetrator of rape. About two in five rape victims (39.1\%) reported injury (e.g., bruises, vaginal tears),, 12.3\% reported a sexually transmitted disease as a result of the rape victimization. Approximately 71.3\% of rape victims (an estimated 16.4 million women) experienced some form of impact as a result of violence by a rape perpetrator. Among U.S. women, the adjusted odds of experiencing asthma, irritable bowel syndrome, frequent headaches, chronic pain, difficulty sleeping, activity limitations, poor physical or mental health,, use of special equipment (e.g., wheelchair) were significantly higher for lifetime rape victims compared with non-victims. This article fills gaps in our understanding of health impacts associated with rape of women, is the only nationally representative source of this information to our knowledge. Primary prevention efforts in youth that seek to prevent the first occurrence of rape, other forms of SV may be most effective for reducing the long-term health effects of this violence.

title: Prevalence of intimate partner reproductive coercion in the United States: Racial, ethnic differences
authors: Basile, Kathleen C, Smith, Sharon G, Liu, Yang, Miller, Elizabeth, Kresnow, Marcie-Jo
keywords: anything related to domestic violence; domestic violence; domestic violence, cultural contexts; sexual assault; sexuality
abstract: Reproductive coercion (RC) is a specific type of intimate partner violence (IPV). Although clinical studies have highlighted women's experiences of RC, we know little about its national prevalence, differences in prevalence by sex category, race/ethnicity. Data are from the National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey (NISVS), years 2010 to 2012. NISVS is an ongoing, nationally representative random-digit-dial telephone survey of the noninstitutionalized English- or Spanish-speaking U.S. adult population. This article reports the national lifetime, 12-month prevalence of two RC victimization measures,, proportions among IPV victims. T tests were used to examine differences in estimates across racial/ethnic groups. In the United States, 9.7\% of men, 8.4\% of women experienced any RC by an intimate partner during their lifetime. Men reported more commonly than women that a partner tried to get pregnant when the man did not want her to; women reported higher prevalence of partner condom refusal. Examination by race/ethnicity revealed that non-Hispanic (NH) Black women, men had significantly higher lifetime prevalence of both RC types than all other groups; in the last 12 months, NH Blacks had significantly higher prevalence across the board than NH Whites. Hispanics had significantly higher lifetime, 12-month prevalence of any RC, partner condom refusal than NH Whites. RC is at the intersection of two public health concerns-IPV, reproductive health. Documenting its prevalence, differences by sex, race/ethnicity may inform prevention efforts to reduce occurrence, negative health outcomes among specific populations.

title: Lifetime number of perpetrators, victim-offender relationship status per U.s. victim of intimate partner, sexual violence, or stalking
authors: Peterson, Cora, Liu, Yang, Merrick, Melissa, Basile, Kathleen C, Simon, Thomas R
keywords: intimate partner violence; sexual violence; stalking
abstract: The aim of this study was to describe the U.S. population-level prevalence of multiple perpetrator types (intimate partner, acquaintance, stranger, person of authority, or family member) per victim, to describe the prevalence of victim-offender relationship status combinations. Authors analyzed U.S. nationally representative data from noninstitutionalized adult respondents with self-reported lifetime exposure to intimate partner violence, sexual violence, or stalking in the 2012 National Intimate Partner, Sexual Violence Survey (NISVS). An estimated 142 million U.S. adults had some lifetime exposure to intimate partner violence, sexual violence, or stalking. An estimated 55 million victims (39\% of total victims) had more than one perpetrator type during their lifetimes. A significantly higher proportion of female victims reported more than one perpetrator type compared with male victims (49\% vs. 27\%). Among both female, male victims with >1 perpetrator type, the most prevalent victim-offender relationship status combinations all included an intimate partner perpetrator. Many victims of interpersonal violence are subject to multiple perpetrator types during their lifetimes. Prevention strategies that address polyvictimization, protect victims from additional perpetrators can have a substantial, beneficial societal impact. Research on victim experiences to inform prevention strategies is strengthened by comprehensively accounting for lifetime victimizations.

title: A university partnership for victim service professional development: Model standards for serving victims, survivors of crime
authors: DeHart, Dana
abstract: This paper describes processes, products of a partnership to promote professionalization of the field of victim services. The National Victim Assistance Standards Consortium was established by the federal Office for Victims of Crime in partnership with the University of South Carolina. The Consortium reached across geographic, philosophical,, disciplinary divides to forge a common ground in professional development, including a definition, mission for the field as well as three sets of model standards for serving victims, survivors. The project included a review of literature on victim services, town hall meetings across the country,, layered review, refinement of standards by approximately 50 professionals working at the local, state,, national levels. The online document, Achieving Excellence: Model Standards for Serving Victims \& Survivors of Crime, will provide standards for promoting competence, ethical integrity as well as quality, consistency of service.

title: Assessing the relevance of statistics, crime analysis courses for working crime analysts
authors: Kringen, Jonathan Allen, Sedelmaier, Christopher M, Elink-Schuurman-Laura, Kristin D
abstract: Crime analysts study criminal activity, police function to improve performance. Analysts inform operations, aid resource allocation,, evaluate programs. These tasks require high levels of statistical literacy. Given that most analysts are college-educated civilians, college coursework in statistics and/or crime analysis may represent the foundational knowledgebase within the profession. However, little research has attempted to determine if coursework teaches the skills needed by analysts. Underlying this issue is a limited understanding about what technical skills crime analysts regularly use. Analyzing parallel surveys of 98 criminal justice educators, 146 crime analysts, this study compares the skills taught in undergraduate-level statistics, crime analysis courses to those used by analysts. Comparisons are made between perceptions of the value of coursework. Results indicate discrepancies between the orientation of coursework, the needs of analysts which underscore differences in the perceived relevance of statistics education. Recommendations are discussed.

title: A preliminary analysis of the factors affecting satisfaction with the police practicum credit program in South Korea
authors: Cho, Joon Tag, Park, Hyeonho
abstract: Numerous studies have been conducted about criminal justice internship programs in western countries, but few have addressed similar types of programs conducted in Eastern countries. To fill this gap in the literature, this study preliminarily analyzed the factors affecting satisfaction with the police practicum credit program in South Korea using data collected from 208 participating students, police officers. The results showed that participants were generally satisfied with the program but had different perceptions about each program component. Focusing on the crucial elements affecting overall satisfaction with the program, the study examined the following factors: the curriculum; the period, practice time; the proportion of on-site practice; teaching material; credits;, police officers’ preparedness, attitudes, information offerings. Our results suggest that the curriculum, preparedness of the officers in charge were significant factors affecting the participants’ satisfaction. Based on the findings, implications for policy recommendations are discussed.

abstract: There has been increasing recognition in Australia of the potential for collaborative research relationships between police, academics. Despite significant improvements in partnership arrangements, research outcomes however, it would be na ve to suggest that the working relationship is always smooth. Drawing on the author's personal experiences, understanding of working with police, the article considers the views of both police, academics working together. It suggests that continuous communication, negotiation, understanding where the other party sits are crucial to productive working relationships.

title: What goes up must come down? 25 years of public trust in the police
authors: Bradford, Ben
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Public trust in the police is an almost ever-present feature of United Kingdom policy, political, indeed cultural debates,, this has been true right across the past quarter century. Concentrating on the population-level picture,, on England, Wales, in this article I outline what we know about changes in ‘trust, confidence’ over the past two decades or so,, make comparison with changes in other, closely associated, indicators. Why it might be that over this period trust in police first increased significantly,, then declined? Answers to this question implicate what might be termed the political economy of trust. Change in public trust may be due to a whole set of factors operating across multiple levels of policing, the society in which it takes place.

title: Predictors of the onset of sexual violence perpetration in adolescence, emerging adulthood
authors: Ybarra, Michele L, Petras, Hanno, Goodman, Kimberly L, Mitchell, Kimberly J
journal: Prevention science: the official journal of the Society for Prevention Research
keywords: Community sample; Longitudinal study; Onset; Sexual violence perpetration; Survival analysis
abstract: To identify factors in adolescence that predict the onset of sexual violence in adolescence, young adulthood. Data were analyzed from six survey waves of the longitudinal Growing up with Media Study (2008-2018) conducted in the USA. Participants were 778 youth 13-18 years old at baseline, who completed online surveys assessing sexual violence behaviors, predictors. Sexual violence perpetration behaviors included sexual assault, rape, attempted rape,, coercive sex. Only 2\% of females, 3\% of males reported their first sexual violence perpetration by age 14. In contrast, by age 18, 6\% of females, 12\% of males had perpetrated their first sexual violence. For both males, females, the rate of the onset seems to plateau by age 22. Predictors of the onset of sexually violent behavior for those who began perpetrating when they were 14-17 years old were largely similar to those who began perpetrating when they were 18-25 years old. Alcohol plus other substance use, aggressive, delinquent behavior, caregiver monitoring, behavior problems at school, externalizing peers, exposure to community violence,, exposure to violent media were all implicated. Early prevention-well before college, perhaps even before high school-is needed to have an impact on the onset of sexual violence perpetration, as most perpetrators of sexual violence will have acted for the first time by age 23. Several modifiable risk factors observed in adolescence could signal the opportunity for targeted prevention to reduce the odds of onset of sexual violence.

title: Co-existence patterns of social norms, positive defending intention among adolescents as school bullying bystanders
authors: Chen, Zhan-Jie, Yu, Jia-Ming, Liu, Fang, Wang, Jing-Xi, Zhen, Rui
keywords: adolescent; bystanders; defending intention; school bullying; social norms;324\_Bystander
abstract: School bullying occurs frequently in primary, secondary schools, which is a global problem, it often brings serious physical, mental harm to the victims. When school bullying occurs, there may be a large number of bystanders in addition to the bullies, victims. What actions bystanders take affects the progress of school bullying. Relevant studies indicate that social norms including how peers around them react (descriptive norms), how important adults such as teachers, parents demand (injunctive norms) play important roles in bystanders' action-taking, but limited studies have considered individual differences. Therefore, this study used a person-centered approach to explore the co-existence patterns of social norms, bystanders' defending intention to further understand their relations. We surveyed 1,384 junior high school students in China by self-report questionnaires,, they were asked to assess their defending intention when witnessing school bullying events under different contexts of social norms. Through latent profiles analysis, five co-existing patterns were identified: no norms-no defending group (4.8\%), parent norms-no defending group (3.6\%), weak norms-low defending group (24.3\%), teacher-peer norms-medium defending group (40.6\%), teacher-peer norms-high defending group (26.7\%). In four out of the five patterns, students' levels of defending intention were highly consistent with the levels of peer, teacher norms, but largely contradicted parent norms. This suggests that descriptive norms from peers, injunctive norms from teachers, other than those from parents are crucial for promoting bystanders' defending intention, which provides important enlightenment for school bullying prevention. These findings provide important enlightenment for the prevention, control of school bullying in the future.

title: Trust in the police, crime reporting: Reassessing assumptions in the context of violent crime in England, Wales
authors: Timukaite, Aiste, Buil-Gil, David
abstract: The reporting of crime to the police is crucial for an efficient functioning of the criminal justice system. It is widely argued that victims’ decision to contact the police is based on considerations of the anticipated costs, benefits of crime reporting. Scholars have previously suggested that victims’ attitudes towards the police may influence their perceptions of the costs, benefits associated with crime reporting. However, victims’ trust in the police as a multidimensional construct has not been empirically tested as a predictor of victims’ crime reporting to the police. This study uses Crime Survey for England, Wales data from 2017/2018 to 2019/2020 to explore the relationship between victims’ trust in police effectiveness, violent crime reporting behaviour. Furthermore, this study examines the influence of victim, situational characteristics on decisions to report victimisation to the police. Our analysis reveals that victims’ trust in police effectiveness does not predict their decision to disclose violent crime victimisation to the police. However, victims’ sex, age significantly influence reporting decisions. Moreover, our findings reveal that situational factors, specifically the presence of a weapon, injury to the victim, are important predictors of violent crime reporting.

title: Examining ransomware payment decision-making among small-, medium-sized enterprises
authors: Matthijsse, Sifra R, Moneva, Asier, van 't Hoff-de Goede, M Susanne, Leukfeldt, E Rutger
abstract: Ransomware is currently one of the most prominent cyberthreats for organizations. Small-, medium-sized enterprises are particularly vulnerable to ransomware victimization, more inclined toward paying the ransom. However, while a few studies have been conducted on victimization of ransomware, little is known about how small-, medium-sized enterprises respond to victimization, what factors contribute to the decision to pay the ransom. This study uses a survey with a vignette experiment conducted among 445 owners, managers of Dutch small-, medium-sized enterprises to gain more insight into the factors that are related to the decision to pay the ransom in the event of ransomware victimization. Findings show that the likelihood that the ransom is paid is low. While the affordability of the ransom demand seems unrelated to the likelihood of paying, being advised by a cybersecurity company to pay the ransom, not having a back-up significantly increases the likelihood of the ransom being paid. The findings provide insight into factors that make ransomware victims vulnerable to extortion. Furthermore, implications for how ransomware attacks can be mitigated are discussed.

title: Disseminating fraud awareness, prevention advice to older adults: perspectives on the most effective means of delivery
authors: Button, Mark, Shepherd, David, Hawkins, Chloe, Tapley, Jacki
abstract: AbstractRaising awareness to combat scams has become a central strategy of fraud/scam prevention. Using data from a wider evaluation of a targeted campaign to improve fraud prevention, awareness for older adults predominantly over 75, this paper offers findings on the most effective means of dissemination of anti-scam communications to this group. The paper draws upon almost 1000 questionnaire responses, qualitative data from older adults, as well as volunteers, workers involved in the project. The research finds many older adults have not received any fraud prevention or awareness communications in the prior six months, illustrating a gap in fraud prevention messaging reaching this group. The paper also shows that the preferred method of dissemination is one-to-one through friends, family, that is also the case for the most isolated. The paper offers some potential solutions to address these gaps, particularly for lonely older adults.

title: How health message framing, targets affect distancing during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Neumer, Anna, Schweizer, Theresa, Bogdanić, Vita, Boecker, Lea, Loschelder, David D
journal: Health psychology: official journal of the Division of Health Psychology, American Psychological Association
keywords: 316\_介入実験\_環境手がかり;05\_リハーサルを用いた行動変容手法;\_\_\_202401\_大津社会実験
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Maintaining safe physical distance is paramount to slowing the spread of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2)/coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), particularly indoors (e.g., while shopping). We used a health message intervention to motivate grocery store customers to engage in distancing behavior. METHOD: In an online experiment (N = 206), a field experiment (N = 268; preregistered on OSF), we used a 2 × 2 between-subjects design, manipulated health messages (a) as gain-framed (``to foster health'') versus loss-framed (``it could be deadly''), (b) as targeting different beneficiaries (customers themselves versus fellow citizens). In the field experiment, observers rated customers' distancing behavior during a random confederate encounter, a subsequent interview. We assessed customers' perceptions of risk, worry, perspective-taking,, state optimism as concurrent psychological processes to investigate customers' distancing behavior in correlational mediation analyses. RESULTS: Contrary to previous research, the intervention was more effective when pertaining to customers themselves than to their fellow citizens (Experiments 1-2). In addition, loss-framed messages were more effective than gain-framed ones (Experiment 2). The former behavioral effect was accompanied (and statistically mediated) by a concurrent psychological increase in customers' perceived risk, worry. CONCLUSIONS: Owing to their low cost, easy implementation, health messages constitute a promising means to promote physical distancing. Our results show that their effectiveness significantly depends on the framing, target of the health behavior. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2022 APA, all rights reserved).

title: Cybercrime Victimization : An examination of Individual, Situational level factors
authors: Ngo, Fawn T
abstract: Using a sample of college students, we apply the general theory of crime, the lifestyle/routine activities framework to assess the effects of individual, situational factors on seven types of cybercrime victimization. The results indicate that neither individual nor situational characteristics consistently impacted the likelihood of being victimized in cyberspace. Self-control was significantly related to only two of the seven types of cybercrime victimizations, although five of the coefficients in the routine activity models were significant, all but one of these significant effects were in the opposite direction to that expected from the theory. At the very least, it would appear that other theoretical frameworks should be appealed to in order to explain victimization in cyberspace.

title: Star wars: The empirics strike back
authors: Brodeur, Abel, Lé, Mathias, Sangnier, Marc, Zylberberg, Yanos
abstract: Using 50,000 tests published in the AER, JPE,, QJE, we identify a residual in the distribution of tests that cannot be explained solely by journals favoring rejection of the null hypothesis. We observe a two-humped camel shape with missing p-values between 0.25, 0.10 that can be retrieved just after the 0.05 threshold, represent 10–20 percent of marginally rejected tests. Our interpretation is that researchers inflate the value of just-rejected tests by choosing “significant” specifications. We propose a method to measure this residual, describe how it varies by article, author characteristics. (JEL A11, C13)

title: Fear, phoning: Telephones, fraud,, older adults in the UK
authors: Button, Mark, Shepherd, David, Hawkins, Chloe, Tapley, Jacki
abstract: This study explores the experiences of attempted frauds, victimisation which use largely telephone-based means of communication on predominantly over 75s in the United Kingdom. Using a postal survey targeted at the clients of a charity working mostly with this age group, two surveys were conducted during the 18-month life of the project, securing almost 2,000 responses, which sought to explore their experience of fraud as part of a wider evaluation of a fraud prevention initiative. The surveys were supported by 18 interviews with clients, 7 interviews with the charity co-ordinator, volunteers. The research found higher rates of victimisation than the norm for this group, combined with a large number of attempted frauds predominantly via the telephone, with 20\% of respondents experiencing at least weekly attempts. The research highlights the first significant evidence of the fears, concerns,, anxieties among a minority of this group of frauds/scams, their impact on their daily lives. The paper also offers insights into telephone fraud, a typology of this crime.

title: Personal theories of police officers about authority
authors: Weber, Matthias, Schophaus, Malte
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Police authority supposedly guides the actions of police officers. This article reconstructs personal theories on the authority of police by means of qualitative interviews with German police officers, police candidates. These personal theories are divided into four self-schemata composed of: dealing effectively, preferably with possible problems occurring with police work; different normative orders that define the relationship between the police, civil society; a reference to desirable personality traits for police officers;, symbolic representations of police authority. Such self-schemata influence police interactions with citizens, disclose a diversity of police ideas about authority. The different self-schemata of authority seem to originate from different backgrounds such as practical experience of policing, formal education in police colleges, compliance with commonly accepted societal norms like fairness, non-violence, respect, personal convictions. It is discussed how these self-schemata can be constructively reflected in formal police education in Germany. This article contributes to a nuanced understanding of police authority, how this might be integrated into training. Further research should investigate how these schemata can be integrated into a dynamic model, carry out a comparative, intercultural analysis of these personal theories.

title: Violence against women, girls in Dorset, United Kingdom: an epidemiological study of perpetrators, locations based on police records
authors: Pearcey, Jessica, Ariel, Barak, Harinam, Vincent, Assaraf, Noy
abstract: AbstractViolence against women, girls (VAWG) continues to be a prevalent phenomenon, yet where it is more likely to occur in the public domain, how offenders assault victims remain understudied areas of interest. This analysis is based on police records on VAWG from Dorset, United Kingdom (UK), using descriptive, spatial statistical methods alongside k-means longitudinal clustering. The spatial analysis uses hexagonal tessellations with a maximum area of 100 m² to identify VAWG hotspots. Findings reveal a significant concentration of public-place VAWG harm in a few spots: half of the reported VAWG occurred within just 2.6\% of these hexagons. The study also illustrates a consistent trend in VAWG occurrences, with areas categorised as low, moderate,, high in VAWG counts, measured harm remaining constant over time. However, offenders responsible for the majority of counts, harm are not predominantly active in the hotspots with the highest counts, harm, which suggests a stochastic modus operandi rather than a fixation on specific locations. The identified VAWG hotspots, patterns in offender behaviour provide valuable insights for implementing targeted crime management strategies,, underscore the need to integrate factors like frequency, recentness, degree of harm,, geographical location to assess, address VAWG risks effectively.

title: Opening the black box of police operations, crime during the COVID-19 pandemic
authors: Koper, Christopher S, Lum, Cynthia, Wu, Xiaoyun, Khatchatourian, Hailey
abstract: This paper documents how a large suburban police department in the United States responded to the COVID-19 pandemic, assesses whether their responses had discernible impacts on crime, disorder. We used time series forecasting, regression approaches with more than six years of data to examine whether calls for police service rose or fell significantly during the pandemic’s first year in response to shifts in police activity (including remote responses to calls, reductions in proactive, community policing,, other shifts in patrol, investigative work), other important events (like government lockdowns, social protests). Call volumes for violent, property,, disorder incidents generally remained within or below normal pre-COVID ranges during the pandemic’s first year, but violence, disorder calls were significantly higher than expected when adjusted for reduced levels of public activity during this time. However, these patterns were not clearly related to reductions in proactive police work or other operational changes by the police during the pandemic. This study provides a more detailed, explicit assessment of policing during the COVID-19 pandemic than has most prior research,, it highlights the need for deeper localized studies of criminal justice policies, operations during COVID-19 to guide practitioners, policymakers in responding to future public health crises.

title: Procedural justice perceptions, legitimacy beliefs,, compliance with the law: a meta-analysis
authors: Walters, Glenn D, Bolger, P Colin
abstract: Objectives The purpose of this study was to compare procedural justice, legitimacy as correlates, predictors of compliance with the law. Methods A literature review produced 64 studies, 95 samples,, 196 effect sizes from studies published or conducted sometime between 1990, February 2018 in which procedural justice was correlated with legitimacy and/or compliance, or legitimacy was correlated with compliance. Fifty samples included all 3 correlations, 3 samples included 2 correlations,, the remaining 42 samples included a single correlation. Two random effects meta-analyses were performed. Results Pooled univariate effects for all three correlations achieved significance. Although there was a high degree of heterogeneity in the results, modest evidence of publication bias in one of the subsamples, sensitivity testing indicated that no one study had an undue influence over the results. Using a generalized least squares (GLS) multivariate approach, a path analysis revealed a significant a path from procedural justice to legitimacy, a significant b path from legitimacy to compliance,, a significant c’ path from procedural justice to compliance, but only the a, b paths were significant when the analysis was restricted to studies with longitudinal data. Conclusions The current findings suggest that legitimacy beliefs are instrumental in promoting compliance with the law, that while procedural justice perceptions also appear to predict compliance, the effect was relatively weak in this meta-analysis, could not be reliably established in longitudinal datasets.

title: The impact of hot spots policing on collective efficacy: Findings from a randomized field trial
authors: Rinehart Kochel, Tammy, Weisburd, David
abstract: In disadvantaged neighborhoods, prior research has found reduced social cohesion, less willingness among residents to address disruptive behaviors, violations of social norms. This deficiency is commonly associated with higher levels of disorder, crime. Therefore, recent scholarship has begun to consider whether police can help foster collective efficacy, especially in places struggling with serious crime problems. Early results are somewhat mixed. Yet the cooperation hypothesis asserts that when neighborhood residents see police as a more viable, reliable resource, residents will be emboldened to exert informal social control to address problems. Over the last two decades, hot spots policing has been recognized as an effective method to reduce crime. At the same time, there have been few rigorous studies of whether this approach impacts collective efficacy at hot spots. To investigate this question, we conducted an experiment in 71 crime hot spots, comparing a collaborative problem solving versus a directed patrol (police presence) approach versus standard policing practices. Over time, a substantial increase in police presence did appear to promote modest improvements in collective efficacy. We attribute this finding to the cooperation hypothesis.

title: The purposes, meanings of surveillance: A case study in a shopping mall in Ankara, Turkey
authors: Akinci, Guliz Mugan
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Security management; Shopping centers; Society; Human rights; Security personnel; Turkey;332\_Retail;Security Journal
abstract: The aim of surveillance in the mall environment is to create a safe, secure place for customers, but it may hence work as an exclusionary tool for some. Armada, a shopping mall in Ankara, was chosen as the site for this research, where the purposes, impacts of surveillance related to safety, exclusion were analyzed from the points of view of mall users, staff. Qualitative interviews were conducted with 43 mall users, seven mall personnel. The results indicated that most of the users, staff perceived surveillance in the mall in relation to the security, safety, comfort of potential customers. Exclusion was considered as a probable, unavoidable outcome of surveillance, not challenged by the users. This finding raises the question of surveillance as a mechanism of intolerance against difference, variety in urban life.

title: Street prostitution zones, crime
authors: Bisschop, Paul, Kastoryano, Stephen, van der Klaauw, Bas
abstract: This paper studies the effects of legal street prostitution zones on registered, perceived crime. We exploit a unique setting in the Netherlands where these tippelzones were opened in nine cities under different regulation systems. Our difference-in-difference analysis of 25 Dutch cities between 1994–2011 shows that opening a tippelzone decreases registered sexual abuse, rape by about 30–40 percent in the first two years. For cities which enforced licensing in tippelzones, we also find reductions in drug-related crime, long-term effects on sexual assaults. Effects on perceived drug nuisance depend on the regulation system, the proximity of respondents to the tippelzone. (JEL J16, J47, K42)

title: What men say when apprehended for kerb crawling: A model of prostitutes clients' talk1
authors: Brooks-Gordon, Belinda, Gelsthorpe, Loraine
abstract: Prostitution research has traditionally focused on women engaged in sex work while the male clients have been so hidden that their characteristics, motives have been difficult for researchers to study. A general confusion exists in parliamentary debates, media,, policy, as to who the clients of prostitutes are,, their purpose for the visit (Carpenter, 2000). Despite the lack of theoretically informed debate about the role of the consumer in the buying, selling of sex, recent policy, legislation in England has continued to criminalize the male customer of on-street sexual practices. This paper presents data from 518 cases in which men were stopped for street soliciting (or ‘kerb crawling’),, contributes to the ongoing prostitution/policing debate by providing an analysis of the language these men use to justify their actions when stopped by the police for soliciting women. From the analysis of such attributional accounts, a new theoretical model of client behaviour is presented. Discussion focuses upon the utility of such a model to further our understanding of prostitutes clients' behaviour, their contact with law enforcement,, their subjective reasons for seeking commercial sex.
