title: Violent, nonviolent crimes against sex workers: The influence of the sex market on reporting practices in the United Kingdom
authors: Connelly, Laura, Kamerāde, Daiga, Sanders, Teela
keywords: policing; reported victimization; sex work; violence;336\_STP
abstract: Previous research has shown that sex workers experience extremely high rates of victimization but are often reluctant to report their experiences to the police. This article explores how the markets in which sex workers operate in the United Kingdom impact upon the violent, nonviolent crimes they report to a national support organization, their willingness to report victimization to the police. We use a secondary quantitative data analysis of 2,056 crime reports submitted to the U.K. National Ugly Mugs (NUM) scheme between 2012, 2016. The findings indicate that although violence is the most common crime type reported to NUM, sex workers operating in different markets report varying relative proportions of different types of victimization. We also argue that there is some variation in the level of willingness to share reports with the police across the different sex markets, even when the types of crime, presence of violence,, other variables are taken into account. Our finding that street sex workers are most likely to report victimization directly to the police challenges previously held assumptions that criminalization is the key factor preventing sex workers from engaging with the police.

title: Vulnerability, involvement in drug use, sex work: (649562007-001)
authors: Cusick, Linda, Martin, Anthea, May, Tiggey
abstract: Recent academic, policy, campaign literature on commercial sex accepts the diff e re n c e between adult, child involvement in prostitution. The Department of Health (2000) Safeguarding children involved in prostitution d i rects the police to treat children (aged under 18) involved in prostitution as victims of abuse. There is also a long-standing debate about the order of involvement in drug use, sex work with some re s e a rch suggesting that, amongst younger sex workers, drug use more frequently pre-dates sex work. A team of re s e a rchers from Imperial College, South Bank University carried out this study between April 2001, October 2002. They examined vulnerability amongst young prostitutes, the relationship between sex work, drug use,, opportunities for leaving sex work, giving up drug use.

title: ‘Trapping’ in drug use, sex work careers
authors: Cusick, Linda, Hickman, Matthew
abstract: This paper examines the reinforcement of sex work, drug use. Data from 92 survey, in-depth interviews were analysed to examine associations between vulnerabilities, ‘trapping’: mutually reinforcing sex work, problematic drug use. Three-quarters of participants had used drugs, half had sold sex before 18. Half had been in care, half had been homeless. One in 5 (21\%) had run away or left home before 16, 80\% had been convicted for acquisitive offences. Nevertheless, these experiences did not explain trapping.There were strong associations between being trapped, convictions (81\%);, being trapped, outdoor/drift sex work (92\%). After adjustment for the other vulnerabilities in the logistic regression only outdoor/drift sex work remained significant: with sex workers involved in outdoor/drift sex-work having an adjusted odds ratio of over 7 (95\% c.i. 1.7–28.3) of being trapped. Moreover, since the sample over-represents the extent of problematic drug use amongst indoor sex workers the study underestimates differences in trapping potential between sex markets. We conclude that outdoor/drift sex markets may reinforce vulnerability, sex work, problematic drug use. Interventions are recommended to disentangle sex, drugs markets,, reduce the sex industry's potential for exploitation, abuse.

title: The impact of observer characteristics on blame assessments of prostituted female youth
authors: Franklin, Cortney A, Menaker, Tasha A
abstract: Currently, two studies have examined perceptions of prostituted youth, factors associated with negative assessments. The male-, majority-race nature of criminal justice agencies, research on rape victim culpability attributions underscores the importance of addressing perceptions of this population as paramount to effective intervention. This research used 357 student survey responses to investigate observer characteristics correlated with blameworthiness assessments. Findings demonstrated sexist attitudes, observer race correlated with blameworthiness directed toward prostituted youth with no victimization history disclosure,, prostitution myth adherence, observer childhood abuse correlated with blameworthiness directed toward prostituted youth whose victimization history was disclosed. Research, policy implications are discussed.

title: Rationalizing Online Romance Fraud: In the Eyes of the Offender
authors: Barnor, Barnor Jonathan Nii, Boateng, Richard, Kolog, Emmanuel Awuni, Afful-Dadzie, Anthony
abstract: This study seeks to understand romance scam from the offenders' perspective, how they rationalize their motivations, opportunities, abilities towards the commission of the crime. To this end, we adopt the Motivation-Opportunity-Ability framework, the Rationalization dimension of the Fraud Triangle Theory. The study employed a qualitative methodological approach to analyze the opportunities presented by emerging technologies to cyber fraudsters amid socio-economic drivers. One is the interplay of various socio-economic factors being a major driving force behind the commission of cybercrime. These include peer recruitment, training, poverty, unemployment, low level of education, low income. The uniqueness of this study stems from the fact that it deviates from previous studies to investigate cybercrime from the perspective of the perpetrators. Again, this study is arguably one of the first to put all three dimensions of the MOA framework, the rationalization dimension of the Fraud Triangle to study romance scammers' behaviors.

title: Do prostitution, social vulnerability go hand in hand? Examining the association between social background, prostitution using register data
authors: Henriksen, Theresa Dyrvig
abstract: This article provides new knowledge on the social background of women involved in indoor prostitution by integrating a novel data source in terms of administrative register data. Questions concerning dynamics of entry, whether sex-sellers have a more socially marginalised position than others have long been debated in research. Based on register data on 1128 female sex-sellers, the article takes an important step towards answering such questions by analysing, comparing the social background of sex-sellers, of a matched sample of Danish women (n = 73,320). The study includes descriptive insights into a number of indicators, including demographics, out-of-home placement, mental health problems, drug problems, incarceration, educational attainment, labour market attachment. Multivariate regression models are used to examine potential predictors of involvement in prostitution. The findings show that indoor sex-sellers often come from a socially marginalised background, experience multiple social vulnerabilities in both childhood, adulthood. Furthermore, the study shows strong associations between indicators of social vulnerability, selling sex. Especially indicators of an unstable childhood environment (e.g. out-of-home placements, mothers’ incarceration), indicators of social marginalisation in adulthood (e.g. incarceration, mental health problems) have proven to have a strong association with involvement in prostitution as an adult.

title: The online dating romance scam: causes, consequences of victimhood
authors: Buchanan, Tom, Whitty, Monica T
abstract: The online dating romance scam is a relatively new, under-reported international crime targeting users of online dating sites. It has serious financial, emotional consequences, affecting hundreds of thousands of people. However, little if anything is known about psychological characteristics that may put people at risk of romance scam victimization, or influence how they react to it. Online daters (N=853), participants recruited from a victim support site (N=397) completed a battery of online questionnaires. High scores on the romantic belief of Idealization were associated with likelihood of being a romance scam victim. Victims experienced significant emotional distress as well as financial losses. Even respondents who reported being fooled by scammers, but who had not lost any money, reported significant distress. Level of emotional distress was associated with high Neuroticism,, also with high Loneliness, low Openness to Experience among victims not losing money. The findings have implications for the feasibility of crime-prevention measures based on victim characteristics,, for treatment of victims by law enforcement, other stakeholders.

title: Meeting you was a fake: investigating the increase in romance fraud during COVID-19
authors: Buil-Gil, David, Zeng, Yongyu
abstract: Purpose Romance fraud refers to situations where an individual is deceived for financial gain by someone with whom the victim perceives to be in a romantic relationship. With the increase in internet use, the growth in loneliness, the increasing engagement in online dating sites during COVID-19, opportunities for romance fraud may have suffered an important increase. This paper aims to analyse changes in romance fraud, loneliness, internet use during the pandemic. Design/methodology/approach Data about romance fraud reported to the police in the UK,, survey data recorded by the Understanding Society longitudinal survey, are used to address our research questions. Auto regressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) modelling is used to analyse whether temporal changes observed are an effect of social changes associated with lockdown, stay-at-home orders. Findings The analysis shows that cyber-enabled romance fraud experienced a large increase after April 2020, which is greatly above any expected crime variation considering known pre-COVID trends. The increase in romance fraud was more abrupt among young adults than older persons. The results also indicate that only young adults experienced a significant increase in loneliness, while older adults reported a large increase in internet use during COVID. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is a first-of-its-kind paper analysing the effect of rapid social changes on a growing type of cyber-enabled fraud. It is likely that the growth in romance fraud during COVID is due to a combined effect of an increase in internet use, growing loneliness rates experienced by many people during the pandemic.

title: Profiling consumers who reported mass marketing scams: demographic characteristics, emotional sentiments associated with victimization
authors: DeLiema, Marguerite, Witt, Paul
abstract: AbstractWe examine the characteristics of consumers who reported scams to the U.S. Federal Trade Commission. We assess how consumers vary demographically across six scam types,, how the overall emotional sentiment of a consumer’s complaint (positive, negative, neutral/mixed) relates to reporting victimization versus attempted fraud (no losses). For romance, tech support,, prize, sweepstakes,, lottery scams, more older than young, middle-aged adults reported victimization. Across all scam types, consumers classified as Black, Hispanic,, Asian/Asian Pacific Islander were more likely than non-Hispanic white consumers to report victimization than attempted fraud. Relative to complaints categorized as emotionally neutral or mixed, we find that emotionally positive complaints, emotionally negative complaints were significantly associated with victimization, but that these relationships differed by scam type. This study helps identify which consumer groups are affected by specific scams, the association between emotion, victimization.

title: A crime script analysis of the Madoff Investment Scheme
authors: Hardy, John, Bell, Peter, Allan, Douglas
abstract: The Madoff Investment Scheme was a long-term, large-scale fraud which involved both an affinity fraud, a Ponzi scheme. Numerous studies have examined financial, legal aspects of the case, but relatively few have explored the case from a criminological perspective. This study applies crime script analysis (CSA) to the Madoff case in order to conceptualise the procedural elements of complex fraud offences, to identify crime prevention opportunities for investigators, regulatory bodies. CSA identifies 12 steps in the offence, occurring in three phases which create a relationship between earlier, later victims, with earlier victims providing credibility to the scheme, later victims generating the resources to sustain it. The study finds that crime prevention techniques which harden targets, extend guardianship could reduce criminal opportunities for offenders, techniques which strengthen formal surveillance, assist natural surveillance could control the capabilities required to perpetrate similar offences.

title: ‘Should’ve known better’: Using Lerner’s Belief in a Just World to understand how the Fraud Justice Network observe victims of online romance, investment frauds
authors: Nataraj-Hansen, Shalini
abstract: This article explores the application of Lerner’s Belief in a Just World (BJW) to online fraud. BJW finds that people tend to blame victims when their sense of justice is threatened, if there is little or no chance of obtaining compensation or justice for the victim. Specifically, BJW suggests that when victims are perceived as acting with agency,, have little chance of compensation, they are blamed for their crime. Online fraud victims are blamed by family, friends, justice agencies,, themselves, for their victimisation. Little is known about why the Fraud Justice Network (FJN), which comprises the multitude of agencies that aim to combat online fraud, blames victims. This article begins to address this gap by presenting findings of qualitative interviews with 14 FJN representatives, using thematic analysis. Three significant themes emerge about victims: ‘agency’, ‘gullibility, compensation’,, ‘deservedness of justice’. This study found that (a) victims are seen as behaviourally responsible, (b) agency is blameworthy,, (c) victims deserve justice. The study also finds evidence of BJW thinking within the FJN. Findings can inform future organisational policies on how victims of online fraud can be more effectively managed, supported, including by financial institutions or law enforcement agencies.

title: It happened again: Differences between single, repeat/poly-victimization among financial fraud victims
authors: Snyder, Jamie A, Golladay, Katelyn A
journal: Journal of White Collar, Corporate Crime
abstract: An increasing number of studies have focused on fraud victimization. However, fewer studies have specifically focused on financial fraud, a unique form of fraud that relies on victim participation. Using the Supplemental Fraud Survey (SFS), the prevalence, differences between single, repeat/poly-victims of financial fraud were examined utilizing state dependence, risk heterogeneity variables to identify potential differences. Overall, some support for state dependence was found, while less support was found for risk heterogeneity. Reporting the victimization to a family member, having a higher income reduced the risk of becoming a repeat/poly-victim, while identifying as a victim, having a higher total monetary loss were associated with increased risk. Implications for policy, theory,, prevention are discussed.

title: Language, psychology,, new new media: The hyperpersonal model of mediated communication at twenty-five years
authors: Walther, Joseph B, Whitty, Monica T
abstract: Research on the hyperpersonal model originally described how the substitution of language for nonverbal cues, necessitated by text-based computer-mediated communication systems, transforms users’ reception, self-presentation, composition,, reciprocal reinforcement of messages in ways that create socially desirable relationships online. This article reviews the model after 25 years. It explicates the original model, mentions a sample of illustrative findings. It reflects on the state of internet diffusion, research traditions in the 1990s that affected the model’s original focus,, how these conditions have changed. It enumerates contexts that continue to meet the model’s original boundary assumptions,, some boundary expansions. It explores ways in which the model’s principles extend into contemporary multi-modal social media. It illustrates the evolutionary applicability of the model through cases of deceptive online romances, including contemporary online romance scams. It concludes by suggesting future research examining how many contemporary social media performances, responses comport with, illustrate the model’s tenets, at scale.

title: Policing advance fee fraud (AFF): Experiences of fraud detectives using a victim-focused approach
authors: Webster, Julianne, Drew, Jacqueline M
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Advance fee fraud (AFF) involves an offender using deceit to obtain a financial gain from the victim. The victim believes that by forwarding a sum of money, there will be a future ‘pay-off’. The most commonly witnessed forms of AFF perpetrated via the Internet include classic ‘Nigerian’ or ‘419’ scams, investment fraud, romance fraud. Because of the largely transnational nature of AFF offending, where the victim, offender typically reside in different parts of the world, police are adapting their traditional, reactive approaches to more innovative strategies to combat this crime more effectively. This article utilises a qualitative, semi-structured interview design to explore the experiences of police detectives involved in the implementation of an early intervention model with victims of AFF. The study highlights the challenges involved in developing effective police strategies to proactively reduce the duration, severity of this type of financial victimisation.

title: Cryptocurrency Ponzi schemes, their modus operandi in South Korea
authors: Choi, Seoung Won, Lee, Julak, Lee, Sang-Hak
abstract: The surge of interest in digital currencies has led to a corresponding global increase in Ponzi schemes associated with cryptocurrencies. Scammers of cryptocurrency Ponzi schemes often target older adults who are cash-rich, have limited knowledge of digital assets. Therefore, to reduce the number of victims, it is imperative to increase the understanding of the crime itself. However, there remains a paucity of scholarly exploration focused on the criminal mechanisms underpinning such schemes, the strategic decision-making process of the perpetrators. This study seeks to address this gap in the literature, enhance the current understanding of cryptocurrency-based Ponzi schemes through an examination of their operational tactics. The methodology employed in this study distinguishes the progression of these schemes into two stages: the pre-crime phase, the criminal event phase, each scripted for further clarity, yielding three scripts for the former, eleven for the latter. Based on these parsed narratives, this research proposes several policy strategies aimed at curtailing the prevalence of cryptocurrency Ponzi schemes.

title: Self, desired partner descriptions in the online romance scam: a linguistic analysis of scammer, general user profiles on online dating portals
authors: Lee, Kam-Fong, Chan, Mei Yuit, Mohamad Ali, Afida
abstract: The online romance scam is a cybercrime that has resulted in substantial impact on victims, both psychologically, financially. The display of a personal advertisement by scammers on online dating websites in the form of the user profile is often the first step in the scam strategy to attract potential victims. This study examined differences in the use of language in self-, desired partner-description found in both the scammer profiles, a set of general user profiles on online dating websites. Using a corpus-based methodology, 500 user profiles identified as having fraudulent characteristics were compared with the same number of user profiles downloaded from five popular dating portals. Words that are statistically different in their frequencies of occurrence in the two sets of data were generated using a corpus analysis software, then categorized based on semantic, contextual criteria. The analysis uncovered linguistic features that are distinctive of the scammer profiles, revealing strategies used by online scammers in constructing, engaging a certain type of victim, by intensively invoking love, romance, commitment,, conjuring hope of a future as a couple through pertinent use of lexical, function words. Implications of the study include its contribution to the understanding, identification of the linguistic indicators of romance fraud user profiles which are important in efforts to raise public awareness, for future development of computerized scam detection tools.

title: Understanding romance scammers through the lens of their victims: Qualitative modeling of risk, protective factors in the online context
authors: Wang, Fangzhou, Topalli, Volkan

title: Resilience in sophisticated financial crime networks: a social network analysis of the Madoff Investment Scheme
authors: Hardy, John, Bell, Peter
abstract: Despite numerous investigations, studies, the resilience of Madoff’s scheme from at least the 1970s until its collapse in 2008 is poorly understood. This study applies social network analysis (SNA) to the Madoff Investment Scheme in order to identify key factors which support resilience in networks that are engaged in a sophisticated criminal enterprise. The SNA identified four clusters of individuals who performed vital functions within the network: a core leadership group, a compliance group, a capital group, a facilitators group. The study then examined the network’s response to exogenous, endogenous shocks, finding that the Madoff network had been resilient to both exogenous shocks, such as Securities, Exchange Commission examinations,, endogenous shocks, such as significant investor withdrawals, prior to its collapse in 2008. These findings suggest that monitoring network responses to exogenous, endogenous shocks could assist investigators in identifying Ponzi schemes in the future.

title: Online romance scams, victimhood
authors: Sorell, Tom, Whitty, Monica
abstract: Online romance scams defraud dating website users of large amounts of money, inflict serious psychological harm. Victims of these scams often blame themselves for their losses, are blamed by others. We consider whether victims actually do share responsibility with the scammer for their losses. Three sorts of cases are particularly relevant: (i) where there are relatively many abortive meetings, even more fruitless money transfers in a single scam; (ii) where someone is a repeat scam victim;, (iii) where the victim has been warned by authorities that they are currently a victim of a scam, pay anyway. We argue that responsibility sometimes is shared, but that losses can be out of proportion to imprudence. Scam victims sometimes violate epistemic norms, but in ways that are peculiar to romantic attachment. The paper combines the methods of qualitative psychological research on scam victims, analytic philosophy (Research for this paper was supported by Grant EP/N028112/1 from the UK Engineering, Physical Sciences Research Council).

title: The online romance scam: A complex two-layer scam
authors: Kopp, Christian, Sillitoe, J, Gondal, I, Layton, R
keywords: Online Romance scam; personal love story; Transtheoretical Model;240800\_Toroma;340\_Frauds;Romance
abstract: Online Romance scams are very successful unethical practices which cause considerable financial, emotional damage to their victims. This paper argues that the success of this scam technique is based on a strategy, similar to that in the Nigerian Letter scam, in which scammers invoke strong emotions in the recipients. We reflected on the notion that strong emotions play an important role in the development of normal romantic relationships,, these emotions are related to personal experiences of the individual which are accumulated in so-called ‘personal love stories’. The personal love story is the individual’s view of the idealized perfect relationship,, as such it impacts on the selection of a partner in the initiation stages of a partnership,, endures through the development of the relationship until its eventual termination. Personal love stories are important for the success of a relationship,, we assert in this paper that these love stories play an important role in the development of romance scam relationships, support the scammer’s eventual demand for financial funds from the victim. This paper presents a theory which attempts to explain the success of romance scams as a ‘two-layer scam’, related first to establishing a faked relationship by addressing strong personal romantic emotions,, second to building spurious reasons to request significant monetary payments.

title: The scammers persuasive techniques model: Development of a stage model to explain the online dating romance scam
authors: Whitty, M T
abstract: This study examined the persuasive techniques employed by criminals in the online dating romance scam. Twenty participants were interviewed, including financial, non-financial victims. The paper first examines errors in decision making, finds victims make similar errors compared with victims of other mass marketing frauds. It is also proposes that the near-win phenomenon is useful in explaining why individuals remain in the scam, why some become re-victimized. A model called the Scammers Persuasive Technique Model is developed to highlight the processes involved in the scam. It provides a description of the victim, highlights how criminals groom victims prior to any financial requests. The various stages that follow to keep the victim involved in the scam are highlighted.

title: The online dating romance scam: The psychological impact on victims – both financial, non-financial
authors: Whitty, Monica T, Buchanan, Tom
journal: Criminology \& criminal justice: the international journal of policy, practice
abstract: This article examines the psychological impact of the online dating romance scam. Unlike other mass-marketing fraud victims, these victims experienced a ‘double hit’ of the scam: a financial loss, the loss of a relationship. For most, the loss of the relationship was more upsetting than their financial losses (many described the loss of the relationship as a ‘death’). Some described their experience as traumatic, all were affected negatively by the crime. Most victims had not found ways to cope given the lack of understanding from family, friends. Denial (e.g. not accepting the scam was real or not being able to separate the fake identity with the criminal) was identified as an ineffective means of coping, leaving the victim vulnerable to a second wave of the scam. Suggestions are made as to how to change policy with regards to law enforcement to deal with this crime.

title: Risky facilities, physical site features,, comparing crime between urban parks
authors: Spencer, M Dylan, Schnell, Cory
abstract: There is much interdisciplinary research on the relationship between urban parks, crime but very little understanding of why some parks experience more crime compared to other parks. This study integrates ecological perspectives to examine crimes reported to the police during the COVID-19 pandemic. We use open data sources to observe the environmental context, physical site features of 110 parks in Charleston, SC. Our findings suggest site features of parks (e.g., playgrounds, restrooms) have a cumulative effect on crime. Both physical, social environmental variables influence why some parks become “risky facilities.” As city planners embrace greening, other climate-friendly solutions to transform urban communities, research needs to further assess the impact of these policies on crime.

title: Identifying the spatial patterns, environmental predictors of card skimming at gas stations: a remote systematic social observation of Google Street View imagery
authors: Sundquist, Hannah, Connealy, Nathan T, Hart, Timothy C, Toohy, Kayla
abstract: An increased reliance on payment system technologies globally has led to the proliferation of card skimming as an unintended consequence. Moreover, skimming prevention has also proved challenging, particularly at lesser supervised public places like gas stations. The current study aims to determine if there are identifiable spatial patterns or environmental characteristics that predict skimming at gas stations. Density analyses, a remote systematic social observation (SSO) of Google Street View imagery were used to assess the environmental contexts associated with high skimming gas stations compared to controls. Results indicate place management features related to increased visibility, lines of sight significantly predict skimming risk. Policy, practice implications are discussed, as well as relevant applications to environmental criminology approaches explaining crime occurrence at the micro-level.

title: The journey-to-crime buffer zone: Measurement issues, methodological challenges
authors: Rossmo, D Kim, Wheeler, Andrew P
keywords: Buffer zone; Crime trips; Distance decay; Environmental criminology; Journey to crime;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose The journey to crime is well-researched in criminology. Fundamental to many of these studies is the offending probability by distance function, a distribution comprised of two key components – distance decay, the buffer zone. However, it is difficult to measure this relationship accurately because of intensive data requirements. Here, we explore this challenge in detail, quantify data requirements. Methods We define, describe the buffer zone, outline two proposed explanations. Using this framework, four critical research considerations that avoid the ecological fallacy are identified,, a testing procedure proposed. Finally, we conduct simulation analyses to establish minimum data requirements. Results We conclude 50 or more observations are needed to reliably determine the shape of an offender's travel distribution, a number much higher than used in previous studies. Two empirical case studies of prolific predatory offenders support these findings. Conclusion Understanding crime journeys is relevant for both theory, practice. Crime travel is central to routine activity, crime pattern theories,, a critical factor in offender decision-making, target choice, spatial displacement, crime scripts, geographic profiling, crime prevention,, risk assessments. The relationship between distance, offending probability must be accurately measured to be properly understood.

title: Crime radiation theory: the co-production of crime patterns through opportunity creation, exploitation
authors: Linning, Shannon J, Bowers, Kate, Eck, John E
abstract: AbstractConsiderable research shows that crime is concentrated at a few proprietary places: addresses, facilities. Emerging research suggests that proprietary places may radiate crime: activities at a place increase the risk of crime in the area around it. Weaknesses in the research create uncertainty about radiation, so we need more rigorous research. To conduct this research, we need a theory of crime radiation that operates at two spatial levels: the proprietary place, the area. This paper describes such a theory. Our theory states that crime radiation stems from the interaction between place management decisions at the place, offenders searching for opportunities in the area. Place managers create crime opportunities inside, outside their places. Offenders exploit place managers’ creations by deliberately searching for opportunities or by chancing upon the opportunities. The ways place managers, offenders interact gives rise to three types of crime radiation: hot dot, veiled dot,, cold dot. Finally, we propose questions crime scientists should answer to better understand crime radiation.

title: From mobility to crime: Collective patterns of human mobility, gun violence in Baltimore City
authors: Situ, Xinyi
keywords: Hotspot; Violence; Mobility; Population; Firearm;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose: In this research, I investigated the link between collective mobility patterns—specifically inward population flow, residential mobility—and changes in reported gun violence incidents in Baltimore City. I also examined whether this relationship differs among various types of gun violence. Furthermore, I explored the potential moderating influence of collective mobility patterns on the relationship between neighborhood hotspot coverage, occurrences of gun violence. Methods: The data were sourced from a blend of mobile device location data, Part 1 crime data from the Baltimore Police Department, the American Community Survey,, the zoning map of Baltimore. I used Poisson regression with Moran Eigenvector Spatial Filtering (MESF) for the analysis. Results: Inward population flow consistently exhibited a positive relationship with gun violence regardless of its subtype, whereas residential mobility demonstrated significant influence primarily on firearm-related robbery incidents. Moderation analysis indicated that depending on the type of gun violence being assessed, either inward population flow or residential mobility could attenuate its association with neighborhoods' crime hotspot coverage. Conclusions: Understanding collective mobility patterns is crucial for comprehending the spread of gun violence. Such insights can assist law enforcement agencies in refining hotspot policing strategies, adapting police tactics accordingly.

title: Individual, neighborhood factors in residence-to-crime distances for property, drug,, violent offenses
authors: Wooldredge, John, Graham, Amanda, Frank, James
keywords: Residence-to-crime distance; Neighborhood disadvantage; Residential instability; Multilevel models;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose Individual, neighborhood level effects on distances separating offenders' residences from their crime locations were compared across property, personal,, drug crimes as well as all offenses combined. Methods Police, court data for 2529 felony arrestees referred to a County Prosecutor's Office in the northern mid-west were examined. Multilevel generalized least squares models were estimated with offenders nested within block groups. Results Residence/crime distances were generally shorter for rape, assault,, homicide relative to burglary, breaking, entering, theft,, robbery. Concentrated economic disadvantage was inversely related to distances for all crimes combined,, for drug crimes, assaults specifically. Significant individual level effects on distances for specific offenses included race (robbery, drugs, assault), prior arrests (theft), offense seriousness (thefts, drug crimes),, victim-related factors (robberies, assaults), but not always in expected directions. Conclusions Relative to offender demographics (age, sex, race), incorporating more proximate hypothesized effects on residence/crime distances in related studies (criminal priors, offense severity, acting alone versus in a group, neighborhood SES, etc.) will be useful for informing crime prevention strategies. More proximate effects on these distances might partially or fully mediate demographic effects.

title: A systematic review of lifestyle-routine activity theory in the context of direct-contact sexual victimization
authors: Hayes, Brittany E, Maher, Cooper A
keywords: exposure to crime; guardianship; routine activity theory; sexual assault; target suitability;\_\_work\_pdf登録;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Studies have extended, applied lifestyle-routine activity theory (L-RAT) to direct-contact sexual violence (SV). Yet, operationalizations of theoretical concepts-exposure, proximity, target suitability,, guardianship-have not been consistent across studies within this context,, therefore the ultimate conclusions on the robustness of the theory remain an open empirical question. In this systematic review, we compile scholarship on the application of L-RAT to direct-contact SV to identify how core concepts have been operationalized as well as their association with SV. Studies met the inclusion criteria if they were published before February 2022, examined direct-contact sexual victimization,, explicitly categorized measures into one of the aforementioned theoretical concepts. Overall, 24 studies met the inclusion criteria. Certain factors, such as alcohol, substance use as well as sex behaviors, emerged as consistent operationalizations of exposure, proximity, target suitability,, guardianship across studies. Alcohol, substance use, sexual orientation, relationship status,, behavioral health conditions were common correlates of SV. Nevertheless, there was considerable variability in measurement, significance, clouding how these factors affect risk of SV. In addition, several operationalizations were unique to single studies, reflecting context-specific operationalizations about the population, research question at hand. Conclusions drawn from this work have implications for the generalizability of the body of knowledge related to the application of L-RAT to SV, identify the need for systematic replication efforts. Implications for future research, especially as it relates to replication efforts, claims around generalizability, are discussed.

title: Deconstructing journey-to-crime's questionable validity in theft-related crimes
authors: Michaud, Patrick, Proulx, Jean
keywords: Journey-to-crime; Home-to-crime; Criminal mobility; Environmental criminology; Construct validity;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose This study empirically quantifies the methodological biases of the journey-to-crime measurement, by investigating the extent to which they affect its ability to estimate the itineraries offenders actually travel during the perpetration of their crimes. Methods With the support of police-arrest records, interviews,, web-mapping technologies, the detailed route taken by 98 offenders during 449 theft-related crimes are reconstructed in order to test some of the key assumptions underlying journey-to-crime research. Results Police data used to compute home-crime distances have been found to provide satisfactorily accurate crime-location addresses, but poorly accurate offender home-addresses. Several explanations of why the police have problems correctly identifying where an offender is truly residing on the day of a given crime are presented. Even if the offender's residence was the most important node in their crime journey, the actual travel undertaken by offenders was much more complex than the home-crime-home itinerary assumed by the journey-to-crime measurement. Conclusions Despite its numerous drawbacks, the traditional journey-to-crime measure is still a valid, useful proxy for the total distance actually traveled by offenders in robbery, “other theft,” but not in burglary, motor-vehicle theft. Implications for criminal mobility research, future studies are discussed.

title: Territory, residency,, routine activities: A typology of gang member mobility patterns with implications for place-based interventions
authors: Valasik, Matthew, Gravel, Jason, Tita, George E, Brantingham, P Jeffrey, Griffiths, Elizabeth
keywords: Street gangs; Mobility polygons; Territoriality; Spatial typology; Gang intervention;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose The current study examines the mobility patterns of gang associates in East Los Angeles using Field Investigation (FI) cards collected by police officers to document informal encounters with civilians. Methods We construct a typology classifying each stop in relation to a gang associate's claimed territory, residence,, the location of the stop. We then report on the distribution of mobility types, describe the individual-, event-,, gang-level characteristics commonly associated with each. Results Our findings suggest that there is significant variability in the mobility patterns of gang associates,, that associates often live outside their gang's turf, sometimes returning to their turf, but often spending time away from their turf. Conclusions These results have implications for place-based gang interventions, suggest that all gangs may not be equally suited to interventions such as civil gang injunctions.

title: Why didn’t you resist? Situational influences on victim resistance during a rape
authors: Chopin, Julien, Beauregard, Eric
abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine factors influencing victim resistance during rape. Specifically, this study aims to understand which factors impact victim resistance using a multivariate approach focused on situational aspects related to offender, victim,, crime context characteristics. The sample includes 2,017 rape cases where victims did not resist, resisted passively, resisted verbally, or resisted physically. The first step of this study uses bivariate analyses to examine the relationship between the different categories of victim resistance, offender, victim,, crime context characteristics. Second, we computed three sequential binomial regressions in order to better understand the impact of each variable in multivariate modeling. The findings suggest that victim resistance is impacted by three main dimensions: victims’ physical, psychological vulnerabilities, the mentalizing of victimization risk,, the analysis of offenders’ vulnerabilities, additional risks to the victim. Both theoretical, practical implications for victims as well as for various actors in the criminal justice system are discussed.

title: Criminal nomadism: A neglected dimension of spatial mobility in sex offending
authors: Michaud, Patrick, Beauregard, Eric, Proulx, Jean
keywords: Crime pattern theory; Criminal career; Criminal nomadism; Geographic mobility; Sex offending; Spatial patterns;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose This study investigates criminal nomadism—an individual's propensity to engage in continuous or intermittent interurban travel as a way to cope with the consequences of their criminal lifestyle and/or as a strategy to adapt to the reality of being a “career criminal.” Methods The criminal-career itinerary across Canada of 448 men convicted of sex offenses was reconstructed through individual interviews, analysis of detailed criminal records. Five distinct components of criminal nomadism (i.e., trips, nodes, paths, range,, mesolevel activity space), inspired by crime pattern theory, are suggested, analyzed. Results Results show that criminal nomadism is the reality of young, educated Whites who have a prolific criminal career interspersed with long incarceration sentences. Nomadic offenders did not wander freely, randomly, but rather seemed to be looking for opportunities, privacy. Sex-offending variables did not make a significant contribution to predictions, suggesting that criminal nomadism is more a general offending phenomenon than something specific to sex offending. Conclusions This study provides supporting evidence that an extensive criminal career is generally associated with a geographically scattered, nomadic lifestyle. Implications for public policies, future studies are discussed.

title: Uncertainty, heuristics in offender decision-making: Deviations from rational choice
authors: Rossmo, D Kim, Summers, Lucia
keywords: Criminological theory; Offender decision-making; Prospect theory; Rational choice theory;J Crim Justice;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Purpose Using perspectives from prospect theory, behavioral economics, we explore examples of offender decision-making that appear inconsistent with rational choice, expected utility theories. Methods Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 200 adult offenders with three or more convictions for predatory property or street crime (theft, burglary, and/or robbery). Subjects were asked to describe situations in which they had encountered crime prevention or control measures,, their relevant responses. Specific questions focused on how offenders assessed the effort, risk,, reward involved. Thematic analysis was employed to identify deviations from rational choice perspectives. Results Offenders, particularly abusers of drugs and/or alcohol, often held distorted perceptions of effort, risk,, reward. Cognitive biases, heuristics influenced logic, many offenders were guided by their intuition, even to the point of superstition. Some had dual motivations (“needs”, “wants”) that resulted in a nonlinear relationship between value, utility. Conclusions Rational choice, expected utility theories do not adequately explain offender decision-making, particularly when drug addiction is involved. Effective crime prevention, control strategies require a more comprehensive understanding of how offenders evaluate costs, benefits,, make situational offending decisions.

title: Sexual victimization of college students in public transport environments: a whole journey approach
authors: Natarajan, Mangai, Schmuhl, Margaret, Sudula, Susruta, Mandala, Marissa
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Harassment; Public transport; Situational prevention; Routine precautions; College students; Victimization; Rape; Risk factors;330\_SAEnv;Journey to crime/victimization;CampusCrime
abstract: Sexual victimization of female students during the commute to college is a common, sometimes serious problem. This small-scale study that gathers victim survey data from a sample of 140 female college students in New York City provides insight into their experiences of sexual victimization during the commute to college. It is informed by a “whole journey” approach that includes walking to, from the bus/subway stops as well as waiting for, riding on the bus or subway. The study findings highlight extensive patterns of victimization during all stages of female students’ subway commute to, from college. It is important for colleges, universities in the cities to learn about, deal with off-campus sexual victimization, work with other stakeholders to enhance the safety of commuting students by developing effective, appropriate measures to reduce the opportunities for sexual victimization.

title: Women’s transit safety: making connections, defining future directions in research, practice
authors: Ceccato, Vania
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Gender violence; Crime in transit settings; Case studies; International perspective; Public transportation; Women; Violent crime;330\_SAEnv;Journey to crime/victimization
abstract: Drawing from a diverse range of examples, the guest editor aims to summarise, reflect upon the key material presented in this special issue. This ‘afterword’ to the special issue also highlights the key messages that emerge from the diverse research techniques, methodologies employed in the varied range of case studies, most of them small-scale studies. This final article identifies the unanswered questions, looks forward discussing future research agendas, policy recommendations that arise from this international, multidisciplinary take on women’s victimisation, perceived safety in transit environments.

title: A psychometric study of information technology risks in the workplace
authors: Coles, Robert, Hodgkinson, Gerard P
journal: Risk analysis: an official publication of the Society for Risk Analysis
abstract: As organizations become increasingly reliant on information technology (IT) they are exposed to a growing number of risks. Surprisingly, however, very few studies to date have investigated the psychometric representation of IT risks,, none have been undertaken in the workplace. Accordingly, the present study was designed to map the judgments of a representative group of workplace IT users. Fifty-seven participants evaluated 18 IT risk scenarios by means of 13 bipolar attribute-rating scales. Profile proximities derived from the raw data were submitted to a weighted multidimensional scaling analysis. The results indicated that a six-dimensional solution was required on both statistical, conceptual grounds to represent adequately the participants' judgments. The dimensions reflected the extent to which the various risk scenarios were perceived as: (1) serious or minor in nature; (2) having a high or low probability of occurrence; (3) causing a high or low degree of stress; (4) deliberate or accidental; (5) having an impact on the organization or on individuals;, (6) the product of human or technological causes. The data were also submitted to a series of hierarchical cluster analyses, using a variety of agglomeration techniques. This second approach revealed a robust structure in which the risk scenarios were grouped into two broad categories, based on whether the events depicted would be likely to have a major or minor impact. The major impact category broke down further, into two subcategories, based on whether the scenarios were seen to arise from deliberate causes or through negligence. In conclusion, we consider the implications of our findings for future research, the refinement of IT risk assessment frameworks, tools,, the training of risk management professionals.

title: The journey to crime: Victims, offenders converge in violent index offences in Chicago
authors: Block, Richard, Galary, Aneta, Brice, Darryl
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Robbery; Shopping; Research \& development--R\&D; Population density; Domestic violence; Costs; Central business districts;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal;Journey to crime/victimization
abstract: In Chicago, most non-lethal violence occurs close to the home of the victim or offender. This research describes the distance between the home of the victim, offender, their meeting in a violent crime. Analysis includes all UCR Index criminal sexual assaults, robberies,, aggravated assaults recorded by the Chicago Police in 1998. Little evidence is found for a zone of reduced crime around the home address of the offender. Predatory violence was most likely to occur in neighbourhoods where many offenders resided. Women were much more likely to be attacked close to their, the offender's home than men. Distance, location,, neighbourhood reflected the routine activities of victims, offender as they converged in a violent incident.

title: Identifying the nature of risky places for sexual crime: The applicability of crime pattern, social disorganization theories in a Canadian context
authors: Hewitt, Ashley N, Beauregard, Eric, Andresen, Martin A, Brantingham, Patricia L
keywords: Sexual crime; Criminogenic environment; Crime pattern theory; Social disorganization; Negative binomial;330\_SAEnv;z\_rural2020;Risky facilities;J Crim Justice
abstract: Using both crime pattern, social disorganization theories, the current study investigates the characteristics of those places that experience high counts of reported sexual crime to police.Socio-demographic factors, land use, specific sexual crime attractors,, ecological variables are used to predict dissemination areas with high counts of sexual crime within a large city using 2180 founded crime events retrieved from a Canadian police database.Socio-demographic, ecological factors, as well as the presence of particular sexual crime attractors, characterize these neighborhoods. For example, dissemination areas that have higher percentages of female, male,, single residents, as well as higher counts of rental units, bars,, schools, experience more sexual crimes. Land use does not predict dissemination areas with high counts of sexual crime.Both crime pattern, social disorganization theories provide a framework within which the nature of sexual crime places can be better understood. This information could be used to empower community members as to the types of places that are the riskiest for crimes of this nature, as well as to create a conversation about interventions that could be put in place at both the secondary, tertiary levels to prevent future occurrences.

title: Bus stops, violence, are risky places really risky?
authors: Gerell, Manne
journal: European journal on criminal policy, research
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; RTM; Risk terrain modeling; Violent crime; Crime forecasting; Public transport; Collective efficacy; Victims; Victimization; Crime; Forecasting; Neighborhoods; Risk factors; Violence; Offenses; Efficacy; Passengers; Fitting;330\_SAEnv;Risky facilities
abstract: Geographic forecasting of crime can be done by considering prior crime or by considering spatial risk factors, e.g., using risk terrain modeling (RTM). The present paper tests both methods, but primarily focuses on RTM, on increasing our understanding of forecasting by attempting to compare the spatial risk factors for where the number of crimes is high with the spatial risk factors for where the risk of victimization is high. This is performed by fitting negative binomial models on crime around bus stops, comparing them to the same models with the number of bus passengers as exposure variable. The models also take the surrounding environment into account by fitting multi-level models with neighborhood level predictors of concentrated disadvantage, collective efficacy. The results show that some types of facilities are risk factors for crime, but not for victimization. This results in new insights into how flows of people impact on forecasting, as for instance a school is a spatial risk factor for crime, while not being associated with an elevated risk per person. The results also show that the neighborhood level of collective efficacy is a stable, significant risk factor both for crime, for risk of victimization, highlighting a potential for better crime forecasting by combining different spatial, theoretical perspectives.

title: Exploring the conditional effects of bus stops on crime
authors: Stucky, Thomas D, Smith, Sarah L
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; public transportation; bus stops; crime; spatial analysis; Criminal statistics; Entrepreneurs;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal;Risky facilities
abstract: Public transportation is a major element of social life in most cities,, the most common mode of public transportation is busing. This study examines whether bus stops are a robust predictor of crime, net of other factors,, whether the effect of bus stops on crime is conditioned by socioeconomic, land use factors. We use geocoded Indianapolis crime, bus stop data for 2010 to predict crime counts in 500-feet × 500-feet square grid cells, using negative binomial models. Net of other factors, bus stops are associated with variation in counts of Uniform Crime Reports reported rape, robbery, aggravated assault, burglary, larceny in a cell. In addition, the effect of bus stops on crime was conditioned by land use characteristics. In particular, the effect of bus stops on crime was greater in commercial, industrial areas, but dampened in areas with high-density residential housing.

title: Crime in São Paulo’s metro system: sexual crimes against women
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Paz, Yuri
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement; Gendered violence; Subway; Transit environments; GIS; Google Street View; Subways; Crime prevention; Women; Sex crimes; Violent crime; Sao Paulo Brazil;330\_SAEnv;public\_transportation\_334;\_2024\_tmg-GIS;Risky facilities;GSV
abstract: The article investigates personal safety conditions in the São Paulo metro, the largest rapid transit system in Brazil. The study looks at all types of crimes, but devotes special attention to the nature, spatio-temporal dynamics of sexual crimes against women while in transit. The methodology combines Geographical Information System, crime records with data collected using Google Street View, other secondary data into a set of regression models. Findings show that sexual violence is concentrated at the busiest central stations; it often takes place during the morning, afternoon rush hours,, at stations that also attract all sorts of violence, events of public disorder. The study finalises with an analysis of the metro’s current prevention practices targeting women’s sexual victimisation.

title: Where do sex crimes occur? How an examination of sex offense location can inform policy, prevention
authors: Calkins, Cynthia, Colombino, Niki, Matsuura, Taiki, Jeglic, Elizabeth
journal: International journal of comparative, applied criminal justice
abstract: Although ample evidence demonstrates that sex crime policies focused on “stranger danger” types of offenses that occur in public places do little, if anything, to reduce sex crime, we have much less data with which to inform primary prevention strategies. Using archival data collected from the files of 1468 sex offenders, this study provides empirical data on offense location, how it varies by victim–offender relationship. Though 4\% of cases occurred in areas normally restricted by residence restrictions or child safety zone legislation, only 0.05\% of the offenses were perpetrated by a stranger against a minor victim in a restricted location. By providing narrative descriptions of the types of sex crimes that occur in child-dense locations, this study provides a richer, more contextualized notion of the nature of risk in public-restricted locations. Given the infrequent occurrence of sex crimes in child-dense locations, it is argued that tertiary sex crime prevention efforts ought to focus on where sex crimes most frequently occur (i.e., in the home, by known perpetrators), that resources be shifted to primary prevention.

title: The nature of rape places
authors: Ceccato, Vania
keywords: Sexual violence; Crime geography; Outdoor environment; Public places; City structure;330\_SAEnv;z\_jsep2015;J Environ Psychol;Risky facilities
abstract: The objective of this article is to characterise the distribution, the urban landscape in which outdoor rapes happen in Stockholm, the capital of Sweden. Geographical Information Systems (GIS) underlie the methodology of this research that combines crime police records, police protocols, information from fieldwork of a sample of rape places. Rapes are concentrated in the inner city areas but follow a patchy pattern in some parts of the periphery. Rapes happen in places with poor visibility but that offer an easy escape for the offender. A large share of them happen in the weekends, holidays, hot months of the year, which can be associated with unstructured leisure routine activities of individuals. Results show that the role of environment on the occurrence of rape varies over time, space – a fact with important implications for research, safety interventions.

title: Limning auditing Indian auditors
authors: Deb, Rajat
abstract: The boom of regulatory agencies is a common global phenomenon,, its basics are deeply rooted in national settings, leading to the setting up of specific regulators. Theoretically, auditors must demonstrate their professional prowess, skepticism,, analytical procedure,, effectively communicate audit outcomes to the stakeholders. Interestingly, the Indian audit profession is at its crossroads: constrained by scams, multiple regulators. Reform initiatives in the wake of corporate shenanigans compelled the creation of the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) under Section 132 of the Companies Act, 2013. However, the accounting profession regulator, the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI), alleges penetration of the former in its regulatory jurisdiction. Against this backdrop, adopting a descriptive approach, the current study attempts to unearth the factors leading to such face-offs for offering an amicable solution. The study concludes that the ICAI’s objections to treating the NFRA as a “super-regulator” cannot be supported. Consequently, the observation of the Committee on Experts constituted by the Supreme Court. Vesting investigating power in the NFRA could be a game changer in regulating auditors, audit firms,, audit networks. In light of the findings, the auditors could motivate to improve the audit quality substantially.

title: Space–time dynamics of crime in transport nodes
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Uittenbogaard, Adriaan Cornelis
journal: Annals of the Association of American Geographers. Association of American Geographers
abstract: This article assesses space–time variations of crime rates in underground stations. Drawing on assumptions from time geography, routine activity principles,, defensible space theory, the study investigates daily, weekly,, seasonal variations of crime at underground stations in the Swedish capital, Stockholm. Data from extensive field work at the stations was combined with crime records, passenger flow to test whether stations’ environmental attributes affect crime at different times. Geographical information systems, spatial statistic techniques,, modeling underpin the methodology used in the study. Findings show that crimes tend to happen more often in the evening, at night, on holidays,, on weekends. There is also evidence of seasonal variations of crime. In the winter, stations with social disturbance, signs of deterioration show high levels of crime, whereas in the summer, offenses are concentrated in stations nearby alcohol selling outlets. Stations with hiding spots are often targeted for crime during daily peak hours, whereas during holidays, crowded stations, those with alcohol selling outlets attract more criminal activities. Results suggest that the role of the stations’ environment on crime causation varies over time—an important fact for safety interventions.

title: Assessing the correlation between bus stop densities, residential crime typologies
authors: Kooi, Brandon R
abstract: Crime, disorder surrounding public transit is a serious problem for most public, private policing agencies. Although terrorism targeting public transportation continues to receive appropriate attention, transit users are far more likely to be impacted by typical UCR crime, general disorder. This study mapped out over 600 bus stop locations throughout a midsize Midwest city, conducted a quasi-experimental design to measure the impact of concentrated bus stop locations on crime. The findings indicate highly concentrated bus stop locations may be facilitating crime statistics in targeted locations. Policy implications are discussed debating the spatial responsibility for public transit security, police strategies that include important community-driven solutions. As part of larger gentrification movements, urban planners are encouraged to look at the availability of potential victims within high-crime areas, determine whether routine pathways of these victims are unnecessarily encountering a large clustering of motivated potential offenders because of where public transportation is located.

title: Areal differentiation in crime in public transit terminals in Ibadan metropolis
authors: Ajayi, Adeyinka Peter, Ajayi, Dickson ‘dare
keywords: Transportation; Studies; Public transportation; Crime; Developing countries--LDCs; Transportation terminals; Public safety; Ibadan Nigeria; 9130:Experimental/theoretical; 1200:Social policy; 8350:Transportation \& travel industry; 9177:Africa;330\_SAEnv;Risky facilities
abstract: The unprecedented rate of urbanization in the twentieth, twenty- first century in most less developed countries (LDC) is coming at a huge cost to cities in these countries chief among which are distorted morphologies, dysfunctional infrastructural system, ever-increasing crime rate, In Ibadan metropolis one of the infrastructure that has been subject of this systemic abuse are the public transit terminals, this study analyses the incidences of crime,the spatial pattern of their occurrences, the nature of crime which are prevalent in, around major road transit terminals, statistical records of crime incidences, data on crime experiences of two hundred, fifty respondents were analyzed statistically, descriptively, the findings revealed that crime rate, the nature, pattern of occurrence varied spatially within the metropolitan parks, recommendations on how best to safe-guard the parks are subsequently made.

title: Security in Stockholm's underground stations: The importance of environmental attributes, context
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Uittenbogaard, Adriaan, Bamzar, Roya
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Assaults; Criminology;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal;\_2024\_tmg-GIS;Risky facilities
abstract: The aim of this article is to report on the security conditions in underground stations, surrounding areas in Stockholm, the capital of Sweden. The study is based on a comprehensive fieldwork combined with Geographical Information Systems techniques, regression models. Findings show that a relatively small share of reported events is crime; acts of public disorder are more common at the stations. Events tend to happen in the evenings – nights, holidays, weekends – and, at least for theft, in the hotter months of the year. Although the highest number of events is found in the central station, the so-called ‘end-stations’ show often higher rates than those located in the inner city. Results show that opportunities for crime are dependent on stations’ environmental attributes, type of neighbourhood in which they are located, city context. These findings lend weight to principles of traditional urban criminology theory such as routine activity, social disorganisation. The article concludes with directions for future research, suggestions for policy.

title: The role of neighborhood parks as crime generators
authors: Groff, Elizabeth, McCord, Eric S
keywords: Criminology And Law Enforcement--Security; Social classes; Data collection; Theory; Public access; Generators;330\_SAEnv;Security Journal;Risky facilities
abstract: Neighborhood parks in urban areas have long been seen as contested spaces. Because they are publically owned, they are at the same time everyone's, no one's. As public resources they have little intrinsic guardianship, thus are susceptible to being taken over for undesirable activities (that is, living spaces for the homeless, markets for drug dealers, delinquent behavior magnets for juveniles). While much has been written about parks, crime, little research exists which empirically examines the topic. The current research examines neighborhood parks in Philadelphia, PA as they relate to crime, disorder that occurs outdoors. We use primary data collection to quantify the number of potential activity generators (recreation centers, pools, playground, night lighting,, so on), other park characteristics. Land use on adjacent streets is also collected. Our analysis finds that neighborhood parks are associated with increased levels of crime in the surrounding area. However, specific characteristics of parks are associated with lower crime levels.

title: The spatial concentration, stability of crime in a South African township
authors: Breetzke, G D, Edelstein, I S
abstract: The law of crime concentration at places motivates that a small number of locations are responsible for a disproportionate amount of crime. Research applying the law has largely been confined to the United States, Europe with much less known about spatial crime concentrations, their stability in less developed contexts, particularly in Africa. In this study, we explore the spatial concentration of crime in a setting axiomatically different from the West, namely Khayelitsha, a township on the outskirts of Cape Town in South Africa. Specifically, we describe rape, robbery, assault concentrations in Khayelitsha from 2008 to 2015, examine the extent to which these concentrations change over time. Similar to international research, we found that crime in Khayelitsha spatially concentrates, that these concentrations are remarkably stable. Practical implications of these findings are discussed in the context of a historically unique post-apartheid South African spatial setting.

title: The impact of the Canterbury Earthquakes on the temporal, spatial patterning of crime in Christchurch, New Zealand
authors: Breetzke, Gregory D, King, Marcus, Fabris-Rotelli, Inger
journal: The Australian \& New Zealand journal of criminology
abstract: The Canterbury Earthquakes struck the Canterbury region of the South Island of New Zealand between September 2010, February 2011. The Earthquakes resulted in widespread structural damage to Christchurch, the main city of the region,, greatly impacted other aspects of society including crime. In this study, we adopt an exploratory approach to investigate the impact that these earthquakes have had on the temporal, spatial patterning of four types of crime in Christchurch: assault, domestic violence, burglary, arson. Overall crime has decreased in post-quake Christchurch with the notable exception of domestic violence. We found remarkably similar temporal signatures of crime for all crime types occurring across both the pre-, post-earthquake periods. Spatially, crime has increased in the majority of neighbourhoods in Christchurch post-quake despite overall crime levels being down. Explanations for this paradoxical, other finding are outlined in the context of a rebuilding, recovering city.

title: The law of crime concentration: An application, recommendations for future research
authors: Levin, Aaron, Rosenfeld, Richard, Deckard, Michael
abstract: Objective We address four outstanding empirical questions related to the “law of crime concentration” (Weisburd in Criminology 53:133–157, 2015 ): (1) Is the spatial concentration of crime stable over time? (2) Do the same places consistently rank among those with the highest crime counts? (3) How much crime concentration would be observed if crimes were distributed randomly over place? (4) To what degree does the spatial concentration of crime depend on places that are crime free? Methods The data are annual counts of violent, property crimes in St. Louis between 2000, 2014. Temporal stability in the spatial inequality of crime is measured by computing the fraction of crimes that occur in the 5\% of street segments with the highest crime frequencies each year. The spatial mobility of crime is measured by computing the number of years each street segment appears in the top 5\% of street segments. Poisson simulations are used to estimate the fraction of crimes that could appear in the top 5\% of street segments on the basis of chance alone. The impact of crime-free locales on the spatial concentration of crime is evaluated by comparing results from analyses that include, exclude crime-free street segments from the crime distributions. Results The concentration of crime is highly unequal, stable over time. The specific street segments with the highest crime frequencies, however, change over time. Nontrivial fractions of street segments may appear among the 5\% with the highest crime frequencies on the basis of chance. Spatial concentration of crime is reduced when crime-free street segments are excluded from the crime distributions. Conclusions The law of crime concentration is not a measurement artifact. Its substantive significance, however, should be assessed in future longitudinal research that replicates the current study across diverse social settings.

title: More places than crimes: Implications for evaluating the law of crime concentration at place
authors: Bernasco, Wim, Steenbeek, Wouter
abstract: Objectives: The crime, place literature lacks a standard methodology for measuring, reporting crime concentration. We suggest that crime concentration be reported with the Lorenz curve, summarized with the Gini coefficient,, we propose generalized versions of the Lorenz curve, the Gini coefficient to correct for bias when crime data are sparse (i.e., fewer crimes than places). Methods: The proposed generalizations are based on the principle that the observed crime concentration should not be compared with perfect equality, but with maximal equality given the data. The generalizations asymptotically approach the original Lorenz curve, the original Gini coefficient as the number of crimes approaches the number of spatial units. Results: Using geocoded crime data on two types of crime in the city of The Hague, we show the differences between the original Lorenz curve, Gini coefficient, the generalized versions. We demonstrate that the generalizations provide a better representation of crime concentration in situations of sparse crime data,, that they improve comparisons of crime concentration if they are sparse. Conclusions: Researchers are advised to use the generalized versions of the Lorenz curve, the Gini coefficient when reporting, summarizing crime concentration at places. When places outnumber crimes, the generalized versions better represent the underlying processes of crime concentration than the original versions. The generalized Lorenz curve, the Gini coefficient, its variance are easy to compute.

title: The law of crime concentration, the criminology of place: The law of crime concentration
authors: Weisburd, David
keywords: crime concentration; crime places; hot spots; microgeographic; unit of analysis;z\_DSSV2019;z\_bsj2019;Space-time Concentration ;criminology
abstract: According to Laub (2004), criminology has a developmental life course with specific turning points that allow for innovations in how we understand, respond to crime. I argue that criminology should take another turn in direction, focusing on microgeographic hot spots. By examining articles published in Criminology, I show that only marginal attention has been paid to this area of study to date—often termed the criminology of place. I illustrate the potential utility of a turning point by examining the law of crime concentration at place, which states that for a defined measure of crime at a specific microgeographic unit, the concentration of crime will fall within a narrow bandwidth of percentages for a defined cumulative proportion of crime. By providing the first cross‐city comparison of crime concentration using a common geographic unit, the same crime type,, examining a general crime measure, I find strong support for a law of crime concentration. I also show that crime concentration stays within a narrow bandwidth across time, despite strong volatility in crime incidents. By drawing from these findings, I identify several key research questions for future study. In conclusion, I argue that a focus on the criminology of place provides significant opportunity for young scholars, has great promise for advancing criminology as a science.

title: The Impact of the 2010 Winter Olympic Games on Crime in Vancouver
authors: Andresen, Martin A, Tong, William
journal: Canadian journal of criminology, criminal justice
abstract: There is little research on exceptional events, crime. Yet exceptional events, such as natural disasters, worldwide political meetings,, international sporting competitions, affect the lifestyles, routines of large numbers of people. In this article, we examine the impact of the 2010 Winter Olympic Games on assault, theft, mischief,, prostitution in Vancouver neighbourhoods. Overall, there is no evidence to support the claim that the Olympic Games affected all crime types, in all places. However, we do find increases in assault that relate to the Olympic Games in a few key neighbourhoods. As with previous research, it appears that the substantial increase in the number of security personnel (police, military, etc.) mitigated the potential increase in crime.

title: Testing the stability of crime patterns: Implications for theory, policy
authors: Andresen, Martin A, Malleson, Nicolas
journal: The journal of research in crime, delinquency
keywords: 308\_STC;Journal of Research in Crime, Delinquency\_Sage;Space-time Concentration
abstract: Recent research in the ‘‘crime at places’’ literature is concerned with smaller units of analysis than conventional spatial criminology. An important issue is whether the spatial patterns observed in conventional spatial criminology focused on neighborhoods remain when the analysis shifts to street segments. In this article, the authors use a new spatial point pattern test that identifies the similarity in spatial point patterns. This test is local in nature such that the output can be mapped showing where differences are present. Using this test, the authors investigate the stability of crime patterns moving from census tracts to dissemination areas to street segments. The authors find that general crime patterns are somewhat similar at all spatial scales, but finer scales of analysis reveal significant variations within larger units. This result demonstrates the importance of analyzing crime patterns at small scales, has important implications for further theoretical development, policy implementation.
