abstract: Modern policing is faced with a rapidly changing landscape which continues to present new challenges, opportunities to policing (NPCC, 2015). With limited resources, it is hoped policing education will support police services to deal with these challenges through embedding evidence-based practices (Mitchell, Lewis, 2017). The large number of new recruits from the police uplift provides an exciting opportunity to incorporate these practices into operational policing (Lum, Koper, 2017; Pepper et al., 2020). The purpose of this study was to investigate evidence-based research projects produced by student police officers, explore whether they provide knowledge that is relevant, embedded into policing practice. Using qualitative methods data was gathered from key informants, graduates from the University of South Wales' five established police partners in England, Wales. The findings identified that knowledge from the projects was being disseminated within the police organisations,, that student police officers were informally applying evidence-based knowledge they had gained from their research projects in their day-to-day operational policing roles,, some were transferring this knowledge as tutors, supervisors. This study concluded that research projects produced by student officers can have a direct impact, contribution to policing practice, policy. However, to capitalise on this opportunity police services would benefit from developing formalised processes to embed this knowledge into practice.

title: Disparity between punitive attitudes toward stranger rape, partner rape: Evidence from cross-national survey data
authors: Uhl, Andrzej, Porębski, Andrzej, Ilczuk, Ewa
abstract: While legally the same, acts of sexual abuse within, outside intimate relationships are not seen as equal by the public,, this distinction might also be reflected in preferred criminal punishment; some people might deem partner rape as deserving less harsh punishment than the rape of a stranger. Our secondary analysis examines differential punitiveness toward these two types of rape among the respondents ( n = 11,383) to a large population survey conducted in 2021 in Austria, Czechia, Germany, Hungary, Poland,, Slovakia. As part of the survey, respondents chose preferred sentences for partner, stranger rape. Using these sentencing questions, we investigate the direction, extent,, demographic distribution of the differential punitiveness toward stranger, partner rape. A large group of respondents (ranging from 31.5\% in Austria to 47.3\% in Czechia) granted greater leniency to partner rape than to stranger rape, the reverse was rarely observed. More severe sentences were chosen for stranger rape more often than for partner rape. The individual bias toward leniency for partner rape was also typically stronger than the rare bias for stranger rape (the difference of 36 vs. 24 months of imprisonment, respectively). Relative leniency toward partner rape was particularly pronounced in Slavic countries, more prevalent among men,, positively correlated with age, right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, rape myth acceptance. Drawing on our results, previous scholarship, we attribute the observed disparities to the persistence of rape myths, the legitimation of intra-relationship sexual violence by conventional belief systems.

title: Exploring the associations between community gun violence exposure, adolescent delinquency: Evidence from the future of families, child wellbeing study
authors: Pei, Fei, Li, Xiaomei, Kang, Luyao, Wang, Chenming
abstract: In the past decades, an increasing body of research has delved into the mechanisms of adolescent delinquency from various perspectives, including individual characteristics, interpersonal relationships, school environments,, community settings. However, limited research focused on its association with community gun violence exposure. Utilizing data from 3,595 adolescents ( M = 15.63, SD = 0.71), their families, we examined how the number of gun violence incidents proximal to adolescents’ homes, schools was linked with their self-reported delinquent behaviors, controlling for other important individual, interpersonal,, community-level predictors of adolescent delinquency. Results revealed relationships between gun violence within 1,000, 500 m of homes (but not schools), adolescent delinquency; yet the direction of the relationship differs by distance.

title: Exploring the perceived impact of a multi-year campus hazing prevention initiative at eight universities
authors: Allan, Elizabeth J, Kerschner, David, Franklin, Devin
abstract: Guided by the Hazing Prevention Framework, this investigation employed quantitative, qualitative methods to examine the perceived impact of a 3-year, multi-campus initiative to implement a comprehensive, public health-based approach to campus hazing prevention. Data were collected from campus staff employed at eight universities participating in the Hazing Prevention Consortium by using the Hazing Prevention Rubric, conducting follow-up interviews. Analysis of rubric scores revealed an average increase of 18.66\%, suggesting overall progression for these campuses. Qualitative analysis illuminated commitment, capacity, assessment, planning, implementation, evaluation, cultural competence,, sustainability themes, provided further context for interpreting rubric scores. Factors perceived to strongly influence the progression of hazing prevention included the presence of a network of peers for collaboration, assessment data to guide prevention, factors perceived to influence regression included the challenges related to COVID-19, the lack of senior leader commitment to hazing prevention. Findings contribute new knowledge, add to the literature about hazing prevention, rubrics for evaluating campus-wide prevention initiatives. Recommendations for research, practice are provided.

title: Using the life history calendar to examine victimization, mental health,, seeking, attaining help among transgender women: An example of a culturally relevant adaptation
authors: Hereth, Jane E, Kennedy, Angie C, Garthe, Rachel C, Durand, Brenna, Morein, Lane, Lunger, Lexy, De Smet, Lucas E, Thornton, Lukas E, Blackburn, Allyson M, Saba, Jessica
abstract: Transgender women are at increased risk for interpersonal violence victimization, including physical, sexual child abuse, mistreatment, intimate partner violence, sexual assault,, transgender-related community violence. Experiencing multiple forms of interpersonal victimization is associated with a range of adverse mental health outcomes. Life course approaches such as the life history calendar (LHC) are useful for examining trajectories of victimization, associated mental health outcomes, yet to date this method has not been used to examine transgender women’s victimization trajectories. In this paper, we describe adapting the LHC to examine transgender women’s experiences of victimization, adverse mental health, help-seeking,, help-attainment ( N = 103),, we share participants’ feedback on the acceptability of the LHC. First, we engaged in an iterative, collaborative process to adapt existing LHCs used in studies on victimization among cisgender women to ensure relevancy for our sample, then we conducted one-on-one interviews with participants using the adapted LHC. At the end of the interview, participants were asked for feedback about their experience. Responses were transcribed verbatim, coded using open, thematic coding methods. Overwhelmingly participants (97.8\%) found the experience to be “positive” (73.0\%) or “neutral” (39.3\%). Just two participants’ responses were coded as only “challenging.” Other themes included enjoying the process of using the calendar to reflect on their life events, feeling good about using their stories to help others. The adaptation, findings from our study demonstrate that despite high levels of victimization, trauma, potential difficulty discussing these topics in a research context, transgender women who participated in this study found the LHC interview to be acceptable and, in many cases, positive. Findings can inform future LHC adaptations, research as well as the development of culturally relevant, effective mental health interventions for transgender women.

title: Mothers' violence experiences, provision of emotional support following child sexual abuse
authors: Rancher, Caitlin, Smith, Daniel W
keywords: emotional support; intimate partner violence; non-offending caregiver; physical abuse; sexual abuse
abstract: Emotional support from a non-offending caregiver, often the child's mother, is theorized to help buffer children from the consequences of child sexual abuse (CSA). However, many mothers struggle to provide effective emotional support, suggesting it may be important to assess for factors related to mothers' abilities to support their child. CSA frequently occurs in families that have experienced other types of violence, including intimate partner violence (IPV),, many mothers have their own personal history of child abuse. This research examined the prevalence, influence of mothers' experiences of child abuse, adult interpersonal violence on the provision of emotional support following their child's CSA disclosure. Participants included 120 mothers, their children (aged 7-17) recruited from a children's advocacy center following the disclosure of CSA. Mothers, children completed convergent measures of emotional support. Mothers also completed semi-structured interviews assessing their experiences of adult IPV, child physical abuse, sexual abuse. Most mothers had experienced IPV (68\%), child physical abuse (87\%). Nearly half (49\%) had experienced CSA. Regression analyses indicated that mothers' experiences of CSA were negatively associated with mother-report of emotional support (partial η2 = .05); however, mothers' experiences of IPV, child physical abuse were positively associated with child-report of emotional support (IPV, partial η2 = .06; physical abuse, partial η2 = .09). The results highlight the importance of assessing for mothers' experiences of violence to best support families receiving services for CSA.

title: Cross-sectional, longitudinal associations between pornography use, dating violence victimization: Are there risks for teenagers?
authors: Martel, Sara, Bergeron, Sophie, Bőthe, Beáta, Vaillancourt-Morel, Marie-Pier, Hébert, Martine, Dion, Jacinthe
keywords: adolescent health; intimate violence; pornography; sexually explicit material
abstract: Dating violence victimization (DVV) is a prevalent public health problem with harmful consequences among adolescents. Pornography use has been identified among the factors associated with DVV. However, most studies have relied on cross-sectional designs, limiting the ability to determine temporal relationships between these variables. The present study assessed bidirectional longitudinal associations between pornography use, DVV (psychological, physical,, sexual), also examining cross-sectional associations, gender differences. Participants' self-report data from two assessments of a longitudinal study were used. The sample consisted of 1,556 teenagers (Mage = 14.55 years, SDage = .630; 51.5\% were girls) having reported an intimate relationship in the past year at the first and/or second time point (T1/T2). Whereas some cross-sectional associations between pornography use, DVV were observed at T1, results from the autoregressive cross-lagged model revealed no significant longitudinal association between pornography use, the three forms of DVV, regardless of gender. Thus, pornography use may not represent a significant risk factor over time for DVV in adolescents. These findings provide additional insights concerning the associations between pornography use, DVV, suggest that emphasis should perhaps be placed on other variables in the study of risk factors for DVV. Still, although modest, transversal links support the importance of interventions that promote healthy intimate relationships in adolescence, education about pornography use.

title: Service providers' attitudes toward mandatory reporting of intimate partner violence: The impact of professional experience
authors: Nordby, Christine, Douglas, Kevin S, Vatnar, Solveig Karin Bø
keywords: disclosure of domestic violence; domestic violence; legal intervention
abstract: Mandatory reporting (MR) among service providers (SP) working with intimate partner violence (IPV) is controversial,, the research is scarce. The potential association of SPs experience with IPV, MR-IPV, their attitudes is the aim of the current study. A total of 374 SPs working with victims, perpetrators (help-seekers) of IPV participated in this study. Factor analysis was conducted to produce a continuous standardized dependent variable as a measure of attitudes toward MR-IPV. Descriptive results indicated that SPs were generally supportive of MR-IPV. Linear regression analyses showed that a higher degree of professional experience with IPV was significantly associated with less skepticism of MR-IPV. The result was significant regardless of (1) severity of violence, (2) category of help-seeker, (3) time of incidents,, (4) number of cases where MR-IPV was considered relevant. Having substantial experience with IPV, MR-IPV remained significant adjusting for the SP category, years in current position, knowledge of MR,, frequency of mandatory reports. Our results indicate that experience is an important part of SPs attitudes toward MR-IPV.

title: Latent classes analysis approach of intimate partner violence victimization, perpetration in emerging adulthood
authors: Cherrier, Chloé, Courtois, Robert, Rusch, Emmanuel, Potard, Catherine
keywords: emerging adulthood; intimate partner violence; latent class analysis; perpetration; psychosocial vulnerabilities; victimization;324\_Bystander
abstract: This study sought to identify classes of intimate partner violence (IPV) among emerging adults reporting both victimization, perpetration, as well as the co-occurrence of multiple forms of violence (i.e., psychological, physical,, sexual), the association of psychosocial vulnerability factors (i.e., parental attachment, childhood abuse, dysfunctional attitudes, sociotropy-autonomy, self-esteem,, problem solving). A total of 363 French emerging adults aged 18 to 30 years (mean age = 24.73; 88.7\% women) responded to self-report questionnaires at 12-month intervals. A latent class analysis identified five classes: low IPV (37.7\%), poly IPV (7.5\%), psychological, sexual IPV (8.9\%), psychological, physical IPV (6.5\%),, psychological IPV (39.4\%). The classes were compared with logistic multinomial regressions, with the low IPV class as a reference. The results revealed that a history of IPV (12 months before) was the most predictive factor of IPV classes. Significant psychosocial vulnerability factors included social problem solving for poly IPV, psychological IPV, attraction to loneliness (dimension of autonomy) for psychological, sexual IPV, high self-esteem for poly IPV,, a secure attachment to the mother for psychological IPV, for psychological, physical IPV. Childhood abuse was not associated with the different classes. Implications for research, prevention programs will be discussed. This includes efforts to empirically integrate life skills with established psychosocial factors,, working on representations of IPV by framing conflicts as interactive interactions, to further improve intervention strategies.

title: A chain mediation model of basic need satisfaction, self-concept clarity between harsh parenting, problematic Internet use among adolescents
authors: Kong, Fanchang, Chen, Shenghan, Tang, Feng, Li, Huizhi
keywords: adolescents; basic need satisfaction; harsh parenting; problematic internet use; self-concept clarity
abstract: This study presents a model of harsh parenting that has an indirect, direct effect on problematic Internet use (PIU) through the mediating process of basic need satisfaction, self-concept clarity. A sample of 490 Chinese middle-school adolescents completed anonymous questionnaires regarding harsh parenting, PIU, basic need satisfaction,, self-concept clarity during class sessions. After controlling the sex, grade,, history of Internet use, harsh parenting was positively related to PIU. Moreover, basic need satisfaction, self-concept clarity mediated the association between harsh parenting, PIU among adolescents. These findings indicate that basic need satisfaction, self-concept clarity are protective factors in reducing the negative effect of harsh parenting on PIU. Theoretical, practical implications are discussed.

title: A model of bystander helping to prevent suicide: Examining, extending the Theory of Planned Behavior
authors: Banyard, Victoria, Mitchell, Kimberly J, Jones, Lisa M, Dunsiger, Shira, Ybarra, Michele L
abstract: Research documents alarmingly high suicidal behavior risk among adolescents, young adults in the United States. A related concern is similarly high rates of exposure to the self-directed violence (SDV) of others. The current study examined how components of the Theory of Planned Behavior explain factors related to helping social network members engaging in SDV. Baseline data (N = 4,982) from the longitudinal study, Project Lift Up, were analyzed cross-sectionally. Young people, ages 13 to 22, were recruited through social media platforms; sexual, gender minority youth were oversampled. Participants answered questions about exposure to other people's SDV, measures of key constructs related to the Theory of Planned Behavior for helping reduce SDV including perceptions of what others think about helping, behavioral control. Three outcomes were assessed: Intent to help someone, proactive behavior to promote the other person's mattering,, proactive behavior to prevent SDV. Measures showed adequate reliability, validity (Cronbach's alphas above .70). Overall, regression analyses across the three outcomes partially supported the Theory of Planned Behavior. Attitudes, confidence explained variance in intent to help, proactive behavior outcomes, whereas intent, social norms showed more mixed associations with the three outcomes. While the Theory of Planned Behavior is useful to explain gatekeeper outcomes for suicide prevention, specific significant factors within the model vary by the specific outcome being examined. Further research to unpack nuances in gatekeeper behaviors is needed, may help design prevention strategies.

title: Social beliefs, attitudes involved in the willingness to intervene in cases of intimate partner violence against women in a Spanish sample
authors: Badenes-Sastre, Marta, García-Sánchez, Efraín, Lorente Acosta, Miguel, Expósito Jiménez, Francisca
keywords: attribution of responsibility; myths; perceived severity; risk assessed; sexism
abstract: Intimate partner violence against women (IPVAW) is a public health, social responsibility issue affecting women worldwide. The role of society is essential to help victims to get out of the violent relationship, reduce their risk of revictimization. In this regard, the social response to IPVAW depends to some extent on public beliefs, attitudes toward IPVAW. Hence, this research explores the direct relationship between sexism, the willingness to intervene in cases of IPVAW, indirectly through acceptance of myths of IPVAW, perceived severity of IPVAW, risk assessed of victims' health, life as well as to the establishment of equal relations, attribution of the responsibility to the aggressor,, victim blaming. A Spanish sample of 487 participants was collected through incidental sampling. Participants responded to an online survey that was disseminated via email, social media. A parallel path analysis model showed that greater sexism was associated with lower willingness to intervene in cases IPVAW, via greater acceptance of the myths of IPVAW, less attribution of responsibility to the aggressor. IPVAW perceived severity, risk assessed,, victim blaming did not explain the effect of sexism on willingness to intervene. This research emphasizes the need to focus on egalitarian education that mitigates sociocultural risk factors such as patriarchal beliefs, attitudes that explain IPVAW, favors a climate of acceptance, tolerance of this problem, making it difficult for victims to break with the violent relationship.

title: Assessing the victim-perpetrator overlap in adolescent dating violence in China: A latent class analysis
authors: Cheung, Nicole W T, Yao, Wei
keywords: cultural contexts; dating violence; domestic violence; youth violence
abstract: There is a limited understanding of the pathways that lead to victim-perpetrator overlap in adolescent dating violence (ADV) particularly in developing countries such as China. Applying a latent class approach, the present study focuses on whether the overlap can be explained by theoretical constructs grounded in social learning, general strain,, social bonding theories,, whether these constructs relate to underexplored mediating mechanisms or are direct precursors. The study sample consisted of 1,787 dating adolescents (39.8\% male; mean age = 17.82 ± 0.92 years) from a population of 5,820 adolescents in 32 high schools in Chinese cities, rural counties. We found a significant victim-perpetrator overlap in controlling, psychological,, physical ADV, with the proclivity increasing with the severity of ADV. Membership of groups engaged in general delinquency, those engaged in dating violence increased the odds of victim-perpetrator overlap. Peer bullying victimization was the most consistent direct predictor of victim-perpetrator overlap in family/peer/community settings; victimization resulting from interparental violence during childhood, peer bullying,, community violence was the most consistent indirect predictor. Neighborhood bonds had a greater impact than social bonds with family, school in terms of direct, indirect protective effects against victim-perpetrator overlap. Patterns of exposure to violent victimization in family/peer/community settings, patterns of social bonds cast new light on the nature of deviant peer (general delinquency vs. ADV) networks, which were found to operate as major mediating mechanisms in victim-perpetrator overlap.

title: Examining the meaning of ``violence'' through machine learning techniques
authors: van Breen, Jolien, Rijcken, Emil, Kantorowicz, Jaroslaw, Liem, Marieke
keywords: social injustice; topic modeling; violence; word embeddings
abstract: This paper examines the meaning of violence in contemporary Western societies. Scholars have argued that in contemporary Western societies, the concept is expanding toward a broader understanding of violence, beyond its ``traditional'' usage in the context of crime, war. The current paper aims to generate empirical evidence that speaks to this question. We take the Netherlands as a case study, apply machine learning techniques to discourse on violence in 80,000 articles published in national newspapers between 2012, 2021. Results show that the public discourse on violence in the Netherlands has a component that can be described as the familiar or ``traditional'' usage of the term violence-referring to violent political conflicts, or interpersonal violence such as child abuse. Beyond this, the term violence is associated with discourse on societal challenges. It appears in discourse on social media, political polarization,, social injustice faced by ethnic minorities, women,, the LGBT+ community. The later stages of the analysis demonstrated that the terms associated with social injustice in particular (e.g., ``racist'') become more closely associated with the concept of violence over time. In short, our findings support the notion that the collective understanding of violence in the Netherlands is developing toward a broader understanding of violence, beyond the context of crime, war. Specifically, in recent years the term violence is increasingly used in association with issues of social injustice.

title: Sexual assault-related interactions, social reactions in the initial months following assault: A daily diary study
authors: Reeves, Jonathan W, Mohr, Jenna, Dworkin, Emily R
keywords: daily diaries; disclosure; sexual assault; social reactions; trauma
abstract: Most sexual assault survivors disclose to informal supporters, receive both negative, positive social reactions. Converging evidence suggests that the first months after sexual assault are a period of increased support-seeking that may be uniquely important to survivors' recovery, especially among survivors at risk of chronic post-traumatic stress, alcohol misuse. However, no research has examined when, how often survivors talk about their assault, what social reactions they receive during this time. As such, the goal of this study was to characterize the day-to-day assault-related interactions, social reactions received by a high-risk group of survivors during the first months following sexual assault. Adult female survivors of past-10-week sexual assault with elevated assault-related post-traumatic stress, alcohol use (N = 41) completed a baseline assessment, daily diaries over 21 days as part of a larger mHealth clinical trial. Results demonstrated that assault-related interactions occurred on an average of 24.4\% of days (range: 1-14 days), were more likely to occur earlier in the daily dairy period,, decreased in frequency over time. Across days, most survivors (75\%) received both positive, negative reactions in these interactions, whereas fewer (20\%) received only positive reactions, no one received only negative reactions. These findings suggest that survivors commonly have assault-related interactions with their supporters in the initial aftermath of the assault, that receiving both positive, negative social reactions is typical. Findings could inform future early interventions aiming to improve supporter reactions, better support survivors' recovery.

title: Criminogenic, noncriminogenic needs in men, women who self-report intimate partner violence
authors: Radatz, Dana L, Hilton, N Zoe
abstract: Little is known regarding the criminogenic needs of men, women who self-report intimate partner violence (IPV). We examined criminogenic, noncriminogenic needs of men, women within the general population who self-reported in three groups: perpetrating physical IPV, perpetrating non-IPV physical violence,, nonviolence perpetration. The sample included 847 men, 1437 women from the Interpersonal Conflict, Resolution (iCOR) Study. Those who self-reported IPV exhibited criminogenic, noncriminogenic needs, ranging from antisocial personality patterns (10\%) to criminal associates (69\%). Participants who self-reported engaging in IPV had the most criminogenic, noncriminogenic needs, had similar needs to those reporting non-IPV violence,, had consistently more needs than the nonviolence group. Overall, women reported more noncriminogenic needs than men. Community-based IPV treatment programs accepting individuals from multiple referral sources should anticipate variation in criminogenic, noncriminogenic needs among participants, especially relative to gender, referral type.

title: Jurisdictional resource factors influencing adoption, implementation of the Public Safety Assessment during pretrial
authors: Grodensky, Catherine A, Comfort, Megan, Trudeau, James, Tibaduiza, Elizabeth, Demichele, Matthew
abstract: Criminal legal systems are increasingly adopting actuarial pretrial assessments which use statistical formulas to estimate individuals’ probability of adhering to pretrial requirements, guide the conditions of their supervision. A large gap in the study of pretrial assessments is due to inattention to implementation of these assessments in real-world settings. We conducted qualitative research examining personnel, data resource factors that influenced adoption, implementation of one pretrial assessment, the Public Safety Assessment (PSA) in seven counties in the United States. Qualitative interviews with legal, community actors were conducted, supplemented with implementation process data to elucidate personnel, data capacity factors impacting PSA adoption, implementation. Findings suggest that generally, jurisdictions with existing pretrial services programs were more likely to adopt the PSA, to encounter fewer barriers to implementation due to personnel, data infrastructure. Implications for PSA adoption, implementation in future pretrial settings are discussed.

title: The addition, expansion of demographic characteristics in the NCVS
authors: Harrell, Erika, Tapp, Susannah N
abstract: One of the advantages of the National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) is that it is a large-scale data collection that allows data to be analyzed on various subpopulations. Since the survey’s inception, there have been changes to the population, law,, areas of public interest. In July of 2016, questions were added to the NCVS on citizenship, veteran status, sexual orientation,, gender identity. In addition, changes were made to existing questions on disability status, household income. This allowed for analysis of criminal victimization against more demographic groups. This article discusses these changes, provides estimates of violent victimization by these demographic characteristics.

title: Prison personnel solutions for reducing, improving the appropriate use, effectiveness of extended restrictive housing
authors: Mears, Daniel P, Pesta, George B, Aranda-Hughes, Vivian
abstract: Critiques of extended restrictive housing (ERH), used to manage incarcerated persons deemed to pose a threat to prison order, safety, have led to calls for reducing its use. There is a need for guidance about how to achieve this goal. Drawing on a qualitative study of restrictive housing in Florida, we glean insights from personnel about (1) how to reduce the need for, use of ERH, (2) how, when needed, to ensure its appropriate use, effectiveness. Findings point to many possible solutions for reducing ERH, facilitating appropriate, effective use of it. They also reveal that personnel support reforms that would reduce ERH, change how it operates. Implications for research, policy are discussed.

title: A comprehensive analysis of labor trafficking cases in the United States: An 11-year review
authors: Dominguez, Ezequiel Y, Sandal, Megan E, Pukalo, Lauren M, Roe-Sepowitz, Dominique
abstract: Despite increasing attention to human trafficking since the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000, knowledge gaps about labor trafficking remain. Issues such as legal inconsistencies, sector-specific vulnerabilities,, limited training for stakeholders hinder effective prosecution, often leading to outcomes that inadequately address the gravity of these crimes. While research has focused primarily on victims, less attention has been given to perpetrators. This exploratory study examines labor trafficking arrests from 2011 to 2022, using descriptive analysis to profile traffickers, assess control methods,, explore trends in criminal prosecution. Findings emphasize the need for targeted interventions, improved data collection,, standardized legal frameworks to better address labor trafficking in the U.S.

title: Assessing the impact of safety interventions on open drug markets in a small Swedish municipality using synthetic control methods
authors: Ceccato, Vania, Jorge, Marco Antonio, Gliori, Gabriel
abstract: Abstract Objectives We analyze the impact of the “Stoppa droghandeln” (“Stop the drug trade”) program, a set of safety interventions aimed at reducing crime, particularly drug-related crimes, in a small Swedish municipality (Österåker) from 2018 to 2023. Methods We use a count-based synthetic control approach to compare police crime data before, after beginning the safety interventions (“Stop the drug trade”). This quasi-experimental design was used to infer the causal effects of “Stop the drug trade” on crime, using an evaluation framework including several robustness tests with different crime types. Cluster detection analysis was also used to monitor potential changes in the geography of open drug markets. Results In 2023, Österåker performed better than 82\% of all Swedish municipalities for drug-related offenses. Estimates indicate that 3221 crimes were prevented in Österåker, including 589 less drug-related offenses. However, the non-significant p-values suggest that Österåker’s crime reduction did not outperform most other municipalities. While this could be due to other municipalities implementing their own interventions, the magnitude, consistency of the treatment effects across crime types in Österåker make it unlikely that these results occurred by chance. In terms of geography, clusters of drug-related offenses were stable,, after the interventions, they became more concentrated in particular places. Conclusions This study’s findings underscore the potential impact of a blend of social, situational crime prevention interventions to reduce drug-related offenses, other crimes in a small municipality. The Österåker case demonstrates that strategies should target specific types of crime, monitor possible shifts in crime concentration across different parts of the study area over time. The synthetic control method helped isolate the impact of safety interventions on drug-related crime, demonstrating its value as a tool for policy evaluation.

title: Revalidation of the First Step Act risk assessment: A test of predictive strength, dynamic validity,, racial/ethnic neutrality
authors: Labrecque, Ryan M, Hester, Rhys, Gwinn, Jason
abstract: The First Step Act mandated the development, implementation a risk, needs assessment system for the Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP). In response, the Prisoner Assessment Tool Targeting Estimated Risk, Needs (PATTERN) was created to assess the risk of recidivism among each person in BOP custody. This investigation represents the first external validation of PATTERN. Results indicated PATTERN is highly predictive of both general, violent recidivism, individuals are capable of changing risk scores, levels while in custody,, changes in risk levels are associated with meaningful differences in recidivism risk. Although PATTERN was accurate in predicting recidivism across all five racial/ethnic groups examined, it also overpredicted recidivism among some groups, underpredicted recidivism for others.

title: The code in the corridors: School victimization, the code of the Street
authors: Erickson, Jacob H, Bryson, Sara L, Sivils, Lucy, Fernandez, Jessica
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: While previous research demonstrates the negative consequences of victimization at school, less research has examined the link between victimization in school, adherence to the code of the street. Using two waves from the Gang Resistance Education, Training (G.R.E.A.T.) data, the current study investigated the impact of school victimization on street code adherence. Results indicated a general measure of school victimization was significantly associated with increased street code adherence at a later wave. We disaggregated this measure to assess the relationship between specific indicators of school victimization, increased street code adherence. Being attacked or threatened while traveling to or from school or while at school, having rumors or lies spread about oneself,, having sexual jokes or gestures directed at youth at school were related to street code adherence. Having things stolen at school, being made fun of for appearance or speech were not significantly associated with street code adherence. We discuss the theoretical, practical implications for these findings.

title: Progressive politics, policy setting: Examining criminal justice reform efforts by Black prosecutors
authors: Henry, Tri Keah S, Fordham, Tyeisha, Mitchell, Julius
abstract: Increasing awareness of racial disparities in case processing, sentencing has led justice reform advocates to challenge locally elected officials, specifically chief prosecutors, to address disparate treatment through criminal justice reforms. Elected prosecutors within across several jurisdictions have attempted to address these concerns by adopting “smart-on-crime” policies. However, the extent to which chief prosecutors have adopted such policies has been unexplored empirically. Additionally, little is known about prosecutors’ support for these changes in smaller jurisdictions. The current study explores the political platforms, reform efforts of progressive-oriented prosecutors, highlighting the reform efforts of Black chief prosecutors. Findings suggest that reformed-minded Black prosecutors adopt policies aimed at addressing disparate treatment, positively influencing public perceptions, legitimacy of the office.

title: Does procedural justice matter in probation? Investigating the relationship between procedural just treatment, law-abiding behavior among a sample of high-risk offenders
authors: Buckner, Zachary, Martin, Shanda, Norris, Katherine, Walker, D'andre
abstract: Community supervision programs are instrumental for reducing the prison population, successfully reintegrating offenders back into society. Prior literature suggests that supportive relationships between legal authorities, their clients may foster law-abiding behavior. Using data from the Serious, Violent Offender Reentry Initiative (SVORI) program (N = 781), the current study investigates whether fair (procedurally just) treatment by community supervision officers is associated with compliance, receiving a formal violation. Findings from multivariate analyses suggest that individuals who perceive their supervising officer as treating them procedurally just are more likely to comply with directives, less likely to receive formal violations. Such findings underscore the importance of legal authorities treating probationers with dignity, respect. Policy implications, limitations are discussed.

title: Policing conspiracy theorists: the importance of procedural justice policing, trust
authors: Murphy, Kristina
abstract: PurposeThe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic brought out the best in people, but it also brought out the worst in people. Authorities grappled with the proliferation of misinformation, belief in conspiracy theories, distrust of authorities, anti-social behaviour. As frontline enforcers of COVID-19 restrictions, police were confronted with these attitudes, behaviours every day. This study examines whether the perceived trustworthiness of police during the pandemic – particularly procedural justice – protected public trust in police, reduced conspiracy theory uptake.Design/methodology/approachThis paper uses survey data collected from 779 Australians during the COVID-19 pandemic.FindingsFindings revealed that individuals who perceived police as untrustworthy during the pandemic, as well as those scoring high on conspiracy propensity, were less likely to trust police, were more likely to endorse COVID-19-specific conspiracy theories. Further, trust mediated the relationship between procedural justice, endorsement of conspiracy theories,, conspiracy propensity moderated the relationship between procedural justice, endorsement of conspiracy theories. Specifically, procedural justice protected trust most strongly for those low on conspiracy propensity, but reduced endorsement of COVID-19 conspiracy theories most strongly for those high on conspiracy propensity. Together, the findings show that procedural justice policing is critical for protecting trust in police, for mitigating conspiracy theory uptake.Originality/valueThe study makes a novel contribution to the policing, trust, conspiracy theory literature as it is the first to test whether conspiracy propensity moderates the relationship between procedural justice on peoples’ trust in police, their endorsement of conspiracy theories.

title: Universal Sexual Violence Intervention effects in a cluster-randomized trial: Moderation by sexual orientation
authors: Coulter, Robert W S, Gartner, Rachel E, Cramer, Casey, Smith, Emil K, Abebe, Kaleab Z, Miller, Elizabeth
keywords: cluster-randomized controlled trial; college health; sexual minority; sexual violence; young adults;CampusCrime;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: Sexual minority (e.g., gay/lesbian, bisexual,, queer) students are more likely than their heterosexual peers to experience sexual violence (SV) during college. Interventions that prevent SV, improve SV care-seeking behaviors for sexual minority students are lacking. Giving Information for Trauma Support, Safety (GIFTSS) is an evidence-based universal SV intervention implemented by providers during college health, counseling visits. Compared to controls, GIFTSS participants reported greater self-efficacy to use SV harm reduction strategies, SV disclosure during clinical visits. However, GIFTSS' effectiveness for sexual minority participants is unknown. The current study examines whether sexual orientation moderates GIFTSS' effects on numerous SV-related outcomes (i.e., to test whether intervention effects at 4, 12 months differed based on sexual orientation). Across 28 college campuses in Pennsylvania, West Virginia, 2,291 students participated in a two-arm cluster-randomized controlled trial. We used mixed models with two-, three-way interaction terms to test whether sexual orientation modified GIFTSS' effects at 4-, 12-month follow-up on participants': SV recognition; knowledge of, self-efficacy to enact SV harm reduction strategies; intentions to intervene; knowledge of, self-efficacy to use SV-related services; SV disclosure during visits;, recent SV exposure. Overall, 22.1\% of participants were sexual minorities (n = 507). Sexual orientation moderated GIFTSS effectiveness as indicated by significant three-way interaction (p = .01) at 12-month follow-up,, knowledge of SV services decreased for heterosexual participants (β = -.23) but increased for sexual minority participants (β = .23). Our study indicates that universal provider-based education may promote greater knowledge of SV services among sexual minority than heterosexual participants,, population-specific interventions are needed that reduce sexual minority students' SV exposure, service utilization,, other critical aspects of SV prevention on university campuses.Clinical Trial Registration: Registry name: College Health Center-based Alcohol, Sexual Violence Intervention (GIFTSS), Registration number: NCT02355470, Web link: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ct2/show/NCT02355470, Deidentified individual participant data will not be made available.

title: We Don't Haze: Testing the effectiveness of a video-based hazing prevention training for college students
authors: Kerschner, David J, Allan, Elizabeth J
keywords: alcohol, drugs; bullying; hazing; prevention; violence;CampusCrime;321\_SA実証研究
abstract: This research reports findings from a study to explore the efficacy of a video-based training with college students to determine the extent to which the training shifted student perceptions of hazing, increased willingness, ability to intervene in situations where hazing is occurring,, altered student perceptions of hazing social norms. The study included two experimental groups, a control group at each of the three data-gathering sessions at three U.S. universities. Each of the universities belonged to the Hazing Prevention Consortium, had demonstrated a willingness to prevent hazing on their campuses. The 17-minute hazing prevention documentary We Don't Haze, developed using a bystander intervention framework, was administered in two experimental conditions: video-only, video plus facilitated discussion. Participants (n = 318) were members of a leadership development program, resident advisors,, club sport athletes, were randomly assigned to one of the two treatment groups or the control group. Students who viewed the video-based training, students who viewed the video, engaged in a follow-up facilitated discussion significantly shifted their perceptions of hazing, indicated an increased willingness, ability to intervene, help others who are experiencing or have experienced hazing, compared to students who viewed a general leadership video. The results of this study indicate that the tested hazing prevention trainings-both the stand-alone video, We Don't Haze,, the video plus discussion-hold promise for strengthening knowledge of the full range of harm associated with hazing, while amplifying perceptions that support hazing prevention, diminishing perceptions that contribute to normalizing hazing.

title: The impact of COVID-19 on crime: A systematic review
authors: Hoeboer, C M, Kitselaar, W M, Henrich, J F, Miedzobrodzka, E J, Wohlstetter, B, Giebels, E, Meynen, G, Kruisbergen, E W, Kempes, M, Olff, M, de Kogel, C H
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: AbstractCOVID-19 caused a great burden on the healthcare system, led to lockdown measures across the globe. These measures are likely to influence crime rates, but a comprehensive overview on the impact of COVID-19 on crime rates is lacking. The aim of the current study was to systematically review evidence on the impact of COVID-19 measures on crime rates across the globe. We conducted a systematic search in several databases to identify eligible studies up until 6–12-2021. A total of 46 studies were identified, reporting on 99 crime rates about robberies (n = 12), property crime (n = 15), drug crime (n = 5), fraud (n = 5), physical violence (n = 15), sexual violence (n = 11), homicides (n = 12), cybercrime (n = 3), domestic violence (n = 3), intimate partner violence (n = 14),, other crimes (n = 4). Overall, studies showed that most types of crime temporarily declined during COVID-19 measures. Homicides, cybercrime were an exception to this rule, did not show significant changes following COVID-19 restrictions. Studies on domestic violence often found increased crime rates,, this was particularly true for studies based on call data rather than crime records. Studies on intimate partner violence reported mixed results. We found an immediate impact of COVID-19 restrictions on almost all crime rates except for homicides, cybercrimes, intimate partner violence.

title: ``everything that is here, I have lived'': A triangulated analysis of an intimate partner violence assessment tool in Curitiba, Brazil
authors: Signorelli, Marcos Claudio, Guimarães da Rocha, Raiza Wallace, Xavier Hall, Casey D, Prado, Sandra Marques, Evans, Dabney P
keywords: Brazil; cross-cultural comparison; intimate partner violence; surveys, questionnaires; violence against women
abstract: Using a mixed-methods triangulation approach we piloted the Composite Abuse Scale-Brazilian version (CAS-Brazil) at the House of the Brazilian Woman of Curitiba among 62 survivors of intimate partner violence, four professionals serving survivors to assess its feasibility for use. Quantitative data were tabulated using descriptive statistics while qualitative data were recorded, coded,, thematically analyzed. Four qualitative domains emerged: (a) conceptual understanding; (b) item definitions; (c) women's experiences;, (d) professionals' perspectives. Comprehension of the CAS-Brazil appeared high across participants from diverse backgrounds. Professionals viewed it as highly feasible for use in Brazilian cross-sectoral services to support survivor decision-making.

title: Social reactions to disclosures of intimate partner stalking, unwanted pursuit behaviors: Associations with PTSD, academic outcomes,, empowerment
authors: Lietzau, Stephanie B, Aiken, Brianne E, Cooney, Caroline C, Dardis, Christina M
keywords: PTSD; academic outcomes; disclosure; empowerment; social reactions; stalking
abstract: Among college survivors of unwanted pursuit behaviors (UPBs; 40.1\%, n = 189) or intimate partner stalking (IPS, i.e., UPBs causing emotional distress; 32.1\%, n = 151), the present study examined effects of social reactions to disclosures on post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptomatology, academic outcomes,, personal empowerment. Compared to UPB survivors, IPS survivors were more likely to disclose, reported higher positive, negative reactions to disclosure as well as greater frequency of UPBs/IPS, IPV,, PTSD symptoms. Among both groups, only negative social reactions were positively associated with PTSD symptoms. However, among IPS (but not UPB) survivors, only positive social reactions were related to academic outcomes, empowerment when controlling for PTSD, IPS frequency. Implications for research, practice are discussed.

title: Ambient temperature, deaths from homicide in Brazil during 2010-2019: A nationwide space-time-stratified case-crossover study
authors: Mahendran, Rahini, Xu, Rongbin, Yu, Pei, Coelho, Micheline S Z S, Saldiva, Paulo H N, Li, Shanshan, Guo, Yuming
keywords: Temperature; case-crossover design; climate change; homicide
abstract: RESEARCH QUESTION: Previous evidence suggests a positive association between temperature, homicide, but the association was less clear in Brazil where homicide is one of the leading causes of death. This study aimed to quantify the association between ambient daily temperature, homicides in Brazil with potential lag effects, to quantify the temperature attributed fractions of homicides in Brazil. METHODS: A space-time-stratified case-crossover design with distributed lag models was used to evaluate the temperature-homicide association from 1·1·2010 to 31·12·2019 in Brazil. The odds ratios (OR), attributable fractions, their confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. RESULTS: Overall every 5°C increase in daily mean temperature was associated with a 10·6\% (OR=1·106, 95\% CI: 1·085-1·127) increase in homicidal deaths at lag 0-8 days. The temperature-homicide association is stronger for females, elderly, homicides by fights, sharp objects or firearm,, in North region. During the study period, 1·8\% (95\% CI: 1·1\%-2·7\%) of homicides could be attributed to temperature above immediate-region-specific median temperature corresponding to 10,921 additional deaths (95\% CI: 6,350-15,372). CONCLUSION: Our nationwide study suggests that the homicides in Brazil may increase with temperature, recommends targeted preventions for certain risk groups to high temperature, considering future climate change circumstances.

title: Techno-digital policing, speculative fictions: Towards a criminology of the future
authors: Campbell, Elaine
abstract: This paper argues for a criminology of the future. This matters at a time when the accelerating use of technologically-supported, digitally enhanced (techno-digital) policing methods outpaces our ability to take stock of their social, criminal justice effects. Criminology, policing studies have been swift to address the organisational, operational complexities of techno-digital transformations,, have raised critical questions of the politico-ethical implications of this qualitatively different paradigm of policing. However, this scholarship remains marginal to,, is eclipsed by futures-facing technoscientific research agendas which continually bring the future into being through practices of building, inventing, designing, experimenting. Criminology steps lightly, if at all, into the future. Trapped by the conventions of retrospective analyses, the discipline has difficulty engaging with uncertainty, the unknown,, is reluctant to speculate on worlds-to-come. This paper works towards a criminology of the future,, does so by firstly, drawing on Jasanoff’s notion of sociotechnical imaginaries to unpack the strategic, forward-looking discourse of contemporary techno-digital policing;, secondly, using science fiction – specifically cyberpunk cinema – as an analytical tool for probing the possible futures of today’s techno-digital investments. The speculative fictions of cyberpunk films can guide, warn against, anticipate, inspire innovative frames of reference which not only raise difficult, incisive questions about the transformative complexities of techno-digital innovation, but also bring criminology into productive alliance with the sub-disciplinary fields of futures, cultural, film, policing, science, technology studies.

title: Citizen empowerment as a police force multiplier: Reproducing social domination through a 21st century personal safety app
authors: Turner, Justin, Milburn, Travis
abstract: Citizen is a digital mapping platform, personal safety app that boasts over 10 million users in the United States. Through the platform, users can report crimes, map safe routes, or rely on the app’s other functions to protect themselves from dangerous situations. Sold on a promise of empowerment, Citizen markets itself as a 21st century technology capable of repairing the ills of our social world. In this article we analyze how Citizen taps into the desire for control, safety, urges its users to actively protect their own communities. As such, we suggest that while surveillant in nature, Citizen revolves around the force inherent to police power, transforming its users via police power by first integrating them into their social platform. Ultimately, Citizen reminds us that police power is not limited to ideological or violent exchanges, but can be a compelling solution to community problems. Rather than a progressive fix to the issues between policing, communities, however, we find that Citizen offers an expansion of police power at the individual scale, reproducing social domination both at the level of capital, the state.

title: Security, suspicion,, surveillance? There’s an app for that
authors: Kennedy, Liam, Coelho, Madelaine
keywords: Security; Apps; Nextdoor; Crime; Neoliberalism; Race;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: Despite the recent rise in popularity of mobile safety applications, social scientists have yet to examine these applications in any considerable depth. In this paper we undertake the case studies of bSafe, Citizen,, Nextdoor – analyzing promotional materials, blog posts – in order to further theorize digital security consumption, the potential concomitant social harms. We find these app companies frame crime, risk in ways that obscure the structural elements that precede crime, encourage social divisions. Drawing from over 30,000 user reviews, we speculate about the ways these apps might shape understandings, feelings,, experiences of risk, crime,, victimization. A closer examination of these apps is particularly urgent given these digital technologies have been mobilized in similar ways to respond to the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: A content analysis of personal safety apps: Are they keeping us safe or making us more vulnerable?
authors: Maxwell, L, Sanders, A, Skues, J, Wise, L
keywords: personal safety apps; public violence; vulnerability;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: Despite personal safety apps claiming to increase safety, few studies have examined the usefulness of such apps in reducing public stranger violence. A content analysis of personal safety apps available in the iTunes store, Google Play identified location-based services, personal alarms, crowd-sourced hot spot data,, geofencing as the most common features. The majority of apps offered interventions either at the time of the event or post-event, suggesting that they may reduce a user's fear of crime but have limited usefulness in reducing vulnerability to victimization. Implications for users, app designers,, key stakeholders are discussed.

title: “Now you’re connected”: Carceral visuality, police power on MobilePatrol
authors: Revier, Kevin
abstract: Police increasingly rely on new media software for public communication, policing operations. One such software is MobilePatrol: Public Safety App, a free to use mobile phone application marketed by data, analytics company Appriss Safety. It compiles information including mug shot photos, sex offender lists,, most wanted profiles for public access. To capture carceral visuality on the application, I conduct an ethnographic content analysis of police use in upstate New York. I penned a daily user log, took in-app “screenshots”,, analyzed user product reviews. I find that MobilePatrol reinforces an emerging new carceral visibility where an assemblage of police records are rapidly disseminated for widespread consumption, further driving data-led state entrenchment into the public sphere.

title: Surveillance does not equal safety: Police, data, consent on dating apps
authors: Stardust, Zahra, Gillett, Rosalie, Albury, Kath
abstract: As dating apps continue to receive pressure from civil society, media, governments to address a range of safety concerns, technology companies have developed, deployed a spate of new safety features. Taken together, these features rely upon increased surveillance, partnerships with both technology start-up companies, law enforcement agencies proposed as responses to sexual harassment, abuse. In this article, we draw on empirical accounts of app use –, popular media reporting – to problematise commonsense assumptions about dating apps, safety, technology, policing, surveillance. Where so-called safety features involve increased surveillance, techno-carceral solutionism, there is potential to make users less safe – particularly for app users who are marginalised or stigmatised on the basis of their race, sexuality, gender, health status, employment or disability. Instead of the impetus to ‘datafy’ consent by documenting evidence of sexual transactions, or to monitor users by sharing data with police, we argue that a more effective approach to safety must extend the notion of ‘consent culture’ to encompass a consent-based approach to collecting, storing,, sharing user data – including seeking consent from users about how, whether their data is sold, monetised or shared with third parties or law enforcement.

title: Weight loss-there is an app for that! But does it adhere to evidence-informed practices?
authors: Breton, Emily R, Fuemmeler, Bernard F, Abroms, Lorien C
abstract: Little is known about how much smartphone apps for weight control adhere to evidence-informed practices. The aim of this study was to review, summarize the content of available weight control apps. Information on content, user rating,, price was extracted from iTunes on September 25, 2009. Apps (n = 204) were coded for adherence to 13 evidence-informed practices for weight control. Latent class analysis was used to identify subgroups of apps based on endorsement practices. Only a small percentage of apps had five or more of the 13 practices (15\%). Latent class analysis revealed three main types of apps: diet, physical activity,, weight journals (19\%); dietary advice, journals (34\%);, weight trackers (46\%). User ratings were not associated with apps from these three classes. Many apps have insufficient evidence-informed content. Research is needed that seeks to develop, improve,, evaluate these apps.

title: Who uses mobile phone health apps, does use matter? A secondary data analytics approach
authors: Carroll, Jennifer K, Moorhead, Anne, Bond, Raymond, LeBlanc, William G, Petrella, Robert J, Fiscella, Kevin
keywords: Internet; cell phone; health behavior; health promotion; mobile applications; smartphone;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: BACKGROUND: Mobile phone use, the adoption of healthy lifestyle software apps (``health apps'') are rapidly proliferating. There is limited information on the users of health apps in terms of their social demographic, health characteristics, intentions to change,, actual health behaviors. OBJECTIVE: The objectives of our study were to (1) to describe the sociodemographic characteristics associated with health app use in a recent US nationally representative sample; (2) to assess the attitudinal, behavioral predictors of the use of health apps for health promotion;, (3) to examine the association between the use of health-related apps, meeting the recommended guidelines for fruit, vegetable intake, physical activity. METHODS: Data on users of mobile devices, health apps were analyzed from the National Cancer Institute's 2015 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS), which was designed to provide nationally representative estimates for health information in the United States, is publicly available on the Internet. We used multivariable logistic regression models to assess sociodemographic predictors of mobile device, health app use, examine the associations between app use, intentions to change behavior,, actual behavioral change for fruit, vegetable consumption, physical activity,, weight loss. RESULTS: From the 3677 total HINTS respondents, older individuals (45-64 years, odds ratio, OR 0.56, 95\% CI 0.47-68; 65+ years, OR 0.19, 95\% CI 0.14-0.24), males (OR 0.80, 95\% CI 0.66-0.94),, having degree (OR 2.83, 95\% CI 2.18-3.70) or less than high school education (OR 0.43, 95\% CI 0.24-0.72) were all significantly associated with a reduced likelihood of having adopted health apps. Similarly, both age, education were significant variables for predicting whether a person had adopted a mobile device, especially if that person was a college graduate (OR 3.30). Individuals with apps were significantly more likely to report intentions to improve fruit (63.8\% with apps vs 58.5\% without apps, P=.01), vegetable (74.9\% vs 64.3\%, P<.01) consumption, physical activity (83.0\% vs 65.4\%, P<.01),, weight loss (83.4\% vs 71.8\%, P<.01). Individuals with apps were also more likely to meet recommendations for physical activity compared with those without a device or health apps (56.2\% with apps vs 47.8\% without apps, P<.01). CONCLUSIONS: The main users of health apps were individuals who were younger, had more education, reported excellent health,, had a higher income. Although differences persist for gender, age,, educational attainment, many individual sociodemographic factors are becoming less potent in influencing engagement with mobile devices, health app use. App use was associated with intentions to change diet, physical activity, meeting physical activity recommendations.

title: The role of lifestyle, personal characteristics on fear of victimization among university students
authors: Lee, Daniel R, Hilinski-Rosick, Carly M
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: The fear of crime has been both theoretically, empirically connected to a complex relationship of situational context (e.g., time of day, location), personal characteristics (e.g., age, race, gender, personal, vicarious victimization). Building off of routine activities, lifestyle-exposure theory, this research extends the understanding of these relationships by examining the impact of lifestyle activities (e.g., consumption of alcohol, illicit drugs,, time away from residence), personal characteristics (e.g., direct, vicarious victimization) on the fear of various crimes across temporal situations, among a sample of college, university students. The results indicate that fear of crime varies by crime type, that certain demographic, lifestyle characteristics, experiences with victimization affect students’ fear of crime. Although no evidence was found to suggest that fear of theft varies by temporal context (i.e., during the day or at night), certain characteristics, such as gender, perceived risk,, avoidance behaviors, have varying relationships with fear of violent crimes when considering time of day. The findings suggest that future research should examine more critically the relationship that lifestyles, personality, gender,, time of day have with the fear of crime.

title: How transport users perceive personal safety apps
authors: McCarthy, Orla Thérèse, Caulfield, Brian, O'Mahony, Margaret
journal: Transportation research. Part F, Traffic psychology, behaviour
abstract: Fear of crime, a perceived sense of being unsafe have the potential to discourage individuals from using public transport. This paper presents analysis of the results of a survey on aspects of personal safety apps, how individuals perceive them in relation to their personal safety, privacy, their preference to purchase them. It explores their willingness to download for free or purchase such an app, their impression of features that an app might include such as revealing their location, how they would rate police force monitoring if included as a feature of the app, finally how they would rate a personal safety app against other technologies used to improve perceived transport user safety. The results show that the majority of respondents would consider downloading a personal safety app. Lower levels of engagement with technology, a higher level of education, being resident in the city of Dublin (as opposed to surrounding regions), privacy concerns tended to make females less likely to consider downloading the app. These findings were not repeated for males. The results suggest that younger respondents were more likely to be negatively impacted by the inclusion of a facility to report location in an emergency on the app, while the older age groups were more likely to be unaffected. For the location tracking feature, cluster membership, gender, resident outside Dublin were significant. Less than half of the respondents would be negatively influenced in their decision to buy the app if a cost of €1.79 were introduced. When respondents were asked about the inclusion of police monitoring as a feature of the app, the results suggested that police monitoring had a more definite effect on perceived personal safety than on privacy.

title: Explaining the gender gap in fear of crime: Assessments of risk, vulnerability among New York City residents
authors: Snedker, Karen A
abstract: In the fear of crime literature, there is a consensus that women consistently report higher levels of fear. I examine how men, women assess their risks in light of prior experience, the environmental conditions that signal risk,, perceived personal vulnerability to provide a more thorough account of the gender disparity. Findings from in-depth interviews with New York City residents suggest that subjective evaluations of vulnerability are strong indicators of fear of crime for men, women. Furthermore, qualitative data reveal that gender assessments of vulnerability are related to issues of socialization, social learning processes, notions of effective agency. Little evidence supports fear of rape as the driving force behind perceived vulnerability for women.

title: The use of mobile phone applications to enhance personal safety from interpersonal violence - an overview of available smartphone applications in the United Kingdom
authors: Ford, Kat, Bellis, Mark A, Judd, Natasha, Griffith, Nel, Hughes, Karen
keywords: Apps; Interpersonal violence; Mobile applications; Mobile technology; Personal safety; Smartphones; Violence prevention;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: BACKGROUND: Interpersonal violence has devastating implications for individuals, families,, communities across the globe, placing a significant burden on health, justice,, social welfare systems. Smartphone technology may provide a platform for violence prevention interventions. However, evidence on the availability, user experience of smartphone applications aimed to prevent violence is underexplored. METHODS: Systematic searches of available smartphone applications marketed for personal safety, violence prevention on the Apple Store (IOS), Google Play (Android) in the United Kingdom were run in May 2021. Relevant applications were downloaded, with data on user reviews, ratings extracted. Included applications were categorised according to their features, functions. Online user reviews were rated according to their sentiment (positive, negative, neutral), thematically analysed. RESULTS: Of 503 applications, 86 apps met review criteria. Only 52 (61\%) apps offered full functionality free of charge. Over half (52\%) of apps were targeted towards the general population, with 16\% targeting women, 13\% targeting families. App functionality varied with 22\% providing an alarm, 71\% sending alerts to pre-designated contacts, 34\% providing evidence capture, 26\% offering educational information. Overall, 71\% of applications had a user rating of four or above. For 61 apps a total of 3,820 user reviews were extracted. Over half (52.4\%) of reviews were rated as having a positive sentiment, with 8.8\% neutral, 38.8\% negative. Key themes across user reviews included positive consequences of app use, technical, usage issues including app reliability, dissatisfaction with the financial cost of some app features, personal data, ethical issues. CONCLUSIONS: Reviews suggest that users find apps for personal safety, violence prevention useful. However, individuals also report them being unreliable, not working as described, having features that others may exploit. Findings have implications for the development of policy on apps to improve personal safety, especially given recent national policy (e.g. UK) discussions about their utility. Without the regulation or accreditation of such technology for quality assurance, reliability, emphasis needs to be placed on ensuring user safety; otherwise vulnerable individuals may continue to place reliance on untested technology in potentially dangerous circumstances.

title: Video games do affect social outcomes: a meta-analytic review of the effects of violent, prosocial video game play: A meta-analytic review of the effects of violent, prosocial video game play
authors: Greitemeyer, Tobias, Mügge, Dirk O
abstract: Whether video game play affects social behavior is a topic of debate. Many argue that aggression, helping are affected by video game play, whereas this stance is disputed by others. The present research provides a meta-analytical test of the idea that depending on their content, video games do affect social outcomes. Data from 98 independent studies with 36,965 participants revealed that for both violent video games, prosocial video games, there was a significant association with social outcomes. Whereas violent video games increase aggression, aggression-related variables, decrease prosocial outcomes, prosocial video games have the opposite effects. These effects were reliable across experimental, correlational,, longitudinal studies, indicating that video game exposure causally affects social outcomes, that there are both short-, long-term effects.

title: Mobile applications addressing violence against women: a systematic review
authors: Eisenhut, Katharina, Sauerborn, Ela, García-Moreno, Claudia, Wild, Verina
keywords: health policy; prevention strategies; public health; systematic review;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: Introduction: Violence against women is a pressing global health problem that is being met with a new intervention strategy-mobile applications. With this systematic review, we provide an initial analysis, functional categorisation of apps addressing violence against women. Methods: We conducted a systematic online search conforming with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews, Meta-Analyses guidelines to identify apps addressing violence against women in five World Bank regions (Europe, Central Asia; North America, Latin America, the Caribbean; Middle East, North Africa; South Asia;, sub-Saharan Africa). Applications with location of initiation in mentioned regions, ≥100 downloads were included. Data on sector, target group(s), year of release, location of initiation, implementation were extracted. By means of a structured qualitative content analysis, applications were then categorised according to their main functions. Results: Of 327 relevant applications, 171 were included into the systematic review, assigned to one of five identified categories of main functions, respectively: emergency, avoidance, education, reporting, evidence building,, supporting apps. The largest proportion (46.78\%) consisted of emergency apps, followed by education, reporting, evidence building, supporting, avoidance apps in descending order. With regards to the geographical distribution of app categories, significant (χ2(20)=58.172; p=0.000) differences among the included regions were found. Conclusion: A vast proportion of apps addressing violence against women primarily draw on one-time emergency or avoidance solutions, as opposed to more preventative approaches. Further research is necessary, critically considering questions of data security, personal safety, efficacy of such mobile health interventions.

title: Comparing crime reporting factors in EU countries
authors: Torrente, Diego, Gallo, Pedro, Oltra, Christian
journal: European journal on criminal policy, research
abstract: Through crime-reporting citizens make their security needs explicit to the police. This information helps the police in the allocation of resources. In the European Union, there are significant differences among countries, both in terms of overall, specific crime-reporting rates. Factors highlighted by the literature that might explain these differences are not entirely satisfactory. There is little comparative research,, most published studies are nation-centred, based on the experience of central, northern European countries,, largely focused on the situational variables related to the criminal incident itself. It is widely assumed that situational variables have a universal explanatory capacity in crime reporting. This article questions this assumption, shows that a number of factors weight differently in explaining national rates. Following a literature review, we identified four groups of causal factors, analysed their explanatory capacity. These are related largely to the incident (rational models), victims’ perception (psychological models). In addition, we also analysed the influence of institutional, community factors. The European Survey on Crime, Safety database was used for our analysis. Results show the existence of two areas in Europe, the north-central area, the south-eastern area, in terms of crime reporting rates, the factors that explain these differences. Rational, psychological models explain crime-reporting practices better in the north-central area. In contrast, socio-demographic variables, social inequalities are more relevant for explaining crime reporting in the south-eastern area of Europe. Institutional variables are also important in eastern countries. Community factors are not significant explanatory variables due to the limitations of indicators available in the database. Our research reveals that crime-reporting is a rather more complex phenomenon than is often assumed,, highlights the limitations of existing knowledge, methodologies on comparative crime-reporting.

title: Rape: is there an app for that? An empirical analysis of the features of anti-rape apps
authors: Bivens, Rena, Hasinoff, Amy Adele
abstract: This study of mobile phone apps designed to prevent sexual violence (n = 215) is a quantitative analysis of all their features (n = 807). We analyze the intended users (victims, bystanders,, perpetrators), rape prevention strategies of each feature, finding that anti-rape app design generally reinforces, reflects pervasive rape myths, by both targeting potential victims, reinforcing stranger-danger. To demonstrate that these limitations are primarily cultural rather than technological, we conclude by imagining apps with similar technical features that resist rather than reinforce rape myths. This study offers an empirical investigation of the relationship between technical design, social norms,, a unique methodology for uncovering the ideologies that underlie design.

title: A survey of the mobile phone-based interventions for violence prevention among women
authors: Sinha, Sunny, Shrivastava, Aviral, Paradis, Christiana
keywords: violence prevention; women; Cellphone-based; ICT; Information Communication Technologies; health; social work practice;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: Information Communication Technologies (ICT), particularly mobile phone technology, has increased the propinquity between individuals by enhancing their ability to frequently communicate with one another through different mediums, like text, audio, video,, emojis. Cell phone technology is being used to combat various social issues, including several public health-related problems such as violence against women. Over the past two decades several cellphone-based apps, including Circle of 6, MyPlan, Panic Button,, Aspire News have been developed in several countries to prevent violence against women. Anecdotal evidence suggests that these apps are effective both as violence prevention, as an intervention tool in public as well as private spaces. However, very little awareness exists among social workers about these mobile phone applications (apps), particularly the capabilities, limitations of these apps. Based on a brief survey, classification of the existing mobile phone apps designed to prevent violence against women, this paper aims to explain how these apps work,, point out their capabilities, limitations so that social workers, public health professionals can better guide their clients in using these technology-based services. It is highly recommended that social workers evaluate how their clients are affected by the use or non-use of violence prevention apps, advocate for their client’s right to digital literacy, internet access.

title: The usage of mobile apps to fight violence against women: A survey on a sample of female students belonging to an Italian university
authors: Tozzo, Pamela, Gabbin, Andrea, Politi, Caterina, Frigo, Anna Chiara, Caenazzo, Luciana
journal: International journal of environmental research, public health
keywords: mobile apps; personal safety; survey; violence against women
abstract: The prevalence of violence against women continues to grow, this plague has had a huge impact from a clinical, social, judicial point of view. For this reason, alongside the efforts made at the legislative level to prevent the phenomenon, to improve assistance to victims in recent years, efforts to contain, better manage this phenomenon have also grown in the extra-legislative sphere: for example, through the application of new technological solutions, safety planning. In recent years, there has been an increase in the marketing of mobile phone apps dedicated to the prevention of violence against women, with different functions, different objectives. The purpose of this study is to investigate the knowledge, propensity to download this type of app in a group of 1782 Italian female university students. This research was performed using an online questionnaire administered to female students attending four different courses (law, medicine, healthcare professionals, political sciences) at one Italian university. Chi-square or Fisher's exact test was used to analyze associations between responses to questionnaire, the type, the year of course. The results show that 62.6\% of our sample are unaware of the existence of these apps, that 79.5\% of the sample would be willing to download one in the future. With regard to whom to turn to after a violent incident, the majority of those interviewed (43.9\%) would turn to the police, not to health facilities. According to our findings, law female students (52.7\%) think, more than any other category, that the most effective way to improve public safety, reduce the number of victims lies in legislative solutions.
