To induce the perception of time pressure, one group was informed that the task would have to be completed under time pressure ( N = 66), whereas the other group did not receive this instruction ( N = 67); although both groups had the same amount of time). Outcomes included the number, quality of hypotheses generated for solving the case. The quality of hypotheses generated was measured against criteria established by expert detectives. Results revealed that time pressure directly decreased the quantity, quality of hypotheses generated. In the relationships, low time urgency moderated the effect of time pressure on the number, quality of hypotheses generated, also low NFC moderated the impact of time pressure on the number of hypotheses generated. Furthermore, the most experienced detectives were least affected by the negative association between time pressure, the quality of hypotheses generated. The findings suggest lower time urgency, lower NFC, more experience are adaptive ‘protective’ factors against the negative impact of time pressure on hypothesis generation within high stakes, uncertain situations such as rape investigations.

title: Policing through social media: a qualitative exploration
authors: Fallik, Seth Wyatt, Deuchar, Ross, Crichlow, Vaughn J, Hodges, Hannah
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Social media, in the past decade, has been used to hold police accountable for their actions. There has been, however, a paucity of empirical research into how law enforcement uses social media. To explore this issue, this paper uses qualitative data emerging from ethnographic research conducted in a Southern American state. Participant observations of police officer deployments were paired with semi-structured interviews with officers from three law enforcement agencies. The extent, ways in which these officers used social media is explored. Findings indicate that social media is used to bring positive attention to law enforcement agencies, aid criminal investigations. Although the positive impact of social media was highlighted in these experiences, persistent problems, challenges also featured in the data. Finally, officer insights were drawn upon to make recommendations for future policing policy, research.

title: Reducing police turnover: Recommendations for the law enforcement agency
authors: Hilal, Susan, Litsey, Bryan
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Law enforcement is a career that offers long-term employment; however, not everyone who enters the profession stays until they retire. Because the costs of employing a police officer can be significant to both the organization, the individual seeking to pursue, maintain a career in law enforcement, identifying ways to reduce police turnover is important. This study captures the experiences of officers who left prematurely, whether voluntarily or involuntarily, to help identify what agencies can do to keep officers long term. Data for this exploratory study was gathered via semi-structured interviews with 36 former police officers. The findings highlighted several common themes that law enforcement agencies could address, including: leadership training, clear, transparent processes, permanent light-duty assignments, shift flexibility, improved morale,, more focus on personal wellness.

title: Police discretion, organizational characteristics,, traffic stops: An analysis of racial disparity in illinois
authors: Nowacki, Jeffrey S, Spencer, Tyrell
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: An important source of racial disparity in policing is traffic enforcement. The level of discretion afforded to officers for traffic enforcement is generally greater than it is for other policing decisions. One way to control misuse of discretion is through minority representation, which is the extent that the racial composition of the police agency matches that of the local community. Using data from the Illinois Department of Transportation (IDOT), the 2013 Law Enforcement Management, Administrative Statistics (LEMAS), this study examines how social context, police organizational variables (e.g., minority representation) relate to enforcement outcomes. We find that organizational measures, including minority representation, relate to written citations, consent search requests. Moreover, non-white population size conditions the effect of minority representation on traffic stops, citations. These results highlight the importance of accounting for both social context, organizational characteristics when research examines discretionary police behavior.

title: A state-of-the-art review on police accountability: What do we know from empirical studies?
authors: Feys, Yinthe, Verhage, Antoinette, Boels, Dominique
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The method, results of a scoping review, based on the principles of a systematic literature review, on police accountability are presented with the aim of providing an overview of the characteristics of empirical research on the topic, the main themes covered in this research tradition. To our knowledge, no systematically conducted review has been undertaken although one could help to identify gaps in the (empirical) literature, give insights into the themes studied in this regard. Three main themes were discovered during the review; aside from police accountability as such, many studies related to police integrity or, to a lesser extent, historical facts concerning police accountability or integrity. Two of the most striking findings were the low number of empirical studies included in our thematic synthesis, the limited amount of methodological information reported in these publications. As such, the authors recommend more empirical research regarding police accountability and, more generally, sufficient methodological reporting when writing a publication.

title: Officer attitudes toward citizen review, professional accountability
authors: Lee, Heeuk D, Collins, Peter A, Hsieh, Ming-Li, Boateng, Francis D, Brody, David
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The practice of citizen review has developed as one method for improving the accountability of law enforcement officers to the general public, to their respective criminal justice organizations. However, little information is available regarding officers’ general perceptions of the citizen review process, as well as the perceptions of those officers who have actually been subject to formal review. This study provides analysis of data collected via a survey of commissioned officers in a large metropolitan police department in the Pacific Northwest. Their attitudes, perceptions of their professional, civilian oversight board, the Offices of Professional Accountability (OPA), were measured,, this study found that police officers with a deeper understating of the OPA system were more willing to report misconduct. Also, police officers who possess higher satisfaction attitudes toward the OPA were more likely to report grievances to it.

title: Good practice case studies in the advancement of women in policing
authors: Ward, Aiyana, Prenzler, Tim
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Research shows that increasing the number of female officers is beneficial to policing. However, women remain a minority in police departments throughout the world,, the better performing departments have, on the whole, achieved female representation at only 25\%, with senior women at 10\%. There is also very little research on effective strategies for making large improvements. Consequently, this study aimed to identify, explain above average achievements in the status of women in policing. Following a worldwide search, five cases were identified: one involved female recruits (North Wales), two involved officer numbers (Cumbria, Surrey),, two involved women in senior ranks (Hertfordshire, South Africa). Efforts to identify possible influences were limited by a lack of information about strategies, including in response to requests for information. However, there were indicators that outcomes were related to senior management commitment, explicit targets, monitoring, flexible employment, a range of support mechanisms such as mentoring, leadership programmes. The findings emphasize the need for more research on what works in optimizing women’s participation in police work.

title: Space, time variations in crime-recording practices within a large municipal police agency
authors: Boivin, Rémi, Ouellet, Frédéric
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: When comparing crime rates across several locations or analysing general trends, it is usually assumed that police statistics are an imperfect, but relatively constant indicator of the phenomenon. ...

title: Source of job satisfaction among South Korean police officers
authors: Jo, Youngoh, Hoover, Larry T
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Studies of police job satisfaction show consistent findings that work-related variables have greater effects than personal demographic factors. Despite the cumulative knowledge about the sources of police officers' job satisfaction, there exist several limitations, including the applicability of the findings drawn from Western studies to the Asian context, differences in the determinants of job satisfaction across organisational subgroups. This study contributes to current literature by examining both phenomena: (1) whether work-related factors dominate for South Korean police officers,, (2) whether determinants of job satisfaction vary across type of duty. Using a sample of 341 Korean police officers, this study found that work-related variables indeed had stronger effects than demographic on job satisfaction in the sample. However, the determinants of job satisfaction differ between patrol officers, clerical officers. Although perceptions of pay, commitment have significant effects on job satisfaction for both groups, autonomy, job security, citizen feedback affect only clerical officers' job satisfaction, but not patrol officers'.

title: Racial profiling in decisions to search: A preliminary analysis using propensity-score matching
authors: Higgins, George E, Jennings, Wesley G, Jordan, Kareem L, Gabbidon, Shaun L
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The objective of the present study was to understand if racial and/or ethnic backgrounds are causal factors in a police officer's decision to search individuals during traffic stops. Using the Police-Public Contact Survey, propensity-score matching, the study results indicate that Blacks are significantly more likely to be searched than Whites. There were no differences, however, in searches between Hispanics, Whites. These findings suggest that race, but not ethnicity, appears to be a causal factor in a police officer's decision to search. The implications of this finding, along with directions for future research, are also discussed.

title: Municipal police officer job satisfaction in Pennsylvania: A study of organisational development in small police departments
authors: Julseth, Jason, Ruiz, James, Hummer, Don
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Current policing literature indicates that the retention rate of patrol officers is in steady decline. On the whole, various policing factors that include fatigue, stress, workload appear to be major reasons for high turnover rates. In order to substantiate patrol officers' views of contemporary policing, we examined their perceptions of issues related to overall job satisfaction, correlating factors. Municipal police officers from 14 south central Pennsylvania police departments located in one mid-size county were surveyed to determine if there were any significant differences or correlations between perceptions of overall job satisfaction, previous research related to satisfaction with administration, shift work, equipment, community support, department morale, policies, procedures. Results indicate that there is an apparent connection between stress, overall job satisfaction. Most notably, higher stress levels, faster rotating shifts, officers' perceptions of department morale were shown to impact the levels of overall job satisfaction.

title: A preliminary examination of crime analysts' views, experiences of comparative Case Analysis
authors: Burrell, Amy, Bull, Ray
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Comparative Case Analysis (CCA), typically conducted by crime analysts, uses crime scene behaviours to try to identify series of crimes committed by the same offender. Accurate identification of series of offences allows the police to pool resources, evidence, thereby boosting the potential to identify, apprehend the offender. This paper discusses the results of a survey of a sample of crime analysts working in two UK police forces about their views, experiences of CCA. The results focus on how CCA is conducted, what evidence, information is considered,, how useful CCA is to criminal investigation. Suggestions for how CCA might be developed further are also included.

title: Comparing the workplace experiences of male, female police officers: Examining workplace problems, stress, jobc satisfaction, consideration of career change
authors: Hassell, Kimberly D, Archbold, Carol A, Stichman, Amy J
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This study examines the interrelationships between four workplace problems, namely the need for mentoring programmes, stress, job satisfaction, consideration of making career changes, to determine whether female officers' workplace experiences differ significantly from male officers. Data were collected from a survey of patrol officers employed in a municipal, Midwestern police department. Surveys were completed by 80 per cent of the sworn patrol officers, producing a sample of 87 officers. The analyses show that police officers who perceive a need for a formal mentoring programme reportedly experience higher levels of workplace stress. The findings also indicate that officers with higher stress levels are less satisfied with their jobs. Further, the analyses indicate that female officers experience their workplaces more similarly to, rather than different from, male officers. To decrease workplace stress, improve job satisfaction in this department, administrators must address the lack of mentoring — for both male, female officers.

title: A comparison of the British Crime Survey, police statistics for a southern English county
authors: Qureshi, Faiza
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The purpose of this research was to examine whether it was possible to use the British Crime Survey (BCS) data on Stop, Search for a southern English police force area (PFA), to compare the findings from the BCS with those from police records. The local-level analysis of the BCS by PFA, recorded police statistics was an attempt to identify the similarities, differences, if any, between the two data sources. The research compares recorded police, BCS statistics for the same geographical police force area of a southern English county, for the period 2003 to 2006. The analysis looks at the number of stops, searches in each data source, presents a comparison of the ratio of persons arrested following a Stop, Search. The distribution of vehicle, pedestrian stops, searches in the two data sources is examined, as well as the demographic characteristics of suspects. The findings show that the BCS is a more accurate measure of stops than police statistics, although both data sources produced a similar pattern in the proportion of searches, arrests. The BCS showed that motor vehicle encounters were the most common form of contact, whereas police statistics showed that it was pedestrian encounters. However, a limited analysis was conducted using the BCS when the data were subdivided to consider age, ethnicity. Above all, the research has drawn attention to the gulf that exists between the two data sources.

title: Police, the reclamation of public places: A study of MacArthur Park in Los Angeles
authors: Sousa, William H, Kelling, George L
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Throughout the 1980s, 1990s, MacArthur Park — a 40-acre public park located near downtown Los Angeles — was widely known to be one of the largest open-air drug markets in Los Angeles. The Alvarado Corridor Initiative, a police-led initiative developed in 2003, was designed to address crime, disorderly behaviour in MacArthur Park through a combination of problem-solving, order-maintenance,, situational crime prevention efforts. This paper assesses the impact of the Alvarado Corridor Initiative using information from interviews, focus groups with neighbourhood residents, business-people, police officers,, other individuals familiar with MacArthur Park. The results suggest that many of the problems in MacArthur Park have been resolved, that the park experienced a turnaround that can be linked to the implementation of the Alvarado Corridor Initiative. In assessing the effectiveness of the Alvarado Corridor Initiative, this paper also provides a commentary on the evolution of public places in the United States, the role that the police can serve in terms of helping to preserve those public places.

title: An empirical study of intelligence strategy implementation
authors: Gottschalk, Petter, Gudmundsen, Yngve Sommerseth
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Strategy implementation suffers from a general lack of academic attention. The need for improved implementation of strategies in law enforcement, policing has been emphasised by both scholars, practitioners. Implementation is important for four reasons. First, the failure to carry out a strategy can cause lost opportunities, duplicated efforts, incompatible organisational units, wasted resources. Second, the extent to which a strategy meets its objectives is determined by implementation. Third, the lack of implementation leaves police officers dissatisfied, reluctant to continue doing strategic planning work. Finally, the lack of implementation creates problems establishing, maintaining priorities in future strategic planning. In this empirical study, implementation of intelligence strategy is studied in a causal relationship with organisation structure, organisation culture. It is found that a knowledge organisation structure has a significant positive influence on the extent of strategy implementation.

title: Examining the link between the forensic quality, customer service quality of police call centre interviews
authors: Leeney, David G, Mueller-Johnson, Katrin
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Police call centre performance is currently assessed using private sector performance measures such as call answer time, customer satisfaction. Police communications, however, place a higher value on the accuracy, efficiency of the caller/call handler interaction than do commercial organisations. This is because the police must also establish, maintain, develop, with the caller, the basis for action to protect the public or bring offenders to justice, in light of the caller's needs, the policing context, resources available at the time. The existing police performance measures for call centre assessment may therefore be inadequate when examined from a forensic perspective. This research fills a gap in the current literature by establishing if a normative evaluation of the police/citizen/call centre interaction was sufficiently linked to the forensic quality of the interview to make the need to secondarily measure forensic quality redundant. This question was explored through an analysis of interview data drawn from two sources: external secondary data relating to service quality, data coded by the researcher relating to forensic quality. Forensic quality of the call was assessed with a newly developed instrument. The research found that real world call centre interviews varied both in terms of service, forensic quality. Furthermore, service quality, forensic quality were statistically unrelated, which means that it did not follow that a call delivering good customer service also delivered a forensically sound call. The implications of this finding for police practice are discussed.

title: Policing, safety, security in public assembly facilities
authors: Frosdick, Steve
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article explores how ‘policing’, in its widest sense, seeks to maintain public safety, security in the places where people gather to view events. The paper begins by clarifying its setting in public assembly facilities, conceiving of ‘policing’ as ‘almost anything done by anyone who controls other people’ (Waddington, 2007). The paper goes on to show how the long history of disasters, disorder in such facilities means that they have to be ‘policed’, outlines the various bodies involved in ‘policing’ them. The paper then discusses the concepts of ‘safety’, ‘security’. ‘Safety’ starts with structural design, maintenance to prevent fire or collapse. It manages capacities, ingress, egress in complex space. It also deals with aspects of human behaviours, emergencies, evacuations. ‘Security’, on the other hand, addresses the prevention, detection of crime, the terrorist threat, the maintenance of public tranquillity. The paper seeks to differentiate the terms ‘safety’, ‘security’ with reference to four alternative models. Two forms of the integrated whole in which ‘security’ is conceived as a subset of ‘safety’, or vice versa, are outlined, commended as best practice. However, the historical practice, current policy reasons why ‘safety’, ‘security’ have been treated as either separate or overlapping concepts are also explored. The discussion refers to various facility disasters to illustrate the serious consequences when policing policy, practice overlooks ‘safety’ or allows ‘security’, ‘safety’ to get out of balance.

title: An exploration of the juxtaposition of professional, political accountability in local law enforcement management
authors: LaFrance, Casey, Allen, Jennifer M
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This study focuses on one arena of public administration in which the balancing act between various accountability considerations is especially visible: local law enforcement management,, one of the many accountability conflicts that law enforcement CEOs face: the intersection of political, professional accountability streams. There are two guiding questions in this study. First, when faced with a choice between political, professional accountability, how do county sheriffs, municipal police chiefs act? Next, what factors do these managers believe to be crucial in the development of their officers' use of professional discretion? This study provides a preliminary glimpse of local law enforcement managers' responses to these questions. Consistent with the literature on officer discretion, these managers' responses cite five factors that affect the development of discretion for new recruits: (1) experience, (2) formal training, (3) community norms, (4) external systemic actors,, (5) peer influence, mentorship conducted in the context of the informal organisation. Analysis of these managers' responses indicates that, in the aggregate, professional autonomy is more highly prized than political deference in each type of department. These findings question the conventional wisdom that suggests sheriffs are less professionally accountable than their police chief counterparts.

title: Felonious line-of-duty officer deaths (1995–1999): The impact of tenure, age
authors: Tucker-Gail, Kasey A, Selman, Donna, Kobolt, James R, Hill, Tara
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article examines officer age, employment tenure variables in the FBI Law Enforcement Officers Killed, Assaulted summary from 1995 to 1999. During this time frame, 309 incidents of felonious officer deaths were reported to the FBI. The purpose of this paper is to identify patterns in the data for application within law enforcement when considering training needs over the life cycle of an officer's career,, to conduct original, exploratory research in the field. The research concludes that the combination of 0–4 years of experience combined with the ages 30–39 years was particularly deadly for the years 1995–1999. Finally, based on the findings, considerations for hiring, training, data collection are made.

title: Emotional labour in the context of policing in Victoria: A preliminary analysis
authors: Chapman, David
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Much research has been undertaken, much has been written about the effects of emotional labour in the service, helping industries. While there has been much conjecture as to the definitions of emotional labour, there has been little serious analysis on the effects on police officers of performing emotional labour. On the one hand, the available evidence suggests police officers are among the most stressed employees of all professions, whilst on the other, the limited research on emotional labour, policing makes only tenuous links possible between the performance of emotional labour, high-stress outcomes in policing. This paper reviews emotional labour theory, past studies of employees, the culture within Victoria Police (Australia), their stress claims data. Further research is required to establish a link between performing emotional labour, the stress of police officers.

title: Policing fraud in the private sector: A survey of the FTSE 100 companies in the UK
authors: Brooks, Graham, Button, Mark, Frimpong, Kwabena
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Fraud has increasingly become recognised as a problem in the private sector, with a growing number of estimates of the size of the problem produced by official government bodies, private professional services companies such as KPMG. There have, however, been fewer surveys of the strategies being used by the private sector to tackle fraud. This paper presents findings from a survey of the UK's FTSE 100 companies which produced 32 responses, the strategies they are using to counter fraud. It demonstrates a mixed picture of both good, bad practice, when benchmarked against well-recognised standards for tackling fraud, on issues such as having: a strategy; a designated person responsible for fraud; regular risk assessments; preventative measures; investigative resources, effective relationships with the police. It also calls for further research to be conducted on private sector counter fraud strategies.

title: Explorations in police organisation: An Indian context
authors: Srivastava, Sweta
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The research is concerned with understanding the role of organisational justice,, the parameters of organisational support mechanisms in the sustenance, enhancement of psychological well-being, which in turn was postulated to contribute to a number of organisationally relevant outcome variables, with a focus upon the target group of a security-service organisation personnel. The sample consisted of 270 male lower, middle level respondents from a government security-service (police) organisation, who were located in the eastern, central,, western parts of a large state of north India. Major findings were that internal motivation, ego-resilience, well-being,, organisational justice were significant positive predictors of organisationally relevant outcome variables. Further, organisational justice,, organisational support were found to be positive contributors to well-being, which apparently was needed to alleviate the sense of a lack of psychological well-being that seemed to prevail among the respondents.

title: Gender, victimisation, perceived risk, perceptions of police performance in disadvantaged neighbourhoods
authors: Gainey, Randy R, Payne, Brian K
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Although research on the public's attitudes towards the police has a long history,, gender has long been considered a potential correlate, theoretical, empirical development concerning the role of gender in forming positive or negative attitudes towards the police is limited. In this paper we approach this issue in three ways to understand better how gender may or may not affect attitudes towards the police among a sample of residents in disadvantaged neighbourhoods in two south-eastern cities. We find that the total bivariate effect of gender in the sample is small, not statistically significant. However, there is some evidence that gender plays a distal causal role because women feel less safe or at greater risk of victimisation, but are less likely to be victimised or confronted with a drug dealer. Theoretical, policy implications are provided.

title: The effect of educational differences on the level of job satisfaction in police officers in turkey
authors: Özel, Ali, Bayındır, Nida, İnan, Hatice Zeynep, Özel, Emine
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: In order to maintain the well-being of a country, it is essential to understand the needs of that country's police officers, what affects their job satisfaction. Current literature shows that there are many factors that can impact on a police officer's job satisfaction. The current research examines the job satisfaction of police working in the city of Kutahya, both in central Kutahya, in the counties of Kutahya. The study focused on the relationship between the level of education, job satisfaction for police in central Kutahya, the counties of Kutahya, as well as if the pleasure, dissatisfaction they experience in the organisation is related to demographic factors. Accordingly, the study examined some factors which are assumed to affect job satisfaction, such as communication gaps, friendship, promotion opportunities, management style, fair wages, fair work assignment. The results showed that the level of education does not affect the job satisfaction of police officers who work in central Kutahya or the counties of Kutahya. Moreover, data analysis showed that the police enjoy their job even though they complain about their job, the negative conditions that they experience in their job.

title: Investigating missing person cases: How can we learn where they go or how far they travel?
authors: Shalev, Karen, Schaefer, Martin, Morgan, Alex
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article discusses the need to improve our understanding of where people go when they go missing, its applications for policing policy. The paper will use a pilot study of 70 solved adult missing person cases. The analysis includes frequencies, a measure of distances travelled by missing persons from the location where they went missing to where they were found. The study explores the demographic background of missing persons, examines a variety of travel patterns. The discussion focuses on explaining the spatial patterns of missing persons, the potential to improve police investigations of missing person cases by reducing search areas. Finally, recommendations are made for policy changes.

title: International comparative perspective of police in schools resulting from a Fulbright Alumni Initiatives Award
authors: Briers, Andrew N, Dickmann, Ellyn M
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article outlines the results of a Fulbright Alumni Initiatives Award 2005–8, which provided resources, support for an international school police officer exchange programme between officers in the United States, the United Kingdom. This multi-year exchange programme had several outcomes including exchange opportunities for 11 officers from London, Colorado; the development of a school/community safety curriculum; international collaborative school safety research project planning, implementation;, programme dissemination opportunities. Extensive knowledge, idea sharing resulted from this exchange programme, current as well as future school policing programmes around the world can benefit from the details outlined in this case study.

title: The best police force in the world will not bring down a high crime rate in a materialistic society
authors: Teh, Yik Koon
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The increasing crime rate in a rapidly developing country like Malaysia has caused its citizens to feel unsafe. The Malaysian Government has to increase the police force, review its training programmes. This paper argues that even with the best trained police force, the crime rate will remain high. This is due to the highly capitalistic, materialistic culture of the Malaysian society that has led to the occurrence of elements of Robert Merton's (1938) theory of Anomie — excessive emphasis on monetary goals regardless of the moral status of the means used to achieve them. Steven Messner, Richard Rosenfeld's (2001) Institutional-Anomie theory states that anomic pressure arises when there is an overemphasis on the market ethic that undermines the regulatory power of social norms. This results in individuals feeling an overriding pressure to achieve, at the same time being confronted with weak normative restraints on legitimate means to achieve. The two theories suggest that certain cultural conditions, in combination with certain structural conditions, generate anomie, a high crime rate. At present, Malaysia's capitalistic, materialistic culture has generated cultural, structural conditions that are highly conducive to a high crime rate. Increasing the police force, improving policing will not be enough to reduce the high crime rate.

title: Policing, procedural fairness, public behaviour: A review, critique
authors: Tankebe, Justice
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper provides a brief review, critique of the procedural fairness conception of police legitimacy. It is argued that the theoretical framework is too limited to constitute the basis for any overall legitimacy-based model of policing. Rather, its potential stands to be greatly enhanced if it incorporates other crucial variables such as the role of police self-legitimating activities in shaping police treatment of the public,, the contexts in which procedural fairness, outcome issues are singularly or collectively influential. It is also argued that, while it is well, good if procedural fairness enhances the quality of public compliance, cooperation with the police, it is unhealthy if procedural fairness is taken seriously only for its utilitarian value. Procedural fairness,, by extension police legitimacy, must be pursued as something of intrinsic value, a good in, of itself; treating people fairly should not be an issue of choice contingent simply on demonstrable evidence of the facilitation of the task of the police in maintaining order.

title: Victims of criminal investigations: Experiences of adults in two communities in Osun State, Nigeria
authors: Agunbiade, Ojo Melvin, Opatola, Mustapha Olayiwola
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Criminal investigation represents a crucial stage in the process of crime management, justice realisation in any modern society; but the criminal investigation process is prone to abuse. This study examines the experiences of adults who have been interrogated for a criminal offence or offences in two communities in Osun State (Southwestern Nigeria). Thirty-five adults within the age range of 18–64 years, who are residents in the two communities (Ile-Ife, Modakeke-Ife) were systematically selected from the police records of investigated criminals, while 15 crime-investigating, experienced police officers were purposively selected from a divisional police headquarters, two police stations within the two communities. A qualitative, in-depth interview technique was used in generating relevant data. The selection of cases was from lists of reported, investigated criminal cases at three police stations namely: a divisional police station, one police station from each of the two communities. Findings revealed that many of the participants are sceptical about the readiness of the Nigerian police to respect, protect the fundamental human rights of suspects. In conclusion, there is a high preponderance of delay in criminal investigations, a lack of adequate training for police officers saddled with the responsibilities of crime investigation in the locality. This finding may be extended to the increasing rate of delay in criminal investigations in Nigeria, the perversion of justice. Hence, urgent attention is needed in addressing the loss of confidence in the Nigerian police by the public especially in crime protection, investigation.

title: Urban, small town comparison of citizen demand for police services
authors: Johnson, Richard R, Rhodes, Trisha N
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Little is known about the similarities, differences that exist between urban, small town police agencies with regard to citizen calls for service. The research about citizen demand for policing services in the USA has focused overwhelmingly on city police agencies, the research methodologies used made direct comparisons with smaller agencies impossible. The present research involved a comparison of calls for service from three urban municipal police departments, three small town departments for the same two-week period of time using identical coding schemes. The findings suggest that urban agencies receive proportionately more order maintenance calls, small town agencies receive proportionately more service calls,, both types of agencies receive similar proportions of law enforcement-related calls. The urban agencies, however, dealt with larger proportions of more serious crimes.

title: Perceptions of police, policing in a rural county of England
authors: Mawby, R I
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Crime, disorder audits provide the opportunity to identify, address the concerns local people express about local policing. This paper discusses the findings of the 2001, 2004 Cornwall Crime Surveys (CCSs), identifies public perceptions of police, policing in the county. The 2004 survey is used to compare those holding more favourable views with those who are critical of the police. The findings are then used to test the hypothesis that those who are more critical of the public police will be more positive about plural policing alternatives. The findings indicate that rural residents' concerns over public safety are accentuated by their concerns that the police in Cornwall are less accessible than those in urban areas, they are generally supportive of increasing the policing mix. However, they clearly see improvements to the public police as the preferred solution.

title: A comprehensive assessment of crime investigation policy in japan, by crime, clearance, criminal rates
authors: Yamamura, T, Kinoshita, H, Hishida, S
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The present study aims to demonstrate the effectiveness of crime investigation policy by crime, clearance, criminal rates, analysed using data published by the Japanese Government. The major findings of the study show that: (1) the crime rate declined steadily between 1945, 1975, but then increased again from 1975 to 2003, accelerating from 1985, with a sharp rise from 1995,, then began to descend again from 2003; (2) considerably better clearance rates were achieved between 1945, 1985, but rates subsequently dropped suddenly in 1985, continue to be sluggish; (3) the criminal rate (the number of persons in custody per 100,000 inhabitants) has shown a decline during the decades since 1945. The study concludes that: (1) there is a misdirected target-setting policy for crime investigation which aggravates the crime rate; (2) an inefficient training programmes for replacement detectives to improve their performance induces a drop in the clearance rate;, (3) the objective of minimising citizens' fear of crime depends on efficient crime investigation by experienced, expert detectives based on best practice at the crime scene, resulting in the arrest of offenders. The implications of these findings are discussed with reference to several policing practices in crime investigation.

title: Early intervention to reduce complaints: An Australian Victoria police initiative
authors: Macintyre, Stuart, Prenzler, Tim, Chapman, Jackie
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: ’Complaints profiling’, ‘early warning’ or ‘early intervention’ systems are currently seen as vital mechanisms for reducing police misconduct, improving police–community relations. This paper reports on the introduction of an early intervention system for police in the State of Victoria, Australia. The findings support the contention that such systems have a demonstrable utility in reducing complaints. A sample of 44 individuals profiled showed that interventions resulted in a 71.07 per cent reduction in complaints, from an expected 121 down to 35 over a two-year period. Additionally, the study showed that the financial cost-benefit effects were very positive, with reduced complaints resulting in an estimated saving of AU$3.2 million over the two years. A study of a sample of nine locations showed a 58.6 per cent reduction in complaints, from a projected number of 60.6 down to 25 over a one-year period, with an estimated saving of AU$1.4 million. The paper also describes the types of interventions used, a number of issues that arise from complaints profiling.

title: Police perceptions of the long-, short-term spatial distribution of residential burglary
authors: McLaughlin, Lindsay M, Johnson, Shane D, Bowers, Kate J, Birks, Dan J, Pease, Ken
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper seeks to explore police officer perception of the spatial distribution of residential burglary over different time periods. Using a survey of officers across three English police basic command units (BCUs), it examines the accuracy of their impressions of the locations of crime over the preceding year, the preceding two weeks. It also explores how these perceptions might affect the deployment of resources, police action. The results suggest that whilst officers have a good idea of where burglary occurred over the preceding year, they are less accurate for the recent distribution of risk because short-term hotspots are indeed significantly more unstable than long-term hotspots. The short-term predictive power of both one-year, two-week retrospective perceptions is very limited. Tactical advantages will only be afforded by the swift, routine identification of emerging short-term hotspots.

title: Occupational stress, coping, personality in the police: An SEM study
authors: Ortega, Adriana, Brenner, Sten-Olof, Leather, Phil
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article explores the relationships among exogenous factors, such as gender, age, rank/grade, tenure, personality, occupational stress, coping strategies, well-being, organisational commitment, job satisfaction. The sample used for this study comprised 1,535 police officers from a British police force, 20.78 per cent of whom were female. It was expected that personality, gender, age, rank, tenure were associated with ***work-related stress; coping; well-being,, work attitudes. More specifically, it was predicted: (1) that there was a correlation among personality, well-being, work attitudes;, (2) that coping strategies were directly associated with well-being, work attitudes. Using LISREL 8.54 these relationships were examined. The resulting model yielded meaningful, significant relationships, fitted the observed data: χ2 (114) = 291.88; p ≤ 0.01; RMSEA = 0.032; AGFI = 0.96; CFI = 0.99; n = 1510. Personality traits were found to be directly related to work-related stress, coping strategies, tension, burn out as well as negatively related to overall job satisfaction. Gender, age, rank did not show meaningful relationship with any of the endogenous variables. Occupational stressors were associated with low organisational commitment, poor overall job satisfaction. Also coping strategies were directly associated with organisational commitment, job satisfaction.

title: The New York City police department's Compstat: Dream or nightmare?
authors: Eterno, John A, Silverman, Eli B
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The Compstat paradigm has revolutionised the way policing is accomplished in democratic countries. Many agencies throughout the world have emulated the Compstat programme which originated in New York City in 1994. The strengths of Compstat have been widely publicised: dramatic reductions in crime, accountability of key staff members,, coordination of various units within an agency. The weaknesses of Compstat are less recognised: due process considerations, community relations, leadership issues, inadequate problemsolving. Weaknesses pose challenges, the authors present an alternative model to address these weaknesses. This model focuses on integrating community policing's essential components within the context of the Compstat paradigm. This provides a more powerful mechanism to combat crime, terrorism.

title: Compstat: The manager's perspective
authors: Vito, Gennaro F, Walsh, William F, Kunselman, Julie
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Originally established by Commissioner William Bratton, his colleagues in the New York City Police Department, Compstat has emerged as a new organisational paradigm in policing. This paper presents data drawn from the written views of police managers from across the USA. The respondents were attending the Administrative Officer's Course at the Southern Police Institute of the University of Louisville, Kentucky. During the course of their studies, they read several works on Compstat, including Silverman's (1999) work, NYPD Battles Crime. Content analysis of their written comments reveals the strengths, weaknesses that they associate with the Compstat model.

title: Police-media relations at critical incidents: Interviews from Oklahoma City
authors: Caeti, Tory J, Liederbach, John, Bellew, Steven S
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The policing of critical incident scenes, including natural disasters, hazardous materials spills, hostage situations,, terrorist attacks, has become an especially salient topic in the post-September 11 environment. Given the attention-grabbing nature of these events, police administrators are often faced with the task of building, maintaining relationships with members of the media at these scenes, primarily reporters, their crews who often pursue goals that are in direct conflict with those of law enforcement. This article examines the issues related to police—media relations at critical incident scenes using interview data from subjects involved in policing the scene of the Oklahoma City bombing, the related trials of Timothy McVeigh, Terry Nichols. These interviews provide a context for the presentation of guidelines important to police administrators who must be able to forge successful relationships with the media at critical incidents.

title: Repeat victimisation, prolific offending: Chance or choice?
authors: Everson, Steve
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article reports the findings of a study that used, as a starting point, two well-established findings. First, that a small proportion of offenders is responsible for a very large proportion of offences and, second, that a small proportion of victims suffers a large proportion of offences. What is the link between these two facts? What role do prolific offenders play in the repeated victimisation of individuals, locations? The study also analysed factors, relating to the offending ‘career’ of a criminal, that might impact upon repeat offending. It went on to examine the transition of offending from one offence to the next by individuals, whether repeat offenders were ‘specialists' or ‘generalists’. The study concluded with a discussion on ways in which the findings might be utilised in crime prevention/reduction efforts.

title: Influencing the police: Local autonomy in policy, practice in England, Wales
authors: Applegate, Richard J
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article assesses the influence of the Home Office; Her Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary; the Association of Chief Police Officers; the Audit Commission; the Local Police Authority, the Chief Constable, on policy makers, implementers of policy from various levels of a police organization. It is based on three policy areas: the Citizens' Charter; Annual Policing (now Performance) Plans;, Domestic Violence Policy in England, Wales. Both policy makers, policy implementers believed that, with the exception of the Association of Chief Police Officers,, the Local Police Authority, there was a strong influence from all these groups in all the policy areas examined. However for police officers directly involved in the implementation process, the Citizens' Charter, Annual Policing (now Performance) Plans had made little difference to the way they carried out their day-to-day work. In these more generic policy areas they saw less influence from these groups, with greater influence coming from consumers, public opinion, colleagues, immediate supervisors. But in the tighter policy area of domestic violence, where there is greater top-down control, the influence of these groups was the strongest, with local autonomy, both in policy, practice, hard to find.

title: School-based police officers: What can the UK learn from the USA?
authors: Briers, Andrew N
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This article is based on the author's experience as Britain's first school-based police officer, his subsequent experience of policing schools in the USA. It outlines the current practices of the Metropolitan Police Service in its quest to introduce the concept of placing police officers on a full-time basis in schools. This is in response to the alarming number of young people becoming involved in crime, is part of the package of measures being taken forward by the Prime Minister's Street Crime Action Team (Home Office, 2003) to combat street robberies, related crime. It highlights the strengths, weaknesses of such a scheme as experienced by the author, the strategies used to address the problems of youth violence, compares, contrasts these findings with those of his experiences in several schools in the US over a five-month period as an observational evaluator. The article also endeavours to look at the different ways in which the work of the schools officer is perceived in the two countries, the support structure which is available in each. The challenges which need to be met in order to form partnerships are outlined. Such efforts can collectively tackle the issue of juvenile delinquency through a common vision. In addition the need for a comprehensive training manual to be developed, implemented to assist these processes is discussed. The paper concludes by considering the extent to which, by combining the good practice from the US with those successful elements of the UK model, school police partnerships can moveorward, embrace the notion of school-based police officers in a positive light.

title: Quality, innovation in the vocational education, training of Dutch police
authors: Ijzerman, Peter D
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: In the Netherlands, a fundamental change in police vocational training is being carried out. This change process is required to equip police officers in a better way for their duties in an increasingly complex society. This paper outlines the explicit contribution Dutch police training is making. First of all, the author makes some observations about important developments in Dutch society relevant to the role, position of the police,, the response given to these developments by the Dutch police. Secondly, he makes some general remarks about the need for professionalisation, on bridging the gap between police education, professional practice. After the introductory paragraphs, the main features of the new concept behind Dutch police training will be described. In conclusion, possible risks involved in the innovation process will be described, some attention will be paid to cultural aspects of the police, significant issues relating to the relationship of the police with the administrative, judicial systems.

title: Polygraphic examinations in Japan: Application of the guilty knowledge test in forensic investigations
authors: Hira, Shinji, Furumitsu, Isato
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: There are two main types of psychophysiological detection of deception in Held practice: the guilty knowledge test (GKT), the control question test (CQT). A survey carried out for members of the American Psychological Association, the Society for Psychophysiological Research proved that many of the members consider that the GKT is superior to the CQT in its validity. Moreover, several experimental studies reported that the GKT produces fewer false positive errors (classifying an innocent suspect as guilty) than the CQT. In spite of these issues, the GKT is used less in North America, there are several researchers who insist that it is inapplicable in real-life criminal investigations. In Japan, however, the GKT has been extensively, successfully used in criminal investigations since the 1950s. Moreover, basic studies of the GKT, such as visual presentations of evidence, an automated diagnostic method by a computer, detecting guilty knowledge by using event-related brain potentials, are actively carried out in many Japanese laboratories to improve the method's reliability. In an effort to encourage the application of the GKT as an effective, scientific method in criminal investigations, this paper describes the status of the GKT in Japan.

title: Computer-based retrieval of suspects using similarity of modus operandi
authors: Yokota, Kaeko, Watanabe, Shoichi
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This report presents the development, evaluation of the suspect retrieval system based on modus operandi developed by the National Research Institute of Police Science in Japan. The database used in the system stores a large number of records consisting of the modus operandi of prior offenders. A score is assigned to each record, where each score represents the similarity of the modus operandi between each record, a crime under investigation. The similarity is statistically calculated based on the choice probability of each modus operandi. Suspects in the database are rank ordered according to scores. The higher a rank is, the more likely a suspect is expected to have committed the crime under investigation. The validity of the system is evaluated with data about Japanese burglars (n = 12,468), some factors influencing the accuracy of the retrieval are discussed.

title: Inconsistent role of the media in criminal profiling in a serial murder case
authors: Yamamura, Takehiko
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: An inspection of media articles about the Kobe serial murder case in 1997 suggests that the media may have several negative effects on criminal profiling in professional criminal investigations. The most worrying aspect of media responses to serious offending is the way they can shape social perception of a crime. In particular, the media focus on narrow aspects of a case, in so doing give a distorted picture of the criminal. Inspection of articles in some newspapers indicate that reporters see themselves as on-lookers rather than as professional investigative journalists. They cling to rumour, the tit-bits of information they can gather, are forced to enlarge them to make a story. By doing so they spread misleading, damaging information about a crime. In conclusion, it is argued that the way the media report serious crime, including serial murder, can be considered counter-productive to a criminal investigation.

title: Reliability of eyewitness testimony: A field experimental approach for a real crime
authors: Itsukushima, Yukio, Nomura, Kouji, Usui, Nobuo
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: To develop a method to assess the reliability of eyewitness testimony in a real criminal case, a field experimental or simulation method was introduced. In that case, an eyewitness witnessed a man at night who was in an escaping vehicle, identified him as a criminal from a photo-spread about two weeks later. The description of the eyewitness was detailed; however, there might be estimator variables that lower his performance of perception, memory. To clarify whether such testimony is trustworthy, a field experimental method was adopted. Results of the experiment showed that almost all subjects of the experiment could not only not recall the details of the events but also could not identify the target person. From these findings it is concluded that the testimony was not reliable enough to convict the suspect. In this paper the usefulness of a field experimental approach is stressed, it is suggested that guidelines such as PACE or recently issued US guidelines for treating eyewitness testimony should be used to prevent miscarriage of justice.

title: The effect of repeated photographic identification, time delay on the accuracy of the final photographic identification, the rating of memory
authors: Naka, Makiko, Itsukushima, Yukio, Itoh, Yuji, Hara, Satoshi
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: In the historically well-known case of Teigin Jiken (the case of Imperial Bank), eyewitnesses were presented with a large number of photos repeatedly, during a six-month investigation, before they finally identified a suspect. In this paper, by partially modelling their study on the investigation after Teigin Jiken, the authors examine the possibly negative effect of repeated photo identification (RPI), time delay on memory for a face,, subjects' ratings of the state of memory, confidence. Undergraduates participated in a staged event followed by a delay with or without RPI,, then the final photo identification. The results showed a cumulative effect of RPI, time delay. In particular, subjects with RPI were less accurate in the final photo identification,, their ratings of the state of memory, confidence were less calibrated to accuracy.

title: False memories in children created through a series of interviews. Who took a boy away?
authors: Takaoka, Masako, Saito, Kenichiro, Wakinaka, Hiroshi, Yamamoto, Toshiya
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: In this paper, the authors demonstrate how false eyewitness testimonies were created through a joint remembering between children, adult interviewers. Jen five-year-old children participated in an event at their kindergarten: a three-year-old boy came to the kindergarten, played with them, but left while they were watching a video. A week later, three pairs of interviewers interviewed children on the event. They repeated the interview five times on different days. The interviewers were misinformed beforehand that Taka, a female adult familiar to the children, took the boy away. Actually, however, the boy was taken away by a teacher. Although the interviewers conducted a fair interview without using leading question, false information was created. The interviewers seemed to pick up the information which was consistent with their knowledge. Also, children's testimonies changed in response to the interviewers' questions, responses. Furthermore, children filled in the gap using their own schema, script.

title: Joint construction of ‘facts’ in court: A case study of microscopic communication
authors: Ohashi, Yasushi, Mori, Naohisa
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Eyewitness testimony is generated through communication between the examiner, non-examiner (eyewitness) in interrogation rooms or public courts. In this analysis, the authors have studied the ‘fact-generating’ process microscopically,, the issue of credibility in testifying from one's experience. Specifically, they examined the Kabutoyama case, in which it took more than 20 years to render a final verdict of not guilty. They closely examined the credibility of testimony made by a key witness in the case. After analysing the testimony both qualitatively, quantitatively, they observed several characteristics in the witness-examiner exchanges, consider that non-empirical eyewitness testimony is a product of witness-examiner interactions. This paper is based on a research project carried out to report on expert opinion regarding credibility of eyewitness testimony. Part of the results of this project have already been published by Mori, Ohashi (1997).

title: Community policing: Fighting crime or fighting colleagues?
authors: Fielding, Nigel
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Community policing continues to enjoy much favour as a principal alternative to traditional, law-enforcement-oriented policing. A large body of research suggests, however, that it confronts a range of organisational obstacles. These obstacles arise largely from the endurance of an organisational form developed to support a law-enforcement-oriented approach,, which has engendered both working practices, an occupational culture inhospitable to the pursuit of community policing. Drawing on field research in the London Metropolitan Police, Surrey police forces, the paper identifies key obstacles to the delivery of community policing. It also indicates some of the conditions under which successful community policing can be achieved. These entail both changes in the organisational environment in which community policing is placed,, changes in prevailing conceptions of the nature, role of community policing. In particular, it is argued that community policing needs to move emphatically away from approaches based on community building, ‘outreach’,, towards a construction of community policing based firmly on its role in crime control.

title: Marksmanship skills of female police recruits: Impact of basic firearms training
authors: Charles, Michael T, Copay, Anne G
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Female police officers generally have a weaker grip strength, are less familiar with firearms than their male counterparts when they enter the police academy. The study examined whether the basic law enforcement firearms class adequately prepared female officers. Police recruits coming to the Police Training Institute (PTI) with no or little firearms training were selected. The grip strength, marksmanship scores of 216 police recruits (185 men, 31 women) were measured. Both male, female recruits significantly improved their marksmanship scores by the end of the training. The female scores remained slightly but significantly lower than the male scores due to their lower grip strength.

title: Policing in a multicultural society: A changing society, a changing police culture?
authors: Srinivasan, Nara, Hearn, Lydia
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: For many years Australia has been known for its all-white policy, but in recent years the government has undertaken a series of radical measures to improve ‘access', ‘equity’ of all groups living in Australia — a process which has involved improving the ability of government bodies to understand the intricate relations which arise within a multicultural society so that they can better attend to the different values, needs of the various groups. In this paper, the authors look at an innovative, proactive programme entitled ‘Policing in a multicultural community’ set up by the Western Australian Police Service, the Department of Multicultural Affairs, the Ethnic Communities Council, Edith Cowan University, in coordination with the Northern Suburbs Migrant Resource Centre. The programme is based on the premise that ‘only through understanding people's needs, expectations, fears can compatibility between police, society be achieved’. The findings of this comprehensive evaluation showed that by fostering a sense of partnership it is possible to achieve significant impacts in terms of promoting an understanding of cultural diversity among police officers,, overcoming issues which in the past have prevented ethnic minority groups from accessing police services.

title: The changing face of policing in Central, Eastern Europe
authors: Mawby, Rob
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: The dramatic social, political changes taking place in Central, Eastern Europe have inevitably influenced the structure, functions of the police, particularly where the police were associated, in the minds of the people, with maintenance of the former regime. To date, however, little systematic research has been done on the police systems of these countries. This paper consequently provides a broad literature review. Following an account of policing in the past, it focuses on the changes that have taken place in recent years. Two issues are of particular note. First, developments,, public perceptions of those developments, vary widely. Secondly, while some aspects of policing, such as victims' perceptions, have been considered in more detail, others, such as police officers' own views, have rarely been considered. There is thus a real need for further research to document, explain the changes that have occurred.

title: Stressor exposure, methods of coping among senior police managers at a time of organisational, management change
authors: Brown, Jennifer, Cooper, Cary, Kirkcaldy, Bruce
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper discusses the context within which British police chief superintendents, superintendents (n = 533) were working as a background to measuring their sources of work-related stress, coping adaptations. Some comparative analyses are presented examining the internationalism of changes in police management, organisation. The results of the empirical investigation into the sources of stress, coping strategies of British police managers are then presented. Superintendents report having too much work to do with too few resources among the most significant stressors. They cope through use of secondary stress management interventions which are task orientated rather than emotion focused. The paper concludes by relating findings to organisational changes occurring within policing elsewhere, makes some recommendations to alleviate stress among police managers.

title: Managing police investigations into burglary
authors: Gill, Martin, Hart, Jerry, Livingstone, Ken
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper reports on findings from a Home Office-funded research project on the management of police investigations. While the original study concerned itself with strategies for dealing with burglary, auto crime, this paper focuses specifically on how the police manage burglary offences. It evaluates police detectives' responses to questions asked in interviews about which actions they felt to be of greatest benefit in achieving a number of pre-defined outcomes. The authors sought to evaluate police results in terms of the recovery of stolen property, victim reassurance, the gathering of information for the purposes of criminal intelligence, in addition to the more conventional measures of success — detections, arrests. This paper will be of interest both to academics wishing to know more about the development of investigative practice, as well as to practitioners seeking a more comprehensive means of evaluating performance.

title: Victim—Offender mediation, the gatekeeping role of police
authors: Prenzler, Tim, Hayes, Hennessey
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper reports on implications for the management of police discretion arising from a Victim—Offender pilot project in Queensland, Australia. The pilot was conducted with juvenile offenders, was highly successful on a range of key outcomes related to restorative justice. However, the project suffered from very low referrals from police,, there were no referrals from the courts, partly because of magistrates' deference to police decisions. As a consequence, many crime victims, young offenders, their caregivers had no opportunity to benefit from reparation. On this basis, a recommendation was made to curtail police discretion severely by building into the case disposition process mandatory consultation regarding mediation with all victims, offenders. This posed a direct challenge to the traditional wide discretionary powers held by police in their gatekeeping role. This research was commissioned by the Queensland Department of Justice. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily those of the Department.

title: Private security, its contribution to policing: Under-researched, under-utilised, underestimated
authors: Button, Mark
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Policing has become increasingly associated with what the police do by academics, practitioners, policy makers. Yet there is a wide range of individuals, organisations, other than the police, engaged in policing. These include other public bodies such as Customs, Excise, trading standards officers, vigilantes, private security firms to name a few. One of the most significant of these is the latter. This paper assesses the contribution of private security to policing by analysing some of the main activities undertaken, comparing them to those pursued by the police. It also argues that private security is under-researched in comparison to the police, particularly given the significant roles that are undertaken. It also argues private security is under-utilised in its potential contribution to policing, crime prevention. Finally, the paper considers how private security is often underestimated when some of the potential causes for concern are considered.

title: Dilemmas confronting female police officer promotional candidates: Glass ceiling, disenfranchisement or satisfaction?
authors: Whetstone, Thomas S, Wilson, Deborah G
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Through an analysis of data from one large Midwestern municipal police agency, this study examined some of the issues affecting the promotion of female police officers. Specifically, the issues examined are those influencing the decision about whether to enter the promotional process and, once a decision is made to enter the process, those factors influencing women during the process. Within the agency under study, the rate of promotion for females still lags behind that for males. The study found that personal ‘choices' constrained by impediments from both within, outside the organisation contributed to the lack of parity. Based on these findings, suggestions are made for strategies to increase the numbers of women, relative to men, in supervisory, managerial positions.

title: Improving police integrity, accountability to the community
authors: Loveday, Barry
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper looks at the implications for police complaints procedures of the Police (Northern Ireland) Act 1998 which establishes under an Ombudsman independent civilian investigation of complaints against the police. The paper also considers the problems surrounding police investigation of complaints, concludes that the move towards shared investigation or civilian investigation of serious complaints against the police has become much more likely. This is in part due to the nature of the evidence given to the recent inquiry into police discipline, complaints by the Home Affairs Committee. The evidence suggested that it was never likely that the police could act independently, wholly objectively in conducting investigations against fellow officers. For these, other reasons it is argued that the Northern Ireland Ombudsman, with civilian investigators given the powers, privileges of the constable, could provide a useful example for future reform of complaints mechanisms in the UK.

title: Comparative models of policing, the role of women officers
authors: Heidensohn, Frances
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper considers the importance of comparative international studies of policing, with some key examples. The neglect of the position of female officers in these accounts is noted and, in the rest of the paper, an attempt is made to redress the balance by comparing the key features of the role of women in policing in Australia, Britain, the USA. The need for analytical models to include gender is noted, with some examples of how this might be done,, the explanatory powers of various taxonomies of policewomen's experiences are tested.

title: Comparing charges: The experience of discrimination, harassment among women police officers serving in Australia, the British Isles, the United States of America
authors: Brown, Jennifer
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper reports the findings of a survey of policewomen serving in Australia (n = 206), the British Isles (n = 176), the United States of America (USA) (n = 186). Problems of undertaking comparative research into policewomen are discussed, caution must be exercised in the interpretation of the results, given the opportunistic nature of the data collection: delegates attending international conferences of policewomen. Notwithstanding limitations of the research design, several observations are drawn from the data: the ubiquitous nature of sex discrimination, sexual harassment in the police service, greater similarities between officers from the British Isles, Australia with greatest divergence evident from those serving in the USA;, variation in terms of the frequency with which support strategies are adopted by policewomen. Explanations in terms of aspects of masculinity, women's networking are offered to account for differences between the policewomen.

title: Gender integration in Australian policing: The evolution of management responsibility
authors: Prenzler, Tim
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: This paper traces the development of women's formal integration into policing in Australia with an emphasis on the role of legislation in affecting change. Grudging compliance with the requirements of anti-discrimination has occurred in the last two decades with a limited application of the more demanding requirements of legislation oriented towards affirmative action. This paper sets up a model for effective management of equal employment opportunity (EEO) responsibilities, tests the level of current application of the model with reference to EEO reports, other data on the status of women. Despite significant progress, specific problems remain, the percentage of sworn female officers will increase only very slowly, will not reach parity with men unless more dynamic efforts are made to improve participation. The main areas of concern are physical ability entry tests, low application rates, lack of union support, managerial indifference, inadequate diagnostic review. Two key strategies for improvement derived from this analysis are targeted promotion in recruitment, the application of a systematic ‘problem oriented’ approach to EEO management.

title: Policing at the Crossroads: Changing directions for the new millennium
authors: Walsh, William F
journal: International journal of police science \& management
abstract: Now is a period of reflection, transition as the last decade of this century draws to an end. Scholars argue that substantial forces are challenging current methods of working, organising, that restructuring is needed to prepare for the future. How then should police administrators prepare their organisations to respond to the challenges of the 21st century? This discussion employs historical, organisational evidence to analyse the critical milestones in the development of policing. It posits that policing has reached an important crossroads with organisational managers dividing their support between traditional or community/problem-solving operational models. It faces the challenge of selecting a pathway for the future. The demands of providing security, order in the emerging information age, with its global, economic order, far exceed present day policing methods. This discussion concludes with suggestions on how to prepare for the future. This paper was originally presented at the 1997 Academy of Criminal Justice Sciences meeting in Louisville, Kentucky.

title: Preventing Violence Against Women in Transport Systems
abstract: As the global community marks Women’s International Day on March 8, the World Bank is putting more emphasis on preventing the potential violence, harassment that women, girls may face while using public transport.

title: Lost in the system: Locating rogue trading incidents in police statistics
authors: Day, Tim
abstract: This research aims to examine police recording of rogue trading. It explores whether this could be improved through a clear definition, specific crime code, or flag, for this type of crime. To examine this, the research compares rogue trading recording practices with those of distraction burglary. Both are similar in victimology, offender profile, but only distraction burglary has a nationally adopted definition, a crime code under which incidents are recorded. The findings indicate that current recording practices make understanding the extent, impact of rogue trading difficult,, victims would therefore be better served through the implementation of a definition, crime code or flag.

title: ABORTION RESTRICTIONS AND INTIMATE PARTNER VIOLENCE IN THE DOBBS ERA
The effects of crime information, response effectiveness on behavioral intentions of coping with crime
authors: Shimada, Takahito, Arai, Takashi
journal: Shinrigaku kenkyu: The Japanese journal of psychology
abstract: A survey, an experiment were conducted about the promotion of behavioral intentions for preventing sexual assaults by strangers.
