title: When abused women decide to seek help from a victims assistance program: Their perceived needs, self-reported mental health symptoms
authors: Mengo, Cecilia, Gidycz, Christine
keywords: help seeking; intimate partner violence; mental health; perceived needs; women;320\_ST実証研究;GSV
abstract: This study examines the nature of perceived needs of women victims of intimate partner violence (IPV), their association with social demographic characteristics, self-reported mental health symptoms. The study uses data from case records of women victims of IPV (n = 154) seeking help from a victim assistance program housed within city police station located in the southwest, United States. The majority of the women in this study reported needs related to counseling, protection orders, Crime Victims' Compensation Rights, legal services,, Temporary Aid for Needy Families. Findings also indicate that perceived needs of women were significantly associated with self-reported mental health symptoms. Some needs had a stronger relationship to women's mental health symptoms than others. Overall these findings suggest that it is imperative to emphasize responses that can address all the needs of women (in addition to stopping IPV) to reduce mental health symptoms.

title: Implementing the LifeSkills Training drug prevention program: factors related to implementation fidelity
authors: Mihalic, Sharon F, Fagan, Abigail A, Argamaso, Susanne
abstract: BACKGROUND: Widespread replication of effective prevention programs is unlikely to affect the incidence of adolescent delinquency, violent crime,, substance use until the quality of implementation of these programs by community-based organizations can be assured. METHODS: This paper presents the results of a process evaluation employing qualitative, quantitative methods to assess the extent to which 432 schools in 105 sites implemented the LifeSkills Training (LST) drug prevention program with fidelity. Regression analysis was used to examine factors influencing four dimensions of fidelity: adherence, dosage, quality of delivery,, student responsiveness. RESULTS: Although most sites faced common barriers, such as finding room in the school schedule for the program, gaining full support from key participants (i.e., site coordinators, principals,, LST teachers), ensuring teacher participation in training workshops,, classroom management difficulties, most schools involved in the project implemented LST with very high levels of fidelity. Across sites, 86\% of program objectives, activities required in the three-year curriculum were delivered to students. Moreover, teachers were observed using all four recommended teaching practices,, 71\% of instructors taught all the required LST lessons. Multivariate analyses found that highly rated LST program characteristics, better student behavior were significantly related to a greater proportion of material taught by teachers (adherence). Instructors who rated the LST program characteristics as ideal were more likely to teach all lessons (dosage). Student behavior, use of interactive teaching techniques (quality of delivery) were positively related. No variables were related to student participation (student responsiveness). CONCLUSION: Although difficult, high implementation fidelity by community-based organizations can be achieved. This study suggests some important factors that organizations should consider to ensure fidelity, such as selecting programs with features that minimize complexity while maximizing flexibility. Time constraints in the classroom should be considered when choosing a program. Student behavior also influences program delivery, so schools should train teachers in the use of classroom management skills. This project involved comprehensive program monitoring, technical assistance that likely facilitated the identification, resolution of problems, contributed to the overall high quality of implementation. Schools should recognize the importance of training, technical assistance to ensure quality program delivery.

title: Rethinking program fidelity for criminal justice: Outcome evaluation program for female offenders
authors: Miller, J Mitchell, Miller, Holly Ventura
abstract: Criminal justice program evaluation has long been oriented around reduction objectives determined through quasi-experimental, related variable analytic designs (Petrosino, Soydan, 2005; Shover, 1979). Such purely quantitative approaches relate program impacts considered indicative of program effectiveness but neglect nonmeasured program drivers informing why or how outcomes are realized. More often than not, outcome evaluation in criminal justice imprudently assumes that program results are a function of treatment or intervention sans empirical confirmation. Helpfully, mixed-methods approaches coupling process, outcome phases have migrated from other disciplines, offer a more rigorous, scientific strategy for determining program efficacy. Mixed-methods research in the milieu of applied criminology, criminal justice science, unfortunately, is generally underutilized as the objectives, design requirements of the process phase are poorly articulated, blurred with the functions of pure qualitative research. Although applied fieldwork enables an exploration of phenomena, contextualization of quantitative findings, process evaluation uses qualitative techniques to capture data for confirmatory as well as ethnographic purposes. Accordingly, the foremost objective of process evaluation is to ascertain program fidelity, a concept informing whether treatment services are delivered consistent with program theory, design.

title: Risk communication: A mental models approach
authors: Granger Morgan, M, Fischhoff, Baruch, Bostrom, Ann, Atman, Cynthia J
abstract: People today must make decisions about many health, safety,, environmental risks. Nuclear power, HIV/AIDS, radon, vaccines, climate change,, emerging infectious diseases are just some issues that may face them in the news media, ballot box, or doctor's office. In order to make sound choices they need to get good information. Because their time is limited, that information has to be carefully selected, clearly presented. This book provides a systematic approach for risk communicators, technical experts, hoping to serve the public by providing information about risks. The procedure uses approaches from risk, decision analysis to identify the most relevant information; it uses approaches from psychology, communication theory to ensure that it is understood. This book is written in nontechnical terms, designed to make the approach feasible for anyone willing to try it. It is illustrated with successful communications, on a variety of topics.

title: Analytical methods for social research: Counterfactuals, causal inference: Methods, principles for social research: Methods, principles for social research
authors: Morgan, Stephen L, Winship, Christopher
abstract: In this second edition of Counterfactuals, Causal Inference, completely revised, expanded, the essential features of the counterfactual approach to observational data analysis are presented with examples from the social, demographic,, health sciences. Alternative estimation techniques are first introduced using both the potential outcome model, causal graphs; after which, conditioning techniques, such as matching, regression, are presented from a potential outcomes perspective. For research scenarios in which important determinants of causal exposure are unobserved, alternative techniques, such as instrumental variable estimators, longitudinal methods,, estimation via causal mechanisms, are then presented. The importance of causal effect heterogeneity is stressed throughout the book,, the need for deep causal explanation via mechanisms is discussed.

title: Modern, postmodern social theorizing: Bridging the divide
authors: Mouzelis, Nicos P
abstract: There is a growing conflict between modern, postmodern social theorists. The latter reject modern approaches as economistic, essentialist, often leading to authoritarian policies. Modernists criticize postmodern approaches for their rejection of holistic conceptual frameworks which facilitate an overall picture of how social wholes (organizations, communities, nation-states, etc.) are constituted, reproduced, transformed. They believe the rejection of holistic methodologies leads to social myopia - a refusal to explore critically the type of broad problems that classical sociology deals with. This book attempts to bridge the divide between these two conflicting perspectives, proposes a novel holistic framework which is neither reductionist/economistic nor essentialist. Modern, Postmodern Social Theorizing will appeal to scholars, students of social theory, of social sciences in general.

title: A leap of faith? Positive illusions in romantic relationships
authors: Murray, S, Holmes, J G
abstract: It is proposed that satisfying, stable relationships reflect intimates' ability to see imperfect relationships in somewhat idealized ways-to make a leap of faith. Both members of dating, married couples completed a measure of relationship illusions, tapping idealized perceptions of the partners' attributes, exaggerated perceptions of control,, unrealistic optimism. Results of concurrent analyses revealed that relationship illusions predicted greater satisfaction, love,, trust,, less conflict, ambivalence in both dating, marital relationships. A longitudinal follow-up of the dating sample revealed that relationships were more likely to persist the stronger individuals' initial illusions. Relationship illusions also predicted increases in later satisfaction but not vice versa. These results suggest that positive illusions capture a prospective sense of conviction or security that is not simply isomorphic with satisfaction.

title: Rapid assessment of “eve teasing” (sexual harassment) of young women during the commute to college In India
authors: Natarajan, Mangai
abstract: Many countries have taken action in recent times to address harassment in the work place, violence in the home, but little attention has been paid to sexual harassment in public places, specifically during women’s journey to work, school. In developing countries, many more women are seeking education, employment than previously, which has increased the opportunity for sexual harassment in public places. In India, the study location, this harassment is known as “eve teasing”. Eve teasing includes cat calling, lewd remarks,, inappropriate sexual contact such as rubbing, fondling. Tolerance of such incidents could lead to more severe forms of abuse, encourage more individuals to participate. Necessary as laws are, they cannot bring about immediate changes in widespread public behaviors, particularly those, such as eve teasing, that are deeply rooted in the culture of a country. To date there is no systematic research on sexual harassment in public places to assist public authorities, town planners with the development of security measures, especially for college-going women in cities, towns in India. Rapid assessment methodology has been used increasingly, especially in the field of public health, to assist decision-making about appropriate interventions for social problems by examining issues within social, cultural contexts in space, time. This paper provides a case study of rapid assessment of so-called “eve teasing” of female college students in Chennai, India. Three methods were employed in this rapid assessment of the problem— focus group discussions with college students, interviews with police officers from stations nearby the campuses, safety audits of the campus surroundings. This small exploratory study of eve teasing in India succeeded in promoting understanding of the problem, in providing many suggestions for reducing it. These latter included an extensive inventory of precautions for students, particularly female students to take in order to protect themselves from eve teasing,, a list of preventive suggestions for other stakeholders—the police, local municipalities, transport agencies, the colleges themselves. The study has wider implications for the study of routine precautions, for crime in public space, for the use of rapid assessment techniques in Crime Science.

title: The offender's perspective on crime: Methods, principles in data collection
authors: Nee, Claire
abstract: This chapter outlines the importance of including the offender’sperspective on his or her own behaviour in any analysis of criminal activity. In particular, it argues that research on specific types of crime, patterns of crime, interventions into offending behaviour must benefit from including this perspective. The first part of the chapter focuses on work done on residential burglary to show how fruitful this ‘grounded’ approach to research can be. It then goes on to discuss how reliant we are on self-report methodologies in this type of research, describes some general principles, recent developments that have improved the validity, reliability of crime data collected in the field.

title: When things turn sour: A network event study of organized crime violence
authors: Niezink, Nynke M D, Campana, Paolo
abstract: Abstract Objective This study examines the mechanisms underpinning the emergence of violence among individuals in the organized crime milieu. Methods Relying on criminal event data recorded by a UK Police Force, we apply a longitudinal network approach to study violent interactions among offenders. The data span the period from 2000 to 2016, include 6,234 offenders, 23,513 organized crime-related events. Instead of aggregating these data over time, we use a relational event-based approach to take into consideration the order of events. We employ an actor-oriented framework to model offenders’ victim choices in 156 violent events in the OC milieu. Results We find that the choice of offenders to target a particular victim is strongly affected by their mutual history. A violent act is often preceded by a previous act of violence, both in the form of repeated violence, reciprocated violence. We show that violence is strongly associated with prior co-offending turning sour. We uncover a strong effect for previous harassment as a retaliation cum escalation mechanism. Finally, we find evidence of conflicts within organized crime groups, of violence being directed to offenders with the same ethnic background. Conclusions Relational effects on victimization are consistently stronger than the effects of individual characteristics. Therefore, from a policy perspective, we believe that relational red flags (or risk factors) should play a more central role. A focus on harassment could be valuable in the development of an early intervention strategy.

title: Subcultural values, violent delinquency: A multilevel analysis in middle schools
authors: Ousey, Graham C, Wilcox, Pamela
abstract: This study extends research in the subculture of violence tradition by examining the simultaneous effects of individual-, aggregate-level proviolence values on violent behavior. With data from a survey of 3,690 seventh-grade students nested within 65 Kentucky schools, we found that an initially observed between-school effect of violent values on in-school violent behavior is not a contextual effect. Rather, the between-school effect of violent values is primarily a reflection of the individual-level association between violent values, violent behavior. Moreover, we found that the effect of individual values remains evident after measures of impulsivity, exposure to violent peers are controlled. No evidence of cross-level interaction effects involving individual values, the school-level violent value context was found.

title: Gender differences in rational decisions on shoplifting
authors: Özaşçılar, Mine
abstract: In line with earlier criminological research on gender differences in criminality, this study investigates gender differences in shoplifting. Using data from 1150 young adults residing in Istanbul, Turkey, it applies rational choice theory (RCT) to shoplifting by men, women. The findings confirm earlier research indicating that rational decisions to commit crimes vary by gender. Shoplifting intentions only vary in terms of guilt. The implications for future studies applying the RCT framework, limitations of the current study are discussed.

title: Security when it is welcome: Exploring device purchase as an opportune moment for security behavior change
authors: Parkin, Simon, Redmiles, Elissa M, Coventry, Lynne, Sasse, M Angela
abstract: Many security experts bemoan that consumers behave insecurely. Yet, current approaches to improving behavior either fail to consider when people may be most receptive to an intervention, or only consider experiences of threat (e.g., getting hacked) when identifying opportune moments for behavior change. We instead explore how an exemplar, positive experience – buying a new device – can serve as a “security trigger moment”. Through in-situ interviews with customers (n=85), sales staff (n=21) across four branches of a major UK retailer, we characterise the potential for behavior change during device purchase. Further, rather than assuming that users are always ready for an intervention, we explore how the abilities, motivations of users, sales staff can influence the power of a security trigger moment to drive behavior change. Our work lays the foundation for identifying additional trigger moments, deploying targeted interventions when they are most welcome

title: The Environmental Satisfaction Scale: A measure of satisfaction with local environmental conditions, government environmental policies
authors: Pelletier, Luc G, Legault, Louise R, Tuson, Kim M
abstract: Satisfaction with environmental conditions, government policies are hypothesized to play an important role in the genesis of proenvironmental behaviors. Given the absence of a scale measuring these constructs, two studies were conducted for the purpose of constructing, vaidating the Environmental Satisfaction Scale (ESS). The ESS consists of two subscales measuring individuals' satisfaction with local environmental conditions, with government policies. In the first study, a prototype of the ESS was constructed,, Its psychometric properties were evaluated. Results supported the factorial structure of the scale, showed satisfactory levels of internal consistency. In the second study, subjects completed the revised ESS, the Motivation Towards the Environment Scale,, various measures of environmental attitudes, behaviors. Results supported the by dimensional factorial structure, construct validity of the scale. Implications for the use of the ESS in future research on the environment are discussed.

title: Territoriality, fear of crime in elderly, nonelderly homeowners
authors: Pollack, L M, Patterson, A H
abstract: Summary Recent studies have shown that fear of crime is a serious problem among older Americans. Newman (25) suggests that such fear can be reduced through manipulation of the designed environment in order to deter criminals. The present study, an extension of the work of Patterson (28), investigates the relationship between territorial marking, fear of theft, assault among elderly (N = 157), nonelderly (N = 88) male, female homeowners. In contrast to the finding that territoriality is associated with reduced fear among the aged, in this study no such relationship was found for a nonelderly sample. Findings are discussed in terms of loss of “active mastery”, control of the environment with age.

title: Global cities, public transportation,, social exclusion: A study of the bus system in Abu Dhabi
authors: Qamhaieh, Abdellatif, Chakravarty, Surajit
abstract: As cities of the Gulf Cooperation Council grow, integrate with global markets, questions relating to their unique social compositions continue to emerge. Abu Dhabi has been competing with other cities in the region through massive investments in infrastructure, megaprojects, including the provision of public transportation. The paper examines the issues of bus ridership in Abu Dhabi, relates it to the broader debates on social exclusion, transportation. As a globalizing city with a majority expatriate population,, with a large presence of blue-collar workers, unique rifts in the society are further complicating the ‘usual’ prejudice against buses. The paper reports on results from fieldwork including surveys, observations. It concludes that the bus system could be more effective in fostering social inclusion if a broader accessibility planning approach is used.

title: Culturing community development, neighborhood open space,, civic agriculture: The case of Latino community gardens in New York City
authors: Saldivar-Tanaka, Laura, Krasny, Marianne E
abstract: To determine the role Latino community gardens play in community development, open space,, civic agriculture, we conducted interviews with 32 community gardeners from 20 gardens,, with staff from 11 community gardening support non-profit organizations, government agencies. We also conducted observations in the gardens,, reviewed documents written by the gardeners, staff from 13 support organizations, agencies. In addition to being sites for production of conventional, ethnic vegetables, herbs, the gardens host numerous social, educational,, cultural events, including neighborhood, church gatherings, holiday parties, children’s activities, school tours, concerts, health fairs,, voter registration drives. In some cases, the gardens also serve to promote community activism. The primary concern of gardeners is to secure land tenure in the face of pressures to develop the garden sites for housing. The support organizations, agencies provide help with land tenure, as well as with advocacy, organization,, horticultural practices. Although the role of the Latino gardens in community development appears to be more important than their role in open space or agricultural production, the gardens can also be viewed as unique “participatory landscapes” that combine aspects of all three movements, as well as provide a connection between immigrants, their cultural heritage.

title: Concern about crime among Montana farmers, ranchers$^1$
authors: Saltiel, John, Gilchrist, Jack, Harvie, Robert
abstract: Abstract The effects of previous victimization, distance from law enforcement, neighbors,, sufficiency of police patrols on fear of crime are estimated using data from Montana farmers, ranchers. Victimization has the strongest direct effect. Distance from police, neighbors seems to heighten sensitivity to lesser police patrol activity in isolated areas, which in turn increases concern about criminal victimization. Fear of crime in rural farm areas reflects, in part, the spatial arrangements, related consequences of living in these regions.

title: Helping women transition out of sex work: study protocol of a mixed-methods process, outcome evaluation of a sex work exiting program
authors: Shareck, Martine, Buhariwala, Pearl, Hassan, Maha, O'Campo, Patricia
keywords: Critical time intervention; Evaluation; Implementation; Outcome; Process; Sex work; Social determinants of health;356\_ProcessEval
abstract: BACKGROUND: For women who want to, exiting sex work can be challenging. Numerous programs strive to help women wanting to exit sex work, secure alternative sources of income by providing targeted support at key moments during the transition, yet few of those initiatives are rigorously evaluated. In 2017 ``Exit Doors Here'', a 9-month sex work exiting program based on the critical time intervention (CTI) approach, was developed to provide wrap-around support services (e.g., health, addiction, housing, education,, employment supports) to women wishing to transition towards exiting sex work. METHODS: We present the design of an evaluation study of Exit Doors Here which combines quantitative, qualitative methods to assess participant recruitment, retention into the program, program fidelity,, relationships with service providers (process evaluation), as well as progress made by participants in terms of strengthening their social support networks, moving closer to achieving their housing, pre-employment (i.e., educational, training, volunteering),, income-related goals, as well as their involvement in sex work (outcome evaluation). Each year for 4 years, between 25, 30 Exit Doors Here clients will be invited to complete an interviewer-administered questionnaire at the beginning, after completing the program,, to share data from their CTI charts, related documentation. Once a year, program staff, peer workers will be interviewed,, service providers will be surveyed. DISCUSSION: Conducting a formative (process) evaluation will allow us to inform program implementation, improve program delivery early on for maximum benefit. The summative (outcome) evaluation will provide much needed evidence on the effectiveness of CTI in supporting a traditionally underserved population to achieve the housing, pre-employment, income-related goals they value,, their progress towards reducing their involvement in,, eventually exiting, sex work.

title: Explaining feast or famine in randomized field trials. Medical science, criminology compared: Medical science, criminology compared
authors: Shepherd, Jonathan P
abstract: A feast of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) in medical science, comparative famine in criminology can be explained in terms of cultural, structural factors. Of central importance is the context in which the evaluation of interventions is done, the difference in status of situational research in the two disciplines. Evaluation of medical interventions has traditionally been led by practitioner (clinical) academics. This is not the case in criminal justice, where theory has had higher status than intervention research. Medical science has advanced in, or closely associated with, university teaching hospitals, but links between criminology, criminal justice services are far more tenuous. The late development of situational crime prevention seems extraordinary from a medical perspective, as does the absence of university police schools in the United Kingdom, elsewhere. These structural, cultural factors explain concentration of expectation, resource,, RCT productivity in medical science. The Campbell Collaboration, the Academy of Experimental Criminology are forces which are reducing this polarization of feast, famine in RCTs. But unless scientific criminology is embedded in university schools which are responsible for the education, training of law, probation,, police practitioners, convergence in terms of RCTs, implementation of findings in practice seems unlikely.

title: The power few: experimental criminology, the reduction of harm: The 2006 Joan McCord Prize Lecture
authors: Sherman, Lawrence W
keywords: CRIMINOLOGY; JUSTICE; EVIDENCE (Law); CRIME forecasting; RECIDIVISTS; VICTIMS of crimes; Crime prevention; Ethics; Experimental criminology; Hot spots; Repeat offenders; Repeat victims;318\_介入実験\_Policing;J Exp Criminol
abstract: The promise of experimental criminology is finding ways to reduce harm from crime, injustice. The problem of experimental criminology is that so few experiments produce evidence of big effects from the interventions they test. One solution to this problem may be concentrating scarce resources for experiments on the “power few:” the small percentage of places, victims, offenders, police officers or other units in any distribution of crime or injustice which produces the greatest amount of harm. By increasing the homogeneity, base rates of the samples enrolled in each experiment, the power few hypothesis predicts increased statistical power to detect program effects. With greater investment of resources,, possibly less variant responses to greater dosages of intervention—especially interventions of support, as distinct from punishment—we may also increase our chances of finding politically acceptable interventions that will work. title: Fairness, Effectiveness in policing: The evidence
authors: National Research Council, Division of Behavioral, Social Sciences, Education, Committee on Law, Justice, Committee to Review Research on Police Policy, Practices
abstract: Because police are the most visible face of government power for most citizens, they are expected to deal effectively with crime, disorder, to be impartial. Producing justice through the fair,, restrained use of their authority. The standards by which the public judges police success have become more exacting, challenging. Fairness, Effectiveness in Policing explores police work in the new century. It replaces myths with research findings, provides recommendations for updated policy, practices to guide it. The book provides answers to the most basic questions: What do police do? It reviews how police work is organized, explores the expanding responsibilities of police, examines the increasing diversity among police employees,, discusses the complex interactions between officers, citizens. It also addresses such topics as community policing, use of force, racial profiling,, evaluates the success of common police techniques, such as focusing on crime ``hot spots.'' It goes on to look at the issue of legitimacyâ€``how the public gets information about police work,, how police are viewed by different groups,, how police can gain community trust. Fairness, Effectiveness in Policing will be important to anyone concerned about police work: policy makers, administrators, educators, police supervisors, officers, journalists,, interested citizens.

title: Qualitative analysis of visual risk communication on twitter during the Covid-19 pandemic
authors: Sleigh, Joanna, Amann, Julia, Schneider, Manuel, Vayena, Effy
keywords: Covid-19; Pandemic; Public health; Risk communication; Twitter; Visuals;361\_SocialMedia
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Covid-19 pandemic is characterized by uncertainty, constant change, forcing governments, health authorities to ramp up risk communication efforts. Consequently, visuality, social media platforms like Twitter have come to play a vital role in disseminating prevention messages widely. Yet to date, only little is known about what characterizes visual risk communication during the Covid-19 pandemic. To address this gap in the literature, this study's objective was to determine how visual risk communication was used on Twitter to promote the World Health Organisations (WHO) recommended preventative behaviours, how this communication changed over time. METHODS: We sourced Twitter's 500 most retweeted Covid-19 messages for each month from January-October 2020 using Crowdbreaks. For inclusion, tweets had to have visuals, be in English, come from verified accounts,, contain one of the keywords 'covid19', 'coronavirus', 'corona', or 'covid'. Following a retrospective approach, we then performed a qualitative content analysis of the 616 tweets meeting inclusion criteria. RESULTS: Our results show communication dynamics changed over the course of the pandemic. At the start, most retweeted preventative messages came from the media, health, government institutions, but overall, personal accounts with many followers (51.3\%) predominated,, their tweets had the highest spread (10.0\%, i.e., retweet count divided by followers). Messages used mostly photographs, images were found to be rich with information. 78.1\% of Tweets contained 1-2 preventative messages, whereby 'stay home', 'wear a mask' frequented most. Although more tweets used health loss framing, health gain messages spread more. CONCLUSION: Our findings can inform the didactics of future crisis communication. The results underscore the value of engaging individuals, particularly influencers, as advocates to spread health risk messages, promote solidarity. Further, our findings on the visual characteristic of the most retweeted tweets highlight factors that health, government organisations should consider when creating visual health messages for Twitter. However, that more tweets used the emotive medium of photographs often combined with health loss framing raises concerns about persuasive tactics. More research is needed to understand the implications of framing, its impact on public perceptions, behaviours.

title: Residents, employees, visitors: Effects of three types of ambient population on theft on weekdays, weekends in Beijing, China
authors: Song, Guangwen, Zhang, Yanji, Bernasco, Wim, Cai, Liang, Liu, Lin, Qin, Bo, Chen, Peng
keywords: Ambient population; Big data; Employees; Residents; Theft; Visitors;330\_SAEnv
abstract: Objectives: The residential population of an area is an incomplete measure of the number of people that are momentarily present in the area,, of limited value as an indicator of exposure to the risk of crime. By accounting for the mobility of the population, measures of ambient population better reflect the momentary presence of people. They have therefore become an alternative indicator of exposure to the risk of crime. This study considers the heterogeneity of the ambient population by distinguishing residents, employees, visitors as different categories,, explores their differential impact on thefts, both on weekdays, weekends. Methods: We analyze one-year of police recorded thefts across 2104 1 km2 grid cells in a central area in Beijing, China. Controlling for the effects of attractiveness, accessibility,, guardianship, we estimate a series of negative binominal models to investigate the differential effects of the three groups (residents, employees, visitors) in the ambient population on crime frequencies, both on weekdays, during weekends, holidays. Results: Overall, larger ambient populations imply larger theft frequencies. The effect of visitors is stronger than the effects of residents, employees. The effects of residents, employees vary over the course of the week. On weekdays, the presence of residents is more important, while the reverse holds true during weekends, holidays. Discussion: The effects of ambient population on thefts vary by its composition in terms of social roles. The larger role of visitors is presumably because in addition to being potential victims, residents, employees may also exercise informal social control. In addition, they spend more time indoors than where risk of theft is lower, while visitors might spend more time outdoors, may also bring about greater anonymity, weaken informal social control.

title: Improving policing through research
authors: Stanko, E A
journal: Policing A Journal of Policy, Practice
abstract: This group of papers is meant to spark further conversation about the role of social science evidence in driving better policing. For many academics, seminars, conferences are common events for on, off line spoken frustration about the failure of policing to take on board ‘good academic evidence’ to improve policing. In many ways such frustration is surprising. In the UK at least, the police service should be advantaged in its ability to harness best academic advice. Senior police officials throughout the UK are exposed to the virtues of what systematic criminological approaches offer during their training for promotion to the most senior management roles.

title: Governance through norms, standards: The normative force behind design-led crime prevention
authors: Stummvoll, Günter
journal: Criminology \& criminal justice: the international journal of policy, practice
abstract: Crime prevention standards in housing have for a long time been limited to target hardening,, in that respect European Norms were developed as guidelines for ‘burglar resistant’ doors, windows, shutters (EN1630). Recent developments include a set of supplementary crime prevention standards in the building sector, which are not limited to technical products but focus on the layout, management of urban environments, their impact on public safety. This article focuses on the problem of systematic Europe-wide implementation of crime prevention standards in urban planning. The attempt to implement common guidelines for design-led crime prevention through the development of a European Norm has failed. In this article I will first introduce the system of standardization, then examine the particular European Standard for Crime Prevention by Urban Planning, Building Design (CEN/TR14383). Instead of a harmonious application of that standard in Europe, a variety of policies have been negotiated, including national standardization, consulting schemes, liaison systems based on rewards. Moreover the standard has been re-interpreted in some jurisdictions as ‘gender mainstreaming’,, it has been adopted by police to organize national training for local governments. I will present, compare examples from Denmark, the UK, the Netherlands, Austria, Poland to show the divergent ways of interpretation, practical implementation of guidelines in design-led crime prevention.

title: Farm crime: Out of sight, out of mind: A study of crime on farms in the county of Rutland, England
authors: Sugden, Gavin
abstract: Reports from a number of informed sources now indicate that British farms are suffering some of the highest levels of crime in their existence. This paper concentrates on one identifiable farming region within the United Kingdom—the county of Rutland—and reports on the findings of a detailed farm crime survey carried out in 1996. The findings reveal a level of crime quite possibly unsuspected even by the farmers themselves.

title: Fraud, the American dream: Toward an understanding of fraud victimization
authors: Trahan, Adam, Marquart, James W, Mullings, Janet
abstract: ABSTRACT American culture, the practices of government focus an overwhelming majority of attention on violent “street” crime. As a result, very little is known about the victims of fraud. In order to contribute to this literature, a case study is provided that examines the victim population of a Ponzi scheme. Data are provided on the general characteristics of the victims, their investments,, the growth of the scheme. A theoretical model is formulated from Messner, Rosenfeld.'s work in Crime, the American Dream. This paper expands the concepts of this theory by providing evidence that it can be used to explain victim behavior.

title: Cambridge studies in criminology: Prisoner reentry, crime in America
authors: Travis, Jeremy, Visher, Christy A
abstract: Prisoner Reentry, Crime in America is intended to shed light on a question that fuels the public's concern about the number of returning prisoners. What are the public safety consequences of the fourfold increase in the number of individuals entering, leaving the nation's prisons each year? Many have speculated about the nexus between prisoner reentry, public safety. Journalistic accounts of the reentry phenomenon have painted a picture of a tidal wave of hardened criminals coming back home to resume their destructive lifestyles. Law enforcement officials have attributed increases in violence in their communities to the influx of returning prisoners. Politicians have recommended policies that keep former prisoners out of high crime neighborhoods in the belief that crime would be reduced. The chapters in this book address these issues, suggest policies that will keep released prisoners from committing new crimes.

title: Fraud victimization: Risky business or just bad luck?
authors: Van Wyk, Judy, Benson, Michael L
journal: American journal of criminal justice: AJCJ
abstract: Victimology theory recognizes that the characteristics, attitudes,, behaviors of potential victims influence the likelihood of criminal victimization. An important question for victimologists is whether potential victims put themselves at risk by engaging in risky behavior or whether victimization is primarily a result of bad luck. While this question has been investigated extensively with respect to street crime victimization, little attempt has been made to apply it to victimization by fraud. This article investigates the influence of attitudes toward financial risk taking on the likelihood of fraud victimization. Using data from a telephone survey of 400 randomly sampled respondents, we find that age, attitudes toward financial risk taking are significantly related to the likelihood of attempted victimizations but not to successful victimizations.

title: Residents' perceptions of satisfaction, safety: A basis for change in multifamily housing
authors: Weidemann, Sue, Anderson, James R, Butterfield, Dorothy I, O'Donnell, Patricia M
abstract: This article reports on the use of the concepts of residential satisfaction, safety in the evaluation of a specific multifamily public housing site, illustrates the potential of these concepts for providing critical information for the future planning, design of that site. The evaluation was primarily based on structured self-reports from residents about perceptions of their housing environment, their expressed satisfaction with that housing. Issues such as privacy, appearance, management, maintenance, safety from crime, resident similarity,, economic value of the residence were among those examined. Two types of analyses are reported: principal component analyses of over 200 items from the questionnaire, multiple regression analyses to determine which principal component factors were predictive of residents' satisfaction, safety. The results of the regression analyses clearly show the interdependence between the physical environment, the residents, managers of that environment. This information resulted in the formulation of general objectives, specific recommendations for change.

title: Use of correlational data to examine the effects of risk perceptions on precautionary behavior
authors: Weinstein, Neil D, Rothman, Alexander J, Nicolich, Mark
keywords: Behavior; Experimentation; Risk Perception;J\_TF1505;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;z\_jpa2009;a\_jpa2012;9\_340\_乗物盗反復被害\_2009\_JPA(9章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;\_\_\_202405\_RV\_Veh
abstract: Abstract The idea that perceptions of high personal risk lead people to adopt precautionary behavior (the “motivational hypothesis”) is mainly tested with correlational data. A review of studies from selective journals reveals a high proportion with methodological, conceptual problems that make them invalid as tests of this hypthesis. Three problems arc emphasized: (1) the misinterpretation of correlations from cross-sectional studies as testing the motivational hypothesis when they actually indicate the accuracy of risk perceptions; (2) the failure to control for prior behavior in prospective studies;, (3) the we of prospective studies in situations of little behavior change. Path models are used to help explain these problems. Recommendations for selecting research designs, for calculating the least problematic correlations are given, along with warnings about the many assumptions needed to interpret even these correlations. Summary Overall, 27 of the 61 cross-sectional analyses listed in Tables 2, 3 were conducted using clearly inappropriate variables. The appropriateness of the remaining correlations rest on one or two rather questionable assumptions: (1) that people do not distort their risk perceptions to justify their behavior or intentions, (2) that negative screening results a problem like breast cancer do not affect perceptions of future risk. The correlations preferred for testing the motivational hypothesis are listed in Table 4. Summary When the amount of precautionary behavior in a population has become relatively stable, behavior at time t+1 is well-predicted from behavior at time t, no independent variable other than Bt will have much predictive value in a prospective design. To avoid this problem, research should be conducted at a time when a substantial change in behavior is occurring, such as soon after the risk is recognized. If this is not possible, interventions that lead people to change their behavior (e.g., by raising risk perceptions or by lowering barriers to action) are required. In effect, they remove the system from equilibrium, allow one to watch what happens as people seek a new equilibrium. The least satisfactory choice is to use a cross-sectional correlation, such as R H∗B, that represents a summation over previous changes in behavior. The assumptions required to interpret such a correlation have been discussed earlier.

title: Cambridge studies in criminology: Police innovation: Contrasting perspectives: Contrasting Perspectives
authors: Weisburd, David L, Braga, Anthony A
abstract: Over the last three decades American policing has gone through a period of significant change, innovation. In what is a relatively short historical time frame the police began to reconsider their fundamental mission, the nature of the core strategies of policing,, the character of their relationships with the communities that they serve. This volume brings together leading police scholars to examine eight major innovations which emerged during this period: community policing, broken windows policing, problem oriented policing, pulling levers policing, third party policing, hot spots policing, Compstat, evidence-based policing. Including advocates, critics of each of the eight police innovations, this comprehensive book assesses the evidence on impacts of police innovation on crime, public safety, the extent of the implementation of these new approaches in police departments,, the dilemmas these approaches have created for police management. This book will appeal to students, scholars, researchers.

title: Effects of improved street lighting on crime
authors: Welsh, Brandon P, Farrington, David C, Wilson, David B, Mason, George
abstract: Improved street lighting serves many functions, is used in both public, private settings. The prevention of personal, property crime is one of its objectives in public space, which is the main focus of this review. There are two main theories of why improved street lighting may cause a reduction in crime. The first suggests that improved lighting leads to increased surveillance of potential offenders (both by improving visibility, by increasing the number of people on the street), hence to increased deterrence of potential offenders. The second suggests that improved lighting signals community investment in the area, that the area is improving, leading to increased community pride, community cohesiveness,, informal social control. The first theory predicts decreases in crime especially during the hours of darkness, while the second theory predicts decreases in crime during both daytime, nighttime. Results of this review indicate that improved street lighting significantly reduces crime. This lends support for the continued use of improved street lighting to prevent crime in public space. The review also found that nighttime crimes did not decrease more than daytime crimes. This suggests that a theory of street lighting focusing on its role in increasing community pride, informal social control may be more plausible than a theory focusing on increased surveillance, increased deterrence. Future research should be designed to test the main theories of the effects of improved street lighting more explicitly,, future lighting schemes should employ high quality evaluation designs with long-term followups.

title: Cluster randomised-control trial for an Australian child protection education program: Study protocol for the Learn to be safe with Emmy, friends™
authors: White, Codi, Shanley, Dianne C, Zimmer-Gembeck, Melanie J, Lines, Katrina, Walsh, Kerryann, Hawkins, Russell
abstract: BACKGROUND: Child maltreatment has severe short-and long-term consequences for children's health, development,, wellbeing. Despite the provision of child protection education programs in many countries, few have been rigorously evaluated to determine their effectiveness. We describe the design of a multi-site gold standard evaluation of an Australian school-based child protection education program. The intervention has been developed by a not-for-profit agency, comprises 5 1-h sessions delivered to first grade students (aged 5-6 years) in their regular classrooms. It incorporates common attributes of effective programs identified in the literature,, aligns with the Australian education curriculum. METHODS/DESIGN: A three-site cluster randomised controlled trial (RCT) of Learn to be safe with Emmy, friends™ will be conducted with children in approximately 72 first grade classrooms in 24 Queensland primary (elementary) schools from three state regions, over a period of 2 years. Entire schools will be randomised, using a computer generated list of random numbers, to intervention, wait-list control conditions, to prevent contamination effects across students, classes. Data will be collected at baseline (pre-assessment), immediately after the intervention (post-assessment),, at 6-, 12-,, 18-months (follow-up assessments). Outcome assessors will be blinded to group membership. Primary outcomes assessed are children's knowledge of program concepts; intentions to use program knowledge, skills,, help-seeking strategies; actual use of program material in a simulated situation;, anxiety arising from program participation. Secondary outcomes include a parent discussion monitor, parent observations of their children's use of program materials, satisfaction with the program,, parental stress. A process evaluation will be conducted concurrently to assess program performance. DISCUSSION: This RCT addresses shortcomings in previous studies, methodologically extends research in this area by randomising at school-level to prevent cross-learning between conditions; providing longer-term outcome assessment than any previous study; examining the degree to which parents/guardians discuss intervention content with children at home; assessing potential moderating/mediating effects of family, child demographic variables; testing an in-vivo measure to assess children's ability to discriminate safe/unsafe situations, disclose to trusted adults;, testing enhancements to existing measures to establish greater internal consistency. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Australian, New Zealand Clinical Trials Register (ACTRN12615000917538). Registered (02/09/2015).

title: Delinquency in a Birth Cohort
authors: Wolfgang, Marvin E, Figlio, Robert M, Sellin, Thorsten
abstract: ``Delinquency in a Birth Cohort is a turning point in criminological research in the United States,'' writes Norval Morris in his foreword. ``What has been completely lacking until this book is an analysis of delinquency in a substantial cohort of youths, the cohort being defined other than by their contact with any part of the criminal justice system.'' This study of a birth cohort was not originally meant to be etiological or predictive. Yet the data bearing on this cohort of nearly ten thousand boys born in 1945, living in Philadelphia gave rise to a model for prediction of delinquency,, thus to the possibility for more efficient planning of programs for intervention. It is expert research yielding significant applications and, though largely statistical, the analysis is accessible to readers without mathematical training. ``No serious scholar of the methods of preventing, treating juvenile delinquency can properly ignore this book.''—LeRoy L. Lamborn, Law Library Journal ``The magnitude of [this] study is awesome. . . . It should be a useful guide for anyone interested in the intricacies of cohort analysis.''—Gary F. Jensen, American Journal of Sociology ``A book the student of juvenile delinquency will find invaluable.''—Criminologist

title: An experimental study of responses to armed police in Great Britain
authors: Yesberg, Julia A, Bradford, Ben, Dawson, Paul
abstract: Abstract Objectives This study tested whether the presence of a firearm changed the way people reacted to police among a British sample. Method In an online study, participants were shown images of armed, unarmed police, rated them on a number of variables. Some participants were primed to think about terrorism,, some participants were exposed to more armed police than others. Results Participants had more negative responses to police when they were armed. We found no effect of the terrorism prime on people’s reactions to images of armed police, no effect of exposure. Yet, unexpectedly, we found a negative effect of the terrorism prime on trust, legitimacy. Conclusions In a country where police have never before been routinely armed, this research raises important questions about how armed police can retain the public’s support when they may no longer be considered ‘prototypical representatives’ of the British people.

title: The relationship between the trust among neighborhood residents, the intention to act for problems in public parks
authors: Amemiya, Mamoru, Shimada, Takahito, Kikuchi, George, Harada, Yutaka
journal: Journal of The Japanese Institute of Landscape Architecture
abstract: In order to create safe public parks that are accessible to everyone, the role of neighborhood residents is important. The aim of this study is to identify the factors that affect the intention of the residents to deal with various problems in public parks, especially in terms of the types, extent of social networks among neighborhood residents, based on a survey conducted in Suma Ward, Kobe City. 837 respondents of the survey were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Three latent variables were set in the model -the trust among neighborhood residents, the size of personal networks in neighborhoods,, the participation in neighborhood activities. Results are as follows. 1)In order to form the intention to act for the problems in public parks, the trust is important. 2)The size of personal networks, the participation in neighborhood activities can stimulate the creation of the trust. 3)The role of the trust is important for large parks while the extent of social networks is important for small parks. Based on these results, this paper discusses the direction of the risk management of public parks by neighborhood residents.

title: The effects of a nearby murder case on residents’ anxiety, crime prevention’s cognition
authors: 桐生, 正幸
abstract: E(その他) 本研究では，身近で発生した殺人事件が，地域防犯への関心や，犯罪に対するリスク認知と不安感に及ぼす影響について検討した。2007年10月に幼女が殺害された加古川市にて活動する防犯ボランティアが研究対象である。この殺人事件は，彼女の家の前にて刃物で刺された未解決事件である。調査は，兵庫県の５市にて行った。加古川市と他の市は，防犯活動が活発な地域である。調査回答者は，全部で361名（女性130名，男性231名。平均年齢67.3歳）のボランティアであった。調査結果は次の通りである。加古川市のボランティアは他の市よりも，１）治安悪化を認識し，２）高い犯罪不安感を感じていた。 This study examined the effect of a neighbouring murder case on risk perception, anxiety about crime,, concerns about crime prevention. A volunteer crime prevention group in Kakogawa city, where a little girl murder occurred in October 2007 was examined. This case involved the stabbing of a victim in front of her home, which has remained unsolved. The investigation involved five cities in Hyogo prefecture. In Kakogawa city, other cities, the anticrime activity was active. There were 361 volunteers involved in the survey. 130 are women while 231 are men, the average age is 67.3 years old. The survey results indicated that the volunteers in Kakogawa had higher perceptions than the volunteers in other cities in 1) recognizing that the public peace has worsened;, 2) feeling of anxiety for the increased in crimes.

title: The effects of information about crime on mother's anxiety about crime
authors: Arai, Takashi, Fuji, Kei, Yoshida, Fujio
journal: Shinrigaku kenkyu: The Japanese journal of psychology
keywords: reactions to crime, information about crime, anxiety about crime, impact of information content;z\_2016\_事典\_08犯罪不安;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章
abstract: This study examined a causal model that the effect of information about crime on risk perception, anxiety about crime,, crime prevention is mediated by the informational content, source. We measured risk perception, anxiety about crime from a social, an individual perspective. A web-based survey was conducted with mothers (N=1040) who have children aged 3-12 years. The results of structural equation modeling indicated the following. (a) Information about crime given by the mass media, Internet,, hearsay increased the risk perception, anxiety about crime through the impact of informational content (i.e., ``feeling that crime is close,'' ``emotional fluctuations,'' ``sympathy for the victims,'', ``remembering a similar crime''). (b) Hearsay information directly controlled optimistic cognitions. (c) Mass media, hearsay information directly promoted crime prevention. (d) Cognition about the deterioration of security advanced cooperative crime prevention in the neighborhood.

title: Determinants of the perceived risk of crime
authors: Sakaguchi, Yusuke
keywords: perceived risk of crime, fear of crime, comparison of Japan, the United States;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;125\_日本の研究;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第1章
abstract: This paper attempts to answer the following question: ``What type of people are likely to perceive the risk of crime victimization,, why?''Empirical research on the fear of crime in the West, which began in the 1960s, indicates that women, old people,, lower socio-economic groups have a tendency to perceive the risk of crime. Researchers have attributed the tendency in these groups to their physical, social vulnerability. In order to find out whether we can apply the results of the research conducted in the West to Japanese society, we compare the determinants of the perceived risk of crime in Japan with those of the perceived risk of crime in the United States. This comparison is conducted by analyzing the data of General Social Surveys (GSS), Japanese General Social Surveys (JGSS) held in 2000.The findings reveal that in the United States, women, old people,, low-income groups are more likely to perceive the risk of crime; this perception can be attributed to their physical, social vulnerability. On the other hand, in Japan, it was found that young women, men having young children,, white-collar or highly educated women are more likely to perceive the risk of crime. However, their risk perception cannot be explained by physical, social vulnerability. This paper illustrates the unique factors underlying the perceived risk of crime in Japan: fear of sexual crime, vulnerability of the significant other, differences in the wording of GSS, JGSS, opportunities of walking alone at night,, the role of the media.

abstract: Little research efforts have been paid to mail survey methodology in a study of survey research. Crucial weakness in mail survey has been low response rate. Many factors have been utilized to boost response rate in Western societies. But little research has been carried out in Japan, though recently a little more effort has been paid to this research. Some results of experiments to boost response rate are presented in this report. It has been shown that cover letter in green color, reminder card have positive effect on response rate. Content of cover letter has no effect, but content of reminder card emphasizing the importance of the study has a little positive effect. Response rate for persons who received questionnaire at their work place is larger than those who received questionnaire at their home address..

title: 犯罪発生要因に関する環境心理学的研究 : 研究の概観と都道府県単位での人口密集と犯罪の関連の検討

keywords: review of studies, determinants of crime, population density, socio-economical factors, social change;2012\_jsep\_review\_root
abstract: 犯罪の環境心理学的研究は, 従来, 犯罪者の人格特性などの主体的要因の分析を主におこなってきた.とくにわが国の場合��うした傾向が強いように思われる.しかし, 行動は通常主体と環境の相互作用の結果として生じるのであり, 犯罪もその例外ではない.このような立場から本研究ではまず, 従来の犯罪研究において環境の関与がどの程度明らかにされてきたのかを概観した.その際, 環境を巨視的環境と微視的環境の二つに分け, それぞれについて概観した.その結果, 所見の不一致や犯罪の分類の不十分さなど, 多くの課題が残されていることを指摘した.次に, わが国の場合, 実証的な研究そのものが不足していることから, 犯罪環境として最もしばしば言及される人口密集と犯罪の関係を都道府県単位で検討した.とくに, 今回の分析では密集を周辺環境の密集と住居内の密集に区分すること, 社会変動の影響の検討も含めて継年的な分析をおこなうことに主眼をおいた.その結果, 人口密集でも, 周辺環境の密集の指標である人口密度は犯罪認知総数, 窃盗, 強盗, 粗暴犯と関連するのに対して, 住居内密集の指標である一人当たりの畳数は殺人と強盗と関連するという違いがみられた.また, 人口密集や求人倍率, 都市公園面積, 転入率などの環境要因は年とともに相関関係が強くなること, 住居内密集度では1980年代後半以降に総数や窃盗との関係が弱まること, 知能犯はバブル景気の時期に当たる1980年代後半の一時期に密集の二つの指標や求人倍率と関連することなど, 年による変化もみられた.これらを踏まえて, 犯罪と環境の問題に関する今後の研究の課題と問題点を指摘した.

title: Youth problems, urban social control
authors: Sugiyama, Kazuaki
keywords: a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;125\_日本の研究;120\_理論検討(2章)\_root
abstract: The aim of this paper is to explain the relationship between youth problems, urban social control in contemporary Japan, taking into consideration my previous research about adolescent social problems in the 1990's, the recent direction of neoliberal social control. The author discusses moral panic derived from particular issues in Japanese social context, making reference to studies on crime, social control, the social construction of problematic youth representation that flourished in Anglophone critical geographies. While there are a lot of other reported problems related to young people in Japan, this paper specifically focuses on social problems concerning the regulation of Telephone Dating Services, which were seen as a new ``harmful'' environment for juveniles by neighborhoods in Toyama prefecture, Japan, from 1993-1998. There is widespread public concern about this problem in almost every prefectures of Japan, many people support the call for the enactment of a regulation act. It became necessary for the local government to protect these juveniles from such a ``harmful'' environment, to interfere with more sound education. The author considers ``moral geographies'' with reference to the policing, surveillance of offenders against the background of the protection act for juveniles,, suggests that this local process relates closely to the recent direction of urban social control from a regional to national scale. It is considered to be a precursor of the conservative youth policy in recent years,, continues with community-based social control in contemporary Japan.

title: An experimental study of victim derogation: The case of victims of ijime
authors: Ono, Toshikazu
journal: THE JAPANESE JOURNAL OF EXPERIMENTAL SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY
abstract: The purpose of this study is to show that the specific form characterizing ijime, a particular type of bullying often observed in classrooms in Japan, facilitates people's common belief that victim of ijime is also to be blamed for inviting it. Specifically, it was hypothesized that a victim of aggression is more likely to be derogated more strongly (1) when the aggression is done by a group than when it is done by a single individual,, (2) when it is done repeatedly than when it is done just once. Results of an experiment confirmed the first hypothesis, but not the second. The paper also reports a finding from another experiment showing that two individual difference variables-confidence in self-efficacy, general distrust of society-are related to the degree of victim derogation.

title: Spatio-temporal three-dimensional mapping of crime events: Visualising spatio-temporal clusters of snatch-and-run offences
authors: Nakaya, Tomoki, Yano, Keiji
abstract: To detect spatio-temporal pattern of crime clusters/hotspots, the possibilities of three-dimensional mapping methodologies for crime event data are explored using two approaches: three dimensional kernel-density mapping using a volume rendering technique, visualisation of cylindrical significant clusters that can be detected by space-time scan statistics. Both approaches are intended to visualise spatio-temporal domains with high densities of crime in a three-dimensional space composed of two geographical dimensions, one time dimension. The proposed three-dimensional mapping methodologies are evaluated through application to a dataset of snatch-and-run offences in Kyoto City during the period 2003-2004. The results are summarized as follows: (a) Three-dimensional crime mapping enables effective visualisation of the geographical extents, duration of crime hotspots simultaneously. This method is particularly useful to identify geographical diffusion, movements of crime clusters/hotspots compared to traditional dynamic analyses of crime mapping using cross-sectional maps with arbitrary time intervals. (b) In practice, the roles of three-dimensional kernel mapping, space-time scan statistics should be complementary. Space-time scan statistics provide clear-cut domains of crime clusters/hotspots that can be used for secondary analyses, such as evaluation of socio-environmental, temporal characteristics focusing on detected domains. However, we should note that the method assumes cylindrical geometrical-constrains of space-time domains. Three-dimensional kernel density mapping provides fuzzy domains with high densities of crime, a useful basis to assess the validity of the assumption of spatial scan statistics, to investigate detailed space-time sequences of crime clusters/hotspots. (c) Empirical analyses of the snatch-and-run offence dataset in Kyoto City revealed constant clusters/hotspots during the study period in central Kyoto, around Kyoto Station as well as transient clusters/hotspots around several railway stations in the suburbs. Temporal differences of transient clusters show geographical movements of hotspots from the north to the south via the west. We also identified that outbreaks of snatch-and-run offences alternated between a pair of cluster areas. These results suggesting so-called displacement phenomena indicate the need to monitor crime events, effects of crime-preventive actions in a widespread space-time context.

keywords: map perception, crime map, spatial smoothing;z\_2009jasc;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_220\_市川第1波\_2010\_犯社研(4章);a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root
abstract: Spatial smoothing is one of the spatial operations in GIS. It makes spatial information vague, ambiguous to some extent, in order to hide the exact location or attribute of spatial objects. Since spatial smoothing is a kind of conversion of spatial data, use of visualized spatial data also changes with spatial smoothing. The degree of smoothing affects the way, result of map use. Though this has been widely recognized in cartography, GIS, few studies have been done in the literature. To fill the gap of the research, this paper analyzes the effect of spatial smoothing in map use. The experiment is performed on the focus to a facility choice on a map. The observed data are used to build, estimate a stochastic model representing the hotel choice behavior. The model serves for not only explaining the choice behavior of a hotel but also discussing it in relation to the degree of spatial smoothing.

title: 近隣での防犯対策が市民の犯罪の知覚に与える影響
authors: 島田, 貴仁, 雨宮, 護, 菊池, 城治
keywords: 近隣での防犯対策, 被害リスク認知, 居住満足感;z\_2018jssc;z\_岩波エビデンス;z\_2011\_小俣本\_第6章;犯罪予防の社会心理学\_230\_市川第2波3波\_2018\_犯社研(5章);z\_2013\_コミュニティの社会心理学;a\_犯罪予防の社会心理学\_root;30\_日本語;32\_日本\_犯罪社会学研究;業績一覧\_01論文
abstract: 近年,日本では,近隣での防犯対策が広く行われるようになったが,これらの防犯対策が一般市民の犯罪の知覚へどう影響しているかの実証研究は少ない.本研究では,近隣での防犯対策として青色防犯パトロールと犯罪発生マップ掲示を実施している首都圏の1市で住民調査(回答数1,171名)を実施し,防犯対策の認知が犯罪の知覚に与える影響を階層的重回帰分析で分析した.犯罪の知覚を個人-地区,認知-感情の2軸からなると考え,個人の被害リスク認知と犯罪不安,地区の治安評価と満足感の4つを目的変数とした.各目的変数を回答者のデモグラフィックなど統制変数のみで説明するモデルと,統制変数に防犯対策の認知を加えて説明するモデルとを比較したところ,防犯対策の認知は被害リスク認知,地区の満足感に対して有意な影響を与えていた.青色防犯パトロールは,パトロール車両を見た回答者の被害リスク認知を高める一方,地区の満足感を低めていた.一方,犯罪発生マップの掲示は,その内容を確認した回答者の地区の満足感に影響していたが,被害リスク認知や犯罪不安には影響していなかった.近隣での防犯対策の選択への含意が議論された.

title: Social attitudes towards sex work, its criminalization: An empirical study with a Spanish sample
authors: Gómez-Bellvís, Ana B, Castro-Toledo, Francisco J, Falces, Carlos
abstract: This article examines social attitudes towards sex work, its regulation in Spain, considering different types of sex work (street, brothel, private house, escort,, online). It also analyses underlying beliefs that have been shown in the literature to be relevant. A questionnaire was administered to 1168 participants (52\% women, 48\% men), with about 50\% aged between 35, 54. The results indicate that attitudes vary depending on the type of sex work, with greater disapproval for more visible or public forms such as street, brothel-based sex work. The beliefs driving this rejection align with the stigmatizing views of these forms. As for the regulatory measures, there is no clear preference for any of the approaches considered, although support for each of them is consistent with the premises of each regulatory framework in terms of freedom, equality, social problems,, the dignity of the activity. These findings suggest that it would be more appropriate to measure attitudes towards sex work by type of sexual services, that further research is needed, particularly if legislative change is sought.

title: EMMIE, the what works centre for crime reduction
authors: Sidebottom, Aiden, Tilley, Nick
abstract: The United Kingdom has made significant investments in promoting, facilitating evidence-based policy, practice. In this chapter our focus is on the What Works Centre for Crime Reduction (WWCCR), in particular EMMIE. EMMIE is a framework denoting five categories of evidence that are important to inform policy, practice decision-making: Effect, Mechanism, Moderator, Implementation,, Economics. As part of the WWCCR, EMMIE was used to populate a toolkit for police, others with crime prevention responsibilities to draw on, in deciding what to do to address crime problems (the “Crime Reduction Toolkit”). Across the range of interventions for which systematic reviews had been undertaken, the toolkit summarizes the quality of both the available evidence, findings in relation to the five domains comprising EMMIE. An appraisal of systematic reviews using EMMIE revealed substantial gaps in the crime reduction evidence base, whose repair will require primary studies, reviews that draw on a wide range of studies using diverse methods.

title: Do increases in the price of fuel increase levels of fuel theft? Evidence from England, Wales
authors: Sidebottom, Aiden, Agar, Iain, Kurland, Justin
keywords: Bilking; Drive-offs; Fuel; Petrol; Price; Theft;20250703\_Aiden
abstract: Fuel prices have increased sharply over the past year. In this study we test the hypothesis that increases in the price of fuel are associated with increases in motorists filling their fuel tank, driving off without paying. We use weekly crime data from six police forces in England, Wales for the period January 2018 to July 2022, combined with regional data on the number of fuel sales, average fuel prices. Our results demonstrate an overall weak price-theft relationship for the 238 week study period, less so than in previous studies. However, we find strong evidence that the recent spike in fuel prices was associated with elevated levels of fuel theft. The implications of our findings for future research, crime prevention are discussed.

title: Police education, democratic policing in Taiwan: a longitudinal quasi-experimental study of the effects of selection, police socialisation on human rights, moral reasoning, prejudice
authors: Lin, Keng-Hui, Sidebottom, Aiden, Wortley, Richard
abstract: Abstract Objectives To investigate the effects of selection, group socialisation on support of human rights, moral reasoning, prejudice in police officers in Taiwan. Methods We used a longitudinal quasi-experimental design to track three cohorts of police officers (n = 585), a comparison group of criminology undergraduates (n = 43). Results There were no statistically significant differences in measures of human rights, moral reasoning, prejudice between new police recruits, the control group. However, time in police education was associated with a statistically significant reduction in police officer support of human rights, moral reasoning, an increase in prejudice. In the control group, the reverse was true. Conclusions Exposure to police education in Taiwan resulted in police officers being significantly more prejudiced, significantly less adherent to the principles of human rights, moral reasoning. These results appear to be attributable to police socialisation rather than selection effects.

title: Police practitioner views on the challenges of analysing, responding to knife crime
authors: Bullock, Karen, Agar, Iain, Ashby, Matt, Brennan, Iain, Hales, Gavin, Sidebottom, Aiden, Tilley, Nick
abstract: AbstractKnife crime remains a major concern in England, Wales. Problem-oriented, public health approaches to tackling knife crime have been widely advocated, but little is known about how these approaches are understood, implemented by police practitioners. To address this knowledge gap, this article draws on semi-structured interviews, focus groups with 44 police personnel to consider the processes, challenges of applying problem-oriented, public health approaches to knife crime. Findings show that knife crime was seen as a complex social problem which would not be solved by ‘silver bullets’; prevention was prioritised, the limitations of enforcement were widely acknowledged; there was an emphasis on understanding, responding to vulnerability, risk; discussion of ‘holistic’, ‘whole systems’ approaches was evident (but these concepts were rarely defined);, the problem of serious violence was viewed as a shared, multi-agency issue that the police could not tackle alone. Various challenges were also evident, most notably around analysis of the drivers, patterns of knife crime, the evaluation of knife crime interventions. The article concludes by discussing the implications of the findings for knife crime prevention, the implementation, advancement of problem-oriented, public health approaches to policing.

title: Further evidence on the extent, time course of repeat missing incidents involving children: A research note
authors: Galiano López, Clara, Hunter, Jane, Davies, Toby, Sidebottom, Aiden
abstract: This study examines the extent, time course of repeat missing incidents involving children. Using data from one UK police force (n = 2,251), we find (1) that the majority (65\%) of missing incidents are repeats, (2) that a small group of repeatedly missing children (n = 43; 6\%) account for a sizable proportion of all missing incidents (n=739, 33\%), (3) that the likelihood of a child going missing repeatedly is elevated in the weeks immediately following a previous missing incident. The implications of our findings for future research, for the prevention of missing incidents are discussed.
